Each expression applies only in its respective finite-moment range. For \(1<\ParetoTailExponent\le2\), the mean exists and the variance is infinite in the unbounded model. For \(\ParetoTailExponent\le1\), even the mean is infinite. A capped variable \(\min(\ParetoTaskDemand,\DemandCap)\) has finite moments for every finite \(\DemandCap\); a finite observed tail cannot establish that an actual deployment has infinite variance.
Step count is also not service time. To use the queueing result in section 1.3.1, the model must describe service at the selected resource boundary. Variable call lengths and external waits can change that distribution even at a fixed number of turns. Capacity planning therefore needs means for average load, measured tails for service targets, and explicit limits for admitted work. No single fitted tail index replaces those three obligations (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-goodput}\)).



Frequent verification consumes resources; delayed detection can waste subsequent work. A cadence model is useful only after identifying which failures a check detects and which work can safely be repeated. It does not schedule mandatory authorization or precondition checks, and it cannot reverse an external effect.


Consider \(\UsefulStepCount\) useful generation steps with homogeneous generation cost \(\StepGenerationCost\) per step and verification cost \(\VerificationCheckCost\) per check. Express both costs in the same unit, such as money or serial elapsed time; do not add money to latency. Suppose checks occur every \(\CheckIntervalStepCount\) steps, errors occur at constant rate \(\GenerationStepErrorRate\) per useful step, and errors are rare within an interval. Assume each check detects the modeled error, the extra work between error and detection averages \(\CheckIntervalStepCount/2\) steps, and recovery costs \(\ErrorRecoveryCost\) per error independently of \(\CheckIntervalStepCount\).
Ignoring partial final intervals and repeated errors during recovery gives the first-order model
\[\VerificationScheduleCost(\CheckIntervalStepCount)\approx
\UsefulStepCount \StepGenerationCost+\frac{\UsefulStepCount}{\CheckIntervalStepCount}\VerificationCheckCost
+\UsefulStepCount\GenerationStepErrorRate
\left(\frac{\CheckIntervalStepCount}{2}\StepGenerationCost+\ErrorRecoveryCost\right).\]
The two cadence-dependent terms vary in opposite directions. Differentiating their sum for positive continuous \(\CheckIntervalStepCount\) gives
\[\frac{d\VerificationScheduleCost}{d\CheckIntervalStepCount}
=-\frac{\UsefulStepCount \VerificationCheckCost}{\CheckIntervalStepCount^2}
+\frac{\UsefulStepCount\GenerationStepErrorRate \StepGenerationCost}{2},
\qquad
\CheckIntervalStepCount^*=\sqrt{\frac{2\VerificationCheckCost}
{\GenerationStepErrorRate \StepGenerationCost}}.\]
Consequently, the relaxed verification count is \(\VerificationCheckCount^*=\UsefulStepCount/\CheckIntervalStepCount^*\). Independence from \(\UsefulStepCount\) follows from the homogeneous, long-run assumptions, not from a universal property of agent tasks. Actual schedules use feasible integer intervals, handle the final partial block, and respect deadlines and mandatory checks. Error bursts, state-dependent check power, and correlated recovery attempts require a different model.



A second model assumes that any erroneous block must be generated again from its start. Partition \(\UsefulStepCount\) useful steps into blocks of \(\CheckIntervalStepCount\) steps, with \(\CheckIntervalStepCount\) dividing \(\UsefulStepCount\). Let each step succeed independently with probability \(0<\StepSuccessProbability<1\), each generation take \(\StepGenerationTime>0\), and each block check take \(\BlockCheckTime>0\). A check perfectly distinguishes successful from failed blocks. Every retry starts from the same recoverable state, draws independent outcomes, and has the same duration; reset overhead is negligible. No attempt has an externally visible effect that a retry would duplicate.
The block succeeds with probability \(\StepSuccessProbability^\CheckIntervalStepCount\), so its number of attempts is geometric with mean \(\StepSuccessProbability^{-\CheckIntervalStepCount}\). The expected completion time is
\[\ExpectedRunCompletionTime(\CheckIntervalStepCount)=\frac{\UsefulStepCount}{\CheckIntervalStepCount}\,
\frac{\CheckIntervalStepCount \StepGenerationTime+\BlockCheckTime}{\StepSuccessProbability^\CheckIntervalStepCount}
=\UsefulStepCount \StepSuccessProbability^{-\CheckIntervalStepCount}\left(\StepGenerationTime+\frac{\BlockCheckTime}{\CheckIntervalStepCount}\right).\]
Set \(\StepFailureHazard=-\ln \StepSuccessProbability>0\). Differentiating \(\ln \ExpectedRunCompletionTime(\CheckIntervalStepCount)\) gives the stationary equation and its positive root:
\[\StepFailureHazard \StepGenerationTime \CheckIntervalStepCount^2+\StepFailureHazard \BlockCheckTime \CheckIntervalStepCount-\BlockCheckTime=0,\]
\[\CheckIntervalStepCount^*=
\frac{-\BlockCheckTime+
\sqrt{\BlockCheckTime^2+4\StepGenerationTime \BlockCheckTime/\StepFailureHazard}}
{2\StepGenerationTime}.\]
The derivative changes from negative to positive at this root. Compare feasible integer block sizes rather than rounding blindly. When \(\StepFailureHazard \BlockCheckTime/\StepGenerationTime\ll1\), the leading approximation is
\[\CheckIntervalStepCount^*\approx\sqrt{\frac{\BlockCheckTime}{\StepFailureHazard \StepGenerationTime}}
\approx\sqrt{\frac{\BlockCheckTime}{(1-\StepSuccessProbability)\StepGenerationTime}},\]
where the second approximation additionally requires \(\StepSuccessProbability\) close to one. If \(\StepSuccessProbability=1\), this model favors the largest permitted block because no regeneration is needed.
The absent factor of two distinguishes complete-block regeneration from a model that charges only average lost or wasted work within an interval. These models cannot be interchanged merely because both have square-root optima. Checkpointing in Checkpoints often reconstructs recorded events instead of regenerating model actions; that runtime must use its actual reconstruction cost and unresolved-effect contract.




A checkpoint can reduce work that must be repeated after a failure, but saving it also interrupts useful execution. Young’s first-order model balances these terms (Young 1974). Let \(\CheckpointInterval>0\) be useful execution time between completed checkpoints, \(\CheckpointWriteTime>0\) their fixed duration, and \(\MeanTimeBetweenFailures\) the mean time between failures. Assume rare Poisson failures independent of progress, small checkpoint overhead, reliable saved state, and restart cost \(\JobRestartTime\) independent of \(\CheckpointInterval\).

Young, John W. 1974. “A First Order Approximation to the Optimum Checkpoint Interval.” Communications of the ACM 17 (9): 530–31. https://doi.org/10.1145/361147.361115.
To first order, failures occur approximately uniformly within a useful-work interval, so each loses an average of \(\CheckpointInterval/2\) work. Ignoring failures during saving and recovery gives approximate overhead per unit useful time
\[\CheckpointOverheadRatio(\CheckpointInterval)\approx
\frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval}
+\frac{\CheckpointInterval}{2\,\MeanTimeBetweenFailures}
+\frac{\JobRestartTime}{\MeanTimeBetweenFailures}.\]
Differentiation isolates the cadence-dependent terms:
\[\CheckpointOverheadRatio'(\CheckpointInterval)=-\frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval^2}
+\frac{1}{2\,\MeanTimeBetweenFailures},
\qquad
\CheckpointOverheadRatio''(\CheckpointInterval)=\frac{2\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval^3}>0.\]
The minimizing interval of this approximate cost function is therefore
\[\OptimalCheckpointInterval=\sqrt{2\,\CheckpointWriteTime\,\MeanTimeBetweenFailures}.\]
Restart cost raises overhead but does not move this optimum because it is constant with respect to \(\CheckpointInterval\). A more complete model can include failures during saving and recovery; Daly (2006) develops such refinements. They do not follow by adding restart time to \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) in the displayed square root.

Daly, J. T. 2006. “A Higher Order Estimate of the Optimum Checkpoint Interval for Restart Dumps.” Future Generation Computer Systems 22 (3): 303–12. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.future.2004.11.016.
This calculation applies only when failure loses work that must be re-executed. A durable agent may instead reconstruct recorded state without resampling its past decisions. Checkpoints models that different cost. Neither a saved state nor this timing calculation rolls back committed external actions; their recovery protocol remains necessary.

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
A release decision requires a declared experiment and criterion. These entries separate sample planning, repeated-run estimands, sequential evidence, and cost-sensitive escalation.


The sampling design determines which uncertainty calculation applies. Tasks and repeated runs distinguishes tasks from repeated runs, and Confidence intervals for acceptance separates a single proportion from a paired candidate–baseline difference. This section gives an approximate sample-size calculation for independent arms, states the paired-score interval that the chapter’s worksheet uses, and gives a bootstrap construction for a declared statistic that lacks an analytic interval.


Suppose two arms contain independent Bernoulli trials, with the same number \(\ComparisonArmTrialCount\) in each arm. Their hypothesized success probabilities are \(\ArmSuccessProbability_1\) and \(\ArmSuccessProbability_2\), with \(0<\ArmSuccessProbability_1<\ArmSuccessProbability_2<1\). Let \(\FiniteChange \ArmSuccessProbability=\ArmSuccessProbability_2-\ArmSuccessProbability_1\) and \(\PooledAcceptanceProbability=(\ArmSuccessProbability_1+\ArmSuccessProbability_2)/2\). Under these assumptions, the difference of sample proportions has alternative variance
\[\frac{\ArmSuccessProbability_1(1-\ArmSuccessProbability_1)+\ArmSuccessProbability_2(1-\ArmSuccessProbability_2)}{\ComparisonArmTrialCount}.\]
For a two-sided normal-approximation test with significance target \(\StatisticalSignificanceLevel\) and power target \(1-\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate\), a common planning approximation places the positive rejection boundary \(\SignificanceCriticalQuantile\sqrt{2\PooledAcceptanceProbability(1-\PooledAcceptanceProbability)/\ComparisonArmTrialCount}\) below the alternative mean by \(\StatisticalPowerQuantile\) alternative standard deviations. Here \(\StandardNormalQuantile\) is the standard normal quantile at probability \(\QuantileProbabilityLevel\). Solving that relation gives
\[\TasksPerComparisonArm=
\left\lceil
\frac{\left[\SignificanceCriticalQuantile\sqrt{2\PooledAcceptanceProbability(1-\PooledAcceptanceProbability)}+
\StatisticalPowerQuantile\sqrt{\ArmSuccessProbability_1(1-\ArmSuccessProbability_1)+\ArmSuccessProbability_2(1-\ArmSuccessProbability_2)}\right]^2}{(\FiniteChange \ArmSuccessProbability)^2}
\right\rceil.\]
This is the equal-arm normal approximation implemented in Brant’s independent-proportion planning calculator (Brant, n.d.). It neglects the far rejection tail under the specified alternative and uses an approximate pooled null variance. It is not an exact power guarantee, a minimum sample size for every useful finding, or a test of already observed results. Rare outcomes, dependence, unequal allocation, missing labels, or a paired design require the corresponding design calculation. Increasing repeats on a fixed task does not create independent tasks.

Brant, Rollin. n.d. Inference for Proportions: Comparing Two Independent Samples. Power/sample size calculator, Department of Statistics, University of British Columbia.

Napkin Math 1.1: Plan two independent armsProblem: For hypothetical success probabilities 0.30 and 0.35, what equal-arm sample count does the approximation give at significance target 0.05 and power target 0.80?
Calculation: Using rounded normal quantiles 1.96 and 0.84, then rounding the result upward, gives 1,375 independent trials per arm.
Scope: This plans a particular independent-arm experiment before its outcomes are observed. It does not establish that an observed difference is significant, and it does not apply to the paired repair comparison by ignoring its within-task dependence. Sampling and grader fidelity still limit the population claim.





Pairing changes the uncertainty of a difference. Each sampled task yields one baseline outcome and one candidate outcome, cross-classified as in Paired task outcomes: \(\ConcordantTaskCount_{11}\) tasks accepted by both configurations, \(\BaselineOnlyAcceptedTaskCount\) by the baseline only, \(\CandidateOnlyAcceptedTaskCount\) by the candidate only, and \(\ConcordantTaskCount_{00}\) by neither, with \(\EvaluationSampleCount=\ConcordantTaskCount_{11}+\BaselineOnlyAcceptedTaskCount+\CandidateOnlyAcceptedTaskCount+\ConcordantTaskCount_{00}\). The marginal estimates are \(\CandidateAcceptanceEstimate=(\ConcordantTaskCount_{11}+\CandidateOnlyAcceptedTaskCount)/\EvaluationSampleCount\) and \(\BaselineAcceptanceEstimate=(\ConcordantTaskCount_{11}+\BaselineOnlyAcceptedTaskCount)/\EvaluationSampleCount\), so \(\EstimatedPairedAcceptanceDifference=(\CandidateOnlyAcceptedTaskCount-\BaselineOnlyAcceptedTaskCount)/\EvaluationSampleCount\). Both proportions are measured on the same tasks, and their sampling errors are correlated. An interval that treated them as independent arms would ignore that dependence.
Newcombe’s method 10 assembles the paired interval from the two single-proportion Wilson intervals (Newcombe 1998). Let \([\CandidateIntervalLowerLimit,\CandidateIntervalUpperLimit]\) and \([\BaselineIntervalLowerLimit,\BaselineIntervalUpperLimit]\) be the intervals of equation 13.2 for the two marginal counts at the same \(\IntervalNormalQuantile\), and write their distances from the point estimates as

Newcombe, Robert G. 1998. “Improved Confidence Intervals for the Difference Between Binomial Proportions Based on Paired Data.” Statistics in Medicine 17 (22): 2635–50. https://doi.org/10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19981130)17:22<2635::AID-SIM954>3.0.CO;2-C.
\[\CandidateLowerLimitDistance=\CandidateAcceptanceEstimate-\CandidateIntervalLowerLimit,\quad
\CandidateUpperLimitDistance=\CandidateIntervalUpperLimit-\CandidateAcceptanceEstimate,\quad
\BaselineLowerLimitDistance=\BaselineAcceptanceEstimate-\BaselineIntervalLowerLimit,\quad
\BaselineUpperLimitDistance=\BaselineIntervalUpperLimit-\BaselineAcceptanceEstimate.\]
The within-pair dependence enters through a phi coefficient whose numerator is continuity corrected when it is positive:
\[\PairedVerdictCorrelation=\frac{\ContinuityCorrectedCrossProduct}{\sqrt{(\ConcordantTaskCount_{11}+\CandidateOnlyAcceptedTaskCount)(\BaselineOnlyAcceptedTaskCount+\ConcordantTaskCount_{00})(\ConcordantTaskCount_{11}+\BaselineOnlyAcceptedTaskCount)(\CandidateOnlyAcceptedTaskCount+\ConcordantTaskCount_{00})}},\qquad
\ContinuityCorrectedCrossProduct=\begin{cases}
\max(\ConcordantTaskCount_{11}\ConcordantTaskCount_{00}-\BaselineOnlyAcceptedTaskCount \CandidateOnlyAcceptedTaskCount-\EvaluationSampleCount/2,\ 0), & \ConcordantTaskCount_{11}\ConcordantTaskCount_{00}>\BaselineOnlyAcceptedTaskCount \CandidateOnlyAcceptedTaskCount,\\
\ConcordantTaskCount_{11}\ConcordantTaskCount_{00}-\BaselineOnlyAcceptedTaskCount \CandidateOnlyAcceptedTaskCount, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}\]
with \(\PairedVerdictCorrelation=0\) when the denominator is zero. The difference is smallest when the candidate proportion is low and the baseline proportion is high, so the lower limit combines the candidate’s downward distance with the baseline’s upward distance, and the upper limit combines the opposite pair:
\[\PairedDifferenceLowerLimit=\EstimatedPairedAcceptanceDifference-\sqrt{\left(\CandidateLowerLimitDistance\right)^2-2\PairedVerdictCorrelation\,\CandidateLowerLimitDistance\BaselineUpperLimitDistance+\left(\BaselineUpperLimitDistance\right)^2},\]
\[\PairedDifferenceUpperLimit=\EstimatedPairedAcceptanceDifference+\sqrt{\left(\CandidateUpperLimitDistance\right)^2-2\PairedVerdictCorrelation\,\CandidateUpperLimitDistance\BaselineLowerLimitDistance+\left(\BaselineLowerLimitDistance\right)^2}.\]
Setting \(\PairedVerdictCorrelation=0\) discards the pairing. A positive \(\PairedVerdictCorrelation\), produced when tasks tend to receive the same verdict under both configurations, subtracts the covariance term and narrows the interval without changing either marginal count. Newcombe’s method 8 uses the same construction with an uncorrected \(\PairedVerdictCorrelation\); in his coverage evaluation, the correction of method 10 removed the most severe coverage shortfalls of method 8. The interval remains nominal and approximate. It assumes independently sampled tasks, one complete verdict per configuration on each task, a level fixed in advance, and a single look at the data. The worksheet in Paired outcome comparison implements this construction and checks it against two of Newcombe’s published examples.



For a statistic without a convenient analytic interval, the nonparametric bootstrap approximates repeated sampling from the observed empirical distribution (Efron and Tibshirani 1994). Let \(\SampledUnit_1,\ldots,\SampledUnit_{\SampledUnitCount}\) be the independent sampled units and \(\SampleStatistic\) the statistic computed from them. Draw \(\SampledUnitCount\) units with replacement, recompute the statistic, and repeat this procedure \(\BootstrapReplicateCount\) times. If a unit is a paired task record, keep both configurations’ outcomes together; independently resampling the two columns destroys the pairing. Clustered observations require a resampling design that preserves the relevant cluster dependence.

Efron, Bradley, and Robert J. Tibshirani. 1994. An Introduction to the Bootstrap. Routledge. https://doi.org/10.1201/9780429246593.
Let \(\BootstrapReplicateCount\ge1\) be an integer. Denote replicate \(\BootstrapReplicateIndex\) by \(\SampleStatistic^{*(\BootstrapReplicateIndex)}\) and sort the bootstrap statistics as \(\SampleStatistic^*_{(1)}\le\cdots\le\SampleStatistic^*_{(\BootstrapReplicateCount)}\). Define their empirical quantile by
\[\BootstrapQuantileFunction^*(\QuantileLevel)=\inf\left\{\QuantileThresholdCandidate:\frac{1}{\BootstrapReplicateCount}
\sum_{\BootstrapReplicateIndex=1}^{\BootstrapReplicateCount}\EventIndicator\{\SampleStatistic^{*(\BootstrapReplicateIndex)}\le \QuantileThresholdCandidate\}\ge \QuantileLevel\right\},
\qquad 0<\QuantileLevel<1.\]
Equivalently, \(\BootstrapQuantileFunction^*(\QuantileLevel)=\SampleStatistic^*_{(\lceil \BootstrapReplicateCount \QuantileLevel\rceil)}\). The one-based index lies between \(1\) and \(\BootstrapReplicateCount\), including for small resample counts; different software may use interpolated quantiles instead.
For \(0<\StatisticalSignificanceLevel<1\), the percentile interval with nominal coverage \(1-\StatisticalSignificanceLevel\) is
\[[\BootstrapQuantileFunction^*(\StatisticalSignificanceLevel/2),\ \BootstrapQuantileFunction^*(1-\StatisticalSignificanceLevel/2)].\]
This definition makes the ordering and finite-resample quantile convention explicit. The SciPy bootstrap documentation (The SciPy community, n.d.) describes percentile intervals and paired resampling; it also distinguishes percentile, basic, and bias-corrected methods. The construction is not a universal coverage guarantee. A small or unrepresentative sample, strong skew, dependence, or a statistic that behaves poorly under resampling can invalidate its interpretation. More bootstrap replicates reduce Monte Carlo variability conditional on the data; they do not supply missing tasks, repair missing outcomes, or establish an unobserved tail. The paired-score interval in Confidence intervals for acceptance is a separate method, not this bootstrap interval.

The SciPy community. n.d. Scipy.stats.bootstrap. SciPy documentation.




Fix one task, its initial-state distribution, the complete run policy, and a binary pass criterion. Suppose the runs are independent and identically distributed conditional on that task, with per-run pass probability \(\AttemptPassProbability\). Among \(\GeneratedSampleCount\ge \IndependentAttemptCount\ge1\) fully graded runs, let \(\PassingSampleCount\) pass. These are integer counts with \(0\le \PassingSampleCount\le \GeneratedSampleCount\). Pending or unavailable labels require the declared missing-outcome policy rather than silent exclusion.


For every subset \(\RunIndexSubset\) of \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) run indices, let \(\SubsetAnyPassIndicator\) indicate that at least one member passed. Averaging these indicators over all \(\binom \GeneratedSampleCount \IndependentAttemptCount\) subsets gives
\[\CandidateAvailabilityEstimate_k=\frac{1}{\binom \GeneratedSampleCount \IndependentAttemptCount}\sum_{|\RunIndexSubset|=k}\SubsetAnyPassIndicator
=1-\frac{\binom{\GeneratedSampleCount-\PassingSampleCount}{\IndependentAttemptCount}}{\binom \GeneratedSampleCount \IndependentAttemptCount}.\]
The failure numerator is zero when \(\GeneratedSampleCount-\PassingSampleCount<\IndependentAttemptCount\). Each subset comprises \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) conditionally independent runs, so \(\mathbb{E}[\SubsetAnyPassIndicator]=1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount\). Linearity of expectation therefore establishes
\[\mathbb{E}[\CandidateAvailabilityEstimate_k]=1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount.\]
The subset indicators need not be mutually independent for this expectation argument. Chen et al. (2021) use this unbiased estimator for test-passing candidate availability. It does not establish that a deployed selector returns a passing candidate within its allowance; Candidate availability under pass@\IndependentAttemptCount develops that distinction. Generating \(\GeneratedSampleCount=\IndependentAttemptCount\) is valid, although its sampling variability must still be assessed.

Chen, Mark, Jerry Tworek, Heewoo Jun, Qiming Yuan, Henrique Ponde de Oliveira Pinto, Jared Kaplan, Harri Edwards, et al. 2021. “Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2107.03374.



For \(\GeneratedSampleCount-\PassingSampleCount\ge \IndependentAttemptCount\), expand the failure ratio as
\[\frac{\binom{\GeneratedSampleCount-\PassingSampleCount}{\IndependentAttemptCount}}{\binom \GeneratedSampleCount \IndependentAttemptCount}
=\prod_{j=0}^{\IndependentAttemptCount-1}\frac{\GeneratedSampleCount-\PassingSampleCount-\ProductFactorIndex}{\GeneratedSampleCount-\ProductFactorIndex}
=\prod_{j=0}^{\IndependentAttemptCount-1}\left(1-\frac{\PassingSampleCount}{\GeneratedSampleCount-\ProductFactorIndex}\right).\]
Direct floating-point factorials can overflow even when the final ratio lies in \([0,1]\). The product avoids those factorials. A log representation also avoids intermediate products of many small factors:
\[\LogFailureRatio=\sum_{j=0}^{\IndependentAttemptCount-1}\log\left(1-\frac{\PassingSampleCount}{\GeneratedSampleCount-\ProductFactorIndex}\right),
\qquad \CandidateAvailabilityEstimate_k=1-\exp(\LogFailureRatio).\]
In floating-point code, log1p(-c / (n-j)) and -expm1(s_fail) reduce cancellation when the ratio is close to one. Handle \(\GeneratedSampleCount-\PassingSampleCount<\IndependentAttemptCount\) before taking logarithms, returning \(\CandidateAvailabilityEstimate_k=1\); \(\PassingSampleCount=0\) gives zero coverage. The arithmetic takes \(\mathcal{O}(\IndependentAttemptCount)\) terms but still has finite-precision limits. Stable evaluation does not remove uncertainty in the measured pass probability.



Let \(\SubsetAllPassIndicator\) indicate that every run in subset \(\RunIndexSubset\) passed. Counting successful subsets and applying the same expectation argument gives
\[\AllRunsPassEstimate_k=\frac{\binom \PassingSampleCount \IndependentAttemptCount}{\binom \GeneratedSampleCount \IndependentAttemptCount},
\qquad \mathbb{E}[\AllRunsPassEstimate_k]=\AttemptPassProbability^\IndependentAttemptCount.\]
The numerator is zero when \(\PassingSampleCount<\IndependentAttemptCount\). Otherwise,
\[\AllRunsPassEstimate_k=\prod_{j=0}^{\IndependentAttemptCount-1}\frac{\PassingSampleCount-\ProductFactorIndex}{\GeneratedSampleCount-\ProductFactorIndex}.\]
This is the task-level repeated-run estimator in equation 13.5. For a declared task distribution with task-specific probabilities \(\AttemptPassProbability_i\), the population quantities are
\[\operatorname{pass@}\IndependentAttemptCount=\mathbb{E}_i[1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability_i)^\IndependentAttemptCount],
\qquad \operatorname{pass}^{\IndependentAttemptCount}=\mathbb{E}_i[\AttemptPassProbability_i^\IndependentAttemptCount].\]
Average the task-level estimates with the declared task weights, not weights proportional to how many repeats a task received. Under independently sampled new tasks and independent runs, the probability that all \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) new tasks pass is instead \((\mathbb{E}_i[\AttemptPassProbability_i])^\IndependentAttemptCount\). That is a different experiment. Shared outages, retained state, or feedback-conditioned revisions can violate the conditional independence used here. Potential and repeated-run consistency states which complete policy, criterion, task distribution and observation cutoff accompany these metrics.




The sequential example in Staged Releases compares two specified Bernoulli distributions (Wald 1945). It is distinct from the chapter’s paired offline comparison. Let independent labels \(\TaskAcceptanceLabel_i\in\{0,1\}\) have a stationary acceptance probability \(\StreamAcceptanceProbability\), with the label and observation policy fixed in advance. The simple hypotheses are

Wald, Abraham. 1945. “Sequential Tests of Statistical Hypotheses.” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 16 (2): 117–86. https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177731118.
\[\StatisticalHypothesis_0:\StreamAcceptanceProbability=\StreamAcceptanceProbability_0,\qquad \StatisticalHypothesis_1:\StreamAcceptanceProbability=\StreamAcceptanceProbability_1,\qquad 0<\StreamAcceptanceProbability_1<\StreamAcceptanceProbability_0<1.\]
Both probabilities are design inputs. Treating an estimated historical baseline as known without accounting for its uncertainty changes this model. With \(\AcceptedLabelCount_n=\sum_{i=1}^{\ObservedLabelCount}\TaskAcceptanceLabel_i\), use the chapter’s log-likelihood ratio in favor of the specified degradation:
\[\CumulativeLogLikelihoodRatio_n=\sum_{i=1}^{\ObservedLabelCount}\log\frac{\Pr(\TaskAcceptanceLabel_i\mid \StreamAcceptanceProbability_1)}{\Pr(\TaskAcceptanceLabel_i\mid \StreamAcceptanceProbability_0)}
=\AcceptedLabelCount_n\log\frac{\StreamAcceptanceProbability_1}{\StreamAcceptanceProbability_0}+(\ObservedLabelCount-\AcceptedLabelCount_n)\log\frac{1-\StreamAcceptanceProbability_1}{1-\StreamAcceptanceProbability_0}.\]
A pass adds a negative increment and a failure a positive one. Stop and select \(\StatisticalHypothesis_1\) at \(\CumulativeLogLikelihoodRatio_n\ge \SprtUpperLogBoundary\), select \(\StatisticalHypothesis_0\) at \(\CumulativeLogLikelihoodRatio_n\le \SprtLowerLogBoundary\), and otherwise continue, with \(\SprtLowerLogBoundary<0<\SprtUpperLogBoundary\). A statistical selection is not itself production authorization. In particular, selecting \(\StreamAcceptanceProbability_0\) against this particular \(\StreamAcceptanceProbability_1\) does not establish general noninferiority or absence of harmful effects.


For the untruncated test, write its realized errors as
\[\RealizedFalseAlarmProbability = \Pr_0(\text{select }\StatisticalHypothesis_1),\qquad
\RealizedMissedDegradationProbability = \Pr_1(\text{select }\StatisticalHypothesis_0).\]
Here \(\Pr_{\HypothesisIndex}\) means probability under \(\StatisticalHypothesis_{\HypothesisIndex}\). At an upper-boundary stopping path, its likelihood under \(\StatisticalHypothesis_1\) is at least \(e^{\SprtUpperLogBoundary}\) times that under \(\StatisticalHypothesis_0\). Summing over all such paths gives
\[1-\RealizedMissedDegradationProbability\ge e^{\SprtUpperLogBoundary} \RealizedFalseAlarmProbability.\]
Likewise, summing over lower-boundary paths gives
\[\RealizedMissedDegradationProbability\le e^{\SprtLowerLogBoundary}(1-\RealizedFalseAlarmProbability).\]
These relations concern realized operating characteristics, not arbitrary target values. Neglecting boundary overshoot replaces the inequalities by equalities. Substituting desired errors \(\StatisticalSignificanceLevel\) and \(\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate\) then yields Wald’s approximate boundaries
\[\SprtUpperLogBoundary=\log\frac{1-\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate}{\StatisticalSignificanceLevel},\qquad
\SprtLowerLogBoundary=\log\frac{\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate}{1-\StatisticalSignificanceLevel},
\qquad 0<\StatisticalSignificanceLevel,\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate<1,\quad\StatisticalSignificanceLevel+\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate<1.\]
The targets have the same meanings as in equation 13.9: \(\StatisticalSignificanceLevel\) targets selecting degradation under \(\StreamAcceptanceProbability_0\), and \(\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate\) targets selecting \(\StreamAcceptanceProbability_0\) under \(\StreamAcceptanceProbability_1\). Discrete observations generally overshoot the boundaries. The approximation does not establish \(\RealizedFalseAlarmProbability\le\StatisticalSignificanceLevel\) and \(\RealizedMissedDegradationProbability\le\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate\) individually; Fischer and Ramdas (2026) analyze that limitation. Validate the operating characteristics under the selected model and actual stopping policy. A sample or time cap introduces another disposition, inconclusive, whose probability must not be folded into favorable selection.

Fischer, Lasse, and Aaditya Ramdas. 2026. “Improving Wald’s (Approximate) Sequential Probability Ratio Test by Avoiding Overshoot.” IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 72 (4): 2457–71. https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.2026.3658855.



Let \(\SprtStoppingSampleCount\) be the untruncated stopping sample count. Under \(\StatisticalHypothesis_1\), the mean increment is
\[\SprtExpectedLogIncrement_1=\StreamAcceptanceProbability_1\log\frac{\StreamAcceptanceProbability_1}{\StreamAcceptanceProbability_0}+(1-\StreamAcceptanceProbability_1)\log\frac{1-\StreamAcceptanceProbability_1}{1-\StreamAcceptanceProbability_0}>0.\]
For these independent, bounded Bernoulli log increments and a stopping time with finite expectation, Wald’s identity gives \(\mathbb{E}_1[\CumulativeLogLikelihoodRatio_{\SprtStoppingSampleCount}]=\SprtExpectedLogIncrement_1\mathbb{E}_1[\SprtStoppingSampleCount]\). If overshoot is neglected, the terminal expectation is approximately \((1-\RealizedMissedDegradationProbability)\SprtUpperLogBoundary+\RealizedMissedDegradationProbability \SprtLowerLogBoundary\). Substituting the design target \(\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate\) for the realized error gives the further planning approximation
\[\mathbb{E}_1[\SprtStoppingSampleCount]\approx\frac{(1-\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate)\SprtUpperLogBoundary+\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate \SprtLowerLogBoundary}{\SprtExpectedLogIncrement_1}.\]
The mixture includes both terminal decisions, including mistaken selection of \(\StatisticalHypothesis_0\), as in the average-sample-number expression of Hory and Hero (2004, eq. 24). It is not the conditional expected sample count until a degradation alarm. Staged Releases computes this approximation and adds an explicit label-delay model; the time conversion does not follow from the probability test alone.

Hory, Cyril, and Alfred O. Hero. 2004. Sequential Probability Ratio Test for the Detection of a Single Electron Spin in the OSCAR Setup. arXiv preprint quant-ph/0402181.
Changing task mix, correlated trials, outcome-dependent completion ordering or missing labels can invalidate the assumed stream. A protocol must state which labels become available and how their order and unresolved cases enter the analysis. Multiple monitored metrics, repeated restarts and hard operational tripwires also change the decision procedure. Expected sample count is neither a maximum traffic exposure nor a harm bound. Admission limits and the recovery of outstanding effects remain separate runtime obligations.




As an optional decision model, when policy permits a choice between automatic execution and human review, that choice can be modeled as a binary decision under uncertainty with asymmetric costs. The approval gate in Approval Gates enforces the selected policy; it does not make prohibited actions eligible for a cost-based exception.
Let \(\PolicyAction\) denote a proposed action, and let \(\DamagingOutcomeIndicator=1\) indicate the modeled damaging outcome if it executes automatically; \(\DamagingOutcomeIndicator=0\) means that particular damage does not occur, not necessarily that the task succeeds. The runtime estimates the conditional probability \(\Pr(\DamagingOutcomeIndicator=1\mid\InputFeatureVector,\PolicyAction)\) from observable features \(\InputFeatureVector\). Write the estimate as \(\EstimatedDamageProbability\); it need not equal the true probability.
We define the loss matrix \(\EscalationLossMatrix(\EscalationDecision,\RealizedDamageOutcome)\) for decision \(\EscalationDecision\in\{\text{Auto},\text{Escalate}\}\). All costs use a common unit, with \(\UnrecoverableDamageCost>0\) and \(\HumanReviewCost\ge0\); any latency penalty must be converted to that unit before addition. This simplified model assumes that review always prevents the modeled damage; the approval mechanism itself supplies no such guarantee:

\(\EscalationLossMatrix(\text{Auto}, 0) = \AutonomousExecutionComputeCost\): The direct token and compute cost of autonomous execution.
\(\EscalationLossMatrix(\text{Auto}, 1) = \AutonomousExecutionComputeCost + \UnrecoverableDamageCost\): The compute cost plus the unrecoverable damage of external failure.
\(\EscalationLossMatrix(\text{Escalate}, 0) = \AutonomousExecutionComputeCost + \HumanReviewCost\): The compute cost plus human supervisor inspection latency and labor cost.
\(\EscalationLossMatrix(\text{Escalate}, 1) = \AutonomousExecutionComputeCost + \HumanReviewCost\): Human intervention prevents the failure, incurring only inspection cost.

Under risk-neutral Bayesian decision theory, the expected risk \(\ExpectedDecisionRisk(\EscalationDecision \mid \EstimatedDamageProbability)\) of each action is:
\[\ExpectedDecisionRisk(\text{Auto} \mid \EstimatedDamageProbability) = (1 - \EstimatedDamageProbability) \AutonomousExecutionComputeCost + \EstimatedDamageProbability (\AutonomousExecutionComputeCost + \UnrecoverableDamageCost) = \AutonomousExecutionComputeCost + \EstimatedDamageProbability \cdot \UnrecoverableDamageCost\]
\[\ExpectedDecisionRisk(\text{Escalate} \mid \EstimatedDamageProbability) = \AutonomousExecutionComputeCost + \HumanReviewCost\]
Using the estimated probability, review has lower modeled expected cost exactly when
\[\EstimatedDamageProbability \cdot \UnrecoverableDamageCost > \HumanReviewCost \iff \EstimatedDamageProbability > \frac{\HumanReviewCost}{\UnrecoverableDamageCost} \equiv \EscalationThresholdProbability\]
At equality, either decision has the same modeled cost. If review has a residual damaging-outcome probability, its expected loss needs that additional term; the displayed threshold no longer applies unchanged.


Estimation variance alone does not establish that \(\EstimatedDamageProbability\) understates risk, nor does it supply a valid upper confidence bound. A bound must follow from a declared sampling model and coverage procedure. Even a valid pointwise bound can lose its advertised coverage when the runtime adaptively selects actions or encounters a different population.
If a procedure supplies an upper bound \(\DamageProbabilityUpperBound\) for the relevant conditional damage probability, replacing \(\EstimatedDamageProbability\) by \(\DamageProbabilityUpperBound\) gives a conservative cost comparison on the event that the bound covers. The result is still a cost rule. It does not by itself prove a specified upper bound on the probability of an unhandled failure.
To see the distinction, suppose a policy separately requires automatic execution only where the true conditional probability satisfies \(\ConditionalDamageProbability(\InputFeatureVector,\PolicyAction)\le\DamageProbabilityTolerance\). Under the declared deployment distribution, that assumption yields
\[\Pr(\DamagingOutcomeIndicator=1,\ \EscalationDecision=\text{Auto})
=\mathbb{E}[\EventIndicator\{\EscalationDecision=\text{Auto}\}\ConditionalDamageProbability(\InputFeatureVector,\PolicyAction)]
\le\DamageProbabilityTolerance\Pr(\EscalationDecision=\text{Auto})\le\DamageProbabilityTolerance.\]
A confidence-bound implementation must account for failures of simultaneous coverage before claiming this result. Distribution shift, imperfect review, and dependence across repeated actions add further obligations. No expected-cost threshold replaces mandatory authority, precondition, or approval checks; Irreversible Commitments develops those checks for partial and uncertain outcomes.

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
A training update changes parameters using finite trajectory evidence. The derivations below distinguish parameterization, estimator properties, and conditional behavior bounds; none substitutes for evaluation of the resulting policy.


Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is one parameter-efficient fine-tuning method. For a frozen weight matrix \(\WeightMatrix_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{\LayerOutputWidth \times \LayerInputWidth}\), it parameterizes an update using trainable factors \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix \in \mathbb{R}^{\LayerOutputWidth \times \AdapterRank}\) and \(\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix \in \mathbb{R}^{\AdapterRank \times \LayerInputWidth}\), typically with \(\AdapterRank \ll \min(\LayerOutputWidth, \LayerInputWidth)\). With the scaling convention used in Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning, the effective matrix is
\[\WeightMatrix = \WeightMatrix_0 + \FiniteChange\WeightMatrix = \WeightMatrix_0 + \frac{\AdapterScalingFactor}{\AdapterRank} \AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix\]
where \(\AdapterScalingFactor\) is a constant scaling hyperparameter.
During forward computation on an input activation vector \(\LayerInputVector\):
\[\HiddenActivation = \WeightMatrix_0 \LayerInputVector + \FiniteChange\WeightMatrix \LayerInputVector = \WeightMatrix_0 \LayerInputVector + \frac{\AdapterScalingFactor}{\AdapterRank} \AdapterUpProjectionMatrix (\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix \LayerInputVector)\]
A common initialization draws \(\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix\) from a Gaussian distribution \(\GaussianDistribution(0, \AdapterInitializationStandardDeviation^2)\) and sets \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\) to zero, giving \(\FiniteChange\WeightMatrix = \ZeroMatrix\) initially. This preserves this layer’s forward mapping when its other components and inputs are unchanged. The factors contain \(\AdapterRank(\LayerOutputWidth + \LayerInputWidth)\) trainable parameters rather than the base matrix’s \(\LayerOutputWidth\LayerInputWidth\). Sharing a base with several adapters is one deployment option, not an isolation boundary between their roles.
During backward propagation, gradients of the scalar loss \(\LossFunction\) with respect to the adapter projection matrices \(\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix\) and \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\) are computed using the matrix chain rule:
\[\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \AdapterDownProjectionMatrix} = \frac{\AdapterScalingFactor}{\AdapterRank} \AdapterUpProjectionMatrix^T \left( \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \HiddenActivation} \right) \LayerInputVector^T, \quad \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \AdapterUpProjectionMatrix} = \frac{\AdapterScalingFactor}{\AdapterRank} \left( \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \HiddenActivation} \right) (\LayerInputVector^T \AdapterDownProjectionMatrix^T)\]
The frozen base weights \(\WeightMatrix_0\) receive zero gradient accumulation, eliminating optimizer state memory for \(\WeightMatrix_0\) while preserving exact activation gradients \(\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \LayerInputVector} = \WeightMatrix_0^T \left( \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \HiddenActivation} \right) + \frac{\AdapterScalingFactor}{\AdapterRank} \AdapterDownProjectionMatrix^T \AdapterUpProjectionMatrix^T \left( \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \HiddenActivation} \right)\) to backpropagate through preceding layers.
At the stated initialization, \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix=\ZeroMatrix\) makes the gradient of \(\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix\) zero, while the gradient of \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\) can be nonzero. Updating \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\) can therefore enable subsequent updates to both factors. Freezing the base eliminates its parameter-update state, not the need to propagate information through the layer or retain the activations required by the chosen backward implementation.



Generalized advantage estimation (GAE) is one way to combine observed rewards with an estimated value function (Schulman et al. 2016). For a finite episode, let \(\DecisionStepIndex=0,\ldots,\TurnHorizon-1\), let \(\InteractionHistory_k\) contain the interaction history and time, and let \(\Reward_k\) be the reward after action \(\TrajectoryAction_k\). For discount \(\DiscountFactor\in[0,1]\), define the remaining return and its conditional expectations:

Schulman, John, Philipp Moritz, Sergey Levine, Michael I. Jordan, and Pieter Abbeel. 2016. “High-Dimensional Continuous Control Using Generalized Advantage Estimation.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
\[\RemainingReturn=\sum_{j=k}^{\TurnHorizon-1}\DiscountFactor^{\LaterStepIndex-\DecisionStepIndex}\Reward_j,\qquad \PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_k)=\mathbb E_\pi[\RemainingReturn\mid \InteractionHistory_k],\qquad \PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\InteractionHistory_k,\TrajectoryAction_k)=\mathbb E_\pi[\RemainingReturn\mid \InteractionHistory_k,\TrajectoryAction_k].\]
The advantage is \(\PolicyHistoryAdvantage(\InteractionHistory_k,\TrajectoryAction_k)=\PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\InteractionHistory_k,\TrajectoryAction_k)-\PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_k)\). With an estimate \(\LearnedRemainingReturnEstimate\) and terminal value \(\LearnedRemainingReturnEstimate(\InteractionHistory_{\TurnHorizon})=0\), the residual and finite-episode GAE recursion are
\[\TemporalDifferenceResidual_k=\Reward_k+\DiscountFactor\LearnedRemainingReturnEstimate(\InteractionHistory_{k+1})-\LearnedRemainingReturnEstimate(\InteractionHistory_k),\qquad
\GaeAdvantageEstimate_k=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\TurnHorizon-1-\DecisionStepIndex}(\DiscountFactor\TraceDecay)^\ell\TemporalDifferenceResidual_{\DecisionStepIndex+\ell}
=\TemporalDifferenceResidual_k+\DiscountFactor\TraceDecay\GaeAdvantageEstimate_{k+1},\qquad
\GaeAdvantageEstimate_{\TurnHorizon}=0.\]
Here \(\TraceDecay\in[0,1]\). At \(\TraceDecay=1\), the sum telescopes to \(\RemainingReturn-\LearnedRemainingReturnEstimate(\InteractionHistory_k)\). At \(\TraceDecay=0\), it uses one residual, whose conditional expectation equals the advantage when the value function is exact. Approximate values introduce a bias–variance trade-off. A computational cutoff is not necessarily a terminal state; its bootstrap convention must match the objective. These estimators do not require an observed context to reveal the full environment state, but their conditioning information must be specified.
A reference-policy penalty answers a separate question: how different are two action distributions at the same input? For a fixed token prefix \(\ConditioningTokenPrefix\), write \(\NextTokenDistribution(\VocabularyToken)=\Policy(\VocabularyToken\mid \ConditioningTokenPrefix)\) and \(\ReferenceNextTokenDistribution(\VocabularyToken)=\pi_{\text{ref}}(\VocabularyToken\mid \ConditioningTokenPrefix)\). Assume positive probabilities on a common finite vocabulary. The exact divergence is
\[\KlDivergence(\NextTokenDistribution\parallel \ReferenceNextTokenDistribution)=\sum_\VocabularyToken \NextTokenDistribution(\VocabularyToken)\log\frac{\NextTokenDistribution(\VocabularyToken)}{\ReferenceNextTokenDistribution(\VocabularyToken)}.\]
The nonnegative quantity \(\KlSampleStatistic(\VocabularyToken)=\ReferenceNextTokenDistribution(\VocabularyToken)/\NextTokenDistribution(\VocabularyToken)-\log(\ReferenceNextTokenDistribution(\VocabularyToken)/\NextTokenDistribution(\VocabularyToken))-1\) is a sample statistic, not the divergence itself. We can check its expectation directly:
\[\mathbb E_{\VocabularyToken\sim \NextTokenDistribution}[\KlSampleStatistic(\VocabularyToken)]
=\sum_\VocabularyToken \ReferenceNextTokenDistribution(\VocabularyToken)-\sum_\VocabularyToken \NextTokenDistribution(\VocabularyToken)-\sum_\VocabularyToken \NextTokenDistribution(\VocabularyToken)\log\frac{\ReferenceNextTokenDistribution(\VocabularyToken)}{\NextTokenDistribution(\VocabularyToken)}
=\KlDivergence(\NextTokenDistribution\parallel \ReferenceNextTokenDistribution).\]
The sampling distribution matters. Tokens collected under an older behavior distribution are not samples from the current \(\NextTokenDistribution\) merely because both probabilities can be evaluated. At a fixed prefix, importance weighting by \(\NextTokenDistribution(\VocabularyToken)/\BehaviorDistribution(\VocabularyToken)\) recovers this expectation from behavior distribution \(\BehaviorDistribution\) when the required support and integrability hold. It does not correct the distribution of prefixes by itself. A sampled training penalty must declare those choices rather than equating every token statistic with exact KL. Neither a penalty nor surrogate clipping grants authority or guarantees that optimization will preserve task behavior; Group Relative Policy Optimization explains their role in the update.



A long trajectory offers more opportunities for a reward to depend on earlier actions, but horizon alone does not determine gradient variance. Consider on-policy sampling with a terminal reward \(\TrajectoryReward\), undiscounted finite horizon \(\TurnHorizon\), policy-independent environment dynamics, and a baseline \(\PolicyGradientBaseline_k(\InteractionHistory_k)\) fixed for the update and independent of the current sampled action conditional on its history. Under the regularity conditions for differentiating the trajectory expectation, a likelihood-ratio estimator is
\[\PolicyGradientEstimate=\sum_{k=0}^{\TurnHorizon-1}\nabla_\ModelParameters\log\Policy(\RolloutAction_k\mid \InteractionHistory_k)\,[\TrajectoryReward-\PolicyGradientBaseline_k(\InteractionHistory_k)].\]
Subtracting the baseline leaves the expectation unchanged because the conditional expected policy score is zero. The baseline changes the estimator, not the reward’s specification. A failed trajectory with \(\TrajectoryReward=0\) has a negative multiplier only where its baseline is positive.
To inspect variance without conflating a vector covariance matrix with a scalar, fix a parameter-space direction \(\ParameterSpaceDirection\) and write
\[\ProjectedTurnGradientContribution_k=\ParameterSpaceDirection^T\nabla_\ModelParameters\log\Policy(\RolloutAction_k\mid \InteractionHistory_k)\,[\TrajectoryReward-\PolicyGradientBaseline_k(\InteractionHistory_k)].\]
For finite second moments, the exact identity is
\[\operatorname{Var}(\ParameterSpaceDirection^T\PolicyGradientEstimate)
=\sum_{k=0}^{\TurnHorizon-1}\operatorname{Var}(\ProjectedTurnGradientContribution_k)
+2\sum_{0\le k<j<\TurnHorizon}\operatorname{Cov}(\ProjectedTurnGradientContribution_k,\ProjectedTurnGradientContribution_j).\]
Shared rewards and dependent interactions can produce nonzero cross terms, but their signs and magnitudes are not fixed by the number of turns. If every \(\operatorname{Var}(\ProjectedTurnGradientContribution_k)\le\TurnContributionDeviationBound^2\), Cauchy–Schwarz gives the conditional upper bound
\[\operatorname{Var}(\ParameterSpaceDirection^T\PolicyGradientEstimate)
\le\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\TurnHorizon-1}\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\ProjectedTurnGradientContribution_k)}\right)^2
\le \TurnHorizon^2\TurnContributionDeviationBound^2.\]
This is an upper bound under a uniform variance assumption, not a prediction of quadratic growth. If cross terms vanish, the bound becomes \(\TurnHorizon\TurnContributionDeviationBound^2\). More generally, the additional assumption \(\lvert\operatorname{Cov}(\ProjectedTurnGradientContribution_k,\ProjectedTurnGradientContribution_j)\rvert\le \TurnCovarianceBoundScale\TurnCovarianceDecayRatio^{\LaterRolloutTurnIndex-\RolloutTurnIndex}\) for constants \(\TurnCovarianceBoundScale\ge0\) and \(0\le\TurnCovarianceDecayRatio<1\) gives
\[\operatorname{Var}(\ParameterSpaceDirection^T\PolicyGradientEstimate)
\le \TurnHorizon\TurnContributionDeviationBound^2+2\TurnCovarianceBoundScale\sum_{\ell=1}^{\TurnHorizon-1}(\TurnHorizon-\ell)\TurnCovarianceDecayRatio^\ell
\le \TurnHorizon\left(\TurnContributionDeviationBound^2+\frac{2\TurnCovarianceBoundScale\TurnCovarianceDecayRatio}{1-\TurnCovarianceDecayRatio}\right).\]
A discount factor or a dense step reward does not establish that covariance assumption. Replacing a terminal criterion with learned process scores can also change the objective and introduce assessment error. The engineering comparison in Credit Across Turns therefore asks what each estimator measures, how its uncertainty is assessed, and what obtaining its evidence costs. It does not infer sample efficiency from horizon or reward density alone.



The bounds in Exposure Bias distinguish errors measured on reference-policy states from errors measured on learner-policy states. Neither bound predicts the realized cost of a particular agent. We derive the distinction for a finite horizon \(\TurnHorizon\), a deterministic reference policy \(\pi^*\), and a possibly stochastic learner \(\pi\) with the same initial-state distribution and environment dynamics.
Let \(\StateDistribution^t\) be the state distribution before decision \(\TurnIndex\) under \(\pi\), and \(\StateDistribution=\TurnHorizon^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^\TurnHorizon \StateDistribution^t\). Include the relevant history in the state where needed. For immediate task cost \(\ImmediateTaskCostScore(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)\in[0,1]\), define
\[\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi)=\sum_{t=1}^\TurnHorizon\mathbb E_{\PolicyObservedState\sim \StateDistribution^t,\;\PolicyAction\sim\pi(\cdot\mid \PolicyObservedState)}[\ImmediateTaskCostScore(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)].\]
Separately, let \(\ReferenceDisagreementProbability(\PolicyObservedState,\pi)=\Pr_{\PolicyAction\sim\pi(\cdot\mid \PolicyObservedState)}[\PolicyAction\ne\pi^*(\PolicyObservedState)]\). This disagreement loss is not necessarily the task cost or the token-level training loss.


Write \(\ReferenceStepDisagreementRate_t=\mathbb E_{\PolicyObservedState\sim \ReferenceStateDistribution^t}[\ReferenceDisagreementProbability(\PolicyObservedState,\pi)]\) and \(\ReferenceStateDisagreementRate=\TurnHorizon^{-1}\sum_t\ReferenceStepDisagreementRate_t\). Couple the two executions so they share environment randomness while their actions agree. Along a reference execution, draw hypothetical learner actions at each visited state. Until the first disagreement, these draws also describe the coupled learner.
By the union bound, the probability of at least one disagreement is at most \(\sum_t\ReferenceStepDisagreementRate_t=\TurnHorizon\ReferenceStateDisagreementRate\). This argument needs no independence between disagreements. Before divergence, the coupled executions incur the same costs; afterward, their total cost difference is at most \(\TurnHorizon\). Therefore
\[\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi)-\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi^*)\le \TurnHorizon\Pr(\text{any disagreement})
\le \min\{\TurnHorizon,\;\TurnHorizon^2\ReferenceStateDisagreementRate\}.\]
This yields the expert-distribution bound of Ross et al. (2011), Theorem 2.1, with the additional trivial horizon cap. Marginal error bounds do not justify replacing the union bound by \(1-(1-\ReferenceStepDisagreementRate)^\TurnHorizon\); that product requires further conditional-probability assumptions.

Ross, Stéphane, Geoffrey Gordon, and J. Andrew Bagnell. 2011. “A Reduction of Imitation Learning and Structured Prediction to No-Regret Online Learning.” Proceedings of the Fourteenth International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS) 15: 627–35.



Now let \(\LearnerStateDisagreementRate=\mathbb E_{\PolicyObservedState\sim \StateDistribution}[\ReferenceDisagreementProbability(\PolicyObservedState,\pi)]\). Define \(\ReferenceCostToGo(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)\) as expected cost from step \(\TurnIndex\) through \(\TurnHorizon\) after taking \(\PolicyAction\) and then following \(\pi^*\). Let
\[\ReferenceActionDisadvantage(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)=\ReferenceCostToGo(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)-\ReferenceCostToGo(\PolicyObservedState,\pi^*(\PolicyObservedState)).\]
Compare policies that switch from the learner to the reference after successively later steps. Their cost differences telescope, giving
\[\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi)-\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi^*)=
\sum_{t=1}^\TurnHorizon\mathbb E_{\PolicyObservedState\sim \StateDistribution^t,\;\PolicyAction\sim\pi(\cdot\mid \PolicyObservedState)}
[\ReferenceActionDisadvantage(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)].\]
Suppose \(\ReferenceActionDisadvantage(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)\le \DeviationDisadvantage\) for every learner-reachable state and action, with \(\DeviationDisadvantage\ge0\). The disadvantage is zero when the action agrees with the reference, so each expectation is at most \(\DeviationDisadvantage\) times the corresponding disagreement probability. Thus
\[\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi)-\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi^*)\le\min\{\TurnHorizon,\;\DeviationDisadvantage \TurnHorizon\LearnerStateDisagreementRate\},\]
as in Theorem 2.2. Linear dependence on \(\TurnHorizon\) requires a horizon-independent \(\DeviationDisadvantage\); in general, \(\DeviationDisadvantage\) can grow with the remaining horizon. If the immediate cost itself is disagreement, the simpler identity \(\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi)=\TurnHorizon\LearnerStateDisagreementRate\) follows directly, but does not describe arbitrary task costs.
DAgger obtains reference labels at states visited during successive policy collections and aggregates the examples for supervised learning. Its guarantees also require the stated learning and sampling assumptions. Collecting such records alone neither proves a small population error for the released policy nor makes the distribution penalty vanish. The chapter uses these bounds to motivate coverage and evaluation, not to promise that a particular training method eliminates compounding errors.

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
More workers can shorten a task, and more reviewers can change an error probability. Both conclusions depend on the overhead and dependence models, not on agent count alone.


The Delegation Trade-Off models the speedup of splitting work across \(\WorkerCount\) workers with a serial fraction and a coordination term (equation 17.1). To examine one possible scaling curve, suppose the normalized overhead is \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)=\CoherencyCoefficient(\WorkerCount-1)+\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient \WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\). This assumption gives
\[\text{Speedup}(\WorkerCount) = \frac{1}{\NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio(\WorkerCount)}, \qquad \NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio(\WorkerCount) = (1 - \ParallelFraction) + \frac{\ParallelFraction}{\WorkerCount} + \CoherencyCoefficient (\WorkerCount - 1) + \PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient \WorkerCount (\WorkerCount - 1)\]
where \(\ParallelFraction \in (0, 1]\) is the fraction of the fixed work that divides across workers. The nonnegative coefficients \(\CoherencyCoefficient\) and \(\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient\), with \(\CoherencyCoefficient+\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient>0\), parameterize the assumed overhead. With \(\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient=0\) and \(\ParallelFraction=1-\ContentionCoefficient\), \(1/\NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio\) is the universal scalability law of equation 17.5, so \(\CoherencyCoefficient\) is its coherency coefficient. The term in \(\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient\) adds overhead that grows with the number of worker pairs. Their values are workload parameters, not universal properties of delegation. The physical domain is integer \(\WorkerCount\ge 1\); on this domain \(\NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio(\WorkerCount)>0\) and \(\NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio(1)=1\). The following continuous relaxation identifies candidate worker counts to test.
Maximizing speedup on the physical domain means minimizing \(\NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio(\WorkerCount)\). Extending the denominator to positive real \(\WorkerCount\) for differentiation gives
\[\frac{d \NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio}{d \WorkerCount} = -\frac{\ParallelFraction}{\WorkerCount^2} + \CoherencyCoefficient + \PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient (2\WorkerCount - 1)\]
and setting the derivative to zero gives the stationary condition
\[\StationaryConditionPolynomial(\WorkerCount) = 2\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient \WorkerCount^3 + (\CoherencyCoefficient - \PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient) \WorkerCount^2 - \ParallelFraction = 0\]

Exactly one positive root. The coefficients of \(\StationaryConditionPolynomial(\WorkerCount)\), in order, are \(2\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient\), \(\CoherencyCoefficient - \PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient\), \(0\), and \(-\ParallelFraction\). Whether \(\CoherencyCoefficient - \PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient\) is positive or negative, the sequence of nonzero signs changes exactly once, so by Descartes’ rule of signs \(\StationaryConditionPolynomial\) has exactly one positive real root \(\WorkerCount^*\). When \(\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient = 0\) the condition reduces to \(\CoherencyCoefficient \WorkerCount^2 = \ParallelFraction\), so \(\WorkerCount^* = \sqrt{\ParallelFraction / \CoherencyCoefficient}\), which with \(\ParallelFraction=1-\ContentionCoefficient\) is the peak of equation 17.6.
The denominator is strictly convex. The second derivative, \[\frac{\DerivativeOperator^2 \NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio}{d \WorkerCount^2} = \frac{2\ParallelFraction}{\WorkerCount^3} + 2\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient,\] is positive for every \(\WorkerCount > 0\), so \(\WorkerCount^*\) uniquely minimizes the extended denominator. If \(\WorkerCount^*<1\), the constrained minimum is at \(\WorkerCount=1\). Otherwise, evaluate the adjacent integers around \(\WorkerCount^*\), subject to available capacity. Maximizing the reciprocal outside the physical domain is unnecessary and need not be valid.

Under this assumed overhead, speedup eventually falls as concurrency grows. A split shortens modeled elapsed time only if \(\NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio(\WorkerCount)<1\) at some feasible integer \(\WorkerCount>1\); that condition says nothing by itself about acceptance or cost. Fit any proposed overhead model to workload measurements, examine variation and fit error, and test its predictions at the contemplated worker counts. A stationary point is a scheduling hypothesis, not a deployment recommendation. Single-Agent Baseline Benchmarking makes the latter decision against the task’s objective and constraints.



The voting example in Correlated Ensemble Failures concerns false approval of a candidate known to violate the assessed criterion. Agreement among reviewers is not the same problem as a distributed protocol choosing one value. To model the former, let \(\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_j=1\) indicate false approval by reviewer \(\ReviewerIndex\), with an odd number \(\WorkerCount\) of reviewers. If these indicators are independent Bernoulli variables with common probability \(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability\), the majority false-approval probability is
\[\Pr\left(\sum_{j=1}^{\WorkerCount}\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_j>\frac{\WorkerCount}{2}\right)
=\sum_{k=(\WorkerCount+1)/2}^{\WorkerCount}\binom{\WorkerCount}{\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount}\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability^\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount(1-\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability)^{\WorkerCount-\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount}.\]
For \(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability<1/2\), this probability tends to zero as odd \(\WorkerCount\) increases. That conclusion depends on the stated joint model; knowing each reviewer’s marginal error rate is not enough.
A latent task propensity gives a different joint model. Let \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\) denote the false-approval probability for a randomly selected candidate in the declared cohort, and assume \(\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_j\mid \FalseApprovalPropensity\) are independent Bernoulli variables with parameter \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\). Conditional independence can describe separate samples at a fixed input even when the reviewers use identical weights. Across candidates with different propensities, however,
\[\mathbb{E}[\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_j]=\mathbb{E}[\FalseApprovalPropensity]=\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability,\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_i,\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_j)=\operatorname{Var}(\FalseApprovalPropensity)\quad (\PeerReviewerIndex\ne \ReviewerIndex).\]
The covariance follows from conditional independence and the law of total covariance. Since each marginal indicator is Bernoulli with probability \(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability\), its variance is \(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability(1-\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability)\). For \(0<\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability<1\), the pairwise correlation is therefore
\[\CorrelationCoefficient=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\FalseApprovalPropensity)}{\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability(1-\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability)}.\]
This dependence arises from shared candidate difficulty in the model, not from an assertion that identical weights force dependent random draws at every fixed input. Communication between reviewers or other shared randomness would require an additional dependence model.
For the chapter’s illustrative beta mixture, assume \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)\) with \(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\PropensityPriorRejectionShape>0\). Its mean and variance give
\[\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability=\frac{\PropensityPriorApprovalShape}{\PropensityPriorApprovalShape+\PropensityPriorRejectionShape},\qquad
\CorrelationCoefficient=\frac{1}{\PropensityPriorApprovalShape+\PropensityPriorRejectionShape+1},\qquad
\PropensityPriorApprovalShape=\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability\left(\frac{1}{\CorrelationCoefficient}-1\right),\qquad
\PropensityPriorRejectionShape=(1-\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability)\left(\frac{1}{\CorrelationCoefficient}-1\right).\]
The parameterization applies for \(0<\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability<1\) and \(0<\CorrelationCoefficient<1\). Independence is the limiting constant-propensity case, not a beta distribution with finite shape parameters and \(\CorrelationCoefficient=0\). Define the beta function locally by
\[\mathrm{B}(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)=\int_0^1 \FalseApprovalPropensityLevel^{\PropensityPriorApprovalShape-1}(1-\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel)^{\PropensityPriorRejectionShape-1}\,d\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel.\]
Integrating the conditional binomial probability over \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\) gives the beta-binomial distribution for the false-approval count \(\FalseApprovalCount=\sum_j\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_j\):
\[\Pr(\FalseApprovalCount=\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount)=
\int_0^1 \binom{\WorkerCount}{\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount}\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel^\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount(1-\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel)^{\WorkerCount-\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount}
\frac{\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel^{\PropensityPriorApprovalShape-1}(1-\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel)^{\PropensityPriorRejectionShape-1}}{\mathrm{B}(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)}\,d\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel
=\binom{\WorkerCount}{\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount}\frac{\mathrm{B}(\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount+\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\WorkerCount-\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount+\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)}{\mathrm{B}(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)}.\]
Summing over \(\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount>\WorkerCount/2\) yields the majority false-approval probability; the \(\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount=\WorkerCount\) term gives unanimous false approval. These are consequences of the full mixture assumption. Other joint distributions can share the same \(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability\) and \(\CorrelationCoefficient\) while producing different majority probabilities.
The asymptotic result also has a precise scope. Conditional on \(\FalseApprovalPropensity=\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel\ne1/2\), the sample fraction converges to \(\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel\). The beta distribution has no point mass at \(1/2\), so bounded convergence gives
\[\lim_{\substack{\WorkerCount\to\infty\\\WorkerCount\ \text{odd}}}
\Pr(\FalseApprovalCount>\WorkerCount/2)=\Pr(\FalseApprovalPropensity>1/2)
=\frac{1}{\mathrm{B}(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)}
\int_{1/2}^{1}\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel^{\PropensityPriorApprovalShape-1}(1-\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel)^{\PropensityPriorRejectionShape-1}\,d\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel.\]
In this model, adding reviewers cannot remove the cohort’s mass of candidates that most reviewers tend to approve incorrectly. The result is not a universal error floor for all model ensembles. Measure the actual review policy on the intended cohort, retain evidence about its errors, and keep runtime authorization and scoped acceptance checks distinct from the vote.

title: 19 Conclusion
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can individually tested components still leave an agent’s task unfinished or its effects unaccounted for?
An autonomous agent unites disparate systems disciplines (foundation models, memory hierarchies, isolated execution sandboxes, transactional event logs, and independent verifiers) into a single closed-loop control architecture. Each individual component can satisfy its local unit tests, yet the integrated system can still fail if the contracts connecting them are ungrounded or ambiguous. The core challenge of agentic systems engineering is designing the deterministic harness that bounds and verifies a stochastic proposer, a problem that larger models and more elaborate prompts do not remove. Across a trajectory horizon, carried working state, and delegated authority, reliable autonomy is achieved only when the runtime enforces invariant closure at every system boundary.

Learning Objectives

Trace an incident-remediation trajectory, identifying the owner and record of each consequential transition
Translate a task contract into bounds and acceptance requirements proportionate to its horizon, state, and authority
Diagnose state and evidence mismatches at subsystem boundaries using the authority and lifetime of each record
Resolve an uncertain external action without confusing a lost response with permission to repeat its effect
Select a system intervention using attributed failures, outcome evidence, and its full deployment cost
Construct a safety case that connects scoped claims to arguments, evidence, assumptions, and residual uncertainty
Distinguish assistance with specifications from authority to adopt them and accept the resulting task






Every mechanism in the book now carries a price in one unit, the cost per accepted task of each lighthouse (Cost per Accepted Task by Archetype), so the last instrument is in place. The introduction to this book posed three foundational architectural questions that every subsequent chapter has addressed in part. With the complete system architecture now assembled and priced, each question admits a concise engineering answer, and each answer represents a concrete design claim that this concluding chapter tests against a live operational workload.


↩︎ The three foundational architectural questions governing agentic design are established in The book's three questions.
The first question asked when an adaptive, model-directed loop earns its cost over a deterministic workflow. The answer cannot be settled globally across an entire application; it must be resolved at each individual decision point by measuring the cost per accepted task under a fixed specification contract. A model should direct the next action only where interpreting dynamic, unstructured evidence improves the task acceptance rate by a larger factor than the added inference calls increase the cost of an attempt. Deterministic software should govern everywhere else. Evaluated by this metric, dynamic model loops can earn their cost at phases such as root-cause diagnosis, where the next diagnostic transition cannot be enumerated in advance, while deterministic control structures manage the predictable orchestration surrounding them. The incident below supplies a cost threshold for that comparison. Its price, worked out in section 19.3.2, shows the model calls to be a small fraction of one remediation attempt’s cost. Whether additional diagnostic calls earn that cost depends on the relative acceptance improvement measured against a matched baseline under the same contract and latency constraints.
The second question asked what operational machinery must surround the model. The answer is strictly proportional to the task’s exposure profile across state, authority, and execution horizon. Managing state requires selectively retrieved context, explicitly budgeted serving state, and durable audit records that preserve source authority. Governing authority demands typed, mediated action interfaces, definitive effect settlement before any retry loop can execute, and process containment enforced within the execution substrate beneath the model. Managing horizon requires a supervisory harness that bounds the total trajectory, a write-ahead log of intent recorded before committing each external side effect, and compensating workflows capable of mitigating actions that cannot be reversed. A read-only lookup requires little of this protective scaffolding, whereas an autonomous remediation agent operating on live production systems demands all of it.
The third question asked how operators verify that a task has actually succeeded. The answer requires objective evidence collected from an authoritative endpoint that directly monitors the target system, evaluated against an explicit contract adopted by system owners before execution began. This verification must satisfy a pre-declared closure evidence level, with any residual uncertainty explicitly quantified and assigned to an accountable owner. A model’s self-generated report never serves as evidence, however coherent or persuasive, because a component executing within the loop cannot certify its own output. Stated as an operational acceptance rule, this is the discipline of invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)).
Each of these answers is straightforward to state for an isolated component, but maintaining them across subsystem boundaries is where agentic architectures most often fail. Individually tested services routinely drop an in-flight task when state, authority, and verification handoffs cross architectural seams. The answers are therefore tested on one complete incident handled by the remediation agent, the lighthouse that exercises horizon, state, and authority at once, followed from its contract across the memory and execution boundaries to the one boundary no runtime can close on the owner’s behalf.



A database service triggers a query-latency alert shortly after a configuration change. An automated remediation agent inspects telemetry, correlates logs, and proposes reverting to the previous known-good settings. The human operator approves the rollback, but the configuration endpoint drops the network connection before returning an acknowledgment. At this moment, the system faces a classic distributed systems dilemma: whether the mutation took effect remains fundamentally unknown. No fluent textual explanation from a language model can resolve that ambiguity. If the runtime interprets the timeout as a failure and retries under a fresh operation identifier, it risks executing the mutation twice. If it optimistically assumes success, it risks closing an incident while degraded queries continue to impact production. If it simply halts, it leaves a live production change in an unverified state with no entity accountable for it. Each failure mode arises by default when every component satisfies its local unit contract, yet no system component owns the distributed boundary between them. This is the end-to-end argument that grounded the closure evidence levels (The invariant closure principle) applied to a single incident: an intermediate success report from a tool or a model call cannot establish acceptance, and only the principal holding the task contract can verify completion against direct evidence from the service.



Horizon, state, and authority return together, and the runtime closes each on one trajectory.
This concrete incident, incident_42 on database service db_primary_01, represents the operational workload of the remediation agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) and supplies the book’s capstone synthesis. The remediation agent is this book’s irreversible actor: it operates over a bounded horizon, mutates shared production state, and exercises real authority over a live service. This single trajectory, from initial diagnostic telemetry through operator approval, execution dispatch, and terminal acceptance, anchors the remainder of the chapter. At every transition, the engineering criterion remains constant: the system must deterministically record what it proposed, what permissions were granted, what physical effects occurred, what evidence validates the outcome, and which principal bears ongoing responsibility. Building an agentic machine learning system means guaranteeing that these accounts are durable and verifiable. In this architecture, the managed database service owns its active configuration, the runtime orchestrator owns execution and control decisions, and the accepting authority verifies whether post-remediation evidence satisfies the delegated operational contract. One named human principal, operations_owner_42, is accountable both for any operation the runtime cannot settle and for the service once the incident is accepted. The runtime’s settlement process, a runtime component rather than a person, reconciles uncertain operations on that owner’s behalf.


The incident lifecycle begins under incident_contract_v1, which grants bounded diagnostic read access and establishes formal gates for proposing, approving, and validating configuration mutations. Initial privileges are strictly observational. The runtime provisions read_scope_42 to query authorized service endpoints, ensuring that telemetry gathering cannot inadvertently trigger state changes or be coerced into production writes. Throughout this trace, identifiers such as read_scope_42 denote durable local record keys rather than opaque cryptographic hashes.
Next, the context manager gathers the initial latency alert, recent time-series metrics, active configuration parameters, and relevant runbook sections into an auditable manifest, context_manifest_42. Every observation in this manifest records its originating source, a version tag when available, and a precise ingestion timestamp. Here, a practical systems hazard appears: while the retrieved runbook suggests a memory-pool misconfiguration, that document might describe a previous software deployment. By diffing the runbook recommendations against the active production configuration (config_v7) and current telemetry, the agent formulates a diagnostic hypothesis. Additional diagnostic queries, constrained by the task’s remaining call budget, must corroborate this hypothesis against alternative explanations such as downstream network congestion or disk saturation.
When the diagnostic evidence converges on a known regression, the model emits change_request_42, which specifies the target configuration keys, the desired values, and the expected baseline version config_v7. In accordance with incident change policy, an authorized human operator reviews the proposed diff and issues approval_42. This record binds the operator’s identity to the request identifier, the target host, the exact payload parameters, the prerequisite baseline config_v7, and an expiration window. The approval records permission for that exact payload and nothing broader; it does not perform the mutation. The model drafts the operational rationale, but it cannot grant itself execution authority. An approval granted minutes before execution is an earlier authorization check, and complete mediation (definition \(\ref{dfn-complete-mediation}\)) requires a fresh one at the moment of use. Prior to network dispatch, the runtime action gate therefore rechecks operator authorization, compares the payload against the approval’s digest, inspects the expiration deadline, confirms resource quotas, and evaluates runtime preconditions. If an operator revokes the ticket or the model generates an altered proposal, the original approval no longer matches and cannot silently apply to a mutated repair payload.


↩︎ Rechecking an approved request’s digest, expiry, budget, and authorization at the dispatch boundary is established in Dispatch-time rechecks.
Even a thorough pre-dispatch check cannot protect against time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) races if a peer operator modifies database settings in the sub-second interval between the gate check and network arrival. The database configuration endpoint closes this concurrency window with the conditional update of Conditional updates, an atomic expected-version check. The endpoint executes the modification if and only if the live configuration version matches config_v7 at the instant of the write; a version conflict triggers an immediate rejection, returning the task to the agent for re-diagnosis rather than applying an outdated patch onto an altered baseline. To survive network instability, the endpoint also makes the write idempotent in the sense of definition \(\ref{dfn-idempotent-action}\): it deduplicates requests by an operation identity bound to the caller, target, and payload, and retains that identity across a window longer than the maximum client retry horizon, so a replayed request inside the window is recognized rather than reapplied. The endpoint also exposes a read-only operation-status lookup. These correctness guarantees must reside at the endpoint implementation itself; client tool schemas or client-side metadata can declare invariants, but only the server endpoint can enforce them. Before transmitting the RPC across the network, the runtime appends an intent record for op_42 to a write-ahead journal at the durability boundary chosen for the deployment, together with its recovery descriptor: the obligation registration of the trajectory saga, here the corrective-action template, the preconditions it must satisfy, and the accountable owner, operations_owner_42. Once both are persistent on disk, the runtime dispatches the request with operation identity op_42 and expected version config_v7.


↩︎ Deduplication by an operation identity bound to caller, target, and payload is established in Operation identity and endpoint contracts.
