Greshake, Kai, Sahar Abdelnabi, Shailesh Mishra, Christoph Endres, Thorsten Holz, and Mario Fritz. 2023. “Not What You’ve Signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection.” Proceedings of the 16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security, 79–90. https://doi.org/10.1145/3605764.3623985.

Hardy, Norm. 1988. “The Confused Deputy: (Or Why Capabilities Might Have Been Invented).” ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 22 (4): 36–38. https://doi.org/10.1145/60609.60611.
Five foundational works trace this lineage from classical systems theory to dependable agent design:

Saltzer et al. (1984) articulates why reliable verification must ultimately reside at the endpoints where application semantics are fully understood. In agentic architectures, it provides the core justification for why task acceptance and completion checks belong to the task owner rather than intermediate execution layers.
Gray (1981) examines the transaction abstraction alongside its operational limits in decentralized, long-running workflows. It clarifies which atomicity and consistency guarantees an agent runtime can inherit directly, and where it must substitute compensation, idempotent retries, and asynchronous settlement.
Brooks (1987) distinguishes between the essential complexity of specifying conceptual structures and the accidental complexity of implementing them. This distinction clarifies what model generation can streamline, such as boilerplate synthesis and API translation, and what remains hard systems engineering: defining crisp specifications, verifying invariants, and validating task contracts.
Sculley et al. (2015) analyzes deployed machine learning through the lens of systems engineering, demonstrating how glue code, configuration drift, and hidden feedback loops dominate operational debt. Its cautionary analysis applies with even greater force when models shift from passive prediction to active tool invocation across production infrastructure.
Kelly and Weaver (2004) introduces the Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) for constructing rigorous, auditable safety arguments. It illustrates how to link an explicit engineering claim directly to empirical evidence, contextual boundaries, and underlying assumptions, the discipline required when validating agent deployments and establishing operational acceptance.


Saltzer, Jerome H., David P. Reed, and David D. Clark. 1984. “End-to-End Arguments in System Design.” ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 2 (4): 277–88. https://doi.org/10.1145/357401.357402.

Gray, Jim. 1981. “The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations.” Proceedings of the Seventh International Conference on Very Large Data Bases (VLDB) 7: 144–54.

Brooks, Frederick P. 1987. “No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering.” Computer 20 (4): 10–19.

Sculley, D., Gary Holt, Daniel Golovin, Eugene Davydov, Todd Phillips, Dietmar Ebner, Vinay Chaudhary, Michael Young, Jean-François Crespo, and Dan Dennison. 2015. “Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 28: 2503–11.



Every given below is a hypothetical problem input, not a measurement of a particular model, service, or deployment. The problems combine mechanisms from several parts of the book, and each asks for numbers and then for the design decision those numbers support.

Spacing checks and checkpoints on a long repair (Basic). A repair agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)) runs a 60-turn trajectory of 15 s turns, and each turn independently proposes a violating step with probability \(\PerStepErrorRate = 0.005\). The runtime can insert a check every \(\CheckWindowTurnCount\) turns that catches any violation in its window. Each check also saves a durable checkpoint of the sandbox (Checkpoints), which takes 3 s, and a caught window is restored from the previous checkpoint and rerun. Operations wants at least 95 percent of windows to pass on the first attempt. When a window fails, finding the responsible step means replaying the alternatives inside it: the agent chooses among 3 candidate actions per turn, each replayed path takes 0.5 s to check, and the attribution budget is 10 minutes.
Use equation 1.1 to compute the probability that the whole trajectory runs free of violations with no intermediate checks, and the per-turn rate a better model would need to lift it to 95 percent. Find the largest \(\CheckWindowTurnCount\) that meets the first-pass target and the largest \(\CheckWindowTurnCount\) that fits the attribution budget. Which constraint binds, and how many checks does the trajectory need? At that spacing, compute the expected wall-clock time including checkpoint saves and reruns, and compare it with rerunning the unchecked trajectory from scratch until it passes. Turn 40 pushes a branch to a shared remote, an effect the sandbox checkpoint cannot restore. Using intent before effect (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}\)) and the commitment region of The commitment region, explain where a check must sit relative to that turn, what the runtime must record before dispatching it, and why the restore-and-rerun arithmetic above no longer covers a violation found after it.
Where the accepted-task cost goes (Basic). A repair attempt runs 30 turns. Each turn reads 8,000 input tokens at $2 per million and generates 400 output tokens at $10 per million, and each attempt also pays $0.25 of sandbox time, $0.15 of test runs, and $1.00 of human review. Half of the attempts are accepted.
Compute the attempt cost and \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) from equation 1.2. Two changes are proposed. Prefix caching bills each turn’s reused prefix at one-fifth of the input price, and without other changes the reused prefix is 7,200 of the 8,000 input tokens. A context fix adds a 2,000-token block of current test output to every turn and raises acceptance to 65 percent. Compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) for each change alone. Then compute it for both together, with the block placed after the stable content so that the 7,200-token reused prefix survives and the block is billed at the full input price. Using principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\), explain why the two changes compound only under that placement (Exercise 7 prices the alternative), and which term of the attempt cost neither change touches.
Pricing a blind retry (Basic). A fleet of remediation agents (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) issues 25,000 mutating configuration calls per day. Requests are lost with probability \(\RequestLossProbability = 0.001\) and replies with probability \(\ReplyLossProbability = 0.004\), and a duplicated change costs $2,000 in expected damage. An operation-status lookup costs $0.01.
Compute the expected number of timeouts per day and, using the settlement relation of notebook \(\ref{nbk-07-settlement-budget}\), the expected duplicates per day under a blind retry with a fresh identity, and their daily cost. Compare that cost with a status lookup on every timeout. An endpoint offers neither deduplication by operation identity nor a status lookup. Using the contract of section 19.3, decide whether the task can be admitted against that endpoint and what the runtime must do after a lost reply.
Serving memory for a support fleet (Intermediate). This problem transfers the chapter’s whole-trajectory sizing to the support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)), whose binding constraint is serving capacity under concurrency rather than the authority that binds the remediation agent. Sessions arrive at 20 per second and last 180 s on average, mostly waiting on the customer. Each session makes 6 model calls of 2 s each, every call reads a 6,000-token context, and attention state costs 0.1 MB per token. The pool has 1,000 GB of accelerator memory for attention state, prefills 400,000 tokens/s in aggregate, and moves 200 GB/s between host memory and accelerators.
Use equation 18.4 to compute the concurrent sessions and the attention state needed to hold every session resident, and compare it with the pool. Compute the state held by sessions inside a model call. Evaluate two policies: evicting a session’s state between calls and recomputing it at the next call, and keeping it in a host-memory tier so that only about 500 new tokens per call are prefilled. For each, compute the load on the binding resource. Choose a policy, and state which workload and fleet measurements are needed before concluding that the remediation agent would encounter a different binding constraint.
Buying release evidence for an adapted model (Intermediate). A team proposes an adapted model for a repair workload that lowers the cost per assigned task from $1.20 to $0.80. Development and training cost $6,000, each release-evaluation task costs $3 per arm, both arms run the same number of tasks, and the workload runs 10,000 tasks per month. Acceptance is about 70 percent. The release test uses \(\SignificanceCriticalQuantile = 1.96\) and \(\StatisticalPowerQuantile = 0.84\).
Use equation 13.3 to compute the tasks per arm needed to detect a 5-point and a 2.5-point acceptance difference, and fold each evaluation bill into \(\AdaptationInvestmentCost\). Use equation 1 to compute \(\BreakEvenTaskCount\) and the payback in months for each. Leadership requires payback within 6 months. Which detectable difference can the team afford? A 3-point regression can hide inside the 5-point test; compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) for both configurations under that regression and decide whether the cost case survives it. Unlike notebook 19.1, the evaluation bill here depends on the decision the team wants to defend; explain why.
Delegating a research question under a deadline (Intermediate). A research agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}\)) answers a question in 40 minutes as a single controller, at a cost of $4.00. The analyst needs the answer in 20 minutes. Of the work, 80 percent splits across workers, and coordination overhead grows as \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount) = 0.02\,(\WorkerCount-1)\) of the single-controller time. A design with \(\WorkerCount \ge 2\) workers costs $4.00 plus $0.60 per worker for repeated context and result integration. The question’s allowance is $10.
Use equation 17.1 to find the smallest \(\WorkerCount\) that meets the deadline, the \(\WorkerCount\) that maximizes speedup, and the cost multiple of each over the single controller. A proposed runtime gives each worker its own $10 ceiling. Compute the worst-case spend at the chosen \(\WorkerCount\) and state the admission rule of principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\) that prevents it. Three workers agree on a source’s claim after reading the same page. Explain why that agreement is weaker evidence than three independent checks, and what the integrating controller must record before accepting it.
Where the fresh evidence goes in the prompt (Intermediate). A remediation trajectory runs 20 turns. Its context starts at 20,000 tokens and grows by 1,000 tokens per turn. A 500-token status block, refreshed from the source on every turn, sits at token position 2,000, right after the system instructions. Uncached input costs $2 per million tokens, a reused prefix costs $0.20 per million, and prefill runs at 10,000 tokens/s.
Using principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\), compute the tokens recomputed on turns 2 to 20 with the block at position 2,000 and with the block moved to the end of the prompt, where each turn recomputes only the block and the new turn’s tokens. Compare the input cost and the average per-turn prefill time of the two layouts. The team then proposes to stop refreshing the block and rely on the cached copy, since a cache hit shows the text is unchanged. Use principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\) to decide whether the saving is admissible, and state which check at the endpoint still protects the change if the status block is stale.
Sizing a whole remediation trajectory (Advanced). A remediation service runs 400 attempts per day, and 80 percent are accepted. An attempt spends $0.60 on 12 model turns, $5.00 on operator approval, and $0.40 on the health-window check. Three failure paths remain.

Each turn proposes a violating action with probability 0.01; the action gate rejects 98 percent of them, and an escaped violation causes $20,000 of damage, of which compensation recovers 75 percent.
In 5 percent of attempts the baseline changes before dispatch. Without an expected-version check the stale change applies, causing $3,000 of damage with 50 percent recovered; with the check the change is rejected and redone at a cost of 4 turns and a new approval.
Each attempt makes one mutation, and its reply is lost with probability 0.005. A blind retry duplicates the change, causing $10,000 of damage with 50 percent recovered; a settlement query costs $0.01.

Use equation 12.5 to compute the expected loss per attempt from each path with all mechanisms in place, then fold it into the attempt cost and compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\). Recompute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) with the gate, the version check, and settlement each removed in turn, and rank the mechanisms by what they save per day. With every mechanism present, which term dominates the cost per accepted task? Find the gate miss rate that brings that term below $1 per attempt and the resulting \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\). Compare the model’s token spend with the expected loss, and explain what the comparison says about where engineering effort on this lighthouse belongs.
Critiquing a research system end to end (Advanced). A team deploys a research agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}\)) that answers 20,000 analyst questions per day. Its design is as follows.

A planner fans each question out to 8 workers, each granted its own copy of the question’s $12 allowance.
Workers fetch 40 pages in total per question and concatenate them into the planner’s context without source labels, and the planner holds a send_report tool that can address any email named in its context.
An answer is accepted when 3 of the 8 workers agree.
A retrieval cache keyed by URL never expires its entries.
Every night, each accepted trajectory becomes a supervised fine-tuning target, and the acceptance grader is reused both as the reward for reinforcement learning and as the release evaluation.
After 24 hours, a generated summary replaces the raw trajectory log.

Assume that 1 page in 500 carries an injected instruction, the planner acts on 2 percent of the injected instructions it reads, and each disclosure costs $5,000. Each question produces one final answer candidate. Before grading, 60 percent of candidates are valid, with \(\VerifierFalseRejectionRate = 0.10\) and \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate = 0.20\). Compute the expected disclosures and their daily cost, the worst-case spend on one question against its allowance, and, by equation 3.3, the invalid share of accepted answers and the invalid answers accepted per day. Map every design choice to the ledger principle of table 2 it violates, rank the defects by expected harm, and propose a redesign that names the owner and the record at each seam of table 4. Defend which two changes ship first, and identify one defect that no number above prices but that would still block a safety case.

title: 19 Conclusion
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can individually tested components still leave an agent’s task unfinished or its effects unaccounted for?
An autonomous agent unites disparate systems disciplines (foundation models, memory hierarchies, isolated execution sandboxes, transactional event logs, and independent verifiers) into a single closed-loop control architecture. Each individual component can satisfy its local unit tests, yet the integrated system can still fail if the contracts connecting them are ungrounded or ambiguous. The core challenge of agentic systems engineering is designing the deterministic harness that bounds and verifies a stochastic proposer, a problem that larger models and more elaborate prompts do not remove. Across a trajectory horizon, carried working state, and delegated authority, reliable autonomy is achieved only when the runtime enforces invariant closure at every system boundary.

Learning Objectives

Trace an incident-remediation trajectory, identifying the owner and record of each consequential transition
Translate a task contract into bounds and acceptance requirements proportionate to its horizon, state, and authority
Diagnose state and evidence mismatches at subsystem boundaries using the authority and lifetime of each record
Resolve an uncertain external action without confusing a lost response with permission to repeat its effect
Select a system intervention using attributed failures, outcome evidence, and its full deployment cost
Construct a safety case that connects scoped claims to arguments, evidence, assumptions, and residual uncertainty
Distinguish assistance with specifications from authority to adopt them and accept the resulting task

title: 19 Conclusion
text:
Every mechanism in the book now carries a price in one unit, the cost per accepted task of each lighthouse (Cost per Accepted Task by Archetype), so the last instrument is in place. The introduction to this book posed three foundational architectural questions that every subsequent chapter has addressed in part. With the complete system architecture now assembled and priced, each question admits a concise engineering answer, and each answer represents a concrete design claim that this concluding chapter tests against a live operational workload.


↩︎ The three foundational architectural questions governing agentic design are established in The book's three questions.
The first question asked when an adaptive, model-directed loop earns its cost over a deterministic workflow. The answer cannot be settled globally across an entire application; it must be resolved at each individual decision point by measuring the cost per accepted task under a fixed specification contract. A model should direct the next action only where interpreting dynamic, unstructured evidence improves the task acceptance rate by a larger factor than the added inference calls increase the cost of an attempt. Deterministic software should govern everywhere else. Evaluated by this metric, dynamic model loops can earn their cost at phases such as root-cause diagnosis, where the next diagnostic transition cannot be enumerated in advance, while deterministic control structures manage the predictable orchestration surrounding them. The incident below supplies a cost threshold for that comparison. Its price, worked out in section 19.3.2, shows the model calls to be a small fraction of one remediation attempt’s cost. Whether additional diagnostic calls earn that cost depends on the relative acceptance improvement measured against a matched baseline under the same contract and latency constraints.
The second question asked what operational machinery must surround the model. The answer is strictly proportional to the task’s exposure profile across state, authority, and execution horizon. Managing state requires selectively retrieved context, explicitly budgeted serving state, and durable audit records that preserve source authority. Governing authority demands typed, mediated action interfaces, definitive effect settlement before any retry loop can execute, and process containment enforced within the execution substrate beneath the model. Managing horizon requires a supervisory harness that bounds the total trajectory, a write-ahead log of intent recorded before committing each external side effect, and compensating workflows capable of mitigating actions that cannot be reversed. A read-only lookup requires little of this protective scaffolding, whereas an autonomous remediation agent operating on live production systems demands all of it.
The third question asked how operators verify that a task has actually succeeded. The answer requires objective evidence collected from an authoritative endpoint that directly monitors the target system, evaluated against an explicit contract adopted by system owners before execution began. This verification must satisfy a pre-declared closure evidence level, with any residual uncertainty explicitly quantified and assigned to an accountable owner. A model’s self-generated report never serves as evidence, however coherent or persuasive, because a component executing within the loop cannot certify its own output. Stated as an operational acceptance rule, this is the discipline of invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)).
Each of these answers is straightforward to state for an isolated component, but maintaining them across subsystem boundaries is where agentic architectures most often fail. Individually tested services routinely drop an in-flight task when state, authority, and verification handoffs cross architectural seams. The answers are therefore tested on one complete incident handled by the remediation agent, the lighthouse that exercises horizon, state, and authority at once, followed from its contract across the memory and execution boundaries to the one boundary no runtime can close on the owner’s behalf.

title: 19 Conclusion
text:
A database service triggers a query-latency alert shortly after a configuration change. An automated remediation agent inspects telemetry, correlates logs, and proposes reverting to the previous known-good settings. The human operator approves the rollback, but the configuration endpoint drops the network connection before returning an acknowledgment. At this moment, the system faces a classic distributed systems dilemma: whether the mutation took effect remains fundamentally unknown. No fluent textual explanation from a language model can resolve that ambiguity. If the runtime interprets the timeout as a failure and retries under a fresh operation identifier, it risks executing the mutation twice. If it optimistically assumes success, it risks closing an incident while degraded queries continue to impact production. If it simply halts, it leaves a live production change in an unverified state with no entity accountable for it. Each failure mode arises by default when every component satisfies its local unit contract, yet no system component owns the distributed boundary between them. This is the end-to-end argument that grounded the closure evidence levels (The invariant closure principle) applied to a single incident: an intermediate success report from a tool or a model call cannot establish acceptance, and only the principal holding the task contract can verify completion against direct evidence from the service.



Horizon, state, and authority return together, and the runtime closes each on one trajectory.
This concrete incident, incident_42 on database service db_primary_01, represents the operational workload of the remediation agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) and supplies the book’s capstone synthesis. The remediation agent is this book’s irreversible actor: it operates over a bounded horizon, mutates shared production state, and exercises real authority over a live service. This single trajectory, from initial diagnostic telemetry through operator approval, execution dispatch, and terminal acceptance, anchors the remainder of the chapter. At every transition, the engineering criterion remains constant: the system must deterministically record what it proposed, what permissions were granted, what physical effects occurred, what evidence validates the outcome, and which principal bears ongoing responsibility. Building an agentic machine learning system means guaranteeing that these accounts are durable and verifiable. In this architecture, the managed database service owns its active configuration, the runtime orchestrator owns execution and control decisions, and the accepting authority verifies whether post-remediation evidence satisfies the delegated operational contract. One named human principal, operations_owner_42, is accountable both for any operation the runtime cannot settle and for the service once the incident is accepted. The runtime’s settlement process, a runtime component rather than a person, reconciles uncertain operations on that owner’s behalf.


The incident lifecycle begins under incident_contract_v1, which grants bounded diagnostic read access and establishes formal gates for proposing, approving, and validating configuration mutations. Initial privileges are strictly observational. The runtime provisions read_scope_42 to query authorized service endpoints, ensuring that telemetry gathering cannot inadvertently trigger state changes or be coerced into production writes. Throughout this trace, identifiers such as read_scope_42 denote durable local record keys rather than opaque cryptographic hashes.
Next, the context manager gathers the initial latency alert, recent time-series metrics, active configuration parameters, and relevant runbook sections into an auditable manifest, context_manifest_42. Every observation in this manifest records its originating source, a version tag when available, and a precise ingestion timestamp. Here, a practical systems hazard appears: while the retrieved runbook suggests a memory-pool misconfiguration, that document might describe a previous software deployment. By diffing the runbook recommendations against the active production configuration (config_v7) and current telemetry, the agent formulates a diagnostic hypothesis. Additional diagnostic queries, constrained by the task’s remaining call budget, must corroborate this hypothesis against alternative explanations such as downstream network congestion or disk saturation.
When the diagnostic evidence converges on a known regression, the model emits change_request_42, which specifies the target configuration keys, the desired values, and the expected baseline version config_v7. In accordance with incident change policy, an authorized human operator reviews the proposed diff and issues approval_42. This record binds the operator’s identity to the request identifier, the target host, the exact payload parameters, the prerequisite baseline config_v7, and an expiration window. The approval records permission for that exact payload and nothing broader; it does not perform the mutation. The model drafts the operational rationale, but it cannot grant itself execution authority. An approval granted minutes before execution is an earlier authorization check, and complete mediation (definition \(\ref{dfn-complete-mediation}\)) requires a fresh one at the moment of use. Prior to network dispatch, the runtime action gate therefore rechecks operator authorization, compares the payload against the approval’s digest, inspects the expiration deadline, confirms resource quotas, and evaluates runtime preconditions. If an operator revokes the ticket or the model generates an altered proposal, the original approval no longer matches and cannot silently apply to a mutated repair payload.


↩︎ Rechecking an approved request’s digest, expiry, budget, and authorization at the dispatch boundary is established in Dispatch-time rechecks.
Even a thorough pre-dispatch check cannot protect against time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) races if a peer operator modifies database settings in the sub-second interval between the gate check and network arrival. The database configuration endpoint closes this concurrency window with the conditional update of Conditional updates, an atomic expected-version check. The endpoint executes the modification if and only if the live configuration version matches config_v7 at the instant of the write; a version conflict triggers an immediate rejection, returning the task to the agent for re-diagnosis rather than applying an outdated patch onto an altered baseline. To survive network instability, the endpoint also makes the write idempotent in the sense of definition \(\ref{dfn-idempotent-action}\): it deduplicates requests by an operation identity bound to the caller, target, and payload, and retains that identity across a window longer than the maximum client retry horizon, so a replayed request inside the window is recognized rather than reapplied. The endpoint also exposes a read-only operation-status lookup. These correctness guarantees must reside at the endpoint implementation itself; client tool schemas or client-side metadata can declare invariants, but only the server endpoint can enforce them. Before transmitting the RPC across the network, the runtime appends an intent record for op_42 to a write-ahead journal at the durability boundary chosen for the deployment, together with its recovery descriptor: the obligation registration of the trajectory saga, here the corrective-action template, the preconditions it must satisfy, and the accountable owner, operations_owner_42. Once both are persistent on disk, the runtime dispatches the request with operation identity op_42 and expected version config_v7.


↩︎ Deduplication by an operation identity bound to caller, target, and payload is established in Operation identity and endpoint contracts.
At this stage, the configuration endpoint’s network response is lost in transit. The client runtime experiences a socket timeout. This is the lost-acknowledgment problem that opened Recovering After Partial Effects: a timeout yields no information about execution state. The network may have dropped the outbound packet, the endpoint may still be executing the transaction, or the endpoint may have committed the write and lost the acknowledgment on the way back. Instead of gambling on a blind retry or prematurely declaring failure, the runtime logs the status of op_42 as unknown and hands it to the settlement process. Rather than dispatching a second mutating RPC, the settlement process issues an authorized status query against the endpoint’s operation registry. In the successful resolution branch of this scenario, this status lookup confirms that op_42 committed the requested payload, transitioning the database configuration to config_v8. The immutable operation identity firmly binds this remote confirmation to the local dispatch record, resolving network ambiguity even if the original RPC suffered significant transmission delays. Conversely, if the status lookup returns an empty record or encounters a transient service outage, the settlement process cannot conclude that the mutation failed; the original request might still be queued in an intermediate network buffer. In that unresolved branch, the operation status remains unknown, preserved through the recovery descriptor as an open obligation of operations_owner_42 rather than swept away by process termination.


↩︎ Registering the recovery obligation alongside the forward intent, before dispatch, is established in Obligation registration.
Confirming that config_v8 committed settles the mechanical outcome of the mutation, but it does not resolve the operational incident. The runtime context manager flushes the stale config_v7 snapshot and assembles fresh post-mutation telemetry to evaluate database performance under live load. Assume that latency percentiles and error budgets gathered across an observation window, health_window_42, successfully satisfy the quantitative performance thresholds specified in incident_contract_v1, and that secondary policy assertions pass. An authorized human principal or automated gatekeeper evaluates this telemetry and signs acceptance_42. This acceptance record explicitly binds together the original incident contract, the operator approval, the settled operation identifier, the new active configuration version (config_v8), and the validated metric window. Only then is the incident formally closed under contract for the evaluated duration. Monitoring the service after the window passes to operations_owner_42, the same owner who would have held op_42 had its status stayed unknown.
Seen from above, this one incident has crossed nearly every part of the book (figure 1). The adopted contract came first; the loop that diagnosed the regression was assembled from the model call, context, tools, and sandbox of Parts I to III; the harness of Part IV wrapped every step; and acceptance rested on external evidence rather than the agent’s report. Learning and delegation never entered, because neither was needed to close this task.






Figure 1: One Trajectory Through the Whole System: A task contract, defined in the introduction and adopted at the specification boundary that Part VII closes on, governs a live loop in which context assembly (Part II) feeds a model call (Part I) whose proposal becomes a validated, authorized tool call run in a sandbox (Part III), with the observation returning to context as data. The harness (Part IV) wraps every step with budgets, the approval gate, the durable log, and recovery. Acceptance rests on scoped external evidence rather than the agent’s report; learning (Part V) and scale (Part VI) are optional lifecycle choices.



The audit chain summarized in table 1 enables an independent auditor or site reliability engineer to reconstruct the causal lineage of the incident without relying on a language model’s retrospective self-report. Structured records expose operational gaps immediately: a successful completion token from a model call cannot settle the network status of op_42, and an unanchored telemetry snapshot lacking a verified observation window cannot validate an acceptance claim.



Table 1: Owners and Records Along One Trajectory: The incident’s consequential transitions remain auditable through explicit owners and linked records. An unresolved outcome remains a recorded obligation rather than disappearing when execution stops.

Real production telemetry is rarely sterile. A diagnostic log entry or an issue tracker comment can carry an indirect prompt injection, instructions written to exfiltrate database credentials to an external server. The payload enters the agent’s context through an authorized diagnostic read, yet the untrusted text inherits none of the operator’s administrative authority; an agent that acted on it would be the confused deputy of definition \(\ref{dfn-confused-deputy}\), spending the operator’s grant on the attacker’s intent. While structured provenance tagging and XML delimiters assist the model in distinguishing ingested data from operational instructions, model-level comprehension provides no security boundary. Strong isolation outside the model runtime must govern what an ostensibly schema-valid tool call can execute using legitimate system privileges.


↩︎ Indirect prompt injection, delivered through an observation the agent reads rather than by the interacting user, is established in Prompt injection entry points.
In this incident scenario, an attempted exfiltration collides with layered architectural barriers. If the manipulated model emits a tool call directed to an unauthorized external IP address, the runtime action gate blocks dispatch, because read_scope_42 grants queries only against the named diagnostic endpoints and an arbitrary address is not among them. Independently of that grant, the sandbox’s egress policy drops unsanctioned outbound sockets at the network layer regardless of what code or parameters the agent generates. The read grant says which services the task may ask; the egress policy says which hosts any process may reach. Allowing unrestricted outbound connections would create an exfiltration channel even with local filesystems mounted read-only.


↩︎ Network egress enforcement placed outside the guest’s control boundary is established in Enforcement outside the guest.
The harder case uses only permitted operations. A diagnostic query to an endpoint inside read_scope_42 can carry a database connection string in one of its arguments, and both the tool and the destination are allowed. The dispatch release check of equation 9.3 catches it. The credential carries a confidentiality label whose recipient set excludes the telemetry service, the label propagates into the query string built from it, and the reference monitor rejects dispatch because the recipient is not in that set. Layered constraints thus bound the blast radius of a successful injection, at the gate, at the network layer, and on the data itself.
When the action gate intercepts an unauthorized or malformed action, it appends the rejection event to the audit journal as an undispatched intent. If an operation has already crossed the network boundary into production, terminating the sandbox process does not neutralize the external state change. operations_owner_42 and the incident-response team must inspect the audit log, determine what side effects materialized in production, and select the appropriate compensatory action. Similarly, if an adversarial prompt leads the model to assert that cluster latency has normalized, the runtime ignores the assertion; model output can never substitute for empirical telemetry verified across health_window_42. Rigorous ownership boundaries govern adversarial attacks and standard component outages with equal fidelity.
The remediation trajectory terminates cleanly using a single model and a single runtime controller. Mining this execution trace for offline post-training or delegating sub-problems across a fleet of specialized sub-agents represent subsequent, optional architectural decisions (section 19.4.4, section 19.6). Neither optimization alters the authorization invariants required to dispatch op_42 or the empirical evidence demanded to seal acceptance_42.



Managing incident_42 integrates engineering responsibilities that were established across individual chapters. The context window must faithfully represent the operational configuration, operator approval must validate the exact mutation diff, and terminal acceptance criteria must verify the operation that actually committed on the remote service. No single theoretical abstraction or isolated mechanism guarantees all three properties. Table 2 compiles the fifteen foundational principles established throughout this book into an operational reference. Each entry presents the governing mathematical formulation or structural contract alongside its concrete design prediction. When a prediction is quantitative, it provides the first-principles scaling law or sizing estimate developed in the corresponding chapter.
The three H·S·A exposures (horizon, state, and authority) structure this ledger. The principles in Part I quantify the computational cost of an isolated model invocation and formalize the statistical limits of verification. Parts II, III, and IV establish operational closure across the three fundamental exposures that a single model call cannot manage on its own: persistent state across conversational turns, mutable authority over external systems, and an execution horizon over which errors compound. Part V refines the policy weights through post-training without expanding authority; fine-tuning alters candidate trajectory distributions but grants no new access rights. Part VI multiplies all three exposures across concurrent sub-agents and distributed execution graphs. Anchoring the ledger, invariant closure marks the boundary that automated computation cannot self-certify: the task contract that defines human acceptance. Although each principle is categorized by its primary exposure, these dimensions inherently interact: persisting state over long horizons demands durable write-ahead logging, while delegating tasks across agents projects state and authority across distributed boundaries.

Checkpoint 19.1: Reading the ledger as a design tool
The mathematical formulations in the ledger provide concrete quantitative estimates for sizing and evaluating real architectures rather than theoretical abstractions.

Horizon budget: Using equation 1.1, what per-step violation rate keeps the chance of any unchecked violation over \(\TurnHorizon\) turns below a target violation probability, and how must that rate change when \(\TurnHorizon\) doubles?
Acceptance vs. price: By equation 1.2, compare cutting the cost per attempt by a fraction \(\RelativeImprovementFraction\) with raising acceptance by the same relative fraction. Which lowers cost per accepted task more, and why does a token discount that touches only part of the attempt cost lose ground to the acceptance gain?
Pass rate vs. acceptance: A change raises the verifier’s pass rate but leaves acceptance under protected checks unchanged. Which two ledger rows explain why cost per accepted task does not fall?



The ledger states what each mechanism guarantees in general. The incident still needs those guarantees written down as the specific terms it runs under: which outcome counts as recovery, which actions are permitted and when, and which evidence closes the task. That is the job of the incident’s task contract.

title: 19 Conclusion
text:
When an automated latency alert fires for incident_42, the runtime dispatches a diagnostic workflow rather than an open-ended authorization to modify the production database. An unconstrained optimization loop might easily restore query throughput by disabling secondary index updates or relaxing data integrity constraints, destroying durability in the name of speed. The deployment therefore grounds this remediation workflow in incident_contract_v1, an adopted task contract that separates the desired service outcome from the permitted mechanisms an agent may use to pursue it.


The five contract components define the operational perimeter for this workload. Rather than describing an abstract agent architecture, they bind a specific incident to an identified service, explicit permission boundaries, and named decision authorities. Table 3 instantiates this contract for this database remediation scenario.


↩︎ The five-part task contract governing an agentic workload is established in The five-part task specification contract.



Table 3: The Incident Contract: The same five components connect this delegated task directly to its operational permissions, evidence records, and accountable owners. Merely identifying a record name does not establish that its underlying validation checks have passed.










Contract field

Restore acceptable query latency for db_primary_01 without violating the required error-rate and change-policy conditions; leave unrelated settings unchanged
incident_contract_v1, adopted by the authorized task owner

op_42, health_window_42, and the adopted decision in acceptance_42






A production goal must encode process constraints alongside target metrics because the validity of an outcome depends on how the system reaches it. In this remediation trace, that dependency surfaces through explicit approval bindings and version preconditions. The contract enforces these preconditions at the infrastructure layer: a configuration endpoint that lacks an atomic compare-and-swap or expected-version check cannot safely host this workflow, regardless of how frequently the agent runtime re-reads config_v7 before issuing a mutation. Without atomic validation at the service boundary, concurrent writes can slip between the runtime’s final read and the update, silently overwriting live state.
Observation boundaries constrain read-only diagnostics just as strictly as write operations. Under read_scope_42, the agent may query telemetry from designated endpoints but cannot inspect customer database rows, application payload logs, or external network destinations. Tool outputs must also enforce truncation and redaction budgets: the harness captures vital status lines, flags truncated payloads explicitly in the telemetry stream, and routes full raw diagnostic output to an isolated log sink with an independent retention policy. Simple heuristic filters, such as stripping known API keys or ANSI escape sequences, mitigate obvious hygiene hazards, but they cannot prove that an arbitrary output string is free of sensitive data or indirect prompt injections. Reliable protection requires structural access boundaries: enforcing what the agent can read, where intermediate context flows, and which endpoints may receive its output.


↩︎ Head-and-tail byte budgets and explicit truncation notices for tool output are established in Bounded output capture.



An H·S·A analysis identifies the concrete operational obligations generated by this contract. The introduction placed the remediation agent at a moderate horizon of tens of turns, mutable shared production state (\(\StateExposureLevel_3\)), and changes that cannot always be compensated (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\)), and incident_42 sits exactly there. Diagnostic investigation demands strict, finite allowances for foundation model inference and tool invocations. Interacting with live service state and maintaining durable audit trails require source-aware state tracking. Finally, transitioning from diagnostic reads to active production modification requires an explicit escalation of authority. The workload contract fixes these obligations; engineers then select the infrastructure mechanisms needed to satisfy them: sandbox boundaries, retry budgets, and model serving configurations.
The operational envelope attached to incident_contract_v1 applies the harness’s trajectory budgets and resource ceilings. This envelope establishes hard caps on agent turns, wall-clock duration, observation buffer sizes, ephemeral disk allocation, and monetary expenditure. The execution harness must reserve the bounded liability of every admitted model call or tool operation in advance, while retaining an emergency reserve for post-incident health checks and graceful recovery routines. Accounting for consumed tokens alone is insufficient: an inference request currently in flight can consume the remainder of a budget, and asynchronous tool routines accumulate cloud compute and storage costs even when no model generation is active. The envelope must therefore distinguish between local resource ceilings enforced by the executor and supervisor-level thresholds that halt task admission and trigger automated operator intervention.


↩︎ Multi-dimensional budget vectors and the advance reservation of each admitted call’s liability are established in Budgets and Ceilings.
Priced on the remediation workload profile used for this lighthouse in Cost per Accepted Task by Archetype, one incident_42 attempt runs about 10 turns and costs $20.45: $0.15 of model calls, $0.10 of telemetry queries and change tools, $0.20 for the health-window check, and $20 of on-call review for the approval. At 70 percent acceptance, each accepted incident costs $29.21 (equation 1.2). The model accounts for 0.7 percent of the attempt, while operator approval takes 97.8 percent of the money and 50 percent of the 30-minute time to mitigate. This profile sets a threshold for additional diagnosis rather than establishing superiority over a fixed workflow. If all other expected attempt costs remain unchanged, doubling the model-call charges raises attempt cost by its existing model share, 0.7 percent. The added calls lower cost per accepted task only if acceptance rises by a greater relative fraction under the same contract and latency limits; that gain must be measured.
The same profile shows where the danger lies. A wrong change, proposed in 4 percent of attempts and costing $12,000 when it fully commits, carries an expected irreversible loss of $480 per attempt if no check stands ahead of the write (equation 12.5), about 23× the cost of the attempt itself. For this workload, then, the envelope’s caps on turns and spend matter less than its gates: the approval binding, the expected-version check, and the health window that bounds how long a wrong change runs before anyone reverses it.
Similarly, the contract lists idempotency, request deduplication, and out-of-band status reconciliation as strict prerequisites before admitting any remediation workload. When a network partition or gateway timeout obscures the fate of a remote call, these guarantees enable the runtime to poll the endpoint for the true state of an operation rather than blindly issuing a duplicate mutation (section 19.5).



Consider what happens when the run approaches its execution deadline while the status of op_42 is still being reconciled. Extending the deadline simply because the model predicts imminent success violates the envelope contract. Conversely, abruptly terminating the process and marking the operation as failed fabricates an unverified outcome. A robust runtime halts further task admission, logs the expiration event, and preserves both the pending operation identifier and its allocated reconciliation quota. Because remote work often persists across downstream systems after a local client times out, operations_owner_42 retains ultimate operational responsibility for reconciling the orphaned operation or executing an explicit administrative handoff when the allocated automated budget expires.
System acceptance operates under fundamentally different boundaries than resource accounting. Operating entirely within budgeted turn and token limits does not prove that database latency has recovered; only rigorous downstream verification recorded in the trace can substantiate recovery. In production architectures, mutating service state, verifying health criteria, and closing an incident ticket are distinct operational milestones with separate evidentiary requirements.
An operational envelope succeeds only when its resource limits align with the physical demands of the workload. It must grant sufficient observation capacity to diagnose the underlying fault, reserve adequate compute and network quota to verify the outcome, and specify a deterministic fallback protocol when execution yields an indeterminate state. Tightening an envelope ceiling reduces blast radius but risks making completion criteria unattainable; expanding it grants greater operational latitude but introduces unhedged liability that demands human oversight. Managing these boundaries across an agent’s lifecycle requires synchronizing task contracts, context windows, cached state, and dynamic system configurations as each evolves along distinct timelines.


↪ A worksheet mapping each contract condition to its design obligation and the evidence to record is developed in Selecting Responsibilities from the Task Contract.

title: 19 Conclusion
text:
Before an incident mitigation applies a configuration update, context_manifest_42 selects diagnostic evidence describing config_v7. Once the configuration endpoint confirms that operation op_42 successfully applied config_v8, any subsequent prompt that continues to present config_v7 as active state provides the model with an incorrect basis for its next decision. The earlier observation remains factually true, but its operational role has shifted: it no longer describes the active system, serving instead as historical evidence of the incident trajectory. Tracing this shift across runtime boundaries illustrates how memory architectures must coordinate with action execution and recovery contracts.


The incident’s records fall into the four roles of an evidence chain, plus one working-context view. The configuration service is the source record, which establishes and owns the applied configuration under its read-and-update contract. The runtime operation log is the observation or event log, which durably captures the agent’s decisions and received evidence, including human approval bindings and the settlement status (whether unresolved or committed) of op_42. Model-generated incident summaries are agent-written memory, and diagnostic vector indices are derived retrieval indexes; both help locate and interpret the other records, but neither can override primary system state. The context manifest belongs to none of these roles. It is the working-context view, the exact prompt payload assembled for the next model invocation from the task contract, live observations, and retrieved artifacts, and it is an ephemeral selection rather than an authoritative replacement for upstream sources.


↩︎ Source records, event logs, agent-written memory, and derived indexes as roles in an evidence chain are established in Record roles.
These roles are distinct positions in an evidence chain rather than hierarchical tiers in a monolithic cache. An external service evolves independently of the agent harness, and artifacts vary widely in lifecycle: some are ephemeral scratchpads, others persist under formal retention policies, and still others vanish during host failures. The operation log is authoritative only for the local events it has durably written; it cannot attest to external system effects that it has not explicitly verified. If a network response is lost, a generated summary asserting that the configuration has been restored provides zero operational proof of success. This scenario directly reflects the distinction between recorded intent and external settlement.


↩︎ The trajectory log, which records observations and decisions but is not proof that an external effect settled, is established in The Trajectory Log.



When the upstream service confirms config_v8, the context assembly pipeline updates the active configuration entry in context_manifest_42. It preserves the preceding config_v7 record if that diagnostic trace is necessary to justify the remediation step. However, any derived artifacts that depend on the superseded configuration, such as diagnostic summaries or precomputed runbook excerpts, require invalidation or re-evaluation, whereas unrelated operational records remain unaffected. If an asynchronous retrieval index lags behind reality, the runtime can issue an authorized direct read to fetch bounded, up-to-date evidence. If direct reads fail or are unavailable, the manifest must explicitly record the omission rather than silently projecting stale data. Explicit tombstones prevent obsolete snapshots from entering the prompt as active state, though fetching the replacement value still requires a distinct read operation.


↩︎ Withdrawing a staged observation’s authority over current state when its source changes is established in Context Invalidation.
The serving system evaluates cache validity through an entirely different lens. Key-value (KV) cache tensors computed for prompt tokens describing config_v7 remain mathematically valid representations of those exact token sequences, regardless of external system state. An upstream configuration change does not automatically evict accelerator-resident tensors by file path or resource identifier. Instead, when context assembly substitutes config_v8 evidence into the prompt, prefix reuse terminates at the first modified token. The leading unchanged tokens remain reusable under the prefix compatibility rules, whereas all downstream positions require fresh KV computation. This architectural seam highlights the tension between two foundational principles: prefix coherence (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\)) dictates mathematical reuse of intermediate activations, while source authority (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)) governs semantic freshness. Consequently, a serving cache hit confirms computational efficiency rather than the freshness or validity of the underlying world state.


↩︎ Reuse of KV state only over an exact token prefix computed under the same weights and execution parameters is established in Prefix compatibility.
Evidence refresh is also bound by temporal reality. Source version checks and retrieval pipeline maintenance ensure that the model receives the freshest available snapshot, but they cannot freeze external services while the model deliberates. Because concurrent systems can drift during generation, the execution pipeline cannot rely solely on prompt-time freshness; it must enforce optimistic concurrency checks at the action endpoint when the mutation is applied.



During incident_42, the runtime platform captures host-level provenance: which authorized endpoint provided an observation under read_scope_42, the corresponding source timestamp and version vector, any payload filtering applied, and the exact model request that consumed the data. The runtime separately logs its own policy admission decisions. These host-verified events are fundamentally distinct from the model’s generated assertions, such as claiming that a specific configuration rollout triggered the latency alert. The model’s reasoning remains an internal hypothesis until substantiated by verifiable system telemetry.
Untrusted data paths, such as prompt injections embedded in external log streams, underscore this separation from the security boundary. Ingesting text from a trusted storage bucket does not endow that text with operational authority or approval status. Provenance tracks the data lineage and origin of tokens, while the security subsystem enforces authorization against explicit, unforgeable capability grants. The agent runtime evaluates permissions against the active execution context and credentials, treating all observed data strictly as passive payload.



The source-to-context example exposes a fundamental failure mode in modular architectures: storage and serving subsystems can both operate strictly within their local specifications while the agent as a whole acts on stale, invalid evidence. Table 4 extends this ownership analysis to five critical subsystem seams encountered during the incident. The final two rows govern scenarios where the architecture incorporates continuous learning or delegated multi-worker execution.

Delegation makes the final row concrete without altering the acceptance contract. A worker may receive a subset of read_scope_42 while the parent retains its broader read permissions. That reusable capability differs fundamentally from a consumable allowance: concurrent workers must coordinate reservations against a shared budget rather than each receiving an independently spendable quota (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\)). Similarly, consensus among multiple diagnostic workers cannot substitute for empirical verification. When workers process identical noisy inputs or observe one another’s intermediate reasoning, their failures correlate; apparent agreement often reflects shared bias rather than independent confirmation. Whether delegation yields a net benefit is the central evaluation question examined in section 19.6, which balances task decomposition against the coordination tax (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}\)) incurred across subagent boundaries.
Taken together, structured boundary records enable an auditor or post-incident review to reconstruct exactly what the runtime observed, what operations it proposed, what authority it possessed, and what state the external world ultimately committed. Converting this body of recorded evidence into an admissible next action, whether settling an ambiguous inflight request or dispatching a compensating repair, is the responsibility of the execution and recovery boundary.

title: 19 Conclusion
text:
The capstone trace resolved its lost reply with a single status query, and it could do so only because every piece of state that query needed was persisted before the network dropped the reply. The sequence is familiar by now. Each step was admissible because of three properties: durability that covers the declared failure domain, evidence states the runtime must keep apart, and obligations that outlive the process that created them. Each binds an abstract intent, such as change_request_42, to the concrete mutation an external endpoint actually applies, without inventing either success or failure when network visibility collapses.


The trace wrote the intent for op_42 and its recovery descriptor before the request left (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}\)), binding the operation to its request, bound approval, endpoint contract, resource reservation, and accountable owner. Registering the descriptor only after a response would have left exactly the gap the lost reply exposed, an active remote mutation with no durable record of who must reconcile it. The ordering is a database write-ahead log applied to an external effect, with one difference that shapes everything after it. A database’s recovery manager can redo or undo a logged update itself, whereas the runtime can neither redo nor undo the endpoint’s mutation; the log tells it which operation to ask about, and only the endpoint can answer.


↩︎ Durable intent, the admitted operation acknowledged by storage that survives the declared failure domain before dispatch, is established in Durable Intent Before Dispatch.
Durable acknowledgments must cover the failure domain declared by the deployment environment. A local fsync on a single host is not a guarantee that the record will survive the loss of the physical storage device or a host-level crash before replication completes. If the required storage acknowledgment is missing or ambiguous, the execution gate must withhold dispatch. Even after an intent is acknowledged to disk, an administrative pause or authority revocation can safely withhold the unsent request, because recording intent commits the system to track the operation, not to execute it unconditionally.



Neither the expired timer nor the surviving intent log can say which of the capstone trace’s three outcomes occurred. Recovery from a lost reply therefore depends entirely on endpoint guarantees, which must reside at the remote service because the agent’s local log and the external configuration service cannot participate in a single atomic transaction. Issuing an idempotent status query rather than dispatching a fresh mutation enforces settlement before retry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}\)). Once correlated evidence confirms that the endpoint applied config_v8, dependent tasks may safely consume the result. Any subsequent replay of the same operation must conform to the endpoint’s repeat contract and pass active admission checks.
Table 5 distinguishes boundary states that naive agent architectures often treat as interchangeable tool errors.
