Confirming that an endpoint applied a change still leaves the acceptance step of the trace incomplete; the runtime must verify downstream service health before declaring success. The operation’s budget reservation likewise stays open until settlement, because a charge for remote work can arrive after its reply, as the canceled child with a late bill showed in Spending Governance.



A recovery contract asks three things of every effect before dispatch: its target state, the recovery action available under the task’s authority, and the evidence that would show recovery worked. For op_42 the answers split across two of the three contracts. The configuration itself is restorable selected state, since the endpoint keeps config_v7 and a further versioned write can return to it. The queries db_primary_01 served while a wrong configuration was live are a commitment that cannot be undone, which is why the health window, not a later rollback, is what limits the damage of a wrong change. The registered recovery descriptor therefore provides an explicit compensation plan rather than an inverse operation guaranteed to rewrite history. A corrective configuration request requires active credentials, relevant approvals, and explicit preconditions verified against the live environment: the same admission checks that the typed action contract (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}\)) enforces on forward actions. Compensations can themselves stall or fail partially. Rolling back a local workspace cannot reverse an external configuration change, just as issuing a network cancellation request cannot guarantee that the remote endpoint terminated execution. All residual obligations remain assigned to operations_owner_42 until an authorized human operator or automated successor explicitly acknowledges the handoff. Even a write that restores config_v7 is, in the vocabulary of the trajectory saga (definition \(\ref{dfn-trajectory-saga}\)), a compensating step: a new forward action that observers may see half-applied, not an erasure of the first. Because op_42 was itself a rollback, restoring config_v7 would reinstate the configuration the incident was opened against, so the useful corrective action after a wrong op_42 is usually a newly diagnosed change, admitted like any forward action.


↩︎ Restoring selected state, compensating a known effect, and managing a commitment that cannot be undone are established as recovery contracts in Recovery contracts.
Semantic watchdog mechanisms and progress monitoring determine when the execution harness must halt ordinary processing to investigate stalls. Detecting semantic livelocks is non-trivial: repeated tool calls and static observations do not definitively prove that an agent is looping, because an asynchronous status query may legitimately return a pending state across multiple polling intervals. To bound the blast radius of heuristic errors, the harness enforces a strict dispatch ceiling on total invocations and token budgets. When an execution hold triggers, the runtime suspends further speculative dispatches while preserving all admitted operations, allowing only separately authorized, budgeted settlement and recovery tasks to proceed.


↩︎ Semantic watchdogs that detect activity without progress are established in Semantic Watchdogs.

Checkpoint 19.2: Auditing the incident's action boundary
Each prompt names a failure at the action boundary; decide which record or check must catch it.

Changed precondition: approval_42 names config_v7, but another operator changes the configuration before application. Which check must prevent the stale proposal from applying, and who may authorize a revised change?
Retry exposure: The log contains the intent for op_42, but no response. If some fraction of lost replies hide an applied change, what fraction of fresh-identity retries duplicate the change, and which endpoint guarantee brings that fraction to zero?
Missing obligation: A design records its recovery descriptor only after receiving success. Identify the failure interval this leaves uncovered and the record and owner that must survive it.
Unresolved exit: The follow-up allowance expires while status remains unknown. Which operation, financial liability, and handoff records must remain even though this continuation ends?



Because every failure in this trace is anchored to a defined boundary and an accountable owner, the record also shows where the next safeguard belongs. Choosing that safeguard is itself a decision that needs evidence.

title: 19 Conclusion
text:
An execution trace supports a far more precise question than whether the agent needs a larger or smarter foundation model. If context_manifest_42 still presents config_v7 as current after settlement confirms config_v8, the defect lies in stale state selection. If the runtime blindly retries op_42 because an initial response timed out, the defect lies in outcome handling and the endpoint’s recovery contract. Additional pretraining or fine-tuning might shift how frequently the model encounters these code paths, but modifying weights cannot repair a missing state transition or make an unsafe non-idempotent retry safe.
Effective intervention selection pairs an attributed failure with a targeted causal remedy. As formalized in the intervention ladder, candidate remedies should be evaluated in order of operational cost and reversibility. Cheap, easily reversible adjustments come first: refining context and retrieval, hardening tool interfaces and schemas, and enforcing deterministic runtime control. Modifying model weights is reserved for residual failures that persist after these structural remedies, and only when evidence shows that the residual stems from the model’s behavior rather than from a missing record or check. This sequence represents a pragmatic default justified by cost and reversibility, not an inflexible ritual that every failure must climb. An urgent authorization bypass, for example, points directly to a runtime enforcement repair rather than a prompt modification.


↩︎ The intervention ladder ordering candidate remedies by operational cost and reversibility is established in The intervention ladder.


Although an execution trace records what transpired, causal attribution requires an experimental hypothesis test. The fault is isolated by reconstructing the initial input, tool contract, runtime state, and observed outcome, and then manipulating only the suspected causal variable under controlled conditions. For instance, supplying a missing configuration version directly into the prompt verifies whether the issue was an information deficit. Similarly, replacing an ambiguous network timeout with an explicit pending status reveals whether the tool interface misled the controller. Once a candidate fix is identified, engineers must evaluate the repair across the entire affected task suite while running regression checks across unrelated workloads to detect secondary side effects.
Table 6 connects candidate intervention rungs to the empirical evidence required to justify them. The first three rows represent low-cost, reversible structural fixes; the two training rows modify model parameters; and the final row addresses the distinct architectural decision of task delegation.



Table 6: Evidence for an Intervention: A causal diagnosis directs the remedy; no row guarantees improvement or removes the obligations enforced elsewhere in the system.










Intervention
Evidence motivating the change
Obligation the change leaves in place




Context and retrieval
Needed facts are absent, stale, or obscured in the actual model input
Validate source versions and preserve current task constraints


Tool interface
Arguments or outcome states are ambiguous to the caller
Enforce authorization and distinguish a rejected request from an unresolved effect


Runtime control
Budgets, action preconditions, or settlement rules are not enforced at the responsible boundary
Test enforcement and recovery under the declared failure model


Supervised fine-tuning
Admitted demonstrations represent a recurring behavior the current policy handles poorly
Supply current contracts and evaluate generalization and regressions


Reward-driven learning
New attempts can be assessed under a useful scoped reward without a demonstrated response at every decision
Protect assessment, inspect reward gaps, and evaluate held-out behavior


Delegated trajectories
Separate ownership and focused contexts may improve a declared task objective
Bound authority and spending, reconcile results, and compare with a capable single controller






Adapting model weights reshapes proposal distributions; it never relieves the system of enforcing contracts, budgets, or security boundaries at runtime. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to imitate demonstrated recovery paths and structured search strategies, whereas reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards optimizes these behaviors through autonomous exploration. Both training paradigms must prove their generalization gains on the true deployment distribution. Even a sandboxed, automated reward evaluator can harbor specification gaming or omit subtle edge cases in task requirements.


↩︎ Reward hacking, which exploits the gap between a verifiable reward and the intended task, is established in The score and the intended outcome.
Delegation occupies a distinct architectural dimension outside the ladder. Partitioning a task across multiple agents alters system topology, ownership boundaries, and communication overhead rather than repairing an individual component failure. A workload decomposed into clear, decoupled subtasks may warrant delegation without any model training whatsoever. When considering delegation, the primary baseline must be a capable single controller equipped with selective retrieval and parallel tool calls. Any architectural comparison must account for what multiple independent trajectories actually cost: the redundant prompt contexts, serialization latencies across inter-agent dependencies, and reconciliation logic that together constitute the coordination tax (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}\)). In the running incident, diagnostic sub-agents inspecting logs in parallel could shorten triage, without any worker holding permission to apply production changes, but only if the serial share of diagnosis and the integration overhead pass the screen of equation 17.1. Because diagnosis takes only 20 percent of this incident’s time to mitigate and approval takes 50 percent, that screen is hard to pass here, which is why incident_42 closed without delegation. That architectural partitioning remains completely orthogonal to whether the underlying model weights require adaptation.


↩︎ Benchmarking a multi-agent design against a single controller with matched tools, budgets, and concurrency limits is established in Matched comparison conditions.



Even when an engineering intervention reliably improves behavioral reliability, it must still survive rigorous economic accounting. Let \(\AdaptationInvestmentCost\) denote the incremental, one-time expenditure incurred for dataset curation, training compute, and offline evaluation. Let \(\BaselineTaskCost\) and \(\AdaptedTaskCost\) represent the expected operating costs per assigned task under the baseline and adapted configurations, respectively. These operational expectations must incorporate the amortized costs of failed attempts, retries, and any downstream human review or recovery workflows. Assuming stationary unit costs over the operational planning horizon, a positive per-task operational saving \(\FiniteChange \TaskCost = \BaselineTaskCost - \AdaptedTaskCost\) yields the continuous break-even threshold:
\[\BreakEvenTaskCount = \frac{\AdaptationInvestmentCost}{\BaselineTaskCost - \AdaptedTaskCost} = \frac{\AdaptationInvestmentCost}{\FiniteChange \TaskCost}, \qquad \FiniteChange \TaskCost > 0. \tag{1}\]
The relation is the payback horizon of context compaction (The price of compaction) moved up one scale. There a one-time summarization surcharge is recovered over the remaining calls of one trajectory; here a one-time engineering investment is recovered over the tasks of a deployment. Because tasks arrive in discrete units, the minimum production volume required to recover the upfront investment is the ceiling integer \(\lceil \BreakEvenTaskCount \rceil\). If the incremental per-task saving is nonpositive (\(\FiniteChange \TaskCost \le 0\)), the investment can never break even on operational execution costs alone under these assumptions. In such cases, adopting a more expensive configuration requires justification along non-monetary axes: higher solution quality, bounded latency tails, non-negotiable autonomous capabilities, or reduced systemic risk. Furthermore, if the two configurations achieve different end-to-end task success rates, calculating cost simply per assigned task becomes misleading. Engineers must instead divide each configuration’s expected attempt cost by its empirical acceptance probability to evaluate the cost per accepted task (equation 1.2).

Napkin Math 19.1: Conditional payback of a smaller adapted modelScenario: The remediation agent is a poor subject for this question, because its model calls are 0.7 percent of an attempt, so a cheaper model offers little scope for reducing its cost. Consider instead a short, high-volume workload in which the token bill is what a smaller model changes: an engineering team evaluating a specialized, smaller fine-tuned model for automated code review. Both candidate configurations must satisfy identical acceptance criteria and latency bounds on the target workload, exhibiting equivalent empirical acceptance rates. Rigorous offline and shadow evaluation must validate this equivalence before cost models can justify a production rollout. All step and token metrics represent empirical averages across all assigned review tasks, including failed attempts and retries, capturing the composite performance of the model and runtime policy.
Variables: The generalist baseline consumes 12,000 billable input tokens and 800 billable output tokens per step across an average of 5 steps. Inference pricing stands at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. In contrast, the smaller adapted model operates with a distilled prompt consuming 1,500 input tokens and 800 output tokens across 4 steps, billed at $1 and $4 per million tokens, respectively. These figures assume standard on-demand token billing without prompt-caching discounts.
The upfront engineering investment entails $4,000 for data collection and curation, $500 for training compute, and $8,000 for rigorous evaluation and benchmark verification, totaling an incremental expenditure of $12,500. The expected deployment workload is 20,000 assigned reviews per month. All ancillary costs (developer tooling, human escalation, and infrastructure maintenance) are assumed equivalent across configurations and cancel out of the marginal equation.
Math: Executing a single step under the baseline policy costs 12,000 × $3 plus 800 × $15 per million tokens, yielding $0.048 per step and an expected task cost of $0.2400. A step under the adapted policy costs $0.0047, totaling $0.0188 per task. Under stationary cost assumptions, the intervention produces an incremental operational saving of $0.2212 per assigned task. Applying equation 1 yields a continuous break-even threshold of approximately 56,509.95 tasks. The discrete integer crossing occurs at 56,510 tasks; at steady monthly volume, this investment pays for itself in approximately 2.83 months.
Systems insight: Because break-even duration equals \(\BreakEvenTaskCount\) divided by monthly volume, the economic horizon is governed by deployment volume and verification overhead rather than raw training compute. Rigorous evaluation accounts for 64 percent of the initial investment, whereas training compute represents just 4 percent. On the operational side, reduced input tokens generate 79 percent of the net per-task savings, meaning the financial viability hinges on the adapted model maintaining competence under a dramatically compacted prompt. If traffic drops to a quarter of anticipated volume (5,000 reviews per month), the payback timeline stretches to 11.3 months. These savings apply per assigned task; they translate to cost per accepted task only as long as end-to-end acceptance rates remain equal (equation 1.2). If the adapted model’s acceptance falls, the comparison must be rerun on cost per accepted task, and the human escalation and review costs assumed above to cancel no longer cancel, because each rejected review now creates human work the baseline did not.


Deciding on a systems intervention therefore synthesizes root-cause attribution, comparative evaluation, and end-to-end resource accounting. The boundaries of authority and the verification of acceptance must remain external to the agent configuration itself. Once an engineering remedy is proposed, the remaining question is what empirical evidence supports releasing that complete configuration within its declared operating envelope.

title: 19 Conclusion
text:
An incident record links an approved configuration change directly to an observed service outcome. Rather than assuming that this connection implies general correctness, systems engineering requires establishing which operational claims the record substantiates, which enforcement mechanisms make those claims trustworthy, and which residual failure modes remain unaddressed. Resolving these requirements demands an empirical safety case: an inspectable, structured argument establishing that specific safety claims hold within a defined operating envelope, rather than an ungrounded certificate asserting that an autonomous agent behaves correctly under all reachable conditions.1
1 Goal Structuring Notation (GSN): Kelly and Weaver (2004) presented a graphical notation for safety arguments that represents the claims being asserted, the strategies that decompose them, the operational context and assumptions under which they hold, and the empirical evidence that supports them. Structuring an argument explicitly uncovers claims lacking supporting evidence or unverified operational assumptions, which are the gaps that table 7 is designed to expose. 
Kelly, Tim, and Rob Weaver. 2004. The Goal Structuring Notation: A Safety Argument Notation.

Lipson, Howard. 2013. Assurance Cases Overview. Software Engineering Institute, Carnegie Mellon University.
In this framework, a claim asserts a specific operational property, such as authorization validity or state idempotency. An argument articulates the causal chain linking the system architecture and runtime mechanisms to that claim. Evidence provides the empirical backing: audit logs, telemetry windows, regression suites, and operator review traces. As the Software Engineering Institute’s assurance-case methodology (Lipson 2013) emphasizes, merely citing a governance tool or testing practice is insufficient. The case must demonstrate concrete enforcement, verifiable coverage, and direct relevance to the deployed release artifact. Documenting assumptions and counterexamples alongside supporting records gives reviewers the context needed to assess the true boundaries of the argument.


Table 7 applies this structure to the operational trace of incident_42. These claims focus strictly on the mediated database modification and its observed outcome, avoiding overgeneralized assertions about agent behavior across arbitrary tasks. The entries combine concrete runtime records with the supplementary validation suites required by a production deployment case; they outline what the safety case must verify rather than asserting that every offline test ran during the live incident itself.



Table 7: An Incident Safety Case in Three Claims: Mechanisms, records, and assumptions support different parts of the argument. Evidence sufficient for one claim does not automatically establish the others.











Scoped claim
Argument and owner
Supporting evidence
Assumptions and residual uncertainty




The mediated change to db_primary_01 requires approval for the exact request and current preconditions
The action gate checks approval_42 against change_request_42, its target, desired settings, expected config_v7, and validity conditions before dispatch
The approval and admission records, together with tests of missing, expired, mismatched, and stale approvals
The argument depends on controlled access paths and endpoint enforcement; an unrelated privileged operator or bypass is outside this particular gate’s claim


The lost response does not justify issuing a fresh duplicate change
The settlement process preserves op_42 for operations_owner_42 and reconciles through the endpoint’s operation-status and deduplication contract
Durable intent and recovery descriptor recorded before dispatch; the lost-response status; the later source confirmation that op_42 applied config_v8
The endpoint must honor the stated identity, atomic version check, and retention contract, including delayed requests; unavailable status leaves the operation unresolved rather than proving failure


The incident meets incident_contract_v1 under the recorded acceptance scope
The acceptance owner checks the applied configuration, required change-policy conditions, and the declared service measurement window
acceptance_42 references op_42, config_v8, health_window_42, required checks, and the authorized adopter
Measurements cover the named service and window, not every future condition; they do not prove the model’s diagnosis, and post-window monitoring remains with operations_owner_42






An agent’s diagnostic report can help engineers pinpoint anomalous telemetry or surface inconsistencies across distributed logs, but it cannot serve as independent proof of its own successful execution. Similarly, recorded operator sign-offs provide valid evidence only when explicitly mandated by contract. Human reviews carry their own failure modes, latency, and cognitive blind spots, requiring the same provenance tracking and scope validation demanded of automated assertions.



Different validation checks address fundamentally different operational questions. An action-gate test exercises deterministic policy enforcement along a single dispatch path, whereas a fault-injection harness evaluates state reconciliation under dropped packets or transient network partitions. Determining how reliably an integrated agent satisfies contracts in production is an aggregate population question. Answering it requires representative task distributions, held-out evaluation environments, and rigorous uncertainty treatment. The statistical cost of that confidence is governed by equation 13.3: because precision scales only with the square root of the task count, halving the minimum detectable difference between two candidate configurations requires quadrupling the evaluation sample size per arm.
Production assessment requires preserving the disposition of every admitted trial at the observation cutoff, including hard timeouts, failed downstream checks, and unresolved outcomes. If an execution path branches into an indeterminate state, the evaluation harness must classify that trial as unresolved, even if subsequent service latency falls within acceptable thresholds. Similarly, verifying operational health for one service leaves pending financial transactions or external side effects unresolved. By explicitly retaining each pending obligation alongside its designated operational owner, the audit trail prevents aggregated health dashboards from obscuring critical unresolved work.
When offline evaluations support staged production exposure, engineering teams must freeze and identify the complete candidate runtime configuration: model weights, context-assembly pipelines, tool definitions, execution harnesses, and the specific validation suites tied to the claim. Before admitting live requests, the deployment protocol must define the eligible workload envelope, canary routing splits, resource limits, and automated circuit-breaker policies. Live canary routing tests agent behaviors under workload conditions that offline benchmarks inevitably omit. However, assigning a small routing fraction does not inherently bound downstream blast radius; asynchronous side effects, queued database operations, and concurrent tool executions continue processing after an operator triggers an emergency stop. Detecting an anomaly, confirming that admission has halted, and settling effects already released are therefore distinct intervals.


↩︎ Tripwires that stop admission, and rollback that leaves transmitted requests and changed objects in place, are established in Operational tripwires.
Revoking API tokens or draining incoming canary traffic halts only future dispatches. Requests already acknowledged by downstream services and state mutations already written to storage persist, together with their designated settlement owners. Rather than relying on the fragile assumption that rolling back a container image restores world state, a production safety case explicitly documents these operational limits and defines containment protocols for partially executed work.



An incident trace does not automatically belong in a continuous learning pipeline. If an engineer proposes extracting an execution segment as training_record_42, training admission predicates govern whether its context, execution targets, access permissions, and provenance satisfy ingestion standards. An unresolved or aborted operational trace is not equivalent to a negative training example; mislabeling it as such biases the learned policy. Furthermore, teams must quarantine validation suites and benchmark distributions away from the training loop. Repeatedly selecting candidate policies against the same evaluation set erodes statistical validity (Dwork et al. 2015). This dynamic exposes the core tension between verification asymmetry under optimization pressure (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)) and independent release evidence (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence}\)): once a verification metric is converted into a training loss or reward signal, it loses its standing as an objective safety assessment. This is Goodhart’s law in the form Selection pressure on imperfect checks met it under search and The score and the intended outcome met it under training: optimization concentrates on the verifier’s blind spots, so release evidence must come from checks the optimization never observed.

Dwork, Cynthia, Vitaly Feldman, Moritz Hardt, Toniann Pitassi, Omer Reingold, and Aaron Roth. 2015. “The Reusable Holdout: Preserving Validity in Adaptive Data Analysis.” Science 349 (6248): 636–38. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaa9375.

↩︎ The admission predicates for a training record, covering record fidelity, permitted use, process and outcome conditions, and target suitability, are established in Admission predicates.

Updating model weights or agent prompts produces an entirely new system configuration that requires fresh release evidence rather than an inherited endorsement from historical incidents. Model updates also break runtime serving state. Identical prompt prefix text does not render key-value cache tensors computed under previous weights valid for an updated model; cache reuse must satisfy the exact prefix-matching and model-versioning contracts. The safety case must therefore bind strictly to the concrete configuration scheduled for deployment, treating the resolution of incident_42 as an audit of a single, immutable execution rather than an open-ended clearance for subsequent model iterations.

Checkpoint 19.3: Defend the incident's acceptance
Each prompt tests whether a piece of evidence supports the claim it is attached to.

Claim scope: Which records establish that the approved change applied, and why is acceptable latency alone insufficient?
Missing evidence: If operation status remains unavailable, what must stay unresolved and who retains responsibility?
Evidence quality: How can a model report or human review contribute without becoming independent proof of every claimed property?
Evidence volume: A team can afford only twice as many release tasks per arm. By equation 13.3, by what factor does the smallest difference it can detect shrink, and is that enough to rank two configurations that differ by a few points?
Changed configuration: Why do stopping candidate admissions and preserving the same prompt establish neither reversal of earlier effects nor compatibility of old KV state with new weights?



By structuring empirical evidence into an inspectable safety case, engineering teams make acceptance decisions transparent while clearly cataloging residual risks. Unmonitored environmental states outside the measurement window, shifting workload distributions, and unverified edge cases are brought to light as explicit design constraints. Stating these boundaries is not an admission of failure; a case that names its limits is the only kind a reviewer can check.

title: 19 Conclusion
text:
The safety case for incident_42 establishes a bounded claim: an approved configuration change produced acceptable service behavior under a declared runtime contract. Even after the runtime enforces every declared policy boundary, sandboxes every tool invocation, and logs every state transition, three fundamental systems questions remain open: how completely the acceptance criteria capture overall service health, how to maintain consistency when external production state mutates during deliberation, and how reliably the execution audit trail supports causal attribution.
Acceptance criteria are inevitably incomplete. In this incident scenario, the telemetry collected during health_window_42 satisfies the latency and error thresholds mandated by incident_contract_v1. In production, however, an engineer’s operational concerns extend well beyond two isolated metrics. A service can report acceptable tail latencies while quietly exhausting background worker pools, corrupting downstream database records, or leaking memory. Structured qualitative reviews guided by explicit rubrics can detect subtle behavioral regressions, but evaluators, whether human operators or secondary judge models, carry their own blind spots and failure modes. Tamper-proofing an automated verification check prevents a buggy or gaming agent from modifying its own evaluation, but tamper resistance does not make the specification complete. Expanding true test coverage requires uncovering unmodeled failure modes and integrating them into the contract; generating dozens of candidate actions against an incomplete check merely overfits the agent’s search to an unrepresentative proxy.


↩︎ Calibrating rubric-based human and model judges, whose shared mistakes survive high agreement, is established in Calibration of qualitative judgment.
Concurrent state drift imposes a second fundamental limit. Production services do not pause while an agent deliberates. While the agent fetches telemetry, executes multi-step model inference, or awaits human authorization, live traffic fluctuates, background autoscalers adjust capacity, and peer services deploy schema updates. An optimistic concurrency guard, such as validating an endpoint version tag at the write, prevents the agent from applying an approved change to a mutated baseline. Rejecting a stale mutation, however, merely resets the execution loop: the agent must re-read service state, synthesize a revised diagnosis, and request a fresh approval. If external churn is rapid or deliberation latency is high, the agent risks operational livelock, burning through its step and token budgets on perpetual retries. Designing protocols that balance evidence freshness, lock granularity, and deliberation latency within bounded incident budgets remains an open systems challenge.
Causal attribution also remains narrower than the execution record. An audit log establishes temporal correlation, not causal proof. For example, evidence confirming that operation op_42 applied config_v8 immediately before health_window_42 recorded healthy telemetry does not prove that the configuration change resolved the incident. A transient network bottleneck may have cleared on its own, an upstream dependency may have recovered, or a client retry storm may have subsided. Controlled comparisons, targeted fault-injection tests, and structural dependency analyses can substantiate causal claims when operational constraints allow them.
A second attribution problem arises inside long trajectories, which incident_42 is too short to show. When a trajectory fails only at its final acceptance check, two different questions follow. Locating the first observable mismatch is a replay problem. Where retained inputs and boundary records support reconstruction, comparing the run step by step against a reference execution finds that mismatch under a declared equivalence relation; it does not by itself establish the responsible step. Showing which step was responsible, that a different choice there would have passed, is a counterfactual problem, and its search space is every untaken branch the agent could have selected. That counterfactual search space grows as the branching factor raised to the task horizon \(\TurnHorizon\), the same exponent that drives the reliability decay of equation 1.1. It is the credit-assignment problem of Baselines and credit assignment seen from the debugging side: one terminal verdict, and every turn a candidate for blame. With an illustrative four candidate actions per step over a fifty-step task, that space spans \(4^{50} \approx 10^{30}\) paths, far beyond any practical replay budget. Passing checks every five steps can change this arithmetic. If check coverage establishes that the defect occurred after the last passing check, and the window’s state is isolated and safely restorable, the bounded illustration enumerates a single five-step window of \(4^{5} = 1,024\) alternatives, requiring about 20 minutes of replay at 1.2 s per check. Check spacing can therefore bound the counterfactual search horizon when check coverage excludes earlier defects and the window’s state is isolated and safely restorable; otherwise the investigation must retain earlier steps and external changes as possible causes.


↩︎ Replaying a recorded run to its first divergence point is established in Locating a Divergence.
This book focuses on digital systems, whose operations routinely produce nonrestorable external effects: consumed cloud compute and API budgets, irreversible third-party financial transactions, communications dispatched to human users, and sensitive credentials leaked to external logs. Physical actuation introduces domain-specific sensing, mechanical kinematics, continuous dynamics, and hard real-time deadlines beyond the scope of this book. The difference between digital software agents and physical robotics is not a clean boundary between reversible simulation and irreversible reality: both execute actions that cross the causal boundary into an external world where state cannot be rolled back simply by terminating a process. In both domains, rigorous systems engineering requires explicitly cataloging what state can be observed, what actions can be controlled, what side effects can be restored, and which residual risks must escalate to an accountable human principal.
These operational boundaries define the scope of an automated acceptance decision and the residual duties it leaves behind. Establishing that scope is a fundamental engineering responsibility. Generative models and autonomous runtimes can propose plausible execution plans, execute diagnostic checks, and optimize candidate actions, but they cannot assume organizational accountability. Deciding which failure modes are acceptable, which invariants must hold, and which operational risks require human oversight remains the non-delegable duty of authorized system architects.

title: 19 Conclusion
text:
Suppose an incident model proposes shortening the observation window so that database service db_primary_01 can be declared recovered sooner. The model can articulate the operational trade-offs, draft the revised acceptance predicate, and identify supporting metric streams. None of those contributions, however, alters incident_contract_v1. Until the authorized contract owner adopts a revision through the established change-management policy, the runtime must evaluate the incident strictly against existing criteria. Assisting in the formulation of a decision is fundamentally different from possessing the authority to make it binding.
Brooks famously separated the essential difficulty of conceptualizing complex software entities from the accidental difficulty of expressing them in a particular programming language or machine environment (Brooks 1987). In automated incident management, producing a configuration change represents accidental mechanics; deciding which service behaviors constitute true recovery, and which operational risks the change may introduce, constitutes the essential engineering work. An agent can generate a syntactically valid configuration payload while the recovery criteria themselves remain poorly specified. Accelerating payload generation does nothing to resolve that underlying ambiguity.
This conceptual boundary does not relegate language models to mere syntax generation. An agent can propose requirements, evaluate trade-offs between designs, expose inconsistent assumptions across services, or draft fault-injection tests. These activities contribute directly to conceptual reasoning rather than routine boilerplate. Even so, their engineering value depends entirely on the verifiable evidence and arguments they produce. If a critical fraction of specification and review remains unaided by models, that work acts as the serial fraction in the Amdahl bound of equation 17.1, here with one human and one model rather than many workers. A task whose specification and review require half of the original effort cannot finish more than twice as fast, however quickly the model produces everything else, so end-to-end turnaround stays dominated by deliberate human specification and review.
The specification boundary separates candidate proposal from authoritative adoption. The engineers and organizations responsible for a service determine who may approve modifications to its goals, permissions, and acceptance conditions; the execution runtime strictly enforces those policies. An agent does not acquire governance authority merely by authoring a new contract, nor can it enlarge its own permissions or relax evaluation standards when an assigned task becomes difficult. This is invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) applied directly to the contract itself: the model can no more alter its own acceptance criteria than it can certify its own execution trace.
Approval bindings and immutable trace acceptance records enforce this boundary in practice, because neither artifact can be created through agent self-declaration. If an agent identifies a genuine flaw or contradiction in the criteria, that finding can initiate an authorized review. The review must preserve an explicit record of which contract governed the attempted execution and which evidence supports any revised claim, rather than allowing the runtime to silently replace an unmet condition with a more lenient target.
The same boundary governs test construction. An agent-written test suite provides real value, even when the model also drafted the implementation, but both artifacts can easily encode the same mistaken requirement. Separating the acceptance decision from candidate generation ensures that candidates are evaluated against the adopted contract, protected regression suites, live service observations, and qualified human review. This structure prevents self-fulfilling validation: internal agreement between a generated candidate and its co-generated tests must never masquerade as independent verification of correctness, regardless of where the evidence originated.
Agentic systems provide powerful support for making accountable decisions about bounded tasks, but deciding what those tasks mean remains the responsibility of system owners. When an agent produces a valuable contractual revision, that proposal must pass through the formal adoption process before it can govern production behavior.

title: 19 Conclusion
text:
Safely accepting an automated incident remediation requires maintaining four fundamental architectural distinctions: capability, enforcement, evidence, and accountability. Even when a foundation model proposes an accurate diagnosis and a valid fix, these four concerns answer fundamentally different operational questions. Conflating them allows a locally successful component to create the illusion of overall task completion, so that the task is closed before the environment has verified the result.

Fallacy: A sufficiently capable model removes the need for explicit runtime boundaries.
Deploying a more capable model improves diagnostic accuracy and produces fewer malformed actions, but training suppresses the rate of violating proposals without driving it to zero. Over multi-step operational horizons, compound probability amplifies whatever residual risk remains, as captured by equation 1.1. Even with a residual violation rate of only 0.1 percent per step, 4.9 percent of 50-turn trajectories generate at least one violating proposal. Across 10,000 daily trajectories in production, that tiny fraction yields roughly 488 hazardous proposals each day. Explicit runtime boundaries determine whether each proposal is safely intercepted or permitted to produce side effects on live infrastructure. In the capstone incident, even an accurate restoration proposal still requires strict approval bindings and version checks; model confidence can never authorize op_42.


Pitfall: Treating passing checks as proof of the entire completion claim.



An accurate check shrinks the invalid share from 70 percent to about one in nine, not to zero.
Observing acceptable service latency does not prove that an approved operation occurred, because external traffic might have simply subsided. Conversely, confirming that a configuration change took effect does not guarantee that the service has returned to healthy operation. A valid completion certificate such as acceptance_42 must assemble evidence of both correct execution and restored service behavior, alongside all mandatory policy checks. Furthermore, passing a verification check provides weaker probabilistic assurance than the raw accuracy of the check suggests. Under Bayesian precision (equation 3.3), base rates dominate posterior confidence. If only 30 percent of proposed candidate actions are valid, a verifier that misses 10 percent of valid proposals while mistakenly passing 5 percent of invalid ones still leaves 11.5 percent of its passing set invalid. This quantification demonstrates the principle of verification asymmetry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)) in practice: high nominal check accuracy does not ensure correctness when candidate quality is low. A defensible safety case must therefore document the explicit scope and blind spots of each verification check, clearly assigning ownership for any residual monitoring duties.


Fallacy: An intervention is justified because it is the next rung of the intervention ladder.
The intervention ladder organizes mitigation strategies by ascending operational cost and decreasing reversibility, but stepping to the next rung does not ensure that the action addresses the underlying defect. A stale context entry, an unconstrained retry loop, and an inaccurate model diagnosis demand fundamentally distinct remedies, and escalating to a heavier mechanism incurs substantial overhead whether or not it fixes the issue. For example, adapting a smaller model (examined in notebook 19.1) demands an upfront investment of $12,500 and requires 56,510 reviews to break even, which translates to 11.3 months at an operating volume of 5,000 reviews per month. That investment yields zero return if the operational failure actually resided in prompt context or the retry policy. Interventions should follow directly from attributed cause, comparative outcome evidence, and total lifecycle costs; model fine-tuning and operational delegation remain specialized tools rather than automatic defaults.


Pitfall: Allowing the component producing a result to redefine the conditions for accepting it.
An agent model can helpfully identify an unstated requirement, draft a new integration test, or propose updating an impractical service-level objective. However, it must never possess the authority to shorten health_window_42, expand its own execution permissions, or unilaterally certify its own completion claim. Redefining acceptance criteria to declare success prematurely imposes a direct statistical penalty. Halving the observation window cuts the number of metric samples in half. For approximately independent measurements, this reduction widens the confidence interval on the service latency estimate by a factor of 1.41. Consequently, the revised claim relies on significantly degraded empirical evidence at the exact moment when the incident is difficult and rigorous verification is critical. Modifying acceptance criteria requires explicit sign-off from the designated system authority, backed by an audit record detailing which contract version governs the work. Delegating automated reasoning or execution to an agent never transfers the ultimate responsibility for accepting the result.

title: 19 Conclusion
text:
The incident connects the book’s components through one concrete task rather than through an abstract reference architecture. A foundation model proposes a diagnosis and a configuration rollback. Context assembly provides relevant telemetry and logs, complete with verifiable provenance and freshness boundaries. The action boundary admits only validated operations into the production environment, while durable execution logs record intent prior to side effects and track unresolved outcomes across network partitions. Finally, runtime service telemetry and automated policy verifiers evaluate the result against an explicit contract before committing to acceptance. Each component fulfills an isolated, local contract; the end-to-end integrity of the system emerges from the records, fences, and ownership chains that bind them together.
Table 8 summarizes the quantitative relations that govern an agentic execution trajectory, linking the compounding error of unchecked steps to the economics of verification, retry safety, and parallel delegation.



Table 8: Key Equations of the Conclusion: Each relation prices one term of an accepted task: unchecked reliability, cost, payback, check precision, retry exposure, irreversible loss, release evidence, delegation, and concurrency. Symbols carry the meanings given where each relation is derived.

Key Takeaways: Own every transition, bound every claim

Every consequential transition requires an explicit owner and a durable record: The request, decision, side effect, and resulting evidence must remain structurally linked throughout the trajectory. An unknown outcome is never a license to retry blindly; an ambiguous operation retains its human or system owner rather than fabricating a premature success or failure.
The contract, not a mechanism catalog, defines system boundaries: Task horizon, mutable state, and delegated authority dictate where a workload is vulnerable, and the formal contract determines which guardrails to deploy. Every telemetry record and intermediate artifact retains its provenance, authority level, and expiration window, ensuring that stale cached data never masquerades as fresh environmental evidence.
Interventions must follow attributed evidence, prioritizing the lowest-cost remedy: Prefer lower-cost, reversible remedies when they address the attributed failure; initiate fine-tuning or model changes only when evidence supports them. Compare candidate mitigations under identical task constraints while accounting for development, inference, verification, and recovery costs. Model fine-tuning and multi-agent delegation must earn their keep through measurable end-to-end gains rather than architectural ambition.
Claims must remain bounded by verifiable evidence, while ultimate adoption remains with human principals: A passing verification check supports acceptance strictly within its specified domain, with residual uncertainty and environmental assumptions made explicit. Models can synthesize specifications, generate test cases, and draft operational contracts, but designated human owners must ratify the governing contracts and acceptance procedures, and they retain accountability for whatever residual risks remain.






Unchecked success decays exponentially as the horizon grows.
This book opened with two foundational pieces of arithmetic, and every subsystem analyzed across these chapters addresses one of them. The first is horizon compounding (equation 1.1): with a per-step correctness rate of 99 percent, an unchecked trajectory succeeds 90.4 percent of the time across 10 turns, but falls to 36.6 percent across 100 turns. Targeted post-training can reduce how often a policy proposes an invalid action, but it cannot guarantee zero violations. Consequently, invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) must remain anchored in external systems mechanisms, regardless of model scale or capability. Runtime admission and verification mechanisms limit unchecked execution or turn detected violations into rejected attempts. Typed action contracts intercept unsafe proposals before they produce side effects. Automated verifiers and execution watchdogs limit error propagation across turns. Finally, durable write-ahead logging and scoped compensation mechanisms (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}\)) bound the cost of recovering from failures, allowing sandbox modifications to be rolled back cleanly while compensating external side effects through explicit, forward-recovering operations.



Raising acceptance cuts cost per accepted task more than halving token price.
The second governing relation is the cost per accepted task (equation 1.2), which charges the compute and operational overhead of every rejected attempt to the few that are accepted. At $2.10 per attempt and a baseline 40 percent acceptance rate, each accepted task costs $5.25. Cutting the raw token price in half reduces this effective cost to $3.63, whereas improving task acceptance to 60 percent drives the cost down further to $3.50. The four lighthouses stress different terms of that balance, as Cost per Accepted Task by Archetype priced them. In those accounts, sandbox holding and tools dominate repair cost; higher acceptance saves more than cheaper tokens when other attempt costs remain fixed. Research spends most on tokens through its sub-agent fan-out. Support spends most on escalation handoffs, while its interactive latency target requires separate capacity checks. Selecting an intervention requires pricing the work needed to improve these outcomes, not merely identifying the largest cost term. Remediation spends most on human approval, and incident_42 showed why: approval is most of each attempt’s cost, and a wrong change costs far more than any attempt. Across all workloads, verification asymmetry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)) keeps the denominator honest, because an attempt counts as accepted only within the explicit bounds validated by an authorized check.
This book began by distinguishing a proposed action from its realized side effect, and an apparently plausible generation from an accepted task. In the end-to-end case study of incident_42, that distinction culminates in an inspectable, auditable decision: acceptance_42 anchors the governing contract to the settled change, the passing verification suite, and scoped telemetry evidence, while operations_owner_42 retains explicit responsibility for post-window operational health. When required evidence cannot be verified, the runtime records an unresolved disposition rather than fabricating completion. Each failure that plagues unprincipled agent deployments has a specific guard in this trace: a duplicated change from a blind retry meets the operation identity and settlement query, an incident closed before its change applied meets the acceptance record, and an untracked production modification with no owner meets the intent log and its accountable owner, operations_owner_42. A defensible audit trail that tracks what the model proposed, what the action boundary permitted, what side effects occurred, what evidence validated the result, and who retains operational responsibility is the true deliverable of an agentic machine learning system.
Every mechanism in this book answers the same limitation, that the model samples stochastic outputs and cannot certify its own correctness. No algorithmic advance in deep learning eliminates that underlying uncertainty. The core contribution of this book is the surrounding systems architecture, the harness and runtime that make a model’s proposals safe to execute, verifiable to accept, and economically viable to operate at scale.

title: 19 Conclusion
text:
The engineering challenges examined throughout this book did not begin with modern foundation models. Computer systems researchers have wrestled with authority, state coordination, and verifiable delegation for decades. Operating systems encountered the problem of authority first. Dennis and Van Horn introduced capabilities to bind access rights directly to unforgeable tokens (Dennis and Van Horn 1966), establishing that components should operate only with explicit, unforgeable references. Saltzer and Schroeder formalized these protection mechanisms into durable design principles (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975), notably least privilege and complete mediation, which govern how an action gate inspects, validates, and filters tool invocations before side effects reach an external environment. Database systems confronted the complementary problem of mutable state and consistent outcomes. Gray established the classical transaction model by pairing write-ahead logging with atomic commit protocols and crash recovery (Gray 1978). Gray also recognized the limits of strict ACID guarantees, however, when coordinating long-running work across autonomous organizations (Gray 1981). That insight led directly to sagas (Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987), which replace distributed locks with sequences of local transactions coupled with compensating steps when an effect cannot be undone cleanly. Saltzer, Reed, and Clark formulated the end-to-end argument (Saltzer et al. 1984), establishing that correctness and final verification must ultimately reside at the application endpoints that understand the semantics of the task. Each domain encountered the same fundamental vulnerability: individual components can succeed locally while the composite system loses track of global state or fails to verify completed work.

Dennis, Jack B., and Earl C. Van Horn. 1966. “Programming Semantics for Multiprogrammed Computations.” Communications of the ACM 9 (3): 143–55. https://doi.org/10.1145/365230.365252.

Saltzer, J. H., and M. D. Schroeder. 1975. “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems.” Proceedings of the IEEE 63 (9): 1278–308. https://doi.org/10.1109/proc.1975.9939.

Gray, Jim. 1978. “Notes on Data Base Operating Systems.” In Operating Systems: An Advanced Course. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-08755-9_9.

Garcia-Molina, Hector, and Kenneth Salem. 1987. “Sagas.” Proceedings of the 1987 ACM SIGMOD International Conference on Management of Data, 249–59. https://doi.org/10.1145/38713.38742.

Minsky, Marvin. 1961. “Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence.” Proceedings of the IRE 49 (1): 8–30. https://doi.org/10.1109/JRPROC.1961.287775.

Smith, Reid G. 1980. “The Contract Net Protocol: High-Level Communication and Distributed Problem Solving in a Distributed Processor.” IEEE Transactions on Computers C-29 (12): 1104–13.

Wooldridge, Michael, and Nicholas R. Jennings. 1995. “Intelligent Agents: Theory and Practice.” The Knowledge Engineering Review 10 (2): 115–52. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0269888900008122.

Parasuraman, Raja, Thomas B. Sheridan, and Christopher D. Wickens. 2000. “A Model for Types and Levels of Human Interaction with Automation.” IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics - Part A: Systems and Humans 30 (3): 286–97. https://doi.org/10.1109/3468.844354.
Artificial intelligence and multi-agent systems research introduced the complementary questions of autonomous decision making and structured delegation. Minsky identified the credit-assignment problem (Minsky 1961), highlighting how difficult it is to determine which intermediate action in an extended horizon caused an ultimate success or failure, a challenge that continues to complicate trajectory optimization and policy evaluation. Smith developed the contract net protocol (Smith 1980), organizing distributed problem solving through an explicit cycle of task announcements, bids, and awards among cooperating nodes. Wooldridge and Jennings characterized intelligent agents through autonomy, reactivity, goal-directed proactiveness, and social ability (Wooldridge and Jennings 1995), defining the behavioral boundaries that separate goal-seeking entities from static programs. In parallel, human-factors research established how to partition control between humans and automated systems. Parasuraman, Sheridan, and Wickens demonstrated that system designers must distinguish which cognitive functions are automated from the level of autonomy granted across each stage (Parasuraman et al. 2000). That operational distinction underpins modern approval gates, where a runtime permits a model to propose a sensitive action while withholding the authority to execute it without operator confirmation.
Modern machine learning systems joined this systems lineage when Sculley et al. (2015) demonstrated that the trained model represents only a small nucleus within a vast, complex harness. Most of the ongoing maintenance debt in production ML stems not from model weights, but from fragile boundary code, configuration debt, and hidden feedback loops. When large language models demonstrated the ability to follow instructions in context (Brown et al. 2020), they provided systems designers with a flexible, general-purpose proposer. Interleaving reasoning traces with concrete actions (Yao et al. 2023) and training models to invoke external tools (Schick et al. 2023) closed the execution loop, transforming passive text predictors into runtime engines that effect change across real environments. With that transition, classic security and reliability hazards reappeared immediately. Indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al. 2023) is simply the classic confused deputy problem (Hardy 1988) arising in a semantic medium: an untrusted input misleads a privileged agent into misusing its authority on behalf of an attacker. Evaluating autonomous workflows, assigning credit across multi-step execution traces, and developing defensible safety cases remain formidable engineering challenges. Lasting progress will come not from superficial metaphors, but from grounding modern agent designs in classical systems principles supported by empirical evidence.

Brown, Tom B., Benjamin Mann, Nick Ryder, Melanie Subbiah, Jared Kaplan, Prafulla Dhariwal, Arvind Neelakantan, et al. 2020. “Language Models Are Few-Shot Learners.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33: 1877–901. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2005.14165.

Yao, Shunyu, Jeffrey Zhao, Dian Yu, Nan Du, Izhak Shafran, Karthik Narasimhan, and Yuan Cao. 2023. “ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Schick, Timo, Jane Dwivedi-Yu, Roberto Dessı̀, Roberta Raileanu, Maria Lomeli, Luke Zettlemoyer, Nicola Cancedda, and Thomas Scialom. 2023. “Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 36: 68539–51.

Greshake, Kai, Sahar Abdelnabi, Shailesh Mishra, Christoph Endres, Thorsten Holz, and Mario Fritz. 2023. “Not What You’ve Signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection.” Proceedings of the 16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security, 79–90. https://doi.org/10.1145/3605764.3623985.

Hardy, Norm. 1988. “The Confused Deputy: (Or Why Capabilities Might Have Been Invented).” ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 22 (4): 36–38. https://doi.org/10.1145/60609.60611.
Five foundational works trace this lineage from classical systems theory to dependable agent design:

Saltzer et al. (1984) articulates why reliable verification must ultimately reside at the endpoints where application semantics are fully understood. In agentic architectures, it provides the core justification for why task acceptance and completion checks belong to the task owner rather than intermediate execution layers.
Gray (1981) examines the transaction abstraction alongside its operational limits in decentralized, long-running workflows. It clarifies which atomicity and consistency guarantees an agent runtime can inherit directly, and where it must substitute compensation, idempotent retries, and asynchronous settlement.
Brooks (1987) distinguishes between the essential complexity of specifying conceptual structures and the accidental complexity of implementing them. This distinction clarifies what model generation can streamline, such as boilerplate synthesis and API translation, and what remains hard systems engineering: defining crisp specifications, verifying invariants, and validating task contracts.
Sculley et al. (2015) analyzes deployed machine learning through the lens of systems engineering, demonstrating how glue code, configuration drift, and hidden feedback loops dominate operational debt. Its cautionary analysis applies with even greater force when models shift from passive prediction to active tool invocation across production infrastructure.
Kelly and Weaver (2004) introduces the Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) for constructing rigorous, auditable safety arguments. It illustrates how to link an explicit engineering claim directly to empirical evidence, contextual boundaries, and underlying assumptions, the discipline required when validating agent deployments and establishing operational acceptance.


Saltzer, Jerome H., David P. Reed, and David D. Clark. 1984. “End-to-End Arguments in System Design.” ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 2 (4): 277–88. https://doi.org/10.1145/357401.357402.

Gray, Jim. 1981. “The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations.” Proceedings of the Seventh International Conference on Very Large Data Bases (VLDB) 7: 144–54.

Brooks, Frederick P. 1987. “No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering.” Computer 20 (4): 10–19.

Sculley, D., Gary Holt, Daniel Golovin, Eugene Davydov, Todd Phillips, Dietmar Ebner, Vinay Chaudhary, Michael Young, Jean-François Crespo, and Dan Dennison. 2015. “Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 28: 2503–11.

title: 19 Conclusion
text:
Every given below is a hypothetical problem input, not a measurement of a particular model, service, or deployment. The problems combine mechanisms from several parts of the book, and each asks for numbers and then for the design decision those numbers support.

Spacing checks and checkpoints on a long repair (Basic). A repair agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)) runs a 60-turn trajectory of 15 s turns, and each turn independently proposes a violating step with probability \(\PerStepErrorRate = 0.005\). The runtime can insert a check every \(\CheckWindowTurnCount\) turns that catches any violation in its window. Each check also saves a durable checkpoint of the sandbox (Checkpoints), which takes 3 s, and a caught window is restored from the previous checkpoint and rerun. Operations wants at least 95 percent of windows to pass on the first attempt. When a window fails, finding the responsible step means replaying the alternatives inside it: the agent chooses among 3 candidate actions per turn, each replayed path takes 0.5 s to check, and the attribution budget is 10 minutes.
Use equation 1.1 to compute the probability that the whole trajectory runs free of violations with no intermediate checks, and the per-turn rate a better model would need to lift it to 95 percent. Find the largest \(\CheckWindowTurnCount\) that meets the first-pass target and the largest \(\CheckWindowTurnCount\) that fits the attribution budget. Which constraint binds, and how many checks does the trajectory need? At that spacing, compute the expected wall-clock time including checkpoint saves and reruns, and compare it with rerunning the unchecked trajectory from scratch until it passes. Turn 40 pushes a branch to a shared remote, an effect the sandbox checkpoint cannot restore. Using intent before effect (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}\)) and the commitment region of The commitment region, explain where a check must sit relative to that turn, what the runtime must record before dispatching it, and why the restore-and-rerun arithmetic above no longer covers a violation found after it.
Where the accepted-task cost goes (Basic). A repair attempt runs 30 turns. Each turn reads 8,000 input tokens at $2 per million and generates 400 output tokens at $10 per million, and each attempt also pays $0.25 of sandbox time, $0.15 of test runs, and $1.00 of human review. Half of the attempts are accepted.
Compute the attempt cost and \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) from equation 1.2. Two changes are proposed. Prefix caching bills each turn’s reused prefix at one-fifth of the input price, and without other changes the reused prefix is 7,200 of the 8,000 input tokens. A context fix adds a 2,000-token block of current test output to every turn and raises acceptance to 65 percent. Compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) for each change alone. Then compute it for both together, with the block placed after the stable content so that the 7,200-token reused prefix survives and the block is billed at the full input price. Using principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\), explain why the two changes compound only under that placement (Exercise 7 prices the alternative), and which term of the attempt cost neither change touches.
Pricing a blind retry (Basic). A fleet of remediation agents (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) issues 25,000 mutating configuration calls per day. Requests are lost with probability \(\RequestLossProbability = 0.001\) and replies with probability \(\ReplyLossProbability = 0.004\), and a duplicated change costs $2,000 in expected damage. An operation-status lookup costs $0.01.
Compute the expected number of timeouts per day and, using the settlement relation of notebook \(\ref{nbk-07-settlement-budget}\), the expected duplicates per day under a blind retry with a fresh identity, and their daily cost. Compare that cost with a status lookup on every timeout. An endpoint offers neither deduplication by operation identity nor a status lookup. Using the contract of section 19.3, decide whether the task can be admitted against that endpoint and what the runtime must do after a lost reply.
Serving memory for a support fleet (Intermediate). This problem transfers the chapter’s whole-trajectory sizing to the support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)), whose binding constraint is serving capacity under concurrency rather than the authority that binds the remediation agent. Sessions arrive at 20 per second and last 180 s on average, mostly waiting on the customer. Each session makes 6 model calls of 2 s each, every call reads a 6,000-token context, and attention state costs 0.1 MB per token. The pool has 1,000 GB of accelerator memory for attention state, prefills 400,000 tokens/s in aggregate, and moves 200 GB/s between host memory and accelerators.
Use equation 18.4 to compute the concurrent sessions and the attention state needed to hold every session resident, and compare it with the pool. Compute the state held by sessions inside a model call. Evaluate two policies: evicting a session’s state between calls and recomputing it at the next call, and keeping it in a host-memory tier so that only about 500 new tokens per call are prefilled. For each, compute the load on the binding resource. Choose a policy, and state which workload and fleet measurements are needed before concluding that the remediation agent would encounter a different binding constraint.
Buying release evidence for an adapted model (Intermediate). A team proposes an adapted model for a repair workload that lowers the cost per assigned task from $1.20 to $0.80. Development and training cost $6,000, each release-evaluation task costs $3 per arm, both arms run the same number of tasks, and the workload runs 10,000 tasks per month. Acceptance is about 70 percent. The release test uses \(\SignificanceCriticalQuantile = 1.96\) and \(\StatisticalPowerQuantile = 0.84\).
Use equation 13.3 to compute the tasks per arm needed to detect a 5-point and a 2.5-point acceptance difference, and fold each evaluation bill into \(\AdaptationInvestmentCost\). Use equation 1 to compute \(\BreakEvenTaskCount\) and the payback in months for each. Leadership requires payback within 6 months. Which detectable difference can the team afford? A 3-point regression can hide inside the 5-point test; compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) for both configurations under that regression and decide whether the cost case survives it. Unlike notebook 19.1, the evaluation bill here depends on the decision the team wants to defend; explain why.
Delegating a research question under a deadline (Intermediate). A research agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}\)) answers a question in 40 minutes as a single controller, at a cost of $4.00. The analyst needs the answer in 20 minutes. Of the work, 80 percent splits across workers, and coordination overhead grows as \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount) = 0.02\,(\WorkerCount-1)\) of the single-controller time. A design with \(\WorkerCount \ge 2\) workers costs $4.00 plus $0.60 per worker for repeated context and result integration. The question’s allowance is $10.
Use equation 17.1 to find the smallest \(\WorkerCount\) that meets the deadline, the \(\WorkerCount\) that maximizes speedup, and the cost multiple of each over the single controller. A proposed runtime gives each worker its own $10 ceiling. Compute the worst-case spend at the chosen \(\WorkerCount\) and state the admission rule of principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\) that prevents it. Three workers agree on a source’s claim after reading the same page. Explain why that agreement is weaker evidence than three independent checks, and what the integrating controller must record before accepting it.
Where the fresh evidence goes in the prompt (Intermediate). A remediation trajectory runs 20 turns. Its context starts at 20,000 tokens and grows by 1,000 tokens per turn. A 500-token status block, refreshed from the source on every turn, sits at token position 2,000, right after the system instructions. Uncached input costs $2 per million tokens, a reused prefix costs $0.20 per million, and prefill runs at 10,000 tokens/s.
Using principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\), compute the tokens recomputed on turns 2 to 20 with the block at position 2,000 and with the block moved to the end of the prompt, where each turn recomputes only the block and the new turn’s tokens. Compare the input cost and the average per-turn prefill time of the two layouts. The team then proposes to stop refreshing the block and rely on the cached copy, since a cache hit shows the text is unchanged. Use principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\) to decide whether the saving is admissible, and state which check at the endpoint still protects the change if the status block is stale.
Sizing a whole remediation trajectory (Advanced). A remediation service runs 400 attempts per day, and 80 percent are accepted. An attempt spends $0.60 on 12 model turns, $5.00 on operator approval, and $0.40 on the health-window check. Three failure paths remain.

Each turn proposes a violating action with probability 0.01; the action gate rejects 98 percent of them, and an escaped violation causes $20,000 of damage, of which compensation recovers 75 percent.
In 5 percent of attempts the baseline changes before dispatch. Without an expected-version check the stale change applies, causing $3,000 of damage with 50 percent recovered; with the check the change is rejected and redone at a cost of 4 turns and a new approval.
Each attempt makes one mutation, and its reply is lost with probability 0.005. A blind retry duplicates the change, causing $10,000 of damage with 50 percent recovered; a settlement query costs $0.01.

Use equation 12.5 to compute the expected loss per attempt from each path with all mechanisms in place, then fold it into the attempt cost and compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\). Recompute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) with the gate, the version check, and settlement each removed in turn, and rank the mechanisms by what they save per day. With every mechanism present, which term dominates the cost per accepted task? Find the gate miss rate that brings that term below $1 per attempt and the resulting \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\). Compare the model’s token spend with the expected loss, and explain what the comparison says about where engineering effort on this lighthouse belongs.
Critiquing a research system end to end (Advanced). A team deploys a research agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}\)) that answers 20,000 analyst questions per day. Its design is as follows.

A planner fans each question out to 8 workers, each granted its own copy of the question’s $12 allowance.
Workers fetch 40 pages in total per question and concatenate them into the planner’s context without source labels, and the planner holds a send_report tool that can address any email named in its context.
An answer is accepted when 3 of the 8 workers agree.
A retrieval cache keyed by URL never expires its entries.
Every night, each accepted trajectory becomes a supervised fine-tuning target, and the acceptance grader is reused both as the reward for reinforcement learning and as the release evaluation.
After 24 hours, a generated summary replaces the raw trajectory log.

Assume that 1 page in 500 carries an injected instruction, the planner acts on 2 percent of the injected instructions it reads, and each disclosure costs $5,000. Each question produces one final answer candidate. Before grading, 60 percent of candidates are valid, with \(\VerifierFalseRejectionRate = 0.10\) and \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate = 0.20\). Compute the expected disclosures and their daily cost, the worst-case spend on one question against its allowance, and, by equation 3.3, the invalid share of accepted answers and the invalid answers accepted per day. Map every design choice to the ledger principle of table 2 it violates, rank the defects by expected harm, and propose a redesign that names the owner and the record at each seam of table 4. Defend which two changes ship first, and identify one defect that no number above prices but that would still block a safety case.

title: 17 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can splitting a task across several agents cost more and deliver less than giving one agent the same resources?
Splitting a task across several agents looks like the natural answer when the work is wide, since each worker can hold a smaller context and pursue its piece in parallel. The split replaces nothing the single agent already had. A capable single controller already runs searches and tests concurrently, keeps its context lean through retrieval and compaction, and holds scoped grants, so delegation must be judged against that baseline rather than against a fragile loop. What delegation adds is a set of boundaries between separately managed trajectories, and each boundary must carry explicitly what one trajectory carried implicitly. A worker can build against an interface that changes before its edit lands, two patches can merge cleanly and still break each other, reviewers that share a model can agree on the same mistake, and a canceled child can leave a container running and a budget half spent. Coordination overhead grows with every worker added, while the serial part of the task caps any speedup the parallel part can buy. Whether to split is therefore a measured decision. A multi-agent design earns its place only when it delivers more accepted tasks per unit of cost, or finishes them sooner in a way the objective values, than a single controller given the same tools and budget. Every handoff multiplies horizon, state, and authority, and the runtime must keep each delegated obligation owned until it settles.
