Even when every child agent operates within its assigned token budget, rate mismatches between pipeline stages can destabilize the system: a fast producer can rapidly overwhelm a slower consumer, causing queues to fill with increasingly stale candidate items.
Consider an upstream agent that lists files and emits candidate diffs at \(\ArrivalRate =\) 5 items per second. A downstream reviewer model generates a 500-token critique for each item at a decode speed of 40 tokens per second, yielding an effective service rate of only \(\ServiceRate =\) 0.08 items per second. In an unconstrained queue, the backlog expands at the net rate \(\ArrivalRate - \ServiceRate\). After 10 minutes, the queue accumulates 2,952 unreviewed items, and a newly submitted diff faces an estimated queue wait of 10.2 hours. Long before process memory is exhausted, the queued items become functionally obsolete: the repository state they reference has diverged, reproducing between agents the stale-observation failure that context invalidation guards against inside one trajectory. Per-agent token budgets fail to prevent this collapse because each individual candidate item is inexpensive to generate.


↩︎ Context invalidation, which withdraws observations that a later change has made stale, is established in Context Invalidation.
A finite credit window prevents this divergence by bounding the number of admitted, in-flight items, much as an aggregate budget caps token expenditure; it is the same mechanism that bounds staged records in trajectory collection. A producer transmits only while it holds a credit the consumer issued for free capacity, so congestion delays the producer but never overflows a buffer. Let \(\CreditWindowCapacity\) denote the fixed credit capacity of the channel, \(\FreeCreditCount\) the unallocated credits held by the producer, and \(\OutstandingItemCount\) the outstanding admitted items currently circulating in the pipeline. The runtime enforces the structural invariant:
\[\FreeCreditCount+\OutstandingItemCount=\CreditWindowCapacity,\qquad \FreeCreditCount\ge0,\quad \OutstandingItemCount\ge0.\]


↩︎ Collection credits, which bound staged trajectories between generation and verification, are established in Collection credits and staging reserves.
Under this discipline, admitting a new work item requires the producer to acquire and attach an available credit. That credit remains tied to the item while it traverses the network, waits in downstream queues, undergoes evaluation, or reserves output buffer space. The runtime returns the credit to the producer’s pool only when the item reaches a designated capacity-release boundary. Credit returns are processed atomically and with at-most-once semantics. A lost return silently shrinks the window, and a duplicated one inflates it, so network disconnections trigger ledger reconciliation against the authoritative runtime state rather than granting producers a fresh batch of credits.
Beyond protecting buffer memory, credit windows provide a sizing model for mean residence at a sustained service rate. Little’s law (theorem \(\ref{thrm-05-littles-law}\), equation 5.7) states that the mean number of items held equals their admitted rate times their mean residence. Applying it to a saturated window takes one mapping. The items held are the outstanding ones, \(\OutstandingItemCount=\CreditWindowCapacity\). The window admits a new item only when the consumer drains one, so the admitted rate is the drain rate \(\ServiceRate\), not the producer’s offered rate \(\ArrivalRate\). Dividing the items held by the admitted rate gives a mean residence of \(\CreditWindowCapacity/\ServiceRate\). With a window of \(\CreditWindowCapacity =\) 8 credits in the pipeline above, a diff that would have waited 10.2 hours behind the unbounded backlog instead resides in the window for 100 seconds on average. A hard freshness requirement additionally needs admission timestamps, deadline checks before service, and bounded service times if timely service must be guaranteed. When credits are exhausted, the producer yields execution instead of flooding the pipeline with artifacts destined to be obsolete upon inspection. Furthermore, if each in-flight payload is constrained to at most \(\DataVolume\) bytes, total memory occupancy cannot exceed \(\CreditWindowCapacity\DataVolume\). This demonstrates why payload return bounds (section 17.4) serve as crucial admission-control parameters rather than mere prompt formatting conventions.
Exhausting data credits, however, must never starve control-plane traffic. Signals such as cancellation commands, credit reconciliation messages, execution status receipts, and financial settlement records travel over reserved out-of-band control channels. The runtime must reject new task admissions whenever doing so would risk exhausting the execution slots reserved for downstream consumers and cleanup handlers; otherwise, upstream producers waiting for credits will block the very consumers needed to release them, deadlocking the system. Finally, releasing a channel credit must not be conflated with releasing an external resource or refunding a financial commitment: credit reclamation restores pipeline capacity, whereas financial settlement accounts for external cost.
Together, cancellation hierarchies and credit-based flow control bound the volume and financial exposure of in-flight work while keeping control paths responsive; credit windows also support mean-residence sizing under the stated service assumptions. Enforcing these boundaries across distributed child agents ultimately hinges on the authority model governing each node: what capabilities each descendant holds, how delegation is verified, and how fresh that authorization must be when validated at a remote gateway (section 17.8).




Suppose worker_caller_01, an agent authorized only to update selected caller functions, spawns a new child task to inspect upstream source code and designates the root orchestrator as that child’s parent. If the runtime naively resolves authority from the client-supplied parent identifier, the inspection child inherits the root’s global authority, including publication credentials intended exclusively for the release integration service. The delegation tree (the supervision tree’s parent-child edges, along which grants now flow) has itself manufactured a confused deputy (definition \(\ref{dfn-confused-deputy}\)). The runtime resolved authority from a name the requester supplied, the parent identifier that the child chose for itself. Similarly, two sibling workers dispatched concurrently might both observe the parent’s uncommitted budget before either issues an external call, overdrawing the task’s shared financial or token allowance. Task cancellation exposes a matching temporal hazard: a descendant grant that was perfectly valid when minted must admit no further work once the runtime revokes an ancestor in its lineage.
Scoped grants and credential brokering establish where authority resides within isolated execution environments. Multi-agent architectures extend this foundation through attenuated delegation: every hop down the task hierarchy passes authority no broader than the delegator’s existing authority. This model enforces the principle of least privilege (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975) with capabilities (definition \(\ref{dfn-capability}\)), so the authority travels in the reference a child holds rather than being looked up from the identity it claims, and confinement survives concurrent spending and ancestor state transitions. While a model may propose spawning a child task and suggest its scope, the runtime supervisor alone assigns the child’s identity, issues its attenuated grant, commits its resource reservation, and binds its lifecycle.

Saltzer, J. H., and M. D. Schroeder. 1975. “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems.” Proceedings of the IEEE 63 (9): 1278–308. https://doi.org/10.1109/proc.1975.9939.


A delegation tree applies the containment relation \(\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ChildCapabilityGrant)\subseteq\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ParentCapabilityGrant)\) established in Attenuation of delegated authority at every hop. In a multi-agent tree the relation governs concrete operations executed on underlying system resources, rather than superficial labels such as tool names or directory prefixes that an agent might attempt to manipulate. For example, an inspection child task may hold permission to inspect a specific interface file, but it must possess no rights to modify caller source files, exfiltrate repository data, or access the parent broker’s credentials for external repositories. The execution boundary enforces these perimeter restrictions directly; the child environment starts without inheriting broader host credentials or open file handles.
Runtimes can implement these bindings using either protected internal kernel handles or cryptographically verifiable bearer tokens. Chained-caveat tokens let a holder attenuate its grant locally without contacting an issuer, because each added restriction extends a keyed hash chain that the holder cannot unwind (Birgisson et al. 2014). Because the runtime supervisor, never the generative model, binds the resulting capability to the specific task execution context, a compromised or malfunctioning worker cannot forge a parent lineage or substitute a token belonging to another task.
Permissions and consumable budgets require fundamentally different delegation mechanics. Permissions are not depleted by use, so they can be shared: a parent that delegates read access retains its own ability to read. Consumable budgets, by contrast, are depletable resources that must be partitioned rather than duplicated, ensuring that each unit of currency or token quota is spent at most once. The admission control gate must therefore enforce conservation laws across the entire delegation hierarchy. Before dispatching a child task, the runtime atomically reserves the child’s admitted liability against the shared allowance, accounting for all concurrent siblings and the parent’s own outstanding work. This atomic reservation prevents two sibling workers from racing to commit the same remaining balance, and it is the shared-allowance rule of trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\)) applied across a tree, under which concurrent holders reserve against one allowance and a derived allowance only narrows. If a child subsequently subdivides its allowance among its descendants, it creates a nested subledger bounded strictly by its initial allocation rather than creating an independent chargeable pool. Upon task completion, formal settlement credits back only the unspent remainder verified by execution receipts; each liability is counted exactly once in a root ledger or delegated subledger, and reserves for finalization routines remain protected.



In a distributed multi-agent system, revocation cannot depend on promptly delivering push notifications to every running child. A robust architectural pattern assigns each task node in the runtime a monotonic generation counter and an operational state (such as active, canceled, or completed). When a grant is issued, the runtime binds it cryptographically to the complete root-to-holder lineage path, recording the exact generation counter of each ancestor at the moment of delegation. Revoking an ancestor marks that node ineligible or advances its generation counter. Node restarts must monotonically advance or preserve generation counters rather than resetting to zero, which would inadvertently revive expired or revoked grants.
When an agent submits an operation to the API gateway, the admission check verifies the grant’s cryptographic integrity, scope, and expiration, while querying the current lifecycle status and generation of every ancestor in the bound lineage path. If any ancestor has been canceled or its generation advanced, the gateway rejects the descendant’s request immediately, even if the worker leaf process itself has not yet received a cancellation signal and still considers itself active.
Traversing a lineage path of depth \(\ell\) directly requires \(\mathcal{O}(\ell)\) ancestor lookups at admission time. Advancing an ancestor’s generation number instantly invalidates the entire subtree of descendant grants in \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) time without requiring the coordinator to track down and rewrite individual token payloads. While gateway caches or indexed summaries can reduce the latency of these lineage checks, they introduce cache invalidation obligations that must be handled carefully.

Enforcing cancellation semantics requires an unambiguous, linearizable ordering point. Under a strict freshness policy, revocation updates and admission checks share an authoritative global order: once a revocation is committed, no subsequent admission check within that scope may evaluate against stale policy state. Because local signature verification and expiry checks establish only that a grant was valid when issued, a replicated gateway that cannot verify current ancestor state must fail closed, withholding admission from new operations.
Alternatively, systems that prioritize availability over strict consistency may permit distributed gateways to evaluate requests against cached ancestor state for a declared interval. This engineering trade-off introduces a stale-policy window, the bounded interval in which an already-revoked grant may still be accepted by an out-of-date gateway. The system designer must explicitly bound this window to account for cache invalidation propagation, token refresh intervals, clock skew assumptions, and network partition timeouts. Furthermore, revocation must actively sever all mediation pathways, including revoking open writable file handles held by running processes; any operations already admitted to external systems prior to revocation remain governed by transactional settlement rules.



During execution, a worker may discover that completing its objective requires an operation that exceeds its delegated authority. Rather than terminating or attempting privilege escalation, the worker generates an authorization request. The runtime intercepts these requests into a bounded approval queue, deduplicates redundant submissions, and routes them to the task owner. In this workflow, any explanatory rationale produced by a root or worker model is treated strictly as unverified commentary. Security decisions cannot bind to natural language explanations; instead, the action-bound approval established in Action-bound approval binds each decision to the exact operation it authorizes.
For a proposed publication operation, the approval interface must present the human operator with immutable, canonical parameters: the originating task identifier (migration_task_01), cryptographic content hashes of the candidate artifact, the target repository destination reference, operational parameters, base-version preconditions, and supporting verification evidence. The approval service then records the authorized approver’s decision against that exact represented operation.
Immediately before dispatching the privileged action, the runtime verifies that the target state has not drifted: the artifact candidate, destination reference, and repository commit preconditions must still match the approved payload, while current grants, lineage generations, and remaining budgets must still permit execution. If an intermediate integration step altered a single byte of the candidate artifact after approval, the runtime rejects the action and requires a fresh approval decision. Single-use approvals must also be atomically consumed upon execution to prevent replay attacks, because a cryptographic signature alone does not enforce exactly-once execution semantics. Passing validation tests in migration_accept_v1, obtaining operator approval, and executing the privileged publication remain three distinct, non-fungible events.

Checkpoint 17.3: Bounding work, authority, and spending after a split

Cancellation scope: The supervisor cancels migration_task_01 after the gateway admitted worker_interface_01’s test operation but before its reply arrives. Which statements can the runtime make truthfully now, and which must wait for further evidence?
Barrier vs. quorum: At a per-worker on-time probability of 90 percent, why can a 6-of-8 stopping rule rescue a read-only analysis but not the two-part migration?
Hedging a mutation: Why is a hedged copy of a mutating tool call a retry before settlement, and what must both attempts share before the runtime may issue it?
Credit window: The reviewer drains 0.08 items per second. What window keeps the modeled mean residence under one minute, and which messages must travel outside the data credits?
Joint allowances and revocation: Two siblings each receive less than the parent’s remaining allowance. What must the runtime do so they cannot jointly overdraw it, and what happens at a remote gateway that cannot confirm an ancestor’s current generation?



Delegation controls conserve authority and spending, distinguish cancellation from completed cleanup, and separate administrative approval from verified success. These safeguards make task decomposition governable. Whether splitting a task across multiple agents is actually useful, however, remains a separate empirical question, answerable only by measurement against a strong single-agent baseline.




A software repair task, such as an authentication migration, can execute under a single agent controller equipped with parallel tool dispatch, or under a multi-agent supervisor coordinating separate workers for interface updates and caller refactoring. If an experimental trial grants parallel tool execution to the supervisor while artificially restricting the single controller to serial execution, the benchmark measures that baseline handicap rather than the true benefit of delegation. A rigorous evaluation begins with an objective declared in advance, such as minimizing cost per accepted task subject to a deadline, or maximizing completed tasks within a fixed operating budget. The coordination tax (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}\)) then appears in three measurements read together: accepted-task rate, elapsed wall-clock time, and cost per accepted task. While a Pareto improvement across all three dimensions is ideal, it is rarely achieved; in practice, delegating work across agents represents an explicit trade of computational cost for lower latency. This trade-off is justified only when the engineering objective values latency reduction and the solution satisfies all quality and budget constraints.


A fair comparison applies the matched-budget comparison established in Matched-budget comparison, which fixes the task distribution, criteria, and resource envelope before policies are compared, against an equally capable baseline: an iterative single controller with parallel tool execution, rather than an isolated, single-turn model call. For delegation, the matched envelope must also fix starting fixtures, evidence access, and identical concurrency limits on both model calls and tool executions. Because either policy may terminate early, unconsumed budget represents an operational outcome rather than an experimental discrepancy. If a delegated design also alters underlying model selections or prompt formulations, the trial evaluates a compound bundle of variables; isolating the architectural impact of delegation requires a controlled ablation. Benchmarks must evaluate and report acceptance on the integrated, end-to-end task. In a multi-file migration, if the interface worker passes its local unit tests while the caller patch introduces breaking signature incompatibilities, the entire task has failed, regardless of the individual success receipts returned by either worker.



Every attempted task must remain in the evaluation denominator; tasks that encounter timeouts, unhandled errors, or indeterminate verdicts cannot be discarded from the benchmark. When the operational contract treats late delivery as an outage, on-time acceptance must be recorded as a distinct metric alongside gross completion. End-to-end latency spans the full execution envelope, measured continuously from task arrival through task decomposition, sub-agent dispatch, intermediate reconciliation, final integration, and automated assessment. Calculating median latency solely over accepted tasks introduces severe survival bias by filtering out prolonged failures. Systems evaluation therefore tracks latency across all arrivals. A task still running at the observation cutoff is right-censored: its latency is known only to exceed the cutoff, so it enters the latency distribution as a lower bound rather than being dropped, the same refusal to discard unresolved outcomes that keeps pending and unknown verdicts in the evaluation denominator (The four-verdict rule).
Cost accounting must encompass the complete system boundary: supervisor orchestration, retrieval queries, verification suites, merge conflict reconciliation, failed exploratory attempts, canceled speculative branches, and environment cleanup. Token expenditures must distinguish input and output tokens at their respective market prices, while concurrent tool invocations must be billed by aggregate worker execution time, which frequently exceeds the wall-clock span of the critical path. The effective cost per accepted task divides this full cohort spend by the accepted count under the same matched-budget accounting, so an architecture with no accepted solutions still reports its spend and the zero count. The dramatic token inflation documented in war story 17.1 illustrates why rigorous cost accounting is essential before committing to a multi-agent deployment.

Napkin Math 17.6: How much acceptance a token multiple must buyProblem: A delegated multi-agent architecture consumes tokens at the ratios reported for the research system: 15× the token volume of a standard chat interaction, compared to 4× for an autonomous single agent. Assuming a constant price per token, how much must task acceptance improve for delegation to break even on cost per accepted task, and over which baseline success rates is break-even mathematically achievable?
Math: Let \(\DelegationTokenMultiple\) be the token multiple, delegated tokens per attempt over single-agent tokens per attempt. Following equation 1.2, with cost proportional to tokens, the delegated cost per accepted task divided by the single-agent cost per accepted task is \(\DelegationTokenMultiple\,\SingleAgentAcceptanceProbability/\MultiAgentAcceptanceProbability\). With \(\DelegationTokenMultiple=\) 15× \(/\) 4× \(=\) 3.75×, economic break-even requires that \(\MultiAgentAcceptanceProbability =\) 3.75× \(\cdot\, \SingleAgentAcceptanceProbability\). Because probability is bounded (\(\MultiAgentAcceptanceProbability \le 1\)), break-even is possible only when the single-agent baseline achieves \(\SingleAgentAcceptanceProbability \le\) 26.7 percent. Even if the reported evaluation score gain of 90.2 percent translated directly into an acceptance rate multiplier of 1.90×, the effective cost per accepted task would remain 2.0× that of the single-agent baseline.
Systems insight: When delegation multiplies token consumption by a factor of \(\DelegationTokenMultiple\), it reduces effective cost \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) if and only if it scales task acceptance by more than \(\DelegationTokenMultiple\). At an expansion ratio of 3.75×, this economic efficiency can materialize only on difficult tasks where the single agent succeeds less than 26.7 percent of the time. On workloads where a single agent already succeeds reliably, delegation cannot be justified by cost efficiency; it must be justified as a purchase of reduced wall-clock latency or broader search coverage, valued explicitly by the system’s operational requirements.








Coherency cost turns added workers into lost capacity past the peak.
A matched trial is expensive, so before running one a team must decide which worker counts deserve a trial at all. The fixed-work scaling model of equation 1 does not replace that benchmarking; its role is to guide the search by identifying promising worker counts. Varying the worker count alters resource contention, sub-task dispatch boundaries, and inter-agent reconciliation costs simultaneously. Consequently, any empirical overhead curve holds strictly within the evaluated range and serves as a hypothesis beyond it. To reason about scaling limits systematically, classical systems engineering separates everything that keeps a fleet from ideal division into work that serializes (undivided planning, and any overhead that queues at a single resource) and pairwise reconciliation, two mechanisms that require fundamentally different architectural remedies.

Theorem 17.1: Universal scalability law
For a fixed amount of work divided among \(\WorkerCount\) equally capable workers, Gunther’s universal scalability law (USL) (Gunther 2008) gives the relative capacity, the speedup over one worker, as equation 5, with its peak at equation 6.
\[
\text{Speedup}(\WorkerCount)=\frac{\WorkerCount}{1+\ContentionCoefficient(\WorkerCount-1)+\CoherencyCoefficient \WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)}
\tag{5}\]
\[
\WorkerCount^*=\sqrt{\frac{1-\ContentionCoefficient}{\CoherencyCoefficient}}
\tag{6}\]

Contention (\(\ContentionCoefficient\)): The share of work that serializes, including undivided planning, final assessment, and queueing at single resources such as the supervisor or the integration queue.
Coherency (\(\CoherencyCoefficient\)): The cost of pairwise reconciliation. Each of the \(\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\) ordered worker pairs may exchange state, re-read a peer’s output, or resolve a conflicting change, the same count as the mesh round in section 17.3.
Amdahl’s law (\(\CoherencyCoefficient=0\)): Capacity saturates at \(1/\ContentionCoefficient\) and never declines.
Retrograde region (\(\WorkerCount>(1-\ContentionCoefficient)/\CoherencyCoefficient\)): A positive \(\CoherencyCoefficient\) makes added workers harmful, not merely useless. Capacity peaks at \(\WorkerCount^*\) and falls below one, slower than a single worker, past this count. With the screening notebook’s \(\ContentionCoefficient=\) 0.20 and \(\CoherencyCoefficient=\) 0.02, every count from 41 workers up finishes later than the serial reference.



Dividing both the numerator and denominator of equation 5 by \(\WorkerCount\) yields \(1/[\ContentionCoefficient+(1-\ContentionCoefficient)/\WorkerCount+\CoherencyCoefficient(\WorkerCount-1)]\). This expression matches equation 1 directly when setting the parallel fraction \(\ParallelFraction=1-\ContentionCoefficient\) and the overhead function \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)=\CoherencyCoefficient(\WorkerCount-1)\), so the screen’s linear penalty \(\WorkerOverheadSlope\) plays the role of the coherency coefficient \(\CoherencyCoefficient\). The match follows from the screen’s assumed linear elapsed penalty; it does not establish that every handoff cost is pairwise. Pairwise state reconciliation across \(\WorkerCount\) workers can produce such a penalty when its quadratic aggregate work is distributed across the workers. Serialized processing of a growing receipt volume can also increase elapsed overhead with worker count. A fitted coefficient therefore nominates a mechanism to investigate rather than identifying its cause. Applying the notebook’s assumed parameters, equation 6 places the continuous theoretical optimum at 6.3 workers, which evaluates to the discrete optimum of 6 workers identified in the screening notebook.

The architectural remedy depends on the measured source of overhead. Supervisor queue time, dependency invalidations, and reconciliation work help distinguish serial processing from cross-worker dependency work, and a matched trial that changes one mechanism can test the diagnosis. A verified serial bottleneck may benefit from pipelining supervisory prompts, sharding shared integration queues, or asynchronous event loops. When dependency reconciliation dominates, a partition that reduces cross-agent synchronization may instead pay. Interface refactoring coupled to caller implementations provides one such dependency hazard; a research query with independent search paths provides a contrasting partition.

Lighthouse 17.1: Research agent (orchestrator-worker fan-out)Workload: The research agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}\)) addresses open-ended, breadth-first queries. A lead orchestrator decomposes the inquiry into independent search paths, dispatches read-only subagents to retrieve and analyze external sources, and synthesizes their condensed findings. The builders of one production research system report that this breadth-first regime is where delegation helps most, in contrast to coding tasks whose tight interdependencies leave less work to run in parallel (Hadfield et al. 2025).
Scenario coefficients: Suppose lead-agent planning and final synthesis serialize \(\ContentionCoefficient=\) 0.10 of total execution, while subagents operate almost entirely without cross-communication (\(\CoherencyCoefficient=\) 0.002). Evaluating the scalability model yields an optimal fan-out of 21 subagents achieving 5.5× relative capacity. In contrast, the code repair agent’s high coherency limits its configuration to 6 workers at 2.3× capacity. Under these assumptions, the research partition permits a 3.5× wider effective worker fan-out. (These stylized coefficients illustrate the scaling regime rather than measured telemetry.)
Local constraint: Low coherency overhead permits wider fan-out under the supplied model, but token expenditure and context trust can still constrain deployment. At fixed per-worker work, token consumption scales linearly with fan-out, so the economic break-even threshold analyzed in notebook 17.6 may cap deployment before the modeled capacity peak \(\WorkerCount^*\). Furthermore, because worker receipts incorporate uncurated text from external web APIs, the bounded receipt protocol of section 17.4 limits returned context and keeps worker claims separate from runtime evidence. Source-derived fields and summaries remain untrusted inputs whose proposed uses require the security checks established for the tool boundary.
Systems insight: Under the supplied coefficients, the research partition supports wider fan-out than the repair partition. Dependency traces can establish whether interface isolation addresses the repair workload’s overhead; matched outcome and cost measurements determine whether wider research fan-out earns its additional spend. Admission controls bound that spend independently of the modeled capacity gain.


In production systems, empirical engineering inverts this analytical workflow. Rather than postulating coefficients, engineers conduct targeted benchmarking trials across a small set of practical worker counts (for example, \(\WorkerCount \in \{1, 2, 4\}\)) to estimate \(\ContentionCoefficient\) and \(\CoherencyCoefficient\). The resulting model fit projects the empirical capacity peak \(\WorkerCount^*\), identifying the next candidate configuration to benchmark. A large fitted coherency parameter \(\CoherencyCoefficient\) warrants inspecting traces and testing targeted interventions. Redesigning the task decomposition is justified when that evidence confirms that dependency reconciliation dominates; the coefficient alone does not establish the remedy.



Once the scalability fit has nominated a configuration, the matched trial decides whether it earns its tax. Consider an evaluation ledger for a representative cohort of software migration tasks patterned after migration_task_01, evaluated under identical automated test suites (migration_accept_v1). Both configurations operate under identical constraints: matching tool and model concurrency limits, identical sandbox permissions, and equivalent token and financial ceilings. The experiment isolates the delegation architecture itself: how work is decomposed, dispatched, and integrated, rather than what the runtime allows.

Every architectural flaw below stems from treating a delegation boundary as an operational guarantee that distributed coordination cannot enforce. In multi-agent architectures, these flawed assumptions carry measurable engineering costs in execution latency, token expenditure, and state consistency.

Fallacy: More workers necessarily improve the task outcome.
Adding parallel workers introduces synchronization overhead, resource contention, and coordination traffic that quickly erode parallel speedup. In the screening notebook (17.1), deploying eight workers consumes 0.440 of the serial execution time, compared to 0.433 achieved at an optimal configuration of 6 workers. Beyond this point, coherency cost dominates: under the universal scalability law with those same coefficients, scaling out to 41 workers runs slower than executing the workload on a single agent. Furthermore, economic cost escalates even when latency stalls. A multi-agent delegation multiple of 3.75× in token consumption pays for itself only on difficult tasks that an isolated single agent completes less than 26.7 percent of the time. Rather than assuming that parallelism is beneficial, system designers must benchmark candidate topologies under identical token budgets and time ceilings against a declared task objective.


Pitfall: Treating a clean merge as evidence that concurrent changes remain compatible.
A successful textual merge only verifies that concurrent workers avoided line collisions in shared files, leaving cross-file semantic dependencies completely unvalidated. Across a repository of 1,000 files where each worker performs 10 edits, two concurrent workers touch completely disjoint files 90.4 percent of the time. As a result, nearly every pair of concurrent patches merges cleanly from the perspective of version control, even when a caller and an interface worker introduce mutually incompatible API contracts. Coordination systems must validate semantic dependencies and test candidate integration trees within an isolated environment before guarded publication (section 17.5).


Fallacy: Agreement among reviewers proves correctness.
Consensus among language-model reviewers reflects the correlation of their errors rather than an objective proof of correctness. When multiple reviewer agents share underlying model families, prompt templates, or reasoning biases, their mistakes correlate positively. For instance, five reviewers with an individual false-approval rate of 20 percent would reach an erroneous majority verdict only 5.79 percent of the time under strict statistical independence. Under the assumed beta mixture, in which reviewers share each candidate’s difficulty, that false-majority rate jumps to 16.68 percent. Adding more homogeneous reviewers cannot eliminate this shared bias, as error rates quickly asymptote toward an irreducible floor of 15.0 percent (section 17.6). Production architectures must treat subjective reviewer voting as an advisory signal and isolate it strictly from deterministic, guarded verification checks.


Pitfall: Closing the parent task and releasing its reservations as soon as cancellation is requested.
A cancellation request immediately closes admission for new subtasks, but active execution, external tool calls, and downstream token charges drain asynchronously. Discarded work is not a rounding error. In the delegation ledger of table 9, failed attempts and canceled speculative branches account for $6 of $18 in delegated spend, and that ledger is complete only because every one of those charges stayed owned until it settled. If the parent task releases its accounting context and budget allocations the moment cancellation is requested, the trailing operations continue running without an owner, and their charges land outside any ledger as untracked spend and leaked resources. Robust orchestrators close admission at the entry gates, broadcast cancellation signals downstream, and maintain accounting context and state reservations until all active operations, diagnostic evidence, and billing charges have fully settled under the settlement rule.


Fallacy: If each worker usually finishes on time, the fan-out usually finishes on time.
Synchronizing multiple concurrent workers behind an all-results barrier compounds tail latency exponentially. Because every worker must complete before the barrier can lift, the overall probability of on-time completion multiplies each individual worker’s success rate. With an individual on-time probability of 90 percent per worker, a fan-out of 8 workers completes within the deadline only 43.05 percent of the time, and barrier success falls below even odds once the fleet reaches 7 workers (section 17.7). Where the system contract accepts interchangeable or quorum-based results, implementing a stopping rule restores 96.19 percent; where every subtask is strictly required, the orchestrator must reduce fan-out width to keep tail latency bounded.




Delegation turns one trajectory into several, and every boundary it adds must carry explicitly what a single trajectory carried implicitly: the inputs a worker may rely on, the authority and allowance it may spend, the evidence it must return, and the obligations that outlive it. The runtime, not the workers, owns those boundaries. It separates claims from execution records, revalidates dependencies before anything publishes, treats agreement among similar reviewers as one correlated signal, and keeps every admitted operation owned until it settles.
Whether those boundaries are worth building is a measurement question. Delegation lowers cost per accepted task only when it raises acceptance by more than it multiplies spend; otherwise it must be bought as reduced wall-clock time or broader coverage that the declared objective explicitly values. Key Takeaways: Delegation must earn and preserve its boundaries

Coordination overhead sets the useful fleet size: Serial execution constraints cap parallel speedup at \(1/\ContentionCoefficient\), while pairwise reconciliation costs cause effective system throughput to fall beyond \(\WorkerCount^*=\sqrt{(1-\ContentionCoefficient)/\CoherencyCoefficient}\). Shrinking serial planning and integration overhead raises the scalability ceiling far more than merely shaving latency off individual handoffs. Empirical profiling across realistic workloads, rather than casual inspection of isolated agent trajectories, must calibrate these parameters.
Task dependencies govern completion makespan: Communication topologies, scheduling precedence, and fault-supervision hierarchies address distinct systems requirements. Once a schedule attains its critical-path bound, further latency reductions require shortening that path; before it does, additional slots or reduced contention may also shorten runtime. Furthermore, any agent endowed with recursive delegation authority requires hard runtime limits on fan-out, nesting depth, and aggregate token reservations.
Delegation handoffs require explicit runtime contracts: A handoff envelope must establish immutable task inputs, granted execution authority, resource budgets, and required evidence before worker execution begins. The returned receipt must strictly isolate ground-truth execution records from the worker’s unverified self-assessment, truncating narrative explanations rather than audit telemetry whenever context limits bind.
Disjoint writes do not guarantee semantic compatibility: Non-overlapping file edits establish only that parallel workers avoided concurrent modification conflicts; they do not prove that combined changes preserve system-wide behavioral invariants. Safe publication requires revalidating dependencies against the latest branch head, testing the integrated candidate in isolation, and advancing branch pointers through conditional atomic updates.
Correlated reviewer errors impose an irreducible accuracy floor: When automated reviewers evaluate an intrinsically challenging artifact, shared model blind spots cause their errors to correlate, preventing majority-voting failure rates from dropping to zero. Beyond this floor, spending additional tokens on homogeneous reviewers yields negligible benefit. Runtimes must instead incorporate independent verification modalities, such as deterministic test suites or formal linters, because peer consensus cannot manufacture authoritative correctness.
Resource obligations outlive parent caller lifecycles: Canceling a parent agent halts the dispatch of new downstream tasks, but it does not automatically terminate remote tool operations, network sockets, or asynchronous child processes already in flight. Each in-flight bound has its own mechanism. Credit windows bound the volume of queued work and support mean-residence sizing, attenuated grants and atomic reservations bound authority and spend, and the settlement record, not cancellation or credit release, keeps every admitted effect owned until its outcome and charges settle.
Multi-agent execution must outperform a capable single-agent baseline: A meaningful evaluation benchmarks multi-agent architectures against an equally optimized single-agent controller provisioned with identical parallel tool access, context allowances, and wall-clock budgets. System accounting must price every failed attempt, speculative invocation, and rollback, justifying multi-agent coordination only when the resulting increase in task success or latency reduction offsets its marginal token overhead.



The coordination tax (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}\)) manifests in the serialized handoffs, validation barriers, and residual dependencies that remain after decomposing a task. Invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) mandates that these architectural boundaries maintain strict external validation and effect gating, ensuring that peer consensus among models is never mistaken for authoritative execution rights. Finally, trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\)) extends from one trajectory to a tree of them. Every child is a separately owned trajectory whose derived grants only narrow, whose consumable allowance is reserved against its ancestors’ shared allowance, and whose unsettled side effects remain accounted for by the runtime after its parent stops.



The question of when dividing computational work yields a net speedup is older than autonomous software agents. Gene Amdahl’s 1967 argument established that serial execution fractions strictly cap the speedup achievable by adding processors (Amdahl 1967). Two years later, Ronald Graham showed that while greedy list scheduling lands close to the theoretical dependency bound, adding parallel resources can paradoxically increase total completion time (Graham 1969). Neil Gunther later unified these dynamics in the universal scalability law, introducing a pairwise coherency penalty to explain how crosstalk and contention turn throughput saturation into outright performance collapse (Gunther 2008). Across successive computing generations, systems architects repeatedly encountered the same hard reality: coordination overhead and coherency penalties, rather than the raw supply of workers, dictate practical scale.

Distributed artificial intelligence confronted the handoff problem in the 1970s. The Hearsay-II speech-understanding system coordinated independent, opportunistic knowledge sources through a shared blackboard (Erman et al. 1980). Carl Hewitt’s actor model abandoned shared memory entirely, giving each autonomous agent private local state and routing interactions through addressed messages (Hewitt et al. 1973). Reid Smith formalized structured delegation in the Contract Net Protocol, turning task announcement, bidding, and award into an explicit, typed exchange between a manager and prospective contractors (Smith 1980).
Over the following decades, classical distributed systems research supplied the precise operational controls that multi-agent architectures require today. Kung and Robinson introduced optimistic concurrency control, permitting workers to execute tentatively against private workspace copies and validate isolation before committing (Kung and Robinson 1981). Birrell and Nelson established typed remote procedure calls with explicit failure semantics, replacing unstructured message passing with formal client-server contracts (Birrell and Nelson 1984). Gray and Cheriton solved distributed state synchronization and lock management through time-bounded leases (Gray and Cheriton 1989). Joe Armstrong formalized supervision trees within Erlang, demonstrating how structured hierarchies and crash-only semantics allow runtimes to restart failed processes from clean, known states (Armstrong 2003). Finally, object-capability systems eliminated ambient authority by embedding access rights directly into object references rather than relying on global identity checks (Dennis and Van Horn 1966; Hardy 1988), an approach later extended through cryptographically attenuable tokens with chained caveats (Birgisson et al. 2014).

Redundancy followed a parallel trajectory of high theoretical promises followed by sobering empirical corrections. The Condorcet jury theorem (Condorcet, Marquis de 1785) and John von Neumann’s multiplexed majority organs (Neumann 1956) demonstrated that aggregating independent votes can synthesize near-perfect reliability from noisy components. Leslie Lamport, Robert Shostak, and Marshall Pease proved the rigorous mathematical bounds of Byzantine fault tolerance, establishing that agreement in the unsigned-message protocol model survives arbitrary, even malicious, faults only while fewer than one third of participants are faulty (Lamport et al. 1982). However, the independence premise behind probabilistic majority-voting guarantees collapsed when applied to software. John Knight and Nancy Leveson demonstrated experimentally that independently written programs fail coincidentally on the same edge cases far more often than chance predicts (Knight and Leveson 1986). Dave Eckhardt and Larry Lee provided the analytical explanation: complex problem domains harbor intrinsically difficult input regions that induce correlated failures across diverse implementations (Eckhardt and Lee 1985).
Modern language-model architectures have revived every one of these paradigms simultaneously. Self-consistency uses majority voting across sampled reasoning paths (Wang et al. 2023), multi-agent debate structures iterative argumentation across model instances (Du et al. 2023), and conversational frameworks coordinate role-playing agents over structured communication graphs (Wu et al. 2023). In production, orchestrator-worker patterns have delivered capability gains on breadth-first research tasks, and their builders report roughly 15× the token consumption of a chat interaction to get them (Hadfield et al. 2025). Systematic empirical analyses of multi-agent failures reveal that the field has re-encountered classical distributed failure modes: ill-defined task boundaries, uncoordinated handoffs, and verification bottlenecks that silently propagate errors rather than catching them (Cemri et al. 2025).

The Contract Net Protocol (Smith 1980). The foundational text on structured delegation. Smith frames task distribution as a typed, negotiated protocol, showing that the essential elements of modern task envelopes, from capability announcements to formal awards, were established long before language models existed.
An Experimental Evaluation of the Assumption of Independence in Multiversion Programming (Knight and Leveson 1986). The landmark controlled experiment that disproved the assumption of independent software failures. This paper provides the standard methodological blueprint for evaluating whether an ensemble of redundant agent reviewers yields genuine reliability gains or merely inflates inference cost.
Making Reliable Distributed Systems in the Presence of Software Errors (Armstrong 2003). Armstrong’s doctoral dissertation detailing the architecture of Erlang. It articulates the operational rationale for supervision trees, fail-stop process isolation, and restart strategies, mapping directly to how orchestrators should manage the lifecycles and blast radiuses of child agent trajectories.
A General Theory of Computational Scalability Based on Rational Functions (Gunther 2008). Gunther derives the universal scalability law directly from queueing models. The derivation clarifies the physical distinction between contention and coherency, explaining why serial bottlenecks and cross-agent communication demand fundamentally different architectural fixes.
Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (Cemri et al. 2025). An extensive empirical taxonomy analyzing real-world multi-agent failure traces. It serves as an indispensable field catalog of the specification gaps, uncoordinated handoffs, and verification failures that production runtime environments must actively prevent.

Every given below is a hypothetical problem input, not a measurement of a real system. Each problem ends in a design decision, and the calculation exists to justify it.

Choosing the lever in a worker-count screen (Basic). A fixed work partition has divisible fraction \(\ParallelFraction=0.9\) and normalized overhead \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)=\WorkerOverheadSlope(\WorkerCount-1)\) with \(\WorkerOverheadSlope=0.01\). The resource ceiling permits at most \(20\) workers, and each added worker adds roughly the same token spend.

Using equation 1, compute the normalized elapsed time at \(\WorkerCount=4\), \(8\), and \(16\), the integer count that minimizes it, and the speedup at that count. Compare the count with \(\sqrt{\ParallelFraction/\WorkerOverheadSlope}\).
Two proposals compete for the same engineering effort: halving the per-worker overhead to \(\WorkerOverheadSlope=0.005\), or halving the serial work so that \(\ParallelFraction=0.95\). Compute the best integer count and its speedup under each proposal.
Decide which proposal to fund once worker spend is counted, and state which proposal alone can ever deliver a speedup above \(10\times\).

Hot files in a shared workspace (Basic). A repository holds \(\RepositoryFileCount=5{,}000\) files, and each worker writes \(\WorkerWrittenFileCount=20\) of them, chosen uniformly and independently.

Using equation 4, compute the probability of at least one shared write for \(\WorkerCount=2\) and \(\WorkerCount=4\) workers, both exactly and by the exponential approximation. Find the smallest fleet for which a shared write is more likely than not.
Each worker also edits one shared dependency manifest with probability \(0.3\), independently of its other writes. For four workers, compute the probability that at least two edit the manifest, and the probability of any shared write at all.
A colleague proposes a single shared working directory for four workers because “collisions are under 40 percent.” Decide, and name the two hazards of section 17.5 that remain even when no two workers write the same file.

Sizing a credit window for staleness (Basic). A producer emits candidate items at \(\ArrivalRate=2\) items per second. A consumer model writes a \(400\)-token critique of each item at \(50\) output tokens per second, and each returned record occupies at most \(\DataVolume=8{,}192\) bytes. An item is useful only if the consumer begins serving it within \(60\) s of admission. For initial sizing, screen a saturated credit window by requiring its modeled mean residence to be no greater than this interval; assume negligible transport time and full utilization at the stated service rate.

Compute the consumer’s service rate \(\ServiceRate\), the backlog of an unbounded queue after five minutes, and the wait of the newest item behind that backlog.
Using the full-window mean residence \(\CreditWindowCapacity/\ServiceRate\), find the largest integer window \(\CreditWindowCapacity\) that passes this sizing screen and its payload bound \(\CreditWindowCapacity\DataVolume\). Does passing the screen establish that every item begins service before its freshness deadline?
Find the minimum number of identical consumers needed to keep pace with the producer and the largest shared window that passes the same mean-residence screen at their aggregate service rate. State how admission timestamps and a freshness check before service should handle an item that has waited too long. Explain why cancellation and settlement traffic must not draw on these data credits.

A fourth slot or a shorter vertex (Intermediate). A migration plan has a shared specification \(\DependencyGraphVertex_1\) (\(30\) s); four module refactors \(\DependencyGraphVertex_2\) through \(\DependencyGraphVertex_5\) (\(60\), \(60\), \(90\), and \(40\) s), each depending only on \(\DependencyGraphVertex_1\); and an integration check \(\DependencyGraphVertex_6\) (\(50\) s) depending on all four refactors. Each vertex occupies one interchangeable slot, with no other delays.

Compute \(\AggregateSlotWork\) and \(\CriticalPathDuration\) from equation 2, and the lower bound of equation 3 for \(\WorkerCount=2\), \(3\), and \(4\) slots.
By assigning the four refactors to slots, find the shortest achievable makespan for each \(\WorkerCount\). Explain why the bound is not attained at \(\WorkerCount=2\).
The team currently runs \(\WorkerCount=3\) and can afford either a fourth slot or engineering that shortens \(\DependencyGraphVertex_4\) to \(60\) s. Decide, and state what shortening \(\DependencyGraphVertex_4\) buys once the fourth slot exists.

Pricing deadline coverage (Intermediate). Under matched resource ceilings, a single controller spends an expected \(\$0.40\) per attempt with \(\AcceptanceProbability=0.60\), and \(40\) of every \(100\) attempts are accepted by the deadline. A delegated configuration spends \(\$0.90\) per attempt with \(\AcceptanceProbability=0.80\), and \(72\) of every \(100\) attempts are accepted by the deadline. Spend includes failed attempts and canceled branches, and cost is proportional to tokens.

Compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) for both configurations from equation 1.2, and their ratio.
Find the token multiple \(\DelegationTokenMultiple\), the delegated acceptance that would restore break-even on \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\), and the largest single-controller acceptance for which break-even is possible at all.
Per \(100\) attempts, compute the marginal cost of each additional on-time acceptance. One service values an on-time accepted migration at \(\$1\), another at \(\$5\). Decide which configuration each should run.

Hedged lookups for the support agent (Intermediate, second-lighthouse transfer). The support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)) answers a refund-eligibility question by dispatching three read-only lookups in parallel: the customer record, the order history, and the governing policy clause. All three are required. Each lookup attempt independently returns an admissible result within \(1\) s with probability \(0.70\) and within \(2\) s with probability \(0.95\). The service target is that at least \(95\) percent of answers have all three results within \(2\) s. Assume \(1{,}000\) sessions dispatch their three initial lookups simultaneously. The lookup pool has \(4{,}000\) slots, and each launched attempt retains its reservation until the \(2\) s observation cutoff, even if its result arrives earlier. An attempt that has not returned an admissible result remains outstanding until that cutoff. Treat the stated completion probabilities as unchanged by load when calculating a policy without admission blocking.

Compute the probability that all three results arrive within \(2\) s without hedging. Explain why the \(\RequiredResultCount\)-of-\(\WorkerCount\) stopping rule of section 17.7 does not rescue this fan-out.
Compare two hedging policies: duplicating every lookup at dispatch, and starting a replacement only for a lookup still outstanding at \(1\) s, which must then itself return within the remaining \(1\) s. Assuming every proposed hedge is admitted, compute the per-lookup and all-three probabilities within \(2\) s. For each policy, compute both expected slot demand and the largest possible slot demand before the cutoff.
Decide whether either calculation establishes that the policy meets the deadline target within the hard slot limit. Propose an admission rule for delayed hedges, and explain why deadline acceptance must be evaluated again when the rule can deny replacements. Contrast the binding constraint here with the coherency limit on the repair agent’s migration, and state what must hold before the same hedging could be applied to issuing the refund itself.

Bounding a remediation delegation tree (Intermediate, second-lighthouse transfer). The remediation agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) is restoring a degraded checkout service. Its root grant permits reading metrics and logs for checkout and scaling the checkout deployment between \(4\) and \(12\) replicas; it permits no configuration writes. The root’s remaining allowance is \(\$50\), of which \(\$5\) is a protected finalization reserve and \(\$6\) is already reserved for the root’s own outstanding work. The model proposes three children, each with a \(\$20\) allowance, “less than the parent’s remaining \(\$50\)”: a metrics worker that reads checkout metrics, a log worker that reads logs for checkout and payments, and a capacity worker that scales checkout between \(4\) and \(16\) replicas.

State which proposed grants violate \(\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ChildCapabilityGrant)\subseteq\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ParentCapabilityGrant)\) and how to narrow them. Compute the worst-case liability if each child’s allowance is copied from the parent’s balance, and which children atomic reservation admits if they are dispatched in the order listed. Find the largest equal allowance that admits all three. The capacity worker then proposes two scale workers at \(\$8\) each; state which the runtime admits and repair the split.
An operator takes over and the runtime cancels the root at \(\TimeInstant=0\). Both scale workers are active, and each submits at most one scale step every \(5\) s to a remote gateway. Under a cached-authorization policy the gateway trusts a lineage record for up to \(18\) s, with a \(2\) s clock-skew allowance. Under a strict policy it looks up the current status and generation of each of the \(3\) nodes in a scale worker’s lineage at \(4\) ms per lookup. Compute the stale-policy window, the most scale steps it can admit after cancellation, and the strict policy’s added latency as a fraction of the step interval. Choose a policy for scale steps and one for metric reads, and state what the strict policy costs if the authoritative store is unreachable for \(30\) s.
Under the policy chosen in part (b), the ledger at cancellation shows: the metrics worker settled \(\$4\) and stopped; the log worker settled \(\$9\), and a log-export job it started before cancellation is still unresolved with a bounded liability of \(\$3\); the first scale worker settled \(\$2\) and was confirmed terminated; the second scale worker settled nothing, and a node-pool scale-up it started before cancellation has an unknown outcome with a bounded liability of \(\$5\); the root’s own work settled \(\$4\). Compute the allowance the runtime may release now, the amount still held, and the release a “cancellation refunds all reservations” rule would claim. A follow-up remediation task needs a \(\$20\) allowance. Decide whether to admit it now, and state who owns the two open operations and what that owner must retain.

Buying evidence past a correlated floor (Advanced). Reviewers each falsely approve a known-invalid candidate with marginal probability \(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability=0.10\), and their errors follow the beta mixture of section 17.6 with \(\CorrelationCoefficient=0.30\). The release rule requires that an invalid candidate be approved with probability at most \(0.01\). A reviewer call costs \(\$0.20\). A protected regression test costs \(\$0.50\) and passes an invalid candidate with probability \(0.05\), assumed independent of the candidate’s reviewer propensity \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\).

Compute the beta parameters \(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape\) and \(\PropensityPriorRejectionShape\), and the majority false-approval probability for three reviewers under independent errors and under the mixture.
Compute the mixture’s majority false approval for seven reviewers and the floor \(\Pr(\FalseApprovalPropensity>1/2)\), numerically. Decide whether any number of reviewers of this kind can meet the release rule.
Price two designs per candidate: seven reviewers under majority vote, and three reviewers plus the protected test, with approval requiring both a reviewer majority and a passing test. Compute each design’s false-approval probability and choose one.
Critique the assumption that the test is independent of \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\). Name a mechanism from this chapter that would correlate the test with the reviewers, and state the measurement that must precede release.

Fitting the scalability law before choosing a fan-out (Advanced, critique and redesign). Trials of a repair-migration partition under matched resources measure relative capacity \(\text{Speedup}(2)=1.835\) and \(\text{Speedup}(4)=2.878\). The serial reference takes \(40\) minutes, and the service requires completion within \(11\) minutes. The expected cost of an attempt grows with worker count as \(\$1.00+\$0.30(\WorkerCount-1)\), and acceptance does not change with \(\WorkerCount\).

Rearrange equation 5 so that it is linear in \(\ContentionCoefficient\) and \(\CoherencyCoefficient\), fit both coefficients from the two measurements, and compute \(\WorkerCount^*\) from equation 6, the best integer count and its capacity, and the smallest count that runs slower than one worker.
A trial at \(\WorkerCount=8\) measures \(2.90\). Compare it with the fitted prediction, and state what the gap implies about using the fit outside the measured range.
The team proposes deploying the best integer count from part (a). Critique the proposal against the deadline. For this calculation, suppose two proposed redesigns have the following responses: sharding the integration queue halves \(\ContentionCoefficient\), and repartitioning the migration so interface changes land before caller work begins halves \(\CoherencyCoefficient\). For each, find the smallest worker count that meets the deadline, if any, and its cost per attempt, and recommend a design under these assumptions. State what trace or matched intervention evidence would establish the assumed coefficient responses in a deployment.



What’s Next: From coordination to costWhen is the time saved by delegation worth its additional resource use? This chapter answered for one stated workload, with a ledger that charged failed attempts and canceled branches to the accepted tasks they served. That ledger is a special case of a question every deployment faces, for one agent or many. The next chapter opens with the repair team offered a model whose tokens cost a tenth as much and asks why the switch can still raise the price of every repair that ships. Answering it means counting what each accepted task costs across all its attempts, how context reuse, retries, and model choice change that cost, and how concurrent trajectories compete for capacity. The same account then prices delegation itself, without dropping the reservations and unresolved obligations established here.

title: 17 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can splitting a task across several agents cost more and deliver less than giving one agent the same resources?
Splitting a task across several agents looks like the natural answer when the work is wide, since each worker can hold a smaller context and pursue its piece in parallel. The split replaces nothing the single agent already had. A capable single controller already runs searches and tests concurrently, keeps its context lean through retrieval and compaction, and holds scoped grants, so delegation must be judged against that baseline rather than against a fragile loop. What delegation adds is a set of boundaries between separately managed trajectories, and each boundary must carry explicitly what one trajectory carried implicitly. A worker can build against an interface that changes before its edit lands, two patches can merge cleanly and still break each other, reviewers that share a model can agree on the same mistake, and a canceled child can leave a container running and a budget half spent. Coordination overhead grows with every worker added, while the serial part of the task caps any speedup the parallel part can buy. Whether to split is therefore a measured decision. A multi-agent design earns its place only when it delivers more accepted tasks per unit of cost, or finishes them sooner in a way the objective values, than a single controller given the same tools and budget. Every handoff multiplies horizon, state, and authority, and the runtime must keep each delegated obligation owned until it settles.

Learning Objectives

Estimate the speedup and useful worker count of a work partition from its serial fraction and coordination overhead
Calculate makespan bounds from a task’s dependency graph to decide whether added slots or shorter tasks pay
Design bounded receipts and credit windows that cap returned context and payload occupancy, and size mean residence under an explicit freshness policy
Apply shared-write collision estimates to justify private workspaces and dependency revalidation before publication
Calculate majority false approval under correlated reviewer errors to choose between more reviewers and a different check
Evaluate fan-out completion rules and hedging under deadline, capacity, and duplicate-effect constraints
Apply attenuated grants and atomic reservations to bound a delegation tree’s authority, spending, and settlement after cancellation
Evaluate delegation against a capable single-controller baseline using a declared objective and matched resource ceilings

title: 17 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
The repair agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)) has so far fixed a connection-pool race, a change confined to one module that a single controller holds comfortably in one context. Its next assignment is wider: migrate an authentication module across a repository, a change that reaches every caller of the module’s interface and is exactly the kind of repair task that tempts a split. The task naturally splits into two coupled changes: revising an internal interface and updating its downstream callers. A single coordinator could retain the entire task, dispatching parallel searches and test runs to collect evidence before synthesizing a unified patch. Alternatively, it could partition the problem, assigning the interface update and caller modifications to separate workers. Each worker operates within a focused context window, editing candidate files and reacting to compiler diagnostics independently. This division introduces an immediate distributed consistency challenge: the caller modifications must remain compatible with the interface that ultimately lands, not merely the snapshot the caller worker read at dispatch.



A fleet multiplies horizon, state, and authority, so every handoff must preserve closure.
The runtime mechanisms established in earlier chapters govern a single execution trajectory at a time. Within that boundary, the harness checks each model and tool invocation against an assigned grant and token budget, durable execution logs one trajectory’s event history, failure recovery settles, repairs, or compensates the effects of that one trajectory, evaluation compares trials of one configuration against another, and curation and post-training improve the policy that drives it. Partitioning the migration preserves these local controls inside each individual worker, but it leaves the coordination space between them unmanaged. A single-agent runtime provides no mechanism to resolve which interface revision the caller worker targets, whether a clean textual merge of two patches preserves semantic correctness, or what consensus among five reviewer agents actually guarantees. Nor does it define who claims an orphaned test container after a coordinator cancels a subtask, or how a parent bounds the authority and compute budget delegated to a child. Without explicit systems controls, every such gap threatens to make the split cost far more than it buys.
This chapter builds the runtime controls that make delegation governable and the empirical framework that decides whether it pays. The required controls are state records and verification gates owned directly by the runtime rather than left to prompt instructions: enforceable task assignments, receipts that separate an agent’s self-reported claims from verified tool evidence, a publication barrier that revalidates cross-module dependencies before any candidate patch merges, clean cancellation paths that account for in-flight work, and authority grants that narrow monotonically at every delegation hop. The chapter pairs these mechanisms with a measurement discipline that compares each multi-agent design against a single agent holding equivalent parallel tools and resource budgets, and that prices every token consumed by failed, retried, or canceled subtasks.
The migration carries the argument from the decision to split through the final accounting, and each control answers a hazard that the previous one exposes. A screen of serial work against coordination overhead first decides whether a partition can pay at all (section 17.2). Dependency, communication, and supervision structures then fix what may run concurrently and who owns each child (section 17.3), and typed envelopes and receipts fix what crosses each handoff (section 17.4). Once workers run in parallel, guarded publication keeps their edits consistent (section 17.5), and a joint error model shows what agreement among reviewers can and cannot certify (section 17.6). Cancellation, hedging, and credit windows bound the work still in flight (section 17.7), attenuated grants and atomic reservations bound authority and spending at every hop (section 17.8), and a matched comparison against a capable single controller decides whether the whole design earns its tax (section 17.9).

title: 17 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
Handing the interface update and the caller update to dedicated workers differs from issuing concurrent model queries, and that difference defines the unit of delegation. A delegated worker owns a bounded child trajectory with its own context window, model-and-tool loop, task contract, and independent lifecycle. Several candidate samples dispatched by one controller, such as the self-consistency votes of test-time compute, are instead parallel calls inside one trajectory. They are the cheapest ensemble an agent can run and also the most correlated, because every sample shares the model, the prompt, and the input’s difficulty, a dependence that section 17.6 quantifies. The architectural shift lies in establishing explicit boundaries between separately managed trajectories, regardless of whether those workers execute on a single host or across a distributed cluster.


↩︎ Self-consistency, which samples several reasoning paths and returns the plurality answer, is established in Selection policies.
The point of comparison throughout this chapter is the capable baseline: the single-agent runtime developed in earlier chapters, which already manages its context window, reserves system resources, verifies proposed tool effects externally, and executes candidate searches and isolated tools concurrently. Delegation retains every one of those operational requirements while introducing new coordination boundaries. The fundamental systems question is whether dividing control and context improves a declared task objective enough to justify the overhead of managing them.


The first motivation is context partitioning: each worker retains only the material strictly necessary for its subtask. In the migration scenario, the interface worker maintains the target API contract and local unit tests without ingesting the intermediate compiler diagnostics of the caller worker, allowing each subsequent model invocation to process substantially fewer prompt tokens. However, the net token savings depend entirely on the structure of the decomposition. If both workers repeatedly require the full repository commit history, separate contexts duplicate prompt state rather than isolating it, a redundancy the single-agent baseline already avoids through retrieval and compaction.
The second motivation is separate task ownership. Workers can pursue multi-turn exploratory investigations through iterative tool feedback and local reasoning loops while a central coordinator tracks inter-task dependencies and orchestrates final integration. Assigning task ownership, however, does not eliminate underlying data dependencies. A caller worker that generates code against an outdated interface must still reconcile its implementation once the interface worker finalizes the new contract. True operational independence derives from the causal graph of the task itself, never from cosmetic role descriptions in prompt templates.
The third motivation is task-scoped authority. Decomposing work across workers binds tools, execution capabilities, and resource budgets directly to individual subtasks. For example, a test-runner worker can be granted execution privileges in an isolated container without granting it credentials to publish pull requests or write to production databases. Even so, process isolation does not eliminate trust boundaries: a child worker’s textual output can still inject unvalidated claims or prompt injections into the parent coordinator’s context, and any external mutations it produces must still be verified and settled by the runtime.
Table 1 separates these opportunities from capabilities already present in the baseline.



Table 1: What Delegation Adds: The comparison preserves the capable single-controller runtime and identifies the extra boundaries a coordinated design must justify.
