These organizational advantages carry concrete systems costs. Every delegation boundary incurs a coordination tax (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}\)).

Definition 17.1: Coordination tax
Coordination tax is the work and elapsed time a delegated design spends on handoffs rather than on the task: preparing and validating envelopes, delivering context, scheduling children, collecting receipts, and reconciling and integrating their results.

Significance: The tax enters both terms of the cost per accepted task, \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) (equation 1.2): its tokens and tool time raise \(\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]\), and the part on the critical path lengthens every attempt against its deadline.
Distinction: While task decomposition aims to reduce makespan by distributing work concurrently, the coordination tax represents the unavoidable friction introduced by that distribution. This tax scales with worker count, communication frequency, and inter-task dependencies.
Common pitfall: Accounting only for the tokens and execution time of successful worker turns. Context re-ingestion, supervisor arbitration turns, failed retries, and abandoned speculative branches all consume model quota and execution budgets.



Coordination tax impacts systems along two distinct dimensions: aggregate resource consumption and end-to-end latency. Duplicated input prompt tokens, redundant tool invocations, and serialize-deserialize cycles increase the total operational cost. Meanwhile, user-perceived delay is governed by makespan, the wall-clock time elapsed from the arrival of a task to the completion and verification of its final artifact. Makespan depends strictly on the operations situated on the critical path. A straggling child worker delays synchronization at the join barrier, while subsequent arbitration and reconciliation turns further inflate the critical path before results can be accepted.
Amdahl’s fixed-work argument1 gives the first screening model (Amdahl 1967). Let \(\SerialReferenceTime\) be the time for a fixed set of operations executed serially, with fraction \(\ParallelFraction\) perfectly divisible among \(\WorkerCount\) equally fast workers and fraction \(1-\ParallelFraction\) remaining serial. Assume enough resources for that division and let \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)\) be the additional elapsed overhead, normalized by \(\SerialReferenceTime\). Then
1 Amdahl’s Argument: Amdahl’s 1967 conference paper contains no equation; it argues in prose that the serial housekeeping of a program limits what any number of parallel processors can deliver, and the familiar formula was written down by later authors. The lesson transfers intact to delegation, where planning, integration, and final assessment are the housekeeping that no added worker absorbs.\[\text{Speedup}(\WorkerCount)=\frac{\SerialReferenceTime}{\Time(\WorkerCount)}=\frac{1}{(1-\ParallelFraction)+\ParallelFraction/\WorkerCount+\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)}. \tag{1}\]
Equation 1 provides a preliminary screening model for a specified work partition. The baseline \(\SerialReferenceTime\) reflects that partition executed sequentially on a single thread of execution, rather than the capable baseline runtime (which already pipelines tool executions and concurrent candidate samplings). In production, an empirical benchmark of the capable baseline must replace \(\SerialReferenceTime\) before finalizing any worker allocation. Within this theoretical formulation, achieving any net speedup over the serial reference requires that:
\[\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)<\ParallelFraction\left(1-\frac{1}{\WorkerCount}\right).\]
The right-hand side represents the theoretical wall-clock time saved by distributing the parallelizable portion across \(\WorkerCount\) workers. Whenever coordination overhead \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)\) exceeds this threshold, the split task takes longer than serial execution. Furthermore, this inequality constrains execution time alone; task acceptance rates, token expenditures, and monetary costs enter the trade-off in section 17.9, which gives serializing work and pairwise reconciliation separate coefficients because their remedies differ (section 17.9.3).

Napkin Math 17.1: Screening a proposed work partitionProblem: A hypothetical fixed workload has \(\ParallelFraction=\) 0.80 and assumed normalized overhead \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)=\WorkerOverheadSlope(\WorkerCount-1)\) with \(\WorkerOverheadSlope=\) 0.02. The resource ceiling permits at most 16 workers. Which integer count minimizes modeled elapsed time?
Math: Evaluating the denominator of equation 1 for each permitted count, four workers require 0.460 of the serial reference time. The minimum occurs at 6 workers, requiring 0.433, a 2.3× speedup; eight workers increase the ratio to 0.440, because the shrinking parallel term \(\ParallelFraction/\WorkerCount\) no longer pays for the added overhead. Halving the overhead coefficient to 0.01 moves the optimum to 9 workers and the speedup to 2.7×.
Systems insight: The serial fraction sets the ceiling and the overhead sets the useful fleet size. No worker count beats \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)=\) 5× here, and the best count sits near \(\sqrt{\ParallelFraction/\WorkerOverheadSlope}\), so halving the per-worker overhead \(\WorkerOverheadSlope\) adds 3 workers but only 0.4 of speedup. Shrinking the serial planning and integration work is the larger lever.


A reduction in modeled makespan does not automatically justify a multi-agent architecture. Production systems optimize under varied constraints: one automated migration service may seek to maximize accepted pull requests prior to a nightly release window subject to a strict token budget, whereas another prioritizes minimizing the total cost per accepted migration. Trading latency for computational overhead is justified only against an explicit, pre-declared optimization objective, and the decision framework of section 17.9 charges that objective for retries and failed executions as well. Before attempting to size or provision an agent pool, a systems architect must map the causal dependency graph of the workload: identifying which subtasks can truly proceed concurrently and determining the exact evidence required at each downstream join. Those fundamental dependencies dictate the coordination topology.

title: 17 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
Consider a codebase migration task (migration_task_01) where an interface worker and a caller worker concurrently inspect a repository (repo_base_01). Even though both agents run in parallel, the caller’s patch fundamentally depends on the interface definitions that its peer is actively modifying. Routing both workers through a single supervisor does not eliminate that underlying causal dependency. A runtime architecture that naively treats the supervisor’s message-routing graph as the true dependency graph will prematurely accept and publish a caller patch built on stale interface assumptions.
To build reliable multi-agent systems, engineers must distinguish three separate structural graphs that govern execution:

The dependency graph defines causal precedence by recording which artifacts, decisions, or validation checks must complete before downstream work can safely proceed.
The communication topology defines the network paths, protocols, and message envelopes through which agents exchange information.
The supervision tree defines operational ownership over agent lifecycles, governing fault isolation, resource reservations, and cancellation cascades.

Because a supervisor frequently manages children whose outputs depend causally on one another, runtime engines must maintain these three structures independently. Conflating message delivery with causal dependency or lifecycle ownership leads directly to race conditions, orphaned processes, and corrupted state.


How work crosses boundaries between agents determines how communication routing and supervision map onto underlying task dependencies (table 2). The most prevalent pattern is the supervisor-worker topology (frequently termed orchestrator-worker). In this model, a centralized coordinator decomposes an incoming task, dispatches subtasks to subordinate workers, and synthesizes their returned receipts. This design directly mirrors the contract net protocol2 originally developed for distributed problem solving (Smith 1980). In production systems, these foundational topologies frequently compose. For example, a supervisor might dispatch parallel analytical investigations, stream their candidate patches through a staged validation pipeline, and persist intermediate progress within a shared task store.
2 Contract Net Protocol: In Smith’s 1980 protocol, a manager node announces a task, idle contractor nodes submit bids, and the manager awards the contract to a chosen bidder, which may subcontract in turn. The award represents the conceptual ancestor of the typed task envelope: it fixes which agent owns the subtask and what structured receipt must return, eliminating the ambiguity inherent in prompt-level delegation.


Table 2: Coordination arrangements and runtime obligations: While routing patterns structure message handoffs, the execution runtime must enforce result validity, resource boundaries, and state consistency across agent boundaries.











Arrangement
How work crosses a boundary
Useful when
Obligation that remains




Supervisor–worker
A coordinator assigns subtasks and collects bounded receipts
A task has separable investigations and an explicit integration decision
Bound dispatch, returned context, and the coordinator’s own work


Pipeline
Each stage receives the artifacts and evidence its predecessor is required to provide
Later work depends on a sequence of transformations or checks
Preserve stage preconditions and bound queues between stages


Shared blackboard
Workers claim tasks and publish versioned artifacts through a shared store
Different workers can contribute as dependencies become available
Enforce claim ownership, publication rules, and dependency validity


Actor messaging
Workers hold local state and exchange addressed messages
Responsibilities require ongoing asynchronous interactions
Define delivery, duplicate handling, ordering, and bounded mailboxes






Each coordination topology makes different trade-offs regarding where state accumulates and where synchronization occurs. A supervisor concentrates integration logic and validation evidence at a single coordinator, requiring compact, structured receipts to prevent prompt context exhaustion. A pipeline structures execution as a sequence of discrete transformations, keeping each stage’s working context tightly focused while streaming items concurrently across stages. By contrast, a shared blackboard3 decouples agents entirely by externalizing coordination into a centralized artifact and task store (Erman et al. 1980). In an actor architecture, originally formulated by Hewitt, Bishop, and Steiger, agents maintain completely isolated private state and communicate exclusively via asynchronous message passing to explicit addresses (Hewitt et al. 1973). Both blackboards and actor meshes shift the coordination burden toward explicit conflict resolution, distributed ordering, and bounded mailbox management.
3 Blackboard Architecture: The Hearsay-II speech-understanding system of the 1970s coordinated independent knowledge sources that never communicated directly with one another, interacting solely by posting and reading hypotheses on a shared global data structure. Its central scheduling challenge, deciding which pending contribution to evaluate next, reappears whenever agent workers claim tasks from a shared operational store.Message counts scale with the communication graph and its interaction protocol. If each of \(\WorkerCount\) participants transmits an update to every other participant during an execution round, the network must handle \(\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\) directed deliveries. With an average payload size of \(\MeanDeliveryPayloadLength\) tokens per delivery, that single round consumes \(\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\MeanDeliveryPayloadLength\) tokens across the system. In contrast, a supervisor managing \(\WorkerCount\) workers requires only \(2\WorkerCount\) deliveries per round (one dispatch envelope and one receipt per worker), consuming \(2\WorkerCount{}\MeanDeliveryPayloadLength\) tokens. The full mesh thus scales quadratically, transmitting \((\WorkerCount-1)/2\) times more messages per round than the centralized coordinator.
Raw transmission volume measures network traffic, not what the receiving models must ingest. In a fully connected mesh where each agent appends every incoming peer message to its prompt history, ingested tokens per round grow as \(\mathcal{O}(\WorkerCount^2)\), and the append-only re-send of equation 2.9 compounds that growth across rounds because each later prompt carries every earlier delivery. Even in a centralized topology, verbose receipts, iterative deliberation rounds, or frequent status polling against a blackboard store can exhaust context windows and inflate inference budgets. Across the four arrangements of figure 1, the supervisor’s round costs \(2\WorkerCount\) deliveries and the actor mesh up to \(\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\), while the pipeline and blackboard replace direct deliveries with bounded queues and versioned claims that the runtime must police.






Figure 1: Four Coordination Arrangements: Each panel shows where work crosses a boundary. A supervisor sends envelopes down and collects receipts, a pipeline passes artifacts through bounded queues, a blackboard mediates claims and versioned publications through a shared store, and actors exchange addressed messages through mailboxes. One supervisor round costs \(2\WorkerCount\) deliveries and a full mesh round \(\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\). Each topology imposes specific runtime obligations for bounding queues, isolating concurrent state, and verifying result correctness.



Architectural design therefore prioritizes explicit, bounded handoffs over minimal edge counts. Each worker must receive only the specific inputs and validation invariants required for its assigned subtask, preventing individual context windows from degrading under cumulative peer histories.



Formal reasoning about execution concurrency models task precedence as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), \((\DependencyGraphVertexSet,\DependencyGraphEdgeSet)\). Each vertex \(\DependencyGraphVertex \in \DependencyGraphVertexSet\) represents a bounded unit of execution, either an autonomous agent trajectory or a deterministic runtime validation check. A directed edge \((\PredecessorGraphVertex,\DependencyGraphVertex) \in \DependencyGraphEdgeSet\) indicates that vertex \(\DependencyGraphVertex\) requires a declared precondition satisfied by vertex \(\PredecessorGraphVertex\), such as an emitted code artifact, a validated test report, or an explicit authorization token. A status message signaling task completion satisfies an incoming edge only when accompanied by verifiable output receipts.
A vertex becomes dependency-ready once every prerequisite predecessor condition has been verified. However, dependency readiness alone does not trigger execution: the runtime dispatcher must additionally verify execution authority, allocate an active worker slot, and secure a bounded token and financial budget reservation. If a predecessor fails or emits invalid artifacts, the control plane either halts downstream successors or transitions execution to an explicit recovery branch. Loops and iterative refinement cycles enter the graph as unrolled, bounded attempts. Because graph acyclicity guarantees only the absence of logical dependency loops, the underlying runtime remains responsible for detecting dynamic deadlocks arising from shared resource locks, exhausted thread pools, or saturated queues.
To estimate the theoretical limits of parallel scheduling, assume each vertex \(\DependencyGraphVertex\) occupies one interchangeable worker slot for a fixed duration \(\VertexSlotTime(\DependencyGraphVertex)\), encompassing both model inference latency and external tool execution. Let \(\WorkerCount\) represent the pool of available parallel worker slots. Under these assumptions, aggregate slot-work \(\AggregateSlotWork\) and critical-path duration \(\CriticalPathDuration\) are defined as
\[
\AggregateSlotWork=\sum_{\DependencyGraphVertex\in \DependencyGraphVertexSet}\VertexSlotTime(\DependencyGraphVertex),\qquad
\CriticalPathDuration=\max_{\pi\in\operatorname{Paths}(\DependencyGraphVertexSet,\DependencyGraphEdgeSet)}\sum_{\DependencyGraphVertex\in\pi}\VertexSlotTime(\DependencyGraphVertex).
\tag{2}\]
Any valid schedule’s total makespan \(\ScheduleFinishTime\) must satisfy the dual lower bounds
\[
\ScheduleFinishTime\ge\max\left(\frac{\AggregateSlotWork}{\WorkerCount},\CriticalPathDuration\right).
\tag{3}\]
The aggregate work bound \(\AggregateSlotWork/\WorkerCount\) reflects the fundamental capacity constraint: \(\WorkerCount\) parallel worker slots cannot complete \(\AggregateSlotWork\) total units of execution time in less than \(\AggregateSlotWork/\WorkerCount\), regardless of schedule structure. The critical-path bound \(\CriticalPathDuration\) reflects the causal precedence constraint: sequential dependencies cannot be parallelized, establishing a lower bound on latency even with infinite worker slots.4 In production environments, resource contention, queuing overhead, payload serialization, and trajectory retries expand the overall makespan well beyond these theoretical minimums unless explicitly incorporated into vertex durations \(\VertexSlotTime(\DependencyGraphVertex)\) and graph edges.
4 Greedy List Scheduling: Graham established that any list schedule which never leaves a worker slot idle while a dependency-ready vertex waits completes within a factor of \(2-1/\WorkerCount\) of the optimal makespan. Graham also demonstrated that such schedules can suffer counterintuitive timing anomalies where adding worker slots or reducing individual task durations actually increases overall completion time (Graham 1969). A runtime dispatcher that greedily schedules ready work is therefore near-optimal relative to the theoretical bound in equation 3, and an observed latency regression after expanding worker pools does not necessarily indicate a scheduler implementation bug.
Graham, Ronald L. 1969. “Bounds on Multiprocessing Timing Anomalies.” SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics 17 (2): 416–29. https://doi.org/10.1137/0117039.

Napkin Math 17.2: DAG scheduling in multi-agent executionProblem: Consider an illustrative repository upgrade with 4 worker slots. Table 3 gives assumed durations for a single successful execution of each node. Each node occupies one slot; there are no additional dispatch delays, resource conflicts, retries, or transfer costs. How much can overlap?

Math: Summing the node durations as in equation 2 gives 275 s of aggregate slot-work. Dividing by the slot count gives the work term in equation 3, 68.75 s. The paths \(\DependencyGraphVertex_1\to \DependencyGraphVertex_2\to \DependencyGraphVertex_5\to \DependencyGraphVertex_7\) and \(\DependencyGraphVertex_1\to \DependencyGraphVertex_3\to \DependencyGraphVertex_5\to \DependencyGraphVertex_7\) tie for the critical path. The table’s schedule uses at most 3 slots, so it is feasible under the stated capacity and attains the path bound.
Result: Completion takes 174.5 s, a 1.58× speedup over executing these same nodes serially, and more slots cannot shorten the remaining chain.
Systems insight: Once a schedule attains the critical-path bound, as this one does, allocating worker slots beyond peak concurrency yields zero latency improvement. The off-critical branch through \(\DependencyGraphVertex_4\) and \(\DependencyGraphVertex_6\) finishes 26.5 s before \(\DependencyGraphVertex_7\) can start, meaning optimizations on that branch do not affect overall makespan. In contrast, shortening \(\DependencyGraphVertex_5\) or \(\DependencyGraphVertex_7\) yields a direct second-for-second reduction in total makespan up to the available slack. Shortening \(\DependencyGraphVertex_2\) in isolation provides no benefit because \(\DependencyGraphVertex_3\) ties it on the critical path. Analyzing production agent traces requires distinguishing a dependency-limited schedule like this one from a capacity-limited schedule, where additional slots or reduced contention can still shorten makespan.





A static plan specifies its stages, conditional branches, validation checkpoints, and retry bounds ahead of execution. Because all artifact dependencies and message routes are declared upfront, operators can inspect handoffs statically and verify safety invariants before dispatch. With enforced per-node work limits, bounded attempts, and stated service or deadline assumptions, the declared graph supports worst-case resource and execution bounds; a termination deadline does not guarantee accepted completion or immediate settlement of external work.
In contrast, dynamic spawning provisions child agents at runtime in response to intermediate observations. For example, during a repository migration, a worker analyzing call sites might uncover an undocumented dependency and request an isolated sub-investigation. While the model proposes this subtask dynamically, the runtime control plane must evaluate and admit it under the prevailing task contract. Dynamic spawning allows systems to adapt flexibly to open-ended workloads, but it introduces non-deterministic execution graphs. When an unconstrained model decides how many child agents to spawn and when to spawn them, combinatorial fan-out can quickly overwhelm system capacity and inflate execution costs.

War Story 17.1: Unbounded fan-out in a multi-agent research system (2025)Context: Anthropic’s engineering team described building an autonomous research system where a lead orchestrator plans an investigation, spawns parallel subagents to search for evidence, and synthesizes their findings (Hadfield et al. 2025).
Mechanism: The lead agent possessed unconstrained authority to determine subagent fan-out. In early prototype versions, the model routinely spawned 50 subagents even for simple queries, searched endlessly for nonexistent sources, and allowed subagents to degrade coordination by flooding one another with excessive updates.
Impact: The engineering team reports that autonomous agents typically consume about 4× more tokens than standard conversational interactions, while multi-agent systems consume roughly 15× more. Although the multi-agent configuration outperformed a single agent by 90.2 percent on the team’s internal research evaluation, the unconstrained fan-out incurred disproportionate resource expenditure on straightforward tasks.
Fix: The team embedded explicit scaling heuristics into the orchestrator’s prompt, instructing the model to calibrate subagent allocation to query complexity, allocating a single agent for direct fact retrieval and scaling upward only for open-ended synthesis. Furthermore, the orchestrator was structured to wait synchronously for each dispatched subagent batch to conclude before initiating subsequent steps, simplifying state synchronization at the cost of pipeline parallelism.
Systems lesson: Dynamic fan-out is fundamentally an architectural resource allocation problem that cannot rely solely on model self-restraint. While prompt-based heuristics guide model proposals, the runtime control plane must enforce hard admission limits on tree breadth, recursion depth, and aggregate budget reservations, directly bounding the token consumption in the effective cost metric \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\).


Uncontrolled fan-out illustrates the necessity of formal admission control in multi-agent architectures. Relying solely on prompt instructions to curb subtask generation is insufficient: an unconstrained model can still propose redundant branches or trigger cascading worker requests. Simply allocating each child a budget fraction smaller than the parent’s remaining funds also fails to protect the system, as a burst of concurrent siblings can issue overlapping claims that collectively exceed available capacity. The runtime admission controller must atomically reserve each child’s maximum potential liability against the shared task budget before dispatching execution, an invariant that section 17.8 formalizes across hierarchical delegation trees. Production runtimes must independently enforce four distinct bounds: fan-out breadth (maximum children per parent), concurrent active slots (maximum parallel executions), recursion depth (maximum delegation layers), and absolute deadlines. A shallow tree can still exhaust resources through excessive breadth, while a strict concurrency cap can still permit an unbounded sequence of sequential worker allocations.


↩︎ Bounded-liability admission, which reserves an operation’s maximum charge before admitting it, is established in Reservation and settlement.



Beyond resource management, dispatching a child agent establishes lifecycle ownership. A child’s running trajectory, pending tool invocations, and uncommitted side effects typically outlive the ephemeral model call that spawned it. The supervision tree defines how the runtime isolates faults and manages recovery when a child encounters an unrecoverable failure. Drawing directly from the battle-tested principles of Erlang/OTP (Open Telecom Platform) supervision trees,5 systems formalize recovery through explicit, per-supervisor restart strategies (Armstrong 2003, 2007):
5 Erlang Supervision Trees: Erlang emerged from a telephone-switching research program initiated in 1981, established on the design principle that systems should allow failing processes to crash cleanly while a designated supervisor restores known-good state, rather than attempting defensive error handling locally (Armstrong 2003). In agentic systems, this principle is even more vital: allowing a confused agent trajectory to attempt local recovery within a contaminated context window frequently compounds its errors, whereas a supervisor restart provisions a clean execution context from recorded inputs.
Armstrong, Joe. 2003. “Making Reliable Distributed Systems in the Presence of Software Errors.” PhD thesis, Royal Institute of Technology (KTH).

Armstrong, Joe. 2007. “A History of Erlang.” Proceedings of the Third ACM SIGPLAN Conference on History of Programming Languages (HOPL III), 6-1-6-26. https://doi.org/10.1145/1238844.1238850.

Under a one_for_one policy, the supervisor restarts only the failed child agent while allowing sibling workers to continue uninterrupted. This strategy is ideal for embarrassingly parallel or loosely coupled subtasks, such as searching disjoint documentation sources, where workers share no mutable intermediate state.
Under a one_for_all policy, the failure of any single child triggers the supervisor to terminate and restart all sibling workers within that supervision group. This approach is essential for tightly coupled collaborative tasks where partial artifacts become invalid upon peer failure. For example, if an interface worker crashes and restarts with an altered API contract, any partial implementation generated by a concurrent caller worker is fundamentally invalidated.

The two policies differ in blast radius (figure 2). One failure under one_for_one costs a single fresh attempt and its reservation, whereas under one_for_all it discards the progress of every coupled sibling, and the whole group restarts from recorded inputs.
To prevent degenerate retry storms, supervision trees enforce a restart intensity bound, the maximum number of restarts permitted within a sliding time window. When a child agent repeatedly fails and breaches this threshold, the supervisor ceases local restarts, aborts its remaining subordinates, and escalates the failure upward to its own parent supervisor. In an agentic system, a restart must never simply continue from the failed worker’s corrupted or circular context window. Instead, the runtime treats each restart as a freshly admitted attempt, provisioning a clean context initialized from recorded input artifacts and acquiring a fresh budget reservation. When aborting sibling processes under one_for_all or escalation, the runtime invokes the structured cancellation and cleanup protocols described in section 17.7.






Figure 2: Restart Policies in a Supervision Tree: Under the one-for-one policy (a), only the failed worker restarts, as a newly admitted attempt with its own reservation, while its siblings continue. Under the one-for-all policy (b), the supervisor stops the coupled siblings through the cancellation protocol and restarts the whole group from recorded inputs, because the caller’s partial work has lost its meaning. Either supervisor that exceeds its declared restart intensity stops restarting and escalates the failure to its parent.




Checkpoint 17.1: Evaluating multi-agent coordination topologies

Dependency vs. routing: The interface and caller workers communicate only through their supervisor. Why can they still produce interdependent patches, and which of the three structures records that?
Critical-path estimate: Using the durations in table 3, estimate how much completion changes if \(\DependencyGraphVertex_6\) takes 20 s less, and how much if \(\DependencyGraphVertex_5\) takes 20 s less. Which node should an engineering team speed up?
Worker-count screen: With \(\ParallelFraction=0.9\) and the notebook’s overhead \(\WorkerOverheadSlope=\) 0.02 per extra worker, estimate the best worker count from \(\sqrt{\ParallelFraction/\WorkerOverheadSlope}\) and the speedup ceiling \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)\). Is it worth halving \(\WorkerOverheadSlope\) or halving \(1-\ParallelFraction\)?
Aggregate admission: Why can granting every child less than its parent’s remaining budget still oversubscribe the task? What must happen atomically?



While the coordination topology delineates how responsibility, messages, and evidence traverse agent boundaries, structural routing alone does not guarantee execution safety. Every boundary crossing requires a formal task envelope that explicitly defines what artifacts the worker receives, what tools and tokens it may consume, and what typed receipts it must return.

title: 17 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
A message asking worker_caller_01 to “update the callers” leaves critical engineering boundaries unspecified: the target interface version, the files permitted to change, the resource budget, and the acceptance criteria for completion. If the worker fills those gaps from its own interpretation of the prompt, that interpretation becomes the de facto contract. While a workflow dependency edge dictates when a child task may begin, the task envelope defines what that child is permitted to read, modify, spend, and return. Delegation therefore requires a typed action contract (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}\)) that extends across the agent boundary, much like a typed interface in a classic remote procedure call establishes formal argument types, return values, and failure semantics before execution begins (Birrell and Nelson 1984).

Definition 17.2: Typed task envelope
A typed task envelope is a versioned assignment record binding a child task to identified inputs, a scoped authority grant, resource and lifecycle limits, completion requirements, and a bounded return format.

Significance: The runtime validates task boundaries before admitting work and verifies returned artifacts against required evidence. In addition, capping the return payload prevents runaway worker outputs from flooding the coordinator’s context window on subsequent execution turns.
Distinction: The envelope defines an operational, enforceable contract for execution and resources; the natural-language prompt merely describes the objective within those constraints.
Common pitfall: Mistaking a syntactically valid envelope for proof of authorization or successful execution. Both authorization and task completion require verification against authoritative state records maintained outside the worker’s control.





When delegating a subtask, the parent agent proposes the work, but the execution runtime authenticates the parent-child relationship, resolves the authority grant, and locks the resource reservation. In the task envelope shown in listing 1, field identifiers point to immutable registry records rather than embedding raw, unverified data. The referenced acceptance contract specifies expected caller behavior, exact test suite versions, the execution environment, and any required human reviews prior to final acceptance.



Listing 1: Bounded Child Assignment: The envelope identifies inputs, authority, resource ownership, acceptance requirements, and limits on the return.


{
  "task_id": "worker_caller_01",
  "parent_task_id": "migration_task_01",
  "envelope_version": "caller_assignment_v1",
  "dispatch_id": "caller_dispatch_01",
  "assignment": "Update the designated authentication callers.",
  "inputs": {"base_ref": "repo_base_01"},
  "authority": {"grant_ref": "caller_private_patch_grant_01"},
  "budget": {"reservation_ref": "caller_reservation_01"},
  "completion": {
    "contract_ref": "migration_accept_v1",
    "required_evidence": [
      "candidate_ref", "write_set_ref", "dependencies_ref",
      "check_report_ref", "usage_ref", "settlement_ref"
    ]
  },
  "return_limits": {
    "receipt_bytes": 8192,
    "optional_summary_tokens": 256,
    "artifact_references": 8
  }
}



The task and dispatch identifiers tie an assignment directly to its execution records, where durable write-ahead log intents preserve dispatch identity so recovery can reconcile unresolved work before any permitted retry. The base reference (base_ref) fixes the immutable repository snapshot exposed to the worker; any reads extending beyond that baseline snapshot (such as queries to external package registries) require their own versioned references. The authority grant restricts the worker to editing designated caller files within an isolated scratch workspace, reading approved paths, and running local verification commands. The capability system enforces parameter-level constraints on each tool invocation rather than granting coarse binary access, and it explicitly withholds publication rights to shared branches. The budget reservation establishes hard limits on consumable resources, including input and output tokens as well as tool execution counts. Because the runtime resolves these records against authoritative registry state before dispatch, a worker cannot expand its privileges or budget by modifying envelope fields in its own context.


↩︎ Durable intent, the admitted request recorded before dispatch so recovery retains its identity and can resolve an uncertain outcome, is established in Durable Intent Before Dispatch.
Completion requirements explicitly enumerate the evidence artifacts the runtime must collect (such as test logs, dependency manifests, and reviewer sign-offs) before considering the task complete. Finally, the return limits enforce strict bounds on the receipt payload and its natural-language summary, ensuring that bulky build outputs remain stored out-of-band rather than polluting the coordinator’s context window.



The return payload in listing 2 describes a candidate change ready for integration review, one step short of an accepted modification. The receipt structure strictly separates verified operational metadata from unverified model commentary: runtime services directly populate and authenticate every field under runtime, whereas assertions generated by the worker model remain isolated under worker_claims.



Listing 2: Bounded Child Receipt: Runtime records and a worker-authored explanation remain distinct; candidate readiness does not authorize publication.


{
  "task_id": "worker_caller_01",
  "envelope_version": "caller_assignment_v1",
  "dispatch_id": "caller_dispatch_01",
  "return_status": "complete",
  "runtime": {
    "status": "candidate_ready",
    "base_ref": "repo_base_01",
    "candidate_ref": "caller_candidate_01",
    "write_set_ref": "caller_writes_01",
    "dependencies_ref": "caller_dependencies_01",
    "check_report_ref": "caller_checks_01",
    "usage_ref": "caller_usage_01",
    "settlement_ref": "caller_settlement_01"
  },
  "worker_claims": {
    "summary": "Updated the designated callers for the migration."
  }
}



The write-set record reflects the diff actually produced in the isolated workspace rather than the worker’s conversational recollection of what it modified. Similarly, the dependency record captures observed file reads, loaded package versions, configuration files, and external environment flags, bounded by explicit tracing coverage. The checker report records the exact candidate hash, the test command, the container environment, and the exit status. This record carries the evidence-scope rule of the tool boundary across the delegation boundary. A single call’s observation confirmed only what that call measured; a check result here establishes an outcome for one identified candidate hash, checker, and environment, and authorizes nothing beyond it. If the runtime cannot produce or verify every piece of mandatory evidence, the return status transitions to evidence_unavailable rather than complete.


↩︎ The evidence-scope rule, under which an observation confirms only what its tool measured during that invocation, is established in Complete mediation.
The usage record accounts for charged and reserved work across tokens, wall-clock time, and tool invocations. The settlement record distinguishes a stop acknowledgment, confirmed resource release, and unresolved background operations with retained owners. A complete return and the final settlement of every operation are therefore distinct statuses. This separation becomes critical when the parent cancels an execution branch (section 17.7), ensuring that task termination does not leave orphaned background processes or dangling locks. Optional prose explanations may be shortened or omitted when space is constrained, with the omission explicitly recorded, while required identities, statuses, and evidence references pass intact. If the mandatory structural fields alone exceed receipt_bytes, the runtime generates an explicit payload-size failure rather than returning a truncated record.



Instead of inlining an entire repository tree into a child task’s context prompt, the parent passes an immutable repository reference (base_ref). The worker then issues targeted read queries to fetch only the source files relevant to its assignment. However, this pass-by-reference pattern yields net token savings only when the child inspects a small fraction of the code base. If the worker iteratively fetches broad directory trees, the combined cost of reference overhead, tool invocation tokens, and repeated context re-reads across turns can quickly outstrip the cost of an upfront payload.

Napkin Math 17.3: Price the reads after the handoffProblem: Each of 6 children receives either a 48,000-token repository slice or a 350-token reference envelope followed by 3,600 tokens of retrieved content. With all other inputs equal, no cache discount, and a hypothetical $3 per million input tokens, how much repository-delivery input does the reference save?
Math: Pasting costs 6 \(\times\) 48,000 \(=\) 288,000 tokens, or $0.864. The reference costs 6 \(\times\) (350 \(+\) 3,600) \(=\) 23,700 tokens, or $0.071, a 12.2× reduction. If every child instead reads the full slice, the reference design consumes 290,100 tokens and loses its saving.
Systems insight: The efficiency of reference passing depends entirely on read selectivity rather than the pointer mechanism alone. In this configuration, each child inspects only 7.5 percent of the slice, keeping reference passing economical until reads exceed 47,650 tokens. Effective multi-agent system design therefore pairs pointer handoffs with precise task scoping and indexing.


Passing a shared base reference also amortizes KV-cache prefill across parallel workers, but only when their prompt prefixes align.


↩︎ Prompt prefix alignment and KV-cache prefill amortization are established in Preserving an exact prefix.
Once execution concludes, the receipt hands the parent coordinator an isolated candidate, its base version, and runtime-recorded evidence. Those records, not the absence of overlapping files, decide whether candidates can merge safely. Two patches that touch disjoint files can still be incompatible, and making that judgment before anything publishes is the job of the next section.

title: 17 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
Consider an authentication migration where the runtime assigns worker_interface_01 to update an interface and worker_caller_01 to adapt a call site. Both workers branch from the same baseline commit, repo_base_01. When the interface worker finishes first, the integration service accepts its patch as repo_head_02. Because the caller worker modifies a different file, a standard three-way textual merge succeeds cleanly without merge conflicts. The caller’s patch, however, still targets the obsolete interface. Modifying separate files prevented a textual collision, but it left the semantic dependency behind the caller’s code unchecked.
Optimistic concurrency control (OCC) resolves this tension by letting each agent work privately against a snapshot and validating every publication prerequisite before the shared branch changes (Kung and Robinson 1981). A transaction runs a read phase against private copies, a validation phase that checks whether concurrent commits invalidated anything it read, and a write phase that commits only after validation succeeds; the expected-version check at the tool boundary is that validation applied to a single file. The scheme pays when conflicts are rare, because it trades lock waiting for occasional discarded work. A worker’s read phase, however, spans minutes of model generation and tool execution rather than the brief life of a database transaction, so a failed validation discards real inference spend, and its prerequisites include dependency freshness and acceptance evidence as well as unchanged files. Instead of holding a repository lock while an agent deliberates, the runtime decouples private execution from integration, which exposes parallelism and converts conflicts into the coordination tax of candidate revalidation and occasional discarded work.

↩︎ Conditional updates that commit only while the target still matches its expected version are established in Conditional updates.



Operating multiple agents within a single shared working directory introduces three immediate failure modes. A lost update occurs when two workers inspect the same file, deliberate over multiple inference turns, and serialize their writes back to disk. The later write silently replaces the earlier contribution, leaving the underlying operating system none the wiser because both operations were syntactically valid. A torn dependency read emerges when an agent executes tests while a peer is actively modifying related files, for example by evaluating code after a new interface has landed but before the caller has been updated. The test runner executes against an incoherent intermediate state that no agent ever intended to propose. Finally, tool-lock contention strikes when concurrent build tools or version-control commands collide on local metadata locks, such as Git’s .git/index.lock. One worker crashes on a locked index even when the underlying edits target entirely disjoint directories.



Shared writes pass even odds at five workers, long before a fleet feels large.
These collisions manifest surprisingly early as agent concurrency grows. Suppose a repository contains \(\RepositoryFileCount\) files and each of \(\WorkerCount\) workers modifies \(\WorkerWrittenFileCount\) distinct files, chosen uniformly and independently at random. Worker \(\EarlierWorkerCount+1\) avoids overlapping with all preceding workers only if it selects its \(\WorkerWrittenFileCount\) files exclusively from the \(\RepositoryFileCount-\EarlierWorkerCount \WorkerWrittenFileCount\) files that earlier workers left untouched. The probability that all \(\WorkerCount\) write sets remain pairwise disjoint is therefore
\[
\Pr(\text{no shared write})=\prod_{k=1}^{\WorkerCount-1}\frac{\binom{\RepositoryFileCount-\EarlierWorkerCount \WorkerWrittenFileCount}{\WorkerWrittenFileCount}}{\binom{\RepositoryFileCount}{\WorkerWrittenFileCount}}\approx\exp\left(-\frac{\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\WorkerWrittenFileCount^2}{2\RepositoryFileCount}\right).
\tag{4}\]
Equation 4 is the birthday bound6 generalized to multi-file write sets. Because the exponent scales quadratically with the number of worker pairs rather than linearly with worker count, collision odds mount rapidly. In a hypothetical repository of 1,000 files where each worker touches 10 files, even 2 concurrent workers collide with probability 9.6 percent. At 5 workers, a write collision becomes more likely than not, and scaling to 8 workers drives the collision probability to 94.4 percent. In practice, uniform random access is an illustrative baseline that can understate risk when writes cluster; actual agent modifications heavily cluster around package manifests, central routing tables, and shared configuration files. Rigorous workspace isolation is therefore an architectural prerequisite for multi-agent coordination, rather than a performance tuning knob reserved for massive worker pools.
6 Birthday Bound: The classical birthday problem calculates the number of people required before two share a birthday. The answer, twenty-three people for even odds across 365 days, often surprises newcomers because the number of potential pairs grows quadratically with group size. Systems designers exploit this same relation to size hash tables and cryptographic identifiers. In multi-agent execution, each worker represents an individual and the repository files represent the calendar, with collision probability amplified because each worker samples \(\WorkerWrittenFileCount\) distinct files simultaneously rather than a single day.Providing each worker with an isolated workspace establishes a stable snapshot baseline and an unshared scratchpad for local modifications. When a worker completes its task, the runtime receives an immutable candidate artifact (identified by a cryptographic commit hash) rather than a reference to a mutable filesystem directory.
Systems engineers implement this isolation through two primary mechanisms: linked Git worktrees and copy-on-write filesystems. Linked worktrees allocate dedicated working trees, indices, and HEAD pointers for each agent while sharing underlying object storage in .git/objects. Copy-on-write filesystems provide instant, block-level cloning with zero-copy snapshotting, governed by runtime pooling lifecycles and reset contracts.


↩︎ Copy-on-write provisioning, which copies only what a task writes over a read-only base, is established in Copy-on-write provisioning.
Neither filesystem mechanism provides security on its own. If an agent executes arbitrary shell commands with unrestricted filesystem permissions, it can traverse parent directories, access peer worktrees, or corrupt the shared Git directory. A robust architecture therefore pairs workspace isolation with an external sandbox and a mediated tool gateway. The gateway confines filesystem writes to the assigned worktree, strips integration credentials, and allocates ephemeral ports and temporary directories for test suites. Furthermore, discarding a worktree cleanly recycles local ephemeral state, but it cannot revoke side effects that an external service has already accepted.



When a worker signals completion, the centralized integration service evaluates the returned execution receipt. The service resolves runtime.base_ref and runtime.candidate_ref, verifies cryptographic commit lineage, and independently derives the modified file paths rather than trusting a worker-reported write set. Beyond commit hashes, the service inspects runtime.dependencies_ref, which records the exact source versions, environmental flags, and file reads underpinning the candidate. Reliable dependency tracking requires runtime instrumentation of mediated filesystem calls, lockfiles, and configuration manifests; subjective, model-generated self-reports cannot be trusted for correctness. Furthermore, negative dependencies require careful tracking: an agent’s code generation may depend on the absence of a conflicting file, meaning that recording only positive file reads yields incomplete dependency graphs. Whenever dependency tracking is partial or ambiguous, the integration service treats an empty dependency manifest as unknown rather than disjoint, triggering a fresh revalidation of the candidate against the current branch head.
Let the commit content hashes \(\WorkerBaseCommitHash\), \(\WorkerCandidateCommitHash\), and \(\IntegrationHeadCommitHash\) identify the worker’s base, its returned candidate, and the integration head captured for this attempt. The protocol has four steps, which listing 3 condenses into the control flow of an integration service.

Revalidate dependencies: Compare dependency versions between \(\WorkerBaseCommitHash\) and \(\IntegrationHeadCommitHash\). Pairwise disjoint file sets demonstrate only textual independence; if a referenced interface or schema changed on the main branch, the runtime must revise or regenerate the candidate before attempting integration.
Build the candidate: Construct an immutable integration candidate \(\IntegrationCandidateCommitHash\). If \(\IntegrationHeadCommitHash\) still matches \(\WorkerBaseCommitHash\), the candidate is simply the worker’s own commit \(\WorkerCandidateCommitHash\) (the fast-forward path). If the head advanced, the service stages a private merge commit combining \(\IntegrationHeadCommitHash\) and \(\WorkerCandidateCommitHash\). Should textual or structural conflicts arise, the service may dispatch a bounded reconciliation task to an agent; the resulting merge artifact is treated as a fresh candidate proposal, subject to the full validation pipeline.
Check the exact candidate: Every integration candidate must pass the scope and quality checks mandated by migration_accept_v1 within the protected assessment sandbox of Grader isolation. Under the evidence-scope rule, verification tests executed on the worker’s private branch do not validate the newly synthesized merge candidate. Acceptance criteria must be evaluated directly on the exact commit hash \(\IntegrationCandidateCommitHash\).
Publish with an expected-head update: Advance the target ref if and only if the current branch pointer still equals the captured \(\IntegrationHeadCommitHash\) and all publication guards remain satisfied. These guards verify active grant authorization, unrevoked task status, comprehensive dependency tracking, and fresh acceptance test evidence. In Git, the low-level update-ref command with an expected old object hash guarantees an atomic compare-and-swap. The runtime sequences authorization guards with this atomic ref update to eliminate race conditions between token revocation and publication, while external dependencies are anchored by their action-time version contracts.

If a concurrent writer advances the branch head before the atomic ref update executes, the integration attempt aborts. Rather than blindly retrying the update against the new head, the service loops back to step 1, revalidating all dependencies against the updated state. If the publication command returns an ambiguous network outcome or timeout, the service must query the authoritative repository log before attempting a retry, preventing duplicate commits. Figure 3 assembles the three ingredients: private worktrees over shared repository storage, a staged merge that is textually clean even though the caller relies on the interface as of \(\WorkerBaseCommitHash\), and the four-step gate whose moved-head exit returns to revalidation.



Listing 3: Guarded Integration of a Worker Candidate: The service revalidates dependencies against the captured head, checks the exact candidate, and publishes with an expected-head update under the task’s publication guard.


def integrate(repo, task, receipt, contract, max_attempts):
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        head = repo.read_ref(TARGET)                          # h_head for this attempt
        stale = changed_dependencies(receipt.dependencies_ref, receipt.base_ref, head)
        if stale:
            return request_revision(task, stale, head)        # regenerate, then return
        if head == receipt.base_ref:
            candidate = receipt.candidate_ref                 # fast-forward case
        else:
            candidate = stage_merge(head, receipt.candidate_ref)
            if candidate is None:
                return request_reconciliation(task, head)     # another proposal
        evidence = run_protected_checks(contract, candidate)  # binds this exact candidate
        if not evidence.accepted:
            return reject(task, candidate, evidence)
        with publication_guard(task) as guard:                # cancellation, grants, lineage
            if not guard.eligible:
                return withdrawn(task)
            outcome = repo.update_ref(TARGET, candidate, expected=head)
        if outcome.uncertain:
            return reconcile_publication(task, candidate)     # never blind-retry the effect
        if outcome.applied:
            return published(task, candidate, evidence)
        # head moved: loop back to dependency validation for the new head
    return unresolved(task, reason="integration_attempts_exhausted")









Figure 3: Private Workspaces and Guarded Publication: Linked worktrees (a) give each worker its own files, index, and HEAD while sharing repository storage; the sandbox around each one, not the worktree, scopes its writes. The caller edits files the interface change never touched (b), so the staged merge is textually clean even though the caller relies on the interface as of \(\WorkerBaseCommitHash\). Publication (c) therefore revalidates dependencies at the captured head, checks the exact integration candidate, and advances the target only if the head is unchanged and the publication guard holds. A moved head returns the attempt to validation, and every other exit returns an explicit status.



Table 4 traces the lifecycle of the caller worker’s patch through each phase of the guarded integration protocol.



Table 4: A Clean Merge with a Stale Dependency: Publication requires current dependency support and exact-candidate evidence, even when the workers edit different files.

Repeated invalidations quickly erode the efficiency gains of parallel delegation. If several agents continuously update overlapping dependencies, workers spend more compute discarding stale rollouts and reconciling candidates than generating productive code. Runtimes mitigate this through bounded retries, exponential backoff, and serialized commit queues, transitioning exhausted attempts into explicitly unresolved task states. However, when invalidation rates remain persistently high, the architectural remedy lies in work decomposition rather than concurrency tuning. Structuring the task graph to sequence interface migrations ahead of dependent caller tasks eliminates the cross-worker hazard entirely, achieving higher net throughput with fewer wasted agent turns.



Repository staging isolates and buffers only local repository state. A failed Git integration rolls back local commits, but it cannot undo mutations already executed on shared relational databases, physical test rigs, or external payment gateways. External resources operate under their own conditional-update and ownership semantics.
When managing unmergeable stateful resources (a live database migration lock, a dedicated test bench, or an embedded hardware debugger), the runtime must decide precisely when to enforce mutual exclusion. A pessimistic lease acquires an exclusive, time-bounded grant before an agent begins work, and the coordinator reclaims an expired grant so that a stalled holder cannot keep the resource indefinitely. Conflicting workers block until the lease holder releases the lock or times out, avoiding conflict-driven discarded work while the lease remains valid, but agent concurrency collapses into serialized execution. Conversely, optimistic control maximizes parallel execution by deferring conflict checks until publication. If validation fails, however, the runtime discards the entire execution trajectory, while any external side effects already dispatched to outside systems remain irreversible. This irreversibility governs the architectural division: optimistic concurrency control excels for private, discardable working trees, whereas the non-mergeable exclusive resources considered here require exclusion established at the target resource before issuing commands. Table 5 compares these operational strategies.


↩︎ Leases, the split-brain they permit when a stalled worker outlives its grant, and epoch fencing at the destination resource are established in Operation identity and endpoint contracts.
