Key Takeaways: Delegation must earn and preserve its boundaries

Coordination overhead sets the useful fleet size: Serial execution constraints cap parallel speedup at \(1/\ContentionCoefficient\), while pairwise reconciliation costs cause effective system throughput to fall beyond \(\WorkerCount^*=\sqrt{(1-\ContentionCoefficient)/\CoherencyCoefficient}\). Shrinking serial planning and integration overhead raises the scalability ceiling far more than merely shaving latency off individual handoffs. Empirical profiling across realistic workloads, rather than casual inspection of isolated agent trajectories, must calibrate these parameters.
Task dependencies govern completion makespan: Communication topologies, scheduling precedence, and fault-supervision hierarchies address distinct systems requirements. Once a schedule attains its critical-path bound, further latency reductions require shortening that path; before it does, additional slots or reduced contention may also shorten runtime. Furthermore, any agent endowed with recursive delegation authority requires hard runtime limits on fan-out, nesting depth, and aggregate token reservations.
Delegation handoffs require explicit runtime contracts: A handoff envelope must establish immutable task inputs, granted execution authority, resource budgets, and required evidence before worker execution begins. The returned receipt must strictly isolate ground-truth execution records from the worker’s unverified self-assessment, truncating narrative explanations rather than audit telemetry whenever context limits bind.
Disjoint writes do not guarantee semantic compatibility: Non-overlapping file edits establish only that parallel workers avoided concurrent modification conflicts; they do not prove that combined changes preserve system-wide behavioral invariants. Safe publication requires revalidating dependencies against the latest branch head, testing the integrated candidate in isolation, and advancing branch pointers through conditional atomic updates.
Correlated reviewer errors impose an irreducible accuracy floor: When automated reviewers evaluate an intrinsically challenging artifact, shared model blind spots cause their errors to correlate, preventing majority-voting failure rates from dropping to zero. Beyond this floor, spending additional tokens on homogeneous reviewers yields negligible benefit. Runtimes must instead incorporate independent verification modalities, such as deterministic test suites or formal linters, because peer consensus cannot manufacture authoritative correctness.
Resource obligations outlive parent caller lifecycles: Canceling a parent agent halts the dispatch of new downstream tasks, but it does not automatically terminate remote tool operations, network sockets, or asynchronous child processes already in flight. Each in-flight bound has its own mechanism. Credit windows bound the volume of queued work and support mean-residence sizing, attenuated grants and atomic reservations bound authority and spend, and the settlement record, not cancellation or credit release, keeps every admitted effect owned until its outcome and charges settle.
Multi-agent execution must outperform a capable single-agent baseline: A meaningful evaluation benchmarks multi-agent architectures against an equally optimized single-agent controller provisioned with identical parallel tool access, context allowances, and wall-clock budgets. System accounting must price every failed attempt, speculative invocation, and rollback, justifying multi-agent coordination only when the resulting increase in task success or latency reduction offsets its marginal token overhead.



The coordination tax (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}\)) manifests in the serialized handoffs, validation barriers, and residual dependencies that remain after decomposing a task. Invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) mandates that these architectural boundaries maintain strict external validation and effect gating, ensuring that peer consensus among models is never mistaken for authoritative execution rights. Finally, trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\)) extends from one trajectory to a tree of them. Every child is a separately owned trajectory whose derived grants only narrow, whose consumable allowance is reserved against its ancestors’ shared allowance, and whose unsettled side effects remain accounted for by the runtime after its parent stops.

title: 17 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
The question of when dividing computational work yields a net speedup is older than autonomous software agents. Gene Amdahl’s 1967 argument established that serial execution fractions strictly cap the speedup achievable by adding processors (Amdahl 1967). Two years later, Ronald Graham showed that while greedy list scheduling lands close to the theoretical dependency bound, adding parallel resources can paradoxically increase total completion time (Graham 1969). Neil Gunther later unified these dynamics in the universal scalability law, introducing a pairwise coherency penalty to explain how crosstalk and contention turn throughput saturation into outright performance collapse (Gunther 2008). Across successive computing generations, systems architects repeatedly encountered the same hard reality: coordination overhead and coherency penalties, rather than the raw supply of workers, dictate practical scale.

Amdahl, Gene M. 1967. “Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities.” Proceedings of the April 18-20, 1967, Spring Joint Computer Conference on - AFIPS ’67 (Spring), AFIPS ’67 (spring), 483–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1465482.1465560.

Erman, Lee D., Frederick Hayes-Roth, Victor R. Lesser, and D. Raj Reddy. 1980. “The Hearsay-II Speech-Understanding System: Integrating Knowledge to Resolve Uncertainty.” ACM Computing Surveys 12 (2): 213–53. https://doi.org/10.1145/356810.356816.

Hewitt, Carl, Peter Bishop, and Richard Steiger. 1973. “A Universal Modular ACTOR Formalism for Artificial Intelligence.” Proceedings of the 3rd International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI), 235–45.
Distributed artificial intelligence confronted the handoff problem in the 1970s. The Hearsay-II speech-understanding system coordinated independent, opportunistic knowledge sources through a shared blackboard (Erman et al. 1980). Carl Hewitt’s actor model abandoned shared memory entirely, giving each autonomous agent private local state and routing interactions through addressed messages (Hewitt et al. 1973). Reid Smith formalized structured delegation in the Contract Net Protocol, turning task announcement, bidding, and award into an explicit, typed exchange between a manager and prospective contractors (Smith 1980).
Over the following decades, classical distributed systems research supplied the precise operational controls that multi-agent architectures require today. Kung and Robinson introduced optimistic concurrency control, permitting workers to execute tentatively against private workspace copies and validate isolation before committing (Kung and Robinson 1981). Birrell and Nelson established typed remote procedure calls with explicit failure semantics, replacing unstructured message passing with formal client-server contracts (Birrell and Nelson 1984). Gray and Cheriton solved distributed state synchronization and lock management through time-bounded leases (Gray and Cheriton 1989). Joe Armstrong formalized supervision trees within Erlang, demonstrating how structured hierarchies and crash-only semantics allow runtimes to restart failed processes from clean, known states (Armstrong 2003). Finally, object-capability systems eliminated ambient authority by embedding access rights directly into object references rather than relying on global identity checks (Dennis and Van Horn 1966; Hardy 1988), an approach later extended through cryptographically attenuable tokens with chained caveats (Birgisson et al. 2014).

Kung, H. T., and John T. Robinson. 1981. “On Optimistic Methods for Concurrency Control.” ACM Transactions on Database Systems 6 (2): 213–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/319566.319567.

Birrell, Andrew D., and Bruce Jay Nelson. 1984. “Implementing Remote Procedure Calls.” ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 2 (1): 39–59. https://doi.org/10.1145/2080.357392.

Gray, Cary G., and David R. Cheriton. 1989. “Leases: An Efficient Fault-Tolerant Mechanism for Distributed File Cache Consistency.” Proceedings of the Twelfth ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP), 202–10. https://doi.org/10.1145/74850.74870.

Dennis, Jack B., and Earl C. Van Horn. 1966. “Programming Semantics for Multiprogrammed Computations.” Communications of the ACM 9 (3): 143–55. https://doi.org/10.1145/365230.365252.

Hardy, Norm. 1988. “The Confused Deputy: (Or Why Capabilities Might Have Been Invented).” ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 22 (4): 36–38. https://doi.org/10.1145/60609.60611.

Birgisson, Arnór, Joseph G. Politz, Úlfar Erlingsson, Ankur Taly, Michael Vrable, and Mark S. Miller. 2014. “Macaroons: Cookies with Contextual Caveats for Decentralized Authorization in the Cloud.” Proceedings of the Network and Distributed System Security Symposium (NDSS).

Condorcet, Marquis de. 1785. Essai Sur l’application de l’analyse à La Probabilité Des décisions Rendues à La Pluralité Des Voix. Imprimerie Royale.

Neumann, John von. 1956. “Probabilistic Logics and the Synthesis of Reliable Organisms from Unreliable Components.” In Automata Studies, edited by Claude E. Shannon and John McCarthy, vol. 34. Annals of Mathematics Studies. Princeton University Press. https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400882618-003.

Eckhardt, Dave E., and Larry D. Lee. 1985. “A Theoretical Basis for the Analysis of Multiversion Software Subject to Coincident Errors.” IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering SE-11 (12): 1511–17. https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.1985.231895.
Redundancy followed a parallel trajectory of high theoretical promises followed by sobering empirical corrections. The Condorcet jury theorem (Condorcet, Marquis de 1785) and John von Neumann’s multiplexed majority organs (Neumann 1956) demonstrated that aggregating independent votes can synthesize near-perfect reliability from noisy components. Leslie Lamport, Robert Shostak, and Marshall Pease proved the rigorous mathematical bounds of Byzantine fault tolerance, establishing that agreement in the unsigned-message protocol model survives arbitrary, even malicious, faults only while fewer than one third of participants are faulty (Lamport et al. 1982). However, the independence premise behind probabilistic majority-voting guarantees collapsed when applied to software. John Knight and Nancy Leveson demonstrated experimentally that independently written programs fail coincidentally on the same edge cases far more often than chance predicts (Knight and Leveson 1986). Dave Eckhardt and Larry Lee provided the analytical explanation: complex problem domains harbor intrinsically difficult input regions that induce correlated failures across diverse implementations (Eckhardt and Lee 1985).
Modern language-model architectures have revived every one of these paradigms simultaneously. Self-consistency uses majority voting across sampled reasoning paths (Wang et al. 2023), multi-agent debate structures iterative argumentation across model instances (Du et al. 2023), and conversational frameworks coordinate role-playing agents over structured communication graphs (Wu et al. 2023). In production, orchestrator-worker patterns have delivered capability gains on breadth-first research tasks, and their builders report roughly 15× the token consumption of a chat interaction to get them (Hadfield et al. 2025). Systematic empirical analyses of multi-agent failures reveal that the field has re-encountered classical distributed failure modes: ill-defined task boundaries, uncoordinated handoffs, and verification bottlenecks that silently propagate errors rather than catching them (Cemri et al. 2025).

Wang, Xuezhi, Jason Wei, Dale Schuurmans, Quoc Le, Ed Chi, Sharan Narang, Aakanksha Chowdhery, and Denny Zhou. 2023. “Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models.” The Eleventh International Conference on Learning Representations.

Du, Yilun, Shuang Li, Antonio Torralba, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, and Igor Mordatch. 2023. “Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models Through Multiagent Debate.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2305.14325.

Wu, Qingyun, Gagan Bansal, Jieyu Zhang, Yiran Wu, Beibin Li, Erkang Zhu, Biyi Gao, et al. 2023. AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation.

Hadfield, Jeremy, Barry Zhang, Kenneth Lien, Florian Scholz, Jeremy Fox, and Daniel Ford. 2025. How We Built Our Multi-Agent Research System. Anthropic Engineering Blog.

The Contract Net Protocol (Smith 1980). The foundational text on structured delegation. Smith frames task distribution as a typed, negotiated protocol, showing that the essential elements of modern task envelopes, from capability announcements to formal awards, were established long before language models existed.
An Experimental Evaluation of the Assumption of Independence in Multiversion Programming (Knight and Leveson 1986). The landmark controlled experiment that disproved the assumption of independent software failures. This paper provides the standard methodological blueprint for evaluating whether an ensemble of redundant agent reviewers yields genuine reliability gains or merely inflates inference cost.
Making Reliable Distributed Systems in the Presence of Software Errors (Armstrong 2003). Armstrong’s doctoral dissertation detailing the architecture of Erlang. It articulates the operational rationale for supervision trees, fail-stop process isolation, and restart strategies, mapping directly to how orchestrators should manage the lifecycles and blast radiuses of child agent trajectories.
A General Theory of Computational Scalability Based on Rational Functions (Gunther 2008). Gunther derives the universal scalability law directly from queueing models. The derivation clarifies the physical distinction between contention and coherency, explaining why serial bottlenecks and cross-agent communication demand fundamentally different architectural fixes.
Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (Cemri et al. 2025). An extensive empirical taxonomy analyzing real-world multi-agent failure traces. It serves as an indispensable field catalog of the specification gaps, uncoordinated handoffs, and verification failures that production runtime environments must actively prevent.


Smith, Reid G. 1980. “The Contract Net Protocol: High-Level Communication and Distributed Problem Solving in a Distributed Processor.” IEEE Transactions on Computers C-29 (12): 1104–13.

Gunther, Neil J. 2008. “A General Theory of Computational Scalability Based on Rational Functions.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:0808.1431.

Cemri, Mert, Melissa Z. Pan, Shuyi Yang, Lakshya A. Agrawal, Bhavya Chopra, Rishabh Tiwari, Kurt Keutzer, et al. 2025. Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?

title: 17 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
Every given below is a hypothetical problem input, not a measurement of a real system. Each problem ends in a design decision, and the calculation exists to justify it.

Choosing the lever in a worker-count screen (Basic). A fixed work partition has divisible fraction \(\ParallelFraction=0.9\) and normalized overhead \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)=\WorkerOverheadSlope(\WorkerCount-1)\) with \(\WorkerOverheadSlope=0.01\). The resource ceiling permits at most \(20\) workers, and each added worker adds roughly the same token spend.

Using equation 1, compute the normalized elapsed time at \(\WorkerCount=4\), \(8\), and \(16\), the integer count that minimizes it, and the speedup at that count. Compare the count with \(\sqrt{\ParallelFraction/\WorkerOverheadSlope}\).
Two proposals compete for the same engineering effort: halving the per-worker overhead to \(\WorkerOverheadSlope=0.005\), or halving the serial work so that \(\ParallelFraction=0.95\). Compute the best integer count and its speedup under each proposal.
Decide which proposal to fund once worker spend is counted, and state which proposal alone can ever deliver a speedup above \(10\times\).

Hot files in a shared workspace (Basic). A repository holds \(\RepositoryFileCount=5{,}000\) files, and each worker writes \(\WorkerWrittenFileCount=20\) of them, chosen uniformly and independently.

Using equation 4, compute the probability of at least one shared write for \(\WorkerCount=2\) and \(\WorkerCount=4\) workers, both exactly and by the exponential approximation. Find the smallest fleet for which a shared write is more likely than not.
Each worker also edits one shared dependency manifest with probability \(0.3\), independently of its other writes. For four workers, compute the probability that at least two edit the manifest, and the probability of any shared write at all.
A colleague proposes a single shared working directory for four workers because “collisions are under 40 percent.” Decide, and name the two hazards of section 17.5 that remain even when no two workers write the same file.

Sizing a credit window for staleness (Basic). A producer emits candidate items at \(\ArrivalRate=2\) items per second. A consumer model writes a \(400\)-token critique of each item at \(50\) output tokens per second, and each returned record occupies at most \(\DataVolume=8{,}192\) bytes. An item is useful only if the consumer begins serving it within \(60\) s of admission. For initial sizing, screen a saturated credit window by requiring its modeled mean residence to be no greater than this interval; assume negligible transport time and full utilization at the stated service rate.

Compute the consumer’s service rate \(\ServiceRate\), the backlog of an unbounded queue after five minutes, and the wait of the newest item behind that backlog.
Using the full-window mean residence \(\CreditWindowCapacity/\ServiceRate\), find the largest integer window \(\CreditWindowCapacity\) that passes this sizing screen and its payload bound \(\CreditWindowCapacity\DataVolume\). Does passing the screen establish that every item begins service before its freshness deadline?
Find the minimum number of identical consumers needed to keep pace with the producer and the largest shared window that passes the same mean-residence screen at their aggregate service rate. State how admission timestamps and a freshness check before service should handle an item that has waited too long. Explain why cancellation and settlement traffic must not draw on these data credits.

A fourth slot or a shorter vertex (Intermediate). A migration plan has a shared specification \(\DependencyGraphVertex_1\) (\(30\) s); four module refactors \(\DependencyGraphVertex_2\) through \(\DependencyGraphVertex_5\) (\(60\), \(60\), \(90\), and \(40\) s), each depending only on \(\DependencyGraphVertex_1\); and an integration check \(\DependencyGraphVertex_6\) (\(50\) s) depending on all four refactors. Each vertex occupies one interchangeable slot, with no other delays.

Compute \(\AggregateSlotWork\) and \(\CriticalPathDuration\) from equation 2, and the lower bound of equation 3 for \(\WorkerCount=2\), \(3\), and \(4\) slots.
By assigning the four refactors to slots, find the shortest achievable makespan for each \(\WorkerCount\). Explain why the bound is not attained at \(\WorkerCount=2\).
The team currently runs \(\WorkerCount=3\) and can afford either a fourth slot or engineering that shortens \(\DependencyGraphVertex_4\) to \(60\) s. Decide, and state what shortening \(\DependencyGraphVertex_4\) buys once the fourth slot exists.

Pricing deadline coverage (Intermediate). Under matched resource ceilings, a single controller spends an expected \(\$0.40\) per attempt with \(\AcceptanceProbability=0.60\), and \(40\) of every \(100\) attempts are accepted by the deadline. A delegated configuration spends \(\$0.90\) per attempt with \(\AcceptanceProbability=0.80\), and \(72\) of every \(100\) attempts are accepted by the deadline. Spend includes failed attempts and canceled branches, and cost is proportional to tokens.

Compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) for both configurations from equation 1.2, and their ratio.
Find the token multiple \(\DelegationTokenMultiple\), the delegated acceptance that would restore break-even on \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\), and the largest single-controller acceptance for which break-even is possible at all.
Per \(100\) attempts, compute the marginal cost of each additional on-time acceptance. One service values an on-time accepted migration at \(\$1\), another at \(\$5\). Decide which configuration each should run.

Hedged lookups for the support agent (Intermediate, second-lighthouse transfer). The support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)) answers a refund-eligibility question by dispatching three read-only lookups in parallel: the customer record, the order history, and the governing policy clause. All three are required. Each lookup attempt independently returns an admissible result within \(1\) s with probability \(0.70\) and within \(2\) s with probability \(0.95\). The service target is that at least \(95\) percent of answers have all three results within \(2\) s. Assume \(1{,}000\) sessions dispatch their three initial lookups simultaneously. The lookup pool has \(4{,}000\) slots, and each launched attempt retains its reservation until the \(2\) s observation cutoff, even if its result arrives earlier. An attempt that has not returned an admissible result remains outstanding until that cutoff. Treat the stated completion probabilities as unchanged by load when calculating a policy without admission blocking.

Compute the probability that all three results arrive within \(2\) s without hedging. Explain why the \(\RequiredResultCount\)-of-\(\WorkerCount\) stopping rule of section 17.7 does not rescue this fan-out.
Compare two hedging policies: duplicating every lookup at dispatch, and starting a replacement only for a lookup still outstanding at \(1\) s, which must then itself return within the remaining \(1\) s. Assuming every proposed hedge is admitted, compute the per-lookup and all-three probabilities within \(2\) s. For each policy, compute both expected slot demand and the largest possible slot demand before the cutoff.
Decide whether either calculation establishes that the policy meets the deadline target within the hard slot limit. Propose an admission rule for delayed hedges, and explain why deadline acceptance must be evaluated again when the rule can deny replacements. Contrast the binding constraint here with the coherency limit on the repair agent’s migration, and state what must hold before the same hedging could be applied to issuing the refund itself.

Bounding a remediation delegation tree (Intermediate, second-lighthouse transfer). The remediation agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) is restoring a degraded checkout service. Its root grant permits reading metrics and logs for checkout and scaling the checkout deployment between \(4\) and \(12\) replicas; it permits no configuration writes. The root’s remaining allowance is \(\$50\), of which \(\$5\) is a protected finalization reserve and \(\$6\) is already reserved for the root’s own outstanding work. The model proposes three children, each with a \(\$20\) allowance, “less than the parent’s remaining \(\$50\)”: a metrics worker that reads checkout metrics, a log worker that reads logs for checkout and payments, and a capacity worker that scales checkout between \(4\) and \(16\) replicas.

State which proposed grants violate \(\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ChildCapabilityGrant)\subseteq\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ParentCapabilityGrant)\) and how to narrow them. Compute the worst-case liability if each child’s allowance is copied from the parent’s balance, and which children atomic reservation admits if they are dispatched in the order listed. Find the largest equal allowance that admits all three. The capacity worker then proposes two scale workers at \(\$8\) each; state which the runtime admits and repair the split.
An operator takes over and the runtime cancels the root at \(\TimeInstant=0\). Both scale workers are active, and each submits at most one scale step every \(5\) s to a remote gateway. Under a cached-authorization policy the gateway trusts a lineage record for up to \(18\) s, with a \(2\) s clock-skew allowance. Under a strict policy it looks up the current status and generation of each of the \(3\) nodes in a scale worker’s lineage at \(4\) ms per lookup. Compute the stale-policy window, the most scale steps it can admit after cancellation, and the strict policy’s added latency as a fraction of the step interval. Choose a policy for scale steps and one for metric reads, and state what the strict policy costs if the authoritative store is unreachable for \(30\) s.
Under the policy chosen in part (b), the ledger at cancellation shows: the metrics worker settled \(\$4\) and stopped; the log worker settled \(\$9\), and a log-export job it started before cancellation is still unresolved with a bounded liability of \(\$3\); the first scale worker settled \(\$2\) and was confirmed terminated; the second scale worker settled nothing, and a node-pool scale-up it started before cancellation has an unknown outcome with a bounded liability of \(\$5\); the root’s own work settled \(\$4\). Compute the allowance the runtime may release now, the amount still held, and the release a “cancellation refunds all reservations” rule would claim. A follow-up remediation task needs a \(\$20\) allowance. Decide whether to admit it now, and state who owns the two open operations and what that owner must retain.

Buying evidence past a correlated floor (Advanced). Reviewers each falsely approve a known-invalid candidate with marginal probability \(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability=0.10\), and their errors follow the beta mixture of section 17.6 with \(\CorrelationCoefficient=0.30\). The release rule requires that an invalid candidate be approved with probability at most \(0.01\). A reviewer call costs \(\$0.20\). A protected regression test costs \(\$0.50\) and passes an invalid candidate with probability \(0.05\), assumed independent of the candidate’s reviewer propensity \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\).

Compute the beta parameters \(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape\) and \(\PropensityPriorRejectionShape\), and the majority false-approval probability for three reviewers under independent errors and under the mixture.
Compute the mixture’s majority false approval for seven reviewers and the floor \(\Pr(\FalseApprovalPropensity>1/2)\), numerically. Decide whether any number of reviewers of this kind can meet the release rule.
Price two designs per candidate: seven reviewers under majority vote, and three reviewers plus the protected test, with approval requiring both a reviewer majority and a passing test. Compute each design’s false-approval probability and choose one.
Critique the assumption that the test is independent of \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\). Name a mechanism from this chapter that would correlate the test with the reviewers, and state the measurement that must precede release.

Fitting the scalability law before choosing a fan-out (Advanced, critique and redesign). Trials of a repair-migration partition under matched resources measure relative capacity \(\text{Speedup}(2)=1.835\) and \(\text{Speedup}(4)=2.878\). The serial reference takes \(40\) minutes, and the service requires completion within \(11\) minutes. The expected cost of an attempt grows with worker count as \(\$1.00+\$0.30(\WorkerCount-1)\), and acceptance does not change with \(\WorkerCount\).

Rearrange equation 5 so that it is linear in \(\ContentionCoefficient\) and \(\CoherencyCoefficient\), fit both coefficients from the two measurements, and compute \(\WorkerCount^*\) from equation 6, the best integer count and its capacity, and the smallest count that runs slower than one worker.
A trial at \(\WorkerCount=8\) measures \(2.90\). Compare it with the fitted prediction, and state what the gap implies about using the fit outside the measured range.
The team proposes deploying the best integer count from part (a). Critique the proposal against the deadline. For this calculation, suppose two proposed redesigns have the following responses: sharding the integration queue halves \(\ContentionCoefficient\), and repartitioning the migration so interface changes land before caller work begins halves \(\CoherencyCoefficient\). For each, find the smallest worker count that meets the deadline, if any, and its cost per attempt, and recommend a design under these assumptions. State what trace or matched intervention evidence would establish the assumed coefficient responses in a deployment.



What’s Next: From coordination to costWhen is the time saved by delegation worth its additional resource use? This chapter answered for one stated workload, with a ledger that charged failed attempts and canceled branches to the accepted tasks they served. That ledger is a special case of a question every deployment faces, for one agent or many. The next chapter opens with the repair team offered a model whose tokens cost a tenth as much and asks why the switch can still raise the price of every repair that ships. Answering it means counting what each accepted task costs across all its attempts, how context reuse, retries, and model choice change that cost, and how concurrent trajectories compete for capacity. The same account then prices delegation itself, without dropping the reservations and unresolved obligations established here.

title: 15 Trajectory Fine-Tuning
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can training on a useful recovery record teach the model to repeat the mistake instead of the correction?
While prompt engineering and runtime guardrails guide an off-the-shelf model, fine-tuning modifies the neural network weights directly, embedding specialized decision policies and tool calling conventions into model parameters. However, training on multi-turn trajectories requires strict separation between agent proposals and external environment observations: for trajectory imitation, loss applies only to selected policy responses, while environment feedback remains conditioning context. Naive fine-tuning can teach a policy to hallucinate its own tool responses or overfit to static workspace layouts, degrading general reasoning and error recovery. Systems engineering governs how datasets are partitioned, how loss masks are applied, and how updated checkpoints are validated against regression suites before deployment. An update is worth releasing only when closed-loop task acceptance improves under the same runtime that still bounds every proposal the model makes, however far its training loss has fallen.

Learning Objectives

Assign agent behavior to weights, context, or runtime, and decide when a failure warrants a weight change
Construct model inputs that preserve intended conditioning and price per-invocation serialization in training tokens
Map admitted response spans to causal token targets, observation masks, and termination policy
Compare loss weighting and construct batches without unintended cross-example dependencies
Calculate imitation regret bounds on reference and learner states to decide when on-policy labeling pays
Calculate preference margins and gradient weights, and distinguish what a comparison measures from task acceptance
Select behavior sources and parameter artifacts using explicit resource and version accounting
Evaluate a versioned policy for release on closed-loop acceptance, cost per accepted task, and schema transfer, while preserving runtime enforcement









Fine-tuning reshapes each model call but leaves every exposure to the runtime.
Consider a recovery demonstration admitted by the curation pipeline for the repair agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)) into repair_demonstrations_v1. During the recorded session, the agent generated a malformed edit proposal that the runtime validator refused prior to tool dispatch. In response to the failure notification, the model inspected the tool schema, generated a corrected edit, and produced candidate patch ws_r20. From this multi-turn trajectory, the target-selection policy recovery_targets_v1 marks three assistant turns as supervised targets: the schema inspection request (e3), the corrected edit (e4), and the scoped final summary (e6). The malformed proposal (e2) and the runtime’s refusal remain in the input history as conditioning context. The member that entered the corpus is the redacted view trace_r19_01_redacted_v1, and the corpus manifest binds it to those role assignments, its lineage, and its split membership.
An admitted record is not yet in a form a training loop can safely ingest. The raw event log is an interleaved transcript of heterogeneous events, recording model generations, runtime observations, and tool responses in the exact sequence they occurred. If a data loader treats every assistant message as a supervised target, it computes loss on the malformed edit proposal alongside the correction, directly reinforcing the initial mistake. If the training pipeline computes loss across all sequence tokens indiscriminately, the model expends parameter capacity predicting deterministic environment replies, such as compiler diagnostics or file directory listings, that the model will never emit during inference. If the batching pipeline packs multiple trajectories into a shared context window without attention masking, self-attention heads attend across sample boundaries, leaking private workspace contents into unrelated training examples. Standard cross-entropy loss fails silently under each of these conditions. The empirical loss decreases steadily as the optimizer fits the data, concealing severe behavioral corruption from offline training metrics. While curation contracts determine which actions demonstrate desirable behavior and evaluation contracts measure the deployed agent, neither specifies how to convert a multi-turn execution trace into isolated, causal gradient updates.
The path from an admitted record to an evaluated policy update begins with a question curation leaves open, namely which parts of the repair behavior belong in weights at all (section 15.2). The answer fixes what the data pipeline must protect. Serialization reconstructs each model input exactly as the agent received it (section 15.3), loss masking places the gradient on the selected responses and nowhere else (section 15.4), and batching shares buffers without letting examples read one another or skew one another’s weight (section 15.5). Masking and batching guard directly against the three silent failures above, and serialization guards the premise both rely on, that each prefix is the one the model actually saw.
A faithful loader still trains on recorded prefixes, and the deployed policy acts on prefixes its own choices produce. Exposure bias prices that gap over the horizon and decides when labeling the learner’s own states pays (section 15.6), and schema robustness asks the same question of the tool interfaces the policy is shown (section 15.7). The remaining sections vary the update itself along three independent choices: the objective, where preference optimization contrasts valid alternatives that imitation cannot rank (section 15.8); the behavior source, where distillation moves a costlier configuration’s behavior into a cheaper one (section 15.9); and the parameter artifact, where adapters change what a run must store (section 15.10). Closed-loop evaluation decides whether any of them earned a release (section 15.11), and a training manifest for the repair policy assembles the whole chain (section 15.12).



Modifying model weights is an expensive, high-blast-radius intervention reserved for specific failure modes. The intervention ladder orders changes by cost and reversibility, so engineers consider cheaper prompt, schema, and runtime mitigations before committing compute to parameter updates, while diagnostic evidence can justify a direct weight update. Supervised fine-tuning can address systematic behavioral defects rooted in the policy itself rather than omitted instructions or missing runtime constraints. The principle of verified trajectory post-training (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training}\)) requires curation to relate the recorded evidence to a declared learning use and distinguish admissible targets from contextual or rejected actions. While this ordering serves as a defensive default justified by operational cost and blast radius, section 15.9 examines the complementary scenario where fine-tuning proves more economical than paying the recurring token latency and cost of carrying lengthy guidance in every prompt.


↩︎ The intervention ladder, which orders context, schema, runtime, and parameter interventions by cost and reversibility, is established in The intervention ladder.
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) adjusts trainable model parameters to maximize the conditional likelihood of selected target tokens given their causal prefix context. When processing an admitted trajectory record such as trace_r19_01_redacted_v1, the training loop must implement the specific recovery sequence defined in recovery_targets_v1 rather than indiscriminately computing loss over every recorded token. The model must observe the historical context and tool outputs that justify a chosen action, yet the data pipeline must strictly censor subsequent execution steps that would prematurely reveal future observations or solutions. Trajectory fine-tuning therefore inherits two distinct data contracts: a target-selection contract that designates which tokens contribute to the loss gradient, and a conditioning contract that governs what causal history the model observes when generating those tokens.
This distinction defines what it means for an agent to learn improved behavior rather than overfit an idiosyncratic run. In an error-recovery trajectory, the true behavioral goal is teaching the model to inspect an updated schema after encountering a refusal, issue a properly formed corrective call, and interpret what the runtime verification check establishes. Merely memorizing the file paths of a specific test fixture or predicting hard-coded test outputs minimizes training loss without acquiring generalizable recovery skills. Evaluating whether the updated policy transfers these procedural habits to unfamiliar environments and novel tasks is precisely what section 15.11 measures.


Every response generated by an agent emerges from two inputs: the model’s static weights and the dynamic context window assembled for that invocation. Because fine-tuning updates only the weights, system architects must divide agent capabilities into three architectural homes, summarized in table 1:

Procedure represents behavior that remains stable across tasks and evolves slowly, such as inspecting diagnostic output before modifying source code or auditing unresolved issues before reporting task completion. Procedure is what model weights can reliably internalize.
Contracts represent the dynamic operational facts that vary across deployments, user sessions, and individual execution turns, such as API tool definitions, schema requirements, environment parameters, and granted permissions. Contracts belong strictly in the prompt context; a model that has memorized an earlier schema will continue emitting obsolete arguments when an interface changes.
Enforcement represents the critical invariants that must hold even when the model generates incorrect or adversarial proposals, such as schema validation, authorization checks, sandbox containment, and execution timeouts. Enforcement must reside in the deterministic runtime harness under invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)).




Table 1: Responsibilities of Weights, Context, and Runtime: Weights hold procedure, context holds the current contract, and the runtime enforces that contract whatever the model proposes.










Home
Intended responsibility
Consequence for fine-tuning




Weights
Learned procedures and response tendencies, including tool selection and recovery behavior
Update the proposal distribution, then measure whether the changed behavior helps under the declared task conditions


Context
Current task facts, tool schemas, observations, and represented scope
Supply the information the policy needs now; do not rely on memorized versions as the authority for current facts or permissions


Runtime
Validation, authorization, containment, resource controls, and evidence collection
Preserve enforcement independently of the learned policy; a model’s predicted result is not an observed external effect






Relying on parameters to store interface contracts creates immediate operational brittleness. When a tool interface adds a required parameter or alters its return structure, a model that relies on memorized signatures will continue generating obsolete calls. Similarly, a revoked authorization remains revoked regardless of how frequently the action appeared in successful training demonstrations. Fine-tuning cannot replace dynamic contracts; what it can teach is the procedural discipline of consulting and adhering to whichever contract the context window specifies.
This architectural boundary disproves the naive view that fine-tuning simply moves the prompt into the weights. Only the procedural components of a prompt (structured reasoning guidelines, diagnostic checklists, or few-shot error recovery examples) can be absorbed into the parameters, saving substantial token overhead on every turn (section 15.9). The contractual components must remain in the prompt context, because omitting them forces the model to guess the operational facts of the current execution environment. Furthermore, the deterministic checks that enforce authorization and boundary invariants cannot reside in either prompts or weights, because probabilistic token distributions cannot guarantee invariant execution.
Fine-tuning alters the policy’s proposal distribution: which tools it requests, how thoroughly it investigates diagnostic evidence, and which execution paths it explores. These behavioral shifts directly influence task success rates, end-to-end latency, and token consumption. Nevertheless, every proposed action executes entirely within the execution horizons, state machines, and authority boundaries established by the runtime harness. This separation is the proposal boundary. Training reshapes what the policy proposes, while the runtime decides which actions are permitted to execute. This principle governs every adaptation strategy in this chapter, culminating in the release verification criteria.



Designing an adaptation pipeline requires making three orthogonal decisions:

Training Objective: The loss formulation that defines the learning signal. Supervised imitation learning maximizes the likelihood of curated target demonstrations, whereas preference learning techniques such as direct preference optimization (section 15.8) optimize policy weights by contrasting preferred trajectories against dispreferred alternatives under an explicit ranking criterion.
Behavior Source: The origin of the demonstrations and environmental conditioning. Traces may be harvested from instrumented production systems and filtered through offline verification, generated by a teacher configuration with privileged context or an expanded search budget (section 15.9), labeled on the states the learner itself reaches, or synthesized by injecting faults the recordings never contained (section 15.6.2).
Parameter Artifact: The physical representation of the updated weights. Teams can fine-tune all model parameters directly or train modular adapter matrices, such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules, that attach to a frozen base checkpoint (section 15.10).

Because these three design dimensions are orthogonal, they combine modularly: a deployment might train a lightweight parameter adapter using a direct preference objective derived from synthetic teacher demonstrations.
Regardless of which combination an architecture adopts, the training process depends fundamentally on how trajectory records are converted into model inputs. Serialization determines tokenization and visibility windows, loss masking isolates the precise prediction targets, and batching schedules balance gradient variance across variable-length interaction turns. When deployed, the trained artifact will inevitably encounter unseen environmental states and revised tool schemas, requiring empirical validation before release. Constructing the prefix input and conditioning window for each targeted response constitutes the initial systems hurdle.




Consider the repair demonstration admitted during curation: it contains a malformed edit proposal, a runtime refusal, a schema inspection, and a corrected edit. A training loader that strips out the refusal fundamentally alters the problem the subsequent correction answered. Similarly, a loader that places a later passing test check before the edit leaks future evidence that the model never possessed when proposing the patch. While curation identifies which model completions are worthy of reinforcement, serialization must reconstruct the exact prompt and observation history that elicited them. This includes preserving any runtime redactions, such as synthetic placeholders substituted for private file paths, so the training example faithfully reflects the environment the model actually encountered.


Runtime event logs record system state transitions, but an event log alone does not guarantee what was present in a model’s context window. System prompts evolve, tool schemas update dynamically, and intermediate messages are often summarized or truncated to fit token budgets. To reconstruct inputs accurately, the training pipeline relies on delivered-input manifests. These manifests identify the exact messages, tool definitions, summaries, and bounded observations dispatched to the model, along with their contents and schema versions. The manifest provides the authoritative record that a specific payload entered an invocation, preventing accidental data leakage or historical revisionism.


↩︎ The delivered-input manifest that records the exact payload sent to the model, rather than mutable paths or references, is established in The log event schema.
When constructing an example that demands historical fidelity, serialize the selected invocation directly from this recorded manifest. The example must preserve the observation exactly as the agent saw it, including partial buffers, truncated outputs, or execution errors, rather than substituting a clean or complete result obtained later in the run. Conversely, when intentionally transforming an example, apply the reviewed transformation systematically to both the prompt and the associated response, retain parent trace references, and recheck schema compatibility. Shortening prompts for context distillation (section 15.9) is one such transformation.
Table 2 outlines how curated responses map to their valid conditioning context in the running repair demonstration. While the table highlights the core causal dependencies, the fully rendered training example incorporates the entire context available at that turn, including system instructions and active tool definitions.



Table 2: Inputs and Selected Responses in the Repair Demonstration: Each row pairs a reviewed response with evidence available to condition it.










Selected response
Relevant conditioning evidence
Response content selected by curation




e3
Earlier delivered task context and the malformed e2 proposal with its pre-dispatch refusal
Request to inspect the available schema


e4
The corresponding returned schema and the retained context supporting the edit
Corrected edit with its version condition


e6
The candidate-specific check summary delivered at e5 and retained evidence for the report’s scope
Final report of the supported result and limitations






Notice the causal boundaries across these turns. The refusal at e2 demonstrates that runtime validation caught the malformed proposal before dispatch; no tool executed on the host. The check summary at e5 arrived only after the agent issued the corrected edit, so it can condition the final report at e6, but cannot appear in the context for e4. Similarly, selecting the schema inspection at e3 isolates the model’s query tokens for training while treating the returned schema as external observation. Maintaining these explicit associations ensures that subsequent loss masking isolates model decisions from environment observations.



Before training begins, structured message objects (system instructions, user prompts, assistant thoughts, tool calls, and environment returns) must be serialized into the token sequence expected by the target model. Chat templates differ substantially across model architectures. Even checkpoints derived from the same base model often disagree on how to format tool schemas, delimit parallel calls, or signal message boundaries. A serialized dataset artifact must therefore record the tokenizer version, template configuration, tool-formatting schema, and response-boundary policy alongside the token arrays. The true model input consists of the message sequence paired with this concrete rendering configuration.
In schematic form, a multi-turn tool-calling example follows the structure shown below. The delimiter strings are illustrative placeholders, as each model family defines its own special tokens. Here, the system segment defines the task contract and tool definitions, the assistant segment emits an optional reasoning trace followed by two parallel tool calls with unique identifiers, and each tool segment returns an observation matched to its corresponding call identifier.
<|system|> task contract; schemas for read_file(target_uri), run_tests(target) <|end|>
<|user|> Fix the connection-pool leak in src/pool.py <|end|>
<|assistant|> <|reasoning|> Reproduce the failure, then read the module. <|end_reasoning|>
  <|call id=c1|> {"name": "read_file", "arguments": {"target_uri": "src/pool.py"}} <|end_call|>
  <|call id=c2|> {"name": "run_tests", "arguments": {"target": "tests/test_pool.py"}} <|end_call|>
<|end_turn|>
<|tool id=c2|> FAILED test_release: pool exhausted <|end|>
<|tool id=c1|> ...file contents... <|end|>
<|assistant|> ...
In this sequence, c2 completes before c1, and this runtime delivers observations in arrival order, so the listing places the c2 reply first because that is the prompt the model actually received at its next turn. The call identifiers keep each observation bound to its original invocation regardless of that order. The error to avoid is re-sorting the replies into call order (c1, then c2) for tidiness, which would invent a prompt the model never saw. Serialization assembles tokens according to how the runtime presented the prompt to the model, whatever order that was. Reordering calls whose arguments or observations depend on one another alters the causal problem; any such permutation constitutes a synthetic data transformation that requires explicit validation. The <|end_turn|> token records where the policy surrendered control to the runtime loop, while all tokens enclosed between <|tool|> and <|end|> constitute external observations.
The training pipeline bundles this rendered dataset as serialization_v1. Its manifest couples the admitted execution records with the active rendering configuration, mapping every selected response span to its exact token offsets. Because tokenization, template injection, and string redaction can shift token boundaries (leading whitespace can merge into an adjacent special token, for example), the pipeline must re-verify all token offsets against the final rendered array. A rigorous pipeline decodes completed examples to inspect task prompts, tool bindings, span boundaries, and end-of-sequence markers. If an example fails boundary alignment or drops content, the pipeline drops the record entirely rather than patching it with synthetic filler.
Role delimiters establish protocol syntax, but they convey no runtime authority. If a model generates text that mimics a <|tool|> delimiter, that text remains model output under the tokenizer’s grammar; the serialization pipeline must never promote unverified generations into genuine environment observations.


↩︎ The rule that model output is a proposal carrying no authority until the runtime validates it is established in The Model Invocation Boundary.



Serving runtimes vary in how they manage conversational history. Some systems preserve full transcripts across iterations, while others prune earlier steps, compact intermediate context, or discard chain-of-thought scratchpads between turns to reduce KV cache footprints. A single concatenated transcript provides a faithful training example only when its causal attention prefixes match what the model actually perceived during online inference. The repair agent’s own runtime compacts history once the working set crosses its watermark, so a turn delivered after compaction saw a digest, not the raw turns that a concatenated transcript would place before it. When serving prunes or compresses history between steps, each invocation must instead be serialized as an independent training example containing its exact delivered prefix.


↩︎ Watermark-triggered compaction, which replaces earlier turns with a digest between invocations, is established in Context Compaction.
This independence incurs a substantial computational penalty, and its arithmetic is the triangular sum that already priced an append-only trajectory at serving time (equation 2.9), now paid in stored training tokens. If a trajectory spans \(\TurnHorizon\) turns and each turn contributes roughly \(\TurnAppendLength\) tokens, the example for turn \(\TurnIndex\) spans approximately \(\TurnIndex\,\TurnAppendLength\) tokens. Serializing all \(\TurnHorizon\) invocations independently requires \(\TurnAppendLength\,\TurnHorizon(\TurnHorizon+1)/2\) tokens, compared to just \(\TurnHorizon\,\TurnAppendLength\) tokens for a unified transcript, an expansion factor of \((\TurnHorizon+1)/2\). Over a stipulated horizon of 30 turns, serializing each invocation separately multiplies the required token volume by 15.5×. An agent system’s history-retention policy is therefore a primary engineering constraint when sizing training compute. The same fidelity rule covers the model’s own reasoning text. If serving discards an earlier turn’s rationale before the next invocation, the reconstructed prefix for that invocation omits it too; whether retained rationale then becomes a target or stays context is a separate choice (section 15.4.4).
With serialization_v1 assembled, the pipeline defines the tokenized sequences, their conditioning evidence, and the response spans selected during curation. The remaining challenge is determining which token predictions contribute to the training loss. Unmasked cross-entropy over entire multi-turn sequences would inadvertently penalize the model for failing to predict external tool outputs or user messages. Observation loss masking converts the curated span boundaries into aligned prediction targets while preserving necessary observations as conditioning context.




A data loader that naively selects every assistant token trains the model on malformed proposals alongside their subsequent corrections, unraveling careful curation decisions. Worse, a loader that computes loss across all tokens asks the policy to predict external environment responses. Serialization structures the input sequence into tokens, but the loss mask determines which of those tokens generate parameter updates.


Let \(\SerializedTrainingExample=(\SequenceToken_1,\ldots,\SequenceToken_{\SequenceLength})\) be one serialized example, with an initial context or boundary token at \(\SequenceToken_1\). Let \(\EligibleTargetPositionSet\subseteq\{2,\ldots,\SequenceLength\}\) contain the eligible policy-token positions selected for imitation. Position eligibility depends on admitted response spans and the specific training objective rather than token authorship alone. The mask is \(\PositionLossMask_{t}=\IndicatorFunction\{\TokenIndex\in\EligibleTargetPositionSet\}\), with \(\PositionLossMask_1=0\). For an example with at least one selected target, the mean masked cross-entropy is
\[\MaskedFinetuningLoss(\ModelParameters)=-\frac{1}{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}\sum_{t=2}^{\SequenceLength}\PositionLossMask_{t}\log\Policy(\SequenceToken_t\mid \TokenPrefix),\qquad \ActiveTargetTokenCount=\sum_{t=2}^{\SequenceLength}\PositionLossMask_{t}>0. \tag{1}\]
Each selected token is predicted from the preceding prefix. During training, the model conditions on the recorded sequence prefix, including earlier actions, observations, and admitted mistakes, rather than sampling fresh rollouts at each step. This training regime is teacher forcing1 (Williams and Zipser 1989). It allows recovery prefixes that contain historical failures to serve as valid conditioning contexts, provided the trajectory satisfies the curation contract.
1 Teacher Forcing: Williams and Zipser named the technique in 1989 for recurrent networks, feeding the recorded target back as the next input instead of the network’s own output. Because every prefix is recorded rather than generated, a causal model computes all of an example’s next-token predictions in one parallel forward pass, which is why imitating a trajectory costs one pass per example rather than one sampled rollout per decision.In the running repair trajectory, target_mask_v1 maps reviewed response spans directly onto the tokens emitted by serialization_v1, distinguishing target tokens from conditioning context (table 3). Modifying a tokenizer vocabulary, adjusting chat formatting templates, or transforming text inputs inevitably alters token alignments. Consequently, the pipeline must regenerate and validate masks against the exact serialization output rather than copying offsets across pipeline stages.

Definition 15.1: Observation loss masking
Observation loss masking excludes supplied observations from the direct token-prediction loss while retaining the permitted observation context needed to train selected policy responses.

Significance: Focuses the optimization objective strictly on the policy’s conditional distribution \(\Policy(\TrajectoryAction_{t}\mid \TrajectoryState_{t})\). Consequently, verbose environment output cannot dilute the gradient signal for policy actions, regardless of how much sequence context observations consume (notebook 15.1 quantifies this dilution).
Distinction: Masked tokens remain in the input context and participate in self-attention; only their next-token loss terms are omitted. Furthermore, policy authorship alone does not qualify a token as a target: rejected attempts or toxic actions require masking even when generated by an assistant role.
Common pitfall: Selecting an entire multi-turn tool exchange simply because the tool call succeeded, inadvertently training the model to predict external environment responses.






In causal autoregressive models,2 the hidden state at input index \(\TokenIndex-1\) generates the logits that predict token \(\SequenceToken_t\). The data loader must therefore align the prediction logits at \(\TokenIndex-1\) with target label \(\SequenceToken_t\) and target mask \(\PositionLossMask_{t}\), rather than attaching the mask of input token \(\SequenceToken_{t-1}\). Table 4 illustrates this boundary alignment. Because several distributed training frameworks perform this causal shift internally within their loss functions, applying a manual shift inside the data loader can silently misalign targets by one token across the entire corpus. Inspect the aligned labels and predicted tokens on a synthetic short example before launching large-scale training runs.
2 Causal Self-Attention: Causal masking in Transformer decoders restricts each token from attending to subsequent positions (Vaswani et al. 2017). This triangular attention structure allows a single forward pass over an input sequence of length \(\SequenceLength\) to compute all next-token predictions in parallel. It also enforces the label shift: the network predicts \(\SequenceToken_t\) using only the representation formed at \(\TokenIndex-1\).

Let \(\VocabularyTokenLogit_{t-1,\VocabularyToken}\) denote the logit for vocabulary token \(\VocabularyToken\) produced from \(\TokenPrefix\), using an ordinary softmax and no label smoothing. Differentiating equation 1 gives
\[\frac{\partial\MaskedFinetuningLoss}{\partial \VocabularyTokenLogit_{t-1,\VocabularyToken}}=\frac{\PositionLossMask_{t}}{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}\left(\Policy(\VocabularyToken\mid \TokenPrefix)-\IndicatorFunction\{\VocabularyToken=\SequenceToken_t\}\right).\]
When \(\PositionLossMask_{t}=0\), the next-token prediction at position \(\TokenIndex-1\) yields zero direct loss derivative. The token nevertheless shapes subsequent representations through causal attention layers, allowing gradients backpropagated from downstream active losses to adjust the parameters that encode it. The model conditions on tool outputs without expending capacity attempting to synthesize them. This mechanism underpins verified trajectory post-training (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training}\)) at token-level precision.
A deployed agent trajectory records an interleaved dialogue between two distinct systems: the agent policy and the external environment. Training without observation masking forces a single parameter set to approximate two conflicting distributions simultaneously:

The agent policy \(\Policy(\TrajectoryAction_{t}\mid \TrajectoryState_{t})\), mapping historical observations and instructions to deliberate tool calls or answers.
An environment dynamics model \(\EnvironmentTransitionDistribution(\TrajectoryState_{t+1}\mid \TrajectoryState_{t}, \TrajectoryAction_{t})\), predicting outputs returned by arbitrary shells, database engines, or remote APIs.

Because real tools execute directly during deployment and supply ground-truth outputs, tasking the policy with predicting environment returns wastes model capacity.
Supervising the environment distribution introduces two severe systems failures:

Loss dilution: Under standard token-averaged cross-entropy, unmasking inflates the normalization denominator from \(\ActiveTargetTokenCount\) to the number of causal prediction terms, \(\SequenceLength-1\), because the initial stored boundary has no preceding-position prediction. As a result, the effective gradient scale on critical decision tokens collapses proportionally to the selected fraction of predicted positions (computed in notebook 15.1). The loss budget then goes to runtime artifacts (file paths, stack traces, compiler dumps, and raw JSON payloads), which pull on the average in two directions. Repetitive parts such as echoed schemas, boilerplate headers, and repeated paths are easy to predict and drag the averaged loss down; novel parts such as a fresh stack trace or unseen file contents are hard to predict and swamp the gradient. Either way, the averaged number stops measuring the policy.
Role confusion: When trained to predict tokens following a tool invocation, the policy learns that tool outputs naturally succeed tool calls within the same autoregressive stream. In production, such a model can continue past its own tool call and write a fabricated tool result instead of ending the turn with the stop reason that hands control back to the runtime. Because the runtime separates generated text from authenticated environment observations (section 15.3), it discards the fabricated result, so every such turn burns output budget on tokens that are thrown away and can stall the trajectory until the runtime intervenes.

Observation masking eliminates both pathologies at the loss level. A validation loss curve cannot reveal how often an unmasked model fabricates environment outputs in practice; that failure mode emerges only during interactive, closed-loop evaluation. While predicting environment transitions is a legitimate goal when training world models or offline tool simulators, it conflicts with the policy imitation objective required for autonomous agents.

Many agent datasets incorporate intermediate reasoning traces, such as chain-of-thought scratchpads or tool-use plans. Deciding how to supervise this intermediate text requires choosing between three distinct data-loading regimes (table 7). Supervising the rationale trains the model to generate its own reasoning before invoking tools. Retaining the rationale under a loss mask treats the reasoning as supplied conditioning context, training the model to act upon plans provided by an external orchestrator or user. Stripping the rationale entirely fundamentally alters the conditional distribution by forcing the policy to act directly from context alone.
Formally, given context prefix \(\TurnContext_{t}\), rationale tokens \(\RationaleTokens\), and action tokens \(\ResponseActionTokens=(\ResponseActionTokens_1,\ldots,\ResponseActionTokens_n)\), response-only supervision models the conditional distribution \(\Policy(\ResponseActionTokens_j\mid \TurnContext_{t}, \RationaleTokens, \ActionTokenPrefix)\). If the production serving environment does not provide \(\RationaleTokens\), the deployed model must evaluate \(\Policy(\ResponseActionTokens_j\mid \TurnContext_{t}, \ActionTokenPrefix)\). Because these represent mathematically distinct conditional distributions, omitting rationale at training time represents an explicit distillation experiment that must be validated directly against the unconditioned serving target.

At inference time, an external planning agent or the policy’s own autoregressive generator can supply the required reasoning text. When the model generates its own rationale, runtime text inevitably diverges from the training demonstration; downstream evaluation must measure this divergence. A rationale segment merits target status only when the system architecture explicitly requires the deployed policy to synthesize its own thoughts under operational latency and token budgets.



To teach an agent when to yield control, the training loss must include the authentic policy-generated termination token (such as <|eom_id|> or <|im_end|>) at the end of each selected response. Host frameworks often insert their own control delimiters to demarcate incoming tool payloads; data loaders must never confuse these host delimiters with genuine policy stop tokens. Excluding termination tokens from the loss mask deprives the model of direct supervision on when to stop. Without that supervision, the policy can generate past the end of its action until the output limit cuts it off. Such calls return TRUNCATED rather than COMPLETED, so the runtime’s quarantining rule withholds a proposal that may have been correct.


↩︎ The normalized TRUNCATED status and the quarantining rule that withholds an incomplete candidate are established in The normalized status envelope.
Truncated responses, where an output was cut short by a context window or a timeout, present a dangerous edge case. A common pipeline flaw is appending a synthetic end-of-turn token to an incomplete response, which trains the policy to end a turn on a partial command. That is the training-side twin of the hazard the quarantining rule blocks at serving time, where a truncated rm -rf argument still parses as a complete and broader command. The training-side version is worse, because a policy that has learned to emit the terminator after a partial command produces a COMPLETED status, which the quarantining rule admits. When encountering truncated turns, engineering pipelines should adopt one of two sound strategies:

Conservative exclusion: Mask the truncated turn entirely (\(\PositionLossMask_{t}=0\)) while preserving preceding successful turns in the trajectory.
Prefix-only supervision: Supervise the valid initial tokens of the truncated turn up to the truncation point, but strictly omit any terminating token.

Whenever trajectories undergo truncation, sliding-window packing, or template transformations, the data pipeline must recompute target masks and verify that \(\ActiveTargetTokenCount > 0\). Robust training loaders implement automated unit assertions on critical boundaries: the first token of an agent response, the closing turn terminator, the transition into tool observations, rejected recovery attempts, and truncated sequences. Validating these boundaries guarantees that the training engine optimizes the exact supervised objective declared by the curation policy.

With per-example loss masking in place, the training loader enforces the exact boundary between conditioning context and imitation targets. Production training, however, batches heterogeneous trajectories across varying sequence lengths and device topologies. The batching and collation mechanisms must uphold this target contract without silently skewing loss weights across sequence lengths.




Consider a batch where a lengthy debugging and code repair trace shares a single training buffer with a brief, unrelated file lookup. Under an ordinary lower-triangular causal mask, the lookup can attend directly to the repair trace’s intermediate file contents and tool outputs, context that the lookup policy will never encounter during online inference. Under token averaging, the multi-turn repair trace will also outweigh the brief lookup by the exact ratio of their active target tokens.
Constructing a batch of variable-length trajectories therefore forces two coupled systems decisions: how much gradient weight each trajectory exerts on the optimization objective, and how multiple sequences share physical buffer memory without leaking information across sequence boundaries. Sequence packing is strictly a memory layout optimization; a correct implementation preserves both the mathematically specified loss and the causal isolation of each sequence’s predictive context.


Let a batch contain \(\BatchSize\) examples. Example \(\BatchExampleIndex\) has stored length \(\SequenceLength^{(\BatchExampleIndex)}\), including context, and \({\ActiveTargetTokenCount}_{\BatchExampleIndex}>0\) selected target tokens under the preceding section’s mask. Let \(\LossFunction_{\BatchExampleIndex}\) be its mean masked negative log-likelihood. Two batch objectives are
\[\TokenAveragedBatchLoss=
\sum_{\BatchExampleIndex=1}^{\BatchSize}\frac{{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}_{\BatchExampleIndex}}{\sum_{k=1}^{\BatchSize}{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}_k}\LossFunction_{\BatchExampleIndex}, \tag{2}\]
\[\ExampleAveragedBatchLoss=\frac{1}{\BatchSize}\sum_{\BatchExampleIndex=1}^{\BatchSize}\LossFunction_{\BatchExampleIndex}. \tag{3}\]
Token averaging in equation 2 assigns equal coefficients to selected token losses. Example averaging in equation 3 assigns equal coefficients to example means. Both count selected targets, never context or padding. A record with no selected targets supplies no \(\LossFunction_{\BatchExampleIndex}\) and is excluded from either objective.
These normalization coefficients govern the loss function directly, though realized gradient magnitudes also depend on prediction errors and parameter sensitivities. Example averaging equalizes serialized example means, not completed interactions or underlying tasks; one example may represent a single invocation. In contrast, token averaging weights each example proportionally to its active target count.
This distinction becomes critical when trajectory serialization splits a multi-turn interaction into separate training records. If one of \(\BatchSize\) initial examples becomes \(\TurnHorizon\) per-invocation examples while every other example remains once, example averaging changes that trajectory’s aggregate share from \(1/\BatchSize\) to \(\TurnHorizon/(\BatchSize-1+\TurnHorizon)\). It has \(\TurnHorizon\) times each unsplit example’s share, rather than \(\TurnHorizon\) times its former normalized share. Under token averaging, the trajectory’s aggregate share remains unchanged only if its selected targets form a disjoint partition, each turn is selected once, and the other batch members and their targets stay unchanged. Repeating prefix context alone does not repeat active targets. Data sampling, trajectory segmentation, and loss normalization therefore jointly dictate how underlying agent capabilities are weighted during optimization. Writing out the coefficients each objective places on an example mean and on a single selected token (table 8) makes the difference exact.

The mathematical equivalence in table 8 requires careful distributed accounting. A large batch is rarely processed in one piece. It is split into microbatches (slices processed one after another before a single parameter update) and spread across data-parallel workers (each holding a copy of the model and processing its own share of the batch). Computing a true global token average requires summing active token losses and token counts across all microbatches and workers before dividing. Averaging local microbatch means directly produces an accurate token average only when active token counts match across all microbatches; otherwise, the workers must combine their raw sums and counts before taking the ratio.




Definition 15.2: Sequence packing
Sequence packing places several variable-length training examples in shared buffers while preserving their intended information boundaries and loss targets.

Significance: Uniform padding allocates the longest example’s length to every row, reducing batch occupancy to the ratio of mean to maximum sequence length. Sequence packing reclaims this wasted capacity (notebook 15.2).
Distinction: Independent trajectories share physical memory buffers without sharing predictive context; multi-turn interactions within an individual trajectory retain access to their complete history.
Common pitfall: Applying a standard causal mask across concatenated sequences, allowing later examples to attend illegitimately to earlier ones.



The file lookup from the section’s opening must never read the repair trace’s file contents or tool observations. Reading them would be cross-contamination,3 the leak a packed layout must prevent (Krell et al. 2021). Let \(\QueryBufferPosition\) and \(\KeyBufferPosition\) denote buffer positions, \(\QueryVector_i\) and \(\KeyVector_j\) their query and key vectors, and \(\AttentionHeadDimension\) the attention-head dimension. The pre-softmax attention scores \(\text{score}_{i,j}\) enforce both causality and example membership:

The equivalence is the property to test: a packed loader that trains faster but lets examples read one another has changed the learning problem, and no loss curve will show it.\[\text{score}_{i,j}=\begin{cases}
\QueryVector_i\KeyVector_j^T/\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension} & \text{if }\operatorname{example}(\QueryBufferPosition)=\operatorname{example}(\KeyBufferPosition)\text{ and }\KeyBufferPosition\le \QueryBufferPosition,\\
-\infty & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases} \tag{4}\]
Under an ordinary causal mask, every query in a later example can score keys in an earlier one; the block-diagonal mask sets each of those cross-example entries to \(-\infty\) before the softmax, and excludes trailing padding keys the same way (figure 3). Variable-length attention kernels (Dao 2023) enforce this without materializing a dense \(-\infty\) matrix. The loader hands the kernel the example boundaries as cumulative offsets, \(0\), \(\PackedExampleLength_1\), \(\PackedExampleLength_1+\PackedExampleLength_2\), and so on through the buffer’s total length (\(\BatchSize+1\) entries for \(\BatchSize\) examples), so that example \(\PackedExampleIndex\) occupies one contiguous interval of positions, and the kernel computes scores only for query and key pairs that fall inside the same interval. Whether a given kernel also skips the computation for cross-example blocks of the score matrix, and how much time that saves, is an implementation property to measure on the target accelerator. The mask is the correctness requirement; skipped work is a throughput bonus that must be shown, not assumed.

One long trajectory holds padded occupancy to 19.1 percent; packing reaches 76.6 percent.
Loss computation requires the same rigorous boundary isolation. In autoregressive language modeling, targets are created by shifting labels by one position. Shifting labels across an entire concatenated buffer inadvertently trains the final token of one example to predict the initial token of the next. Each example’s initial prompt context remains unselected as a target, and shifted prediction-target pairs must stay strictly inside their parent example. Attention masks and target masks enforce distinct systems constraints: attention masks isolate visible context, while target masks isolate supervised loss gradients. Both must be implemented correctly.
