An argument schema constrains the syntactic format of a request, but it cannot constrain the underlying code execution. A specialized symbol-renaming tool may parse external ASTs, inspect secondary source trees, or execute defective third-party libraries. A narrow signature provides safety only when the implementation and its surrounding execution sandbox enforce that advertised boundary. Conversely, a shell runner’s blast radius is defined by its working directory, operating-system privileges, credential access, and network egress rules. Because the side effects of an expressive shell command cannot be reliably determined by inspecting its arguments, the runtime must rely on containment to enforce isolation.


↪ The isolation envelope that enforces a command’s reach regardless of its arguments is developed in Choosing an Isolation Envelope.
Tool implementations should also adopt defensive defaults that fail visibly. When an agent provides an ambiguous file path or target identifier, rejecting the call with an informative diagnostic is far safer than guessing or silently appending data, as appending is a stateful mutation that can silently duplicate configuration entries. A dry-run mode allows the model to inspect a proposed diff against the current workspace state before committing changes; the runtime must still enforce approval gates and verify preconditions at execution time. These defensive defaults make operational failures interpretable, but engineers should remember that rollback capabilities and high-fidelity simulation are properties of the underlying tool implementation, not inherent guarantees of the interface.



Rigorous evaluation of toolkit designs requires isolating the effects of granularity and staging policy by holding all other experimental factors constant: the benchmark task distribution, initial workspace snapshots, model checkpoints, generation parameters, token budgets, and verification suites. In the connection-pool repair workload, test trials must exercise realistic failure modes: locating relevant source files across deep directory hierarchies, applying patches against concurrently modified buffers, interpreting noisy test failure logs, and recovering gracefully when a necessary tool descriptor is omitted from the initial active toolkit. These targeted trials disentangle catalog coverage limitations from model selection errors, and separate model selection accuracy from execution-time runtime failures.
Comprehensive evaluation logs must record selection errors, malformed arguments, rejected preconditions, unnecessary discovery calls, recovery turns, and uncontained side effects alongside binary task completion. Cost accounting should measure serialized descriptor tokens, retrieval and reranking latency, execution sandbox compute time, observation overhead, and cumulative tokens wasted on failed trajectories. A recovered tool selection error costs inference turns and latency, whereas an unrecovered error aborts the task; consequently, toolkits are ranked by total cost per accepted task rather than the simple probability of avoiding selection errors. Furthermore, when comparing designs that require fundamentally different security postures, such as an unconstrained command runner vs. a constrained AST manipulation tool, evaluations must report those privilege differences explicitly rather than attributing performance gaps solely to catalog size.
The ultimate objective of toolkit engineering is an active catalog whose contracts align with workload demands while keeping execution costs and failure modes transparent. Static staging, on-demand selection, task-level abstractions, and expressive command runners represent trade-offs to evaluate against these cost and reliability metrics. The same engineering principles apply when an agent interacts with a graphical user interface instead of a programmatic API: mouse clicks, keyboard events, and visual screen parsers impose their own granularity challenges, prefill budgets, and containment boundaries.




Consider the staging-container restart scenario when an administrative web dashboard provides no programmatic API. A computer-use tool bridges this interface gap by rendering visual screenshots to the model and translating model-generated targets into synthetic mouse clicks, keystrokes, or scrolling gestures, the low-level input space pioneered in early web-agent research (Shi et al. 2017). Operating on raw pixels does not relax system invariants. While the model proposes an interaction based on an observed frame, the execution runtime retains responsibility for validating arguments, enforcing authorization, dispatching OS events, and interpreting observations. A coordinate within display boundaries merely confirms that an event can reach the window manager, offering no assurance about the state mutation that the event will trigger.


Suppose an agent session possesses authorization to restart the staging container srv-stage-04, but security policies strictly forbid modifying production workloads. The agent observes a confirmation modal that identifies the staging container and renders a clickable Restart button. Controlling this workflow requires the same rigorous interface contract used for structured tool calls, adapted for spatial and temporal dynamism.
When the runtime captures an observation, it records the application and window identifier, a unique capture identifier, an observation timestamp, and the exact geometric frame presented to the model. If the runtime downsamples, pads, or crops the image before model ingestion, it must retain the crop offsets and scaling factors needed to project a proposed coordinate back into the native display coordinate space. Raw screenshot pixels, application-relative window coordinates, and virtual desktop coordinates represent distinct spatial reference frames. The runtime adapter must validate all proposed points against the active viewport; silently clamping out-of-bounds coordinates to the nearest edge risks turning an invalid model hallucination into a destructive click on an unintended adjacent control.
Now suppose the model proposes clicking the Restart button based on that observation. Prior to event dispatch, the adapter must recheck the current application focus, active window state, and target dialog parameters using platform accessibility or windowing APIs. In a dynamic desktop environment, state changes rapidly. A background network event or concurrent operator action might bring a production container dialog into the foreground at those exact screen coordinates. In this scenario, valid spatial coordinates no longer justify executing the model’s proposal. The runtime must detect the stale precondition, abort the pending dispatch, and request a fresh visual observation. While benign updates such as a ticking taskbar clock do not invalidate a target, any modification to a resource identifier, modal overlay, or button layout alters the operational effect.
Once the staging dialog is re-verified, the policy engine must evaluate the session grant against the intended container restart rather than checking a generic permission to emit mouse clicks. If the interface cannot establish which backend operation the click will execute with the confidence required by the security policy, the runtime must block dispatch and escalate the decision to an authorized operator. Otherwise, the adapter dispatches the bounded input event and records its immediate outcome. Structured endpoints enforce resource identity and action preconditions directly at the server interface, providing a robust execution boundary. By contrast, visual actuation cannot achieve atomic execution: capturing a fresh screenshot reduces staleness, but it cannot prevent a concurrent state change from slipping between the observation capture and the event dispatch.
After dispatching the input event, the subsequent observation must verify operational progress rather than mere input delivery. A disappearing confirmation modal might indicate that the server accepted the restart command, but it might also mean that a network timeout dismissed the dialog without action. The runtime must gather corroborating evidence of the restart, either by inspecting a refreshed dashboard status indicator or by issuing an authorized read-only status query. If the click produces no visible change and the dashboard continues displaying the previous state, the requested operation might still be processing asynchronously. Under these conditions, the execution yields an uncertain outcome (definition 7.4), which the runtime must resolve through the idempotency and reconciliation protocols detailed in section 7.5 rather than by repeatedly firing redundant clicks.



Visual observations require the same rigorous resource accounting as textual tool payloads. Vision encoders partition input images into fixed-size grid patches, converting high-resolution screenshots into thousands of visual tokens. Because visual token consumption directly inflates inference latency and per-turn billing, systems engineers must monitor both the raw byte representation submitted to the model and its resulting token allocation. A screenshot is priced like any other staged observation: its token count plays the role of \(\ShapedObservationSize\) in notebook 7.2, and every later call that retains it multiplies that count by \(\RetainingCallCount\). One screenshot per turn, each retained, therefore grows carried input with every step of a computer-use trajectory, which is why the techniques below shrink the per-frame count and why retention policy matters as much as resolution.


↩︎ How a vision front-end turns an image into reserved context positions, and how one image can overflow a request’s headroom, is established in Multimodal input accounting.
Naively compressing visual inputs introduces sharp engineering trade-offs. Downscaling an entire screen capture reduces token consumption, but blurs fine visual details such as container names, port numbers, or warning banners until they become unreadable. Conversely, tightly cropping the image preserves full pixel resolution around a candidate button, but strips away peripheral context, concealing modal warning banners or active window titles that are essential for correct interpretation.
A resilient architecture balances these demands through hierarchical visual sampling: capturing a low-resolution full-screen overview to establish window layout and focus, paired with an on-demand, high-resolution crop around the target interaction zone. Each visual artifact must retain its parent observation identifier and affine coordinate mapping so the runtime can translate local crop coordinates back to native display space. Similarly, transmitting visual diffs of modified screen regions reduces payload size during iterative tasks, provided the diff retains sufficient surrounding landmark geometry for the vision model to orient itself. Because large language model inference engines rely on exact prefix matching for KV-cache reuse, altering a visual frame across turns invalidates cached prefixes for all subsequent tokens. A well-designed observation budget delivers the minimal visual evidence necessary to authorize and execute the next operational decision while keeping token consumption bounded.

Checkpoint 7.4: A click is still a tool call
A dashboard changes after the model observes a staging restart dialog. The adapter can capture the display and send a click, but cannot atomically bind that click to the displayed resource.

Target identity: Which changes require rejecting the old proposal, and why is a coordinate-range check insufficient?
Observation geometry: What information must accompany a resized crop so a proposed point can be mapped to the intended surface?
Authority and freshness: What does a new screenshot establish, and which action-time uncertainty remains before dispatch?
Effect evidence: If the click times out and the old status remains visible, why is another click not automatically justified? What evidence would support the intended restart without claiming the whole task is complete?







The tool boundary fails when evidence about one stage is treated as a guarantee about another. These misconceptions recur across structured, terminal, and visual interfaces.

Fallacy: A schema-valid call is safe to execute.
Structural validity checks the shape of a request; the session’s grant, the current domain preconditions, and resource limits are separate checks (section 7.3). In the GitHub MCP leak (war story 7.1), every call the agent made was schema-valid and within its credential’s reach. The call that exceeded the task’s grants was the first private-repository read, and no check compared it with the task.


Pitfall: Treating a timeout as permission to retry.
A timeout records missing knowledge, not a failure. Under the blind-retry model of notebook 7.1, a per-call duplicate probability of 1.9208 percent becomes about 3,842 duplicate effects a day across 200,000 mutating calls. Retry only on safe operation semantics, an endpoint that honors the operation ID, or reconciliation evidence (section 7.5); otherwise record the effect as unresolved.


Fallacy: A zero exit status establishes task completion.
Exit status is the invoked program’s convention. A runner that discovers zero tests, a script without pipefail, and a client that prints its error and exits normally all return zero (section 7.7). The r18 reproducer pass supports one exercised connection-pool case; acceptance follows the task’s evidence standard (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)).


Pitfall: Shrinking an observation without recording what was dropped.
Truncation itself is unavoidable, since the illustrative log in notebook 7.2 is 62.5× the entire context window. The mistake is losing the record of omission. A head-only policy applied to listing 4 keeps the banner and passing tests and drops the one panic that explains the failure. The head, notice, and tail of equation 2 keep it within the same byte budget, and an inspection handle recovers the middle on request.


Fallacy: Staging every registered tool is harmless because each descriptor is short.
Descriptors add up, and they recur on every call. In notebook 7.4, a 50-tool catalog occupies 15,000 tokens of each request, while the 6 tools a step needs, with selection overhead, use 2,200. Over a trajectory that difference is paid once per turn, in capacity taken from task evidence (section 7.9).


Pitfall: Letting the model poll a long-running job.
Each “still running” answer is a full model call. In notebook 7.3, a 300 s job checked every 5 s costs 59 extra model calls and $0.8764 in tokens that change no decision. Runtime polling or a completion notification detects the change without inference and wakes the model only when the result can alter the next action (section 7.8.3).




Every runtime mechanism in this chapter enforces one discipline. An agent may base its next decision only on what returning evidence directly confirms. A schema validates the syntactic shape of a request, an authorization grant restricts its permissible targets, an endpoint check enforces execution preconditions and timing, and an observation reports what the tool actually measured. None of these mechanisms assumes that a proposed operation successfully altered external state, nor does a completed execution guarantee that the broader task has succeeded. When evidence is missing, as it was after the timed-out staging restart, the runtime must record the evidentiary gap explicitly rather than interpolating an assumed outcome.

Key Takeaways: A tool call includes its returning evidence

A call ends at its observation, not its dispatch: The runtime matches each returning result to its corresponding invocation, recording whether the proposal was rejected, dispatched, completed, or left in an indeterminate state. Subsequent planning must reason strictly from this confirmed disposition rather than assuming an action succeeded simply because the host dispatched it.
Schemas shape requests; enforcement governs effects: Type signatures and parameter descriptions guide the model to structure valid calls, but authorization grants, resource quotas, and precondition checks govern actual execution. Any mutation that depends on an unchanged target resource must verify preconditions atomically alongside the write, rather than relying on stale observations from an earlier read.
Discovery does not confer permission: Exposing a tool interface in the context window reveals structural syntax, but connectivity and schema compliance never imply authorization. The host runtime must validate every invocation against task-scoped grants, including read-only queries, while the remote endpoint enforces its own perimeter independently.
An unknown effect forbids blind repetition: Because a timed-out attempt may have committed before network acknowledgment was lost, duplicate side effects track reply loss rather than request loss. The runtime may retry an unacknowledged invocation only under provably idempotent semantics, an endpoint deduplication contract, or explicit probe reconciliation. Otherwise, it must preserve the operation as an unresolved effect.
Truncation must disclose what it dropped: Buffer limits and model context windows constrain distinct physical resources, yet both force data omission. An observation payload that incorporates execution status, provenance metadata, and a measured omission counter preserves diagnostic integrity, whereas silent head truncation often discards the terminal error or stack trace needed to diagnose a fault.
Acknowledgment is not completion: Long-running jobs require durable handles, scoped inspection, authorized input channels, and unambiguous cancellation outcomes. Event-driven runtime detection re-awakens the model only when a state change can alter the next action, preventing empty polling loops that burn inference budgets on uninformative checks.
No toolkit size is universally optimal: Catalog staging and API granularity navigate a fundamental trade-off among context overhead, selection accuracy, expressiveness, and security boundaries, while visual interfaces introduce freshness and target-geometry constraints. System designers must evaluate a toolkit by its total cost per accepted task and the precision of the authority it leaves bounded.



The typed action contract (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}\)) cleanly separates an interpretable proposal emitted by the model from the authorization required to execute it. When network drops or timeouts leave an outcome ambiguous, settlement before retry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}\)) extends that discipline to prevent silent state corruption: the runtime must either establish that repeating the call is safe or record an unresolved effect. A tool’s completion report, however, confirms only that an operation finished, not that the overall task succeeded. Final acceptance always demands invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)), verifying that the system’s operational requirements hold in reality before declaring success.



The tool execution boundary is the modern incarnation of a problem operating systems encountered half a century ago, when an untrusted program requested an operation the system could not let it perform directly. In a 1972 computer security planning study for the U.S. Air Force, Anderson introduced the concept of the reference monitor, establishing three non-negotiable requirements for access control: the monitor must be tamper-proof, always invoked, and small enough to be subjected to rigorous analysis and verification (Anderson 1972). Saltzer and Schroeder synthesized these insights into foundational design principles, most notably complete mediation, least privilege, and economy of mechanism, which dictate that every access path must be validated and that protection mechanisms should remain minimal and transparent (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975). Dennis and Van Horn had earlier introduced capability-based addressing, wherein possession of an unforgeable token directly conveys the authority to act (Dennis and Van Horn 1966), while Lampson formalized access policies into a canonical matrix defining the rights held by subjects over system objects (Lampson 1974). Hardy’s 1988 analysis of the confused deputy problem revealed the hazards of ambient authority, showing what goes wrong when a privileged service executes operations on behalf of an unprivileged client without checking the client’s authority (Hardy 1988). In agent runtimes, this exact vulnerability manifests whenever a model holding private credentials executes operations triggered by untrusted user prompts or retrieved external content.

Lampson, Butler W. 1974. “Protection.” ACM Operating Systems Review 8 (1): 18–24. https://doi.org/10.1145/775265.775268.

Saltzer, Jerome H., David P. Reed, and David D. Clark. 1984. “End-to-End Arguments in System Design.” ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 2 (4): 277–88. https://doi.org/10.1145/357401.357402.

Kung, H. T., and John T. Robinson. 1981. “On Optimistic Methods for Concurrency Control.” ACM Transactions on Database Systems 6 (2): 213–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/319566.319567.

Garcia-Molina, Hector, and Kenneth Salem. 1987. “Sagas.” Proceedings of the 1987 ACM SIGMOD International Conference on Management of Data, 249–59. https://doi.org/10.1145/38713.38742.

Gray, Cary G., and David R. Cheriton. 1989. “Leases: An Efficient Fault-Tolerant Mechanism for Distributed File Cache Consistency.” Proceedings of the Twelfth ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP), 202–10. https://doi.org/10.1145/74850.74870.
A second historical lineage governs operations that cross network boundaries. Birrell and Nelson designed the Remote Procedure Call (RPC) to make remote invocations feel as natural as local function calls, but they documented the fundamental tension of distributed execution: during network partitions or server crashes, a caller cannot know whether a request succeeded, failed, or stalled midway through execution (Birrell and Nelson 1984). In the same year, Saltzer, Reed, and Clark articulated the end-to-end argument, demonstrating that reliability and correctness cannot be guaranteed solely by intermediate communication layers and must ultimately be validated by the endpoints themselves (Saltzer et al. 1984). Distributed systems researchers developed several robust patterns to handle this inherent ambiguity. Kung and Robinson introduced optimistic concurrency control, allowing transactions to proceed without heavy upfront locking and validating serializability before commit (Kung and Robinson 1981). For distributed operations that cannot be rolled back atomically, Garcia-Molina and Salem formulated sagas, coordinating sequences of local transactions coupled with compensating actions to undo partially completed work (Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987). Gray and Cheriton introduced leases, using time-bounded grants to manage shared resources without requiring indefinite locks (Gray and Cheriton 1989). Finally, Helland made the practical case that reliable distributed systems must push retry safety into the receiver by enforcing endpoint idempotence (Helland 2012), a requirement that directly informs how tool runtimes deduplicate requests and handle agent retries.
Language models converged on tool execution from the opposite direction, evolving from passive sequence predictors into interactive system callers. Early modular architectures routed model queries to external calculators, symbolic solvers, and database interfaces (Karpas et al. 2022). Yao et al. (2023) established the ReAct paradigm, demonstrating that interleaving explicit reasoning traces with concrete actions and environment feedback dramatically improves multi-step problem solving. Schick et al. (2023) showed with Toolformer that models could learn in a self-supervised manner to propose external API calls spontaneously, complete with appropriate arguments, during standard text generation. As the scope of external tools expanded, retrieval-augmented tool selection helped eliminate hallucinated function signatures by fetching accurate documentation on demand (Patil et al. 2023), while large-scale instruction tuning exposed models to thousands of diverse, real-world REST APIs (Qin et al. 2024). Interacting with external environments also has roots in web agents that manipulate user interfaces through simulated keyboard and mouse events (Shi et al. 2017). However, designing interfaces specifically tailored to language models proved even more effective: Yang et al. (2024) demonstrated with SWE-agent that structuring the agent-computer interface around model-friendly commands, such as concise file viewers with line numbers and restricted editing primitives, substantially lifted task success on complex software engineering benchmarks. To manage the proliferation of heterogeneous tools, open specifications like the Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardized the boundary between host runtimes and external tool servers (Model Context Protocol 2025). As tool calling gained ubiquity, however, it exposed a unique vulnerability: an agent interprets untrusted external text within the same context window that guides its decisions, allowing adversarial inputs to steer the model into executing unintended tool invocations (Greshake et al. 2023). Because the language model is an untrusted caller that can be influenced by malicious prompts, the enclosing systems runtime must enforce complete mediation and least privilege on every operation, and permit retries of uncertain effects only when their repetition is safe.

For further reading:

Saltzer and Schroeder, “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems” (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975). The canonical catalog of security principles for computer systems. Read through the lens of agent execution, principles like complete mediation, least privilege, and economy of mechanism serve as a direct checklist for designing secure tool boundaries.
Birrell and Nelson, “Implementing Remote Procedure Calls” (Birrell and Nelson 1984). The foundational paper on RPC and the clearest exposition of distributed failure semantics. It establishes why a caller can never be completely certain whether an unacknowledged remote call executed, providing the theoretical basis for retry budgets and timeout policies.
Hardy, “The Confused Deputy” (Hardy 1988). A concise, three-page paper that identifies how an entity with broad ambient authority becomes an unwitting tool for attackers. It represents required reading for understanding why language agents must never carry ambient credentials across security domains.
Helland, “Idempotence Is Not a Medical Condition” (Helland 2012). A practical guide to designing distributed systems that survive retries by pushing deduplication and idempotence keys into receiver interfaces, directly applicable to tool runtime dispatch.
Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design (Ousterhout 2018). A compact treatment of interface design and deep modules. The book’s criteria for module depth and interface complexity provide concrete guidance for sizing tool APIs so models can invoke them effectively without leaking implementation details.
Yang et al., “SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering” (Yang et al. 2024). An empirical demonstration that designing clean, model-oriented tool interfaces is just as vital to agent performance as scaling the underlying language model.

All quantities below are hypothetical problem givens, chosen to be round, and describe no particular provider, protocol version, or deployment. Assume message losses are independent unless a problem says otherwise.
1. Blind retry at fleet volume (Basic). A tool fleet issues 120,000 mutating calls a day to an endpoint with no deduplication. Each request is lost with probability 1 percent and each reply with probability 3 percent; lost messages never arrive later, and every timeout triggers exactly one retry.

Compute the per-call timeout probability, the per-call duplicate-effect probability, and the expected duplicates per day.
A network team offers two upgrades: halve reply loss, or halve request loss. Compute the daily duplicates under each and explain why one of them slightly increases duplicates.
Name the change that removes the duplicate path rather than shrinking it, and state what the endpoint must bind the identifier to for that change to hold.

2. Sizing the tail (Basic). An adapter stages test logs with a head-and-tail policy under \(\ObservationByteBudget = 16{,}384\) bytes, with \(\NoticeByteAllocation = 256\) bytes and \(\HeadByteAllocation = 4{,}096\) bytes. A failing run writes 9,000,000 bytes in total. Its only diagnostic is a 2,400-byte panic block, followed by 11,000 bytes of teardown output and a 600-byte final summary.

Compute \(\TailByteAllocation\) and determine whether the whole panic block reaches the model.
Keeping \(\ObservationByteBudget\) and \(\NoticeByteAllocation\) fixed, find the largest \(\HeadByteAllocation\) that keeps the entire panic block in the tail. How many bytes does the omission notice report in either configuration?
The same runner sometimes prints the panic before 200,000 bytes of teardown output. Explain why no split of this \(\ObservationByteBudget\) fixes that case, and name the mechanism from section 7.6 that does.

3. When catalog selection pays (Basic). A repair harness registers 80 tools, each contributing 420 tokens to the final serialized request. On-demand staging exposes 8 of them plus 900 tokens of selection interface and metadata, and the runtime selects without an extra model call. A trajectory makes 40 model calls, and uncached input costs $3 per million tokens.

Compute the catalog input of one call under each layout, the capacity released per call, and the break-even number of unused descriptors.
Compute the tokens and uncached dollars released over the trajectory.
In one trajectory out of five, a needed tool was not staged and the agent spends one extra model call of 30,000 input tokens rediscovering it. Does selection still pay? State the condition under which the comparison would flip.
The 80 descriptors come from three interoperable tool servers discovered at session start. One of them advertises delete_branch with a description stating that it is approved for all repositories, and the task’s grants do not include branch deletion. Does staging or omitting that descriptor change what the agent may do? Name the check that governs the call if the model proposes it anyway, where each part of that check runs, and what the returned observation should report.

4. The price of asking whether a job finished (Intermediate). A repair agent’s test suite completes after 1,500 s. Under model-directed polling, the model checks every 30 s, starting one interval after dispatch, with each status call reading a 48,000-token selected input and generating 60 tokens. The cache covers 90 percent of that input. Hypothetical prices per million tokens are $3 uncached input, $0.30 cached input, and $15 output. The fleet runs 2,000 such jobs a day.

Compute the pending-status calls per job, the incremental cost per job, and the daily fleet cost of polling.
Product management caps model-directed polling at $0.10 per job. Find the minimum poll interval that meets the cap, and the worst-case delay between completion and detection at that interval for a job whose completion time is not known in advance.
Runtime polling every 10 s costs no inference. Compare its worst-case detection delay and token cost with the answer to (b), then choose a design to ship and state what model-directed inspection remains useful for.

5. Retrying a refund (Intermediate; second lighthouse). The support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)) issues refunds through a payment endpoint that offers no deduplication contract. It sends 40,000 refund calls a day, each averaging $60. Requests are lost with probability 0.5 percent and replies with probability 1.5 percent. The alternative to blind retry is an authorized reconciliation probe written before dispatch (equation 1), which adds 4 s to the customer’s wait on every timed-out call. For parts (a) and (b), assume lost messages never arrive later and every delivered refund request executes successfully.

Under one blind retry per timeout, compute the expected duplicate refunds per day and their dollar exposure.
Under the probe policy, compute the fraction of sessions that incur the extra wait and the total added customer wait per day.
Compare the duplicate-refund exposure with the added customer wait. State what operation-specific evidence or endpoint guarantee would make the probe sufficient to settle the original refund or permit a retry, including how it rules out an attempt that could still execute before authorizing another execution. If the probe is inconclusive or the allowed wait expires, specify the recorded outcome and escalation. What response-latency limit would be needed to decide whether this policy meets the service target? Explain why a refund’s operation ID must not be a hash of the customer and amount.

6. Carry, drop, or re-read (Intermediate). A repair agent stages a 6,000-token test observation that stays in context for its remaining 45 model calls. Uncached input costs $3 per million tokens. An alternative policy keeps the observation for the 5 calls in which it informs a decision, then replaces it with a 300-token summary carrying an inspection handle for the rest of the trajectory. Each later re-read through the handle costs one extra model call with 40,000 input tokens and returns a 2,000-token slice that stays in context for 5 calls.

Compute the carried input tokens and uncached cost of keeping the observation, and the same for dropping it with no re-reads.
Find the number of re-reads at which dropping stops being cheaper.
Tokens are not the only cost of a re-read. Identify one latency cost and one evidence risk the ledger in (a) omits, and state which of them would change the policy for a log whose failure sits in the omitted middle.

7. Scheduling a batch by footprint (Intermediate). A response proposes five calls for the connection-pool repair, listed with durations and declared footprints. read_source(pool.py) takes 2 s and reads pool.py. read_source(config.py) takes 2 s and reads config.py. apply_patch(pool.py) takes 1 s, reads and writes pool.py, and uses the version returned by the first read. run_tests takes 30 s, reads pool.py, config.py, and tests/, and writes .cache. lint(pool.py) takes 5 s, reads pool.py, and writes .cache. The workflow requires tests and lint to see the patched file.

Apply the noninterference condition to find which pairs may overlap, then give the shortest schedule and its makespan. Compare with fully serial dispatch.
Changing the linter to write .lintcache instead is a one-line configuration change. Compute the new makespan.
The model proposes replacing lint and run_tests with one bash -c "make check" call that runs both in sequence for 35 s and whose footprint is undeclared. What must the runtime do with it, and what does that cost in makespan relative to (b)?
Between the read of pool.py and apply_patch, a teammate commits a change to the same file. The patch arguments still pass schema validation. State which descriptor field and which endpoint operation reject the stale patch, why a separate version check before the write is insufficient, and what the rejection returned to the model should contain.

8. Retention windows and delayed attempts (Advanced). A runtime retries a mutating call against an endpoint that deduplicates by operation ID. Each attempt waits a 10 s timeout, then backs off 1, 2, 4, and 8 s before attempts two through five. The network can delay a request by up to 120 s before delivery. The endpoint retains operation IDs for 60 s after first receipt.

Compute the send time of each attempt and the retention window needed so that no delivered attempt of this operation can execute a second time.
The endpoint’s retention is fixed at 60 s. Show that no schedule containing even one retry closes the gap, then redesign the contract so every attempt carries the original logical operation’s admission timestamp and the endpoint rejects the operation more than 45 s after that timestamp. Assuming clocks agree within 2 s, which attempts may the runtime still send while preserving that expiry bound?
Critique the redesign. What new failure mode does request expiry introduce, what outcome must the runtime record when every permitted attempt times out, and which settlement mechanism from section 7.5 takes over?

9. One shell or twelve tools (Advanced; second lighthouse). A team proposes giving the remediation agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) a single run_shell tool with a 500-token descriptor in place of 12 structured tools of 350 tokens each, citing fewer selection errors. A trajectory makes 30 model calls at $3 per million uncached input tokens. With structured tools, an attempt costs $1.20, is accepted with probability 0.80, and causes an unconfined production change with probability 0.001; with the shell those figures are an attempt cost reduced by the descriptor savings, acceptance probability 0.78, and unconfined-change probability 0.004. Each unconfined change costs $2,000 to detect and repair.

Compute the per-trajectory descriptor savings and \(\CostPerAcceptedTask = \mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability\) for each design, first from token costs alone and then including expected change losses in the attempt cost.
Find the unconfined-change probability the shell design would need to match the structured design’s \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\).
Critique the team’s evaluation metric, and propose a toolkit that keeps most of the descriptor savings without the loss. Say which mechanism bounds the shell’s reach and which staging policy recovers context capacity.


What’s Next: From tool interfaces to execution isolationA well-specified, authorized tool can still execute faulty or untrusted code. The boundary checks a call’s arguments against the task’s grants, but a general-purpose command runner such as run_shell accepts commands whose effects no argument check can bound, and even a narrow tool’s implementation can reach whatever its host process can. A descriptor does not limit which files the running code reads, which external services it contacts, or how many resources it consumes. Agent Sandboxes develops the execution envelope that enforces those limits beneath the running code, extending the tool contract from permitted requests to contained execution.

title: 7 Tool Calling
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why does a tool call that parses cleanly still need a runtime between it and the world?
A tool call is the first point at which a model’s output can change something outside the conversation. A proposal that parses cleanly can still name a target the task was never granted, act on a file that has changed since the model read it, or repeat an operation whose first attempt already took effect. Generating the call therefore cannot be what authorizes it. The runtime must stand between proposal and effect, validating each call against its schema, checking it against the grants the task holds, dispatching it, and recording what is actually known about the result. That record is often incomplete. A request that times out may have been lost, may still be running, or may have succeeded without a delivered reply, and a blind retry can restart healthy workers or apply the same change twice. The outcome has to stay explicitly unknown until the runtime settles it, rather than be filled in by the model’s account or the runtime’s optimism. What returns to the model is itself a design decision, because a log far longer than the next call can hold must be cut down without hiding the line that matters, and a job that outlives one turn must report back without being mistaken for a finished one. Tool calling keeps the model a proposer and leaves authority with the runtime, which exercises it only on evidence it can check.

Learning Objectives

Trace a proposed tool call through validation, authorization, dispatch, and a correlated observation into the next model call
Design a tool descriptor that separates structural validation from action-time preconditions enforced with the effect
Distinguish tool discovery and connectivity from the grants required to invoke an operation
Select blind retry, endpoint deduplication, or reconciliation for an uncertain effect from operation semantics and loss rates
Design bounded observations that preserve execution status, omission information, and the scope of available evidence
Compare waiting and resumption strategies for long-running tools by detection delay, inference cost, and retained supervision
Evaluate toolkit granularity by context cost, cost per accepted task, and enforced reach across structured, general-purpose, and computer-use interfaces

title: 7 Tool Calling
text:
An agent asked to restart a container on a staging server, the kind of infrastructure change the remediation agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) makes, emits a short tool call. The host runtime checks the call against the tool’s schema, confirms that this session may restart that container, and sends POST /containers/srv-stage-04/restart. Two seconds later the socket times out. The request may be lost, delayed, still executing, or completed without a delivered reply. A retry could restart healthy workers, and the first attempt can still take effect after the timeout.



The Authority axis, closed at the tool boundary by mediating every proposed call.
Nothing about this failure is exotic. The repair agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)) meets the same questions on every turn of the connection-pool repair. It reads src/pool.py, replaces text derived from the version it read, runs the test suite, and receives a log far longer than the next model call can hold. Each step is a tool call, and each can be rejected, left running, completed without a reply, or answered with more output than the model should see.
The pieces built so far do not settle these questions. Messages and tool definitions gave the model a structured way to propose a call, and the memory chapters already relied on tools to read sources, search indexes, and update records without examining what happens between a proposal and its result. A retrieval result identifies the version it observed, but whether the file still has that version when a later edit commits is an action-time precondition that something must enforce. A proposal names an operation and its arguments. It does not decide whether this task may run the operation, whether an earlier attempt already ran it, or what the next model call should receive.
This chapter builds the runtime’s tool boundary, the path between a proposed call and the environment it would change. The boundary validates each proposal, checks it against the task’s grants, dispatches it, tracks what is known about its effect, and returns a bounded observation matched to the call. Throughout, it keeps apart the three things the timeout blurs: what the model proposed, what effect the operation had, and what evidence the runtime holds about either.


↩︎ The separation of proposal, effect, and observation is established in The trajectory as the systems management boundary.
The chapter follows one call from proposal to observation, then widens to effects whose outcome stays uncertain, to output too large to return whole, to jobs that outlive a model turn, and finally to the catalog of tools the model sees.

title: 7 Tool Calling
text:
Listing 1 shows the staging restart as one turn of the loop, in a provider-neutral form. The runtime reports what it knows about this attempt, and the next model call receives that result together with the earlier request and proposal.



Listing 1: One turn of the tool-call loop: A call identifier correlates the proposed call with its result. The next model call receives the timeout as an unknown effect, not as evidence that the restart did not happen.


[
  {"role": "user",
   "content": "Stage-04 is serving a stale config. Restart it."},
  {"role": "assistant",
   "content": [
     {"type": "tool_call", "id": "call_1", "name": "restart_container",
      "arguments": {"container_id": "srv-stage-04"}}]},
  {"role": "tool",
   "content": [
     {"type": "tool_result", "call_id": "call_1",
      "content": {"transport_status": "timeout", "effect_status": "unknown"}}]}
]



The runtime correlates each result with its corresponding call using an explicit identifier rather than message order alone. That identifier establishes message lineage across asynchronous turns, but correlation alone does not resolve whether the target service completed the requested mutation. Preventing duplicate restarts requires an operational contract for idempotency, developed in section 7.5. Even if the subsequent model turn assumes that the service recovered, the runtime preserves the underlying uncertainty. It authorizes a retry only when idempotent semantics, an endpoint deduplication contract, or reconciliation evidence that also rules out a still-delayed attempt supports it; fresh evidence that the container looks unchanged is not enough on its own (section 7.5.1).


At the model-side call surface, an inference engine emits structured invocation blocks rather than unstructured natural text. Once the model outputs a proposal, the runtime assumes full custody of execution. Between the moment a tool call leaves the model and the moment an observation enters the context of the next turn, the runtime mediates the entire round trip across the four coordinated stages in figure 1: argument validation screens inputs against tool schemas, policy authorization verifies security grants, dispatch executes the permitted operation while tracking outcomes, and observation shaping normalizes raw results into bounded prompt payloads.


↩︎ The six-phase turn lifecycle, whose validation, execution, and observation phases these four stages refine, is established in The six-phase turn execution lifecycle.
Request validation parses proposed arguments against the tool’s declared schema, verifying required fields, data types, value ranges, and relational invariants among parameters. Dynamic constraints that depend on volatile environment state cannot be settled at this boundary; the system must evaluate them at the execution boundary rather than inferring them from historical context. Next, operation authorization verifies the active session’s security grants and access policies against the targeted resource, for read operations as well as state mutations, and admits the call against its concurrency budgets and rate limits.
Following authorization, dispatch submits the permitted operation to the underlying execution provider while outcome tracking maintains execution identity and status. This tracking distinguishes cleanly among pre-dispatch rejections, active background tasks, successfully reported results, and unconfirmed execution states. A transport timeout simply indicates that the runtime exceeded its waiting deadline, leaving the remote execution state unconfirmed. Finally, observation shaping maps the raw return value back to the originating call identifier, truncating payloads to fit context budgets, sanitizing terminal escape sequences, and tagging the output with accurate status metadata. If log output must be truncated, the payload explicitly discloses the omission; if a system returns an asynchronous job ticket, observation shaping reports it as an acknowledgment rather than a completed effect.
Certain validation checks must execute at the remote endpoint because safety requires atomicity with the state change itself; for example, an edit conditioned on a source version requires the version check to occur in lockstep with the update. Consequently, the host runtime and the remote endpoint each enforce their respective boundaries. The endpoint checks access independently, even for requests that the host runtime already cleared. This division reflects the end-to-end argument applied to system protection: an authorization check that depends on private endpoint state can be finalized only at that endpoint, making preliminary host-level checks useful performance optimizations rather than authoritative substitutes (Saltzer et al. 1984).






Figure 1: The tool-call loop: Validation and authorization can reject a proposed call before dispatch. For a dispatched call, the runtime tracks the available outcome and shapes the return into a bounded observation matched to its call identifier. An unknown effect remains unknown in that observation.



When the serving interface returns native structured call blocks, the runtime extracts the proposed operation and arguments directly. When a model emits proposals within unstructured free text, the runtime must first detect and parse those fragments before validation can proceed. Constrained decoding eliminates syntactic parsing failures by enforcing grammar rules directly during token generation. However, syntax alone never establishes operational safety: whether the target resource exists, whether the observed version remains current, and whether the current session holds execution privileges remain runtime checks that no decoding grammar can verify.



Securing the tool interface rests on complete mediation (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975), the protection principle that already required the tool handler of Likelihood and checked properties to check a validated path again when the read executes. At the tool boundary, mediation must govern both reads and mutations. Emitting a tool name does not grant the model ambient runtime authority, nor does receiving an observation make external data trusted.

Definition 7.1: Complete mediation
Complete mediation requires every proposed access to pass through an enforced authorization boundary before it reaches the protected resource. In an agent runtime, the return path is also mediated so that observations enter context under explicit access, payload, and status contracts.

Significance: A valid-looking call cannot bypass the checks governing what the session may read, change, or disclose.
Distinction: Schema validation establishes structural admissibility, not permission. Observation normalization establishes a usable representation, not the truth of its contents or immunity to prompt injection, attacker-controlled content that attempts to redirect the model.
Common pitfall: Treating a prompt instruction such as “never delete production data” as an access barrier. The runtime must enforce the restriction even when the model proposes the prohibited action.



Anderson formalized the architectural component required to enforce complete mediation: the reference monitor (Anderson 1972).

Definition 7.2: Reference monitor
Reference monitor is the enforcement component through which every access to a protected resource passes. It must be tamper-proof, always invoked, and small enough to verify. In an agent runtime, the host’s validation and authorization path is the reference monitor for proposed tool calls, and each endpoint’s access check is a second monitor for the resources that endpoint owns.

Significance: The three requirements turn complete mediation from an intention into a checkable property of the runtime’s structure.
Distinction: The policy specifies permitted accesses, whereas the reference monitor provides the non-bypassable mechanism that evaluates and enforces those rules on every attempt.
Common pitfall: Adding a tool route that does not pass through the monitor, such as an unrestricted shell with network access beside a checked file adapter, which makes the adapter’s checks advisory.



These three requirements dictate concrete architectural choices at the tool boundary. Tamper-proofing ensures that neither generated model tokens nor untrusted data ingested from external systems can alter the authorization rules enforced by the runtime. Always-invoked mandates that every operational path pass through the monitor without exception. Exposing an unrestricted shell runner alongside a sandboxed file tool, for example, completely undermines the protection boundary, because the agent can bypass file restrictions by issuing shell commands. Finally, verifiability requires policy decisions to be deterministic, auditable software checks. Although an auxiliary classifier or guardrail model can score operational risk, probabilistic inference cannot be verified in the strict systems sense; the monitor itself must enforce deterministic access boundaries.
Two operational rules follow directly from complete mediation, and this chapter applies them systematically. The grant rule establishes that execution authority derives solely from the session’s active security grants, re-evaluated on every invocation. Read operations demand the same rigorous mediation as state mutations, because returning private records discloses sensitive data even when environment state remains unchanged. Nothing the model sees or emits enlarges those grants, whether a schema-valid call or a tool description claiming broad permission; later sections apply the rule to each new artifact they introduce. The evidence-scope rule establishes that an observation confirms only the specific metric or condition measured by the tool during that invocation. Reporting that an operating system process exited with code zero confirms only process termination; it does not prove overall task completion, which remains a distinct judgment governed by invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)). Furthermore, raw output text remains untrusted data even after the runtime strips terminal formatting and normalizes metadata; observations supply empirical evidence of state, but they carry no ambient authority to dictate subsequent actions.



A single model response can propose multiple tool calls simultaneously, such as reading three source files in parallel. When operations are strictly read-only and independent, the runtime can dispatch them concurrently, correlating each returned observation with its respective call identifier. A failure in one read does not invalidate concurrent operations that succeeded. Nevertheless, every invocation in the batch must individually pass validation and authorization, and the combined batch consumes from a shared resource and rate-limit budget.
State mutations complicate concurrent execution. For example, reading src/pool.py concurrently with another call that edits it yields non-deterministic results depending on scheduling race conditions. When tools declare a trustworthy resource footprint, the explicit read set \(\ToolCallReadSet_i\) and write set \(\ToolCallWriteSet_i\) of each call \(\ToolCallIndex\), the runtime can evaluate potential data hazards. Calls \(\ToolCallIndex\) and \(\PeerToolCallIndex\) may run concurrently when neither writes state the other reads or writes, \(\ToolCallWriteSet_i \cap (\ToolCallReadSet_j \cup \ToolCallWriteSet_j) = \emptyset\) and \(\ToolCallWriteSet_j \cap \ToolCallReadSet_i = \emptyset\), which are Bernstein’s conditions for noninterference (Bernstein 1966). Reads of two different files pass both conditions; a read and an edit of src/pool.py fail the first, because the edit writes the file the read reads. This guarantee, however, relies entirely on the completeness of footprint declarations; any hidden side effect or undeclared shared dependency invalidates the concurrency guarantee.

Bernstein, Arthur J. 1966. “Program Analysis for Parallel Processing.” IEEE Transactions on Electronic Computers EC-15 (5): 757–62. https://doi.org/10.1109/PGEC.1966.264565.
Operations with opaque side effects, such as arbitrary shell commands, possess unknown footprints. In such cases, the runtime must either isolate the execution environment, serialize calls conservatively, or reject batched execution in favor of fine-grained tools. Furthermore, when operations exhibit causal dependencies, those ordering constraints must originate from the workflow policy or an explicit dependency graph; the sequential order of tokens generated by the model does not constitute reliable evidence of intended execution order. Batching also does not imply atomicity: a batch forms a transaction only when the underlying tool substrate explicitly provides transactional all-or-nothing rollback semantics.
The runtime can also govern whether the model proposes an action. Using serving-level tool-choice control, the runtime can configure tool calling as optional, mandate that the model invoke at least one tool, restrict selection to a specific named operation, or forbid tool execution altogether. Orchestration engines use these constraints to guide execution phases, for instance forcing a diagnostic read before permitting an edit, or disallowing tool calls to force a final textual summary. Tool-choice controls, however, only shape model generation; under the grant rule, forcing a tool choice confers no operational authorization. Executing each stage of this mediated round trip requires an unambiguous request representation, establishing a strict operational boundary between static schema validation and dynamic preconditions verified at dispatch time.

title: 7 Tool Calling
text:
Recall the connection-pool repair (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)) right at the transition from revision r17 to r18. The model has inspected src/pool.py and emitted a proposed patch. Before applying that modification to real infrastructure, the host runtime must resolve four fundamental questions: which tool operation the model selected, what its arguments denote, whether the current task possesses the authority required to execute the mutation, and whether the underlying target file still matches the exact source state on which the model based its proposal. A well-formed JSON payload satisfies syntactic structure, but syntax alone cannot answer these operational questions.
A tool descriptor defines an operation’s functional purpose, input parameters, expected return values, and execution side effects. Within that descriptor, the argument schema codifies machine-checkable constraints: required fields, primitive types, permitted enumerations, and supported size bounds. These specifications serve two distinct audiences: natural-language descriptions guide the language model in selecting and parameterizing tools, while the surrounding runtime and downstream service endpoints validate and enforce the interface contract.


To make these guarantees concrete, consider a tool named conditional_replace_file. This tool replaces a single file in the task’s designated workspace, but commits the change only if that file still matches the expected source version. The descriptor must establish several semantic invariants: path resolves strictly relative to the designated workspace rather than an arbitrary host location; expected_version identifies the baseline source revision the model inspected; and replacement supplies the complete replacement content encoded in the endpoint’s documented format. Under this specification, passing an empty replacement string explicitly truncates the file to zero bytes instead of serving as a shorthand instruction to leave contents unmodified.
Full file replacement keeps this precondition example transparent, though production runtimes often prefer line-anchored patches or structured diffs to minimize token generation overhead. The interface comparison in Interface Benchmarking shows that localized edits reduce generated output; they still demand identical coordination between precondition verification and atomic mutation.
Listing 2 illustrates the machine-checkable argument structure. The request payload contains neither a credential token nor a privilege flag through which the model might expand its access rights. The host runtime independently binds the invocation to the task’s authorized execution context.



Listing 2: Conditional file replacement arguments: The schema describes the request’s structure. Its descriptions do not implement path confinement, authorization, or atomic version checking.


{
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["path", "expected_version", "replacement"],
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "path": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 1,
      "description": "File path relative to the designated workspace."
    },
    "expected_version": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 1,
      "description": "Source version returned with the inspected file."
    },
    "replacement": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "Complete replacement text, written as UTF-8."
    }
  }
}



The descriptor’s result contract requires equal precision. A completed replacement reports the affected path and its newly assigned revision token. A version conflict explicitly reports that the target diverged and the replacement was not applied. Furthermore, the runtime must clearly distinguish deterministic client errors (malformed arguments or insufficient authority) from indeterminate transport failures where the endpoint’s state remains unknown after a dropped connection. A comprehensive descriptor explicitly models all four outcomes, including network timeouts where no acknowledgment arrives.
Precise field names and descriptions eliminate avoidable ambiguity during generation. For example, a file-reading tool should state whether its offset argument counts bytes, characters, or lines. Similarly, a timeout parameter must state its measurement units and specify whether it bounds connection establishment, remote execution, or end-to-end response delivery. While clear documentation guides the model toward valid parameters, the execution runtime must programmatically enforce all defaults, enumeration sets, and numerical bounds. Grounding model generation in explicit tool documentation yields measurable reliability improvements: Patil et al. (2023) demonstrated that models trained to condition tool invocations on retrieved API documentation invent nonexistent operations and hallucinate invalid arguments far less frequently than models relying solely on unconditioned prompting.



When processing a tool call, the runtime first verifies that the model produced a fully completed candidate, adhering to the invocation contract defined in The Invocation Contract. If generation halted prematurely due to token limits or client disconnection, the runtime aborts immediately; a partial payload that happens to form syntactically valid JSON cannot be trusted as an intentional tool request. Once execution status confirms a complete output, the runtime parses the candidate and validates its arguments against the tool’s registered JSON schema before performing any domain checks.
In this replacement example, omitting expected_version or supplying a numeric path fails structural validation immediately. Setting "additionalProperties": false in listing 2 likewise causes the parser to reject hallucinated arguments such as force or recursive. However, structural conformance resolves only syntax. Verifying whether the path resides within the task’s assigned sandbox, and determining whether the target still contains the inspected source revision, require distinct evaluation steps. As summarized in table 1, the runtime enforces these guarantees across layered boundaries.



Table 1: Checks at the tool boundary: Each check establishes a different part of the action contract. Rows follow the round trip; domain preconditions come last because the endpoint enforces them together with the effect, so source-dependent checks remain valid through the operation they protect.










Check
Question for the proposed edit
What passing does not establish




Argument structure
Are the required fields present with the declared types and supported constraints?
The path is permitted, the version is current, or the replacement is a correct repair.


Authority
Do the task’s current grants permit this operation on the resolved target?
The arguments fit resource limits or the operation will succeed.


Resource limits
Does the request fit enforced payload, execution, and result limits?
The target still satisfies the operation’s preconditions when the effect happens.


Domain preconditions
Does the target support this operation, and does its version match when the update takes effect?
The returned evidence will establish task acceptance.






A string formatted as a file path does not constitute a confined resource reference.1 The tool implementation must canonicalize and resolve the target inside the authorized workspace, accounting for symlinks, directory traversal escapes, and path alias changes that could redirect the operation. Similarly, declaring replacement as a string does not bound its encoded memory footprint. Production adapters enforce explicit byte-size limits on incoming payloads, bound the volume of captured diagnostic output, and apply strict execution timeouts. Static schema validation handles input syntax, whereas dynamic state verification, path confinement, and resource throttling remain runtime obligations. Schema Rules for Tool Definitions supplies a bounded edit descriptor along with schema rules for required fields, size limits, explicit units, and variant semantics.
1 Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use: Bishop and Dilger analyzed the UNIX file-access race in which the binding of a name to an object changes between a program’s check and its later use, so a privileged program can be steered onto a file it never checked (Bishop and Dilger 1996). A tool adapter that validates src/pool.py and then reopens the path by name inherits the same window: a symbolic link swapped in between turns a permitted edit into an edit elsewhere. Resolving the path once and operating on the resolved object, rather than re-resolving the string, is what closes it. 
Bishop, Matt, and Michael Dilger. 1996. “Checking for Race Conditions in File Accesses.” Computing Systems 9 (2): 131–52.
Grammar-guided decoding does not change this division of labor. A token-level mask removes syntax errors before the candidate exists, but it cannot resolve a filesystem reference, evaluate an access policy, or compare a version tag with the file’s current revision. The host runtime validates the materialized request, and the endpoint verifies dynamic preconditions at the moment the effect happens. This separation instantiates the typed action contract (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}\)), which admits a call to the environment only after validation, precondition, and authorization checks, with the version precondition enforced together with the mutation rather than during an earlier read.


↩︎ The structural guarantee of grammar-guided decoding, and the reference and permission checks it leaves open, are established in Scope of the structural guarantee.



The expected_version parameter binds the retrieval contract of The Retrieval Contract directly to the mutation contract enforced here. An earlier read operation confirmed only that src/pool.py matched revision r17 at the specific instant of observation; that read did not lock or reserve the file for future modification. If a concurrent process or another agent alters src/pool.py before the edit request arrives, applying a patch derived from r17 would silently overwrite those intervening modifications, causing a classic lost-update anomaly.
To prevent the lost update, the storage service must verify the expected version and commit the replacement as a single atomic conditional update, the storage equivalent of a hardware compare-and-swap (CAS) primitive.2 In this example, the workspace source service executes the entire sequence inside a single coordination boundary: it resolves the target file, verifies that its current revision matches expected_version, writes the new content, and publishes the resulting revision token. Decomposing this sequence into non-atomic operations (reading the revision, verifying it in user space, then issuing a write) reopens a race window where concurrent writers can intervene. The atomic conditional update closes this time-of-check to time-of-use gap.
2 Optimistic Validation Under Contention: The expected-version check is commit-time validation from optimistic concurrency control, applied to one file. What is new at the tool boundary is the price of a conflict: each failed validation costs the agent a fresh read and a new proposal, paid in model turns rather than in microseconds. 
↩︎ Why context engineering cannot close the refresh-to-execute race, and leaves the revision check to the tool boundary, is established in Detecting change and bounding uncertainty.

This execution branch yields two distinct operational outcomes:

If the current source revision remains r17, the update commits the replacement and returns r18, identifying the new revision produced by the edit.
If another writer modified the source first, the version check fails. The service rejects the replacement, leaves the storage state unaltered, and returns an explicit version-conflict status.

Following a conflict, the runtime directs the agent to perform an authorized read of the updated source file and synthesize a fresh proposal, rather than blindly overwriting the intervening modifications.
This concurrency guarantee holds only as long as all mutations route through the shared coordination boundary. If external processes or unmanaged scripts modify files directly on disk, bypassing the version service, version tokens offer no protection and the endpoint cannot ensure integrity. Dry-run previews follow the identical principle. A dry run confirms that a proposed patch applies cleanly against revision r17 at the moment of evaluation, but it establishes no lock on that revision. The runtime must re-verify all preconditions, permissions, and version tokens when executing the live write.
Receiving a successful r18 confirmation verifies that the file modification committed to disk, but it does not establish that the underlying connection-pool bug has been resolved. Demonstrating functional correctness requires empirical validation. A subsequent passing run of test_waiter_notified_on_return is evidence that the patch fixes the exercised case of the race, while broader task acceptance continues to follow the project’s verification suite. At the network layer, a dropped reply leaves the caller uncertain whether the server committed the edit or failed before processing the payload. The retry and idempotency contracts analyzed in section 7.5 resolve this operational uncertainty.



When an operation fails, the runtime must return a structured, bounded diagnostic that isolates the failure condition without leaking information beyond the task’s authorized grants. For example, a structural rejection should identify the missing expected_version property, and a concurrency conflict should state that revision r17 has been superseded. Conversely, permission rejections must refuse access cleanly without exposing directory structures, environment variables, or path hints that an agent might probe. The runtime logs whether a rejection originated locally during client-side schema validation or remotely at the service endpoint, allowing downstream decision logic to distinguish between an unattempted proposal and a failed remote mutation. Clear, bounded diagnostics provide the model with the exact evidence needed to synthesize a valid revision, which must then traverse the same validation pipeline.
The descriptor, its layered checks, and its diagnostics together define one tool’s contract, and every check so far has assumed that the runtime already holds that contract and knows which endpoint implements it. In a real deployment the contract arrives from elsewhere: a repository server, another team’s service, a vendor’s integration. How the runtime learns which operations exist, and why learning that an operation exists confers nothing, is the next problem; how many of the discovered descriptors to stage on each turn is a separate budget question that section 7.9 takes up.

title: 7 Tool Calling
text:
In practice, a tool implementation such as conditional_replace_file can live in several environments: an in-process adapter compiled into the application, a standalone background daemon, or a remote microservice managed by another team. Before the model can propose a valid call, the host runtime must determine which operations that endpoint exposes and how to encode their arguments. This discovery phase supplies that interface metadata. Under the grant rule, however, learning that an operation exists confers no authority to execute it: discovery defines interface syntax, whereas authorization governs execution rights.


When building a self-contained agent with a small, static set of tools, registering local functions directly in-process is simple and fast. However, when multiple host applications must connect to independently maintained tool services, custom point-to-point integration quickly becomes impractical. The underlying challenge is combinatorial. Without a shared interface, \(\HostRuntimeCount\) host runtimes integrating \(\ToolServiceCount\) tool services require up to \(\HostRuntimeCount \times \ToolServiceCount\) bespoke adapters. Standardizing on a common protocol reduces this burden to \(\HostRuntimeCount + \ToolServiceCount\) implementations, allowing each side to build to the specification once.



A shared protocol turns pairwise adapters into one implementation per side.
Decoupling tools across a protocol boundary also introduces critical fault isolation. When a tool runs in a separate process, a memory leak, segmentation fault, or unhandled blocking call crashes only the tool server rather than tearing down the primary agent orchestration loop. Even so, protocol standardization does not eliminate engineering responsibilities: integrators must still define tool semantics, audit version compatibility, and enforce security policies. Local in-process plugins and out-of-process tool servers represent deliberate deployment trade-offs rather than mutually exclusive or evolutionary stages.
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) exemplifies this architecture. MCP structures integrations across three distinct entities: a host application (such as an interactive environment or agent runtime), clients that manage connections, and servers that expose capabilities. The host runs one client per connected server, and each client speaks the protocol on the host’s behalf. Servers can run as local child processes or as remote network services. This architectural division clarifies integration responsibilities rather than prescribing a specific execution sandbox (Model Context Protocol 2025).
Each deployment model matches different operational demands. A local child process keeps filesystem operations adjacent to the working copy and simplifies process lifecycle management. Conversely, a remote service can centralize credential storage, connection pooling, and backend access without replicating sensitive configurations across every host machine. Both options, however, introduce distinct failure modes and resource boundaries: an unconfined local process still reaches whatever local filesystem it is granted, while a severed network link can leave an in-flight operation executing invisibly on a remote server. Architects must choose deployments based on where resource governance and policy enforcement belong, evaluating transport latency relative to tool execution duration rather than presuming any transport topology is universally superior.



MCP defines two primary wire operations for tool interaction: tools/list to discover available tool definitions and tools/call for execution.3 Each definition advertises a unique name, a natural-language description, and a JSON Schema governing accepted arguments; an invocation names the target tool and supplies a matching argument dictionary. These messages establish the mechanics of interface exchange rather than a task’s execution rights. The MCP tools specification (Model Context Protocol 2025) defines these message formats and explicitly mandates server-side input validation and access controls.
3 JSON-RPC Request Identifiers: MCP frames these messages as JSON-RPC 2.0 requests, each carrying an id that its response echoes (Model Context Protocol 2025). That identifier does the work of this chapter’s call identifier, matching a reply to its request on one connection. It says nothing about whether a second tools/call with the same arguments is the same intended effect, which is why retry safety needs the separate operation identity developed in section 7.5. 
Model Context Protocol. 2025. Model Context Protocol Specification, Version 2025-11-25. Protocol specification.
To trace where policy boundaries sit during execution, consider a repository server advertising two illustrative operations: read_source and apply_patch. A concrete integration sequence proceeds through several verification checkpoints:

The host’s client queries tools/list, and the host admits each returned schema only if its own policy allows it (for example, because the server and its version are on an allowlist), binding each admitted schema explicitly to that server instance and its locally governed tool policy. Explicit binding ensures that an identically named tool advertised by another server cannot silently shadow or replace the expected implementation.
The host determines which admitted definitions to expose in the model context for the connection-pool repair task.
When the model proposes an operation, the host runtime validates the arguments against the schema and verifies task-level authorization before transmitting the request.
Upon receiving tools/call, the endpoint independently verifies the request against the underlying operating system permissions and data access controls it manages.

For the connection-pool repair, discovering that apply_patch exists leaves the permitted edit paths and the expected-version preconditions unchanged. The guarantee of atomic, conditional updates derives entirely from the server implementation, never from an encouraging function name. If an endpoint fails to provide conditional-update guarantees, the runtime must reject it as incompatible with the task’s safety contract.



Tool descriptions provided during discovery are untrusted external inputs. A description might accurately summarize an operation, omit critical failure modes, or embed prompt instructions that attempt to steer model behavior. Even an authenticated server can supply a misleading description, because verifying a server’s identity does not imply endorsing every claim it emits. A host runtime must never promote claims such as “approved for all workspaces” into an authorization grant.
Filtering which tools appear in the model prompt narrows the attack surface, but catalog filtering alone cannot replace per-call enforcement. Task grants evolve dynamically, and call arguments select specific resources at runtime. Authorizing an agent to inspect src/pool.py does not permit it to read unrelated credentials or transmit private source code to an external service.
