title: 7 Tool Calling
text:
All quantities below are hypothetical problem givens, chosen to be round, and describe no particular provider, protocol version, or deployment. Assume message losses are independent unless a problem says otherwise.
1. Blind retry at fleet volume (Basic). A tool fleet issues 120,000 mutating calls a day to an endpoint with no deduplication. Each request is lost with probability 1 percent and each reply with probability 3 percent; lost messages never arrive later, and every timeout triggers exactly one retry.

Compute the per-call timeout probability, the per-call duplicate-effect probability, and the expected duplicates per day.
A network team offers two upgrades: halve reply loss, or halve request loss. Compute the daily duplicates under each and explain why one of them slightly increases duplicates.
Name the change that removes the duplicate path rather than shrinking it, and state what the endpoint must bind the identifier to for that change to hold.

2. Sizing the tail (Basic). An adapter stages test logs with a head-and-tail policy under \(\ObservationByteBudget = 16{,}384\) bytes, with \(\NoticeByteAllocation = 256\) bytes and \(\HeadByteAllocation = 4{,}096\) bytes. A failing run writes 9,000,000 bytes in total. Its only diagnostic is a 2,400-byte panic block, followed by 11,000 bytes of teardown output and a 600-byte final summary.

Compute \(\TailByteAllocation\) and determine whether the whole panic block reaches the model.
Keeping \(\ObservationByteBudget\) and \(\NoticeByteAllocation\) fixed, find the largest \(\HeadByteAllocation\) that keeps the entire panic block in the tail. How many bytes does the omission notice report in either configuration?
The same runner sometimes prints the panic before 200,000 bytes of teardown output. Explain why no split of this \(\ObservationByteBudget\) fixes that case, and name the mechanism from section 7.6 that does.

3. When catalog selection pays (Basic). A repair harness registers 80 tools, each contributing 420 tokens to the final serialized request. On-demand staging exposes 8 of them plus 900 tokens of selection interface and metadata, and the runtime selects without an extra model call. A trajectory makes 40 model calls, and uncached input costs $3 per million tokens.

Compute the catalog input of one call under each layout, the capacity released per call, and the break-even number of unused descriptors.
Compute the tokens and uncached dollars released over the trajectory.
In one trajectory out of five, a needed tool was not staged and the agent spends one extra model call of 30,000 input tokens rediscovering it. Does selection still pay? State the condition under which the comparison would flip.
The 80 descriptors come from three interoperable tool servers discovered at session start. One of them advertises delete_branch with a description stating that it is approved for all repositories, and the task’s grants do not include branch deletion. Does staging or omitting that descriptor change what the agent may do? Name the check that governs the call if the model proposes it anyway, where each part of that check runs, and what the returned observation should report.

4. The price of asking whether a job finished (Intermediate). A repair agent’s test suite completes after 1,500 s. Under model-directed polling, the model checks every 30 s, starting one interval after dispatch, with each status call reading a 48,000-token selected input and generating 60 tokens. The cache covers 90 percent of that input. Hypothetical prices per million tokens are $3 uncached input, $0.30 cached input, and $15 output. The fleet runs 2,000 such jobs a day.

Compute the pending-status calls per job, the incremental cost per job, and the daily fleet cost of polling.
Product management caps model-directed polling at $0.10 per job. Find the minimum poll interval that meets the cap, and the worst-case delay between completion and detection at that interval for a job whose completion time is not known in advance.
Runtime polling every 10 s costs no inference. Compare its worst-case detection delay and token cost with the answer to (b), then choose a design to ship and state what model-directed inspection remains useful for.

5. Retrying a refund (Intermediate; second lighthouse). The support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)) issues refunds through a payment endpoint that offers no deduplication contract. It sends 40,000 refund calls a day, each averaging $60. Requests are lost with probability 0.5 percent and replies with probability 1.5 percent. The alternative to blind retry is an authorized reconciliation probe written before dispatch (equation 1), which adds 4 s to the customer’s wait on every timed-out call. For parts (a) and (b), assume lost messages never arrive later and every delivered refund request executes successfully.

Under one blind retry per timeout, compute the expected duplicate refunds per day and their dollar exposure.
Under the probe policy, compute the fraction of sessions that incur the extra wait and the total added customer wait per day.
Compare the duplicate-refund exposure with the added customer wait. State what operation-specific evidence or endpoint guarantee would make the probe sufficient to settle the original refund or permit a retry, including how it rules out an attempt that could still execute before authorizing another execution. If the probe is inconclusive or the allowed wait expires, specify the recorded outcome and escalation. What response-latency limit would be needed to decide whether this policy meets the service target? Explain why a refund’s operation ID must not be a hash of the customer and amount.

6. Carry, drop, or re-read (Intermediate). A repair agent stages a 6,000-token test observation that stays in context for its remaining 45 model calls. Uncached input costs $3 per million tokens. An alternative policy keeps the observation for the 5 calls in which it informs a decision, then replaces it with a 300-token summary carrying an inspection handle for the rest of the trajectory. Each later re-read through the handle costs one extra model call with 40,000 input tokens and returns a 2,000-token slice that stays in context for 5 calls.

Compute the carried input tokens and uncached cost of keeping the observation, and the same for dropping it with no re-reads.
Find the number of re-reads at which dropping stops being cheaper.
Tokens are not the only cost of a re-read. Identify one latency cost and one evidence risk the ledger in (a) omits, and state which of them would change the policy for a log whose failure sits in the omitted middle.

7. Scheduling a batch by footprint (Intermediate). A response proposes five calls for the connection-pool repair, listed with durations and declared footprints. read_source(pool.py) takes 2 s and reads pool.py. read_source(config.py) takes 2 s and reads config.py. apply_patch(pool.py) takes 1 s, reads and writes pool.py, and uses the version returned by the first read. run_tests takes 30 s, reads pool.py, config.py, and tests/, and writes .cache. lint(pool.py) takes 5 s, reads pool.py, and writes .cache. The workflow requires tests and lint to see the patched file.

Apply the noninterference condition to find which pairs may overlap, then give the shortest schedule and its makespan. Compare with fully serial dispatch.
Changing the linter to write .lintcache instead is a one-line configuration change. Compute the new makespan.
The model proposes replacing lint and run_tests with one bash -c "make check" call that runs both in sequence for 35 s and whose footprint is undeclared. What must the runtime do with it, and what does that cost in makespan relative to (b)?
Between the read of pool.py and apply_patch, a teammate commits a change to the same file. The patch arguments still pass schema validation. State which descriptor field and which endpoint operation reject the stale patch, why a separate version check before the write is insufficient, and what the rejection returned to the model should contain.

8. Retention windows and delayed attempts (Advanced). A runtime retries a mutating call against an endpoint that deduplicates by operation ID. Each attempt waits a 10 s timeout, then backs off 1, 2, 4, and 8 s before attempts two through five. The network can delay a request by up to 120 s before delivery. The endpoint retains operation IDs for 60 s after first receipt.

Compute the send time of each attempt and the retention window needed so that no delivered attempt of this operation can execute a second time.
The endpoint’s retention is fixed at 60 s. Show that no schedule containing even one retry closes the gap, then redesign the contract so every attempt carries the original logical operation’s admission timestamp and the endpoint rejects the operation more than 45 s after that timestamp. Assuming clocks agree within 2 s, which attempts may the runtime still send while preserving that expiry bound?
Critique the redesign. What new failure mode does request expiry introduce, what outcome must the runtime record when every permitted attempt times out, and which settlement mechanism from section 7.5 takes over?

9. One shell or twelve tools (Advanced; second lighthouse). A team proposes giving the remediation agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) a single run_shell tool with a 500-token descriptor in place of 12 structured tools of 350 tokens each, citing fewer selection errors. A trajectory makes 30 model calls at $3 per million uncached input tokens. With structured tools, an attempt costs $1.20, is accepted with probability 0.80, and causes an unconfined production change with probability 0.001; with the shell those figures are an attempt cost reduced by the descriptor savings, acceptance probability 0.78, and unconfined-change probability 0.004. Each unconfined change costs $2,000 to detect and repair.

Compute the per-trajectory descriptor savings and \(\CostPerAcceptedTask = \mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability\) for each design, first from token costs alone and then including expected change losses in the attempt cost.
Find the unconfined-change probability the shell design would need to match the structured design’s \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\).
Critique the team’s evaluation metric, and propose a toolkit that keeps most of the descriptor savings without the loss. Say which mechanism bounds the shell’s reach and which staging policy recovers context capacity.


What’s Next: From tool interfaces to execution isolationA well-specified, authorized tool can still execute faulty or untrusted code. The boundary checks a call’s arguments against the task’s grants, but a general-purpose command runner such as run_shell accepts commands whose effects no argument check can bound, and even a narrow tool’s implementation can reach whatever its host process can. A descriptor does not limit which files the running code reads, which external services it contacts, or how many resources it consumes. Agent Sandboxes develops the execution envelope that enforces those limits beneath the running code, extending the tool contract from permitted requests to contained execution.

title: 5 KV Cache Management
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can an agent that is generating nothing still exhaust the memory of the machine serving it?
An agent spends much of its life waiting. While a test suite runs or a remote service responds, the model generates nothing, yet the attention state computed from the request’s prefix can stay resident in accelerator memory, holding capacity that another request could put to work. That state is large, it grows with every token the trajectory carries, and its size is fixed by the model’s geometry rather than by any choice the agent makes. A serving engine that reserves room for the longest request it might see strands much of its memory, and one that copies a shared prefix into every branch pays for the same state many times over. At each pause the engine must choose among keeping the state resident, moving it to slower memory, and dropping it to rebuild from the tokens when the agent resumes. Each option trades memory against the delay before the next output token, and the right one depends on how long the wait will last. Capacity is therefore set less by how many contexts fit at once than by how long each one stays, because a context that holds memory through a long tool wait serves no turns while it keeps its place. Managing retained attention state turns the state an agent carries into a priced claim on the machine serving it, sized against the turn rate the service must sustain.

Learning Objectives

Calculate retained attention-state memory and resident fit from model geometry, token count, and storage precision
Calculate the memory that block allocation and prefix sharing recover from full-cap reservation and duplicated prefixes
Distinguish compatible, available prefix reuse from the applicability of the underlying information
Select a chunked-prefill token budget that bounds the gap between output tokens for ongoing requests
Evaluate keep, move, and recompute policies for paused state against memory pressure and resume latency
Analyze how residence time converts a memory-fit bound into a sustainable turn rate






The connection-pool repair agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)) has reached a candidate revision, r18. Its targeted reproducer passes, prompting the harness to submit a fully serialized request of 32,768 tokens and launch an integration test suite that runs for 45 seconds. That length, a power of two that keeps the block and pool arithmetic round, is shorter than the staged request of the context-engineering examples, and every per-request footprint and transfer time below scales linearly with it. If the serving engine holds the request’s attention state in accelerator memory throughout that entire wait, the device does no work for that workflow. The model generates zero tokens during the test suite, yet its retained state pins memory that another concurrent request could put to work. This is the tool-wait problem named in the turn lifecycle of The six-phase turn execution lifecycle. Preserving that state is a deliberate systems policy, and running an agentic service requires pricing that policy against its alternatives.



State becomes a physical resource claim inside the serving system.
Earlier abstractions stop short of that physical commitment. Context Engineering established how the harness selects and refreshes prompt context for each call, and its prefix-layout calculation priced a cached prefix as a discounted line on the bill. Neither abstraction captures the physical footprint of the underlying computation: how many gigabytes of memory that retained attention state consumes, how many concurrent trajectories an accelerator can hold at once, or what the serving engine should do with that state when an agent pauses to await tool execution. Those mechanical questions dictate whether an inference node that comfortably supports a single repair workflow can scale to sustain dozens.


↩︎ Pricing a reused prompt prefix at a discounted cached-input rate is established in Preserving an exact prefix.
Managing retained attention state is not solely an internal serving problem; it spans an operational boundary between two parties. The application caller controls its submitted context, tool execution timing, and any cache-management hints the serving API exposes. The serving operator controls physical device allocation, memory placement, compute scheduling, and retention policies. When the two belong to separate organizations, as with hosted commercial model APIs, the caller cannot manage physical accelerator memory directly. Instead, the application influences retention only through the interfaces and pricing tiers the service exposes. Distinguishing where these responsibilities divide clarifies which performance levers belong to the agent harness and which belong to the serving engine, the inference software that executes model calls and manages accelerator memory. The word “runtime” keeps its earlier meaning here, the agent runtime that runs the loop around the model.
The chapter follows the r18 request’s attention state through its life in the serving engine, and each stage raises the question the next one answers. Sizing the state from model geometry shows how few 32,768-token contexts fit in the memory left after the weights (section 5.2). Allocating that state naively strands much of the pool (section 5.3), which fixed-size blocks recover while letting forked candidates share a prefix (section 5.4). Sharing within one request invites reuse across turns, which needs an index over retained prefixes and a rule for what to evict (section 5.5). Whatever the cache misses must be prefilled without stalling other requests’ generation (section 5.6). The test wait itself forces a choice among keeping, moving, and dropping the paused state (section 5.7). Finally, residence time turns a count of resident contexts into a sustainable turn rate (section 5.8).



The r18 request’s 32,768 tokens do not reach the accelerator as raw text. During causal self-attention in a Transformer decoder, each newly generated token attends to earlier tokens through their key and value projections (Vaswani et al. 2017). Recomputing these projections at every decode step would repeat the linear transformations over the entire historical prefix, creating an unsustainable quadratic compute bottleneck. Serving engines avoid this recomputation by retaining the computed key and value tensors in accelerator memory across decode cycles.1 While autoregressive decoding relies on retained attention state, sustaining long-horizon agent execution requires managing its physical capacity, allocation overhead, and multi-tenant residency.
1 Memory-Limited Inference: Caching keys and values trades quadratic recomputation for persistent memory capacity, and that memory quickly becomes the primary serving bottleneck. An analytical study of large-model serving revealed that sharing a single key-value head across all query heads allowed an identical deployment to serve contexts more than an order of magnitude longer, precisely because retained attention state, rather than compute throughput, bounded context length and batch concurrency (Pope et al. 2023). Managing this memory footprint determines whether an agent deployment scales. 
Pope, Reiner, Sholto Douglas, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Jacob Devlin, James Bradbury, Jonathan Heek, Kefan Xiao, Shivani Agrawal, and Jeff Dean. 2023. “Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference.” Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems (MLSys) 5: 606–24.

↩︎ Retained attention state in autoregressive decoding is established in Conditional token selection.


Definition 5.1: KV cache
KV cache is the per-sequence store of attention keys and values that the model has computed for already processed tokens, retained so that later tokens can attend to them without recomputing their projections.

Significance: Its payload scales linearly with retained tokens; consequently, sequence context length, rather than static model parameter count, determines how many concurrent requests can share the memory pool remaining after loading model weights.
Distinction: It represents intermediate projected state rather than a raw copy or semantic compression of input text. Reconstructing it requires executing the exact token sequence through identical model weights and layer configurations.
Common pitfall: Budgeting only for input prompts. Every newly decoded output token appends key and value states at every layer, so a request reaches its maximum memory footprint at completion rather than during initial prefill.



For a decoder employing causal self-attention with uniform layer geometry, every retained token contributes both a key vector and a value vector across all layers. Let \(\LayerCount\) represent the number of layers, \(\KvHeadCount\) the number of key-value heads per layer, \(\AttentionHeadDimension\) the dimension of each head, and \(\ElementStorageSize\) the storage size in bytes per element. Accounting for both vectors yields the memory footprint per token:
\[\KvCacheBytesPerToken = 2 \cdot \LayerCount \cdot \KvHeadCount \cdot \AttentionHeadDimension \cdot \ElementStorageSize \tag{1}\]
A sequence retaining attention state across \(\SequenceLength\) tokens requires an aggregate cache payload of \(\KvCacheMemory = \SequenceLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\). Here \(\SequenceLength\) counts only the tokens whose keys and values have already been evaluated; each newly sampled token increments \(\SequenceLength\) once the model completes its forward pass.
The key-value head count \(\KvHeadCount\) in equation 1 represents the number of stored attention heads, which often falls below the query head count. Multi-query attention pushed this reduction to its structural extreme by sharing a single key-value head across all query heads2 (Shazeer 2019). Grouped-query attention strikes an intermediate balance: several query heads share one key-value head, dividing the stored key-value head count by the group size relative to a standard multi-head design (Ainslie et al. 2023), a scaling quantified across attention designs in Attention State by Attention Design. Because this head grouping is established during pretraining, a serving allocator cannot dynamically drop heads from an existing checkpoint without fundamentally altering the model’s computations.
2 Multi-Query Attention: Motivated primarily by memory bandwidth rather than storage capacity (incremental decoding reloads stored key and value tensors at each generation step), sharing key-value tensors across query heads drastically reduces memory bus traffic alongside physical storage with minimal quality loss (Shazeer 2019). Grouped-query attention subsequently recovered nearly all multi-head attention quality while preserving the bulk of these memory savings (Ainslie et al. 2023). Consequently, the head count \(\KvHeadCount\) in equation 1 is an architectural parameter established at pretraining. 
Shazeer, Noam. 2019. “Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head Is All You Need.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1911.02150.

Ainslie, Joshua, James Lee-Thorp, Michiel de Jong, Yury Zemlyanskiy, Federico Lebr’on, and Sumit Sanghai. 2023. “GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints.” Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP).
While equation 1 accounts for the raw tensor payload under dense causal attention, physical memory consumption in production serving engines exceeds this theoretical bound. Allocation block granularities, memory alignment, page table metadata, and quantization scales all add runtime overhead. Non-uniform architectures, such as sliding-window attention or compressed latent representations, require their own capacity models.
The worked estimate uses a representative configuration: the Llama 3 70B model geometry, with 70.6B parameters, and a DGX H100 node containing 8 accelerators. While specific hardware platforms and checkpoint dimensions vary, the underlying capacity arithmetic remains unchanged. Unlike the single-device, 8-bit illustration in Per-call work estimate, both weights and KV cache tensors use 16-bit storage here, with the model weights sharded across the node’s accelerators by tensor parallelism. The aggregate high-bandwidth memory remaining after provisioning model weights and a runtime reserve constitutes the KV pool. The number of active sequences whose KV payloads can reside simultaneously within this pool defines the resident-fit bound. This aggregate derivation assumes perfectly balanced shards without redundant weight replication; in production, memory limits must be satisfied on every individual accelerator device. None of the r18 context’s internal structure survives into this accounting: system prompt, tool schemas, workspace state, turn history, and latest observation all become key and value tensors at every layer, so the whole 32,768-token context costs 10.7 GB whatever its zones contain (figure 1). The figure’s zones follow the change-rate order of context staging. Its shared invariant prefix is the root of instructions and tool schemas together with the slow-changing workspace description, its growing trajectory state is the rest of the trunk, and its active turn is the leaf.






Figure 1: From Agent Context to KV State: A 32,768-token agent context (a), divided into system prompt, tool schemas, workspace, turn history, and the latest observation, becomes key and value tensors at every layer (b). The grouped-query model’s per-token footprint then sets how many such contexts fit in the node’s KV pool, before allocator overhead and headroom.




Napkin Math 5.1: Sizing the attention state of an agent trajectoryProblem: Consider a server node of 8 accelerators, each with 80 GB (vendor-rated in binary gigabytes, about 85.9 GB in the decimal units used throughout this chapter), for 687.2 GB of aggregate accelerator memory. Model weights occupy 141.2 GB, and the runtime reserves 20 GB for dynamic activations and scratch buffers. Under full causal attention without prefix sharing, how many independent sequences can simultaneously reside in the remaining memory across different context lengths?
Math: Evaluating equation 1 for this architecture yields \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken = 2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 327,680\;\text{bytes/token}\). For an agent trajectory retaining 32,768 tokens, the footprint becomes \(\KvCacheMemory = 32,768 \times 327,680\;\text{bytes} \approx 10.7\;\text{GB}\).
Subtracting model parameters and runtime buffers isolates the usable capacity: \(687.2 - 141.2 - 20 \approx 526.0\;\text{GB}\). Dividing this available pool by the footprint per sequence and taking the floor determines the resident-fit bound. Using exact floating-point values prior to display rounding yields \(\left\lfloor 525.994767360 / 10.737418240 \right\rfloor = 48\). Table 1 evaluates this bound across three operational context regimes.



Table 1: Payload and resident fit: Each sequence stores its own full-attention state; the calculation excludes allocator overhead and additional headroom.










Retained tokens
KV payload per sequence
Sequences that fit




8,192
2.7 GB
195


32,768
10.7 GB
48


131,072
42.9 GB
12






Systems insight: Resident capacity scales inversely with retained context length. Because model weights occupy a fixed memory slice regardless of context, expanding sequence length directly cannibalizes the cache pool. Each fourfold increase in sequence length (from 8,192 to 32,768, and onward to 131,072 tokens) reduces the resident sequence capacity by roughly 75 percent. Retained context length is the primary control lever governing serving capacity, and the agent runtime directly governs it. Maintaining an active working set rather than accumulating unbounded historical observations (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}\)) keeps requests operating in the high-density rows of table 1. These figures are raw tensor payloads; physical memory allocators, page fragmentation, and safety headroom further reduce actual capacity, while translating instantaneous resident capacity into sustainable request throughput requires analyzing sequence residence times (section 5.8.2).


Model weights incur a one-time memory cost that is amortized across all concurrent requests, whereas every independent sequence imposes an additive burden through its private attention state. Common prefixes across requests reduce this marginal cost only when the serving engine systematically caches and reuses identical attention prefixes across turns.
Both model architecture and numerical precision dictate the per-token payload before memory allocation even begins. An architecture trained with fewer key-value heads or compressed latent representations3 reduces the state generated per token. Similarly, quantizing keys and values to 8-bit or 4-bit representations halves or quarters the raw element bytes \(\ElementStorageSize\), though it introduces dequantization scale metadata and potential numerical degradation that engineers must validate against target task benchmarks. Regardless of compression, every retained byte represents allocated physical memory tied to an ongoing execution lifecycle.
3 Latent KV Compression: Multi-head latent attention compresses keys and values into a single low-rank latent vector per token and dynamically reconstructs per-head tensors during attention, exchanging additional projection arithmetic for a substantially smaller memory footprint (DeepSeek-AI et al. 2024). Although this technique modifies the calculation of \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\) in equation 1, it preserves the fundamental system dynamics: latent cache tensors must still be paged, allocated, retained across idle periods, and evicted under memory pressure. 
DeepSeek-AI, Aixin Liu, Bei Feng, Bin Wang, Bingxuan Wang, et al. 2024. “DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2405.04434, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2405.04434.
How much the architecture moves the payload is easiest to see across published geometries. Figure 2 evaluates equation 1, and its latent-attention counterpart, for six registered models: one with full multi-head attention, four with grouped-query attention, and one with multi-head latent attention.














Figure 2: Attention Architecture Sets the KV Payload: (a) Bytes retained per token at 16-bit precision for six published model geometries, on a logarithmic axis, colored by attention design. (b) One session’s KV payload against retained tokens for one model of each design, beside the memory of a single accelerator. Parameter count barely predicts the payload: the latent-attention model, the largest of the three in panel (b), caches the least. The dotted segment extends the multi-head model past its trained window for scale only.



The spread in figure 2 is fixed at pretraining; the serving engine can work within it but cannot change it. Full multi-head attention in the GPT-3 (175B) geometry retains 4,718.6 KB per token, 67× the 70.3 KB of the latent-attention DeepSeek-V3; even the grouped-query Llama-3.1-70B of the worked estimate retains 4.7× as much. At the 131,072 tokens of the long regime, that is 42.9 GB against 9.2 GB for one session. The choice of model therefore fixes the slope of every capacity line in this chapter, and the runtime’s levers (retained tokens, sharing, precision, and eviction) act only along that slope. Whatever the slope, each retained byte stays allocated for as long as its sequence holds the prefix, which is where the lifecycle decisions begin.
In the running repair agent scenario, deciding whether to keep attention state resident while waiting for an external test suite to run exemplifies this lifecycle tension. Holding the attention state in accelerator memory avoids restoration of the retained prefix when the tool returns observations, but keeping gigabytes of memory pinned for an idle agent deprives concurrent requests of accelerator resources. Before exploring eviction and caching policies, however, the serving engine must translate theoretical tensor footprints into physical memory allocations. Statically pre-allocating contiguous buffers for a sequence’s maximum potential context wastes the memory pool through severe internal fragmentation long before actual tensor payloads fill device capacity.



In an agentic workflow, request lengths are dynamic and fundamentally unpredictable. When an automated repair agent executes an integration test and receives a compiler traceback or test log, its next generation step requires KV cache space for both the accumulated history and the newly ingested tool output. The serving system must accommodate this growth on the fly, without knowing in advance how many tokens the model will generate or how many tool-call iterations will follow. While a static footprint calculation determines the memory consumed by tokens processed so far, the memory allocation policy governs runtime behavior: how much spare buffer to reserve at admission, whether an expanding sequence must be relocated in memory, and how rapidly reclaimed capacity returns to the shared pool.


The simplest allocation strategy is static reservation, which provisions a contiguous memory buffer sized to the configured token cap (\(\ContextWindow\)) the moment a request is admitted. Static reservation eliminates reallocation stalls and out-of-memory errors during generation: because the maximum possible buffer is already secured, the sequence expands within its pre-allocated envelope without moving. However, this safety incurs severe structural waste. Any unpopulated buffer capacity remains locked for the entire lifetime of the request, completely inaccessible to concurrent sequences. This reservation accounts solely for KV cache state; activation tensors and ephemeral runtime scratchpads draw from separate memory pools.
In the 526.0 GB KV pool modeled above, an admission cap of 32,768 tokens requires 10.74 GB for each reservation. Dividing the pool by this single-request footprint bounds concurrency to at most 48 resident reservations, assuming balanced tensor-parallel sharding across accelerators and no auxiliary overhead beyond the baseline runtime reserve. The count matches the 32,768-token row of table 1 because a full-cap reservation is exactly that context’s footprint, whether or not the tokens ever arrive.
Now consider the resulting capacity utilization for a mixed request population, mostly short turns with occasional long trajectories like r18, all admitted under the same cap. If those requests finish at a mean length of 2,048 tokens, each reservation is only 6.25 percent populated even upon completion, holding 2,048 valid token states out of 32,768 allocated slots. During earlier decoding steps, utilization is lower still. Empirical evaluations confirm that this structural waste dominates naive serving systems: when Kwon et al. (2023) profiled early systems, actual token state accounted for only 20.4 to 38.2 percent of allocated KV memory, with the remainder lost to reservation slack and fragmentation.
A second strategy grows a contiguous allocation incrementally as tokens arrive. When adjacent capacity is unavailable in the allocator’s address space, the memory manager cannot simply extend the buffer in place. Instead, it must allocate a larger buffer elsewhere, copy all existing key and value entries from the old buffer to the new buffer, and then release the original space. This approach incurs two severe penalties: the allocator must hold both buffers simultaneously during the transfer, causing transient memory spikes, and the synchronous copy consumes substantial memory bandwidth. Contiguity here refers to an unbroken span in the allocator’s virtual address space, which the accelerator already translates to physical memory in hardware. The restriction therefore comes from software, not from the memory hardware. Standard attention kernels locate a token’s keys and values by a fixed stride from the start of one buffer, so each sequence’s KV tensor must occupy a single span. Removing that requirement calls for an indirection the serving engine itself controls, because the decisions that matter belong to the engine: how many tokens a unit of allocation holds, how many sequences reference each unit, and when a shared unit must be copied before a write. The remedy is a software table the attention kernel reads directly (section 5.4).



Unused slots inside an active reservation constitute internal fragmentation; free capacity split across disconnected extents too small to satisfy a contiguous request constitutes external fragmentation. This classic distinction originates in early storage allocation research for multiprogrammed systems4 (Randell 1969). Table 2 separates them because each condition demands a distinct systems remedy: eliminating reservation slack cures the first, whereas changing the allocation granularity cures the second.
4 Internal and External Fragmentation: The analysis of storage allocation that named the two losses also measured their trade: rounding requests up to fewer standard sizes cost more storage in internal fragmentation than it recovered in external fragmentation (Randell 1969). Paged KV allocation makes the same trade on purpose, accepting at most one partial block per sequence in exchange for a pool in which any free block fits any request. 
Randell, Brian. 1969. “A Note on Storage Fragmentation and Program Segmentation.” Communications of the ACM 12 (7): 365–69, 372. https://doi.org/10.1145/363156.363158.



Table 2: Unused KV capacity: Reservation slack belongs to an allocation; external fragmentation concerns free space that cannot satisfy a particular contiguous request.










Condition
Where capacity is unavailable
Consequence




Internal fragmentation
Inside an allocation, beyond its initialized entries
Other requests cannot use the reserved slots


External fragmentation
In separate free extents of a variable-size allocation pool
A contiguous request can fail even when aggregate free capacity is sufficient






Consider a concrete example of external fragmentation. Suppose an allocator has three free extents of exactly 256 token slots each, separated by live allocations. A new sequence requiring 512 contiguous slots arrives. Even though the allocator holds 768 free slots in aggregate (more than enough capacity to satisfy the request), the allocation fails because no individual extent can accommodate 512 contiguous slots. The failure stems entirely from the contiguity requirement rather than an absolute shortage of memory.
In an agentic repair workload, this memory pressure becomes acute because a paused trajectory retains its allocation under naive retention policies while waiting for tool execution, even as concurrent requests demand memory to grow. A robust serving system therefore requires two complementary architectural mechanisms: first, a space-efficient allocation unit, which fixed-size blocks provide, and second, an explicit lifecycle and eviction policy, which section 5.7 develops.




When an integration-test log extends an agent’s repair context, the serving engine need not relocate the existing KV tensor to find a larger contiguous buffer. Instead, it allocates additional fixed-size physical blocks and appends their identifiers to the request’s block table. The attention kernel dereferences that table when reading earlier token positions. PagedAttention demonstrated this combination of dynamic block allocation and noncontiguous attention over KV storage (Kwon et al. 2023). Its lineage traces directly to paged virtual memory. The Manchester Atlas one-level store introduced paging in 1962 to decouple a program’s contiguous virtual address space from scattered physical page frames (Kilburn et al. 1962). The block table applies this same indirection to token positions, allowing sequences to grow dynamically without requiring contiguous physical allocations.

Definition 5.2: Paged KV block table
Paged KV block table is a per-sequence software mapping from logical token blocks to the physical KV blocks that store their initialized key and value entries.

Significance: A sequence can grow by acquiring another block without relocating its existing blocks.
Distinction: The table maps token positions for the attention kernel; it is not the accelerator’s hardware page table.
Common pitfall: A mapped block has allocated capacity, but only its initialized token entries may be read as valid KV state.





Consider an illustrative block size of four tokens, chosen to make the mapping concrete rather than to recommend a production configuration. A ten-token prefix occupies logical blocks 0, 1, and 2. Its block table contains [3, 7, 9]: token positions 0–3 reside in physical block 3, positions 4–7 in block 7, and positions 8–9 in the first two slots of block 9. Physical block IDs are pool indices managed by the allocator, not raw memory addresses or token sequence numbers.
For any token position, the attention kernel determines its logical block index via integer division by the block size, consults the block table to locate the physical block, and calculates the token’s offset within that block using the modulo remainder. For token position 9 with a four-token block size, the kernel calculates logical block \(\lfloor 9 / 4 \rfloor = 2\), looks up physical block 9, and determines offset \(9 \bmod 4 = 1\) (the second slot). Computing the final byte offset in device memory incorporates the model layer, KV head index, and tensor stride conventions. This software lookup preserves logical sequence ordering even when physical blocks are scattered across high-bandwidth memory among other requests’ blocks, as panel (a) of figure 3 traces for position 9.






Figure 3: Block Table Indirection and Tail Copy-on-Write: Panel (a) follows each logical block through its table entry to a physical block scattered among other requests’ blocks; position 9 resolves to logical block 2, then to physical block 9, slot 1. Panel (b) shows two candidates that share the full blocks 3 and 7, while candidate B’s private append first copies the two initialized entries of the shared tail into block 14.



Because every block in the allocator’s pool is interchangeable and of identical size, any free block satisfies an allocation request. Paging thereby eliminates external memory fragmentation at block granularity. The remaining memory overhead consists of block-table metadata, temporary scratchpad buffers, and unallocated slots in each sequence’s final block.



Because sequence lengths rarely align with block boundaries, the final block of a sequence typically contains uninitialized slots. This internal fragmentation constitutes the tail waste \(\KvBlockTailWaste\). For a block holding \(\KvBlockSize\) tokens, tail waste is bounded by \(0 \leq \KvBlockTailWaste \leq \KvBlockSize-1\), with an expected value of \((\KvBlockSize-1)/2\) when sequence lengths yield uniformly distributed remainders modulo \(\KvBlockSize\). A sequence whose length is an exact multiple of \(\KvBlockSize\) incurs zero tail waste.
Block size presents a fundamental systems trade-off:

Smaller blocks (for example, 16 tokens) reduce worst-case tail waste and permit fine-grained prefix sharing and copy-on-write duplication. However, they inflate block-table metadata and increase indexing overhead for the attention kernel.
Larger blocks (for example, 64 tokens) amortize bookkeeping costs and align more effectively with memory bus transactions and tensor core tile dimensions on modern accelerators, but they increase tail waste and copy overhead during branch forks.

Selecting an appropriate block size therefore requires balancing sequence length distributions, tree-search branching patterns, and hardware memory access characteristics.

These values are node-wide footprints summed across all model shards, not the local allocation on a single accelerator.
The maximum unused tail contains one fewer slot than a full block. A 16-token block can therefore leave at most 15 slots (4.92 MB) unutilized, while a 64-token block can leave at most 63 slots (20.64 MB) unutilized.
For a 32,768-token agent context, even the larger block’s worst-case tail waste represents only 0.2 percent of the sequence’s total memory footprint.
Systems insight: Because tail slack is bounded by at most one block per unshared sequence, its relative overhead diminishes as sequence length increases. At multi-thousand-token agent context lengths, tail waste ceases to be the governing constraint. Engineers should select block sizes primarily to optimize attention kernel throughput and sharing granularity, revisiting tail waste only when serving workloads dominated by short sequences.





The final-length snapshot estimate is about 16× the full-cap reservation count.
Translating these worst-case bounds into expected memory overhead requires evaluating the workload’s sequence length distribution. Consider final sequence lengths modeled as a capped exponential distribution with a mean of 2,048 tokens, bounded by the 32,768-token ceiling established for static reservation. Under this distribution, 16-token blocks leave 0.4 percent of allocated KV memory unutilized, whereas 64-token blocks leave 1.5 percent.
Dividing the same pool, which accommodated only 48 static worst-case reservations, by the expected paged footprint gives a planning estimate of approximately 780 final-length request snapshots, a 16× increase over full-cap reservation. This capacity multiplier represents the core payoff of paging: memory allocation expands incrementally as tokens are generated, rather than reserving buffer space for an upper bound that most requests never reach. This estimate describes a hypothetical population sampled at completion; the requests resident in a running service have a length distribution that also depends on growth and residence time. Actual admission must account for current unique blocks and the generation growth the controller promises. The gain is close to the ratio of the cap to the mean final length, 32,768 to 2,048, so it measures how far the population falls short of the cap. A request like r18 that actually grows to the cap gains no resident capacity from paging. What paging still buys it is growth without relocation, block-level sharing with forked candidates, and memory that is claimed only as tokens arrive rather than at admission.



Agent workflows that sample parallel candidates to gather empirical verification (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)) make context branching frequent. Multiple candidate actions or code patches branch from an identical prompt and tool-execution prefix, diverging only in their subsequent generations. The breadth allocation of Parallel sampling along the breadth axis already priced this branching in memory. With the prompt stored once, peak KV demand grows as the prompt plus each candidate’s own tokens; without sharing, every candidate carries its own copy of the prompt. Paging is the mechanism that delivers the first form. In a paged KV cache, the candidates’ block tables point to the same physical blocks for all shared prefix tokens, provided the model architecture and runtime configuration allow block sharing.
The difference is large at agent context scales. Under contiguous allocation, giving each of four candidate branches its own copy of an 8,192-token prefix requires writing 10.7 GB of KV state for the Llama 3 70B geometry, counting the four new copies and not the parent’s original. That is the footprint of one full 32,768-token context, since four copies of 8,192 tokens hold that many token positions. Under paged allocation, duplicating the block tables avoids copying any tensor payload whatsoever. The engine merely updates software metadata and increments reference counters; cloning a block table requires work proportional to the number of block entries rather than the roughly ten gigabytes of underlying KV data.
A shared sequence tail requires special handling when branches diverge. If the final block of a shared prefix is only partially filled, two concurrent candidates cannot independently append new tokens into its remaining empty slots without overwriting each other. In the ten-token example, both candidates initially share the block table [3, 7, 9]. Physical block 9 contains only two valid tokens (positions 8 and 9 in slots 0 and 1). Before candidate B writes token position 10, the engine allocates a fresh physical block 14, copies the two initialized entries from block 9 into block 14, and updates candidate B’s final block-table entry to point to block 14. Candidate B then writes token 10 into slot 2 of its private block 14. This copy-on-write5 operation leaves candidate A’s state unchanged, as panel (b) of figure 3 draws. Table 3 records the ownership transition, assuming these two candidates are the sole owners of the prefix.

Copy-on-write is necessary only when mutating a shared, partially filled block. When a candidate branches at an exact block boundary—for instance, after a twelve-token prefix using four-token blocks—token position 12 initiates a new logical block (\(\lfloor 12 / 4 \rfloor = 3\)). The generating candidate simply allocates an unshared block from the free pool and appends its ID to its block table, requiring no data copying. Similarly, if a partial tail block is already privately owned (reference count of 1), the candidate appends subsequent tokens directly into the remaining slots without allocation or copying. The engine selects the appropriate operation based on two state variables: the occupancy of the target block and its current reference count.
When an agent discards an unpromising candidate trajectory, the engine decrements the reference counts of its constituent physical blocks. A block returns to the free pool when its reference count reaches zero and all outstanding device operations (tracked via asynchronous completion events) have finished. Furthermore, as discussed in the next section, a dormant prefix-cache entry may retain physical blocks even after an active request completes, preserving them across subsequent agent turns. Total physical memory consumption is therefore governed by the number of unique physical blocks resident on the accelerator, not the aggregate logical token count across all active candidates.

Checkpoint 5.1: Reasoning about KV allocation
The allocation policy must preserve each sequence’s state while managing capacity shared by many requests.

Reservation estimate: If the hypothetical mean final length doubled to 4,096 tokens under the same 32,768-token cap, what fraction of each static reservation would be populated at completion, and would static reservation admit any more sequences?
External fragmentation: Identify why the three free extents in the example cannot satisfy its contiguous request, and why a fixed-size block pool changes that condition.
Tail ownership: Trace a private append to a shared partial tail and distinguish it from an append at a full-block boundary.
Reclamation: Explain why ending an active request does not always make its blocks immediately reusable.



Paged allocation decouples logical sequence expansion from physical memory layout, eliminating external fragmentation while enabling zero-copy prefix sharing across concurrent trajectories. However, sharing state across independent requests or across subsequent turns of an agent session requires a complementary mechanism: the serving engine must identify matching historical prefixes across disparate requests and manage cache retention under memory pressure. That capability is the domain of prefix caching.




In the connection-pool repair scenario, the agent invocation that processes an integration-test result often begins with the identical system prompt, tool definitions, and historical observations present in the preceding turn. If the serving engine retained the corresponding key-value (KV) activations from that earlier call, it can attach those existing tensors directly to the new request, prefilling only the newly arrived tokens. On the bill, this saving appears as a discounted cached-input rate; in system implementation, it translates into a concrete serving architecture governed by an index, an explicit ownership contract, and an eviction policy.

Definition 5.3: Prefix cache
Prefix cache is the serving system’s index of retained KV state, keyed by exact token prefix and computation configuration, allowing subsequent requests sharing that initial sequence to attach existing state instead of recomputing it during prefill.

Significance: It converts repeated prefill work into an index lookup across request boundaries. The computational savings grow with the length of the matched prefix and recur on every turn that preserves that prefix, making stable prompt layouts essential across long trajectories.
Distinction: Block sharing reuses state among candidates that the engine forks from one request and therefore knows to be related; a prefix cache must find reusable state, by content, for requests that arrive independently over time, and it can offer only what memory pressure and eviction have left resident.
Common pitfall: Assuming a cache hit guarantees semantic freshness. Matching cached tokens verifies identical historical inputs and execution settings, but it does not check whether the real-world state described by those tokens has changed.





In causal full-attention architectures, reusable KV state requires an exact, contiguous token prefix starting from the very first position of the sequence, rather than semantically similar phrasing, because attention state is derived from the token prefix (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\)). Matching token identifiers is merely the first prerequisite. The cached KV tensors remain mathematically valid only when generated under identical execution parameters: the same base model weights, active low-rank adaptation (LoRA) adapters (lightweight fine-tuned weight adjustments), positional encodings, and attention masks. For multimodal requests containing images, audio, or structured embeddings, matching the synthetic placeholder tokens in the text prompt is insufficient; the underlying tensor inputs and projection parameters must match exactly. A production serving engine must encode these operational dependencies directly into its cache keys or validate them before binding cached blocks to a request.
Compatibility, physical availability, and tenant isolation represent three distinct verification boundaries. Computationally compatible tensors may have already been evicted from accelerator high-bandwidth memory (HBM), or they may reside in host memory or on solid-state drives, requiring an explicit page-in transfer before the model can consume them. Conversely, tensors residing directly in local accelerator memory may belong to a different tenant or security domain, making them ineligible for sharing under isolation rules. The reusable prefix length is the longest contiguous token sequence that simultaneously satisfies compatibility, physical residency, and access permissions. That sequence is frequently shorter than the longest match found in the prefix tree. Furthermore, newly generated tokens qualify for subsequent prefix matching only after their corresponding KV blocks have been fully materialized in memory and committed to the index.
These structural requirements operate independently of semantic validity. Updating a target repository from commit r17 to r18 does not alter or invalidate the KV activations previously computed for an older prompt describing r17. Those tensors remain numerically identical and computationally compatible with the stale prompt, even though the context no longer reflects the current state of the code. The harness’s context-selection policies govern which evidence to provide to the model. When the agent harness updates or replaces outdated logs in the serialized prompt, the prefix matcher detects the divergence, immediately terminates the match at the first altered token, and triggers a fresh prefill for the updated text. The prompt layout, rather than the cache layer, enforces freshness.


↩︎ How the harness withdraws a stale observation, such as the r17 test failure, while keeping it as history is established in Context Invalidation.



A radix prefix cache organizes stored token sequences using a compressed prefix tree (a radix tree), where each edge represents a variable-length sequence of tokens rather than a single symbol (Zheng et al. 2024).6 To resolve a cache match, the scheduler walks the tree from the root, matching prompt tokens along successive edges until reaching a divergence point. This traversal simultaneously identifies the longest common prefix and the physical KV blocks storing its activations. Once a match is identified, the engine must acquire explicit ownership of those memory blocks before the background eviction thread can reclaim them. Lookup overhead scales with the prefix length examined, remaining on the order of microseconds on host CPUs. Alternatively, systems can implement an equivalent reuse contract using chained hash tables, where each fixed-size block is keyed by a cryptographic hash of its token content concatenated with the hash of its parent prefix.
6 Compressed Prefix Tree: The trie stored one symbol per edge, so a shared prefix was found by walking from the root (Fredkin 1960). PATRICIA collapsed chains of single-child nodes into one edge, so index size grows with the number of stored keys rather than their length (Morrison 1968). The same compression matters for KV reuse, because agent prefixes run to thousands of tokens and a one-token-per-edge index would spend a node on each of them.

Morrison, Donald R. 1968. “PATRICIA—Practical Algorithm To Retrieve Information Coded in Alphanumeric.” Journal of the ACM 15 (4): 514–34. https://doi.org/10.1145/321479.321481.
The tree’s shape follows from the causal dependence that context staging already turned into a layout rule. Every position’s keys and values depend on the full history before it, so a node’s KV state is valid only beneath its exact ancestors, and an identical passage that follows a modified token lives on a different branch with no reusable state. The layout rule is the harness’s half of the same constraint. Staging volatile components (dynamic counters, tool outputs, scratchpad notes) toward the end of the prompt keeps the long invariant prefix on one path from the root, and compaction that rewrites only trailing turns leaves that path intact.

Physical memory allocation introduces a practical policy choice at block boundaries without altering the underlying definition of compatibility. Suppose a later request matches the ten-token prefix whose blocks [3, 7, 9] were traced earlier, with block 9 holding two initialized entries. A serving engine that supports partial-tail reuse preserves all ten tokens and resolves the new turn’s divergent append with the same copy-on-write step recorded in table 3. An engine that caches only complete blocks reuses eight tokens and prefills the remaining two. Both designs are valid: the partial-tail strategy minimizes redundant prefill at the expense of copy-on-write buffer management, while the full-block strategy simplifies allocation by trading a modest amount of recomputation for uniform block lifecycles.



When an inference request finishes, the serving engine releases the request’s execution handles on the allocated KV blocks. The cache manager, however, retains its own structural references to those blocks, keeping them in memory as dormant state in case a subsequent request can reuse them. The system’s retention policy determines whether the next turn finds that KV state immediately resident in accelerator memory, must page it back from host RAM, or must recompute it entirely.
Reusing and reclaiming memory blocks requires strict ownership tracking across concurrent threads and hardware streams. When a request matches a cached prefix, the memory manager increments reference counts on the corresponding blocks before dispatching execution kernels. Conversely, before reclaiming a physical block under memory pressure, the allocator must sever the cache’s indexing reference, confirm that active execution references have dropped to zero, and synchronize with outstanding device streams that might still be reading or writing those memory addresses. The allocator must also synchronize index modifications and reference changes so that a concurrent lookup cannot bind to a block while background eviction is tearing it down.
In tree-structured prefix caches, leaf-first eviction maintains structural consistency by preserving contiguous paths from the root and evicting unused leaf nodes first. Because internal nodes store common prefix state shared across multiple conversation branches, evicting an ancestor would invalidate all of its downstream descendants. An internal node becomes eligible for reclamation only after all of its descendant children have been evicted. Within the set of eligible leaves, systems frequently adopt a least-recently-used (LRU) policy (Zheng et al. 2024), operating on the premise that recent access predicts near-term reuse (Belady 1966).7 Reclamation therefore cascades upward. An inactive parent cannot be reclaimed while its child remains cached, but once the child leaf is evicted, the parent itself becomes an eligible leaf and can be freed if memory pressure persists (figure 4).
7 Replacement with Foresight: The classic study of page replacement showed that the optimal policy evicts the page whose next use lies furthest in the future, a rule no online system can apply because it needs the future reference string (Belady 1966). Recency-based policies approximate it. An agent harness sometimes holds part of that future, such as a tool launch that will idle a prefix for minutes, which is why a retention hint from the caller can beat recency alone.

Leaf-first eviction keeps residency prefix-closed, meaning that every resident node’s ancestors are also resident, and in full-attention models that property is an operational necessity. While freeing an upstream prefix block leaves the numeric values of a retained downstream suffix physically untouched, causal attention requires the entire preceding context to evaluate subsequent tokens. An orphaned suffix block is useless on the accelerator until its missing ancestral prefix is either reloaded from auxiliary storage or recomputed through a new prefill pass.
Retention policies therefore balance occupied accelerator capacity against the computational cost a future hit would eliminate. Recency alone provides an imperfect signal: an agent may generate a speculative branch that is never visited again, whereas a system prompt shared by hundreds of concurrent agent workers remains valuable despite sporadic gaps between calls. More resilient eviction schemes score cached nodes by balancing their expected reuse probability and recomputation cost against their physical memory footprint, adapting the retention weights to match dynamic workload demands.



Counting raw matching tokens in a prompt overstates real-world system benefits whenever matching blocks have been evicted, tenant isolation policies prohibit sharing, or memory allocators round matches down to physical block boundaries. Systems engineers evaluate caching efficacy by measuring the tokens actually served from reusable KV state without recomputation. Across a specified workload window, the token-weighted prefix hit rate is defined as
\[\PrefixHitRate = \frac{\sum_{i} \ReusedPrefixLength^{(\WorkloadRequestIndex)}}{\sum_{i} \PromptLength^{(\WorkloadRequestIndex)}} \tag{2}\]
where \(\PromptLength^{(\WorkloadRequestIndex)}\) represents the prompt token count of request \(\WorkloadRequestIndex\), and \(\ReusedPrefixLength^{(\WorkloadRequestIndex)}\) counts the prompt tokens whose compatible KV activations were attached without recomputation after enforcing availability, security permissions, and block-alignment constraints. In the earlier four-token block example, a request matching ten tokens under a full-block-only caching policy yields \(\ReusedPrefixLength = 8\), leaving two tokens to be prefilled. A production telemetry pipeline should also distinguish warm hits (state already resident in accelerator HBM) from cold hits (state that must be restored across PCIe from host memory).
The concrete computational value of a prefix hit follows directly from prefill arithmetic. Consider a deliberately small 4,096-token prefix of invariant system instructions and tool definitions; the longer shared zone of the r18 context would save more. Retaining this sequence in memory occupies 1.34 GB of KV activations distributed across the server node. Reconstructing that state from scratch requires roughly 578 trillion operations for linear projection layers, plus approximately 22 trillion operations for causal self-attention (equation 4). If the node sustains 45 percent of its peak 16-bit floating-point throughput (about 3,560 trillion operations per second), rebuilding that prefix incurs 169 ms of prefill latency on every single cache miss. In contrast, a turn that scores a cache hit and appends only a 32-token suffix bypasses the prefix prefill entirely, requiring only a single memory-bandwidth-bound pass over the model weights. Because a 32-token suffix provides too little parallel arithmetic to saturate the accelerator’s matrix units, execution time is bounded by the weight-read floor of roughly 5 ms. Both numbers come from one step-time model that the rest of the chapter reuses. A forward pass over \(\ForwardPassTokenCount\) token positions takes \(\WeightOnlyStepTime(\ForwardPassTokenCount) = \max\left(\PerDeviceWeightReadTime,\; 2\Parameters \ForwardPassTokenCount/\AttainableComputeRate\right)\), the larger of the time \(\PerDeviceWeightReadTime\) to read the weights once from accelerator memory and the time to perform \(2\Parameters \ForwardPassTokenCount\) weight operations at the sustained rate \(\AttainableComputeRate\). These are the two per-token floors of equation 2.7 applied to a whole pass; equation 5 derives the bound and its assumptions. The rebuild estimate above adds the attention term, which this weight-only model omits. The hit thus replaces 169 ms of prefix prefill with a pass of about 5 ms, and a trajectory that keeps its invariant prefix stable collects that saving on every turn, in both latency and aggregate prefill work.
Although equation 2 measures the computational work avoided during prefill, end-to-end request latency also includes novel suffix prefill, autoregressive token generation, batch scheduling delays, and memory transfers. Once a hit eliminates prefix compute, any of these can dominate total response time. When monitoring production clusters, a declining prefix hit rate warrants investigating both sides of the client-service interface. On the client side, minor modifications in prompt serialization—such as altered whitespace, injected timestamps, or reordered JSON schema keys—prematurely truncate prefix matches. On the server side, heightened memory pressure, poor cross-node routing, or mismatched runtime configurations can render compatible state unavailable or physically inaccessible.
When using hosted model APIs, application developers require an explicit reuse contract rather than relying on unverified assumptions about the provider’s internal memory allocator. This contract must clearly define eligible token inputs, compatible execution configurations, tenant isolation boundaries, and supported retention lifetimes. In agentic workflows, cache expiration tightly couples this reuse contract to tool execution latency. If an external tool call blocks longer than the provider’s idle eviction threshold, the subsequent turn discovers that its cached prefix has been purged and incurs a full prefill penalty, the remote equivalent of the drop-and-recompute policy described in section 5.7. An agent harness aware of these eviction horizons can anticipate cache misses during long tool waits rather than absorbing unexpected latency spikes. The cached-token metric returned in API usage records is the client’s primary telemetry signal, though interpreting it requires understanding its precise operational scope.

Systems Perspective 5.1: Reading a cached-token countA usage record that reports cached input tokens indicates how many prompt tokens the provider served from reusable KV state, which is the numerator of equation 2 for that specific request. However, this metric remains silent on where those tensors resided (accelerator HBM vs. host DRAM), how the provider indexed them, or how long they will remain unevicted before the next invocation.
Its diagnostic value emerges when tracked across successive turns of an agent trajectory. Dividing the cached-token count by the total prompt tokens yields the caller’s observed prefix hit rate. A count that abruptly plunges to zero following an extended tool execution is consistent with cache expiration under idle eviction, but memory pressure, routing changes, and incompatible execution settings can produce the same observation. A count that stabilizes below the expected value may indicate an early prompt serialization divergence. Comparing submitted token prefixes and checking request routing and execution settings helps distinguish that client-side cause from unavailable or ineligible cached state. A confirmed layout divergence is an issue the client application can resolve directly in its prompt assembly pipeline.


An agent application must maintain functional correctness regardless of whether a request hits or misses the cache; the serialized context, not the cache, dictates the model’s true prompt input. A cache hit simply eliminates redundant arithmetic. When an agent turn introduces a voluminous test log or extensive retrieval chunk, it inevitably injects new prefill compute into the execution engine. Scheduling that compute-intensive prefill phase alongside latency-sensitive, memory-bandwidth-bound token generation for existing requests constitutes the fundamental serving challenge addressed next.




Prefix reuse eliminates redundant computation on shared prompt prefixes, but new observations inevitably introduce fresh work. When the repair agent submits selected integration-test output, the serving engine must process the uncached suffix of the serialized request before generating the next response token. Other requests may already be generating tokens on the same accelerators. If the engine schedules the entire new prefill as one uninterrupted monolithic batch, those ongoing decode streams must wait for that pass to finish before executing their next decode step. In interactive agent workflows, that stall translates directly into noticeable inter-token latency spikes.
Trimming the observation reduces the raw number of tokens to process, but once the request reaches the server, scheduling determines how execution time is shared among active streams. The engine does not need to execute a long prefill as an all-or-nothing unit. Continuous batching already re-forms the batch at every forward step, admitting and retiring requests between token-generation steps (Yu et al. 2022), and that per-iteration boundary is exactly where a slice of one request’s prefill can be combined with other requests’ decodes. By splitting long prefills into smaller token chunks that co-run alongside ongoing decodes, the scheduler bounds how long any single iteration can stall active generation streams (Agrawal et al. 2023, 2024).

Definition 5.4: Chunked prefill
Chunked prefill is a scheduling policy that splits a request’s uncached prompt into token spans processed over several engine iterations, each iteration also advancing ongoing decodes, while preserving causal order.

Significance: It bounds the gap between consecutive output tokens for ongoing requests to the duration of a single chunked iteration rather than a full monolithic prefill, at the expense of a modest delay in time to first token for the new request.
Distinction: A chunk represents an execution quantum for the scheduler rather than a physical storage layout. The memory allocator maps the resulting KV activations into memory blocks whose page sizes operate independently of chunk boundaries.
Common pitfall: Treating the per-iteration token budget as an exact wall-clock time limit. Iteration latency depends on attended context length, memory bandwidth, and batch composition, so operators must calibrate the budget against measured gaps between output tokens under realistic workloads.





Under autoregressive causal attention, processing a later chunk requires access to the compatible per-layer KV state generated by earlier prefixes. Each query token in the active chunk attends to all preceding prompt tokens as well as prior and concurrent tokens within its own chunk, enforced by the causal mask, while remaining blind to subsequent tokens. The engine preserves correct positional encodings and mask logic as it extends the stored KV state, loading previously computed keys and values from memory rather than recomputing their projections from raw token embeddings.
Chunking therefore alters the temporal execution schedule while preserving exact causal semantics, modulo minor floating-point non-associativity across kernel tiling and batching configurations. This scheduling flexibility incurs two physical costs: subsequent chunks must repeatedly stream earlier KV activations from high-bandwidth memory, increasing aggregate memory traffic, and smaller prefill slices introduce additional kernel-launch and scheduling overheads.



To balance throughput and latency, a scheduler establishes an iteration-level token budget \(\IterationTokenBudget\). In standard autoregressive decoding, each scheduled decode request contributes exactly one token position, whereas each scheduled prefill contributes the token count of its next chunk. An engine iteration admitting prefill chunks of size \(\PrefillAllocatedTokenCount_i\) alongside a set \(\DecodeRequestSet\) of active decode requests must satisfy
\[\sum_{i} \PrefillAllocatedTokenCount_i + \lvert\DecodeRequestSet\rvert \le \IterationTokenBudget \tag{3}\]
while ensuring that the admitted combination fits within available accelerator memory. A request whose prompt spans multiple chunks retains its partially computed prefix KV state in memory across iterations while waiting for its subsequent slices to run.
A common scheduling policy prioritizes ongoing decoding requests by reserving \(\lvert\DecodeRequestSet\rvert\) slots first, dedicating the remaining capacity \(\IterationTokenBudget - \lvert\DecodeRequestSet\rvert\) to prefill chunks. This decoding-first priority ensures steady token generation for active streams without requiring them to wait for an entire multi-thousand-token prompt. However, the arriving request may require several iterations to complete its prefill, particularly if heavy decode traffic restricts the available chunk size. Conversely, allocating too much budget to prefill chunks can starve decode streams and trigger latency spikes. A robust scheduler must balance decode responsiveness against prefill completion progress to avoid both stream stalls and prompt starvation.
The weight-only step-time model \(\WeightOnlyStepTime(\ForwardPassTokenCount)\) of the prefix-hit estimate gives the scale of this trade-off, with \(\ForwardPassTokenCount\) the token positions that equation 3 admits in one iteration. With 32 ongoing decodes and nothing else, each step sits at the weight-read floor of about 5 ms. Admitting a 4,096-token prefill as one unit adds about 162 ms of arithmetic before those decodes run again (weight work only, so slightly below the 169 ms prefix rebuild, which includes attention), stretching their gap between tokens to about 168 ms.
Dividing that prompt into 512-token chunks reshapes execution. Each iteration now carries 544 positions and takes about 22 ms. Because the decodes advance in each of the eight iterations, their worst gap is about 8× smaller, while the new prompt completes after about 173 ms instead of 162 ms. Chunking buys existing streams a much shorter gap for a modest delay in the new request’s first token.
On one time axis, the monolithic schedule leaves a single long gap between two output tokens, while the chunked schedule places a token at every iteration boundary and finishes the prompt only slightly later (figure 5). Both schedules omit attention traffic, which grows with each chunk’s context, and per-iteration overhead, so measured iterations run longer and the budget must come from measurement.

Admitted as one unit (a), the prefill separates two decode tokens by about 168 ms. Split into 512-token chunks (b), every iteration also advances the decodes, so the gap is one iteration of about 22 ms, and the prompt finishes slightly later.
