Characterizing these trade-offs requires replaying representative arrival traces across candidate token budgets while tracking key systems metrics: time to first token for newly admitted requests, inter-token latency for active decode streams, aggregate token throughput, and accelerator memory occupancy. High-percentile latency measurements, such as the p99 inter-token gap, expose transient scheduling hiccups far better than arithmetic averages, which easily conceal the disruptive stalls of occasional large prefills. Systems designers must also distinguish server iteration step times from client-perceived streaming intervals; downstream buffering, transport serialization, and network round-trip times introduce variances that server-side metrics do not capture.
Selecting the token budget \(\IterationTokenBudget\) ultimately balances hardware execution efficiency against service responsiveness. Smaller chunks provide frequent scheduling checkpoints that protect inter-token deadlines, yet they extend total prompt completion times and add kernel-launch overhead. Larger chunks maximize tensor-core utilization by providing wider matrix dimensions during attention and feed-forward operations, but they penalize concurrent decode streams with longer stalls. In practice, operators configure the token budget to the largest chunk size whose corresponding iteration duration comfortably satisfies the target inter-token latency objective for active streams. On the reference node, the weight-only estimate gives the starting point. An inter-token target comfortably above 22 ms admits the 512-token chunk alongside 32 decodes. A tighter target forces smaller chunks and a later first token for the new request, while running the prompt unchunked exposes the decodes to the full 168 ms gap. Measured attention traffic and per-iteration overhead then shrink the admissible chunk from that estimate.



Chunking resolves prefill-decode contention by time-slicing compute on a single worker node. Prefill-decode disaggregation, the disaggregated serving that the call-latency decomposition introduced as a way to meet time-to-first-token and per-token objectives separately, takes the structural alternative and decouples the two phases across distinct pools of specialized workers (Patel et al. 2024; Zhong et al. 2024). Because prefill is compute bound and decode is memory bandwidth bound, disaggregation allows operators to tailor parallelism strategies independently, allocating tensor parallelism across high-throughput accelerators for prefills while grouping decodes onto workers optimized for high-bandwidth memory capacity. These architectures compose: a separated prefill worker can still process prompts in chunks to manage memory footprint and smooth its pipeline.
Decoupling the execution phases replaces intra-node compute contention with an inter-node network handoff. When a prefill worker finishes processing a prompt, it must transfer the resulting KV activations to an assigned decode worker before autoregressive generation can start. This handoff requires preallocating compatible cache blocks on the destination accelerator, aligning memory layouts across heterogeneous attention kernels, and streaming tensors over high-speed interconnects. If network fabrics saturate or queueing builds up at either worker pool, the latency of this state transfer can quickly exceed the compute savings gained from phase isolation.
Systems architects must therefore evaluate disaggregation across the full end-to-end path—accounting for queueing delays at both stages, serialization overheads, and network transfer latencies—rather than evaluating isolation against idealized peak interconnect speeds. For an agent interacting with a hosted model endpoint, these internal cluster topologies remain abstracted behind the serving API. The agent experiences their consequences indirectly through overall request latency, streaming variance, and concurrency limits.
Chunking and disaggregation govern how active requests share compute resources during model execution. Once generation completes and an agent suspends execution to invoke an external tool or inspect an environment, the operational challenge changes from scheduling compute to managing idle memory. Deciding whether that trajectory’s KV state remains resident in accelerator memory, spills to host memory, or evicts entirely becomes the governing concern.




The r18 request’s 45-second integration test is the tool-wait problem in its plainest form. When an agent invokes an external tool, such as a long-running test or a query to a remote database, the serving system faces an extended idle period before the tool returns its output. Although the model performs no active generation during this pause, retaining its key-value cache in accelerator memory ties up scarce HBM. To prevent idle requests from starving active generation, the serving engine must execute a paused-state policy: retain the state in device memory, offload it to host memory or secondary storage, or drop it entirely and reconstruct it when the tool output arrives. Systems research on tool-augmented generation evaluated these same three mechanisms—preserve, swap, and discard—selecting dynamically among them per request to minimize wasted accelerator memory (Abhyankar et al. 2024). This choice balances device memory capacity against host storage, interconnect transfer time, and recomputation latency. It belongs below the model. Invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) closes mechanical bounds below the model, and the pool is such a bound. The model cannot observe how full the pool is, nothing in a proposal can enforce a release, and the correctness of the next turn never depends on where the state was kept. The serving engine therefore executes the policy and decides keep, move, or drop. The agent runtime may supply hints, such as the expected length of the wait or whether the trajectory is likely to resume at all, and a hosted service exposes them only through its API. The model neither makes the decision nor supplies the hints, and its proposals never touch the lifecycle.

Evaluating a pause policy begins by measuring the physical memory that the policy can actually free. In a paged KV cache, an agent’s logical sequence length does not map directly to reclaimable capacity. Prefix blocks shared with active concurrent trajectories, such as common system prompts or branching execution paths, must remain allocated on the accelerator as long as another request holds a valid reference. Similarly, blocks currently committed to in-flight asynchronous direct memory access (DMA) copies or active kernel operations cannot be freed until those transfers complete. The uniquely reclaimable footprint consists solely of unshared blocks with no pending operations, and every pause calculation must use this footprint as its baseline.
Offloading state requires available capacity at the target tier and a coordinated handoff protocol. To maintain memory safety, the engine must preserve source blocks in accelerator memory until the outbound DMA transfer to host memory verifies successfully. During the transfer window, the state consumes both device HBM and host DRAM concurrently. The host-memory budget must therefore accommodate these transient transfer buffers alongside already parked trajectories. Upon resumption, the sequence reverses: the scheduler must allocate accelerator blocks, initiate an inward transfer, and update page tables before attention kernels can resume execution.
Discarding the KV cache relinquishes the computed state while preserving the underlying information, provided the raw input sequence and environment observations remain recorded in durable logs. Because attention state is derived from the token prefix (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\)), state lost this way can be derived again. If the request resumes, the engine reconstructs the missing attention state by re-running prefill across the historical prompt. This reconstruction requires exact provenance: the precise token sequence, active LoRA adapters, position encodings, attention masks, and multimodal embeddings. A compressed conversation summary cannot substitute for the raw token history. Reconstruction typically reuses any compatible prefix blocks that remain in memory and prefills only the missing suffix. In managed inference platforms, callers can exploit these trade-offs only to the degree that the hosting service exposes explicit prefix caching or session controls.

Each policy targets a distinct operational regime:

Keep: Retaining state on the accelerator is optimal when the memory pool has ample headroom and the agent anticipates an immediate return. Holding the blocks incurs zero marginal cost if no competing work requires memory, and it guarantees zero restoration latency when generation resumes.
Move: Under memory pressure, offloading state to host DRAM releases critical accelerator capacity without discarding the completed prefill computation.
Drop: Discarding state becomes the preferred choice when the probability of resumption is low, host DRAM is exhausted, or the context is short enough that recomputing prefill is faster than transferring the data across the bus. Every policy must also enforce memory isolation boundaries so that evicted or offloaded blocks remain protected from unauthorized access by other tenants.

When pause durations extend across minutes or hours, as for workflows waiting for human approval, the engine can migrate state beyond host DRAM to non-volatile storage. Hierarchical serving systems organize storage across host memory and NVMe drives, prefetching cached layers sequentially so that retrieval from disk overlaps with execution of earlier layers (Gao et al. 2024). At data center scale, distributed architectures pool the host memory and solid-state storage of thousands of nodes into a shared cluster-wide KV cache (Qin et al. 2024). Across all storage tiers, cached attention tensors represent derived, transient state; the durable history of user inputs, tool actions, and execution evidence resides in the runtime’s authoritative event log.



To quantify these choices, consider an agent holding 32,768 tokens of context while pausing for a 45 s integration test on an eight-accelerator node. In this scenario, all historical KV entries have already been materialized, each 16-token block is completely filled, and no blocks are shared or committed to in-flight transfers. The uniquely reclaimable cache footprint is therefore 10.74 GB (excluding auxiliary page tables and transfer buffers, which the runtime budgets separately).
The transfer and recompute durations derive directly from hardware specifications. Because tensor parallelism partitions key-value heads evenly across the eight accelerators, each device holds one-eighth of the total state and transfers data over its own 64 GB/s PCIe link. When all eight links operate concurrently, the node moves state at an aggregate bandwidth of \(\HostLinkBandwidth =\) 512 GB/s. Offloading the complete 10.74 GB payload across this interface requires 21 ms, and restoring it upon resumption takes an identical 21 ms.
Reconstruction instead repeats the prefill pass. For a model with \(\Parameters\) parameters and a sequence of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens, evaluating the feed-forward and projection weights requires \(2\Parameters \SequenceLength\) floating-point operations. At the sustained prefill rate assumed for the reference system, recomputing this context demands 1.3 s, and including the quadratic attention term of equation 4 would lengthen it further. (Because every policy must eventually process the incoming test observation once the wait concludes, that downstream prefill is common to all policies and omitted from this comparison.)
In this weight-only comparison, both transfer duration and recompute duration scale linearly with sequence length \(\SequenceLength\), so their ratio is independent of context size:
\[\frac{\KvReloadTime}{\KvRecomputeTime} = \frac{\SequenceLength \, \KvCacheBytesPerToken / \HostLinkBandwidth}{2 \Parameters \SequenceLength / \AttainableComputeRate} = \frac{\KvCacheBytesPerToken \, \AttainableComputeRate}{2 \Parameters \, \HostLinkBandwidth} \tag{4}\]



Reloading paused state beats rebuilding it by about 62× in the linear reference comparison.
Here \(\AttainableComputeRate\) represents the sustained prefill throughput, and \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\) is the cache footprint per token. Equation 4 applies the reload-versus-reconstruction comparison of Queueing for Trajectories to this reference architecture. Reloading retained state is approximately 62× faster than recomputing from raw tokens. Even when heavy bus contention degrades link bandwidth to a quarter of its rated capacity, reloading remains 15× faster than prefill. Under this linear reference comparison, recomputation becomes advantageous when host DRAM capacity or PCIe bandwidth is sufficiently constrained by competing workloads, leaving accelerator compute as the less congested resource.
Retaining the cache on-chip throughout the 45 s wait ties up 10.74 GB \(\times\) 45 s \(\approx\) 483.18 GB·s of memory-time capacity (calculated using the unrounded payload). This cumulative occupancy translates into lost serving capacity whenever concurrent requests queue for device memory. Counted in request slots rather than bytes, it is the residence that Little’s law converts into a lost turn rate in section 5.8.2, where the same wait divides the memory-bound rate by the ratio of the whole turn cycle to its generation time.
Moving the state to host memory immediately upon entering the pause releases those accelerator blocks as soon as the 21 ms outbound copy completes. The freed blocks can serve other queries for 45 s \(-\) 21 ms \(=\) 44.98 s before the test returns. The policy incurs 42 ms of total transfer work across the bus, but only the inbound reload sits on the critical path of the resuming query, adding 21 ms of restoration delay. Dropping the state avoids bus transfer entirely, but forces 1.3 s of prefill work onto the critical path before generation can restart.
If the engine can predict the tool completion timestamp accurately, typically from a hint the agent runtime supplies, asynchronous prefetching can schedule the inward transfer to complete precisely as the test finishes. Reserving the destination device blocks at the start of that inbound copy yields an accelerator release window of 45 s \(-\) 21 ms \(-\) 21 ms \(=\) 44.96 s. Prefetching hides restoration latency completely while maintaining both transfer stages, though it requires reliable advance knowledge of return times.
The same reasoning extends to every context length and wait. The round-trip transfer time, which scales linearly with context length and equals 42 ms in this configuration, sets a necessary condition. A pause shorter than the round trip ends before offloading can move the state out and back without delaying resumption. Keeping it avoids restoration work when memory permits; under pressure, moving or dropping it may still be necessary. Above the round trip, offloading becomes possible, and whether it pays depends on whether other requests are queued for the freed memory and how much reload delay the resuming turn tolerates. For long pauses under memory pressure, offloading reclaims device memory for almost the entire wait at the cost of a sub-second reload. The worked 32,768-token, 45 s test sits far beyond that round trip. It also sits short of the much longer waits at which parked state accumulates enough to fill host memory, a boundary set by host capacity and by how fast paused trajectories arrive rather than by a fixed duration. The example therefore falls squarely in the offload regime (figure 6). When pauses stretch into minutes or hours, as for operations awaiting human review, parked state accumulates in host memory, and the decision turns on host capacity, secondary storage bandwidth, or eventual recomputation.

External tool executions exhibit significant runtime variance: a test suite may fail immediately on a syntax error, finish early, or stall on an environmental hang. This variance complicates offload and prefetch decisions:

If a tool completes earlier than forecasted while offloading is still in flight, the engine must either wait for the outbound transfer to finalize before reloading or cancel the transfer mid-stream, exposing unbuffered restoration latency.
Premature prefetching followed by a delayed return re-occupies accelerator memory while the model remains idle, negating the capacity reclaimed during the pause.
If a paused trajectory is cancelled or times out, an anticipatory inward reload wastes interconnect bandwidth.

A robust pause policy must therefore evaluate the full probability distribution of return times alongside client latency service-level objectives (SLOs), rather than relying on mean wait times and uncontended transfer estimates.
Furthermore, transfers rarely occur in isolation. Multiple paused trajectories frequently finish their external tasks in close temporal proximity, triggering a surge of concurrent reloads across shared host-memory buses, PCIe switches, and storage links. Summing nominal per-accelerator link rates is valid only if interconnect topologies and memory controllers maintain non-blocking throughput under concurrent load.
Suppose 32 paused repairs on a node finish their external tasks simultaneously. Their combined attention state totals 344 GB, which requires at least 0.67 s to reload even when the eight host links sustain their maximum aggregate throughput. The final reload in the queue therefore experiences a restoration delay roughly 32× longer than the isolated 21 ms reload latency, and any congestion on shared bus root complexes lengthens the tail further. System engineers must provision transfer queues, admission controls, and accelerator headroom specifically to absorb these burst-induced restoration delays.
Pipelining can overlap data transfers with computation, but strict causal dependencies dictate which operations can run concurrently. In standard full-attention models, generating or processing new observation tokens requires access to all historical key and value tensors. An engine cannot compute attention for layer \(\LayerIndex\) until the historical KV blocks for layer \(\LayerIndex\) reside in accelerator memory. Transfer latency can therefore be hidden only if the engine streams state in layer by layer (reloading layer \(\LayerIndex+1\) while executing attention on layer \(\LayerIndex\)) or if the node schedules unrelated generation requests while the paused state reloads in the background. Both techniques require careful engine coordination: layer-wise streaming requires fine-grained synchronization across DMA engines, while concurrent execution requires reserve accelerator memory to host the in-flight requests alongside incoming reload buffers.



Keeping, offloading, and recomputing all preserve the exact mathematical semantics of full attention. A distinct family of policies reduces memory occupancy by approximating the cache: evicting tokens selectively, restricting attention to a local window, or quantizing key and value tensors to lower precision. Because these strategies alter the underlying model computation, their efficacy cannot be judged by memory savings alone; they require empirical validation against task accuracy. In agentic workflows, an eviction policy cannot assume that low attention weight during past decoding steps implies irrelevance in future turns.
The mechanics of attention sinks demonstrate why naive eviction schemes break down. Because softmax normalizes attention weights to sum to one across the sequence, transformer layers deposit residual attention mass on the initial sequence positions whenever a query has no strong semantic match among current tokens. A sliding-window policy that evicts those initial tokens removes this stabilizing mass, causing generation perplexity to degrade sharply once context length exceeds the window size. Retaining a small set of initial sink tokens alongside the sliding window restores numerical stability across long sequence streams (Xiao et al. 2024). More sophisticated pruning strategies retain tokens that accumulate high cumulative attention mass (Zhang et al. 2023) or that receive significant attention within a recent temporal window (Liu et al. 2023).

Liu, Zichang, Aditya Desai, Fangshuo Liao, Weitao Wang, Victor Xie, Zhaozhuo Xu, Anastasia Mazur, Chen Dun, and Anshumali Shrivastava. 2023. “Scissorhands: Exploiting the Persistence of Importance Hypothesis for LLM KV Cache Compression.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS).
While past attention predicts future utility reasonably well in conventional conversation, agent trajectories routinely violate this assumption in three distinct ways:

Dormant constraints: Instructions defined early in an execution trace—such as environment constraints, security policies, or API rules—often receive negligible attention across dozens of intermediate tool turns. When the agent produces its final edit or synthesis, violating those dormant instructions causes silent task failure.
Exact identifiers: Unique entities like commit hashes, process IDs, file paths, and cryptographic nonces may appear once during environment exploration and remain unreferenced for many turns. If an eviction heuristic prunes these tokens because intermediate turns ignored them, the agent cannot quote them accurately in subsequent shell or API calls.
Tool-schema syntax: Schema definitions and JSON delimiters in the system prompt govern the grammar of every tool call. Individual decoding steps frequently assign weak attention mass to structural delimiters like brackets and colons. Pruning them produces malformed syntax that crashes downstream parsers rather than a graceful degradation in output quality.

Cache approximation in agentic systems must therefore be evaluated against hard semantic dependencies rather than aggregate perplexity. The lossless policies (keep, move, and drop) cost interconnect bandwidth and tiered memory capacity, but they preserve the full-attention computation for the same recorded inputs and compatible configuration, subject to numerical differences across implementations. They decide where one paused trajectory’s state lives. They leave open how many trajectories a node can carry when each one holds memory for its whole residence, waits included, and answering that requires putting time into the capacity accounting.




A paused repair task can hold key-value state in accelerator memory for minutes without executing a single forward pass, while an incoming request demands both memory capacity and execution time immediately. How an engine handles paused state dictates how many concurrent agent trajectories can fit in memory. Converting that static concurrency into a sustainable throughput, however, requires modeling how long each session holds its memory. Capacity planning must therefore tackle both dimensions: first establishing physical occupancy bounds, and then coupling those bounds to residence time.
Tracking memory demand in agentic serving is fundamentally different from tracking standard batch inference workloads. In standard inference, every active sequence holds a private cache. With agents, logical contexts frequently overlap through shared system prompts and tool descriptions, while continuations require private allocations, and dormant prefixes can be discarded or paged out without stalling active execution. Simply summing the logical key-value footprints of all active trajectories double-counts shared prefix blocks. Conversely, counting only the requests currently decoding tokens ignores the dormant KV state that still occupies HBM. Rigorous capacity planning therefore begins with the physical pool: determining how many unique physical blocks the serving system must retain to satisfy its workload.


To build a tractable capacity model, consider a set of equal-length requests with input prompt length \(\SequenceLength\) and a maximum generation allowance of \(\OutputLimit\) tokens. Because paged allocation hands out fixed-size blocks of \(\KvBlockSize\) tokens, each private allocation rounds up to the nearest whole block. Without prefix sharing, every resident request must independently provision memory for its full prompt and output allowance. When requests share an identical, compatible prefix, however, the memory pool allocates those prefix blocks once and pays only for each request’s private remainder. For this simple decomposition, assume that the common prefix aligns cleanly with a block boundary; any trailing partial block follows the copy-on-write accounting described earlier.
The memory available for key-value caching is whatever high-bandwidth memory remains after allocating model weights and reserving memory for execution runtimes:
\[\KvPoolMemory = \NodeHbmCapacity - \WeightMemory - \RuntimeReserveMemory \tag{5}\]
Production deployments typically withhold an additional headroom fraction \(\KvPoolHeadroomFraction\) of this pool to absorb bursty intermediate activations and memory fragmentation. Given block size \(\KvBlockSize\), a block-aligned common prefix of \(\SharedPrefixLength\) tokens, and a cache footprint of \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\) bytes per token across all layers, the total physical block demand across \(\BatchSize\) resident requests (every request whose state is resident, whether decoding or paused) must satisfy
\[\left\lceil \frac{\SharedPrefixLength}{\KvBlockSize} \right\rceil + \BatchSize \left\lceil \frac{\SequenceLength + \OutputLimit - \SharedPrefixLength}{\KvBlockSize} \right\rceil \le \left\lfloor \frac{(1-\KvPoolHeadroomFraction)\, \KvPoolMemory}{\KvBlockSize \, \KvCacheBytesPerToken} \right\rfloor \tag{6}\]
The resident-fit bound of section 5.2, refined for blocks, headroom, and sharing, is the maximum integer \(\BatchSize\) that satisfies equation 6. Setting \(\SharedPrefixLength = 0\) yields the unshared baseline. Because the common prefix is allocated only once, sharing delivers its largest gains when common instructions represent a dominant fraction of the total prompt, and when private working memory—the unique turn history and generation allowance—remains small.
Notebook 5.3 grounds these formulations on the same eight-accelerator DGX H100 node serving Llama 3 70B. Rather than optimistically assuming an average generation length, the sizing calculation reserves the full \(\OutputLimit\) token allowance to guarantee that resident requests cannot trigger out-of-memory aborts during decoding, treating the headroom fraction as a deliberate provisioning reserve.

The sharing gain \(1/(1-\SharedPrefixFraction)\) steepens as the shared fraction of each request grows.
In production environments, requests arrive with heterogeneous lengths and variable prefix overlap. An admission controller must therefore balance committed blocks, anticipated generation growth, and temporary staging buffers required during KV transfers or eviction copies. Furthermore, an aggregate node-wide memory bound is necessary but not sufficient: multi-GPU deployments distribute KV cache blocks across tensor-parallel shards, meaning a free physical block on one accelerator cannot alleviate memory exhaustion on another. Admission decisions must satisfy physical capacity constraints across every individual device.



A static fit bound defines instantaneous capacity, the number of slots that can exist in memory simultaneously. Translating that capacity into sustainable throughput requires adding time to the accounting, and classical queueing theory supplies the identity that links capacity, residence, and throughput.

Theorem 5.1: Occupancy equals rate times residence (Little's law)In any stable system where items arrive, reside for a while, and leave, the long-run averages obey one identity, whatever the arrival pattern, service order, or residence distribution. Little’s law (Little 1961) states
\[\MeanSlotOccupancy = \ArrivalRate \MeanHoldTime \tag{7}\]

Mean occupancy (\(\MeanSlotOccupancy\)): average number of items resident, here KV slots held.
Throughput (\(\ArrivalRate\)): long-run arrival rate, equal to the completion rate when unfinished work does not accumulate.
Mean residence (\(\MeanHoldTime\)): average time an item holds its slot, counting every phase in which the slot stays allocated.

A slot held in accelerator memory while an agent waits for external tool execution remains resident throughout that wait; omitting idle waiting time from \(\MeanHoldTime\) artificially deflates the denominator and drastically overstates sustainable system throughput.
The law’s generality has a price. Its proof assumes nothing about how items arrive or how long they stay, only that the long-run averages exist, and for that reason it fixes the mean occupancy and says nothing about the peak. A burst of arrivals, or residences that end together, can hold far more slots than \(\MeanSlotOccupancy\) for as long as the backlog lasts, so capacity is sized from the arrival and residence patterns, not from the mean identity alone.



Little, John D. C. 1961. “A Proof for the Queuing Formula: \(L = \lambda W\).” Operations Research 9 (3): 383–87. https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383.
Rearranging the relation as \(\ArrivalRate = \MeanSlotOccupancy/\MeanHoldTime\) expresses the achievable service rate as a function of allocated capacity and residence duration. Here each resident item is one turn’s generation-and-tool-wait cycle, not a complete multi-turn trajectory. Let \(\ModelTime\) be the time a turn spends generating and \(\ToolTime\) the time it then waits on its tool. A slot kept through the wait resides for \(\ModelTime + \ToolTime\), while a slot released for the wait resides for \(\ModelTime\) alone, so for the same number of slots the two policies’ turn rates differ by the factor \(1 + \ToolTime/\ModelTime\). That factor is the residency tax of a synchronous tool wait, and notebook 5.4 prices it for the repair turn.

Each repair turn resides 5 s while generating and, under the keep policy, another 45 s while its integration test runs. What turn rate can memory sustain with the wait held resident, and with the slot released for the wait?
Math: By equation 7, \(\ArrivalRate = \MeanSlotOccupancy/\MeanHoldTime\). Keeping state through the wait gives \(\MeanHoldTime =\) 50 s and \(\ArrivalRate =\) 0.82 turns/s. Releasing the slot for the wait gives \(\MeanHoldTime =\) 5 s and \(\ArrivalRate =\) 8.2 turns/s. The ratio is \(1 + \ToolTime/\ModelTime\), or 10×.
Systems insight: Holding paused state through an idle tool wait penalizes the memory-bound turn rate by a factor of \(1 + \ToolTime/\ModelTime\). The economic viability of keeping state in accelerator memory depends on the ratio of wait duration to generation time, not the wait duration alone. Once the wait dominates, moving the state out to host memory, at a restoration latency of about 21 ms, becomes the better default whenever memory is contested. This same factor scales the memory term of every attempt’s cost, expanding \(\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]\) in equation 1.2 across the entire unevicted residence.





A kept slot is paid for across the whole cycle, rather than only while it generates.
The turn rate calculated from releasing slots is an ideal upper bound imposed strictly by memory capacity. In practice, prefill computation, state restoration bandwidth, PCIe bus contention, and scheduling queues introduce additional bottlenecks; compute throughput or interconnect bandwidth often saturates before memory is fully exhausted. Furthermore, if multiple trajectories share prefix blocks, those blocks remain pinned in memory even if one trajectory enters an idle wait.
Because Little’s law fixes only the mean, the residency calculation also hides the peaks that agent workloads produce. Tool executions frequently complete together, as in the correlated return burst of section 5.7.4, and tree-search agents fan out into many candidate paths at once, so instantaneous memory demand rises well above the average for as long as the burst lasts. Robust capacity planning must therefore stress-test the empirical distributions of prompt length, dynamic output expansion, search branching, and tool latencies against both device-level physical boundaries and strict service-level latency objectives.
These dynamics manifest differently across agent architectures. The software repair agent operates in a batch-like regime characterized by deep context windows and prolonged tool waits during test suite runs. By contrast, the customer support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)) services numerous concurrent, short sessions where users wait interactively for low-latency responses. These contrasting profiles place divergent demands on the key-value pool and require distinct sharing and retention strategies.

While both workloads pay a similar residency tax, the optimal pause policy diverges based on who waits for the resume. The repair agent should migrate its state to host memory during tests, as the regime analysis of figure 6 recommends, and it can fall back to dropping the state when host memory is tight, since recomputation adds only 2.6 percent to a 50 s turn cycle where an automated test harness waits. In contrast, the support agent should keep or move its state and avoid dropping it, because recomputation lands directly in front of an interactive user as added delay to the first token. For support workloads, the decision that matters most is therefore what happens to each session’s private history beyond the shared prefix. Rebuilding that history is what the customer waits for, so keeping or moving it, not enlarging the shared prefix, protects the first token.





A single aggregate metric such as occupied pool fraction cannot distinguish healthy, amortized caching from an impending allocation failure. A memory pool at high utilization composed mostly of discardable dormant prefixes can easily admit a new request through cheap reclamation. Conversely, that same utilization level with all blocks pinned by active decoding leaves no headroom for context expansion. Table 6 establishes the physical categories required to interpret these operational states.



Table 6: Physical pool accounting: Apply the rows in order so each block belongs to exactly one category at a given instant. Logical references are tracked separately from physical storage.









Pool state
Accounting and consequence




Active or pinned
Count each physical block once, even when several requests reference it. It cannot be reclaimed while any required owner or operation still uses it.

Evaluating blocks in this strict order ensures that every physical block belongs to exactly one state at any given instant. For instance, while a paused trajectory’s private blocks are being copied out to host memory, each source block stays in the first row, pinned by the transfer that still reads it, and becomes reclaimable only when the copy completes. On the return trip, the device blocks allocated to receive the reload sit in the second row until the transfer lands. Similarly, a dormant prefix is reclaimable only when all dependent references and asynchronous operations have cleared. This taxonomy exposes true admission capacity without double-counting shared blocks or assuming that eviction requests free memory instantaneously.
Physical pool accounting provides only the static half of the operational picture; it must be coupled with continuous telemetry on throughput, work volume, and latency. A production telemetry pipeline should record offered request rates, prompt and completion token volumes, the token-weighted prefix hit rate of equation 2, eviction and restoration bandwidth, recomputed tokens, and the distribution of tool wait and resumption intervals. Operators must evaluate these metrics alongside concrete latency targets: admission delay in the scheduling queue, time to first token, inter-token latency, and state resumption delay. Relying on hit rates in isolation can be deceiving: a high reuse fraction can coexist with long scheduling queues, while high eviction counts may be entirely benign if the discarded prefixes represent cold sessions that will never be queried again.
The definitive signature of memory thrashing is cache churn: the rapid cycle of evicting blocks only to reload or recompute them shortly thereafter.8 When cache churn coincides with degrading tail latency or falling completed work under sustained offered load, it signals that the aggregate working set of active trajectories has overrun physical memory capacity. Resolving this collapse requires adjusting admission policies, offload thresholds, or scheduling priorities. Because the critical memory occupancy threshold at which churn begins varies across allocators and workload compositions, operators must correlate physical pool states with queue dynamics rather than relying on a static utilization ceiling. Furthermore, this diagnostic boundary matters across system layers: client applications consuming remote API endpoints observe only black-box latency and error codes, whereas infrastructure operators have access to the physical block states, page tables, and transfer telemetry required to perform root-cause remediation.
8 Thrashing: Multiprogrammed virtual-memory systems of the 1960s encountered this exact pathology: when the aggregate working sets of resident programs exceeded main memory, page faults forced continuous eviction of recently used pages, and processors spent their execution cycles servicing I/O rather than executing instructions (Denning 1968b). The solution was explicit load control: restricting the multiprogramming level until the working sets of admitted programs fit comfortably in physical memory. In agentic KV cache serving, the corresponding remedy is admission control against the retained state of active trajectories, rather than tuning eviction algorithms to page faster.

Engineering high-performance KV cache management requires navigating subtle interactions among memory geometry, request scheduling, and agent lifecycle dynamics. Many common architectural missteps stem from conflating raw memory capacity with sustained serving throughput, or mistaking cached intermediate activations for semantic ground truth. The following fallacies and pitfalls highlight where system designers frequently misjudge these trade-offs, along with the costs estimated on the reference node.

Fallacy: Model size, not retained context, decides how many sequences a node can serve.
Static model weights consume a fixed footprint allocated at initialization, leaving a 526.0 GB pool dedicated to dynamic attention state on the reference node. While model parameters establish the initial baseline headroom, the active context length of running sequences overwhelmingly governs dynamic memory consumption. Holding the model constant, that memory pool accommodates 195 unshared sequences when context is kept to 8,192 tokens, but capacity plunges to just 12 concurrent sequences once context expands to 131,072 tokens (section 5.2). Retained context length serves as the primary operational lever governing system concurrency, and the agent harness dictates that length through its prompt construction, tool history, and conversation buffering. Swapping in a smaller model only increases concurrent serving capacity to the extent that it reduces the per-token memory footprint \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\) or frees up additional accelerator memory for the KV pool.


Pitfall: Reserving every request’s maximum context.
Allocating contiguous memory upfront for each request’s worst-case context length severely throttles system throughput through internal fragmentation. When a serving system sizes every slot for a 32,768-token cap while requests average a final length of only 2,048 tokens, barely 6.25 percent of the allocated memory actually holds valid attention state upon completion. Under this static reservation regime, the reference pool can admit only 48 concurrent sequences. In contrast, paged virtual memory allocation dynamically allocates physical blocks on demand, giving the final-length snapshot estimate of approximately 780 over the same physical memory (section 5.4). Systems should allocate memory blocks incrementally as tokens arrive during prefill and generation, reserving the output allowance the admission controller promises, as the capacity notebook does, rather than the full context cap.


Fallacy: Compatible cached attention state proves that its evidence is current.
Prefix caching operates strictly at the level of token identifiers and model configurations, without semantic awareness of environment state or external reality. On the reference node, a prefix match on the agent repair loop’s 4,096-token invariant prompt saves roughly 169 ms of prefill computation per turn (section 5.5). The inference engine achieves that speedup regardless of whether those cached tokens reflect stale diagnostics from revision 17 (r17) or up-to-date observations from the current repository source. Prefix match compatibility only confirms that the token sequence and attention architecture match bit-for-bit. Determining whether an earlier r17 failure supports a claim about revision 18 (r18) requires semantic validation in the agent harness before serializing the prompt. Updating the prompt with fresh r18 observations breaks prefix reuse at the first modified token and forfeits part of that computational saving. That forfeited saving is the correct price of grounding the next decision in current evidence (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)).


Pitfall: Always moving paused state out of accelerator memory.
Blindly offloading KV cache blocks to host memory whenever an agent pauses to execute an external tool wastes interconnect bandwidth and inflates resumption latency. Evacuating the 10.74 GB attention state for a paused repair agent requires 42 ms of link transfer, which adds 21 ms of overhead before the model can resume generation. When the memory pool contains plenty of free blocks, this offload latency provides zero benefit to the system. Conversely, under heavy contention, offloading that same state frees valuable high-bandwidth accelerator memory for 44.98 s across an extended 45 s tool invocation (section 5.7). Serving schedulers must evaluate eviction dynamically based on uniquely reclaimable blocks, active queue pressure, and expected resumption deadlines. An external tool call marks an opportunity for scheduling decisions rather than an automatic eviction trigger.


Fallacy: A resident-fit count is a throughput guarantee.
Calculating how many concurrent request snapshots fit into physical accelerator memory establishes an instantaneous capacity limit, not a sustained throughput guarantee. The reference node fits 41 unshared repair trajectories in memory simultaneously. However, if those sessions hold their memory allocations across an idle 45 s tool pause, the node sustains a maximum of only 0.82 turns/s from memory alone. If the engine instead releases those memory slots during the pause, the memory-only throughput bound rises to 8.2 turns/s (notebook 5.4). Memory fit dictates maximum concurrency (\(\MeanSlotOccupancy\)), but Little’s law (\(\MeanSlotOccupancy = \ArrivalRate \MeanHoldTime\)) dictates that arrival throughput (\(\ArrivalRate\)) is governed equally by mean residence time (\(\MeanHoldTime\)). When agent turns involve long execution pauses or queueing delays, residence time inflates and throughput collapses even though memory looks full. Occupancy stays high, but most of the resident state is idle, so the turn rate is low. Schedulers must validate admission against offered traffic distributions, burst arrivals, and latency targets rather than relying on static slot counts.


Pitfall: Treating KV storage as the authoritative task record.
The KV cache is a hardware-bound optimization artifact, not a durable system of record. Dropping the 10.74 GB repair state from accelerator memory costs approximately 1.3 s of prefill compute to rebuild from raw tokens, and it forfeits zero evidence needed by the task. Retaining or serializing KV cache tensors merely preserves intermediate, activation-level computation tied to a specific hardware layout, model architecture, and numerical precision. It does not record the authoritative code revisions, environment observations, or validation evidence that govern an agent’s task progression. Systems must persist trajectory history, tool outputs, and verification state in a durable application runtime. The KV cache should always be treated as an ephemeral, recomputable cache over that authoritative token log, reproducible up to floating-point differences across distinct implementations.




Retained key-value (KV) attention state is fundamentally a cache of intermediate computation. Like any cache in a computer system, its cost has two dimensions: capacity and residency. Capacity represents the physical bytes allocated in high-bandwidth memory, determined by the model’s tensor geometry and active sequence length. Residency represents the duration for which a sequence occupies those bytes across token generation cycles and tool execution stalls. Allocation granularity and prefix sharing dictate how many bytes are stranded by internal fragmentation or duplicated across concurrent branches. Meanwhile, residency converts raw physical capacity into sustainable system throughput: an agent blocked on an external tool environment still occupies accelerator memory, reducing the concurrent request load a serving node can support. Every memory management policy examined in this chapter (paged block tables, tree-based prefix eviction, offloading, and recomputation) navigates this trade-off between memory footprint, recomputation overhead, and scheduling delay. Cache mechanisms manage physical storage, but they cannot assess whether cached tokens remain semantically valid; context validity remains strictly the responsibility of the agent harness and the context it supplies.

Key Takeaways: Managing derived attention state

Retained length is the capacity knob: With model weights occupying a static allocation, resident capacity scales inversely with retained sequence length, falling from 195 sequences at 8,192 tokens down to 12 sequences at 131,072 tokens on the reference node. A context length that easily satisfies the model architecture’s maximum context window can still quickly exhaust the serving node’s physical memory pool.
Physical blocks, not logical references, consume capacity: Paged attention rounds private sequence state up to fixed-size blocks, whereas identical prefix sequences share physical blocks through reference counting. Reclaiming a finished trajectory frees only those physical blocks whose reference count drops to zero, ensuring active sequences and asynchronous transfer operations remain protected.
Prefix reuse requires both structural compatibility and memory availability: Matching token prefixes permit KV cache reuse only when the corresponding physical blocks remain resident and accessible under tenant-isolation rules. A cache hit guarantees neither the freshness of underlying external data nor the semantic validity of the trajectory; preserving cache affinity must never prevent an agent harness from invalidating stale context.
Retention policies and compute schedulers manage complementary resources: Chunked prefill schedules incoming prompt tokens alongside active decodes to prevent high latency spikes during token generation. Similarly, each way of handling a paused agent trajectory (retaining its blocks in accelerator memory, offloading them to host RAM or secondary storage, or recomputing them on demand) exchanges memory footprint for interconnect bandwidth and resumption latency. The optimal strategy depends on the link bandwidth and the expected wait duration.
Idle tool waits impose a severe residency tax on throughput: Static resident-fit bounds govern instantaneous occupancy rather than sustained request throughput. Holding physical cache blocks resident while an agent waits on external tools or human feedback depresses sustainable turn throughput by the residency tax factor \(1 + \ToolTime/\ModelTime\). Production admission and eviction policies must therefore optimize for end-to-end task completion rates and tail latency rather than raw accelerator memory utilization.



Attention state derived from the token prefix (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\)) enables the serving engine to reuse previous computation rather than evaluating redundant prompt tokens. Precise block tracking and residency accounting quantify the trade-off between retaining that state and freeing high-bandwidth memory for active generation. Throughout these optimizations, source authority remains paramount (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)): an inexpensive continuation never justifies serving an obsolete observation when the underlying system or environment has changed.



Almost every memory management technique in this chapter resolves an architectural problem that time-sharing operating systems encountered decades ago. When early programs outgrew physical core memory, the Manchester Atlas one-level store introduced paging (Kilburn et al. 1962): an address translation table mapped a program’s contiguous virtual address space onto scattered physical page frames, freeing programmers from managing manual overlays and allowing memory to allocate without contiguous physical reservations. Decoupling virtual addresses from physical layout promptly exposed new systems trade-offs. Randell (1969) formalized the distinction between internal fragmentation (storage lost inside rounded-up allocations) and external fragmentation, where free memory sits stranded between allocations. Belady (1966) demonstrated that optimal offline page replacement requires clairvoyant knowledge of future memory references, establishing that practical online policies must rely on heuristics. When memory pressure mounted, time-sharing systems routinely collapsed into thrashing, spending virtually all cycles swapping pages rather than executing user code. Denning’s working-set model clarified the dynamics of this failure and proved that the only dependable remedy was admission control: admitting fewer concurrent processes rather than swapping pages more aggressively (Denning 1968a, 1968b). Operating systems also pioneered fine-grained memory sharing. The TENEX system introduced copy-on-write sharing so that multiple processes could reference identical pages safely until one attempted a mutation (Bobrow et al. 1972), while Morrison’s PATRICIA trees indexed strings through shared prefixes (Morrison 1968). Denning (1970) gathered these foundations into the virtual-memory discipline that computer systems curricula teach to this day.

Subsequent innovations in serving systems recapitulated the operating-systems lineage directly. Orca introduced iteration-level scheduling, enabling fine-grained preemption and dynamic batching where requests join and leave running batches on individual token boundaries (Yu et al. 2022). Agent workloads introduce the memory dilemma at the center of this chapter: execution state that idles during tool execution and subsequently resumes. When an agent invokes an external tool, its execution thread pauses while waiting for external API responses or environment feedback. During this idle window, the retained KV cache ties up expensive accelerator high-bandwidth memory. Work on tool interception formalized this challenge by framing KV cache lifecycle management around three primary operations: keeping the state resident in device memory, swapping it to host memory or storage, or dropping it entirely to recompute upon resumption (Abhyankar et al. 2024). This trade-off balances idle memory capacity against host-to-device transfer bandwidth and compute recomputation costs. Multi-turn serving systems such as CachedAttention and Mooncake expanded this design space into multi-tier memory hierarchies, paging dormant KV caches out to host DRAM and disaggregated solid-state storage clusters (Gao et al. 2024; Qin et al. 2024). Lossy approximation techniques pursued an alternative path, trading mathematical fidelity for reduced memory footprints through attention sinks (Xiao et al. 2024) and score-based eviction policies (Zhang et al. 2023). However, whether lossy cache approximation can reliably preserve the intricate, long-range dependencies required across extended agent trajectories remains an open systems and modeling challenge.
For readers seeking to trace the lineage from classical memory management to agent serving infrastructure, six works are especially illuminating:

Denning (1970) provides the foundational survey of paging, replacement algorithms, and locality of reference, showing how modern KV-cache management problems mirror classical virtual memory challenges transposed onto a new architectural storage unit.
Denning (1968a) introduces the working-set model, establishing the formal link between program locality and resource allocation. It provides the theoretical foundation for admission control, explaining why multi-tenant model servers must reject or queue requests when aggregate memory demand exceeds physical accelerator capacity.
Pope et al. (2023) develops an analytical model for large-model inference, demonstrating rigorously how attention head sharing, tensor partitioning, and memory bandwidth dictate whether a deployment is bounded by arithmetic throughput or memory capacity.
Kwon et al. (2023) introduces PagedAttention, adapting classical operating system paging, virtual block tables, and copy-on-write mechanisms to eliminate KV cache fragmentation in serving engines. It serves as an exemplary case study in translating classical systems principles to modern accelerator architectures.
Zheng et al. (2024) structures prompt cache management through radix trees, treating token prefix reuse as a first-class scheduling and eviction problem in multi-turn and agentic serving workloads.
Abhyankar et al. (2024) formalizes the tool-wait problem in agent workloads, quantifying the engineering trade-offs among retaining, swapping, and discarding KV cache state during external tool execution.

Below what sustained link bandwidth would recomputation become the faster way back?
Forty paused sessions of 32,768 tokens each return at the same instant. Compute each session’s state, its isolated reload time, the reload completion time of the last session when reloads share the full aggregate link rate, and the time to recompute all forty sequentially from weight work alone.
Each returning session must be restored within 250 ms. How many of the forty meet that target if reloads share the link fairly, and how many if they are served one at a time in arrival order at the full link rate? Propose two design changes that would serve the rest.

6. Shared prefix and residence time (Intermediate). Requests carry 24,576 prompt tokens and an output allowance \(\OutputLimit = 1{,}024\). A block-aligned common prefix of 16,384 tokens is compatible and shareable across all of them. Blocks hold \(\KvBlockSize = 16\) tokens, and the planner withholds headroom \(\KvPoolHeadroomFraction = 0.10\). Each turn generates for 4 s and then waits 36 s for a tool.

Using equation 6, compute the usable blocks and the resident-fit bound without and with sharing. Compare the gain with \(1/(1-\SharedPrefixFraction)\).
The operator wants memory to sustain 10 turns/s. Using the shared fit and equation 7, what rate does keeping state through the wait sustain, and how many resident slots would the target require under that policy?
Instead, each paused turn moves its private blocks to host memory and reloads them when the tool returns, while the common prefix stays resident for the other requests. Compute the memory-bound rate, the host-link traffic at 10 turns/s, and the restoration delay per turn. Is the link the binding resource?

7. Fan-out over a shared source bundle (Advanced). The research agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}\)) retrieves a 60,000-token bundle of source documents and fans the question out to 12 workers. Each worker’s input is the bundle followed by a 2,000-token private instruction, and each may generate up to 3,000 tokens. A synthesis call then reads the bundle followed by all 12 worker outputs. Ignore block rounding and headroom.

A contiguous allocator deep-copies the bundle’s state into every worker. How much KV state does it copy? Compute the KV footprint of one question with and without block sharing, and how many questions each policy keeps resident in the pool.
A developer serializes each worker’s private instruction before the bundle so that the model reads its task first. What happens to the shared footprint in (a), and what layout serves both goals?
For the synthesis call, how much weight-only prefill does a hit on the bundle avoid, and how much new prefill remains? Contrast the constraint that binds this workload with the one that binds the repair agent in this chapter.
A platform team proposes reusing the bundle’s KV state across different users’ questions that retrieve the same documents. State the conditions under which that reuse is compatible, available, and permitted, and explain why a hit says nothing about whether the documents are current or trustworthy.

8. Paused state through a human approval (Advanced). The remediation agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) proposes a production change and waits for human approval. During a major incident, 60 trajectories await approval at once. Each retains 20,000 tokens: an 8,000-token invariant prefix, identical and shareable across trajectories, followed by 12,000 tokens of incident-specific diagnostics. Each turn generates for 6 s, approval takes 10 minutes, and the host can hold 1 TB of parked state.

Under the keep policy, what share of the pool do the 60 trajectories hold without sharing and with the prefix shared, and what residency tax does the approval wait impose?
Suppose the private blocks move to host memory and the shared prefix stays resident. Compute the host footprint, and compare the time to restore 20 trajectories whose approvals arrive together by reload with the time to recompute their private regions sequentially.
Before acting on an approval, the harness must re-observe production state (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)), and the refreshed observations replace the diagnostics from token 8,000 onward. How much of the parked state remains usable? Recommend a paused-state policy, and say how the recommendation changes if refreshed observations were only appended after the existing diagnostics.
Compared with the repair agent, what binds this workload, and how large is its restoration cost relative to the wait?


What’s Next: From reusable computation to durable informationDropping the r18 request’s attention state forfeits no evidence, because the serving engine can rebuild it from the token log. The repair’s next session still needs that evidence once this serving session ends: the candidate at r18, the r17 failure, the passing reproducer, and the integration checks that remain unresolved. KV state can itself be moved or serialized, so storage location alone does not separate a cache from a memory. The unresolved problem is which information should persist, how it is identified and updated as its sources change, and how a later session retrieves evidence appropriate to its task. Long-Term Memory develops that durable-information contract.

title: 5 KV Cache Management
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can an agent that is generating nothing still exhaust the memory of the machine serving it?
An agent spends much of its life waiting. While a test suite runs or a remote service responds, the model generates nothing, yet the attention state computed from the request’s prefix can stay resident in accelerator memory, holding capacity that another request could put to work. That state is large, it grows with every token the trajectory carries, and its size is fixed by the model’s geometry rather than by any choice the agent makes. A serving engine that reserves room for the longest request it might see strands much of its memory, and one that copies a shared prefix into every branch pays for the same state many times over. At each pause the engine must choose among keeping the state resident, moving it to slower memory, and dropping it to rebuild from the tokens when the agent resumes. Each option trades memory against the delay before the next output token, and the right one depends on how long the wait will last. Capacity is therefore set less by how many contexts fit at once than by how long each one stays, because a context that holds memory through a long tool wait serves no turns while it keeps its place. Managing retained attention state turns the state an agent carries into a priced claim on the machine serving it, sized against the turn rate the service must sustain.

Learning Objectives

Calculate retained attention-state memory and resident fit from model geometry, token count, and storage precision
Calculate the memory that block allocation and prefix sharing recover from full-cap reservation and duplicated prefixes
Distinguish compatible, available prefix reuse from the applicability of the underlying information
Select a chunked-prefill token budget that bounds the gap between output tokens for ongoing requests
Evaluate keep, move, and recompute policies for paused state against memory pressure and resume latency
Analyze how residence time converts a memory-fit bound into a sustainable turn rate

title: 5 KV Cache Management
text:
The connection-pool repair agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)) has reached a candidate revision, r18. Its targeted reproducer passes, prompting the harness to submit a fully serialized request of 32,768 tokens and launch an integration test suite that runs for 45 seconds. That length, a power of two that keeps the block and pool arithmetic round, is shorter than the staged request of the context-engineering examples, and every per-request footprint and transfer time below scales linearly with it. If the serving engine holds the request’s attention state in accelerator memory throughout that entire wait, the device does no work for that workflow. The model generates zero tokens during the test suite, yet its retained state pins memory that another concurrent request could put to work. This is the tool-wait problem named in the turn lifecycle of The six-phase turn execution lifecycle. Preserving that state is a deliberate systems policy, and running an agentic service requires pricing that policy against its alternatives.



State becomes a physical resource claim inside the serving system.
Earlier abstractions stop short of that physical commitment. Context Engineering established how the harness selects and refreshes prompt context for each call, and its prefix-layout calculation priced a cached prefix as a discounted line on the bill. Neither abstraction captures the physical footprint of the underlying computation: how many gigabytes of memory that retained attention state consumes, how many concurrent trajectories an accelerator can hold at once, or what the serving engine should do with that state when an agent pauses to await tool execution. Those mechanical questions dictate whether an inference node that comfortably supports a single repair workflow can scale to sustain dozens.


↩︎ Pricing a reused prompt prefix at a discounted cached-input rate is established in Preserving an exact prefix.
Managing retained attention state is not solely an internal serving problem; it spans an operational boundary between two parties. The application caller controls its submitted context, tool execution timing, and any cache-management hints the serving API exposes. The serving operator controls physical device allocation, memory placement, compute scheduling, and retention policies. When the two belong to separate organizations, as with hosted commercial model APIs, the caller cannot manage physical accelerator memory directly. Instead, the application influences retention only through the interfaces and pricing tiers the service exposes. Distinguishing where these responsibilities divide clarifies which performance levers belong to the agent harness and which belong to the serving engine, the inference software that executes model calls and manages accelerator memory. The word “runtime” keeps its earlier meaning here, the agent runtime that runs the loop around the model.
The chapter follows the r18 request’s attention state through its life in the serving engine, and each stage raises the question the next one answers. Sizing the state from model geometry shows how few 32,768-token contexts fit in the memory left after the weights (section 5.2). Allocating that state naively strands much of the pool (section 5.3), which fixed-size blocks recover while letting forked candidates share a prefix (section 5.4). Sharing within one request invites reuse across turns, which needs an index over retained prefixes and a rule for what to evict (section 5.5). Whatever the cache misses must be prefilled without stalling other requests’ generation (section 5.6). The test wait itself forces a choice among keeping, moving, and dropping the paused state (section 5.7). Finally, residence time turns a count of resident contexts into a sustainable turn rate (section 5.8).

title: 5 KV Cache Management
text:
The r18 request’s 32,768 tokens do not reach the accelerator as raw text. During causal self-attention in a Transformer decoder, each newly generated token attends to earlier tokens through their key and value projections (Vaswani et al. 2017). Recomputing these projections at every decode step would repeat the linear transformations over the entire historical prefix, creating an unsustainable quadratic compute bottleneck. Serving engines avoid this recomputation by retaining the computed key and value tensors in accelerator memory across decode cycles.1 While autoregressive decoding relies on retained attention state, sustaining long-horizon agent execution requires managing its physical capacity, allocation overhead, and multi-tenant residency.
1 Memory-Limited Inference: Caching keys and values trades quadratic recomputation for persistent memory capacity, and that memory quickly becomes the primary serving bottleneck. An analytical study of large-model serving revealed that sharing a single key-value head across all query heads allowed an identical deployment to serve contexts more than an order of magnitude longer, precisely because retained attention state, rather than compute throughput, bounded context length and batch concurrency (Pope et al. 2023). Managing this memory footprint determines whether an agent deployment scales. 
Pope, Reiner, Sholto Douglas, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Jacob Devlin, James Bradbury, Jonathan Heek, Kefan Xiao, Shivani Agrawal, and Jeff Dean. 2023. “Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference.” Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems (MLSys) 5: 606–24.

↩︎ Retained attention state in autoregressive decoding is established in Conditional token selection.


Definition 5.1: KV cache
KV cache is the per-sequence store of attention keys and values that the model has computed for already processed tokens, retained so that later tokens can attend to them without recomputing their projections.

Significance: Its payload scales linearly with retained tokens; consequently, sequence context length, rather than static model parameter count, determines how many concurrent requests can share the memory pool remaining after loading model weights.
Distinction: It represents intermediate projected state rather than a raw copy or semantic compression of input text. Reconstructing it requires executing the exact token sequence through identical model weights and layer configurations.
Common pitfall: Budgeting only for input prompts. Every newly decoded output token appends key and value states at every layer, so a request reaches its maximum memory footprint at completion rather than during initial prefill.



For a decoder employing causal self-attention with uniform layer geometry, every retained token contributes both a key vector and a value vector across all layers. Let \(\LayerCount\) represent the number of layers, \(\KvHeadCount\) the number of key-value heads per layer, \(\AttentionHeadDimension\) the dimension of each head, and \(\ElementStorageSize\) the storage size in bytes per element. Accounting for both vectors yields the memory footprint per token:
\[\KvCacheBytesPerToken = 2 \cdot \LayerCount \cdot \KvHeadCount \cdot \AttentionHeadDimension \cdot \ElementStorageSize \tag{1}\]
A sequence retaining attention state across \(\SequenceLength\) tokens requires an aggregate cache payload of \(\KvCacheMemory = \SequenceLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\). Here \(\SequenceLength\) counts only the tokens whose keys and values have already been evaluated; each newly sampled token increments \(\SequenceLength\) once the model completes its forward pass.
The key-value head count \(\KvHeadCount\) in equation 1 represents the number of stored attention heads, which often falls below the query head count. Multi-query attention pushed this reduction to its structural extreme by sharing a single key-value head across all query heads2 (Shazeer 2019). Grouped-query attention strikes an intermediate balance: several query heads share one key-value head, dividing the stored key-value head count by the group size relative to a standard multi-head design (Ainslie et al. 2023), a scaling quantified across attention designs in Attention State by Attention Design. Because this head grouping is established during pretraining, a serving allocator cannot dynamically drop heads from an existing checkpoint without fundamentally altering the model’s computations.
2 Multi-Query Attention: Motivated primarily by memory bandwidth rather than storage capacity (incremental decoding reloads stored key and value tensors at each generation step), sharing key-value tensors across query heads drastically reduces memory bus traffic alongside physical storage with minimal quality loss (Shazeer 2019). Grouped-query attention subsequently recovered nearly all multi-head attention quality while preserving the bulk of these memory savings (Ainslie et al. 2023). Consequently, the head count \(\KvHeadCount\) in equation 1 is an architectural parameter established at pretraining. 
Shazeer, Noam. 2019. “Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head Is All You Need.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1911.02150.

Ainslie, Joshua, James Lee-Thorp, Michiel de Jong, Yury Zemlyanskiy, Federico Lebr’on, and Sumit Sanghai. 2023. “GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints.” Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP).
While equation 1 accounts for the raw tensor payload under dense causal attention, physical memory consumption in production serving engines exceeds this theoretical bound. Allocation block granularities, memory alignment, page table metadata, and quantization scales all add runtime overhead. Non-uniform architectures, such as sliding-window attention or compressed latent representations, require their own capacity models.
The worked estimate uses a representative configuration: the Llama 3 70B model geometry, with 70.6B parameters, and a DGX H100 node containing 8 accelerators. While specific hardware platforms and checkpoint dimensions vary, the underlying capacity arithmetic remains unchanged. Unlike the single-device, 8-bit illustration in Per-call work estimate, both weights and KV cache tensors use 16-bit storage here, with the model weights sharded across the node’s accelerators by tensor parallelism. The aggregate high-bandwidth memory remaining after provisioning model weights and a runtime reserve constitutes the KV pool. The number of active sequences whose KV payloads can reside simultaneously within this pool defines the resident-fit bound. This aggregate derivation assumes perfectly balanced shards without redundant weight replication; in production, memory limits must be satisfied on every individual accelerator device. None of the r18 context’s internal structure survives into this accounting: system prompt, tool schemas, workspace state, turn history, and latest observation all become key and value tensors at every layer, so the whole 32,768-token context costs 10.7 GB whatever its zones contain (figure 1). The figure’s zones follow the change-rate order of context staging. Its shared invariant prefix is the root of instructions and tool schemas together with the slow-changing workspace description, its growing trajectory state is the rest of the trunk, and its active turn is the leaf.






Figure 1: From Agent Context to KV State: A 32,768-token agent context (a), divided into system prompt, tool schemas, workspace, turn history, and the latest observation, becomes key and value tensors at every layer (b). The grouped-query model’s per-token footprint then sets how many such contexts fit in the node’s KV pool, before allocator overhead and headroom.




Napkin Math 5.1: Sizing the attention state of an agent trajectoryProblem: Consider a server node of 8 accelerators, each with 80 GB (vendor-rated in binary gigabytes, about 85.9 GB in the decimal units used throughout this chapter), for 687.2 GB of aggregate accelerator memory. Model weights occupy 141.2 GB, and the runtime reserves 20 GB for dynamic activations and scratch buffers. Under full causal attention without prefix sharing, how many independent sequences can simultaneously reside in the remaining memory across different context lengths?
Math: Evaluating equation 1 for this architecture yields \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken = 2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 327,680\;\text{bytes/token}\). For an agent trajectory retaining 32,768 tokens, the footprint becomes \(\KvCacheMemory = 32,768 \times 327,680\;\text{bytes} \approx 10.7\;\text{GB}\).
Subtracting model parameters and runtime buffers isolates the usable capacity: \(687.2 - 141.2 - 20 \approx 526.0\;\text{GB}\). Dividing this available pool by the footprint per sequence and taking the floor determines the resident-fit bound. Using exact floating-point values prior to display rounding yields \(\left\lfloor 525.994767360 / 10.737418240 \right\rfloor = 48\). Table 1 evaluates this bound across three operational context regimes.



Table 1: Payload and resident fit: Each sequence stores its own full-attention state; the calculation excludes allocator overhead and additional headroom.
