Moving from conversational token generation to autonomous goal execution transforms the systems engineering contract between the model, the runtime, and the surrounding environment.

Definition 1.1: Agentic system
Agentic system is an autonomous software system in which a runtime places a foundation model in a closed control loop with context, state, tools, and an environment, dispatching the model’s authorized proposals and returning their environmental observations to subsequent calls until the task is accepted, halted, or escalated.

Significance: The unit of systems optimization shifts from the isolated model call to the complete task trajectory. Unchecked errors compound exponentially across sequential turns (section 1.6), and every attempt, accepted or aborted, is charged to the task’s cost per accepted result.
Distinction: In conversational interfaces, a human executes tools, verifies output, and bridges state between turns. In an agentic system, software executes these operations under delegated authority, meaning the model’s output is strictly a proposal that holds no standing authority of its own.
Common pitfall: Treating agency as a capability inherent to the model’s weights. A more capable model produces more accurate candidate actions, but permission enforcement, sandbox isolation, durable state persistence, and completion verification belong entirely to the surrounding software runtime.



This architectural shift forces a fundamental recalculation of core systems metrics. In classical model serving, infrastructure teams optimize for tokens per second, tail latency percentiles, and accelerator utilization. In agentic systems, the governing metrics become task completion rate, cost per accepted task, and reliability across multi-turn horizons. An isolated-request baseline bounds and accounts for each call separately, retains no task state after the response, and treats an HTTP 200 status as successful request completion. Those choices do not establish completion of a delegated task: an execution spans dozens of dependent steps, accumulates context and tool output that the serving system must keep available between calls (the attention key-value cache it retains for the growing prefix, so the next turn need not recompute it, can occupy gigabytes of accelerator memory), and triggers side effects that permanently alter external systems.

title: 1 Introduction
text:
Consider a concrete engineering challenge: diagnosing and repairing an intermittent race condition in a distributed key-value store.1 A foundation model2 can inspect the issue description and propose an edit to the connection-pool locking logic. Emitting that patch text, however, leaves the repository completely untouched. Resolving the defect requires an agent to locate the relevant source files, draft an edit, execute compilers and test runners inside an isolated environment, interpret diagnostic logs when a build fails, and verify that the resulting code satisfies the repository’s regression test suite.
1 Repository Repair as a Benchmark Task: SWE-bench established repository repair as a standard benchmark for agentic systems: each instance pairs a real GitHub issue with the unit and integration tests from the patch that fixed it (Jimenez et al. 2024). A candidate patch is evaluated by whether those tests pass after application. The model is never permitted to inspect the evaluation tests directly, ensuring that acceptance rests on independent, untampered evidence rather than self-reported success. 
Jimenez, Carlos E., John Yang, Alexander Wettig, Shunyu Yao, Kexin Pei, Ofir Press, and Karthik Narasimhan. 2024. “SWE-Bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
2 Foundation Model: Bommasani and colleagues introduced the term in 2021 to describe models trained on massive, diverse datasets at scale that can be adapted to an expansive range of downstream tasks (Bommasani et al. 2021). Because a foundation model is general-purpose, its weights encode neither the security permissions nor the specific acceptance criteria of a given production task; those boundaries must be defined and enforced by the surrounding runtime. 
Bommasani, Rishi, Drew A. Hudson, Ehsan Adeli, Russ Altman, Simran Arora, Sydney von Arx, Michael S. Bernstein, et al. 2021. “On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2108.07258.
An agentic system comes into existence precisely when software closes this interaction loop. Rather than relying on an engineer to copy prompts and error traces back and forth, the surrounding software feeds the foundation model an objective alongside fresh environmental observations, captures the model’s proposed action, dispatches that action, and returns structured execution feedback to guide the next decision.
The surrounding software, the runtime, enforces the operational boundary between model reasoning and environment mutation. All execution authority resides permanently with the runtime. Because a model outputs only unstructured text or token streams, generating an operation’s name confers no inherent permission to run it. The runtime parses the proposed action, verifies that it complies with current access policies, and dispatches the call through a designated tool. A tool provides a structured interface to an environmental capability, such as reading file contents, editing source code, executing a shell command, or running a test suite. The part of the runtime that drives this loop is often called the agent harness, and The Agent Harness develops it as a component of the runtime rather than a separate system. Figure 1 sets the two arrangements side by side. In panel A a developer carries every command and every error by hand; in panel B the runtime dispatches only the actions it grants and routes verifier evidence back to itself rather than trusting the model’s account of what happened.






Figure 1: A Person or a Runtime Closes the Loop: In the conversational arrangement (A), the model answers and the developer runs every tool and carries each error back by hand. In the agentic arrangement (B), the runtime assembles context, receives the model’s proposal, and dispatches only actions it grants; the model holds no authority, and verifier evidence returns to the runtime rather than to the model’s own report.



Panel B represents the architectural foundation of this book. High-parameter foundation models paired with optimized inference engines provide essential proposal capabilities, but they supply only the raw computational engine. A model cannot manage its own execution authority, maintain state across tool failures, or verify the correctness of its actions against external reality. Those responsibilities fall entirely on the surrounding software architecture. Engineering an agent is therefore the discipline of designing, securing, and operating the complete closed-loop system that surrounds the model.
Analyzing and building these systems requires four foundational instruments:

The Stochastic Computer: An architectural mapping that models an agentic system after classical computer architecture, treating the foundation model as a probabilistic execution unit, the context window and external stores as a memory hierarchy, tools as input/output interfaces, and the runtime as the operating system kernel (section 1.3).
The H·S·A Exposure Space: An analytical coordinate system that measures how far a delegated task departs from stateless model inference along three operational dimensions: execution horizon (\(\TurnHorizon\)), persistent state (\(\StateExposureLevel_0\) to \(\StateExposureLevel_3\)), and external authority (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\) to \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\)) (section 1.4).
The Invariant Closure Principle: A governance rule stipulating that safety and security invariants must be mechanically enforced by the runtime below the model, while task acceptance must be verified against independent evidence above the model (section 1.5). Below the model means between its proposal and the environment, where the runtime decides what may execute; above it means between the finished result and whoever accepts it, where the runtime decides what counts as done.
Horizon Reliability and Cost Arithmetic: Mathematical formulations that quantify how single-step error rates compound across multi-turn trajectories, demonstrating how retry budgets and recovery mechanisms dictate the true compute cost per accepted task (section 1.6).

Section 1.4 also places four recurring reference workloads, which the book calls lighthouses, in the exposure space; the repair task is one of them. Once all four instruments are in hand, section 1.7 follows the repair task turn by turn to show where each one acts, and section 1.8 maps the instruments onto the structure of the book.

title: 1 Introduction
text:
To understand how the disparate subsystems of an agentic architecture collaborate, we can look to an architecture familiar to every systems engineer: the classical computer. An autonomous task requires computational execution, working and persistent memory, interfaces to perceive and manipulate the external world, supervisory control, and mechanisms to optimize future executions from past runs. Taken together, these requirements map directly onto the classical hardware-software hierarchy.
We formalize this mapping as the stochastic computer (figure 2).3 Its upper band is the live execution loop of a single task, and its lower band acts across tasks. In the live band, the foundation model acts as the central processing unit (CPU). Context engineering and external datastores represent the memory hierarchy, spanning working registers (the active context window) to secondary storage (long-term retrieval indices). Tool invocation functions as input/output (I/O) bus communication with external peripheral devices. The agent runtime serves as the operating system kernel: it schedules model calls, mediates every privileged operation, manages execution state, and enforces access control. Across tasks, learning from recorded runs plays the role of a profile-guided optimizing compiler (one that recompiles a program using measurements taken from its earlier executions), refining the model’s policy from traces of prior runs without modifying underlying safety boundaries. Finally, coordinating many agents mirrors scale-out across a network fabric, where several agents divide one workload and contend for shared state and resource limits.
3 The Stored-Program Organization: Von Neumann’s 1945 draft report on the EDVAC partitioned a computer into central arithmetic, central control, memory, and input/output organs (Neumann 1945). In von Neumann’s architecture, central control holds the absolute authority to fetch and execute instructions. In an agentic system, that authority is deliberately inverted: authority resides strictly within the surrounding runtime, while the learned model only proposes actions. Trust is decided outside the processor. 
Neumann, John von. 1945. First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC. Moore School of Electrical Engineering, University of Pennsylvania.






Figure 2: The Stochastic Computer as an Architectural Map: The agent stack structured around traditional computing layers (marked with ≈). The live execution loop (top) executes one task trajectory turn by turn. The across-task loop (bottom) compiles evaluated trajectories into updated model policies and coordinates multi-agent scale. While the architectural analogy provides intuition, the chapters develop each subsystem through its own rigorous systems mechanisms.



The analogy breaks down at the processor, and that divergence defines the core discipline of agentic systems engineering. A conventional CPU executes instructions deterministically. Given identical registers and machine state, execution is repeatable and auditable. A foundation model, by contrast, operates stochastically by sampling tokens from a distribution learned during training and conditioned on the observations supplied in its context. That conditioning guarantees neither that the observations are complete and current nor that the proposed action is correct. Its outputs are candidate proposals, not certified computations. A generated response can be eloquently phrased yet factually wrong, syntactically correct yet semantically catastrophic, and nothing within the generated text itself can vouch for its own validity.
In a classical operating system, the kernel trusts the CPU to execute instructions faithfully. In an agentic system, the runtime cannot trust its processor even to report its own status accurately. Conditioning on observations does not certify an execution result, so a model may hallucinate a successful return code or report actions it never took. The runtime must therefore close the control loop independently: it mechanically enforces permissions below the model and verifies results against external ground truth above the model (section 1.5.2). Memory relationships diverge just as sharply. While a physical CPU addresses memory directly, the context presented to a model is merely a selective, lossy projection of the environment’s state. Authoritative state resides in external databases, filesystems, and version-control trees; the agent’s memory holds only transient working representations.
Viewing the agent as a stochastic computer clarifies where traditional systems guarantees hold and where new abstractions are required. The primary systems challenge is not simply invoking a model, but building the deterministic runtime (the memory virtualization, execution sandboxes, and verification pipelines) that allows an unreliable cognitive core to drive reliable, autonomous computation.

title: 1 Introduction
text:
Agents depart from a single model call along horizon, state, and authority.
While the architecture of a stochastic computer identifies the structural components of an agentic system, the H·S·A exposure space quantifies the runtime machinery that a specific workload demands. It measures how far a delegated assignment departs from an elementary, single-turn model invocation. The fundamental unit of that measurement is the primary runtime artifact of this book: the trajectory.

Definition 1.2: Trajectory
Trajectory is the ordered sequence of recorded states, proposed actions, runtime decisions, and observations through which one delegated task proceeds, from its initial context to its ultimate acceptance, termination, or escalation.

Significance: The trajectory length defines the operational horizon \(\TurnHorizon\), which governs how compounding errors degrade system reliability. Furthermore, its complete span (encompassing rejected actions, retries, and failed branches) establishes the true accounting boundary when computing cost and latency per accepted task.
Distinction: While a conversational transcript merely captures the tokens exchanged between a model and a user, a trajectory preserves the full causal history of execution. It records which action proposals the runtime approved, modified, or rejected, alongside the raw observations returned by external tools, linking every decision to the exact evidence available at that step.
Common pitfall: Preserving only the final deliverable. Storing just the accepted patch or completed document hides the computational cost of discarded attempts, masks transient faults, and discards the intermediate verification evidence that justified accepting the work.



We formalize this sequence using the compact notation
\[\Trajectory = (\TrajectoryState_0, \TrajectoryAction_0, \TrajectoryObservation_1, \TrajectoryState_1, \TrajectoryAction_1, \TrajectoryObservation_2, \dots, \TrajectoryState_{\TurnHorizon})\]
where \(\TrajectoryState_{t}\) represents the recorded state available at decision step \(\TurnIndex\), \(\TrajectoryAction_{t}\) is the proposed action emitted by the model, and \(\TrajectoryObservation_{t+1}\) is the subsequent observation returned by the execution environment. Each transition from \(\TrajectoryState_{t}\) to \(\TrajectoryState_{t+1}\) constitutes a single turn: one model invocation paired with the runtime’s mediation of the resulting proposal. The notation establishes a total ordering across interactions, where each \(\TrajectoryState_{t}\) reflects the runtime’s partially observed view of the broader environment.
A standard model invocation is isolated: it consumes a static prompt and returns a completion. Extending that single call into an autonomous trajectory exposes the system to progressive operational risk along three physical and architectural dimensions: how long execution continues, what state persists across steps, and what external side effects the system can trigger. This book models these dimensions as the Horizon, State, and Authority (H·S·A) exposure space.

Definition 1.3: H·S·A exposure space
H·S·A exposure space is the three-dimensional coordinate system quantifying how far a delegated task departs from an isolated model call: its horizon \(\TurnHorizon\) measured in sequential turns, the state \(\StateExposureLevel_0\) through \(\StateExposureLevel_3\) carried between invocations, and the authority \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\) through \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\) exercised over external systems.

Significance: Each axis identifies a concrete operational exposure that the runtime must bound. Horizon determines how rapidly unverified errors compound, state dictates the working memory and durable artifacts carried forward, and authority establishes the maximum blast radius of an errant action. Later divisions of this book systematically address how to close these exposures: Part II governs state, Part III controls authority, and Part IV bounds horizon.
Distinction: A coordinate in this space describes the exposure a task carries, which is a property of the task and its environment. The runtime’s validation gates, sandboxes, and compensating operations are its response to that exposure, which section 1.5 develops as closure. Closure is what the runtime builds; the coordinate is where the task sits.
Common pitfall: Inferring authority from syntax or command names alone. Authority reflects the operational consequence of an action within its specific environment; an identical file deletion is discardable inside an ephemeral sandbox, but irreversible when executed directly against an unversioned production datastore.



Horizon \(\TurnHorizon\) tracks the duration of execution in discrete sequential turns. Every additional turn provides another opportunity for invalid tool invocations, stale environment observations, and context drift; section 1.6 models mathematically how unchecked step-level failure rates compound into severe task-level unreliability across extended sequences. Crucially, turn count and wall-clock latency represent distinct operational budgets that require independent management. A three-turn workflow that triggers a large remote build cluster can run for hours, whereas a hundred-turn in-memory code refactoring completes in seconds. Production runtimes must meter both metrics, bounding turns to restrict error compounding and bounding wall-clock time to release compute and network resources.
State (\(\StateExposureLevel_0\) to \(\StateExposureLevel_3\)) characterizes the data, memory, and environmental artifacts that persist across turns. At \(\StateExposureLevel_0\), the system operates completely statelessly, carrying no task context past a single invocation. At \(\StateExposureLevel_1\), the runtime maintains conversational working state; this includes the tokenized context window as well as inference-tier serving state, such as cached key-value (KV) attention pairs. At \(\StateExposureLevel_2\), the agent manages task-local working artifacts within an isolated workspace, such as a private source tree, an ephemeral container, or an in-memory scratchpad. At \(\StateExposureLevel_3\), execution interfaces with durable shared state that outlives the individual task session, such as an authoritative database, a shared object store, or a central code repository. Because realistic workloads routinely span several tiers at once, this classification establishes what data the runtime must checkpoint or isolate, determines cache invalidation boundaries, and dictates which storage system remains authoritative when local scratchpad views diverge.
Authority (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\) to \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\)) defines the blast radius of actions delegated to the task. At \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\), access is strictly read-only, although exfiltration remains a risk if retrieved secrets leak into output text. At \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_1\), mutations are confined entirely to a disposable workspace where unintended modifications carry zero external impact. At \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_2\), actions affect external systems, but every mutating operation has an explicit compensating transaction4 executed under verified preconditions, with a separate retry policy preventing duplicate effects. At \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\), the task executes non-compensable actions (such as modifying unversioned production records, issuing financial transactions, or publishing public communications) for which no automated reversal exists. Authority reflects the operational consequence within the specific execution environment rather than cosmetic command syntax. Because a trusted runtime mediates every action against an explicit per-task capability grant, restricting this grant provides the first and most cost-effective line of defense before deploying complex validation machinery.5
4 Compensating Transactions: Garcia-Molina and Salem introduced sagas for long-lived distributed transactions where holding locks across the entire workflow is impractical: a saga consists of a sequence of local transactions, each paired with a compensating transaction that semantically undoes earlier steps if the overall workflow aborts (Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987). Compensation is an active forward recovery action rather than an atomic rollback; concurrent processes can observe intermediate states, and the compensating action itself may fail. An \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_2\) capability grant therefore requires an executable compensation handler before dispatching the initial mutating effect. 
Garcia-Molina, Hector, and Kenneth Salem. 1987. “Sagas.” Proceedings of the 1987 ACM SIGMOD International Conference on Management of Data, 249–59. https://doi.org/10.1145/38713.38742.
5 Least Privilege and Complete Mediation: Saltzer and Schroeder’s foundational protection principles dictate that every program must operate using the smallest set of privileges necessary to complete its task (least privilege), and that every access to every object must be systematically validated (complete mediation) (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975). Validating capability grants on every tool invocation applies both principles to a non-deterministic model whose proposals cannot be inherently trusted. Restricting the task’s initial capability grant remains the most dependable technique for minimizing potential damage when runtime verification checks fail to intercept an unsafe request. 
Saltzer, J. H., and M. D. Schroeder. 1975. “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems.” Proceedings of the IEEE 63 (9): 1278–308. https://doi.org/10.1109/proc.1975.9939.
The coordinate space in figure 3 maps agentic workloads across three operational exposure axes: horizon (\(\TurnHorizon\), turns along the horizontal), authority (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\) to \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\) on the vertical), and carried state (\(\StateExposureLevel_0\) to \(\StateExposureLevel_3\) on the depth axis). This space functions as an analytical lens rather than a rigid taxonomy: two workloads occupying the exact same cell may still demand different runtime controls if their data sensitivity, tool reliability, or catastrophic failure thresholds diverge. Furthermore, altering the execution environment can shift a task into a completely different cell even when its foundation model and turn horizon remain identical, as demonstrated in example 1.1. The four workloads plotted in the space are the book’s lighthouse workloads, described in section 1.4.1.






Figure 3: The H·S·A Exposure Space: Horizon (\(\TurnHorizon\), turns), carried state (\(\StateExposureLevel_0\) to \(\StateExposureLevel_3\)), and authority (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\) to \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\)) map the operational departures of an agent from an isolated model call. Plotted positions represent illustrative task configurations rather than intrinsic properties of each workload class. The formal task contract and failure consequences dictate necessary runtime controls. System closure represents the engineering response to these exposures rather than an independent coordinate axis.




Example 1.1: A working copy and the only copyScenario: A coding assistant must repair a software defect while preserving adjacent, uncommitted edits authored by a developer. Consider two execution environments: an isolated, ephemeral sandbox containing a working copy of the project vs. direct access to the developer’s sole authoritative workspace. The foundation model, repair objective, and expected turn horizon remain identical in both configurations. In each case, the assistant issues a command to delete files while cleaning up intermediate build artifacts.
Diagnosis: Inside the ephemeral sandbox, the source files constitute \(\StateExposureLevel_2\) working state and the mutation authority is bounded at \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_1\). Tearing down the sandbox discards any erroneous modifications without corrupting the developer’s original files. In the authoritative workspace, however, that identical command targets \(\StateExposureLevel_3\) state. Although one person uses it, the workspace is durable state the task shares with its developer, it outlives the task, and it holds the only copy of the developer’s edits. If the deleted files contain unique, unstaged edits missing from version control history, the operation immediately escalates to \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\) irreversible data destruction. Version control alone does not prevent this loss, as uncommitted working-tree changes lack snapshots. A resilient systems contract grants the agent access strictly to an isolated clone, excludes unrelated edits from the agent’s context, and reserves the integration of reviewed patches for a separate gate. The runtime must enforce that isolation boundary through tool authorization rather than relying on prompt instructions asking the model to exercise caution.
Systems lesson: The failure boundary shifted fundamentally even though the model, prompt, and turn horizon remained unchanged. Automated test suites evaluate functional behavior, and diff reviews verify patch cleanliness, but neither technique prevents an unauthorized deletion command from obliterating working state. Sound systems engineering enforces safety at the infrastructure boundary, preventing destructive operations from reaching authoritative state, rather than relying on post-hoc verification to detect irreversible side effects.




The four workloads plotted across the H·S·A exposure space of figure 3 define this book’s lighthouses: the support agent, remediation agent, repository repair agent, and research agent. Like a lighthouse, each is a fixed reference point that the reader can steer by as the mechanisms change from chapter to chapter. They represent four distinct architectural archetypes chosen because each is bounded by a fundamentally different systems bottleneck; an optimization that halves latency for one workload may be entirely irrelevant to another. Automated repository repair serves as our primary running example, while the other three appear whenever a chapter explores failure modes or constraints that repository repair does not trigger.

Lighthouse 1.1: Repair agent (long-horizon worker)Workload: A repository coding agent diagnoses and fixes a defect in an isolated working copy, submitting a verified patch for review. The connection-pool race condition in this chapter serves as the concrete running example; its reference harness budgets 30 steps inside a 128,000-token context window.
Exposure: Long horizon (tens to hundreds of turns), a task-local working copy (\(\StateExposureLevel_2\)), and filesystem edits confined strictly to that disposable sandbox (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_1\)) until a human-reviewed patch is exported.
Binding constraint: Compounding errors across the trajectory, and repeated input whose token count grows quadratically when every turn resends the full history. Without compatible prefix reuse, this repeated input can dominate aggregate inference work and cost, while acceptance depends strictly on immutable test suites that the agent cannot modify.



Lighthouse 1.2: Research agent (untrusted reader)Workload: A deep-research agent answers an open-ended question by querying, retrieving, and synthesizing external web sources, frequently delegating sub-queries to parallel worker agents.
Exposure: Horizons from tens of turns for one question to thousands for a standing crawl, an expanding knowledge store of ingested documents (\(\StateExposureLevel_3\)), and read-only authority (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\)).
Binding constraint: Ingested content is untrusted data. Through indirect prompt injection, in which a retrieved page carries text the model may follow as an instruction, it can redirect the trajectory or exfiltrate private context (Greshake et al. 2023), so read-only access is still a serious security exposure. Aggregate token consumption from retrieved documents and worker fan-out dominates total execution cost.



Lighthouse 1.3: Remediation agent (irreversible actor)Workload: An automated site-reliability agent diagnoses a live production incident and applies configuration or infrastructure changes to restore service. One Incident Through the System analyzes one such remediation end to end.
Exposure: A moderate horizon (tens of turns), mutable shared production infrastructure (\(\StateExposureLevel_3\)), and non-compensable or irreversible operations (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\)).
Binding constraint: A single erroneous action can incur outages costing orders of magnitude more than all trajectory compute combined. Human-in-the-loop approval latency and the blast radius of incorrect decisions dominate systems design, necessitating strict approval gates, compensating actions, and explicit points of no return before execution begins.



Lighthouse 1.4: Support agent (interactive responder)Workload: A customer-operations agent resolves billing and booking inquiries while the user waits synchronously.
Exposure: Short sessions of a few turns each across thousands of concurrent users, session context combined with sensitive enterprise database records (\(\StateExposureLevel_1\) with \(\StateExposureLevel_3\)), and authority that escalates from read-only queries (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\)) to compensable updates such as a seat hold that can be released (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_2\)), and on to actions with no automated reversal such as a refund paid out to an external account (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\)).
Binding constraint: Strict tail latency under high concurrency, combined with verifiable adherence to enterprise policy. Serving throughput and the aggregate memory overhead of retaining active session state across thousands of simultaneous connections dominate systems cost.


Comparing these four lighthouses demonstrates why systems mechanisms cannot be evaluated in the abstract. Proactive context summarization is vital for a multi-turn repository repair agent but largely superfluous for a three-turn support session. An on-call remediation agent can read diagnostic telemetry under a prior grant while requiring explicit approval for consequential production changes. A read-only researcher can likewise operate under a bounded grant, but disclosure of sensitive context may still require approval. The task boundary, rather than the workload label, determines where those gates belong. Each subsequent chapter links its proposed mechanisms directly to the lighthouse whose binding constraints they resolve. Placing a workload in the space shows where it is exposed; how the runtime closes each exposure without trusting the model to do so is the subject of invariant closure.

title: 1 Introduction
text:
A foundation model operating within an agentic loop generates fluent, plausible proposals, but it cannot certify their safety or correctness. This limitation creates the central governance challenge of agentic architecture. When the model cannot validate its own outputs, the surrounding system must guarantee operational integrity, and invariant closure divides that responsibility between two sides of the model. Safety constraints are mechanically enforced below it, and task completion is verified against independent evidence above it.


Invariant closure primarily defends against the fail-plausible fault: the output appears well formed and credible while the intended property remains unsatisfied.6 Consider an autonomous repository repair loop: an agent terminates its execution with a confident, well-reasoned summary declaring that a race condition is fixed, even though the underlying defect persists. The generated patch might be syntactically immaculate yet eliminate thread safety by deleting a critical synchronization lock. Alternatively, a test suite might exit with return code zero only because the model commented out failing assertions. In both cases, the system encounters a fault that appears completely credible to superficial inspection.
6 Signaled and Unsignaled Failures: The standard dependability taxonomy classifies failures by detectability as well as by kind: a signaled failure raises a warning when the service goes wrong, and an unsignaled one does not (Avizienis et al. 2004). A fail-plausible fault is an unsignaled content failure (the delivered result is wrong and nothing announces it), so a runtime that watches only for crashes, timeouts, and error codes will record it as a success. 
Avizienis, Algirdas, Jean-Claude Laprie, Brian Randell, and Carl Landwehr. 2004. “Basic Concepts and Taxonomy of Dependable and Secure Computing.” IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing 1 (1): 11–33. https://doi.org/10.1109/TDSC.2004.2.
7 Fail-Stop and Byzantine Faults: Schlichting and Schneider defined a fail-stop processor as one that halts on failure without first making an erroneous state transition, so that other processors can detect the halt (Schlichting and Schneider 1983). Lamport, Shostak, and Pease showed that reaching agreement when some components may send arbitrary, conflicting messages requires more than two-thirds of the components to be correct, the origin of the \(3\ByzantineFaultCount+1\) replica bound for tolerating \(\ByzantineFaultCount\) such faults (Lamport et al. 1982). 
Schlichting, Richard D., and Fred B. Schneider. 1983. “Fail-Stop Processors: An Approach to Designing Fault-Tolerant Computing Systems.” ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 1 (3): 222–38. https://doi.org/10.1145/3149.3150.

Lamport, Leslie, Robert Shostak, and Marshall Pease. 1982. “The Byzantine Generals Problem.” ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems 4 (3): 382–401. https://doi.org/10.1145/357172.357176.
Classical fault models highlight why this failure pattern demands a distinct systems category. In distributed systems, a fail-stop component halts when it faults, enabling a supervisor to detect the failure through missing heartbeats or nonzero exit codes (Schlichting and Schneider 1983). A Byzantine component may exhibit arbitrary or deceptive behavior, but Byzantine fault-tolerant agreement uses redundancy under a stated bound on the number of faulty replicas (Lamport et al. 1982).7 A plausible wrong answer can evade crash monitoring and agreement among model samples. Because the model process neither crashes nor halts, fail-stop monitors register success. Furthermore, sampling repeatedly from the same foundation model establishes no bound on how many samples are wrong: shared systematic blind spots can produce agreement on an incorrect answer. The fail-plausible fault is thus an unsignaled semantic failure that looks like success on the surface.



Crash detection and agreement leave plausible wrong answers needing an outside check.
8 The Confused Deputy: Hardy described a compiler that held a license to write files in its own directory; a user passed it the name of the billing file as an output path, and the compiler, acting with its own authority rather than the user’s, overwrote the billing records (Hardy 1988). Authority that comes from where a program runs rather than from the request it serves can be steered by whoever supplies the names, which is exactly the position of a model whose tool calls run with host credentials while it reads untrusted text. 
Hardy, Norm. 1988. “The Confused Deputy: (Or Why Capabilities Might Have Been Invented).” ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 22 (4): 36–38. https://doi.org/10.1145/60609.60611.
To prevent fail-plausible faults from corrupting system state, the execution environment enforces zero ambient authority: the model holds no standing privileges of its own, and every external side effect must pass through an explicit grant checked by the runtime.8 Generated tokens cannot authorize commands, alter the runtime’s execution records, or declare acceptance. Instead, the runtime gathers environmental evidence strictly through designated tools and deterministic checks. For repository repair, this requires separating the raw patch text the model proposed from the diff the runtime actually applied on disk (the two differ whenever a patch fails to apply cleanly), as well as isolating model-authored summaries of test execution from actual process exit codes.
Every external check establishes a bounded claim that is narrower than the overarching task objective. A clean compilation step demonstrates only that the program conforms to grammar and type rules under a specific build configuration. A passing regression test records only that the implementation executed successfully for the specific inputs and thread schedules tested. As Dijkstra observed, testing can reveal the presence of defects, but never prove their absence (Dijkstra 1970).



The working-copy comparison in example 1.1 separates preventing an unauthorized action from deciding whether an outcome meets engineering requirements. A filesystem boundary mechanically prevents writes outside the assigned workspace. Whether a patch inside that workspace repairs a race condition is a distinct assertion requiring empirical evidence of program behavior. Invariant closure assigns both responsibilities to explicit mechanisms around the model rather than relying on model self-assurance. Limits are enforced mechanically below the model, and acceptance rests on evidence gathered above it. The principle below measures both against the task contract, the explicit specification of what may execute and what counts as done, which section 1.5.3 defines. It also states the cost of leaving steps unchecked in terms of a per-step error rate \(\PerStepErrorRate\), a result that section 1.6 derives.

Principle 1: Invariant closureInvariant: Constraints never rest on the model; bounds close mechanically below it, acceptance on evidence above it. Each enforced bound names the property and assumptions under which it holds, and each acceptance decision names the evidence standard it applies. Without either, a trajectory of \(\TurnHorizon\) independent steps, each correct with probability \(1-\PerStepErrorRate\), succeeds only with probability \[ \Pr(\text{success}) = (1-\PerStepErrorRate)^{\TurnHorizon} \] while an enforced bound rejects the violations it blocks, and a check rejects those it detects.
Implication: Under the independent-step model without recovery, unchecked reliability decays exponentially with horizon; raising step accuracy does not remove the need for runtime bounds and checks. The runtime mediates permitted effects and resource use independently of the model’s compliance. It accepts completion only when evidence meets the task contract, preserving the distinction between a passing check and a guarantee beyond that check’s coverage. The contract itself is adopted by authorized people: the model can draft it but cannot adopt, relax, or certify against it. Greater operational exposure requires stronger justification for both the boundaries and the evidence.


Mechanical enforcement establishes concrete execution boundaries. A filesystem restriction prevents writes to protected paths, provided all file operations pass through the enforcement layer and its isolation assumptions hold. This mechanism governs where modifications land, but leaves the correctness of those modifications as a separate question. Similarly, schema validation confirms that a tool request is syntactically well formed, while authorization remains an independent check. The systems design rule is to keep each enforced property narrower than the complete task claim and explicitly name the guarantee it provides.
Acceptance decisions rely on evidence organized across distinct closure evidence levels. The classical end-to-end argument explains why the levels differ (Saltzer et al. 1984). An end-to-end task property can be validated only by an endpoint equipped with complete task requirements, so correct behavior at a lower layer, such as generating well-typed code, cannot certify end-to-end correctness. Ordered from the weakest default grounding to the strongest, the five levels are:

Self-report: The agent’s own account is an unverified claim rather than an empirical observation of the environment.
Static analysis: Analysis checks structural and type invariants without executing the code.
Visible tests: Tests execute cases that the agent can inspect directly. They are valuable for iterative diagnosis, but they expose test cases that candidate solutions can overfit against.
Sealed tests: Tests withhold their definitions from the agent and run within tamper-proof sandboxes, preserving evaluation integrity.
Formal verification: A proof establishes that an implementation satisfies an explicit mathematical model, though confirming that the specification reflects true user intent remains an external human judgment.

The ordering is a default rather than an absolute ranking, because a level’s strength also depends on how complete its tests or its specification are. An exhaustive sealed test suite provides more practical confidence than a mathematical proof derived from an incomplete specification.
In the race-condition repair, passing a sequential unit test yields evidence only for single-threaded execution. Sealing that test protects the assertions from modification, but does not broaden its coverage. Establishing that the concurrency defect is resolved requires running multi-threaded stress workloads that force thread interleavings under varied execution schedules. Human code review then examines operational assumptions that the test harness cannot probe. Because an automated verdict can be fully repeatable yet structurally incomplete, acceptance claims must remain strictly bounded by what the test infrastructure measured.
Certain completion criteria cannot be reduced to executable boolean predicates and require qualitative evaluation. An automated or human evaluator scores these outcomes against an explicit rubric, documenting decision ownership and epistemic uncertainty while mechanical permission bounds remain in force. When candidate evidence falls short of the task contract, the runtime reports an unresolved outcome or escalates to human operators; it never treats a plausible narrative as a substitute for verified completion. Validation mechanisms also differ in how often they accept an outcome that is in fact wrong, a rate that must be measured rather than assumed. Intermediate checks paired with repair or restoration can shorten the unchecked horizon for the properties they reliably detect. Undetected errors still carry forward, so the compounding analyzed in section 1.6 depends on both check coverage and recovery.


↪ Measuring a grader’s false-acceptance rate against independent reference assessment is developed in Grader error rates.



A simple instruction such as “repair the race condition” leaves critical engineering boundaries undefined. A proposed patch might remove thread synchronization entirely, passing a sequential regression check while exacerbating concurrency failures under production load. Similarly, an agent issued a cleanup directive might purge scratch files in a disposable sandbox, or inadvertently delete uncommitted source files in a shared repository. An unadorned goal cannot distinguish constructive solutions from catastrophic side effects. Before an execution engine dispatches any autonomous action, the system requires an explicit specification defining what resources may be mutated and what evidence is required to accept the final output.9
9 Wiener’s Warning on Delegated Purpose: In 1960 Wiener argued that when a mechanical agency acts too fast and irrevocably for anyone to intervene before the action completes, “we had better be quite sure that the purpose put into the machine is the purpose which we really desire” (Wiener 1960). The warning binds hardest where authority is irreversible, which is why the contract that follows is written and adopted before the loop runs rather than repaired after an effect lands. 
Wiener, N. 1960. “Some Moral and Technical Consequences of Automation: As Machines Learn They May Develop Unforeseen Strategies at Rates That Baffle Their Programmers.” Science 131 (3410): 1355–58. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.131.3410.1355.
10 Design by Contract: Meyer framed a software component’s interface as a contract of preconditions the caller must establish, postconditions the supplier guarantees, and invariants both preserve, each written as a checkable assertion (Meyer 1992). The task contract borrows the structure but not the trust: in classical design by contract the supplier’s own code checks its postconditions, whereas here the supplier is the model, so the completion criteria must be checked by the runtime and tools rather than asserted by the component that produced the result. 
Meyer, Bertrand. 1992. “Applying ‘Design by Contract’.” Computer 25 (10): 40–51. https://doi.org/10.1109/2.161279.
A task specification transforms underspecified intent into an enforceable systems contract. We formulate this as a five-part tuple, \(\TaskContract = \langle \TaskContractGoal, \TaskEnvironment, \PermittedActions, \AvailableObservations, \CompletionCriteria \rangle\), which cleanly separates the desired objective from the execution environment, delegated permissions, permitted observations, and acceptance criteria. This structural separation is necessary because natural language instructions communicate intent without providing the runtime mechanisms required to authorize execution or verify task fulfillment.10

Definition 1.4: Task contract
Task contract is the explicit specification of a delegated task that separates its goal, environment, permitted actions, available observations, and completion criteria, so that the runtime, not the model, decides what may execute and when the task is done.

Significance: The completion criteria define what counts as accepted, which fixes the denominator of cost per accepted task. Two systems, or two versions of one system, can be compared only under the same contract.
Distinction: A prompt communicates intent to the model; a contract is enforced by the runtime and the tool environment. The same sentence can appear in both, but only the contract constrains what executes.
Common pitfall: Writing the permitted actions into the prompt alone. The model reads the limit, and the host process still allows everything its credentials allow.



In the repository repair task, the goal \(\TaskContractGoal\) includes an explicit negative scope, the set of existing system behaviors and invariants that must remain undisturbed outside the reported defect. The environment \(\TaskEnvironment\) identifies the source baseline, runtime dependencies, and the designated workspace where edits occur. Permitted actions \(\PermittedActions\) authorize bounded file edits, directory inspection, and test runner invocations, while denying network egress and write access to parent directories. Available observations \(\AvailableObservations\) restrict returned payloads to source excerpts, bounded test logs, and Git diffs. Finally, completion criteria \(\CompletionCriteria\) define the sealed test suites that must pass alongside human review gates for unmeasured behaviors. Table 2 grounds these five components in concrete systems artifacts.



Table 2: Five-Part Task Specification Contract: Each component answers a distinct systems question for the repair task, cleanly decoupling intent, execution context, authority, visibility, and verification.

Each component of the contract prevents a specific systems failure mode. Omitting a negative scope from the goal invites degenerative solutions, such as silencing a concurrency bug by removing the failing assertion or deleting multi-threaded access paths altogether. Lacking an isolated environment specification, agent edits and ad hoc dependency installations pollute shared host state, destroying experimental reproducibility. Without explicit action boundaries, tool dispatch defaults to the ambient authority of the host process. Unbounded observations permit sprawling search outputs that flood the model’s context window, degrading reasoning performance and evicting critical instructions. Finally, omitting formal completion criteria forces the runtime to rely on the model’s self-reported success as its termination signal.
Environments that keep changing on their own require the contract to separate what the agent changed from what the world changed. During live incident triage by the remediation agent (lighthouse 1.3), traffic and error rates keep shifting while the agent works. Unless the contract records which observations follow from the agent’s own configuration change and which reflect outside load, a coincidental drop in traffic reads as a successful fix. Observation constraints must also differentiate empty query results from truncated responses. If the runtime truncates a voluminous test log to fit token budgets, it must inject explicit truncation metadata into the prompt; otherwise, the model may treat the omission of an error message as proof that no error occurred.
Operational resource bounds and termination rules necessarily accompany the contract. Every delegated task requires turn budgets, wall-clock execution deadlines, monetary token spend limits, and deterministic error-handling policies for resource exhaustion. Halting on an exhausted resource budget produces an unresolved outcome, meaning that the evidence gathered so far neither accepts nor rejects the work. That differs from a failure, where evidence shows the attempt did not meet the contract, and from silent termination, which leaves no record at all. The runtime preserves the intermediate diff, logs the incomplete verification checks, and escalates to human engineers for intervention.
Drafting a contract also exposes the boundaries of what can be safely delegated. Subjective directives such as “improve maintainability” cannot be evaluated by automated predicates alone. In such cases, the system architect must establish measurable proxy metrics, assign a qualified human reviewer, or exclude the subjective decision from autonomous execution entirely. The primary function of the task contract is to make these operational boundaries explicit so that the runtime can enforce them deterministically.
Subsequent chapters implement each facet of this architecture. In Tool Calling, we formalize permitted actions and structured observation schemas. In Agent Sandboxes, we design isolated container and virtual machine environments to safely execute untrusted side effects. In The Agent Harness, we construct the harness at the core of the runtime that enforces task goals, operational budgets, and stopping rules. Finally, Agent Evaluation establishes the statistical and empirical evidence pipelines required by formal completion criteria.
The invariant closure principle and the five-part task contract establish the governance framework required for autonomous execution. Mechanically enforcing isolation below the foundation model protects shared infrastructure, while verifying empirical evidence above the model supports acceptance under the task contract. Yet rigorous governance introduces concrete systems overhead: running sealed regression suites, provisioning ephemeral execution sandboxes, and verifying intermediate invariants consume runtime latency and compute budgets. Evaluating these engineering trade-offs requires analyzing the quantitative dynamics of multi-turn execution, where horizon compounding and verification economics determine the ultimate cost per accepted task.

title: 1 Introduction
text:
A realistic agentic trajectory spans dozens of sequential turns, with each turn building directly on observations and state modifications from the preceding step. A misdiagnosed deadlock trace leads the model to inspect the wrong source file; an erroneous patch to that file cascades into compilation failures or silently corrupts unrelated business logic. Because foundation models generate fluent rationalizations even when mistaken, nothing in the model’s generated text signals the exact moment execution derailed. An extended autonomous task can easily fail even when individual per-turn accuracy appears exceptionally high.
The invariant closure principle (1) stated the cost of leaving steps unchecked without deriving it. Elementary probability supplies the derivation and shows why the principle places verifiers inside the execution loop. Suppose each of \(\TurnHorizon\) sequential steps is correct with probability \(1-\PerStepErrorRate\), errors are statistically independent, and no step is verified before subsequent steps build upon it. The overall task succeeds only if every intermediate step succeeds:
\[\Pr(\text{success}) = (1-\PerStepErrorRate)^{\TurnHorizon} \tag{1}\]
Equation 1 applies classic series-reliability analysis11 to the sequential turns of a trajectory. We call the resulting reliability collapse horizon compounding. Statistical independence is an idealization; in practice, errors correlate and models occasionally recover from bad states. Under the independent-step model without recovery, unchecked success decays exponentially with horizon length (notebook 1.1); correlation and recovery can change the shape of that decline.
11 Reliable Systems from Unreliable Components: Von Neumann posed the problem in 1956 for logic networks whose every element errs with some fixed probability, so that errors accumulate through the depth of the computation (Neumann 1956). His remedy interleaved redundant computation with “restoring organs” that re-establish a correct signal at intervals, keeping the error bounded however deep the network grows. Checks paired with restoration play the same structural role for the errors they detect, limiting their accumulation to the distance between successful restorations. 
Neumann, John von. 1956. “Probabilistic Logics and the Synthesis of Reliable Organisms from Unreliable Components.” In Automata Studies, edited by Claude E. Shannon and John McCarthy, vol. 34. Annals of Mathematics Studies. Princeton University Press. https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400882618-003.


Under the independent-step model without recovery, unchecked success falls exponentially with the horizon.


Napkin Math 1.1: Horizon compoundingProblem: Each step of a repair agent is correct with probability 99 percent, independently, and no step is checked before the next one builds on it. What fraction of tasks succeed at horizons of 10 and 100 turns, and what per-step error rate would hold the longer horizon at 90 percent success?
Math: By equation 1, \(0.99^{10} \approx 0.904\), so 90.4 percent of tasks succeed at 10 turns, while \(0.99^{100} \approx 0.366\) leaves 36.6 percent at 100 turns. Holding 90 percent at 100 turns requires \(\PerStepErrorRate = 1 - 0.90^{1/100} \approx 0.00105\), about 0.11 percent per step and 9.5× lower than the assumed 1 percent. For small \(\PerStepErrorRate\), \((1-\PerStepErrorRate)^\TurnHorizon \approx e^{-\PerStepErrorRate \TurnHorizon}\), and the requirement reads \(\PerStepErrorRate \TurnHorizon \approx 0.105\) at any horizon.
Systems insight: The product \(\PerStepErrorRate \TurnHorizon\), not step accuracy alone, sets task reliability. A tenfold longer horizon demands a tenfold lower per-step error to hold the same success rate. The cheaper engineering knob is usually the unchecked horizon itself: a check that reliably detects an error, followed by restoration and a successful retry, bounds the segment over which that error can compound. Under the notebook’s independence assumption, perfect detection and restoration turn the extended task into a sequence of short segments. Supplying and enforcing those checks is the primary responsibility of the runtime, as formalized by the invariant closure principle (1).


The horizon in equation 1 belongs to the delegated task, and the tasks delegated to agents have lengthened quickly. Kwa et al. (2025) express that length in human terms. They time people with the relevant expertise on a suite of software and research tasks, then report each model’s 50 percent time horizon, the length of task, in expert time, that an agent built on the model completes in half its attempts. Figure 4 plots that horizon for every model the study evaluates, at the model’s release date.














Figure 4: Measured Task Horizon: Each point is one model’s 50 percent time horizon, the expert-time length of task its agent completes in half its attempts, against the model’s release date. The vertical axis is logarithmic, so the straight dashed fit to frontier models released since 2023 is exponential growth, doubling about every 4.2 months. Filled points were the frontier at release, open points were not, and bars are 95 percent confidence intervals. Data from Kwa et al. (2025) (Time Horizon v1.1).


Kwa, Thomas, Ben West, Joel Becker, Amy Deng, Katharyn Garcia, Max Hasin, Sami Jawhar, et al. 2025. “Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2503.14499.


Among the frontier models in figure 4, the 50 percent horizon grew from about 3 seconds to about 17 hours, a factor of roughly 19,000, doubling every 6.2 months across the whole period and every 4.2 months since 2023. Equation 1 turns that trend into an engineering obligation. A task that occupies an expert for hours instead of minutes spans many more dependent steps, and at a fixed per-step error, doubling the unchecked horizon squares the probability of success. Each doubling of the delegated task therefore requires either halving the per-step error or inserting checks that halve the unchecked segment between them. Model improvement supplies the first; only the runtime can supply the second, and the measured horizon is itself a reminder that half the attempts at that length still fail.
Checking converts a silent failure into an explicit, rejected attempt, and a rejected attempt still consumes real resources. Suppose each attempt at a task is accepted with probability \(\AcceptanceProbability\), independently of earlier attempts, and the runtime retries until one is accepted. The number of attempts follows a geometric distribution with mean \(1/\AcceptanceProbability\). Each attempt costs \(\AttemptCost\) in expectation, tallying model tokens, tool execution, test sandboxes, and human review, all of which a failed attempt consumes as completely as a successful one. The expected cost per accepted task is therefore
\[\CostPerAcceptedTask = \frac{\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]}{\AcceptanceProbability} \tag{2}\]
Production runtimes bound the retry budget, so some tasks end without acceptance, and their spend must still be charged to the tasks that were accepted. Measured over a cohort, cost per accepted task is therefore the total spend of every initiated task divided by the number accepted; the accounting pitfall in section 1.9 prices what omitting the failed attempts hides. Even in its expected-value form, equation 2 exposes a trade-off between unit model pricing and acceptance, which notebook 1.2 prices for the repair task.


↪ Whole-trajectory cost and the cohort cost per accepted task, which charges failed and abandoned attempts to the accepted ones, are developed in Cost per Accepted Task.

Napkin Math 1.2: Cheaper tokens or more acceptancesProblem: An attempt at the repair task spends $1.30 on model tokens and $0.80 on the sandbox, tests, and review, and is accepted with probability 40 percent. Which lowers cost per accepted task more: halving the token price, or raising acceptance to 60 percent through a context or tool improvement?
Math: The baseline attempt costs $2.10, and the task needs 2.5 attempts on average, so equation 2 gives \(2.10 / 0.40 = 5.25\) dollars per accepted task. Halving the token price lowers the attempt to $1.45, giving \(1.45 / 0.40 \approx 3.63\) dollars. Raising acceptance at the original attempt cost gives \(2.10 / 0.60 = 3.50\) dollars. To find the acceptance that the price cut is worth, set the cheaper attempt’s cost per accepted task, \(\AttemptCost(1 - \text{cut} \times \text{share})/\AcceptanceProbability\), equal to \(\AttemptCost/\BreakEvenAcceptanceProbability\) at the original attempt cost, where cut is the fraction of the token price removed and share is the tokens’ share of the attempt cost. Solving gives \(\BreakEvenAcceptanceProbability = \AcceptanceProbability/(1 - \text{cut} \times \text{share})\). Tokens are 62 percent of the attempt, so the price cut matches an acceptance of \(0.40 / (1 - 0.5 \times 0.62) \approx 0.58\).
Systems insight: The two levers act on different amounts. A price cut can remove at most the share of the attempt that the cheaper component represents, whereas acceptance divides the whole attempt cost (sandbox, tests, and review included). Halving the token price removes half of the tokens’ 62 percent share, which is worth the same as gaining 18 percentage points of acceptance (40 percent to 58 percent). Here the two options land close together, and the acceptance gain wins only narrowly. Any context enhancement or tool refinement that lifts acceptance beyond that threshold outperforms the price cut, because higher acceptance amortizes sandbox overhead, environment setup, and verification spend across fewer discarded runs. Systems engineers must evaluate interventions by their net effect on \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) under a rigorous acceptance contract, never by inference tariffs alone.





Acceptance divides every cost in an attempt, so a modest gain in it can outweigh halving the token price.
Equation 1 and equation 2 form the quantitative bedrock for systems design throughout this book. Equation 1 governs how rapidly reliability deteriorates across unchecked trajectories, while equation 2 establishes the economic threshold for architectural mechanisms. An intermediate check, a sandbox boundary, or a prompt cache (which reuses the serving state already computed for a repeated prompt prefix, so later calls skip recomputing it) changes both terms of that ratio. Writing \(\MechanismAttemptCost\) and \(\MechanismAcceptanceProbability\) for the attempt cost and acceptance with the mechanism in place, the mechanism justifies its overhead only when \(\MechanismAttemptCost/\MechanismAcceptanceProbability < \AttemptCost/\AcceptanceProbability\). Equivalently, it must lower \(\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]\) by a larger ratio than it degrades \(\AcceptanceProbability\), or raise \(\AcceptanceProbability\) by a factor that outstrips its added per-attempt cost.
Neither equation depends on how control decisions are generated. Both apply equally to deterministic programs with hardcoded control flow and to autonomous loops where foundation models choose each subsequent action. That structural neutrality makes them the decisive instrument for choosing between static workflows and dynamic agentic loops.


The software repair task illustrates both predictable mechanics and dynamic exploration. Initializing a working copy, fetching dependencies, and executing static analysis can follow a fixed workflow, where the sequence of operations is specified in advance. In contrast, diagnosing an intermittent race condition requires inspecting arbitrary source files, formulating test hypotheses, and evaluating runtime logs based on observations that unfold dynamically. A model-directed loop, in which the model chooses its next tool invocation based on intermediate trajectory observations, becomes valuable at these divergent branches, provided its acceptance gains exceed the variance and token overhead it introduces.
A fixed workflow is not limited to static linear scripts: it can evaluate conditional branches, manage retries, and dispatch parallel tasks, provided its control graph is defined in advance. Because the model calls embedded within a workflow remain stochastic, a deterministic control graph guarantees neither reproducible outputs nor bounded wall-clock latencies. When comparing a fixed workflow against a model-directed loop, systems architects must evaluate both under identical task contracts and acceptance verifiers. By equation 2, a model-directed loop is justified only when its open-ended exploration raises \(\AcceptanceProbability\) by a greater proportion than its additional model calls inflate \(\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]\).


↪ Economic feasibility envelopes for choosing between deterministic workflows and model-directed loops are developed in Economic feasibility envelopes for agentic loops.
Authorization policies must be decoupled from the control architecture that selects the steps. A fixed workflow can require human authorization before executing an external side effect, just as an autonomous diagnostic loop can operate entirely unprompted within an isolated sandbox. The runtime permits exploratory actions within a constrained boundary while gatekeeping irreversible operations such as production deployment. An approved execution grant merely authorizes an action to run; it does not validate the correctness of the resulting state, which still requires independent post-condition verification.

Checkpoint 1.1: Changing the task boundary
A repair agent can inspect and edit a disposable working copy and return a patch for review. Its contract grants no access to the deployment service.
Reading the boundary

Authority: The task now includes deployment. Which authority level does it move to, and which permission decision must be added that no passing test can supply?
State: The workspace turns out to hold the only copy of unrelated edits. Which exposure changes, and which single change to the grant removes it?
Acceptance evidence: A sealed sequential test passes after the race-condition repair. Which claim does it support, and what further evidence would you require before accepting?
Control policy: Which steps of the repair would you assign to a fixed workflow, and which decision must stay model-directed?

Pricing the choice

Cost per accepted task estimate: An attempt costs $2.10, of which $0.80 is sandbox, tests, and review, and 40 percent of attempts are accepted. Estimate the cost per accepted task if you halve that $0.80, and again if a tool change raises acceptance by 10 percentage points. Which would you fund?



Treating agent reliability and execution cost as coupled functions of trajectory length and acceptance probability establishes a rigorous baseline for system design. These quantitative trade-offs explain why real-world agent architectures depend less on unconstrained model autonomy than on bounded execution graphs, robust intermediate verifiers, and disciplined resource accounting across realistic workloads.

title: 1 Introduction
text:
The four instruments have so far been developed one at a time. Following the repair task of section 1.2 through its actual turns shows where each one acts: which component holds authority at each step, where evidence enters, and why the unit the runtime manages is the whole trajectory rather than the individual call.


Execution begins when the runtime provisions an isolated working copy of the repository and supplies the initial task description. The model proposes running the failing test. After validating that this command is authorized, the runtime invokes the test runner and records its output. When the runner reports a deadlock, the runtime supplies the diagnostic output to the next model call. The model then proposes inspecting the connection-pool implementation, and the returned source code reveals the locking logic that requires repair.
Guided by this inspection, the model proposes a patch. As section 1.3 established, that patch is a candidate rather than a certified computation. Before modifying the working copy, the runtime verifies that the edit targets permitted files. That path check is a mechanical bound below the model, and it is what keeps this \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_1\) edit inside the \(\StateExposureLevel_2\) working copy. The step also underscores a foundational separation of concerns. The model’s generated diff is merely a proposal, the modified file is an effect, and the tool’s execution report is an observation. When a subsequent compilation attempt reports an unclosed bracket, that observation directly steers the next decision. The model proposes a corrected patch, which the runtime applies before rerunning the build. The compiler has acted as an intermediate check in the sense of the horizon notebook (1.1), catching the syntax error one turn after it happened; the corrected patch and successful rebuild prevent that error from carrying into the remaining turns. Once compilation succeeds and visible unit tests pass, the runtime collects regression evidence from the contract’s sealed suite, which the editing tools cannot touch, raising the closure evidence above the model from visible tests to sealed tests. It then records the resulting deliverable alongside these verification records. If the results satisfy the contract’s acceptance criteria, the runtime submits the repair; otherwise, it can continue iterating, abort, or escalate to a human engineer.
Dynamic observations dictate subsequent action: a thread deadlock demands different remediation than a syntax error, and a clean build never proves that a race condition has disappeared. Even a comprehensive regression test can miss an interleaving that triggers the defect under concurrency. Consequently, an agent runtime requires both a mechanism to incorporate incoming evidence and a rigorous policy for deciding when that evidence justifies termination. The loop itself is old, since feedback control12 and reinforcement learning have long organized action around observations of an environment (Wiener 1948; Sutton and Barto 2018), and ReAct showed foundation models interleaving reasoning, actions, and observations in the same way (Yao et al. 2023). What the runtime adds is accountability for that loop, which is why fault isolation, access control, and recovery remain essential when a generated proposal can be wrong or destructive.
12 Cybernetics: Wiener’s 1948 book named the study of control through feedback, in which a system measures the result of its own action and uses the difference from its goal to choose the next one (Wiener 1948). The loop corrects errors only if the measurement comes from the environment; a runtime that feeds back the model’s own account of what it did has closed a loop around a claim rather than around the result. 
Wiener, Norbert. 1948. Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine. Wiley.
The multi-turn trajectory serves as the primary systems management boundary because operational dependencies span individual invocations. The corrected patch depends on compiler diagnostics emitted several turns earlier. Each edit consumes part of the task’s cumulative token and financial budget, and every operation must be evaluated against the task’s security permissions. A single model request ends the moment its response stream finishes; the delegated task, along with any background tool execution, completes only when the runtime explicitly settles it. The runtime must therefore manage state, resource quotas, and lifetime policies at the granularity of the entire task rather than the individual call.
This boundary explains why a service that manages only isolated requests needs additional task-level mechanisms to host a multi-turn trajectory. Table 3 compares a deliberately simple stateless-request baseline with the requirements of the repair trajectory and identifies the chapters that address them. Stateful services may already supply some of these mechanisms; the comparison identifies responsibilities rather than limitations inherent to web services.
