Four recurring workloads, each bound by a different exposure, keep the argument concrete. A repair agent that fixes a defect in an isolated working copy over a long horizon is the running example in every chapter. A research agent that reads untrusted sources, a remediation agent whose actions on production systems can be irreversible, and a support agent that serves many short interactive sessions at once return wherever the repair agent cannot exercise a constraint. A mechanism that is central for one of these workloads can be pure overhead for another, which is why the book prices mechanisms against a workload rather than ranking them in the abstract.

title: Preface
text:
The book builds understanding in dependency order: model, memory, tools, runtime, measure, learn, scale. Each part adds responsibilities that the preceding material prepares the reader to evaluate. This teaching sequence is not a requirement to deploy every mechanism. When an agent fails, a related ordering governs the response. The intervention ladder ranks remedies by cost and reversibility. Once a failure is attributed to a measured cause, changes to context, to tools and their schemas, and to runtime control come before changes to the model’s weights, which are reserved for the failure that survives them and made only on evidence that the change helps. The ladder is a default order rather than a sequence every failure must climb, and The intervention ladder develops it.
Introduction opens the book. It defines the agentic system and the trajectory, names the fail-plausible faults that make agents hard to trust, states the invariant closure principle, and turns a task into a contract. Horizon, state, and authority then help the reader judge the runtime responsibilities needed and choose between a fixed workflow and a model-directed loop. It draws the whole system once, as a single map, and then leaves the analogy behind.

Part I: The Model studies the component every agent is built around through a single call. The Foundation Model establishes what a call reads, returns, and costs, and why its output is a proposal the runtime must check rather than a result. Test-Time Compute asks when longer reasoning, additional candidates, or check-and-revise rounds improve the selected result within a bounded budget, and what evidence supports accepting it.
Part II: Agent Memory governs the state exposure. Context Engineering decides what each call sees under a fixed budget, KV Cache Management prices what holding that context costs in the serving system, and Long-Term Memory governs what persists across sessions and returns only through retrieval.
Part III: Tool Use governs the authority exposure. Tool Calling separates proposal validation, authorization, dispatch, and evidence of the resulting effect, including cases where a timeout leaves the outcome uncertain. Agent Sandboxes bounds the reach of executing code, while Agent Security addresses how untrusted information can misuse otherwise legitimate access.
Part IV: The Agent Runtime governs the horizon exposure. The Agent Harness runs the loop under budgets and approvals, Durable Execution preserves progress across stated failure conditions, and Failure Recovery chooses among repair, compensation, containment, and escalation. The part ends with Agent Evaluation, which measures the whole single-agent system and establishes the evidence needed to judge later learning and scaling decisions.
Part V: Learning from Trajectories changes model behavior when evaluation justifies that intervention; it does not replace the runtime’s boundaries. Trajectory Curation decides when a failure warrants changing the weights at all, then selects and prepares records for different learning objectives, including demonstrations of recovery. Trajectory Fine-Tuning teaches behavior from those records, and Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards optimizes against verifiable rewards while examining the limits and protection of the reward checks.
Part VI: Agents at Scale multiplies all three exposures. Multi-Agent Coordination splits a task across agents only when the coordination pays for itself, and Agent Economics prices and provisions agents per accepted task.
Part VII: Synthesis follows a production incident-remediation task through the system in Conclusion. It ends at the specification boundary, where defining success, judging whether the evidence is sufficient, and answering for the result stay with the engineer.

Reference appendices collect material that supports the chapters without interrupting them: the mathematical background, the inference cost derivations behind the book’s serving estimates, the distributed-state guarantees behind durable execution and coordination, a reference architecture, typed tool interfaces, a failure taxonomy, and a glossary.

title: Preface
text:
The book is written to be read in order. Each chapter uses only ideas introduced earlier in the book or defined where they appear, and each owns its concepts, so a mechanism is taught once and cited afterward. Every chapter opens with the agent problem it solves, introduces the mechanism as the answer to that problem, and closes with a summary and a handoff to the next chapter. Classical systems ideas, such as write-ahead logs, compensating transactions, idempotency keys, and capabilities, appear where they are the real engineering, introduced as the fix for an agent failure rather than as a lesson in their own right.
Readers with a particular role can weight their reading after the introduction. Engineers who build serving and execution infrastructure will lean on the chapters on the model, the KV cache, sandboxes, durable execution, and economics. Engineers who build agent platforms will lean on context engineering, tool calling, security, the harness, failure recovery, evaluation, and multi-agent coordination. Researchers and post-training teams will lean on the model, test-time compute, evaluation, and all of Part V. These emphases do not remove prerequisites established by earlier chapters. Every path begins with Introduction and ends with Conclusion.
Figure 1 diagrams these pedagogical pathways across eight horizontal part bands: solid blue boxes and directed edges trace the linear core path culminating in the conclusion, while dashed gray boxes isolate the optional post-training and test-time compute track (Test-Time Compute and Part V). The detailed test-time compute and post-training methods form an optional branch, so a course on building and operating agents can follow the core path. A course on post-training keeps that branch and still needs Parts I through IV beneath it, because Trajectory Curation starts from the evidence that Agent Evaluation defines.






Figure 1: Chapter Dependency Map: Each arrow points from a chapter to a later chapter that consumes its results, derived from the book’s cross-references with transitive links omitted. Solid chapters form the core path the conclusion builds on; the dashed branch through test-time compute and Part V can be skipped by a course that does not cover post-training.





The margins carry unnumbered marginal navigation pointers that trace dependencies between chapters without interrupting the flow of the prose:

↩︎ Backward pointer: Directs the reader back to the earlier chapter where a contract, check, or cost model was established.
↪ Forward pointer: Directs the reader ahead to the later chapter, or to the appendix, where the current idea is developed, measured, or enforced.
⇄ Contrast: Marks a place where two chapters treat the same problem differently, so the comparison is visible at a glance.

A pointer only orients. When a sentence depends on another chapter, the reference stays in the text.

title: Preface
text: This is not a prompt-engineering guide. Prompts matter, but the book treats them as one input the runtime assembles, and it never relies on an instruction to the model where a mechanical check is possible. It is not a tutorial for any agent framework, protocol implementation, or model provider, and it does not rank this year’s models or benchmarks. Products and benchmarks appear only as examples of a technique or a class of evaluation, with citations. It is not a book about the internals of accelerators. It develops the serving relationships an agent engineer needs, including how prompt processing differs from output generation and when shared-prefix reuse reduces repeated work, with detailed derivations collected in an appendix. Finally, it covers software agents that act through tools on digital systems. Agents that act on the physical world raise problems of their own and are outside its scope.

title: Preface
text: Frameworks, protocols, and model weights will change, some of them before this book reaches print. The text therefore emphasizes the ideas that survive those changes, such as the trajectory as the unit of work, the three exposures and the closure against them, the separation between a model that proposes and a runtime that decides, and the discipline of measuring before changing anything. Current protocols and systems appear throughout to make the ideas concrete, but the principles stand independently of any vendor or tool. Where a question is still open, such as how best to evaluate systems that act or how to structure an agent’s long-term memory, the book says so and presents the question as an open problem rather than a settled method.

title: Agentic Machine Learning Systems
text:
Vijay Janapa Reddi

October 13, 2026




  
    This is a working volume. Agentic machine learning systems turn model inference into a stateful control loop that observes, decides, acts, verifies, and adapts. The managed trajectory, rather than the isolated request, is the central unit of engineering.
    The volume builds an agentic system in the order its dependencies impose, model, memory, tools, runtime, measurement, learning, and scale, and treats unsettled mechanisms as open design questions rather than fixed doctrine.
  

  
    
      
    
    Agentic Machine Learning Systems
    Vijay Janapa Reddi
    
      📖 Download PDF
      ·
      📱 Download EPUB
    
  


What You Will Learn

The book opens with an introduction that defines the agentic system, its unit of work (the trajectory), and the three exposures an agent adds beyond a single model call: horizon, state, and authority. Seven parts then build the system in order.

  Part I: The Model. The foundation model and test-time compute.
  Part II: Agent Memory. Context engineering, KV cache management, and long-term memory.
  Part III: Tool Use. Tool calling, agent sandboxes, and agent security.
  Part IV: The Agent Runtime. The agent harness, durable execution, failure recovery, and agent evaluation.
  Part V: Learning from Trajectories. Trajectory curation, trajectory fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards.
  Part VI: Agents at Scale. Multi-agent coordination and agent economics.
  Part VII: Synthesis. One trajectory through every part, and the specification boundary.


Prerequisites

Readers should be familiar with foundation models and large language models, including prompting and token generation, and with software systems concepts such as APIs, state management, concurrency, and process isolation. Programming experience and undergraduate-level probability provide the remaining foundations. The book assumes no earlier volume of this series and develops the agentic and serving concepts it needs.

title: Author’s Note
text:
Author’s Note

When an AI answers a question, the interaction is over. When an AI takes an action, the real engineering has only just begun.
A prompt-and-response model in a stateless, text-only interaction is an oracle behind glass: it answers when spoken to, carries no action privileges, and leaves no session state for the next call. But when you give that intelligence tools, memory, and a delegated goal, it ceases to be an oracle. It becomes an actor.
My curiosity about agentic systems began during a National Science Foundation (NSF) workshop on AI efficiency. As someone whose work has long focused on benchmarking and quantitative systems evaluation, including the initialization of MLPerf, I found myself asking a fundamental systems question: how do we benchmark and evaluate the efficiency of these actors?
At the algorithmic and application layers, the community has introduced a vibrant lexicon of techniques: “prompt engineering,” “prompt chaining,” “in-context reflection,” and “agentic workflows.” These ideas are genuinely creative and impactful. They show us what is possible when models interact iteratively with task environments. But as a computer systems architect, I found myself asking a complementary question: what is the fundamental machine required to build, benchmark, and scale these ideas? When you hear these exotic-sounding terms at the application level, what is the actual system you have to construct underneath?
To measure and engineer these workflows, we have to break them down to their fundamentals. And when you look at them from first principles, an agentic system is not an alien artifact. It is a machine built around a foundation model, and its parts are ones a systems engineer recognizes.

The foundation model reads a context and proposes the next action.
Agent memory decides what each call sees and keeps what must outlast the session.
Tools carry approved proposals into the environment under scoped permissions, with sandboxes containing the reach of executable code.
The agent runtime mediates proposals, records execution, and coordinates recovery or escalation when something goes wrong.

The introduction draws this machine once, as a single map that I call the Stochastic Computer. After that, the book argues each part in its own terms, because a model is not a processor and a context window is not a cache.
Yet this machine carries a profound systems twist: it is stochastic. A deterministic program repeats its result when its inputs and execution conditions remain fixed. A sampling foundation model can propose a different action under the same context. Even when generation is repeatable, the proposal can still be wrong. Repeated success is no substitute for bounding what the next action may reach.
I experienced this firsthand while drafting these chapters. Working alongside an autonomous coding assistant with direct terminal access, the agent took an unexpected turn and executed an rm -f directly in the directory containing my active edits. To compound the disaster, in an unthinking moment of late-night muscle memory, I committed and pushed the changes upstream. In an instant, days of work across a holiday weekend evaporated into git history.
You would think a computer systems professor would know better than to give an unconstrained actor raw effector privileges without an isolated sandbox, or to blindly push a tree without auditing the diff. But that is the precise nature of the trap: autonomy is seductive right up until an irreversible mutation occurs.
The introduction returns to the boundary this incident exposed by comparing a disposable working copy with an author’s sole authoritative workspace (example \(\ref{exmp-01-hsa-incident}\)). The task needed only reversible authority over a copy of my files, and the environment granted irreversible authority over the only one.
Reliability has always required more than debugging individual components. When the component proposing actions is learned, we must also account for proposals that look plausible while violating the task. We cannot rely on human vigilance or prompt cleverness alone to guarantee safety. The runtime around the model must bound what each call sees, contain what each action can reach, preserve the records needed for recovery, and escalate when an effect cannot be safely repaired.
I write these chapters as a student of a discipline in motion. Putting this book together, shuttling between Cambridge and Zurich, has been my way of distilling the durable first principles that will still govern these systems a decade from now, the three exposures of horizon, state, and authority and the closure the runtime builds against them.
I hope you find it helpful.
— Vijay Janapa Reddi
Cambridge, Massachusetts & Zurich, Switzerland
2026

title: Notation
text:
An agentic system places a foundation model inside a loop: the model proposes an action, the runtime decides whether to admit it, a tool executes it, and the observation that comes back shapes the next call. Describing that loop requires notation for trajectories, task contracts, budgets, verification, and coordination, alongside the model and serving quantities underneath them. Machine learning, computer systems, and control each developed their notation independently, and several letters arrive with conflicting meanings.
In control and robotics, \(\Glyph{\tau}\) is a torque or a time constant; in this book bare \(\Glyph{\tau}\) is always a trajectory, \(\Trajectory= (\TrajectoryState_0, \TrajectoryAction_0, \TrajectoryObservation_1, \TrajectoryState_1, \dots, \TrajectoryState_{\TurnHorizon})\). In transformer notation \(\Glyph{H}\) often counts attention heads; here \(\Glyph{H}\) is the horizon in turns, and heads are \(\AttentionHeadCount\). In machine learning \(\Glyph{B}\) is batch size, and it remains batch size here; the trajectory budget is bold \(\TrajectoryBudget\). The conventions below keep one meaning per symbol, and the collision tables at the end of this section resolve the remaining cases. A symbol that appears only inside one derivation is defined where it is used and is not listed here.


Five relationships recur across the chapters of this book. They link a trajectory’s structure to its elapsed time, its reliability, its cost, and the speedup available from splitting it across workers. Each is derived in the section cited with it; the forms below fix the symbols those chapters use.


A trajectory, the ordered record of one delegated task, is formalized in The H·S·A Exposure Space as:
\[\Trajectory= (\TrajectoryState_0, \TrajectoryAction_0, \TrajectoryObservation_1, \TrajectoryState_1, \TrajectoryAction_1, \TrajectoryObservation_2, \dots, \TrajectoryState_{\TurnHorizon})\]
where \(\TrajectoryState_{t}\) is the assembled context state, \(\TrajectoryAction_{t}\) is the action the model proposes on turn \(\TurnIndex\), and \(\TrajectoryObservation_{t+1}\) is the environment observation returned to the agent.



The wall-clock duration of a trajectory over a horizon of \(\TurnHorizon\) turns, indexed \(\TurnIndex= 0, \dots, \TurnHorizon-1\), is in the simplest case the sum of its model calls and tool operations (Queueing for Trajectories):
\[\TrajectoryDuration = \sum_{t=0}^{\TurnHorizon-1} \left( \ModelTime^{(t)} + \ToolTime^{(t)} \right)\]
The sum assumes that model calls and tool operations run one after another with no other delay. A turn that also waits on a remote service or on a person’s approval adds that wait, \(\ExternalWait\), as a further interval. The sum applies only when the included intervals are nonoverlapping and cover the measured duration. For overlapping work, measure elapsed time between the declared endpoints and analyze the dependency critical path; summing enclosing spans and their children double-counts time.
Each model call is itself an inference pass on an accelerator, and its time \(\Time\) obeys the iron law of ML Systems:
\[\Time = \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} + \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} + \Latency\]
The first term charges the bytes the call moves against memory bandwidth, the second charges its operations against the sustained compute rate, and the third is fixed per-call overhead. The floors the first two terms set for prompt processing and output generation follow from the roofline in Cost Asymmetry Between Input Prefill and Output Generation.



Agentic systems are measured per accepted task completion rather than raw requests. Trajectory goodput counts distinct task completions accepted under a declared contract per unit of elapsed observation time \(\ObservationIntervalLength>0\) (Release measurements):
\[\TrajectoryGoodput = \frac{\AcceptedTasks}{\ObservationIntervalLength}\]
Goodput per dollar instead divides the same accepted count by the full included cost. Neither measure is the fraction of resources spent on accepted trajectories; that fraction answers a different accounting question.
The cost per accepted task divides the included monetary costs of all \(\InitiatedTasks\) distinct initiated tasks, including their attempts and branches, by the \(\AcceptedTasks>0\) distinct tasks accepted under the same contract (Cohort cost per accepted task):
\[\CostPerAcceptedTask = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{\InitiatedTasks} {\TaskCost}_i}{\AcceptedTasks}\]
When every attempt is accepted independently with probability \(\AcceptanceProbability\) and a task retries until one is, the same ratio takes the per-attempt form \(\CostPerAcceptedTask = \mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability\) (Reliability and Cost over a Horizon). With no accepted tasks, report total spend and the zero accepted count rather than a finite unit cost. Report unsettled liability separately from known charges.



A trajectory executing \(\TurnHorizon\) sequential turns without intermediate verification, where each turn is correct with probability \(1 - \PerStepErrorRate\) independently of the others, compounds its errors and succeeds with probability (Reliability and Cost over a Horizon):
\[\Pr(\text{success}) = (1 - \PerStepErrorRate)^{\TurnHorizon}\]
An intermediate check can interrupt error propagation when it detects an error and the runtime prevents later turns from building on it. Training on trajectories can lower \(\PerStepErrorRate\), but it supplies no such check.



Splitting a fixed task across \(\WorkerCount\) equally capable workers shortens it only as far as its parallel fraction and the cost of coordinating the workers allow (The coordination tax):
\[\text{Speedup}(\WorkerCount) = \frac{1}{(1-\ParallelFraction) + \ParallelFraction/\WorkerCount + \CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)}\]
where \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)\) is the added coordination overhead as a fraction of serial time. With no overhead the bound is Amdahl’s law. Once \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)\) exceeds the time the split saves, \(\ParallelFraction(1 - 1/\WorkerCount)\), the split task takes longer than serial execution.




The loop symbols describe one turn of a trajectory: the context assembled by the runtime, the proposal generated by the model, the decision made by the runtime harness, and the resulting observation.


A trajectory advances one turn at a time, and every turn is written with the same few parts, each carrying the turn index.










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\Trajectory\)
Trajectory
Tuple
Ordered record of one delegated task, \(\Trajectory= (\TrajectoryState_0, \TrajectoryAction_0, \TrajectoryObservation_1, \dots, \TrajectoryState_{\TurnHorizon})\). Bare \(\Glyph{\tau}\) always means a trajectory in this book.


\(\TurnIndex\)
Turn index
Integer
Counts turns within a trajectory from \(\TurnIndex= 0\), so \(\TrajectoryState_{\TurnHorizon}\) is the state after the final turn. Inside a per-token loss such as \(\MaskedFinetuningLoss\), \(\Glyph{t}\) indexes token positions instead. Positions in a durable log use \(\Glyph{j}\).


\(\TurnContext_{t}\)
Context
Tokens
What the runtime assembles and sends on turn \(\TurnIndex\): instructions, goal, tool definitions, and the history of actions, observations, and evidence.


\(\TrajectoryState_{t}\)
State at turn \(\TurnIndex\)
Record
The context state the model saw on turn \(\TurnIndex\). In Part V, the state a policy conditions on.


\(\TrajectoryAction_{t}\)
Action proposal
Text or tool call
What the model proposed on turn \(\TurnIndex\). Nothing happens until the runtime admits it.


\(\TrajectoryObservation_{t}\)
Observation
Typed result
What an action returned, such as an exit code, captured output, a response body, or a status.


\(\Policy\)
Policy
Distribution
The model viewed as a distribution over proposals given a context, with parameters \(\ModelParameters\).


\(\bot\)
Rejection
Symbol
A proposal withheld through the admission gate, recorded with its reason. This does not undo earlier attempts or establish that outstanding external work has stopped.







A task contract fixes what a trajectory is for, where it runs, what it may do and see, and what ends it.










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\TaskContract\)
Task contract
Tuple
\(\TaskContract = \langle \TaskContractGoal, \TaskEnvironment, \PermittedActions, \AvailableObservations, \CompletionCriteria \rangle\).


\(\TaskContractGoal\)
Goal
Text
Desired end state, with explicit negative scope.


\(\TaskEnvironment\)
Environment
Specification
Reproducible place the work happens: base commit, image, configuration, network rules.


\(\PermittedActions\)
Permitted actions
Set
Tools the task may call and the limits on each. Least privilege stated per task.


\(\AvailableObservations\)
Available observations
Specification
What the agent may see, and how much, including truncation and redaction rules.


\(\CompletionCriteria\)
Completion criteria
Set of checks
Checks that decide when the task is done, at a stated closure evidence level. The model’s claim of completion is never one of them.







H·S·A names the three exposures an agentic task adds beyond a single model call. A task’s position says how exposed it is. The closure the runtime must supply against that exposure is governed by the invariant closure principle and is not a fourth axis. Zero ambient authority describes the model at every authority level and has no symbol.










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\TurnHorizon\)
Horizon
Turns
Number of turns a trajectory runs: \(\TurnHorizon= 1\) (single call), \(\TurnHorizon\approx 10\) (short loop), \(\TurnHorizon\ge 100\) (minutes to hours). Wall-clock duration given \(\TurnHorizon\) is \(\TrajectoryDuration\).


\(\StateExposureLevel_0\) to \(\StateExposureLevel_3\)
State
Level
What the task carries between turns: \(\StateExposureLevel_0\) (nothing), \(\StateExposureLevel_1\) (context window and KV cache), \(\StateExposureLevel_2\) (sandboxed working files), \(\StateExposureLevel_3\) (durable state that outlives the session or is shared beyond it). Written with its level, because bare \(\Glyph{S}\) is sequence length.


\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\) to \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\)
Authority
Level
What the task may do through its tools: \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\) (read access), \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_1\) (mutation confined to a discardable sandbox), \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_2\) (external action that is retry-safe or compensable), \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\) (irreversible external action). Covers confidentiality as well as integrity, so \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\) is not a zero blast radius.




Forms of closure evidence are named in words and carry no symbol: self-report, static checks, visible tests, sealed tests, and formal proof. They support different claims under different assumptions, not a universal weakest-to-strongest ranking. Protecting a check does not establish complete coverage.



A capability grant bounds what an operation may reach. An information-flow policy attaches two labels to every record, propagates them through each transformation, and checks them against each operation before dispatch.










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\CapabilityGrant\)
Capability Grant
Tuple
\(\CapabilityGrant = (\GrantRights, \mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant, \GrantCondition, \GrantExpiryTime)\): rights, objects, the condition predicate on an access, and expiry time. Derived grants carry a subscript, as in \(\ChildCapabilityGrant \sqsubseteq \ParentCapabilityGrant\). Not \(\Glyph{C}\), which is always a cost.


\(\GrantExpiryTime\)
Grant expiry time
Seconds (timestamp)
Time after which a grant admits nothing; an access at time \(\TimeInstant\) is admitted only if \(\TimeInstant< \GrantExpiryTime\). A derived grant expires no later than its parent.


\(\IntegrityProvenance(\LabeledRecord)\)
Integrity provenance
Set of sources
Sources whose content may have influenced record \(\LabeledRecord\). A derived record takes the union of its inputs’ provenance.


\(\ConfidentialityLabel(\LabeledRecord)\)
Confidentiality
Set of recipients
Recipients permitted to receive record \(\LabeledRecord\). A derived record takes the intersection of its inputs’ labels. In the evaluation chapter, \(\Glyph{\kappa}\) is Cohen’s kappa, a local agreement statistic.


\(\AcceptedInfluences(\ProposedOperation)\)
Accepted influences
Set of sources
Sources the task policy accepts as influences on operation \(\ProposedOperation\); the evidence check is \(\IntegrityProvenance(\LabeledRecord) \subseteq \AcceptedInfluences(\ProposedOperation)\). Upright, to stay distinct from the environment \(\Glyph{\mathcal{E}}\).


\(\ChildCapabilityGrant\)
Child capability grant
Tuple
Capability grant derived from a parent grant, which may permit no more than its parent does. Attenuation orders the two grants, child below parent.


\(\GrantAllowedAccesses\)
Allowed accesses of a grant
Set
Set of accesses a capability grant allows, written as a function of the grant. Attenuation requires the child’s set to lie inside the parent’s. Not an advantage or an action set.


\(\GrantCondition\)
Grant condition
Predicate
Condition a capability grant attaches to an access, such as binding its use to one task or recipient; third component of \(\CapabilityGrant\), applied to an access as a predicate. May carry an aggregate resource budget.


\(\GrantRights\)
Grant rights
Set
Set of operations a capability grant permits its holder to perform; first component of \(\CapabilityGrant\). An access is admissible only if its operation lies in this set.


\(\AccessAttemptTime\)
Access attempt time
Seconds
Timestamp at which a proposed access is checked against a capability grant. The access is admissible only if this time precedes \(\GrantExpiryTime\). Not the turn index \(\TurnIndex\).


\(\ParentCapabilityGrant\)
Parent capability grant
Tuple
Capability grant from which a narrower child grant \(\ChildCapabilityGrant\) is derived. It stays usable after the derivation unless the runtime withdraws it.


\(\ProposedAccess\)
Proposed access
Record
Access a tool call proposes, naming an operation, a target, and its arguments, which an enforcement point admits or refuses under a capability grant \(\CapabilityGrant\).








Agent workflows spend compute and memory budgets across iterative model calls, context accumulations, and generation streams.


A model call is bounded by its window and by limits the runtime sets on each request. A trajectory is bounded by a budget under runtime-owned accounting; model visibility does not confer authority to change the meter.










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\SequenceLength\)
Sequence length
Tokens
The shared symbol for sequence length, used here for the prompt a call reads. The State exposure is always written with a level, \(\StateExposureLevel_0\) to \(\StateExposureLevel_3\).


\(\BasePromptLength\)
Base prompt length
Tokens
First prompt of a trajectory before any turn appends to it, as in the resend sum. Subscripted because \(\StateExposureLevel_0\) is a State level.


\(\TurnAppendLength\)
Per-turn append
Tokens
Tokens one turn adds to the next prompt: the action, its observation, and any evidence kept in context.


\(\PromptTokensSent\)
Prompt tokens sent
Tokens
Cumulative prompt tokens a trajectory sends across its calls. With a fixed append and no compaction, the resend sum is \(\PromptTokensSent = \TurnHorizon\,\BasePromptLength + \TurnAppendLength\,\TurnHorizon(\TurnHorizon-1)/2\).


\(\OutputLength\)
Output length
Tokens
Tokens a call generates; \(\OutputLength_t\) is the output of turn \(\TurnIndex\). Lowercase \(\Glyph{k}\) counts samples, as in pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\).


\(\TokenVocabulary\)
Vocabulary
Set of tokens
The token set a call samples from; \(\lvert\TokenVocabulary\rvert\) is the vocabulary size.


\(\ContextWindow\)
Context window
Tokens
Hard per-call context limit; when inputs and outputs share it, \(\SequenceLength+ \OutputLimit \le \ContextWindow\).


\(\OutputLimit\)
Output limit
Tokens
Maximum tokens the runtime lets a call generate.


\(\PerTokenDecodeTime\)
Per-token decode time
Seconds
Time to generate one output token on a single stream. A call’s whole decode interval is \(\DecodeInterval\).


\(\DecodeInterval\)
Decode interval
Seconds
A call’s whole output-generation interval, \(\DecodeInterval(\OutputLength) \approx \OutputLength\,\PerTokenDecodeTime\) at a stable per-token time. One term of the call latency \(\CallLatency\).


\(\CallLatency\)
Call latency
Seconds
Elapsed time from request preparation to normalized response, the sum of nonoverlapping intervals \(\CallLatency = \CallPreparationTime+ \RequestQueueTime+ \PrefillTime+ \DecodeInterval + \CallPostprocessingTime\). \(\RequestQueueTime\) is the wait before service that the queueing models compute.


\(\CompletionDeadline\)
Deadline
Seconds
Wall-clock ceiling enforced by the runtime, on one call or on a whole trajectory. The text names the scope. Inside the budget \(\TrajectoryBudget\) the trajectory deadline is written \(\TrajectoryTimeLimit\); everywhere else a deadline is \(\CompletionDeadline\).


\(\CostCeiling\)
Cost ceiling
Dollars
Cost allowance checked against actual consumption, outstanding liability, and newly proposed work while preserving finalization resources.


\(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\)
KV bytes per token
Bytes per token
\(\KvCacheBytesPerToken = 2 \cdot \LayerCount\cdot \KvHeadCount \cdot \AttentionHeadDimension \cdot \ElementStorageSize\), in the shared symbols for layers, KV heads, head dimension, and element size.


\(\KvCacheMemory\)
KV-Cache Memory
bytes
Logical full-attention state (\(\KvCacheMemory = \SequenceLength\cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\)) at the specified geometry and precision. Allocation overhead and shared physical ownership require separate accounting.


\(\KvBlockSize\)
KV block size
Tokens
Token positions per fixed block in paged KV storage. Not \(\Glyph{p}\), which is a probability, or \(\Glyph{B}\), which is batch size.


\(\MemoryHoldDuringWait\)
Memory held during a wait
Byte-seconds
Constant uniquely resident bytes multiplied by wait duration; \(\KvCacheMemory \cdot \ExternalWait\) applies when that payload is fully resident and unshared. Pool accounting counts shared blocks once.


\(\ObservationTokenCount\)
Observation tokens per call
Tokens
Tokens one call devotes to immediate tool observations and user steering: the observation buffer, one partition term of the context budget.


\(\ConditioningTokenPrefix\)
Conditioning token prefix
Token sequence
Token prefix a language-model policy conditions on when it chooses the next token, such as the context delivered before one sampled token of a rollout. Written without a position index; the same prefix written relative to a position carries \(\Glyph{x_{<t}}\).


\(\DecodingConstraintState\)
Decoding constraint state
State
State of the parser or output-constraint automaton that constrains decoding, indexed by decoding step; the initial state carries index zero. Elements of the automaton’s state set \(\AutomatonStateSet\).


\(\AutomatonStateSet\)
Constraint automaton state set
Set
Finite set of states of an output-constraint automaton. The appendix on inference sizes a dense mask table from its cardinality and the vocabulary size.


\(\MaskedTokenLogit\)
Masked token logit
Scalar
Logit of one vocabulary token at a decoding step after the constraint mask: its raw logit when the token is allowed and negative infinity otherwise. Written with step and token indices. Dimensionless.


\(\NormalizerTokenIndex\)
Normalizer token index
Token
Token of the vocabulary that a softmax normalizer sums over. Bound variable of the normalizing sum, kept distinct from the evaluated token.


\(\ActiveTargetTokenCount\)
Active target token count
Tokens
Number of token positions in one example that the loss mask \(\PositionLossMask_{t}\) selects as training targets; required positive. The normalizer of \(\MaskedFinetuningLoss\). Not the Little’s-law count of leases held at once, \(\ActiveLeaseCount\), which shares the glyph.


\(\CallPreparationTime\)
Call preparation time
Seconds
Time a runtime spends preparing a model call: assembling context, serializing the payload, and dispatching it. First term of \(\CallLatency\). Not the host-side preparation time of a serving node, which shares the glyph.


\(\CallPostprocessingTime\)
Call postprocessing time
Seconds
Time after generation until a model call’s normalized response is ready: response transfer, deserialization, and schema validation. Last term of \(\CallLatency\).


\(\SystemInstructionTokenCount\)
System instruction tokens per call
Tokens
Tokens one call devotes to static system instructions, one term of the context budget partition.


\(\ToolDeclarationTokenCount\)
Tool declaration tokens per call
Tokens
Tokens one call devotes to API schemas and tool declarations, one term of the context budget partition.


\(\TaskStateTokenCount\)
Task state tokens per call
Tokens
Tokens one call devotes to task state such as constraints, progress records, and source or test excerpts, one term of the context budget partition.


\(\TrajectoryTurnLimit\)
Trajectory turn limit
Turns
Largest number of turns the harness admits for one trajectory; the first element of \(\TrajectoryBudget\). Each admitted model call increments the turn meter. It caps \(\TurnHorizon\), the number of turns actually run.


\(\TrajectoryTokenLimit\)
Trajectory token limit
Tokens
Largest cumulative number of tokens, input plus output, one trajectory may consume; the second element of \(\TrajectoryBudget\). The meter counts every input token, cached or not. Not the per-call limits \(\ContextWindow\) or \(\OutputLimit\).


\(\TrajectoryTimeLimit\)
Trajectory time limit
Seconds
Elapsed wall-clock time a trajectory budget allows; the third element of \(\TrajectoryBudget\). Outside the budget a deadline is \(\CompletionDeadline\).


\(\SequenceToken\)
Sequence token
Token
One token of a serialized input sequence, written with its position as an index. Its prefix before a position is \(\TokenPrefix\). Not an input feature vector.


\(\TokenPrefix\)
Token prefix
Token sequence
Tokens of a sequence that precede the current position, the context an autoregressive model conditions on. The range is part of the symbol, not an index, so the prefix has its own row.


\(\VocabularyToken\)
Vocabulary token
Token
One token of the model vocabulary \(\TokenVocabulary\), the variable a next-token distribution, a logit, or a sum over candidate tokens ranges over. Not the verification evidence \(\Glyph{v_t}\).


\(\ValidTokenSet\)
Valid token set
Set of tokens
Vocabulary tokens whose decoded strings keep the output a viable prefix of the target grammar from a parser state. Written with its constraint state as argument; a subset of \(\TokenVocabulary\).


\(\SamplingTemperature\)
Sampling temperature
Dimensionless
Positive scalar that divides the logits before the softmax at sampling time, sharpening the distribution below one and flattening it above. Zero means greedy decoding, not a division. Bare \(\Glyph{\tau}\) is still a trajectory.


\(\PerTokenPrefillTime\)
Per-token prefill time
Seconds
Time prefill spends per prompt token at the compute-bound floor, about two operations per parameter at the peak rate \(\PeakRate\). Pairs with \(\PerTokenDecodeTime\).


\(\PrefillTime\)
Prefill time
Seconds
Time a model call spends processing its whole prompt, about the sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) times \(\PerTokenPrefillTime\).


\(\WeightOnlyStepTime\)
Weight-only step time
Seconds
Estimate of one serving forward pass: the larger of the weight-read time and the time for two weight operations per parameter per token position. Written with the token count as argument; omits attention traffic and per-iteration overhead. Not the turn index \(\TurnIndex\).


\(\RuntimeReserveMemory\)
Runtime reserve memory
Bytes
Accelerator memory a serving runtime reserves for dynamic activations and scratch buffers, excluded from the KV pool \(\KvPoolMemory\).


\(\PrefixHitRate\)
Prefix hit rate
Fraction
Token-weighted share of prompt tokens over a workload window whose compatible key-value state was attached without recomputation. Counts tokens actually served, not potential matches. Not the serving utilization \(\ServingUtilization\).







Agentic systems are measured per accepted task, not per request. The time terms decompose one turn, the cost terms price attempts and the accepted results they buy, and the capacity terms size the pools that serve them.










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\ModelTime\)
Model time
Seconds
Time spent in model calls during a turn.


\(\ToolTime\)
Tool time
Seconds
Time a tool takes to execute, such as a build or a test run.


\(\ExternalWait\)
External wait
Seconds
Time spent waiting on a remote service or a person’s approval.


\(\TrajectoryDuration\)
Trajectory duration
Seconds
Elapsed time between declared endpoints. A component sum applies only to disjoint intervals covering that duration.


\(\TrajectoryGoodput\)
Trajectory goodput
Tasks/time
Distinct accepted task completions per elapsed observation interval under the declared contract. Sustaining it at acceptance fraction \(\AcceptanceFraction\) requires the admission rate \(\TrajectoryAdmissionRate = \TrajectoryGoodput/\AcceptanceFraction\).


\(\TrajectoryBudget\)
Trajectory budget
Vector
\(\TrajectoryBudget = \langle \TrajectoryTurnLimit, \TrajectoryTokenLimit, \TrajectoryTimeLimit, \CostCeiling \rangle\), allowances on turns, tokens, elapsed time, and dollars. Admission accounts for actual consumption and reserved bounded liability. The time allowance \(\TrajectoryTimeLimit\) is the trajectory’s deadline. Bold, to stay distinct from batch size \(\BatchSize\).


\(\ConcurrentTrajectories\), \(\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\)
Concurrent trajectories, admission rate
Count, trajectories/s
Little’s law for trajectories, \(\ConcurrentTrajectories = \TrajectoryAdmissionRate\,\mathbb{E}[\TrajectoryDuration]\), with \(\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\) the shared arrival rate \(\ArrivalRate\) counted in trajectories. Other held resources follow the same pattern, as in \(\ActiveLeaseCount= \ArrivalRate\,\LeaseHoldTime\).


\(\LeaseHoldTime\)
Lease holding time
Seconds
Mean time a trajectory holds a sandbox lease, the residence term in \(\ActiveLeaseCount= \ArrivalRate\,\LeaseHoldTime\).


\(\TaskCost\)
Task cost
Dollars
Included monetary cost of all attempts and branches for one distinct initiated task.


\(\AttemptCost\)
Attempt cost
Dollars
Full cost of one attempt: input and output tokens, tool fees, sandbox time, verification, and human review.


\(\InputTokenPrice\), \(\OutputTokenPrice\), \(\CachedInputTokenPrice\)
Per-token prices
Dollars/token
Prices of an uncached input token, an output token, and a cached input token. Lowercase \(\Glyph{c}\) is a unit price that an uppercase \(\Glyph{C}\) totals; \(\Glyph{p}\) stays a probability.


\(\ExpectedCheckingTime\)
Expected checking time
Seconds
Expected verifier slot time per attempted record under a short-circuit check cascade. A time, distinct from the attempt cost \(\AttemptCost\) in dollars.


\(\AcceptedTasks\)
Accepted tasks
Count
Distinct tasks satisfying the declared acceptance criteria by the observation cutoff; pending and unknown verdicts remain separately reported.


\(\InitiatedTasks\)
Initiated tasks
Count
Size of a settled cohort of distinct initiated tasks, whatever their outcome. It is the range of the cost sum in \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) and the denominator of \(\AcceptanceFraction\).


\(\AcceptanceFraction\)
Acceptance fraction
Fraction
\(\AcceptanceFraction = \AcceptedTasks/\InitiatedTasks\) over a fully classified cohort, so \(\CostPerAcceptedTask = \AcceptedTaskMeanCost+ \frac{1-\AcceptanceFraction}{\AcceptanceFraction} \UnacceptedTaskMeanCost\), where \(\AcceptedTaskMeanCost\) and \(\UnacceptedTaskMeanCost\) are the mean included costs of an accepted and an unaccepted task. It counts tasks, whereas \(\AcceptanceProbability\) counts attempts.


\(\AcceptanceProbability\)
Acceptance probability
Probability
Per-attempt probability of acceptance; with independent retries, \(\CostPerAcceptedTask = \mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability\).


\(\CostPerAcceptedTask\)
Cost per accepted task
Dollars/task
Total included monetary cost divided by \(\AcceptedTasks>0\), including failed attempts. No finite ratio exists when none are accepted.


\(\BreakEvenTaskCount\)
Break-even task volume
Tasks
Tasks an adaptation must serve before its per-task saving recovers its one-time cost, \(\BreakEvenTaskCount = \AdaptationInvestmentCost/\FiniteChange\TaskCost\) for \(\FiniteChange\TaskCost > 0\).


\(\WorkerCount\)
Worker count
Count
Equally capable agents, model workers, or verifier slots in one pool. Never bare \(\Glyph{M}\) or \(\Glyph{P}\), which the shared tables assign to memory and parameter count.


\(\ServiceRate\)
Service rate
Items/s
Rate at which one server (a worker, consumer, or model endpoint) completes items or calls, so a pool of \(\WorkerCount\) servers has capacity \(\WorkerCount\ServiceRate\). Subscripted rates such as \(\Glyph{\mu_{\text{out}}}\), and a statistical mean \(\Glyph{\mu}\), are distinct.


\(\ParallelFraction\)
Parallel fraction
Fraction
Share of the work that divides among workers in the coordination bound, \(\text{Speedup}(\WorkerCount) = 1/\big((1-\ParallelFraction) + \ParallelFraction/\WorkerCount + \CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)\big)\).


\(\CoordinationOverhead\)
Coordination overhead
Fraction of serial time
Added elapsed cost of coordinating \(\WorkerCount\) workers, normalized by serial time and always written with its argument, \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)\). Distinct from the interaction history \(\InteractionHistory_k\).


\(\ContentionCoefficient\), \(\CoherencyCoefficient\)
Contention and coherency coefficients
Fraction
The universal scalability law’s serialized share and pairwise reconciliation cost, \(\text{Speedup}(\WorkerCount) = \WorkerCount/\big(1 + \ContentionCoefficient(\WorkerCount-1) + \CoherencyCoefficient\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\big)\). Subscripted, because bare \(\Glyph{\kappa}\) is the confidentiality label.


\(\AcceptedTaskMeanCost\)
Mean cost of accepted tasks
dollars
Mean task-account cost of the accepted tasks in a settled cohort. With the mean cost of unaccepted tasks it partitions \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\).


\(\AdaptationInvestmentCost\)
Adaptation investment cost
dollars
Incremental one-time cost of an intervention such as an adaptation, covering data curation, training compute, and offline evaluation. Numerator of the break-even task count \(\BreakEvenTaskCount\).


\(\HumanReviewCost\)
Human review cost
dollars
Cost of the human review that an escalated action or a rejected attempt triggers, inspection and labor included. Latency must be converted to this common cost unit before addition.


\(\MeanAttemptCost\)
Mean attempt cost
dollars
Expected all-inclusive monetary cost of one attempt at a task, the same for every attempt under the independent-trials model. Equals the expectation of \(\AttemptCost\) when attempts are identical; the planning ratio divides it by \(\AttemptPassProbability\).


\(\CriticalPathDuration\)
Critical-path duration
Seconds
Duration of the longest source-to-sink path through a dependency graph, summing the durations of the vertices on it. A lower bound on makespan however many workers run, since sequential dependencies cannot overlap.


\(\DependencyGraphVertex\)
Dependency-graph vertex
Vertex
One vertex of a task-precedence graph: a bounded unit of execution that occupies one worker slot. Numbered vertices name the nodes of a specific plan. Not a version or a velocity.


\(\VertexSlotTime\)
Vertex slot time
Seconds
Time one vertex of a task-precedence graph occupies a worker slot, including model inference and tool execution. Written with its vertex as argument.


\(\UnacceptedTaskMeanCost\)
Mean cost of unaccepted tasks
dollars
Mean task-account cost of the unaccepted tasks in a settled cohort: failures, cancellations, and timeouts. Pairs with \(\AcceptedTaskMeanCost\).








Recovery, evaluation, and learning attach their own quantities to a trajectory: what a sample or a search buys, what a check establishes, what a stored entry may still support, what a retry may repeat, and which tokens a training objective selects.


Test-time compute spends extra samples or search on one decision, and a verifier decides which result to keep. Two different events share the letter \(\Glyph{p}\) in these chapters, so each has its own symbol, and each chapter states which one it means where it introduces it.










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\PerStepErrorRate\)
Per-step error rate
Probability
Probability that one unchecked turn is wrong, assumed independent across turns, so an unchecked horizon succeeds with \((1-\PerStepErrorRate)^{\TurnHorizon}\). Verifier error rates and the stale-support rate carry subscripts.


\(\CandidatePoolSize\)
Candidate pool size
Count
Candidates generated for one decision in best-of-\(\CandidatePoolSize\) sampling, or the breadth of concurrent candidate streams. A search tree’s visit count \(\Glyph{N}(\Glyph{s},\Glyph{a})\) is local to its derivation.


\(\AttemptPassProbability\)
Per-attempt pass probability
Probability
Probability that one independent attempt on a given task passes its check, so that \(\text{pass@}\IndependentAttemptCount= 1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount\) and a sequential retry costs about \(\MeanAttemptCost/\AttemptPassProbability\) per success. A per-task quantity; the workload-level per-attempt rate is \(\AcceptanceProbability\).


\(\ValidCandidateRate\)
Valid-candidate rate
Probability
Base rate \(\Pr(\text{Valid})\) of candidates that meet the specification before any check; with \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\) and \(\VerifierFalseRejectionRate\) it sets verifier precision \(\VerifierPrecision\). Same letter as \(\AttemptPassProbability\), but a different event.


\(\SearchDepth\)
Search depth limit
Steps
Maximum depth a tree search expands; the depth index is \(\Glyph{d}\). Not \(\Glyph{D}\), which is dataset size.


pass@\(\Glyph{k}\)
Pass at k
Probability
At least one of \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) runs of the same task passes the criterion, averaged over tasks. Candidate availability is distinct from selected acceptance.


pass\(^{\Glyph{k}}\)
Pass to the k
Probability
All \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) runs of the same task pass, averaged over tasks. Under conditional independence this is \(\mathbb E_i[\AttemptPassProbability_i^\IndependentAttemptCount]\), not \((\mathbb E_i[\AttemptPassProbability_i])^\IndependentAttemptCount\) for independent new tasks.


\(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\), \(\VerifierFalseRejectionRate\)
Verifier false-acceptance, false-rejection rates
Probability
\(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate = \Pr(\text{PASS}\mid\neg\text{Valid})\) and \(\VerifierFalseRejectionRate = \Pr(\neg\text{PASS}\mid\text{Valid})\). Subscripted to stay distinct from the per-step error rate \(\PerStepErrorRate\) of horizon compounding.


\(\CandidateUtility\)
Candidate utility
Scalar
Genuine task utility, the true quality, of one candidate, which a scorer estimates with error. Indexed by candidate. Not the unlabeled pool or resource utilization that share the letter elsewhere.


\(\ChildPruningProbability\)
Child pruning probability
Probability
Probability that an intermediate check prunes one proposed child of a search node, independently of its siblings. Not the weight-pruning threshold of compression.


\(\GeneratedSampleCount\)
Generated sample count
Integer
Number of candidates generated for one task when estimating pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\), from which subsets of \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) runs are drawn. Must be at least \(\IndependentAttemptCount\).


\(\IndependentAttemptCount\)
Independent attempt count
Integer
Number of independent attempts or runs at one task, such as the attempts a retry budget allows or the runs that pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\) and pass\(^{\IndependentAttemptCount}\) score. At least one of them is accepted with probability \(1-(1-\AcceptanceProbability)^{\IndependentAttemptCount}\).


\(\FusionInputRank\)
Fusion input rank
Integer
One-based rank of a candidate within one retrieval method’s ranked list, as reciprocal rank fusion reads it. Indexed by method.


\(\GroupContrastProbability\)
Group contrast probability
Probability
Probability that a group of independent rollouts on one task contains at least one pass and at least one failure, so that its reward contrast is nonzero. Written with its arguments \(\GroupSize\) and \(\AttemptPassProbability\); rollouts per informative group are \(\GroupSize\) divided by this probability.


\(\FalseApprovalCount\)
False approval count
Count
Number of reviewers in an ensemble that approve a candidate known to be invalid. Binomial under independent errors, beta-binomial under the shared-difficulty mixture.


\(\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount\)
False approval outcome count
Integer
A particular number of falsely approving reviewers, the value at which the false-approval count’s distribution is evaluated or summed. Ranges from zero to \(\WorkerCount\); a majority exceeds half of \(\WorkerCount\).


\(\FalseApprovalPropensity\)
False approval propensity
Probability
Probability, intrinsic to one candidate, that a randomly chosen reviewer falsely approves it, treated as a random variable over the candidate population. Under shared difficulty, reviewers are independent given the propensity but correlated across candidates.


\(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability\)
Marginal false-approval probability
Probability
Probability that one model reviewer approves a candidate known to be invalid, averaged over the candidate population. The mean of \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\) in the latent-propensity model. Compare \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\), a single verifier’s false-acceptance rate.


\(\ReviewerIndex\)
Reviewer index
Index
Index of one reviewer in a review ensemble. The other reviewer of a pair is \(\PeerReviewerIndex\).


\(\PeerReviewerIndex\)
Peer reviewer index
Index
Index of the other reviewer of a pair whose errors are compared with those of the reviewer \(\ReviewerIndex\). Distinct from it in a pairwise covariance.


\(\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator\)
Reviewer false-approval indicator
0 or 1
Indicator that one reviewer approves a candidate known to violate its acceptance criterion: one when it falsely approves, zero otherwise. Indexed by reviewer; the false approval count \(\FalseApprovalCount\) sums them.


\(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape\)
Propensity prior approval shape
Dimensionless
First shape parameter of the beta distribution assumed for the false-approval propensity \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\), the pseudo-count weighting approval. Set from the marginal rate and the correlation.


\(\PropensityPriorRejectionShape\)
Propensity prior rejection shape
Dimensionless
Second shape parameter of the same beta distribution, the pseudo-count weighting correct rejection. Not a batch size.


\(\PassAtKEstimate\)
Pass-at-k estimate
Probability
Unbiased estimate of pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\) for one task from a set of generated candidates: one minus the share of size-\(\IndependentAttemptCount\) subsets with no passing candidate. The plug-in form is biased.


\(\PassingSampleCount\)
Passing sample count
Count
Number of the \(\GeneratedSampleCount\) candidates generated for one task that pass the test criterion. At most \(\GeneratedSampleCount\).


\(\SearchBranchingFactor\)
Search branching factor
Count
Number of candidate extensions each expanded node of a search tree proposes before any pruning. Not the survivors per node after pruning.


\(\RankFusionSmoothingConstant\)
Rank-fusion smoothing constant
Dimensionless
Positive constant that reciprocal rank fusion adds to each rank before taking the reciprocal, compressing score differences between adjacent ranks. The usual choice is 60.


\(\SearchQueryEmbedding\)
Search query embedding
Vector
Embedding of a search query, the full-precision vector a vector index compares with its stored vectors. Not the attention query.


\(\StoredIndexVector\)
Stored index vector
Vector
One vector stored in a vector index, scored against the search query embedding \(\SearchQueryEmbedding\).


\(\TrialPassProbability\)
Trial pass probability
Probability
Probability that a fixed candidate passes one verification trial under a specified protocol. It varies run to run only through flakiness.


\(\VerificationTrialCount\)
Verification trial count
Integer
Number of verification trials an all-pass rule requires of one candidate, counting the first. Acceptance needs every one of them to pass.


\(\VerifierPrecision\)
Verifier precision
Probability
Probability that a candidate meets the specification given that the verifier passed it. Set by Bayes’ rule from the valid-candidate rate \(\ValidCandidateRate\) and the verifier error rates \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\) and \(\VerifierFalseRejectionRate\). Not a product operator.


\(\NucleusProbabilityMass\)
Nucleus probability mass
Probability
Cumulative probability mass of the smallest high-probability token set that nucleus sampling draws from, between zero and one.


\(\TopTokenSampleCount\)
Top-token sample count
Count
Number of highest-probability tokens top-k sampling keeps as candidates at each decoding step. Not the number of attempts \(\IndependentAttemptCount\).

Generation index

Independent probabilities that a call’s request, or its reply, is lost in transit.

Probability

Named probabilities use lowercase \(\Glyph{p}\), as \(\AcceptanceProbability\) does.

Repair cap
Count
Configured bound on admitted forward-repair attempts in a declared scope; exhaustion withholds further repair and selects permitted recovery or handoff, not proof that repair is impossible.


\(\CheckpointInterval\)
Checkpoint Interval
Seconds
Useful-work interval chosen between durable checkpoints. Not \(\Glyph{\tau}\), which is a trajectory.


\(\OptimalCheckpointInterval\)
Optimal checkpoint interval
Seconds
The interval \(\CheckpointInterval\) that minimizes expected overhead, \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval \approx \sqrt{2\,\CheckpointWriteTime\,\MeanTimeBetweenFailures}\) under Young’s approximation.


\(\CheckpointWriteTime\)
Checkpoint write time
Seconds
Pause to persist one checkpoint, during which useful work stops.


\(\MeanTimeBetweenFailures\), \(\TurnFailureRate\)
Mean time between failures, failure rate
Seconds, failures/time
Mean useful time between failures that lose work, and its reciprocal \(\TurnFailureRate= 1/\MeanTimeBetweenFailures\). A failure rate counted per turn or per step states that unit. An upright acronym, not the memory root \(\Glyph{M}\).


\(\ExpectedIrreversibleLoss\)
Expected irreversible loss
Consequence units
\(\ExpectedIrreversibleLoss= \sum_\PolicyAction\Pr(\text{bad}\ \PolicyAction)\cdot \text{consequence}(\PolicyAction)\cdot(1-\ActionRecoverableFraction)\), where \(\ActionRecoverableFraction\) is the recoverable fraction of action \(\PolicyAction\)’s consequence. A check before a pivot raises \(\ActionRecoverableFraction\); one after it does not.


\(\TasksPerComparisonArm\)
Tasks per comparison arm
Tasks
Sample size per arm for a two-proportion release comparison, \(\TasksPerComparisonArm \approx 2(\SignificanceCriticalQuantile+\StatisticalPowerQuantile)^2\,\PooledAcceptanceProbability(1-\PooledAcceptanceProbability)/\TargetAcceptanceDifference^2\); the Type II error rate \(\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate\) and the pooled acceptance rate \(\PooledAcceptanceProbability\) are local to the formula.


\(\StatisticalSignificanceLevel\)
Significance level
Probability
Type I error target of a release test or a sequential test, and \(1-\StatisticalSignificanceLevel\) the coverage of a confidence interval. Subscripted so that bare \(\Glyph{\alpha}\) stays the acceptance fraction \(\AcceptanceFraction\).


\(\PositionLossMask_{t}\)
Loss mask
Binary \(\{0,1\}\)
Selects eligible policy-response targets under the declared objective, with \(\TokenIndex\) a token position. Supplied prompts, observations, initial context seeds, and unselected policy responses have \(\PositionLossMask_{t}=0\).


\(\MaskedFinetuningLoss\)
Masked fine-tuning loss
Cross-entropy
Mean selected-token loss for one example: \(-\frac{1}{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}\sum_t \PositionLossMask_{t}\log\Policy(\SequenceToken_t\mid \TokenPrefix)\), with \(\ActiveTargetTokenCount=\sum_t \PositionLossMask_{t}>0\). Batch aggregation is specified separately.


\(\TrajectoryReward(\Trajectory)\)
Trajectory reward
Scalar
Reward a verifier assigns to a whole trajectory.


\(\ActionRecoverableFraction\)
Recoverable fraction of an action
Fraction
Fraction of an action’s consequence that compensation can restore if the action proves bad. Zero for an action past a pivot; a pre-pivot check gives the product of its catch rate and the fidelity of the revert. Not server utilization \(\ServingUtilization\).


\(\EvidenceRecordEvent\)
Evidence record event
Event
Logged event that durably records evidence received about a dispatched operation, whose status may still be pending, partial, or unknown. Last event of the intent-before-effect ordering. Not the observation a model sees.


\(\AdmissionDecisionEvent\)
Admission decision event
Event
Event at which the runtime admits a proposed external effect, recording its authorization and budget-reservation decision. Second event of the write-ahead dispatch ordering, after the proposal and before the flush.


\(\IntentAcknowledgmentEvent\)
Intent acknowledgment event
Event
Event at which the log durably acknowledges an operation’s recoverable intent record, and the records before it, under the declared failure domain. The durability barrier: dispatch may follow only after it.


\(\ExternalDispatchAction\)
External dispatch action
Action
Dispatch of an admitted operation to an external endpoint, which is not its completion. Follows the acknowledgment event in the intent-before-effect ordering. Not the proposed or permitted action of the same turn.


\(\LogPositionIndex\)
Log position index
Integer
Position of one entry or boundary in a trajectory’s durable append-only log, counted from one. Distinct from the turn index \(\TurnIndex\): one turn can append several log records.


\(\CheckpointLogPosition\)
Checkpoint log position
Integer
Authoritative log position to which a published checkpoint binds its record and workspace snapshots. A log position like \(\LogPositionIndex\), not a turn index.


\(\IntegrationHeadCommitHash\)
Integration head commit hash
Hash
Content hash of the integration branch head captured for one integration attempt. A content hash names an immutable commit; the integration gate compares hashes, never mutable directory references.


\(\BlockingCallTimeout\)
Blocking call timeout
Seconds
Hard timeout after which a call blocked on an unresponsive dependency gives up the worker slot it occupies. With arrivals at \(\ArrivalRate\), the product of the two is the number of slots held in steady state (Little’s law).


\(\EvaluationTrialCount\)
Evaluation trial count
Integer
Number of trials assigned to an evaluation cohort, including incomplete, timed-out, crashed, and budget-exhausted runs. Denominator of \(\EstimatedAcceptanceProbability\).


\(\EstimatedAcceptanceProbability\)
Estimated acceptance probability
Probability
Sample estimate of a configuration’s acceptance probability from an evaluation, such as accepted trials over assigned trials or the task-averaged share of accepted runs. With one run per task it is the observed acceptance share around which Wald and Wilson intervals are built.


\(\IntervalNormalQuantile\)
Interval normal quantile
Dimensionless
Positive standard-normal quantile that sets the width of a two-sided confidence interval at its stated nominal confidence, written bare inside interval formulas. About 1.96 for a nominal 95% interval, a quantile at one minus half of \(\StatisticalSignificanceLevel\).


\(\HypothesizedAcceptanceProbability\)
Hypothesized acceptance probability
Probability
Acceptance probability a sequential probability ratio test specifies under one of its two simple hypotheses, indexed zero for the baseline and one for the degraded alternative; the degraded value is the smaller, and both are design inputs. Not \(\AttemptPassProbability\), the per-attempt pass probability.


\(\ObservedLabelCount\)
Observed label count
Integer
Number of task labels a sequential test has observed so far. Indexes the running statistics \(\CumulativeLogLikelihoodRatio\) and \(\AcceptedLabelCount\).


\(\AcceptedLabelCount\)
Accepted label count
Integer
Number of accepted labels among the observations a sequential test has collected so far, indexed by the observation count. The running sum of the accepted indicators; it enters the log-likelihood ratio.


\(\CumulativeLogLikelihoodRatio\)
Cumulative log-likelihood ratio
Dimensionless
Cumulative log-likelihood ratio of the specified degradation against the baseline after the labels observed so far in a sequential test. Indexed by label count, or by the stopping count.


\(\EventIndicator\)
Event indicator
0 or 1
Indicator of an event: one when the braced condition holds and zero otherwise, written with the condition in braces. Same meaning as the blackboard-bold indicator \(\Glyph{\mathbb{I}}\), kept in bold-one rendering for this book. Not the all-ones vector.


\(\AllRunsPassEstimate\)
All-runs-pass estimate
Probability
Unbiased estimate, for one task, of the probability that all of a claimed number of runs pass: the share of subsets of the graded runs in which every run passed. Carries task and claim-size indices; averaged over tasks it estimates the all-runs-pass probability.


\(\ConcordantTaskCount\)
Concordant task count
Integer
Number of sampled tasks on which the baseline and candidate configurations receive the same verdict in a paired comparison. Always written with a two-digit index giving the baseline outcome then the candidate outcome: 11 accepted by both, 00 by neither. The discordant cells are \(\BaselineOnlyAcceptedTaskCount\) and \(\CandidateOnlyAcceptedTaskCount\).


\(\BaselineOnlyAcceptedTaskCount\)
Baseline-only accepted tasks
Integer
Number of tasks in a paired comparison that the baseline accepts and the candidate does not, one of the two discordant counts. With \(\CandidateOnlyAcceptedTaskCount\) it forms the discordant pairs of McNemar’s test and the paired difference.


\(\CandidateOnlyAcceptedTaskCount\)
Candidate-only accepted tasks
Integer
Number of tasks in a paired comparison that the candidate accepts and the baseline does not, the other discordant count. Not a queue server count or a speed of light.


\(\BaselineAcceptanceEstimate\)
Baseline acceptance estimate
Probability
Observed acceptance share of the baseline configuration over the tasks of a paired comparison: its accepted count divided by the task count. Pairs with \(\CandidateAcceptanceEstimate\).


\(\CandidateAcceptanceEstimate\)
Candidate acceptance estimate
Probability
Observed acceptance share of the candidate configuration over the tasks of a paired comparison: its accepted count divided by the task count. With \(\BaselineAcceptanceEstimate\) it gives the paired difference \(\EstimatedPairedAcceptanceDifference\).


\(\EstimatedPairedAcceptanceDifference\)
Estimated paired acceptance difference
Dimensionless
Observed difference between the candidate’s and the baseline’s acceptance shares on the same sampled tasks: the discordant-count difference divided by the task count. The paired interval is built around it.


\(\PairedDifferenceLowerLimit\)
Paired difference lower limit
Dimensionless
Lower endpoint of a confidence interval for the paired acceptance difference between a candidate and its baseline. The noninferiority gate checks it against the negated tolerance. Computed by Newcombe’s paired-score method in the mathematical appendix.


\(\PairedDifferenceUpperLimit\)
Paired difference upper limit
Dimensionless
Upper endpoint of a confidence interval for the paired acceptance difference between a candidate and its baseline. Pairs with \(\PairedDifferenceLowerLimit\); the mathematical appendix gives its Newcombe formula.


\(\ReferenceAssessedFailure\)
Reference-assessed failure
Event
Event that a trial fails its specified criterion according to an independent reference assessment, the conditioning event of a grader’s false-acceptance rate.


\(\PairedOutcomeCellCount\)
Paired outcome cell count
Integer
Number of paired tasks in one cell of the baseline-by-candidate outcome table, indexed by the baseline outcome then the candidate outcome (one for accepted, zero for rejected). The off-diagonal cells have their own rows, \(\BaselineOnlyAcceptedTaskCount\) and \(\CandidateOnlyAcceptedTaskCount\).


\(\StreamAcceptanceProbability\)
Stream acceptance probability
Probability
Stationary probability that one monitored task is accepted, the Bernoulli parameter a sequential release test compares at two hypothesized values. The same quantity as \(\AcceptanceProbability\), written bare as the release chapter does.


\(\TaskAcceptanceLabel\)
Task acceptance label
0 or 1
Binary label recording whether one monitored task was accepted, one for acceptance. Indexed by arrival order; the sequential test sums them.


\(\SprtExpectedLogIncrement\)
SPRT expected log increment
Nats
Expected increment of a sequential probability ratio test’s log-likelihood ratio per labeled observation, under the hypothesis its index names. Divides the boundary average in the expected stopping count.


\(\SprtLowerLogBoundary\)
SPRT lower log boundary
Nats
Lower stopping boundary on the log-likelihood ratio, at or below which the test selects the baseline hypothesis. Negative.


\(\SprtUpperLogBoundary\)
SPRT upper log boundary
Nats
Upper stopping boundary on the log-likelihood ratio, at or above which the test selects the degraded hypothesis. Positive.


\(\SprtStoppingSampleCount\)
SPRT stopping sample count
Integer
Random number of labeled observations a sequential probability ratio test takes before its statistic first crosses a boundary, without truncation.


\(\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate\)
Statistical false-negative rate
Probability
Allowed probability of a type II error, a release comparison missing a true difference of the target size. One minus it is the statistical power. Pairs with \(\StatisticalSignificanceLevel\).


\(\SignificanceCriticalQuantile\)
Significance critical quantile
Dimensionless
Standard-normal quantile at one minus half the significance level \(\StatisticalSignificanceLevel\), the two-sided critical value of a release test. About 1.96 at a level of 0.05.


\(\StatisticalPowerQuantile\)
Statistical power quantile
Dimensionless
Standard-normal quantile at the target statistical power of a release test, one minus the type II error rate \(\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate\). About 0.84 at 80% power.


\(\TargetAcceptanceDifference\)
Target acceptance difference
Dimensionless
Difference in acceptance probability between two system versions that a release comparison is planned to detect. It appears squared in the denominator of \(\TasksPerComparisonArm\), so halving it quadruples the tasks per arm.


\(\PooledAcceptanceProbability\)
Pooled acceptance probability
Probability
Average of the acceptance probabilities of the two system versions a comparison tests, used as the pooled variance estimate in planning. It pools planned probabilities, not observed shares.


\(\ToolTargetState\)
Tool target state
Record
State of the external system or resource a tool operation reads or mutates, such as a remote file or service record. The baseline captured just before dispatch is what a reconciliation probe compares against. Not the trajectory state \(\TrajectoryState_{t}\).


\(\PlanAction\)
Plan action
Record
One action of an execution plan, the summation variable when the expected irreversible loss \(\ExpectedIrreversibleLoss\) sums over the plan. Not the per-turn proposal \(\TrajectoryAction_{t}\).


\(\ValidatedProposalEvent\)
Validated proposal event
Event
Event at which the runtime holds a validated, complete proposal for an external effect, first in the write-ahead dispatch ordering: intent before effect. Distinct from the proposed action itself.


\(\WorkerBaseCommitHash\)
Worker base commit hash
Hash
Content hash of the commit a worker started from. A content hash names an immutable commit; the integration gate compares hashes, never mutable directory references.


\(\ConfidenceCriticalQuantile\)
Confidence critical quantile
Dimensionless
Positive standard-Normal critical value for a two-sided test at the chosen confidence level, about 1.96 at 95% confidence.


\(\PowerCriticalQuantile\)
Power critical quantile
Dimensionless
Positive standard-Normal critical value corresponding to the chosen statistical power of a test, about 0.84 at 80% power.


\(\HypothesisTestFalseNegativeRate\)
Test false-negative rate
Probability
Probability that a hypothesis test misses a true effect; one minus it is the statistical power. Not the link bandwidth, which shares the glyph \(\Glyph{\beta}\).


\(\EvaluationSampleCount\)
Evaluation sample count
Count
Number of examples in the evaluation set over which an accuracy or calibration metric is computed. It sets the sampling error of an accuracy estimate. Not the training-set size \(\DatasetSize\).


\(\SequentialTestObservation\)
Sequential-test observation
Record
One observation a sequential test collects, indexed in arrival order, so the observations run from the first to the latest.


\(\CorrelationCoefficient\)
Correlation coefficient
Dimensionless
Pearson correlation coefficient between two random quantities, between minus one and one. Shares the glyph \(\Glyph{\rho}\) with the communication-to-compute ratio and the serving utilization.


\(\GaussianDistribution\)
Gaussian distribution
Distribution
Gaussian (normal) distribution with the mean and covariance given as its arguments, written \(\GaussianDistribution(\Glyph{\mu}, \Glyph{\Sigma})\).


\(\IndicatorFunction\)
Indicator function
Function
Function equal to one when its condition holds and zero otherwise.


\(\FiniteChange\)
Finite change
Operator
Prefix operator for the finite change in the quantity it prefixes, between two states, configurations, or points in time. Differs from a \(\Glyph{\Delta}\) fused into a named entry.


\(\StateOperation\)
State operation
Function
Operation that maps a system’s stored state to a new state, such as one pipeline write. Idempotent when applying it twice gives the same result as applying it once.

The generalized advantage estimator’s decay factor, \(\TraceDecay\in [0,1]\). Elsewhere a rate carries a subscript, as \(\ArrivalRate\) and \(\TurnFailureRate\) do.

\(\EnvironmentTransitionDistribution\)
