Incomplete candidate that may nevertheless parse
Withhold from action; record the limit and diagnose


REFUSED
The model or service explicitly declines the request or response
Refusal notice, partial content, or no payload
Handle under the task’s refusal policy; do not treat as an action


TRANSPORT_FAILURE
Delivery fails or the local deadline expires without accepted completion
Missing or partial content; remote outcome may be unknown
Record uncertainty and apply bounded failure handling


REJECTED
A runtime monitor rejects the response during reception
Content observed before rejection
Withhold from action; record the rejection and request cancellation


CANCELED
Discretionary runtime or operator cancellation before accepted completion
Partial, missing, or otherwise unusable as a completed candidate
Stop local candidate processing; track remote termination separately


FAULTED
The service reports an execution failure
Missing, partial, or diagnostic content
Record the reported fault and route to failure handling






For an artifact such as a read_file request, kind="tool_request" instructs the runtime which candidate representation to validate, while status="COMPLETED" confirms that generation finished under the interface contract. Neither field confirms that the host dispatched the tool or that the filesystem operation succeeded; completion tracks protocol generation, whereas execution and task acceptance remain separate host decisions.
Applying invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) to the status field establishes a mandatory gate: the quarantining rule. Under this rule, any payload whose invocation envelope reports a status other than COMPLETED cannot pass into the candidate execution pipeline. The runtime must verify the status flag before admitting content to downstream parsing or action dispatch. While the system may inspect malformed or interrupted output inside an isolated diagnostic sandbox, that inspection cannot authorize tool dispatch or silently reclassify the fragment as a finished proposal. When later chapters sample several candidates for one task, a candidate cut off by a token limit obeys the same rule. Under the quarantining rule, a truncated payload is treated as a diagnosable failure rather than a partial action.
The cleanup command introduced earlier demonstrates why structural parsing alone cannot replace this status check. Suppose the complete intended command is
rm -rf /tmp/scratch/cache_dir
If an exhausted token quota truncates generation midway through the path, the resulting prefix is
rm -rf /tmp/scratch
The truncated string parses as valid shell syntax, but it broadens the deletion scope to the entire parent directory. If the envelope marks this output as TRUNCATED, the quarantining rule holds the command in quarantine, preventing accidental execution. Conversely, receiving status="COMPLETED" does not grant execution authority; it merely establishes that the model finished generating its proposal. Neither command represents an approved cleanup policy on its own; the comparison underscores that syntactic validity cannot substitute for verified completion evidence.
Listing 3 implements this admission check. The gate admits only completed generations to downstream processing, leaving syntax validation, permission checks, and task-level verification to subsequent stages.



Listing 3: Completed-candidate admission: The status check admits only completed generations to the candidate path. Returning the payload grants no execution authority.


def completed_candidate(envelope):
    if envelope["status"] != "COMPLETED":
        raise ValueError("Response is not a completed candidate")
    # Syntax, permission, and task evidence remain unchecked.
    return envelope["payload"]



Incomplete payloads are redirected to a dedicated diagnostic log governed by its own memory and access bounds. This log retains the partial byte stream alongside the observed stop_reason to assist failure analysis. Attempting to “repair” a truncated fragment by appending guessed arguments or synthetic delimiters produces an entirely new candidate devoid of generation provenance; such synthetic patches can never inherit the COMPLETED status of the original call.



Streaming delivers incremental response fragments across an active network connection before generation finishes. A delivery chunk can contain part of a decoded sub-word, several tokens, or an application-layer framing event. The host runtime must adhere to the provider’s framing protocol rather than assuming a one-to-one correspondence between chunks and tokens. Incremental inspection allows the runtime to discover early structural violations; if a prefix violates format constraints, the monitor halts waiting immediately rather than buffering unusable tokens. Because generation is ongoing, the monitor evaluates whether the prefix can transition to a valid completion, rather than testing whether the prefix is already complete.
Rejection and cancellation represent distinct operational events. When an incremental monitor detects a structural violation, the host runtime sets the call status to REJECTED and issues a cancellation signal to the remote endpoint. If an operator or runtime policy cancels an otherwise compliant response before accepting completion, the runtime marks the status as CANCELED. A local deadline expiry without accepted completion instead maps to TRANSPORT_FAILURE, as in table 2; the runtime may then request cancellation while tracking remote termination separately. Withholding the partial payload from tool dispatch is an invariant the host enforces locally in each case. However, halting remote decode loops and reclaiming accelerator memory require the serving engine to process and honor the cancellation request. Simply closing a TCP socket provides no guarantee that remote execution has ceased.
Consider a call with an output allowance of 4,096 tokens whose stream validator detects a schema violation at step \(\RejectionDecodeStep =\) 96. The runtime’s part of the response finishes at once. It records the rejection, discards the partial proposal, and sends a cancel request. The service’s part depends on whether that request is honored (figure 3).






Figure 3: Reject, Then Cancel: The runtime’s stream validator advances a parser state as each prefix arrives and holds the output rather than acting on it. At step 96 the proposal introduces a key outside the schema, so the runtime records a rejection, discards the partial proposal, and sends a cancel request. The runtime outcomes on the left hold regardless of the service; the service outcomes on the right hold only if the service receives and honors the cancel request.



The skipped-step count shown is an upper bound that requires provider cooperation. If the serving engine processes the cancellation promptly, it skips up to \(\OutputLimit - \RejectionDecodeStep =\) 4,000 autoregressive decode steps. In the reference unbatched deployment, each plain autoregressive decode step reads the model weights from accelerator memory, so the step takes at least the weight bytes divided by the memory bandwidth; for the reference deployment of section 2.8, that floor is 21.075 ms per generated token. At that reference floor, skipping all these steps avoids 84.3 s of estimated decode work. An honored cancellation also frees the request’s slot among the requests the serving engine decodes together and releases the call’s KV-cache allocations. If the remote service fails to honor the cancellation, the host runtime still quarantines the rejected payload locally, but the remote service may continue generating up to its token allowance.
Nonstreaming invocations enforce the same admission barrier once the whole response arrives. Streaming moves the observation boundary earlier in the call, enabling rapid rejection and resource recovery without relaxing the rule that incomplete prefixes never trigger external side effects. Either way, the status gate settles only whether a complete candidate exists. A COMPLETED read_file proposal can still name a missing file or a path outside the workspace, so the next question is which property each subsequent check on that candidate can establish.

title: 2 The Foundation Model
text:
Suppose the status gate has admitted a completed read_file proposal with path set to src/pool.py. Completion says only that generation finished, and, as the validation and authorization stages in section 2.2.2 showed, schema conformance says nothing about whether the file exists or lies inside the workspace. Generative inference produces a candidate token sequence; neither high statistical likelihood nor schema conformance determines whether the runtime environment can safely act on it.
The same distinction applies when the model emits a source code patch rather than an inspection request. A candidate patch can parse cleanly, compile against existing headers, and pass a sequential unit test while leaving the underlying race condition untouched. Each verification check answers a narrow, specific question rather than certifying overall task satisfaction. Robust candidate verification systems must track these separate dimensions of evidence explicitly rather than collapsing them into a single, undifferentiated notion of validity.


Autoregressive generation assigns probabilities based on patterns in training data and context tokens, reflecting linguistic familiarity rather than operational truth. Whether a generated path exists on disk, whether the caller holds read permissions, and whether an altered function preserves system invariants depend entirely on the operational environment and the task contract. An obsolete or nonexistent path often receives substantial model probability simply because it matches common directory conventions in the training corpus.
Sound verification begins by pairing each concrete property with the precise evidence required to validate it. For a read_file invocation, a schema validator checks that the payload contains only supported keys and provides a string-valued path. A passing result proves syntactic schema membership, provided the validator implements the schema dialect faithfully and inspects the exact object forwarded to execution. Proving that the target file exists requires probing the filesystem, while establishing access rights requires evaluating the task’s current capability grant against host operating system policies.
Static analysis and dynamic testing support fundamentally different operational claims. A compiler verifies type consistency and language constraints under fixed configuration flags, whereas a linter detects anti-patterns through static heuristic rules. Dynamic test suites execute concrete code paths and record runtime assertions, so a passing single-threaded checkout test says nothing about the connection pool under concurrent contention.


↩︎ The closure evidence levels, from self-report and static checks through visible and sealed tests to formal proof, are established in The invariant closure principle.
8 Complete Mediation: One of the design principles that Saltzer and Schroeder (1975) set out for protection systems: every access to every object is checked against current authority at the moment of access, not remembered from an earlier decision. The tool handler applies the same rule to a model’s proposal, so a path validated when the request was composed is checked again when the read executes, closing the gap in which the grant or the file could have changed. 
Saltzer, J. H., and M. D. Schroeder. 1975. “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems.” Proceedings of the IEEE 63 (9): 1278–308. https://doi.org/10.1109/proc.1975.9939.
Architecturally, these boundaries require the execution runtime to treat generated model output strictly as untrusted data rather than direct control flow. A candidate tool call remains passive data until an authorized tool handler ingests, verifies, and dispatches it. That handler enforces access boundaries at execution time,8 completely independent of any self-assertions the model makes regarding its own permissions. Similarly, evaluating an untrusted patch requires running arbitrary machine instructions, demanding isolated execution sandboxes even during preliminary test runs.



Prompts that instruct a model to inspect or refine its own patch can surface shallow syntax errors or expose omitted edge cases. Model-based self-review, however, is simply another autoregressive generation step sampled from the same parameter distribution and conditioned on the same incomplete context. When the generator operates under an incorrect assumption about an API or concurrency model, a self-review prompt typically reinforces that assumption rather than exposing it. Re-prompting does not create statistical independence. Empirical evaluations of self-correction without external grounding demonstrate this limit clearly: across complex reasoning tasks, models prompted to inspect their own answers rarely improve their accuracy and frequently introduce regressions (Huang et al. 2024).

Huang, Jie, Xinyun Chen, Swaroop Mishra, Huaixiu Steven Zheng, Adams Wei Yu, Xinying Song, and Denny Zhou. 2024. “Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Zheng, Lianmin, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ying Sheng, Siyuan Zhuang, Hao Wu, Yonghao Zhuang, Zi Lin, et al. 2023. “Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 36: 46595–623.
Engineers must maintain a firm conceptual separation between candidate refinement and formal property certification. A model-generated critique can guide iterative search, but external tools (compilers, linters, sandboxed test harnesses, and kernel access-control checks) must provide evidence for the specific properties they check. No critique emitted by a model, whether self-generated or evaluated by an auxiliary judge model, carries the authority to validate a security boundary or approve deployment. When a system does use a learned judge (a second model prompted or trained to grade the first model’s output) as a secondary evaluator, its verdicts must be treated as noisy signals with measurable false-positive rates and known systematic biases, such as preferences for verbose explanations or specific candidate positions (Zheng et al. 2023).
A conditional-probability calculation clarifies why fallible verification gates leave residual risk. The following model parameters reflect a hypothetical scenario evaluating a candidate patch against a concurrency specification:

Systems Perspective 2.1: What a passing verdict leaves unresolvedLet \(\CandidateDefectRate\) denote the defect rate, the share of generated patches that violate a specified behavioral property (a local symbol here, distinct from the per-turn error rate of horizon compounding), and let \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\) denote the checker’s false-accept rate, the probability that it passes a defective patch. Suppose \(\CandidateDefectRate =\) 18 percent, \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate =\) 0.65, and the checker passes valid patches with probability 0.85. Bayes’ rule gives the fraction of defective patches among the passing results:
\[\Pr(\text{Defective} \mid \text{PASS}) = \frac{\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate \cdot \CandidateDefectRate}{\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate \cdot \CandidateDefectRate + \Pr(\text{PASS} \mid \text{Valid}) \cdot (1 - \CandidateDefectRate)} \tag{4}\]
Substituting the assumed rates gives \(\frac{0.65 \times 0.18}{(0.65 \times 0.18) + (0.85 \times (1 - 0.18))}\approx 14.37\%\). The defect share among passing patches falls only from 18 percent to 14.37 percent, because the checker rejects 35 percent of defective patches while also rejecting 15 percent of valid ones. The lever is \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\): a checker with half the false-accept rate, 0.325, lowers the residual to 7.7 percent. Repeating the same check buys no such guarantee, because its behavior on the surviving candidates is correlated with the first pass. Every defective patch that passes also inflates the apparent acceptance probability \(\AcceptanceProbability\) in the cost per accepted task (equation 1.2).
A sound checker for the exact property drives \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\) to zero under its assumptions. Determinism alone does not supply soundness, and soundness for schema membership does not extend to patch behavior. The residual in equation 4 is one minus the precision \(\VerifierPrecision\) of a passing verdict in the verification asymmetry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)), written there with valid-candidate rate \(\ValidCandidateRate = 1 - \CandidateDefectRate\) and false-reject rate \(\VerifierFalseRejectionRate = 1 - \Pr(\text{PASS} \mid \text{Valid})\). That principle holds that producing a candidate, selecting it, and establishing that it satisfies the task are different events, and it yields a design rule. Select each validation gate for the specific property it establishes and its false-accept rate, and let the task contract determine what residual defect rate the system can tolerate.





In production systems, executing full end-to-end integration tests or sandboxed reproduction scripts is orders of magnitude more expensive than parsing JSON or running a static linter. Consequently, the runtime organizes candidate verification into an ascending cascade, rejecting malformed or unauthorized requests early before spending compute on deep behavioral evaluation. Staging checks by cost optimizes throughput, but each gate validates an orthogonal property rather than an increasingly strict approximation of overall correctness. Table 3 categorizes these verification layers alongside their computational overhead and formal evidentiary boundaries.



Table 3: Scoped candidate checks: A passing result supports a named claim, not every property needed for task acceptance. The runtime preserves these distinctions when composing the checks.












Verification layer
Gate mechanism
Property or evidence
Cost to account for
Limit of the claim




Syntax and schema
Parser and schema validator
Required fields, supported types, and declared value constraints
Parsing and validation
Does not establish permission or correct values beyond the schema


Authorization
Task permission check and enforcing tool handler
Requested operation and target fall within the current grant
Policy lookup and mediation
Permission does not establish that the operation serves the goal


Static analysis
Compiler, type checker, or linter
Properties covered by the selected analysis and configuration
Analysis of the candidate and its dependencies
Coverage depends on the checker and language assumptions


Behavioral evaluation
Controlled execution and designated tests
Observed outcomes for the exercised inputs and conditions
Environment preparation and execution
Passing cases do not establish untested behavior






Consider how this tiered pipeline evaluates an inspection request. Behind the status gate of section 2.5, a read_file proposal needs only the first two rows of table 3 before dispatch. Executing the read operation simply feeds environmental state back to the agent for subsequent reasoning cycles rather than completing the overall bug fix. Conversely, when evaluating a proposed patch, the pipeline validates patch syntax and file targets, applies the diff inside an isolated scratch workspace, and triggers targeted unit tests. Final acceptance adheres to the task contract’s explicit evidentiary standard, escalating to human review when automated checks cannot decisively settle safety or correctness criteria.
The verification cascade inspects output the model has already generated. A streaming monitor can reject an invalid prefix before the response finishes, but the offending token has already been emitted, and recovering still costs a fresh call. When the required output structure is known before the call, the syntax constraint can move inside generation and prevent the malformed token instead of rejecting it after emission.

title: 2 The Foundation Model
text:
Consider a software repair agent attempting to inspect an unfamiliar module by calling read_file(path) with argument "src/pool.py". If the model’s generated text omits the closing quotation mark before emitting an end-of-turn token, the runtime parser encounters malformed JSON and rejects the payload before dispatching the call. That parser check shields the execution boundary from syntactic corruption, yet resolving the failure demands another full call: queueing, prefill, and every decode step again, with a fresh chance of a different error. When the system knows the target output structure ahead of time, the inference engine can instead remove the tokens that would violate the required syntax during generation, so the defect never reaches the tool boundary.

Definition 2.3: Grammar-constrained decoding
Grammar-constrained decoding restricts next-token selection during autoregressive generation to tokens whose decoded text preserves a viable prefix of a target formal grammar.

Significance: Dynamic token masking guarantees that any completed generation sequence strictly satisfies the structural grammar, eliminating syntax errors at the model boundary when the constraint parser covers the target schema.
Distinction: Post-generation validation inspects an already emitted sequence and discards invalid payloads after full generation. Constrained decoding actively shapes the vocabulary distribution at every generation step. Even so, neither approach verifies whether a syntactically correct payload contains sensible parameter values or possesses valid execution permissions.
Common pitfall: Mistaking a viable prefix for a completed data structure. If token limits, request timeouts, or connection failures truncate generation early, the emitted sequence remains an unfinished prefix that cannot be safely dispatched.





The constraint engine maintains a running parse state synchronized with the sequence generated so far. Consider a schema expecting a string-valued path parameter. Once the prefix {"path": appears in the decoding buffer, the grammar allows optional whitespace followed by an opening quotation mark, but forbids unquoted booleans, numbers, or bare identifiers. When the generator emits {"path":"src/, the text represents a viable prefix:9 while incomplete as a JSON document, it can still transition into a valid object through subsequent string and delimiter tokens. The fundamental mechanism of constrained decoding relies on evaluating whether a candidate token can extend the current prefix toward an accepting grammar state.
9 Legal (Viable) Prefix: The viable-prefix concept stems from classical compiler theory. The LR parsers introduced by Knuth (1965) read input strings left to right, identifying an error at the exact first symbol that cannot extend the sequence into any valid sentence of the language. A grammar mask applies this principle constructively: instead of catching syntax violations after generation finishes, the engine prunes invalid transition tokens from the vocabulary before sampling. 
Knuth, Donald E. 1965. “On the Translation of Languages from Left to Right.” Information and Control 8 (6): 607–39. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0019-9958(65)90426-2.
At generation step \(\TokenIndex\), let \(\DecodingConstraintState_t\) represent the parser’s internal state, including nested scope tracking for recursive structures. Let \(\ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)\) denote the set of vocabulary tokens whose decoded strings maintain a viable prefix under the target grammar. Because modern language models operate on subword tokens rather than individual characters, a single token can span multiple characters, punctuation marks, or whitespace segments (for example, a single token .py"} that finishes the extension, closes the string, and closes the object). The engine must therefore simulate the parser across the token’s full decoded byte sequence to confirm that every character transition is valid.
Incremental parsing demonstrates that pruning invalid tokens at each decoding step produces syntactically flawless outputs for domain-specific languages such as SQL (Scholak et al. 2021). To minimize per-step latency, guided-generation frameworks precompute transition tables between the target grammar and the model vocabulary, converting the valid-token search into an efficient table lookup during the forward pass (Willard and Louf 2023).
For each token index \(\MaskTokenIndex\) in vocabulary \(\TokenVocabulary\), the constraint engine constructs an additive logit mask:
\[\LogitMaskEntry_i(\DecodingConstraintState_t) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \MaskTokenIndex \in \ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t) \\ -\infty & \text{if } \MaskTokenIndex \notin \ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t) \end{cases}\]
Adding this mask to the unnormalized logit vector \(\LogitVector_t\) produces the filtered logit vector \(\MaskedLogitVector_t = \LogitVector_t + \LogitMask(\DecodingConstraintState_t)\). At unit temperature, the resulting softmax distribution becomes
\[\SoftmaxOutputProbability_{t, i} = \frac{\exp(\MaskedTokenLogit_{t, i})}{\sum_{j \in \TokenVocabulary} \exp(\MaskedTokenLogit_{t, j})} = \begin{cases} \frac{\exp(\OutputLogit_{t, i})}{\sum_{k \in \ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)} \exp(\OutputLogit_{t, k})} & \text{if } \MaskTokenIndex \in \ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t) \\ 0 & \text{if } \MaskTokenIndex \notin \ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t) \end{cases} \tag{5}\]
Setting the logits of invalid tokens to \(-\infty\) forces their sampling probabilities to zero, renormalizing the distribution entirely across viable continuations. Once the sampler draws a token from this restricted set, the engine consumes that token’s characters and advances the parser to state \(\DecodingConstraintState_{t+1}\). This formulation assumes that \(\ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)\) remains nonempty and that the sampling configuration respects the mask. The engine applies the grammar mask before top-\(\TopTokenSampleCount\) or nucleus truncation so that these filters select among legal continuations. If an implementation instead truncates support first and no retained token belongs to \(\ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)\), the serving runtime must raise an explicit constraint-satisfaction error rather than silently disabling the mask. Positive finite temperature rescales the remaining probabilities without removing their support.
Recomputing \(\ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)\) from scratch at every step would cost a scan of the whole vocabulary per token. Engines therefore compile the tool schema once into an automaton whose states each carry a precomputed mask \(\LogitMask(\DecodingConstraintState_t)\), so that each step is a lookup followed by a state transition. The automaton in figure 4 is compiled for a query tool with two fields, query and limit, rather than for read_file; the mechanism is identical.






Figure 4: Grammar-Constrained Decoding: A tool schema compiles once into an automaton whose states each carry a token mask. At every step the mask sets illegal tokens to \(-\infty\) before normalization, so only a legal continuation can be drawn, and the drawn token advances the automaton. The logit values are illustrative: a fluent but illegal continuation can outscore the legal one and still receive zero probability. A precomputed per-state mask suits a finite-state constraint; nested structures need additional parser state. The strip along the bottom lists what the mask leaves unchecked.



Generating viable prefixes guarantees that the output will not contain invalid syntax, but it does not guarantee that generation finishes cleanly. For the output to form a complete, usable payload, two operational conditions must hold: the parser must reach an accepting state, and the generation sequence must terminate according to the protocol rules. The constraint engine must disallow end-of-sequence (<eos>) tokens whenever required fields or closing delimiters remain unwritten. As a result, maintaining viable prefixes provides a conditional guarantee: completed outputs are structurally sound, but the system cannot assume that every generation request finishes within its allocated token budget.


↪ The automaton behind the token mask, and the induction showing that a constrained output ending in a permitted end token belongs to the grammar, are developed in Finite-state constrained decoding.
Consider what happens when an inference request hits its maximum output token limit while emitting arguments, leaving the decoding buffer at {"path":"src/po. The string is a viable prefix under the schema, yet the envelope reports status: TRUNCATED, and the quarantining rule of section 2.5.2 applies exactly as it did to the shortened rm -rf path. A heuristic repair parser that appends the closing quote and brace would fabricate the call read_file("src/po"), which the model never finished and which names a file nobody asked for. The mask governs which tokens can appear; it never promotes an interrupted generation to a completed one.



Grammar masking moves the first row of table 3 into generation and leaves every other row where it was. A masked {"path":"src/pool.py"} still names a file that may not exist or may lie outside the grant, because the mask operates strictly on the textual representation and never queries repository state or security policy. Property by property, the mask’s own reach is narrow (table 4).



Table 4: Reach of the grammar mask: A completed constrained output establishes membership in the enforced output language. Every other property keeps the check it needed without the mask.










Verification dimension
What the grammar mask establishes
Evidence still required




Syntactic conformance
All of it for the enforced grammar, once generation accepts
A COMPLETED status, since a legal prefix may be unfinished


Schema completeness
Only the constraints its compiler supports, at accepting completion
A final validation pass against the authoritative schema


Referential integrity
Nothing
Observation of the named resource in the relevant environment


Semantic invariants
Nothing
Checks or judgments covering the task property


Authorization bounds
Nothing; generated text grants no authority
A runtime permission decision for the proposed operation






The strength of the structural guarantee depends directly on the formal expressive power of the enforced grammar. Enforcing a general JSON grammar guarantees only that the output obeys RFC 8259 syntax (balanced braces, legal numeric formats, and escaped strings) without constraining object keys or data types. In contrast, compiling a specific JSON Schema into the constraint engine allows the runtime to enforce required properties, restrict types (such as distinguishing floating-point numbers from integers), and constrain string values to specific regular expressions or enumerations.
Engineering challenges arise when a schema relies on advanced features that the constraint compiler cannot translate into finite-state or pushdown automata. For example, schema keywords enforcing cross-field conditional dependencies (if/then/else), unique array elements, or complex lookahead assertions often exceed the capabilities of precomputed token masks. If an execution engine encounters unsupported schema features, an improper grammar compiler, or divergent type interpretations between the generator and consumer, the structural guarantee collapses. To maintain system integrity, the runtime must document which schema features its engine enforces and perform a final validation pass against its authoritative interface before dispatch. Logit masking acts as a mechanical filter situated below the model in the hierarchy of invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)): it guarantees syntactic conformance without requiring model cooperation, leaving semantic acceptance and authorization to verification layers situated above the model.
Schema structure directly influences how an agent handles ambiguity or missing context. When a schema strictly mandates a file path with no alternative representations, every accepted completion must provide a path string, even when the prompt context provides no reasonable clue about which file to inspect. By stripping away all tokens outside the target structure, an over-constrained mask removes the agent’s ability to communicate that critical information is missing. Under these conditions, the model has no choice but to invent a plausible file path to reach an accepting parser state.
Systems engineers can prevent this forced confabulation by designing schemas that incorporate explicit fallback variants, such as an unknown payload variant or a structured error field. Providing an unknown branch allows the agent to signal insufficient information directly within the schema without inventing fictitious data. These variants represent distinct semantic branches within the model’s output payload; they should not be confused with transport-level invocation statuses or runtime tool execution failures.
Engineers must also recognize that introducing fallback branches does not prevent semantic misuse. An agent might still output a fabricated file path when an unknown variant is available, or falsely trigger an error state when sufficient context exists. The execution runtime must evaluate each payload variant according to the application’s task contract, gathering targeted observations or asking for user clarification when uncertainty arises. The schema provides the expressiveness necessary for honest reporting; external system observations determine whether the agent’s reported choice is justified.



Supervised fine-tuning (further training on curated example responses, developed in Trajectory Fine-Tuning) and instruction tuning teach models to associate natural language prompts with specific tool definitions, biasing generation toward well-structured function arguments (Schick et al. 2023). Runtime logit masking operates at a different systems layer: it determines the exact mathematical support of the vocabulary distribution at each generation step. Learned formatting shifts probability mass toward expected syntax, while masking reduces the probability of every illegal token strictly to zero. These two strategies reinforce each other. A model tuned for structured calling reliably allocates high logits to semantically appropriate tokens, while the runtime mask guarantees that subtle sampling variations or long-context degradations cannot produce malformed syntax.

Schick, Timo, Jane Dwivedi-Yu, Roberto Dessı̀, Roberta Raileanu, Maria Lomeli, Luke Zettlemoyer, Nicola Cancedda, and Thomas Scialom. 2023. “Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 36: 68539–51.
Neither approach substitutes for the other. Statistical alignment alone yields no formal guarantee against syntax violations, while a grammar mask contributes zero domain knowledge toward selecting the correct file path. The overall reliability of the agent depends on the synergy between training fidelity, expressive schema definitions, and robust runtime constraints.
Furthermore, deploying grammar constraints introduces concrete systems trade-offs that engineers must measure across the end-to-end request lifecycle. Compiling complex regular expressions or nested JSON schemas into deterministic automata consumes CPU time and memory. In dynamic environments where agents construct ad hoc schemas per request, compilation latency can offset the latency saved by avoiding syntax retries. Similarly, tracking parse states and computing masks across large vocabularies (\(|\TokenVocabulary| \ge 128{,}000\) tokens) adds per-token decoding overhead unless supported by precomputed lookup indices or bitmasks applied on the accelerator. A systems engineer must evaluate compilation cost, serving memory footprint, and decoding throughput together, rather than assuming that eliminating syntax retries automatically reduces total operational cost.

Checkpoint 2.2: Evaluating schema-constrained decoding
A repair agent uses constrained decoding for file-reading proposals. Its runtime records response kind and invocation status separately.

Completion: If an output ceiling interrupts a legal JSON prefix, can you explain why grammar masking does not permit dispatch of the fragment?
Constraint scope: If a completed request satisfies the schema but names a nonexistent file, can you identify which property was enforced and which observation is still needed?
Response variants: A completed, schema-valid response selects the unknown variant. Decide what the runtime does next, and name the observation it should obtain before calling the model again.
Combined mechanisms: Can you explain why a model trained for tool use can still benefit from runtime masks without either mechanism granting execution authority?



Constrained decoding eliminates an entire class of syntax failures before dispatch, but a structurally valid invocation still requires sufficient compute budget to reach completion and external empirical evidence to justify execution. An agent architecture must account for schema compilation, input prompt processing, and token generation as distinct latency and cost factors. Balancing these overheads against the risk of unconstrained retries determines whether grammar-guided decoding delivers a net performance and reliability gain for a given task.

title: 2 The Foundation Model
text:
When an automated repair agent requests a code fix, it can ask the model for a localized diff or for the entire modified file. Both formats describe the same underlying patch, but the full-file approach forces the model to regenerate hundreds of lines of unchanged syntax alongside the edit. The runtime absorbs the latency and compute cost of generating those redundant tokens long before a compiler or test runner can validate the candidate patch. An effective invocation contract must therefore budget prompt reading and output writing explicitly, rather than treating every model invocation as a uniform, black-box unit of work.
Input length and output length stress distinct subsystems in the inference serving stack. Prompt ingestion exposes many known token positions to parallel matrix computation across the accelerator’s execution units. Conversely, autoregressive token generation executes as a strictly sequential loop, where each new token depends on the hidden state of all preceding positions. Because hardware architectures handle these two phases under vastly different physical constraints, output length serves as the primary software lever for controlling generation latency. However, an excessively large prompt, an undersized reply, or a congested service queue can quickly shift the latency bottleneck elsewhere.


From the perspective of an agent runtime, a model invocation begins when the runtime prepares the outbound request and ends when the normalized response is ready for dispatch to a tool or validation check. Within this end-to-end boundary, preparation spans local context assembly, payload serialization, and network dispatch; queueing measures the idle wait in the serving system’s admission queue; prefill processes the supplied prompt tokens in a single parallel forward pass; decode generates completion tokens through an autoregressive sequence of forward passes; and postprocessing encompasses network response transfer, wire deserialization, and schema validation. A non-overlapping accounting of these phases yields
\[\CallLatency = \CallPreparationTime + \RequestQueueTime + \PrefillTime + \DecodeInterval + \CallPostprocessingTime \tag{6}\]
Each term in equation 6 represents an elapsed duration in seconds, captured via high-resolution timestamps rather than derived backward from token counts. When preparation or network transfer overlaps with server-side execution, telemetry spans must track concurrent execution explicitly to avoid double-counting. An agent runtime that instruments only aggregate wall-clock duration cannot diagnose whether an unexpected latency spike stems from a bloated prompt, a saturated inference queue, or an excessively verbose generation, and each of those causes demands a different fix.
Accounting for the first generated token requires special care. In a standard Transformer architecture, the prefill pass processes the entire prompt and produces the initial logit distribution from which the first output token is sampled. From the client’s perspective, the elapsed time between dispatching the request and receiving that initial token constitutes the time to first token (TTFT), whereas the average delay between subsequent tokens defines the time per output token (TPOT). Production serving systems treat TTFT and TPOT as separate service-level objectives because prefill and decode compete directly for shared accelerator compute and memory bandwidth. Indeed, disaggregated serving architectures separate prefill and decode onto physically distinct accelerator pools to isolate these workloads and meet each objective independently (Zhong et al. 2024).

Zhong, Yinmin, Shengyu Liu, Junda Chen, Jianbo Hu, Yibo Zhu, Xuanzhe Liu, Xin Jin, and Hao Zhang. 2024. “DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-Optimized Large Language Model Serving.” 18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 24), July, 193–210.
When telemetry includes the sampling and transmission of the first token in TTFT, the remaining decode phase accounts for only the subsequent \(\OutputLength-1\) tokens in a completion of total length \(\OutputLength\). For a streamed response, adding client-measured TTFT, the inter-token arrival intervals across the remaining \(\OutputLength-1\) tokens, and trailing response deserialization captures total call latency without charging the first token twice. Client-observed TTFT differs substantially from server-side prefill execution time because it also absorbs network transit and queueing delay. Furthermore, because network transports and serving runtimes frequently batch streamed tokens into multi-token network chunks, observed chunk-arrival intervals do not always reflect raw token-generation intervals on the accelerator.
Setting an output token limit caps generation volume rather than execution speed; an overloaded inference queue can easily consume an agent’s entire timeout budget before prefill even completes. Meaningful latency benchmarks must therefore explicitly record the model architecture, prompt and completion lengths, prefix-cache conditions, and cluster load. Even when an agent executes single-threaded, sequential turns, the underlying serving system rarely processes that agent in isolation. Modern inference engines employ continuous batching to schedule, admit, and retire individual requests at the granularity of single token-generation steps (Yu et al. 2022), interleaving the agent’s decode steps with requests from dozens of other concurrent clients.



A baseline analytical model of per-call execution gives input processing and output generation separate per-token time floors, because different physical constraints govern the two phases. A dense Transformer with \(\Parameters\) parameters executes approximately \(2\Parameters\) floating-point operations for each token it processes, in prefill and decode alike. What differs is how often the weights must be read. Prefill reads each weight tensor from accelerator memory once per call and reuses it across all \(\SequenceLength\) prompt positions, so a long prompt spreads one weight read over thousands of tokens of arithmetic, and each prompt token costs about \(2\Parameters\) operations at the peak arithmetic rate \(\PeakRate\). Single-stream decode produces one token per step, so it reads every weight once per generated token. Each output token therefore moves the full weight payload of \(\Parameters\,\ElementStorageSize\) bytes (with \(\ElementStorageSize\) bytes per parameter) across a memory interface of bandwidth \(\Bandwidth\), and its arithmetic finishes long before those bytes arrive.
These two regimes are the two limbs of the roofline model (Williams et al. 2009), which bounds attainable throughput by the lesser of the peak arithmetic rate and the memory bandwidth multiplied by the work done per byte moved. Prefill does much work per byte and sits under the arithmetic limb; low-batch decode does little and sits under the bandwidth limb, a split that empirical evaluations of Transformer inference confirm (Pope et al. 2023). The two floors are

Williams, Samuel, Andrew Waterman, and David Patterson. 2009. “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” Communications of the ACM 52 (4): 65–76. https://doi.org/10.1145/1498765.1498785.
\[\PerTokenPrefillTime \approx \frac{2\Parameters}{\PeakRate}, \qquad \PerTokenDecodeTime \ge \frac{\Parameters\,\ElementStorageSize}{\Bandwidth} \tag{7}\]
The lowercase symbols are per-token floors. Under this model the phase durations of equation 6 are \(\PrefillTime \approx \SequenceLength\,\PerTokenPrefillTime\) and \(\DecodeInterval \approx \OutputLength\,\PerTokenDecodeTime\). Dividing the two floors cancels the parameter count \(\Parameters\):
\[\frac{\PerTokenDecodeTime}{\PerTokenPrefillTime} \approx \frac{\PeakRate \, \ElementStorageSize}{2 \, \Bandwidth} \tag{8}\]
Consider a concrete reference deployment: a dense model with 70.6B parameters stored in 8-bit precision (\(\ElementStorageSize = 1\) byte) on a single accelerator with an 8-bit peak rate of 1,979 TFLOP/s and a memory bandwidth of 3.35 TB/s. Each token costs 141.2 GFLOP of arithmetic, and dividing by the peak rate gives a prefill floor of 71.35 μs per prompt token. Each decode step reads 70.6 GB of weights, and dividing by the bandwidth gives a decode floor of 21.075 ms per generated token. Under equation 8, decoding a single output token therefore takes the same hardware time as ingesting roughly 295 prompt tokens. This asymmetry is the content of output-bound latency (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}\)), under which each plain, unbatched decode step incurs a full weight read in this model, so output volume can dominate call latency. The ratio reflects weight-dominated, unbatched decode against peak-throughput prefill, not a measured cloud service rate or a commercial billing tier.


↪ Both execution floors and their operating boundaries are developed in Cost Asymmetry Between Input Prefill and Output Generation.
This analytical budget charges each prompt token once at the prefill floor and reserves one decode floor step for each generated token. It is an idealized hardware baseline rather than a substitute for wall-clock measurement: it omits network transit, queueing delay, attention quadratics, and runtime software overhead. It also assumes standard autoregressive generation without speculative decoding. In production, a serving system that batches concurrent client requests, distributes model weights across tensor-parallel accelerators (sharding individual weight matrices across multiple devices), or reuses cached attention state substantially alters the relationship between token count and elapsed time. The analytical estimate is therefore ideal for comparing interface formats and output volumes, but certifying a production deadline requires measuring latency directly under realistic serving load.
Applying this baseline to the first repair turn demonstrates the structural dominance of output tokens. A prompt of 8,000 tokens contributes 0.571 s of prefill work, while generating a reply of 200 tokens contributes 4.215 s of decode execution. The total call estimate is 4.786 s. Although output constitutes only 2.4 percent of the call’s total tokens, it accounts for 88.1 percent of the required processing time. Pruning redundant output tokens therefore reduces overall latency far more effectively than removing an identical number of prompt tokens. At the same time, an agent benefits from a cheaper invocation only if the model still receives sufficient diagnostic context to generate a correct candidate; engineers must prune verbosity from the output format, not critical evidence from the prompt.



Even when individual turns produce concise outputs, a multi-turn trajectory can still generate an immense prompt ingestion workload. Consider an agent runtime that maintains an append-only execution log and re-transmits the full cumulative history on every invocation. If the initial turn contains \(\BasePromptLength\) prompt tokens and each subsequent turn appends \(\TurnAppendLength\) tokens of combined model output and tool observations, a trajectory spanning a horizon of \(\TurnHorizon\) turns submits:
\[\PromptTokensSent = \sum_{j=0}^{\TurnHorizon-1} \left(\BasePromptLength + \PriorTurnCount\,\TurnAppendLength\right) = \TurnHorizon \BasePromptLength + \TurnAppendLength \frac{\TurnHorizon(\TurnHorizon-1)}{2} \tag{9}\]
prompt tokens in total. The quadratic growth in equation 9 arises directly from the naive strategy of repeatedly re-sending accumulated history, rather than from an intrinsic requirement of agentic reasoning. Implementing sliding-window context buffers, trimming redundant tool payloads, or summarizing historical turns transforms this workload. Furthermore, a stateful serving interface can maintain conversation state on the server, avoiding redundant network re-transmission even when the model’s active attention window spans the full trajectory.



Re-sent input grows with the square of the horizon; prefix reuse keeps fresh prefill linear.
Fortunately, repeated prompt input does not necessitate repeated matrix computation. Prefix caching enables the inference engine to retain and reuse previously computed Key-Value (KV) activations for prompt prefixes that remain identical across consecutive requests (Zheng et al. 2024). Successful KV reuse requires an exact match across token IDs, model weights, and positional encodings, as well as sufficient accelerator memory to retain the cache blocks. Modifying an early system prompt instruction or altering a tool schema invalidates all downstream cached activations from that modification point onward. Even identical source text fails to hit the cache if tokenizer configurations, chat templates, or special tokens diverge.
To quantify the benefits of prefix reuse, assume an inference service that caches all preceding prompt prefixes but runs fresh prefill over each newly appended turn suffix. This newly appended suffix contains the model’s previous response and the subsequent tool output. Across all \(\TurnHorizon\) turns, the cumulative number of prompt tokens requiring fresh prefill drops to \(\BasePromptLength + (\TurnHorizon-1)\,\TurnAppendLength\). This baseline conservatively assumes the runtime does not preserve the KV activations generated during decoding; advanced engines can retain those generated activations as well, avoiding fresh prefill over earlier model outputs. Holding these assumptions constant isolates the exact architectural benefit of prefix caching.

Napkin Math 2.2: The price of an append-only trajectoryProblem: A coding agent runs 30 turns. Its first prompt has 8,000 tokens, each turn appends 1,500 tokens, and each call emits 200 output tokens. Assume that every prompt fits the service’s context limit and that compatible earlier prompt state remains available for reuse. How much input does the trajectory supply, and how does prompt-prefix reuse change its estimated processing work?
Math: Applying the arithmetic series in equation 9 gives \(30\times 8,000+1,500\times\frac{30\times 29}{2}=892,500\) prompt tokens. Total output is \(30\times 200=6,000\) tokens. Without reuse, input therefore accounts for 99.3 percent of the combined input and output token count, although it does not account for that share of processing time.
With prompt-prefix reuse, fresh prefill covers \(8,000+29\times 1,500=51,500\) tokens. Dividing the original input count by this fresh-prefill count gives a 17.3× reduction. At the reference prefill floor, the prefill-work estimate falls from 63.68 s to 3.67 s. Decode work stays at 126.45 s; caching earlier input does not remove the task’s new responses.
Systems insight: Append-only context makes input work grow with the square of the horizon. Doubling the trajectory to 60 turns multiplies re-sent input by 3.5× but fresh prefill under prefix reuse by only 1.9×, because reuse converts quadratic growth into a linear trajectory. Prefix reuse therefore serves as the primary lever for minimizing the input component of \(\AttemptCost\) in the cost per accepted task (equation 1.2), with its value compounding as horizons lengthen. While caching preserves the full decision context without loss of information, cache eviction and cross-worker request routing can dilute these theoretical savings in production.


In the illustrated repair turn, output length dominates the single-call estimate. For the append-only workload under high batching described here, uncached prefill can dominate aggregate serving work. Prefix reuse acts directly on the input component; its effect on end-to-end latency depends on how much that component contributes. Wall-clock latency governs the end-to-end responsiveness experienced by a single agent trajectory. Because each sequential turn depends strictly on the outcome of prior tool executions, an agent cannot parallelize its own dependent turns; every output token remains a sequential step on the critical execution path, even when the server concurrently batches that step with other requests. Computational work, by contrast, dictates cluster throughput, hardware provisioning, and aggregate operational expenditure. When a serving cluster batches dozens of concurrent streams, the memory weight reads are amortized across requests. Under high batching, the amortized service time per decoded token drops from the memory-bandwidth floor toward the compute-bound arithmetic limit \(2\Parameters/\PeakRate\) of equation 7, the same efficiency as prompt prefill, as the batched-step bound derived in Cost Asymmetry Between Input Prefill and Output Generation shows. In this regime, total cluster workload scales directly with aggregate token volume. For an append-only agent, that token volume is overwhelmingly dominated by re-sent prompt history, so uncached prefill dominates the aggregate work estimate for this workload when the cluster maintains high batching and has memory for the attention state.
Which term an engineer should attack therefore depends on who waits for the output, and the repair agent alone cannot show the contrast. Its consumer is a compilation and test pipeline that must wait for a syntactically complete response. The support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)) instead streams output tokens to a person reading as they arrive. The consumer requirements determine which latency terms these two illustrated workloads prioritize.

Lighthouse 2.1: Call latency for two lighthousesSupport agent: A customer-operations turn submits an 8,192-token prompt (consisting of policy documentation, customer account history, and recent dialogue) and streams an 150-token response to a human user in a live chat interface. At the chapter’s reference hardware floors, prefill takes 0.58 s and generating the full reply requires 3.2 s. However, token streaming displays the initial words immediately following queueing and prefill; the remaining tokens arrive at approximately 47 tokens per second, which easily outpaces human reading speed. Under these lengths and streaming rates, TTFT governs how soon the user can begin reading. When 6,144 prompt tokens represent a common prefix of system instructions, organizational policies, and tool definitions shared across all concurrent sessions, prefix caching leaves only 2,048 tokens of fresh prefill, which takes just 0.15 s. In a loaded cluster, admission queueing rapidly becomes the dominant contributor to first-token latency.
Repair agent: The initial repair turn commits 88.1 percent of its estimated hardware work to generating a 200-token response. The agent runtime can parse, validate, and execute the generated patch only after receiving the entire payload. Decode duration dominates this repair estimate, making the compactness of the requested code representation its primary optimization lever.
Systems insight: The illustrated support turn prioritizes TTFT because the user can read while the remaining tokens arrive, whereas output volume dominates the illustrated repair call, whose consumer waits for a complete patch. Shortening the support reply does not directly remove queueing or prefill from first-token latency. Caching the repair prompt reduces its input work and input cost, but that saving contributes little to this output-dominated estimate. Different prompt lengths, streaming rates, or serving load can change the binding term; measured phase durations and queueing determine which intervention improves the latency the consumer waits on.


Retaining intermediate activations in memory introduces an explicit storage cost. Caching a long prefix occupies accelerator high-bandwidth memory that cannot be allocated to concurrent request batches. Holding that KV state active across long external tool invocations pins memory that no generation is using. When memory pressure triggers cache eviction, the serving system discards intermediate attention activations rather than the underlying context; the agent runtime can always reconstruct the prompt from its local logs, albeit at the cost of recomputing the prefill forward pass. Context selection and KV-cache management thus represent two distinct system decisions: context engineering determines what evidence the model observes, whereas cache retention policies govern whether storing derived attention state is worth the memory footprint.


↪ The choice to keep, move, or drop attention state held through a tool wait is developed in Paused-State Policies.
Wall-clock latency, hardware compute work, and billed API cost represent distinct accounting dimensions. Commercial inference providers typically bill uncached prompt tokens, cached prompt tokens, and generated completion tokens at widely divergent rates, whereas on-premise infrastructure amortizes fixed hardware acquisition and power costs across dynamic utilization. Consequently, token-count ratios do not directly mirror monetary expense. At the full task horizon, end-to-end expenditure also encompasses failed tool executions, retry attempts, sandboxed validation runs, and idle accelerator reservations during tool waits. The analytical per-call estimate provides only one fundamental building block of this comprehensive systems budget.

Checkpoint 2.3: Pricing calls and trajectories
A call’s token count and its elapsed execution time quantify distinct facets of the overall system budget.

Measurement boundary: If the time to first token already accounts for sampling and delivering the initial token, how many subsequent token-generation intervals remain in a completed completion of length \(\OutputLength\)?
Horizon estimate: If an agent trajectory triples to 90 turns under fixed \(\BasePromptLength\) and \(\TurnAppendLength\), estimate the growth factor for uncached re-sent input vs. fresh prefill under prefix caching. Which term dictates whether scaling to longer trajectories remains computationally viable?
Reuse assumptions: How does the analytical work estimate change if the inference server evicts the cached prefix from accelerator memory during a blocking tool execution?
Cost denominator: Why does an overwhelming majority of input tokens fail to produce an equivalent majority of financial cost when providers bill cached input and generated output at starkly different rates?
Interface estimate: A full-file replacement requires 1,850 output tokens, whereas a localized diff requires only 80. At the reference decode floor, which interface alternative can realistically operate within a 15 s latency deadline? Why is this analytical roofline model insufficient on its own to guarantee real-world service-level agreement (SLA) compliance?



Deconstructing the model invocation budget exposes two primary sources of computational waste: generating superfluous tokens that the downstream interface does not require, and recomputing prompt representations that the serving system could readily cache. Optimizing these efficiency levers does not guarantee task success, however; a compact diff that fails to compile or a cached prompt that leads to an incorrect edit wastes the entire invocation. Selecting an optimal agent interface demands evaluating candidate patch quality, downstream failure modes, and end-to-end resource consumption under identical operational benchmarks.

title: 2 The Foundation Model
text:
When an automated repair agent modifies connection-pool locking logic, its output payload does not need to repeat the entire source file. The model could emit a fully rewritten file, or it could target a specific code block and emit only the replacement text. Emitting a localized edit consumes far fewer generation tokens by omitting unchanged code, but it creates an operational dependency: the execution runtime must locate the exact target coordinates in the target file. Choosing an interface is therefore not a superficial formatting choice; it directly determines both the computational cost of generating a candidate and the operational preconditions required for the runtime to apply it.
High schema parse rates alone cannot validate an interface design. A whole-file replacement might parse into valid JSON yet arrive long after the service deadline because the model spent tens of seconds generating unchanged lines. Conversely, a compact diff might arrive in about 2.3 s yet fail to match its target anchors against current repository state. Neither outcome delivers an accepted repair. A rigorous empirical comparison must track the model call’s completion status, account for all compute resources consumed across retries, and validate the resulting artifact against uniform acceptance criteria.


Representation granularity dictates how much context the model must emit to describe a mutation. At one extreme, a whole-file representation returns the entire file content, re-emitting hundreds of lines of untouched code alongside the modification. At the other extreme, a localized edit supplies only a target locator and the delta relative to the baseline file. Consider an anchored search-and-replace edit: it specifies an exact snippet of source text to find and the replacement text to substitute. If that anchor string is missing from the file or matches multiple locations, the runtime cannot infer a unique mutation. Rewriting the entire file eliminates anchor-matching ambiguities, but it introduces a different validation burden: the runtime must ensure the model did not silently overwrite unrelated functions or drop concurrent modifications made by other processes.
Serialization represents a distinct and orthogonal design dimension. Either granularity can use JSON: one object might store a target path and complete source buffer, while another stores a path, a search block, and a replacement snippet. Custom delimiters, such as Markdown code fences or unified diff headers, can frame either payload just as easily. The actual token overhead depends on tokenizer vocabulary and structural markers, not on common folklore that JSON is inherently bloated while patch syntax is always compact. Emitting thousands of tokens for an unmodified file is a penalty imposed by coarse representation granularity, not by the serialization format wrapping it.
The constraint mechanism introduces a third independent axis. An agent architecture can elicit structured outputs through fine-tuning, in-context demonstrations, or runtime grammar masking during token decoding. These mechanisms can also operate together; for example, fine-tuned models frequently run under grammar masks to prevent syntax drift. The formal language guarantees established in section 2.7 ensure that generated tokens conform to a specified grammar, but they guarantee grammatical form, not execution semantics. A grammar mask cannot guarantee that an anchor snippet exists within the repository, nor that the proposed patch repairs the underlying race condition. If an evaluation alters both serialization framing and constraint methods simultaneously, it benchmarks bundled interface variants rather than isolating the causal impact of any single architectural choice.



To evaluate competing interfaces fairly, an experimental harness must enforce matched budgets across all trials. In the connection-pool repair benchmark, every trial starts from an identical repository snapshot and defect description, and the harness holds constant the model weights, sampling parameters, diagnostic tooling, and acceptance test suites. Each interface also operates under identical resource ceilings (such as maximum wall-clock time and token allocations) and the same retry policy. Instruction prompts and response payloads will naturally exhibit different token counts, because prompt overhead and verbosity are intrinsic properties of the interface under test. Matched budgets do not require equal token consumption across designs; rather, they subject each candidate to identical operating boundaries and accounting rules.


↪ Matched-budget comparison of complete agent policies, charging every initiated trial to the cost per accepted task, is developed in Matched-budget comparison.
The accounting boundary must be defined explicitly. An invocation deadline measures single-turn inference latency, concluding when the runtime receives and normalizes the model’s generated response. A task deadline governs the complete agent lifecycle, including payload parsing, workspace patching, test compilation, and test execution. Every retry, unparsable output, and failing test execution draws against this cumulative task budget. Benchmarks that grant free retries following malformed responses subsidize brittle interfaces and corrupt comparative latency metrics.
To pinpoint system failures without masking catastrophic errors, the benchmark harness must decouple intermediate execution stages from final task acceptance (table 5). The total number of initiated trials must remain the denominator for all top-level success metrics. Discarding unparsable responses or timed-out calls artificially inflates reported accuracy. Conditional rates, such as the proportion of cleanly applied edits that pass functional tests, serve as valuable diagnostic telemetry, but engineers must always state the conditioning filter explicitly.



Table 5: Interface evaluation measurements: Distinct observations prevent a formatting improvement from being mistaken for a task-level improvement. The same task fixtures, acceptance standard, and resource ceilings govern each design.










Measurement
What the trial records
What it does not establish




Invocation outcome
Completion status, elapsed time, and token usage
That a delivered candidate is valid


Structural validity
Whether a completed payload parses and satisfies the required schema
That its values describe the current environment


Applicability
Whether the authorized edit identifies its target and can be applied to the expected version
That the resulting program repairs the defect


Acceptance evidence
Results of the same required checks on the resulting artifact
Correctness beyond the checks’ coverage


Resource use
All calls and checks charged to the trial, including failed attempts
A benefit unless accepted outcomes justify the expenditure






Production serving conditions must also be recorded alongside payload statistics. Shared inference infrastructure introduces substantial latency variance: KV-cache hits, dynamic batching contention, and host-level queueing delays alter observed wall-clock execution even when prompt and completion lengths remain constant. A few favorable measurements during quiet periods do not prove deadline reliability. In shared production clusters, tail latency governs service-level objective violations, because the slowest requests dictate pipeline throughput (Dean and Barroso 2013). The immediate engineering question is whether an interface representation leaves sufficient headroom under the tail-latency envelope to generate and validate candidate fixes.

Dean, Jeffrey, and Luiz André Barroso. 2013. “The Tail at Scale.” Communications of the ACM 56 (2): 74–80.



Applying the per-token cost model highlights the severe latency penalty of emitting unchanged text, tracing performance bottlenecks directly to interface granularity rather than serialization envelopes.



Generating unchanged code, not reading the prompt, pushes the whole file past the deadline.

Napkin Math 2.3: A repair representation under an invocation deadlineProblem: A repair invocation begins with 8,000 baseline context tokens and operates under an invocation deadline of 15 s. Emitting a whole-file replacement requires 350 additional instruction tokens and 1,850 output tokens. Emitting a localized edit requires 120 additional instruction tokens and 80 output tokens. These token counts represent scenario parameters. Using the prefill and autoregressive decoding rates established earlier, which interface representation fits within the simplified service-work budget?
Math: The service-work model charges prompt prefill at 71.35 μs per token and autoregressive decoding at 21.075 ms per token. To isolate inference execution, this baseline calculation omits request serialization, network transit, server-side queueing, and subsequent validation runs. Multiplying each interface’s token profile by these unit costs yields:
\((8,000+350)\times 0.00007135\,\text{s}+1,850\times 0.021075\,\text{s}\approx 39.58\,\text{s}\)
\((8,000+120)\times 0.00007135\,\text{s}+80\times 0.021075\,\text{s}\approx 2.27\,\text{s}\)
The whole-file estimate exceeds the deadline by a wide margin, whereas the localized edit finishes well within the allocated budget. The localized representation provides a 17.5× reduction in estimated service work, with token decoding accounting for 98.5 percent of the whole-file latency. In production, normalized invocation outcomes and observed wall-clock times determine whether the candidate arrived before deadline expiration.
To evaluate downstream yield, consider a second hypothetical scenario where localized edits complete on time with valid syntax, but only 95 percent resolve to an applicable edit on the codebase. Among those applicable edits, assume 60 percent pass the required test suite. The fraction of all initiated trials that yield an accepted repair is:
\(0.95\times 0.60=0.57\)
This 57 percent yield is the product of the applicability rate and the conditional test-pass rate, requiring no independence assumption between stages. Invocations that miss deadlines or emit invalid syntax reduce this end-to-end yield even further.
Systems insight: When output generation threatens an invocation deadline, shrinking representation granularity is the primary engineering lever. Because autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, each generated token costs roughly 295 prompt prefill tokens at hardware reference floors (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}\)). Whole-file generation squanders almost all of its 39.6 s runtime emitting unchanged code, while the localized edit meets the deadline with a 6.6× safety margin. However, compact representations trade decoding latency for applicability risk: localized edits require exact anchor matching, which restricts the passing yield to 57 percent in this scenario. That hypothetical yield forms the acceptance probability \(\AcceptanceProbability\) that governs the amortized cost per accepted task (equation 1.2).


The invocation deadline functions as an absolute admission filter. Under these timing parameters, a whole-file response cannot even enter evaluation, rendering its potential code quality irrelevant. If system designers relax the deadline beyond the whole-file threshold, the trade-off shifts: applicability and patch correctness become decisive. Under generous latency budgets, a localized representation that frequently targets stale anchors or ambiguous line offsets quickly loses its advantage over a whole-file approach that reliably delivers an integrated solution.

Checkpoint 2.4: Reconsidering the interface when conditions change
The repair interface must be reassessed whenever the workspace state or resource budget shifts.

Applicability: If the source file changes after the prompt is assembled, which measurement in the benchmark pipeline changes, and what preconditions must the runtime verify before applying either representation?
Deadline: If the invocation deadline doubles while token lengths and accounting rates stay fixed, which representations fit the budget, and how do you distinguish that analytical estimate from an empirical completion guarantee?
Serialization: If the localized edit is encoded as a JSON object rather than plain text delimiters, which latency benefits survive and which token counts must be re-profiled?
Admission: How do you distinguish a COMPLETED but malformed request from a syntactically valid but TRUNCATED request? Which specific check prevents each from triggering downstream tool execution?
Acceptance evidence: If an edit applies cleanly and passes a sequential test suite, what additional runtime evidence does a race-condition task still require before acceptance?



Rigorous interface benchmarking unifies model call contracts with systems economics. The request specifies the context and output allowances; the normalized response confirms whether the model delivered a completed payload before the deadline; and tiered evaluation metrics determine whether the proposed mutation reliably solves the task within resource constraints. Assuming that a valid schema implies an applicable patch, or that a fast diff implies defect-free code, collapses these stages into one, and that confusion remains among the most common failure modes in agent systems design.

title: 2 The Foundation Model
text:
A code repair request can return promptly yet name the wrong file, or return the right patch long after its latency budget has expired. In autonomous execution loops, engineers frequently conflate distinct operational boundaries, confusing inference execution with total round-trip latency, syntactic validity with semantic correctness, and transport success with task completion. These failures expose several persistent mistaken assumptions about the model call.

Fallacy: One model response has a fixed cost.
Output length governs the bulk of execution time in the illustrated unbatched interface comparison. At its reference hardware floors, sequentially decoding a token takes far more time than processing a prompt token in parallel. In the interface comparison, regenerating a whole-file representation requires 39.6 s, whereas emitting a localized patch for the identical bug requires only 2.3 s, a 17.5× speedup that arises almost entirely during token generation (section 2.8). Engineers must therefore budget input and output tokens as separate resource dimensions rather than treating an invocation as an atomic unit of cost. Furthermore, wall-clock budgets must span the entire invocation boundary, including admission queueing and network transport; setting a maximum token limit bounds generation volume, but it does not control the time at which a response finally arrives.


Pitfall: Treating a completed invocation as a completed task.
A status of COMPLETED merely indicates that the serving engine finished generating tokens within the parameters of its invocation contract. It does not mean the produced output is correct or even usable. In the hypothetical interface scenario, every localized call completed on time, yet only 57 percent of those trials produced patches that passed the automated repair checks. Similarly, an agent may emit a syntactically parseable file path right before being cut off by a context limit, illustrating why downstream execution must verify generation status before triggering actions. Robust systems explicitly record two distinct facts for every invocation: whether a complete candidate artifact arrived from the generator, and whether independent verification evidence confirms that the artifact satisfies the task’s acceptance standard.


Fallacy: Valid JSON means a safe and correct tool call.
A JSON object satisfies its schema as long as its fields match the declared types, regardless of whether the payload is safe, authorized, or logically sound. A tool call containing a file path string conforms to schema validation whether that path names the intended target, an outdated file, or an unauthorized directory outside the permitted workspace. As table 3 lays out, schema checks establish structural validity, whereas authorization policies and task evidence govern security boundaries and functional correctness. The same gap recurs at the behavioral level: a test checker that exhibits a false accept rate of 0.65 on defective patches still leaves 14.37 percent of its passing candidates defective under these assumed rates. Furthermore, under grammar-constrained decoding, an interrupted sequence remains an incomplete, broken payload even if every token emitted prior to truncation was structurally legal.


Pitfall: Collapsing every unsuccessful outcome into the same retry.
Blindly retrying a failed call repeats the underlying root cause alongside the request. If a whole-file generation request misses a 15 s deadline, immediately resending the identical prompt spends another 39.6 s of estimated compute only to time out once again. Similarly, a response that exceeds its output budget truncates at the exact same token allowance, and a request that triggers a safety refusal elicits the same refusal on retry. Rather than treating all failures as transient network errors, an agent runtime must normalize execution status codes and dispatch targeted recovery policies: a bounded exponential backoff for transient service outages, a larger token allowance or more compact prompt representation for truncation, and a fresh environment observation when an edit fails to match its target.


Fallacy: Greedy decoding makes a served call reproducible.
Greedy selection fixes the token choice for a given logit vector, but the serving infrastructure computes that vector, and two distinct causes can change it. The first operates even on a healthy serving path, where batch-dependent floating-point reduction order shifts closely contested logits in their least significant bits, enough to flip an argmax and redirect every later token. The second is a change to the serving path itself. In war story 2.1, misrouting and a miscompiled top-\(\TopTokenSampleCount\) operation changed model outputs for identical requests, affecting 16 percent of one model’s requests at peak impact, so an identical prompt succeeded on one attempt and failed on the next. Pinning the temperature addresses neither cause.
