A simplistic filter that retains only lines matching FAILED captures the terminal assertion failure but drops the event sequence that explains it. Without seeing that waiter_registered_before_return and connection_available_after_return both evaluated to true, the model cannot deduce whether the failure stemmed from a race during registration, an unavailable resource, or a missed notification. A structured, compact observation preserves this causal chain: “At r17, test_waiter_notified_on_return registered the waiter before returning a connection. The connection became available, but assert waiter_resumed_at_notification_check failed at the notification check.” Alongside this narrative digest, the context retains the revision identifiers (src/pool.py@r17, tests/test_pool.py@r17), the execution schedule, and a pointer handle to the raw execution trace for on-demand debugging.
This concise record provides empirical backing for the missed-notification hypothesis under the tested conditions while maintaining a strict boundary between raw observations and diagnostic conjectures. When a subsequent patch yields revision r18, the runtime must record the new test outcome against r18 rather than overwriting or conflating it with the historical r17 failure. A compaction step that collapses both runs into an unqualified summary such as “the bug is fixed” erases the provenance needed to verify that the repair actually resolved the underlying race condition.



To prevent compaction passes from stripping decision-critical data, the runtime designates an invariant set of protected fields that must survive any transformation. Before committing an updated working context, the system validates that these fields are present and unaltered. In our pool-repair scenario, the protected set includes the revision identifiers (pool.py@r17), the test identifier (test_waiter_notified_on_return), the concurrent scheduling flags, the failed assertion statement, and the exit status. Global task constraints must also remain pinned: preserving public API compatibility, confining edits to the designated repository directory, and blocking production deployment commands. Later execution stages might require specific function implementations or configuration values that this compact digest omits, but those can be paged in as needed.
Field protection must be dynamically scoped to the task phase. Pinning every historical line number, diff chunk, and identifier defeats the purpose of compaction by quickly exhausting the context budget. Conversely, enforcing an overly rigid, global schema risks dropping domain-specific diagnostic relationships. An assertion message copied verbatim without its corresponding commit hash or concurrency configuration is useless or misleading. Similarly, runtime filtering must scrub credentials, authentication tokens, and private keys; sensitive literals must never be retained simply because a filter rule matches string literals.
Furthermore, protected fields are not restricted to static configuration parameters; agents frequently uncover new invariants during execution. Suppose our concurrency reproducer fails consistently under the controlled waiter-before-return schedule but passes nondeterministically under the default operating system thread scheduler. The initial task specification contains no mention of this dependency; the relationship surfaces only within tool output. A naive summarizer that records “the waiter test failed” while discarding the scheduling flag permits subsequent turns to re-run tests under the default scheduler, observe an accidental pass on buggy code, and prematurely claim success. When tool feedback demonstrates that an outcome depends strictly on an experimental parameter, the runtime must promote that parameter into the protected-field inventory alongside the empirical observation supporting it. Once promoted, the parameter undergoes the same integrity checks as the original contract constraints.
Automated validation catches missing test identifiers, modified literals, or results misattributed to the wrong revision. However, validating schema conformance does not ensure that the designer selected all necessary fields or that the model will attend to them in later decisions. Section 4.8 measures both. Before evicting any uncompressed payload, the runtime must assign a clear disposition to the omitted information: either it is demonstrably irrelevant to downstream tasks, it remains retrievable via an external handle, or it is permanently pruned, marking an explicit epistemic boundary. If a future reasoning step demands an evicted detail and external retrieval fails, the agent must rerun the tool or acknowledge the knowledge gap rather than hallucinating plausible execution history.



Between passes, new observations accumulate in the leaf, and a compaction pass folds them into the trunk’s progress record, which is why every pass costs a trunk rewrite. To avoid invoking compaction after every small tool observation, systems decouple the trigger threshold from the target compaction length. This dual-threshold technique, known as hysteresis,8 allows new observations to accumulate across multiple turns before the runtime rewrites the context buffer. A narrow gap between thresholds causes frequent, expensive compaction cycles. Conversely, raising the high watermark permits longer operational trajectories between passes, while lowering the target length creates substantial token headroom by forcing aggressive compression. The optimal watermark separation reflects both token geometry and information utility. Compressing too deeply risks stripping subtle evidence, while compressing too conservatively causes thrashing.
8 Watermark Pairs: Operating-system page reclaim uses the same two-threshold pattern. A reclaim thread wakes when free memory falls below a low watermark and stops only after restoring a higher one, allowing reclamation to run in batches rather than on every allocation. The gap balances batch size against invocation frequency, a trade-off that equation 3 quantifies for context compaction. Let \(\CompactionTriggerLength\) and \(\CompactionTargetLength\) denote the upper trigger threshold and the post-compaction target, respectively, measured in total serialized input tokens. Because the system must reserve capacity for model generation, these watermarks satisfy the strict inequality \(\CompactionTargetLength < \CompactionTriggerLength \le \ContextWindow - \OutputLimit\), where \(\ContextWindow\) is the context window limit and \(\OutputLimit\) is the reserved output allowance. These thresholds represent explicit runtime policy choices rather than physical model limitations.
Assuming an idealized cycle where each compaction pass resets the request exactly to \(\CompactionTargetLength\) and each subsequent turn appends a net volume of \(\TurnAppendLength > 0\) input tokens, the runtime inspects context size after each addition before issuing the next model call. The integer number of turns between compaction passes is
\[
\CompactionCycleTurnCount = \left\lceil \frac{\CompactionTriggerLength - \CompactionTargetLength}{\TurnAppendLength} \right\rceil.
\tag{3}\]



Hysteresis turns compaction into a sawtooth whose gap sets the cadence.
Because context length is evaluated at discrete turn boundaries, the actual serialized length immediately prior to compaction is \(\CompactionTargetLength + \CompactionCycleTurnCount\TurnAppendLength\). This quantity can overshoot \(\CompactionTriggerLength\) by up to \(\TurnAppendLength - 1\) tokens, making \(\CompactionTriggerLength\) a soft operational threshold. When arrival sizes vary wildly across tool calls, the runtime must either truncate individual observation payloads or stage them in a temporary buffer to prevent an unexpected payload from exceeding the hard ceiling \(\ContextWindow - \OutputLimit\). Furthermore, if the runtime invokes a secondary language model to execute the compaction pass, that summarization call requires its own dedicated input and output token budgets.
Compaction interacts directly with prompt cache economics. A compaction pass that modifies the prefix trunk invalidates KV-cache reuse downstream from the rewrite point, triggering the trunk recomputation penalty modeled in Call \(\Glyph{n}+2\) of figure 3. For a cycle comprising \(\CompactionCycleTurnCount\) task turns and one compaction pass, let \({\TaskTurnCost}_{\CompactionCycleTurnIndex}\) represent the total cost of task turn \(\CompactionCycleTurnIndex\) (encompassing both cached and uncached input tokens alongside generated output tokens). Let \(\CompactionPassCost\) denote the complete cost of the compaction pass under the same billing boundary. The amortized financial cost per task turn is
\[
\AmortizedTurnCost = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{\CompactionCycleTurnCount} {\TaskTurnCost}_{i} + \CompactionPassCost}{\CompactionCycleTurnCount}.
\tag{4}\]
Any cache misses resulting from an altered prefix are already reflected in the uncached token rates of subsequent \({\TaskTurnCost}_{\CompactionCycleTurnIndex}\) terms; introducing a separate cache-invalidation penalty would double-count those costs. Evaluating compaction policies requires accounting for system-level costs beyond prompt tokens, including artifact storage, secondary retrieval latency, redundant verification reruns, and trajectory failures caused by prematurely evicted context. A compaction schedule that minimizes prompt token expenditure may inflate total task cost if excessive compression forces the agent into exploratory dead ends. Runtimes must therefore optimize for the effective cost per completed task (\(\CostPerAcceptedTask\)) rather than local turn cost \(\AmortizedTurnCost\). The watermark gap \((\CompactionTriggerLength - \CompactionTargetLength)\) directly determines \(\CompactionCycleTurnCount\), establishing how frequently the system amortizes \(\CompactionPassCost\).

Napkin Math 4.3: Spacing compaction passesProblem: The repair agent from notebook 4.1 appends each 4,000-token tool result and compacts instead of overflowing. Its 128,000-token context window, minus the 8,000-token output reserve, leaves 120,000 tokens for serialized input. Each compaction pass resets the prompt back to 47,000 tokens (matching the baseline selecting policy’s request size), and the subsequent pass triggers upon reaching 92,000 tokens. How often does compaction occur, and how many passes does the agent execute across its 30-turn step budget?
Variables: Every compaction pass resets the prompt to the exact target \(\CompactionTargetLength\). Turn-by-turn additions \(\TurnAppendLength\) remain constant at 4,000 tokens. The runtime evaluates buffer length after each tool addition and before dispatching the next model inference. The configured watermarks are operational policy choices rather than empirical performance limits.
Math: Applying equation 3 yields \(\CompactionCycleTurnCount = \lceil (92{,}000 - 47{,}000) / 4{,}000 \rceil = 12\) additions between successive compaction passes. The system hits the trigger at 95,000 input tokens, overshooting \(\CompactionTriggerLength\) by 3,000 tokens. Adding the reserved output capacity requires 103,000 tokens, safely within the window limit prior to compaction. Over the complete 30-turn trajectory budget, the runtime triggers 2 compaction passes, and each pass rewrites the trunk. These are the trunk rewrites that notebook 4.2 counted. Only the count carries over, because that notebook priced a fixed request with its leaf replaced on every call, whereas here the leaf grows between passes. If the post-compaction target instead rises to 81,000 tokens under identical arrival rates, the operational interval collapses to 3 additions.
Systems insight: Compaction frequency scales directly with the token arrival rate divided by the watermark gap. Narrowing that gap from 12 arrivals down to 3 forces compaction 4× as often. The per-turn amortized compaction overhead in equation 4 scales proportionally; setting a gap smaller than a single turn’s arrival causes thrashing, compacting on every step. Systems designers should size the watermark gap to span multiple arrivals and compress toward \(\CompactionTargetLength\) only as far as protected-field constraints permit, leaving the boundary between necessary context and dispensable detail to empirical validation.


A compressed observation captures only one facet of task progression. Driving an agentic repair to completion also requires maintaining the current candidate patch, the empirical checks validating it, the remaining test obligations, and the immediate next action. Because unstructured narrative summaries easily lose these dependency chains during aggressive compaction, the runtime must formalize them within an explicit, structured progress ledger.




The repair has now moved through three events. First, at r17, the controlled test failed. Second, the agent’s candidate patch wrote r18. Third, the reproducer passed on r18. Once the third event has happened, the runtime must carry all three across the next compaction. A naive compaction summary that claims “fixed the notification bug” discards the precise distinctions the agent needs to plan its next action. In r17, a controlled diagnostic test observed a released connection returning to the pool while a waiting thread remained blocked. In r18, a targeted reproducer passed, establishing that the waiter is now awakened under those specific test conditions. That passing check provides evidence for the patch under an isolated scenario, but it proves nothing about full regression behavior or public API compatibility. Once the raw diagnostic exchanges are pruned from the context window, the next model call must still differentiate between verified empirical observations, working diagnostic hypotheses, and a fully validated repair.
A structured progress record maintains this operational state across context evictions using explicitly defined fields. Rather than replaying verbose conversational transcripts, the record encapsulates active task constraints, empirical observations, diagnostic hypotheses, artifact identifiers, and pending obligations. This schema exposes missing fields and internal contradictions to automated validation, though verifying whether those fields accurately reflect reality requires host-side auditing. This mechanism serves as a continuation record rather than an execution checkpoint: it conveys what the subsequent model invocation must know to proceed. The mechanical responsibilities of snapshotting running processes, tracking dirty workspace files, and supervising in-flight tool executions remain the domain of execution persistence.


↪ Execution checkpoints, which bind workspace snapshots and in-flight operations to a committed log position, are developed in Checkpoints.


A reliable progress record strictly partitions objective facts that the host runtime can verify from interpretive claims generated by the model. Active operational constraints originate in the initial task specification, not in a model’s fallible summary. Similarly, artifact versions and tool outcomes stem directly from host execution logs rather than free-form prose. A diagnostic narrative remains a hypothesis even when it cleanly accounts for observed symptoms. Enforcing explicit boundaries between these categories prevents a summarization step from silently mutating an exploratory directive like “test this repair” into an authoritative assertion that “this repair passed.”


↩︎ The five-part task specification contract, the source of a task’s binding constraints, is established in The five-part task specification contract.
In the connection-pool example, the agent must not have the authority to relax public API contracts, expand workspace boundaries, or bypass deployment restrictions simply by rewording its progress record. If a human operator alters the task parameters, the runtime injects the updated contract directly instead of retaining stale instructions to preserve a prompt prefix. Consequently, every progress record explicitly references the contract version against which it was constructed, enabling the runtime to validate its contents against currently authorized constraints. Each observation entry obeys the scope rule, so the r17 failure and the r18 pass each characterize only their own revision. Milestones must therefore record the exact operation executed and its empirical outcome rather than claiming generalized resolution. Stating that “reproducer passed on r18” records a verifiable event; asserting that “the race condition is eliminated” overstates what that single check proved. Similarly, the handle row implements the handle rule. Whenever the agent requires an exact assertion diff or full test trace to take its next step, the runtime can fetch the raw payload through its stored reference without polluting the ongoing prompt with unneeded detail.



A model-generated progress record represents an untrusted candidate transformation of the conversation history. Before substituting this summary into the active prompt, the runtime must validate both its structural representation and its underlying claims. Schema enforcement guarantees that an observation field contains an outcome status, an artifact identifier, and an evidence pointer, but syntax checking cannot confirm that the reported outcome corresponds to an actual tool execution. The distinction between structural validity and value correctness applies as directly to context summaries as it does to tool invocations.


↩︎ The gap between a schema-valid payload and a correct one is established for tool calls in Scope of the structural guarantee.
To prevent circular reasoning, the audit must evaluate candidate records against an external required-field inventory maintained by the host runtime. If the runtime trusted an internal checklist generated by the model itself, a hallucinating summarizer could omit a vital deployment constraint from both the record and its verification checklist while passing self-consistency checks. Instead, the runtime injects active constraints directly from the task specification and compares artifact hashes and test assertions against authoritative logs. Because this inventory is scoped to explicit task requirements, anticipating every latent detail a future step might need remains a context-selection challenge rather than an automatic benefit of schema validation.
When evaluating claimed progress, the runtime resolves every evidence pointer against the system execution log, matching the reported command, exit code, and artifact version against reality. A missing tool result must remain recorded as unknown; a failed execution remains failed regardless of whether the model frames the outcome optimistically; and a nonzero exit code records an unsuccessful execution without establishing its cause. Any diagnostic milestone must be supported by recorded evidence, and incomplete investigations must remain explicitly designated as open hypotheses.
Suppose a candidate record claims that the entire regression test suite passed on r18, yet host records show that the model only ran test_waiter_notified_on_return. The audit detects this factual conflict immediately and rejects the record. Broader questions (whether the single test provides sufficient coverage, whether edge cases lurk in unexercised modules, whether subsequent actions comply with system policies) are managed through automated test execution and policy enforcement rather than the summarization audit itself.
Version tracking is how the audit enforces the scope rule. A historical finding may name r17, but a claim about the current pool needs evidence recorded against r18. The audit distinguishes cleanly between a missing historical payload, a valid historical observation, and an unverified assertion about current code. Treating all three indiscriminately as version mismatches would discard valuable diagnostic context while failing to confirm whether the present codebase actually functions.
Listing 2 collects these checks into one host-side function. It runs as ordinary code outside the model, and every value it compares comes from a source the candidate record did not write: the runtime-owned inventory, the recorded tool events, and the current workspace. Each observation claim names its event, target artifact, revision, and execution scope, including the selected test and its recorded configuration. Current-state claims receive the same evidence check as historical milestones before their applicability to the present workspace is checked.



Listing 2: Auditing a candidate progress record: Every comparison uses evidence the summarizer did not produce. An empty result permits replacement; any finding rejects the candidate.


def audit_record(record, inventory, events, workspace):
    findings = []

    # 1. Required fields: contract constraints plus promoted discoveries,
    #    such as the controlled waiter-before-return schedule.
    for field in inventory.required_fields():
        if record.value_of(field.name) != field.value:
            findings.append(("missing_or_altered", field.name))

    # 2. Historical and current claims must match recorded evidence.
    for claim in (*record.milestones, *record.current_state_claims):
        event = events.get(claim.event_id)
        if event is None:
            findings.append(("no_evidence", claim))
        elif (claim.operation, claim.result, claim.artifact,
              claim.artifact_version, claim.scope) != \
             (event.operation, event.result, event.artifact,
              event.artifact_version, event.scope):
            findings.append(("contradicts_event", claim))

    # 3. Scope: history may name r17; a current-state claim needs support
    #    recorded at the version the workspace holds now.
    for claim in record.current_state_claims:
        if claim.artifact_version != workspace.version_of(claim.artifact):
            findings.append(("needs_current_evidence", claim))

    return findings



When applied to our candidate record, Check 2 rejects the assertion that the full regression suite passed on r18 because the event log documents only a single test execution. It also rejects a current-version claim with no corresponding event or with a different artifact or execution scope. Check 1 catches any omission of the no-deployment constraint or the controlled test schedule. Check 3 allows the r17 failure to persist as an immutable historical observation while preventing the model from presenting that diagnostic failure as a description of the current r18 workspace.
The runtime retains all raw tool logs and source diffs until the candidate record is either validated or rejected; pruning conversational turns from the prompt context does not imply purging raw payloads from backing storage. If the audit flags discrepancies, the runtime can supply the specific failure diagnostics back to the model for a targeted correction attempt, or it can bypass the model and synthesize a minimal, verified record directly from known-good state. Because iterative repair calls consume both token budgets and wall-clock latency, the system enforces a strict retry policy capping correction attempts, tool retrievals, and execution time rather than retrying indefinitely until a model output happens to pass. If repeated retries fail to yield a verified summary, the runtime must retain a larger slice of raw context (if token capacity allows), fetch essential artifacts on demand, or abort with an explicit handoff exception. Blindly accepting an unverified summary is unacceptable in production systems, and exhausting a retry budget establishes neither factual accuracy nor operational success.



Once validated, the progress record anchors the next model invocation. The runtime composes the prompt by combining the active contract, the audited record, and the immediate observations or code excerpts required for the upcoming decision. Staging these segments in canonical root, trunk, and leaf order allows the audited record to reside in a reusable prompt trunk, maximizing KV-cache prefix sharing across turns until an altered constraint or new execution result invalidates it. The entire prompt assembly, including structural framing and payloads retrieved via handles, must satisfy admission bounds, reserving sufficient context capacity for model generation.
In the connection-pool scenario, the subsequent call evaluates the r18 patch with the passing reproducer and unresolved API compatibility obligations clearly visible, without re-reading pages of discarded diagnostic tangents concerning thread timeouts. If a later debugging phase requires specific details omitted during compaction, the runtime retrieves the original artifacts through their handles or surfaces the missing evidence as an explicit knowledge gap. Compaction behaves like a staged cache rather than an irreversible, lossy step only under two conditions: the raw payloads stay retained, and each pass is rebuilt from them rather than from the previous summary. A pass that summarizes the last summary inherits every loss before it, and that recursive case is where small per-round losses compound (section 4.8.2).
Persisting a structured record to disk guarantees that summary state survives process crashes, but context availability alone does not render an interrupted agent fully resumable. Restoring workspace files, synchronizing git worktrees, and reconciling in-flight tool calls with indeterminate outcomes demand comprehensive execution-recovery mechanisms. Context continuation fulfills a more bounded contract. It guarantees that the next model invocation receives an accurate, verified representation of task state and empirical observations under documented operational conditions.

Checkpoint 4.2: Continuing after compaction
A candidate progress record says the repair is complete, while the retained evidence contains only a passing reproducer on r18.

Evidence scope: Which claim should the audit reject, and which historical result should it retain?
Constraint preservation: How can the runtime check for a missing no-deployment requirement without relying on the summary’s own checklist?
Missing detail: What conditions must hold before a raw-payload handle can supply an omitted assertion to the next call?
Correction budget: If each rejected record costs one more call as large as the compaction pass and the policy caps corrections at two, what is the worst-case multiple on \(\CompactionPassCost\) in equation 4, and which outcomes remain permissible once the cap is reached?



A structured progress record preserves the vital technical distinctions that an agent needs to continue operating after conversational history has been pruned. However, the operational utility of these recorded observations depends entirely on whether their environmental assumptions remain valid. When a developer modifies a source file, updates a configuration, or alters a test fixture, the runtime must determine which findings remain trustworthy without erasing the immutable history of what was previously observed. Reconciling active state changes with historical evidence is the core responsibility of context invalidation.




Invalidation acts on the second event of the repair’s timeline, the write that turns r17 into r18, before the reproducer runs again. At that moment the working context holds the r17 source excerpt, the r17 test failure, and the missed-notification hypothesis built on both. The failure accurately documents how the unpatched system behaved under the earlier source, test harness, and configuration. It reveals nothing, however, about whether the patched implementation in r18 resolves the bug.
The same boundary separates historical source excerpts from active working state. An excerpt of src/pool.py captured at r17 may explain why the agent formed its original missed-notification hypothesis, but planning a subsequent patch against r18 requires inspecting the actual code at r18. When constructing the next model prompt, the runtime faces an explicit architectural choice: retain the earlier excerpt as immutable history, overwrite it with current source text, or evict it entirely because the upcoming decision no longer depends on it.

Definition 4.3: Context invalidation
Context invalidation withdraws a staged observation’s authority to support claims about current state whenever an underlying artifact or operational precondition changes, while preserving that observation as historical evidence of the state it originally recorded.

Significance: When a superseded observation leaks into a decision prompt, it introduces an unchecked step error that compounds across multi-step execution horizons (equation 1.1). Invalidation intercepts this drift by converting stale state into an explicit refresh operation scheduled before the model acts.
Distinction: Invalidation alters an observation’s applicability to the present, not its historical truth. It also differs from context deletion, which merely removes tokens from the request payload. The test failure at r17 remains an immutable, accurate record of revision r17.
Common pitfall: Treating a fresh timestamp or an unexpired polling interval as a guarantee that an in-context observation matches the current artifact on disk.



When a runtime neglects context invalidation, stale observations corrupt agent decisions through three distinct failure modes. In offset drift, the model plans an edit against line numbers or byte offsets retrieved at r17. Because the patch that created r18 shifted the surrounding file, the patch tool rejects the edit or, worse, fuzzy-matches the hunk into an unintended function. In ghost-symptom chasing, the r17 failure trace remains active in the prompt, leading the model to diagnose and attempt to repair defects that the candidate patch already resolved. In regression from old negative evidence, a verbose early failure log overpowers a concise passing notification from a later run; the model then unnecessarily reverts or complicates an edit that the current build actually validates. Listing 3 shows how offset drift manifests at the tool execution boundary. Each failure mode conflates historical observation with current truth, a confusion that dependency tracking turns into an explicit refresh decision.

Test-time deliberation already bound each observation to the content of what it read and propagated lost support through a candidate plan’s dependency graph (Evidence preconditions). Context invalidation applies the same machinery to the working context, with two differences. The graph now covers the observations staged in the request rather than uncommitted candidate artifacts, and its usual trigger is a write the agent itself executed against the workspace. The observations that write reaches are retained as history rather than retracted. Each observation therefore needs provenance that describes both its origin and the conditions under which it was collected. For a source code excerpt, this provenance includes the file path, repository revision, and specific line span or abstract syntax tree (AST) symbol. For a test execution, it encompasses the exact commit hash of the source, the revision of the test suite, the selected test case, runtime environment variables, and the exit status. Timestamps capture only temporal sequence; establishing what was observed requires tying the data directly to immutable content identifiers.
Derived conclusions inherit dependencies directly from their supporting observations. When the candidate patch generated r18, the missed-notification hypothesis rested solely on traces collected at r17 rather than representing an invariant fact about the codebase. Consequently, the actual runtime behavior of the patched implementation became an open question requiring fresh experimental validation. The runtime maintains this manifest deterministically rather than delegating bookkeeping to model attention. Every staged observation \(\TrajectoryObservation_{t}\) binds to its target artifact through an observation binding:
\[
\ObservationBinding(\TrajectoryObservation_{t}) = \langle \text{artifact}, \text{kind}, \text{revision}, \text{range}, \text{content id} \rangle,
\tag{5}\]
where \(\ObservationBinding(\TrajectoryObservation_{t})\) records the artifact identifier, its type (such as a source file, test execution, daemon process, or build artifact), the revision observed, the specific byte range or symbol queried, and a cryptographic hash of the content ingested. Derived entries (diagnostic hypotheses and test summaries) maintain directed edges to each underlying observation. Together, these bindings and edges construct an in-memory dependency graph.9 When a tool write mutates an artifact, the runtime flags all directly bound observations as historical, traverses the outgoing edges, and marks every downstream conclusion for reassessment. The r17 excerpt and test trace become historical and the working hypothesis is flagged for reassessment, while a documentation excerpt and the note derived from it keep their status because nothing they depend on changed (figure 4).

A dependency record makes invalidation selective. Modifying an unrelated documentation file leaves execution traces applicable to the unchanged binary or script. Conversely, editing a test assertion, adjusting a timeout configuration, or altering the core data structure immediately invalidates dependent execution claims. Whenever dependency edges are ambiguous or coarse-grained, safety dictates conservative over-invalidation. Marking a broader set of entries for refresh avoids reasoning over silent regressions, because an unrecorded dependency does not guarantee freshness.
Cryptographic content identifiers verify whether input artifacts remain identical across execution steps.10 When validating a derived result, the runtime compares the current content hashes of its direct dependencies against their recorded values at execution time. Even with perfectly stable inputs, nondeterministic software behaviors (such as thread interleaving or network timeouts) mean that a single passing test run remains merely a sample of system behavior. The runtime’s manifest must therefore track artifact identities, spatial observation scopes, and empirical uncertainty as distinct metadata dimensions.
10 Timestamps vs. Content Hashes: Make’s timestamp rule (Feldman 1979) rebuilds a target whose file was touched but not changed and can miss a real change whose timestamp moved backward. Modern build engines record cryptographic hashes of input contents and rebuild only when a dependency hash diverges (Mokhov et al. 2018). Context runtimes face the same trade-off: a timestamp records when an inspection occurred, while a content hash confirms whether the artifact is unchanged.

Mokhov, Andrey, Neil Mitchell, and Simon Peyton Jones. 2018. “Build Systems à La Carte.” Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 2 (ICFP): 79:1–29. https://doi.org/10.1145/3236774.



The most direct signal of state mutation is a verified write executed through a runtime tool. When a file-editing tool successfully writes r18, the runtime immediately marks all r17 source excerpts as historical and registers pending test obligations for the updated code. A tool invocation that fails or raises an exception may leave partial writes on disk. The runtime must inspect affected artifacts as well as tool exit statuses and return payloads, marking dependent observations for revalidation until the resulting state is established. Furthermore, state tracking must reside in the runtime’s authoritative metadata graph, never in conversational prompt nudges that urge the model to remember what changed.
External processes can also mutate the workspace behind the runtime’s back. Inexpensive filesystem metadata (file size and modification timestamps) provides lightweight heuristics suggesting a refresh, but authoritative validation requires inspecting content hashes or cryptographic commit identifiers. Kernel-level filesystem watchers (such as Linux’s inotify subsystem) reduce change-detection latency, yet queue overflows, unmonitored mount boundaries, and dropped events can silently leave a cached view stale (Linux man-pages project 2026). Robust runtimes treat watcher events as hints to trigger revalidation rather than as infallible event streams.

11 Leases: Gray and Cheriton (1989) converted temporal bounds into formal consistency guarantees through leases. In a distributed cache, a lease grants a client exclusive or shared read rights over a datum for a fixed term, during which the server guarantees it will not permit conflicting writes until every lease expires or is explicitly released. This guarantee hinges on server-coordinated consensus. Because standard filesystems and external web services provide no such cooperative write locks to an agent runtime, a local observation TTL remains a purely speculative heuristic. 
Gray, Cary G., and David R. Cheriton. 1989. “Leases: An Efficient Fault-Tolerant Mechanism for Distributed File Cache Consistency.” Proceedings of the Twelfth ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP), 202–10. https://doi.org/10.1145/74850.74870.
To bound uncertainty over dynamic external resources, runtimes often configure a time-to-live (TTL) policy that forces a fresh read after an observation exceeds a specified duration. A TTL operates as an operational heuristic calibrated to the environment’s volatility and the cost of acting on stale data, rather than as a formal proof of correctness.11 An observation younger than the TTL window can become invalid microseconds after retrieval, while an expired observation may reflect perfectly static content. For mission-critical actions, the runtime must bypass TTL caches entirely and perform an eager, synchronous read.
Even when the runtime refreshes context immediately before generating a prompt, an unavoidable race window remains, because the external system can mutate between prompt construction and tool execution. Context engineering cannot close this window in the model’s token space. Guarding against concurrent mutation requires execution-time preconditions at the tool boundary, such as atomic compare-and-swap operations or optimistic revision checks.12 The context assembly layer’s responsibility is to record the exact revision identifier on which the model’s generated plan rests, allowing the tool execution layer to validate that precondition before committing destructive changes.
12 Optimistic Validation: In optimistic concurrency control, transactions execute reads and computations without acquiring locks, validating prior to commit that no conflicting transaction mutated their read set (Kung and Robinson 1981). If the validation check fails, the transaction aborts. Preconditions at the agent tool boundary follow this exact structure: the assembled prompt supplies the version snapshot the model evaluated, and the tool runner verifies that version’s integrity before applying side effects to disk.

Once an observation no longer validates a claim about current state, the runtime must decide how to represent that invalidation in the subsequent prompt. Table 9 contrasts three fundamental strategies: evicting the outdated payload entirely, replacing it in place with a lightweight tombstone or fresh read, or appending an advisory notice to the end of the context. These strategies govern both what the model perceives and how much of the prompt can reuse the KV-cache prefix.



Table 9: Invalidation representation choices: Removing a payload, replacing it in place, and appending a notice are different operations, even when each is described informally as tombstoning, the practice of leaving a marker where deleted content stood.










Policy
What the next request contains
Limitation




Remove the old payload
Other selected material, without the outdated excerpt
The request no longer supplies that historical detail; provenance must be retained elsewhere if needed.


Replace the old payload
Current evidence, or a short marker that identifies the superseded entry and pending refresh
A marker is not fresh evidence; changing earlier tokens also changes the reusable prefix boundary.


Append a superseding notice
The unchanged old payload plus a notice describing its status
The outdated material remains visible and occupies capacity; the notice does not enforce correct use.






In the connection-pool scenario, an in-place replacement marker can state explicitly that the previously displayed source belongs to r17 and that the agent must inspect r18 before attempting another edit. If the earlier test failure provides valuable diagnostic history, the runtime can retain a compact summary of that failure alongside the pending check status. This architecture maintains the continuity of the investigation without misrepresenting stale code as current reality; storing a handle to the full r17 excerpt preserves auditability without wasting working-set capacity.
Appending an advisory notice to the prompt conserves the KV-cache prefix across turns, but it forces the model to arbitrate between the original payload and the superseding correction.13 Merely placing the notice at the end of the context or emphasizing it with system directives provides no architectural guarantee that attention will prioritize the update over the vivid, detailed error text above it. Conversely, outright payload deletion purges the raw tokens but risks leaving orphan hypotheses or derived conclusions intact unless the runtime explicitly propagates retraction across the dependency graph. Both payload removal and in-place replacement invalidate the KV-cache prefix at the point of mutation. Because prefix caching matches token sequences from left to right, altering even a single token forces the inference engine to recompute the entire subsequent suffix, regardless of whether the token count changed.
13 Tombstones in Storage Engines: Log-structured storage engines like Bigtable record deletions by writing tombstones, which actively mask superseded values during read scans until major compaction discards both the tombstone and the deleted record (Chang et al. 2008). The storage engine’s read path mechanically enforces this masking. In contrast, an appended advisory notice in a language model prompt enjoys no mechanical read filter: the superseded text remains fully visible in the attention matrix, leaving the model to heuristically resolve the contradiction.

Napkin Math 4.4: Token accounting for invalidationProblem: How do payload removal, in-place replacement, and appended notices alter resident token counts and the uncached suffix that the inference engine must recompute?
Variables: The baseline prompt is the 47,000-token request configured under the selecting policy of notebook 4.1. An outdated 850-token source excerpt from r17 sits at the start of the dynamic trunk, leaving the 15,000-token root (system instructions and tool declarations) as the unchanged prefix. An in-place tombstone marker consumes 24 tokens; an appended advisory notice, including its role and message framing, consumes 128 tokens. These quantities represent serialized token counts assuming isolated modifications without cross-boundary BPE re-tokenization. The comparison isolates the invalidation edit itself. The leaf is held unchanged from the previous call, and the notice is appended at the end of the request, after the leaf. Removal and replacement both diverge from the baseline at the end of the root prefix, terminating KV-cache reuse at that boundary.
Math: Evicting the excerpt yields 47,000 − 850 = 46,150 resident tokens. Subtracting the reusable prefix leaves 46,150 − 15,000 = 31,150 tokens in the uncached suffix that requires prefill computation.
Replacing the excerpt with a tombstone leaves 46,150 + 24 = 46,174 resident tokens, creating an uncached suffix of 46,174 − 15,000 = 31,174 tokens. In contrast, appending an advisory notice leaves all earlier tokens untouched, yielding 47,000 + 128 = 47,128 resident tokens; here, only the new 128-token tail extends beyond the cached prefix.
Systems insight: Appending preserves KV cache locality across the turn, forcing prefill across only 128 tokens compared to 31,174 tokens under in-place replacement, roughly 244× fewer for the edit itself. On a real next call that also replaces the leaf, as the selecting policy does, both representations prefill the new 8,000-token leaf as well, so the per-call gap narrows to the trunk that replacement recomputes. The saving also recurs as a cost on every later call, because all 850 superseded tokens stay resident, dilute the target evidence’s share of attention (equation 2), and invite ghost-symptom chasing. Systems architects should apply a hybrid policy informed by the dependency graph: append an advisory notice for inert historical context that the agent might cite as rationale, but replace or tombstone code regions that subsequent edits target, or defer that replacement to the next scheduled trunk rewrite, when the prefix is lost anyway (notebook 4.2). Because none of these three strategies fetches fresh source, the subsequent read of r18 and the agent’s output reserve must be budgeted separately.


Context invalidation preserves the essential boundary between historical observation and actionable present truth. An effective runtime policy unifies deterministic dependency tracking, bounded freshness heuristics, and deliberate context representations that balance attention hygiene against prefix-cache hit rates. The primary engineering objective is empirical, namely that context updates supply sufficient evidence for correct, constraint-respecting actions while minimizing token expenditure and prefill latency across multi-step execution horizons. Determining whether an assembled context policy achieves that balance without silently dropping constraints or acting on stale evidence requires evaluating the complete context lifecycle under realistic task workloads.




Evaluation returns to the end of the repair’s timeline. The reproducer has passed on r18, the history has been compacted, and the next request must carry the task constraints, the r17 failure of test_waiter_notified_on_return, and the r18 pass, each with its scope. At this junction, the context policy succeeds only if the subsequent prompt provides sufficient evidence to distinguish the active candidate patch from the earlier failure, while identifying which verification checks remain outstanding. Token reduction alone is never evidence of success. When compaction erases version boundaries, an agent can mistake an obsolete diagnostic failure for current reality, or mistake a partial reproducer pass for complete task success, which example 4.1 dissects.

Example 4.1: A passing test without its versionScenario: The repair stands where this chapter left it. test_waiter_notified_on_return failed at r17 and passes at r18 under the recorded configuration, and broader behavior is unverified. Before the next call, a naive compaction policy replaces these entries with one summary: “The waiter test passed; the repair is complete.” The API constraint and the deployment prohibition survive verbatim.
Diagnosis: A schema validator checking for a string-valued test_status accepts the summary without error, and a rule-based constraint check confirms that both negative constraints remain present. Neither check, however, detects that a localized, single-case observation was erroneously promoted into an assertion of complete task success. An evidence probe addresses this gap by freezing the execution history and inspecting the assembled prompt and the subsequent model decision. It verifies candidate and test identities, reproducer scope, and unresolved acceptance obligations. In a controlled variant, the evaluator mutates a relevant test or source file after the passing run. An effective context policy must prompt the agent to recognize that the earlier pass no longer characterizes the mutated candidate, compelling it to collect fresh evidence before reporting the repair complete. Conversely, an unrelated file modification provides a contrasting control where the evaluator ensures the policy does not trigger indiscriminate context invalidation.
Systems lesson: A context policy must preserve causal relationships and version bindings, not merely isolated field names. A test result has meaning only relative to the exact artifact and execution conditions under which it was produced, and subsequent decisions must respect those boundaries. Targeted evidence probes pinpoint semantic information loss, while repeated dynamic trials verify whether the agent acts on those preserved distinctions during execution.


Every mechanism in context engineering converges on failures of this kind. Selection determines which material enters the working prompt; staging establishes representation and ordering; compaction and progress ledgers govern what survives across context boundaries; and invalidation dictates when stale support must be refreshed. Evaluating context quality by summary length alone ignores the subtle semantic failure modes that emerge at these architectural joins. Evaluation therefore compares the complete context policy (its external source retrieval, schema transforms, and fallback paths included) under the operational constraints and resource limits of the target task.


A controlled comparison starts each repair trial from the identical source snapshot, task contract, and baseline observations. The evaluation harness holds the model configuration, sampling parameters, tool interfaces, and acceptance tests fixed while varying only the context policy. Each candidate policy operates under identical resource ceilings, such as the 128,000-token window and the 30-turn step budget of the benchmark scenario. However, identical limits do not yield identical resource consumption. A policy that executes supplementary source reads or invokes an auxiliary model for recursive summarization pays for that compute against the shared task budget.
An honest policy specification must account for operational decisions that otherwise introduce unmeasured advantages. A sliding-window policy requires an explicit retention rule for pinned system instructions and base constraints. A summarizing policy requires an explicit trigger threshold, a target compaction ratio, a protected-field schema, and defined fallback behavior when summary validation fails. Similarly, any policy that replaces raw payloads with external database handles must specify how the runtime responds to retrieval misses. Vague labels like “sliding window,” “summarizer,” or “structured ledger” obscure these operational mechanics, yet fallback paths frequently decide whether an agent recovers or terminates prematurely due to missing context.
Repeated trials across cohorts remain essential even with greedy decoding or fixed random seeds. In distributed inference systems, model serving engines, low-level kernel non-determinism, and asynchronous environment scheduling introduce subtle run-to-run variations. Benchmark protocols must log exact model versions, serving infrastructure revisions, sampling hyperparameters, sandbox environments, and KV-cache settings. Confounding context policy changes with serving infrastructure updates obscures causality, measuring artifact shifts across the combined system rather than context selection. A single successful trajectory provides an existential proof of capability, not a reliable performance estimate.

An evaluation harness must separate an information omission in the prompt from a model’s failure to attend to an available field. For every probe, define the required information schema against the task fixture before inspecting candidate outputs. In the software repair scenario, this manifest includes public API constraints, the designated workspace directory, deployment prohibitions, exact source and test identities, and the recorded scope of test executions. This inventory forms an explicit evaluation criterion, strictly bounded by the conditions anticipated in the fixture.
Required-field retention measures the ratio of correctly represented required items to total required items assessed. A field counts as retained only when its value, scope, and provenance agree with the ground-truth fixture; the mere appearance of a key named test_status is insufficient. Exact identifiers or compiler diagnostics can be verified through deterministic string equality. Paraphrased claims, by contrast, require semantic validation rules that account for annotator disagreement or evaluation uncertainty. Diagnostic logs should categorize omitted, corrupted, and unsupported fields separately whenever those distinctions alter the systems diagnosis.
Retention across successive compaction cycles is a much stricter property than retention after a single round. An item can vanish from context during intermediate steps and subsequently reappear through an expensive re-fetch. The benchmark specification must declare whether it measures instantaneous presence at each compaction boundary, uninterrupted retention across the entire episode, or just-in-time recovery prior to decision execution. In equation 6, \(\TaskContract\) stands for the set of critical constraints drawn from the task contract (the negative scope of its goal and the limits on its permitted actions), not for the five-part tuple itself, and \(|\TaskContract|\) counts them. The index \(\CompactionBoundaryCount\) counts compaction boundaries, not samples or retries. For uninterrupted retention of that set across \(\CompactionBoundaryCount\) compaction boundaries, the empirical retention metric is
\[
\ConstraintRetentionFraction(\CompactionBoundaryCount) = \frac{1}{|\TaskContract|} \sum_{\CriticalConstraint \in \TaskContract} \prod_{i=1}^{\CompactionBoundaryCount} \IndicatorFunction\left[\CriticalConstraint \text{ correctly retained at boundary } \CompactionBoundaryIndex\right].
\tag{6}\]



A small per-round loss compounds geometrically over repeated compactions.
The product in equation 6 demonstrates why recursive context compaction poses severe reliability hazards. When a required constraint or fact survives an individual compaction step independently with probability \(1-\CompactionLossProbability\), its survival probability across \(\CompactionBoundaryCount\) successive compactions compounds to \((1-\CompactionLossProbability)^\CompactionBoundaryCount\), mirroring the horizon-compounding dynamics of equation 1.1 with compaction intervals replacing raw decision turns. For example, with an apparently modest per-round loss rate of 5 percent, a constraint survives 10 compaction rounds with probability 59.9 percent, but survives 40 rounds with probability only 12.9 percent. An information loss rate that appears negligible during a single compaction benchmark quickly erodes system constraints over extended executions. This exponential decay explains why robust production systems validate protected schema fields programmatically at every compaction boundary rather than trusting an unconstrained neural summarizer. Scaling this analytical model across the complete working set requires modeling joint survival distributions, as real-world compaction failures often exhibit strong cross-field correlations within a round.
Behavioral metrics require precisely defined denominators. For example, a constraint-violation rate must measure the proportion of violating actions specifically against the subset of decision points where that constraint was applicable. Diagnostic harnesses must record proposed actions rejected by safety filters without executing them, separating generation errors from downstream enforcement failures. Similarly, the stale-support rate
\[
\StaleSupportRate = \frac{\text{decisions that treat superseded support as current}}{\text{decisions that require current evidence}}
\tag{7}\]
restricts its denominator strictly to decisions where evidence currency affects execution validity. Under the scope rule, citing the r17 failure after the move to r18 is not a stale-support decision; treating it as evidence about r18 without a fresh check is. Test fixtures and execution trace audits must codify these classification boundaries explicitly.
Task acceptance supplies the primary end-to-end evaluation metric:
\[
\EstimatedAcceptanceProbability = \frac{\AcceptedTasks}{\EvaluationTrialCount},
\tag{8}\]
estimating the true acceptance probability \(\AcceptanceProbability\) defined in equation 1.2. Here, \(\AcceptedTasks\) represents the count of trials that successfully satisfy the verification standard within allocated resource budgets, while \(\EvaluationTrialCount\) represents the total cohort of assigned trials. Passing a localized reproducer test is merely an intermediate observation within that standard; it does not constitute general proof of patch correctness. Incomplete runs, policy timeouts, tool execution crashes, and context budget exhaustion must remain in the denominator \(\EvaluationTrialCount\) rather than being silently discarded. The measurement contract outlined in table 10 organizes these complementary evaluation tiers, with equation 7 and equation 8 establishing precise denominator definitions for behavioral and end-to-end evaluation.

Compression measures representation volume rather than decision quality. To calculate compression at a given decision step, serialize two alternative prompts using an identical tokenizer: an uncompacted reference prompt containing the complete raw history, and the candidate prompt produced by the context policy. Both serializations must include system instructions, tool declarations, structured schemas, and framing delimiters. The request compression ratio is defined as
\[
\RequestCompressionRatio = \frac{\ReferenceRequestLength}{\PolicyRequestLength},
\tag{9}\]
where \(\ReferenceRequestLength\) and \(\PolicyRequestLength\) represent the token counts of the uncompacted reference request and the policy-generated request, respectively. The uncompacted baseline \(\ReferenceRequestLength\) serves as an analytical reference and may exceed the context window of the model serving engine; measuring it does not require executing it. Under this formulation, values of equation 9 exceeding \(1.0\) indicate token reduction. Evaluators must maintain consistent token accounting across both terms, because dividing raw observation tokens by a fully serialized prompt introduces measurement asymmetry and invalidates comparative analysis.
Compression ratios are also sensitive to trajectory variance. In static-trace probes where every policy ingests an identical historical trace, request lengths compare directly. In dynamic closed-loop trials, however, a deceptively high compression ratio often signals that an ineffective policy generated extraneous exploratory steps that had to be compressed away. Engineering reports should pair compression ratios with absolute token counts and aggregate system expenditure. This accounting must incorporate the auxiliary compute required to generate summaries, execute external retrieval queries, and reload evicted payloads from secondary storage. Neglecting these overheads creates an illusion of efficiency by transferring token expenditure from the main context window into external auxiliary calls.
Verifying that an agent actually uses retained context requires methods beyond static inspection. Token presence in a prompt does not guarantee downstream attention, and internal attention weights or verbatim identifier quotations offer only correlational evidence. Diagnostic interventions provide much stronger causal verification. By systematically ablating or mutating a critical task variable within a controlled fixture while leaving surrounding context unchanged, an evaluator can probe whether model decisions change in response. If mutating the active branch identifier or test status does not alter subsequent tool calls, the model is insensitive to that state variable under the current prompt structure. Static ablations must still be coupled with end-to-end task trials, as an adaptive agent in a dynamic environment may successfully compensate for an omitted context field by re-querying the environment via tool calls.
While example 4.1 diagnoses the overstatement of unverified claims, counterfactual probes evaluate context omissions just as effectively. Suppose a compaction policy strips raw execution logs from the working prompt, leaving only an external storage handle. This optimization preserves fidelity only if the backing storage is reachable, indexed, and cheap enough to query on demand. Evaluating the agent with the storage handle temporarily disabled reveals whether the policy includes a fallback, a failure mode invisible to simple field-presence checks. When an agent cannot reconstruct necessary evidentiary context, aborting the task gracefully or requesting operator intervention is far safer than proceeding on hallucinated assumptions.
Selecting a production context policy requires balancing these interdependent metrics across the entire execution lifecycle. Systems architects must compare candidates across task acceptance rates, failure classifications, end-to-end latency, and cumulative dollar cost under identical operating constraints. A structured ledger policy that boasts flawless schema retention but repeatedly prompts unsupported task completions fails in its core systems objective. The optimal policy for production deployment is the feasible configuration that minimizes the effective cost per accepted task, \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\), computed across the entire cohort of assigned trials. Shrinking context size reduces individual invocation costs, but if aggressive truncation degrades \(\AcceptanceProbability\) by precipitating unresolved trials or runtime crashes, the effective cost per completed task escalates rapidly. Only rigorous end-to-end economic accounting resolves this engineering trade-off.

Checkpoint 4.3: Testing what survives compaction
A candidate policy preserves the manifest’s field names but drops specific values and version relationships. Its resulting request is measurably shorter than the uncompacted reference prompt.

Retention: How does an automated validation check distinguish mere field key presence from the semantic retention of the r18 reproducer test outcome?
Evidence scope: How does an intervention probe distinguish a valid historical reference to the r17 failure from an unsupported assertion about the r18 workspace?
Cost boundary: If the runtime fetches an evicted diagnostic log on every subsequent turn via tool calls, which metrics reveal whether compaction achieved a net resource reduction?
Retention estimate: Using the hypothetical per-round loss rate from equation 6, after how many compaction rounds does a single constraint’s survival probability fall below even odds (50 percent), and what does this imply for where protected-field validation must execute?
Controlled comparison: Why can a fixed-trace probe isolate representation defects without predicting dynamic end-to-end task completion rates?



Rigorous evaluation transforms context engineering from ad hoc prompt tuning into an empirical systems discipline. Every empirical result remains bounded by the realism of the test fixtures, the precision of evidence criteria, and the completeness of resource accounting. The most dangerous engineering pitfalls arise when single-tier metrics are conflated with system efficacy, such as treating reduced prompt length as proof of information density, or mistaking the syntactic presence of safety instructions for enforceable behavioral boundaries.




Context engineering failures typically arise when system designers confuse the token payload presented to a model with the state, memory, and safety guarantees of the broader system. A prompt can be aggressively compressed yet silently drop a decisive operational constraint, or it can preserve an exhaustive transcript that presents superseded tool outputs alongside active state. Designing robust agent architectures requires identifying where context assembly breaks down under operational scale.

Fallacy: If every token fits, every needed fact is usable.
Admitting a prompt within the interface’s context window does not ensure that the model can effectively attend to and extract every critical fact (section 4.3). Token capacity defines only an upper bound on ingestion, whereas evidence retrieval remains an empirical property of attention allocation. For example, under fixed logits, the toy attention head in equation 2 assigns 96.8 percent of its attention weight to the target token across a sequence of 100 keys, but this share declines to 2.9 percent when distributed across 100,000 keys, even though all 100,000 keys fit within the context limit. Reliable context validation therefore requires varying information density and layout alongside sequence length, measuring actual task completion on realistic workloads rather than relying on raw token budgets.


Pitfall: Treating deterministic extraction as lossless task understanding.
Deterministic filters and parsers guarantee reproducibility, but reproducibility is not semantic comprehension. A heuristic parser consistently extracts the same error lines while silently dropping the decisive warning that preceded them. For example, filtering exclusively for FAILED status lines in listing 1 isolates the failing assertion while discarding the chronological event sequence that makes the failure actionable. Deterministic pipelines make transformations inspectable and debuggable, yet they remain vulnerable to silent data loss. Resilient runtimes guard against this by marking protected fields that summarization passes cannot discard, annotating omitted spans, and retaining content-addressed handles to raw payloads so that an agent can re-read original data when ambiguity arises.


Fallacy: A valid progress-record schema guarantees continued compliance.
A structured schema verifies syntactic presence, but it cannot guarantee that semantic constraints survive repeated compaction cycles. Under the hypothetical 5 percent per-round loss rate modeled in equation 6, an operational policy constraint survives 40 iterative compaction steps with only 12.9 percent probability, even though every intermediate serialized record validates cleanly against the schema. Systems engineers must treat prompt context as an advisory communication channel rather than an authoritative enforcement layer. Runtimes must validate protected fields against ground-truth sources at every compaction boundary (section 4.6), assess subsequent agent actions against security policies, and enforce hard execution boundaries through external middleware rather than relying on in-context reminders.


Pitfall: Keeping obsolete support solely to preserve a prefix hit.
Appending corrections to the end of a transcript preserves prefix-cache hits for the next immediate inference step. In notebook 4.4, the invalidation edit alone makes in-place replacement reprocess roughly 244× as many tokens beyond the prefix, a gap that narrows to the size of the trunk once the next call’s new leaf is counted. However, prioritizing short-term cache hits retains 850 superseded tokens across all subsequent requests, forcing the model to repeatedly reconcile stale text with appended errata. The dependency graph decides which rule applies. Evidence in any region that a later edit or current-state decision targets should be replaced, and appended notices reserved for inert history that the agent cites only as rationale (section 4.7).


Fallacy: A larger context window removes the need to select and compact.
Expanding context windows raises physical token limits, but it does not eliminate the compounding latency, cost, and attention degradation of unmanaged histories. As demonstrated in notebook 4.1, an append-only transcript policy running across a 30-turn horizon requires 167,000 tokens by its final request. While an expanded window accommodates this trajectory, it bills 3,030,000 input tokens compared to 1,410,000 tokens for a selective policy that maintains a compact working set of 8,000 observation tokens, a factor of 2.1× in token volume. The extraneous tokens also dilute attention over the exact evidence required for subsequent tool invocations. Structured selection and compaction remain indispensable, reducing both the effective trial cost \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) and the distraction within the request regardless of window capacity.


Pitfall: Placing unnecessary volatile fields before reusable content.
Prefix-caching engines match sequence tokens strictly from left to right. Inserting dynamic values (timestamps, request identifiers, ephemeral counters) near the start of a prompt breaks cache reuse across turns, even when the system prompt, schemas, and task instructions that follow are completely unchanged. In notebook 4.2, this volatile layout increases the input bill so that it is 3.2× that of the stable layout under explicit reuse and pricing assumptions. Exact-prefix matching halts at the very first differing token, regardless of message roles or field semantics. System architects should structure prompts hierarchically, pinning invariant instructions and tools at the root prefix and deferring volatile, per-call parameters to the leaves.

These pitfalls reflect a shared architectural mistake: treating the context window as a monolithic store for evidence, control state, and execution enforcement. Robust context engineering separates these responsibilities across distinct system tiers. The working context supplies curated, task-relevant evidence for immediate model decisions, authoritative datastores track verified environment history, and external runtime monitors enforce execution invariants. A context management policy succeeds when it preserves these boundaries within operational cost and latency budgets, rather than attempting to make the prompt self-sufficient at all costs.



Fitting an execution trace within a model’s context window does not ensure that the model will make a sound decision. Throughout this chapter, the repair agent’s most instructive failures rarely stemmed from context window exhaustion. Instead, they occurred when the context representation severed critical causal relationships: a discarded hypothesis remained displayed alongside contradictory evidence, a passing reproducer lost its revision metadata, an automated summary silently dropped an operational constraint, and a cached code excerpt persisted after the underlying file had changed. Each case reflects a failure of context state management rather than token capacity. Solving these breakdowns requires runtime bookkeeping outside the model (explicit working-set management, dependency tracking, cache-aware layout, and artifact versioning), not a larger context window or more elaborate prompt engineering.

Key Takeaways: Context is selected information for the next decision

Context budgets require explicit working-set management: Every serialized request must preserve sufficient headroom for generation, but staying within token limits does not guarantee that the prompt supplies the necessary evidence. Naively appending every tool observation quickly exhausts the context window: in our reference repair agent, uncontrolled logging overflows the context window at turn 21 of 30. Effective runtimes actively bound and select per-turn observations to match the execution horizon while measuring decision quality directly.
Prefix stability governs cache reuse rather than semantic authority: Placing static instructions and tool definitions in a stable prefix eliminates redundant prefill computation through KV-cache reuse. Across the repair trajectory, under the chapter’s stated reuse and price assumptions, an unstable layout’s input bill came to 3.2× that of a cache-aligned layout. However, cache layout should never be confused with authority: message roles, cache boundaries, and data provenance are separate architectural concerns, and staging content in a privileged prefix does not validate untrusted tool outputs.
Compaction mechanisms must enforce strict schema retention: Truncation and summarization inevitably discard detail. Because small per-round losses compound geometrically over long trajectories, compaction policies must explicitly safeguard the exact fields required by downstream tools and decisions. Runtimes should validate generated summaries against their original records at every compaction boundary, retaining raw-payload handles so the agent can deterministically retrieve omitted evidence on demand.
Observation validity must be bound to artifact versions: Every tool observation reflects the specific system environment and artifact revision present when the tool ran. When an agent modifies source code or configuration files, earlier test results cease to validate claims about the current state, even though they remain historically accurate records of prior turns. Runtime managers must track revisions explicitly, invalidating stale claims while preserving observations that remain tied to untouched components.
Context policies must be evaluated on end-to-end task outcomes: Intermediate metrics such as compression ratio, token count, and field retention provide useful diagnostics, but they do not measure decision quality. A compaction or retrieval strategy improves a system only if it reduces the effective cost per accepted task completion, accounting for the overhead of compaction calls, retries, and failed trajectories across all evaluated trials.



Treating prompt context as an active working set (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}\)) transforms context engineering from intuitive prompt assembly into a rigorous systems discipline. Rather than assuming that a larger window will resolve ambiguity, engineers must verify whether an assembled prompt contains the precise dependencies needed for the next decision step. Scoping observations by artifact revision reinforces the rule that authority remains with the external source of truth (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)), enabling the runtime to invalidate superseded evidence without corrupting historical audit logs. Working together, these principles ensure that context preparation is transparent about its cache costs, accountable for the evidence it provides, and explicit about unresolved dependencies.



Managing bounded fast memory against a much larger backing store is one of the foundational challenges of computer systems. When virtual memory decoupled address spaces from physical DRAM, Belady established the theoretical ceiling for page replacement by comparing online policies against an optimal offline algorithm with clairvoyant knowledge of future memory accesses (Belady 1966). Denning grounded this theory in measurable program behavior with the working-set model (Denning 1968), defining an empirical working set over a sliding time window to prevent thrashing. Context engineering confronts an analogous capacity constraint, but operates under a critical systems difference: unlike hardware architectures with memory management units, a transformer forward pass yields no access traces or page faults. The runtime cannot passively observe token reuse. Instead, it must actively predict and assemble the relevant working set before issuing each model call. Virtual context management systems such as MemGPT (Packer et al. 2023) directly adopted this hierarchical mindset, paging structured dialogue and retrieved facts between the active context window and external persistent storage.

O’Neil, Patrick, Edward Cheng, Dieter Gawlick, and Elizabeth O’Neil. 1996. “The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree).” Acta Informatica 33 (4): 351–85.
The mechanisms required to maintain consistency across derived agent state draw from decades of research in automated reasoning, software build systems, and distributed storage. Classical truth maintenance systems established early formalisms for tracking dependencies: Doyle (Doyle 1979) recorded explicit justifications for each maintained belief, automatically propagating invalidations whenever an underlying premise collapsed. Software build tools addressed the same synchronization challenge at the filesystem boundary. Feldman’s make (Feldman 1979) reconciled targets with dependencies using file modification timestamps, a strategy that modern build architectures subsequently generalized by tracking cryptographic content hashes and execution traces (Mokhov et al. 2018). In distributed systems and databases, optimistic concurrency control (Kung and Robinson 1981) protected state validity by verifying at commit time that underlying read sets remained unaltered, while cache leases (Gray and Cheriton 1989) bound staleness through time-limited writer contracts. Similarly, data provenance research clarified how derived views inherit lineage from source records (Buneman et al. 2001), and log-structured storage engines established how to compact and tombstone superseded records without stalling active reads (O’Neil et al. 1996; Chang et al. 2008). Agent runtimes encounter this identical systems dilemma: intermediate summaries and cached observations inevitably outlive their inputs unless governed by explicit dependency tracking and proactive eviction.
The foundation model layer introduced its own distinct set of systems bottlenecks. Transformer attention (Vaswani et al. 2017) structured every input sequence as an all-to-all competition for weight, making sequence length a quadratic compute and linear memory cost during inference. Retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al. 2020) brought dynamic document chunks into this input space, while reasoning-and-acting frameworks such as ReAct (Yao et al. 2023) established the now-standard agent loop of interleaved reasoning, tool invocation, and environment observations. As multi-turn interaction traces expanded, empirical evaluation began to distinguish nominal context capacity from usable context quality. Liu et al. (2024) documented the U-shaped “lost-in-the-middle” phenomenon, showing that retrieval performance falls when critical evidence sits in the interior of a long prompt. Shi et al. (2023) demonstrated that even benign, irrelevant context distracts model attention and degrades task accuracy, while Hsieh et al. (2024) revealed that basic needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks substantially overestimate real-world context utilization on complex multi-hop queries. At the serving layer, systems such as vLLM (Kwon et al. 2023) and SGLang (Zheng et al. 2024) introduced paged attention and prefix caching to share key-value tensors across requests, turning prompt structure into a primary determinant of accelerator memory footprint and time-to-first-token latency. Finally, because naive history compaction can distort the evidence it keeps, findings by Maynez et al. (2020) on widespread hallucination in abstractive summaries underscore why runtime compaction requires verifiable provenance audits.

8. Freshness through a human approval (Advanced). The remediation agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) decides on a production change from 5 observations of shared state.
