Compute the probability that one observation still describes its resource at decision time and the probability that all 5 do. If every decision requires current evidence for all 5, estimate \(\StaleSupportRate\) from equation 7.
A teammate proposes refreshing all 5 observations immediately before each model call. The call takes 30 seconds, and the action executes after a human approval that takes 10 minutes. Compute the probability that at least one of the 5 resources changes between refresh and execution, first ignoring the approval and then including it. What does the result show about the limit of any context-refresh policy for this workload?
Only one observation, the configuration version the change edits, determines whether the action is safe; the other four were diagnostic. Redesign the policy around the binding \(\ObservationBinding(\TrajectoryObservation_{t})\) of equation 5 and an action-time precondition at the tool boundary that re-observes and re-requests approval when the precondition fails. Compute the probability that the precondition holds at execution and the expected number of approval rounds, and compare with a precondition on all 5 observations. Contrast the change signal available here with the one the repair agent uses after its own patch.


What’s Next: From selected tokens to physical attention stateThe runtime has chosen the token sequence for the next call, and the prefix-layout calculation priced its reused prefix as a discounted line on the bill. Behind that discount sits physical state. The serving system must decide whether to retain the attention state computed from earlier compatible prefixes, and holding it occupies accelerator memory even while the agent generates nothing and waits on a tool, memory that competing requests could use. KV Cache Management sizes that state and develops the storage, sharing, and retention decisions for it. Those decisions can change execution cost without changing which observations belong in the logical working context.

title: 4 Context Engineering
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can an agent lose the thread of a task even when its entire history still fits?
An agent’s context window is a finite and expensive resource, not an unbounded repository for raw text. Naively accumulating tool outputs, conversational turns, and retrieved snippets exhausts token capacity, inflates prefill latency, and spreads attention across material the next decision does not need. Fitting is not the same as being usable. A request that fits can still place a refuted hypothesis beside the test that refuted it, or present a result from an earlier revision as a fact about the current one. Effective context engineering treats each request as a deliberately selected working set, in which relevant state is compacted without losing its provenance, superseded observations are withdrawn, and bulky artifacts stay in durable storage behind handles. Stale or truncated evidence that does reach the model produces errors that compound across later turns. The systems challenge is to carry an accurate, minimal projection of the environment within the token budget, so that the state an agent carries bounds its uncertainty rather than compounding it.

Learning Objectives

Distinguish nominal request capacity from usable working context and explain why admitted tokens dilute needed evidence
Allocate the next request’s input budget while preserving output headroom and task-relevant evidence
Design a context layout that separates source roles from change rate and supports compatible prefix reuse
Compare compaction policies by information loss, recovery requirements, and the cost of repeated transformations
Audit a progress record against runtime-owned sources and quantify how unchecked per-round constraint loss compounds across compaction cycles
Apply dependency-aware invalidation without treating historical observations as proof of current state
Evaluate context policies by decision quality, accepted outcomes, and total resource use under common limits

title: 4 Context Engineering
text:
The repair agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)) has spent several turns investigating a connection-pool defect. It has inspected the pool implementation, executed a reproduction test, and revised its initial diagnosis, and deliberation has left behind candidate versions, a refuted timeout hypothesis, test observations, and the dependency records that tie them together (Revisable Candidate Plans). None of that progress lives inside the model. Because foundation models are stateless functions across turns, every call begins and ends with the payload assembled by the host runtime. The agent can use the test trace, honor public API constraints, and avoid revisiting a rejected hypothesis only if the runtime includes them in the upcoming request, structured so that the status and role of each artifact remain unambiguous.



Working context governs the within-session state exposure by selecting, representing, and refreshing what each call carries.
The token accounting of Discrete Token Representation settles two questions for an individual request: whether the payload satisfies the admission bound, and what its tokens cost (The Cost of a Model Call). Accounting bounds, however, do not dictate semantic utility. A prompt can fit well within token limits and still fail to guide the agent toward a valid repair. The simplest agent architectures evade this problem by treating context as an append-only log, concatenating every observation, tool execution, and partial response into an expanding transcript. That policy breaks down almost immediately. Even while the transcript fits within physical limits, the runtime pays repeatedly for obsolete tokens that the next decision no longer requires. Stale code snippets sit alongside their replacements, and refuted hypotheses linger alongside the test results that disproved them, diluting the model’s attention. When an extended trajectory inevitably exhausts the context window, an unmanaged runtime is forced into blind truncation, evicting vital instructions or early constraints without any principled criteria for what to preserve.


↩︎ The quadratic input cost of resending an append-only history on every call is established in Multi-turn trajectory cost accumulation.
This chapter develops the agent’s working context: the runtime subsystem that decides what each model call receives. Rather than treating context as a passive transcript, this subsystem constructs a bounded working set tailored to a single decision. It establishes token budgets for each distinct role in the prompt, arranges data layouts so unchanged prefixes can be reused across turns, compacts historical evidence without corrupting its factual validity, maintains structured progress records that resist summarization drift, and enforces invalidation rules whenever external actions alter environment state. The host runtime owns assembly, token budgets, records, and execution gates. Selection and compaction can use heuristics or model-generated candidates, which the runtime must check against the task’s requirements and retained evidence before admission.
The chapter follows the repair agent through its next decision, and each section answers the question the previous one leaves open. The runtime first decides which evidence the next step needs and how the input allowance divides among competing roles (section 4.2). Admitting that evidence does not mean the model can use it, so section 4.3 separates the window an interface accepts from the context a model reliably acts on. The selected items then need a layout that keeps their sources distinct and their stable prefix reusable across turns (section 4.4). When history outgrows the budget, compaction (section 4.5) and audited progress records (section 4.6) shorten it without erasing causal evidence or refuted hypotheses. When the agent’s own edits change the workspace, invalidation (section 4.7) withdraws the observations that no longer describe it. Evaluation (section 4.8) then asks how to show that a complete policy lowers the cost per accepted task.

title: 4 Context Engineering
text:
As our connection-pool investigation unfolds, the runtime accumulates far more information than was present at initialization. A controlled test has demonstrated that a connection returned to the pool while a waiting client remained blocked. Consequently, the initial timeout hypothesis has been undermined, leaving missed notification as the leading candidate explanation. The next model invocation must capitalize on this empirical progress. If the runtime blindly replays the entire conversational history without distinguishing raw observations from superseded hypotheses, it forces the model to re-evaluate discounted failure modes alongside the very evidence that disproved them.
Consider the state of the codebase at version r17, where the relevant files are src/pool.py and tests/test_pool.py, and the failure is captured by the reproducer test_waiter_notified_on_return. Before prompting the model for a candidate patch, the runtime must determine precisely which source excerpts, empirical test results, architectural constraints, and unresolved questions are required in the upcoming prompt. We call this choice the working-set decision: the runtime must select the bounded subset of task information necessary to execute the next concrete step. The decision is the first obligation of treating context as a selected working set (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}\)).
The term draws inspiration from Denning’s classic working-set model of program behavior (Denning 1968). Over any temporal window, an executing program references only a fraction of its total address space. By keeping this active working set resident in physical page frames, an operating system avoids thrashing while relegating dormant pages to backing storage. An agent runtime faces an analogous residency challenge, since it must stage the right tokens in context to support the immediate operation without exhausting its prompt budget. A fundamental architectural divergence, however, distinguishes context engineering from virtual memory. Denning’s working set is measured dynamically from page references the program has already issued. An agent runtime, by contrast, must construct the context working set before issuing the model call, relying on a predictive judgment about what the upcoming decision will require.1 Furthermore, standard foundation model interfaces report only generated tokens; they emit no hardware-style reference bits or access telemetry to indicate which staged context tokens the model actually used during inference.
1 Optimal Replacement (MIN): Belady (1966) evaluated page-replacement algorithms against an optimal offline baseline that evicts the page whose next reference lies farthest in the future. Practical operating systems approximate this unrealizable clairvoyance using historical access patterns such as least recently used (LRU). An agent context runtime lacks even that access history: because the model interface reports no reference bits for the tokens it processes, working-set selection must rely on explicit domain heuristics and structured task state rather than on observed cache reuse. 
Belady, Laszlo A. 1966. “A Study of Replacement Algorithms for a Virtual-Storage Computer.” IBM Systems Journal 5 (2): 78–101. https://doi.org/10.1147/sj.52.0078.
In context management, relevance must govern selection rather than chronological recency. Core user constraints established at the start of a session remain binding after dozens of intermediate tool invocations, whereas a lengthy test log generated moments ago may offer only a single diagnostic status code. Moreover, candidate information extends far beyond the linear dialogue history. System instructions, schema declarations for available tools, newly inspected source files, and dynamically retrieved reference documents (Lewis et al. 2020) all compete for space in the assembled request. The runtime must synthesize an operational representation from these disparate sources without letting any staged copy outrank its origin, because authority stays with the source (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)). The environment remains the only authority on system state, and runtime policy, not the model, governs which actions are permissible.
To structure this selection, the runtime compiles a context manifest, a structured inventory that enumerates each artifact designated for the upcoming request alongside the rationale for its inclusion. The manifest for the connection-pool repair’s next request (table 1) reads as an architectural specification rather than a raw byte serialization: each row names an entry and the content the next step needs from it. Artifacts such as code snippets and test logs are itemized with their contextual provenance, ensuring that their substantive contents are injected only where directly relevant to the pending decision.



Table 1: Selecting the next request: Each entry supplies a distinct part of the illustrative connection-pool decision. Version labels identify the example’s artifacts, not measured repository revisions.









Selected entry
Content needed for the next step




Goal and constraints
Repair waiter notification; preserve the public API; remain within the approved workspace; do not deploy to production.


Current artifacts
Relevant source and test excerpts from src/pool.py and tests/test_pool.py at r17, together with the configuration used by the controlled test.


Observed result
On r17, the controlled waiter/return test recorded an available connection while a waiter remained blocked. Keep the test identity and conditions attached to the result.


Hypothesis status
The timeout explanation has lost support. Missed notification remains a hypothesis, not an established cause.


Repair and check status
No candidate patch has yet been checked. Behavior outside the controlled reproducer remains unresolved.


Next bounded step
Propose a candidate change to the notification path using the current excerpts; do not report the defect as repaired.






Curating this manifest demands disciplined relevance filtering. Retaining an empirical failure log without binding it to its source commit (r17) risks contaminating later turns, where an obsolete error trace might be mistaken for evidence against a newly patched implementation. Similarly, recording an abbreviated label like “notification bug” without qualifying its uncertainty prematurely elevates a working hypothesis to an established root cause. Conversely, retaining the full conversational history of rejected theories wastes valuable context capacity; once the runtime records that the timeout hypothesis was refuted by specific test evidence, the multi-turn deliberations that led to that hypothesis can be safely discarded. While a foundation model can assist in summarizing past turns to build this representation, the runtime must validate those synthesized summaries against ground-truth environmental observations before admitting them into the prompt.
The active working context must also be decoupled from durable records stored in external backing storage. For instance, rather than inlining a verbose test log into the prompt, the runtime can provide a raw-payload handle, a compact reference pointing to an external record that an authorized tool can dereference on demand, subject to access controls and retention policies. This architecture enforces the handle rule: once a payload has been moved behind a handle, it re-enters the active working context only through an explicit, validated retrieval operation. If downstream reasoning requires a specific stack trace line or configuration parameter omitted from the initial prompt, the model can invoke a dedicated retrieval tool to bring that specific slice into the context.
Every working-set candidate must satisfy hard context admission bounds. When an inference endpoint enforces a shared context window across inputs and outputs, the serialized prompt length \(\SequenceLength\) must obey the constraint \(\SequenceLength \le \ContextWindow - \OutputLimit\), where \(\OutputLimit\) denotes the token budget reserved for model generation. When providers enforce separate input and output limits, \(\SequenceLength \le \ContextWindow\) applies directly. The runtime must measure token consumption against the fully formatted wire payload (system envelopes, chat formatting markers, and JSON tool schemas included) rather than summing isolated string fragments. Because tokenizer merges and protocol framing introduce serialization overhead, token savings achieved by compressing an evidence block can easily be erased if surrounding wrappers expand.


↩︎ The admission bound and the output headroom \(\OutputLimit\) it reserves are established in Output headroom.
While this inequality sets the global ceiling, the runtime must allocate the available token space across the distinct functional roles identified in the manifest. We model this distribution through a planning budget:
\[
\SystemInstructionTokenCount + \ToolDeclarationTokenCount + \TaskStateTokenCount + \ObservationTokenCount \le \ContextWindow - \OutputLimit.
\tag{1}\]
In this budget partition, \(\SystemInstructionTokenCount\) encompasses the static system instructions, \(\ToolDeclarationTokenCount\) accounts for API schemas and tool declarations, \(\TaskStateTokenCount\) covers ongoing task constraints, historical progress logs, and active source or test excerpts, and \(\ObservationTokenCount\) accommodates immediate tool execution feedback and user steering. Because these terms compete for a strictly bounded total, any expansion in one component forces an immediate contraction elsewhere. An uncurated runtime that blindly appends every raw tool observation2 allows \(\ObservationTokenCount\) to expand monotonically with every turn. Each new line of command-line output then crowds out \(\TaskStateTokenCount\), the task constraints and code excerpts on which the next decision depends. Under appending, the observation share grows on every request until it displaces that state; selection holds each share fixed by moving older results into retained records that a handle can still reach (figure 1).
2 Interleaved Observations: ReAct prompting interleaves reasoning traces, tool actions, and observation payloads within an ever-expanding prompt transcript (Yao et al. 2023). While keeping full execution history visible simplifies early prototyping, it incurs a steep systemic penalty: the unchecked growth of \(\ObservationTokenCount\) consumes prompt capacity and inflates input token costs across every subsequent inference step. 
Yao, Shunyu, Jeffrey Zhao, Dian Yu, Nan Du, Izhak Shafran, Karthik Narasimhan, and Yuan Cao. 2023. “ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
Equation 1 serves as an architectural planning guide rather than an exact arithmetic identity. Because sub-word tokenization of concatenated strings does not strictly equal the sum of independently tokenized substrings, the runtime must validate the fully assembled wire payload against the provider’s token limit. When the assembled request exceeds the bound, the budget partition sets priority by telling the runtime which component (typically the observation buffer or historical context) must be pruned or summarized. Prompt staging (section 4.4) orders these same four components by their rate of modification to maximize prefix (KV-cache) reuse.






Figure 1: Selection Protects the State Budget: Each bar is one serialized request, stacked by the four terms of equation 1 beneath the input limit \(\ContextWindow-\OutputLimit\), with the output reserve \(\OutputLimit\) hatched above it. Appending every tool result (A) lets \(\ObservationTokenCount\) grow until it displaces the task state the next decision needs. Selection (B) keeps each term’s share by moving older results into retained records outside the request, where a handle can reach them if a later decision needs them. Segment heights are schematic, not measured token counts.




Napkin Math 4.1: How much of the window is evidenceProblem: In our reference repository-repair harness, an agent executes within a 128,000-token context window under a 30-turn step budget. The runtime reserves 8,000 tokens for generation (\(\OutputLimit\)) and allocates 3,000 tokens to system instructions (\(\SystemInstructionTokenCount\)) and 12,000 tokens to tool declarations (\(\ToolDeclarationTokenCount\)). Dynamic task state (constraints, progress logs, and active code excerpts) consumes 24,000 tokens (\(\TaskStateTokenCount\)). If every raw tool result is appended directly at 4,000 tokens per turn, how many turns fit within the window, and what maximum per-turn observation size would allow the execution to complete the entire step budget?
Variables: The context window and step horizon reflect the registry’s repository-repair harness profile. Component sizes and per-turn observation rates represent operational stipulations for fully serialized wire requests.
Math: Applying equation 1, the usable input capacity is 128,000 − 8,000 = 120,000 tokens. Deducting system instructions and tool declarations leaves 105,000 tokens (82.0 percent of the context window) available for state and observations. Subtracting the 24,000 tokens required for state yields an observation budget of 81,000 tokens. Under naive appending, this budget accommodates 81,000 / 4,000 = 20 turns. Sustaining all 30 turns requires constraining the per-turn observation payload to at most 81,000 / 30 = 2,700 tokens.
Result: The appending policy exhausts the context window at turn 21, failing well before reaching the 30-turn budget.
Systems insight: The number of feasible turns is bounded directly by the observation budget divided by the per-turn observation size, making observation volume the primary design lever. Compressing each result into an informative 2,000-token digest extends endurance to 40 turns, clearing the step budget. Context capacity, however, is only the baseline constraint. Because an appending policy re-reads every accumulated token on each call, its cumulative input bill grows quadratically in \(\TurnHorizon\). This is the re-send pattern of equation 2.9 with a per-turn append \(\TurnAppendLength\) of 4,000 tokens. Here the first request already holds one tool result, so the base length \(\BasePromptLength\) is the fixed terms plus one \(\TurnAppendLength\), and the appended sum runs to \(\TurnHorizon(\TurnHorizon+1)/2\) rather than \(\TurnHorizon(\TurnHorizon-1)/2\). Selection, by contrast, keeps the bill linear. Over this step budget, and even granting the appending policy a window large enough to admit its last request, it bills 3,030,000 input tokens against 1,410,000 for selection, 2.1× as many. That excess enters the numerator of \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) (equation 1.2) on every attempt, accepted or not.





Appending re-reads every result, so its bill bends upward; selection stays linear.
The notebooks throughout this chapter reuse this baseline scenario, adopting the 128,000-token window, the 30-turn step budget, and the component token allocations defined above. The repair agent binds on one term of the partition, the growth of \(\ObservationTokenCount\) against \(\TaskStateTokenCount\). The other three lighthouses fill the same request with different material.

Lighthouse 4.1: Context by archetype
Each recurring workload places pressure on a distinct component of the context budget in equation 1, requiring a specialized mitigation strategy (table 2).



Table 2: Context by archetype: The four recurring workloads bind on different terms of the same input budget.

Systems insight: The same budget equation binds on different constraints across workloads: token accumulation for the repair agent, provenance tracking for the research agent, temporal freshness for the remediation agent, and prefix cache amortization for the customer support agent. Engineering techniques rarely transfer across archetypes without adaptation. Compaction algorithms that keep a software repair agent within its token allocation do not resolve the primary vulnerability of a research agent, whose chief challenge is filtering untrusted external input rather than managing context length.


Every one of these budgets governs admission, ensuring that a serialized payload physically fits within the provider’s context limit, but admission does not guarantee semantic adequacy. A prompt may strictly obey the budget yet omit the critical return path needed to formulate a patch, or conversely, it may incorporate every relevant code excerpt while burying crucial version distinctions beneath superseded error logs. Sizing a context budget is therefore only the first architectural challenge; an effective runtime must also evaluate how effectively the downstream model can retrieve and reason over the tokens admitted into that window.

title: 4 Context Engineering
text:
In notebook 4.1, the 128,000-token window admits the investigation’s complete transcript for its first 20 turns. Fitting an entire history within the sequence window does not mean an agent should include every interaction; utility depends entirely on what the added material contributes to the pending decision. An omitted synchronization contract will invalidate a proposed repair, whereas ten pages of repeated timeout speculation will not improve it. Raw request length cannot distinguish essential evidence from noisy distraction.
The nominal context capacity specifies the maximum sequence length that the configured model interface physically accepts, bounded by its input and generation limits. How effectively the model reasons over a specific collection of instructions and evidence is a separate question, answered only by evaluating concrete tasks under explicit quality criteria (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}\)).

Definition 4.1: Usable working context
Usable working context is the context content, organization, and length with which a specified model and invocation configuration meet a chosen quality criterion on a stated workload.

Significance: Usable working context, rather than the nominal window, determines how much of the input allowance \(\ContextWindow-\OutputLimit\) effectively supports decisions. It dictates how many turns an execution trajectory can sustain before selection or compaction must intervene, directly setting the input token cost per accepted task in \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\).
Distinction: Nominal capacity is an architectural boundary of the serving interface that admits a request; usable working context is an empirical property of a task, model, and representation that only rigorous evaluation can establish.
Common pitfall: Treating a fixed fraction of the nominal window, or success on an isolated synthetic retrieval probe, as a universal guarantee of usable context for a production workload.



For a software repair workload, that criterion might require candidate patches to pass designated regression tests while strictly honoring a permitted edit scope, with the test suite and its coverage explicitly declared. In contrast, an information extraction workload demands high precision and recall against structured schemas. Because failure modes diverge across tasks, usable context must be measured independently for each workload.


An isolated retrieval probe3 asks whether specified information can be found in an input. An agentic repair decision demands more. The model must relate newly observed symptoms to source artifacts, preserve system invariants, and distinguish an empirical measurement from an unverified hypothesis. These are different evaluation obligations (table 3). While a synthetic retrieval probe quickly flags basic architectural blind spots, validating a runtime context policy requires decision-level verification under realistic operating conditions.
3 Needle-in-a-Haystack Probes: The best-known isolated retrieval probe plants a short fact, the needle, in long distractor text and asks the model to return it. Hsieh et al. (2024) found that models scoring nearly perfectly on this probe degraded sharply as length grew on tasks that require multi-hop tracing and aggregation, and that only about half of the models tested held satisfactory performance at the context length all of them claimed to support. The gap between the probe and the harder tasks is the gap between nominal capacity and usable working context. 
Hsieh, Cheng-Ping, Simeng Sun, Samuel Kriman, Shantanu Acharya, Dima Rekesh, Fei Jia, Yang Zhang, and Boris Ginsburg. 2024. “RULER: What’s the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models?” Conference on Language Modeling (COLM).



Table 3: Retrieval and decision scope: A simple retrieval probe and the running repair example test different capabilities.










Test obligation
Isolated key-retrieval probe
Connection-pool repair decision




Identify relevant content
Return the requested planted value.
Find the source, test conditions, and observation relevant to the notification path.


Interpret relationships
Match the queried key to its value.
Tie the failure to r17 and distinguish the missed-notification hypothesis from the observed blocked waiter.


Respect task constraints
Meet the probe’s answer requirements.
Propose a scoped change while preserving the public API and leaving untested behavior unresolved.


Establish success
Compare the returned value with the probe’s target.
Apply the chosen candidate checks and scope criteria; report only what they establish.






Context organization directly influences task success even when all required facts are present in the prompt. Evaluating multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval, Liu et al. (2024) reported marked sensitivity to the position of relevant information across model architectures, with accuracy dropping substantially when key facts appeared in the middle of the input. This position sensitivity, known as lost in the middle, means systems engineers cannot treat context as an unordered bag of tokens. Placement policies must be validated against the target workload, as positional degradation profiles vary across model families and prompt geometries.
Length degrades comprehension even when every required fact remains in the input. One long-context benchmark isolates that effect by rewriting each of its stories at lengths from a few hundred tokens to the full text while preserving the details its questions depend on, so a change in score across lengths reflects the surrounding material rather than missing evidence (Fiction.live 2025). Answering requires following the order of events and drawing inferences from implicitly stated information, a task closer to a repair decision than to returning a planted value. Figure 2 plots the scores against the length of story in context, as aggregated by Epoch AI (2026).














Figure 2: Comprehension Falls with Context Length: Accuracy on the same stories as the version placed in context grows from the shortest rewrite to 192K tokens. The shaded band spans the middle half of the 53 models scored at every length through 60K tokens; colored lines trace six individual models. A few models stay near the top at every length, while the median model loses more than a third of its accuracy by 60K tokens. Each point rests on 36 questions, so single-length wiggles are within sampling noise. Data from Fiction.live (2025) via Epoch AI (2026).


Fiction.live. 2025. Fiction.LiveBench.

Epoch AI. 2026. Capabilities and Benchmarking.


Two features of figure 2 bear on the working budget. The decline starts early and runs deep. Across the 53 fully scored models, the median falls from 100 percent on the shortest version to 58 percent at 8K tokens and 56 percent at 60K, and only 3 stay at or above 90 percent at 60K. The models also differ widely at a single length, from 22 to 100 percent at 60K tokens, which is the empirical content of the definition above. Usable working context belongs to a specified model, configuration, and workload, and the budget is found by evaluation rather than read from the window.
A first-order mechanism explains why appending distractor tokens cannot be treated as free. Within an individual attention head, a query assigns weight to each visible key through a softmax operation (Vaswani et al. 2017). For a target key with scaled logit \(\TargetKeyLogit\) alongside \(\CompetingKeyCount\) other keys with logits \(\CompetingKeyLogit_j = \QueryVector\cdot\KeyVector_j/\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}\) for head dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension\), the target’s weight is
\[
\TargetKeyAttentionWeight = \frac{e^{\TargetKeyLogit}}{e^{\TargetKeyLogit} + \sum_{j=1}^{\CompetingKeyCount} e^{\CompetingKeyLogit_j}}.
\tag{2}\]



Fixed-logit distractors shrink the target’s share of one normalizer.
All weights share a single normalizer. Because each additional key contributes a strictly positive term \(e^{\CompetingKeyLogit_j}\) to the denominator of equation 2, expanding the sequence length while holding logits constant depresses the target key’s share of attention. This structural decay is attention dilution. In a toy head with a target logit of 6 and every background logit at -2, the target commands 96.8 percent of the weight among 100 keys. When the context expands to 100,000 keys, that same target’s share falls to 2.9 percent, even though no single background key is individually competitive.
In agent execution, this effect is often worse than unrelated filler would produce.4 Stale tool executions, superseded logs, and earlier source reads share identifiers such as waiter, connection, and timeout with the evidence that matters. Because these semantically related tokens produce substantial inner products with query vectors, their logits remain elevated. This dynamic is a sufficient condition for dilution under fixed logits, not a deterministic forecast of failure. Production models sharpen logits, route evidence across multiple attention heads and layers, and learn position-dependent retrieval behaviors, which is why Liu et al. (2024) measured degradation empirically rather than deriving it analytically. Trained models also show a second consequence of the shared normalizer. Because the weights must sum to one, a query with no strong match deposits its residual weight on the first few positions, which then act as attention sinks regardless of their content (Xiao et al. 2024). Sinks change where leftover weight goes, not the dilution argument. For context selection, the lesson of equation 2 stands, and every staged token adds a term to the normalizer that the evidence for the next decision must compete against.
4 Distracting Context: Shi et al. (2023) added irrelevant sentences to grade-school arithmetic problems and found that model accuracy fell dramatically, although the added text changed nothing about the answer. Because the distractors were irrelevant by construction, the drop measures interference rather than missing information. That interference is the cost an agent pays for every superseded log line and stale file read it keeps in the request. 
Shi, Freda, Xinyun Chen, Kanishka Misra, Nathan Scales, David Dohan, Ed H. Chi, Nathanael Schärli, and Denny Zhou. 2023. “Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of machine learning research, vol. 202: 31210–27.

Xiao, Guangxuan, Yuandong Tian, Beidi Chen, Song Han, and Mike Lewis. 2024. “Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

↪ Why cache eviction policies must retain attention-sink tokens is developed in Reclamation vs. approximation.




Choosing a working budget takes two steps, and only the first can be computed from the window. The admission bound gives a ceiling. In notebook 4.1, it leaves 81,000 tokens for observations in any one request. An appending policy must hold each result to 2,700 tokens to last all 30 turns, whereas a selecting policy can spend up to that whole share on every request, because it does not accumulate. The ceiling says what fits, not what the next decision can use, so the second step searches beneath it empirically. Systems engineers evaluate complete context policies against representative task suites, the method section 4.8 develops, and adopt the budget that meets the workload’s quality criterion at the lowest effective cost. A context policy specifies far more than a simple token limit. It determines which material is retrieved, how structured data is represented, and where each component appears within the prompt layout. Decision quality must be evaluated alongside input size, inference latency, and token cost. Because additional context can provide essential grounding, introduce benign noise, or actively degrade reasoning through dilution, the resulting quality curve is rarely monotonic and seldom offers a single clean optimum. A documented operating envelope must therefore specify the workload, model configuration, quality threshold, and measured experimental conditions.
These decisions carry direct resource consequences under model-call cost accounting. Processing uncached tokens incurs prefill latency and compute charges, whereas aligned prefix caching amortizes prompt costs across repeated steps. High cache hit rates or discounted per-token pricing mean little if stale context degrades agent decisions. Conversely, pruning context too aggressively to reduce prefill costs risks stripping away vital constraints. Systems optimization targets meeting the task quality threshold at minimal effective cost, captured by the effective cost metric \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) from equation 1.2. Pruning unnecessary tokens lowers the raw attempt cost in the numerator, but omitting an indispensable fact degrades the acceptance probability \(\AcceptanceProbability\) in the denominator, inflating overall expenditures across failed trajectories.
In the connection-pool repair example, retaining the full transcript of early exploratory turns wastes capacity once distilled diagnostic observations, code snippets, interface invariants, and active hypotheses are available to guide the next patch. Stripping away a required interface contract or error log simply to compress the prompt into an arbitrary sub-budget, however, represents an equally counterproductive optimization. When no evaluated policy meets both the task criterion and the available budget, the runtime must obtain the missing information, narrow the scope of the next permitted action, or report the limitation; a successful request-admission check never certifies adequate context.
Once the runtime selects the working set and bounds its token footprint, it must assemble those items into a concrete prompt layout that preserves source roles and evidence relationships while cleanly separating stable prefix content from dynamic step updates to maximize inference cache reuse.

title: 4 Context Engineering
text:
Once a context selection policy identifies the relevant working set for an upcoming invocation, the runtime must translate those disparate entries into a concrete request payload. In our connection-pool repair task, the selected manifest contains distinct classes of information: inviolable public API constraints, source code excerpts from src/pool.py at revision r17, execution results from test_waiter_notified_on_return, and the missed-notification working hypothesis alongside an abandoned timeout conjecture. Merging these items into a flat, undifferentiated string would obscure the critical distinctions that govern the model’s next decision. Staging is the disciplined process of converting selected entries into a structured request. It preserves the semantic source, authority, and revision of every item so that the model can differentiate policy instructions from empirical evidence and tentative hypotheses, while arranging content in an order that minimizes unnecessary token churn across consecutive calls.


A well-engineered context layout stratifies information by its rate of change, placing static material before volatile content. We partition the serialized prompt into three functional regions: the root, the trunk, and the leaf. These zones classify content strictly by its mutation frequency during an agent’s trajectory, rather than by message role or semantic authority. Table 4 maps the repair agent’s selected working set into this operational order. In the running scenario from notebook 4.1, the root holds 3,000 tokens of system instructions alongside 12,000 tokens of tool declarations. The trunk incorporates 24,000 tokens of evolving task state, and the leaf receives 8,000 tokens of freshly retained observations.



Table 4: Context ordered by change rate: The zones help preserve a stable request prefix. Message roles and source metadata remain separate from these placement choices.










Zone
Contents in the repair request
When it changes




Root
Application instructions and available tool definitions
The application contract or tool interface changes


Trunk
Task constraints, the current progress record, and selected source and test content at r17
A task constraint changes, an artifact is edited, or the progress record is refreshed


Leaf
The latest scoped test observation and the next bounded step, here proposing a candidate change to the notification path
New evidence or a new next-step decision arrives






Prefix stability must never supersede correctness. The root remains stable only as long as its specifications remain accurate; if a tool definition changes during a session, the runtime must update the root in the next invocation, accepting the cache miss. Similarly, when a candidate patch advances the repository from revision r17 to r18, the runtime cannot continue staging r17 source code simply to keep the trunk prefix warm. The earlier test failure remains valid historical evidence regarding r17, but verifying whether it persists on the patched workspace requires fresh execution. Section 4.7 formalizes how invalidation policies govern this transition.
Information can also migrate between zones as task execution unfolds. An observation initially staged in the leaf may graduate into the trunk’s summarized progress record during a planned refresh, provided its provenance, version bounds, and execution scope remain intact. Conversely, if an application instruction must be injected dynamically on a per-step basis, it resides in the leaf without forfeiting its normative authority. Zone placement dictates the physical order of tokens to optimize change frequency; structural schemas and message roles establish provenance and semantic interpretation.



When staging an observation, the host runtime must bind sufficient provenance metadata to interpret the underlying payload. For our failing test case, the host attaches the test identifier, the workspace revision (r17), the execution environment configuration, and a unique run identifier. This discipline embodies the scope rule:5 an observation provides valid evidence exclusively for the specific artifact versions and execution conditions under which it was gathered. Every subsequent context transformation (summarization, compaction, and invalidation alike) must preserve these provenance boundaries.
5 Why- and Where-Provenance: Database research distinguishes why-provenance, the source records that justify a result’s existence, from where-provenance, the source locations its values were copied from (Buneman et al. 2001). The scope rule demands both for every observation: which execution and artifact versions justify its existence, and which payload spans supplied its values. A result that loses either becomes an unattributed claim that later compaction can silently generalize. 
Buneman, Peter, Sanjeev Khanna, and Wang-Chiew Tan. 2001. “Why and Where: A Characterization of Data Provenance.” Database Theory – ICDT 2001, Lecture notes in computer science, vol. 1973: 316–30. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-44503-X_20.

Greshake, Kai, Sahar Abdelnabi, Shailesh Mishra, Christoph Endres, Thorsten Holz, and Mario Fritz. 2023. “Not What You’ve Signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection.” Proceedings of the 16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security, 79–90. https://doi.org/10.1145/3605764.3623985.
The runtime synthesizes this framing externally rather than extracting it from text inside the observation. A robust serializer treats raw tool output strictly as a literal data value within a structured envelope, preventing mismatched quotes, markdown delimiters, or control characters from corrupting the surrounding schema. Despite this structural isolation, the payload itself remains an untrusted span: arbitrary text whose arrival the runtime can document, but whose semantic claims it cannot verify. While rigorous encoding prevents format-injection attacks, it cannot prevent the underlying language model from attending to and executing adversarial instructions embedded within the text (Greshake et al. 2023).
Consequently, provenance labeling serves semantic interpretation rather than security enforcement. Tagging a tool output as untrusted data guides the model’s reasoning, but it does not restrict the model’s capabilities. If an observation instructs the agent to delete a database or overwrite production credentials, the model might still attempt that operation. Security boundaries (file system sandboxing, read-only workspace mounts, and deployment blocks) must execute deterministically in the host runtime, entirely outside the model’s prompt interpretation. Staging maintains the architectural boundary between instructions and observational evidence, while host execution gates enforce operational safety.


↪ The host-side information-flow policy that limits what untrusted context may influence and where private data may flow is enforced in Information-Flow Policy.
How much weight this distinction carries depends on the workload. The repair agent’s observations come mostly from its own workspace, whose files change only when the agent or its tests change them. The research agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}\)) fills its requests with third-party text, so its \(\ObservationTokenCount\) consists mostly of untrusted spans (lighthouse 4.1). For that workload the untrusted-span boundary, not token growth, is the binding concern.



Request organization directly governs inference performance and operational cost in modern serving infrastructure. Serving engines equipped with prefix caching6 bypass redundant transformer prefill computation by reusing intermediate key-value (KV) activations for identical leading token sequences. Because causal self-attention calculates each token’s key and value representations conditionally on all preceding tokens, any divergence in the prefix invalidates the KV cache for all subsequent positions. Even if two prompts share thousands of identical trailing tokens, the serving engine cannot reuse the suffix cache if a single token near the beginning has changed, because attention state is derived from the token prefix (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\)). Ordering the zones by change rate is what turns this rule into savings. A call that changes only the leaf reuses the root and trunk, whereas a compaction that rewrites the trunk ends reuse at the root boundary and forces recomputation of every later token (figure 3).
6 Automatic Prefix Reuse: Serving systems such as SGLang index cached attention state by token prefix within a radix tree, allowing an incoming request that shares an existing token prefix to reuse cached KV blocks transparently (Zheng et al. 2024). Because radix tree lookups evaluate exact token equality rather than semantic equivalence, two requests that diverge on an early timestamp share zero cache entries past that offset. Layout discipline directly determines cache hit rates. 
Zheng, Lianmin, Liangsheng Ying, Zhenghao Yin, Cody Hao Liu, Eric Yu, Prakhar Patel, Zhipeng Yang, Anthony K. Joseph, and Ion Stoica. 2024. “SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2312.07104, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2312.07104.






Figure 3: Reuse Ends at the First Changed Token: Three consecutive requests follow the root, trunk, and leaf order of table 4, with the output reserve \(\OutputLimit\) beyond the input limit \(\ContextWindow-\OutputLimit\). A new observation changes only the leaf, so the root and trunk remain a reusable prefix. Refreshing the trunk to r18 moves the first changed token to the end of the root, and every later token is processed again. The figure assumes compatible cached state on the serving side; an identical prefix alone does not guarantee reuse.



Cache equality depends strictly on the final serialized token sequence rather than abstract application state. Serialization details (JSON dictionary key ordering, whitespace padding, system prompt templating, and token merges across boundaries) can inadvertently mutate the token stream. For instance, byte-pair encodings (BPE) frequently merge trailing whitespace with leading characters of subsequent strings, creating different token IDs across zone boundaries. Prefix stability can therefore be verified only on the fully assembled, tokenized prompt.
An identical token prefix is necessary for cache reuse, but it is not sufficient. The serving infrastructure must still retain compatible cache blocks in accelerator memory, configured for the identical model weight snapshot, positional encoding offsets, and attention mechanisms. Memory pressure, LRU evictions, or node autoscaling can purge cached state between agent turns despite byte-level request stability. While serving engines manage and evict these internal tensors, the agent runtime bears the responsibility of maintaining stable prefixes for static material while accurately refreshing data essential to the next decision.


↪ Prefix compatibility and the retention and eviction of cached KV blocks in the serving engine are developed in Prefix Caching Across Turns.
Placing high-frequency metadata near the start of a request destroys prefix reuse for zero operational gain. Moving dynamic elements (request IDs, wall-clock timestamps, invocation counters) into the leaf preserves prefix continuity across the root and trunk. If an application requires a timestamp, isolating it in the leaf prevents it from evicting tens of thousands of reusable root tokens. When an early field diverges, cache sharing collapses at the first differing token. The following calculation takes the extreme case, where divergence occurs at the very first token, to establish an upper bound on the cost penalty of placing volatile fields at the front of a request.

Napkin Math 4.2: Pricing a context layout across one trajectoryProblem: The repair agent of notebook 4.1 runs its full 30-turn step budget under the selecting policy, executing one call per turn. Each request carries a 15,000-token root of instructions and tool declarations, a 24,000-token trunk of task state, and an 8,000-token leaf of selected observations, measured after serialization. The leaf is replaced on each call rather than appended. The trunk is rewritten on 2 calls after the first, one for each compaction pass that notebook 4.3 finds this step budget triggers. Input tokens cost a hypothetical $3 per million tokens, with cached reads billed at 10 percent of that price. What input bill follows from each layout?
Variables: Both layouts have 47,000 tokens per request and 1,410,000 input tokens across the trajectory, matching the selecting policy budget from notebook 4.1. In the unstable layout, the first token differs on every invocation and no prefix is reused. In the stable layout, the first call is cold; the 2 trunk rewrites first differ immediately after the root; and the remaining 27 calls first differ immediately after the trunk. Compatible cached state remains available for every matching prefix. This calculation isolates input token pricing, omitting generation charges and cache storage fees.
Math: The unstable layout processes all input without reuse, incurring $4.23. In the stable layout, the initial cold call processes the entire request, each trunk rewrite prefills only the trunk and leaf, and every warm call processes only the leaf. The total uncached volume is \(47{,}000 + 2 \times 32{,}000 + 27 \times 8{,}000 = 327{,}000\) tokens. The remaining 1,083,000 tokens hit the prefix cache, achieving an aggregate cache hit rate of 76.8 percent. Billing uncached tokens at full price and reused tokens at the reduced rate yields $1.31 for the trajectory.
Result: Average input cost drops from $0.141 per call in the unstable layout to $0.044 in the stable layout. An unstable layout bills 3.2× the stable layout and requires 4.3× more uncached prefill tokens. These figures represent billing and token volume ratios, not end-to-end execution speedups.
Systems insight: With a stable prefix, the size of the volatile leaf determines the marginal input cost of each invocation. Rewriting the trunk requires prefilling 32,000 tokens, the prefill of 4 leaf-only calls. Systems engineers should place all per-call dynamic fields strictly in the leaf and restrict trunk rewrites to moments when underlying workspace artifacts or active task constraints change. This layout reduces the input component of attempt cost within the effective cost equation \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) by the ratio above. Task accuracy (\(\AcceptanceProbability\)) remains intact only as long as staged context remains faithful to real environment state: preserving a high cache hit rate never justifies retaining stale context.



Checkpoint 4.1: Checking the staged request
A candidate patch has just moved the workspace from r17 to r18, and the runtime is staging the next request.

Provenance after promotion: If a test result moves from the leaf into a refreshed progress record, what source, version, and scope must remain attached to it?
Volatile fields: Why does a changing field near the start shorten prefix reuse without necessarily eliminating it, and where should a per-call request identifier go?
Trunk refresh estimate: With the layout notebook’s zone sizes, how many uncached input tokens does the trajectory pay if the trunk is rewritten on every fourth call after the first instead of twice? Compare the result with the unstable layout’s count.
Stale trunk: After the source changes from r17 to r18, why is keeping the old source in the trunk an incorrect optimization even when it raises the hit rate?



Staging ensures that selected evidence enters the prompt in an interpretable schema and an order engineered for prefix cache reuse. However, ordering alone does not compress verbose outputs; an oversized test log or sprawling source file still consumes its full allocation of the token budget. When the required working set exceeds available context limits, the runtime must alter the underlying representation to preserve key decision evidence within fewer tokens. That compression challenge motivates compaction.

title: 4 Context Engineering
text:
A multi-turn task such as our connection-pool repair rapidly accumulates repeated source listings, boilerplate test setup output, and sprawling execution traces. Retaining every line in every prompt consumes capacity that downstream reasoning steps need for patch analysis and test verification. Aggressively compressing that trace into a generic note like “the test failed,” however, discards the diagnostic clues that matter, because the model loses track of which source revision failed, which thread interleaving was executed, and which assertion failed. Compaction must compress the working context without corrupting or discarding the causal evidence that future decisions depend on.

Definition 4.2: Context compaction
Context compaction replaces material in a working context with a shorter representation chosen for the task’s next decisions.

Significance: It creates room for new observations inside the fixed input allowance \(\ContextWindow-\OutputLimit\), allowing an agent trajectory to run past the turn at which appending would overflow while retaining critical evidence, constraints, and unresolved obligations.
Distinction: A compressed representation is inherently lossy or access-deferred. Keeping a handle to omitted material makes recovery conditional on an explicit retrieval step.
Common pitfall: Assuming that a deterministic extractor, or a summary mentioning all required field names, guarantees that no decision-critical information was lost.





No single compaction strategy fits all runtime data; every representation forces a trade-off between prompt compression, downstream validation overhead, and the risk of silent information loss. A regular expression provides deterministic filtering, but it can easily drop the single line that explains an intermittent fault. A source-code skeleton preserves API signatures, yet it strips the concurrency logic needed to diagnose a missed wakeup. Conversely, delegating compaction to an LLM-written summary can preserve high-level diagnostic intent, but models frequently hallucinate or misstate whether a verification check actually passed.7
7 Unfaithful Summaries: In a human evaluation of neural abstractive summarizers, Maynez et al. (2020) found hallucinated content (statements unsupported by the source document) in the output of every model studied. A progress record written by a model inherits this failure mode. The audit developed later in this chapter therefore compares each claimed milestone with its recorded event instead of trusting the summarizer’s account. 
Maynez, Joshua, Shashi Narayan, Bernd Bohnet, and Ryan McDonald. 2020. “On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization.” Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL), 1906–19. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2020.acl-main.173.
Table 5 compares the choices by their preservation obligations rather than by fixed reduction ratios. The appropriate representation depends on the immediate downstream operation. Inspecting an interface requires only an outline, whereas debugging a race condition demands exact function bodies and thread-interleaving logs.



Table 5: Compaction representation choices: Trade-offs between prompt reduction, residual prompt contents, and the downstream validation required to prevent silent information loss.










Representation
What remains in the request
What must be checked




Normalized or deduplicated text
Selected text with repeated output or formatting removed
Whether repetition, ordering, timing, or formatting carries task evidence


Tool-result digest and raw handle
Status, selected evidence, source identity, and a retrieval reference
Whether the digest supports the next decision and the omitted payload remains accessible


Deterministic extraction
Matched log records, selected fields, source excerpts, or code outlines
Whether the extraction rule omitted relevant context, relationships, or implementation details


Model-written summary
A generated account of observations, hypotheses, and progress
Whether each retained claim is supported and required details and uncertainty remain explicit






The first three representation classes rely on deterministic transformations executed entirely by the runtime without invoking a language model. Table 6 breaks those three rows into the concrete techniques a runtime implements and asks a sharper question of each. Where the first table names what must be checked, the second names the specific evidence each technique can drop without any error being raised. While deterministic filtering guarantees computational repeatability, it cannot guarantee semantic sufficiency; an operation is safe only when downstream decisions do not depend on the omitted lines.



Table 6: Deterministic compaction techniques: Specific evidence dropped by programmatic pruning methods. The trace in listing 1 demonstrates how naive failure-marker slicing discards the causal ordering behind a test failure.










Technique
What it keeps
What it can silently drop




Repeated-poll deduplication
One copy of an unchanged status output and a repetition count
A brief change between polls, or the timing of repetitions


Terminal-control stripping
Plain text without escape codes, progress redraws, or spinners
Timing or ordering signals carried only by the redraws


Diff hunk folding
Changed lines, their location, and a marker for unchanged context
Surrounding code needed to judge whether the change is correct


Superseded-read replacement
A pointer from an old file read to the edit that replaced its source
Old text a later decision needs to explain what changed


Head, tail, and failure-marker slicing
Setup lines, final lines, and lines matching failure patterns
An intermediate warning or event ordering that matches no pattern


Source outline
Signatures, types, and docstrings, with bodies folded
The implementation a repair must read, such as the notification path


Tool-result digest
Status, exit code, payload size, and a handle to the retained output
Every detail of the payload until the handle is retrieved






Lossless byte compression offers no shortcut, because the model reads only decoded tokens. The alternative that loses nothing is the handle rule from the working-set decision, which pairs a digest in the request with a handle to the retained payload. The raw payload stays in an external artifact store, and the cost of that choice falls on the later step that needs the payload, which pays a read’s latency and the tokens of whatever it brings back.
Consider our connection-pool repair task. When executing a controlled regression test at revision r17, the runtime captures the log excerpt shown in listing 1 (where repetitive polling lines have been stripped for clarity).



Listing 1: Observation before compaction: The event ordering and failed assertion together identify what the controlled test observed at r17.


source=src/pool.py@r17 test=tests/test_pool.py@r17
test_name=test_waiter_notified_on_return
configuration=controlled waiter-before-return schedule
... repeated worker progress messages ...
waiter_registered_before_return=true
connection_available_after_return=true
waiter_resumed_at_notification_check=false
FAILED: assert waiter_resumed_at_notification_check



A simplistic filter that retains only lines matching FAILED captures the terminal assertion failure but drops the event sequence that explains it. Without seeing that waiter_registered_before_return and connection_available_after_return both evaluated to true, the model cannot deduce whether the failure stemmed from a race during registration, an unavailable resource, or a missed notification. A structured, compact observation preserves this causal chain: “At r17, test_waiter_notified_on_return registered the waiter before returning a connection. The connection became available, but assert waiter_resumed_at_notification_check failed at the notification check.” Alongside this narrative digest, the context retains the revision identifiers (src/pool.py@r17, tests/test_pool.py@r17), the execution schedule, and a pointer handle to the raw execution trace for on-demand debugging.
This concise record provides empirical backing for the missed-notification hypothesis under the tested conditions while maintaining a strict boundary between raw observations and diagnostic conjectures. When a subsequent patch yields revision r18, the runtime must record the new test outcome against r18 rather than overwriting or conflating it with the historical r17 failure. A compaction step that collapses both runs into an unqualified summary such as “the bug is fixed” erases the provenance needed to verify that the repair actually resolved the underlying race condition.



To prevent compaction passes from stripping decision-critical data, the runtime designates an invariant set of protected fields that must survive any transformation. Before committing an updated working context, the system validates that these fields are present and unaltered. In our pool-repair scenario, the protected set includes the revision identifiers (pool.py@r17), the test identifier (test_waiter_notified_on_return), the concurrent scheduling flags, the failed assertion statement, and the exit status. Global task constraints must also remain pinned: preserving public API compatibility, confining edits to the designated repository directory, and blocking production deployment commands. Later execution stages might require specific function implementations or configuration values that this compact digest omits, but those can be paged in as needed.
Field protection must be dynamically scoped to the task phase. Pinning every historical line number, diff chunk, and identifier defeats the purpose of compaction by quickly exhausting the context budget. Conversely, enforcing an overly rigid, global schema risks dropping domain-specific diagnostic relationships. An assertion message copied verbatim without its corresponding commit hash or concurrency configuration is useless or misleading. Similarly, runtime filtering must scrub credentials, authentication tokens, and private keys; sensitive literals must never be retained simply because a filter rule matches string literals.
Furthermore, protected fields are not restricted to static configuration parameters; agents frequently uncover new invariants during execution. Suppose our concurrency reproducer fails consistently under the controlled waiter-before-return schedule but passes nondeterministically under the default operating system thread scheduler. The initial task specification contains no mention of this dependency; the relationship surfaces only within tool output. A naive summarizer that records “the waiter test failed” while discarding the scheduling flag permits subsequent turns to re-run tests under the default scheduler, observe an accidental pass on buggy code, and prematurely claim success. When tool feedback demonstrates that an outcome depends strictly on an experimental parameter, the runtime must promote that parameter into the protected-field inventory alongside the empirical observation supporting it. Once promoted, the parameter undergoes the same integrity checks as the original contract constraints.
Automated validation catches missing test identifiers, modified literals, or results misattributed to the wrong revision. However, validating schema conformance does not ensure that the designer selected all necessary fields or that the model will attend to them in later decisions. Section 4.8 measures both. Before evicting any uncompressed payload, the runtime must assign a clear disposition to the omitted information: either it is demonstrably irrelevant to downstream tasks, it remains retrievable via an external handle, or it is permanently pruned, marking an explicit epistemic boundary. If a future reasoning step demands an evicted detail and external retrieval fails, the agent must rerun the tool or acknowledge the knowledge gap rather than hallucinating plausible execution history.



Between passes, new observations accumulate in the leaf, and a compaction pass folds them into the trunk’s progress record, which is why every pass costs a trunk rewrite. To avoid invoking compaction after every small tool observation, systems decouple the trigger threshold from the target compaction length. This dual-threshold technique, known as hysteresis,8 allows new observations to accumulate across multiple turns before the runtime rewrites the context buffer. A narrow gap between thresholds causes frequent, expensive compaction cycles. Conversely, raising the high watermark permits longer operational trajectories between passes, while lowering the target length creates substantial token headroom by forcing aggressive compression. The optimal watermark separation reflects both token geometry and information utility. Compressing too deeply risks stripping subtle evidence, while compressing too conservatively causes thrashing.
8 Watermark Pairs: Operating-system page reclaim uses the same two-threshold pattern. A reclaim thread wakes when free memory falls below a low watermark and stops only after restoring a higher one, allowing reclamation to run in batches rather than on every allocation. The gap balances batch size against invocation frequency, a trade-off that equation 3 quantifies for context compaction. Let \(\CompactionTriggerLength\) and \(\CompactionTargetLength\) denote the upper trigger threshold and the post-compaction target, respectively, measured in total serialized input tokens. Because the system must reserve capacity for model generation, these watermarks satisfy the strict inequality \(\CompactionTargetLength < \CompactionTriggerLength \le \ContextWindow - \OutputLimit\), where \(\ContextWindow\) is the context window limit and \(\OutputLimit\) is the reserved output allowance. These thresholds represent explicit runtime policy choices rather than physical model limitations.
Assuming an idealized cycle where each compaction pass resets the request exactly to \(\CompactionTargetLength\) and each subsequent turn appends a net volume of \(\TurnAppendLength > 0\) input tokens, the runtime inspects context size after each addition before issuing the next model call. The integer number of turns between compaction passes is
\[
\CompactionCycleTurnCount = \left\lceil \frac{\CompactionTriggerLength - \CompactionTargetLength}{\TurnAppendLength} \right\rceil.
\tag{3}\]



Hysteresis turns compaction into a sawtooth whose gap sets the cadence.
Because context length is evaluated at discrete turn boundaries, the actual serialized length immediately prior to compaction is \(\CompactionTargetLength + \CompactionCycleTurnCount\TurnAppendLength\). This quantity can overshoot \(\CompactionTriggerLength\) by up to \(\TurnAppendLength - 1\) tokens, making \(\CompactionTriggerLength\) a soft operational threshold. When arrival sizes vary wildly across tool calls, the runtime must either truncate individual observation payloads or stage them in a temporary buffer to prevent an unexpected payload from exceeding the hard ceiling \(\ContextWindow - \OutputLimit\). Furthermore, if the runtime invokes a secondary language model to execute the compaction pass, that summarization call requires its own dedicated input and output token budgets.
Compaction interacts directly with prompt cache economics. A compaction pass that modifies the prefix trunk invalidates KV-cache reuse downstream from the rewrite point, triggering the trunk recomputation penalty modeled in Call \(\Glyph{n}+2\) of figure 3. For a cycle comprising \(\CompactionCycleTurnCount\) task turns and one compaction pass, let \({\TaskTurnCost}_{\CompactionCycleTurnIndex}\) represent the total cost of task turn \(\CompactionCycleTurnIndex\) (encompassing both cached and uncached input tokens alongside generated output tokens). Let \(\CompactionPassCost\) denote the complete cost of the compaction pass under the same billing boundary. The amortized financial cost per task turn is
\[
\AmortizedTurnCost = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{\CompactionCycleTurnCount} {\TaskTurnCost}_{i} + \CompactionPassCost}{\CompactionCycleTurnCount}.
\tag{4}\]
Any cache misses resulting from an altered prefix are already reflected in the uncached token rates of subsequent \({\TaskTurnCost}_{\CompactionCycleTurnIndex}\) terms; introducing a separate cache-invalidation penalty would double-count those costs. Evaluating compaction policies requires accounting for system-level costs beyond prompt tokens, including artifact storage, secondary retrieval latency, redundant verification reruns, and trajectory failures caused by prematurely evicted context. A compaction schedule that minimizes prompt token expenditure may inflate total task cost if excessive compression forces the agent into exploratory dead ends. Runtimes must therefore optimize for the effective cost per completed task (\(\CostPerAcceptedTask\)) rather than local turn cost \(\AmortizedTurnCost\). The watermark gap \((\CompactionTriggerLength - \CompactionTargetLength)\) directly determines \(\CompactionCycleTurnCount\), establishing how frequently the system amortizes \(\CompactionPassCost\).

Napkin Math 4.3: Spacing compaction passesProblem: The repair agent from notebook 4.1 appends each 4,000-token tool result and compacts instead of overflowing. Its 128,000-token context window, minus the 8,000-token output reserve, leaves 120,000 tokens for serialized input. Each compaction pass resets the prompt back to 47,000 tokens (matching the baseline selecting policy’s request size), and the subsequent pass triggers upon reaching 92,000 tokens. How often does compaction occur, and how many passes does the agent execute across its 30-turn step budget?
Variables: Every compaction pass resets the prompt to the exact target \(\CompactionTargetLength\). Turn-by-turn additions \(\TurnAppendLength\) remain constant at 4,000 tokens. The runtime evaluates buffer length after each tool addition and before dispatching the next model inference. The configured watermarks are operational policy choices rather than empirical performance limits.
Math: Applying equation 3 yields \(\CompactionCycleTurnCount = \lceil (92{,}000 - 47{,}000) / 4{,}000 \rceil = 12\) additions between successive compaction passes. The system hits the trigger at 95,000 input tokens, overshooting \(\CompactionTriggerLength\) by 3,000 tokens. Adding the reserved output capacity requires 103,000 tokens, safely within the window limit prior to compaction. Over the complete 30-turn trajectory budget, the runtime triggers 2 compaction passes, and each pass rewrites the trunk. These are the trunk rewrites that notebook 4.2 counted. Only the count carries over, because that notebook priced a fixed request with its leaf replaced on every call, whereas here the leaf grows between passes. If the post-compaction target instead rises to 81,000 tokens under identical arrival rates, the operational interval collapses to 3 additions.
Systems insight: Compaction frequency scales directly with the token arrival rate divided by the watermark gap. Narrowing that gap from 12 arrivals down to 3 forces compaction 4× as often. The per-turn amortized compaction overhead in equation 4 scales proportionally; setting a gap smaller than a single turn’s arrival causes thrashing, compacting on every step. Systems designers should size the watermark gap to span multiple arrivals and compress toward \(\CompactionTargetLength\) only as far as protected-field constraints permit, leaving the boundary between necessary context and dispensable detail to empirical validation.


A compressed observation captures only one facet of task progression. Driving an agentic repair to completion also requires maintaining the current candidate patch, the empirical checks validating it, the remaining test obligations, and the immediate next action. Because unstructured narrative summaries easily lose these dependency chains during aggressive compaction, the runtime must formalize them within an explicit, structured progress ledger.

title: 4 Context Engineering
text:
The repair has now moved through three events. First, at r17, the controlled test failed. Second, the agent’s candidate patch wrote r18. Third, the reproducer passed on r18. Once the third event has happened, the runtime must carry all three across the next compaction. A naive compaction summary that claims “fixed the notification bug” discards the precise distinctions the agent needs to plan its next action. In r17, a controlled diagnostic test observed a released connection returning to the pool while a waiting thread remained blocked. In r18, a targeted reproducer passed, establishing that the waiter is now awakened under those specific test conditions. That passing check provides evidence for the patch under an isolated scenario, but it proves nothing about full regression behavior or public API compatibility. Once the raw diagnostic exchanges are pruned from the context window, the next model call must still differentiate between verified empirical observations, working diagnostic hypotheses, and a fully validated repair.
A structured progress record maintains this operational state across context evictions using explicitly defined fields. Rather than replaying verbose conversational transcripts, the record encapsulates active task constraints, empirical observations, diagnostic hypotheses, artifact identifiers, and pending obligations. This schema exposes missing fields and internal contradictions to automated validation, though verifying whether those fields accurately reflect reality requires host-side auditing. This mechanism serves as a continuation record rather than an execution checkpoint: it conveys what the subsequent model invocation must know to proceed. The mechanical responsibilities of snapshotting running processes, tracking dirty workspace files, and supervising in-flight tool executions remain the domain of execution persistence.


↪ Execution checkpoints, which bind workspace snapshots and in-flight operations to a committed log position, are developed in Checkpoints.


A reliable progress record strictly partitions objective facts that the host runtime can verify from interpretive claims generated by the model. Active operational constraints originate in the initial task specification, not in a model’s fallible summary. Similarly, artifact versions and tool outcomes stem directly from host execution logs rather than free-form prose. A diagnostic narrative remains a hypothesis even when it cleanly accounts for observed symptoms. Enforcing explicit boundaries between these categories prevents a summarization step from silently mutating an exploratory directive like “test this repair” into an authoritative assertion that “this repair passed.”


↩︎ The five-part task specification contract, the source of a task’s binding constraints, is established in The five-part task specification contract.
In the connection-pool example, the agent must not have the authority to relax public API contracts, expand workspace boundaries, or bypass deployment restrictions simply by rewording its progress record. If a human operator alters the task parameters, the runtime injects the updated contract directly instead of retaining stale instructions to preserve a prompt prefix. Consequently, every progress record explicitly references the contract version against which it was constructed, enabling the runtime to validate its contents against currently authorized constraints. Table 7 illustrates how a structured manifest governs context continuation, defining the necessary contents and verification baselines for each field.



Table 7: A progress record for continuation: Named fields preserve the difference between historical evidence, the current candidate, and work still needed. Field presence alone does not establish semantic fidelity.










Record field
Repair information to retain
Basis for checking it




Task and constraints
Repair waiter notification; preserve the public API; approved workspace only; no production deployment
Current task contract and explicit authorized updates


Artifact identities
