Which removal should the runtime make first, and which measurement from section 4.8 would confirm the choice on a trained model?

4. Choosing a watermark gap (Intermediate). A noisier test suite raises arrivals to \(\TurnAppendLength = 6{,}000\) tokens. Compaction returns the request to \(\CompactionTargetLength = 47{,}000\) tokens: a 15,000-token root, a 24,000-token trunk, and an 8,000-token leaf. The output reserve is \(\OutputLimit = 8{,}000\). Two triggers are proposed, \(\CompactionTriggerLength = 92{,}000\) and \(\CompactionTriggerLength = 68{,}000\). Model each cycle as \(\CompactionCycleTurnCount\) ordinary calls at request lengths \(\CompactionTargetLength + \CompactionCycleTurnIndex \, \TurnAppendLength\) for \(\CompactionCycleTurnIndex = 1, \ldots, \CompactionCycleTurnCount\), the last of which triggers a compaction pass over the same request. The first ordinary call after a pass reuses only the root, because the pass rewrote the trunk; every later call reuses the whole previous request. Each ordinary call generates 1,000 output tokens. The compaction pass processes its entire input uncached and generates a 6,000-token record.

For each trigger, compute \(\CompactionCycleTurnCount\) from equation 3, the trigger length and overshoot, whether the trigger request plus \(\OutputLimit\) fits the window, and the number of passes within \(\TurnHorizon\).
Compute \(\CompactionPassCost\), the mean ordinary-call cost, and \(\AmortizedTurnCost\) from equation 4 for each trigger.
Each pass independently loses each of 10 unprotected constraints with probability 0.02. Compute the probability that all 10 survive every pass of the step budget under each trigger.
Choose a trigger and explain why the narrow gap loses on both cost and retention even though each of its passes is cheaper. What measured property of the workload would justify the narrow gap anyway?

5. Replace now, or ride the next rewrite? (Intermediate). Start from the request of notebook 4.4: 47,000 tokens behind a 15,000-token root, with an 850-token r17 excerpt opening the trunk, a 24-token replacement marker, and a 128-token appended notice. Twenty calls remain, and each later call reuses the whole previous request; the new leaf content is the same under both policies and can be ignored.

Compute the input cost of the next call under replacement and under an appended notice.
How many more tokens does the appended policy keep resident on every later call, what do they cost per call at the reused-prefix price, and after how many calls would the two policies break even on price alone?
A compaction pass is scheduled six calls from now and will rewrite the trunk regardless. Propose an invalidation policy that uses this fact, and state the condition under which it must replace the excerpt immediately anyway. Using equation 7, identify which of the next six decisions belong in the denominator and how the policy keeps the numerator at zero.

6. Paying for a protected-field check (Intermediate). A model-written progress record loses each of 12 required constraints independently with probability \(\CompactionLossProbability = 0.03\) per compaction round, and the trajectory runs 3 rounds. A lost constraint makes the task unacceptable; with every constraint intact, \(\AcceptanceProbability = 0.6\). An attempt costs $2. A protected-field check in the style of listing 2 detects 90 percent of losses and repairs each detected loss; budget it as one $0.05 correction call per round.

Without the check, compute the probability that all 12 constraints survive, the resulting \(\AcceptanceProbability\), and \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\).
Repeat with the check, treating undetected losses as the new per-round loss.
What per-round loss would an unchecked summarizer need to keep all-constraint survival at or above 95 percent over 3 rounds?
With the check in place, after how many rounds does all-constraint survival first fall below 50 percent? The runtime in section 4.6 copies contract constraints directly from the task contract. What does that change, and which protected fields remain exposed to \(\CompactionLossProbability\)?

7. A stable root for short sessions (Advanced). The support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)) serves 50,000 sessions a day. Each request carries a 20,000-token root of policy instructions and tool declarations and a 2,000-token customer record. A session makes 6 calls; before call \(\TurnIndex\) the request has grown by 1,500 tokens per turn to \(22{,}000 + 1{,}500\,\TurnIndex\) tokens, and each call generates 300 output tokens. Sessions arrive often enough that compatible root state is always resident. Layout A places the customer record and a session timestamp ahead of the root; Layout B places the root first. Within a session, every call after the first reuses the whole previous request under either layout.

Compute the input and output cost per session, the daily bill, and the token-weighted prefix hit rate under each layout.
Show that the entire difference arises on the first call of each session. Which term of equation 1 binds here, and how does that differ from what binds the repair agent over its step budget?
A developer templates the customer’s name into the first line of the policy instructions to personalize the tone. Which layout does that recreate, and what does it cost per day?
A cost review proposes cutting the root to 10,000 tokens by removing policy text. Under Layout B, compute the saving per session. With a 90 percent resolution rate at the full root, and each unresolved session escalating to a human at $4, how many percentage points of resolution can the cut lose before it costs more than it saves? What evidence should the proposal present before it ships?

8. Freshness through a human approval (Advanced). The remediation agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) decides on a production change from 5 observations of shared state. Other actors change each observed resource independently, as a Poisson process with mean rate \(\ResourceChangeRate\) of one change per 20 minutes. The runtime refreshes an observation only when it is older than a 10-minute time-to-live, so at decision time each observation’s age is uniformly distributed between 0 and 10 minutes.

Compute the probability that one observation still describes its resource at decision time and the probability that all 5 do. If every decision requires current evidence for all 5, estimate \(\StaleSupportRate\) from equation 7.
A teammate proposes refreshing all 5 observations immediately before each model call. The call takes 30 seconds, and the action executes after a human approval that takes 10 minutes. Compute the probability that at least one of the 5 resources changes between refresh and execution, first ignoring the approval and then including it. What does the result show about the limit of any context-refresh policy for this workload?
Only one observation, the configuration version the change edits, determines whether the action is safe; the other four were diagnostic. Redesign the policy around the binding \(\ObservationBinding(\TrajectoryObservation_{t})\) of equation 5 and an action-time precondition at the tool boundary that re-observes and re-requests approval when the precondition fails. Compute the probability that the precondition holds at execution and the expected number of approval rounds, and compare with a precondition on all 5 observations. Contrast the change signal available here with the one the repair agent uses after its own patch.


What’s Next: From selected tokens to physical attention stateThe runtime has chosen the token sequence for the next call, and the prefix-layout calculation priced its reused prefix as a discounted line on the bill. Behind that discount sits physical state. The serving system must decide whether to retain the attention state computed from earlier compatible prefixes, and holding it occupies accelerator memory even while the agent generates nothing and waits on a tool, memory that competing requests could use. KV Cache Management sizes that state and develops the storage, sharing, and retention decisions for it. Those decisions can change execution cost without changing which observations belong in the logical working context.

title: 6 Long-Term Memory
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why does an agent that can search everything it has ever stored still act on the wrong facts?
A context window holds the working state of one model call, and retained attention state only accelerates computation over that same prefix. Neither decides what an agent should still know across sessions, system restarts, or extended operational horizons. Providing an agent with persistent memory requires an external storage architecture that can index heterogeneous experiences, retrieve relevant historical context without polluting active prompts, and resolve conflicting observations over time. However, semantic vector retrieval alone provides no temporal guarantees. Stale facts, superseded code versions, and contradicted preferences score just as highly in cosine similarity as fresh ground truth. The runtime must therefore treat every stored memory as a fallible claim that carries its provenance, the versions for which it holds, and an explicit path to invalidation. Reliability depends on keeping persistent state behind explicit consistency rules rather than trusting the model to reconcile contradictory historical evidence.

Learning Objectives

Classify persistent records by their source, evidential role, and relationship to derived search representations
Specify a retrieval contract that bounds access, returned content, resource use, and required freshness
Choose among pre-staged evidence, a direct read, and model-directed search from how much of the need the task names
Select retrieval methods for an information need, use a bandwidth floor to screen exact vector scans against a latency budget, and estimate multi-hop evidence against a serialized-token budget
Design a memory write policy for admission, correction, supersession, expiry, and deletion
Explain version-aware exclusion and fallback without mistaking removal of stale candidates for complete fresh retrieval
Evaluate cross-session memory policies by task outcomes, update behavior, and total resource cost






Consider the repair agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)) working on its connection-pool defect across several sessions. When the initial session terminates, the subsequent run must reconstruct the operational state: the candidate source tree at revision r18, the diagnostic failure observed at r17, the passing run of test_waiter_notified_on_return, the integration checks that remain unresolved, and an operational note indicating where to resume execution. None of this state survives inside a transient context window once the process exits. Persisting only the final summary message discards critical supporting evidence. Conversely, retaining raw message transcripts without explicit scope creates confusion; an agent reading an unannotated log can easily mistake an earlier failure under r17 for an error in the new candidate patch.



Durable State, closed by checking each retrieved record against its source.
Standard runtime mechanisms do not bridge this gap. Context engineering selects among information already staged for a single model call, while the inference serving system maintains key-value (KV) attention cache state purely to accelerate that computation. Although a prefix cache can outlive an individual request, it remains a derived acceleration structure for a compatible prompt prefix (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\)), regardless of the storage medium holding it. Long-term memory addresses a different systems problem, preserving information that must govern decisions across distinct invocations. A durable memory system must explicitly resolve what records to retain, how to index and retrieve them efficiently, and how to update or invalidate them when external sources change. In the formal framing of The H·S·A Exposure Space, these records constitute durable State (\(\StateExposureLevel_3\)), persisting across session boundaries.
Architecting persistent memory for an agent requires solving three interconnected systems problems. First, the data model must establish explicit record roles that keep external sources, tool observations, and agent-authored notes strictly differentiated, ensuring that subsequent sessions recognize what evidence each record supports. Second, the system requires a retrieval contract. Regardless of the candidate generation mechanism, every read must report its query scope, the snapshot versions it admitted, and whether the search terminated cleanly or degraded under resource budgets. Third, the storage engine needs a write lifecycle that admits, updates, supersedes, expires, and deletes records while propagating those mutations to downstream indexes and summaries.
The chapter takes these problems in the order a read depends on them. Record roles come first (section 6.2), because every later indexing, retrieval, and invalidation policy depends on knowing what authority a stored record carries. The retrieval contract (section 6.3) then fixes what any read must specify and report, whatever index sits behind it, and the choice between pre-staged and model-directed retrieval (section 6.4) decides which component formulates the query. Three method sections match index structures to information needs, moving from names and syntax (section 6.5) through learned representations and fused rankings (section 6.6) to chains of related evidence (section 6.7). The write path (section 6.8) and storage invalidation (section 6.9) keep the store and its derived indexes truthful as sources change, and the final section (section 6.10) judges a complete memory policy by the tasks it helps finish across sessions.



When an autonomous agent repairs a system across multiple sessions, it relies on records that serve different operational purposes. The repository source defines what the code looks like at a given commit; an execution log records how a test behaved under specific runtime parameters; a progress note guides the subsequent session on where to resume work. Systems designers must distinguish these roles explicitly. Retrieval strategies, cache validation, and deletion policies all depend on the operational function of the record in question.


Most persistent state an agent consumes originates outside its execution loop, in version-controlled repositories, production databases, system configurations, and user profiles. Other records arise during execution, including raw environment observations, tool output traces, synthesized progress summaries, and speculative heuristics. Treating these diverse artifacts as undifferentiated “agent memory” obscures the critical distinction between a verifiable ground truth and a derived claim. Table 1 categorizes these records by their architectural role in the evidence chain.



Table 1: Roles of persistent records: These are roles in an evidence chain, not a hierarchy of storage devices or universal levels of trust. One record can serve more than one role.










Record role
Example
What a later use must preserve




Source record
src/pool.py at a specified revision; the user’s stated scheduling preference
The designated source, applicable version or scope, and access conditions


Observation or event log
The outcome of test_waiter_notified_on_return under recorded source, test, and configuration
What was observed, when, and under which conditions; gaps in the retained history


Agent-written memory
A progress note, session summary, or proposed repair lesson
Supporting records, uncertainty, intended scope, and the policy for correction or removal


Derived retrieval index
Search entries over source files, logs, or notes
Which source generation produced the entry and how changes affect its use






A source of record is the designated authoritative origin for a specific claim. For example, the Git tree serves as the source of record for a file’s contents at a particular commit hash, while an authenticated user message serves as the source of record for that user’s operational constraints. Establishing a source of record defines where any downstream assertion must be validated. It confers evidential provenance rather than correctness. A repository commit may harbor a regression, and an inline code comment may contain unauthorized instructions. Under the principle that authority stays with the source (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)), authority describes an evidentiary relationship between a claim and its origin, never an unconstrained permission grant. When an agent’s generated output drifts from its source of record, the output still binds whoever deployed the agent, as one tribunal made explicit in the case that follows. For a memory system, the further question is what happens when such an answer is kept and read again.

War Story 6.1: A support chatbot contradicts its policy page (2024)Context: In November 2022, following the death of his grandmother, passenger Jake Moffatt consulted the customer-support chatbot on Air Canada’s website regarding bereavement fares (Civil Resolution Tribunal of British Columbia 2024). Air Canada’s formal bereavement policy, published on a separate page of the website, explicitly prohibited retroactive bereavement fare adjustments once travel was completed.
Mechanism: The chatbot erroneously informed Moffatt that he could purchase regular-fare tickets immediately and submit a bereavement refund claim within 90 days of ticket issuance, directly contradicting the airline’s published policy. When Moffatt submitted his claim, Air Canada denied it based on the static policy page. Before the British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal, Air Canada argued that the chatbot was an independent legal entity responsible for its own actions.
Impact: The tribunal rejected Air Canada’s argument, finding that the chatbot was an integral component of Air Canada’s website and that the airline remained liable for all information published through it. Finding Air Canada liable for negligent misrepresentation, the tribunal ordered the airline to pay CA$650.88 in damages (representing the difference between the full fare and the bereavement rate), alongside interest and statutory tribunal fees.
Fix: The tribunal dismissed the assertion that customers must independently reconcile conflicting guidance across different website pages, holding that deployers bear full responsibility for auditing and aligning interactive automated assistants with published corporate policies.
Systems lesson: A generated response is a derived artifact, yet users and legal frameworks treat it as an authoritative corporate commitment. The engineering remedy is to stage the versioned source of record into the model call and constrain the answer to claims that text supports, which is the job of the retrieval contract developed below. Model fluency provides neither evidentiary validity nor legal protection.



Civil Resolution Tribunal of British Columbia. 2024. Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149. CanLII.
Through the taxonomy of table 1, the published policy page functioned as the source of record, while the chatbot’s generated response was a derived artifact that diverged from ground truth. If a customer-support system logs its previous dialogue turns to inform future responses, those conversational turns become agent-written memory. They document past interactions, but they never constitute organizational policy. A store that kept the chatbot’s wrong answer and retrieved it for the next bereavement question would repeat the error with the apparent weight of precedent, unless the record carried its role as a derived answer and a link to the policy version it claimed to reflect.
Observation logs capture empirical execution history. When an agent tests a connection pool, an execution log showing a failure at revision r17 remains invaluable diagnostic history even after revision r18 resolves the bug. The subsequent passing run confirms that the specific reproducer succeeded under that exact environment configuration. An execution log provides primary evidence of what the system observed during a run, rather than proving the universal validity of any underlying program assertion. Retaining this historical record across machine restarts or worker failures requires durable persistence guarantees.


↪ Durable, replicated logs that survive worker and machine failures are developed in The Trajectory Log.
Agent-written memory synthesizes raw observations into structured artifacts for future execution steps, taking the form of scratchpad notes, session summaries, or learned heuristics. Condensing raw traces prevents repetitive computation and conserves context window capacity. However, summarization introduces its own failure modes, because compression can strip vital boundary conditions or fabricate causal explanations. For instance, the observation that the targeted reproducer passed at r18 is strictly justified by the execution log. In contrast, the generalized claim that connection-pool timeouts always stem from missed thread notifications asserts a universal rule that a single test execution cannot substantiate. Storing an unsupported generalization in a persistent database creates compounding errors in subsequent planning steps.
This divergence mirrors the foundational distinction from cognitive psychology (Tulving 1972) adopted by agent architectures: episodic memory captures discrete, time-stamped events anchored to specific execution contexts, whereas semantic memory stores generalized knowledge, rules, and abstractions extracted across multiple episodes, complemented by procedural memory that preserves executable workflows, tool scripts, and operational runbooks. In the terms of table 1, observation logs and episode summaries are episodic records, generated lessons and reference facts are semantic records, and reusable repair workflows represent procedural records. In an engineered system, semantic and procedural records are therefore derived artifacts whose epistemic validity depends entirely on the fidelity and scope of the underlying episodic records.

Tulving, Endel. 1972. “Episodic and Semantic Memory.” In Organization of Memory, edited by Endel Tulving and Wayne Donaldson. Academic Press.
A retrieval index serves as an auxiliary acceleration structure for locating information across storage tiers. Whether an index stores term postings, learned vector embeddings, or graph edges over source files, logs, and agent notes (structures this chapter develops in turn), indexing only facilitates discovery. When a search query matches an index entry, a high similarity score demonstrates lexical or semantic affinity to the query string, but provides no assurance of operational applicability to the current task. Operational applicability depends on whether the referenced record matches the current system state, schema revision, and environment constraints.



Consider the state of a code-repair agent immediately after it writes revision r18. If its vector or keyword index was generated from revision r17, a retrieval query for src/pool.py will return the unpatched file. While that record remains an accurate historical reflection of r17, serving it as current context leads the model to believe the bug persists, prompting redundant or conflicting edits. The staleness that context invalidation guards against thus extends beyond the active prompt into the persistent storage tiers that feed subsequent inference calls.


↩︎ Context invalidation, which withdraws a staged observation’s authority over current state once its source changes, is established in Context Invalidation.
Precomputing search indexes eliminates the need to scan large repositories or execution histories during inference. However, this optimization incurs an ongoing synchronization cost. Every update to a source file requires indexing new content and invalidating or evicting obsolete embeddings. Executing these updates synchronously blocks read or write operations, while background asynchronous indexing opens a lag window in which the index still answers from r17 although the file is already at r18. A query that arrives inside that window needs an explicit rule for what it may return, which section 6.9.2 supplies.
Conversational agents meet the same consistency problem in user state. A user who said “Schedule no meetings before 10:00 AM” later says “before 11:00 AM.” The two directives are nearly identical as text, yet their intent is mutually exclusive. A store that treats the second as a duplicate keeps the stale behavior, and one that appends it without retiring the first leaves a contradiction in every later prompt. Telling a complementary fact from a superseding one requires explicit lifecycle metadata, which the write path (section 6.8) supplies and carries to every derived index, alongside validation, time-to-live (TTL) expiration, and cascade deletion.
The read side comes first, because lifecycle metadata protects the agent only if every read reports it. A retrieval interface must therefore return candidate text alongside the provenance, version, and completeness information on which safe execution depends.




Diagnosing the connection pool’s stalled waiter requires both the current implementation in src/pool.py and the test telemetry associated with test_waiter_notified_on_return. A search across repository history can easily return both an r17 test failure and an r18 reproducer pass. While both records are genuine, they answer distinct questions: one documents the defect that triggered the investigation, whereas the other evaluates a candidate patch. Before choosing an index structure or a similarity metric, a system must specify what the agent’s next decision demands and what guarantees a returned record actually establishes.

Definition 6.1: Retrieval contract
A retrieval contract specifies the information requested, the permitted scope and resource limits of the read, and the provenance, applicability, and completion information returned with its results.

Significance: It ensures a bounded search result remains interpretable before that result enters the next model invocation. A misread or misattributed result exacts a double penalty in the cost per accepted task (equation 1.2): its tokens consume prompt budget and inference cost during the attempt, while the mistaken decision it induces drives down the acceptance probability.
Distinction: Ranking algorithms merely score and order candidate items under a specific relevance heuristic. The retrieval contract establishes authorization boundaries, version constraints, serialization budgets, and explicit completion semantics.
Common pitfall: Mistaking an empty result or a truncated scan for definitive proof that the requested data does not exist.



This contract applies uniformly whether the agent executes an index search, a relational database query, or a direct filesystem read; it mandates no single storage layout or similarity threshold. It divides the work among three parties (figure 1). The runtime sets the request’s bounds, the retrieval service checks access and searches within them, and the result envelope reports status, provenance, and limitations before the runtime stages any evidence for the next model call.






Figure 1: The Retrieval Contract: The runtime sets the request’s scope, version requirement, and limits; the model may propose search terms but cannot widen those bounds. The retrieval service checks access, searches, and excludes inapplicable versions, and the envelope reports what was searched and whether the operation completed, returned a partial result, or was unavailable. Only then does the runtime stage selected evidence, with its source and version labels, within the payload budget.





A raw information need such as “find the notification logic” underspecifies the retrieval operation. It leaves undefined whether the caller requires the active workspace, an earlier Git revision, or a diff between them; it says nothing about which repositories the principal may access; and it ignores how many tokens the caller’s remaining context window can accommodate. As summarized in table 2, framing retrieval as a bounded request separates these operational constraints from the underlying index mechanics.



Table 2: A bounded retrieval request: The runtime can supply task-wide defaults, while each query specializes the information need within those limits.










Request field
Meaning in the repair task
Boundary it establishes




Query or information need
Locate the waiter-notification implementation or the recorded reproducer result
The requested match or observation, not a promise that it exists


Authorized scope and principal
The designated repair workspace and the identity under which it is read
The runtime checks permitted paths and records; a scope string alone grants no access


Version or freshness requirement
Read r18, compare r17 with r18, or read the current source under stated snapshot semantics
Which state can answer the question


Result-count and payload limits
Bound returned items and their serialized representation
Count and content size are separate limits


Execution limits
Deadline and supported bounds on scans, expansions, or other search work
When to stop waiting or searching and report incomplete work


Optional filters
Restrict file type, symbol kind, or other relevant metadata
Narrow the information need without replacing authorization






A version requirement differs fundamentally from a wall-clock freshness heuristic. An index entry for revision r17 remains invalid as current r18 source code even if an indexing worker refreshed it seconds ago. Wall-clock TTLs merely trigger periodic reindexing, whereas explicit version tokens establish whether a cached representation strictly matches its underlying source snapshot. When the retrieval service cannot fulfill the requested version from its precomputed index, it must either fall back to an authorized direct read of the primary store or return an explicit incomplete status. Section 6.9 develops this trade-off once the index itself can lag its source.
Similarly, result-count, payload-size, and compute limits constrain different dimensions of system resource consumption. Ten complete source files consume far more serialized tokens than ten function docstrings, yet returning a single item might still require scanning millions of candidate records. The payload limit protects the caller’s downstream context window, search-work budgets (such as graph traversal caps or posting-list scan limits) constrain retrieval service compute, and execution deadlines prevent the agent runtime from blocking indefinitely. Client timeouts must also propagate cancellation signals to the underlying storage engines; uncancelled background queries continue to consume backend resources and inflate total execution cost.



A production retrieval service returns metadata describing the search execution alongside the matching records. At the response level, the result envelope specifies the repository scope and snapshot revision actually searched, the terminal execution status, and any operational constraints that qualify the results:

complete confirms that the declared search algorithm ran to conclusion under its stated semantics. It is a mechanical guarantee about the search performed, not a claim to have found every relevant fact.
partial indicates that the operation halted before exhaustive evaluation, explicitly recording the abort reason (such as an expired deadline, an unavailable index partition, or an output payload cap).
unavailable signals that the retrieval subsystem failed to return usable data, whether due to network partitions, authorization failures, or service crashes.

When an operation yields partial results or truncates output to respect payload limits, the envelope provides an opaque continuation cursor so subsequent bounded requests can resume paging without re-executing the entire query.
These statuses decide what the runtime may infer when a query returns zero hits, a rule this chapter calls the absence rule. An empty result proves nonexistence if and only if a fully completed exhaustive scan produced it, and even then only within the scanned scope and revision snapshot. A completed literal string search across the repository showing that a symbol does not occur in revision r18 meets this standard. A truncated or partial scan that returns zero matches proves nothing, because the target may reside in an unvisited partition. An approximate index (section 6.6.2) offers no absence guarantee even when it completes, because it deliberately skips most of the candidate space to save work; a result set that lacks the relevant record may reflect that skipped region rather than the record’s absence from the corpus.
At the item level, every returned record carries structured metadata alongside its raw content: a persistent URI or path, byte or line ranges, the exact source commit or snapshot identifier, and a content hash of the returned bytes. When an item represents an empirical observation, such as a test execution log, the record must document the runtime configuration, environment variables, test revision, and terminal outcome. If an item stores a derived lesson or summary synthesized by an agent in an earlier session, its envelope must link to the primary records supporting that inference and flag its status as a derived model output. If the retrieval engine attaches a relevance score, it must name the algorithm that produced it (a lexical ranking function, a vector similarity, or a learned reranker, each developed later in this chapter). Ranking scores exist on their algorithm’s internal scale; systems must not treat them as calibrated probabilities.



Listing 1: A serialized result envelope: The response-level fields report what was searched and how the search ended; each item carries its role, location, version, and hash beside its content. Symbolic values stand for settings and contents chosen by the runtime; the field names do not prescribe a storage API.


status: complete
scope: {workspace: repair, principal: repair-agent, source_snapshot: r18}
items:
  - role: source_record
    path: src/pool.py
    lines: [a, b]
    revision: r18
    content_hash: h18
    score: {method: lexical_rank, value: s}
    content: <slice of the return path>
  - role: observation
    test: test_waiter_notified_on_return
    revision: r17
    configuration: c17
    outcome: failed
    content: <recorded failure trace>



In the connection-pool repair task, the staged payload might pair a slice of src/pool.py from revision r18 with an error trace recorded under revision r17, as in listing 1, where the fields outside the two content bodies count against the payload budget just as the bodies do. The r17 trace explains why the repair was initiated, but it provides zero evidence regarding the behavior of the r18 candidate. By packaging each record in an explicit envelope, the retrieval subsystem preserves these applicability distinctions across the boundary between persistent storage and the working context. Envelope labels, however, record provenance without certifying veracity. A cryptographic content hash verifies only that the byte sequence matches a specific snapshot; it does not validate the factual correctness of the text. Similarly, categorizing a record as user input or agent-written memory confers no administrative authority on any instructions embedded within that content.



The agent runtime, never the retrieval backend or an uncalibrated ranking score, determines which records enter the downstream prompt. The runtime curates evidence tailored to the immediate decision, preserves the source and version tags necessary for correct interpretation, and measures the token footprint of the serialized payload. Staging is where invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) reaches the durable read boundary. The bound below the model is mechanical, because a runtime rule rather than the model or the ranker decides what is admitted, and the version labels it preserves are the evidence a later acceptance check needs to tell an r17 observation from an r18 one.
Returned text remains untrusted data, even when fetched from a local repository. While defensive serialization formats cleanly separate retrieved payloads from system instructions, language models can still be misled by adversarial or malformed text embedded inside document bodies. This hazard, prompt injection, occurs when retrieved text hijacks the agent’s control flow, attempting to redirect execution away from the authorized task.


↪ Indirect prompt injection, delivered through retrieved documents and other observations an agent reads, is developed in Prompt injection entry points.
Accurate payload accounting must measure the entire serialized envelope, including wrapper tags, source paths, version identifiers, and status headers, alongside the raw text bodies. Underestimating this structural overhead leads directly to context exhaustion. The ledger in notebook 6.1 demonstrates how metadata overhead alters the number of complete records an agent can stage within a fixed prompt allocation.

Napkin Math 6.1: Making room for retrieved evidenceProblem: A hypothetical model call permits 32,768 tokens in total. Reserving 2,048 tokens for generation leaves the remainder for input. If baseline system prompts, tool schemas, and conversation history occupy 24,576 tokens, how many complete retrieval records can the prompt accommodate?
Math: The retrieval allowance is \(32,768 - 2,048 - 24,576 = 6,144\) tokens. Assume a 128-token response envelope and records that each contain 512 body tokens plus 64 metadata tokens, giving 576 tokens per record.
The maximum number of complete records that fit is 10. Staging these records alongside their envelope consumes \(128 + 10 \times 576 = 5,888\) tokens, leaving a remainder of 256 tokens, too few to hold another complete record.
A naive sizing policy that accounts only for raw document bodies would admit 12 records. When serialized with metadata and envelopes, however, those records require 7,040 tokens, overshooting the allocated retrieval budget by 896 tokens.
Systems insight: Metadata and envelope framing consume context capacity just as surely as document bodies. In this configuration, each record dedicates 64 of its 576 tokens to provenance, causing a body-only heuristic to overcommit the prompt by 2 records. Systems runtimes must reserve capacity for output tokens and the global envelope first, then admit \(\lfloor(\text{allowance} - \text{envelope})/(\text{body} + \text{metadata})\rfloor\) records, remembering that every token assigned to system instructions or tool definitions shrinks the retrieval allowance one for one.


Because subword tokenizers (such as Byte-Pair Encoding) merge tokens across string boundaries, tokenizing text fragments in isolation and summing their counts yields an inaccurate total. Runtimes must measure token lengths on the final, fully serialized prompt structure using the target model’s tokenizer. When a critical record exceeds the remaining budget, the runtime must not silently truncate the text. Instead, it should stage a syntactically coherent excerpt with explicit truncation markers, defer the item to a subsequent retrieval pass, or return an opaque handle that the model can resolve on demand.
Every staged token also incurs concrete inference engine overhead beyond occupying space in the context window. Retrieved context must be processed through the model’s compute-intensive prefill phase and then pinned in accelerator memory as key-value (KV) cache tensors for the duration of the generation cycle or prefix cache retention window. Staging more records increases the token volume that the serving engine must process and retain, although the resulting prefill latency depends on the model, prefix reuse, and serving configuration. Every retained token counts against the resident-fit bound of the serving node’s KV pool, so a generous staging policy reduces how many trajectories the node can serve concurrently.


↩︎ The per-sequence footprint of key-value cache state, and how it limits the number of sequences a node can serve concurrently, is established in The Footprint of Retained Attention State.

Checkpoint 6.1: Interpreting a bounded result
Each question presents a retrieval outcome; decide what operational conclusions it licenses.

Stale excerpt: A query for current source returns an r17 excerpt after the workspace reaches r18. Which historical diagnostic inferences remain valid, and what must happen before the excerpt informs an r18 edit?
Deadline vs. completion: A search reaches its deadline with no matches. Which status does it return, and which conclusion that a completed literal scan of the same snapshot would support is unavailable here?
Payload estimate: If per-record metadata doubled from the value in notebook 6.1, how many complete records would fit the same allowance, and what must the runtime measure before dispatching the call?



The retrieval contract establishes the operational bounds, provenance requirements, and payload limits for each read, but it leaves open an architectural question, namely which component formulates the query. A runtime can predict needed evidence and pre-stage it before invoking the model, or it can equip the agent with search tools to probe the store interactively as discoveries unfold.




When the repair agent diagnoses the stalled waiter in its connection pool, the runtime must decide how to supply the model with relevant evidence. Two distinct retrieval architectures address this challenge. In a pre-staged architecture, the runtime predicts which artifacts will be necessary (such as src/pool.py, tests/test_pool.py, and a stack trace from a prior run) and injects them directly into the prompt before model execution begins. In an agentic architecture, the runtime equips the model with bounded text search, file reading, and symbol-navigation tools, allowing the agent to locate notification logic, inspect the test harness, and follow cross-file references as intermediate discoveries dictate. Both architectures operate over the same underlying storage systems and share identical security boundaries. They differ in when the information need is resolved and which component formulates the retrieval queries.
Pre-staging implements standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where the host system selects external documents and packages them alongside the prompt before inference begins (Lewis et al. 2020). By contrast, agentic retrieval delegates query formulation to the model during the execution loop, interleaving environment observations with subsequent reasoning and action steps (Yao et al. 2023). Autonomous systems designed for repository-scale software engineering (Jimenez et al. 2024) rely heavily on this interactive paradigm, because providing the model with search and navigation commands shaped for code inspection proves far more adaptable than staging a single, static set of top-\(\RetrievalCutoffCount\) retrieved passages up front (Yang et al. 2024). Rather than mutually exclusive alternatives, these two patterns represent complementary policies operating over the same underlying data stores.

Jimenez, Carlos E., John Yang, Alexander Wettig, Shunyu Yao, Kexin Pei, Ofir Press, and Karthik Narasimhan. 2024. “SWE-Bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Yang, John, Carlos E Jimenez, Alexander Wettig, Kilian Lieret, Shunyu Yao, Karthik Narasimhan, and Ofir Press. 2024. “SWE-Agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems.
Pre-staging excels when the evidence required for the next decision is predictable. Loading src/pool.py and tests/test_pool.py directly into the prompt eliminates the latency and inference cost of an exploratory turn spent locating those files. However, pre-staging carries operational risks. It can consume scarce context capacity with irrelevant code, or conversely, miss transitively imported dependencies that only become apparent upon inspecting the source. Model-directed iterative search resolves this rigidity by allowing each discovery to reshape subsequent queries. For example, a failing assertion in a test file might name an internal helper function, prompting the agent to inspect that specific definition next. Interactive exploration, however, introduces its own failure modes. An agent can chase unpromising leads, execute redundant searches across familiar directories, or terminate its investigation prematurely before gathering sufficient evidence.
Before introducing an auxiliary index, such as an inverted text index or a vector store, an engineer should benchmark against a live-source baseline. Bounded substring searches and direct file reads inspect the target workspace directly on disk, introducing no external index that can lag behind ongoing edits. When a problem description already specifies exact filenames or literal error strings, these live-source primitives often supply all the retrieval capability the agent requires. Direct filesystem access, however, presents distinct systems trade-offs. Live reads observe whichever version of a file exists at the exact moment of execution; if concurrent processes modify the workspace, separate reads executed across successive turns can straddle modifications and observe inconsistent snapshots. Furthermore, raw literal searches locate character matches without semantic awareness, failing to distinguish an active symbol definition from an obsolete comment or an unrelated log message. An auxiliary index justifies its memory footprint, construction time, and synchronization overhead only when it measurably amortizes repetitive scanning costs across long trajectories, resolves vocabulary mismatches through semantic embeddings, or accelerates traversal over structural relationships such as call graphs derived from abstract syntax trees (ASTs). An evaluation must charge the cost of building and refreshing the index directly against its query-time savings, a charge the chapter prices at its end, once lexical, dense, and graph indexes are in hand (notebook 6.5).
When an agent probes its environment, the runtime can optimize query execution through parallelism. A single model turn can emit several independent tool calls that the runtime batches or executes concurrently across threads; only queries that strictly depend on earlier observations must block for sequential resolution. Under both paradigms, the execution runtime retains authority over security boundaries and resource consumption. The model acts strictly as an untrusted query generator. It may propose a narrower search path, supply query strings, or request specific filters, but it can never expand the authorized workspace, assume a different principal identity, or increase its own resource ceilings. The runtime enforces these boundaries at the tool interface. Tool calling schemas define and constrain the supported request parameters, while tool execution results transmit truncation warnings, resource limits, and continuation tokens back to the agent.


↪ Tool interface schemas that bound which request parameters a model may supply are developed in Tool Interface Schemas.
In production systems, these two strategies often merge into a tiered hybrid policy. The runtime pre-stages a compact workspace outline, an architectural summary, or persistent user preferences directly into the initial context window, giving the model immediate structural grounding. The agent then issues targeted tool calls to inspect specific function implementations or test traces only when those details become necessary. Evaluating such a hybrid design requires balancing the upfront token overhead of pre-staging against the inference latency and token expenditure of avoided tool turns.
The choice among a direct read, pre-staging, and directed probing follows from how much of the information need the task itself names. When the task names its targets, such as src/pool.py or a pinned note, a direct read stages exactly those records and spends no ranking or exploratory turn. When the needed evidence is predictable but unnamed, such as the tests that usually accompany a module, pre-staging captures it in one step at the price of some irrelevant tokens. When each needed item can be found only from the one before, as when a failing assertion names a helper whose definition names a lock, no pre-staged set can anticipate the chain, and model-directed probing pays one model round per dependent hop. A hybrid seeds the first hop by pre-staging or direct read and leaves the remaining hops to probing. Whichever component formulates the query, what comes back depends on the matching mechanism behind the read, whether lexical matching, learned similarity, or structural traversal, and each mechanism answers a different kind of information need.



When the repair agent investigates its stalled waiter, it faces distinct information needs: locating tests/test_pool.py, finding references to test_waiter_notified_on_return, and isolating the function enclosing a suspect synchronization statement. A well-designed retrieval contract does not force these varied tasks through a single mechanism. A known file path requires only a direct file read. A specific identifier calls for literal text search or symbol lookup. A broad symptom description requires ranking multiple candidate passages before the agent can decide which source files merit inspection.


Exact path lookup retrieves a named object directly from an authorized repository snapshot. Literal text search scans for exact character sequences under declared matching rules such as case sensitivity and boundary delimiters. Neither mechanism interprets semantic role: a match on a test identifier might point to its primary definition, a passing mention in a comment, an import statement, or an entry in an archived failure log.
To support repeated lexical queries across large corpora without scanning every byte on disk, retrieval systems rely on an inverted index (Zobel and Moffat 2006). The index maps each distinct term to a postings list containing every document where the term appears. Beyond the document identifier, each posting typically stores the term’s in-document frequency and position offsets. How source text maps into postings depends entirely on the index’s analyzer. The analyzer determines token boundaries: whether it preserves full identifier tokens, splits snake_case and camelCase identifiers, normalizes letter case, or strips inflectional affixes through stemming. Consequently, a ranked match on an analyzed identifier behaves differently from an exact match on the raw string. When an agent requires an exact literal hit, it must either query an unanalyzed exact-match field or verify the returned source snippet directly.
1 BM25 (Best Match 25): The name records one weighting in the “Best Match” series of the Okapi retrieval system, built on the simple approximations to a two-Poisson model of term occurrence that Robertson and Walker (1994) derived. The formula survived decades of learned rankers because it needs no training data, only corpus statistics an index already keeps, which is why it remains the baseline a repository agent can deploy on the day its workspace is created. 
Robertson, Stephen E., and Steve Walker. 1994. “Some Simple Effective Approximations to the 2-Poisson Model for Probabilistic Weighted Retrieval.” SIGIR ’94, 232–41. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4471-2099-5_24.
2 Inverse Document Frequency (IDF): Spärck Jones (1972) proposed weighting a term by how few documents contain it, on the argument that a term shared by most documents cannot tell them apart. In a repository that argument favors exactly the tokens an agent searches for, such as a unique test name or error string, and discounts keywords every file shares, which is why a rare identifier ranks sharply under BM25 while a vague symptom description does not. 
Spärck Jones, Karen. 1972. “A Statistical Interpretation of Term Specificity and Its Application in Retrieval.” Journal of Documentation 28 (1): 11–21. https://doi.org/10.1108/eb026526.
When a query matches dozens or hundreds of candidates, ranking determines which documents enter the agent’s bounded context window. The BM251 scoring function balances three factors: term rarity across the corpus,2 sub-linear term frequency saturation within each candidate, and document-length normalization (Robertson and Zaragoza 2009):
\[
\operatorname{score}(\LexicalDocument,\LexicalQuery)=\sum_{\QueryWord\in \LexicalQuery}\operatorname{IDF}(\QueryWord)
\frac{\QueryWordFrequency(\QueryWord,\LexicalDocument)(\LexicalFrequencySaturation+1)}{\QueryWordFrequency(\QueryWord,\LexicalDocument)+\LexicalFrequencySaturation(1-\LexicalLengthNormalization+\LexicalLengthNormalization\lvert \LexicalDocument\rvert/\MeanDocumentLength)},
\qquad
\operatorname{IDF}(\QueryWord)=\ln\left(1+\frac{\IndexedDocumentCount-\QueryWordDocumentFrequency(\QueryWord)+0.5}{\QueryWordDocumentFrequency(\QueryWord)+0.5}\right).
\tag{1}\]
Here \(\LexicalQuery\) contains the query terms, \(\LexicalDocument\) is an indexed document, \(\QueryWordFrequency(\QueryWord,\LexicalDocument)\) is the term frequency of \(\QueryWord\) in \(\LexicalDocument\), \(\lvert \LexicalDocument\rvert\) is the document length in analyzer terms, and \(\MeanDocumentLength\) is the collection’s mean document length. The corpus contains \(\IndexedDocumentCount\) documents in total, of which \(\QueryWordDocumentFrequency(\QueryWord)\) contain query term \(\QueryWord\). These lengths are analyzer counts, not the foundation model’s token counts. These symbols are local to lexical ranking; in particular, \(\LexicalDocument\) and \(\LexicalLengthNormalization\) do not carry the meanings earlier chapters gave those letters. The tuning parameter \(\LexicalFrequencySaturation>0\) controls term-frequency saturation. At a fixed document length, the frequency factor rises toward \(\LexicalFrequencySaturation+1\) as \(\QueryWordFrequency(\QueryWord,\LexicalDocument)\) grows, so each additional occurrence adds less to the score than the one before. The parameter \(\LexicalLengthNormalization\in[0,1]\) modulates document-length normalization, with \(\LexicalLengthNormalization=1\) fully penalizing documents proportional to their relative length and \(\LexicalLengthNormalization=0\) disabling length normalization entirely. Because ranking depends on these mechanics, document chunk boundaries, analyzer choices, and parameter settings alter candidate scores even when the underlying source text remains unchanged.

Example 6.1: A higher lexical score is a ranking decisionScenario: Consider a hypothetical index of 100,000 documents with a mean length of 400 analyzer terms. A single query term appears in 5 documents. With \(\LexicalFrequencySaturation=\) 1.2 and \(\LexicalLengthNormalization=\) 0.75, its inverse document frequency is 9.808.
Analysis: A short candidate contains 80 terms and 1 occurrence of the query term; a long candidate contains 4,000 terms and 6 occurrences. The length term \(\LexicalFrequencySaturation(1-\LexicalLengthNormalization+\LexicalLengthNormalization\lvert \LexicalDocument\rvert/\MeanDocumentLength)\) in the denominator of equation 1 is 0.48 for the short candidate but 9.3 for the long one, so the long candidate’s extra occurrences are divided by a far larger denominator. Substituting these counts into the scoring rule gives 14.58 for the short candidate and 8.46 for the long candidate. Repetition alone does not determine their order: saturation and length normalization outweigh the long candidate’s additional occurrences.
Systems lesson: Rank orders candidates for inspection. If the short candidate is a comment while the long one holds the implementation, the agent still needs source inspection or structural information, and choosing whole files rather than functions as documents would change both scores.





Lexical matches identify raw text occurrences. Structural retrieval distinguishes program organization: the enclosing function, type declarations, lexical scopes, and identifiers in call expressions. A parser translates source text into abstract syntax trees with explicit spans, while symbol resolution and semantic analysis establish directed relationships between definitions and call sites. While parsing a call expression identifies the call site syntactically, resolving which concrete implementation executes at runtime requires interprocedural analysis.
During the connection-pool repair, a structural query can return the entire function containing a notification call in src/pool.py rather than an arbitrary fragment, and a reference query can subsequently identify its callers across the codebase. Static coverage depends on language semantics, dependencies, and build configuration; dynamic dispatch, reflection, generated code, and cross-process calls frequently escape static resolution. In a structural index, a missing edge indicates a gap in static coverage rather than an unreachable path, while a static call edge records a potential invocation rather than an executed one. The two representations see the pool’s sources differently (figure 2). A lexical index finds the term notify in the pool source and the r17 failure log alike, whereas a structural index records that the waiter test calls the pool’s return method, which in turn calls the notification, a caller-callee chain that string matching cannot recover.






Figure 2: Occurrences vs. Relationships: A lexical index (A) maps each analyzed term to postings of documents and frequencies, so the term notify matches the pool source and the r17 failure log alike. A structural index (B) records parsed containment and resolved calls, here from the waiter test to the pool’s return method and on to its notification call. Its coverage is declared rather than complete, because a dynamic call can leave a target unresolved.

Restricting an initial probe to src/pool.py and tests/test_pool.py focuses the evidence and limits noise, provided the retrieval interface explicitly reports that bounded scope; a subsequent probe can widen the scope to investigate callers across the repository.
Filtering and ranking interact directly. A service that selects its top-ranked candidates globally and only then discards those outside the requested paths (post-filtering) can easily return an empty set while eligible matches sit farther down the global ranking. Restricting candidates before final scoring (pre-filtering) avoids this loss, as does continuing postings traversal until the requested quota of filtered documents is filled. When query budgets or latency limits terminate the search early, the result remains partial.
Choosing the evaluation order is a cost-based optimization decision analogous to access path selection in relational database optimizers (Selinger et al. 1979).3 The decision balances the filter’s selectivity against the rarity of the query terms. A selective filter, such as one that isolates two files in a repository of thousands, favors pre-filtering candidate documents and evaluating BM25 scores only on the survivors. Conversely, a broad filter paired with a rare identifier favors scoring first, because the rare term’s postings list is already short, provided the search engine continues scanning until enough eligible results remain. This trade-off reemerges with even sharper operational hazards when searching vector proximity graphs (section 6.6).
3 Cost-Based Access Path Selection: The System R optimizer chose among index scans, sequential scans, and join orders by estimating each predicate’s selectivity and the pages each plan would touch (Selinger et al. 1979). A retrieval gateway faces the same estimate with a scope filter as the predicate and a postings list or vector index as the access path, and a wrong estimate costs either a scan of the whole corpus or an empty result that looks like absence.

Exact and structural lookups succeed when the agent already possesses informative names or file locations. Early in an investigation, however, the agent may know only an observed symptom: “a connection is returned, but another caller keeps waiting,” phrased in words the source code never uses. This is the vocabulary mismatch problem, where system designers and users formulate identical concepts using distinct vocabularies (Furnas et al. 1987). Heuristic techniques like identifier splitting, synonym expansion, or query reformulation can recover some lexical matches; once an exploratory search identifies a concrete test name, literal lookup is far more direct than further conceptual search.
When lexical heuristics still leave the candidate set inadequate, the agent needs a representation that maps descriptive prose to differently worded source implementations, along with hybrid rankers that combine dense semantic similarity with exact lexical precision without mistaking similarity for verification.




When an agent investigates a bug report describing a caller that hangs indefinitely, lexical search across the repository can easily rank the critical return path in src/pool.py low or miss it entirely. The line that matters executes notify(), but the report describes a caller that keeps waiting. Dense retrieval supplies a complementary candidate-generation mechanism, using learned representations to match a query against records that share underlying meaning rather than literal tokens. Because dense and lexical methods fail in different places, production systems usually run both and combine their rankings, which is where this section ends.


Dense retrieval encodes a query and each searchable record as vectors using a learned model, ranking records by vector similarity.4 In a bi-encoder architecture, records are embedded offline before a request arrives, leaving only the query to be encoded online at request time (Karpukhin et al. 2020). This separation removes heavy embedding inference from the critical query path. However, offline encoding remains an ongoing operational requirement. Newly inserted or modified records require fresh vector generation, and upgrading or fine-tuning the underlying encoder invalidates the entire index, demanding a complete corpus re-embedding.
4 Vector Space Model: Ranking documents by the angle between a query vector and each document vector predates learned encoders; Salton et al. (1975) represented every document as a vector of term weights and scored it by cosine similarity. Dense retrieval keeps the geometry and replaces sparse, interpretable term weights with learned components, which is what lets it bridge vocabulary and also why no single component explains a match. 
Salton, G., A. Wong, and C. S. Yang. 1975. “A Vector Space Model for Automatic Indexing.” Communications of the ACM 18 (11): 613–20. https://doi.org/10.1145/361219.361220.
The distance metric is defined by the interaction between the encoder and index configurations. For example, inner product search is mathematically identical to cosine similarity when vectors are unit-normalized (\(\ell_2 = 1.0\)), which shifts the computational cost of vector normalization to indexing time rather than paying for vector division on the query path. Neither metric, however, produces a calibrated probability that a candidate record answers the agent’s question; they represent uncalibrated geometric affinities.
In the software repair task, a dense retriever can readily connect the symptom of a waiting caller to the return-and-notify implementation, yielding a promising candidate for inspection rather than proof of a defect. The semantic abstraction that bridges vocabulary gaps, however, can also blur fine syntactic distinctions on which code execution depends. Consider a concrete case in src/pool.py: the return path invokes self._available.notify(), the shutdown routine invokes self._available.notify_all(), and acquisition invokes self._available.wait(timeout). All three statements share the same condition variable, module context, and conceptual vocabulary of thread synchronization. Consequently, an encoder often maps all three to neighboring points in vector space when queried about thread unblocking. Their operational semantics are nonetheless entirely distinct: one wakes a single waiter, another wakes every waiter, and the third blocks. An exact lexical search for notify( isolates the call site immediately, and BM25 assigns the rare identifier a high inverse document frequency (IDF). The systems challenge is therefore determining which retrieval mechanism surfaces the precise evidence the workload requires.



An exact vector scan scores every vector in the eligible search set under the chosen distance metric. It serves as the baseline ground truth for measuring what an approximate search misses, and it remains a practical serving method whenever the eligible candidate set is small.
The fundamental resource requirements of an exact scan follow directly from dimensional arithmetic, independent of any specific hardware architecture. Let \(\EligibleVectorCount\) be the number of eligible vectors, \(\EmbeddingDimension\) their dimension, and \(\ElementStorageSize\) the storage width in bytes per component; like the ranking symbols before them, these letters are local to vector search. Traversing the stored vectors requires streaming \(\EligibleVectorCount \EmbeddingDimension\ElementStorageSize\) bytes from memory, so on a memory system that sustains bandwidth \(\Bandwidth\) one scan takes at least \(\EligibleVectorCount \EmbeddingDimension\ElementStorageSize/\Bandwidth\). Counting two floating-point operations per multiply-accumulate operation, dot-product scoring requires approximately \(2\EligibleVectorCount \EmbeddingDimension\) FLOPs. These totals account only for the vector inner products; they exclude the latency of query embedding, top-\(\RetrievalCutoffCount\) heap maintenance, and fetching the full record payloads from persistent storage.


↪ The roofline model and the ridge point that separates bandwidth-bound from compute-bound work are developed in Cost Asymmetry Between Input Prefill and Output Generation.

Napkin Math 6.2: Why an exact vector scan is bandwidth-boundProblem: Consider a hypothetical searchable set of 10,000,000 vectors, each with 768 components stored in FP16 at 2 bytes per component, held in the main memory of a reference server CPU. Which resource limits one exact dot-product scan, and what floor does it set?
Math: Multiply the vector count by the dimension and component width:
\[
\EligibleVectorCount \EmbeddingDimension\ElementStorageSize = 10^7 \times 768 \times 2\ \text{bytes}.
\]
The raw vectors occupy 15.36 GB. Counting two FLOPs per multiply-add gives \(2\EligibleVectorCount \EmbeddingDimension\), or 15.36 GFLOP per scan. Arithmetic intensity, the FLOPs performed per byte moved from memory, is therefore \(2\EligibleVectorCount \EmbeddingDimension/(\EligibleVectorCount \EmbeddingDimension\ElementStorageSize) = 2/\ElementStorageSize\), which is 1 FLOP/byte at FP16 whatever the corpus size or dimension. The reference host delivers 1 TFLOP/s and 50 GB/s, a ridge point of 20 FLOP/byte, the intensity below which memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic limits the rate. The scan sits far below the ridge, so bandwidth sets its floor. Streaming the vectors takes at least 307.2 ms, while the arithmetic alone would take 15.36 ms. A trajectory that issues 20 such searches spends at least 6.1 s moving vectors. Because the floor is linear in the eligible count, a scope filter that leaves 10,000 vectors has a streaming floor of 0.31 ms. A 10 ms search budget sets an optimistic maximum of ~326,000 vectors on this host before accounting for the rest of the request.
Systems insight: The intensity of an exact scan is fixed by the component width, so added arithmetic never speeds it up, and an accelerator’s higher ridge leaves it bandwidth-bound there too. The levers are fewer bytes per vector (compression) and fewer vectors touched (a narrower eligible set or an approximate index). The bandwidth floor screens out exact scans that cannot meet the search budget. When that floor fits, benchmark the complete request, including query encoding, top-\(\RetrievalCutoffCount\) selection, and record fetches. Choose an exact scan when its measured request latency meets the budget; an approximate index must justify its maintenance cost and recall loss against that baseline.


The memory-bandwidth limit behind output-bound latency (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}\)) therefore reappears in retrieval, because an exact scan, like a decode step, performs only a few operations for each byte it streams. The analysis also establishes where an exact scan remains the right architectural choice. When selective metadata filters restrict the search space to thousands of eligible vectors, an exact scan streams megabytes rather than gigabytes, reducing the streaming floor to sub-millisecond times without the operational overhead of graph maintenance or quantization codebooks. Whether the complete request meets its latency budget still requires measurement. Furthermore, because an exact scan provides perfect recall under the chosen distance metric, it serves as the essential ground truth for evaluating any approximate index.



The exact-scan streaming floor grows with eligible vectors; the search budget sets an optimistic candidate ceiling.
5 Approximate Nearest Neighbors: Exact nearest-neighbor structures that work well in two or three dimensions degrade toward a full scan as dimension grows, the curse of dimensionality. Indyk and Motwani (1998) relaxed the problem to returning a point within a factor of the true nearest distance and showed, through locality-sensitive hashing, that the relaxation admits sublinear query time. Every ANN index an agent uses makes the same bargain, so its misses are part of the contract, measured as recall, never a defect to be tuned away. 
Indyk, Piotr, and Rajeev Motwani. 1998. “Approximate Nearest Neighbors: Towards Removing the Curse of Dimensionality.” Proceedings of the Thirtieth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC), 604–13. https://doi.org/10.1145/276698.276876.
When candidate sets grow into millions of vectors and queries must return within tight latency budgets, scanning the entire corpus becomes prohibitive. Approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search5 trades mathematical exactness for orders-of-magnitude reductions in latency and memory traffic, pruning the search space at the cost of occasionally missing true nearest neighbors. Systems cut memory traffic in one of two fundamental ways: by traversing a proximity graph to evaluate only a tiny fraction of the vector population, or by partitioning the space and compressing vector representations with quantization codes.
A hierarchical navigable small-world (HNSW) index organizes high-dimensional vectors into a multi-layer proximity graph (Malkov and Yashunin 2018). Layer 0 contains every vector in the dataset. Each inserted vector is also assigned a maximum layer \(\ell = \lfloor -\ln \HnswLevelDraw \cdot \HnswLevelNormalization \rfloor\), where \(\HnswLevelDraw\) is drawn uniformly from \((0, 1]\) and \(\HnswLevelNormalization = 1 / \ln \HnswMaximumConnectionCount\), with \(\HnswMaximumConnectionCount\) defining the maximum number of bidirectional connections per node per layer. The assignment gives each vector probability \(\HnswMaximumConnectionCount^{-\HnswLayerIndex}\) of reaching layer \(\HnswLayerIndex\) or above, so each layer holds roughly \(1/\HnswMaximumConnectionCount\) as many nodes as the one beneath it, an exponentially thinning hierarchy that mirrors the express transit lanes of a skip list (Pugh 1990). Traversal begins at an entry point in the sparsest top layer, greedily hopping to whichever neighbor minimizes distance to the query vector \(\SearchQueryEmbedding\). When no neighbor yields further progress, the search drops down to that node’s counterpart in the next layer and resumes the greedy walk. Upon reaching layer 0, the traversal switches from greedy routing to a beam search that maintains a priority queue of the \(\HnswSearchBeamWidth\) closest candidates discovered so far. The search terminates when the closest unexplored neighbor cannot improve the current candidate set, returning the top \(\RetrievalCutoffCount\) vectors. The parameter \(\HnswSearchBeamWidth\) serves as the primary query-time recall knob. A vector the beam never visits cannot be returned (figure 3), so widening the beam evaluates more distances and recovers more true neighbors at the cost of higher query latency.

Pugh, William. 1990. “Skip Lists: A Probabilistic Alternative to Balanced Trees.” Communications of the ACM 33 (6): 668–76. https://doi.org/10.1145/78973.78977.
Constructing an HNSW graph requires executing this layered search for every incoming vector and establishing bidirectional links to its nearest neighbors in each layer. This graph topology incurs substantial memory overhead beyond the raw vectors. Deletions are harder still, because severing a node without reconstructing edge paths among its neighbors risks partitioning the graph and stranding downstream vectors. Production systems therefore mark a deleted node with a tombstone, an exclusion marker that hides it from results while its links stay in place, and section 6.9 examines how the cost of that compromise compounds.






Figure 3: Searching an HNSW Graph: Each upper layer holds a geometrically smaller subset of the vectors. The query enters at the top, hops greedily toward \(\SearchQueryEmbedding\) until no neighbor is closer, and drops a layer from that node. In layer 0 the walk widens into a beam of width \(\HnswSearchBeamWidth\) that visits more nodes than it returns and yields the best \(\RetrievalCutoffCount\). A vector the beam never visits cannot be returned, which is where approximate search misses come from.



Rather than navigating a graph over full-precision vectors, an inverted file index combined with product quantization (IVF-PQ) reduces memory traffic by partitioning the vector space and lossily compressing the stored representations (Jégou et al. 2011), with an offline build pipeline and an online query pipeline (figure 4). During index construction, coarse \(\Glyph{k}\)-means clusters the corpus into \(\CoarseCellCount\) Voronoi cells (each cell is the region of vectors nearer its centroid than any other centroid), each backed by an inverted list of vector identifiers. At query time, the system computes the distance from the uncompressed query vector to all \(\CoarseCellCount\) coarse centroids and evaluates only the vectors residing in the \(\ProbedCellCount\) closest cells.
Product quantization then compresses every stored vector. It splits the \(\EmbeddingDimension\) dimensions into \(\PqSubvectorCount\) distinct subvectors of dimension \(\EmbeddingDimension/\PqSubvectorCount\). For each subspace, \(\Glyph{k}\)-means trains a codebook of 256 centroids, allowing any subvector to be represented by a single one-byte index \(\PqCentroidCode_j \in [0, 255]\) indicating its nearest centroid. Storing a compressed vector therefore requires only \(\PqSubvectorCount\) bytes. At query time, the uncompressed query vector \(\SearchQueryEmbedding\) is segmented into the same \(\PqSubvectorCount\) subspaces. The runtime precomputes an asymmetric distance lookup table \(\text{LUT}[\PqSubspaceIndex, \PqCentroidCode]\), which stores the squared Euclidean distance between the query’s \(\PqSubspaceIndex\)-th subvector and centroid \(\PqCentroidCode\) in subspace \(\PqSubspaceIndex\). The approximate distance between the query \(\SearchQueryEmbedding\) and a stored quantized vector \(\StoredIndexVector\) with codes \(\PqCentroidCode_1, \dots, \PqCentroidCode_{\PqSubvectorCount}\) reduces to summing table lookups:
\[
\PqApproximateDistance(\SearchQueryEmbedding, \StoredIndexVector) = \sum_{j=1}^{\PqSubvectorCount} \text{LUT}[\PqSubspaceIndex, \PqCentroidCode_j].
\tag{2}\]
Equation 2 transforms a bandwidth-bound \(\EmbeddingDimension\)-component dot product into \(\PqSubvectorCount\) single-byte reads and table lookups. Because the lookup table is small enough to stay in processor cache, each scored vector costs \(\PqSubvectorCount\) bytes of memory traffic instead of \(\EmbeddingDimension\ElementStorageSize\), a reduction by the factor \(\EmbeddingDimension\ElementStorageSize/\PqSubvectorCount\) in exactly the term that bounded the exact scan. The parameter \(\ProbedCellCount\) balances recall against the number of cells scanned, while the subvector count \(\PqSubvectorCount\) trades distance fidelity against bytes per code. Systems commonly recover distance accuracy by re-scoring a short candidate list against full-precision vectors stored on secondary media or remote memory. This architecture scales gracefully to billions of vectors on accelerators (Johnson et al. 2019). However, the quantization codebooks and coarse centroids are calibrated on the vector distribution present during index construction; as the corpus drifts or if the embedding model changes, quantization error compounds until the index is retrained.






Figure 4: IVF-PQ Build and Query: At build time each stored vector is split into \(\PqSubvectorCount = 64\) subvectors, each replaced by the one-byte index of its nearest centroid in that subspace’s codebook, and the code is appended to the inverted list of its nearest coarse cell. At query time the full-precision query selects the \(\ProbedCellCount\) nearest cells, fills a table of distances to every subspace centroid, and scores each stored code with \(\PqSubvectorCount\) table lookups. Sizes follow the exact-scan notebook’s corpus.

Product quantization with 64 subvectors of 12 dimensions stores 0.64 GB of codes, 24× smaller than the FP16 vectors, and its per-query lookup table occupies only 65.5 KB.
