Selecting among these index structures requires evaluating them against the specific record volumes, query distributions, and latency budgets the agent encounters. Systems engineers must also distinguish two evaluation metrics. Recall against an exact scan measures algorithmic fidelity to the mathematical distance metric, whereas end-to-end task success measures whether the retrieved records contain the requisite causal evidence to resolve the agent’s objective.
The filtering hazard from lexical search (section 6.5.3) returns here in sharper form, because scope filters present greater friction on a graph index than on inverted postings lists. In lexical retrieval, intersecting a postings list with an eligibility bitset prunes unauthorized documents without altering how the remaining documents are traversed. In an HNSW graph, restricting search during traversal (pre-filtering) forces the beam to step exclusively onto eligible nodes. If a tenant boundary or file path mask isolates regions of the graph, the greedy walk stalls at a local minimum when all outgoing links lead to masked nodes. The search terminates prematurely and returns incomplete results, even when highly relevant eligible nodes exist just beyond the masked barrier. Conversely, filtering after an unconstrained search (post-filtering) risks returning an empty set whenever the top-\(\RetrievalCutoffCount\) candidates fall outside the authorized scope. Systems escape the dilemma in one of three ways (figure 5). They partition the index into scope-isolated subgraphs, seed extra entry points inside the authorized region, or fall back to an exact scan when the filter is selective enough that the measured full request meets the budget, using the floor in notebook 6.2 as an initial feasibility screen.






Figure 5: Filtering Inside a Graph Walk: A scope mask applied during traversal (A) removes the only links between the entry region and the eligible vectors nearest \(\SearchQueryEmbedding\), so the greedy walk stops at a local minimum and returns too few results even though eligible neighbors exist. The three responses (B) partition the index along scope boundaries, restart the walk from an entry point inside the eligible region, or, when the filter is selective, score every eligible vector exactly.






Production systems frequently combine multiple candidate-generation mechanisms through hybrid retrieval, pairing lexical keyword search with dense semantic retrieval. Before merging candidate lists, however, the runtime must establish unambiguous candidate identity based on tenant scope, source path, commit or version identifier, and span coordinates. Strict identity resolution ensures that an r17 passage never erroneously merges with its modified r18 counterpart, and that identical code in another tenant is never treated as authorized local evidence.
Because lexical scores (such as unbounded BM25 values) and dense similarity scores (such as cosine values in \([-1, 1]\)) reside on non-comparable scales, directly normalizing or adding raw scores introduces calibration instability. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) bypasses score calibration by combining ranked lists based solely on candidate ordinal positions (Cormack et al. 2009). Let \(\FusionInputList_i\) denote the list returned by method \(\RetrievalMethodIndex\), and let \(\FusionInputRank_i(\FusionCandidate)\) represent the 1-based rank of candidate \(\FusionCandidate\) within that list. For a positive smoothing parameter \(\RankFusionSmoothingConstant\), the truncated RRF score is defined as:
\[
\operatorname{RRF}(\FusionCandidate) = \sum_{i:\,\FusionCandidate\in \FusionInputList_i} \frac{1}{\RankFusionSmoothingConstant + \FusionInputRank_i(\FusionCandidate)}.
\tag{3}\]
A candidate absent from a given list contributes zero from that source. Increasing \(\RankFusionSmoothingConstant\) compresses the score differential between adjacent ranks without making the method entirely parameter-free;6 the runtime must also define an explicit tie-breaking convention and configure candidate cutoff depths for each retrieval path.
6 RRF score monotonicity: With fixed \(\RankFusionSmoothingConstant > 0\), moving an item from rank \(\FusionInputRank\) to \(\PromotedFusionInputRank < \FusionInputRank\) in one input list increases its contribution by \(1/(\RankFusionSmoothingConstant+\PromotedFusionInputRank)-1/(\RankFusionSmoothingConstant+\FusionInputRank)>0\) (Cormack et al. 2009). If its contributions from other lists do not decrease, its total score increases. This is a property of the item’s score, not a guarantee of improved final rank when other candidates also change, or of relevant evidence.
Cormack, Gordon V, Charles LA Clarke, and Stefan Buettcher. 2009. “Reciprocal Rank Fusion Outperforms Condorcet and Individual Rank Learning Methods.” Proceedings of the 32nd International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval, 758–59.

Dual consensus elevates candidate A for closer inspection, but agreement across two candidate generators remains an incomplete guarantee of relevance when both retrievers share systematic blind spots. To establish higher precision before staging evidence into the agent’s context window, systems employ a cross-encoder reranker (Nogueira and Cho 2019). Rather than scoring query and document independently, a cross-encoder runs the query and the candidate through the model together as one input, so every query token can attend to every candidate token. Because each score depends on a specific query and candidate pair, nothing can be computed before the query arrives, and this joint pass captures fine-grained token interactions at substantial query-time cost. A reranker can only reorder candidates already surfaced by upstream generators; it cannot retrieve missing records, and its score reflects structural and semantic resemblance rather than verified task applicability.

Nogueira, Rodrigo, and Kyunghyun Cho. 2019. “Passage Re-Ranking with BERT.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1901.04085, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1901.04085.
The substantial computational demand of this joint pass is why rerankers operate exclusively on short candidate pools. In a bi-encoder design, candidate vectors are computed offline, reducing query-time evaluation to a lightweight vector dot product. In a cross-encoder, query and candidate tokens must be processed jointly through the transformer layers, preventing offline precomputation. Computational cost scales with both candidate pool depth and token sequence length. For example, reranking a pool of 50 candidates of 300 tokens each against a 100-token query requires processing 20,000 tokens, a prefill load comparable to a substantial model call, spent entirely on ordering. Systems manage this latency budget by constraining candidate pool sizes, invoking rerankers conditionally based on query ambiguity, or executing reranking asynchronously off the interactive path. The complete hybrid pipeline therefore narrows as it proceeds (figure 6). Two candidate generators feed a fusion step that needs only ranks, the costly reranker sees only the short fused pool, and the runtime stages a small labeled set within the payload budget.






Figure 6: From Candidate Lists to Staged Evidence: Lexical and dense retrieval each rank candidates for the repair symptom. Candidates are joined on their full identity, so an r17 span never merges with its r18 counterpart, and reciprocal rank fusion combines ranks rather than raw scores, with the smoothing parameter \(\RankFusionSmoothingConstant\) still a design choice. A cross-encoder reorders only a short pool, because its work grows with both pool size and pair length, and the runtime stages a small labeled set within the payload budget.



Once reranked, top-ranked candidates pass into the staging pipeline (section 6.3.3), where their provenance and authority are verified before injection into the agent’s context payload. Even an optimally ranked evidence set, however, provides bounded guarantees. Retrieving the r18 implementation and a passing reproducer confirms local syntax and isolated test execution, but it cannot prove that all concurrent caller paths remain race-free. Validating broader system properties requires corroborating records, such as runtime execution traces and multi-threaded test outcomes, that no single ranked list assembles on its own.




A single ranked passage often identifies an initial point of entry without delivering all the evidence an agent needs to make an informed engineering decision. In the connection-pool repair, the core implementation, the waiter-notification test, and the recorded test execution logs answer entirely distinct questions. Examining the pool implementation in isolation cannot reveal which execution paths the test actually exercised. Conversely, inspecting a passing test log leaves unanswered whether the change preserved wider public interface guarantees. Multi-hop retrieval addresses this gap by traversing explicit relationships between evidence items, assembling an explanatory chain that no individual passage’s retrieval score could justify alone.
Implementing multi-hop retrieval does not necessarily demand a dedicated graph database. An agent can inspect a retrieved passage, extract an unresolved reference, and issue a targeted tool call to fetch the next source artifact. Alternatively, an execution runtime can resolve known references ahead of time before invoking the model. Precomputing and maintaining explicit entity relationships pays off only when downstream queries reuse those links frequently enough to amortize the parsing and indexing overhead.


In diagnosing the connection pool bug, an effective evidence path originates at the recorded failure of test_waiter_notified_on_return under revision r17, explicitly scoped by its test revision and runtime environment. From there, the traversal traces from the test assertion in tests/test_pool.py directly into the pool operations exercised by the waiter-return scenario in src/pool.py. It then compares those source regions against the candidate patch in revision r18 and its corresponding reproducer execution. Public interface contracts and unrelated callers remain isolated for subsequent targeted queries.
The edges along this path carry fundamentally distinct semantics. A link from a test run to a commit hash binds an outcome to an exact observed artifact; a static symbol reference in test code points to an implementation entity awaiting inspection; and a diff between revisions isolates textual code modifications. A robust retrieval payload preserves these labeled edge semantics alongside precise source locations and commit hashes. The runtime must also expose unresolved or broken links, such as a missing test log, an ambiguous dynamic dispatch target, or a traversal halted by a token budget. A static evidence path highlights plausible candidate root causes, but it cannot prove that those specific statements executed during the failing run, nor does it guarantee that all contributing dependencies were discovered.



While a simple structural index records basic symbol definitions and usages, richer reasoning over software repositories demands structured relational models. A code property graph unifies abstract syntax trees, control-flow graphs, and program-dependence graphs into a single directed graph of program entities connected by typed edges (Yamaguchi et al. 2014). The edge types most relevant to software agents include syntactic containment and declaration, call edges connecting call sites to function targets, data-dependence edges tracking value definitions to their uses, type inheritance, and module-level imports.

Yamaguchi, Fabian, Nico Golde, Daniel Arp, and Konrad Rieck. 2014. “Modeling and Discovering Vulnerabilities with Code Property Graphs.” 2014 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 590–604.
Edge typing is what makes multi-hop graph traversal selective rather than combinatorial. In the connection-pool repair, restricting a search to invocation and mutation edges guides the traversal directly from test_waiter_notified_on_return to the pool’s resource-return method, and onward to the waiter queue that the method mutates, skipping the dozens of unrelated files that merely import the pool module. The entry point for such a traversal, the seed node, can be resolved via an exact symbol lookup, an initial ranked passage retrieval, or an explicit file and line coordinate from an execution trace.
However, an edge is only as reliable as its underlying extraction mechanism. Lexical parsing reliably identifies declared syntax; resolving cross-file call targets requires complete type information and build configuration; dynamic execution traces observe only the concrete paths taken during a specific invocation. Systems graphs must therefore track provenance on every edge, ensuring the runtime never presents a statically inferred call as an observed runtime event. Furthermore, maintaining these graphs introduces ongoing invalidation overhead as the codebase evolves. A local edit to a method signature might invalidate caller graphs and dependent summaries across multiple repositories, whereas modifying an internal comment leaves structural edges unchanged. When source artifacts shift, any relationship whose underlying evidence has changed must be pruned or marked stale according to the update contracts established in section 6.9.



Unconstrained expansion from a seed node quickly pulls in vastly more context than a downstream language model can process or attend to effectively. Traversal routines require strict operational guards: filtering permitted edge types, restricting traversal direction, capping maximum search depth, and bounding the total number of visited nodes. Tracking visited entity identifiers is essential to prevent cyclic loops from triggering infinite expansion. Even with structural bounds, context packing limits remain binding because a small handful of large code or documentation nodes can easily overrun the prompt budget.
Within these operational boundaries, the runtime can prioritize candidate nodes using semantic relevance, edge type affinities, or graph-centrality algorithms like Personalized PageRank (Page et al. 1999), which concentrates random-walk probability around the initial seed nodes. However, applying a naive score threshold across candidate nodes risks fragmenting the evidence chain. Preserving a coherent explanation often requires retaining an intermediate node with a lower individual query score simply to maintain topological connectivity between the seed and high-value leaf evidence, while compensating by pruning non-essential nodes elsewhere.

Page, Lawrence, Sergey Brin, Rajeev Motwani, and Terry Winograd. 1999. The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web. Nos. 1999-66. Stanford InfoLab.

One more level of depth turns a comfortable fit into an overflow.


Depth, more than node size, decides whether a neighborhood fits, and a tree simple enough to count exactly shows how sharply.

Variables: Suppose the neighborhood is a tree with exactly 3 children per internal node, explored through depth 3, with the seed at depth zero and no repeated nodes. Each complete node record occupies 180 serialized tokens, including its local provenance. Reserve 100 tokens total for edge descriptions and the result envelope. All counts are hypothetical fixed serialization sizes.
Math: Counting the seed and all levels gives the geometric sum \(1 + 3 + 9 + 27 = (3^{4}-1)/(3-1) =\) 40 nodes, in general \((\text{children}^{\text{depth}+1}-1)/(\text{children}-1)\). Staging them requires 40 \(\times\) 180 \(+\) 100 \(=\) 7,300 tokens, exceeding the allowance. With the same envelope reservation, the maximum number of complete equal-sized nodes is \(\lfloor(6{,}144 - 100)/180\rfloor =\) 33.
Stopping one level earlier, at depth 2, stages all 13 nodes in 2,440 tokens.
Systems insight: Depth dominates traversal cost because every additional hop multiplies the expansion frontier by the graph’s branching factor. A single extra level separates an evidence payload that comfortably fits the context window from one that overflows the allocation. Traversal engines must bound depth and filter edge types before ranking nodes; within those limits, scoring should prioritize nodes that preserve path connectivity rather than greedily selecting disconnected high-scoring fragments.


Production code graphs exhibit clustered communities, cycles, and heavily skewed degree distributions. Consequently, calculating reachable nodes by raising an average branching factor to a traversal depth typically overestimates distinct reachable entities while underestimating the local search work required to evaluate candidate edges. When an evidence path exceeds the staging budget, the runtime must either narrow the query scope, return a truncated subgraph accompanied by an explicit continuation cursor, or defer downstream expansion to subsequent interactive agent turns. Under the absence rule, any traversal halted by an engineering limit must be explicitly reported as partial rather than exhausted.



Not every agent question resolves to a single evidence path. High-level architectural queries often span entire subsystems, for example how connection pooling, HTTP request dispatching, and transaction lifecycles interact across a service framework. Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) addresses these broader questions by constructing an entity knowledge graph and precomputing hierarchical summaries over densely connected subgraphs, or communities (Edge et al. 2024). Unsupervised community detection7 clusters related nodes based on network topology. However, whether a detected topological cluster corresponds to a true architectural boundary, and whether its generated natural-language summary remains technically accurate, are separate verification concerns.

Edge, Darren, Ha Trinh, Newman Cheng, Joshua Bradley, Alex Chao, Apurva Mody, Steven Truitt, and Jonathan Larson. 2024. “From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2404.16130.
7 Community Detection: GraphRAG partitions its entity graph using the Leiden algorithm, which refines modularity-based clustering to ensure that every detected community is well-separated and internally connected (Traag et al. 2019). Modularity optimization rewards groups with higher internal edge density than an equivalent random network. A detected community reflects entity co-occurrence density within the extracted corpora; whether that topological cluster corresponds to a logical module boundary recognized by system maintainers must be verified against actual source architecture. 
Traag, Vincent A., Ludo Waltman, and Nees Jan van Eck. 2019. “From Louvain to Leiden: Guaranteeing Well-Connected Communities.” Scientific Reports 9 (1). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-41695-z.
A derived summary amortizes token costs by synthesizing scattered facts into a concise artifact, but it remains a lossy, secondary representation. Every generated summary must retain bidirectional links to its source evidence, record the precise artifact revisions and operating parameters it describes, and inherit the most restrictive access label among its underlying inputs, so that a summary built partly from records restricted to one tenant is itself restricted to that tenant. Detailed execution plans should inspect the authoritative underlying records; the summary serves primarily as an indexed navigational map.


↪ How labels propagate through summaries and other transformations under an information-flow policy is developed in Label propagation through transformations.
For instance, an automated repair summary might record that revision r18 passed test_waiter_notified_on_return under a specific thread-concurrency configuration. Because an observation is scoped to its tested configuration, this fact cannot be generalized into an assertion that “the connection pool is thread-safe.” Moreover, precomputed summaries incur ongoing invalidation debt. Persisting an explicit dependency manifest between source files, detected communities, and generated summaries turns invalidation into a traversal of recorded dependencies rather than a guess. Any code modification flags all dependent summaries (and any higher-level rollups derived from them) as dirty. The runtime can continue to serve a dirty summary as a labeled historical snapshot until an offline job or on-demand trigger recompiles or invalidates it.

Checkpoint 6.2: Choosing and bounding related evidence
Apply these retrieval strategies to the running connection-pool repair.

Method choice: A debugging query begins with an exact test identifier, but the subsequent inquiry requires identifying all upstream callers of the modified pool method. Which indexes or direct reads best support each step, and under what workload conditions does maintaining a persistent code property graph justify its synchronization overhead?
Evidence path: Why does a static dependency path from a failing test to a pool implementation fail to prove the runtime root cause or guarantee the general correctness of patch r18?
Expansion estimate: In the tree expansion model from notebook 6.3, if each node record shrank by half, how many levels could traversal proceed before exceeding the retrieval budget, and what computational search overhead would that additional level incur that serialization bounds fail to capture?
Derived summaries: What provenance links and execution constraints must accompany a synthetic summary of a passing reproducer run to prevent a subsequent agent session from drawing invalid conclusions?



Deciding whether to retain a detailed path explanation or a high-level subsystem summary is a write-policy decision, and that policy dictates the fidelity, staleness, and cost of the evidence that every subsequent agent session can retrieve.




Retrieval can return only what the system has retained. An assistant that carries the directive “no meetings before 10:00” strictly within its current context window loses that constraint the moment the session terminates. Persisting the preference into long-term storage solves immediate conversational volatility, but it introduces the consistency challenge previewed in section 6.2. When the user later moves the boundary to 11:00, the runtime must ensure the earlier record stops governing new scheduling decisions without corrupting the historical audit trail.
The distinction between authoritative sources and derived records governs writes just as it governed reads (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)). A user’s explicit directive provides direct evidence of an intent within a specific operational scope; an agent’s internal paraphrase constitutes a lossy derived representation; and an automated rationale explaining why the user dislikes morning meetings is an ungrounded secondary inference. Storing all three artifacts as interchangeable assertions flattens evidentiary weight, depriving downstream retrieval pipelines of the ability to distinguish verified user intent from speculative model summaries.

Definition 6.2: Memory write policy
A memory write policy is the runtime rule governing which proposed records enter durable storage, what claims and operational scopes they carry, and how the system subsequently corrects, supersedes, revalidates, expires, or deletes those records and their downstream derivations.

Significance: Every admitted record becomes a candidate for retrieval in subsequent agent sessions. An unverified lesson admitted into storage can degrade the execution accuracy of every future task that retrieves it. The write path provides the most economical barrier against memory pollution because admission checks execute once per write rather than amortizing filtering costs across thousands of subsequent retrieval queries.
Distinction: Storage retention simply preserves raw bytes in a database or index. The memory write policy governs the operational authority of those bytes, defining what claims an entry can justify and when it must stop influencing execution decisions.
Common pitfall: Deduplicating writes based purely on embedding similarity, which erroneously discards near-identical updates (such as a revised meeting time or flipped boolean flag) as redundant duplicates.





Every candidate memory record requires a concrete provenance tuple: an identifiable owner, an intended operational role, a bounded applicability scope, and verifiable backing evidence. For a scheduling preference, the scope must record the user identity, the target calendar, and explicit time zone constraints rather than leaving the runtime to guess ambient execution conditions. Furthermore, the runtime must enforce explicit consent boundaries: permission to inspect user messages during active reasoning does not grant permission to commit those details into durable storage.
Software repair trajectories generate a different class of evidence. For example, test execution records showing a failure at revision r17 and a pass at revision r18 represent immutable historical observations, but neither result justifies an unconditioned assertion about the codebase. A synthesized rule such as “inspect the return path when a waiter remains blocked” represents a heuristic hypothesis derived from that sequence, not a proven invariant. Systems insight: The repair agent’s memory hazard comes from its own writes, the research agent’s from other people’s text, and the support agent’s from time. One retrieval contract serves all three, and the write policy is where they diverge.





An agent model may propose a memory write, but the runtime storage layer decides whether and how to persist it. Even when an architecture allows the language model to manage its active context by paging memory entries explicitly (Packer et al. 2023), context paging controls only working set occupancy; durable admission remains the exclusive responsibility of the storage runtime. The admission gate validates write permissions, confirms that the target store allows persistent retention for the active session, classifies the record type, and verifies that attached evidence satisfies the schema. Structural schema validation checks required fields such as timestamps and provenance identifiers.
Semantic fidelity, the requirement that the proposed record asserts nothing absent from the raw transcript, needs a check of its own, and that check is a verifier with error rates like any other. A deterministic check can validate a constrained structured input against the proposed record’s owner, relation, value, and scope. Finding “11:00” in free-form text establishes only its occurrence; “11:00 applies only on Fridays” does not support an unrestricted scheduling preference. For free-text summaries, a calibrated model-based judge is one fallible fidelity check, and its false acceptance rate (Check precision and the candidate pool) measures how often unsupported claims pass that check into durable storage, where every later session can retrieve them. Generating a summary and establishing that it is faithful are different events, which is the verification asymmetry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)) applied to memory admission. Sensitive data (such as credentials and private identifiers) demands strict classification and scrubbing policies; simple regular expression filters reliably fail on unstructured disclosures that match no standard secret pattern. When an agent proposes an interpretive conclusion lacking direct observational backing, the admission gate must either reject the candidate or downgrade it to an explicitly tagged hypothesis, preventing it from masquerading as a validated preference or concrete observation.
Only after passing admission validation does the runtime evaluate whether the candidate record inserts a new entry, updates an existing record, or duplicates existing knowledge. Vector similarity in an embedding space is useful for candidate retrieval, but it cannot resolve write semantics. If a user modifies a preference from “no meetings before 10:00” to “no meetings before 11:00,” the semantic embedding vectors are nearly identical. Relying on distance thresholds for deduplication would discard the update as an uninformative repeat, quietly dropping the user’s explicit correction.
When an admitted record targets an existing entity under an identical scope, the runtime executes supersession. The runtime creates a newly versioned record and marks the prior entry as superseded. This terminates the prior record’s eligibility for active decision-making while preserving it in historical logs for auditing and provenance tracing. When scopes differ (for example, if the 11:00 restriction applies only to Fridays), both records remain valid within their respective domains. When scopes overlap ambiguously, the runtime must flag an unresolved conflict or prompt the user for clarification; heuristically synthesizing conflicting records into a fuzzy compromise produces brittle, ungrounded behavior. Furthermore, systems must distinguish an in-place correction from a true state transition. Fixing a transcription error that corrupted “10:00” repairs the fidelity of an existing record, whereas accepting an 11:00 update documents an authentic change in preference.
Concurrent updates demand explicit coordination primitives at the storage layer. A proposed supersession must carry the base version identifier against which it was generated. The store then evaluates and applies the update atomically through a compare-and-swap or conditional write, the same optimistic validation that context engineering applied to tool preconditions, closing the race inherent in separate read and write phases. Optimistic validation suits memory writes particularly well. Two sessions seldom revise the same preference concurrently, so conflicts are rare, and a model call lasting several seconds makes a pessimistic lock impractical to hold across the invocation that proposes the write. When a collision does occur, the runtime must abort the write, reload the latest state, and re-evaluate the update against an explicit conflict resolution policy. Handing the conflict back to the model to blend the two states without transactional guarantees invites silent corruption.


↩︎ Optimistic validation, which checks at commit that the state a decision read is unchanged and aborts otherwise, is established in Detecting change and bounding uncertainty.



Decoupling raw observational writes from downstream inductive derivation is essential for maintaining both prompt responsiveness and data integrity. When an agent executes an action, the runtime immediately writes the raw observation (the execution context, task ID, source revision, tool parameters, and raw output status) to durable storage. Only after this initial write does the runtime schedule background pipelines for summarization, embedding generation, and heuristic reflection. This separation guarantees that hard evidence persists even if downstream inference fails or crashes, while avoiding costly synchronous model calls on every execution step. Generating reflective summaries has demonstrated substantial empirical gains in autonomous error recovery (Shinn et al. 2023); nonetheless, the resulting verbal reflections must enter the store strictly as generated hypotheses (table 7), maintaining explicit foreign-key links to the raw observations from which they were induced.
Write acknowledgments must explicitly report the durability boundary achieved. Systems must distinguish among three distinct guarantees: buffered in memory (queued in an ephemeral local ring buffer), committed to durable storage (flushed to non-volatile disk or replicated across storage nodes under the durability contract), and indexed for search (visible to vector and keyword retrieval engines). Merely enqueuing an event into an in-memory worker queue provides zero crash durability. If a task requires strict persistence guarantees before taking non-reversible external actions, the runtime must block on storage confirmation rather than proceeding optimistically. Moreover, background indexing and reflection pipelines consume significant accelerator cycles and storage I/O; system schedulers must explicitly account for these background workloads to prevent asynchronous memory indexing from starving user-facing interactive inference.



A retained record changes status as its supporting evidence and operational context evolve. The superseded 10:00 preference and the r17 test failure both remain valid historical records while losing eligibility for current decisions, and retaining historical snapshots remains a deliberate architectural policy choice.
Revalidation refreshes the empirical support for an existing record. For instance, asking the user to confirm that the 11:00 scheduling boundary remains active provides authoritative fresh evidence. In contrast, repeatedly retrieving an entry across dozens of successful runs indicates frequent utilization, not revalidation. Confusing usage frequency with validity is dangerous, because an unchecked error that is retrieved often is simply reused often, and each retrieval adds no evidence. Consequently, storage schemas must maintain distinct timestamps for record creation, last access, and last authoritative confirmation. Similarly, revalidating an automated diagnosis or heuristic rule derived from revision r18 requires evaluating it against the current source code tree and active test environment, rather than treating age-based decay as a proxy for correctness.
Expiration revokes a record’s eligibility for decision-making once an expiration timestamp passes or a defined system condition is triggered. An expired temporary directive, such as an out-of-office scheduling window, must not govern subsequent actions without explicit reconfirmation. Some memory systems rank records by similarity multiplied by a recency factor that shrinks with age. Penalizing an expired record this way is inadequate, because if a query has few close semantic matches, an expired record with a penalized score can still surface in the top-\(\RetrievalCutoffCount\) retrieval set and contaminate the prompt. Robust write paths enforce hard filtering, partitioning or tagging expired records so that operational retrieval filters exclude them unconditionally while retaining the payload for compliance auditing.
Deletion addresses the physical and logical lifecycle of the stored data. When a user revokes consent or asks to delete a preference, purging the primary database row is only the initial step. Stale representations frequently linger in secondary indexes, dense vector stores, consolidated episodic summaries, key-value caches, and pre-staged prompt templates managed by the runtime. The key-value case is easy to miss, because a cached prefix that contains the deleted preference still matches any request that repeats those tokens, and a prefix match certifies identical tokens, not current facts. The runtime must therefore evict that prefix or change the prompt so it no longer matches. A comprehensive deletion procedure must identify every downstream derivative, revoke its retrieval eligibility immediately, and schedule background reclamation or re-indexing under the governing data retention policy. To bridge the latency between request receipt and asynchronous garbage collection, systems write the storage counterpart of the marker that context invalidation places in a prompt. This tombstone8 is a durable exclusion record that filters the entity out of all active query paths before physical purging completes.

In an agent memory architecture, lagging asynchronous indexers, pipeline queues, and restored snapshots function just like stale replicas, making durable tombstone markers necessary prior to physical deletion.

A deletion receipt must specify the exact boundary of guarantees achieved. Immutable cold backups, out-of-band external audit logs, and in-flight API payloads dispatched to third-party model providers lie outside the synchronous deletion perimeter. Deleting a record from runtime memory cannot retract a prompt token that an external foundation model has already processed, nor can it un-schedule a calendar invite already sent across an enterprise network. What the runtime can and must guarantee is that every internal index, cache, and prompt assembly buffer within its trust domain immediately ceases to use the deleted entity in future reasoning cycles.



Consolidation compresses clusters of related, fine-grained records into structured, high-level representations optimized for future retrieval. For instance, across a dozen debugging sessions on an asynchronous runtime, several granular test traces and failed stack frames can be consolidated into an architectural summary documenting which notification paths were evaluated, which revisions broke invariants, and which hypotheses remain open. Autonomous agent architectures frequently employ background workers to synthesize episodic observations into higher-level reflections (Park et al. 2023). From a systems perspective, every consolidated reflection is a generated lesson (table 7). Clustering records by embedding proximity helps identify candidate groups for consolidation, but vector similarity alone cannot establish causal relationships; verifying that two failures share an underlying defect requires structural evidence that semantic proximity cannot supply.
When generating consolidated records, the write pipeline must preserve provenance graphs, explicitly recording references to the constituent raw records, boundary conditions, and any observed counterexamples. Synthesizing multiple successful execution traces into an unconditioned, global procedure risks overgeneralizing domain-specific behavior. Furthermore, retaining the underlying source observations alongside the consolidated abstraction remains a deliberate architectural decision. Consolidated summaries minimize prompt tokens during inference, but stripping the raw logs removes the granular execution traces necessary for deep auditing and subsequent re-indexing.



When an unverified hypothesis enters durable memory, subsequent summarization cycles risk treating the stored conjecture as an established premise, echoing and amplifying the error across successive generations of context. Under formal evidentiary rules, repeated retrieval and re-summarization provide zero independent validation. A faulty diagnostic guess that is copied into an episode summary, absorbed into a weekly milestone report, and ultimately consolidated into a cross-project heuristic still rests entirely on the original faulty inference. To prevent memory poisoning, the storage engine must maintain rigorous dependency provenance across all derived artifacts. When an operator or verification pass invalidates a poisoned record, the invalidation must cascade through the entire dependency graph, retracting or marking as suspect every downstream summary and derived lesson. Merely down-ranking or tombstoning the root record is insufficient if derivative summaries continue circulating through retrieval indexes. Finally, even a fully validated, un-poisoned lesson functions merely as a candidate action suggestion; the execution engine must still enforce strict runtime authorization policies and environmental preconditions whenever an agent attempts to act on retrieved memories.

A user changes “no meetings before 10:00” to “no meetings before 11:00” for the same calendar and later requests deletion of the preference. An index and a session summary still contain the original value.

Withdrawal: Enumerate all storage and cache representations that must stop influencing downstream prompts, and specify what guarantees the deletion acknowledgment can truthfully report if an immutable backup retains the raw record for 90 days.
Claim scope: Contrast the evidentiary threshold required for an explicit user constraint against that required for an inductively generated scheduling heuristic.



The memory write path establishes what a stored record claims, what evidence supports it, and when its operational validity ends. Those decisions reach the agent, however, only through derived indexes and caches that are rebuilt after the store changes, and until a lagging index catches up it can still answer with the record the write path just retired.




The connection-pool repair has reached revision r18, yet a subsequent search can still return an excerpt of src/pool.py indexed at r17. Consider how a single stale read unravels an otherwise systematic debugging trajectory:

At turn 12, the agent edits the return path in src/pool.py, and the workspace edit tool confirms the updated file at r18.
At turn 13, a search for the notification logic retrieves the r17 chunk, which still contains the buggy line replaced in the previous turn, without a version label.
At turn 14, the model infers that its earlier modification was lost and reissues the edit. The edit tool rejects the request because the target snippet no longer exists in the current file.
At turn 15, the model confronts conflicting signals: a confirmed write, an excerpt contradicting that write, and a failed re-edit. It concludes that the workspace filesystem is corrupted and begins issuing speculative, wide-ranging edits. Each action burns context tokens and tool budget while driving the repository further from a reviewed state.

The unlabeled stale read initiates this failure by presenting an accurate historical excerpt as current state. The conflicting evidence does not establish filesystem corruption; a direct read of the current source could expose the mismatch. Model reasoning cannot reliably compensate for a retrieval layer that conceals which version its evidence describes. Each turn the trace wasted also lengthens the horizon over which per-turn errors compound (equation 1.1).
Maintaining a persistent index forces a clean separation between two operations that an ephemeral staged prompt naturally couples: withholding obsolete records and generating their replacements.

Definition 6.3: Storage invalidation
Storage invalidation is the exclusion of a derived record (an index entry, vector, summary, or cached result) from current-state retrieval once a relevant change to its source makes it inapplicable, independent of when a replacement is built.

Significance: Coordinating exclusion with the source commit prevents known-obsolete entries from remaining eligible while their replacements are built. Notebook 6.4 compares the additional metadata and indexing work, separately from the common durable commit and coordination costs. In the trace above, one unlabeled stale read cost three turns of the repair’s budget.
Distinction: Rebuilding synthesizes a replacement representation, whereas invalidation merely suppresses the obsolete one. This ensures that any query arriving during the rebuild window receives either an authoritative direct read or an explicit incomplete result rather than stale data.
Common pitfall: Tracking staleness with an ephemeral dirty flag that clears automatically when a background job finishes. If an uncoordinated indexing worker completes late or a retrieval gateway restarts without durable tombstone state, obsolete entries can be erroneously readmitted.





To guarantee freshness, an index entry must explicitly record the source generation from which it was derived. A source generation is a monotonic version identity defined by the storage system’s write contract, providing ordering guarantees that volatile filesystem modification timestamps cannot match. In the connection-pool repair, r17 and r18 denote successive repository states. Once the runtime establishes r18 as the active generation, any query seeking current code must systematically discard entries tagged with r17.
Deciding which derived records an edit affects is the dependency tracking that context invalidation applied to staged observations, now applied to records that persist in the store and its indexes. What is new at this layer is that generations make the tracking durable across sessions, and that some derived records cannot be patched in place. Data dependencies often span beyond individual files. A raw code excerpt depends solely on its source file revision; a call-graph edge depends on multiple source files alongside the static-analysis configuration; an episodic summary depends on the tool outputs and diagnostic logs it consolidates. When an underlying artifact changes, the runtime must invalidate all affected downstream records while keeping unrelated entries intact. If the dependency graph is coarse or incomplete, the runtime must conservatively widen the invalidation boundary or explicitly report retrieval uncertainty. A missing dependency link must never be treated as proof of validity.


↩︎ Tracking which claims depend on which observations, and propagating invalidation through that record, is established in Tracking claim dependencies.
From a systems standpoint, every retrieval index is a materialized view over base data, a problem relational database management systems have addressed for decades. Classical incremental view maintenance computes updates to a view algebraically from delta changes in base relations, bypassing the need to re-evaluate the full query (Blakeley et al. 1986; Gupta and Mumick 1995). Unstructured retrieval indexes, however, resist algebraic delta maintenance. Under fixed-size chunking schemes, inserting even two lines near the beginning of a source file shifts the token boundaries of every subsequent chunk. Furthermore, deep neural embedding models are non-linear, so an updated vector cannot be synthesized from a vector subtraction and a text diff. Consequently, changed text requires discarding existing entries and running end-to-end forward passes to re-embed the new chunks. Practical retrieval architectures therefore decouple invalidation, a metadata exclusion coordinated with the source commit, from index rebuilding, which consumes substantial compute and network latency.
Beyond source generations, an embedding record must also encode the model identifier, tokenization pipeline, and preprocessing hyperparameters that generated it. A valid source generation confirms only that the underlying text is up to date; it does not indicate whether the vector remains compatible with the active retrieval model and query encoder.



Operationalizing this distinction requires a coordinated protocol among the storage coordinator, the indexing pipeline, and the retrieval gateway. This protocol assumes that the agent runtime governs workspace modifications, that the retrieval gateway can query an authoritative source generation along with its content, and that writes, index publications, and query admission share a coordination boundary, such as an atomic database transaction, a conditional write to a strongly consistent store whose replicas agree on a single commit order, or a local mutex. During an in-flight write, the gateway either holds queries within a tight latency deadline or marks the affected file scope as temporarily unavailable. A message queue or publish-subscribe broker alone cannot enforce these properties, because delivering a message is a separate event from committing the write it announces. A notice that r18 committed can reach the gateway after a query has already been admitted against r17, and in that interval the gateway serves r17 as current. The coordination sequence orchestrates a source modification while a straggling index worker remains active:

The source coordinator commits the patch as generation r18 and atomically updates the active generation watermark for admission checks. Here a watermark is a position marker, the highest generation the gateway treats as current, not one of the compaction thresholds of context engineering. This prevents a visibility split where newly committed code is readable from disk while an out-of-band index registry continues to treat r17 as current.
A subsequent query for src/pool.py retrieves candidate vectors derived from r17 from the background index. The retrieval gateway checks their embedded generation tag against the active watermark (r18) and suppresses them. This exclusion signals index lag rather than a missing file or a failed edit.
An indexing job started prior to the commit finishes late. During index publication, the worker checks its captured generation within the coordination boundary. Recognizing that generation r18 has superseded its input, the coordinator discards the stale output or redirects it to an archival store.
A fresh worker generates replacement vectors from an r18 snapshot. It publishes them conditionally, committing the batch only if the workspace generation and index configuration remain unchanged throughout the indexing window.
Inbound queries continuously evaluate candidate generations against the active watermark. Publishing r18 records never reactivates older r17 entries, and background garbage collectors reclaim retired vectors on an independent schedule.

Publication validation and index installation must occur as a single atomic operation, because checking generation validity first and writing later introduces a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition that allows concurrent edits to invalidate the payload. In-memory and durable tombstones record excluded generations while background workers rebuild representations. Because query admission enforces generation checks on every lookup, old candidates remain excluded even if temporary dirty flags clear prematurely. Similarly, deleting a source file installs a versioned tombstone, preventing delayed workers from accidentally resurrecting an obsolete record from an earlier snapshot.
Source generations allow the exclusion policy to be expressed in a compact, interval-based form. Each derived entry \(\DerivedMemoryEntry\) carries a valid lifetime \([\MemoryEntryBirthGeneration(\DerivedMemoryEntry), \MemoryEntryDeathGeneration(\DerivedMemoryEntry))\), where \(\MemoryEntryDeathGeneration(\DerivedMemoryEntry)\) remains open until a subsequent edit to that source scope closes the interval. A query evaluating workspace generation \(\QueryWorkspaceGeneration\) admits candidate entry \(\DerivedMemoryEntry\) if and only if
\[
\text{IsValid}(\DerivedMemoryEntry, \QueryWorkspaceGeneration) = \big(\MemoryEntryBirthGeneration(\DerivedMemoryEntry) \le \QueryWorkspaceGeneration < \MemoryEntryDeathGeneration(\DerivedMemoryEntry)\big).
\tag{4}\]
For current-state execution, the runtime sets \(\QueryWorkspaceGeneration\) to the active workspace generation. For historical diagnostics, such as an agent reviewing why an execution failed at revision r17, the query sets \(\QueryWorkspaceGeneration\) to that historical revision. Subject to retention policies, equation 4 serves both use cases uniformly, preventing historical data from masquerading as current state.
Exclusion solves freshness, but it introduces an efficiency trade-off that compounds over time. Suppressed records continue to occupy memory. In an HNSW graph, tombstoned nodes remain embedded in their neighbors’ adjacency lists. Because greedy graph traversal continues to visit and evaluate these dead nodes before filtering them out at the admission boundary, a search with a fixed beam width explores fewer live items, degrading overall recall. To bound that loss, a background compaction process tracks the ratio of tombstoned records, \(\TombstonedRecordFraction = \lvert \TombstonedNodeSet\rvert/\lvert \IndexGraphNodeSet\rvert\). When this ratio crosses a tuned threshold, the system builds a compacted graph: it purges unreferenced records, recomputes neighbor connections among surviving nodes, rebuilds navigation entry points, and atomically swaps the compacted index into memory. This workflow adopts the compaction design of log-structured merge-trees (O’Neil et al. 1996), balancing query latency and retrieval recall against the compute cost of background rebuilds. This is compaction in the storage-engine sense, rewriting a structure without its dead entries, not the summarization that context compaction performs on a prompt.
This coordination contract must remain robust against system restarts and uncoordinated writers. When a retrieval gateway restarts, it must reconstruct its authoritative generation state from durable storage before accepting queries; an empty in-memory tombstone table must never be treated as evidence that the index is fresh. Furthermore, if external tools or developers modify files without routing through the runtime coordinator, filesystem watcher events may arrive out of order or be dropped. In response, the gateway must fall back to direct, version-validated reads against the filesystem. If it cannot verify whether an indexed chunk matches disk before its query deadline expires, it must flag the result envelope as unverified rather than returning potentially stale data.
Replicated retrieval topologies require explicit read-your-writes9 guarantees, ensuring that an agent always observes the outcomes of its own preceding actions (Terry et al. 1994). When an agent issues a search following an edit, the query carries the log sequence number (LSN) corresponding to that write. A replica whose replay position (the last log entry it has applied) lags that LSN must pause execution within a bounded wait window. If the replica does not catch up before the deadline elapses, the gateway either routes the request to an authoritative primary or returns an explicit partial-status response.
9 Session Guarantees: The Bayou project established four foundational client-centric guarantees for weakly consistent distributed storage: read your writes, monotonic reads, writes follow reads, and monotonic writes (Terry et al. 1994). An agentic system requires more than simple read-your-writes behavior. For example, if an agent reads r18 from an up-to-date replica and subsequently retrieves r17 from a lagging node on the next step, the system violates monotonic reads, and the agent’s view of workspace history moves backward.

Excluding an obsolete candidate prevents an agent from consuming erroneous data, but it does not fulfill the retrieval layer’s contract to return actionable context. When invalidation suppresses a record, the gateway must return an honest assessment of available evidence. As outlined in table 9, a production retrieval layer can respond with one of three outcomes.

The appropriate fallback depends on query structure. For an explicit target path like src/pool.py, the gateway can execute an authorized direct source read, returning the live r18 text while background embedding jobs run. Conversely, a broad semantic query, such as a search for all modules affected by a modified locking interface, cannot be answered by reading a single file. Answering it accurately requires either a refreshed semantic index or comprehensive static analysis across many files. If bounded direct reads cannot resolve the query within the execution budget, the gateway must return an explicit incomplete result. Artificially inflating candidate limits (such as expanding \(\RetrievalCutoffCount\) during top-\(\RetrievalCutoffCount\) nearest-neighbor retrieval) does not solve this problem: an unindexed record does not exist in the vector index, and no search depth can retrieve missing points.
Systems architects must decide where to place this maintenance overhead. Synchronous re-indexing moves parsing, chunking, and embedding directly onto the write path, guaranteeing that fresh representations exist before any subsequent tool executes. Background re-indexing acknowledges writes after the required durable source commit and coordinated exclusion, allowing tools to return before rebuilding finishes while relying on the gateway to manage queries during the refresh window. This architectural trade-off depends on workspace edit frequency and whether bounded direct reads can satisfy immediate downstream queries. As notebook 6.4 quantifies, their additional indexing and local metadata work can differ by several orders of magnitude, and they also differ in what a query during the rebuild sees (figure 7). Synchronous re-indexing never exposes that interval but stalls the write, unchecked background indexing serves r17 entries as current, and background indexing with exclusion suppresses r17 and answers the query with a direct read or a partial result.

Retrieved evidence represents the source state observed at the moment of the read. In an agentic system, a concurrent write can land before the model finishes deliberating and invokes its chosen action. Any tool call whose correctness depends on an unmodified workspace must therefore enforce an execution-time precondition, such as an optimistic version check, at the tool boundary. The storage subsystem’s core duty is to preserve and surface the exact generation metadata that this precondition requires.

Source-generation checks suppress obsolete records, atomic publication prevents straggling workers from reinstating stale representations, and explicit fallback contracts clarify whether fresh evidence is available. Together, these mechanisms enforce internal storage consistency rather than task success. In accordance with the end-to-end argument (Saltzer et al. 1984), whether the r18 patch truly resolves the stalled waiter can be established only at the system boundary through integration tests executed against the real runtime environment. What the storage layer guarantees to that boundary is an uncompromised, auditable record of the exact source generation reflected in every retrieved fact.




Excluding a stale failure trace from an earlier run keeps an outdated representation out of the agent’s next request, but it does not ensure that the agent finds the fresh evidence needed to effect a repair. Conversely, a stored reflection might reproduce a recent passing test run accurately while overstating what the pass proves. Rigorous evaluation cannot treat memory as a static lookup table. It must follow information across its full lifecycle: from initial admission into persistent storage, through indexing, retrieval, and prompt staging, to the subsequent updates, supersessions, and deletions that maintain consistency as the environment evolves.
The appropriate unit of comparison is the memory policy. A memory policy encompasses what an agent writes, how it indexes and retrieves records, how it stages evidence in the prompt, and how it maintains that evidence across sessions. The retrieval index is merely one component of that policy. Component-level microbenchmarks help locate failures in search precision or index latency, but task-level outcomes ultimately decide whether the assembled policy satisfies operational acceptance criteria.


A controlled cross-session trial begins with a fixed source snapshot and an identical initial memory store. Evaluators provision each policy with an isolated environment, identical task sequences, and identical constraints on model inference, tool execution, and compute budgets. Records generated during one trial session may influence subsequent sessions within that same trial, since that cross-session behavior is what the trial measures, but they must never contaminate a parallel trial. Ground-truth reference answers, test fixtures, and evaluator annotations must remain strictly outside both writable and retrievable stores. If an agent can access evaluation artifacts, a policy can easily appear to learn when it is merely caching the answers to the test suite.
The comparison in table 10 isolates the baseline benefit of raw persistence from the operational benefit of governing what persists. Across all experimental conditions, the system enforces identical access controls and action permissions. The “unchecked” condition isolates content admission alone, while all conditions experience external source modifications and user updates on the same synchronized fixture schedule.

The scheduling preference supplies a concrete lifecycle fixture: an initial preference recorded at 10:00, an explicit supersession at 11:00, and a user deletion request in a subsequent session. The evaluation tests whether the agent applies the active preference before deletion and complies with post-deletion invariants afterward. This requires inspecting every storage tier: primary vector and keyword indices, consolidated summaries, and staged prompt templates. An agent that suppresses the primary record from raw search results but still retrieves an unpruned summary containing the old preference violates its withdrawal contract. Furthermore, system backups or audit logs retained for regulatory compliance must fall under an explicit data-retention policy rather than being counted as active working memory.
Similarly, an iterative software-repair fixture retains the failing run at r17, records the subsequent passing run at r18, and then challenges a future agent session to distinguish historical debugging context from the current state of the implementation without inappropriately broadening the reproducer’s scope. When source files change, the fixture tests two critical behaviors: a relevant source edit should trigger revalidation of dependent records, while an unrelated source edit tests whether the policy mistakenly discards valid, useful evidence.
Deterministic fixed-record probes isolate specific defects in admission filtering, retrieval ranking, or cache invalidation. Full task trials then allow policies to accumulate their own records across multi-turn interactions, causing their execution trajectories to diverge naturally over time. Evaluators must hold initial conditions and scoring rubrics constant across runs. When stochastic generation or environment variations introduce noise, evaluations must report the number of independent trials alongside the full distribution of outcomes rather than relying solely on mean performance.



Standard retrieval metrics depend on unambiguous relevance judgments. For each test query, the benchmark must define the eligible source snapshot, the authorized access scope, and the specific records relevant to the agent’s immediate task. Relevance is temporal and context-dependent: the log of the failing run at r17 may be relevant when an agent explains the history of a bug, but it is invalid evidence for whether the candidate at r18 passes. Evaluation fixtures must explicitly label these distinctions rather than expecting an embedding model’s similarity score to capture temporal validity.
Let \(\RetrievedRecordSet_k\) be the set of distinct records returned up to cutoff \(\RetrievalCutoffCount\), and let \(\RelevantRecordSet\) be the set of labeled relevant records in the eligible snapshot. Precision at cutoff \(\RetrievalCutoffCount\) is defined as
\[
\text{P}@\RetrievalCutoffCount = \frac{\lvert\RetrievedRecordSet_k \cap \RelevantRecordSet\rvert}{\RetrievalCutoffCount},
\qquad \RetrievalCutoffCount > 0.
\tag{5}\]
The denominator is the target cutoff \(\RetrievalCutoffCount\), not the number of records the retriever actually returned. Unfilled result positions receive zero credit. Under this formulation, an empty result set scores zero, ensuring that a policy that underfills its staged context cannot artificially outscore a policy that retrieves a broader set of useful evidence. In contrast, calculating precision strictly over the returned records (with \(\lvert\RetrievedRecordSet_k\rvert\) in the denominator) can invert these rankings. Evaluators must explicitly declare their denominator convention and report the raw count of returned records alongside precision scores.
Recall measures the fraction of relevant evidence retrieved from the eligible store:
\[
\text{Recall}@\RetrievalCutoffCount = \frac{\lvert\RetrievedRecordSet_k \cap \RelevantRecordSet\rvert}{\lvert\RelevantRecordSet\rvert}.
\tag{6}\]
When the relevant set \(\RelevantRecordSet\) is empty, recall is mathematically undefined (\(0/0\)). Evaluators should isolate unanswerable queries into a dedicated reporting cohort, assessing whether the agent correctly recognizes the absence of supporting evidence or fabricates an unsupported claim. Keeping the completion status of every evaluation query visible ensures that such boundary conditions are not swept into an aggregate average.
When surfacing an immediate answer is paramount, Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) evaluates how quickly the system finds its first hit. MRR computes the arithmetic mean of the reciprocal rank of the first relevant record across all evaluated queries, scoring zero whenever no relevant item appears within cutoff \(\RetrievalCutoffCount\). However, MRR is insensitive to whether the complete evidence required for a multi-hop reasoning chain was assembled. Multi-hop evaluation fixtures must separately verify that all required entity relationships and source versions are present.
Temporal applicability demands a separate metric. The stale-return rate is the fraction of current-state queries that return at least one record invalidated by subsequent source modifications. It measures the store one layer below the stale-support rate of context engineering (equation 4.7): stale-return counts what retrieval hands back, while stale-support counts decisions that rest on superseded evidence once it is in context, so a stale record that the runtime labels or excludes at staging raises the first without raising the second. Historical retrospective queries must be evaluated and reported separately. Because a retriever that returns nothing returns no stale records, a degenerate policy that returns zero results achieves a perfect stale-return rate of zero while completely failing the task. Consequently, stale-return rates must always be reported alongside recall and evidence coverage.



A comprehensive evaluation must account for the full operational lifecycle of memory updates. In supersession and deletion trials, evaluators track whether an updated or deleted record, along with all its downstream representations (index postings, graph edges, and cached summaries), reached the declared target state within an established deadline. The benchmark logs update latency, queue backlogs, and unresolved timeouts. In this analysis, expiring a record from active retrieval and physically purging it from persistent storage are distinct operations that require distinct accounting; describing a record loosely as “forgotten” obscures whether data was merely hidden from the read path or permanently deleted from the database.
End-to-end task acceptance remains the ultimate arbiter of system quality. The acceptance rate must be calculated across all admitted task trials, explicitly including timeouts, uncaught exceptions, and partial completions in the denominator. Satisfying an obsolete constraint is an operational failure, even if the retriever achieved high precision against a stale label set.
System resource accounting must respect the same strict evaluation boundaries. Cost accounting aggregates the end-to-end compute footprint: query generation, keyword search, dense similarity computation, cross-encoder reranking, model token usage, memory writes, offline consolidation, and background index compaction. This ledger must include asynchronous background operations that do not directly block foreground user requests, as well as deferred maintenance tasks lingering at the end of the evaluation window. Dividing the total expenditure by the number of successfully completed tasks yields the cost per accepted task (equation 1.2). If a system completes zero tasks, evaluators must report total expenditure and zero successes rather than computing an undefined or misleading ratio.
Storage measurements require equally clear accounting boundaries. Benchmarks should report raw source bytes separately from auxiliary structures, including inverted index postings, dense vector tables, graph adjacency lists, version metadata, and durability replicas. Authors must explicitly define whether their reported storage amplification represents auxiliary bytes divided by raw source bytes, or total stored bytes (source plus auxiliary) divided by raw source bytes. Similarly, update-latency benchmarks must compare equivalent operations: a full index rebuild against a full index rebuild, rather than comparing a complete re-indexing pass against an asynchronous tombstone lookup. Notebook 6.5 compares both metrics across two representative store architectures.



Dense vectors multiply a store’s auxiliary bytes by an order of magnitude.

Store A adds a BM25 index and a structural graph with 4 edges per file. Store B adds the same BM25 index plus 100-token chunks embedded as 768-dimensional vectors under an HNSW graph shaped like the one in table 5. The vectors are kept at full FP32 width, twice the FP16 width of the exact-scan corpus, and the encoder is stipulated to be slower than the local batch of notebook 6.4. How do their auxiliary bytes and re-index times compare?
Math: Store A’s auxiliary structures occupy 14.4 MB, an auxiliary ratio of 0.36× over the raw source (total ratio 1.36×). Store B’s occupy 340.8 MB, of which the vectors alone are 307.2 MB, an auxiliary ratio of 8.52× (total 9.52×). After an edit to 15 files, at stipulated throughputs for postings updates and parsing, Store A re-indexes in 34.1 ms. Store B must re-embed 30 chunks; at 50 chunks per second it needs 612 ms.
Store B carries ~24× the auxiliary bytes of Store A and takes ~18× as long to re-index.
Systems insight: Dense vectors dominate both the bytes and the maintenance time, because each chunk becomes hundreds of floating-point components produced by a model pass. Compressing the vectors attacks the byte term, and storing them at FP16 would halve the vector bytes; only a faster encoder or fewer re-embedded chunks attacks the time term, which sets the stale window after every edit. The time ratio therefore depends on the stipulated encoder throughput and shrinks with a faster encoder, while the byte ratio does not depend on it. A dense index is worth its order of magnitude only when it raises task acceptance enough to repay that maintenance in the cost per accepted task. The live-source baseline of section 6.4 pays neither term, which is why it is the comparison every added index must beat.


Staging depth warrants independent empirical measurement because task success does not increase monotonically with the retrieval cutoff \(\RetrievalCutoffCount\). Recall@\(\RetrievalCutoffCount\) (equation 6) cannot decrease as \(\RetrievalCutoffCount\) increases, but every added record changes the prompt the model must use. Two effects that limit usable working context act together here. Each superficially similar but irrelevant passage adds to the softmax normalizer and so dilutes the attention the critical evidence receives (attention dilution), and a larger staged set pushes some of that evidence toward the middle of the prompt, where models use it least reliably (lost in the middle) (Liu et al. 2024). Too few records starve the decision of evidence; too many bury it. The optimal operating range depends heavily on the model’s attention architecture, task complexity, and reranker quality. This mirrors the working-set view of context (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}\)). In practice, systems engineers should configure candidate retrieval to maximize recall, use a precise reranker to stage only a compact working set into the prompt, and systematically sweep staging depth across evaluation trials rather than assuming a single static cutoff.

Ultimately, memory evaluation yields a multidimensional trade-off space rather than a single scalar benchmark score. A more expansive memory store retains helpful edge-case experiences, but it also accumulates obsolete or contradictory records. Conversely, a strict admission gate shields the agent from spurious lessons at the expense of rejecting valuable domain context. Systems architects must systematically vary read and write policies under identical operational budgets, evaluating whether variations in accepted task outcomes stem from evidence coverage, temporal applicability, lifecycle maintenance failures, or compute and storage costs.



A complete evaluation suite must subject the memory system to adversarial boundary tests. In an isolated evaluation sandbox, test harnesses inject synthetic credentials, probe unauthorized namespace boundaries, and retrieve documents embedded with indirect prompt injections (Greshake et al. 2023). The test suite evaluates two critical enforcement layers: whether the runtime intercepts and suppresses unauthorized reads and writes, and whether an adversarial payload survives in downstream consolidated summaries after the primary source document has been withdrawn.

Evaluators must capture both the model’s proposed actions and the runtime’s actual execution disposition. Logging both stages ensures that the evaluation distinguishes an attempted security breach from an executed vulnerability. The memory policy is accountable for the records it admits, indexes, and stages; the tool and runtime authorization subsystems are accountable for governing what the agent is permitted to execute against the external environment.

Checkpoint 6.4: Evidence across sessions
A proposed memory policy raises retrieval scores on a static snapshot. Its authors have not tested updates, deletion, or later task outcomes.

Trial isolation: How can an evaluation harness prevent one policy’s stored reflections or reference answers from contaminating another policy’s trial?
Update semantics: Which later-session probes would distinguish successful preference supersession from keeping both conflicting preferences?
Withdrawal scope: What must be inspected beyond the original record after a deletion request, and what retention limits must the result disclose?
Metric boundary: Why can a zero stale-return rate coexist with failed retrieval, and which task and cost measurements would reveal the failure?
Cost per accepted task: Policy B raises acceptance from 50 percent to 60 percent but adds background maintenance equal to a tenth of Policy A’s attempt cost. Estimate whether its cost per accepted task rises or falls, and find the acceptance rate at which the two policies break even.







Persistent memory systems fail when they grant a stored representation more operational authority than its underlying provenance supports, or when they treat write-time admission as a permanent guarantee of validity. The misconceptions below represent common architectural traps where design shortcuts produce silent state corruption, latency spikes, or degraded reasoning fidelity. Each item highlights an engineering trade-off whose quantitative systems cost is demonstrated in this chapter’s accompanying notebooks.

Fallacy: A near-duplicate memory carries no new information.
The 10:00-to-11:00 revision at the admission gate (section 6.8.2) is one instance of a wider class. A flipped flag (“notify me of failures” becoming “do not notify me of failures”) and a scoped exception (“no meetings before 11:00 on Fridays”) also land beside the record they modify in embedding space, yet the first reverses it and the second must coexist with it. A similarity threshold fails differently on each, dropping the reversal as a repeat and collapsing the exception into the general rule, so the agent either keeps the prohibited behavior or loses the narrower constraint. High geometric proximity does not imply semantic equivalence. An admission pipeline must first establish entity identity, scope, record kind, and explicit update semantics; geometric similarity should deduplicate storage only after verifying that the new record asserts no state change and no change of scope.


Pitfall: Treating a high-ranked record as current.
Vector similarity scores indicate semantic or topical affinity with a query, but they convey nothing about temporal freshness, transactional validity, or operational authority. In the trace that opens section 6.9, the outdated r17 excerpt of src/pool.py ranks first for the notification query. At turn 13 the agent consumed it without a version label, concluded that its own completed edit had been lost, and spent the following turns re-issuing that edit and then making speculative changes that pushed the repository further from a reviewed state. Coordinated generation checks prevent this particular cascade. Filtering 50 candidates adds 1.5 μs of local metadata lookup work under the stipulated scenario, excluding the durable coordination and fallback costs (notebook 6.4). While index rank identifies candidate relevance, the runtime must rely on provenance, version tags, visibility scope, and completion status to govern how a retrieved record is applied.


Fallacy: Staging more retrieved records gives the model more evidence.
Recall@\(\RetrievalCutoffCount\) cannot decrease as \(\RetrievalCutoffCount\) grows, but task success does not follow it (Liu et al. 2024). In notebook 6.1, a staging policy that counts only raw document bodies admits 12 records that serialize to 7,040 tokens, overrunning a 6,144-token allowance before any of it reaches the model. Even within the allowance, the dilution and position effects that make staging depth a measured quantity rather than a maximum still apply. Systems architects must calibrate retrieval staging depth against downstream task completion and execution budgets rather than optimizing recall in isolation (section 6.10).
