Selecting an envelope depends on three characteristics of the agent’s action: the code it runs, the authority it holds, and how long it holds the envelope.

Workload profile: Pure computation over deterministic inputs maps directly to restricted bytecode. Arbitrary POSIX binaries, package managers, and shell scripts require the broader interface of a user-space kernel or a dedicated microVM. A shared-kernel container remains eligible when its configured boundary and trusted host kernel satisfy the declared threat model; it does not contain compromise of that shared kernel.
Authority level: At \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_1\), where mutation is confined to a discardable sandbox, tool admission checks only the request, so once code runs the envelope must enforce the boundary against the assumed attacker. The repair scenario assumes arbitrary native code, including a compromised guest kernel, must not control host enforcement; this warrants the separate guest kernel of a microVM under that threat model. At \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_2\) and \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\), where actions reach external infrastructure, the envelope must be coupled with credential brokers and approval gates, because local containment cannot stop an authorized external call from altering remote state.
Execution horizon: The time over which an envelope is retained decides how its setup is amortized. A setup of 15 ms is prohibitive for a 3 ms parser invoked hundreds of times, but negligible across a multi-turn repair trajectory that runs for minutes (Notebook 8.1).

Applying these criteria to the three workloads that opened the section gives three different envelopes:

The structured log parser executes in a lightweight bytecode sandbox created on demand per invocation.
The connection-pool repair agent retains a dedicated microVM throughout its entire multi-turn trajectory. A user-space kernel is an alternative under a narrower threat model that keeps the emulator trusted, provided its interfaces and performance support the toolchain.
The customer-uploaded binary runs in an ephemeral microVM stripped of all credentials with outbound egress unconditionally denied. A binary that needs more than this profile allows is refused rather than granted relaxed host privileges.

In every case, the security guarantee is defined by the concrete mounts, virtual devices, packet filters, and resource ceilings applied to that envelope.
Performance evaluations must measure the complete lifecycle: admission latency, time to first useful work, steady-state throughput, and final teardown overhead under realistic concurrency. A runtime that advertises instant container creation often defers storage setup or package initialization to the first execution turn. Furthermore, startup costs interact directly with envelope lifecycle policies: allocating a fresh envelope for every atomic step trades initialization latency for clean-slate isolation, whereas retaining an envelope across turns amortizes startup at the cost of managing accumulated state.



Setup occupies a smaller share of a fresh call as useful work increases.

Napkin Math 8.1: Paying setup once or repeatedlyProblem: A hypothetical trajectory performs 100 sequential parser calls, each requiring 3 ms of useful execution, and preparing the envelope through readiness for useful work costs 15 ms in the chapter’s illustrative sandbox profile. How much elapsed time does a fresh envelope per call add over one envelope retained for the trajectory, and at what per-call work does the fresh envelope become affordable?
Math: For \(\EnvelopeCallCount\) calls, setup time \(\EnvelopeSetupTime\), and useful work \(\CallUsefulWorkTime\) per call, fresh-per-call execution takes \(\EnvelopeCallCount(\EnvelopeSetupTime+\CallUsefulWorkTime)\) and trajectory reuse takes \(\EnvelopeSetupTime+\EnvelopeCallCount \CallUsefulWorkTime\). Both perform 300 ms of useful work. Fresh-per-call execution adds 1500 ms of setup, totaling 1800 ms; reuse adds one 15 ms setup, totaling 315 ms, a 5.7× difference. Setup is \(\EnvelopeSetupTime/(\EnvelopeSetupTime+\CallUsefulWorkTime)\) = 83.3 percent of every fresh call. Holding setup to at most 10 percent of a fresh call requires \(\CallUsefulWorkTime \ge \EnvelopeSetupTime(1-\SetupShareCap)/\SetupShareCap\) for a cap \(\SetupShareCap\), here 135 ms of work per call.
Systems insight: The ratio \(\CallUsefulWorkTime/\EnvelopeSetupTime\) determines the setup-cost trade-off. Calls with at least 135 ms of useful work can afford a fresh envelope each; below that, retaining one envelope for the trajectory reduces overhead when the within-task trust policy permits reuse. The price of reuse is a within-task trust policy, since state from earlier calls reaches later ones. Reuse never crosses tenants: ready capacity for the next task comes from pooling and verified reset (section 8.8). The comparison counts setup and useful work only, excluding model calls, queueing, and teardown.





Choosing an envelope settles what code can reach, not how much it may consume, so isolation also requires resource governance alongside namespace and instruction boundaries. An untrusted program can degrade host availability through CPU starvation, memory exhaustion, fork bombs, disk thrashing, or unbounded standard output streaming. Resource limits must encompass the entire workload, including host-side helper threads and emulator processes, measured from the host kernel’s perspective rather than trusting guest-reported statistics. While quotas cap total resource consumption, noisy-neighbor contention across shared CPU caches, memory channels, and storage buses requires independent monitoring and isolation. Engineering validation suites should test excessive memory allocation and runaway output streams alongside access-control denials, recording expected failure-handling behavior.
On Linux systems, cgroups v2 provides the unified control hierarchy needed to govern these execution trees, whether managing container processes or microVM monitor and vCPU threads (The Linux Kernel Documentation Project 2024a). The cpu.max controller enforces strict CPU quotas per scheduling period, automatically throttling the control group once its allocation is exhausted. Process creation is bounded by pids.max to prevent thread-exhaustion attacks. Memory management benefits from graduated enforcement thresholds: when usage exceeds memory.high, the kernel proactively throttles allocating threads and triggers synchronous page reclaim without terminating processes. Only when memory reaches memory.max and reclaim attempts fail does the out-of-memory (OOM) killer terminate tasks within the group. This graduated behavior is vital for agent systems, as an unannounced OOM termination destroys transient diagnostic traces and execution state before the supervisory agent can capture them.

The Linux Kernel Documentation Project. 2024a. Control Group V2. Linux kernel documentation.

The Linux Kernel Documentation Project. 2024d. PSI: Pressure Stall Information. Linux kernel documentation.
To intervene proactively before resource starvation triggers a hard failure, supervisors use Pressure Stall Information (PSI) (The Linux Kernel Documentation Project 2024d). PSI tracks the percentage of elapsed time that threads spend stalled on CPU runqueues, memory page allocation, or blocking disk I/O. By registering custom stall thresholds with epoll, a supervisor receives early warning notifications when a sandbox enters severe resource contention. The supervisor can then initiate memory compaction, capture the sandbox’s diagnostic state, or gracefully terminate the failing agent with an explicit diagnostic reason code, avoiding silent process dropouts.



Suppose the repository under repair contains compiled tensor kernels, so its test suite needs an accelerator to run. The candidate code the agent wrote now drives a physical device that another tenant will use next, and that device joins the isolation boundary. Integrating accelerators introduces four core systems challenges:

Auditing the host driver and ioctl surface exposed to the sandbox.
Enforcing compute and device-memory partitioning.
Containing device-level faults to prevent cascading crashes across adjacent tenants.
Ensuring deterministic memory scrubbing and state reset between workload reassignments, which the reset contract of section 8.8.1 must cover.

Offloading accelerator tasks to a remote microservice replaces direct hardware passthrough with a structured RPC interface, shifting the isolation burden to service-side multi-tenancy and admission controls.
Direct hardware assignment exposes the host to device direct memory access (DMA), enabling peripheral devices to read and write arbitrary host physical addresses independently of CPU page tables. Standard CPU address-space isolation provides no protection against rogue DMA transactions. As detailed in the Linux VFIO framework (The Linux Kernel Documentation Project 2024e), secure device assignment requires an I/O Memory Management Unit (IOMMU) to translate and restrict device DMA requests through dedicated I/O page tables. The IOMMU cannot always separate two devices, because devices that can exchange traffic directly over the PCIe fabric, without the bridge’s access control services forcing that traffic up through the IOMMU, share one isolation group, so the true physical boundary often encompasses several slots rather than one device. Hardware features that split one device among tenants narrow the sharing but do not remove the obligation. The fault domain, the driver’s exposure, and the device memory left behind must still be validated, because CPU-level virtualization guarantees end at the PCIe bus. The last of these is the device row of the reset contract (section 8.8.1).

The Linux Kernel Documentation Project. 2024e. VFIO: Virtual Function I/O. Linux kernel documentation.
The selected envelope establishes a rigorous execution boundary, resource policy, and lifecycle for compute. Multi-turn workflows, however, impose a parallel state continuity requirement: iterative test cycles require access to code modifications and intermediate artifacts generated across preceding turns. Decoupling this persistent filesystem state from the transient lifecycle of worker processes and sandboxes requires a dedicated task-local workspace architecture governed by explicit retention and export policies.

title: 8 Agent Sandboxes
text:
Multi-step agent tasks require files to persist across individual tool invocations. In a software repair task, for example, an agent generates an edit to create candidate patch r18, executes a subsequent shell command to compile the code, and finally runs a test suite that produces an evaluation report. Spawning a fresh process for every command protects the host from runaway memory allocations or lingering background jobs, but those separate processes must still view and modify a shared, continuous filesystem state. Conversely, keeping a single process alive does not establish boundaries around which files the agent may alter. An agent execution environment therefore requires an explicit workspace policy independent of its execution envelope.
That workspace policy delineates four critical boundaries: the immutable source baseline, the task’s private modifications, temporary scratch space, and the artifacts eligible for final export. Generated commands execute strictly within a designated task workspace, isolated entirely from the host’s primary working tree or operational directories. For a code repair run, candidate edits and intermediate build artifacts reside inside this task workspace. At the same time, authoritative acceptance test suites, benchmark harnesses, and reporting mechanisms remain strictly outside the agent’s writable scope, even when the agent is permitted to write temporary test output into a monitored scratch directory.


A full private copy offers a straightforward way to provision an agent workspace, but creating duplicate copies of large source repositories, compilers, language runtimes, and dependencies introduces severe storage and I/O bottlenecks. Copy-on-write solves this by decoupling the immutable base environment from the modifications generated by individual tasks. The runtime pins a read-only base image and exposes a private, writable view for each trajectory. Read requests transparently access the shared base contents, while write operations allocate private storage on demand according to the underlying filesystem’s copying rules. Workspaces sharing the same underlying base remain completely isolated from each other’s mutations.



Copy-on-write provisioning moves what tasks write, not what they can see.

The Linux Kernel Documentation Project. 2024c. Overlay Filesystem. Linux kernel documentation.
A layered filesystem provides a standard implementation of this pattern at the file level. A read-only lower directory tree supplies the baseline repository, while a private, writable upper directory tree stores newly created, modified, or overwritten files. A union mount combines these two layers into a single merged namespace visible to the executing agent. When an agent deletes a file that exists in the read-only lower layer, the filesystem cannot remove the shared file; instead, it writes a special deletion marker into the upper layer to hide the lower entry. In Linux OverlayFS, this marker is known as a whiteout (The Linux Kernel Documentation Project 2024c). Because copy-up operations, directory merges, and whiteouts involve kernel metadata and filesystem-specific structures, the upper tree does not represent a clean, ready-to-commit source tree or patch.
Furthermore, copy-on-write is fundamentally a storage optimization, not an execution isolation boundary. Preventing concurrently executing tasks from modifying the shared base or reading each other’s private layers remains the duty of the sandbox execution envelope. For example, a microVM sandbox might attach an independent copy-on-write block snapshot rather than mounting a host-level filesystem overlay. The choice between block-level and file-level mechanisms directly affects memory and cache utilization, determining whether guest operating systems share a single host page cache or duplicate cached pages across virtual machines.



Copy-on-write defers data copying from workspace creation to the exact instant an agent mutates a file. Consequently, the granularity of that copy operation determines runtime latency and storage overhead. Under a file-level scheme like OverlayFS, modifying a single byte in a large test fixture forces the filesystem to copy the entire file into the private upper layer before applying the write. In contrast, a block-level storage mechanism or an extent-sharing filesystem allocates private storage only for the modified blocks or extents, preserving shared pointers for the rest. While finer granularity drastically cuts payload transfer for localized edits, no storage design eliminates overhead entirely: metadata allocation, journaling, and page-cache management prevent even a one-byte modification from becoming a one-byte physical write.

Napkin Math 8.2: Provisioning by copy, and the granularity of a first modificationProblem: An evaluation host starts 32 workspaces for the same task. The pinned base (repository, toolchain, and dependencies) is 2.4 GB, and each task writes about 40 MB of edits and build outputs. The workspaces share one local drive with a sequential rate of 7 GB/s. How much payload does a full private copy move compared with a copy-on-write view, and what does a later one-byte change to a shared file cost?
Provisioning: A full copy moves 32 × 2.4 GB = 76.8 GB before any agent runs, at least 11.0 s of drive time even at the sequential rate. A copy-on-write view starts as a mount, and only written data acquires private storage, 1.28 GB across all tasks, at least 0.18 s. The copy moves 60× as many bytes, and the ratio is simply the base size over the bytes each task writes. Copy-on-write makes provisioning cost track what the agent changes, not what it can see.
First modification: Each of 32 independent workspaces initially shares an unchanged 1.2 GB binary fixture. Each task overwrites 1 byte within that fixture. Compare two hypothetical implementations: the first copies the entire file’s payload into private storage before modifying it; the second copies only the one 64 KB block containing the update. Assume that block was shared before the update and that no other block needs copying. Neither implementation uses a copy offload or compression in this accounting.
Math: File-granularity copying moves 32 × 1.2 GB = 38.4 GB of payload. Under the stipulated block-copy rule, the corresponding total is 32 × 64 KB = 2,048 KB. Both support the same 32 bytes of requested logical changes, and the file-granularity payload is about 19,000× larger.
Systems insight: Two ratios set the storage bill. Provisioning cost scales with the base size over the bytes each task writes (60× here), so copy-on-write wins whenever tasks change a small fraction of what they can see and loses its advantage as that fraction approaches one. First-write cost scales with the fixture size over the copying unit (about 19,000× here), independent of the edit’s size, so large mutable fixtures belong on block-granular storage and large immutable ones stay read-only. The totals count payload only; metadata, journaling, and caching add traffic, so the drive-time figures are lower bounds.


These quantitative dynamics dictate clear systems engineering practices:

Mount immutable fixtures read-only: Large test fixtures, model weights, and compiler binaries should remain strictly read-only whenever tasks do not require in-place mutation. Read-only mounts prevent inadvertent copy-up operations while allowing multiple concurrent sandboxes to share host page-cache entries.
Redirect volatile outputs to scratch volumes: Build outputs, compiler intermediate files, and execution logs should write directly to dedicated, bounded scratch storage rather than triggering copy-up chains within the primary workspace overlay.
Align storage granularity with access patterns: If tasks must perform localized edits on massive files or databases, systems should deploy block-level snapshotting or extent-sharing filesystems. Copy-on-write provides massive I/O savings when an agent mutates a minor fraction of the workspace, but its performance advantage diminishes rapidly as modifications approach the size of the base image.

Even with copy-on-write efficiency, private task storage requires hard bounds. Unconstrained agent execution can quickly exhaust host disk capacity through runaway build logs, recursive file generation, or massive cache directories. The runtime must enforce quotas on both total storage bytes and inode counts, while accounting for I/O operations per second alongside compute limits. Crucially, when an agent reaches a storage quota, the runtime must surface this condition explicitly as a resource exhaustion error rather than allowing a tool call to fail silently with partial writes or corrupt state. Finally, per-workspace quotas must integrate into host-level admission control: dozens of sandboxes that each respect an individual 10 GB quota can collectively exhaust physical drive capacity if provisioned without aggregate admission limits.



A workspace lease establishes a formal contract binding a provisioned workspace to a specific task, owner, authorized execution envelope, and operational lifetime. In multi-turn agent workflows, an agent relies on intermediate build caches, compiler outputs, and preliminary code edits surviving between turns. The workspace lease ensures this private state persists across sequential tool calls without exposing those modifications to subsequent or concurrent tenants. When an agent dispatches a new command within its assigned turn, the runtime attaches the executing process to the leased workspace; conversely, a new task receives an entirely separate, freshly provisioned environment.


↪ Checkpoints that bind the lease’s workspace files to a committed log position, so private state survives a worker crash as well as a turn boundary, are developed in Checkpoints.
The lease serves strictly as an ownership and lifetime contract, not as a synchronization mechanism. It differs from the scheduler’s lease of Operation identity and endpoint contracts, where a stale worker may still be running somewhere else and the destination must fence its writes with an epoch. A workspace is attached to one envelope, so a stale holder is fenced by the supervisor itself, which revokes the envelope’s access when the lease ends (section 8.8.1). Granting a lease confirms which tenant owns a storage volume, but it does not indicate whether a previous asynchronous command has finished writing or whether orphaned background processes continue to hold open file handles. The runtime must enforce operational quiescence by terminating lingering background jobs and flushing pending I/O operations before concluding a tool turn or handing off workspace state.


↩︎ Supervision and cancellation of background jobs that outlive a tool turn are established in Job supervision and cancellation.
When a task concludes, the runtime must extract permissible deliverables before tearing down private state. For a code repair agent, valid deliverables typically include a unified patch relative to the pinned baseline, a cryptographic hash or manifest of the resulting source tree, and structured execution logs from verification suites. To ensure consistency, the export pipeline must generate deliverables from a stable snapshot or after all writer processes have completely halted, guaranteeing that the exported patch matches the exact version validated by the test suite. Furthermore, the export system must canonicalize and validate all file paths within the workspace boundary; otherwise, symbolic links crafted by an untrusted agent could trick an export routine into reading and leaking sensitive host files.
Runtimes must never simply archive the raw upper filesystem layer as the task deliverable. In an overlay filesystem, the upper layer contains kernel whiteout markers, internal metadata, compiler caches, temporary build artifacts, and potentially leaked environment secrets. Export pipelines must explicitly parse, filter, and validate deliverables into clean formats, such as standard diffs and vetted test reports. Even then, an exported patch represents only a candidate proposal rather than proof of correctness. Downstream release engineering pipelines must independently verify that the patch applies cleanly to trunk and passes authoritative continuous integration checks under trusted credentials before merging into a production repository.
Once legitimate deliverables are extracted, the runtime discards the remaining private state following the sandbox pooling and recycling policies developed in section 8.8.
Regulating artifact export secures the primary file-based egress channel from the workspace. However, arbitrary code executing inside a sandbox can also open network sockets to exfiltrate proprietary source code, internal test fixtures, or discovered security vulnerabilities. Maintaining storage isolation across turns addresses only half the containment challenge; robust sandboxing architectures must enforce strict network egress controls independently of storage continuity.

title: 8 Agent Sandboxes
text:
Consider the threat model where credential brokering is fully operational: an untrusted script triggered by an injected README cannot read the host’s authentication token from guest memory. However, the executing code still holds legitimate read access to the local source files required to complete its software repair task. If that code opens an outbound socket and transmits the repository contents to an unapproved external server, proprietary intellectual property is disclosed immediately. This exfiltration succeeds without breaking the hypervisor envelope or extracting cryptographic keys. Egress control governs the communication channels directed outward from the execution sandbox. A robust security architecture must strictly enforce outbound boundaries on the physical and virtual network data path, rather than trusting guest-level processes or client configurations to behave cooperatively.


The cleanest defense against network exfiltration is running code without an outbound network interface. Tasks that evaluate self-contained code, run localized test suites, or analyze static data require only a loopback interface inside an isolated network namespace. However, agentic tasks frequently require external communication: pulling language dependencies, fetching remote git commits, or submitting job telemetry. For these workloads, the host runtime must provide tightly scoped network access through a task-specific service adapter or a restricted egress gateway, ensuring the guest possesses no unchecked secondary route to external networks.
For any networked guest, routing and protocol enforcement must reside strictly outside the guest’s control boundary. Relying on guest-side environment variables such as HTTP_PROXY or HTTPS_PROXY fails because an untrusted process can simply ignore them, bind raw sockets, or establish unauthorized tunnels. Genuine isolation requires the host virtualization layer (using tools such as Linux network namespaces, virtual ethernet pairs, and nftables or eBPF cgroup filters) to govern all outbound traffic before it reaches external fabrics.
A comprehensive network boundary reviews every communication vector: direct IP sockets, alternate address families such as IPv6, recursive name-resolution queries, and host services exposed across local virtual bridges. In practice, egress enforcement requires two complementary layers operating in tandem. At the transport and network layer, a packet filter evaluates IP addresses and port numbers. It permits traffic destined exclusively for a designated mediation gateway and drops any direct connection attempt to raw IP literals or external resolvers. At the application layer, a dedicated mediator inspects requested protocols, service paths, and specific operations. Verifying this defense-in-depth architecture demands adversarial testing: validating that attempted bypasses, such as direct socket connections and unbrokered DNS queries, are dropped, rather than merely confirming that well-behaved HTTP clients succeed. The two layers fail differently (figure 5): the packet filter cannot tell a fetch from a push to the same address, and the mediator never sees a direct socket that the filter has already dropped, so each covers the other’s blind spot.






Figure 5: Two Enforcement Points Outside the Guest: The packet filter sees only addresses and ports, so it admits connections to the mediator and drops a direct socket or a lookup sent toward an outside resolver, whatever name the program had in mind. The mediator interprets the request. It resolves its own fixed destinations, admits the repository fetch, and adds the brokered credential, while a push or a request for another repository fails the operation grant at the same hostname. A mediator can inspect or change methods, paths, and bodies only if it makes the upstream request itself or terminates TLS; a proxy that merely forwards encrypted traffic cannot.






Allowing an agent to contact a specific network endpoint answers only the coarsest part of the access control question. Modern cloud services serve vastly different operations beneath a single hostname. For example, a code hosting platform exposes read-only repository clones, branch pushes, pull-request commentary, and public asset uploads through the exact same HTTPS endpoint. Granting an agent permission to fetch a specific git repository should not grant it permission to push arbitrary commits or post internal file contents to a public issue tracker. As outlined in table 6, robust egress governance separates policy decisions into three hierarchical scopes: destination endpoints, permitted operations and resources, and the data submitted within those operations.



Table 6: Three scopes of egress policy: Destination restrictions, operation grants, and disclosure decisions constrain different aspects of an outbound request.










Policy scope
Question
What the restriction does not establish




Destination
Which service and network endpoint may this task reach?
Every operation offered by that service is permitted.


Operation and resource
Which action may it perform on which repository, object, or endpoint?
Every submitted field or body is appropriate to disclose.


Submitted data
Which information may leave through the allowed operation?
A scanner can recognize every sensitive encoding or misuse.






A host-owned service adapter embodies this separation by acting as a dedicated API mediator. When an agent requests a repository checkout, the adapter verifies the task’s identity, confirms that the targeted repository matches the approved task scope, and ensures the requested operation is strictly read-only before attaching upstream credentials held securely on the host. The guest receives the resulting files without ever seeing the authentication token. A subsequent request attempting to push code or query an unapproved repository fails immediately at the adapter, even though the remote hostname is identical. Moreover, the adapter must inspect query parameters and request structures; otherwise, an attacker could smuggle arbitrary outbound data inside the parameter fields of an ostensibly permitted GET request.
Standard forward proxies offer significantly less semantic visibility. When a proxy handles HTTPS traffic using the HTTP CONNECT tunnel method, it merely relays an encrypted byte stream between the guest and the destination server. In this mode, the proxy can inspect only the initial transport-layer destination and the Server Name Indication (SNI) header. It cannot see HTTP verbs, URL request paths, request headers, or body payloads. Enforcing operation-level or data-level policies on encrypted traffic requires terminating TLS at the egress gateway. The gateway decrypts the payload, validates the request against fine-grained policy rules, and establishes an independent upstream TLS connection. This inspection architecture requires injecting a private root certificate authority into the guest trust store. However, tools that employ certificate pinning or custom trust stores, including various package managers and language runtimes, will reject these intercepted connections, making host-managed service adapters the more reliable pattern for fine-grained egress mediation.



Restricting network destinations by hostname introduces subtle binding vulnerabilities between name resolution and connection establishment. If a policy engine validates a domain name using a separate DNS query before the guest connects, a malicious DNS server can exploit a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap via DNS rebinding. The resolver returns an authorized public address during the policy check, but subsequently returns a restricted private address when the guest application establishes its socket. To prevent rebinding exploits, the egress mediator must bind destination approvals directly to the physical IP addresses used for the connection, validate every enabled address family (including IPv6), and reject resolved targets that fall outside the approved scope. Similarly, the mediator must strictly intercept HTTP redirects (301 and 302 response codes), subjecting every redirection target to a fresh policy evaluation to avoid server-side request forgery (SSRF).
Host-local interfaces, private subnets (such as RFC 1918 allocations), and link-local addresses represent especially dangerous egress targets. In cloud virtualization environments, instances access local metadata services across link-local addresses such as 169.254.169.254. These metadata endpoints frequently return short-lived identity and access management (IAM) credentials, hypervisor configuration data, and bootstrap tokens without requiring prior authentication. If egress rules filter only public internet ranges while overlooking link-local and internal bridge traffic, an agent can query the cloud metadata service to compromise the host platform. A secure network sandbox must drop all traffic to private, loopback, and link-local ranges by default, permitting communication only toward explicit, authorized host endpoints.
Furthermore, DNS resolution functions as an outbound signaling channel in its own right.8 If a guest environment can dispatch arbitrary queries to a recursive DNS resolver, an agent can exfiltrate sensitive data by encoding byte sequences into subdomain labels (such as data-payload.attacker-domain.com). Even when all TCP and UDP egress traffic to the internet is blocked, the recursive resolver will forward the query to an authoritative nameserver controlled by an adversary, successfully transmitting the payload outside the perimeter. Sandboxes must therefore enforce strict name resolution controls. Rather than granting the guest access to an unrestricted recursive resolver, the runtime should route DNS through an internal adapter that resolves only fixed, allowlisted hosts. Where dynamic resolution is strictly necessary, allowlists must enforce fully qualified domain names rather than broad domain wildcards, since wildcards leave subdomain labels available for data signaling. Complementary controls, such as query-rate throttling and entropy monitoring, constrain channel throughput and expose suspicious lookup patterns, bounding the rate of potential exfiltration.
8 The Confinement Problem: Lampson (1973) posed the problem of running a borrowed program so that it cannot leak its caller’s data, and observed that a program can signal through channels never intended for communication, such as its use of shared resources. Name lookups are such a channel for a guest whose web requests are blocked. Confinement has to account for every externally observable effect of the code, and a rate limit narrows a channel’s bandwidth without closing it.
Lampson, Butler W. 1973. “A Note on the Confinement Problem.” Communications of the ACM 16 (10): 613–15.



Even when network filters, TLS proxies, destination allowlists, and operation grants function exactly as designed, sensitive data can still escape through permitted payload channels. Suppose an agent repair task is authorized to transmit automated diagnostic summaries to an internal issue tracker. The runtime enforces transport isolation, contacts only the approved tracking endpoint, and invokes the permitted submit_report operation. However, an adversarial instruction embedded in the input repository causes the agent model to append proprietary source files or environment variables into the diagnostic report. In this scenario, every structural containment boundary operates correctly, yet the payload discloses sensitive information beyond the task’s intended scope.
Mitigating disclosure through legitimate channels requires layered payload validation. The mediation layer should enforce strict schema constraints on outbound requests, limiting payloads to structured key-value pairs and restricting free-form text fields. Applying tight payload size limits prevents bulk exfiltration attempts. In addition, secret scanners and content inspectors embedded in the egress path can analyze outbound buffers for high-entropy strings, cryptographic keys, and recognized token formats before releasing requests upstream. Nevertheless, automated content scanning remains inherently heuristic; transformed source code, obfuscated strings, and subtle data encodings can bypass signature-based filters. A comprehensive defense requires combining structural payload restrictions with prompt-injection defenses and semantic policy enforcement.
Finally, outbound communication channels must adhere to strict temporal lifecycles. When a task execution lease expires, its corresponding network identity and authorization tokens must be revoked immediately. The sandbox runtime must terminate active TCP connections, reset virtual network interfaces, drop lingering keep-alive sockets, and abort pending brokered requests. Because network egress creates permanent external side effects that cannot be undone by rolling back local disk state, restoring an execution environment for subsequent tasks requires comprehensive network teardown alongside workspace sanitization.

title: 8 Agent Sandboxes
text:
The workspace lease keeps the repair’s edits, build artifacts, and helper processes alive across turns, and the egress controls bound what they can send. When the trajectory ends, a platform serving many tasks must provision the next tenant’s environment without delay. The next tenant must inherit none of the modified files, background daemons, open sockets, or credentials the repair left behind, yet it should not wait for a cold boot either. Sandbox pooling reconciles these requirements. The pool keeps a standby reserve of clean, pre-warmed instances to absorb arrivals, and an instance whose lease has ended rejoins the ready fleet only after a complete, verified reset, regardless of what status code its final tool returned.
Two naive extremes bracket this design space. At one end, a fresh envelope for every tool call carries no state between calls, but every call pays the full setup (Notebook 8.1 found setup to be 83.3 percent of each short parser call), and the control plane must pass the whole workspace across the boundary on every turn. At the other end, one long-lived environment reused across tasks pays no setup between trajectories, but mutable state accumulates in the guest, from stray files and corrupted configurations to backdoors planted by a prompt injection. A sandbox pool takes the middle path. It initializes instances in advance, holds them in a standby reserve, leases each instance to a single trajectory for that trajectory’s entire lifespan (section 8.6.3), and flags the instance as tainted the moment the lease expires. The tainted instance remains strictly unavailable until external hypervisor or operating system mechanisms either restore it to a verified baseline or destroy it entirely.


A reset contract defines the precise conditions under which an execution environment may be cleared to serve a new lease, cataloging all state that teardown or restoration must cover. In practice, this boundary extends far beyond the workspace directory on disk. A command executed by an agent can spawn background processes, leave network connections half-open, alter kernel-level runtime parameters, or enqueue asynchronous tasks inside host-managed services. Simply removing the files that the agent was expected to modify leaves these residual objects untouched. Standard operating-system primitives provide numerous avenues for state to elude naive file-based scrubbing: a rogue daemon can double-fork to detach from the task’s process group, an abstract Unix domain socket leaves no entry in the filesystem, tokens can linger in the kernel keyring, scheduled cron jobs can trigger after the lease has completed, or modified helper scripts can shadow tools earlier on the search path.
To eliminate cross-tenant leakage, the supervisor immediately fences an expiring lease before cleanup begins. It halts incoming tool invocations under that lease and revokes its communication channels, credentials, and network authority. Next, the supervisor quiesces and terminates all owned execution, including child processes, background workers, and pending host-side tasks bound to the environment. A wall-clock timeout, error condition, or explicit cancellation signal initiates this sequence, but teardown requires positive confirmation from the enforcement layer rather than assumptions based on elapsed time. If the virtualization layer cannot conclusively verify that all execution has ceased or that shared hardware resources have been cleanly severed, the supervisor isolates and destroys the instance rather than returning it to the pool.
Once all writers inside the sandbox are confirmed quiescent, the supervisor extracts and persists only those outputs explicitly permitted by the task’s export policy. In a code repair scenario, these artifacts typically include the unified git diff of candidate edits and bounded test execution logs linked to the target repository commit. If an implementation attempts to export artifacts while the guest is still executing, it must enforce an explicit consistency boundary so that concurrent, in-flight writes cannot silently alter or corrupt the data being exported.
With permitted artifacts preserved, the supervisor discards private mutable state or restores the environment from a trusted baseline, verifying readiness before assigning the sandbox to a new tenant. In the pool’s lifecycle (figure 6), the only path back to standby runs through that verification; every other exit from reclaiming ends in destruction. To prevent a generic “reset complete” signal from obscuring unhandled state, table 7 categorizes the required disposition across four distinct operational domains.



Table 7: Reset spans the owned state: An implementation must specify which objects its teardown or rollback covers and how it handles the remainder. Guest reset does not reverse effects already issued to external systems.









State domain
Required disposition before reuse




Guest execution and memory
Stop owned work; destroy and recreate the execution instance or restore the defined memory, processor, and device state.


Workspace and storage
Preserve eligible outputs, release old handles and mounts, and discard or restore the private state without modifying the trusted base.


Network and broker authority
Retire old sessions and lease identities; prevent delayed work from using the next tenant’s resources or grants.


Host services and attached devices
Account for queued work, buffers, and device state that guest-memory rollback does not cover; complete their separate reset or keep them unavailable.












Figure 6: A Pooled Instance from Baseline to Reuse: Instances are restored from a trusted baseline into standby, leased to one trajectory, and marked tainted when the lease ends. Reclaiming then follows the reset contract in order: fence the lease’s authority, quiesce owned work, export permitted outputs, discard or restore the covered state, and verify that contract. Passing checks return the instance to standby, and a failed check or an incomplete teardown removes it from service. The checks test a defined contract; a clean scan for known residue does not by itself show that every mutable object was covered.



Destroying a used execution instance and constructing a replacement from a trusted baseline eliminates reliance on brittle denylists of files, process names, or network sockets. Restoring an existing instance in place can also satisfy the reset contract, but only when restoration comprehensively resets all mutable layers and cleanly severs external dependencies. Restoring guest memory pages and CPU registers does nothing to purge pending messages from a host broker queue or reverse an external database mutation. Because local sandboxing cannot retroactively erase network traffic or side effects emitted outside the boundary, unresolved external operations remain unsettled after the reset.
The fourth accelerator challenge of section 8.5.7, scrubbing device state between tenants, lands here as the device row of table 7. Terminating guest processes leaves their allocations intact in accelerator memory, where a later tenant can read leftover activations or model weights through unzeroed allocations or through inter-process memory handles that outlive the process. Before the accelerator rejoins standby, the supervisor must therefore run a device-level reset it can confirm, such as a PCIe function-level reset or a driver-mediated memory scrub, that zeroes device memory, invalidates the device’s page tables, and severs shared handles. A device whose reset cannot be confirmed stays out of service, exactly like a guest whose teardown cannot be verified.
A fundamental asymmetry governs sandbox validation: discovering a single residual artifact proves that reset failed, but a scan that fails to find known artifacts cannot prove that every mutable object was reset. A checklist scan only proves the absence of the specific artifacts it sought. Readiness checks must therefore verify that the defined restoration mechanism executed completely, rather than attempting to inspect the interior of the guest after the fact. Any failed validation check or incomplete teardown must immediately route the instance to quarantine and destruction.



Snapshotting removes repetitive, high-latency initialization from the sandbox admission path. The runtime prepares a golden environment containing the required operating-system packages, language interpreters, compilers, and project dependencies. Once initialized, the runtime captures the virtual machine’s memory, processor registers, and virtual device states into a trusted baseline snapshot. When tasks arrive, the pool restores fresh execution instances directly from this snapshot. The golden baseline must remain compatible with host execution machinery and must never incorporate a prior tenant’s private files, active credentials, or in-flight task residue. Furthermore, snapshots demand active lifecycle management: upstream security patches, compiler updates, and library revisions can render an older snapshot obsolete even when restoration continues to succeed without error.
The scope of a snapshot depends heavily on the underlying virtualization mechanism. Ephemeral storage, virtual device queues, network socket connections, message broker states, system clocks, and hardware entropy sources often require dedicated reset procedures outside memory restoration. When cloning a running guest image, the supervisor must never duplicate a live tenant identity or assume that restored pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) states will generate cryptographically independent secrets. Before granting a lease to an incoming agent, the supervisor binds a fresh tenant identity, mounts private workspaces, configures isolated network namespaces, and programs hardware resource limits. These initialization steps constitute the prerequisites of readiness and cannot be postponed until after untrusted agent code begins executing.
A standard optimization maps the snapshot’s memory file into each new virtual machine using private copy-on-write semantics (mmap with MAP_PRIVATE). The host kernel points the new virtual memory mappings directly at the snapshot’s cached physical pages without duplicating them in RAM. Pages that remain unwritten, such as guest kernel text, shared libraries, and precompiled bytecode, exist as a single physical copy in host memory shared across the entire pool. Only when an instance writes to a page does the CPU trigger a write fault, prompting the host kernel to allocate and populate a private copy of that specific page.9 This mechanism drastically reduces host memory consumption compared to provisioning fully private guest images. However, memory ledgers must account for both shared and private allocations: hypervisor control blocks, extended page tables, writable workspace pages, and virtual device states still consume private host RAM. The size of a snapshot image on disk is not an accurate indicator of the active pool’s resident memory footprint.
9 Content-Dependent Memory Sharing: Sharing a selected read-only baseline differs from dynamically merging private pages because their contents happen to match, the content-based page sharing introduced for hypervisor memory management (Waldspurger 2002). With cross-tenant merging, the copy-on-write delay on a write can reveal that a matching page exists in another guest, a timing channel that was shown to detect which applications and files a neighboring virtual machine had loaded (Suzaki et al. 2011). A pool’s memory ledger must therefore state which pages may be shared; baseline sharing is not a general guarantee against timing channels.
Waldspurger, Carl A. 2002. “Memory Resource Management in VMware ESX Server.” Proceedings of the 5th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 02), 181–94. https://doi.org/10.1145/844128.844146.

Suzaki, Kuniyasu, Kengo Iijima, Toshiki Yagi, and Cyrille Artho. 2011. “Memory Deduplication as a Threat to the Guest OS.” Proceedings of the Fourth European Workshop on System Security (EuroSec), 1–6. https://doi.org/10.1145/1972551.1972552.
10 Lazy Snapshot Restore: A study of serverless functions restored from microVM snapshots attributed their high startup latency to page faults that bring guest memory in from disk one page at a time (Ustiugov et al. 2021). Recording the stable working set of pages a function touches after restore and prefetching it in one pass substantially reduced that latency. For an agent pool, the analogous working set is the interpreter, toolchain, and dependency pages the first tool call touches, and its size, not the snapshot’s, sets the first command’s latency.
Ustiugov, Dmitrii, Plamen Petrov, Marios Kogias, Edouard Bugnion, and Boris Grot. 2021. “Benchmarking, Analysis, and Optimization of Serverless Function Snapshots.” Proceedings of the 26th ACM International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS), 559–72. https://doi.org/10.1145/3445814.3446714.
Lazy restoration techniques defer paging memory into RAM until the guest explicitly accesses it.10 While lazy paging minimizes reported sandbox creation times, it shifts significant paging overhead into the initial tool call, especially when multiple newly admitted instances simultaneously access disk or network backing stores. Systems architects must evaluate both the time required to return an active lease handle and the end-to-end latency to first productive tool execution. Fleet readiness, copy-on-write sharing efficiency, and restoration latency represent distinct engineering trade-offs that must be profiled independently.



To absorb traffic without incurring cold-boot delays, a pool maintains a standby reserve of clean, unassigned instances. Admitting a new trajectory consumes one standby instance and binds it to the task. Concurrently, the provisioning engine replenishes the reserve, while expired leases remain quarantined until fulfilling their reset contract. The pool’s operational policy must explicitly define whether waiting tasks take scheduling precedence over rebuilding standby instances, how many parallel snapshot restorations the host can sustain without thrashing memory buses, and how the admission controller responds when physical memory or CPU capacity is exhausted. These operational rules give concrete meaning to the reserve sizing calculation.
Dimensioning a sandbox pool requires reasoning across two distinct timescales: long-run fleet capacity and short-run burst readiness. Little’s law (theorem \(\ref{thrm-05-littles-law}\)) governs long-run fleet sizing. Under a steady flow with an admitted arrival rate \(\ArrivalRate\) and a mean lease holding duration \(\LeaseHoldTime\), the average number of active sandbox leases is
\[
\ActiveLeaseCount = \ArrivalRate \, \LeaseHoldTime
\tag{4}\]


↩︎ Little’s law, and the residency tax a tool wait imposes on retained attention state, are established in Residence time and service rate.
Because an agent sandbox lease spans the complete multi-turn trajectory rather than an individual tool execution, the agent’s deliberative horizon sets the holding duration. An environment remains occupied while the model samples tokens, waits on inference queues, and executes test suites. This is the mirror image of the residency tax that retained attention state pays during a tool wait: there the attention state sits idle while a test runs, and here the sandbox sits idle while the model deliberates, so the same long horizon inflates both resident footprints. Little’s law defines the average concurrency, but it provides neither a hard ceiling on concurrent resource consumption nor a guarantee that a newly arrived task will find a warm instance waiting. Variable trajectory lengths, sudden arrival bursts, and teardown latencies necessitate strict admission limits alongside explicit queueing, rejection, or backpressure policies.
The standby reserve addresses the short timescale: the replenishment window \(\InstanceReplenishTime\) required to prepare a single clean instance. The instance provisioning architecture dictates this duration. A cold boot pays the cumulative latencies of virtual machine monitor startup, guest kernel initialization, and user-space runtime setup: \(\SandboxColdBootTime = \MonitorStartupTime + \GuestKernelBootTime + \UserSpaceSetupTime\). For agent environments, \(\UserSpaceSetupTime\) dominates because starting language runtimes, importing heavy libraries, and warming compiler caches take on the order of seconds. Restoring from a pre-initialized snapshot replaces kernel boot and user-space configuration with the restoration of memory mappings, processor registers, and device states, reducing \(\InstanceReplenishTime\) to milliseconds (15 ms in the chapter’s illustrative profile). Snapshotting also restructures memory bus traffic during arrival bursts. With \(\GuestImageMemory\) the full memory image of one guest and \(\LeaseDirtyMemory\) the private pages one instance actually writes, cold-booting \(\BurstArrivalCount\) instances forces the host memory system to populate \(\BurstArrivalCount \GuestImageMemory\) bytes within \(\SandboxColdBootTime\), whereas \(\BurstArrivalCount\) restored instances allocate only their \(\BurstArrivalCount \LeaseDirtyMemory\) private pages, spreading write bandwidth across the duration of the trajectory rather than concentrating it at startup.
A request-level reserve estimate needs a declared replenishment policy. Suppose offered requests form a stationary Poisson stream, and every offered request immediately orders one clean replacement, including a request that must wait. Each replacement becomes ready after the same \(\InstanceReplenishTime\), with unlimited restore concurrency and no active-lease or memory admission limit in this idealization. No request is lost; completions serve waiting requests in arrival order before rebuilding standby. Eventual admitted throughput therefore equals offered throughput in steady flow, permitting the same \(\ArrivalRate\) in the separate active-lease estimate. Ended leases do not supply extra ready instances until reset and are not counted again as replenishment.
Just before a request arrives, outstanding replacement orders correspond to prior offered arrivals during the last \(\InstanceReplenishTime\), excluding the current request. Ready inventory minus waiting demand equals \(\StandbyReserveCount\) minus that outstanding count. The arriving request waits when the count is at least \(\StandbyReserveCount\), so its miss probability is the Poisson tail at or above the reserve. With one standby, the first request consumes it and orders a replacement; a second request before that replacement returns already waits. Poisson arrivals sample the stationary inventory state, making this tail the request-level miss probability under the stated policy. Lost requests, admitted-only replenishment, finite restore workers, variable lead times, and resource admission limits require a different calculation. To screen a reserve against a miss target \(\StockoutProbabilityTarget\) (chosen by the operator, unrelated to the per-turn error rate of horizon compounding), a large-mean normal approximation yields
\[
\StandbyReserveCount \ge \ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime + \StockoutNormalQuantile\sqrt{\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime}
\tag{5}\]
where \(\StockoutNormalQuantile\) denotes the standard normal quantile.11 Round this screening estimate upward, then check the discrete Poisson tail at or above the chosen reserve; the quantile expression is not an exact guarantee. At small means the normal approximation is unsuitable. A guest-page memory ledger follows from copy-on-write page sharing across one golden template, private dirty pages accumulated by active leases, and base overheads for standby instances:
11 Square-Root Staffing: The reserve rule has the form of the square-root staffing rule for many-server queues, which provisions the mean load plus a margin proportional to its square root. Halfin and Whitt (1981) showed that holding the margin’s coefficient fixed keeps the probability of waiting at a stable value strictly between zero and one as the offered load grows. The relative margin shrinks as \(1/\sqrt{\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime}\). That resemblance motivates a sizing screen; the many-server waiting theorem does not establish a miss guarantee for this replenishment policy.
Halfin, Shlomo, and Ward Whitt. 1981. “Heavy-Traffic Limits for Queues with Many Exponential Servers.” Operations Research 29 (3): 567–88. https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.29.3.567.
\[
\PoolResidentMemory = \TemplateSharedMemory + \ActiveLeaseCount \, \LeaseDirtyMemory + \StandbyReserveCount \, \StandbyInstanceMemory
\tag{6}\]
The equation combines mean active guest pages with the configured standby allowance; it is not an instantaneous bound. It excludes waiting demand, transient restores, quarantine, and host monitor, page-table, and control state. A real budget also sets aside headroom; Notebook 8.4 charges both explicitly. Notebook 8.3 applies these sizing relationships to a steady arrival stream.

Napkin Math 8.3: Sizing a pool from its arrival rateProblem: A platform receives 2 offered coding trajectories per second under the no-loss, constant-lead-time policy, and each holds its lease for 300 s. In the chapter’s illustrative sandbox profile, restoring one clean instance from its snapshot takes 15 ms and a full guest image is 512 MB. Each active lease writes about 64 MB of private pages, and each standby keeps 8 MB. Does one standby meet the request-level miss target of 0.1 percent, what is the smallest supported reserve, and what guest-page allowance covers mean active leases and that reserve?
Math: By equation 4, active leases average \(\ArrivalRate \LeaseHoldTime\) = 2 per second × 300 s = 600. Arrivals during one restore average \(\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime\) = 0.03, far too small a mean for the normal approximation in equation 5, so the Poisson tail is read directly. One standby misses when at least one prior replacement remains outstanding, with probability 2.96 percent, above the target. The smallest supported reserve is 2; its miss event requires at least two prior outstanding replacements, with probability \(1 - e^{-\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime}(1 + \ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime) \approx\) 0.044 percent, below the target. Private guest images for every active lease would occupy about 322.1 GB. With copy-on-write, equation 6 gives about 39.0 GB, 8.3× less.
Systems insight: The agent’s trajectory horizon, rather than the latency of individual tool calls, dictates overall fleet cost. Active leases and their resident memory grow linearly in \(\LeaseHoldTime\), so doubling trajectory length doubles the memory term, while copy-on-write sharing keeps a fleet of per-trajectory microVMs affordable. The reserve is governed instead by \(\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime\) and is sharply sensitive to it: the selected reserve of 2 meets the target only while restore stays below about 22 ms, and a 10× slower cold boot (\(\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime\) = 0.3) needs a reserve of 4. Because every attempt holds its sandbox for \(\LeaseHoldTime\), sandbox residency is part of \(\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]\) in the cost per accepted task \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) (equation 1.2), and a rejected attempt pays it again. The estimate assumes the declared no-loss replenishment policy with constant lead time and unlimited restore concurrency; the next notebook treats a finite-worker burst.





Two standby instances meet the request-level target only while restore stays fast.
While steady Poisson arrivals provide a baseline for continuous operations, agent workloads frequently experience sudden synchronized surges, such as a continuous-integration suite launching parallel repair tasks. A burst also breaks an assumption behind equation 5, because a host can run only a fixed number of restores at once, so replenishments queue instead of all finishing within \(\InstanceReplenishTime\). Notebook 8.4 analyzes a deterministic burst under that limit to trace standby consumption, queue draining, and memory budgeting when arrival volume temporarily outstrips replenishment capacity.

Napkin Math 8.4: Consuming and replenishing a ready reserveProblem: How long does a specified burst wait for clean environments, and what resident-memory allowance supports the resulting active leases and rebuilt reserve?
Variables: A hypothetical pool starts with 4 clean standby instances and no active leases. At the initial instant, 12 tasks arrive together. The supervisor admits as many as standby permits, then prioritizes queued tasks over rebuilding the reserve. It can restore 2 instances concurrently, each taking exactly 15 ms to become ready under that concurrency. Assume sufficient execution slots for all tasks, no other arrivals, no lease returns during the calculation, and no restore failures. Handoff and dispatch time are negligible in this model; the restore interval includes the required readiness work.
Math: Initial admission consumes the reserve, leaving 12 − 4 = 8 tasks waiting. The workers serve those tasks in 4 rounds of 15 ms, so the last admission occurs at 60 ms. Rebuilding the original reserve takes another 2 rounds. The pool has its full reserve again at 90 ms, while all 12 admitted leases remain active. Admitting the burst finishes allocating the environments, but the trajectories themselves continue executing.
For an illustrative memory allowance at that final state, suppose immutable resident pages consume 1,000 MB shared across the pool. Each active instance has 64 MB of additional private resident state, and each standby has 8 MB. The resulting 16 instances each require 8 MB for monitor, page-table, and control state. Reserve another 256 MB of headroom. The ledger is in decimal megabytes and sums the exact byte quantities.
1,000 MB shared + 768 MB active-private + 32 MB standby-private + 128 MB control + 256 MB headroom = 2,184 MB.
The private-state terms include resident writable workspace pages, so the workspace is charged once. The total is a pool-residency allowance: host and broker services, storage caches, disk, and accelerator memory sit outside it, transient restore buffers must fit the stated headroom, and enforcement uses exact byte counts.
Systems insight: The standby reserve governs instantaneous admission capacity, while restoration concurrency dictates queue drainage rate. The last admission waits \(\lceil (\BurstArrivalCount - \StandbyReserveCount)/\RestoreWorkerCount \rceil \, \InstanceReplenishTime\) for a burst of \(\BurstArrivalCount\) tasks, a reserve of \(\StandbyReserveCount\), and \(\RestoreWorkerCount\) restore workers, so 4 workers instead of 2 cut the wait from 60 ms to 30 ms, provided restores do not slow under the added concurrency. Each added standby admits one more task immediately and costs 8 MB of idle private memory. The trace is deterministic; a different arrival pattern needs its own calculation.


An exhausted reserve must trigger explicit queueing, deferral, or rejection signals; it must never license the supervisor to lease an unreset or unverified sandbox to bypass admission bottlenecks. Admission control must also track physical resource headroom across active execution and background restoration. Instances awaiting teardown or memory scrubbing continue to occupy host memory and hypervisor tracking tables without providing usable standby capacity. Delays in resetting expired leases therefore represent hidden capacity drains that systems architects must measure alongside restore latency and trajectory duration.

Checkpoint 8.2: Sizing and reclaiming a pool
The pool equations and the reset contract answer each of these.

Active-lease estimate: Arrivals double while trajectories become half as long. Estimate the change in mean active leases, and name which term of equation 6 moves.
Reserve sensitivity: A cold boot replaces snapshot restore and takes an order of magnitude longer. Estimate \(\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime\) from the inputs of Notebook 8.3 and compare the minimum reserves that meet the request-level miss target at the baseline and tenfold lead times.
Reset coverage: A reclaimed instance passed a scan for leftover files, but a daemon from the previous lease still holds a socket. Which state domain of table 7 failed, and may the instance return to standby?






The same lifecycle serves two consumers beyond production traffic: agent evaluation, and training runs that execute many sampled attempts (rollouts) and learn from their outcomes. Benchmarks that evaluate code-generation agents by executing a target repository’s native test suite, such as SWE-bench (Jimenez et al. 2024), depend directly on this substrate. A pinned baseline snapshot and a rigorous reset protocol eliminate cross-test contamination from prior agent attempts, while mounting test runners under read-only permissions prevents candidate patches from modifying the acceptance checks. Sandboxed tests retain access to private writable scratch storage and controlled logging channels. However, systems engineers must decouple execution guarantees from task semantics: the sandbox provides isolated execution from a controlled baseline, but it cannot ensure that a test suite provides comprehensive code coverage or that external dependencies, non-deterministic timers, and floating-point variations will not alter benchmark outcomes.

Jimenez, Carlos E., John Yang, Alexander Wettig, Shunyu Yao, Kexin Pei, Ofir Press, and Karthik Narasimhan. 2024. “SWE-Bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

↪ Repeated runs, confidence intervals, and paired comparisons for agents evaluated on this substrate are developed in Statistical Evaluation Rigor.

Whether the pool serves production, evaluation, or training, its guarantee has the same shape: a contained execution with task-local continuity, starting from a verified baseline. What happens inside that boundary, including which permitted channels the code uses and what it sends through them, lies outside that guarantee, which is why a sandbox that passes every reset check can still host a task that discloses what it was allowed to read.

title: 8 Agent Sandboxes
text:
Robust containment requires both a sound enforcement boundary and sufficient host capacity to sustain that boundary under load. When deploying agent sandboxes, engineering teams often confuse practical filtering heuristics with architectural guarantees, or mistake microbenchmark startup latencies for the true operational cost of isolation.

Fallacy: Removing dangerous names removes the process’s authority.
Stripping dangerous symbols from an execution namespace hides convenient entry points, but it leaves the underlying runtime authority intact (section 8.3). Reachable object graphs, open file descriptors, and native extensions remain within the interpreter’s shared address space. For example, a caller can traverse an ordinary reference like total.__globals__ to retrieve the supervisor’s unredacted module namespace from an allowed helper function. Rice’s theorem rules out a sound and complete semantic classifier for unrestricted programs; it does not cause this reachable-reference escape or prohibit conservative safe subsets. While a specialized, deliberately restricted language can enforce safety invariants through its own formal semantics, executing untrusted code inside the supervisor’s process forces both into a single failure domain. True containment and resource limits must be enforced by the host operating system outside that interpreter process.


Pitfall: Choosing an envelope from a platform label alone.
Architectural labels like “container” or “microVM” specify virtualization mechanisms, not actual security boundaries (section 8.5). While a container shares the host kernel and a microVM interposes a guest kernel beneath a hypervisor monitor, the true blast radius depends on how the runtime environment is configured: filesystem mounts, virtualized devices, egress network routes, control groups, and trusted helper daemons. The same user-space kernel changed its trusted file-access path between releases without changing its name (section 8.5.1), and a microVM given a writable host mount or an unfiltered network route exposes exactly what its label suggests it hides. Systems engineers must evaluate the complete execution configuration against specific threat models and operational workloads. Lower startup latency indicates a lighter initialization path, not stronger isolation.


Fallacy: The cost of strong isolation is its startup latency.
Snapshot restoration reduces guest startup overhead to milliseconds, 15 ms in the chapter’s illustrative profile. However, boot latency is rarely the dominant infrastructure expense. The primary cost of sandboxing stems from cumulative memory residency across the lease horizon. At an arrival rate of 2 trajectories per second and lease durations of 300 s, the pool averages 600 active leases. Even with copy-on-write page sharing, mean active guest pages plus the configured reserve occupy roughly 39.0 GB, compared to the 322.1 GB required by isolated private images (Notebook 8.3). Sandbox provisioning must be budgeted by memory-seconds per trajectory, a quantity that scales directly with the lease hold time \(\LeaseHoldTime\), rather than evaluated solely by boot time.


Pitfall: Treating an allowed destination as approval of everything sent there.
A network egress rule restricts traffic to approved remote endpoints, but it cannot verify whether the payload in a request body is safe (table 6). Credential brokering keeps long-lived tokens and secret keys outside the guest environment while still allowing sandboxed code to request operations against authorized services. Under this design, an agent can use an approved outbound channel to exfiltrate private task data or modify remote state without ever extracting a credential or escaping the sandbox envelope. Preventing this residual abuse is an information-flow and semantic authorization challenge, rather than a perimeter-bypass flaw in the network sandbox.


Fallacy: An empty workspace proves that a used envelope is ready for another tenant.
Files represent only one of the four state domains cataloged in table 7. Even if a cleanup script successfully wipes every file, lingering processes from double-forked daemons, abstract Unix domain sockets, kernel keyring credentials, or modified environment search paths continue persisting. Any leftover artifact across these state domains compromises the next tenant. Multi-tenant recycling demands an explicit reset contract that accounts for every state domain an incoming lease could inspect, destroys or reinitializes that state to a known golden baseline, and validates isolation before reassignment. Moreover, no local cleanup protocol can undo external side effects already committed to remote APIs during the lease.


Pitfall: Sizing the standby reserve from a restore time measured on an idle host.
Determining standby pool capacity from initialization benchmarks gathered on an unloaded system severely underestimates provisioning requirements. Reserve sizing is governed by the traffic intensity parameter \(\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime\), where the request-level miss probability under the stated replenishment policy follows a steep Poisson tail. In the chapter’s illustrative profile, the selected reserve of 2 instances satisfies a 0.1 percent request-level miss objective only as long as snapshot restore completes in under 22 ms. If initialization degrades by a factor of 10×, as an unoptimized cold boot can, the required reserve jumps to 4 instances. Under burst traffic, concurrent VM restoration, host cache contention, and lazy demand paging across copy-on-write regions degrade \(\InstanceReplenishTime\) precisely when capacity is most critical. Sizing calculations must measure initialization latency under the target concurrency of the anticipated burst rather than in quiescent conditions (Notebook 8.4).

title: 8 Agent Sandboxes
text:
A sandbox is an enforceable contract defining the boundaries of execution. It specifies precisely which hardware and operating system resources untrusted code can touch, which platform components form the trusted computing base, and how long both the execution environment and its delegated privileges endure. Because these limits are enforced beneath the executing process, the boundary never depends on model compliance. However, strong isolation introduces concrete operational costs: every admitted trajectory incurs startup latency, memory footprint, and environment reset overhead. In the chapter’s README attack scenario, containment succeeds through architectural enforcement rather than prompt adherence. The injected command cannot read the host’s credentials or open a route to an unapproved destination, although the same instructions can still misuse a channel the task was permitted, as the submit_report request showed.
In the connection-pool repair scenario, this architecture preserves candidate patches and test artifacts while denying the agent access to the host account or the mutable state of concurrent tasks. The evaluation harness keeps validation suites outside the writable workspace, giving the test runner bounded scratch storage. This separation protects the integrity of gathered evidence, even though accepting the repair requires end-to-end evaluation beyond the targeted regression checks run against candidate r18.
Table 8 summarizes the mathematical foundations established across the chapter, connecting access authorization and boundary overhead to the queueing models that govern warm-pool capacity.



Table 8: Key equations of agent sandboxing: Each relation formalizes an access decision or provisioning boundary; the final four equations size warm sandbox pools from arrival rate, task horizon, and environment restore latency.
