Key Takeaways: Containment includes reach and lifetime

Execution environments define blast radius: Tool declarations specify intended interfaces, but the execution environment determines the files, sockets, and memory addresses a process can actually touch. The blast radius of an agent action spans everything its running code can read, mutate, exfiltrate, or consume. Consequently, robust isolation must be enforced by the operating system or hypervisor beneath the process.
In-process filtering cannot guarantee isolation: Code executing inside the supervisor’s runtime can reach the supervisor’s objects through attribute traversal and subclass walks, and native libraries share its address space and identity. The shown escape follows from shared object reach. A process or virtual machine boundary can govern that reach, while a purpose-built language can instead bound its operands, operations, and cost by construction.
Capabilities bound reach to what the task was handed: A capability binds authority to an unforgeable reference with an enforced lifetime instead of to ambient user identity. Attenuation can narrow a grant but never widen it, and deriving a child leaves the parent usable until the runtime withdraws it. Brokers let code request credentialed operations without holding the secret.
Envelope selection balances isolation against performance: Containers, user-space kernels, microVMs, and bytecode runtimes place trust boundaries at different system layers and pay the system-call tax on different calls. A call-heavy build favors a guest kernel over an emulating one. Retaining an envelope for the trajectory amortizes setup when the within-task trust policy permits reuse. A policy that requires fresh state between calls can justify per-call setup even when it dominates useful work.
Permitted egress channels create exfiltration risks: Network policies restrict unapproved endpoints, but permitted traffic, including API requests, artifact uploads, and DNS queries, can still carry sensitive task state outward. Once transport-level isolation is in place, safeguarding sensitive data becomes an information-flow tracking challenge.
Trajectory duration dictates pool capacity: By Little’s law, active sandbox leases scale with arrival rate and total trajectory length rather than individual tool execution time. Copy-on-write memory sharing can reduce the resident footprint of concurrent agent workloads. Strict reset contracts must scrub compute, storage, and network state before an instance returns to the standby pool.



Enforcing containment beneath the model (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-zero-trust-sandboxing}\)) ensures that execution boundaries remain intact regardless of model instructions or prompt injection attempts. This boundary complements the typed action contract (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}\)), separating the admission of a tool request from the confinement of the code that fulfills it. Under invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)), these guarantees must reside below the model, in the supervisor and the envelope it configures, rather than in prompting guidelines. Ultimately, any isolation boundary protects only the specific resources its enforcement mechanisms monitor and reset across successive tool invocations.

title: 8 Agent Sandboxes
text:
Running a stranger’s program on a machine that holds something valuable is the oldest problem in operating-system protection. In the 1960s, multiprogrammed mainframes forced systems designers to isolate mutually suspicious users sharing a single CPU and physical memory. Dennis and Van Horn addressed this challenge by introducing capabilities: unforgeable tokens that bundle the identity of an object with the explicit rights granted to operate on it (Dennis and Van Horn 1966). This design departed fundamentally from ambient, identity-based permissions. Lampson’s access matrix (Lampson 1974) then placed capability lists and access control lists in one model. To enforce such policies, Anderson established the concept of the reference monitor, a compact, tamper-proof mechanism that must mediate every access request between a subject and an object (Anderson 1972). Saltzer and Schroeder subsequently synthesized these insights into an enduring canon of security design principles, establishing least privilege, complete mediation, and fail-safe defaults as non-negotiable engineering requirements (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975). These principles apply directly to tool execution in agent runtimes, where tool code must never inherit the broad ambient authority of the host environment. Furthermore, Lampson recognized early that even when direct access is barred, confinement can fail through subtle covert channels that no designer intentionally provisioned (Lampson 1973). Hardy’s confused deputy (Hardy 1988) later gave ambient authority’s characteristic failure its name, and it reappears whenever an agent invokes external tools using ambient platform credentials.

Dennis, Jack B., and Earl C. Van Horn. 1966. “Programming Semantics for Multiprogrammed Computations.” Communications of the ACM 9 (3): 143–55. https://doi.org/10.1145/365230.365252.

Anderson, James P. 1972. Computer Security Technology Planning Study. ESD-TR-73-51. Deputy for Command; Management Systems, Electronic Systems Division, Air Force Systems Command.

Kivity, Avi, Yaniv Kamay, Dor Laor, Uri Lublin, and Anthony Liguori. 2007. Kvm: The Linux Virtual Machine Monitor.

Kamp, Poul-Henning, and Robert N. M. Watson. 2000. Jails: Confining the Omnipotent Root.
Each isolation envelope examined in this chapter descends from decades of mechanism design. Popek and Goldberg (1974) established the formal requirements for efficient, recursive virtualization, proving that all sensitive processor instructions must trap when executed in an unprivileged mode so that a virtual machine monitor can intercept and emulate them. For decades, commodity architectures like x86 violated these conditions because certain sensitive instructions failed silently rather than trapping. Hardware vendors resolved this deficit only when Intel (VT-x) and AMD (AMD-V) introduced hardware-assisted virtualization extensions with dedicated guest execution modes (Uhlig et al. 2005). Building on these CPU extensions, KVM integrated hypervisor capabilities directly into the Linux kernel, turning guest virtual machines into standard schedulable threads (Kivity et al. 2007). Along a parallel track, systems researchers pursued in-process isolation to eliminate hardware context-switching overhead: Wahbe and colleagues introduced software fault isolation (SFI), rewriting untrusted binary instructions to enforce memory safety within a single address space (Wahbe et al. 1993), an approach that WebAssembly later standardized into a portable, verifiable bytecode (Haas et al. 2017). Between hardware virtualization and language runtimes lies the shared-kernel lineage. System-call interposition initially promised lightweight confinement for unmodified binaries (Goldberg et al. 1996), but Garfinkel systematically cataloged the traps and pitfalls of user-level mediation, demonstrating how time-of-check to time-of-use races and incomplete kernel semantics inevitably compromise user-space monitors (Garfinkel 2003) and pushing security mediation back into the kernel. Concurrently, FreeBSD Jails partitioned a single kernel among mutually untrusted tenants (Kamp and Watson 2000), establishing the shared-kernel foundation that Linux namespaces and control groups later expanded into modern container runtimes, while Capsicum proved that capability discipline could be retrofitted onto standard UNIX processes by restricting system calls and mediating access exclusively through file descriptors (Watson et al. 2010).
Multi-tenant cloud platforms subsequently transformed isolation into an engineering economics problem. Running untrusted, short-lived functions at massive multi-tenant density exposed the memory footprint and startup latencies of conventional hypervisors. This friction drove the development of lightweight virtual machines that could boot in tens of milliseconds, matching container agility while preserving hardware-level isolation (Manco et al. 2017). Firecracker pushed this optimization further by stripping away legacy PC devices such as ACPI tables, IDE controllers, and PCI buses in favor of a minimal virtio device model and a lean, memory-safe implementation tailored specifically for transient workloads (Agache et al. 2020). To eliminate guest boot overhead entirely, systems engineers elevated microVM snapshotting and state restoration into a precise latency-engineering discipline, finding that the page faults that bring a restored guest’s memory in from disk dominate its startup and cutting them by prefetching the working set each function touches (Ustiugov et al. 2021).

Manco, Filipe, Costin Lupu, Florian Schmidt, Jose Mendes, Simon Kuenzer, Sumit Sati, Kenichi Yasukata, Costin Raiciu, and Felipe Huici. 2017. “My VM Is Lighter (and Safer) Than Your Container.” Proceedings of the 26th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP), 218–33. https://doi.org/10.1145/3132747.3132763.

Greshake, Kai, Sahar Abdelnabi, Shailesh Mishra, Christoph Endres, Thorsten Holz, and Mario Fritz. 2023. “Not What You’ve Signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection.” Proceedings of the 16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security, 79–90. https://doi.org/10.1145/3605764.3623985.
Agent systems inherit this entire architectural foundation, but they fundamentally overturn a core operational assumption. In conventional serverless platforms, an untrusted author uploads fixed code in advance, and the runtime executes that code across isolated, stateless invocations. In an agent runtime, by contrast, the untrusted author sits directly inside the execution loop: an autonomous model generates and executes code dynamically at each step of an iterative trajectory. This code is steered by external, untrusted content retrieved from web pages, databases, or third-party tools, content that an adversary can deliberately manipulate through indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al. 2023). Furthermore, while a serverless function discards its environment after a brief invocation, an agent maintains a mutable, stateful environment across an extended multi-step problem-solving sequence. This persistent lifecycle turns state isolation, residual-data scrubbing, and network egress control from occasional provisioning tasks into continuous operational requirements.

Saltzer and Schroeder (1975), The Protection of Information in Computer Systems. The classical foundation of security engineering. It defines the core principles of least privilege, complete mediation, economy of mechanism, and fail-safe defaults. Reading it today reveals how directly five-decade-old operating system principles govern modern agent sandbox design.
Lampson (1973), A Note on the Confinement Problem. A landmark three-page paper that defines confinement and formalizes how untrusted programs leak information across covert channels. This analysis provides the conceptual framework for modern egress filtering, rate limiting, and residual-state scrubbing in agent sandboxes.
Hardy (1988), The Confused Deputy. An influential case study demonstrating how ambient authority causes security boundaries to collapse when a privileged service executes tasks on behalf of an unprivileged requester. It remains the canonical justification for capability-based security, demonstrating why agent tools must receive scoped authorization tokens rather than ambient platform credentials.
Popek and Goldberg (1974), Formal Requirements for Virtualizable Third Generation Architectures. The foundational formalization of trap-and-emulate virtualization. It defines the precise conditions under which sensitive instructions must trap, establishing the theoretical guarantees that allow modern hypervisors and microVM boundaries to contain arbitrary guest code.
Garfinkel (2003), Traps and Pitfalls. An indispensable catalog of failure modes in user-level system-call mediation, analyzing race conditions, path aliasing, and the difficulty of tracking kernel state from user space. It remains an essential checklist for evaluating sandboxes built from ptrace or seccomp filters.
Agache et al. (2020), Firecracker. The production architecture of a minimalist microVM monitor built in Rust for dense multi-tenant workloads. Read it for the concrete engineering trade-offs among device surface, boot latency, and memory overhead that dictate how to size and manage an agent sandbox pool.


Saltzer, J. H., and M. D. Schroeder. 1975. “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems.” Proceedings of the IEEE 63 (9): 1278–308. https://doi.org/10.1109/proc.1975.9939.

Hardy, Norm. 1988. “The Confused Deputy: (Or Why Capabilities Might Have Been Invented).” ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 22 (4): 36–38. https://doi.org/10.1145/60609.60611.

Agache, Alexandru, Marc Brooker, Andreea Florescu, Alexandra Iordache, Anthony Liguori, Rolf Neugebauer, Phil Piwonka, and Diana-Maria Popa. 2020. “Firecracker: Lightweight Virtualization for Serverless Applications.” Proceedings of the 17th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI 20), 419–34.

title: 8 Agent Sandboxes
text:
All givens below are hypothetical problem inputs, not measurements of any product. Decimal units apply throughout these problems (1 GB is \(10^9\) bytes and 1 KB is \(10^3\) bytes), while configured guest memory in the worked notebooks is a binary capacity quoted in conventional megabytes, so a problem’s answer need not reproduce a notebook value digit for digit.
Problem 1 (Basic): Splitting a repair grant across test shards. A repair task holds \(\RepairCapabilityGrant = (\GrantRights=\{\text{read}, \text{write}, \text{execute}\},\ \mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant=\texttt{repo/},\ \GrantCondition,\ \GrantExpiryTime=\GrantIssueTime_0 + 900\,\text{s})\), where \(\GrantCondition\) binds use to this task and carries an aggregate budget of 600 CPU-seconds. The controller proposes three children for parallel test shards: \(\TestsDirectoryShardGrant = (\{\text{read}, \text{execute}\},\ \texttt{repo/tests/},\ 250\ \text{CPU-s},\ \GrantIssueTime_0 + 600\,\text{s})\), \(\WholeRepositoryShardGrant = (\{\text{read}, \text{execute}\},\ \texttt{repo/},\ 200\ \text{CPU-s},\ \GrantIssueTime_0 + 1200\,\text{s})\), and \(\SourceWriteShardGrant = (\{\text{read}, \text{write}\},\ \texttt{repo/src/},\ 200\ \text{CPU-s},\ \GrantIssueTime_0 + 600\,\text{s})\). (a) Apply the component-wise attenuation check to each child and decide which may be issued. (b) The parent keeps 150 CPU-seconds for its own work. Decide whether the valid children fit the aggregate budget, and whether they would still fit if \(\WholeRepositoryShardGrant\) were corrected to expire at \(\GrantIssueTime_0 + 900\,\text{s}\). (c) At \(\GrantIssueTime_0 + 700\,\text{s}\) a shard holding \(\TestsDirectoryShardGrant\) requests execute on repo/tests/run.sh. Evaluate equation 1 term by term and state the verdict.
Problem 2 (Basic): Resident memory of a repair pool. A platform admits repair trajectories at \(\ArrivalRate = 0.25\ \text{s}^{-1}\), each holding its lease for \(\LeaseHoldTime = 1600\,\text{s}\). The shared template occupies 0.5 GB, each active lease writes 96 MB of private pages, three standby instances hold 16 MB each, and a full private guest image would be 0.5 GB. The pool host has 64 GB for sandbox residency. (a) Compute \(\ActiveLeaseCount\) and \(\PoolResidentMemory\) by equation 6, and compare with private images. (b) Trajectories double in length. Recompute \(\PoolResidentMemory\) and decide whether the host still fits. (c) If it does not, find the largest admission rate the host supports at the longer horizon and state the admission policy that enforces it.
Problem 3 (Basic): Paying the system-call tax on a build. An untrusted dependency build performs 30 s of useful computation and issues \(2 \times 10^{6}\) system calls, of which \(5 \times 10^{4}\) touch a virtual device. Take these per-call costs as givens: a shared-kernel container pays \(\PrivilegeTrapTime = 0.1\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) and \(\SystemCallFilterTime = 0.05\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) on every call; a user-space kernel pays \(0.1\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) trap, \(1.5\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) emulation, and \(2.0\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) switch on every call; a microVM pays a \(0.1\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) native trap on ordinary calls and \(5.1\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) in total on each device call. (a) Using equation 3, compute each envelope’s added time and its overhead relative to the useful work. (b) Find the system-call count at which the user-space kernel’s overhead reaches 10 percent. (c) The build holds no credentials but runs code nobody reviewed. Choose the envelope and justify the choice by both cost and trusted components.
Problem 4 (Intermediate): Guard checks for the remediation agent. The remediation agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) attaches a model-written guard to each proposed configuration change, such as p99_ms < 400 and error_rate < 0.01. The supervisor, which holds the agent’s production-change credentials, evaluates the guard on 500 service samples per second, with a 10 ms deadline per sample and a budget of 0.5 CPU cores for guard checks. Three options are available. The first is an in-process evaluator for a purpose-built expression language whose only operands are the supplied metric values and numeric literals, with arithmetic, comparisons, and, and or, no attribute access, subscripts, calls, or loops, and at most 200 syntax nodes at no more than 0.2 µs each. The others are a fresh bytecode sandbox per sample (0.5 ms setup) and a fresh microVM per sample (20 ms setup). (a) Compute each option’s worst-case time per sample and the CPU cores it consumes, and decide which options meet the deadline and the budget. (b) The agent asks for a matches(line, pattern) operator over log lines of up to 200 characters. A backtracking matcher can take \(2^\AdversarialInputLength\) steps of 10 ns on an adversarial \(\AdversarialInputLength\)-character input; a linear-time automaton matcher, with patterns capped at 100 states, takes at most one 10 ns step per state per character. Compute the backtracking time on a 40-character line and the longest input that stays within the evaluator’s 40 µs bound, then the linear matcher’s worst case and the resulting CPU cores. Decide which matcher, if either, may run inside the supervisor, and explain why the supervisor cannot simply stop a runaway match. (c) The agent next proposes replacing guards with a model-written Python script that parses the last minute of logs through a native parsing library, running once per minute with 2 s of useful work. Test the script against each condition that made the guard safe to evaluate in-process, choose its envelope and whether to start one per run under a 10 percent setup cap, and state which authority that envelope may hold.
Problem 5 (Intermediate): Per-document envelopes for the research agent. The research agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}\)) parses 400 retrieved pages while answering one question, each parse needing 2 ms of useful work and no filesystem or network access. The task requires mutable parser and module state from each independently hostile page to be inaccessible to the next; sharing a trusted read-only baseline is permitted. The options are a fresh bytecode sandbox per page (0.5 ms setup), a fresh microVM per page (20 ms setup), or one microVM retained for the whole question (20 ms setup once). (a) Compute the elapsed setup plus work for each option and each option’s setup share of a fresh call. (b) For a cap of \(\SetupShareCap = 10\) percent, compute the minimum per-call work for each fresh-per-call option. (c) The retained microVM is fastest. Apply the stated freshness requirement to decide whether the retained microVM is eligible, and decide which option to deploy even though it misses the 10 percent cap.
Problem 6 (Intermediate): Sizing the reserve under load, not at idle. A repair pool receives offered Poisson requests at \(\ArrivalRate = 0.5\ \text{s}^{-1}\) under the no-loss, constant-lead-time replenishment policy of section 8.8.3, with a request-level miss target \(\StockoutProbabilityTarget = 10^{-3}\). Snapshot restore takes 40 ms on an idle host but 200 ms at the restore concurrency a burst produces. (a) For each restore time, compute \(\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime\) and the smallest reserve whose Poisson tail at or above the reserve meets the target. (b) Find the largest \(\InstanceReplenishTime\) each of the reserves one and two tolerates. (c) Evaluate the normal approximation of equation 5 at the loaded mean, explain why its answer should not be trusted here, and decide the reserve to provision.
Problem 7 (Intermediate): Draining a burst of repair tasks. A continuous-integration trigger releases forty repair tasks at once into a pool holding eight standby instances. With up to four concurrent restore workers each restore takes 25 ms; with eight workers restores contend and each takes 40 ms. Queued tasks take precedence over rebuilding the reserve, and each standby holds 16 MB of private memory. (a) Compute the last admission’s wait and the time at which the reserve of eight is rebuilt with four workers. (b) The platform requires every task in such a burst to start within 100 ms. Decide whether doubling the workers meets the requirement. (c) Find the smallest reserve that meets it with four workers, its standing memory cost, and the time at which that larger reserve is rebuilt.
Problem 8 (Intermediate): When copy-on-write stops paying. An evaluation host starts sixty-four workspaces from a 6 GB pinned base; each task writes 150 MB of edits and build outputs, and the shared drive sustains 5 GB/s. (a) Compute provisioning payload and drive-time lower bounds for full private copies and for a copy-on-write view. (b) The test suite then modifies a 3 GB database fixture in place once per task, and the storage copies whole files on first write. Recompute the copy-on-write payload and its advantage over full copies. (c) Redesign the fixture’s storage so that the advantage returns, given that the tests touch 2,000 blocks of 64 KB. Compute the resulting payload, drive time, and advantage, and name one alternative that avoids copying altogether.
Problem 9 (Advanced): Admission latency for the support agent. The support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)) runs each customer session in its own sandbox. At peak it receives offered Poisson sessions at \(\ArrivalRate = 40\ \text{s}^{-1}\) under the same no-loss, constant-lead-time replenishment policy, so eventual admitted throughput equals that rate; each admitted lease lasts \(\LeaseHoldTime = 45\,\text{s}\), and a customer waiting for a sandbox counts against a 1 s first-response budget. Two provisioning paths exist: snapshot restore at 50 ms, or cold boot at 1.5 s. Use \(\StockoutProbabilityTarget = 10^{-3}\), a 0.5 GB template, 24 MB of private pages per active session, and 16 MB per standby. (a) Compute \(\ActiveLeaseCount\) and, for each path, \(\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime\), the reserve from equation 5, and the smallest reserve from the exact Poisson tail at or above the reserve. (b) Compute \(\PoolResidentMemory\) for each path and the relative margin \(\StockoutNormalQuantile\sqrt{\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime}/(\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime)\). (c) Compare with Problem 2. Identify which term binds the repair pool and which binds the support pool, and recommend a provisioning path and reserve conditional on the declared policy. State why the miss target alone does not prove the 1 s end-to-end response budget, and identify the remaining response-work and waiting-time evidence needed.
Problem 10 (Advanced): Critique a rate-limited resolver. A design review proposes letting repair guests resolve any name under the package mirror’s domain subtree, limited to 20 queries per second, and claims the limit “bounds exfiltration.” Each query name can carry 120 base32 characters of attacker-chosen labels (5 bits each), and a trajectory lasts 1200 s. A legitimate dependency install needs about 400 lookups. (a) Compute the channel’s payload per query, its rate at the limit, the time to leak a 40 KB file, and the total a trajectory could leak. (b) Compute the query budget per trajectory that would hold leakage below 1 KB, and compare it with the install’s legitimate lookups. (c) State what the rate limit actually bounds, then redesign name resolution so the guest’s lookups stop being a channel while installs still work, and say which residual channel the redesign leaves.
Problem 11 (Advanced): Suspend the sandbox while the model deliberates. Extend Problem 2 at the doubled horizon (\(\LeaseHoldTime = 3200\,\text{s}\)). Each trajectory runs forty turns, and 70 percent of every lease is spent waiting for model calls. A proposal suspends the guest to the shared 5 GB/s drive at the start of each model call and resumes it after, writing and then reading its 96 MB of private pages every turn; suspended guests hold no host memory. (a) Compute the admission rate the 64 GB host supports with suspension, the admission rate at which the drive saturates, and the resulting gain over Problem 2(c). (b) Compute the lower bound on added resume latency per turn and per trajectory, and choose an operating admission rate that leaves the drive 20 percent headroom for provisioning traffic. (c) The binding constraint has moved. Name it, and list the reset-contract and authority conditions a suspended guest must satisfy (which work may be running, what happens to its broker sessions, and where its image may go) before the proposal can ship.

What’s Next: From contained code to a defended agentThe submit_report request that passed every boundary in this chapter is not an isolated gap. The same README text can persuade the model to place a private test fixture in the query of a permitted package search. The query reaches an approved registry, the broker keeps its credential, and the code never leaves its envelope, yet the registry receives information the task was never authorized to share. The README can also simply claim that the test suite passed, and no envelope stops the agent from recording that claim as evidence. Agent Security opens with these attacks through permitted operations and builds the runtime checks that decide which data may cross an approved boundary and which sources may justify a consequential decision.

title: 10 The Agent Harness
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why must the decision to continue an agent live outside the model that proposes its next step?
A single model invocation succeeds or fails on its own, but an autonomous agent runs across a horizon of many turns, and per-step errors compound with every turn. Over dozens of sequential tool interactions, a malformed call, a stale observation, or an unhandled exception can carry an unsupervised trajectory into a failure or a loop that no single step reveals. The agent harness is the runtime component that owns this loop: it schedules model calls, enforces the rules for moving between states, tracks task budgets, and holds sensitive actions for human approval. A model can be asked to pause, wait, or stay within an allowance, but a request it honors on almost every turn still fails across a long run, so the decision to continue must rest with deterministic supervision outside the model. Engineering the harness turns stochastic token generation into task execution that stays bounded, interruptible, and accountable across the whole horizon.

Learning Objectives

Design a runtime-owned trajectory record that tracks live plans, grants, consumption, and outstanding obligations
Construct guarded state transitions that keep stale observations out of the next turn while preserving unresolved effects
Calculate how long a control request waits for a turn boundary, and apply pause, cancel, or kill without dispatching incomplete output
Explain which resources an asynchronous wait releases and which the trajectory still owns and pays for
Design an approval gate with expiry and dispatch-time rechecks, and size the resources its held trajectories retain
Allocate shared model-call service by weighted deficit round-robin while keeping provider quotas separate from trajectory budgets
Apply bounded-liability admission before dispatch and select a budget ceiling by cost per accepted task









The horizon exposure, bounded by a harness that keeps control outside the model.
Consider the connection-pool repair agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)) at the moment it produces candidate patch r18. A test job is actively running against a fixed snapshot of that revision when an operator requests a pause for manual inspection. Simultaneously, an independent interactive task queues for model service, and the repair trajectory approaches its allocated budget. Even if the test job finishes cleanly and the next model reply is syntactically flawless, neither event answers whether the repair should proceed right now. That continuation decision depends on operational conditions outside the model: the operator’s pending signal, current task states, shared cluster capacity, and the allowance remaining once in-flight work is accounted for.
The runtime components examined so far each address part of this operational environment. The tool layer tracks job handles and operation repeat contracts, the sandbox isolates execution and bounds workspace lifetimes, and the security checks test each dispatch against its confidentiality and provenance labels and bind each approval to the exact action it covers. Each of these mechanisms, however, operates at the boundary of a single invocation, resource, or decision; none possesses the context or authority to decide whether the trajectory as a whole may take another step. That decision cannot be delegated to the model either. An agent instructed to self-regulate (to pause on request, or to halt before exceeding an allowance) evaluates that rule afresh on every turn. Because of horizon compounding (equation 1.1), even a high per-turn compliance rate decays across an extended run, so a constraint the model honors on almost every turn is still violated in a predictable share of long trajectories. Operational control also requires state that cannot live in an ephemeral context window. An operator needs immediate status without reconstructing the conversation transcript; a scheduler must distinguish between work waiting on background jobs and work eligible to run; and the dispatch path must enforce security grants and token allowances before invoking downstream tools. All three operations demand a single, authoritative account of the trajectory that an unstructured message list cannot maintain.
The agent harness provides this missing supervisory layer by taking ownership of the execution loop for an individual trajectory. The agent proposes candidate actions; the harness determines whether each step runs immediately, yields to other work, or halts, and it enforces those decisions against an execution record that only the runtime can modify. This is trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\)): the runtime governs each model call as one step of a whole trajectory, which advances only through transitions and admissions the runtime’s guards permit, because the trajectory cannot be relied on to yield, to stop, or to notice that it has stopped making progress. Invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) says that bounds belong below the model; this principle names the unit those bounds must cover, the whole trajectory rather than the single call. The chapter turns it into two working rules. First, every outbound model call or tool dispatch must pass an explicit admission check (active operator signals, capability grants, shared capacity, and remaining budget) at the instant it would execute. Second, in-flight work stays accountable: no pause signal, timeout, or cancellation proves that running work has stopped or that its cost is settled, so every outstanding operation keeps a named owner until evidence settles it.
The harness develops in the order these decisions arise in one repair turn. The runtime first needs an authoritative account of the trajectory (section 10.3) and rules for how that account may change (section 10.4). Operators then need a way to stop or redirect it (section 10.5), and long tool jobs and human reviews need waits that keep supervision intact (section 10.6, section 10.7). Across many trajectories, shared model service must be divided (section 10.8), and across many turns, cumulative consumption must be bounded (section 10.9). The record described here lives in host memory; making its guarantees survive host failure is the work of durable execution (Durable Execution).



When an autonomous agent runs inside a bare execution loop, an unexpected operator pause or an unconstrained retry cycle immediately exposes the lack of an external control plane: a path, separate from the one that performs model calls and tool work, that decides whether that work may proceed. An unmanaged loop treats model completions as direct execution instructions; a harness treats them as untrusted proposals, evaluating every action against explicit admission policies, budget constraints, and external supervisory signals.


The unmediated while-loop of An Unmediated Agent Loop is the pattern most prototype agents still use, popularized by ReAct (Yao et al. 2023): invoke a foundation model, dispatch the tools requested in its completion, append the results to the message history, and repeat until the model emits a stopping condition. The introduction also divided a turn into six phases, from context assembly to assessment against the task contract, and observed that some phases wait on tools or people. What the loop lacks for production operation is a place for those phases’ decisions to live. It confines all operational state to the message list and the local call stack of the client process.

↩︎ The six-phase turn lifecycle, including the phases that pause a turn for tools and approvals, is established in The six-phase turn execution lifecycle.

Because an unmanaged loop lacks an independent, externally accessible control state, it cannot support the operational requirements of production systems. If an operator must pause an execution run while a long test suite executes, the runtime provides no interface to receive that command. If cumulative token consumption exhausts the allocated budget, the loop cannot withhold the next model call without terminating abruptly and abandoning in-flight work. Any tool invocation proposed by the model also executes immediately under ambient authority, bypassing policy checks or human review. Although a supervised harness may also execute as a loop or coroutine, it wraps that loop in an explicit state machine with invariant rules governing every continuation path, so that every proposal is filtered before any tool call is admitted (figure 1).






Figure 1: The Prototype Loop vs. the Agent Harness: Panel (a) runs the model’s proposed call directly and keeps all state in the message list, so an outside request has nowhere to land, nothing bounds cumulative spend, and calls that policy would gate run at once. Panel (b) wraps the same loop in a harness whose trajectory record, guarded transitions, control and approval paths, and reserved budgets decide what is admitted. The model only proposes, and the tool layer settles the outcomes of admitted calls.



In an unmanaged system, execution context is scattered across disparate subsystems: host operating systems track local processes, remote clusters hold asynchronous job handles, storage systems manage workspace leases, and identity providers track credential expirations. Panel (b) consolidates these responsibilities into a single runtime-owned record for each trajectory. Operators, cluster schedulers, and dispatch paths all consult this authoritative record before initiating state changes. While a system may pass budget constraints to the model in the prompt and the model may cooperate with pause requests, actual enforcement remains strictly with the runtime. Relying on model cooperation violates invariant closure; the runtime itself must guarantee that system safety invariants hold under all execution paths (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)).

Definition 10.1: Agent harness
Agent harness is the runtime component that owns the agent loop for one trajectory, assembling each model call, interpreting the reply, deciding whether and when each proposed tool call is dispatched, and keeping the record through which outside components inspect, pause, bound, or stop continuation.

Significance: It keeps continuation decisions independent of model cooperation while preserving the grants, consumption, and outstanding work those decisions must respect.
Distinction: The tool layer mediates calls and tracks their outcomes, and the sandbox bounds execution under its policy. The harness composes those mechanisms with control requests, waiting, scheduling, and lifetime budgets.
Common pitfall: Keeping status and pending obligations only in prompt text or inaccessible execution-local state, so a separate control path cannot inspect them or prevent further dispatch.






A software repair workflow illustrates how this division of labor operates in practice. Table 1 traces an illustrative sequence of events around a single execution turn, from the moment the repair becomes eligible for another model call, through the model’s proposal to run the regression test against candidate r18, to the operator’s resume. The cells describe each decision in plain terms; the sections that follow supply the mechanism behind each one. The lifecycle states record whether the trajectory is eligible for continuation (READY), actively querying the model (CALLING_MODEL), awaiting tool completion (WAITING_TOOL), or suspended by an operator (PAUSED).



Table 1: A repair trajectory under supervision: An illustrative control trace. A paused trajectory admits no new work, yet its outstanding job and charges keep an owner.









Event
Harness decision and recorded obligation




The repair is eligible for another model call
From READY, confirm that no operator request is pending, that shared model capacity is available, and that the budget covers the most this call could cost. Set that amount aside, then enter CALLING_MODEL and send the call


A complete reply proposes the test of r18
Record what the call actually used. Check the proposed test against the task’s permissions and the remaining budget, set aside the test’s maximum cost, and record the test as running before sending it. Enter WAITING_TOOL


The operator requests a pause while the test runs
Stop admitting new work. Keep tracking the running test and its cost, but no longer let its result restart the model; then step through READY to PAUSED with no moment at which new work could start


The test result arrives during the pause
Confirm that the result is genuine and belongs to this test of r18. Record its outcome and cost, but leave the trajectory paused and the model’s context unchanged


The operator requests resume
Recheck task state, permissions, the recorded evidence, and the budget before returning to READY. The scheduler may then admit another call; the result supports only the test and revision it actually checked






Three features of the trace recur through the rest of the chapter. First, every row that admits work reserves before it sends. Affordability cannot be judged from settled charges alone, because the running test job may still bill and the proposed call may generate up to its full output allowance; the harness therefore reserves each operation’s worst-case liability at admission and reconciles reported usage afterward. Notebook 10.2 later prices a call that a check of settled spend admits and this reservation test refuses. Second, the pause and the test result are independent events. The pause stops new admission without stopping the job, and the job’s result settles its ledger entry without resuming the turn. Third, the reply’s content never acts on its own: a truncated or canceled reply yields nothing to dispatch, a claim of completion triggers an independent check rather than ending the task, and an action that policy requires a human to review waits in a dedicated hold with its own expiry. Each of these needs runtime state that the message list does not have.
The trace also separates the decision to continue from the resources an agent holds. While the repair trajectory sits in PAUSED or WAITING_TOOL, it keeps its workspace, its cached repository state, and its running test job, but it does not hold a worker thread or a place in the queue for model calls. Because the harness, not the repair loop, decides when the trajectory next calls the model, an interactive trajectory can take the next model-call slot without waiting for the repair to give it up. Which resources a wait releases, and which it keeps, is the subject of supervised waiting (section 10.6); how model calls are divided among trajectories is the subject of scheduling (section 10.8).




When an operator issues a pause request, the conversation transcript cannot answer the questions the harness must resolve. The transcript records what the user and model said, but runtime decisions require knowing the state of the underlying system: which candidate revision is under test, whether a background validation job has finished, how much compute budget remains once outstanding asynchronous tasks are accounted for, and whether any external side effects are still in flight. Simultaneously, the cluster scheduler must distinguish a trajectory blocked on a container execution from one actively waiting for its next inference turn. None of these operational facts belong in the prompt. Resolving them requires runtime-owned control state that the harness can inspect, mutate, and enforce directly without relying on the foundation model to reconstruct its own execution history.

Definition 10.2: Trajectory record
Trajectory record is the per-trajectory control state owned and maintained by the harness. It encapsulates identity and task scope, lifecycle state, resource limits and financial accounting, security grants and workspace leases, pending asynchronous operations, and references to prompt context, the live execution plan, container environments, and verified evidence.

Significance: It provides the harness with an authoritative, centralized structure to inspect and govern the entire trajectory, tracking resource consumption, pending asynchronous operations, and security grants across inference calls.
Distinction: While the conversation transcript records user-model message exchanges, the trajectory record tracks the operational state required to govern execution across multiple turns. A live in-memory record represents active control state, not a durable audit log or proof that external claims are verified.
Common pitfall: Treating a model’s generated text or self-reported progress as an authoritative update to consumed budget, granted capabilities, tool execution results, or task completion.



Table 2 organizes these fields by the supervisory decisions they support. In practice, this structure represents a logical schema: a distributed runtime may partition these field groups across different storage backends, for example keeping ephemeral context references in memory while persisting financial ledgers to an external store, provided each group retains a single authoritative writer and a well-defined update protocol.



Table 2: Trajectory Record Fields: Each field group supports a control decision; references preserve access to larger state without implying that the referenced resources are free or absent.










Field group
Contents
Supervisory use




Identity and task
Trajectory, requester, tenant, optional parent, task contract and version
Bind requests and charges to the right task and authority


Control
state, record_version, control_epoch, pending_control, exit reason
Decide whether a continuation or state change is current and permitted


Continuation
Context reference and version, live-plan reference and revision, candidate workspace and evidence references
Assemble the next call from the intended task state


Limits and accounting
Per-call limits, actual_consumption, outstanding_reservations, finalization_reserve, and deadline
Check new liability against the remaining allowance and preserve funds for final work


Authority and resources
Current grants, workspace leases, credential-broker references, resource owners
Check accessible operations and identify resources requiring release or transfer


Current invocation and observations
current_model_call, observation_eligible_calls, attempt IDs, job handles, deadlines, and expected versions
Correlate events and decide which may inform the current continuation


Held approval
held_approval: exact proposal reference, applicable task and plan versions, approval status and expiry
Keep a proposed action undispatched while its decision is pending


Outstanding obligations
operation_ledger reference, unresolved outcomes and charges, settlement owner
Preserve responsibility after a timeout, plan revision, pause, or scheduling exit






Two questions about a running operation must be answered separately: whether its result may still inform the model, and whether the harness still owes anything for it. The first is observation eligibility, which defines whether the output of an operation is permitted to enter the prompt context for the next model invocation. The second is an outstanding obligation, and the two can come apart. A tool call can lose observation eligibility (when an invocation step times out, or the user cancels a subtask) even while the remote execution continues running in a backend container. To prevent orphaned side effects and resource leaks, the operation ledger tracks every logical operation across its entire lifecycle: transport retries, incoming execution evidence, and the specific subsystem responsible for final settlement.
The trajectory record manages this lifecycle through two versioning counters. While record_version increments on every serialized update to provide optimistic concurrency control, the control epoch (control_epoch) tracks the specific planning and invocation cycle against which proposals and observations are validated. The epoch does not advance on every turn; it advances when the harness withdraws a continuation’s claim on outstanding results, as when a wait deadline expires, an operator interrupts, or a plan revision supersedes pending work. Each call records the epoch current at its registration, so an ordinary result from this turn’s dispatch still matches. Incrementing the epoch invalidates in-flight observations registered under the earlier epoch without breaking the underlying operation’s idempotency contract. As a result, the harness continues tracking background tasks and their external side effects even after the agent has stopped waiting for their immediate output.


↩︎ The operation idempotency contract and retry semantics are established in Retrying Uncertain Actions.
A parallel discipline governs resource accounting. The harness separates settled usage (actual_consumption) from provisional allocations (outstanding_reservations), which represent admitted operations whose compute or financial costs have not yet been finalized. The harness withholds a dedicated finalization reserve from general exploratory steps. This reserve guarantees that the runtime retains sufficient budget to execute mandated cleanup tasks, release sandboxes, and run deterministic verification suites before the trajectory terminates. Wall-clock deadlines operate independently of token limits, because waiting on remote containers or human reviewers consumes real time even when token generation is idle. Section 10.9 formalizes this admission test; the trajectory record provides the live metrics required to enforce it.
These lifecycle and accounting guarantees unite under one working rule, the settlement rule. It is the trajectory-level form of settlement before retry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}\)). That principle says a timeout does not establish whether an effect occurred, so a blind retry is unsafe; the settlement rule adds that losing interest in a result does not release the effect’s charge or its owner either. Under this rule, withdrawing an operation’s observation eligibility, whether through a timeout, a plan revision, an operator pause, or trajectory cancellation, never clears the operation or refunds its financial reservation from the ledger. Only authenticated, correlated evidence can settle an outcome, confirm completion, or release reserved budget. Until that proof arrives, the outstanding obligation retains a designated settlement owner responsible for reconciling its ultimate state.


Only the harness possesses write authority over the trajectory record. While the model can propose plan changes, tool calls, or completion assertions, the harness treats these outputs strictly as unverified proposals. Each update must pass admission checks before the runtime commits it to the record. Provider billing APIs and tool execution metrics supply authoritative consumption figures, cryptographically signed or authenticated tool events supply operational evidence, and control APIs supply verified operator intent. Decoupling this control plane from prompt text ensures strict enforceability: an agent may receive read-only notifications of its remaining budget, but it can never manipulate the meter.
To keep control operations lightweight and prevent multi-megabyte state copies during routine scheduler queries, the trajectory record stores references (content hashes, storage URIs, and job identifiers) rather than deep-copying full prompt contexts, workspace filesystems, or observation payloads. However, these references represent real underlying resource commitments. A paused or waiting trajectory continues to consume resources across distributed subsystems: KV-cache allocations in inference engines, isolated container environments and disk volumes, and open network sockets. The trajectory record holds the authoritative handles to these external assets and signals lifecycle transitions to their respective managers.
All mechanisms discussed in this section assume an active in-memory host. Preserving this control state across process crashes and ensuring that record updates remain strictly serialized with respect to external side effects requires write-ahead logging and durable execution protocols. A dedicated durable-log offset in the control record binds the volatile runtime state to its persistent backing log.


↪ Committing each admitted operation and its reservation to durable storage before dispatch is developed in Durable Intent Before Dispatch.



While test-time compute strategies use dependency graphs over candidate artifacts to explore solutions, runtime execution demands a live plan. A live plan is a dependency-ordered directed acyclic graph of execution steps that explicitly separates proposed actions from operations currently in flight and evidence already verified. Each step in the plan defines a unique identifier, explicit prerequisite steps or evidence dependencies, the target candidate artifact and operating conditions to which it applies, and its current execution status. When the harness admits a step, it binds that step directly to an entry in the operation ledger. Similarly, when a step completes, the harness links it to the immutable evidence supporting that completion, never to an unverified checkbox emitted in model text.


⇄ Contrast: The revisable candidate plan established in Revisable Candidate Plans tracks only unexecuted candidate operations and their supporting evidence; the live plan also records operations in flight.
Consider a practical software repair workflow where candidate r18 has just been generated. The live plan differentiates between the source edit that produced candidate r18, the targeted unit test running against that specific revision, and the broader integration suite required by the task contract. While the test runner executes in a background container, the plan records the step as in-flight rather than optimistically assuming success. When the test runner completes, a passing status validates only that targeted test against candidate r18 under those exact container flags; the remaining verification steps and final acceptance criteria remain unfulfilled. An operator’s pause request arriving mid-test acts as an independent supervisory event, interrupting further dispatch without corrupting the historical inputs or the validity of the ongoing test execution.
When incoming observations demonstrate that a strategy is failing, the model may propose a plan revision to alter downstream tasks. Before adopting any revised plan, the harness validates it against the overarching task contract, current evidence dependencies, remaining budget, and security grants. Adopting the revision advances the plan revision counter and invalidates pending, undispatched proposals and held approvals whose underlying assumptions have changed. Existing verified evidence remains valid under its original operating conditions. The harness synchronizes plan adoption with the tool dispatcher to prevent race conditions where a stale proposal might pass admission against a superseded plan.
Now consider what happens if a plan revision modifies the source code while the targeted test for candidate r18 is still running in the background. The active container job is testing candidate r18, not the new revision. Relabeling the step in the plan cannot convert those eventual test results into evidence for the modified code. Deleting the step from the plan likewise does not abort the remote job, reverse its external side effects, or automatically refund its compute reservation. Instead, the harness preserves the active operation in the ledger under its original settlement owner, blocks downstream steps whose prerequisites are no longer satisfied, and evaluates the replacement work through a fresh admission check. In robust systems, recovering from external operations requires explicit compensation and failure-handling logic rather than retroactively editing plan text.
By maintaining an explicit, dependency-tracked live plan, the trajectory record delineates what the agent has proposed, what the harness has admitted to the execution plane, and what obligations remain outstanding. Preserving consistency across concurrent tool events, asynchronous worker callbacks, and operator interruptions requires the harness to strictly govern how this record evolves, binding all lifecycle mutations to formal, guarded state transitions.




Consider an automated software repair trajectory that submits a suite of test cases for candidate r18. If the wait deadline elapses before a result arrives, the harness must record the outcome as unknown and proceed. One minute later, the test service returns a success report. Both statements reflect reality: the outcome was indeed unknown when the deadline expired, and the tests ultimately passed. The failure occurs if the harness splices that late result into an obsolete turn as though the model had possessed the evidence when selecting its next action. This defect, known as observation crossing, conflates the asynchronous physical history of an operation with the causal evidence admitted to a particular continuation. Preventing it takes two pieces developed in this section: guarded transitions that decide when a continuation may advance, and an epoch fence that decides which late results may still inform it (section 10.4.2).
A state machine with guarded transitions1 makes every such admission explicit. Beyond resolving observation races, guarded transitions prevent scheduling anomalies, such as mistaking a trajectory held for human approval as idle and erroneously dispatching another model call. The runtime control plane, rather than generated model output, governs all state transitions. Table 3 defines this supervisory state machine, organized around five live states, a finalizing state through which every exit must pass, and three terminal absorbing outcomes.
1 Guarded Transition: Harel’s statecharts (Harel 1987) labeled each transition with the event that triggers it and a condition that must hold for it to fire, and added hierarchy and concurrency so that reactive controllers stayed readable as their state counts grew. The harness uses the flat core of that formalism: an event proposes an edge, and the guard, evaluated against the record at that moment, decides whether it fires. Keeping the guard on the edge, rather than in whichever handler happens to receive the event, is what lets one table govern every path into CALLING_MODEL. 
Harel, David. 1987. “Statecharts: A Visual Formalism for Complex Systems.” Science of Computer Programming 8 (3): 231–74. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-6423(87)90035-9.



Table 3: Guarded Trajectory States: An edge permits consideration of a transition, not unconditional execution. Events can update accounting or evidence without changing state.










State
Meaning
Legal next states




READY
Eligible to be considered for the next model call; admission guards still apply.
CALLING_MODEL, PAUSED, FINALIZING


CALLING_MODEL
A model invocation is registered for the current continuation.
READY, WAITING_TOOL, AWAITING_APPROVAL, FINALIZING


WAITING_TOOL

READY, FINALIZING

WAITING_TOOL, READY, FINALIZING

The continuation is held at a local boundary; no new model or tool work is admitted.
READY, FINALIZING

None






The normal operational cycle follows READY → CALLING_MODEL → WAITING_TOOL → READY, tracing through the five live states and guarded transitions shown in figure 2: proposals requiring review divert into AWAITING_APPROVAL, pause commands transition to PAUSED exclusively from READY, and all termination triggers (completion requests, cancellations, or exhausted budgets) route through FINALIZING before reaching absorbing terminal states (COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELED). During execution, a model response may produce no admissible action, request task completion, or propose an action requiring operator approval. While the normalized invocation status defined in Normalized invocation status envelope fixes how the runtime processes individual call outcomes, table 4 specifies how each outcome shifts the overall trajectory state. Two names appear in both vocabularies with different meanings: a reply status of COMPLETED or CANCELED describes one model call, while the terminal states of the same names describe the whole trajectory. A completed reply ends a call, not the task. Only a reply whose status is COMPLETED proceeds to tool candidate validation. The harness must never convert a malformed, truncated, or canceled partial stream into an actionable tool invocation simply because a parser managed to salvage partial arguments from the payload.



Table 4: Reply Status and Next State: Every non-completed status returns to a state that admits no dispatch from the failed reply; reservations for failed or faulted calls stay outstanding until usage settles.

For bounded failure handling while the budget permits, FINALIZING otherwise






Action approval introduces a controlled detour to this cycle. An approved action transitions from AWAITING_APPROVAL to WAITING_TOOL only when its active dispatch guards pass; recording operator approval does not automatically execute the tool. Conversely, a denial, expiration, or operator withdrawal emits a refusal observation back to READY.

The ordinary cycle runs from READY through CALLING_MODEL and WAITING_TOOL back to READY; a proposal that policy requires reviewed is held in AWAITING_APPROVAL, and pause is entered only from READY. Every exit passes through FINALIZING, which stops admission and resolves or transfers remaining duties before an absorbing terminal state. Navigating a legal edge in the state machine is merely a necessary condition for progress, not an unconditional entitlement to execute. Before the runtime admits new work, whether invoking a model or dispatching a tool, it evaluates a comprehensive set of predicates known as the admission check. This check enforces several simultaneous invariants: no pending control holds may exist; the active context, credentials, and required action approvals must remain valid; upstream data dependencies must be resolved; and adequate deadline slack and downstream service capacity must be confirmed. The runtime must also reserve the operation’s bounded financial liability from the task budget without encroaching on the dedicated finalization reserve (section 10.9). For tool calls, the admission check also verifies that arguments are structurally complete. Because system state evolves continuously, this evaluation holds only for the instant it executes. An approval granted seconds earlier or a scheduling decision made on a previous tick does not carry forward; if an unresolved prior operation blocks a dependent mutation, the trajectory cannot dispatch that mutation even if it remains in READY for independent work.
The admission check and its state updates execute as a single atomic transaction. Protected by the trajectory record lock,2 the harness evaluates the guard predicates, reserves the required liability, registers the outgoing invocation or attempt ID, marks the expected observation as eligible, and commits the state transition. After releasing the record lock, the runtime passes the admitted request to a release gate that serializes the final release-or-withhold decision with control updates. This gate rechecks current controls and the existing admission without reserving liability twice; slow network I/O remains outside the record lock. This design enforces the register-before-send rule. Registering state prior to dispatch ensures that ultra-low-latency responses never arrive before the local record exists to receive them. Conversely, transmitting requests strictly outside the critical section prevents slow network I/O, stalled inference endpoints, or lagging tool services from blocking concurrent control actions, scheduler ticks, or arriving results from other workers.
2 Record Lock as a Monitor: Hoare’s monitors (Hoare 1974) bundled shared data with the only procedures allowed to touch it and ran those procedures one at a time, so every invariant on the data could be checked at procedure entry and exit. The trajectory record is a monitor in this sense: controllers, schedulers, and result handlers all reach it through short guarded procedures. The register-before-send rule adds one constraint for a record whose procedures front slow remote services: no procedure waits on a model or tool call while holding the lock. 
Hoare, Charles Antony Richard. 1974. “Monitors: An Operating System Structuring Concept.” Communications of the ACM 17 (10): 549–57. https://doi.org/10.1145/355620.361161.
Because external control requests acquire this same monitor lock, stops and admissions are strictly serialized. This sequencing establishes the admission-order rule. If a pause, cancellation, or kill command commits before an admission check runs, it immediately blocks new outbound work. Conversely, if admission commits first, the operation becomes owned work with a registered identity and reservation. A later control cannot erase that record or refund its liability on intent alone. The release gate can still withhold a definitely unsent attempt, but settlement requires authoritative evidence that release did not occur and that no remote liability remains. Once release may have occurred, a cancellation request cannot establish not_sent; remote evidence must settle the outcome. A volatile withheld flag alone cannot establish non-release after a host crash. Tool-side idempotency and stale-lease fencing still require the endpoint contracts detailed in Operation identity and endpoint contracts.
To coordinate concurrent state access without heavyweight distributed locks, the harness pairs optimistic concurrency validation with epoch fencing. The record_version field detects competing updates at the point of commit, implementing the validation step of optimistic concurrency control (Kung and Robinson 1981). In parallel, increments to control_epoch fence out stale asynchronous responses, the same generation-number check that the tool layer applies to superseded workers at the endpoint. Here the fenced party is an observation: a response stamped with an old epoch cannot advance the current continuation, however well formed it is. These control plane identifiers operate alongside, rather than replace, logical operation identifiers and transport attempt counters. A network retry generates a new attempt ID under the same logical operation, whereas an operator interruption bumps the control epoch to invalidate pending replies without erasing the operation’s accounting ledger.

Listing 1 expresses these rules as a single supervisory procedure. The legal edges match table 3, and any edge without a registered guard predicate is rejected by default. The caller provides the record_version it observed when formulating its transition request; a concurrent modification by another worker causes the version check to fail. Similarly, duplicate deliveries of an event fail either the version check or the edge guard, guaranteeing that no action is admitted twice.



Listing 1: Guarded Transitions: Every state change checks the legal edge, its explicit guard, and the record version under the record lock, then performs admission bookkeeping before the state changes; the admitted request is sent only after the lock is released.


LIVE = {"READY", "CALLING_MODEL", "WAITING_TOOL",
        "AWAITING_APPROVAL", "PAUSED"}
LEGAL = {("READY", "CALLING_MODEL"), ("READY", "PAUSED"),
         ("CALLING_MODEL", "READY"), ("CALLING_MODEL", "WAITING_TOOL"),
         ("CALLING_MODEL", "AWAITING_APPROVAL"), ("WAITING_TOOL", "READY"),
         ("AWAITING_APPROVAL", "WAITING_TOOL"),
         ("AWAITING_APPROVAL", "READY"), ("PAUSED", "READY")}
LEGAL |= {(s, "FINALIZING") for s in LIVE}
LEGAL |= {("FINALIZING", t) for t in ("COMPLETED", "FAILED", "CANCELED")}
# GUARDS maps each edge to a predicate over (record, decision).

def transition(rec, new_state, decision, admit=None):
    with rec.lock:                            # the local decision only
        edge = (rec.state, new_state)
        guard = GUARDS.get(edge)              # no guard, no permission
        if edge not in LEGAL or guard is None or not guard(rec, decision):
            raise IllegalTransition(edge, decision.id)
        if decision.seen_version != rec.record_version:
            raise StaleDecision(decision.id)  # a competing update won
        if admit is not None:
            admit(rec)                        # reserve, register, set eligibility
        rec.state = new_state
        rec.record_version += 1
        rec.history.append((edge, decision.id, rec.record_version))
    # The caller passes admitted work to the serialized release gate outside this lock.



Here, the guard registered on the READY → CALLING_MODEL edge executes the complete admission check, while admit performs the liability reservations and bookkeeping required by the register-before-send rule. Because the monitor lock protects only in-memory lookups, state updates, and an array append, lock contention remains negligible compared to the hundreds of milliseconds consumed by remote inference or tool execution.



When an asynchronous tool result arrives, the harness must reconcile financial and physical state without corrupting the prompt history of an active turn. Upon reception, the runtime authenticates the payload and correlates its task identifier, logical operation ID, and attempt number against the trajectory record. Mismatched or unauthenticated messages are logged for audit and dropped. Valid results immediately update the trajectory’s persistent ledger: the runtime records raw execution evidence and converts reserved financial liabilities into settled resource usage.
However, updating the operational ledger does not imply that the result belongs in the model’s current prompt context. As demonstrated in listing 2, the runtime splits incoming evidence into two separate paths: universal ledger settlement and epoch-fenced observation staging. While every authentic result records evidence and settles any confirmed usage, an observation is staged for immediate prompt injection only if its call ID remains registered in observation_eligible_calls and the epoch recorded with the call at registration matches the active control_epoch. The remote service never sees the epoch; when the harness correlates the result, it looks up the epoch by call ID and attaches it to the local result envelope as result.epoch. This field comes from the registration record, not the remote payload. The two checks fail in different ways. The eligibility set is the per-call statement of which results the current wait expects, and removing an entry after staging is what stops a redelivery from being staged twice. The epoch is a bulk fence: a timeout or operator interrupt advances it once and thereby invalidates every call registered under the old epoch, including any whose removal from the set was missed. If an operation timed out or an operator intervened, its recorded epoch is obsolete. The harness settles the financial balance but refuses to inject the result into the current turn, which eliminates observation crossing. Should that late evidence prove relevant to future turns, the runtime can re-evaluate and stage it during subsequent guarded context assembly. Staging a result does not by itself end the wait. A declared wait policy establishes the criteria required to return from WAITING_TOOL to READY, and the handler requests that transition only when the policy is satisfied.



Listing 2: Routing a Tool Result: Authenticated evidence always reaches the operation ledger and settles usage, while only a currently eligible result under the current control epoch is staged for the waiting continuation.


def on_tool_result(rec, result):
    if not authenticate(result):
        return audit(rec, "unauthenticated_result", result)
    with rec.lock:
        op = rec.operation_ledger.get(result.operation_id)
        if op is None or result.attempt_id not in op.attempts:
            return audit(rec, "unknown_operation", result)
        if not op.record_evidence(result):  # already recorded: duplicate
            return
        settle(rec, op, result.usage)       # reserved -> actual; rest stays owed
        eligible = (result.call_id in rec.observation_eligible_calls
                    and result.epoch == rec.control_epoch)
        if eligible:
            rec.observation_eligible_calls.discard(result.call_id)
            stage_observation(rec, result)  # for the current wait only
        rec.record_version += 1
        seen = rec.record_version
    if eligible and wait_policy_satisfied(rec):  # the guard rechecks it
        transition(rec, "READY", Decision(result.id, seen))



Systems typically implement one of four wait policies: all required results arrive, an acceptable partial batch completes, a wait deadline expires, or an operator triggers an explicit withdrawal. The trajectory record carefully distinguishes confirmed evidence from unreturned, unresolved calls. In the candidate r18 repair scenario, a timeout records that the outcome was unknown at the deadline; it cannot justify inferring that the test suite failed. When the test service eventually reports that candidate r18 passed, the ledger records that verified outcome with its exact scope. A timeout likewise never authorizes an uncoordinated re-execution of a non-idempotent operation. Dependent actions must still satisfy all guard preconditions and adhere to the tool’s mutation safety contract.



To maintain a clean supervisory contract, the state machine permits entry into PAUSED exclusively from READY. If a pause command arrives while the trajectory is in CALLING_MODEL or WAITING_TOOL, the runtime cannot abruptly discard the state of remote interactions. Instead, it asserts a pending_control hold, which prevents the admission of any subsequent work. The harness revokes observation eligibility for active model streams, invalidates any pending approval requests, and terminates the active observation wait; for a trajectory in WAITING_TOOL, this is the explicit-withdrawal wait policy, and it is what permits the WAITING_TOOL → READY step. If policy dictates, the control plane issues cancellation requests to remote workers; under the settlement rule, these operations remain registered in the ledger until remote confirmation arrives. Any partial token stream received from a canceled model call is preserved solely for diagnostic logging, never stitched together to form a valid dispatch.
Once these local eligibility revocations are logged, the trajectory steps through READY directly into PAUSED under the existing admission hold. Because the lock prevents concurrent scheduling during this step-down, no runnable window opens between the transitions. Entering PAUSED halts continuation progress, ensuring that neither pending responses nor held proposals can advance the continuation. However, background tools already running in external systems may continue their physical execution. For example, the remote test execution for candidate r18 can complete while the trajectory remains paused; its completion payload updates the ledger and settles liability without triggering a new inference cycle.
Resuming execution requires a guarded PAUSED → READY transition, followed by a brand-new admission check that reconciles all ledger evidence accumulated during the pause. Resumption is not an automated rollback of pause-time revocations; state withdrawn during a pause is never restored. Expired authorization tokens remain expired, withdrawn approvals require fresh operator authorization, and canceled partial responses are permanently abandoned. If an earlier operation remains unconfirmed, its unresolved state continues to block dependent actions even if unrelated steps are eligible. Meanwhile, physical resource retention operates under independent lifecycles: sandboxed workspace leases, buffer allocations, compute reservations, and model context caches persist or expire according to their respective lifetime policies rather than the trajectory’s instantaneous state.



Every exit path passes through FINALIZING. Upon entering this state, the runtime immediately suspends standard work admission, records the exit reason, revokes unused delegation authority where supported, and triggers the task completion check when completion is claimed. An end-of-turn token emitted by a model merely requests this validation; genuine task completion requires an independent completion check, such as the task contract’s acceptance tests, run outside the model. All finalization checks and mandatory cleanup routines draw from their dedicated, pre-funded reserve.
During finalization, the control plane may block to await pending results, report verification failures, or hand off outstanding cancellation, billing reconciliation, and resource reclamation tasks to an external supervisor. The transition guard into any terminal state requires that every outstanding obligation be either definitively settled or explicitly transferred to an accepting upstream owner. Simply clearing an unresolved task from a local tracking set violates the guard. To effect a legitimate transfer, the runtime must transmit complete metadata (operation IDs, ledger evidence, and funding allocations), allowing the recipient service to assume supervisory responsibility.
All terminal states (COMPLETED, FAILED, and CANCELED) are strictly absorbing. Once a trajectory enters a terminal state, its continuation terminates permanently. Late-arriving tool results or ledger settlements can still update archived historical records through the designated supervisory owner, but no event can transition the continuation back to READY. Resuming an investigation or re-attempting a task requires instantiating a fresh trajectory with a new identifier linked back to the prior run. Within this architecture, COMPLETED denotes solely that the programmatic completion criteria configured for the harness were met. Whether those criteria demonstrate true task competence is an empirical systems question addressed in The Evaluation Problem.
