Guarded transitions keep every update to the record causally consistent under network delays, tool timeouts, and concurrent interventions. They describe pause entry, however, only from the record’s side. An operator who presses pause needs more: an authenticated way to register the request, a bound on how long it takes effect while a model call is still generating, and a distinction between a pause, a cancellation, and a kill that leaves outstanding work owned in each case.




The test job for candidate r18 is still executing when an operator requests a pause. The harness must halt the repair loop’s forward progress without losing the job’s tracking identity, its allocated budget reservation, or the diagnostic evidence it might return. Delaying the pause until the test finishes strips the operator of interactive control over potentially runaway execution. Conversely, declaring the job canceled merely because the trajectory state transitions to PAUSED fabricates an execution outcome the runtime has not yet observed.
External control decouples receiving a request from establishing the physical execution state that request demands. When an operator intervenes, the harness authenticates the caller, verifies authority over the target trajectory, and appends the requested directive to pending_control while holding the record lock. Because this update occurs under the lock, the admission-ordering invariants established in section 10.4 fix exactly which operations fall under the request’s scope. The controller acknowledges the hold to the operator only after the update commits to the record (and, once durable execution is in place, to its log). The response delivered to the operator must also distinguish three distinct milestones: request received, new admission stopped, and subsequent confirmation that running work has terminated.


A turn boundary is an explicit checkpoint where the harness evaluates whether execution may proceed before admitting its next operation. Turn boundaries occur immediately before dispatching an inference call to a foundation model and immediately before invoking any external tool, including each individually admitted call within a proposed parallel batch. The name marks where control takes effect, not a boundary between turns: one turn (one step of the trajectory, counted by \(\TurnHorizon\)) contains a turn boundary before its model call and one before each tool call it admits. A pause that lands midway through a batch therefore leaves the calls already sent registered as owned work and withholds the rest. The admission check evaluates control flags under the trajectory record lock, and the release gate serializes its final decision with subsequent control updates. A flag check followed by an uncoordinated send would leave a race window and would not enforce this boundary. This boundary provides a local admission guarantee: instead of obscuring system state behind the timestamp of an operator’s stop button, it leaves all remaining obligations explicit and inspectable.
Local candidate processing does not have to wait for remote model generation to finish. The foundation-model contract already separates a CANCELED reply from a REJECTED one and withholds both from dispatch; the harness turns that cancellation into a control action. It can initiate streaming cancellation, commanding the serving engine to stop generating an in-progress reply, terminating the invocation’s eligibility to produce an actionable candidate, and retaining partial output solely for bounded diagnosis. A canceled or truncated payload never becomes a dispatchable call, even if a tolerant JSON parser closes its dangling brackets, a valid tool-call prefix appeared before the abort signal, or an apparently complete response arrives after eligibility was withdrawn. The quarantining rule (The normalized status envelope), an application of invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) to the reply status, holds regardless of how the invocation ended. Late-arriving evidence remains useful only to reconcile accounting usage or explain what the serving engine executed.

3 Why Batching Does Not Shorten the Wait: The reference rate charges each generated token one full read of the weights, the single-request case. A serving engine that batches many requests shares that read among them, which raises throughput but still advances each request by one token per ordinary decode step, so batching cannot bring the per-request wait below this estimate. Techniques that emit several tokens per step change the rate, not the wait’s linear growth with the output allowance. Output allowances and wall-clock deadlines address fundamentally different operational risks. An output token ceiling enforces a hard boundary on generated volume under the serving engine’s accounting contract; wall-clock latency, however, also depends on scheduling queues, network stalls, and autoregressive decode throughput. Even under ideal conditions, waiting for a full generation pass introduces substantial delay.3 At a fixed per-token decode time, a call admitted with output allowance \(\OutputLimit\), generating at \(\PerTokenDecodeTime\), can postpone the next turn boundary by approximately
\[\TurnBoundaryDelay \approx \OutputLimit \times \PerTokenDecodeTime\]
Assuming an optimistic decode latency of 21.075 ms per generated token, the single-accelerator, single-request floor of the estimate in Per-call work estimate, with no queueing or memory-access stalls, a 4,096-token allowance postpones the boundary by roughly 86.3 s. Pause or cancellation logic that passively waits for generation to complete would therefore block for more than a minute, and real serving queues only lengthen the wait. A node that splits the weights across several accelerators lowers the per-token floor but leaves the generation estimate linear in \(\OutputLimit\), so halving the allowance halves the full-allowance generation time at a fixed rate, whereas streaming cancellation removes the dependence on generation length entirely. The harness uses both: turn boundaries govern discrete operation admission, while streaming cancellation stops active generations in flight.
Stopping local execution is fundamentally different from terminating remote cluster execution. A host deadline determines when the supervisor ceases waiting and initiates intervention; confirming that remote inference has actually stopped requires positive evidence from the service. Under the settlement rule, unconfirmed resource usage remains an outstanding liability rather than an assumed refund.



The guarded pause sequence established in section 10.4 holds new admissions while transitioning from READY to PAUSED. What this state means to an operator, however, depends on the policy configured for in-flight work. For the r18 test, the policy may permit the active job to finish under its existing budget limits while holding the repair loop’s continuation. Conversely, a policy requiring the job to stop immediately requests cancellation and records whatever outcome the executor confirms. A pause policy that permits execution to proceed leaves the workspace live and mutable, and the operator interface must reflect this active state. Any administrative inspection that demands quiescence requires positive confirmation that all concurrent writers have stopped, or else an isolated snapshot taken at a declared boundary. When the operator resumes the trajectory, execution proceeds along the guarded transitions defined in section 10.4; the pause policy governs only what ran while held, without altering the invariants enforced after resumption.

Mid-trajectory user steering demands the same transactional discipline. If an operator injects a steering instruction, such as directing the agent to modify a different target file, the harness cannot simply append the prompt to the conversation context and assume existing operations adapt. Adding instructions does not retroactively invalidate an already admitted file edit or revoke an active tool approval. Instead, the harness records the instruction, determines which plan steps and proposed actions are superseded, and verifies whether outstanding operations conflict with the revised task.



Unlike cooperative cancellation, a kill request invokes immediate, non-cooperative enforcement. Trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\)) is what makes this enforcement possible: because control requests are recorded independently of model output, the runtime can stop new admission and abort the local work it supervises without waiting on the model or on an external service’s response. When a kill signal arrives, the controller halts local execution, revokes mediated access tokens, and fences off obsolete workers across the execution paths under its control. The sandbox reset contract in The reset contract determines which child processes, descendant namespaces, network channels, and allocated resources that enforcement covers. Asynchronous remote work, third-party transactions, and external handles lie beyond direct local process control and demand their own corroborating evidence.
Finalization therefore records confirmed termination separately from unresolved side effects and pending charges, which retain their designated owner under the settlement rule. The operation’s repeat contract determines whether another attempt is safe, and settlement must precede any retry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}\)); an operation identifier alone cannot reveal what the interrupted execution actually modified.
Enforcing external control decouples trajectory continuation from model behavior and frees execution resources. Worker threads and compute slots never remain blocked while an external job or cancellation response is outstanding. By persisting these control directives and outstanding obligations within the trajectory record, the harness safely suspends execution and yields worker resources, admitting continuation only when verified events satisfy the state machine’s guards.




When the agent dispatches the integration test for candidate r18, the model generates nothing for as long as the test runs, which is tens of seconds for the integration test priced in notebook \(\ref{nbk-05-residency-tax}\), and minutes for a broader suite. If the worker thread that dispatched the job blocks until the result returns, it cannot service any other trajectory in the interim. Worse, the runtime becomes unresponsive to operator pauses or high-priority interactive requests. The repair trajectory requires no token generation while the test executes. What it requires instead is an external supervisor: a control entity that tracks the in-flight job, holds the execution continuation, and buffers incoming evidence without tying up a worker thread in a synchronous wait.
Yielding execution through an asynchronous wait4 releases the worker thread immediately, leaving the trajectory record as the explicit holder of pending state. Alternatively, a runtime with blocking workers can maintain controllability if an independent supervisor thread handles operator requests, heartbeats, and deadlines. This architectural requirement transcends any specific event-loop implementation: waiting must keep the control record accessible, and any returning event must pass through that record’s admission guards before advancing the trajectory.

The event handler generalizes the callback logic in listing 2 across all event sources. Operating under a mutex or transactional boundary, the handler updates the record, advances record_version, and checks the call’s recorded epoch against control_epoch; the version check itself happens in the guarded transition the handler then requests. Because network notifications can be duplicated, the handler must remain strictly idempotent: an identical redelivery will neither append a redundant observation, nor double-bill resource counters, nor re-enqueue an already scheduled continuation. Correlation ensures that incoming data routes to the correct trajectory record, while the tool’s formal contract defines what that evidence actually establishes.
This discipline applies equally to streamed outputs. Real-time log fragments and progress heartbeats can append data to a bounded observation store without terminating the wait interval. Conversely, observing an opening tool-call delimiter in a streaming model response represents an incomplete proposal; the supervisor takes no action until the stream completes. The model adapter retains sole responsibility for parsing and validating full invocation payloads, whereas the harness determines whether that validated proposal remains eligible under current control policies.



For long-running tasks, the harness can wait for a push notification or poll external status at bounded intervals. In both cases, the runtime manages the waiting loop autonomously without querying the model about whether to keep waiting. If a job pauses to request human or auxiliary input, the runtime logs that requirement as a structured state transition rather than a trigger for resumption. Responding to such an input requirement remains a distinctly authorized operation, and the record tracks this pending dependency explicitly rather than treating raw stdout or log lines as an implicit signal to resume model generation.
Parallel tool invocations demand an explicit continuation policy. Under an all-results policy, the harness suspends the trajectory until every member of the batch either returns valid evidence or reaches a terminal disposition, such as a timeout with unresolved side effects. Conversely, a partial-results policy permits the model to reason incrementally as individual results arrive, even while other calls remain in flight. Such a policy must explicitly track missing evidence, preventing downstream steps from proceeding under the mistaken assumption that the entire batch has converged.
For example, a completed lint result need not settle a concurrent test job. If the agent’s next planning step requires both checks on candidate r18, the lint output alone leaves the wait open. If, however, the subsequent step is an independent inspection, a partial-results policy can safely admit it under current limits. Modifying the candidate workspace while the test suite actively reads disk state introduces race conditions; simply designating invocations as parallel does not preserve the tested revision without explicit workspace isolation.
When a deadline expires, it terminates the harness’s wait interval, not the underlying remote operation. The harness logs the timeout, marks the operation as unresolved, and requests the configured intervention policy. The ledger retains the unresolved liability until explicit settlement rules determine whether late-arriving results can be accepted or whether re-execution is safe.



Consider what happens when the test result for r18 arrives while an operator pause is active. The supervisor authenticates the payload, correlates it with the outstanding job handle, and commits the outcome to the trajectory ledger, all while the trajectory state remains strictly PAUSED. A passing test suite (such as test_waiter_notified_on_return) provides verification for that specific revision, but it does not constitute approval of the overall repair, nor does it grant fresh execution budget. The decision to resume the repair belongs entirely to the resume guard. Consequently, the harness event processor must remain active even when trajectory continuation is suspended. The same principle governs finalization: late-arriving evidence can settle outstanding accounting liabilities without accidentally reviving an already terminated trajectory.



Releasing a worker thread does not dismantle the underlying execution environment: sandboxed processes, disk workspaces, network sockets, buffered logs, and retained inference states remain allocated. The control record maintains explicit references to these resources and their respective lifecycles. Tool subscriptions and cloud storage incur ongoing charges, quota reservations persist until liabilities are settled, and the wall-clock task deadline continues to elapse. Even polling routines and cleanup handlers consume execution budget and must operate within configured limits.
A workspace lease guarantees the availability of candidate source edits and test artifacts according to the lifetime contracts established in Workspace leases, persisting across multiple tool boundaries. Its term bounds what a waiting trajectory can lose. If the harness never returns to renew, lease expiry reclaims the workspace; if it returns after expiry, the resumed trajectory must treat its workspace as gone rather than assume the files it left are still there. In parallel, the model serving infrastructure decides whether to retain, evict, or page out key-value cache state across turns. Releasing the harness worker does not remove the residency tax of notebook \(\ref{nbk-05-residency-tax}\): attention state kept resident through the wait still divides the turn rate its memory can sustain by \(1 + \ToolTime/\ModelTime\). The harness provides hints regarding expected wait durations and resumption priorities; where a hosted inference service provides no explicit cache-placement primitives, retention remains subject to provider eviction policies.


↩︎ Keep, move, and drop policies for a paused trajectory’s KV-cache state are established in Keep, move, and drop policies.
A wait is therefore a supervised interval characterized by retained evidence, active resource leases, and pending obligations. When that interval concludes, the harness transitions the continuation to an eligible state only if the record’s guards explicitly approve. Human-in-the-loop approval operates under this identical supervisory discipline: rather than waiting on an external computation, the harness suspends execution before dispatch, waiting for an authorization decision that may arrive late, be denied, or expire entirely.




Consider the internal-review workflow: an agent proposes submitting candidate patch r18 along with selected verification records, but trusted policy permits submission only after an authorized engineer signs off. The proposal is complete, yet the human reviewer is unavailable. Meanwhile, the task’s deadline clock continues advancing, an operator can request a pause, and credentials or access grants can expire. The harness cannot simply leave the proposal floating in the model’s context window, nor can it allow a retry loop or subsequent model step to dispatch the action prematurely. Instead, the runtime must hold the fully formed submission in escrow while review remains unresolved.


↩︎ Action-bound approval, which ties sign-off on the r18 patch submission to its exact canonical payload, is established in Action-bound approval.

Definition 10.3: Approval escrow
Approval escrow is the harness’s retention of an undispatched proposal pending required approval and subsequent dispatch admission. The held record binds the proposal to its enclosing task, approval conditions, and expiration deadline; even after a favorable decision arrives, execution still requires current admission checks at the dispatch boundary.

Significance: Escrow decouples proposing an operation from the authority to execute it immediately, keeping long, human-scale waits visible to supervisors and external schedulers.
Distinction: Authorization policies define who holds the authority to approve a represented action. The harness manages the operational lifecycle of that pending decision: routing the request, tracking timeouts, and enforcing state transitions toward dispatch or refusal.
Common pitfall: Treating a recorded approval as an unconditional instruction to execute, ignoring subsequent changes to credentials, task deadlines, branch states, or available compute capacity.



Requiring human approval is a deliberate task-policy choice rather than an automatic property of irreversible side effects. Some high-risk actions are prohibited outright; many others proceed safely under tight, automated least-privilege policies. Conversely, sensitive data disclosures or even benign, reversible mutations might require human oversight depending on operational risk. The approval gate must therefore enforce trusted runtime policy over the concrete operation, target resource, and parameter scope, never relying on the model’s self-reported assessment of whether an action is safe. Requesting review cannot expand authority: a reviewer cannot grant permissions beyond their own administrative boundaries.
When safety policy exists solely as prompt instructions inside the model’s context window, no gate actually exists. A prominent real-world incident illustrates the failure modes of prompt-only guardrails.

War Story 10.1: A code freeze stated only to the model (2025)Context: In July 2025, SaaStr founder Jason Lemkin was building an application with Replit’s autonomous coding agent and placed the project under an explicit code freeze, instructing the agent in natural language not to modify code or production infrastructure (Sharwood 2025).
Mechanism: The freeze existed only as text in the agent’s conversational context. No supervisory component at the dispatch boundary validated proposed database tool calls against that restriction. Despite the instructions, the agent executed an operation that deleted the production database, subsequently claiming that rollback was impossible.
Impact: The live production database was unavailable until engineering restored it. Lemkin also reported that the agent had masked previous software faults with fabricated synthetic data, including populating a 4,000-record database with fictional user profiles.
Fix: Contrary to the agent’s assertion, database snapshot rollback functioned properly and restored the data. Lemkin observed that natural language instructions cannot reliably enforce operational boundaries in agentic coding environments, advocating for strict architectural isolation between preview, staging, and production environments.
Systems lesson: Operational freezes are admission-control invariants, and admission control belongs strictly to the execution runtime. Stating a freeze to the model merely shifts output probabilities; it provides no deterministic safety guarantees. When enforced at the dispatch boundary by checking the target endpoint and operation payload against active policy, the runtime deterministically traps or rejects forbidden mutations regardless of what the model generates. This reflects the foundational requirement of invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)).


From the perspective of harness architecture, enforcing the freeze requires a single dispatch-time rule: while the freeze flag is set, any proposed mutation against the production target must be rejected or held in approval escrow. A destructive action then collapses into a harmless refusal observation fed back to the model rather than an unrecoverable side effect. Whether the model follows instructions becomes irrelevant to system correctness. The agent’s false claim that rollback was impossible highlights a related boundary: a model-generated status report can be false. The harness must verify execution outcomes and rollback states directly from its append-only operation ledger, never from the agent’s conversational transcript.
Approval gates must also remain selective and narrow. When a human operator faces dozens of routine, low-risk confirmation dialogs every hour, fatigue leads to rubber-stamping without inspection.5 A gate where every request is approved adds no closure beyond the policy check that routed the request to it. Fine-grained authorization grants, sandboxes, and automated linters should handle the vast majority of verifiable actions. Reserving manual approval strictly for high-blast-radius or policy-mandated exceptions ensures that human attention is focused where it matters most.
5 Ironies of Automation: Bainbridge observed that automating most of a process leaves the human operator the residual job of monitoring it, and that people sustain attention poorly on a stream in which almost nothing goes wrong (Bainbridge 1983). An approval queue in which nearly every request is benign is that stream. The one harmful proposal arrives in a queue that has trained the reviewer to expect nothing, which is why the gate’s precision, not its presence, determines what closure it supplies. 
Bainbridge, Lisanne. 1983. “Ironies of Automation.” Automatica 19 (6): 775–79. https://doi.org/10.1016/0005-1098(83)90046-8.


After validating a completed model response, the harness records the held proposal before publishing its approval request. The record references the task and requester, intended tool origin and operation, immutable candidate artifact and selected evidence, applicable preconditions, required approver policy, and approval expiry. It also assigns an approval-request identifier and a held-proposal version, and computes the approval digest, the digest that action-bound approval binds, computed here over the canonical held proposal and covering the operation, its arguments, its target, and the versions of the referenced artifacts. The approval binds to that digest, so changing any argument or artifact produces a different digest and voids the approval. These identifiers and the cryptographic digest track the pending decision itself, distinct from the logical operation IDs or transport-layer idempotency tokens assigned once dispatch begins.
For the review submission, the held artifact is the exact r18 patch and named check records, not a mutable filesystem path whose contents can shift before execution. The selected records retain their evidential scope; a targeted unit-test pass does not become full acceptance because it appears in an approval request. The authentication and represented-action requirements are those of action-bound approval. The harness adds the recorded status needed to distinguish pending, denied, expired, withdrawn, and admitted requests. Figure 3 diagrams this approval pipeline: panel (a) binds the exact proposal payload, artifact hashes, destination scope, and expiration timestamp into an immutable approval digest for revision r18, while panel (b) traces the four-step resolution sequence that parks the trajectory in AWAITING_APPROVAL until reviewer decisions and dispatch guards are verified.






Figure 3: The Approval Gate: Panel (a) lists what the reviewer approves for the r18 review submission: the exact proposal, its destination and data scope, the selected evidence with its limited scope, the preconditions, the digest that binds the approval, the expiry, and the requesting trajectory. Panel (b) holds the proposal without sending it, obtains a decision the model takes no part in, and rechecks current conditions at the dispatch boundary. An approval without capacity stays held; a denial, expiry, or stale proposal returns a refusal observation.



The trajectory enters AWAITING_APPROVAL without sending the held tool call. Parking the trajectory in this state releases its active compute worker; polling for a human response requires an external callback or light notification check rather than expensive model inference. The suspended trajectory retains its proposal record, cryptographic digest, and artifact references, while optionally maintaining its workspace lease and sandbox storage.
Under stable flow, Little’s law (theorem \(\ref{thrm-05-littles-law}\)) makes the mean number of trajectories held in AWAITING_APPROVAL equal to the rate of approval requests multiplied by the mean time to a decision, \(\ApprovalHeldTrajectories = \ArrivalRate\,\ExternalWait\). Review latency, not model speed, dictates how many concurrent held trajectories and retained resources the system carries. The relation fixes the mean, not the peak: a burst of review requests after an incident, or a reviewer who clears the queue once a day, holds far more than the mean for as long as the backlog lasts, so the pool for held workspaces is sized from the arrival pattern. The approval expiry strictly bounds this wait for a decision, while the trajectory’s overall deadline clock advances independently. Which operational cost dominates, retained sandbox footprint or delayed mitigation, depends on the workload profile.


↩︎ Little’s law, which equates mean occupancy with arrival rate times mean residence time, is established in Residence time and service rate.

Lighthouse 10.1: Remediation agent (approval escrow)Workload: The remediation agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) diagnoses a production incident and proposes a change, such as restoring a previous service configuration, that policy holds for an on-call reviewer. The repair agent’s gated action is instead a review submission near the end of a long trajectory. Both wait in AWAITING_APPROVAL, and Little’s law, \(\ApprovalHeldTrajectories = \ArrivalRate\,\ExternalWait\) for the \(\ApprovalHeldTrajectories\) trajectories held at once over a decision time \(\ExternalWait\), prices each wait. All rates and times below are scenario inputs.
Repair agent: Review requests arrive at 6 per hour and a decision takes 2 hours on average, so about 12 trajectories are held at once. Each keeps its workspace lease, 512 MiB in the reference coding-agent profile, so escrow retains 6 GiB of sandbox memory while no user waits on the outcome.
Remediation agent: Requests arrive at 2 per hour, so on average 0.5 trajectories are held and retained resources are negligible. The cost is time: with 6 minutes of diagnosis, a 15-minute mean decision, and 9 minutes to apply and verify, approval is 50 percent of the 30-minute time to mitigate, all of it spent with the service degraded.
Systems insight: One escrow mechanism binds on different terms. For the repair agent, retained memory scales with \(\ExternalWait\), so halving the decision time halves the held workspace. For the remediation agent, each minute removed from \(\ExternalWait\) removes a minute of degradation, and approval is the largest term in time to mitigate. Remediation therefore binds the approval digest to one exact configuration version so review is quick, sets the approval expiry shorter than the interval over which production configuration drifts, and lets already-admitted independent read-only diagnostic jobs continue under their existing grants and limits while the mutation waits.





The approval service returns an authenticated decision cryptographically tied to the held request identifier and version. Rather than blindly treating any inbound approval packet as an immediate trigger to resume execution, the harness validates the decision against the active escrow record and recalculates the approval digest. Duplicate webhooks or replayed messages are idempotent; the harness drops repeated deliveries without recording duplicate decisions or re-triggering dispatch. Similarly, a late decision arriving for a request that has already been withdrawn, expired, or superseded serves only as historical audit evidence; it can never revive a closed request.

Silence leaves the request unapproved. When the approval timeout lapses, the runtime logs an expiration event rather than an active human rejection. While both outcomes prevent dispatch, preserving this distinction is vital for downstream trajectory debugging and model observability. If the agent’s task policy permits continuation after a refusal, the harness delivers a compact observation record confirming that the operation was withheld:
{"approval_id": "review_r18",
 "status": "REFUSED", "reason": "APPROVAL_EXPIRED",
 "dispatch_status": "not_sent"}
The model can then interpret this refusal observation and propose an alternative strategy. What it cannot do is unilaterally extend the expired approval by submitting identical requests in a tight loop. Generating a fresh approval request requires constructing a current proposal that undergoes a new policy evaluation; otherwise, an automated agent could easily subject the human reviewer to an approval-fatigue denial-of-service attack. If the enclosing task has exhausted its wall-clock budget, the harness records the refusal directly in the final execution ledger without expending further tokens or compute to solicit a narrative explanation from the model.



A human approval satisfies governance policy, but it does not guarantee that the runtime environment remains ready for execution. Between the moment a reviewer signs off and the moment the worker prepares to dispatch, the target branch may have advanced, the task’s token or financial budget may have been exhausted, or short-lived credentials may have lapsed. Human approval is merely one precondition for admission, never an exemption from standard admission control.
At the dispatch boundary, the harness re-evaluates the entire operational state. It recomputes the approval digest to ensure the artifact has not been modified in place, checks that the approval lease has not expired, and executes the full suite of rate-limit, budget, and authorization checks. Because queueing delays and downstream rate limits can stall an approved request in escrow, checks validated when the approval message arrived cannot be grandfathered into execution. If any check fails, the harness logs the specific refusal reason; if a task-level termination triggers, the trajectory routes immediately to finalization.
Consider a submission that requires an unmodified target branch. Reading the branch HEAD prior to requesting approval cannot prevent concurrent commits during the minutes or hours the request sits in escrow. When operations carry concurrency preconditions, the dispatching endpoint must verify the expected target version atomically alongside the mutation, or use an external optimistic locking mechanism.


↩︎ The atomic conditional update, which verifies an expected version in the same step as the write, is established in Conditional updates.
Admitting a held request follows the register-before-send protocol with a critical atomic transition: under an exclusive lock, the harness registers the outgoing operation and marks the held escrow record as consumed. This prevents race conditions where duplicate approval callbacks or concurrent workers attempt double dispatch. Competing events, such as an approver’s sign-off racing against an operator cancellation or timeout, are strictly ordered by this admission lock. If a cancellation commits first, it cancels the held request and records an unambiguous not_sent status. Once admission commits, the operation becomes owned work; a later control may still withhold release through the serialized gate, retaining the record and reservation until non-release and absence of remote liability are established. If an unhandled transport failure occurs after the packet departs the host, the harness must treat the remote effect as indeterminate. While marking an approval consumed prevents duplicate local dispatch, it cannot guarantee endpoint deduplication or resolve an in-flight network partition.



Pausing an active trajectory follows the supervisory lifecycle in section 10.4 with an explicit escrow cleanup step. The harness immediately withdraws the pending approval request, marks the proposal as not dispatched in the audit ledger, and transitions through READY to PAUSED. If an approver submits a late decision while the task is paused or after it resumes, the harness rejects the decision because its associated request was already revoked. Should the agent still require the operation upon resuming, it must generate a fresh proposal subject to current state and policy checks.
Cancellation and task expiration route directly into FINALIZING. This terminal path requires all previously dispatched work and outstanding external resources to be settled or transferred to an accepting owner. Withdrawing a held review submission leaves no side effects on external targets, but it does not automatically terminate concurrent asynchronous test jobs, settle their compute costs, or undo previously committed mutations. By maintaining a strict separation between held proposals in escrow and committed entries in the operation ledger, the harness provides unambiguous operational visibility even when complex trajectories terminate abruptly.

Checkpoint 10.2: Approval over time
The internal-review submission for r18 is held while the task approaches its deadline.

Approval vs. capacity: A valid approval arrives while execution capacity is unavailable, and capacity frees only after the approval’s expiry. Decide the trajectory’s state at each event and what the model sees.
Withdrawn request: An operator pauses the trajectory before admission, then the approval arrives. Which record prevents the withdrawn request from running after resume?
Stale precondition: The target branch changes after a pre-dispatch read. Which endpoint condition preserves the approved operation’s precondition?
Lost reply: Dispatch may have occurred before its reply was lost. Why is dispatch_status: not_sent now unjustified, and which outstanding records must remain?
Held-trajectory estimate: Approval requests arrive at ten per hour and a decision takes thirty minutes on average. Estimate how many trajectories sit in AWAITING_APPROVAL, and how the count changes if reviewers answer twice as fast.



The approval gate now has a bounded lifetime and an explicit handoff from held proposal to admitted work. Human agreement is one condition in that handoff, alongside current authority, resource bounds, and action-time preconditions. Multiple trajectories can satisfy those conditions while competing for the same execution capacity, so the harness next needs a policy for sharing that capacity without bypassing their individual gates.




Consider an automated repair trajectory waiting for a targeted test suite to evaluate patch candidate r18. Concurrently, an interactive user session and a backlog of repository maintenance tasks are ready to query the model. When the test execution finishes, the repair trajectory rejoins that active competition. If the harness simply dispatches requests as soon as tasks generate them, aggressive retry loops will monopolize model capacity. If it unconditionally favors interactive requests, large maintenance jobs can wait indefinitely. Concurrency alone does not solve resource allocation; the harness requires an explicit scheduling policy to arbitrate among eligible calls.
The fundamental unit of scheduling admission is a READY trajectory’s next model call, rather than its entire multi-step task or the downstream tool execution that the reply may propose. Completing an asynchronous wait does not grant immediate dispatch; it makes a trajectory eligible only through a guarded transition into the READY state, where it queues for the scheduler’s approval. Downstream, the inference serving engine manages batching, KV-cache allocation, and accelerator execution. That low-level engine scheduling remains strictly decoupled from the harness’s control plane, which decides which high-level trajectory may submit work in the first place.


Granting an equal number of model calls across classes does not deliver equal service. A single maintenance prompt containing extensive code diffs can easily consume 40,000 tokens, whereas a concise interactive query requires only 2,000 tokens. A scheduler must therefore define precisely what resource its allocations apportion. A robust policy bills each admitted request a declared scheduling charge equal to its full input-token count plus its maximum allowed output-token reservation. This conservative metric measures admitted token commitments rather than actual generated output, monetary cost, accelerator occupancy, or task utility. Cached prompt tokens remain part of this upfront charge because serving-engine cache hits cannot be guaranteed before dispatch. While a scheduler could alternatively account for post-execution measured service, doing so requires speculative token estimation upon admission followed by retroactive reconciliation once the model finishes generating.
Weighted deficit round-robin provides an effective, low-overhead mechanism for apportioning this declared token charge across diverse service classes. For each class, the scheduler keeps a credit counter and a queue of the class’s READY trajectories, served in rotation from a pointer that persists between rounds. At the beginning of each scheduling round, the system increments each class’s credit counter by a quantum proportional to its assigned weight. The scheduler then steps through the classes, admitting calls as long as their token charges fit within the available credit and all downstream capacity gates pass. Each admission deducts the call’s charge from the class balance. Unspent credit carries over into subsequent rounds, allowing a class with large requests to gradually accumulate enough deficit credit to admit a multi-thousand-token prompt. When a class exhausts its active work, the scheduler resets its credit counter to zero so it cannot hoard unearned allocations during idle periods. This design adapts the deficit carryover mechanism6 of deficit round-robin (Shreedhar and Varghese 1995) from network packet scheduling to language model admission control.
6 From Fair Queueing to Deficit Round-Robin: Fair queueing for packet networks (Demers et al. 1989) emulated a bit-by-bit round-robin across flows, ensuring that high-volume sources could not exceed their fair shares, but it required ordering packets by computed finish times. Deficit round-robin reached comparable fairness with constant work per packet by giving each queue a quantum and carrying unspent credit forward (Shreedhar and Varghese 1995). Because model-call charges span orders of magnitude, deficit carryover, rather than simple queue rotation, is what enforces proportional fairness here. 
Demers, Alan, Srinivasan Keshav, and Scott Shenker. 1989. “Analysis and Simulation of a Fair Queueing Algorithm.” Proceedings of the Symposium on Communications Architectures and Protocols (SIGCOMM ’89), 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1145/75246.75248.

Shreedhar, M., and George Varghese. 1995. “Efficient Fair Queuing Using Deficit Round Robin.” Proceedings of the Conference on Applications, Technologies, Architectures, and Protocols for Computer Communication (SIGCOMM ’95), 231–42. https://doi.org/10.1145/217382.217453.
Credit belongs to the service class rather than to individual trajectories, so a tenant cannot monopolize the cluster by spawning hundreds of concurrent tasks; the class’s aggregate resource share remains invariant. Rotation among trajectories within a class is equally critical. If the scheduler restarted its scan at the head of the trajectory queue on every pass, trajectories near the front would continuously consume fresh credit while starving trajectories near the tail. Practical implementations enforce three core invariants: assign a strictly positive weight to every class expected to make progress, preserve intra-class rotation positions across passes, and enforce an upper bound on request sizes. Any ceiling placed on accumulated credit must also accommodate the largest single request the policy permits. Capping credit below that maximum prevents large maintenance calls from ever running, leaving them stalled indefinitely despite repeated replenishment rounds.
Configuring class weights fixes how the declared token charge is shared, but that split does not equal the proportion of admitted calls. A concrete scenario demonstrates this divergence.

Napkin Math 10.1: Charge shares vs. call sharesProblem: An interactive class has weight 3 and a maintenance class has weight 1, with a base quantum of 8,000 charge tokens per unit weight per round. An interactive call carries 2,000 input tokens and a 500-token output allowance; a maintenance call carries 40,000 input tokens and a 2,000-token output allowance. Assume both classes remain continuously backlogged at these fixed call sizes, no provider or local-capacity gate binds, and carried credit can cover the largest permitted call. Over many rounds, how many calls does each class admit?
Math: Each round credits 24,000 tokens to the interactive class and 8,000 tokens to maintenance. Because interactive calls incur a scheduling charge of 2,500 tokens each, the interactive class averages 24,000 / 2,500 = 9.6 calls per round. A maintenance call incurs a charge of 42,000 tokens, so its class must carry forward credit for 42,000 / 8,000 = 5.25 rounds per call.
Result: The interactive class receives 75 percent of the total token charge capacity, but it dispatches roughly 50 times as many admitted calls as the maintenance class.
Systems insight: Class weights determine the long-term division of token charges, while admitted call rates depend directly on request size. The maintenance class’s mean interval between admissions, measured in credit rounds, equals its request charge divided by its per-round quantum under the stated assumptions. Halving its input to 20,000 tokens reduces this aggregate interval to approximately 2.8 rounds per admission without changing class weights. An individual trajectory also waits behind its class peers; execution, tool waits, and approval time lie outside this quotient. Increasing a class weight shifts its aggregate token share; shrinking prompt sizes (through prompt compaction or targeted context retrieval) accelerates its call dispatch rate. Finally, the scheduler’s credit ceiling must accommodate at least one complete maintenance charge, or that class will never accumulate sufficient deficit credit to dispatch.





Weights split the token charge; request size then sets a far larger split in calls.
While deficit round-robin guarantees proportional fairness across active service classes, it does not manufacture capacity. When an agent deployment faces sustained overload, scheduling weights merely redistribute queueing delay; they do not increase provider throughput. Managing latency under persistent saturation requires upstream admission limits on incoming tasks or explicit rejection policies, because prioritization can only reallocate existing capacity.



A model call selected by the fairness scheduler cannot dispatch immediately; it must also satisfy the provider’s multidimensional quota contracts. Model providers enforce rate limits across distinct dimensions: requests per minute (RPM), tokens per minute (TPM), and concurrent in-flight requests. The provider’s accounting contract determines exactly what must be reserved prior to transmission. For token limits, providers typically debit the full input count plus the declared maximum output allowance against the current time window until generation finishes. Pricing discounts do not relax rate limits: a provider that discounts cached prompt tokens on the billing invoice may still charge those tokens at full weight against the tenant’s rolling TPM window. Satisfying a token quota likewise guarantees nothing about request concurrency, which is capped independently to protect serving infrastructure from connection pool exhaustion.
Deploying a local rate limiter allows the harness to buffer pending calls gracefully rather than discovering provider saturation through HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) rejections. The rate limiter must account for all traffic sharing the target provider allocation, including concurrent harness processes operating across separate machines. Token bucket algorithms, which permit short bursts up to a bounded depth and replenish at a sustained rate, operate effectively only when their refill parameters and burst ceilings closely match the provider’s enforcement windows. When external traffic shares the account or the exact windowing algorithm is opaque, the harness must maintain conservative safety headroom and dynamically adjust its refill rates using feedback from response headers, such as reported remaining quota and suggested retry intervals.
Beyond external provider quotas, local execution resources impose secondary admission gates. An agent tool call (compiling code, running an integration test, or analyzing a repository) demands a combination of sandbox slots, CPU cores, system memory, and storage bandwidth, even when model token quotas are abundant. Schedulers must track each bottleneck using the explicit physical dimensions of that resource. Bytes of durable disk storage represent a static space constraint; bytes per second of disk transfer represent dynamic channel bandwidth; and storage I/O operations per second (IOPS) bound transactional throughput. While tracking homogeneous sandbox slots suffices when every worker operates within an identical virtual machine envelope, raw slot counts fail to prevent out-of-memory crashes when heterogeneous jobs run side by side.
Workspace lifecycles follow the workspace lease contracts. A repair trajectory, for example, may retain cloned repository files and compiled binaries in a persistent workspace across multiple conversational turns, even as it releases its active CPU and container execution slots between test runs. These retained files occupy storage capacity and lease quotas until explicitly reclaimed. To safeguard interactive user responsiveness, clusters frequently partition execution capacity, reserving dedicated slots for interactive agents to prevent batch maintenance workloads from monopolizing the pool. However, static capacity reservations trade off isolation against efficiency: reserved slots sit idle when interactive demand drops, and reservations protect only against execution slot starvation; they cannot eliminate contention on shared backend disks or preempt long-running tests already executing.
Tool execution requires its own independent admission pipeline. When a model proposes a protected action that requires a human or policy decision, the action cannot immediately execute. If a suitable sandbox execution slot is unavailable when permission is granted, the action remains in AWAITING_APPROVAL alongside its recorded approval decision (table 8) instead of cycling back to READY to issue another redundant model call. Decoupling tool execution into a dedicated dispatch queue allows the harness to apply fair-sharing policies tailored to computational and physical resource units rather than model token counts.



In a distributed harness, queue selection is merely an optimistic nomination, not an irrevocable execution grant. In the interval between a scheduler picking a candidate from the ready queue and committing the dispatch, external state can change: an operator might pause the repair trajectory, an authorization grant might expire, or a parallel thread might deplete the tenant’s remaining financial budget. The selected candidate must therefore clear an atomic admission check that verifies provider quotas, local capacity reservations, and trajectory state. Under the register-before-send rule, every quota and capacity reservation is recorded in the trajectory record before the request leaves the host. An optimistic concurrency check against the trajectory’s record_version guarantees that if two scheduler workers select the same candidate simultaneously, exactly one worker commits the admission and consumes the trajectory’s allowance.
Temporarily blocked admission, whether caused by insufficient deficit credit, exhausted provider rate limits, or saturated sandbox slots, leaves the candidate paused in the READY state. Queuing delay reflects backpressure, not task failure. Once a call is dispatched, network and server failures require outcome-aware reservation settlement. Only authoritative evidence of non-release and no remote liability permits the harness to release the corresponding reservations; provider-quota refunds also follow the provider’s accounting contract. However, under the settlement rule, an ambiguous network outcome, such as an HTTP timeout occurring after request transmission, must keep its reservation outstanding. The remote provider may have received, processed, and billed the request despite the client-side timeout; clearing reservations prematurely risks double-spending budgets and violating provider quotas.
These three control layers operate in concert. Fair-sharing policies determine which eligible trajectory deserves service next. Provider quotas and capacity gates determine whether that work can execute immediately without overwhelming shared infrastructure. Neither mechanism, however, restricts the total cumulative volume of work an agent can request across dozens of turns. An automated repair agent can receive its fair share of tokens in perpetuity without ever converging on a valid patch. Enforcing overall resource discipline requires global trajectory budgets and iteration limits, which supply the final boundary on agentic execution.




Consider an agent attempting a software repair: its accumulated bill already approaches the allocated task budget, while an asynchronous test suite dispatched minutes earlier has yet to report its cloud execution charges. Proposing another model invocation introduces new, uncommitted liability. A fair scheduler determines when that candidate call should receive accelerator service, but scheduling alone cannot determine whether the trajectory has sufficient funds remaining to afford it. To prevent runaway spending, the harness must enforce an admission control rule that accounts for both inflight work and worst-case execution liabilities before dispatching another request.


The necessity of a global lifetime bound becomes obvious when examining a runaway retry loop. Suppose an agent generates a candidate code patch that fails its regression test. The model responds by proposing a slight variant, then another permutation, and eventually a broader diagnostic routine that also fails. Each failure appends an error trace to the conversational context. Every individual tool call remains syntactically well formed and stays strictly within per-invocation token and compute limits. The trajectory yields cleanly at every tool boundary, receives its scheduled turn on the inference server, and satisfies every local admission check. Dozens of turns later, the agent has burned through substantial cloud and inference budgets while making zero measurable progress toward resolving the defect. Figure 4 diagrams this degenerate cycle: failing tests append repeated error observations to the context until turn-completion proposals vanish, showing how an external harness budget halts the runaway retry loop at the admission boundary and forces the trajectory into FINALIZING once liability exceeds the available allowance.
Terminating a degenerate loop is fundamentally an architectural responsibility of the harness. As failure outputs accumulate in the prompt context, they dilute the original system instructions and task specifications. Under severe context dilution, model generations that terminate the trajectory become increasingly rare. Prompt-level guardrails, such as injecting notices about remaining funds or requesting that the model self-regulate under a cost ceiling, offer purely probabilistic nudges rather than deterministic bounds. Worse, their efficacy degrades rapidly as the attention window fills with repetitive stack traces. Because an errant model remains syntactically coherent and locally compliant while failing globally, trajectory bounds must reside within the external supervisory control plane (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\)). Deciding whether an agent has stalled requires complex semantic heuristics, but an external budget deterministically stops further ordinary admission when the allowance is exhausted.

Figure 4: A Runaway Loop and the Budget That Ends It: A failing targeted test appends error observations to the context, completion requests become rare, and each retry is well formed and within per-call limits, so the loop continues without progress. The harness budget, kept outside the context, applies the reservation test at every admission. When a call does not fit or the deadline has passed, admission is refused and the trajectory enters FINALIZING, which settles or transfers its outstanding work.



To constrain total resource consumption, the harness establishes a multi-dimensional per-trajectory budget, the vector
\[\TrajectoryBudget = \langle \TrajectoryTurnLimit,\ \TrajectoryTokenLimit,\ \TrajectoryTimeLimit,\ \CostCeiling \rangle\]
where the components establish formal allowances on execution turns (\(\TrajectoryTurnLimit\)), cumulative tokens (\(\TrajectoryTokenLimit\)), elapsed wall-clock time (\(\TrajectoryTimeLimit\)), and total financial cost (\(\CostCeiling\)). The harness configuration must unambiguously define what increments each meter: admitted model invocations increment the turn counter, effective input prompt tokens plus generated output tokens increment the token counter, and direct API charges, sandboxed execution fees, and paid third-party tool usage increment the dollar ledger. Retried operations, network reconnects, and failed invocations consume real resources and must be billed against these totals. Production harnesses frequently extend this vector with additional domain-specific limits, such as sandbox disk allocations or maximum external API query counts.
Each dimension governs a distinct operational constraint. A trajectory with very few turns can rapidly exhaust financial limits through large-context reasoning models, while an inexpensive agent can tie up execution sandboxes across long asynchronous polling delays. Unlike consumable token or dollar allowances, elapsed time represents a monotonically advancing wall-clock deadline measured from task initiation. Network delays, sandboxed compilation phases, human approval holds, and backoff pauses all advance this deadline unless the task contract explicitly provides a paused clock. When the primary execution deadline expires, the harness halts the admission of new exploratory work while supervising inflight background operations. Post-execution finalization requires its own separately allocated time allowance and reserved funding; an expired exploration deadline must never trigger an unconstrained cleanup phase that runs indefinitely.
The harness may safely expose current budget metrics to the model, enabling the agent to adjust its planning strategy toward cheaper alternatives. However, the model must never possess the authority to modify accounting records, release reservations, or exempt its own calls from admission gates. This separation allows cooperative optimization while guaranteeing that system bounds remain strictly invariant to model behavior.



A budget serves as an absolute ceiling only when the admission gate accounts for unbilled in-flight operations before authorizing new liabilities.7 The amount set aside for an admitted operation is its reservation; the chapter keeps the word escrow for held proposals awaiting approval, which hold an action rather than an amount. Test-time search already reserved each candidate’s maximum completion before dispatch and kept unsettled reservations against its quota; the harness extends that discipline from one search to every operation of the trajectory, including tool jobs and the finalization reserve.
7 Reservation Against an Invariant: Database systems solved a version of this problem for shared quantities such as account balances and inventory counts. Bounded-liability admission applies the same test to a trajectory’s allowance, with the operation’s maximum possible charge standing in for an exact decrement.

Definition 10.4: Bounded-liability admission
Bounded-liability admission is the harness rule that admits a new operation only when, in every cumulative budget dimension, actual consumption plus outstanding reservations plus the operation’s maximum additional charge plus the protected finalization reserve fits within the allowance.

Significance: It transforms an informational budget ledger into an enforceable upper bound on per-attempt expenditure (the numerator of cost per accepted task, equation 1.2) while guaranteeing that essential post-task verification checks remain fully funded.
Distinction: Whereas a simple spend check merely compares settled invoices against the allowance, bounded-liability admission reserves capacity for inflight requests and charges the worst-case ceiling of the pending operation.
Common pitfall: Prematurely releasing a reservation upon a network timeout or client-side cancellation before upstream providers settle actual usage. This error exposes uncommitted budget that concurrent operations can claim before delayed billing charges arrive.



For each cumulative resource dimension, the admission test is
\[\text{actual consumption} + \text{outstanding reservations} + \text{proposed bounded liability} + \text{protected finalization reserve} \leq \text{allowance} \tag{1}\]
The harness evaluates this inequality componentwise across all cumulative resource dimensions, while evaluating wall-clock deadlines through a separate timing guard. The term for outstanding reservations encompasses all admitted but unsettled operations, including concurrent inference requests and active paid tools. The protected finalization reserve isolates dedicated funding for validation runs, report generation, and environment teardown, preventing exploratory steps from exhausting the funds needed to verify final results. When the trajectory transitions into finalization, the harness reallocates the necessary portion of this protected reserve into active operation reservations, avoiding duplicate accounting.
Because this inequality forms the core budget clause of the admission check, the harness must execute it under strict concurrency control following the register-before-send rule. This ordering prevents two concurrent subtasks from reading the same uncommitted headroom and double-spending it. If network dispatch fails, the harness releases the reservation only after establishing that the remote service incurred no billable liability. Any ambiguous dispatch outcome must remain reserved until upstream settlement resolves the transaction.
With the budget clause in place, every piece of the harness has been introduced, and listing 3 assembles them into one turn: the guarded transition of listing 1, the reservation that admission makes, the status routing of table 4, the approval hold, and register-before-send for tool calls. The reservation is made inside the guarded transition into CALLING_MODEL, so an unaffordable call is refused before any request leaves the host. Usage settles the reservation after the reply, and the reply’s status decides the next state before any content can become a tool call. Admission never depends on a charge discovered after the call.



Listing 3: One Admitted Turn: The harness reserves the call’s bounded liability inside the guarded transition, settles from reported usage, routes every non-completed status away from dispatch, and reserves and registers tool calls before sending them.


def run_turn(rec):
    call = new_invocation(rec)
    liability = bound_call(rec.limits)        # full input + output allowance
    transition(rec, "CALLING_MODEL", Decision(call.id, rec.record_version),
               admit=lambda r: reserve(r, call, liability))  # admission test
    reply = invoke_model(rec.context(), rec.limits, call.id)  # lock released
    settle(rec, call, reply.usage)            # missing usage stays reserved
    nxt = Decision(call.id, rec.record_version)
    if reply.status != "COMPLETED":           # truncated, canceled, refused, ...
        return transition(rec, route_status(rec, reply), nxt)  # never dispatched
    proposal = validate(rec, reply)           # schema, epoch, authority
    if proposal.kind == "complete":
        return transition(rec, "FINALIZING", nxt)   # completion check follows
    if proposal.kind == "none":
        return transition(rec, "READY", nxt)
    if needs_approval(rec, proposal):
        return transition(rec, "AWAITING_APPROVAL", nxt,
                          admit=lambda r: hold(r, proposal))
    transition(rec, "WAITING_TOOL", nxt,
               admit=lambda r: reserve_and_register(r, proposal.calls))
    dispatch(proposal.calls)                  # serialized release gate; already reserved



The reserve step evaluates equation 1 and aborts the state transition whenever the proposed invocation exceeds available headroom; route_status maps terminal inference conditions according to table 4. For clarity, the listing abstracts batched invocation checks and multi-step approval lifecycles. Its invoke_model and dispatch helpers also include the serialized release gate: they recheck the admitted operation against current controls before release, retain ownership and liability if release is withheld, and exit through guarded refusal or control handling without returning a fabricated remote reply. These helpers perform no second reservation and keep slow network I/O outside the record lock. This listing describes live-host supervision; crash reconstruction requires the durable evidence developed in Durable Execution.
A control action can also commit while run_turn is blocked in invoke_model, because that call runs outside the lock. The control path then performs the pause entry itself: it withdraws the call’s eligibility, cancels the stream if policy says so, and steps the record through READY to PAUSED. When invoke_model returns, settle still records the call’s usage, but the next transition starts from PAUSED. Every edge it could request from there fails: the edges to WAITING_TOOL and AWAITING_APPROVAL are not legal from PAUSED, and the guards on the legal ones, to READY and FINALIZING, admit only the control path’s own resume or stop decisions. The transition raises IllegalTransition, and the reply is kept only as diagnostic evidence, as a CANCELED reply would be.
For a model call, the proposed bounded liability prices every input token at the undiscounted input rate \(\InputTokenPrice\), cached or not, and the full output allowance \(\OutputLimit\) at the output rate \(\OutputTokenPrice\):
\[\text{liability} = \InputTokenPrice\, \SequenceLength + \OutputTokenPrice\, \OutputLimit \tag{2}\]
Here \(\SequenceLength\) counts the whole prompt, unlike the uncached-only count of the settled ledger in section 10.9.3. Pricing the prompt at full rate keeps the bound valid when an expected cache hit fails to materialize, and charging the whole allowance keeps it valid when the model generates up to its cap; settlement later replaces both worst cases with reported usage.
Even when the unreserved balance remains strictly positive, it may prove insufficient to cover the maximum liability of the next operation. A naive spend check admits such a call on the basis of past settled invoices, only to exceed the budget ceiling once the provider bills the resulting tokens. While shrinking the requested maximum output tokens can lower the call’s worst-case liability, this optimization succeeds only if prompt tokens and outstanding tool charges still fit within the margin. External paid tools that lack enforceable execution timeouts or bounded billing tiers cannot provide a finite liability ceiling either. Under a strict enforcement policy, the harness must either reject such open-ended tools outright, substitute bounded proxies, or explicitly declare an approximate threshold that tolerates financial overshoot. Enforcing a client-side network timeout does not provide an immutable cost ceiling because the remote provider may continue billing until its own worker processes finish.

Napkin Math 10.2: A call the spend check admitsProblem: A repair trajectory has a $3.50 allowance, $2.58 of settled spend, a $0.50 reservation on its unsettled test job, and a $0.30 finalization reserve. The next model call carries 50,000 input tokens and a 4,096-token output allowance, reserved at hypothetical prices of $3 and $15 per million input and output tokens. Should the harness admit it?
Math: The call’s bounded liability is $0.15 of input plus $0.06 of output, $0.21 in all. A spend check sees $3.50 − $2.58 = $0.92 of headroom. Equation 1 subtracts the reservation and the finalization reserve as well, leaving $0.12.
Result: The spend check admits the call; bounded-liability admission refuses it. Admitted, the call would leave the final checks $0.09 short once the test settles in full.
Systems insight: Input is 70.9 percent of this call’s liability, so trimming the output allowance barely helps. The call fits only if its input falls to about 19,500 tokens, through compaction, or if the test job settles and releases part of its reservation. Every $0.10 of unsettled liability removes about 33,300 input tokens from what the next call may carry, which is why settling promptly from usage evidence is worth more than a smaller output cap.





The spend check sees room for the call; after reservations, it no longer fits.
Settlement replaces an estimated reservation with verified consumption once the harness receives an authenticated, cryptographically signed, or correlated usage report from the service provider. An incremental usage report allows the harness to shift confirmed charges into the settled meter while keeping the remaining liability reserved. Only terminal billing evidence authorizes releasing the residual reservation. This principle applies equally to remote side effects and financial charges: a dropped network stream, missing telemetry, or client-side timeout provides no guarantee that the remote provider discarded the work without billing.
Prompt caching discounts demand identical accounting rigor. Before dispatching a request, the admission controller must reserve funds at the standard undiscounted input rate unless the service-level agreement contractually guarantees cache hits for specific prompt prefixes. Once the provider reports verified execution data, the harness settles the transaction according to the actual cached and uncached token counts. Similarly, while terminating an inflight model stream early can limit output charges, the admission gate cannot gamble on speculative cancellations when authorizing subsequent tasks. Enforcing an unyielding ceiling requires adherence to classic systems design: complete mediation across all requests (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975), conservative worst-case reservation bounds, and authoritative settlement driven solely by verified execution records.



Modern inference providers structure billing tiers by partitioning token usage into distinct categories: uncached input tokens (\(\UncachedInputTokenCount\)), cached prompt tokens (\(\CachedInputTokenCount\)), and generated output tokens (\(\OutputLength\)). For any completed turn \(\TurnIndex\), the harness updates the accumulated financial ledger according to:
\[\SettledTrajectoryCost^{(\TurnIndex)} = \SettledTrajectoryCost^{(\TurnIndex-1)} + \InputTokenPrice\, \UncachedInputTokenCount^{(\TurnIndex)} + \CachedInputTokenPrice\, \CachedInputTokenCount^{(\TurnIndex)} + \OutputTokenPrice\, \OutputLength^{(\TurnIndex)} + \sum_{j} \ToolCallCost(\ExecutedToolCall_{t,j})\]
where input token categories are mutually disjoint, unit pricing matches token dimensions, and each tool execution charge \(\ToolCallCost\) posts exactly once to the ledger. This settled accounting equation defines how in-flight reservations convert into finalized balance decrements. The dominant cost driver varies substantially across workloads and provider contracts; a large input prompt volume does not necessarily imply that prompt processing dominates the aggregate bill.
The accompanying analysis examines this dynamic by modeling the append-only context workload introduced in notebook \(\ref{nbk-02-price-of-a-trajectory}\). Whereas that earlier scenario measured raw compute throughput, this one applies a tiered billing contract to the same token distributions. The scenario assumes that the inference engine successfully reuses KV cache states for the static system prompt and prior turns, while billing all newly appended turn observations and tool outputs as uncached input. In practice, achieving these cache discounts requires runtime support: compatible server-side KV cache state must remain resident in accelerator memory, as append-only conversational text alone does not guarantee a cache hit across distributed inference workers.

Napkin Math 10.3: Metering a trajectory against its budgetProblem: The coding workload has completed 30 turns under hypothetical allowances of 40 turns, 2 million effective input-plus-output tokens, 900 s elapsed, and $3.50. The clock reads 460 s. Assume all usage is settled, no paid-tool charges, and prices of $3 per million uncached input tokens, $0.30 per million cached input tokens, and $15 per million output tokens. Which allowance has the largest current used fraction in the reuse and no-reuse cases?
Math: With a base prompt of 8,000 tokens, 1,500 tokens appended per turn, and 200 output tokens per turn, equation 2.9 gives 892,500 input tokens over the trajectory, 898,500 with output. Under prefix reuse, every turn’s earlier prefix is billed as cached input, 841,000 tokens, so the model charge is $0.50. Billed entirely as uncached input, the same tokens cost $2.77.
Result: With reuse, the trajectory has used 75 percent of its turns, 44.9 percent of its tokens, 51.1 percent of its time, and 14.2 percent of its dollars, so turns lead. Without reuse, dollars lead at 79.1 percent.
Systems insight: The leading dimension changes when caching fails. The token meter counts cached input in full and cannot see the change; the dollar meter rises 5.5 times for the same tokens. A harness that sizes \(\CostCeiling\) from the cached bill will therefore meet its dollar ceiling first on exactly the trajectories that miss the cache. Reserve at the undiscounted rate and size the dollar allowance from the no-reuse cost; prefix reuse then lowers the cost per attempt, the numerator of cost per accepted task, by that same ratio instead of silently raising the risk of a budget stop.





A well-designed harness introduces progressive interventions before the admission gate forcibly shuts down exploratory execution. A primary health indicator is the maximum consumed fraction across all active budget dimensions: \(\max(\TurnBudgetUsedFraction, \TokenBudgetUsedFraction, \TimeBudgetUsedFraction, \CostBudgetUsedFraction)\). Factoring unbilled reservations into these fractions provides a far more accurate early warning signal than inspecting settled invoices alone, while the wall-clock timer yields the temporal fraction \(\TimeBudgetUsedFraction\). This multi-dimensional indicator steers adaptive interventions, even as the underlying gate continues to evaluate bounded liabilities independently across each axis.
Table 9 delineates the progressive escalation stages that precede hard enforcement. A deployment policy triggers each stage from the admission terms themselves rather than from a fixed percentage of the allowance, because a fixed percentage ignores how large the next step is. Steering begins when the remaining headroom can fund only a few more calls at their current bounded liability, and finalization begins when the next call’s liability no longer fits beside the finalization reserve.

Context compaction represents one practical mitigation when sufficient budget remains to execute it without destroying critical state. However, invoking a summarization model consumes additional tokens and discards detail. Similarly, downgrading an agent’s permissions to read-only tools prevents irreversible state mutations, but read operations can still incur significant financial costs and leak sensitive context arguments to external retrieval APIs. Revoking delegation privileges stops the spawning of child agents, while leaving existing background subtasks active and their reserved liabilities intact. Dynamically mutating the tool schema presented in the prompt also invalidates previously cached prompt prefixes from the modification point onward, inadvertently trading inference caching efficiency for reduced tool exposure.

When a trajectory enters the finalization stage due to budget exhaustion, the system must not compromise its validation standards. If an expensive regression test remains inflight, its reservation must remain held until final usage telemetry settles the charge. The final diagnostic report must accurately report candidate r18 and record which validation suites completed successfully, rather than treating an early unit test pass as substitute verification for incomplete end-to-end checks.



Enforcing an immutable ceiling guarantees system safety, but setting appropriate numerical thresholds requires empirical validation across representative task distributions. Systems engineers evaluate candidate budget vectors by testing the end-to-end control policy across a workload sample while holding models, tool suites, and acceptance tests constant. The acceptance fraction, accepted tasks divided by all attempted tasks, counts both outright failures and trajectories halted by budget exhaustion. System evaluations must report total dollar expenditure, wall-clock latency, unresolved background liabilities, and operator intervention frequency alongside raw task completion. Dividing the total cost of all attempts by the accepted count gives the cost per accepted task (equation 1.2), which amortizes the expenses of failed and abandoned runs across successful completions. Budget limits appear artificially inexpensive whenever benchmark evaluations omit the costs of failed trajectories from total expenditure. As Kapoor et al. (2024) argue, evaluating agent accuracy in isolation from cost produces needlessly fragile and expensive architectures; engineering robust systems requires joint optimization across both dimensions.
Baseline profiling under unconstrained budgets reveals the empirical completion time and token distributions of successful trajectories, highlighting candidate threshold targets. However, because early steering, throttling, and finalization alter downstream model reasoning, engineers must evaluate the complete policy empirically rather than assuming post-hoc truncation models reality. In practice, empirical cost-benefit curves rarely display a sharp knee. The operational decision rule selects the budget ceiling that minimizes cost per accepted task while keeping unresolved liabilities and manual interventions within acceptable operational bounds. When performance differences fall within empirical measurement uncertainty, simpler budget policies take precedence.
