Key Takeaways: Control lives outside the model

Instructions cannot substitute for architectural controls: A freeze directive honored on 99 percent of individual turns survives across a 30-turn trajectory only 74 percent of the time. In contrast, an invariant enforced at the dispatch boundary holds across every turn because the harness inspects the concrete operation rather than relying on model compliance.
Control signals must decouple from generation completion: Checking for pause or cancellation signals only after a generation finishes can delay a pause by approximately 86.3 s for a 4,096-token allowance, even under zero queueing. Turn boundaries combined with streaming cancellation decouple supervisory latency from generation length.
Halting execution does not settle in-flight obligations: A pause, timeout, or cancellation revokes an operation’s permission to advance the trajectory into the next turn, but it neither terminates external execution nor refunds committed spend. Only correlated, authenticated evidence from the remote provider can formally settle the liability; until that evidence arrives, the harness must preserve explicit ownership and state tracking for the outstanding task.
Asynchronous waits release execution threads, not system resources: Moving a trajectory into an asynchronous wait or human approval queue releases the active worker thread, but the trajectory retains proposal and evidence references, unresolved reservations, and its advancing deadline. Workspace and KV-cache residency continue only under their respective lease and cache policies. By Little’s law (\(\ApprovalHeldTrajectories = \ArrivalRate\,\ExternalWait\)), human review latency multiplies directly into the volume of concurrently suspended trajectories and their retained resource footprints.
Fairness, quota allocation, and budget affordability operate as independent gates: Scheduling weights allocate relative shares of provider capacity, meaning that request payload sizes rather than weights alone determine invocation frequency under deficit round-robin. Provider rate limits protect shared infrastructure against burst exhaustion, whereas task-level budget ceilings bound total lifetime consumption for an individual agent run.
Budget ceilings require upfront reservation of in-flight liabilities: A naive retrospective spend check reports $0.92 of available headroom, whereas bounded-liability admission, which counts unsettled in-flight tool executions and the finalization reserve, reveals only $0.12. Reserving conservative worst-case liabilities prior to dispatch is the only mechanism that converts an informational budget tracker into an enforceable upper bound.
Size budget ceilings by cost per accepted task: A restrictive budget ceiling appears deceptively economical if failed and exhausted runs are omitted from post hoc accounting. Sizing budget ceilings by effective cost per accepted task (\(\CostPerAcceptedTask = \mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability\)), which amortizes failed attempts over accepted outcomes, and treating differences within measurement error as ties, aligns harness admission thresholds with production economics.



Trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\)) establishes the runtime-owned record as the authoritative foundation for supervision. By storing immutable references to external state rather than attempting to duplicate it, the harness decouples admission control and execution governance from model cooperation. Both responsibilities function within explicit resource and evidence boundaries, ensuring that every transition (a normal dispatch, a staged escalation, or an ungraceful abort) preserves an unambiguous owner for every effect still in flight.

title: 10 The Agent Harness
text:
An agent harness synthesizes classical ideas that operating systems, databases, and computer networks developed when shared infrastructure encountered clients that could not be trusted to self-regulate or terminate. In operating systems, Hoare introduced monitors to provide shared mutable state with a single serialized entry point (Hoare 1974). In reactive systems, Harel formalized statecharts with guarded transitions so that valid controller behavior could be rigorously defined and checked (Harel 1987). Concurrently, Saltzer and Schroeder articulated the foundational design principles of computer protection (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975), establishing the requirement of complete mediation: every access must pass through an authoritative check that the client cannot bypass. The trajectory record, its serialization lock, and its guarded transition table apply these three concepts directly to the execution of an autonomous agent run.

Kung, H. T., and John T. Robinson. 1981. “On Optimistic Methods for Concurrency Control.” ACM Transactions on Database Systems 6 (2): 213–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/319566.319567.

Gray, Cary G., and David R. Cheriton. 1989. “Leases: An Efficient Fault-Tolerant Mechanism for Distributed File Cache Consistency.” Proceedings of the Twelfth ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP), 202–10. https://doi.org/10.1145/74850.74870.
Concurrency control and resource accounting soon followed. Optimistic concurrency control (Kung and Robinson 1981) demonstrated that systems can validate updates against previously read versions rather than holding exclusive locks across slow, unpredictable external operations. The harness’s record_version check adopts this exact pattern, allowing an agent to plan or invoke external tools without blocking concurrent readers. O’Neil’s escrow method (O’Neil 1986) partitioned shared quantities by pre-allocating portions against an aggregate invariant that survives concurrent execution; its escrow is a reserved amount, the sense this chapter calls a reservation. It is the direct intellectual ancestor of bounded-liability admission, which admits an agent step only if the worst-case financial or token liability remains safe. Similarly, Gray and Cheriton introduced leases (Gray and Cheriton 1989) to ensure that distributed locks and allocated resources expire automatically if a client crashes or stalls, preventing abandoned runs from holding shared resources indefinitely.
Networking and distributed systems contributed robust mechanisms for queue management and fairness under contention. Demers, Keshav, and Shenker developed fair queueing (Demers et al. 1989), and Shreedhar and Varghese later introduced deficit round-robin (Shreedhar and Varghese 1995) to allocate link capacity equitably across flows of unequal packet size without expensive per-packet accounting. In an agent platform, where requests vary wildly in token counts and latency, carried deficit credits prevent heavy agent runs from starving interactive workloads. Little’s law (Little 1961) relates the mean number of items waiting to their arrival rate and mean residence time, the relation needed to size these waiting queues. When agent steps involve slow tool execution or external inspection, staged event-driven architectures (Welsh et al. 2001) showed how to keep long waits from pinning execution threads by making queues explicit and enforcing localized admission controls at each processing stage.

Little, John D. C. 1961. “A Proof for the Queuing Formula: \(L = \lambda W\).” Operations Research 9 (3): 383–87. https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383.

Parasuraman, Raja, Thomas B. Sheridan, and Christopher D. Wickens. 2000. “A Model for Types and Levels of Human Interaction with Automation.” IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics - Part A: Systems and Humans 30 (3): 286–97. https://doi.org/10.1109/3468.844354.
System safety also relies on decades of human-factors research into supervisory control. Bainbridge’s classic analysis of the ironies of automation (Bainbridge 1983) showed that humans perform poorly when tasked with passively monitoring highly reliable automated systems, precisely because human vigilance deteriorates when intervention is rarely needed. Parasuraman, Sheridan, and Wickens (Parasuraman et al. 2000) subsequently classified automation into explicit operational levels based on the degree to which an autonomous system decides and acts without human intervention. These insights explain why agent approval gates cannot rely on casual human oversight, but instead require explicit, structured pauses that supply unambiguous context before an action proceeds.
Modern language-model agents encountered all of these classical systems challenges simultaneously. Yao et al. (2023) framed agent execution as an interleaved loop of chain-of-thought reasoning and external tool actions with ReAct. Yang et al. (2024) brought this pattern into real software repositories with SWE-agent, demonstrating that purpose-built agent-computer interfaces could resolve real bugs, while also showing that execution cost, waiting latencies, and tool interruptions were no longer edge cases. The hazard of relying on prompt instructions alone became apparent when an autonomous agent deleted a production database during an instructed code freeze (Sharwood 2025), illustrating that a safety invariant stated only in natural language is not enforced. In parallel, systematic benchmarks that measure accuracy without tracking cost (Kapoor et al. 2024) obscure critical engineering trade-offs, which is why resource ceilings should be derived from measured cost distributions rather than optimistic assumptions. The harness developed in this chapter is the systems response to these operational pressures, enforcing classical guarantees directly at the agent trajectory.

Yao, Shunyu, Jeffrey Zhao, Dian Yu, Nan Du, Izhak Shafran, Karthik Narasimhan, and Yuan Cao. 2023. “ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Sharwood, Simon. 2025. Vibe Coding Service Replit Deleted User’s Production Database, Faked Data, Told Fibs Galore. The Register.

Kapoor, Sayash, Benedikt Stroebl, Zachary S. Siegel, Nitya Nadgir, and Arvind Narayanan. 2024. “AI Agents That Matter.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2407.01502.
For further reading:

Saltzer and Schroeder, “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems” (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975): foundational security principles, including complete mediation, that govern every admission check and authorization boundary in the harness.
Hoare, “Monitors: An Operating System Structuring Concept” (Hoare 1974): the classical formulation of serialized access to shared state, providing the conceptual model for trajectory record locking.
O’Neil, “The Escrow Transactional Method” (O’Neil 1986): reservations against an aggregate invariant under concurrency, the intellectual foundation for bounded-liability admission.
Shreedhar and Varghese, “Efficient Fair Queuing Using Deficit Round Robin” (Shreedhar and Varghese 1995): a concise, elegant paper demonstrating how carried credit enables lightweight, \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) fair scheduling across work items of variable size.
Bainbridge, “Ironies of Automation” (Bainbridge 1983): a classic analysis of why human monitoring of reliable automation degrades, essential reading before designing human approval gates.
Yang et al., “SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering” (Yang et al. 2024): a concrete account of command-and-feedback loops in real software repositories, illustrating where model autonomy ends and harness infrastructure must take over.


Saltzer, J. H., and M. D. Schroeder. 1975. “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems.” Proceedings of the IEEE 63 (9): 1278–308. https://doi.org/10.1109/proc.1975.9939.

Yang, John, Carlos E Jimenez, Alexander Wettig, Kilian Lieret, Shunyu Yao, Karthik Narasimhan, and Ofir Press. 2024. “SWE-Agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems.

title: 10 The Agent Harness
text:
Every given below is a hypothetical problem input, not a measurement of a particular model, provider, or service. Prices are in dollars per million tokens unless stated otherwise. Each problem asks for a number and then for the decision the number supports.

Where a pause lands (Basic). A repair harness checks pending_control only when a model reply ends. Generation takes 20 ms per output token with no queueing, and each call’s output allowance is \(\OutputLimit = 8{,}000\) tokens. The operator requirement is that a pause stop new admission within 15 s of its request.
Compute the worst-case wait before the pause takes effect, and the largest \(\OutputLimit\) that meets the requirement without streaming cancellation. For this hypothetical problem, assume a 3,000-token patch can be partitioned into independently complete, validated edit proposals, each no larger than the reduced output cap. Their complete serialization totals 3,000 output tokens with no added proposal overhead, and each call carries the same 40,000-token context without a cache discount. If \(\OutputLimit\) is lowered to meet the requirement, what is the minimum number of complete calls, and how many extra input tokens, at $3 per million, does resending the context cost compared with one call? Explain why an indivisible proposal cannot instead be completed by concatenating truncated replies. The serving service acknowledges a streaming cancellation within 2 s. Decide between the lower cap and streaming cancellation, and state what the pause must still leave in the ledger for a test job already running.
Admission after settlement (Basic). A repair trajectory has a $5.00 allowance, $4.05 of settled spend, a $0.25 reservation on an unsettled test job, and a $0.40 finalization reserve. The next model call carries 80,000 input tokens and \(\OutputLimit = 2{,}000\), at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.
Use equation 1 to decide whether the call is admitted, and compare the spend-check headroom. The call settles with 20,000 uncached input tokens, 60,000 cached input tokens at $0.20 per million, and 900 output tokens. How much reservation does settlement release? The reply proposes paid tool calls bounded at $0.10 each; how many can the harness admit? A defective harness had instead released the test job’s reservation when its wait timed out. How many tool calls would it admit, and by how much would the finalization reserve fall short once the test’s full $0.25 charge arrives?
Workspaces held in escrow (Basic). Review requests for repair submissions arrive at 12 per hour, and reviewers take 45 minutes on average to decide. Each held trajectory keeps a workspace lease of 4 GB, and the pool reserves 24 GB for held workspaces.
Use Little’s law to compute the mean number of held trajectories and the memory they retain. What mean decision time would fit the reserved pool? An alternative snapshots each workspace to storage on entering AWAITING_APPROVAL, keeping 0.25 GB resident, and restores it in 40 s at dispatch. Compute its resident memory and the restore delay as a fraction of the mean decision time. Recommend one design, and explain why a pool sized from the mean alone would still fail after an incident that produces a burst of review requests.
Three classes under deficit round-robin (Intermediate). A harness schedules three classes with quantum 10,000 charge tokens per unit weight per round: support calls (weight 4; 3,000 input tokens and a 500-token output allowance), repair calls (weight 2; 30,000 and 4,000), and maintenance calls (weight 1; 60,000 and 4,000). Assume all classes remain continuously backlogged at the stated call sizes, no provider or local-capacity gate binds, and carried credit has a ceiling large enough for the largest permitted call. One round takes 2 s.
Compute each class’s share of the scheduling charge, its long-run calls per round, and the rounds of credit one call needs. What is the mean interval between maintenance-class admissions in seconds? An engineer caps every class’s carried credit at 50,000 tokens to limit bursts. Determine which class stops running and why. To increase maintenance-class admission frequency, one proposal raises the maintenance weight to 3; another compacts maintenance inputs to 20,000 tokens. Compute the rounds per call and the support class’s charge share under each proposal, and choose the one that leaves support service unchanged.
Sizing a dollar ceiling for cache misses (Intermediate). A repair trajectory runs 25 turns with a 10,000-token base prompt, 2,000 tokens appended per turn, and 300 output tokens per turn; each call’s output allowance is 4,000 tokens. Prices are $3 per million uncached input tokens, $0.30 per million cached input tokens, and $15 per million output tokens, and each turn’s earlier prefix is billed as cached input.
Use equation 2.9 to compute the total input tokens, and the settled cost with and without prefix reuse. The team set \(\CostCeiling = \$1.00\) from the cached bill with a $0.15 finalization reserve, and the harness reserves each call at the undiscounted input rate and full output allowance. After 24 cached turns, is the 25th call admitted, and with what headroom? A long approval wait evicts the cache before one turn, so that turn’s whole input is billed uncached and later turns hit the cache again. Compute the extra charge for an eviction before the 6th turn and before the 24th turn, and state how many of each the trajectory can absorb before the 25th call is refused. What \(\CostCeiling\) guarantees admission of all 25 calls if every turn misses? Recommend how to size the ceiling.
Which allowance binds the research agent (Intermediate). The research agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}\)) starts from a 6,000-token base prompt, appends 12,000 tokens of bounded page observations per turn, and generates 400 output tokens per turn with a 2,000-token output allowance. Each turn takes 45 s. Its budget is \(\TrajectoryBudget = \langle 40 \text{ turns},\ 1.5 \text{ million tokens},\ 1{,}800 \text{ s},\ \$3.00 \rangle\), where the token meter counts cached input in full, and prices match problem 5.
Admitting a turn requires its input plus its output allowance to fit the remaining token allowance. Find the last admitted turn, and compute the used fraction of every dimension at that point with prefix reuse. Which allowance binds, and how does that differ from the repair trajectory of notebook 10.3? A compaction policy runs after every fifth turn: a compaction call reads the full context and writes 2,000 tokens, and the context then restarts from the base prompt plus an 8,000-token summary. Find how many turns the agent now completes before a turn or compaction is refused. Compare this with the token allowance needed to reach 30 turns without compaction. Decide between compaction and a larger \(\TrajectoryTokenLimit\), naming the evidence a summary of untrusted pages must keep by reference.
Choosing a ceiling from a trial (Advanced). A generous-budget run of 100 repair tasks, capped at $10, gives the following outcomes: 30 tasks accepted at about $0.50 each, 25 at about $1.50, 15 at about $3.00, and 5 at about $6.00; the remaining 25 never reached acceptance and spent the full $10. Assume that under a lower cap a task that the generous run accepted at or below the cap is still accepted at the same cost, and every other task spends exactly the cap.
Compute the accepted count and cost per accepted task (equation 1.2) for caps of $1, $2, $4, and $10. A colleague proposes $10 because it maximizes acceptance; critique the proposal. Treating the acceptance count as binomial and freezing each policy’s total cost, estimate the marginal relative standard error of \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) at each cap. Use the first-order approximation that the relative standard error of inverse acceptance equals the acceptance-rate standard error divided by the estimated acceptance fraction. Is the gap between the two lowest-cost caps large compared with each policy’s marginal error? State which paired cost and outcome records, and which declared comparison criterion, a formal verdict would require; these marginal errors alone do not establish distinguishability. How many tasks would bring the relative error to 3 percent at the $2 cap’s acceptance fraction? Finally, explain why a policy that steers or compacts near its cap must be tested as a policy, and why these numbers cannot simply be read from the generous run for it.
Settling timed-out test jobs (Advanced). Each repair trajectory dispatches six test jobs to a metered runner that charges $0.01 per second and enforces a 90 s cap. The harness waits 30 s per job, and 70 percent of jobs finish within the wait at an average of 20 s; the rest run on, averaging 60 s in total. The trajectory allowance is \(\CostCeiling = \$4.00\). The current harness releases a job’s whole reservation when its wait times out and books nothing until the charge arrives.
Compute each job’s bounded liability, the expected late charge per trajectory that the defective harness leaves uncovered, the worst case, and both as fractions of \(\CostCeiling\). Under the settlement rule, how much allowance does a timed-out job hold beyond its eventual charge, on average, while it runs? The runner also supports confirmed cancellation, which stops a job within 5 s and reports its final usage. Compute the charge and the released reservation for a job canceled at its timeout, and the expected test cost per trajectory under “cancel at timeout” and “let it run.” Redesign the timeout policy for the repair agent, stating which evidence releases each reservation and what a canceled job’s missing result costs the repair.


What’s Next: From a live record to a durable oneIf the host fails after reserving and dispatching the test job but before recording its response, the live record alone cannot preserve the admitted operation, its reservation, the held approval, or the evidence needed to resume. Durable Execution develops the history and ordering needed to reconstruct selected control state and distinguish recorded outcomes from unresolved operations after a crash. Rebuilding the record does not itself prove that a remote effect failed, so resumption must preserve the tool’s settlement contract rather than blindly repeat the call.

title: 12 Failure Recovery
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can an agent that records every step it takes still leave the world half changed?
A durable record tells a restarted agent what it intended and what it observed, but the record does not change the world. A provisioning request whose reply was lost may have created a billed environment or nothing at all, and no amount of replay settles which. Restoring a workspace snapshot resets local files, while the remote environment the agent created keeps running and keeps charging. Recovery therefore begins where recording ends, with decisions made on incomplete evidence. A runtime that reads a timeout as failure sends a second request and can leak a second resource, and one that reads it as success builds on an effect that may never have happened. Some effects can be undone only by a new operation that can itself fail, and some cannot be undone at all, so the cheapest place to stop a bad change is before the step that commits it. Other failures raise no error. A trajectory can alternate between two edits for dozens of turns, every call returning success and every health check green, while each turn resends a longer context and the bill grows faster than the turn count. Retries that every layer grants on its own allowance multiply against a dependency that is already failing, so one slow service can stall the shared worker pool. A warning in the prompt does not contain any of these hazards, because the model may ignore advice that a runtime bound would enforce. The runtime must record the cleanup it owes before it acts, keep unknown outcomes owned rather than guessed, weigh another attempt against unwinding by the cost still ahead rather than the cost already spent, and halt work that makes no progress at the gate where new actions are admitted. Over a long horizon, the authority an agent has already exercised becomes a set of obligations the runtime must settle.

Learning Objectives

Classify each tool effect as established, established absent, or unknown, and determine which recovery actions that evidence permits
Register compensations before forward dispatch and order their execution with a dependency-based cleanup graph
Compare one bounded forward repair against compensation and rebuilding, in time and dollars, at the same endpoint
Analyze how checks placed before an irreversible commitment reduce expected loss while cleanup and residual duties remain
Construct progress detectors and price detection latency against a cumulative budget ceiling
Design dependency containment with a single retry owner, scoped circuit breakers, and a capped worker share
Design an incident containment order that limits blast radius while preserving evidence and cleanup
Evaluate recovery policies by accepted tasks, residual obligations, and unresolved outcomes rather than local status









Over a long horizon, authority becomes a recovery problem for the runtime.
When a replacement worker takes over the repair agent’s failed connection-pool repair (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)), it reconstructs the execution log and restores the candidate workspace snapshot ws_r18. The surviving history records an intent to run test_r18, but contains no evidence confirming whether the test passed, failed, or ever ran. As Resuming a Trajectory demonstrated, the worker cannot treat missing evidence as a clean slate; it must retain that uncertainty alongside the unresolved liability. State reconstruction recovers the factual foundation of the execution, but facts alone do not dictate the next step. The runtime’s recovery policy must decide whether to wait for delayed evidence, attempt a targeted repair of the candidate snapshot, or abort the task entirely.
Now expand the scope of the repair to include an external side effect. Besides the unresolved test_r18, which remains a separate operation whose outcome is still owed, the repair provisions an isolated, temporary integration-test environment and runs a new integration suite against ws_r18 inside it. The agent’s authorization grant covers this ephemeral environment and nothing else. Production deployments, public network routing, payment processing, and the deletion of unrelated cloud resources remain strictly beyond its authority.
If a network timeout or process crash drops the provisioning reply, the worker faces an immediate impasse: it cannot know whether the remote environment was successfully allocated or never created.1 Suppose instead that telemetry confirms creation, but the integration suite subsequently crashes. Rolling back the local workspace to snapshot ws_r18 resets internal state, yet the external environment remains active and billing charges continue to accumulate. Local rollback does not undo distributed side effects. Reclaiming those external resources requires an explicit compensating cleanup operation, followed by concrete evidence that the operation satisfied its declared postconditions.
1 Lost acknowledgment: Gray named this the generals paradox in his 1978 notes on database operating systems: over a channel that can lose messages, no finite exchange lets both parties know that the last message arrived (Gray 1978). Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson later proved that in a fully asynchronous system no deterministic consensus protocol can guarantee termination while preserving agreement and validity if even one process may crash, since a crashed process cannot be told apart from a slow one (Fischer et al. 1985). A tool-call timeout inherits the same ambiguity, which is why the settlement rule keeps the outcome unknown rather than guessing. 
Gray, Jim. 1978. “Notes on Data Base Operating Systems.” In Operating Systems: An Advanced Course. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-08755-9_9.

Fischer, Michael J., Nancy A. Lynch, and Michael S. Paterson. 1985. “Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process.” Journal of the ACM 32 (2): 374–82.
Durable logs, checkpoints, and deterministic replay reconstruct what the runtime intended and what it observed. That historical reconstruction provides the essential evidence for recovery, but passive logs cannot alter the outside world. An execution ledger does not tear down an orphaned test cluster, resolve a lost network acknowledgment, or evaluate whether a subsequent attempt justifies its operational cost.


↩︎ Durable logs, checkpoints, and deterministic replay are established in Durable Execution.
Complicating matters further, agent failures frequently manifest without throwing runtime exceptions. An agent trajectory can issue structurally valid tool calls while drifting into destructive patterns: alternating indefinitely between two conflicting edits, bombarding a degraded testing service with aggressive retries, or attempting to transmit private credentials after parsing an untrusted document. Every network call returns a successful status, every worker health check reports green, yet the agent either makes zero forward progress or actively threatens system integrity.
This chapter establishes the runtime recovery policies required to govern these distributed interactions. The recovery architecture records every compensating cleanup obligation before dispatching the operation that produces an external side effect. When an operation is interrupted, the runtime evaluates the surviving evidence alongside projected forward costs, ignoring sunk expenses, to choose whether to retry the operation, repair the proposal within a bound, run compensating actions that unwind external side effects, or hand control to an authorized human operator. Furthermore, the architecture bounds ongoing executions even when no component raises an explicit error. By intercepting actions at the admission gate where new tool calls are scheduled, the runtime halts infinite loops, throttles retries against saturated dependencies, and quarantines suspicious behaviors, rather than relying on prompt warnings that an agent model might overlook or ignore.
The architectural design begins with foundational guarantees. Section 12.2 demonstrates why the environment service and runtime log in this workflow share no atomic commit boundary, carrying forward from the harness the two rules that govern every subsequent recovery decision. Section 12.3 translates these invariants into an executable saga pattern, tracking compensation obligations as explicit, dependency-ordered records. Where an execution encounters partial failure, section 12.4 formalizes how to evaluate the marginal cost of forward repair against backward unwinding, while section 12.5 governs the critical transition across irreversible commitment points.
To address failures that emerge without explicit error signals, the runtime introduces three dedicated containment boundaries: progress watchdogs that identify trajectory stagnation and oscillatory loops (section 12.6), dependency controls that insulate shared backend services from retry cascades (section 12.7), and automated quarantine policies that isolate suspected security incidents (section 12.8). Finally, section 12.9 unites these control loops in a recovery worksheet for a degraded connection-pool repair, detailing the fault-injection test harness required to verify recovery correctness under real-world failures.



The environment service and the runtime’s log commit separately. Although an external service might execute internal database transactions with strict ACID guarantees, no unified atomic boundary encompasses both that remote service and the agent runtime in this workflow. A locking-based transaction can retain exclusive locks until commit or abort to enforce its chosen isolation contract. Two-phase commit coordinates an atomic decision among cooperating resource managers: during preparation each participant preserves the recovery state needed to honor that decision (Gray 1981). A prepared participant may have to wait when the coordinator’s decision is unavailable, retaining resources for recovery. The environment service and runtime log do not participate in such a common protocol. The external endpoints an agent invokes rarely expose a prepare phase or accept this runtime as their coordinator. Even where participants cooperate, retaining transaction resources across model generation, long tests, or asynchronous human review can block competing work for unacceptable periods. A runtime crash while a participant remains prepared can prolong that wait; it does not establish that blocking is necessarily permanent. For the independently administered services in this workflow, recovery therefore uses tentative operations, explicit cancellations, and idempotent exchanges rather than assuming a shared transaction (Helland 2007).
2 Compensating transaction: Gray’s 1981 travel-agent example exhibited this exact structure (Gray 1981). Because each flight or hotel reservation commits at an independent organization, canceling the itinerary requires executing a compensating transaction. Gray proposed that each nested step return the name and parameters of its compensator for the parent coordinator to log, falling back to human intervention as a last resort. However, Gray’s coordinator logs the compensator only after the forward step successfully returns. A trajectory saga must instead record the recovery obligation before dispatching the request over the network, because a dropped connection or lost acknowledgment would otherwise leave unmanaged side effects with no corresponding recovery record. 
Gray, Jim. 1981. “The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations.” Proceedings of the Seventh International Conference on Very Large Data Bases (VLDB) 7: 144–54.
When atomic rollback across independent boundaries is impossible, systems must rely on compensation:2 a forward-executing operation that establishes acceptable postconditions after a prior effect has already committed. Compensation does not erase history or restore the universe to its pristine pre-transaction state. For example, releasing a cloud-hosted development environment deallocates its virtual compute instances and stops active billing meters, but the provisioning event, network ingress logs, and financial charges already accrued remain permanent, and the teardown request itself may fail on an unreachable network. To structure multi-step workflows without global isolation, Garcia-Molina and Salem introduced the saga pattern for long-lived transactions (Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987). Rather than treating the entire trajectory as a single atomic unit, a saga partitions execution into a sequence of smaller, independently committed steps, pairing each forward step with a corresponding compensating action designed to mitigate its side effects if a later step fails.


↪ Two-phase commit’s blocking behavior and the original saga abstraction are developed in Classical Transaction Background.
Compensation is not the only recovery strategy. Apart from a plain retry of an operation whose repeat contract permits one, an agent runtime chooses among three families of response:

Compensation: execute explicit counteracting operations to neutralize partial side effects.
Forward repair: preserve valid intermediate artifacts, such as a successfully compiled binary or a provisioned database schema, and adjust subsequent steps rather than discarding completed progress.
Escalated handoff: halt autonomous dispatch and transfer unresolved obligations, active resource handles, and diagnostic logs to an authorized human operator.

The runtime balances available evidence against projected forward costs to choose among these alternatives; capital and compute time already expended are sunk costs that must not distort future recovery decisions. Whichever path it selects, two rules that the harness already enforces govern the choice, and recovery is where both are tested hardest.
The settlement rule governs what the runtime may believe about an external effect. The harness stated it as a ledger discipline, under which withdrawing an operation’s observation eligibility never settles the operation and only authenticated, correlated evidence does. Recovery needs the rule in a sharper form, as three mutually exclusive evidence states for every dispatched operation: established, established absent, or unknown. An outcome begins as unknown, and only evidence correlated with that specific operation, interpreted through the target endpoint’s contract, can move it to established or established absent. A dropped TCP acknowledgment, an HTTP gateway timeout, an asynchronous accepted-but-pending status, or a status query that returns nothing while the original request may still be in transit all leave the outcome unknown. An unknown outcome keeps its liability reservation against the task budget, keeps a durable record with a named owner, and blocks any forward action that presupposes either success or failure. The runtime may repeat the dispatch only when the endpoint’s verified repeat contract makes re-execution safe, which is settlement before retry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}\)).


↩︎ The settlement rule, which separates observation eligibility from ledger settlement, is established in The Trajectory Record.
The admission check governs what the runtime may do next. Every candidate operation, whether forward progress, a retry, an environment repair, a status probe, or a cleanup action, passes the same predicates the harness applies to ordinary work: valid authority and approval, satisfied dependencies, available capacity, enough time before the deadline, and a reservation whose bounded liability fits beside actual consumption, outstanding liability from unsettled operations, and the protected finalization reserve. The check is re-evaluated at the dispatch boundary immediately before transmission, so a plan-time approval or an earlier durable intent cannot override a later administrative hold, a revoked token, or a depleted budget. Recovery operations receive no exemption. Organizational liability for remote infrastructure does, however, outlive the agent’s reasoning loop, so administrative cleanup backed by independent operational credentials can still pass admission and decommission orphaned resources long after model-directed continuation has ended.


↩︎ The admission check and the finalization reserve it protects are established in Transition guards and the admission check.
A naive undo stack, such as a reversed list of tool invocations that maps server creation to server deletion, is too brittle to satisfy either the settlement rule or the admission check. In-flight operations fail asynchronously, remote endpoints drop responses, and partial writes leave external resources in states that cannot be resolved by simply replaying inverse functions with original arguments. Instead, the runtime must persist a structured recovery obligation before allowing any request to cross the network boundary. This obligation captures correlation identifiers, parent-child causal links, parameter snapshots, timeout thresholds, and settlement state, providing the durable bookkeeping needed to navigate partial failure without leaking resources. The trajectory saga pattern formalizes this durable ledger.



In classical distributed databases, a saga coordinates a long-lived transaction across independent services by assuming that each local transaction either commits cleanly or aborts cleanly. Agentic tool calls break this binary assumption. When an agent provisions a remote resource, the provisioning request may succeed on the remote server even if a network partition drops the return acknowledgment. The runtime is left with an active cleanup obligation whose target resource identifier remains unknown. When applied to an agent trajectory, the saga pattern cannot merely record completed actions; it must durably track unresolved obligations and explicitly account for what the runtime does not yet know.

Definition 12.1: Trajectory saga
Trajectory saga is a recovery pattern that durably records constituent tool actions and coordinates compensating actions when established external effects must be remediated, while explicitly preserving unresolved outcomes and inter-action dependencies.

Significance: Enables systematic recovery across heterogeneous external tools and services that share no common distributed transaction boundary.
Distinction: Compensation represents new forward execution that produces its own observable outcome, rather than an atomic rollback or physical reversal of the environment.
Common pitfall: Deferring cleanup registration until after receiving a successful forward response, creating a crash window where external resources leak without any durable record of their recovery obligation.



In its classical formulation, a saga consists of a sequence of separately committed forward steps \(\SagaForwardStep_1, \dots, \SagaForwardStep_n\), each paired with a compensating step \(\SagaCompensatingStep_i\) that the runtime executes if downstream failures require remediating earlier effects (Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987). A forward action that produces no external side effect requires no compensation. When every forward step succeeds, the saga completes execution as \(\SagaForwardStep_1, \dots, \SagaForwardStep_n\). If step \(\SagaForwardStep_k\) fails, a linear saga unwinds by executing compensating actions in reverse order:
\[\SagaForwardStep_1, \dots, \SagaForwardStep_{k-1}, \SagaFailedForwardStep, \SagaCompensatingStep_k, \SagaCompensatingStep_{k-1}, \dots, \SagaCompensatingStep_1, \tag{1}\]
where \(\SagaCompensatingStep_k\) runs only when evidence confirms that the failed step actually produced an external effect. If the outcome of \(\SagaForwardStep_k\) remains unknown, the runtime’s settlement rules keep the obligation for \(\SagaCompensatingStep_k\) open rather than guessing. While equation 1 models an idealized sequential workflow, non-linear trajectories require a generalized directed cleanup graph. Each compensating step \(\SagaCompensatingStep_i\) is itself an independent, separately committed operation with its own execution outcome; an unwind can stall partway through, leaving certain compensations settled while others remain pending or in flight.


To understand how a runtime manages this uncertainty, consider an agent workflow managing temporary test infrastructure. Let provision_test_env_r18 be the stable logical operation that provisions an isolated test environment, and let release_test_env_r18 be its corresponding cleanup operation, a distinct logical identity that remains stable across retries and restarts. Neither identity should be confused with the endpoint-generated environment identifier. That system handle, denoted env_r18_01 in a successful provisioning run, becomes known to the runtime only after correlated response evidence settles the forward operation.
If the runtime waited until after receiving a successful provisioning reply to register cleanup, a crash during or immediately following dispatch would orphan the remote resource without any local recovery record. The runtime eliminates this crash window by durably registering a cleanup template before forward dispatch. This record includes the exact forward operation and payload, authorized capability scope, execution preconditions, dependencies, and an explicit rule for binding the returned environment identifier. Appended directly to the write-ahead log alongside the forward admission record, this registration shares the forward attempt’s storage acknowledgment and resource reservation, avoiding the overhead and complexity of an independent state machine. Registering the cleanup before the effect it cleans up applies intent before effect (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}\)) to the recovery obligation itself.


↩︎ The durable intent record written before dispatch is established in Durable Intent Before Dispatch.
The resulting template binds cleanup to the specific environment instantiated by this provisioning operation, rather than relying on transient metadata like display names. Durably registering this template establishes a binding commitment for future recovery rather than asserting that the resource already exists. Table 1 follows this distinction across each phase of the crash boundary.



Table 1: Registration and deferred result binding: The recovery obligation precedes the forward effect, while an endpoint-generated resource identifier is bound only when the evidence supports it.










Boundary
Durable obligation and available evidence
Permitted interpretation

provision_test_env_r18, exact request and scope, admission and reservation, and template for release_test_env_r18 with an unbound environment field

The request may be delayed, running, or completed; missing evidence does not authorize another creation or settle cleanup

The evidence binds env_r18_01 to provision_test_env_r18; the binding is durably recorded

When an acknowledgment is lost following dispatch, an idempotent result-recovery probe may retrieve the missing outcome. For a mutating tool without endpoint deduplication, this is the probe that the tool contract of equation 7.1 ships beside its actuate and compensate routines, and the template registered here instantiates that contract’s compensate routine for one specific, bound resource. If probing is unsupported or inconclusive, settlement rules mandate that the operation remain open with an assigned recovery owner. A naive runtime might query the external service, observe that the environment is absent, and prematurely close the cleanup record on the assumption that creation failed. Doing so creates a dangerous race condition: if the original provisioning request was merely delayed in transit, the remote service may instantiate the environment seconds later, leaving an orphaned resource that accrues compute charges indefinitely without any controlling process. If the endpoint supports explicit request cancellation, the runtime can invoke that contract to terminate the pending creation, provided the endpoint guarantees that canceled requests will not take effect downstream.


↪ Result recovery, as distinct from repeated execution, is developed in Repetition and Result Recovery.




Definition 12.2: Semantic compensation
Semantic compensation is an independent forward action designed to establish declared application postconditions following an earlier side effect, without claiming to erase execution history or restore every dimension of the external environment.

Significance: Provides a verifiable, checkable objective for recovery when exact physical or historical reversal is impossible.
Distinction: Releasing a temporary environment terminates its active allocation; it does not un-send network packets, erase system audit logs, or refund consumed compute charges.
Common pitfall: Treating an endpoint’s asynchronous acceptance response as proof that declared postconditions have been achieved when only request receipt has occurred.



In our running example, the compensation contract stipulates that the task-owned environment must no longer be allocated and that no active integration test may still depend on it, requiring any diagnostic artifacts to be transferred to durable storage prior to deallocation. The contract also defines what evidence the endpoint must supply to demonstrate successful release. Because final billing charges often settle asynchronously hours after an environment is torn down, the runtime decouples the physical resource obligation from financial settlement.
Formally, let \(\PreForwardEnvironmentState\) represent the state of the environment prior to executing forward step \(\SagaForwardStep\), and let \(\CompensatedEnvironmentState\) denote the state after executing \(\SagaForwardStep\) followed by its compensating action \(\SagaCompensatingStep\). Because physical time cannot be reversed and side effects alter audit trails and financial balances, \(\CompensatedEnvironmentState\) and \(\PreForwardEnvironmentState\) inevitably differ. Compensation guarantees equivalence only with respect to an explicitly declared set of postcondition predicates \(\CompensationPostconditionSet\). The compensation succeeds if and only if both states agree on every predicate in \(\CompensationPostconditionSet\):
\[\CompensatedEnvironmentState \equiv_{\CompensationPostconditionSet} \PreForwardEnvironmentState \iff \forall \CompensationPostcondition \in \CompensationPostconditionSet:\ \CompensationPostcondition(\CompensatedEnvironmentState) = \CompensationPostcondition(\PreForwardEnvironmentState). \tag{2}\]
Here, predicates such as “the environment is allocated” and “an admitted test depends on it” belong to \(\CompensationPostconditionSet\), and both evaluate to false in \(\PreForwardEnvironmentState\) and \(\CompensatedEnvironmentState\). In contrast, billing ledgers and audit histories lie outside \(\CompensationPostconditionSet\), which is why financial reconciliation requires an independent settlement lifecycle. A compensation contract claims to satisfy only the predicates explicitly declared in \(\CompensationPostconditionSet\); unmodeled side effects remain unaddressed.
Compensation inevitably operates on an environment that has moved on. External services or human operators may have observed the intermediate state, consumed compute seconds cannot be un-billed, and concurrent processes can alter cleanup preconditions. For instance, if a peer workflow has attached to the temporary environment for joint debugging, the originating agent cannot unilaterally destroy the resource simply because its own plan stalled. The runtime’s admission control boundary must inspect live ownership and active dependency graphs at the moment of compensation, rather than blindly following stale planning text.
Local workspace restoration plays a complementary but narrower role. A compatible checkpoint restores only the local workspace projection managed directly by the runtime. Checkpoints cannot reset remote cloud environments, running external daemons, dispatched batch jobs, or accrued service charges. Those external side effects demand semantic compensation. When recovery requires both local rollback and remote compensation, the runtime orchestrates both mechanisms, verifying the independent outcome of each path before declaring the system recovered.


↩︎ Checkpoint restoration, which reinstates the record and workspace without re-executing external actions, is established in Consistent recovery boundaries.



Because cleanup actions cross the same external tool boundaries as forward actions, they encounter the same failure modes: network drops, rate limits, and remote service outages. Consequently, every compensating operation must pass admission control, and its intent must be durably committed before dispatch. When retrying a failed cleanup call, the runtime assigns each transport attempt a unique attempt identifier, while release_test_env_r18 continues to designate the persistent logical operation. Retries adhere to the endpoint’s repeat contract; the stable logical key ensures that duplicate deletion requests execute safely without targeting a different resource if the external system reuses names or identifiers.


↩︎ Stable operation identities, with a fresh attempt identity for each retry under the endpoint’s repeat contract, are established in Operation identity and endpoint contracts.
The coordinator retires a compensation entry only upon receiving verifiable outcome evidence, rather than assuming success simply because a remote call returned without a transport error. If a release call times out, three states remain possible: the environment may be gone, it may still be undergoing deallocation, or it may remain allocated. The settlement rules keep all three possibilities open. Furthermore, cleanup actions consume quota and wall-clock execution budget; a timed-out call refunds nothing. If cleanup cannot progress further within its assigned budget, the obligation remains recorded in the ledger alongside accumulated evidence and an assigned escalation owner. In this way, a failed agent trajectory can terminate safely without masking unresolved external leaks.
Preregistered cleanup templates execute under the supervision of the trusted runtime coordinator without invoking another model inference step. This separation enforces least-privilege control: even if the model’s forward execution authority is revoked following an anomaly or budget exhaustion, a narrowly scoped cleanup grant remains accessible to the coordinator to tear down provisioned resources. If remediation requires operations beyond this pre-authorized grant, the runtime does not guess; it halts and issues an explicitly owned handoff. Later authenticated evidence or manual operator actions can settle the obligation without restarting the obsolete agent trajectory.



A simple last-in, first-out (LIFO) unwind stack is adequate only when an agent executes a strictly linear sequence and every cleanup precondition follows that reverse order. When an agent invokes tools concurrently, triggers asynchronous background tasks, or branches across speculative plans, recovery requires tracking explicit causal dependencies. This structure is a directed cleanup graph \((\CleanupGraphVertexSet,\CleanupGraphEdgeSet)\), where each vertex represents an admitted cleanup operation and a directed edge
\[\SagaCompensatingStep_j \rightarrow \SagaCompensatingStep_k\]
signifies that compensating operation \(\SagaCompensatingStep_j\) must establish its declared settlement conditions before \(\SagaCompensatingStep_k\) is permitted to dispatch. Declared cleanup dependencies must form a directed acyclic graph (DAG); cyclical dependencies represent contradictory recovery requirements that demand explicit operator intervention rather than an arbitrary stack ordering.
In our temporary environment scenario, an active integration test may still be executing when a failure is detected. Confirming that the test process has stopped, or canceling it and verifying that it stopped, must precede release_test_env_r18. Similarly, extracting and preserving diagnostic test artifacts outside the sandbox must occur before deprovisioning the virtual machine. By contrast, removing an unrelated local scratch directory can proceed independently, provided no active test or pending evidence collection depends on it. The cleanup graph answers what must happen first, settlement rules determine what has been empirically verified, and admission control determines which operations may run next. The graph cannot be sequenced until provisioning evidence has bound its target, which is why figure 1 draws the release ordering beneath the registration step it depends on.

The dashed link shows the binding supplying the target of the registered cleanup. In the cleanup lane, release_test_env_r18 waits for its predecessors, and its own outcome either closes the obligation or remains owned, so no path ends in an assumed clean state.



Structuring cleanup as a DAG isolates failures and enables concurrent unwinding. An unresolved or failed cleanup node blocks only its transitive dependents in \((\CleanupGraphVertexSet,\CleanupGraphEdgeSet)\); independent recovery subgraphs can proceed immediately once their predecessors settle, their preconditions hold, and they clear admission control. Executing independent cleanup actions in parallel significantly reduces overall recovery latency.
The cleanup graph enforces ordering without erasing historical accountability. Settled nodes retain their verification evidence, while failed or ambiguous nodes remain bound to their assigned owners. While an authorized administrator may deliberately accept residual risk to unblock downstream execution, the system never silently records an unconfirmed release as clean.



During tree searches, speculative execution, or multi-candidate exploration, an agent system frequently preserves a shared trajectory prefix while exploring several alternative continuations in parallel. While branch ancestry tracks where model execution diverged, it reveals nothing about which external resources each branch currently claims. If an agent creates a cloud test sandbox during the common prefix before branching into three separate test configurations, tearing down that sandbox because Candidate B failed would sabotage the active experiments in Candidates A and C.
The runtime therefore decouples resource ownership from logical branch history by tracking effects and cleanup obligations through reference-counted dependency graphs. When the runtime abandons a speculative branch, it reclaims only those resources owned exclusively by that branch, once its outstanding work has settled or stopped cleanly. Shared resources remain allocated until all surviving dependencies permit release. Furthermore, if an abandoned branch dispatched a provisioning request whose outcome remains unknown, that request remains recorded in the durable ledger; pruning a branch from the scheduler does not erase an unresolved external obligation.
Restoring a branch’s local workspace or context window does not rewind the external environment to the branch point, and evidence gathered from an abandoned candidate cannot be assumed valid for a sibling branch merely because they share an ancestor. During counterfactual execution, local workspaces can be rolled back to earlier checkpoints, but external networks, databases, and billing meters cannot. Enforcing this distinction ensures that speculative branch pruning never silently discards external recovery duties.

While semantic compensation systematically remediates partial effects, unwinding external work can discard valuable intermediate state that could have salvaged the task. If a provisioned test environment is healthy and only the agent’s proposed test configuration was malformed, tearing down the sandbox wastes time and budget that a bounded in-place correction could preserve. Deciding whether to tear down that environment or repair the configuration in place requires comparing the expected cost of forward correction against the expense of backward unwinding and rebuilding.




Take the branch in which provisioning evidence did arrive. The separately authorized operation provision_test_env_r18 has settled, binding the temporary integration-test environment env_r18_01. Before dispatching the integration test, the runtime validates the proposed test configuration and rejects it because a field requiring an integer contains a string. The candidate workspace remains ws_r18, and no integration test has started. Releasing the environment through release_test_env_r18 would discard expensive, fully functional preparation. Conversely, a bounded correction of the configuration can restore readiness without rebuilding the environment from scratch.
This situation differs fundamentally from the unresolved test_r18 intent that the replacement worker recovered. When the runtime rejects a proposal before dispatch, it establishes definitive evidence that the executor never launched the action. A missing result under the settlement rule provides no such assurance; the operation might have succeeded, failed, or stalled midway through execution.
In dependable system design, forward recovery modifies the current state or repairs a proposed action to restore an admissible path toward completing the task. By contrast, backward recovery returns the system to an earlier saved state. The classical dependability taxonomy formalizes these strategies as rollforward and rollback, where rollback restores a previously captured checkpoint (Avizienis et al. 2004).3 Forward repair, the response family named earlier, is the agent runtime’s form of forward recovery, which keeps valid intermediate artifacts and corrects the proposal that failed. In an agentic system, restoring a workspace checkpoint performs backward recovery for the local filesystem and memory state that the checkpoint covers. External systems, however, rarely support true rollback, and compensation sits across the divide. In intent it is backward recovery, because it moves the environment back toward the pre-effect predicates of equation 2. In execution it is forward, a new operation with its own outcome, which is why the trajectory saga definition calls it new forward execution. It achieves semantic equivalence rather than physical restoration.

The colloquial instruction to “try again” blurs a plain retry and the three families of response into one gesture. Separated by the evidence each requires, they become five choices, because forward repair splits into two forms while retry, compensation, and escalation each remain one. Forward repair takes two forms: resampling requests an entirely fresh candidate proposal from the model, while feedback-based repair (Madaan et al. 2023; Shinn et al. 2023) supplies targeted diagnostics to prompt a revised proposal. Compensation executes registered actions to establish fallback postconditions, and escalation transfers decision authority or unresolved obligations to an authorized supervisor. A network timeout raises an effect-status question before any model-repair question can be addressed, and the runtime relies on the settlement rule to resolve whether external state was altered. Similarly, an HTTP 429 rate-limit response proves only what the external service contract guarantees; it does not prove that an attempted state mutation was rejected before execution. Exponential backoff regulates the timing and throughput of a permitted retry, but no backoff schedule can transform an unsafe, non-idempotent repeat into a safe operation.
In contrast to an ambiguous timeout, a pre-dispatch configuration rejection provides a well-defined basis for repair. Because the schema validator rejected the payload locally, the runtime establishes that the proposed action never reached the executor or modified remote state. The runtime can therefore supply the original request, the target schema, the field-level diagnostic, and the task scope within a bounded repair prompt, validating the revised proposal before admitting any side effect. If the repair instead modifies source code rather than an ephemeral test configuration, the modified artifact constitutes a new candidate revision requiring fresh test evidence; previous test passes for ws_r18 cannot certify altered code.

Accumulating failed responses and diagnostic traces across successive attempts also inflates the prompt for subsequent calls. Runtimes must manage two distinct resource boundaries: the per-invocation context window capacity and the cumulative task token meter. Context assembly must fit relevant diagnostic evidence within a single invocation’s context limit, whereas the billing meter charges for all input and output tokens consumed across the full sequence of repair calls. While context compaction can summarize historical attempts to fit within the context window, compaction consumes additional model calls, adds latency, and discards fine-grained diagnostic detail. Before evaluating the economic trade-offs of recovery, the runtime eliminates any candidate action that fails admission control. For instance, an authentication failure never grants permission to synthesize an unauthorized bypass; instead, the runtime must either request an authorized credential refresh, locate a permitted fallback operation, or pause execution and escalate. Financial and latency budgets enforce hard ceilings. Even when a proposed repair is inexpensive in expectation, the runtime admits it only if its maximum bounded liability fits within the remaining allowance. Furthermore, the assembled repair context must separately fit within the target model’s context capacity.


↩︎ Bounded-liability admission, which admits an operation only when its maximum charge fits the remaining allowance, is established in Reservation and settlement.
Expected cost guides the recovery policy only among candidate actions that have cleared admission. Historical expenditures are sunk costs; recovery decisions must depend strictly on forward-looking costs and risks: the cost of retaining useful state, rebuilding that state from scratch, attempting repair, and managing secondary failure. While expensive earlier preparation often implies costly reconstruction, past spending alone never justifies continuing down a failing path. Ongoing resource holding fees, unsafe residual side effects, or task deadline expirations often dictate that discarding partially completed work is preferable to attempting a repair.



Consider the trade-off between attempting a bounded repair and executing an immediate fallback that unwinds and rebuilds the required state. Let \(\FallbackCost\) denote the future cost of compensating existing side effects and rebuilding to a declared readiness endpoint, and let one bounded repair attempt cost \(\RepairAttemptCost\) with probability \(\RepairSuccessProbability\) of reaching that same endpoint. Assuming that an unsuccessful repair leaves the original fallback pathway available at unchanged cost, the expected total cost of attempting repair before falling back is
\[\mathbb{E}[\RepairFirstCost] = \RepairAttemptCost + (1-\RepairSuccessProbability)\FallbackCost. \tag{3}\]
For any strictly positive fallback cost, attempting repair first yields a lower expected cost than an immediate fallback whenever
\[\RepairSuccessProbability > \RepairSuccessProbability^* = \frac{\RepairAttemptCost}{\FallbackCost}. \tag{4}\]
Engineers must evaluate this comparison independently for latency (in seconds) and monetary expense (in model dollars), as their respective break-even thresholds \(\RepairSuccessProbability^*\) often diverge. If \(\RepairAttemptCost \ge \FallbackCost\), no success probability below one can make repair cheaper on that resource axis. Furthermore, if a failed repair alters residual side effects, extends resource holding times, or increases fallback complexity, the term \((1-\RepairSuccessProbability)\FallbackCost\) must be replaced by the corresponding conditional fallback cost. Expected cost is the last of three gates, not the first. Evidence class decides which candidates exist at all, admissibility removes those that authority, allowance, or the deadline forbids, and only then does equation 4 rank the survivors; figure 2 lays out that order.






Figure 2: Recovery Decision Order: Evidence class comes first, because an unknown outcome admits only a retry of the same operation under its repeat contract (a result-recovery probe or a wait gathers evidence that moves the outcome out of this branch rather than acting on it), while a rejected proposal or an established effect opens new proposals, repair, and compensation. Admissibility then removes candidates that lack authority, allowance with the finalization reserve intact, or time; if none remain, the runtime holds or escalates. Expected cost at a matched endpoint chooses only among the admissible survivors, and applies separately to seconds and dollars.

An agent runtime cannot know in advance whether a given failure is repairable, but it can enforce rigorous operational bounds on the recovery process. The primary unit of bounded recovery is the repair episode.5 Each episode maintains a unique identity, records the task and candidate versions it governs, and tracks an attempt counter against an explicit allowance, the repair cap \(\RepairCap\). Every corrective model invocation or tool dispatch must pass admission control and reserve its liability against that allowance. Because the counter increments upon admission rather than success, failed, timed-out, or aborted executions cannot evade the limit. Furthermore, transport retries and secondary proposals remain explicitly tied to their parent operations, ensuring that underlying retry mechanisms cannot silently consume a fresh allowance.
5 Recovery blocks: Randell’s classic recovery block architecture structured fault tolerance around a primary routine, an acceptance test, and a fixed sequence of alternates, each executed from a restored checkpoint until one passed or the sequence was exhausted (Randell 1975). An agentic repair episode preserves the acceptance test and finite iteration, but its alternates are dynamically sampled from a language model rather than written in advance. Consequently, exhausting an episode signals an exhausted recovery budget rather than proof that no feasible solution exists.

Because the attempt limit is an operational policy parameter, exhausting it provides no proof that the underlying problem is unsolvable. A task’s cumulative financial budget and outstanding obligations carry across any revised plan or renamed operation; only an authorized policy modification can initiate a new repair episode, and that new episode inherits all previous telemetry and resource consumption.
Observing repeated errors or identical candidate states justifies early runtime inspection, but repetition alone does not constitute definitive proof of non-progress: an unchanged error diagnostic can follow valuable internal context pruning, and revisiting an earlier state may represent a deliberate search backtrack. Section 12.6 formalizes dedicated watchdog mechanisms to detect these stalls. The governing runtime rule remains direct: once the episode allowance is exhausted or an admission check fails, the runtime denies further repair attempts and selects among still-permitted compensation, a paused continuation awaiting operator inspection, or an explicit escalation.

The break-even analysis in section 12.4.3 assumed that compensation remains an available fallback pathway throughout repair. Certain external commitments, however, irreversibly alter outside state, permanently foreclosing compensation and demanding fundamentally different safety guarantees.




When an agent abandons an in-flight repair task, releasing a temporary integration-test environment deallocates its virtual infrastructure while leaving behind only the accumulated compute charges. Other operations alter the external world in ways that no recovery action within the agent’s authority can reverse. A sound recovery policy must therefore distinguish which postconditions the runtime can reliably reestablish from the residual side effects that will inevitably remain.
The property of reversibility is always relative to a specified subsystem and an explicit boundary of control. For example, a local filesystem snapshot restores the directories it tracks and nothing beyond them. Likewise, invoking an API endpoint named delete or dispatching an action granted only low authority guarantees no stronger recovery semantics than the underlying implementation actually provides.


Before initiating any state modification, the execution runtime must determine three properties for each proposed effect: the precise target state, the recovery action available under the task’s granted authority, and the concrete evidence needed to verify that the recovery postcondition holds. These contracts represent intrinsic semantic properties of the underlying operation rather than superficial endpoint names or the coarse authority levels \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\) to \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\).

Definition 12.3: Pivot action
A pivot action is the designated irreversible commitment within a bounded region of a plan, after which restoring the region’s precommitment state is no longer an available recovery strategy.

Significance: The pivot splits a plan region into two distinct phases: a compensable preparation phase before it and an irreversible phase after it. Hoisting validation checks ahead of the pivot is the primary systems mechanism for preventing defective actions from becoming permanent damages.
Distinction: Being a pivot is an architectural property of an action within a plan region under a specific authority grant, rather than an intrinsic attribute of an API endpoint name. The same API call may be compensable under an administrative role with rollback privileges, yet act as a pivot under a restricted operational grant.
Common pitfall: Delaying checks until after the pivot when they could have run before it. Executing validation late converts failures that compensation could have cleanly resolved into committed production outages.



A commitment region encompasses the span of an execution plan structured around a single pivot: preparatory work that compensation can still unwind, the pivot action itself, and the follow-up obligations that remain afterward. Commitment regions carry intent before effect (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}\)) across a step that compensation cannot reach: everything the runtime must check and record is settled before the irreversible action.
Within each commitment region, the agent must perform every validation check that can legitimately precede commitment before releasing the irreversible action. The runtime must preserve all necessary artifacts, validate their versions and dependencies, and record the authorized intent, resource reservations, recovery metadata, and follow-up obligations to durable storage under the failure-domain contract of Acknowledgment and the failure domain. Only after crossing this durable boundary does the pivot action face its final admission check at dispatch time.
Limiting each region to a single pivot is an architectural discipline rather than a restriction that an entire task trajectory contain only one irreversible action. When a complex workload requires several independent state changes, the plan decomposes into a sequence of distinct commitment regions.
To see this discipline in practice, consider an authorized publishing agent tasked with deploying an approved artifact to an external registry and notifying downstream recipients. A naive plan publishes the artifact first, validates signatures and dependency versions second, drafts release notes third, and sends notifications fourth. If validation fails at the second step, an invalid artifact is already publicly visible, and no recovery action within the agent’s authority can withdraw every distributed copy. Table 4 illustrates how reordering hoists every check and compensable preparation step ahead of publication, isolating publication as the single commitment of its region.

True data and control dependencies fundamentally bound how aggressively the runtime can hoist operations. For example, a validation check that depends on the published artifact, such as confirming that a public package mirror resolves its new identifier, cannot run before release. That verification must remain after the commitment, tracked as an explicit operational risk assigned to a designated owner.
Executing a commitment does not terminate cleanup. When an agent allocates independent temporary resources that are no longer needed by subsequent duties, the runtime must still release them. The orchestrator maintains the compensation ledger across the commitment boundary, withholding only those recovery actions whose preconditions no longer hold or whose execution would directly contradict the committed state.
The software repair agent encounters few pivots within its typical grant, because even submitting a pull request for review can be withdrawn or closed. In contrast, the on-call remediation agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) encounters a pivot in nearly every incident it handles, because it operates at authority level \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\) against shared production infrastructure.

Lighthouse 12.1: Remediation agent (pivot and compensation)Workload: The remediation agent responds to production alerts when a service’s error rate spikes following a configuration change. Its task contract permits querying telemetry systems, staging a candidate configuration on a canary slice (the small fraction of servers that receives traffic first), and rolling that configuration out fleet-wide after obtaining approval. Its operational horizon is tight, and any state modification directly affects live traffic across shared production infrastructure.
Recovery contracts: Querying telemetry metrics and reading logs produces no state changes to compensate. Staging a correction on the canary slice is fully compensable: reverting the canary restores the declared routing and configuration predicates, even though client requests already processed by the canary cannot be recalled. Scaling server replicas is compensable, leaving behind only the accumulated cloud charges. Rolling the configuration across the fleet alongside a rolling service restart constitutes the commitment region’s pivot action: severed TCP connections, invalidated cache entries, and requests dropped during the restart lie beyond any recovery action permitted by the agent’s grant.
Binding constraint: While the software repair agent’s recovery budget is dominated by token re-reads during prompt reconstruction, the remediation agent’s recovery cost is dominated by expected irreversible loss. Every diagnostic check and synthetic test that can evaluate the canary belongs before the fleet rollout. Furthermore, the human-in-the-loop approval gate described in Approval Gates must sit directly at this pivot boundary, maximizing the operational loss prevented per minute of engineer review.


The lighthouse’s ordering rule can be priced. The expected irreversible loss of an execution plan, \(\ExpectedIrreversibleLoss\) (the subscript is part of the symbol’s name, not an authority level), sums over every proposed action \(\PlanAction\) the product of the probability that the action is defective, its blast-radius consequence if committed, and the unrecoverable fraction \(1-\ActionRecoverableFraction\) that compensation cannot restore:
\[\ExpectedIrreversibleLoss = \sum_\PlanAction \Pr(\text{bad}\ \PlanAction)\cdot \text{consequence}(\PlanAction)\cdot(1-\ActionRecoverableFraction). \tag{5}\]



After reordering, changes the canary misses dominate the remaining loss.
Hoisting a diagnostic check ahead of the pivot transforms an unrecoverable failure mode (\(\ActionRecoverableFraction = 0\)) into a partially compensable canary rollback (\(\ActionRecoverableFraction > 0\)). Conversely, scheduling that same validation check after the pivot leaves \(\ActionRecoverableFraction = 0\), forfeiting any loss reduction. A real pre-pivot check recovers through two separate factors. It catches only a fraction \(\PrePivotCatchRate\) of defective actions, and reverting a caught action avoids only a fraction \(\RevertFidelity\) of its consequence, while a missed action recovers nothing. The action’s recoverable fraction in equation 5 is therefore the product \(\ActionRecoverableFraction = \PrePivotCatchRate\,\RevertFidelity\), and keeping the factors apart shows which one an engineering investment moves.

A wrong change that commits at the pivot inflicts \(\text{consequence}(\PlanAction)\) = $12,000.
