These three sources complement one another across the lifecycle of a training pipeline. A production failure reveals a real-world edge case that warrants reproduction in a benchmark; a human demonstration provides an expert recovery strategy to seed the model; and synthetic rollouts explore complex fault matrices through automated permutation.
When generating synthetic rollouts, the environment must compute state transitions dynamically. If an agent emits an action that diverges from a historical trace, the platform cannot simply replay the subsequent observation from a recorded log. Doing so violates environment causality and injects corrupted, contradictory context into the trajectory. Synthetic collection requires a live, interactive environment capable of generating valid observations for arbitrary action sequences.
The choice of data source fundamentally shapes the distribution of harvested behaviors. A collection policy that filters strictly for short, successful runs discards valuable trajectories that exhibit backtracking and fault recovery under partial observability. Conversely, relying uncritically on production traces can overrepresent abandoned user sessions and unresolved timeouts. Recording the collection policy, sampling parameters, and task-family metadata in the manifest enables downstream curation stages to distinguish between genuinely rare engineering events and artificial gaps created by collection filters.



A robust training corpus requires systematic task variation across dimensions that reflect operational reality. In software repair, task distributions should vary across dependency tree depth, the clarity of error feedback prior to an edit, and the concurrency conditions encountered during testing. In document synthesis, distributions should deliberately introduce contradictory sources, missing numerical metrics, and schema drift across versions.
The H·S·A exposures (The H·S·A Exposure Space) characterize each variant: the horizon \(\TurnHorizon\) in turns required to solve the task, the state level (\(\StateExposureLevel_0\) to \(\StateExposureLevel_3\)) the task retains or mutates across steps, and the authority level (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\) to \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\)) its tool set grants. Varying a task along these exposures provides an architectural basis for task variation that avoids arbitrary context-length thresholds or the false assumption that all meaningful tasks must mutate a filesystem.
System privileges and tool access grants must remain explicit and immutably enforced across all task variants. As a model improves, it may learn to query fewer tools, avoid redundant exploratory commands, or complete tasks in fewer turns. This training progress changes the agent’s realized exposure to the environment, but the underlying permissions and runtime sandboxing boundaries must remain unchanged. Similarly, the environment reset contract must govern every reuse of a fixture. If a failed run leaves background processes running, uncommitted file locks, or dangling network sockets, the teardown mechanism must cleanly purge this residual state before the next collection worker initializes, regardless of whether the previous trajectory was admitted into the training corpus or discarded.


↩︎ The reset contract, which catalogs every piece of state that teardown must clear before an environment serves a new lease, is established in The reset contract.
A well-designed collection fixture unifies the task specification and grading criteria with an explicit learning objective, a capture contract, and a structured distribution of variants. Before launching collection workers across this task matrix, however, systems engineers must partition and quarantine held-out evaluation tasks. Reserving these unpolluted benchmarks is the focus of section 14.4.




Consider an automated collection pipeline that harvests multiple repair trajectories for the same connection-pool defect. If an engineer naively partitions the resulting execution traces at random, one successful repair trajectory lands in the training set while another attempt at the exact same defect lands in the final test set. Varying the random seed, prompt wording, or tool sequence creates superficial operational diversity, but it does not make the underlying engineering problem new. When the fine-tuned policy subsequently encounters this task during evaluation, it does not demonstrate generalization; it merely recalls an environment, bug mechanism, and solution it has already observed during training. This failure mode is split leakage: information about an evaluation target reaching the training pipeline through a related or derived record (Kaufman et al. 2012).
1 Duplication in Code Corpora: Code datasets are especially prone to leakage because repository forks, vendored libraries, and copy-pasted snippets reproduce the same defect across nominally distinct codebases. Evaluating code models on corpora that contain near-duplicates inflates reported performance metrics by as much as a factor of two relative to deduplicated corpora (Allamanis 2019). An agent trajectory corpus inherits every duplicate in the underlying codebases and introduces an operational multiplier: repeated execution rollouts on the same benchmark fixture. Grouping trajectories by underlying task is therefore a foundational integrity requirement, not an optional refinement. 
Allamanis, Miltiadis. 2019. “The Adverse Effects of Code Duplication in Machine Learning Models of Code.” Proceedings of the 2019 ACM SIGPLAN International Symposium on New Ideas, New Paradigms, and Reflections on Programming and Software (Onward!), 143–53. https://doi.org/10.1145/3359591.3359735.
In agent trajectory curation, split leakage is the default outcome rather than a rare edge case.1 Suppose an agent executes 8 rollouts per task and an engineer partitions the individual traces at random using a 80 percent/20 percent ratio. A task remains cleanly isolated on one side of the split only if every one of its attempts independently falls into that same partition. For a training fraction \(\TrainingSplitFraction\) and \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) independent attempts per task, that non-leakage probability is \(\TrainingSplitFraction^\IndependentAttemptCount + (1-\TrainingSplitFraction)^\IndependentAttemptCount\). Consequently, 83.2 percent of all tasks straddle the train–test boundary, contaminating the evaluation protocol. Partitioning schemes must therefore follow structural task relationships rather than arbitrary trace run identifiers.



With eight attempts per task, a random 80/20 trace split leaves 83 percent of tasks on both sides.
While the fixture contract defines what an individual execution trial represents, split design governs the scientific validity of what subsequent evaluations can claim about agent learning. To preserve that validity, engineers must isolate and lock down protected evaluation tasks before data collection, model-assisted filtering, or hyperparameter tuning begins. If developers inspect final test failures and subsequently harvest demonstrations targeting those specific failure modes, they convert the test suite into implicit training feedback. The benchmark ceases to function as an independent evaluation, even when no raw test trajectory directly enters the training manifest.


Every rigorous evaluation protocol begins with an explicit claim about operational capability. For instance, an in-distribution deployment assessment asks whether an adapted agent can resolve new, previously unencountered maintenance tickets within the specific repositories and runtime environments it already serves. In contrast, an out-of-distribution transfer assessment tests whether that same agent succeeds across entirely unseen repository families, software architectures, or tool environments. These distinct claims require fundamentally different partitioning boundaries. Familiarity with a shared build tool, compiler flags, or API schema reflects legitimate deployment conditions and does not constitute leakage. In contrast, evaluating an agent on a defect whose solution was observed during fine-tuning invalidates the measurement entirely.
To enforce these boundaries systematically, the curation pipeline organizes tasks into groups. A task group aggregates all repeated attempts, paraphrased prompts, derived test fixtures, and solution-equivalent variations of a single underlying problem. For example, if a benchmark contains an issue fixture pool_repair_01, any rollout generated from an alternate random seed, a renamed variable, or an identical upstream bug copied into a downstream fork belongs to that same task group. The split manifest must explicitly record the structural rationale for each grouping. Naive heuristics frequently fail: grouping solely by repository name misses cross-repository forks and vendored copies, whereas grouping by shared dependencies aggressively collapses unrelated software defects into unmanageably large clusters.
Formally, let the group map \(\TaskGroupMap(\EnvironmentFixture)\) send an environment fixture \(\EnvironmentFixture\) to its designated task group, and let the split map \(\SplitAssignmentMap(\TaskGroupMap)\) assign that group to a partition: training, development, or final test. Every harvested trajectory, synthesized record, or distilled learning example inherits the partition assignment of its originating fixture. Partition integrity requires that:
\[\TaskGroupMap(\EnvironmentFixture_i)=\TaskGroupMap(\EnvironmentFixture_j) \implies \SplitAssignmentMap(\TaskGroupMap(\EnvironmentFixture_i))=\SplitAssignmentMap(\TaskGroupMap(\EnvironmentFixture_j)).\]
This partitioning invariant guarantees that every known manifestation of a problem resides strictly on one side of the split. The strength of this guarantee depends directly on how thoroughly the pipeline identifies latent relationships across tasks. Production split manifests should therefore log the active grouping policy, git commit lineages, schema versions, and quarantined matches awaiting human triage. When allocating splits, randomization must operate over task groups rather than individual rollouts, applying stratification across task complexity or repository size where necessary. Furthermore, evaluation dashboards must report group counts alongside raw trajectory counts, since running dozens of stochastic rollouts against a single fixture still represents only one evaluation point.

Engineering teams must maintain strict discipline between development and final-test partitions. Development tasks guide daily iteration: tuning agent prompts, calibrating trajectory filters, and optimizing fine-tuning data mixtures. In contrast, final-test tasks provide a one-shot measurement of the finalized system under the declared evaluation protocol. Repeatedly evaluating candidate checkpoints against the final test suite and adjusting data mixtures based on those scores effectively bleeds test information into the training loop, invalidating the test’s neutrality. When an engineering team inspects a final-test failure to diagnose a model flaw or create a training demonstration, they must reclassify that task group as a development asset and sample an entirely fresh, unseen task group to replace it in the test partition.



A partition boundary is an architectural firewall across information paths, not merely a directory tag on a storage volume. Reference patches, ground-truth task specifications, hidden unit tests, and final evaluation outcomes must remain strictly isolated from every upstream system component. They must not appear in trajectory harvesting prompts, vector retrieval indexes, shared cross-session agent memories, synthetic problem generators, or model-based selection filters. If a synthetic generator consumes a held-out test problem, it inevitably weaves the target logic into nominally novel training fixtures. Similarly, if an automated trajectory ranker scores candidates by their downstream performance on the final test suite, it overfits the corpus to that test set without directly copying a single token.
During evaluation, an agent naturally receives problem descriptions and the runtime feedback permitted by the test protocol. For example, a code repair agent may execute local development unit tests to verify its progress, but it must never access the hidden acceptance suite used by the evaluation harness. Furthermore, the evaluation harness must prevent the agent’s code from introspecting on the grading infrastructure or reading test assertions from disk during trial execution. Protecting held-out evidence requires explicitly specifying and auditing these boundary access paths.
Whenever new candidate fixtures enter the curation pipeline, automated ingestion checks compare them against reserved task groups using task identifiers, git commit histories, patch hashes, and structural syntax trees. Any fixture with ambiguous lineage routes directly to a quarantine queue for manual review rather than receiving a fresh, unvetted identifier. Applying redaction, variable renaming, or schema transformations does not break provenance; derived records always inherit their parent fixture’s group assignment. If a post-hoc audit reveals that training data inadvertently leaked information about a final-test task, simply deleting the offending record from the data lake is insufficient. Because the leaked data is already baked into the model weights, the team must invalidate the current checkpoint, reassess all affected evaluation claims, and retrain from a clean corpus snapshot.
Even when local split boundaries are airtight, pipelines remain vulnerable to contamination: the prior appearance of evaluation tasks or solutions within the foundational model’s pretraining web crawl.2 Public benchmarks such as standard competitive programming suites or popular open-source repositories often suffer from pretraining contamination, rendering local zero-shot or few-shot claims suspect. To establish defensible evaluation claims, engineering organizations must develop private evaluation fixtures authored behind internal firewalls, audit repository commit timestamps against model training cutoffs, and explicitly document known data provenance.
2 Benchmark Contamination: Measurement validity degraded significantly when web-scale pretraining corpora grew to encompass public benchmarks, leading to models inadvertently trained directly on the test splits used to grade them (Sainz et al. 2023). Because foundational model providers rarely publish exhaustive token-level manifests of their pretraining data, downstream practitioners must rely on n-gram overlap probes and verbatim memorization heuristics to detect contamination. For an agent trajectory curation pipeline, the only robust defense is structural: maintain proprietary, internal fixtures whose code and solutions have never been published to the open internet, and clearly delineate which benchmark results rely on these private evaluations.

While structural group assignments catch known relationships, heuristic deduplication discovers latent similarities that slip past git lineage or issue tracking. Deduplication serves two critical roles: it flags suspicious cross-partition leaks between training and evaluation splits, and it controls redundancy within the training corpus itself. In foundational language modeling, removing near-duplicate documents substantially curtails verbatim memorization while enhancing downstream generalization (Lee et al. 2022). In agent trajectory curation, however, similarity screening is inherently representation-dependent, and syntactic metrics can mislead in both directions. Two distinct repairs can solve the exact same concurrency race condition with almost zero textual overlap in their patch diffs. Conversely, two trajectories might execute identical shell commands or test invocations yet diverge completely in how they interpret terminal output and choose subsequent recovery actions.

Lee, Katherine, Daphne Ippolito, Andrew Nystrom, Chiyuan Zhang, Douglas Eck, Chris Callison-Burch, and Nicholas Carlini. 2022. “Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better.” Proceedings of the 60th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), 8424–45. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2022.acl-long.577.
3 MinHash: Minwise independent permutations were introduced to detect near-duplicate web pages at search-engine scale, where exhaustive all-pairs comparison is computationally prohibitive (Broder 1997). MinHash maps an arbitrary-sized feature set to a fixed-size signature such that the probability of two signatures matching on any given component equals the Jaccard similarity of their underlying sets. At a fixed signature length, signature storage grows linearly with record count. Indexing narrows the pairs sent for review, but candidate volume and review work still depend on corpus size and similarity structure. 
Broder, A. Z. 1997. “On the Resemblance and Containment of Documents.” Proceedings. Compression and Complexity of SEQUENCES 1997 (Cat. No.97TB100171), 21–29. https://doi.org/10.1109/sequen.1997.666900.
To capture meaningful similarity in agent trajectories, feature extraction must combine textual shingles, parsed code syntax, and tool-call invocation sequences. A shingle is a localized feature extracted from a document or trace, such as an n-gram of command tokens or a sub-tree from an abstract syntax tree (AST). While parsing code into an AST strips away superficial formatting differences, aggressive canonicalization (discarding variable identifiers, literal constants, or statement order) can obscure the subtle difference between a working patch and a broken one. Curation pipelines must therefore version their normalization policies and treat high similarity scores as triggers for contextual inspection rather than automatic deletion. To scale set comparisons across hundreds of thousands of trajectories, pipelines use MinHash (Broder 1997),3 which compresses high-dimensional feature sets into compact signatures using the minimum hash values under random permutations. Because standard MinHash treats feature sets as binary indicators and ignores feature frequencies, workloads that require count sensitivity rely on weighted or bag-based estimators.
For nonempty finite feature sets \(\ScreenedFeatureSet_1\) and \(\ScreenedFeatureSet_2\), the Jaccard similarity \(\JaccardSimilarity(\ScreenedFeatureSet_1,\ScreenedFeatureSet_2)\) and the theoretical MinHash collision probability satisfy:
\[\JaccardSimilarity(\ScreenedFeatureSet_1,\ScreenedFeatureSet_2)=\frac{|\ScreenedFeatureSet_1\cap \ScreenedFeatureSet_2|}{|\ScreenedFeatureSet_1\cup \ScreenedFeatureSet_2|}, \qquad
\Pr\!\left(\min_{\ScreenedFeature\in \ScreenedFeatureSet_1}\MinHashPermutation(\ScreenedFeature)=\min_{\ScreenedFeature\in \ScreenedFeatureSet_2}\MinHashPermutation(\ScreenedFeature)\right)=\JaccardSimilarity(\ScreenedFeatureSet_1,\ScreenedFeatureSet_2).\]
Here, \(\MinHashPermutation\) denotes a uniformly random permutation of the universal feature vocabulary. The minimum hash values under \(\MinHashPermutation\) coincide precisely when the first element of \(\ScreenedFeatureSet_1\cup \ScreenedFeatureSet_2\) ordered by \(\MinHashPermutation\) lies within their intersection \(\ScreenedFeatureSet_1\cap \ScreenedFeatureSet_2\). By drawing \(\MinHashPermutationCount\) independent random permutations, the fraction of matching signature components serves as an unbiased estimator of \(\JaccardSimilarity(\ScreenedFeatureSet_1,\ScreenedFeatureSet_2)\) with estimation variance \(\JaccardSimilarity(1-\JaccardSimilarity)/\MinHashPermutationCount\) (Li and Li 2022). In production implementations, families of pseudo-random universal hash functions approximate true random permutations, and ingestion filters must supply explicit fallback rules for empty feature sets.

Li, Xiaoyun, and Ping Li. 2022. “C-MinHash: Improving Minwise Hashing with Circulant Permutation.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 162: 12857–87.
4 Locality-Sensitive Hashing: A hashing framework where collision probability monotonically increases with item similarity, designed for sublinear approximate nearest-neighbor search in high-dimensional spaces (Indyk and Motwani 1998). Banding MinHash signatures implements LSH for Jaccard similarity. Engineers tune parameters \(\SignatureBandCount\) and \(\LshRowsPerBand\) to control candidate generation against available downstream verification bandwidth; large collision buckets can still make pair-review work grow sharply with corpus size. 
Indyk, Piotr, and Rajeev Motwani. 1998. “Approximate Nearest Neighbors: Towards Removing the Curse of Dimensionality.” Proceedings of the Thirtieth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC), 604–13. https://doi.org/10.1145/276698.276876.
To avoid evaluating pairwise MinHash distances across all records, pipelines index signatures using Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH).4 An LSH index partitions an \(\MinHashPermutationCount\)-dimensional signature into \(\SignatureBandCount\) bands containing \(\LshRowsPerBand\) rows each, such that \(\MinHashPermutationCount = \SignatureBandCount \LshRowsPerBand\). Two trajectories become candidate near-duplicates if their signatures match identically across all \(\LshRowsPerBand\) rows in at least one band. Under the assumption of independent hash components, a pair with Jaccard similarity \(\JaccardSimilarity\) matches across all rows of a single band with probability \(\JaccardSimilarity^{\LshRowsPerBand}\). The probability that the pair collides in at least one of the \(\SignatureBandCount\) bands is:
\[\LshCandidateProbability=1-(1-\JaccardSimilarity^{\LshRowsPerBand})^\SignatureBandCount.\]
This function produces an S-shaped selection curve rather than a discontinuous threshold, with its steep region near the similarity \((1/\SignatureBandCount)^{1/\LshRowsPerBand}\). With the signature length \(\MinHashPermutationCount = \SignatureBandCount \LshRowsPerBand\) held fixed, the two parameters trade against each other. Moving components out of rows and into bands (fewer rows per band, more bands) shifts the curve toward lower similarities, capturing more potential duplicates at the cost of larger collision buckets and more downstream verification. Adding bands without removing rows has the same effect but lengthens every signature.



Banding transforms candidate retrieval into an S-shaped probability curve governed by the number of bands and rows.
With \(\MinHashPermutationCount =\) 128 independent ideal components, the variance \(\JaccardSimilarity(1-\JaccardSimilarity)/\MinHashPermutationCount\) peaks at \(\JaccardSimilarity = 0.5\), so the standard error is at most \(0.5/\sqrt{\MinHashPermutationCount}\), or 0.0442 on the Jaccard scale. Storing each component in 4 bytes requires 512 bytes per signature and 51.2 MB for 100,000 records. While this raw matrix excludes the feature inverted index, metadata storage, and candidate staging buffers, it demonstrates that signature storage overhead is trivial even for large corpora.
The index configuration of 32 bands with 4 rows retrieves a pair with similarity \(\JaccardSimilarity =\) 0.5 with candidate probability 87.3 percent, and candidate retrieval becomes virtually certain at \(\JaccardSimilarity =\) 0.8. Downstream review capacity, whether automated AST diff verification or human inspection, is the true systems bottleneck. Because this configuration routes the vast majority of moderately similar pairs to verification, engineers tune the band geometry to match their review budget. At a fixed signature length, moving components into rows (fewer bands of more rows) raises the effective similarity threshold and suppresses candidate volume, whereas moving them into bands lowers the threshold to catch marginal duplicates.
Engineers must inspect candidate pairs in context before merging task groups or discarding trajectories from the corpus. Trajectory deduplication differs fundamentally from document deduplication: a concise, three-step execution trace is not inherently superior to an extended trajectory demonstrating successful error recovery, and two agents producing identical code patches may have navigated entirely distinct decision paths with unique pedagogical value. By establishing defensible evaluation claims, enforcing task-group isolation invariants, and instituting scalable similarity screening, split design creates the foundation for rigorous curation. With these partition boundaries secured, the admission cascade can evaluate candidate trajectories on their individual merits.




A trajectory record can faithfully capture a bug fix yet remain unusable for imitation learning if its data licensing review is incomplete or its execution trace contains unredacted credentials. Running a heavy, multi-minute containerized test suite before verifying those compliance gates wastes expensive verification slots on candidates the system must ultimately reject. Robust curation architectures separate two concerns: they define the required admission criteria for each learning objective first, and then schedule an economical predicate order to evaluate those criteria second.5
5 Classifier Cascade: An ordered sequence of tests that discards unpromising candidates through early, low-cost evaluations gained prominence in real-time object detection, where a cascade of boosted classifiers rejected background image regions after computing just a few features (Viola and Jones 2001). A curation cascade adopts the same computational economics, but operates under fundamentally different error tolerances. While a visual detector tolerates minor classification errors to maximize evaluation throughput, loosening an admission predicate in a curation cascade pollutes the training distribution and degrades downstream model behavior.

Definition 14.1: Verifier cascade
Verifier cascade, also called an admission cascade, is an ordered sequence of declared verification predicates that screens a candidate trajectory for inclusion in a specific learning dataset, terminating evaluation along that route at the first unsatisfied predicate.

Significance: It governs curation throughput and verification cost. The expected validation work per admitted record equals the reach-weighted sum of predicate costs divided by the overall route yield, the same cost-over-acceptance form as cost per accepted task (equation 1.2). Reordering independent predicates dramatically cuts computation time without altering the final admitted set.
Distinction: Rejection is route-specific. A trajectory that fails the strict criteria of an end-to-end demonstration route remains fully available for error diagnosis, preference pair generation, or rollout fixture synthesis, each governed by its own independent predicate sequence.
Common pitfall: Attempting to accelerate validation by dropping or weakening admission predicates. Relaxing a predicate alters the admitted population rather than optimizing evaluation order, converting an efficiency optimization into an unvetted shift in training criteria.





Table 5 partitions the admission decision into five core predicate families. These families represent logical questions rather than dedicated microservices, and concrete implementations vary depending on the destination artifact: a complete demonstration, an isolated recovery segment, a preference pair, or an evaluation fixture for fresh rollouts.

\(\text{chk}_{\text{record}}\): record adequacy and fidelity

Distinguish a malformed tool call rejected before dispatch from an executed patch; bind test outcomes strictly to the evaluated candidate.


\(\text{chk}_{\text{use}}\): permitted use

For an end-to-end demonstration route, admission requires satisfying the conjunction \(\text{chk}_{\text{record}} \land \text{chk}_{\text{use}} \land \text{chk}_{\text{proc,demo}} \land \text{chk}_{\text{out,demo}} \land \text{chk}_{\text{target,demo}}\). The subscripts emphasize that predicates are consumer-specific: a candidate that fails the final repair objective fails this route’s outcome condition (\(\text{chk}_{\text{out,demo}}\)), whereas an isolated error-recovery segment within that same run can easily satisfy the outcome check of a recovery-learning route. Any action designated as an imitation target must be justifiable strictly from the observation context the agent possessed at that step, without lookahead leakage or hindsight annotations injected from subsequent checks. These target designations determine the token-level loss masks during supervised fine-tuning.


↪ Token-level loss masking and target designation mechanisms are operationalized in Observation Loss Masking.
Engineers must separate record validity from action validity. A log that accurately captures a malformed tool call and the runtime’s immediate pre-dispatch refusal satisfies record adequacy (\(\text{chk}_{\text{record}}\)); the logging subsystem functioned correctly even though the model made an error. Conversely, missing environment observations or disordered tool responses render a trajectory inadequate for imitation learning, even if the candidate code ultimately passed all tests. Pipelines can route truncated or imperfect records to diagnostic stores for offline failure analysis, but must never package them as valid behavioral demonstrations.
A preference route adds the shared-context and justified-ordering conditions that define a preference comparison (section 14.2.3) to its outcome and target predicates. Until paired with an appropriate winning rollout, a failed attempt remains merely an unassigned comparison candidate. For reinforcement learning pipelines, curation delivers versioned task definitions, deterministic environment fixtures, and automated grading harnesses for fresh rollouts rather than static records of historical failures. While these downstream applications share uniform requirements for permitted use (\(\text{chk}_{\text{use}}\)) and record adequacy (\(\text{chk}_{\text{record}}\)), they diverge sharply in how they evaluate outcomes (\(\text{chk}_{\text{out}}\)) and assign target labels (\(\text{chk}_{\text{target}}\)).
Each predicate evaluates to one of four canonical states: pass, fail, pending, or unknown, aligning with the four-verdict rule formalized in The four-verdict rule. An explicit fail immediately halts evaluation along that route and keeps the record for diagnosis or another route (figure 2). A missing or timed-out check never defaults to a pass; unverified candidates move to an unresolved quarantine holding queue, tagged with the missing evidence and execution logs required for resolution. Curation telemetry tracks the counts of evaluated, admitted, rejected, and unresolved records per route, ensuring that trajectories redirected to diagnostic pools never inflate the reported yield of production demonstrations.






Figure 2: One Admission Route: A collection record meets the five predicates in execution order and is admitted to the route only if every one passes. The first result other than a pass stops that route’s checks. A failure rejects the record for this route without deleting it, and a pending or unknown result goes to an unresolved hold instead of counting as a pass. Other routes evaluate the same record under their own conditions.






The grading boundary established for evaluation applies with equal force during data curation, where a security breach causes far greater damage than a miscounted evaluation metric. If an agent tampers with grading harnesses during evaluation, it merely skews a benchmark score; if it tampers with grading during data collection, the pipeline ingests corrupt demonstrations that train subsequent models to reproduce the exploit. Listing 1 illustrates a classic failure mode: an agent resolves a failing test suite by rewriting the test assertion rather than fixing the underlying race condition.

--- a/tests/test_pool_wakeup.py

@@ def test_waiter_wakes_after_release():

-    waiter = pool.acquire_async()
-    pool.release(pool.acquire())

Replacing the assertion generates a zero exit code from the test runner while leaving the concurrency bug untouched. In a robust cascade, this patch fails on two separate counts: the candidate diff violates the task’s allowed-path policy (failing process condition \(\text{chk}_{\text{proc}}\)), and running the code against clean, unedited test harnesses reproduces the deadlock (failing outcome condition \(\text{chk}_{\text{out}}\)). An agent’s self-reported success or passing local exit code must never override authoritative verifiers.

Definition 14.2: Test-tampering defense
Test-tampering defense encompasses the architectural controls, permission boundaries, and isolation mechanisms that protect evaluation harnesses, test inputs, and verification results from modification or subversion by the candidate solution or the acting agent.

Significance: It preserves the validity of the outcome predicate \(\text{chk}_{\text{out}}\). Because downstream fine-tuning trains subsequent policy checkpoints on admitted trajectories, an undetected test bypass is actively reinforced across training iterations rather than isolated as an anomalous benchmark trial.
Distinction: Tamper defense protects the integrity of the measurement, not its semantic breadth. A tamper-proof test suite still evaluates only what its assertions cover; verifying whether a passing solution generalizes appropriately remains the responsibility of the target suitability predicate \(\text{chk}_{\text{target}}\).
Common pitfall: Relying solely on in-tree file permissions or clean interpreter processes. If candidate code executes in the same operating-system container or environment as the test runner, it can manipulate runtime assertion hooks, spoof return codes, or inspect privileged test fixtures in memory.



The failure modes that tamper defense addresses are not hypothetical; they have been documented in production frontier models during agentic training.

War Story 14.1: Special-cased tests in agentic coding (2025)Context: Anthropic’s system card for Claude 3.7 Sonnet documents strategic evaluation gaming observed during agentic coding evaluations (Anthropic 2025).
Mechanism: When faced with difficult programming tasks after repeated unsuccessful attempts, the model occasionally resorted to reward hacking, exploiting discrepancies between the empirical reward signal and true task completion. Specifically, the model hardcoded expected return values for known test cases or modified unit test assertions directly so that the suite matched its incorrect implementation.
Impact: Standard user testing failed to catch the behavior because it appeared rarely during straightforward interactions, emerging primarily after extended, multi-turn troubleshooting cycles in specialized programming sandboxes.
Fix: The team deployed transcript classifiers to detect gaming patterns in training runs and applied targeted mitigations prior to model deployment. For production agentic environments, the report advises monitoring for repetitive edit-and-test loops on individual files, code comments indicating test-specific overrides, and unauthorized diffs against test suites.
Systems lesson: An exit code produced inside an execution environment accessible to untrusted agent code is unverified telemetry. A curation pipeline that blindly admits trajectories based on local test passes ingests the exact gaming behavior that monitoring seeks to eradicate. Tamper verification must therefore run as an immutable gate in the cascade before any trajectory can serve as a training target.



Anthropic. 2025. Claude 3.7 Sonnet System Card.
Three defense-in-depth mechanisms place verifier execution beyond the reach of candidate code, extending containment beneath the model (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-zero-trust-sandboxing}\)) into the evaluation harness itself:

Out-of-tree test fixtures: Authoritative evaluation tests reside strictly outside the candidate’s writable workspace, mounted into the container as read-only volumes or injected by the supervisory harness only after the candidate repository snapshot is cryptographically hashed and frozen.
Protected-path manifests: The supervisory pipeline computes the repository diff against the base commit and checks all modified files against a protected-path manifest. Any unauthorized modification to test suites, continuous integration configurations, or build dependencies immediately fails process predicate \(\text{chk}_{\text{proc}}\), irrespective of the test runner’s exit code.
Isolated runner supervision: The test harness executes within a fresh container or sandboxed sub-process orchestrated by a supervisory daemon. Candidate code running in the application runtime cannot monkey-patch assertion libraries, overwrite runtime exception hooks, or capture testing tokens.

Each mechanism is necessary, yet none alone is sufficient. Even with read-only file systems, untrusted code executed during evaluation could exhaust file descriptors, consume excessive memory, or exploit timing side channels to alter execution outcomes. Full execution isolation of the grading harness is therefore mandatory.
A task’s patch-admission policy explicitly defines permitted edits, accommodating legitimate development workflows where tasks require adding regression tests or updating package manifests. Post-hoc audit logs record all execution telemetry but cannot substitute for preventative sandbox boundaries. Containment and authorization checks must always precede the execution of untrusted code, regardless of how other admission predicates are scheduled.
When evaluating non-deterministic tasks, verification harnesses must enforce a declared repetition protocol that specifies environmental seeds, maximum retry bounds, and aggregation rules for inconsistent trials. Repeatedly running a flaky test until it passes once merely samples from favorable noise. If a defective candidate passes a flaky test with probability \(\AttemptPassProbability\) per run, rerunning it up to \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) times reports a pass with probability \(1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount\), the at-least-one form of pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\) applied here to false passes. Similarly, timeouts must be recorded as unresolved outcomes (pending or unknown) and routed to an inspection queue rather than silently treated as deterministic model errors or transient infrastructure hiccups.



For a given admission route, let \(\text{chk}_1,\ldots,\text{chk}_{\AdmissionCheckCount}\) represent the sequence of admission predicates in execution order. Define \(\CheckPassProbability_i=\Pr(\text{chk}_i\text{ passes}\mid \text{chk}_1,\ldots,\text{chk}_{i-1}\text{ pass})\) as the conditional pass probability of predicate \(\text{chk}_i\), with \(\CheckPassProbability_1\) denoting the unconditional pass probability of the initial check. Let \(\CheckSlotTime_i\) represent the expected verifier slot time conditional on reaching that check, measured in seconds. Under short-circuit evaluation, which stops at the first non-passing predicate, the expected verification time per attempted record is:
\[\ExpectedCheckingTime=\sum_{i=1}^{\AdmissionCheckCount} \CheckSlotTime_i\prod_{j=1}^{\AdmissionCheckIndex-1}\CheckPassProbability_j, \tag{1}\]
where the empty product evaluates to one. The overall route yield \(\AdmissionRouteYield\) represents the joint probability that a candidate passes all \(\AdmissionCheckCount\) predicates:
\[\AdmissionRouteYield=\Pr(\text{chk}_1\land\cdots\land \text{chk}_{\AdmissionCheckCount})=\prod_{i=1}^{\AdmissionCheckCount}\CheckPassProbability_i.\]
For routes with nonzero yield (\(\AdmissionRouteYield > 0\)), the ratio \(\ExpectedCheckingTime/\AdmissionRouteYield\) represents the expected verification slot time invested per admitted trajectory. Here, the yield \(\AdmissionRouteYield\) fulfills the role of acceptance probability in the cost-per-accepted-task formulation of equation 1.2. Because this ratio represents expectations across large sample limits, a batch with zero admitted records should report total slot time consumed rather than an undefined ratio. Upstream rollout generation, retry loops, and downstream storage costs are accounted outside this verifier cascade.
Permuting the execution order of these predicates preserves the exact admitted population, provided their definitions, inputs, and evaluations remain unchanged. However, conditional pass probabilities must be re-estimated for each permutation because each check observes a different pre-filtered candidate subset. In practice, operational dependencies and containment constraints restrict permissible evaluation orders; for example, data governance and containment audits must always run before executing untrusted code in sandbox environments.
When two adjacent predicates \(\text{chk}_\FirstAdjacentCheckIndex\) and \(\text{chk}_\SecondAdjacentCheckIndex\) are statistically independent, identifying the optimal execution sequence admits an exact closed form. Evaluating \(\text{chk}_\FirstAdjacentCheckIndex\) before \(\text{chk}_\SecondAdjacentCheckIndex\) incurs an expected local cost of \(\FirstAdjacentCheckSlotTime + \FirstAdjacentCheckPassProbability \SecondAdjacentCheckSlotTime\). Reversing the order to evaluate \(\text{chk}_\SecondAdjacentCheckIndex\) before \(\text{chk}_\FirstAdjacentCheckIndex\) incurs \(\SecondAdjacentCheckSlotTime + \SecondAdjacentCheckPassProbability \FirstAdjacentCheckSlotTime\). Evaluating \(\text{chk}_\FirstAdjacentCheckIndex\) first is strictly more economical whenever \(\FirstAdjacentCheckSlotTime + \FirstAdjacentCheckPassProbability \SecondAdjacentCheckSlotTime < \SecondAdjacentCheckSlotTime + \SecondAdjacentCheckPassProbability \FirstAdjacentCheckSlotTime\), which simplifies directly to:
\[\frac{\FirstAdjacentCheckSlotTime}{1-\FirstAdjacentCheckPassProbability} < \frac{\SecondAdjacentCheckSlotTime}{1-\SecondAdjacentCheckPassProbability}. \tag{2}\]
Consequently, the optimal evaluation sequence ranks independent predicates in ascending order of their cost per rejection, \(\CheckSlotTime_i / (1 - \CheckPassProbability_i)\), executing the most cost-effective rejection filter first. This ordering rule corresponds to the predicate-ranking algorithms developed for relational database query optimizers handling costly user-defined selection filters (Hellerstein and Stonebraker 1993).6
6 Predicate Rank: Relational database query optimizers encountered this challenge when selection predicates began executing computationally expensive user-defined functions. Ordering filters purely by selectivity executed heavy evaluations on tuples that a cheaper predicate would have discarded. Sorting independent filters by rank, defined as per-row cost divided by rejection probability \((1 - \CheckPassProbability_i)\), minimizes total execution work, mirroring the exchange argument in equation 2. In agent curation cascades, where verification steps range from sub-millisecond AST audits to multi-minute integration tests and human evaluations, rank ordering dictates where the majority of the verification compute budget is spent.

Learned scoring models can rank candidate trajectories for manual review or sub-sample from a pool of eligible examples to optimize diversity or stylistic conciseness. For instance, process reward models evaluate individual reasoning steps and intermediate tool calls rather than relying solely on terminal execution outcomes (Uesato et al. 2022; Lightman et al. 2024). While a step-level reward signal highlights likely points of failure, pinpointing the root causal error still requires retrospective human or symbolic review. Furthermore, filtering heavily for trajectory brevity alters the underlying data distribution in subtle ways; curation pipelines must not inadvertently purge the very multi-turn recovery sequences that the model needs to learn robust error-correction.
When tasks require evaluating open-ended prose, user interactions, or design quality, human raters or judge models supply scores governed by explicit rubrics and calibration standards. The verification asymmetry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)) bounds what such a score can do inside a cascade. A learned assessment can rank candidates or supply scoped evidence for one qualitative criterion, but it is not an independent guarantee, and when valid records are rare, even a small false-accept rate fills the admitted set with invalid ones. The judge’s input must therefore be limited to the evidence its criterion names and kept away from anything the candidate wrote to influence its grader. Deterministic verifiers require identical scoping. Every verifier execution must persist metadata identifying the assessor version, rubric hash, extracted evidence, confidence scores, and explicit abstentions. Under no circumstances may an exceptionally high qualitative rating override an unsatisfied deterministic predicate.


↩︎ Qualitative rubrics and grader calibration standards are established in Calibration of qualitative judgment.
Iterated selection against automated scorers concentrates grader blind spots. Repeatedly selecting training data against a learned proxy score initially improves output quality, but excessive optimization eventually leads to proxy collapse: the proxy score continues to rise while true downstream task quality deteriorates (Gao et al. 2023). This is the divergence that best-of-N selection produces against an imperfect check at inference time (Selection pressure on imperfect checks), except that curation writes the winners into the next policy’s weights. When subsequent policy generations train on these curated datasets, idiosyncratic biases in the ranker become baked into model behavior. Mitigating this feedback loop requires periodic double-blind audits of both accepted and rejected records, continuous recalibration against held-out ground truth data that is never used for training, and mandatory re-scoring whenever policy architectures or task domains shift. Any data augmentation or trajectory transformation requires fresh verification of its modified payload and token masks, a provenance boundary that section 14.9 develops.

A route is defensible when each predicate’s verdict and the order of checking can both be justified.

Incomplete outcome: A new collection run has only a targeted pass for its candidate under repair_accept_v1. Decide which route it can enter now, and name the evidence the full demonstration route still needs.

Pricing the cascade

Order estimate: Retaining the notebook’s independence and fixed-duration premises, suppose the process audit \(\text{chk}_{\text{proc}}\) instead costs 2 s and passes 95 percent of records, with \(\text{chk}_{\text{out}}\) unchanged at 8 s and 40 percent. By evaluating trajectories through staged, consumer-specific cascades rather than forcing all data through a monolithic cleanliness filter, the curation infrastructure yields precisely verified datasets tailored to distinct imitation, preference, and rollout objectives. Verifying clean executions, however, solves only half the data problem: production agents inevitably encounter disruptions, and training policies to recover requires capturing and curating traces that contain mistakes without teaching models to repeat them.




When an agent operates in real environments, failures are inevitable. Consider an execution trace where an agent issues a malformed tool call, receives a rejection from the environment runtime, and subsequently inspects the schema to produce a successful patch. A naive curation pipeline might discard this trace because it contains a failed step, or scrub the error to make the agent appear prescient. Doing so discards the most valuable training signal in autonomous systems: learning how to recover from an imperfect prefix. The curation cascade can admit the successful repair while preserving the original misstep as necessary context. The core systems questions then become which recovery trajectories to harvest, how to curate them safely, and how much training capacity to allocate to them.
A training corpus composed solely of pristine, error-free trajectories teaches an agent how to act only when prior steps succeeded flawlessly. In production, however, stochastic tool outputs, transient network glitches, and early reasoning missteps inevitably push an agent off the nominal path. Once off that path, a model trained only on clean prefixes faces states it never saw in training, and over a long horizon a recoverable detour becomes a failed task. This distribution mismatch7 drives the need for recovery demonstrations. The curation system’s practical responsibility is to capture, validate, and package these recovery episodes with their conditioning evidence fully intact.
7 Compounding Imitation Error: A policy trained only on states visited by an expert can turn a per-step error rate \(\PerStepErrorRate\) (the per-step error rate of horizon compounding, equation 1.1) into as many as \(\TurnHorizon^2\PerStepErrorRate\) mistakes over an \(\TurnHorizon\)-step task, because an early error exposes the policy to states absent from its training distribution. Interactively querying an expert on learner-visited states, the core mechanism of DAgger, restores an error bound that scales linearly in \(\TurnHorizon\) (Ross et al. 2011). Recovery demonstrations serve as the offline curation counterpart: they inject supervised repair targets on the flawed state prefixes that direct-success collection inevitably omits.

Definition 14.3: Recovery demonstration
A recovery demonstration is a curated trajectory record or isolated sequence segment that pairs the context of an operational disruption (a model mistake, environment fault, or partial observation) with an action assessed as correct under the task specification and runtime authority boundaries.

Significance: Recovery demonstrations directly address long-horizon execution stability. Under horizon compounding (equation 1.1), any step-level error that the policy can successfully remediate becomes a temporary detour rather than an irrecoverable task failure. Direct-success harvesting systematically starves the training distribution of these pivotal recovery branches.
Distinction: An appropriate recovery action depends on context: it may diagnose an exception, retry with corrected parameters, back off, or hand off control to a human supervisor. It does not demand that the agent heroically overcome impossible environment outages or exceed its security clearance to finish the task.
Common pitfall: Treating every token in an eventually successful trajectory as a positive imitation target, thereby inadvertently teaching the model to repeat the initial mistake.





Direct success, recovery, and negative are descriptive behavioral labels rather than blanket permissions for training. A single extended trajectory may begin with straightforward progress, encounter an unexpected environment error, execute a clean recovery, and later stall on an unrelated tool failure. Discarding that entire trajectory wastes genuine engineering signal; conversely, training uncritically on all its tokens teaches the model to replicate its bugs. The predicates of table 5 already separate the two kinds of decision: record adequacy and permitted use are shared across routes, while the process, outcome, and target predicates are set by the consumer, so a role label only says which consumer-specific checks a segment might pass.
Table 8 maps these behavioral categories to their valid learning applications, emphasizing that taxonomy labels describe behavioral evidence rather than granting unconditional admission.

A hard negative is an action or plan that appears plausible under surface-level heuristics, such as generating valid syntax or matching expected keyword patterns, yet fails rigorous functional validation. Its difficulty stems from this superficial plausibility. However, pinpointing the precise moment of failure in an agentic trace is subtle. A failed assertion downstream confirms that an error occurred, but it rarely reveals the initial root cause. Similarly, repeated tool calls may suggest an infinite loop, yet an iterative polling loop might be entirely justified under asynchronous conditions. Robust curation systems therefore record, for each candidate divergence step, the failure signal that implicates it and an explicit note that the step is uncertain, rather than asserting an unverified divergence point.
Engineering teams also often assume that any recorded negative can be paired immediately with a success to train a preference objective, or replayed as a baseline for reinforcement learning against a verifiable reward. This assumption is hazardous. A negative becomes a comparison only under the shared-context condition of section 14.2.3, which a success that benefited from a different prompt, an extra hint, or updated tool outputs does not meet. A reinforcement learning baseline needs a resettable fixture rather than the stored record.

Systems Perspective 14.1: A recorded mistake is context, not a targetA pervasive misconception in trajectory engineering is that an imitation training set must consist exclusively of pristine, error-free transcripts. In reality, a curated training dataset consists of complete conversational contexts coupled with explicit target masks, and these two components serve fundamentally different purposes.
A flawed model response should receive no direct positive imitation target loss. Nevertheless, that erroneous response must remain in the prompt history if subsequent recovery actions are to make any sense; a correction is meaningful only in the context of the error it resolves. Conversely, an execution trace that ultimately timed out or failed an integration test often contains early sub-tasks solved with exemplary precision. The curation pipeline marks which spans represent valid targets and which represent conditioning context; the loss-masking subsystem then omits their direct next-token loss terms while retaining them as conditioning during fine-tuning. Masking errors out of the loss while retaining them in the attention context teaches the model how to react to a failure without training it to generate one.





To see how target selection operates in practice, trace a concrete collection run, collection_run_r19_01, executing task pool_repair_01 inside test environment pool_fixture_v1. The run yields workspace candidate ws_r20 and captures raw trace trace_r19_01. The numbering differs because workspace identifiers count candidate revisions (ws_r20 is the revision after the evaluation trial’s ws_r19), while run and trace identifiers count collection batches. In this run, end-to-end evaluation confirms that the candidate satisfies acceptance specification repair_accept_v1, fulfilling all process constraints, resource ceilings, and residual cleanup duties.
The run belongs to a campaign whose declared learning use is recovery from harness refusals. Unlike the truncated observation that opened the chapter, this behavior is collected on the premise, recorded in the collection manifest, that the ladder’s probes left it with the model. Supplying the schema in the delivered context and validating proposals against a strict schema still produced malformed edits that the runtime had to refuse. What remains to teach is the response after a refusal.
The event sequence illustrates the recovery dynamics:

Event e1 delivers the task prompt, tool definitions, and repository context.
At event e2, the model generates a file edit containing a malformed argument. Because the tool runtime validates inputs locally before dispatch, it rejects the request immediately; the trace faithfully records this refusal without falsely logging an applied write.
At event e3, the model recognizes the syntax rejection, requests the API schema documentation, and reads the returned specification.
At event e4, the model issues a corrected, schema-compliant edit. The tool enforces an atomic version check alongside the update rather than relying on a stale prior read.
At event e5, the harness runs the required checks on the edited workspace and returns their summary as an observation.
At event e6, the model summarizes the validated changes, documents the patch scope, and concludes the session.

Under curation policy repair_accept_v1, an initial syntax rejection that is promptly diagnosed and corrected is permissible. A target-selection manifest isolates the actions worth imitating without altering the actual sequence of events:

The underlying source trace continues to preserve the original task prompt, tool definitions, intermediate observations, and evaluation logs. Notice that target selection flags only the reviewed policy generation tokens within events e3, e4, and e6, rather than every token generated across the environment interaction. The rejected proposal (e2) and test output (e5) remain in the sequence as conditioning context, providing the causal backdrop that makes the agent’s schema lookup and repair intelligible. An end-to-end task success does not automatically justify supervising every intermediate action; each selected step must represent a sound decision conditioned on what the agent knew at that exact juncture. Set beside the other two record roles, the recovery record sits between a direct success, whose supported responses can all be targets, and a hard negative, whose deficient response is never one (figure 3).

A hard-negative candidate looks adequate under a targeted check and fails a required one. Its deficient response is never an imitation target, and where it went wrong is recorded with its basis rather than fixed at an exact step.



When only a localized recovery window contains sound evidence, the curation harness can admit that isolated segment while marking broader task outcomes as unverified. Furthermore, if post-processing sanitizes credentials or strips sensitive data into trace_r19_01_redacted_v1, the curation pipeline must revalidate target spans against the modified tokens. Pruning the malformed call, inserting future validation outputs into an early prompt, or truncating intermediate observations fundamentally alters the causal reasoning problem the model is being trained to solve.



In production, natural execution occasionally exposes an agent to network drops, service timeouts, and tool errors. However, relying solely on spontaneous operational failures leaves massive blind spots in the training distribution. Systematic fault injection8 proactively bridges these coverage gaps. A rigorous collection protocol logs the injection configuration version, the targeted tool invocation or observation stream, the simulated system state, and the expected remediation policy. Crucially, fault injection operates strictly within established security constraints: injecting a network timeout or file lock grants the agent no auxiliary privileges to install unapproved packages, escalate filesystem permissions, or circumvent human approval barriers. Each condition in table 9 names the causal distinction the fixture must preserve and the response a curator should assess.

Curation adopts the methodological rigor rather than the live production venue. Faults are introduced within versioned, hermetic test fixtures where every injected condition is recorded and environment semantics remain deterministic. This ensures that synthesized demonstrations teach genuine fault recovery rather than learning to exploit idiosyncrasies of the simulation harness.

Consider the lost-acknowledgment scenario in table 9. When a mock harness drops an acknowledgment after committing a mutating remote procedure call, the simulated environment must faithfully retain the side effects of that committed call in its subsequent state. If the mock were to return a connection reset while silently rolling back the server state to a clean slate, it would misrepresent the distributed systems challenge, teaching the agent a naive retry pattern that causes double-execution bugs in production. Replay determinism requires that subsequent model actions receive state observations strictly consistent with prior mutations.
Similarly, an engineering team must differentiate between tasks designed for autonomous remediation and those designed for graceful degradation. A recovery objective requires an authorized, reachable remediation path within the test environment; a safe-stopping objective, by contrast, deliberately closes all remediation paths to teach the agent to halt cleanly and notify an operator. These represent two distinct behavioral objectives with separate evaluation rubrics. Reliability coverage must therefore be tracked separately across unprompted agent mistakes and declared synthetic faults, while documenting any production failure modes that the collection fixture cannot replicate.



Because a recovery trajectory contains multiple diagnostic cycles, failed attempts, and environment feedbacks, it is substantially longer than a direct-success path. Consequently, the fraction of recovery trajectories in a dataset does not equal its fraction of stored disk tokens, nor does it equal its fraction of active training tokens. Curation accounting begins with a global repository of retained trajectories, from which downstream pipelines sample subsets tailored to specific training artifacts. A single retained trace may supply conditioning context to an imitation fine-tuning corpus while contributing preference pairs to a reward modeling set; in both cases, it represents a single underlying task execution.



One recovery class, three shares: records, stored tokens, targets.
For a trajectory category \(\TrajectoryCategoryIndex\), let \(\CategoryRecordCount_j\) denote the number of retained records, \(\MeanStoredTokensPerRecord^{(\TrajectoryCategoryIndex)}\) denote the average stored tokens per record under the active tokenizer, and \(\MeanTargetTokensPerRecord_j\) denote the average selected target tokens per record admitted into a specific imitation fine-tuning artifact. The total stored token volume \(\StoredTokenVolume_j\) and total target token volume \(\TargetTokenVolume_j\) are:
\[\StoredTokenVolume_j=\CategoryRecordCount_j\MeanStoredTokensPerRecord^{(\TrajectoryCategoryIndex)},\qquad \TargetTokenVolume_j=\CategoryRecordCount_j\MeanTargetTokensPerRecord_j.\]
The stored token share measures \(\StoredTokenVolume_j\) relative to the aggregate token footprint of the entire repository, whereas the target token share measures \(\TargetTokenVolume_j\) relative to the active supervision tokens across the training dataset. This distinction carries severe systems implications: processed tokens (context plus targets) dictate transformer attention compute and memory bandwidth during forward-backward passes, whereas selected target tokens determine which direct supervised loss terms enter the objective. Gradients from those terms still pass through context representations. Specifying a dataset mixture in one metric while budgeting accelerator infrastructure in another leads to severe scheduling mismatches, particularly when multi-turn serialization or prefix caching enters the pipeline.

Systems insight: Always formulate training mixtures in terms of target tokens while budgeting accelerator compute and memory in terms of processed context tokens. The operational multiplier separating these two metrics is the context-to-target ratio: 9.25 stored context tokens per target token for recovery traces, compared to 6 for direct successes. Increasing the recovery proportion inflates processed context volume far faster than supervised gradient signal. An engineering team that configures a mixture purely by record count will request a 25 percent recovery ratio but will end up committing 44.97 percent of repository storage and 49.70 percent of processed training tokens to recovery records. Naive multi-turn serialization that repeatedly unrolls conversational prefixes amplifies this computational overhead even further.





While token accounting quantifies the compute and memory footprint of a corpus, empirical mixture experiments determine its practical operational value. A mixture experiment establishes a fixed evaluation protocol, selects a baseline architecture, and evaluates training cohorts across controlled recovery ratios. For example, an ablation study might compare a direct-success baseline against recovery-augmented corpora while holding task domains, base model checkpoints, target-masking criteria, and total training schedules constant. Curation engineers must track trajectory deduplication and replacement meticulously: expanding the recovery fraction under a constrained training budget inevitably reduces coverage of nominal, direct-path tasks.
Rigorous experimental designs declare their budgeting units explicitly and report performance across both metrics. If an experiment fixes total supervised target tokens, the recovery-heavy training arm processes substantially more prompt context tokens, increasing training wall-clock time and FLOPs. Conversely, if an experiment fixes total processed tokens, the recovery-heavy arm receives fewer supervised target updates. When hardware budgets or training schedules represent hard constraints, engineers must evaluate trade-offs directly against wall-clock training time or financial cost.
Model selection proceeds by screening candidate mixtures on a held-out development suite and validating the top configurations against an isolated evaluation benchmark. To prevent high-level aggregate metrics from masking systematic failure modes, evaluation reports must decompose outcomes across nominal workflows, synthesized fault conditions, and out-of-distribution transfer tasks before synthesizing composite scores. Diagnostic tracking must measure end-to-end task completion alongside hallucinated tool claims, superfluous execution steps, clean termination decisions, and cumulative API token expenditure.
Once an optimal mixture is established, its parameters are locked into the corpus manifest, the machine-readable, versioned record that publishes a corpus and that a trainer reads to learn what each member is and how it may be used.9 The mixture is only one of its contents. The manifest records the immutable provenance of the published dataset: input trajectory pool identifiers, selection filter versions, sampling weight distributions, token accounting denominators, test coverage matrices, and audit logs. Its per-record lineage and its publication are developed in section 14.9 and section 14.10.2. Deploying a model trained on this manifest alters the operational distribution of subsequent production trajectories, feeding fresh failure modes and successful recoveries back into the harvesting pipeline. That return path closes a loop in which the policy being improved also generates the data that improves it.
9 Dataset Documentation: Documenting datasets via structured records that detail their creation, composition, collection boundaries, and intended operational envelope originated by analogy to hardware datasheets in electronic engineering (Gebru et al. 2021). A corpus manifest serves as the machine-verifiable incarnation of this standard for agentic systems: its attributes bind cryptographically to dataset versions, filter code, and empirical validation logs, enabling downstream training pipelines to verify corpus invariants automatically rather than relying on informal documentation.

Corpus selection directly shapes the distribution of behaviors the next model generation learns. Consider a curation round for an automated connection-pool repair agent that retains only straight-line, nominal executions while discarding messier traces where the agent recovers from misleading test diagnostics. Fine-tuning on that corpus reinforces straightforward repairs but leaves recovery capabilities unimproved. In the subsequent iteration, a higher nominal acceptance rate masks that vulnerability rather than rectifying it. To maintain system reliability across iterations, curators must track three distinct signals each round: what the current policy sampled, what the curation cascade retained, and how the resulting model performs under independent, held-out evaluation.


A generate–select–train loop begins with a versioned policy sampling executions across a suite of task fixtures within a defined compute budget. A validation cascade routes the resulting trajectories to their respective destinations: clean demonstrations feed supervised imitation buffers, branched pairs populate preference datasets, and unresolved traces enter diagnostic storage. Training on these curated records produces a candidate policy, which offline evaluation tests to decide whether it should become the generator for the next collection cycle. That promotion decision remains an internal development step rather than a production release. Recording attempted, rejected, and unverified traces alongside retained examples guarantees that an apparent gain in corpus quality reflects genuine policy improvement rather than an artificially relaxed acceptance filter.
Selecting sampled successes for imitation is rejection-sampling fine-tuning.10 The Self-Taught Reasoner (STaR) demonstrates this pattern in bootstrapped reasoning by generating candidate rationales, retaining those that yield correct answers, fine-tuning on them, and using ground-truth answers to provide rationales after failed initial attempts (Zelikman et al. 2022). An automated verifier confirms that an execution satisfies its declared acceptance criteria, but trajectory review must still assess whether the intermediate tool calls and intermediate states reflect robust problem-solving worth imitating.
10 Expert Iteration: The generate–select–train loop predates language models. In expert iteration, a search procedure guided by the current network produces stronger decisions than the network alone, the network is trained to imitate them, and the improved network then guides the next round of search (Anthony et al. 2017). Rejection-sampling fine-tuning replaces the search with repeated sampling and the expert’s judgment with a check, which is why the check’s blind spots become the loop’s habits. 
Anthony, Thomas, Zheng Tian, and David Barber. 2017. “Thinking Fast and Slow with Deep Learning and Tree Search.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 30.
Learning does not require mixed outcomes across every task. An all-success batch supplies prime imitation targets, demonstrating efficient paths through complex tools. Conversely, an all-failure collection yields no end-to-end demonstrations under a success filter, yet it still offers valuable intermediate artifacts: corrective segments that isolate where an execution derailed, justified comparisons for preference modeling, and new failure traces that can be promoted to regression fixtures. Group-relative training objectives, by contrast, rely on within-group contrast. Such an objective scores each rollout by its reward minus the mean reward of the rollouts sampled for the same fixture, so when all rollouts receive identical rewards every score is zero and the group contributes no reward-surrogate gradient.


↪ Group relative policy optimization, which scores each rollout against the other rollouts sampled for the same task, is developed in Group Relative Policy Optimization.
The sampling budget required to harvest these different data types follows from the per-attempt pass rate. Suppose the collection policy succeeds on a fixture with probability \(\AttemptPassProbability\) per attempt, with each of the \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) attempts executed independently. A simple success filter extracts a demonstration from the fixture if at least one attempt succeeds, an event that occurs with probability \(1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount\). This expected yield sets the baseline compute cost per retained trajectory when the collector keeps at most one success from each full batch. For preference comparisons based on binary task acceptance and group-relative objectives with binary rewards, useful within-group contrast requires at least one success and at least one failure. Subtracting both the all-failure probability \((1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount\) and the all-success probability \(\AttemptPassProbability^{\IndependentAttemptCount}\) yields the informative-task fraction:
\[\InformativeTaskFraction(\AttemptPassProbability,\IndependentAttemptCount)=1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount-\AttemptPassProbability^{\IndependentAttemptCount}. \tag{3}\]
With 8 attempts, a fixture the policy solves 5 percent of the time yields a success with probability only 0.34, requiring an average of about 24 attempts to harvest a single successful trajectory. That same fixture forms a mixed group of successes and failures with probability 0.34. At 50 percent, where the task is moderately difficult, the mixed fraction reaches 0.99, providing abundant pairwise contrast. When the pass rate reaches 95 percent, nearly every fixture yields a success, but the mixed fraction drops back to 0.34 because batches rarely include a failing attempt. Crucially, equation 3 measures contrast rather than general utility. All-success groups remain valid demonstrations for imitation learning, whereas Zero-contrast groups applies the \(\AttemptPassProbability^{\IndependentAttemptCount}\) and \((1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount\) terms to isolate groups whose uniform rewards offer zero reward-surrogate gradient in group-relative optimization.



Easy fixtures yield successes most often; mid-difficulty fixtures yield contrast most often.
Collection difficulty is fundamentally a resource allocation decision. Hard fixtures cost about 24 attempts per harvested success, but they force the agent into unfamiliar execution paths and expose missing recovery behaviors. Easy fixtures cost almost nothing per success, acting as low-cost regression anchors that preserve core competencies. For rare or mission-critical task families, low harvest yields represent an acceptable engineering expense necessary to maintain comprehensive coverage. Storing the exact sampling and retention policies directly alongside the corpus ensures that distribution shifts remain auditable across retraining cycles.



In an evolving agent system, staleness measures architectural incompatibility rather than chronological age. A trajectory generated by an older policy can remain an exemplary demonstration if the underlying tools and environment semantics are unchanged. Conversely, a trace generated minutes ago is stale if recorded against a deprecated tool schema or evaluated by a flawed grader. Trajectory stores prevent silent corruption by recording four explicit provenance fields: the generating policy, the environment fixture, the tool interface schema, and the grading criteria. When verification criteria evolve, the pipeline triggers automated re-evaluation. When tool schemas change, existing trajectories must undergo schema migration and revalidation. Finally, as policy capability advances, the pipeline focuses sampling on the novel edge cases and failure modes the updated agent actually encounters.
Iterative filtering also risks coverage narrowing. Because strategies that successfully cleared earlier filters appear more frequently in fine-tuning data, the policy is conditioned to reproduce those specific paths, sampling them even more heavily in subsequent rounds. Left unchecked, recursive training on self-generated outputs degrades distributional breadth, mirroring the model-collapse phenomena analyzed by Shumailov et al. (2024). In production architectures, allowing a model’s outputs to dictate its future training distribution introduces the classic hidden feedback loop identified by Sculley et al. (2015), quietly compounding technical debt across generations. Automated verifiers reject failures covered by their declared checks, but filtering alone cannot break the self-referential loop; engineering teams must track and bound this drift through explicit diversity metrics.
Coverage narrowing manifests in three observable telemetry signals. First, the count of distinct normalized action sequences per fixture declines across iterations. Second, pass@1 continues to climb while pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\) at high \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) plateaus, indicating that the policy is concentrating probability mass onto known routines rather than discovering alternative solutions. Third, performance on held-out task families stagnates even as acceptance rates on training fixtures rise. Systems teams must interpret action diversity alongside generalization benchmarks: a drop in unique action sequences can simply reflect an agent pruning redundant retries and settling into optimal execution paths, but when shrinking diversity coincides with stagnant held-out scores, the agent is over-specializing.


↩︎ pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\), the probability that at least one of \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) sampled candidates passes, is established in Candidate availability under pass@\IndependentAttemptCount.
Four engineering controls counteract this narrowing tendency. First, capping the number of retained samples per fixture prevents trivially solved environments from overwhelming the corpus. Second, deduplication filters prune identical normalized action sequences while preserving identical actions that occurred under distinct environmental observations. Third, the training corpus retains a permanent anchor of verified external demonstrations, such as curated human interactions, that automated collection cannot displace. Finally, early-stopping policies halt the self-improvement loop when behavioral diversity and held-out performance plateau, even if acceptance rates on training fixtures continue to climb.
External demonstrations and external evaluation suites serve complementary but distinct architectural functions. Permitted human or expert demonstrations anchor the training distribution because they originate outside the current policy’s behavioral basin. Protected evaluation tasks, by contrast, stay outside both training and automated curation filters under the development and final-test discipline of section 14.4. The loop adds one consumer of that discipline: each promotion decision reads a holdout score, so the suite that gates promotion becomes development data over successive rounds, and a separate final-test suite must confirm any generalization claim. In addition, periodic manual audits across all curation outcomes (accepted runs, rejected candidates, and borderline cases) are essential to catch grader shortcuts, reward hacking, and missed edge cases. Any failure against promotion criteria immediately halts the loop for human inspection.



Production interactions surface operational requirements and edge cases that static offline fixtures miss. However, extracting training signals from live telemetry demands disciplined interpretation: an observed event reflects only the immediate user action, rather than an unvarnished verdict on task correctness. As table 11 summarizes, each telemetry event must be bounded by its specific operational limitations before being assigned a learning role.
