Misinterpreting these signals distorts the training distribution. For instance, when a user edits an agent’s response to introduce a new constraint, the resulting text satisfies an altered prompt rather than the original query. Using that edited response as a supervised target without updating the prompt trains the model on incomplete specifications. Similarly, preference pairs comparing the model’s output against a user edit are valid only when the environmental context and task goals remain identical across both versions. Telemetry pipelines must also treat missing feedback as unobserved data rather than tacit endorsement, verify user consent and data governance permissions before ingestion, and convert critical production errors into graded regression fixtures before recycling them into the training loop.
These operational safeguards translate high-level self-improvement goals into a concrete systems collection plan with explicit sampling budgets, automated validation stages, and mandatory human review gates. Because distributed rollout generation scales horizontally while high-assurance verification and human inspection remain strictly throughput-constrained, the curation pipeline must balance sampling volume against bounded downstream validation capacity, preventing unvetted executions from overwhelming the training loop.




A trajectory collection pipeline must record and audit every curation decision even as generation, verification, and dataset publication execute at drastically different rates. For instance, an agent rollout may finish while downstream verifiers are fully saturated, or a multi-predicate evaluation may stall waiting on a single lagging checker after earlier checks have already passed. Structuring collection as an asynchronous pipeline decouples these stages and allows each to proceed independently within explicit capacity limits. When downstream stages become congested, backpressure propagates upstream to throttle or halt new rollouts, preventing in-flight work from exhausting system memory.

At each stage boundary, the pipeline validates explicit contracts. The verification cascade applies the evaluation criteria of section 14.5, decoupling whether a rollout solved the underlying task from whether it qualifies as a training demonstration, a preference comparison, or an evaluation fixture. If a specific predicate cannot be evaluated immediately, the pipeline marks that result as pending or unknown rather than silently assuming failure. Computationally expensive stages, such as human-in-the-loop review or formal verification, pull tasks from a dedicated, bounded queue. Transferring a case to that queue requires an acknowledged recipient with verified buffer capacity, ensuring that ambiguous or stalled evaluations cannot accumulate indefinitely and exhaust staging storage.
Because distributed workers and network connections inevitably fail, message delivery is retried. Each submission is therefore cryptographically bound to its unique collection run identifier, artifact version, and assessment policy. When the pipeline receives a duplicate identifier with an identical payload, it reuses the existing evaluation decision; if an incoming payload conflicts with an earlier submission under the same identifier, the system diverts the record to an operator investigation queue. Under no circumstances may a transient retry publish duplicate training examples or release a staging reservation twice. Durable ownership and idempotency primitives enforce this invariant without requiring an ad hoc recovery protocol.


↩︎ Semantic deduplication of retried writes, which acknowledges an identical retry and rejects a conflicting payload under the same identity, is established in The storage engine contract.



Staging needs hard admission bounds because how much it holds depends on verifier service time, and service time can collapse. Suppose completed rollouts arrive at verification at an average rate \(\ArrivalRate\), and \(\WorkerCount\) equivalent verifier slots each require a mean service time \(\MeanVerifierServiceTime\) per record. The pool provides an aggregate service capacity of \(\WorkerCount/\MeanVerifierServiceTime\) records per second, operating at nominal utilization \(\ServingUtilization=\ArrivalRate \MeanVerifierServiceTime/\WorkerCount\). In steady state, Little’s law (theorem \(\ref{thrm-05-littles-law}\)) gives the mean number of records in service as \(\ArrivalRate \MeanVerifierServiceTime = \ServingUtilization \WorkerCount\), so the nominal utilization is also the fraction of slots occupied on average. That baseline holds only while the service time does, and the hazard that staging must be dimensioned for is the moment it stops holding.


↩︎ Little’s law, which ties mean occupancy to arrival rate and residence time, is established in Residence time and service rate.
The most acute operational hazard is not an unexpected surge in rollout generation, but a sudden collapse in verifier service rate. Consider a defective test fixture or an unresponsive environment that forces every verifier execution to block until hitting its hard timeout \(\VerifierTimeout\). When this occurs, aggregate checking capacity instantly plummets from \(\WorkerCount/\MeanVerifierServiceTime\) to \(\WorkerCount/\VerifierTimeout\). If rollouts continue arriving at rate \(\ArrivalRate\), unassessed records accumulate in staging at a net rate of \(\ArrivalRate - \WorkerCount/\VerifierTimeout\) records per second. If each record reserves buffer space up to a maximum per-record ceiling \(\RecordSizeCeiling\), a staging storage pool of total capacity \(\StagingStoreCapacity\) that is empty when the burst begins is completely exhausted after
\[\StagingExhaustionTime=\frac{\StagingStoreCapacity}{\left(\ArrivalRate-\WorkerCount/\VerifierTimeout\right)\RecordSizeCeiling}.\]
A store that already holds records at onset is exhausted sooner, in proportion to the space they occupy. Stopping dispatch does not stop growth at once, because rollouts already running still emit records. If those in-flight rollouts can reserve \(\InflightRolloutReservation\) and the controller needs \(\ControllerReactionDelay\) to act, the high watermark, the fraction of the store at which dispatch stops, must satisfy
\[\text{watermark} \le 1-\frac{\InflightRolloutReservation + \ControllerReactionDelay\left(\ArrivalRate-\WorkerCount/\VerifierTimeout\right)\RecordSizeCeiling}{\StagingStoreCapacity}.\]
Notebook 14.4 evaluates this failure mode on a representative verification fleet.

Napkin Math 14.4: How long a staging store survives a timeout burstProblem: A hypothetical collector runs 1,024 concurrent rollouts that each take 45 s. 512 verifier slots take 16.875 s per record on average. Each record reserves a ceiling of 8 MB in a 32 GB staging store. Treat completions as a steady flow and all slots as interchangeable. A defective fixture then makes every test run to its 120 s timeout. How long until the store is fully reserved, and where must dispatch stop if the controller needs 30 s to act?
Math: Rollouts complete at 22.8 records per second against a nominal capacity of 30.3, giving a utilization of 0.75; by Little’s law, that is also the average fraction of the 512 slots in use. During the burst, capacity falls to 4.3 records per second, so staging grows by 18.5 records, or 147.9 MB/s of reservations, every second. Starting from an empty store, it is fully reserved after 216.3 s, about 3.6 min. When dispatch stops, the rollouts already running still hold up to 8.2 GB of reservations, and growth over the 30 s reaction delay adds 4.4 GB. Subtracting both from the 32 GB store places the high watermark at or below 60 percent of the store.
Systems insight: Size staging buffers for service-time collapses rather than nominal steady-state utilization. Even at a modest nominal utilization of 0.75, a verifier stall fills available storage in only 3.6 min. The exhaustion time \(\StagingExhaustionTime\) shrinks proportionally as the record ceiling \(\RecordSizeCeiling\) increases and scales linearly with total store size \(\StagingStoreCapacity\). Watermarks must account for work already in flight and controller reaction latency, backed by hard credit caps when feedback loops lag.


The in-flight rollouts captured in that headroom calculation demonstrate why admission control must account for unfinished work rather than simple queue depth. Instantaneous queue length reflects past arrivals, not committed future occupancy. Rollouts admitted prior to a downstream verifier stall will complete and emit outputs long after the dispatcher stops issuing new work. Admission controllers must therefore enforce concurrent limits on both the total count of active records and their aggregate reserved bytes. Furthermore, these byte reservations must be dimensioned against the maximum per-record ceiling (\(\RecordSizeCeiling\)) rather than the mean record size; while mean sizes dictate steady-state storage requirements, maximum bounds protect the system against worst-case allocation bursts.
A collection credit11 operationalizes both constraints. Every admitted rollout acquires a single credit from a shared pool, reserving storage for its maximum possible payload throughout rollout execution, intermediate staging, and downstream assessment. The credit returns to the pool only when the record reaches a durable terminal disposition or completes an acknowledged handoff to another capacity-controlled queue. Consequently, every unit of pending work is explicitly accounted for across the entire cluster. When a trajectory exceeds its expected allocation, the capture harness enforces an explicit truncation policy rather than silently clipping required state, for example by recording the partial execution trace with marked omissions and flagging the artifact as ineligible for training regimes that require full fidelity. Because one credit spans all four responsibilities, the pool also bounds work that has left the collector but not yet reached a disposition (figure 4).
11 Credit-Based Flow Control: The mechanism originates in hardware network switches, where a transmitter may forward a packet cell only while holding an explicit credit for an available downstream buffer slot, mathematically guaranteeing that buffers never overflow regardless of traffic burstiness (Kung et al. 1994). The receiver returns the credit only after draining the slot, the exact analog of returning a collection credit upon durable disposition. In both domains, the trade-off is identical: aggregate throughput is bounded by total outstanding credits divided by their round-trip return latency, ensuring that a slow downstream stage smoothly throttles upstream generation rather than causing buffer overruns. 
Kung, Hsiang-Tsung, Trevor Blackwell, and Alan Chapman. 1994. “Credit-Based Flow Control for ATM Networks: Credit Update Protocol, Adaptive Credit Allocation, and Statistical Multiplexing.” Proceedings of the Conference on Communications Architectures, Protocols and Applications (SIGCOMM), 101–14. https://doi.org/10.1145/190809.190324.






Figure 4: Collection Credits Across Four Responsibilities: Each admitted run holds one credit through rollout, capture, staging, and assessment. The credit returns to the pool only when the record reaches a durable disposition or an acknowledged transfer to another bounded owner, such as the review queue. A watermark derived from in-flight work slows dispatch before the pool is exhausted, and a hard limit stops admission when that feedback arrives late.



The credit pool directly bounds the count and aggregate record volume of all outstanding runs. This mechanism governs staging buffers, not auxiliary execution resources. Accelerator memory for model inference, sandbox container filesystems, verifier scratch disks, and external object stores each require separate capacity pools with independent accounting; storing a lightweight URI reference in a message queue does not magically bound the multi-gigabyte container image or execution trace to which it points. Robust admission controllers verify reservations across all requisite resource pools up front. This pre-allocation invariant ensures that a pipeline stage never acquires one scarce resource, such as an accelerator slot, only to block indefinitely waiting for an unreserved downstream buffer.
Notebook 14.5 demonstrates how credit bounds insulate a pipeline against a sudden completion burst.

Napkin Math 14.5: Reserve capacity before the completion burstProblem: A hypothetical collector provisions 12 end-to-end credits, each reserving a per-record ceiling of about 2.10 MB. Currently, 4 records sit staged in storage and 8 rollouts are actively executing, each holding an allocated credit while verification is temporarily paused. May the dispatcher admit an additional rollout? Furthermore, once all active rollouts finish and verification resumes, how long will this accumulated cohort take to drain?
Variables: 2 verifiers each assess one record at a time in exactly 10 s, including durable disposition; no new rollout is admitted during the drain, and transfer and publication add no delay.
Math: The 12 outstanding runs hold every credit: staged records reserve 8.39 MB and running rollouts 16.78 MB, for 25.17 MB (exactly 25165824 bytes) with 0 credits free, so the dispatcher admits nothing. Draining the queue takes ⌈12 / 2⌉ = 6 waves of 10 s, or 60 s.
Systems insight: Total byte consumption is strictly bounded by credits multiplied by the ceiling (\(\RecordSizeCeiling\)), independent of arrival timing, while drain latency scales as ⌈credits / verifiers⌉ times service time. Adding verifiers accelerates queue drainage without increasing the byte bound; expanding credits raises both. Engineers should dimension credit pools against physical staging limits and scale verifiers to meet drain deadlines, treating a slower assessment as a longer drain with the reservation still actively held.


Together, these analytical models establish complementary operational bounds: arrival and service rates govern how rapidly an outage consumes available headroom, while credit limits enforce an absolute ceiling on total buffer consumption. Production telemetry must continuously track queue depths, allocated vs. physically consumed bytes, the age of the oldest pending assessment, verification pass rates, and downstream sink throughput. Retries, escalated evaluations, and diagnostic reviews must all consume allocations from this same credit pool. When external dependencies fail, failure containment mechanisms prevent repeated re-verification attempts from amplifying an isolated service outage into cluster-wide failure.


↩︎ Circuit breakers, coordinated retries, and bulkheads that keep retry amplification from spreading a dependency outage are established in Tool Circuit Breakers.



While credit controls prevent staging buffers from overflowing during an outage, steady-state capacity planning compares generation, verification, and storage. With \(\AcceleratorCount\) accelerators each spending \(\AttemptGenerationTime\) accelerator-seconds per attempt, generation has a service ceiling of \(\AcceleratorCount / \AttemptGenerationTime\) attempts per second. With \(\WorkerCount\) verifier slots and expected slot service time \(\ExpectedCheckingTime\) per attempt from equation 1, assessment has a service ceiling of \(\WorkerCount / \ExpectedCheckingTime\). Charging every write at its per-record ceiling \(\RecordSizeCeiling\) gives a conservative provisioned storage rate of \(\DurableStoreWriteBandwidth / \RecordSizeCeiling\) for sustained write bandwidth \(\DurableStoreWriteBandwidth\). With enough credits, work, and scheduling capacity to saturate the stages, the idealized planning rate \(\SustainableAttemptRate\) is:
\[\SustainableAttemptRate=\min\left(\frac{\AcceleratorCount}{\AttemptGenerationTime},\ \frac{\WorkerCount}{\ExpectedCheckingTime},\ \frac{\DurableStoreWriteBandwidth}{\RecordSizeCeiling}\right). \tag{4}\]
Equation 4 identifies the binding stage in this stipulated model. Its planned admitted-record rate is \(\SustainableAttemptRate \cdot \AdmissionRouteYield\), where \(\AdmissionRouteYield\) is the route yield. Actual throughput can be lower because of credits, scheduling, or another shared service. Smaller writes can exceed the conservative storage term, so that term alone does not diagnose an observed storage bottleneck.
This formulation reveals an asymmetric operational trap regarding resource economics. In the illustrated low-priced deterministic route, verifiers occupy CPU slots that cost pennies per hour compared with accelerator instances. Under-provisioning that verifier pool, however, throttles the entire accelerator fleet, causing expensive generation hardware to sit idle. Under the notebook’s active-resource accounting, unused capacity is redeployed or unbilled, and generation compute and task yield dominate the charge per admitted record. A dedicated fleet billed during idle wall time has a different cost boundary. Deterministic verification is not inexpensive for every workload. A model judge or a human reviewer can change that split, and Exercise 5 in section 14.14 prices a route in which human review dominates. Notebook 14.6 evaluates this economic trade-off on a representative deployment.

Napkin Math 14.6: The cheapest stage can set the rateProblem: A hypothetical collector uses 64 accelerators, each spending 60 s of accelerator time per attempt at $2.50 per hour. It checks attempts with the admission route of notebook 14.2, whose cheaper order occupies 6.24 s of slot time per attempt and admits 20.52 percent of attempts, on 4 verifier slots priced at $0.04 per slot-hour. Records of at most 8 MB go to a store that sustains 200 MB/s. Assume sufficient end-to-end credits and no further shared service bottleneck, charge each write at its record ceiling, and bill only active accelerator and occupied verifier time, with unused capacity redeployed or unbilled. Which stage binds this planning model, and what is the active-resource charge per admitted record?
Math: By equation 4, generation supports 64 / 60 s = 1.07 attempts per second, assessment 4 / 6.24 s = 0.64, and conservative provisioned storage supports 200 MB/s / 8 MB = 25. Assessment binds in this model, and matching generation needs 1.07 × 6.24 s, rounded up to 7 slots. Generation costs $0.042 per attempt; adding checking and dividing by the yield gives $0.20 per admitted record, of which checking is 0.2 percent.
Systems insight: Throughput bottlenecks and cost drivers are often decoupled. In this scenario, running only 4 inexpensive verifier slots leaves 39.9 percent of generation capacity unused. Despite this bottleneck, the financial cost of an admitted record is dominated by generation expense divided by yield, following the cost per accepted task formulation (equation 1.2). Adding verifier slots raises the idealized rate until generation saturates while leaving the active-resource charge per record unchanged. With a dedicated fleet billed during idle wall time, greater utilization can instead lower the bill per emitted record. Holding active work per attempt and resource rates fixed, halving the yield to 10.26 percent doubles the unrounded cost per admitted record, displayed to the nearest cent as $0.41. Fixture design and sampling policy control that yield; their measured cost and coverage consequences determine whether a change is worthwhile.





Collection pipelines inherit the sandbox lifecycle and reset contracts. Rollout workers must persist all candidate artifacts, interaction traces, and evaluation evidence to durable storage before tearing down the execution sandbox containing their only ephemeral copy. A pooled execution environment cannot be reassigned to a new rollout until all background writer processes terminate, stale network credentials and access tokens are revoked, and sandbox filesystem reset postconditions are validated. If a downstream verification stage requires interactive access to unpersisted sandbox state, it must hold that environment under an explicit time-bounded lease and operational budget; otherwise, the checker must log the assessment as unavailable and release the host.
When a worker’s dispatch lease expires, expiration does not instantly terminate the executing process or roll back its external side effects. A replacement worker must therefore establish explicit ownership and verify fresh admission checks, while late-arriving outputs from the orphaned worker remain strictly quarantined to their original run. Similarly, if container cleanup fails or an external side effect leaves an indeterminate state, the owning process retains responsibility under the trajectory saga, even if the associated trajectory is discarded from training. Releasing a collection credit frees buffer staging, but it does not absolve the runtime of its teardown and cleanup obligations.


↩︎ The trajectory saga, which keeps a compensation obligation open while an external effect remains unresolved, is established in The Trajectory Saga Pattern.
Once physical movement from execution to durable disposition is bounded and accounted for, data governance determines artifact admissibility: which upstream source versions justify inclusion, what lossy or privacy-preserving transformations were applied, and which dataset split partitions and license restrictions govern the resulting weights.




Months after an execution trace enters a training corpus, curators must resolve critical systems questions regarding its origin, validity, and rights. They must determine which collection run produced the sequence, which validation criteria were verified against specific environment fixtures, whether the organization retains legal permission to train on the incorporated source code or API payloads, and whether a sanitization pass that stripped an API token or network address invalidated the runtime state that justified the agent’s subsequent action.
A preserved execution trace and its evaluation scores cannot answer these questions on their own. In a production curation pipeline, provenance provides the immutable, versioned record that answers them across every derivation of a trace. Consider a concrete recovery pipeline: a raw collection record, trace_r19_01, originates from collection run collection_run_r19_01 and candidate workspace ws_r20. If an automated scrubbing pass removes sensitive network addresses to create trace_r19_01_redacted_v1, the transformed artifact must receive an independent identity and its own admission decision instead of silently replacing the source record and inheriting its labels.


A lineage envelope12 records the origin, dependencies, transformations, and admission decisions of an individual record version. Table 13 outlines its conceptual dimensions. In a robust systems architecture, envelope fields point to content-addressed, access-controlled artifacts rather than embedding inline copies of sensitive or high-volume execution state.
12 Why- and Where-Provenance: Database research distinguished two questions about a derived datum: which source records justify its existence (why-provenance) and which source locations its values were copied from (where-provenance) (Buneman et al. 2001). A trajectory record needs both. Where-provenance traces each retained field to the run, event, and transformation that produced it, and why-provenance traces its admission to the assessments that justified it, so a withdrawn source or a revised criterion can be followed to every affected corpus member.

The envelope must record only what the runtime interfaces actually reveal. When an agent executes against locally controlled model weights, the envelope binds the loaded base model and adapter checkpoint digests. Hosted inference endpoints, however, typically expose only a reported version string and request configuration; in those cases, the envelope documents those exact parameters rather than fabricating an unverifiable weight hash. Similarly, a prompt-template identifier fails to capture dynamic context injected at runtime, and a container base-image digest omits mutable mounted volumes or external network state. Systems engineers must document omissions explicitly rather than relying on identifiers of ambiguous scope.
Evaluation assessments bind directly to the exact byte representation tested. If a trajectory earns a passing score on a targeted capability test, that verdict applies only to that evaluated representation; any pending criterion remains pending when the record enters cold storage. The downstream evaluation cascade alone determines whether the available evidence authorizes a specific learning use.



A trainer decides what to train on by reading the corpus manifest, so it must be able to confirm two things before the first gradient: that the manifest is the one curation issued, and that no record was altered or swapped after admission, whether by a broken pipeline script or by anyone with write access to the store. Integrity mechanisms answer exactly those questions. They establish unmodified bytes, not correct content or permitted use. A cryptographic digest identifies a specified byte representation under standard collision-resistance assumptions. For that digest to remain meaningful across different system components, the lineage envelope must fix both the canonical serialization scheme and the schema version over which the hash was calculated. Comparing an artifact against an expected digest reliably detects bit corruption and unauthorized modifications. Storing an unauthenticated digest directly beside mutable content in an object store, however, provides zero security: an adversary or a broken pipeline script can overwrite the data and the digest simultaneously.
To guarantee authenticity, an authenticated manifest cryptographically binds expected artifact digests and associated metadata to a trusted issuing authority. Systems frequently use a message authentication code (MAC), such as HMAC as specified in RFC 2104 (Krawczyk et al. 1997), computed with a secret key held securely outside the dataset in a dedicated key management service. Because any party possessing a shared symmetric key can forge a valid MAC, production architectures often prefer asymmetric digital signatures (such as Ed25519) when datasets are distributed across multiple worker nodes. The manifest must record the cryptographic algorithm, key version, and authorized issuing scope, and key rotation policies must align with the operational lifetime of the corpus. Verification confirms only that the authenticated byte representation has not been altered since issuance; it covers nothing outside that boundary.

Krawczyk, Hugo, Mihir Bellare, and Ran Canetti. 1997. HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication. RFC 2104. Internet Engineering Task Force. https://doi.org/10.17487/RFC2104.
13 Merkle Tree: A tree in which each internal node holds the hash of its children, introduced to build digital signatures from a conventional one-way function (Merkle 1988). Its useful property is that proving one leaf belongs under a trusted root needs only the sibling hashes along one path, logarithmic in the number of leaves. A corpus manifest can therefore commit to millions of record digests under one root and still verify a single member cheaply, but the root commits only to the leaves that were hashed. 
Merkle, Ralph C. 1988. “A Digital Signature Based on a Conventional Encryption Function.” Advances in Cryptology — CRYPTO ’87, Lecture notes in computer science, vol. 293: 369–78. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-48184-2_32.
Cryptographic integrity must not be confused with semantic correctness. A faithfully authenticated trajectory trace can encapsulate hallucinated model outputs, an erroneous grader verdict, or private data that downstream consumers are legally prohibited from seeing. Similarly, computing a Merkle root13 over captured execution events proves that a given event belongs to the recorded tree, but it proves nothing about execution events that the logging harness dropped or failed to observe. Claims regarding trajectory reproducibility must therefore adhere to the reconstruction and re-execution boundaries established in Recorded Trajectory Replay.



The data minimization and disclosure boundaries established in Disclosure minimization must be enforced before trajectory content enters an ingestion queue, a model-assisted curation worker, or a training store. In curation pipelines, data transformation introduces an immediate systems trade-off: sanitization and redaction modify the training distribution, and stripping an essential field can sever the causal relationship that justified an agent’s subsequent decision.
A derived record must always be created as a new version rather than an in-place modification. The derived record binds a reference to its parent trace, the versioned redaction policy and implementation, the explicit set of altered or excised fields, and any intentionally withheld content. Lineage references do not grant read authorization to restricted raw data, and systems must store original raw bytes only where retention policies explicitly permit them. When source records reach their retention expiration limit and are purged, the lineage envelope documents that boundary directly; retaining a cryptographic hash is not the same as retaining the source data. The source also keeps a reverse reference to each derived version, so that a later correction or withdrawal at the source reaches every artifact derived from it (figure 5).






Figure 5: A Derived Record and Its Lineage: Redaction produces a new record version instead of editing the source. The derived record carries its parent reference, the fields its transformation changed or omitted, and the source’s split group, but its assessment is pending until revalidation decides what the new view still supports. The source keeps a reverse reference, so a later correction or withdrawal can reach every derived version.



Heuristic pattern matching and named-entity recognition models act as screening mechanisms rather than complete sanitization guarantees. Engineers must validate these detectors across the full output pipeline using realistic end-to-end test cases, including deeply nested payloads and generated metadata. Synthetic canaries provide an empirical measure of detector recall: the curation audit log must record how many canaries were injected, how many escaped detection, which semantic classes and text transformations were tested, and where the inspection boundary was applied. Observing zero canary escapes bounds the leak probability only for the evaluated canary distribution. Furthermore, false positives impose a severe systems cost, as over-aggressive scrubbing strips necessary context and distorts the training signal.


↩︎ Canary values, planted synthetic secrets whose escape reveals a leaking path, are established in Detectors and canary values.
When scrubbing identifiers across multi-step interactions, curators use consistent pseudonyms to preserve relational dependencies across turns while preventing identity linkage beyond the access scope that the trace’s disclosure boundary permits. Tokenization effects require careful handling: replacing an identifier with a fixed-width placeholder often alters the sequence’s token count and attention boundaries. Similarly, reserializing a structured payload can preserve outer JSON or YAML formatting while silently breaking nested shell escaping, regular expression matches, or tool invocation syntax. Consequently, checking that an artifact parses successfully is entirely distinct from verifying that it still supports the intended learning target.


↪ Re-verifying selected response spans against token offsets after templating or redaction shifts token boundaries is operationalized in Rendering with versioned templates.
Revalidation must systematically test every property that the transformation could have influenced. This includes validating record structure, ensuring action-observation consistency, verifying that the sanitized context still justifies the target action, and re-evaluating any criteria whose supporting evidence was altered. If a transformation modifies executable code or environment-dependent identifiers, the pipeline must execute the code against an isolated, authorized test fixture to obtain fresh runtime evidence, while archiving prior execution logs as historical artifacts.

Example 14.1: A transformed record needs a new decisionScenario: During a collection run, an agent’s observation records a private system path that a subsequent diagnostic command references, and the source trace captures the successful output of that command. The curation pipeline replaces the path with a sanitized placeholder throughout trace_r19_01_redacted_v1.
Diagnosis: The recorded execution output remains valid evidence only for the original run bound to trace_r19_01; the agent never executed the sanitized placeholder path. The curator must determine whether the sanitized observation and the subsequent command still constitute a coherent learning example. A consistent placeholder can teach an agent how to parse and inspect arbitrary paths without exposing production directory structures. However, replaying the trajectory against an active execution harness requires an authorized, compatible mock fixture; otherwise, the substituted path fails to resolve. If the substitution obscures the causal distinction that prompted the agent’s action, the pipeline must reject the target for supervised training or withhold the record. The derived record inherits the source’s task grouping and train/test split assignment, while all pending evaluation verdicts remain pending until formal revalidation completes.
Systems lesson: Cryptographic integrity establishes which source artifact was transformed, whereas revalidation establishes what the transformed trajectory teaches. Neither operation can alter what physically occurred during the original execution run.





Permission to execute an agent against a task fixture or inspect an internal repository does not convey permission to retain its artifacts, fine-tune models on its data, or publish the resulting corpus. The lineage envelope must record the explicit licensing constraints, the evidentiary basis for data retention, and the designated policy authority or human reviewer who approved data usage. This accounting must cover both the primary task assets and all third-party software dependencies pulled into the environment during execution. Automated license detectors and embedding-based similarity screens help identify suspect components, but they serve as screening tools rather than autonomous legal adjudicators.
When provenance evidence is ambiguous or incomplete, the curation pipeline must withhold the record from downstream consumers while logging the specific withholding rationale. This quarantine is use-specific: an asset held from public pretraining might remain eligible for internal safety evaluations. Furthermore, use-permission holds operate independently of task failure labels, confidentiality tiers, and fault-containment quarantine. Resolving a safety fault or task defect does not automatically grant data-usage clearance.


⇄ Contrast: Incident containment, which holds the work a suspect trajectory might touch rather than withholding a record from one use, is established in Incident Containment.
Approved data permissions operate under strict temporal and organizational scopes. To enforce policy changes, reverse references must connect each source record to its derived views, tokenized dataset partitions, and published corpus manifests. When an upstream data provider revokes permission, or when an organization updates its privacy policies, the system must propagate the restriction or withdrawal to every downstream artifact. The ingestion pipeline immediately halts new admissions under the revoked policy, while the catalog traces all distributed artifacts. Simply deleting a record from an active storage bucket leaves distributed offline copies and completed model parameter updates intact; managing those downstream exposures requires explicit operational ownership, retraining schedules, and audited unlearning procedures.

Checkpoint 14.2: Defend a derived record's use
Each bullet asks for a decision a curator makes before a derived record ships.

Integrity vs. truth: A manifest’s MAC verifies. Decide which of these it establishes: the bytes are unmodified, the grader verdict is correct, the record is permitted for training.
Transformation: A replacement preserves JSON parsing but changes a path used by a later action. Which historical evidence remains valid, and which learning-use checks must be repeated before admission?
Screening: A detector test inserts canaries of three classes and observes zero escapes. What claim can the report make, and which record classes remain untested?
Lineage: A redacted record’s source task is in the final-test group. Decide whether the redacted version may enter training, and name what must happen when an admitted source is later withdrawn.



A well-architected trajectory record possesses a verifiable origin, an explicit transformation history, a legally scoped permission envelope, and strictly preserved evaluation boundaries. Connecting an execution trace through this provenance graph into a corpus manifest gives membership a precise meaning, verified fitness for a declared learning consumer. One record carried through every stage shows how these decisions compose.




To see how the curation stages compose, return to the recovery run collection_run_r19_01 whose targets section 14.6.2 selected. Its refused edit, schema inspection, and corrected edit produced ws_r20, which satisfied repair_accept_v1. The raw trace trace_r19_01 records that sequence without altering any earlier record, neither the pending trial verdict on ws_r19 nor the unresolved earlier test operation test_r18. The curation question is which parts of this record may enter a learning artifact, for which consumer, and on what evidence.
The training objective is recovery from harness refusals, the residual behavior that the campaign’s probes left with the model, and the target policy recovery_targets_v1 already fixed which tokens contribute direct supervised loss: the schema query e3, the corrected edit e4, and the final summary e6, with the refused proposal e2, the test summary e5, the task prompt, and the intermediate tool responses kept as conditioning context. Target selection is only the first stage of admission. The record that actually enters a corpus is a transformed view of trace_r19_01, so the remaining stages must verify that view, bind its provenance, and publish it to a manifest.


Before raw traces enter a training corpus, data hygiene and privacy policies often require sanitization. Here, an authorized transformation creates trace_r19_01_redacted_v1 by scrubbing sensitive fixture paths and replacing them with standardized synthetic references. While the underlying execution stems directly from the original run, admission filtering evaluates whether this sanitized view preserves the technical validity of the recovery lesson. The admission pipeline does not demand byte-for-byte fidelity with historical environment state; it requires that the transformed trace faithfully represent the causal chain needed for supervised imitation.

Because each predicate evaluates to true, the pipeline admits the transformed example as a verified decision demonstration. If path substitution had stripped file names essential for the agent to deduce the correct schema, target suitability (\(\text{chk}_{\text{target,demo}}\)) would have failed immediately. Furthermore, while this redacted trace is fully valid for token-level imitation learning, it cannot serve a downstream consumer that requires executable replay; executing the synthetic paths would require spinning up a fresh environment with matching mock fixtures. Once admitted, the curated trajectory enters the corpus release repair_demonstrations_v1. To guarantee end-to-end reproducibility, the corpus manifest explicitly records every link in the artifact’s provenance chain. For this member, the manifest binds the record to its originating run (collection_run_r19_01), task identifier, fixture snapshot, candidate code patch, and evaluation grader versions. It references both the transformed trace (trace_r19_01_redacted_v1) and the target selection policy (recovery_targets_v1), while logging the specific data governance approvals, task group assignments, and split partition versions. Any missing metadata or inactive model dependencies are explicitly tagged as unavailable rather than omitted.
At the corpus level, the manifest catalogs the source data pools, sampling weights, token accounting budgets, domain coverage metrics, and the formal evaluation protocol. Maintaining clear distinctions among raw interaction counts, stored trace tokens, and selected supervised target tokens prevents deceptive accounting. During training, serialization formats and loss masks enforce these target boundaries, ensuring that future trajectory steps never leak into earlier conditioning windows.
This curated trajectory yields a single demonstration artifact. It cannot be repurposed as a preference pair, because the rejected proposal e2 and the later edit e4 follow different prefixes (e4 comes after the refusal and the schema lookup), so they are not alternative continuations of one context. A preference artifact would need competing completions sampled from one saved branch point. Similarly, publishing an environment for reinforcement learning rollouts requires exporting the task fixture, harness configurations, and dynamic graders, rather than static token sequences.
Publishing an immutable corpus manifest establishes a versioned training baseline, which remains separate from deployment governance for any resulting model. Tracking lineage guarantees that if an upstream fixture defect or data privacy request emerges later, pipeline operators can cleanly trace and purge all derived artifacts across downstream model versions. At the infrastructure layer, ephemeral execution sandboxes are destroyed and billed compute charges are settled independently of whether a trace reaches the corpus manifest.



In agentic data collection, raw trial volume is a deceptive metric. A pipeline may execute thousands of autonomous interactions yet emit only a small handful of usable training samples. Trajectories routinely fail safety filters, duplicate existing task solutions, crash during tool dispatch, or remain stalled in asynchronous evaluation queues. Consequently, systems engineers must evaluate collection economics using the cost per emitted artifact, amortizing all spent compute and infrastructure overhead across the accepted dataset.
For a given collection cohort and accounting cutoff, let \(\CollectionCohortCost\) represent the total monetary expenditure incurred across environment provisioning, inference generation, tool sandbox execution, automated verification, human review, redaction transformations, and storage. Let \(\EmittedArtifactCount\) denote the number of valid artifacts emitted for a designated consumer by that cutoff. The cost per emitted artifact is defined as
\[\CostPerEmittedArtifact=\frac{\CollectionCohortCost}{\EmittedArtifactCount},\qquad \EmittedArtifactCount>0. \tag{5}\]
The numerator \(\CollectionCohortCost\) captures all unproductive runs, rejected proposals, and pipeline failures; if a cohort yields zero usable artifacts (\(\EmittedArtifactCount = 0\)), the pipeline registers the incurred financial loss without dividing by zero. Structurally, equation 5 mirrors the cost per accepted task formulation (equation 1.2): the unit cost equals the average cost per attempt divided by the end-to-end emission yield. This metric isolates data acquisition efficiency, distinguishing curation costs from both runtime inference serving and subsequent model fine-tuning.

The demonstration selector emits at most one artifact per task. What does each emitted artifact cost, and which operational lever most effectively reduces that price?

Math: The selected-and-emitted row of table 15 yields an emission rate of 15 / 500 = 3 percent. The average cost per attempt is $300 / 500 = $0.60. Applying equation 5 yields $0.60 / 3 percent = $20 per emitted artifact. This emission yield differs from a task-completion rate, because the curator caps repeated solutions for the same task and several nonselected runs successfully resolved their repair targets. It is also far below the route yield of notebook 14.2, which counts the records that pass one route’s predicates. Emission yield charges every initiated attempt with the per-task cap, redundancy decisions, ineligibility, and whatever is still pending at the cutoff.
Systems insight: Because unit cost equals attempt cost divided by emission yield, curation yield serves as the primary economic lever. For example, raising yield to 6 percent cuts the unit price in half to $10. With 97 percent of attempts failing to emit a usable artifact, engineering effort should focus on diagnosing nonselection causes before purchasing additional generation compute. High redundancy indicates that the system should launch fewer attempts per task; ineligibility points to split or permission defects caught too late; and backlogged pending evaluations point to verification bottlenecks.


A published manifest documents exactly what was emitted, verifies eligibility across all admission gates, isolates supervision targets, and tallies total acquisition cost. Operational efficiency and curation hygiene, however, are prerequisites rather than guarantees of model improvement. The ultimate test of a curated corpus lies in offline empirical evaluation: measuring the fine-tuned policy against holdout task distributions under controlled benchmark protocols, where neither a low cost per artifact nor a high emission yield can substitute for genuine downstream task performance.




A data collection pipeline can preserve every execution record faithfully and still assemble a counterproductive training set. The mistakes below stem from confusing raw trace telemetry with the deliberate pedagogical choices required to train an agent, and each carries tangible computational or behavioral costs.

Fallacy: A successful task makes every action in its trace a suitable demonstration.
Task acceptance evaluates end-to-end task completion, whereas target selection decides which specific token sequences should receive gradient supervision. Consider an agent that successfully debugs a codebase after several stumbling attempts. Its transcript might include an initial malformed JSON tool call, a parser rejection from the runtime environment, and a subsequent correction. While that malformed call must remain in the transcript as conditioning context so the agent understands the environment’s feedback, it must never be included in the training loss as a target. In the recovery worksheet, a typical recovery trajectory contains 18,500 stored tokens, but only 2,000 of those tokens are designated as supervised targets (section 14.6). Supervising the entire accepted trace forces the model to memorize and reproduce its own intermediate errors. In a sound curation pipeline, record validity (whether the telemetry accurately reflects what happened), task acceptance (whether the agent fulfilled its objective), and target eligibility (whether an action should be reinforced) are three distinct filtering decisions.


Pitfall: Fine-tuning on every failure before probing its cause.
When an agent fails, the easiest operational reaction is often to bundle the failed trajectories into a fine-tuning dataset. In the intervention ladder worksheet, systematic counterfactual probes demonstrate that 90 percent of observed failures originate in the supporting infrastructure below the model weights, such as malformed tool schemas, missing environment variables, or overly aggressive sandbox timeouts (section 14.2.2). Retraining the model across the entire failure corpus requires only $58 of accelerator time, and that modest price creates a dangerous illusion of progress. Fine-tuning merely encourages the model to memorize ad hoc compensations for broken tooling. As soon as an external API changes or the brittle workaround misfires, the failure resurfaces. Systems engineers should run counterfactual probes first, fix defects in tools and runtime environments directly, and restrict fine-tuning to the remaining 300 genuine behavioral failures.


Fallacy: A random split of collected traces holds out unseen tasks.
Applying uniform random sampling across collected trajectories partitions individual attempts rather than underlying problem instances. When an evaluation harness collects 8 attempts per task and allocates a 80 percent fraction to training, 83.2 percent of the tasks end up present in both the training and test sets (section 14.4). Under this configuration, test metrics reflect the agent’s ability to recall previously seen problem setups rather than its capability to generalize to novel tasks. Data splitting must occur at the granularity of task groups, with environment-seed variants inheriting their group’s assignment. Furthermore, any downstream derivatives (redacted transcripts, paraphrased prompts, or deduplicated variants) must inherit the assignment of their source task so that syntactic transformations do not accidentally leak problem state across the evaluation boundary.


Pitfall: Cheapening the verifier cascade by dropping or loosening a predicate.
When verification overhead begins to strain cluster budgets, engineers often attempt to reduce costs by removing expensive check predicates or loosening test assertions. This strategy alters the semantic definition of success rather than optimizing the system. In the cascade worksheet, simply reordering evaluation stages based on their computational cost per rejected candidate saved 16.9 percent of total verification work while maintaining the exact same candidate yield of 20.52 percent (section 14.5.3). Dropping a verification check or silently discarding unresolved edge cases shifts the distribution of accepted trajectories, degrading the downstream training corpus. Performance optimizations should focus on scheduling predicates efficiently under fixed acceptance criteria. In addition, execution pipelines must isolate and report inconclusive runs separately rather than collapsing them into either rejections or unqualified admissions.


Fallacy: Setting a recovery percentage by record count fixes the training mixture.
Trajectory counts provide an unreliable unit of measure when balancing mixed training datasets. A curation system operates across three distinct metrics: raw trajectory records, total stored context tokens, and actively supervised target tokens. In the token budget worksheet, recovery trajectories make up 25 percent of total records, but they represent 44.97 percent of stored tokens and 39.06 percent of selected training targets (section 14.6). Because recovery sequences involve multi-step error correction and verbose environment feedback, their token footprint differs substantially from standard trajectories. Specifying mixture proportions solely by record count miscalculates both the gradient signal allocated to recovery behaviors and the computational budget required for training. Engineers must define training mixtures in terms of supervised target tokens, and validate the resulting policy resilience against held-out task benchmarks under a declared compute budget.


Pitfall: Sizing collection staging from average verifier utilization.
Dimensioning staging storage against average verification throughput invites buffer exhaustion during outages. A verifier pool running at an average utilization of 0.75 appears to have substantial headroom during normal operation. However, automated verification runtimes suffer from bimodal service times. When a faulty test fixture, infrastructure timeout, or broken container environment forces every evaluation to run until its hard execution deadline, service throughput collapses while incoming agent trajectories continue to arrive. In the burst exhaustion worksheet, this prolonged tail latency exhausts the staging store in approximately 3.6 min (section 14.8). Buffer capacity must be bounded by worst-case service latency rather than nominal arrival rates. Robust ingestion architectures use credit-based flow control to restrict outstanding verifier reservations, sizing storage watermarks to absorb both in-flight execution bursts and downstream controller response delays.





A trajectory record and a training example answer different questions. The record says what happened under stated conditions. The example asserts that some part of what happened is worth reproducing, for a named learner, and will be judged against evidence that learner never saw. Every mechanism in the chapter keeps those two apart: probes keep system defects out of the weights, task-group splits keep evaluation evidence out of selection, target selection keeps a faithfully recorded mistake in context and out of the loss, and lineage keeps a transformed record from inheriting a decision made about its source.
Collection credits, lineage envelopes, and the corpus manifest make those decisions operational. The price of the result follows the book’s cost-per-accepted-task form twice over: checking work per admitted record is cascade cost divided by yield, and cost per emitted artifact is attempt cost divided by emission yield, so yield is the lever in both. Self-improvement changes the source distribution with every round, which is why the manifest keeps demonstrations, comparisons, and rollout fixtures distinct and why external assessment stays outside the loop.
The quantitative decisions of the chapter rest on the relations collected in table 16.

Key Takeaways: Give every learning artifact a declared use

Weights are the last remedy, not the first: Counterfactual probes place many failures in context, schemas, or the runtime, where a reversible repair removes them for every model version. Training earns only the residual that survives, and demonstrations, preference comparisons, and rollout fixtures each carry their own admission conditions.
A split protects a claim, not a file: With several attempts per task, a random split over traces puts most tasks on both sides, so the test score rewards recall of solved siblings. Assign whole task groups, carry the assignment into every derived record, and fix it before collection begins.
Cheaper checking must admit the same corpus: Ordering independent, fixed-cost predicates within permissible orders by cost per rejection, \(\CheckSlotTime_i/(1-\CheckPassProbability_i)\), cuts verification work at an unchanged accepted set. Dropping or loosening a predicate buys a different corpus, so its lower unit price is not a saving.
A recorded mistake is context, not a target: Recovery records keep the error and its refusal as conditioning history and select only the assessed correction as supervision. Mixtures are specified in selected targets and budgeted in stored tokens, because context per target differs by class.
Self-selected data narrows what it rewards: When the policy supplies its own records, rising acceptance can hide the recoveries the selector rarely keeps. Distinct action sequences per fixture, pass@1 against pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\), and an external anchor show whether the loop is still learning or only repeating itself.
Staging is sized for the burst, not the average: A verifier timeout burst, not average utilization, exhausts reserved staging, so each run holds a credit at the record ceiling until durable disposition. The cheapest stage can bind the illustrated planning rate while generation divided by yield sets its active-resource price.
The manifest is the contract the trainer reads: Records and derived artifacts bind to source versions, checks, transformations, permissions, split membership, and intended consumers. Integrity proves unmodified bytes, not truth or permission, so every derived record earns its own admission decision.



Verified trajectory post-training (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training}\)) now has a concrete decision boundary: evidence supports a specified learning use, and the corpus manifest carries that decision through selection and transformation so the trainer can tell context from targets. The trained policy still faces evaluation and still runs under the runtime’s authority and resource controls.



The principles governing trajectory curation did not emerge in a vacuum; they adapt hard-won lessons from data mining, information retrieval, and relational databases. Data mining first identified data leakage as a systemic failure mode where information about an evaluation target inadvertently reaches the learner through correlated records (Kaufman et al. 2012). In software modeling, duplicated source files were shown to inflate benchmark accuracy artificially until evaluation splits underwent thorough deduplication (Allamanis 2019). Modern screening pipelines borrow directly from web search, where minwise hashing estimated document resemblance from compact signatures (Broder 1997) and locality-sensitive hashing reduced high-dimensional similarity search to sublinear time (Indyk and Motwani 1998). Database query processing supplied the twin mechanisms of admission control and data provenance: optimizers established how to order expensive filter predicates by their cost-to-selectivity rank to minimize wasted computation (Hellerstein and Stonebraker 1993), while provenance frameworks formalized exactly which source records produced a derived value and why (Buneman et al. 2001).

Kaufman, Shachar, Saharon Rosset, Claudia Perlich, and Ori Stitelman. 2012. “Leakage in Data Mining: Formulation, Detection, and Avoidance.” ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data (TKDD) 6 (4): 1–21.

Zelikman, Eric, Yuhuai Wu, Jesse Mu, and Noah D. Goodman. 2022. “STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning with Reasoning.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35: 15476–88.

Uesato, Jonathan, Nate Kushman, Ramana Kumar, Francis Song, Noah Siegel, Lisa Wang, Antonia Creswell, Geoffrey Irving, and Irina Higgins. 2022. “Solving Math Word Problems with Process- and Outcome-Based Feedback.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2211.14275, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2211.14275.

Lightman, Hunter, Vineet Kosaraju, Yura Burda, Harri Edwards, Bowen Baker, Teddy Lee, Jan Leike, John Schulman, Ilya Sutskever, and Karl Cobbe. 2024. “Let’s Verify Step by Step.” The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
Learning from self-generated execution traces shares an equally deep lineage in reinforcement learning and symbolic reasoning. Classical imitation learning demonstrated that a policy trained exclusively on expert demonstrations compounds its errors when deployed, because small mistakes push the agent into unfamiliar states where it cannot recover (Ross et al. 2011). Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell showed that querying an expert on the learner’s own visited states restores linear error bounds; recovery demonstrations are the systems realization of that theoretical remedy. Expert iteration formalized this dynamic into an alternating loop of generation, search-based selection, and retraining, using tree search to discover improved decisions for a neural network to imitate (Anthony et al. 2017). Bootstrapped reasoning extended this loop to language models by sampling reasoning paths and filtering for traces that reached correct answers (Zelikman et al. 2022). Process supervision then tightened verification from coarse terminal outcomes down to individual reasoning steps (Uesato et al. 2022; Lightman et al. 2024).
Every self-training paradigm eventually encounters the same fundamental challenge: the filtering mechanism is itself an imperfect component of the system being improved. Production machine learning pipelines first exposed the systemic risks of hidden feedback loops, where an operational model’s outputs silently shape its own subsequent training distribution (Sculley et al. 2015). Reward modeling revealed Goodhart’s law in full force: excessive optimization against a learned proxy drives reward scores up while true task quality deteriorates (Gao et al. 2023). Unchecked recursive training on synthetic outputs further accelerates model collapse, progressively eroding diversity and extinguishing the distribution’s tail (Shumailov et al. 2024). Agentic execution sharpens each of these failure modes because trajectories do not exist in isolation. They execute stateful tool calls, operate under specific environment permissions, and can inadvertently manipulate or game their own evaluation harnesses. The safeguards of this chapter, from verifier cascades and disjoint task-group splits to lineage envelopes and dataset manifests (Gebru et al. 2021), apply classical systems isolation and provenance guarantees directly to the trajectory as the atomic unit of machine learning data.

Shumailov, Ilia, Zakhar Shumaylov, Yiren Zhao, Nicolas Papernot, Ross Anderson, and Yarin Gal. 2024. “AI Models Collapse When Trained on Recursively Generated Data.” Nature 631 (8022): 755–59. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07566-y.
For further reading, start with these:

End-to-end arguments (Saltzer et al. 1984): The classic statement of why a function belongs where it can be implemented completely and correctly. In trajectory curation, this principle argues for repairing tool interfaces and runtime environments directly rather than training model weights to work around platform flaws.
Predicate migration (Hellerstein and Stonebraker 1993): The foundational database paper on ordering expensive filter checks by cost per rejection, formalizing the exchange argument used to structure multi-stage verifier cascades.
Imitation learning as no-regret online learning (Ross et al. 2011): The analysis demonstrating why training exclusively on clean expert prefixes leaves an agent unprepared for its own mistakes, establishing the theoretical rationale for recovery demonstrations.
Hidden technical debt in machine learning systems (Sculley et al. 2015): A comprehensive systems catalog of data dependencies and feedback loops that any self-improving corpus pipeline inherits.
Datasheets for datasets (Gebru et al. 2021): The documentation discipline that a corpus manifest adapts into versioned, machine-auditable metadata fields.
Reward-model overoptimization (Gao et al. 2023): A controlled empirical study showing how aggressive optimization against a learned proxy reward drives proxy scores up while true task quality degrades.

Every given below is a hypothetical problem input chosen for round arithmetic, not a measurement of any system. Each problem asks for a calculation and the curation or collection decision it supports.

Sizing a protected split (Basic). A collection job makes \(\IndependentAttemptCount=5\) attempts on each of 2,000 repair tasks. A colleague proposes assigning individual traces to training with probability \(\TrainingSplitFraction=0.9\) and to the final test otherwise.

Compute the fraction and number of tasks whose attempts straddle the partition, and the smallest \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) at which a majority of tasks straddle.
Compute the probability that a given test attempt has at least one sibling attempt of the same task in training, and state what the resulting test score measures.
The team switches to a group split (section 14.4). Treating tasks as independent trials with an acceptance rate near one half, compute how many task groups the final test must hold for the standard error of its task-level acceptance rate to be at most 0.025, and what fraction of the 2,000 tasks that reserves.

Ordering an admission route (Basic). A demonstration route has three independent predicates beyond record adequacy: a permitted-use lookup \(\text{chk}_{\text{use}}\) that takes 0.05 s and passes 70 percent of records, a sandboxed test run \(\text{chk}_{\text{out}}\) that takes 30 s and passes 50 percent, and a model-judged target review \(\text{chk}_{\text{target}}\) that takes 4 s and passes 80 percent. Target review does not need the test result, and the current order is \(\text{chk}_{\text{use}}\to \text{chk}_{\text{out}}\to \text{chk}_{\text{target}}\).

Rank the predicates by cost per rejection (equation 2) and choose the order.
Compute \(\ExpectedCheckingTime\) per attempted record and per admitted record for the current and chosen orders (equation 1), and the fraction of verifier-slot work the change saves.
A colleague proposes dropping \(\text{chk}_{\text{target}}\) instead, because it lowers checking time per admitted record further. Compute that figure and the new yield, and explain why the comparison with part (b) is not a cost comparison at all.

Three denominators for one mixture (Basic). A retained demonstration pool holds 20,000 direct-success records averaging 6,000 stored tokens and 1,000 selected target tokens, and 5,000 recovery records averaging 30,000 stored tokens and 2,500 selected target tokens.

Compute the recovery class’s share of records, stored tokens, and selected targets, and the context per target token for each class.
The team wants recovery to supply half of the selected targets. Holding total selected targets at the current value, compute the presentations each class needs, how many recovery records must repeat, and the change in processed tokens.
Holding processed tokens at the current value instead, compute the total selected targets at the same half-and-half mixture. State which budget this team should fix when training time is the scarce resource, and what the arithmetic cannot decide.

Spending a sampling budget on contrast (Intermediate). A collector has 8,000 attempts for 1,000 repair fixtures in three difficulty bands: 400 fixtures with per-attempt pass rate \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.1\), 400 with \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.5\), and 200 with \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.9\). Attempts are independent, and each fixture receives \(\IndependentAttemptCount=8\).

For each band and in total, compute the expected number of fixtures that yield at least one success and the expected number of mixed groups (equation 3). Compute the attempts spent per mixed group.
A colleague proposes dropping the easy band and spending its 1,600 attempts on the hard band at \(\IndependentAttemptCount=12\). Compute the new expected number of mixed groups and state what the imitation corpus loses.
Decide whether to adopt the proposal for a group-relative objective and for an imitation artifact, and explain why the easy band’s all-success groups are not wasted attempts.

Reviewing after selection (Intermediate). A cohort makes \(\IndependentAttemptCount=10\) independent attempts on each of 200 tasks. Each attempt succeeds with probability 0.2 and costs $0.50 for generation, verification, and storage. Every successful attempt goes to human target review at $6, which passes 75 percent of the successes it sees, independently. The selector emits at most one artifact per task, the first passing success in attempt order.

Compute the expected number of emitted artifacts, the cohort cost, and \(\CostPerEmittedArtifact\) (equation 5).
The team instead reviews a task’s successes in attempt order and stops at its first pass. Show that the set of emitting tasks is unchanged, and compute the expected reviews per task, the new cohort cost, and \(\CostPerEmittedArtifact\).
A second proposal halves \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) to 5 with the stopping review in place. Compute \(\CostPerEmittedArtifact\) and the emitted count, and decide between the two proposals, naming what the cheaper unit price costs the corpus.

The research agent’s collector (Intermediate). The research agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}\)) reads untrusted sources, so each collection record keeps the retrieved pages that its claims cite, and the permitted-use review of that retained content is expensive. A collector runs 32 accelerators at 40 accelerator-seconds per attempt, checks attempts on 16 verifier slots, and writes records of at most 1 GB to a store that sustains 500 MB/s (decimal units). The independent predicates take and pass as follows: record adequacy \(\text{chk}_{\text{record}}\), 0.02 s and 98 percent; permitted use \(\text{chk}_{\text{use}}\), 6 s and 60 percent; citation grounding \(\text{chk}_{\text{out}}\), 3 s and 70 percent; target review \(\text{chk}_{\text{target}}\), 2 s and 90 percent. No predicate depends on another’s result. Use the saturated planning model with sufficient end-to-end credits, no additional shared service bottleneck, and each write charged at its record ceiling; the calculated rate is not a measurement of actual collector throughput.

Order the predicates by equation 2 and compute \(\ExpectedCheckingTime\) and the yield \(\AdmissionRouteYield\).
Evaluate equation 4, name the binding stage in this model, and compute its planned admitted records per hour. Compute the write bandwidth that would let generation bind, and the admitted rate then.
The binding stage differs from the repair collector of notebook 14.6. Explain why, and evaluate a proposal to cut the record ceiling to 100 MB by truncating retrieved pages. Propose a design that lowers stored bytes without weakening \(\text{chk}_{\text{record}}\) or \(\text{chk}_{\text{use}}\).

Staging production feedback for the support agent (Advanced). The support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)) serves customers who are waiting, so its collector captures production sessions it cannot delay or pause. Sessions finish at \(\ArrivalRate=50\) per second and last 120 s, with capture running throughout. A policy-grounding judge assesses each captured record on \(\WorkerCount=40\) slots in a mean of 0.6 s. Records have a ceiling of 250 KB, and staging holds \(\StagingStoreCapacity=4\) GB and at most 10,000 outstanding records (decimal units). During an incident the judge’s endpoint degrades and every assessment runs to its 10 s timeout. The controller needs 20 s to act, and staging starts nearly empty.

Compute the nominal utilization, the degraded capacity, and the staging growth rate. Compute the time until the byte limit and until the record-count limit is reached, and state which binds.
Size the high watermark on the binding limit, counting records from sessions already capturing and growth during the controller’s delay.
Backpressure on the source is unavailable here, unlike in the repair collector. Compute the capture fraction that holds staging steady during the incident, and critique a proposal to keep capturing only the shortest sessions. State what the corpus manifest must record about the uncaptured sessions.

Designing a leakage screen within a review budget (Advanced). A corpus of 100,000 records is screened with 128-component MinHash signatures before split assignment (section 14.4.3). Assume that 2,000 record pairs are true relatives with Jaccard similarity 0.8 and that every other pair has similarity 0.1. Reviewers can inspect 20,000 candidate pairs per screening pass.

For banding designs of 32 bands of 4 rows, 16 of 8, and 8 of 16, compute the expected false candidates among unrelated pairs and the recall of true relatives. Decide which designs fit the review budget.
Redesign the screen so that it keeps the recall of the 32-by-4 design and fits the budget, using the full signature. Justify the chosen threshold with the estimator’s standard error, and estimate the machine work it adds.
Name a relationship that no choice of bands will catch, and the mechanism that must catch it instead.



What’s Next: From corpus membership to learning targetsTranslating an admitted recovery record into a gradient update requires reinforcing the correction rather than the refused proposal it conditions on. Trajectory Fine-Tuning opens with the record this chapter published to repair_demonstrations_v1, whose targets recovery_targets_v1 already fixed. It first asks which parts of the repair behavior belong in weights at all, then turns the curation contract into training examples. Serialization must reconstruct each prefix exactly as the agent received it, loss masking must assign direct supervised loss terms to the selected targets alone, and batching must keep independent examples from reading one another. Preference learning applies a different objective to justified comparisons. Curation decides which material is eligible and why, and the next chapter decides how that material shapes an update and whether the changed policy earns a release under the same runtime controls.

title: 14 Trajectory Curation
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why is an accepted agent trajectory not automatically a good training example?
Every agent run leaves a durable record of what it saw, proposed, and achieved, and a team preparing the next policy is tempted to train on that record directly. A record, however, answers a different question than a training example does. An accepted trial can contain a malformed call that the runtime refused, a failure can stem from a broken tool schema that no weight update repairs, and two attempts at the same task split across training and evaluation turn a test score into a measure of recall. Imitating such records teaches the model its own mistakes and workarounds, and filtering them by outcome alone narrows behavior toward whatever the filter happens to reward. Curation therefore decides, before any gradient is computed, whether a failure belongs in the weights at all, which records may serve which learner, which tokens are targets and which are context, and what evidence and permissions travel with every record derived from the original run.

Learning Objectives

Justify a learning use for a residual failure and distinguish imitation material, preference comparisons, and rollout fixtures
Design versioned collection fixtures and protected splits for a stated generalization claim
Construct admission predicates and compare verification costs without changing their criteria
Assign recovery and negative records to appropriate roles while distinguishing trajectory counts, stored tokens, and loss-bearing tokens
Assess how selection rules and sampling budgets change the diversity and yield of a self-improvement loop
Size bounded collection flow against downstream capacity, and price an emitted artifact by attempt cost and emission yield
Defend a versioned corpus manifest with transformation lineage, permitted uses, and intended consumers

title: 14 Trajectory Curation
text:
The evaluation harness of Agent Evaluation produced more than a release decision. While it judged the repair agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)) over repeated attempts on the connection-pool repair task, it also accumulated a durable trajectory log that captures every trial in granular detail: the environment observations delivered to the model, the code edits it proposed, the invalid tool calls rejected by the runtime, the subsequent recovery steps, and the final verdict scored against the task acceptance criteria. Some runs passed cleanly, others failed outright, and several remain stalled in pending states because regression suites or accounting checks timed out. To an engineering team preparing the next iteration of the policy, these accumulated interaction logs look like the natural, abundant raw material for fine-tuning.



Curation changes what the policy learns from its records and leaves every exposure where the runtime closes it.
The machinery built so far, however, does not specify how to translate raw logs into training data. The acceptance contract defined in The Task Acceptance Contract evaluates the final outcome of an entire trial rather than assigning credit to individual tokens or tool calls within it. Consequently, an accepted verdict alone cannot distinguish between an optimal tool call and an accidental stumble that the agent managed to survive. Imitating raw logs reproduces whatever they contain. If an agent wastes ten calls exploring invalid syntax before hitting the correct command, blind imitation trains the next model to repeat that exploratory churn. Furthermore, rigorous evaluation requires held-out task distributions that the training process never touches. If an engineer partitions data naively at the trace level, different attempts on the same underlying task fixture land on both sides of the train-test split, silently destroying evaluation integrity. Finally, because the agent generated these records under its own behavioral distribution, any filtering rule directly shapes what the subsequent policy will produce, inducing feedback dynamics across training generations.
Bridging the gap between raw execution logs and active model training requires a dedicated systems stage. Trajectory curation selects, labels, and transforms recorded interactions for a declared learning use while preserving the evidence and constraints that justify that use. Where evaluation establishes whether a trial satisfied its specification under fixed conditions, curation resolves a different operational question: which behaviors and tasks the learning process should absorb, which steps must be masked or rewritten, and how to preserve statistical isolation across splits. The end product of this pipeline is a versioned, reproducible corpus tailored to specific training consumers, accompanied by strict provenance records rather than an ad hoc collection of success flags. Transforming these admitted records into tokenized inputs and loss objectives becomes the downstream responsibility of Trajectory Fine-Tuning.
This chapter follows the repair agent from diagnosis to a published corpus. A failure caused by a truncated observation is the case whose remedy lies outside the weights, and a recovery from a refused edit becomes the record carried all the way into a corpus. The stages run in the order the risks arise. Before anything is collected, the failure must be shown to belong in the weights (section 14.2), and the evidence that will later judge the trained model must be fixed and protected (section 14.3, section 14.4). Collected records then pass admission checks specific to the learner that will consume them (section 14.5), recovery records are divided into context and targets (section 14.6), and the feedback created when a policy generates its own data is bounded (section 14.7). The remaining sections keep the collector within its capacity (section 14.8), bind every record to its lineage (section 14.9), and carry one record through the whole chain (section 14.10). The first decision is triage, because a failure that does not belong to the model should never reach a corpus.

title: 14 Trajectory Curation
text:
An execution failure enters the trajectory curation pipeline only after systematic diagnosis confirms that model weights are the appropriate target for remediation. The repair agent’s evaluation history for pool_repair_01 illustrates why diagnostic triage must precede dataset collection. In Agent Evaluation, the candidate configuration’s trial submitted workspace ws_r19.
