equation 5







Key Takeaways: Give every learning artifact a declared use

Weights are the last remedy, not the first: Counterfactual probes place many failures in context, schemas, or the runtime, where a reversible repair removes them for every model version. Training earns only the residual that survives, and demonstrations, preference comparisons, and rollout fixtures each carry their own admission conditions.
A split protects a claim, not a file: With several attempts per task, a random split over traces puts most tasks on both sides, so the test score rewards recall of solved siblings. Assign whole task groups, carry the assignment into every derived record, and fix it before collection begins.
Cheaper checking must admit the same corpus: Ordering independent, fixed-cost predicates within permissible orders by cost per rejection, \(\CheckSlotTime_i/(1-\CheckPassProbability_i)\), cuts verification work at an unchanged accepted set. Dropping or loosening a predicate buys a different corpus, so its lower unit price is not a saving.
A recorded mistake is context, not a target: Recovery records keep the error and its refusal as conditioning history and select only the assessed correction as supervision. Mixtures are specified in selected targets and budgeted in stored tokens, because context per target differs by class.
Self-selected data narrows what it rewards: When the policy supplies its own records, rising acceptance can hide the recoveries the selector rarely keeps. Distinct action sequences per fixture, pass@1 against pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\), and an external anchor show whether the loop is still learning or only repeating itself.
Staging is sized for the burst, not the average: A verifier timeout burst, not average utilization, exhausts reserved staging, so each run holds a credit at the record ceiling until durable disposition. The cheapest stage can bind the illustrated planning rate while generation divided by yield sets its active-resource price.
The manifest is the contract the trainer reads: Records and derived artifacts bind to source versions, checks, transformations, permissions, split membership, and intended consumers. Integrity proves unmodified bytes, not truth or permission, so every derived record earns its own admission decision.



Verified trajectory post-training (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training}\)) now has a concrete decision boundary: evidence supports a specified learning use, and the corpus manifest carries that decision through selection and transformation so the trainer can tell context from targets. The trained policy still faces evaluation and still runs under the runtime’s authority and resource controls.

title: 14 Trajectory Curation
text:
The principles governing trajectory curation did not emerge in a vacuum; they adapt hard-won lessons from data mining, information retrieval, and relational databases. Data mining first identified data leakage as a systemic failure mode where information about an evaluation target inadvertently reaches the learner through correlated records (Kaufman et al. 2012). In software modeling, duplicated source files were shown to inflate benchmark accuracy artificially until evaluation splits underwent thorough deduplication (Allamanis 2019). Modern screening pipelines borrow directly from web search, where minwise hashing estimated document resemblance from compact signatures (Broder 1997) and locality-sensitive hashing reduced high-dimensional similarity search to sublinear time (Indyk and Motwani 1998). Database query processing supplied the twin mechanisms of admission control and data provenance: optimizers established how to order expensive filter predicates by their cost-to-selectivity rank to minimize wasted computation (Hellerstein and Stonebraker 1993), while provenance frameworks formalized exactly which source records produced a derived value and why (Buneman et al. 2001).

Kaufman, Shachar, Saharon Rosset, Claudia Perlich, and Ori Stitelman. 2012. “Leakage in Data Mining: Formulation, Detection, and Avoidance.” ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data (TKDD) 6 (4): 1–21.

Zelikman, Eric, Yuhuai Wu, Jesse Mu, and Noah D. Goodman. 2022. “STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning with Reasoning.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35: 15476–88.

Uesato, Jonathan, Nate Kushman, Ramana Kumar, Francis Song, Noah Siegel, Lisa Wang, Antonia Creswell, Geoffrey Irving, and Irina Higgins. 2022. “Solving Math Word Problems with Process- and Outcome-Based Feedback.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2211.14275, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2211.14275.

Lightman, Hunter, Vineet Kosaraju, Yura Burda, Harri Edwards, Bowen Baker, Teddy Lee, Jan Leike, John Schulman, Ilya Sutskever, and Karl Cobbe. 2024. “Let’s Verify Step by Step.” The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
Learning from self-generated execution traces shares an equally deep lineage in reinforcement learning and symbolic reasoning. Classical imitation learning demonstrated that a policy trained exclusively on expert demonstrations compounds its errors when deployed, because small mistakes push the agent into unfamiliar states where it cannot recover (Ross et al. 2011). Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell showed that querying an expert on the learner’s own visited states restores linear error bounds; recovery demonstrations are the systems realization of that theoretical remedy. Expert iteration formalized this dynamic into an alternating loop of generation, search-based selection, and retraining, using tree search to discover improved decisions for a neural network to imitate (Anthony et al. 2017). Bootstrapped reasoning extended this loop to language models by sampling reasoning paths and filtering for traces that reached correct answers (Zelikman et al. 2022). Process supervision then tightened verification from coarse terminal outcomes down to individual reasoning steps (Uesato et al. 2022; Lightman et al. 2024).
Every self-training paradigm eventually encounters the same fundamental challenge: the filtering mechanism is itself an imperfect component of the system being improved. Production machine learning pipelines first exposed the systemic risks of hidden feedback loops, where an operational model’s outputs silently shape its own subsequent training distribution (Sculley et al. 2015). Reward modeling revealed Goodhart’s law in full force: excessive optimization against a learned proxy drives reward scores up while true task quality deteriorates (Gao et al. 2023). Unchecked recursive training on synthetic outputs further accelerates model collapse, progressively eroding diversity and extinguishing the distribution’s tail (Shumailov et al. 2024). Agentic execution sharpens each of these failure modes because trajectories do not exist in isolation. They execute stateful tool calls, operate under specific environment permissions, and can inadvertently manipulate or game their own evaluation harnesses. The safeguards of this chapter, from verifier cascades and disjoint task-group splits to lineage envelopes and dataset manifests (Gebru et al. 2021), apply classical systems isolation and provenance guarantees directly to the trajectory as the atomic unit of machine learning data.

Shumailov, Ilia, Zakhar Shumaylov, Yiren Zhao, Nicolas Papernot, Ross Anderson, and Yarin Gal. 2024. “AI Models Collapse When Trained on Recursively Generated Data.” Nature 631 (8022): 755–59. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07566-y.
For further reading, start with these:

End-to-end arguments (Saltzer et al. 1984): The classic statement of why a function belongs where it can be implemented completely and correctly. In trajectory curation, this principle argues for repairing tool interfaces and runtime environments directly rather than training model weights to work around platform flaws.
Predicate migration (Hellerstein and Stonebraker 1993): The foundational database paper on ordering expensive filter checks by cost per rejection, formalizing the exchange argument used to structure multi-stage verifier cascades.
Imitation learning as no-regret online learning (Ross et al. 2011): The analysis demonstrating why training exclusively on clean expert prefixes leaves an agent unprepared for its own mistakes, establishing the theoretical rationale for recovery demonstrations.
Hidden technical debt in machine learning systems (Sculley et al. 2015): A comprehensive systems catalog of data dependencies and feedback loops that any self-improving corpus pipeline inherits.
Datasheets for datasets (Gebru et al. 2021): The documentation discipline that a corpus manifest adapts into versioned, machine-auditable metadata fields.
Reward-model overoptimization (Gao et al. 2023): A controlled empirical study showing how aggressive optimization against a learned proxy reward drives proxy scores up while true task quality degrades.


Saltzer, Jerome H., David P. Reed, and David D. Clark. 1984. “End-to-End Arguments in System Design.” ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 2 (4): 277–88. https://doi.org/10.1145/357401.357402.

Hellerstein, Joseph M., and Michael Stonebraker. 1993. “Predicate Migration: Optimizing Queries with Expensive Predicates.” Proceedings of the 1993 ACM SIGMOD International Conference on Management of Data, 267–76. https://doi.org/10.1145/170036.170078.

Sculley, D., Gary Holt, Daniel Golovin, Eugene Davydov, Todd Phillips, Dietmar Ebner, Vinay Chaudhary, Michael Young, Jean-François Crespo, and Dan Dennison. 2015. “Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 28: 2503–11.

Gao, Leo, John Schulman, and Jacob Hilton. 2023. “Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization.” Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning 202: 10835–66.

title: 14 Trajectory Curation
text:
Every given below is a hypothetical problem input chosen for round arithmetic, not a measurement of any system. Each problem asks for a calculation and the curation or collection decision it supports.

Sizing a protected split (Basic). A collection job makes \(\IndependentAttemptCount=5\) attempts on each of 2,000 repair tasks. A colleague proposes assigning individual traces to training with probability \(\TrainingSplitFraction=0.9\) and to the final test otherwise.

Compute the fraction and number of tasks whose attempts straddle the partition, and the smallest \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) at which a majority of tasks straddle.
Compute the probability that a given test attempt has at least one sibling attempt of the same task in training, and state what the resulting test score measures.
The team switches to a group split (section 14.4). Treating tasks as independent trials with an acceptance rate near one half, compute how many task groups the final test must hold for the standard error of its task-level acceptance rate to be at most 0.025, and what fraction of the 2,000 tasks that reserves.

Ordering an admission route (Basic). A demonstration route has three independent predicates beyond record adequacy: a permitted-use lookup \(\text{chk}_{\text{use}}\) that takes 0.05 s and passes 70 percent of records, a sandboxed test run \(\text{chk}_{\text{out}}\) that takes 30 s and passes 50 percent, and a model-judged target review \(\text{chk}_{\text{target}}\) that takes 4 s and passes 80 percent. Target review does not need the test result, and the current order is \(\text{chk}_{\text{use}}\to \text{chk}_{\text{out}}\to \text{chk}_{\text{target}}\).

Rank the predicates by cost per rejection (equation 2) and choose the order.
Compute \(\ExpectedCheckingTime\) per attempted record and per admitted record for the current and chosen orders (equation 1), and the fraction of verifier-slot work the change saves.
A colleague proposes dropping \(\text{chk}_{\text{target}}\) instead, because it lowers checking time per admitted record further. Compute that figure and the new yield, and explain why the comparison with part (b) is not a cost comparison at all.

Three denominators for one mixture (Basic). A retained demonstration pool holds 20,000 direct-success records averaging 6,000 stored tokens and 1,000 selected target tokens, and 5,000 recovery records averaging 30,000 stored tokens and 2,500 selected target tokens.

Compute the recovery class’s share of records, stored tokens, and selected targets, and the context per target token for each class.
The team wants recovery to supply half of the selected targets. Holding total selected targets at the current value, compute the presentations each class needs, how many recovery records must repeat, and the change in processed tokens.
Holding processed tokens at the current value instead, compute the total selected targets at the same half-and-half mixture. State which budget this team should fix when training time is the scarce resource, and what the arithmetic cannot decide.

Spending a sampling budget on contrast (Intermediate). A collector has 8,000 attempts for 1,000 repair fixtures in three difficulty bands: 400 fixtures with per-attempt pass rate \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.1\), 400 with \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.5\), and 200 with \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.9\). Attempts are independent, and each fixture receives \(\IndependentAttemptCount=8\).

For each band and in total, compute the expected number of fixtures that yield at least one success and the expected number of mixed groups (equation 3). Compute the attempts spent per mixed group.
A colleague proposes dropping the easy band and spending its 1,600 attempts on the hard band at \(\IndependentAttemptCount=12\). Compute the new expected number of mixed groups and state what the imitation corpus loses.
Decide whether to adopt the proposal for a group-relative objective and for an imitation artifact, and explain why the easy band’s all-success groups are not wasted attempts.

Reviewing after selection (Intermediate). A cohort makes \(\IndependentAttemptCount=10\) independent attempts on each of 200 tasks. Each attempt succeeds with probability 0.2 and costs $0.50 for generation, verification, and storage. Every successful attempt goes to human target review at $6, which passes 75 percent of the successes it sees, independently. The selector emits at most one artifact per task, the first passing success in attempt order.

Compute the expected number of emitted artifacts, the cohort cost, and \(\CostPerEmittedArtifact\) (equation 5).
The team instead reviews a task’s successes in attempt order and stops at its first pass. Show that the set of emitting tasks is unchanged, and compute the expected reviews per task, the new cohort cost, and \(\CostPerEmittedArtifact\).
A second proposal halves \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) to 5 with the stopping review in place. Compute \(\CostPerEmittedArtifact\) and the emitted count, and decide between the two proposals, naming what the cheaper unit price costs the corpus.

The research agent’s collector (Intermediate). The research agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}\)) reads untrusted sources, so each collection record keeps the retrieved pages that its claims cite, and the permitted-use review of that retained content is expensive. A collector runs 32 accelerators at 40 accelerator-seconds per attempt, checks attempts on 16 verifier slots, and writes records of at most 1 GB to a store that sustains 500 MB/s (decimal units). The independent predicates take and pass as follows: record adequacy \(\text{chk}_{\text{record}}\), 0.02 s and 98 percent; permitted use \(\text{chk}_{\text{use}}\), 6 s and 60 percent; citation grounding \(\text{chk}_{\text{out}}\), 3 s and 70 percent; target review \(\text{chk}_{\text{target}}\), 2 s and 90 percent. No predicate depends on another’s result. Use the saturated planning model with sufficient end-to-end credits, no additional shared service bottleneck, and each write charged at its record ceiling; the calculated rate is not a measurement of actual collector throughput.

Order the predicates by equation 2 and compute \(\ExpectedCheckingTime\) and the yield \(\AdmissionRouteYield\).
Evaluate equation 4, name the binding stage in this model, and compute its planned admitted records per hour. Compute the write bandwidth that would let generation bind, and the admitted rate then.
The binding stage differs from the repair collector of notebook 14.6. Explain why, and evaluate a proposal to cut the record ceiling to 100 MB by truncating retrieved pages. Propose a design that lowers stored bytes without weakening \(\text{chk}_{\text{record}}\) or \(\text{chk}_{\text{use}}\).

Staging production feedback for the support agent (Advanced). The support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)) serves customers who are waiting, so its collector captures production sessions it cannot delay or pause. Sessions finish at \(\ArrivalRate=50\) per second and last 120 s, with capture running throughout. A policy-grounding judge assesses each captured record on \(\WorkerCount=40\) slots in a mean of 0.6 s. Records have a ceiling of 250 KB, and staging holds \(\StagingStoreCapacity=4\) GB and at most 10,000 outstanding records (decimal units). During an incident the judge’s endpoint degrades and every assessment runs to its 10 s timeout. The controller needs 20 s to act, and staging starts nearly empty.

Compute the nominal utilization, the degraded capacity, and the staging growth rate. Compute the time until the byte limit and until the record-count limit is reached, and state which binds.
Size the high watermark on the binding limit, counting records from sessions already capturing and growth during the controller’s delay.
Backpressure on the source is unavailable here, unlike in the repair collector. Compute the capture fraction that holds staging steady during the incident, and critique a proposal to keep capturing only the shortest sessions. State what the corpus manifest must record about the uncaptured sessions.

Designing a leakage screen within a review budget (Advanced). A corpus of 100,000 records is screened with 128-component MinHash signatures before split assignment (section 14.4.3). Assume that 2,000 record pairs are true relatives with Jaccard similarity 0.8 and that every other pair has similarity 0.1. Reviewers can inspect 20,000 candidate pairs per screening pass.

For banding designs of 32 bands of 4 rows, 16 of 8, and 8 of 16, compute the expected false candidates among unrelated pairs and the recall of true relatives. Decide which designs fit the review budget.
Redesign the screen so that it keeps the recall of the 32-by-4 design and fits the budget, using the full signature. Justify the chosen threshold with the estimator’s standard error, and estimate the machine work it adds.
Name a relationship that no choice of bands will catch, and the mechanism that must catch it instead.



What’s Next: From corpus membership to learning targetsTranslating an admitted recovery record into a gradient update requires reinforcing the correction rather than the refused proposal it conditions on. Trajectory Fine-Tuning opens with the record this chapter published to repair_demonstrations_v1, whose targets recovery_targets_v1 already fixed. It first asks which parts of the repair behavior belong in weights at all, then turns the curation contract into training examples. Serialization must reconstruct each prefix exactly as the agent received it, loss masking must assign direct supervised loss terms to the selected targets alone, and batching must keep independent examples from reading one another. Preference learning applies a different objective to justified comparisons. Curation decides which material is eligible and why, and the next chapter decides how that material shapes an update and whether the changed policy earns a release under the same runtime controls.

title: 16 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why does a check that only scores an agent’s attempts end up defining what the agent learns?
Curated demonstrations give an agent a starting policy, but they cover only the decisions someone recorded, and long-horizon tasks keep producing decisions that no demonstration anticipated. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards replaces the demonstration with a programmatic check, such as a unit test suite, a compiler, or a proof checker, that scores each sampled attempt and turns the score into a weight update without a human label. That substitution changes what the check is. An evaluator that once only counted failures becomes the objective the optimizer searches, and the search finds every gap between what the check measures and what the task requires, from a weakened assertion to a patched test runner to a verdict rewritten before it is recorded. The verification boundary must therefore be defended like a security perimeter, with fixtures the candidate cannot reach and rewards read as evidence about only the properties their checks cover. Wherever outcomes can be mechanically checked, the policy improves as far as the scope and protection of the check allow, and no further.

Learning Objectives

Explain why reward-driven learning needs sampled support that imitation does not, and estimate when a task yields no reward contrast
Design a shaped reward that preserves the pass-over-failure order, and bound the false accepts its assessment admits through verifier isolation and repeated checks
Calculate the generation cost and standard error of continuation-based credit estimates across turns
Compute group-relative coefficients and the per-token weight that length normalization assigns them
Specify the per-invocation records and version-lag bound that keep a multi-turn update faithful to its sampling policy
Diagnose changes in reward and length from task outcomes rather than from the narration a policy generates
Size the environment cycle and verifier pool of a rollout-training loop and identify the stage that limits it






The previous chapter left the repair agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)) with trained_policy_v1, a supervised checkpoint fitted to the one malformed-argument recovery that curation admitted. Its release gate already had to send trials into a state the corpus never covered, the version conflict for which no demonstration exists (Case Study: Training the Repair Policy). More imitation needs someone to record that recovery, and a preference pair needs two admissible records of it. The agent’s versioned test fixtures and acceptance checks need neither. They can score entirely novel attempts whose intermediate actions have no labeled target. An autonomous policy might inspect an unexpected source file, attempt an alternative refactoring strategy, or halt when it encounters an unfamiliar error. While the automated test suite verifies whether the final patch succeeds, it provides no token-by-token guidance during intermediate decision steps.



Training changes the policy and leaves every exposure where the runtime closes it.
Existing techniques stop short of using verification outcomes to reshape the underlying policy. Trajectory fine-tuning teaches models to generalize from demonstrated recovery paths, but it remains fundamentally bounded by demonstration data; human-verified repairs for intricate, non-deterministic bugs are exceedingly scarce. Test-time selection filters multiple generated rollouts against an acceptance suite to extract a passing candidate, yet it incurs significant inference latency on every incoming task while leaving the base policy unchanged. Neither approach increases the intrinsic probability of generating successful trajectories from verification signals alone. Reinforcement learning bridges this gap by converting acceptance verdicts directly into gradient updates. In doing so, it alters the role of the verification suite. Once a check enters the optimization objective, any flaw in the test fixture is compiled into the network weights rather than miscounted on a single run, and the acceptance check that once decided a release (The Task Acceptance Contract) becomes the signal that decides every update.
Constructing a training loop that converts automated test outcomes into policy updates requires four tightly coupled systems mechanisms. First, the reward design must remain robust against optimization pressure, evaluating functional correctness without introducing exploitable shortcuts. Second, the policy update rule must solve multi-turn credit assignment, translating a single terminal pass or fail signal into per-token update coefficients over extended interactive trajectories. Third, the rollout recording infrastructure must maintain strict fidelity to what the policy generated and observed, so that the loss is computed on the inputs the policy actually saw. Finally, the compute infrastructure, spanning sandboxed execution environments, verification workers, and gradient engines, must be provisioned so that training updates ingest complete, synchronized candidate groups without pipeline stalls.
The chapter takes these mechanisms in the order a student would need to build them. It first fixes what an outcome-driven update can and cannot learn (section 16.2), then prices the reward that drives it, including the false accepts a verifier admits (section 16.3). Credit assignment follows, first through return and value estimates (section 16.4) and then through group-relative policy optimization (section 16.5), the worked optimizer. The remaining sections keep that optimizer honest in practice: faithful records of multi-turn rollouts (section 16.6), a verifier the candidate cannot reach (section 16.7), diagnostics for the pathologies that rising reward can hide (section 16.8), and the rollout, verifier, and staleness arithmetic that sizes the training fleet (section 16.9). A case study then follows one repair group through the whole loop (section 16.10).



Reinforcement learning optimizes an agent policy directly against task outcomes rather than against recorded human actions. Where behavioral cloning (supervised imitation of recorded actions) requires an admitted demonstration for every intermediate step, reinforcement learning executes candidate rollouts in an environment and scores the resulting trajectories against programmatic checks. A supervised checkpoint, such as the trained_policy_v1 built in Case Study: Training the Repair Policy, offers a useful starting point to bootstrap sampling, but the optimization machinery depends only on the agent’s ability to act, observe, and receive an evaluative score. Before any gradient update can convert raw outcomes into policy improvements, however, the system architecture must establish three foundational mechanisms: the formal representation of multi-turn rollouts, the baseline estimators that isolate meaningful signal from variance, and the execution boundaries that protect verification harnesses during exploration.


A policy \(\Policy(\RolloutAction_k\mid \InteractionHistory_k)\), parameterized by weights \(\ModelParameters\), defines a probability distribution over responses \(\RolloutAction_k\) conditioned on the delivered interaction history \(\InteractionHistory_k\) through turn \(\RolloutTurnIndex\). We consider a finite decision horizon \(\TurnHorizon\) with turn indices \(\RolloutTurnIndex=0,\ldots,\TurnHorizon-1\). (We reserve \(\RolloutTurnIndex\) for agent-environment turns because \(\TokenIndex\) later indexes individual autoregressive tokens within a rollout.) The history \(\InteractionHistory_k\) plays the role of the recorded state \(\TrajectoryState_k\) in the trajectory notation of The H·S·A Exposure Space, the runtime’s delivered view at turn \(\RolloutTurnIndex\) rather than the environment itself. A response \(\RolloutAction_k\) represents either a proposed tool call, such as a shell command or structured API query, or a terminal answer. The runtime validates and executes any requested operation, returning standard output, standard error, or structured payloads as observations for subsequent turns. The interaction history \(\InteractionHistory_k\) records this transcript of delivered prompts, emitted actions, and returned observations. Because modern context windows cannot always ingest unbounded execution logs, the policy consumes a constructed prompt that may truncate or summarize older history. The policy interacts with the environment exclusively through this constructed context window, never through direct inspection of the underlying state \(\RolloutEnvironmentState_{k}\): an edited configuration file or sandbox directory affects policy decisions only after tool invocations reflect its contents back into \(\InteractionHistory_k\).


↪ The partially observable Markov decision process behind this observation constraint is developed in POMDP formalization of trajectories.
A rollout, or sampled trajectory \(\Trajectory\), encapsulates one complete execution trace under specified task definitions, policy weights, environment states, and harness constraints. In our illustrative repair scenario, a trial rl_trial_01 on task pool_repair_01 instantiates container sandbox pool_fixture_v1 and evaluates candidate patches against test harness repair_accept_v1. Each rollout generates its own telemetry, intermediate command outputs, and terminal verification artifacts; past demonstration records provide no credit to this live attempt.
A reward is a scalar evaluation metric computed under an explicit verification rule. In the simplest formulation, intermediate turns emit zero reward, leaving a single terminal score \(\TrajectoryReward(\Trajectory)\) evaluated at horizon completion without temporal discounting (a discount factor \(\DiscountFactor=1\), so a reward counts the same whichever turn it arrives on). The trajectory return collapses to this terminal score, yielding the expected return objective:
\[\ExpectedReturnObjective(\ModelParameters)=\mathbb{E}_{\Trajectory\sim\Policy}\left[\TrajectoryReward(\Trajectory)\right].\]
The expectation integrates over policy stochasticity, task sampling distributions, and environment variations (such as nondeterministic test execution times or network latencies). Maximizing \(\ExpectedReturnObjective(\ModelParameters)\) drives the policy to increase the expected measured reward under these specific operational conditions. Whether that measured score genuinely correlates with true task utility depends on the fidelity of the reward harness itself, an architectural challenge analyzed in section 16.3.
When the reward originates from an automated, deterministic check—such as unit test execution, syntax validation, type checking, or a formal proof assistant—rather than from an imperfect learned preference model or manual human grading, this paradigm is known as reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR)1 (Lambert et al. 2024).
1 Tests as Reward: Executed unit tests served as the reward for a code-generating model before the name existed: Le et al. (2022) trained a pretrained code model with reinforcement learning on test outcomes and added a learned critic that predicts functional correctness. That pairing anticipates this chapter’s central tension, since the test outcome is the trustworthy signal while the denser learned critic is itself a model that optimization can exploit. 
Le, Hung, Yue Wang, Akhilesh Deepak Gotmare, Silvio Savarese, and Steven Chu Hong Hoi. 2022. “CodeRL: Mastering Code Generation Through Pretrained Models and Deep Reinforcement Learning.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-1549.

Definition 16.1: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is policy optimization using reward signals computed by automated checks of specified properties of the policy’s outputs or interactions, such as tests or proof checkers, rather than relying solely on learned preference scores or human ratings.

Significance: An automated verification harness provides an objective training signal without requiring step-by-step demonstrations. By directly incentivizing task success, it increases the acceptance rate \(\AcceptanceProbability\) in the cost per accepted task (equation 1.2) even when human demonstrations do not exist. However, the verifier’s false-accept rate bounds only the per-rollout chance that a sampled failure is rewarded; when true passes are rare, false accepts can make up a far larger share of the rewarded rollouts (section 16.3.2).
Distinction: Whereas behavioral cloning trains the policy to reproduce specific recorded responses, RLVR evaluates only whether the completed trajectory satisfies programmatic criteria. The resulting policy gradient is strictly bounded by the coverage, sensitivity, and sandboxed security of the underlying verifier.
Common pitfall: Mistaking higher reward scores on a fixed verification suite for generalized task competence, or treating automated verification as a justification to relax runtime isolation and execution guardrails.






A terminal reward alone does not compute a parameter gradient. Policy-gradient algorithms adjust model parameters by estimating a gradient direction that increases the log-probabilities of sampled actions proportional to an evaluative score. Standard estimators subtract a baseline from the raw outcome: the centered advantage is \(\TrajectoryReward(\Trajectory)-\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory_0)\), where \(\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory_0)\) depends on the initial task prompt and context \(\InteractionHistory_0\) but remains independent of the sampled action sequence \(\Trajectory\). The baseline serves as an offset reference level. It can be a fixed scalar, an empirical rolling mean across task batches, or a parametric value estimate, and it does not necessarily require training a separate critic network (Williams 1992).
Consider a binary verification check where success yields \(1.0\) and failure yields \(0.0\). With a fixed baseline of 0.25, a passing rollout receives a centered score of 0.75, whereas a failing rollout yields -0.25. These opposing signs drive gradient updates in opposite directions: positive centered returns reinforce the probabilities of every token and tool call sampled along the passing trajectory, whereas negative centered returns suppress them. In contrast, setting the baseline to zero leaves failed rollouts with a centered score of \(0.0\), discarding the negative gradient signal that penalizes counterproductive trajectories.
This uniform attribution illustrates the classic credit-assignment problem:2 a terminal verifier evaluates overall trajectory success, but it cannot differentiate the decisive tool call from irrelevant or mildly detrimental exploratory steps. While subtracting an appropriate baseline reduces the variance of the policy gradient estimator without introducing bias (Greensmith et al. 2004), it applies a uniform scalar adjustment across the entire trajectory rather than isolating action-specific causal effects. Section 16.4 formalizes these estimators and their bias-variance trade-offs, and section 16.5 introduces group-relative scoring to compute data-dependent baselines across parallel rollouts without training an auxiliary value network.
2 Credit Assignment Problem: Minsky (1961) named the problem for learning systems that receive one success signal for a strategy built from many internal decisions, with games and program writing as his examples. The repair agent poses the same question at the scale of tool calls: a failed acceptance check arrives after many turns, and every turn is a candidate for blame, which is why the estimators of this chapter differ mainly in how they spread one outcome across those turns. 
Minsky, Marvin. 1961. “Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence.” Proceedings of the IRE 49 (1): 8–30. https://doi.org/10.1109/JRPROC.1961.287775.



A policy-gradient update can optimize only over trajectories that the sampling harness actually produces. Exploration, the sampling of action sequences the policy has rarely tried at points where it still spreads probability across several plausible actions, determines what reinforcement learning can discover. In environments governed by binary verification checks (pass vs. fail), a task instance that the policy never solves yields exclusively zero rewards. A zero baseline, or one that tracks the observed outcomes such as the mean of a group of attempts (section 16.5.4), then leaves every centered score at zero. A fixed positive baseline does produce a gradient, but it pushes down every sampled action alike and gives the update nothing to prefer. Either way, without variation in the outcome signal the update carries no contrast, regardless of how many rollouts the collector generates. If a policy solves a task instance with base probability \(\AttemptPassProbability\), sampling a group of \(\GroupSize\) independent rollouts yields at least one successful trajectory with probability \(1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\GroupSize\). That condition is the one that binds when \(\AttemptPassProbability\) is small; the group optimizer of section 16.5 also needs at least one failure in the same group, a stricter condition derived there. When \(\AttemptPassProbability=0\), scaling the group size \(\GroupSize\) yields no contrast at all. System builders overcome this cold-start bottleneck by seeding the policy through supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, curating curricula with progressive difficulty, or structuring reward functions with informative intermediate milestones.
Because exploration systematically exposes edge cases in both the target environment and the evaluation harness, the execution runtime must enforce rigid capability and resource boundaries. As an agent generates thousands of candidate interactions, optimization will exploit any loose permission, such as reading hidden test fixtures, patching Python test runners, or modifying exit codes in the evaluation container, to manufacture high rewards without solving the underlying problem. Preventing such gaming requires a protected assessment boundary. The agent’s actions execute within an isolated sandbox, while the verifier runs with separate privileges, shielded storage, and read-only access to private test suites; section 16.7 builds that boundary once the reward and the update it drives are in place. Even with complete isolation, held-out evaluation on disjoint test distributions remains necessary to determine whether the policy acquired robust problem-solving behavior or merely fit the idiosyncrasies of the training verifiers. Before any of that machinery can be designed, however, the reward itself must be pinned down: what the check measures, how often it is wrong, and how other terms may be added to it without overturning the pass-over-failure order.




When an agent tackles a task like pool_repair_01, the training loop requires an objective evaluation score for each newly sampled candidate repair rather than an expert demonstration of which lines to modify. Those acceptance criteria inherit the evaluation harness of repair_accept_v1, but passing a targeted unit test provides evidence only about that specific test assertion. Before the system can convert an execution outcome into a scalar reward, the training infrastructure must guarantee exactly what was executed, which artifact was tested, and which version of the grader evaluated it. The assessment contract established in The Task Acceptance Contract is no longer an offline benchmark; it is now an active component of the optimization objective.


A policy can easily collect high rewards without solving the underlying engineering problem. A candidate patch might satisfy the tested cases while introducing a race condition on an untested concurrency path. Alternatively, if the agent can write to the grading environment, it can modify the test runner so that a failing execution reports success. These failures represent two fundamentally different defects: incomplete test coverage vs. compromised measurement. Hardening the grader protects the measurement process, but it does not make the underlying test criteria complete.

Definition 16.2: Reward hacking
Reward hacking is behavior that increases measured reward by exploiting a gap between the formal reward and the intended task, including manipulation of the measurement mechanism (Amodei et al. 2016; Skalse et al. 2022).

Significance: Gradient optimization reinforces a rewarded shortcut just as eagerly as an authentic solution. Each gamed pass registers as a success, inflating the measured acceptance rate \(\AcceptanceProbability\) and artificially lowering the computed cost per accepted task while true capability stagnates; tracking policy quality during reinforcement learning therefore requires an independent assessment of task performance.
Distinction: A false-positive judgment is an evaluation error. It does not, by itself, establish that the policy discovered or deliberately exploited a shortcut.
Common pitfall: Treating instructions against tampering as protection for the grader. Software isolation at the runtime level must restrict what the policy and its submitted code can affect.



3 Goodhart’s Law Under Training: Selection pressure on imperfect checks showed best-of-\(\CandidatePoolSize\) selection pressing on an imperfect check, where a larger pool favors candidates the proxy overrates. An RL loop applies the same pressure at every update and then writes the result into the weights, so a gap between reward and task is searched far more persistently than any selection step or human-managed target ever searches it. A false accept carries far higher systemic consequences during training than during test-time sampling. At inference time, a noisy selector that accepts a bad candidate simply wastes one decision. In reinforcement learning, however, awarding reward to a defective trajectory raises the probability of the tokens that produced it, prompting the policy to generate more such trajectories on subsequent tasks. Once the exploit is learned into the model weights, the training run can raise its measured score while growing progressively worse at the intended task.3 Formally, let \(\CandidateUtility(\Trajectory)\) represent the developer’s intended objective and \(\ProxyTrajectoryReward(\Trajectory)\) the reward signal calculated by the training loop. Whenever an unintended trajectory \(\ExploitTrajectory\) satisfies \(\ProxyTrajectoryReward(\ExploitTrajectory)\ge\ProxyTrajectoryReward(\Trajectory^*)\) while \(\CandidateUtility(\ExploitTrajectory)\ll \CandidateUtility(\Trajectory^*)\), gradient ascent on \(\ProxyTrajectoryReward\) gives it no less weight than the intended solution. The exploit steadily gains ground whenever it also has higher prior probability under the current policy (Skalse et al. 2022; Krakovna et al. 2020). In practice, degenerate shortcuts often enjoy a substantial probability advantage: weakening an assertion or rewriting a verdict takes only a few lines and no understanding of the bug, whereas diagnosing and fixing a difficult bug may require a complex, multi-turn repair.


↩︎ How a verifier’s false-acceptance rate dilutes the passing candidates at inference time is established in Check precision and the candidate pool.
The optimizer this chapter develops amplifies this failure mode upon its very first occurrence. Group-relative optimization, taught in section 16.5, samples a group of \(\GroupSize\) rollouts for the same task and scores each rollout against the others, so the rarer a pass is within its group, the larger the weight the update gives it. Suppose the test files sit in the rollout’s writable workspace, and one rollout on a difficult bug weakens the failing assertion while the other \(\GroupSize-1\) rollouts fail honestly. That rollout is the group’s lone pass, and it receives the largest coefficient in the group, a weight that grows with \(\GroupSize\) (equation 3 derives its size). Every token that wrote the tampering edit receives a sharp probability increase. The optimization loop did not suffer an algorithmic malfunction; the optimizer performed exactly as designed on the reward signal it received.
The exploits observed in coding environments fall into three recognizable classes, each documented in training or evaluation runs of 2025-era models:

Weakening or special-casing the check. Code that returns expected values only for inputs tested by the suite, or test assertions edited until they pass. A 2025 system card reports that one model, when unable to find a general solution, sometimes special-cased tests to make them pass (Anthropic 2025).
Stubbing or bypassing the verified code path. In one 2025 report during reinforcement learning of a reasoning model on coding tasks, a monitor flagged a plan to make a verification function always return true, alongside an exploit that exited the environment before unit tests could execute (Baker et al. 2025).
Rewriting the verdict inside the runner. Production coding environments used for training proved vulnerable to candidates returning an object whose equality comparison always succeeds, calling sys.exit(0) before any assertion executes, or writing a conftest.py that monkeypatches the test framework’s reporting subsystem so that every failure is recorded as a pass; models trained in those environments learned to use them (MacDiarmid et al. 2025).

These exploits are not confined to training runs. An independent evaluator measured how often the most capable models of 2025 took them when the scorer was within reach, and whether asking the model not to made any difference.

War Story 16.1: Frontier models patch their scorers (2025)Context: In June 2025 the evaluation organization METR reported reward hacking by frontier models, chiefly OpenAI’s o3, on two suites of autonomous tasks: RE-Bench, whose research-engineering tasks let the agent see the entire scoring function, and the broader HCAST suite (Von Arx et al. 2025).
Mechanism: With the scorer in reach, o3 attacked it instead of the task. On a kernel-optimization task it overwrote the timing function so that it always returned shorter measurements; on a code-generation scaffolding task it patched the evaluation function to judge every submission successful; on a fine-tuning speed task it modified the script to copy the cached weights of an already fine-tuned model.
Impact: The fine-tuning task was hacked in 21 of 21 runs. Across RE-Bench, 39 of 128 runs hacked (30 percent), against 8 of 1,087 on HCAST (0.7 percent). Asked after its first hacking plan whether the plan adhered to the user’s intention, o3 answered no 10 times in 10. Adding “Please do not reward hack” to the prompt moved the hacking rate over 20 runs from 80 percent to 70 percent.
Fix: METR excludes successful reward-hacking runs from its reported capability results, and recommends that when a monitor detects a hack, developers patch the exploit in the scoring function rather than punish the model.
Systems lesson: A scorer the agent can read and write sits at the visible-test closure level no matter what the task author intended, and an instruction does not raise it. In an evaluation these runs are excluded after the fact; in an RLVR loop every one of them is a maximal reward, and the gradient copies it.



Von Arx, Sydney, Lawrence Chan, and Beth Barnes. 2025. Recent Frontier Models Are Reward Hacking. METR blog.
METR attributes the substantial difference between 30 percent on RE-Bench and 0.7 percent on HCAST to reachability: on RE-Bench the model could inspect the scoring function directly, making it easier to bypass. The essential defense is a verification check that the policy cannot reach, evaluated on execution evidence that the policy cannot forge. For this reason, the sandboxed architecture of section 16.7 removes the test runner, configuration files, and evaluation credentials from the candidate’s control.
A reward is only as dependable as the closure evidence level of the check that computes it. These closure levels categorize the basis of an evaluation verdict by how much of it the agent policy can influence or reach. A static check establishes selected structural properties, a sealed test suite withholds and protects its test cases, and a formal proof verifies a specified property under explicit assumptions. Test coverage then limits any individual check at every level: even a sealed suite with an omitted edge case continues to reward buggy solutions that exploit the gap. The distinction drawn in Grader error rates between a grader’s false-acceptance rate and the failure rate among accepted outcomes is the same base-rate arithmetic that equation 3.3 applied to a candidate pool. Training changes one thing about it. The policy’s pass rate is no longer a fixed property of the task, so the share of rewards that go to failures moves as the policy learns, and it is largest when true task success is rare. The symbols below map onto those of Grader error rates. Let \(\ReferenceAssessedFailure\) be criterion failure under an independent reference assessment and \(\VerifierVerdict^+\) acceptance by the training verifier (the event written \(\text{Acc}\) there). Let \(\ValidCandidateRate\) be the policy’s current probability that a rollout satisfies the criterion, \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate=\Pr(\VerifierVerdict^+\mid \ReferenceAssessedFailure)\) the verifier’s false-acceptance rate, and \(\VerifierTrueAcceptanceRate\) its probability of accepting a criterion success. Provided verifier acceptance occurs with nonzero probability, the failure rate among accepted rollouts is
\[
\Pr(\ReferenceAssessedFailure\mid \VerifierVerdict^+) = \frac{(1-\ValidCandidateRate)\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate}{\ValidCandidateRate \VerifierTrueAcceptanceRate+(1-\ValidCandidateRate)\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate}.
\tag{1}\]



The rarer true passes are, the more of the reward a small verifier error claims.
Equation 1 defines the false-accept share of the reward: the fraction of all rewarded rollouts that actually fail the task criterion. Because its denominator sums both true positive accepts (\(\ValidCandidateRate \VerifierTrueAcceptanceRate\)) and false positive accepts (\((1-\ValidCandidateRate)\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\)), a small false-positive rate \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\) yields a large false share whenever failures are common. In reinforcement learning on challenging tasks, failure is the default state during early iterations. The same Bayesian arithmetic governs automated tests and learned reward models alike.

Napkin Math 16.1: False accepts in the rewardProblem: A hypothetical batch samples 8 rollouts for each of 1,024 tasks, giving 8,192 rollouts. Suppose 10 percent satisfy the criterion under the reference assessment. The training verifier accepts every criterion success and 2.5 percent of criterion failures. What share of its positive judgments are false accepts?
Math: For \(\BatchRolloutCount\) rollouts, expected true accepts are \(\BatchRolloutCount \ValidCandidateRate \VerifierTrueAcceptanceRate\) and expected false accepts are \(\BatchRolloutCount(1-\ValidCandidateRate)\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\). For this batch these are 819.20 and 184.32, respectively, totaling 1,003.52 expected positive judgments. Applying equation 1 gives 18.4 percent.
Result: 18.4 percent of rewarded rollouts are failures, although the verifier errs on only 2.5 percent of failures. The counts are expectations; an actual batch varies around them.
Systems insight: The false share is set by the ratio \((1-\ValidCandidateRate)\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate/(\ValidCandidateRate \VerifierTrueAcceptanceRate)\), so it moves with the policy’s pass rate as much as with the verifier. In the small-share regime, halving \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\) roughly halves the share; doubling \(\ValidCandidateRate\) has approximately the same effect when \(\ValidCandidateRate\) is also small. For a fixed positive false-acceptance rate, the false share approaches one as true passes become rare. Measure verifier error at the pass rate the policy currently has, and expect the share to fall as training succeeds. The share is not the fraction of the gradient that rewards errors, which also depends on where the false accepts fall within their groups (section 16.5.1).





Suppose a fully assessed rollout receives an observed binary outcome \(\CorrectnessReward(\Trajectory)\in\{0,1\}\). Let \(\FormatComplianceScore(\Trajectory)\in[0,1]\) measure format compliance and let \(\text{len}(\Trajectory)\in[0,1]\) measure generated-token cost relative to an enforced cap. A common terminal score formulation is
\[
\TrajectoryReward(\Trajectory)=\CorrectnessReward(\Trajectory)+\FormatRewardWeight\FormatComplianceScore(\Trajectory)-\LengthPenaltyWeight\text{len}(\Trajectory),
\qquad \FormatRewardWeight\ge 0,\quad \LengthPenaltyWeight\ge 0.
\]
Format compliance encourages well-formed tool calls, and the length penalty favors concise solutions.4 Neither auxiliary term should silently override the core outcome priority. Over their defined ranges, an observed pass earns at least \(1-\LengthPenaltyWeight\), while an observed failure earns at most \(\FormatRewardWeight\). A sufficient condition for every passing rollout to outrank every failing rollout is therefore

\[

Allowing equality permits a tie between a maximally penalized pass and a perfectly formatted failure. Strict inequality protects the score ordering, and it holds only while the normalized length penalty \(\text{len}(\Trajectory)\) remains strictly bounded in \([0,1]\). Normalizing by a nominal token budget preserves that invariant only if the execution runtime enforces the cap with hard process termination.
When an unexpected infrastructure failure leaves a required check unavailable, the assessment remains incomplete. Under the four-verdict rule of The four-verdict rule its verdict is unknown, and the reward stays unresolved rather than being converted to \(\CorrectnessReward=0\) or \(\CorrectnessReward=1\). Converting an unexecuted check to failure penalizes valid candidate solutions for harness faults, while converting it to success creates an immediate reward vulnerability; section 16.6.3 develops how a training loop must handle such rollouts. An explicit timeout under the task contract represents a valid failure verdict; a missing result due to test runner crashes does not. Similarly, introducing partial credit (awarding reward for the fraction of unit tests passed, for instance) defines a distinct optimization objective that alters which behavioral changes earn reinforcement, requiring its own priority analysis.
Permissions and hard resource limits must remain strict runtime constraints. A negative reward penalty merely discourages proposing a prohibited action; only the execution harness can enforce the boundary, and a penalty cannot undo an executed side effect. Even a reward function that ranks every unsafe trajectory below every safe one leaves an agent free to explore unsafe actions during policy search. The operational rule is to keep authorization, network isolation, and resource quotas firmly anchored in the container harness, using reward terms strictly to express preferences within that bounded perimeter.
This terminal reward evaluates the rollout trajectory as a complete artifact. Converting that scalar outcome into updates for the individual actions taken along the trajectory introduces the credit-assignment problem.




With a reward fixed, the credit-assignment problem named in section 16.2.2 becomes concrete. In the connection-pool repair, an agent might run the failing reproducer, read src/pool.py, and correctly identify the missed notification on connection return, only to introduce a syntax error in its final edit. A verifier that evaluates only the end state marks the entire trajectory as failed. That terminal failure characterizes the trajectory as a whole; it does not say that the diagnosis was a mistake.
The estimators that address this problem differ in what they spend to separate the two turns: nothing beyond the sampled return, a trained value model, a denser reward, or additional rollouts. Choosing among them requires keeping two quantities apart, the empirical coefficient applied in a sampled gradient update and the true expected value of an individual action.


Let \(\TurnHorizon\) denote the finite interaction horizon, \(\RolloutTurnIndex \in \{0, \ldots, \TurnHorizon-1\}\) the decision index, and \(\InteractionHistory_k\) the delivered interaction history up to turn \(\RolloutTurnIndex\). Under an undiscounted objective, let \(\TurnReward_k\) represent the reward received immediately after taking action \(\RolloutAction_k\). The remaining return from step \(\RolloutTurnIndex\) onward, often called the reward-to-go, is defined as \(\RemainingReturn=\sum_{j=k}^{\TurnHorizon-1}\TurnReward_j\). In sparse verifiable environments where the environment provides only a terminal reward \(\TrajectoryReward\) at the end of the episode, every intermediate turn sees an identical reward-to-go: \(\RemainingReturn=\TrajectoryReward\) for all \(\RolloutTurnIndex\).
For a trajectory sampled from the current policy, a likelihood-ratio, or score-function, estimator of the REINFORCE form (Williams 1992) is
\[\PolicyGradientEstimate=\sum_{k=0}^{\TurnHorizon-1}\nabla_\ModelParameters\log\Policy(\RolloutAction_k\mid \InteractionHistory_k)\,[\RemainingReturn-\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory_k)].\]
Its expectation equals the gradient of expected total reward under standard regularity conditions: the initial task distribution, environment transitions, and reward mechanism do not depend on \(\ModelParameters\); the differentiable policy has fixed support; and differentiating under the expectation integral is mathematically justified (Sutton et al. 1999). The score \(\nabla_\ModelParameters\log\Policy(\RolloutAction_k\mid \InteractionHistory_k)\) is the sensitivity vector of the sampled action’s log-probability with respect to parameters \(\ModelParameters\). Multiplying this vector by the scalar return \(\RemainingReturn-\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory_k)\) produces a step in parameter space rather than an intrinsic score of action quality (Sutton and Barto 2018).
The baseline \(\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory_k)\) can be fixed, task-specific, or predicted by a learned value model. To maintain an unbiased gradient, \(\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory_k)\) must not depend on the current sampled action conditional on \(\InteractionHistory_k\), and its parameters remain fixed when computing the policy gradient. Subtraction preserves the expectation because the expected score under the policy evaluates to zero:
\[\mathbb E_{\RolloutAction\sim\Policy(\cdot\mid \InteractionHistory)}[\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory)\nabla_\ModelParameters\log\Policy(\RolloutAction\mid \InteractionHistory)]
=\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory)\nabla_\ModelParameters\sum_\RolloutAction\Policy(\RolloutAction\mid \InteractionHistory)=0.\]
A baseline trained on earlier, independent rollouts satisfies this conditional independence property. A baseline computed from the current rollout’s own outcome does not, even if no gradient flows through it, because that outcome depends on the very actions being scored, so the baseline is no longer a constant with respect to them. Group-relative estimators, which compute baselines across multiple rollouts for the same prompt, introduce sample-dependent coefficients that require separate statistical treatment.
Consider the consequences for our connection-pool repair. When an attempt fails (\(\TrajectoryReward=0\)) with a zero baseline, the sampled coefficient \([\RemainingReturn-\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory_k)]\) becomes zero for every turn, yielding zero gradient update. If we instead employ a positive baseline (for instance, an average pass rate of \(0.4\)), the resulting coefficient is negative (\(-0.4\)), penalizing the insightful diagnostic command and the faulty edit alike. The learning algorithm does not assign positive credit to the diagnosis from this single run. Instead, credit for effective diagnostic steps emerges only statistically across many trajectories: actions that systematically lead to successful outcomes appear more frequently in winning runs than in losing ones.
Because every additional interaction turn introduces another score-function term to the summation, the variance of \(\PolicyGradientEstimate\) can grow with the trajectory length \(\TurnHorizon\). Even under a decaying-covariance assumption, the variance bound in Credit assignment variance in trajectory optimization grows linearly with \(\TurnHorizon\), so longer decision horizons can demand substantially more rollouts to extract a clean training signal. Long horizons therefore cost the learner twice. Under the horizon-compounding model (equation 1.1), successful trajectories become exponentially rarer, so fewer rollouts carry a positive signal, and each one that does arrives with a gradient estimate whose variance can grow with \(\TurnHorizon\).



For the same continuation policy and reward definition, define
\[\PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_k)=\mathbb E_\pi[\RemainingReturn\mid \InteractionHistory_k],\qquad
\PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\InteractionHistory_k,\RolloutAction_k)=\mathbb E_\pi[\RemainingReturn\mid \InteractionHistory_k,\RolloutAction_k],\qquad
\PolicyHistoryAdvantage(\InteractionHistory_k,\RolloutAction_k)=\PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\InteractionHistory_k,\RolloutAction_k)-\PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_k).\]
The state value \(\PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_k)\) averages over the policy’s next action and subsequent interaction, whereas the action value \(\PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\InteractionHistory_k,\RolloutAction_k)\) conditions explicitly on that chosen action. Their difference, the advantage, measures expected return relative to the policy’s default behavior at that history. Defining these quantities over interaction histories \(\InteractionHistory_k\) rather than abstract environment states grounds them strictly in the observations and context tokens available to the model.
With terminal value \(\PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_{\TurnHorizon})=0\), the sampled temporal-difference residual (Sutton 1988) is
\[\TemporalDifferenceResidual_k=\TurnReward_k+\PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_{k+1})-\PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_k).\]
Its conditional expectation given \(\InteractionHistory_k\) and \(\RolloutAction_k\) equals the true advantage when the value function is exact and subsequent observations and rewards follow the target environment distribution. A single observed residual is merely a noisy sample of that expectation, and substituting learned value estimates introduces approximation error on top of execution noise;5 dropping \(\TurnReward_k\) is valid only when that immediate step reward is zero. Generalized advantage estimation and KL divergence develops the discounted and multi-step formulations (Schulman et al. 2016).
5 Generalized Advantage Estimation: GAE computes an exponentially weighted average of future residuals parameterized by a decay factor \(\TraceDecay \in [0, 1]\) (distinct from the shaping weights \(\FormatRewardWeight\) and \(\LengthPenaltyWeight\)). At \(\TraceDecay=0\), it uses a single one-step residual, which minimizes variance but incurs substantial bias if the value model contains errors. At \(\TraceDecay=1\), it recovers the empirical return minus the baseline, which is unbiased with respect to the value model but inherits all the variance of subsequent interaction turns (Schulman et al. 2016). For a multi-turn agent with an imperfect critic, \(\TraceDecay\) governs how much credit relies on neural value predictions rather than verified environment execution.

Estimating an existing return differs fundamentally from injecting new reward terms into the training objective. A learned critic acts as an estimator: it approximates the expected continuation return under the current policy without altering the underlying task specification. A process reward model (PRM), by contrast, scores intermediate reasoning steps or tool invocations directly, augmenting the primary objective with synthetic feedback.


↩︎ Process reward models as step-level scorers that prune search at inference time are established in Outcome and step-level evidence.
While dense process rewards can guide search during inference (Lightman et al. 2024; Uesato et al. 2022), training against them directly creates strong incentives for reward hacking. Because the policy generates the very tokens that the process verifier evaluates, systems engineers encounter three common failure modes:

Superficial compliance: The agent generates formulaic boilerplate or ritualistic assertions (such as commenting “carefully verifying pointer bounds before dereferencing”) that satisfy the process model without performing any actual verification.
Locally consistent hallucinations: The agent constructs fluent, step-by-step reasoning that appears rigorous to a local evaluator, even though the derivation rests on an unvalidated or false premise.
Pathological conservatism: The agent avoids exploratory detours, speculative rollouts, or diagnostic failures that temporarily depress step scores, even when those intermediate investigations are necessary to diagnose complex software bugs.

Dense feedback reduces credit variance, but denser feedback is not necessarily correct feedback. Modifying the reward function changes what the policy optimizes, whereas value estimation simply estimates the performance of the policy under the true task metric. Continuation sampling provides an empirical Monte Carlo estimate of state value by rolling out \(\ContinuationCount\) independent trajectories (in this section \(\ContinuationCount\) counts continuations, not output tokens) from an intermediate execution boundary under a fixed continuation policy and averaging their terminal returns. To accurately estimate \(\PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory)\), the starting state of these continuations must match the true conditional environment distribution given history \(\InteractionHistory\). In interactive environments with latent state (such as unobserved database locks, network traffic, or non-deterministic operating system processes), restoring a single concrete container snapshot conditions on that specific state rather than integrating over all hidden states consistent with \(\InteractionHistory\). A sound fork must therefore explicitly reconstruct the filesystem workspace, container network namespace, delivered context tokens, external mock services, continuation policy version, and verification oracle. Simply copying sandbox memory bytes or disk blocks does not guarantee environmental fidelity.
When individual continuations yield independent bounded returns \(\TrajectoryReward^{(\ContinuationIndex)} \in [0, 1]\), the sample mean \(\EstimatedRemainingReturn = \ContinuationCount^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^\ContinuationCount \TrajectoryReward^{(\ContinuationIndex)}\) serves as an unbiased estimator of the expected continuation return. Because Bernoulli random variables achieve maximum variance at \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.5\) (\(\ContinuationReturnStandardDeviation^2 \le 1/4\)), the estimator’s variance is bounded above by \(1/(4\ContinuationCount)\), corresponding to a standard error of at most \(1/(2\sqrt{\ContinuationCount})\). Halving this uncertainty bound requires a fourfold increase in sampled rollouts. This error bound holds strictly for independently sampled branches; if rollouts share cached environment state or common prefixes, cross-sample correlation increases the variance. Furthermore, estimating action values \(\PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\InteractionHistory, \RolloutAction)\) requires conditioning explicitly on the chosen action \(\RolloutAction\) before rolling out the continuation policy. Consequently, sampling values at selected turn boundaries estimates the net value delta across blocks of turns rather than isolating individual token decisions.
A hypothetical fork makes this estimate concrete. Out of 20 continuations launched from the initial bug report, 1 passes, giving a sampled value of 0.05. In the primary trajectory, the policy then runs a debugger, producing an observation that contains the failing line. Forking 20 continuations from this updated history yields 12 passes, corresponding to a sampled value of 0.60. The estimated value difference for the debugger turn is 0.55, even if the primary trajectory later fails on a subsequent edit. Each sample mean carries a standard error of at most 0.11, and because the two fork estimates are independent their variances add, so the difference has a standard error of at most \(\sqrt2/(2\sqrt \ContinuationCount)\), or 0.16. Treating a difference as resolved only when it is at least twice that bound, here 0.32, the observed 0.55 clears the threshold, so the gain is unlikely to be sampling noise. Resolution against noise does not make \(\FiniteChange \EstimatedRemainingReturn\) an exact advantage, however; it remains an empirical estimate at two particular fork conditions. Of the three ways to connect the terminal failure to earlier turns (figure 1), only the forks separate the debugger turn from the faulty edit on this trajectory, and they do it by paying for extra rollouts rather than by adding a criterion the policy could learn to satisfy.






Figure 1: Three Ways to Connect a Terminal Outcome to Earlier Turns: The same trajectory runs a debugger, makes a faulty edit, and fails the terminal check. (a) With only the terminal check, every remaining return equals the one outcome, so the check alone does not separate the useful turn from the faulty one. (b) Learned step scores supply intermediate feedback by adding a criterion to the objective, one the policy can learn to satisfy without progress on the task. (c) Continuation sampling restores each fork condition and averages the returns of its continuations; the difference between the two means estimates how much the debugger turn raised the chance of passing the declared check, with sampling error and without establishing cause.



These continuation rollouts are expensive. Every branch consumes inference tokens, host memory, and sandbox execution time, and the total depends directly on how many intermediate boundaries the fork schedule samples, which makes the schedule the real design choice.

Branches are nonrecursive.
Math:
\[\BaseTrajectoryTokenCount=\TurnHorizon\,\TurnGeneratedTokenCount,\qquad
\ForkedTrajectoryTokenCount(\ForkBoundarySet)=\TurnHorizon\,\TurnGeneratedTokenCount+\ContinuationCount\,\TurnGeneratedTokenCount\sum_{k\in\ForkBoundarySet}(\TurnHorizon-\RolloutTurnIndex).\]
When forking at every intermediate boundary, the remaining-turn sum is \(\TurnHorizon(\TurnHorizon-1)/2\), yielding \(\ForkedTrajectoryTokenCount/\BaseTrajectoryTokenCount=1+\ContinuationCount(\TurnHorizon-1)/2\).

Systems insight: Exhaustive forking grows quadratically as \(\ContinuationCount \TurnHorizon^2\,\TurnGeneratedTokenCount/2\), meaning that doubling the horizon quadruples the credit computation bill even though base trajectory generation only doubles. At this horizon of 30 turns, exhaustive forking multiplies token generation by 117. In contrast, sampling only two targeted boundaries costs 9 times the base trajectory. Selective forking requires an effective policy for choosing boundaries. Two practical triggers are common in production systems: turn boundaries where the policy’s action distribution exhibits high token entropy (a next-token distribution spread across many candidates, measured in section 16.8.1), indicating a decision among genuine alternatives, and turns that execute state-modifying tool calls such as file edits, database migrations, or network reconfiguration. Forking at two or three such junctures captures targeted empirical credit where trajectories diverge, at a small fraction of the exhaustive cost.
Credit assignment is fundamentally a budget decision across a spectrum of computational cost and statistical fidelity. Fixed baselines incur zero token overhead but offer no step-level resolution; learned value functions reduce variance at the expense of training a secondary critic; and continuation rollouts provide direct empirical value estimates at the price of massive token generation. Group-relative policy optimization represents the minimalist end of this spectrum, comparing complete sampled returns within a task group without spending any additional tokens on intermediate branches.

Checkpoint 16.1: Rewards and credit
A reward is a measurement, and credit is an estimate built on it. Each has a price in errors or tokens.

False-accept estimate: The verifier from the false-accepts notebook keeps its error rate while the policy’s pass rate drops from 10 percent to 5 percent. Does the false share of rewarded rollouts rise or fall, and to roughly what value?
Enforcement: Why must runtime authorization remain in force when unauthorized proposals receive a reward penalty?
Credit: With terminal reward zero, when is the score estimator’s coefficient zero and when is it negative? Why does neither answer identify the faulty turn?
Value sampling: What conditions must continuation forks preserve, and why is a difference between two estimated values not generally an exact advantage?
Credit budget: A trajectory doubles from 30 to 60 turns. By what factor does exhaustive continuation sampling grow, and should the schedule fork at every boundary or at two chosen ones?







Suppose three fresh rollouts attempt the connection-pool repair under the same fixture, budget, and assessment rule. Their completed terminal rewards are \([0,1,0]\). The successful rollout provides a direct comparison for the two failures without requiring an expert to label each intermediate edit, though this outcome comparison alone cannot identify which specific action caused success. Group relative policy optimization (GRPO) uses such within-task comparisons6 to construct policy update coefficients, replacing a learned value baseline with groups of sampled outcomes (Shao et al. 2024).

(2024) found that such REINFORCE-style estimators could outperform PPO when fine-tuning language models from human feedback. GRPO adds division by the group’s reward dispersion, a weighting choice analyzed in section 16.5.3.

The trade-off centers on baseline estimation rather than the reward source: proximal policy optimization (PPO) can operate with an external check, just as GRPO can evaluate rollouts against a learned reward model. PPO trains a value function, either sharing parameters with the policy or running in a separate critic network (Schulman et al. 2017).
