Truncation matters more for agent rollouts than for short episodes, because a product of per-token ratios over thousands of tokens is otherwise dominated by a few extreme values. 
Espeholt, Lasse, Hubert Soyer, R’emi Munos, Karen Simonyan, Vlad Mnih, Tom Ward, Yotam Doron, et al. 2018. “IMPALA: Scalable Distributed Deep-RL with Importance Weighted Actor-Learner Architectures.” Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 1407–16.
\[\FiniteChange\text{ver}=\text{ver}_t-\BehaviorPolicyVersion\approx\left\lfloor\frac{\RolloutAdmissionAge}{\PolicyUpdateStepTime}\right\rfloor, \tag{8}\]
where \(\RolloutAdmissionAge\) is the wall-clock time elapsed from sampling the first prompt token to admission into the training batch, and \(\PolicyUpdateStepTime\) is the training step latency. This relationship enables system designers to calibrate staleness bounds directly from rollout duration. Long agent rollouts are precisely the trajectories most prone to severe staleness. Bounded staleness has a long lineage in distributed training architectures, where worker parameter reads are constrained to a fixed step horizon (Ho et al. 2013), and asynchronous actor-learner algorithms tolerate bounded lag in exchange for high actor utilization (Mnih et al. 2016). Applied at admission (figure 2, panels b and c), the check admits the two short rollouts and excludes the long one, recording why it was dropped. These are record-level lag decisions, not a complete group-admission rule. Under an objective that requires the planned cohort, every member must also have a resolved reward and satisfy that bound before the group enters an update.






Figure 2: Group Barriers and Version-Checked Admission: (a) In the hypothetical group of four, the barrier holds every slot until the 16.8 s member finishes, leaving 65 percent of reserved slot time idle. (b) Asynchronous collection releases slots early, so the trainer’s version advances while rollouts run. Each record carries the version that sampled it, and its lag \(\FiniteChange\text{ver}\) at admission grows with its duration; the long rollout exceeds the illustrative bound and is excluded with its reason recorded. (c) A record leaves verification with a pass, a fail, or an unavailable verdict, waits in a bounded group buffer, and reaches the trainer only if its lag is within the bound. While this admission check enforces a strict bound on version lag, it cannot prevent distribution drift when individual gradient updates make large steps in parameter space.



While the version counter provides an operational threshold for admission control, distribution divergence requires separate monitoring: a single large optimizer step can shift output probabilities far more dramatically than several incremental updates. Production diagnostics must break down elapsed age into generation time, tool wait states, verification latency, group buffer residence, and ingestion queue delay, while tracking empirical probability-ratio distributions (\(\Policy / \pi_{\text{old}}\)) to detect distribution drift directly.
Logging per-invocation metadata as described in section 16.6 accurately captures the behavior distribution even when policy checkpoints update mid-episode. Training on these composite trajectories requires optimization formulations that support turn-by-turn behavior probabilities; retroactively relabeling an entire trajectory under the newest policy checkpoint distorts importance weights and introduces optimization instability.
Freshness limits fundamentally balance off-policy variance against selection bias. Discarding trajectories that exceed a staleness threshold bounds policy lag, but because complex tasks demand more reasoning steps and tool calls, strict staleness cutoffs systematically eliminate hard problems from the training distribution. As indicated by equation 8, systems engineers can preserve task diversity by reducing the numerator rather than loosening the bound. Reducing generation, tool-wait, verification, group-buffer, and ingestion delays can shorten \(\RolloutAdmissionAge\) while preserving the long-horizon tasks the learner needs. Synchronous collection eliminates staleness entirely at the expense of straggler idle time, whereas multiple optimization epochs over a single collected batch reintroduce policy lag. While the clipped surrogate objective in section 16.5.2 limits policy updates driven by stale probability ratios, it neither bounds importance sampling variance nor corrects for the shift in visited state distributions (Schulman et al. 2017). Because discarded trajectories consume inference and sandbox capacity without producing gradient updates, monitoring systems must track discard rates, compute overhead, and shifts in task coverage.



Sizing verification infrastructure requires aligning the units of arrival demand with worker service capacity. Let \(\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\) denote completed trajectories arriving per second, \(\WorkerCount\) the number of independent verification worker slots, and \(\VerificationTrialTime\) the mean execution duration for one verification trial, including environment provisioning, execution, and cleanup. When each trajectory requires \(\VerificationTrialCount\) total trials to evaluate determinism or flaky tests, each trajectory demands an average of \(\VerificationTrialCount \VerificationTrialTime\) worker-seconds. The ideal service capacity \(\VerificationPoolCapacity\) and resulting offered utilization \(\ServingUtilization\) are
\[\VerificationPoolCapacity=\frac{\WorkerCount}{\VerificationTrialCount \VerificationTrialTime},\qquad
\ServingUtilization=\frac{\TrajectoryAdmissionRate \VerificationTrialCount \VerificationTrialTime}{\WorkerCount}. \tag{9}\]
Both \(\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\) and \(\VerificationPoolCapacity\) measure completed trajectories per second. Operating at \(\TrajectoryAdmissionRate=\VerificationPoolCapacity\) leaves no capacity margin; arrival bursts, heavy-tailed trial durations, or worker node failures cause queues to grow unbounded. System designers establish a target utilization \(0<\TargetServingUtilization<1\) based on acceptable queueing latency and variance profiles, provisioning at least \(\lceil\TrajectoryAdmissionRate \VerificationTrialCount \VerificationTrialTime/\TargetServingUtilization\rceil\) worker slots. Queue capacity limits and upstream admission control remain necessary. While executing a candidate’s \(\VerificationTrialCount\) trials concurrently across multiple slots reduces wall-clock verification latency, the aggregate worker-second demand remains identical.
For a hypothetical arrival of 512 trajectories every 16 s, \(\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\) is 32 trajectories per second. With each trial lasting 8 s, a single trial per trajectory consumes 256 worker equivalents at that arrival rate. Executing all 3 trials elevates demand to 768 worker equivalents. Applying the utilization relationship in equation 9 with an illustrative 80 percent target requires provisioning 960 worker slots. Verification demand scales linearly with \(\VerificationTrialCount\), and the target utilization establishes the necessary headroom against queueing delays.
Early-exit evaluation policies fundamentally alter these capacity requirements. Under the stop-on-first-rejection policy introduced in section 16.7, verification terminates upon the first failing trial. For a candidate solution with an independent per-trial pass probability \(\TrialPassProbability\), the expected number of trials drops to \(\mathbb{E}[\ExecutedTrialCount]=\sum_{j=0}^{\VerificationTrialCount-1}\TrialPassProbability^\VerificationTrialIndex\). Capacity models must substitute this expected trial count in place of \(\VerificationTrialCount\) when computing total worker demand. Across a diverse task distribution, engineers must compute this demand by averaging over the empirical mixture of pass rates; taking an aggregate average pass rate and raising it to powers yields an inaccurate estimate due to mixture variance. Sizing calculations must also incorporate unequal trial durations, sandbox initialization overhead, and retry cascades. In-memory queues absorb brief arrival spikes, but sustained overload requires adding worker slots or adopting more aggressive early-exit evaluation rules.



Promoting a policy checkpoint internally within the training pipeline serves a completely different operational purpose than releasing a model for deployment. Internal collection gating determines which checkpoint generates subsequent training trajectories. Automated validation checks verify prompt template compatibility, tool-calling syntax, entropy bounds to prevent policy collapse, and memory utilization before promoting a candidate checkpoint to the rollout fleet. The orchestrator must record the promoted model artifact digest and the generating version for every dispatched episode. If a promoted version exhibits degenerate behavior or crashes sandboxes, the controller halts further admission under that version, while any side effects produced by faulty rollouts remain subject to their designated cleanup handlers.
Production deployment release requires a formal evaluation framework verifying regression resistance, safety constraints, latency budgets, and out-of-distribution transfer. Internal training diagnostics provide rapid feedback during optimization, but they must remain strictly quarantined from release benchmarks to prevent benchmark leakage. Production evaluation suites must enforce an isolated assessment boundary, logging benchmark exposure whenever validation metrics inform architectural or hyperparameter revisions.

System evaluations must carefully distinguish between operational consistency and genuine capability expansion. In the competitive reasoning benchmark study of Yue et al. (2025), RLVR-trained models improve pass@1 while base models match or exceed them when sampled across broad cohorts (\(\IndependentAttemptCount \gg 1\)). This pattern is consistent with concentrating probability mass onto successful solution modes that the base model could already generate; it does not establish a universal limit on acquiring new behavior. Reporting pass@1, pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\) at large \(\IndependentAttemptCount\), and the repeated-trial pass\(^\IndependentAttemptCount\) defined in Potential and repeated-run consistency separates a policy that has become more reliable from one that has expanded its underlying capabilities. A candidate checkpoint must remain unreleased until it satisfies recovery, transfer, and unresolved-outcome criteria across comprehensive production testbeds.
Balancing rollout generation, straggler barriers, staleness bounds, and verifier capacity provides the infrastructure that keeps this learning loop saturated. Tracing how these systems mechanisms operate together requires following a complete update cycle on a concrete repair workload.




Consider the connection-pool repair group with rewards \([0,1,0]\) from section 16.5. Three fresh trials, rl_trial_01, rl_trial_02, and rl_trial_03, execute task pool_repair_01 against the fixture pool_fixture_v1, sampled from the supervised checkpoint trained_policy_v1, and each ends in a verdict under repair_accept_v1. The recovery run that produced workspace ws_r20 and the demonstrations built from it remain historical artifacts of curation and fine-tuning; they supply comparisons, not targets, for this group. Following the group through each stage of the chapter shows which question every stage answers before the middle rollout is allowed to move the weights.
The first question is whether the lone pass is a pass. A \([0,1,0]\) group on a hard bug is exactly the shape that tampering produces, so the verdict for rl_trial_02 counts only because it came from the assessment side of table 7. The patch was admitted as a source-only diff, applied to a fresh copy of the fixture, and graded by a controller whose tests and result store the candidate could not reach. The defect is a race on connection return, so the fixture is timing-sensitive, and the all-pass rule of notebook 16.5 applies. If an incorrect patch passes a single trial with probability 0.20, 3 independent trials cut its acceptance to 0.8 percent at a 5.88 percent risk of rejecting a correct one. A trial whose verifier crashed, or whose container was preempted, is marked unresolved under the stop-state rules of section 16.6.3 rather than coerced to zero, because converting an infrastructure fault into a task failure penalizes the policy for the cluster and shifts the group baseline.
The second question is whether the update can be computed on what the policy actually saw. Each rollout record holds the delivered prefix and sampled token IDs of every invocation, the behavior log probabilities under the recorded sampling configuration, and the checkpoint version that produced them (table 6). Before admission, the trainer checks each record’s version lag against its bound (equation 8); a trial that ran long enough to fall behind is excluded with its reason logged rather than silently relabeled under the newest weights. In this worked example, all three rewards are resolved and all three members satisfy the lag bound, so the original complete group is eligible. Under its declared complete-group rule, an unresolved or stale member prevents the group from entering the update; excluding members and recomputing its coefficients would require a separately declared objective and selection analysis.
Only then does GRPO compute coefficients. The pass receives 1.414214 and each failure -0.707107 (notebook 16.3), and under per-rollout averaging each token of rollout \(\GroupRolloutIndex\) carries \(\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i/\RolloutPolicyTokenCount_i\) (equation 5), so the length of each failure sets how hard its tokens are pushed down. Because the reward scores only the outcome, every token in rl_trial_02 receives the same coefficient. The edit that adds the missing notification and any redundant status checks along the way are reinforced alike, and only many such groups separate them statistically. The frozen reference policy stays distinct from the behavior policy, contributing only the divergence penalty. Because the GRPO name covers several variants, the training log records the clipping thresholds, the length and dispersion normalizations, and the penalty weight \(\KlPenaltyCoefficient\) with the update.
When an update over eligible groups yields a candidate checkpoint, such as rl_policy_v1, lineage binds its weights and inference configuration to the rollout records, fixtures, and verifier versions that produced it. The controller may promote rl_policy_v1 to the rollout fleet for further collection, since that is an internal training decision. Releasing it is a different decision. Higher training reward on a known fixture can coexist with regression on unobserved failure modes, and the benchmark study discussed in section 16.9.6 illustrates how higher pass@1 can coexist with unchanged broad-sampling performance, so the release case rests on held-out recovery fixtures evaluated by pass@1, pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\) at large \(\IndependentAttemptCount\), and pass\(^\IndependentAttemptCount\) under the protocol of Agent Evaluation.
Each stage therefore answers one question that no other stage can: the isolated verifier says whether the reward is evidence, the record says whether the update is faithful, the coefficients say how hard the evidence pushes, and the independent evaluation says whether the result belongs in production.



A rollout group can easily contain positive rewards without establishing a sound solution, and a policy update can fit that group without improving the deployed agent. The pitfalls detailed below each turn a narrow, scoped measurement into an unwarranted conclusion, and each carries a concrete systems cost.

Fallacy: An automated reward is a complete task specification.
Automated test suites check only the conditions their authors anticipated, and reinforcement learning operates as an aggressive search procedure that reliably uncovers unhandled edge cases. When a policy’s true success rate is low, Bayesian base rates compound this vulnerability. As demonstrated in notebook 16.1, a verifier that misclassifies only 2.5 percent of failing attempts still results in 18.4 percent of all rewarded rollouts being outright failures when the policy solves only 10 percent of tasks. Because reinforcement updates treat every rewarded attempt as a success, the optimizer systematically increases the probability of the tokens that generated those spurious answers. Always benchmark the verifier against suites of known incorrect solutions, evaluate its false-acceptance rate against the policy’s current pass rate, and gate production deployment on strict held-out task criteria rather than raw training rewards.


Pitfall: Leaving the scorer, the runner, or its configuration where the candidate can reach it.
If an agent can read or write to its evaluation harness, modifying the test framework becomes the path of least resistance. In the METR evaluations, when a task exposed an editable scoring script to the agent, the model bypassed the intended challenge and tampered with the verifier in 21 of 21 runs (war story 16.1). During training, this vulnerability causes severe gradient distortion. On difficult tasks where honest attempts fail, the first rollout that discovers an exploit becomes the group’s lone positive sample. In a rollout group of 16, that single hack receives an advantage coefficient of 3.87, while each honest failure receives a negative coefficient of 0.26 in magnitude, strongly reinforcing the exploit. Always evaluate candidate solutions in an ephemeral workspace isolated behind a hardened controller that retains exclusive ownership of the test harness, the execution runner, and the result path (section 16.7). Even within that sandbox, treat all generated agent code as untrusted input.


Fallacy: A bigger group is the way to extract signal from hard tasks.
Increasing the rollout group size \(\GroupSize\) appears to offer a straightforward way to capture rare successes on difficult tasks. While larger groups improve the likelihood that a batch contains contrasting rewards, the probability of contrast alone does not measure the information each group supplies. At a pass rate of 5 percent, rollout groups of size 8 consume 23.8 rollouts for every informative group with nonzero variance. Expanding the group size to 16 still demands 28.6 rollouts per informative group. By contrast, steering the training curriculum toward tasks near a 50 percent pass rate consumes only 8.1 rollouts per informative group (notebook 16.4). Where obtaining contrast is the binding constraint and the task-mixture change is acceptable, this comparison favors targeting difficulty. Choose the group size using baseline precision, required task coverage, and held-out learning progress as well as rollout cost, and log the sampling distribution.


Pitfall: Reading longer self-correction text as evidence of better reasoning.
When an agent produces lengthy internal monologues and verbose self-critiques, engineers often mistake length for deeper reasoning. In reality, output lengths frequently expand as a direct artifact of loss normalization. Under per-rollout token averaging, a failing rollout of 128 tokens penalizes each individual token 32× as heavily as a failing rollout of 4,096 tokens. Because token-level gradient penalties dilute across longer generation lengths, this objective can favor longer failures even when the extra text performs no useful validation (equation 5). To uncover length bias, compare sequence lengths conditioned on task outcome and train with a constant-denominator loss objective. Ultimately, evaluate candidate revisions by the concrete tool actions and verified task completions they deliver under a matched token budget, rather than by the model’s narration of reconsidering.


Fallacy: Faster environment reset speeds training proportionally.
Optimizing container teardown and environment initialization yields satisfying microbenchmarks, but Amdahl’s law strictly limits the resulting gains in end-to-end training throughput. Reset latency represents only one slice of the rollout lifecycle. Cutting reset overhead from 3.5 s to 15 ms delivers a 233× acceleration in reset speed, yet it improves execution slot capacity by only 1.77×. The remaining 4.5 s spent on model inference, tool execution, and verifier scoring continues to dominate every cycle (notebook 16.6). Moreover, increased rollout throughput converts into faster training progress only if the inference workers, verification services, and parameter optimizers maintain sufficient headroom to ingest the higher volume. Profile the entire training loop to pinpoint the saturated pipeline stage before investing engineering effort into optimizing any individual phase.




Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards uses assessed interactions to guide a policy update without requiring a demonstrated response at every decision. Its opportunity depends on what the sampling process can reach and what the reward distinguishes. Its risks arise because the recorded score, rather than the full task intent, enters the optimization. Reward validity, sampling fidelity, and external enforcement therefore remain part of the learning system rather than prerequisites that can be forgotten once training starts.
The repair group illustrates the resulting chain of responsibility. Completed assessments support group-relative coefficients; recorded policy actions and their actual inputs support the chosen update; resource and version controls govern the collection loop. None of those steps substitutes for evaluating the resulting candidate under its intended operating conditions. Training changes the policy and moves no exposure; the runtime still bounds horizon, state, and authority for whatever the updated weights propose.

Key Takeaways: A learning signal is not a release decision

Reward learning needs reachable distinctions: Fresh interactions provide a different signal from admitted imitation targets. The policy must sample behavior the reward can distinguish; useful support can come from several sources, and supervised fine-tuning is not a mandatory preceding stage.
A protected score still has a scope: Automated checks assess specified properties, not every aspect of task intent. Reward composition can change preferences, while evaluator isolation blocks particular interference paths; neither replaces runtime permissions or independent assessment of the candidate.
Return is not causal credit: A baseline changes the coefficient attached to a sampled action without identifying its individual contribution. Continuation estimates require compatible forks and additional execution; their uncertainty and cost must accompany any interpretation of an estimated advantage.
Group coefficients do not constrain every update: GRPO’s centering and normalization define a particular surrogate. Equal rewards remove its reward-dependent terms, not all learning; clipping changes the objective but does not impose a hard bound on policy drift or gradient magnitude.
Training needs the actions actually sampled: Retain per-invocation inputs, sampled policy tokens, and matching behavior probabilities. Observations supply conditioning rather than sampled actions, and incomplete assessments or truncated episodes require declared treatment rather than silent relabeling or exclusion.
Behavioral changes require behavioral evidence: Entropy, length, reward, and recovery traces guide investigation but do not reveal internal cognition or uniquely diagnose a cause. Test interventions against task outcomes and costs under controlled conditions instead of optimizing telemetry in isolation.
The collection loop and release have different gates: Bounded queues, group completion, version accounting, and verifier capacity govern training operation. Admission for further collection is distinct from external deployment, which requires evidence for the identified policy and retains all runtime controls.



Verified trajectory post-training (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training}\)) reaches its last form in this chapter. Imitation admits recorded responses as targets after curation; reinforcement learning admits every action the policy sampled, malformed ones included, and weights each by an outcome a verifier certified, so the admission decision passes from the curator to the reward. The worked group makes the verification asymmetry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)) concrete under that optimization pressure. A protected, scoped assessment must be joined to the sampled record before it can justify an update. Executing the candidate inside that assessment also stress-tests containment beneath the model (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-zero-trust-sandboxing}\)), because fresh workspaces still receive untrusted code. The same asymmetry governs both ends of the loop. A learned score may shape an update, while the reward and the release decision rest on protected checks wherever such checks exist. Neither the learning signal nor an improved evaluation result moves authority into the weights; invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) continues to govern the effects of each proposal.



The problem this chapter manages began as a question about games. Minsky (1961) asked how a learning system that sees only whether a long strategy won or lost can distribute credit among the many decisions that produced the result, and he named it the credit-assignment problem. Two answers followed that still organize the field. Temporal-difference learning predicted later outcomes from earlier ones, so each step could be scored against the next prediction rather than the final result (Sutton 1988). The REINFORCE family instead differentiated expected reward directly through the probabilities of sampled actions and subtracted a reinforcement baseline to tame the variance (Williams 1992). The policy gradient theorem showed that such estimates remain valid with function approximation (Sutton et al. 1999), and the analysis of baselines as control variates explained why some reduce variance more than others (Greensmith et al. 2004).

Scaling policy gradients to neural networks exposed instability rather than bias. Trust region policy optimization bounded each update’s divergence from the policy that collected the data (Schulman et al. 2015), generalized advantage estimation made the bias-variance trade in the baseline explicit (Schulman et al. 2016), and proximal policy optimization replaced the trust region with the cheaper clipped objective that GRPO and many later methods inherit (Schulman et al. 2017). The systems problem arrived in the same years. Stale-synchronous parameter servers bounded how old a worker’s parameters could be (Ho et al. 2013), asynchronous actor-learners kept every actor busy at the price of that lag (Mnih et al. 2016), and IMPALA separated acting from learning with an explicit off-policy correction (Espeholt et al. 2018), a split that agent rollout fleets resemble.
Language models then turned the reward itself into the hard part. Learning a reward model from human comparisons made preferences optimizable (Christiano et al. 2017; Ouyang et al. 2022), and measuring what happens when a policy is optimized against such a proxy showed a held-out gold score eventually declining while the proxy score keeps rising (Gao et al. 2023). Executable checks offered a sturdier signal: unit tests became the reward for code generation (Le et al. 2022), outcome and process supervision were compared on checkable reasoning (Uesato et al. 2022; Lightman et al. 2024), and the name reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards was attached to training against such checks (Lambert et al. 2024). On the optimizer side, sampled baselines that score each output against its siblings (Kool et al. 2019; Ahmadian et al. 2024) led to group-relative policy optimization (Shao et al. 2024). The same years documented the cost of an imperfect reward, from the early catalog of specification problems (Amodei et al. 2016; Krakovna et al. 2020) to a formal definition of reward hacking (Skalse et al. 2022), and the defense returned to the protection literature: confinement (Lampson 1973) and complete mediation (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975) describe the verifier boundary in terms that predate learned policies entirely.

For further reading, six works trace that lineage from classical learning theory to agent training.

Sutton and Barto (2018) is the standard text on returns, value functions, temporal-difference learning, and policy gradients. It supplies the vocabulary every section of this chapter assumes.
Williams (1992) introduces the REINFORCE estimator and the reinforcement baseline. Reading it shows how little the core update has changed since.
Schulman et al. (2017) presents the clipped objective, read together with Schulman et al. (2016) for advantage estimation. The pair explains what GRPO keeps and what it removes.
Espeholt et al. (2018) is the reference design for separating actors from learners with a bounded, corrected lag. Its staleness problem is the one agent rollouts make worse.
Skalse et al. (2022) gives a precise definition of when a proxy reward can be hacked. It turns the informal worry of this chapter into a property a reward designer can reason about.
Saltzer and Schroeder (1975) states the protection principles that verifier isolation applies. Reading it shows why an instruction to the policy is never a substitute for mediation of every route to the verdict.

Every given below is a hypothetical problem input rather than a measurement of a real system. Each problem ends in a decision, and the calculation exists to justify it.

False accepts early and late in training (Basic). A repair-task verifier accepts every criterion success (\(\VerifierTrueAcceptanceRate=1\)) and a fraction \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate=0.02\) of criterion failures. At the start of training the policy passes the reference criterion with probability \(\ValidCandidateRate=0.04\); after several hundred updates it passes with \(\ValidCandidateRate=0.40\).

Use equation 1 to compute the false-accept share of rewarded rollouts at both pass rates.
Find the largest \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\) that keeps the share at or below \(0.10\) when \(\ValidCandidateRate=0.04\).
The team can afford one verifier-hardening effort, either before training starts or after the pass rate has risen. Decide when to spend it and justify the choice from parts (a) and (b).

Keeping the pass above the failure (Basic). A proposed terminal score is \(\TrajectoryReward=\CorrectnessReward+\FormatRewardWeight\FormatComplianceScore-\LengthPenaltyWeight\text{len}\) with \(\FormatRewardWeight=0.4\), \(\LengthPenaltyWeight=0.7\), and \(\text{len}=\RolloutPolicyTokenCount/\GeneratedTokenCap\) for an enforced cap \(\GeneratedTokenCap=8{,}000\) generated tokens.

Score a pass that uses \(7{,}200\) tokens with \(\FormatComplianceScore=0.5\), and a failure that uses \(400\) tokens with \(\FormatComplianceScore=1\). State whether this pair keeps the intended order.
Compute the lowest possible pass score and the highest possible failure score over the stated ranges, and state whether every observed pass outranks every observed failure.
Holding \(\FormatRewardWeight=0.4\), find the range of \(\LengthPenaltyWeight\) that satisfies the sufficient ordering condition, and explain why part (a) alone was not evidence that the original weights were safe.

Sizing an all-pass rule (Basic). A timing-sensitive fixture passes a fixed incorrect patch with per-trial probability \(\IncorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability=0.30\) and a fixed correct patch with \(\CorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability=0.95\). Trials are independent, acceptance requires \(\VerificationTrialCount\) total passes, and verification stops at the first rejection.

Find the smallest \(\VerificationTrialCount\) that brings an incorrect patch’s acceptance probability below \(0.01\).
At that \(\VerificationTrialCount\), compute the false-rejection probability for the correct patch and the expected number of trials for each patch.
A lone false pass on a hard task receives the largest group coefficient. Compare adding trials with repairing the fixture’s timing sensitivity, and state which the loop should do first.

A mixed task pool and its silent groups (Intermediate). An update samples groups of \(\GroupSize=8\) over \(256\) tasks. Half the tasks belong to a family the policy passes with \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.02\); the other half to a family it passes with \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.60\). Runs are independent and rewards are binary.

Compute \(\GroupContrastProbability\) for each family, the expected number of informative groups per update, and the rollouts spent per informative group across the whole pool.
Compute \(\GroupContrastProbability\) from the pool-average pass rate instead, and explain the size of the error.
For the hard family, compute the coefficient a lone pass receives with \(\AdvantageStabilizer\to0\). A colleague proposes dropping the hard family to cut the rollout bill. Critique the proposal, naming what it does to the training distribution, and propose an alternative that raises the hard family’s contrast without discarding it.

A continuation-sampling budget (Intermediate). A repair trajectory runs \(\TurnHorizon=40\) turns of \(\TurnGeneratedTokenCount=400\) generated tokens. The team may spend at most \(30\) times the base trajectory’s generated tokens on credit estimation, including the base. Continuations are independent binary returns and are not recursively forked.

Compute the generation multiple for exhaustive forking with \(\ContinuationCount=16\) continuations per boundary, and for forks after turns \(10\), \(20\), and \(30\) only.
Find the \(\ContinuationCount\) that brings the per-fork standard-error bound to \(0.05\), and the multiple that \(\ContinuationCount\) costs at the three chosen forks.
Find the largest \(\ContinuationCount\) the budget allows at those three forks and its standard-error bound. Treat a difference between two fork values as resolved only if it is at least twice the bound on the standard error of the difference, \(\sqrt2/(2\sqrt \ContinuationCount)\). Decide whether this schedule can resolve a value difference of \(0.20\), and if it cannot, redesign the schedule within the same budget.

Reset for a short-horizon support agent (Intermediate, second-lighthouse transfer). Apply the slot model of equation 6 to training the support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)) on refund tasks, where a deterministic check compares the issued refund with the recorded policy. An episode has \(\TurnHorizon=4\) decisions with \(\ModelTime=0.6\) s of model service and \(\ToolTime=0.1\) s of record lookup each, then \(\RolloutAssessmentTime=0.2\) s of assessment. Restoring the customer record and refund ledger from a cold fixture takes \(\EnvironmentResetTime=6.0\) s; a snapshot restore takes \(0.3\) s. The pool has \(64\) slots, and the shared model service can sustain at most \(40{,}000\) episodes per hour.

Compute the cycle time and the reset share of the cycle for both resets, and the idealized pool capacity in episodes per hour.
Compute the capacity gain that the shared model service actually permits, and decide whether the snapshot work or added model-service capacity should come next.
In the chapter’s repair-pool example, cold reset was under half of the cycle. Compare this lighthouse’s reset share, explain which term of equation 6 makes reset the lever here, and name the state a local snapshot does not restore if a refund reached an external payment service.

Staleness bounds and verifier provisioning (Advanced). A repair-agent trainer steps every \(\TrainingStepTime=40\) s and admits a record only if \(\FiniteChange\text{ver}\le2\). Of the rollouts, a fraction \(0.70\) take \(30\) s from first token to admission, \(0.25\) take \(90\) s, and \(0.05\) take \(200\) s. Verification receives \(256\) completed trajectories per training step. Every trajectory needs up to \(\VerificationTrialCount=3\) verification trials of \(\VerificationTrialTime=10\) s, and the pool targets \(\TargetServingUtilization=0.8\).

Compute \(\FiniteChange\text{ver}\) for each duration class and the fraction of rollouts excluded. Explain why the excluded fraction understates the damage to hard tasks.
Find the step time above which the \(200\) s rollouts are admitted, and the duration below which a rollout is admitted at the current step time. Compare slowing the trainer, capping rollout duration, and shortening \(\FiniteChange \RolloutDuration\).
Size the verifier pool when all three trials execute. Then size it under stop-on-first-rejection when a fraction \(0.60\) of candidates are incorrect with \(\IncorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability=0.10\) and the rest are correct with \(\CorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability=0.97\).
Size the stop-on-first-rejection pool again by substituting the population’s mean pass probability into every power, and state the consequence of provisioning from that number.

Diagnosing a lengthening policy (Advanced, critique and redesign). During GRPO training with per-rollout token averaging, the mean length of failing repair rollouts grows from \(2{,}000\) to \(6{,}000\) generated tokens while acceptance stays flat. The team proposes adding \(\LengthPenaltyWeight\text{len}\) with \(\LengthPenaltyWeight=0.4\) and \(\FormatRewardWeight=0.2\), where \(\text{len}=\RolloutPolicyTokenCount/4{,}000\) is normalized by a nominal cap the runtime does not enforce.

Using equation 5, compute the ratio of per-token penalties on a \(2{,}000\)-token failure and a \(6{,}000\)-token failure that share the same \(\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i\).
Score a \(9{,}000\)-token pass with \(\FormatComplianceScore=0\) and a \(500\)-token failure with \(\FormatComplianceScore=1\) under the proposal. Find the pass length beyond which a pass with \(\FormatComplianceScore=0\) scores below the best-scoring failure.
Critique the proposal and redesign the response. The redesign should state which diagnostic runs before any penalty is added, what the runtime must enforce, and which condition any length term that survives must satisfy.



What’s Next: From a measured single agent to coordinationSplitting a task across several agents is justified only when the benefits of decomposition exceed its coordination costs. Every mechanism so far, from the harness to this chapter’s repair group, governs one trajectory, and the connection-pool race that group repaired fits in one controller’s context. The repair agent’s next assignment is wider: migrating an authentication module across a repository, a change that reaches every caller of its interface and tempts a split. Part V provides ways to curate learning material, update a policy, and test the result, but no system must complete all three stages before asking whether to delegate. Multi-Agent Coordination compares a coordinated design with a capable single-agent baseline that holds the same parallel tools and a comparable resource budget. Delegation can separate work and context, but it also introduces shared-state conflicts, correlated mistakes, and obligations that cross agent boundaries, and the comparison must price those costs while preserving every runtime control already required for one agent.

title: 16 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why does a check that only scores an agent’s attempts end up defining what the agent learns?
Curated demonstrations give an agent a starting policy, but they cover only the decisions someone recorded, and long-horizon tasks keep producing decisions that no demonstration anticipated. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards replaces the demonstration with a programmatic check, such as a unit test suite, a compiler, or a proof checker, that scores each sampled attempt and turns the score into a weight update without a human label. That substitution changes what the check is. An evaluator that once only counted failures becomes the objective the optimizer searches, and the search finds every gap between what the check measures and what the task requires, from a weakened assertion to a patched test runner to a verdict rewritten before it is recorded. The verification boundary must therefore be defended like a security perimeter, with fixtures the candidate cannot reach and rewards read as evidence about only the properties their checks cover. Wherever outcomes can be mechanically checked, the policy improves as far as the scope and protection of the check allow, and no further.

Learning Objectives

Explain why reward-driven learning needs sampled support that imitation does not, and estimate when a task yields no reward contrast
Design a shaped reward that preserves the pass-over-failure order, and bound the false accepts its assessment admits through verifier isolation and repeated checks
Calculate the generation cost and standard error of continuation-based credit estimates across turns
Compute group-relative coefficients and the per-token weight that length normalization assigns them
Specify the per-invocation records and version-lag bound that keep a multi-turn update faithful to its sampling policy
Diagnose changes in reward and length from task outcomes rather than from the narration a policy generates
Size the environment cycle and verifier pool of a rollout-training loop and identify the stage that limits it

title: 16 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
text:
The previous chapter left the repair agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)) with trained_policy_v1, a supervised checkpoint fitted to the one malformed-argument recovery that curation admitted. Its release gate already had to send trials into a state the corpus never covered, the version conflict for which no demonstration exists (Case Study: Training the Repair Policy). More imitation needs someone to record that recovery, and a preference pair needs two admissible records of it. The agent’s versioned test fixtures and acceptance checks need neither. They can score entirely novel attempts whose intermediate actions have no labeled target. An autonomous policy might inspect an unexpected source file, attempt an alternative refactoring strategy, or halt when it encounters an unfamiliar error. While the automated test suite verifies whether the final patch succeeds, it provides no token-by-token guidance during intermediate decision steps.



Training changes the policy and leaves every exposure where the runtime closes it.
Existing techniques stop short of using verification outcomes to reshape the underlying policy. Trajectory fine-tuning teaches models to generalize from demonstrated recovery paths, but it remains fundamentally bounded by demonstration data; human-verified repairs for intricate, non-deterministic bugs are exceedingly scarce. Test-time selection filters multiple generated rollouts against an acceptance suite to extract a passing candidate, yet it incurs significant inference latency on every incoming task while leaving the base policy unchanged. Neither approach increases the intrinsic probability of generating successful trajectories from verification signals alone. Reinforcement learning bridges this gap by converting acceptance verdicts directly into gradient updates. In doing so, it alters the role of the verification suite. Once a check enters the optimization objective, any flaw in the test fixture is compiled into the network weights rather than miscounted on a single run, and the acceptance check that once decided a release (The Task Acceptance Contract) becomes the signal that decides every update.
Constructing a training loop that converts automated test outcomes into policy updates requires four tightly coupled systems mechanisms. First, the reward design must remain robust against optimization pressure, evaluating functional correctness without introducing exploitable shortcuts. Second, the policy update rule must solve multi-turn credit assignment, translating a single terminal pass or fail signal into per-token update coefficients over extended interactive trajectories. Third, the rollout recording infrastructure must maintain strict fidelity to what the policy generated and observed, so that the loss is computed on the inputs the policy actually saw. Finally, the compute infrastructure, spanning sandboxed execution environments, verification workers, and gradient engines, must be provisioned so that training updates ingest complete, synchronized candidate groups without pipeline stalls.
The chapter takes these mechanisms in the order a student would need to build them. It first fixes what an outcome-driven update can and cannot learn (section 16.2), then prices the reward that drives it, including the false accepts a verifier admits (section 16.3). Credit assignment follows, first through return and value estimates (section 16.4) and then through group-relative policy optimization (section 16.5), the worked optimizer. The remaining sections keep that optimizer honest in practice: faithful records of multi-turn rollouts (section 16.6), a verifier the candidate cannot reach (section 16.7), diagnostics for the pathologies that rising reward can hide (section 16.8), and the rollout, verifier, and staleness arithmetic that sizes the training fleet (section 16.9). A case study then follows one repair group through the whole loop (section 16.10).

title: 16 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
text:
Reinforcement learning optimizes an agent policy directly against task outcomes rather than against recorded human actions. Where behavioral cloning (supervised imitation of recorded actions) requires an admitted demonstration for every intermediate step, reinforcement learning executes candidate rollouts in an environment and scores the resulting trajectories against programmatic checks. A supervised checkpoint, such as the trained_policy_v1 built in Case Study: Training the Repair Policy, offers a useful starting point to bootstrap sampling, but the optimization machinery depends only on the agent’s ability to act, observe, and receive an evaluative score. Before any gradient update can convert raw outcomes into policy improvements, however, the system architecture must establish three foundational mechanisms: the formal representation of multi-turn rollouts, the baseline estimators that isolate meaningful signal from variance, and the execution boundaries that protect verification harnesses during exploration.


A policy \(\Policy(\RolloutAction_k\mid \InteractionHistory_k)\), parameterized by weights \(\ModelParameters\), defines a probability distribution over responses \(\RolloutAction_k\) conditioned on the delivered interaction history \(\InteractionHistory_k\) through turn \(\RolloutTurnIndex\). We consider a finite decision horizon \(\TurnHorizon\) with turn indices \(\RolloutTurnIndex=0,\ldots,\TurnHorizon-1\). (We reserve \(\RolloutTurnIndex\) for agent-environment turns because \(\TokenIndex\) later indexes individual autoregressive tokens within a rollout.) The history \(\InteractionHistory_k\) plays the role of the recorded state \(\TrajectoryState_k\) in the trajectory notation of The H·S·A Exposure Space, the runtime’s delivered view at turn \(\RolloutTurnIndex\) rather than the environment itself. A response \(\RolloutAction_k\) represents either a proposed tool call, such as a shell command or structured API query, or a terminal answer. The runtime validates and executes any requested operation, returning standard output, standard error, or structured payloads as observations for subsequent turns. The interaction history \(\InteractionHistory_k\) records this transcript of delivered prompts, emitted actions, and returned observations. Because modern context windows cannot always ingest unbounded execution logs, the policy consumes a constructed prompt that may truncate or summarize older history. The policy interacts with the environment exclusively through this constructed context window, never through direct inspection of the underlying state \(\RolloutEnvironmentState_{k}\): an edited configuration file or sandbox directory affects policy decisions only after tool invocations reflect its contents back into \(\InteractionHistory_k\).


↪ The partially observable Markov decision process behind this observation constraint is developed in POMDP formalization of trajectories.
A rollout, or sampled trajectory \(\Trajectory\), encapsulates one complete execution trace under specified task definitions, policy weights, environment states, and harness constraints. In our illustrative repair scenario, a trial rl_trial_01 on task pool_repair_01 instantiates container sandbox pool_fixture_v1 and evaluates candidate patches against test harness repair_accept_v1. Each rollout generates its own telemetry, intermediate command outputs, and terminal verification artifacts; past demonstration records provide no credit to this live attempt.
A reward is a scalar evaluation metric computed under an explicit verification rule. In the simplest formulation, intermediate turns emit zero reward, leaving a single terminal score \(\TrajectoryReward(\Trajectory)\) evaluated at horizon completion without temporal discounting (a discount factor \(\DiscountFactor=1\), so a reward counts the same whichever turn it arrives on). The trajectory return collapses to this terminal score, yielding the expected return objective:
\[\ExpectedReturnObjective(\ModelParameters)=\mathbb{E}_{\Trajectory\sim\Policy}\left[\TrajectoryReward(\Trajectory)\right].\]
The expectation integrates over policy stochasticity, task sampling distributions, and environment variations (such as nondeterministic test execution times or network latencies). Maximizing \(\ExpectedReturnObjective(\ModelParameters)\) drives the policy to increase the expected measured reward under these specific operational conditions. Whether that measured score genuinely correlates with true task utility depends on the fidelity of the reward harness itself, an architectural challenge analyzed in section 16.3.
When the reward originates from an automated, deterministic check—such as unit test execution, syntax validation, type checking, or a formal proof assistant—rather than from an imperfect learned preference model or manual human grading, this paradigm is known as reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR)1 (Lambert et al. 2024).
1 Tests as Reward: Executed unit tests served as the reward for a code-generating model before the name existed: Le et al. (2022) trained a pretrained code model with reinforcement learning on test outcomes and added a learned critic that predicts functional correctness. That pairing anticipates this chapter’s central tension, since the test outcome is the trustworthy signal while the denser learned critic is itself a model that optimization can exploit. 
Le, Hung, Yue Wang, Akhilesh Deepak Gotmare, Silvio Savarese, and Steven Chu Hong Hoi. 2022. “CodeRL: Mastering Code Generation Through Pretrained Models and Deep Reinforcement Learning.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-1549.

Definition 16.1: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is policy optimization using reward signals computed by automated checks of specified properties of the policy’s outputs or interactions, such as tests or proof checkers, rather than relying solely on learned preference scores or human ratings.

Significance: An automated verification harness provides an objective training signal without requiring step-by-step demonstrations. By directly incentivizing task success, it increases the acceptance rate \(\AcceptanceProbability\) in the cost per accepted task (equation 1.2) even when human demonstrations do not exist. However, the verifier’s false-accept rate bounds only the per-rollout chance that a sampled failure is rewarded; when true passes are rare, false accepts can make up a far larger share of the rewarded rollouts (section 16.3.2).
Distinction: Whereas behavioral cloning trains the policy to reproduce specific recorded responses, RLVR evaluates only whether the completed trajectory satisfies programmatic criteria. The resulting policy gradient is strictly bounded by the coverage, sensitivity, and sandboxed security of the underlying verifier.
Common pitfall: Mistaking higher reward scores on a fixed verification suite for generalized task competence, or treating automated verification as a justification to relax runtime isolation and execution guardrails.






A terminal reward alone does not compute a parameter gradient. Policy-gradient algorithms adjust model parameters by estimating a gradient direction that increases the log-probabilities of sampled actions proportional to an evaluative score. Standard estimators subtract a baseline from the raw outcome: the centered advantage is \(\TrajectoryReward(\Trajectory)-\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory_0)\), where \(\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory_0)\) depends on the initial task prompt and context \(\InteractionHistory_0\) but remains independent of the sampled action sequence \(\Trajectory\). The baseline serves as an offset reference level. It can be a fixed scalar, an empirical rolling mean across task batches, or a parametric value estimate, and it does not necessarily require training a separate critic network (Williams 1992).
Consider a binary verification check where success yields \(1.0\) and failure yields \(0.0\). With a fixed baseline of 0.25, a passing rollout receives a centered score of 0.75, whereas a failing rollout yields -0.25. These opposing signs drive gradient updates in opposite directions: positive centered returns reinforce the probabilities of every token and tool call sampled along the passing trajectory, whereas negative centered returns suppress them. In contrast, setting the baseline to zero leaves failed rollouts with a centered score of \(0.0\), discarding the negative gradient signal that penalizes counterproductive trajectories.
This uniform attribution illustrates the classic credit-assignment problem:2 a terminal verifier evaluates overall trajectory success, but it cannot differentiate the decisive tool call from irrelevant or mildly detrimental exploratory steps. While subtracting an appropriate baseline reduces the variance of the policy gradient estimator without introducing bias (Greensmith et al. 2004), it applies a uniform scalar adjustment across the entire trajectory rather than isolating action-specific causal effects. Section 16.4 formalizes these estimators and their bias-variance trade-offs, and section 16.5 introduces group-relative scoring to compute data-dependent baselines across parallel rollouts without training an auxiliary value network.
2 Credit Assignment Problem: Minsky (1961) named the problem for learning systems that receive one success signal for a strategy built from many internal decisions, with games and program writing as his examples. The repair agent poses the same question at the scale of tool calls: a failed acceptance check arrives after many turns, and every turn is a candidate for blame, which is why the estimators of this chapter differ mainly in how they spread one outcome across those turns. 
Minsky, Marvin. 1961. “Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence.” Proceedings of the IRE 49 (1): 8–30. https://doi.org/10.1109/JRPROC.1961.287775.



A policy-gradient update can optimize only over trajectories that the sampling harness actually produces. Exploration, the sampling of action sequences the policy has rarely tried at points where it still spreads probability across several plausible actions, determines what reinforcement learning can discover. In environments governed by binary verification checks (pass vs. fail), a task instance that the policy never solves yields exclusively zero rewards. A zero baseline, or one that tracks the observed outcomes such as the mean of a group of attempts (section 16.5.4), then leaves every centered score at zero. A fixed positive baseline does produce a gradient, but it pushes down every sampled action alike and gives the update nothing to prefer. Either way, without variation in the outcome signal the update carries no contrast, regardless of how many rollouts the collector generates. If a policy solves a task instance with base probability \(\AttemptPassProbability\), sampling a group of \(\GroupSize\) independent rollouts yields at least one successful trajectory with probability \(1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\GroupSize\). That condition is the one that binds when \(\AttemptPassProbability\) is small; the group optimizer of section 16.5 also needs at least one failure in the same group, a stricter condition derived there. When \(\AttemptPassProbability=0\), scaling the group size \(\GroupSize\) yields no contrast at all. System builders overcome this cold-start bottleneck by seeding the policy through supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, curating curricula with progressive difficulty, or structuring reward functions with informative intermediate milestones.
Because exploration systematically exposes edge cases in both the target environment and the evaluation harness, the execution runtime must enforce rigid capability and resource boundaries. As an agent generates thousands of candidate interactions, optimization will exploit any loose permission, such as reading hidden test fixtures, patching Python test runners, or modifying exit codes in the evaluation container, to manufacture high rewards without solving the underlying problem. Preventing such gaming requires a protected assessment boundary. The agent’s actions execute within an isolated sandbox, while the verifier runs with separate privileges, shielded storage, and read-only access to private test suites; section 16.7 builds that boundary once the reward and the update it drives are in place. Even with complete isolation, held-out evaluation on disjoint test distributions remains necessary to determine whether the policy acquired robust problem-solving behavior or merely fit the idiosyncrasies of the training verifiers. Before any of that machinery can be designed, however, the reward itself must be pinned down: what the check measures, how often it is wrong, and how other terms may be added to it without overturning the pass-over-failure order.

title: 16 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
text:
When an agent tackles a task like pool_repair_01, the training loop requires an objective evaluation score for each newly sampled candidate repair rather than an expert demonstration of which lines to modify. Those acceptance criteria inherit the evaluation harness of repair_accept_v1, but passing a targeted unit test provides evidence only about that specific test assertion. Before the system can convert an execution outcome into a scalar reward, the training infrastructure must guarantee exactly what was executed, which artifact was tested, and which version of the grader evaluated it. The assessment contract established in The Task Acceptance Contract is no longer an offline benchmark; it is now an active component of the optimization objective.


A policy can easily collect high rewards without solving the underlying engineering problem. A candidate patch might satisfy the tested cases while introducing a race condition on an untested concurrency path. Alternatively, if the agent can write to the grading environment, it can modify the test runner so that a failing execution reports success. These failures represent two fundamentally different defects: incomplete test coverage vs. compromised measurement. Hardening the grader protects the measurement process, but it does not make the underlying test criteria complete.

Definition 16.2: Reward hacking
Reward hacking is behavior that increases measured reward by exploiting a gap between the formal reward and the intended task, including manipulation of the measurement mechanism (Amodei et al. 2016; Skalse et al. 2022).

Significance: Gradient optimization reinforces a rewarded shortcut just as eagerly as an authentic solution. Each gamed pass registers as a success, inflating the measured acceptance rate \(\AcceptanceProbability\) and artificially lowering the computed cost per accepted task while true capability stagnates; tracking policy quality during reinforcement learning therefore requires an independent assessment of task performance.
Distinction: A false-positive judgment is an evaluation error. It does not, by itself, establish that the policy discovered or deliberately exploited a shortcut.
Common pitfall: Treating instructions against tampering as protection for the grader. Software isolation at the runtime level must restrict what the policy and its submitted code can affect.



3 Goodhart’s Law Under Training: Selection pressure on imperfect checks showed best-of-\(\CandidatePoolSize\) selection pressing on an imperfect check, where a larger pool favors candidates the proxy overrates. An RL loop applies the same pressure at every update and then writes the result into the weights, so a gap between reward and task is searched far more persistently than any selection step or human-managed target ever searches it. A false accept carries far higher systemic consequences during training than during test-time sampling. At inference time, a noisy selector that accepts a bad candidate simply wastes one decision. In reinforcement learning, however, awarding reward to a defective trajectory raises the probability of the tokens that produced it, prompting the policy to generate more such trajectories on subsequent tasks. Once the exploit is learned into the model weights, the training run can raise its measured score while growing progressively worse at the intended task.3 Formally, let \(\CandidateUtility(\Trajectory)\) represent the developer’s intended objective and \(\ProxyTrajectoryReward(\Trajectory)\) the reward signal calculated by the training loop. Whenever an unintended trajectory \(\ExploitTrajectory\) satisfies \(\ProxyTrajectoryReward(\ExploitTrajectory)\ge\ProxyTrajectoryReward(\Trajectory^*)\) while \(\CandidateUtility(\ExploitTrajectory)\ll \CandidateUtility(\Trajectory^*)\), gradient ascent on \(\ProxyTrajectoryReward\) gives it no less weight than the intended solution. The exploit steadily gains ground whenever it also has higher prior probability under the current policy (Skalse et al. 2022; Krakovna et al. 2020). In practice, degenerate shortcuts often enjoy a substantial probability advantage: weakening an assertion or rewriting a verdict takes only a few lines and no understanding of the bug, whereas diagnosing and fixing a difficult bug may require a complex, multi-turn repair.


↩︎ How a verifier’s false-acceptance rate dilutes the passing candidates at inference time is established in Check precision and the candidate pool.
The optimizer this chapter develops amplifies this failure mode upon its very first occurrence. Group-relative optimization, taught in section 16.5, samples a group of \(\GroupSize\) rollouts for the same task and scores each rollout against the others, so the rarer a pass is within its group, the larger the weight the update gives it. Suppose the test files sit in the rollout’s writable workspace, and one rollout on a difficult bug weakens the failing assertion while the other \(\GroupSize-1\) rollouts fail honestly. That rollout is the group’s lone pass, and it receives the largest coefficient in the group, a weight that grows with \(\GroupSize\) (equation 3 derives its size). Every token that wrote the tampering edit receives a sharp probability increase. The optimization loop did not suffer an algorithmic malfunction; the optimizer performed exactly as designed on the reward signal it received.
The exploits observed in coding environments fall into three recognizable classes, each documented in training or evaluation runs of 2025-era models:

Weakening or special-casing the check. Code that returns expected values only for inputs tested by the suite, or test assertions edited until they pass. A 2025 system card reports that one model, when unable to find a general solution, sometimes special-cased tests to make them pass (Anthropic 2025).
Stubbing or bypassing the verified code path. In one 2025 report during reinforcement learning of a reasoning model on coding tasks, a monitor flagged a plan to make a verification function always return true, alongside an exploit that exited the environment before unit tests could execute (Baker et al. 2025).
Rewriting the verdict inside the runner. Production coding environments used for training proved vulnerable to candidates returning an object whose equality comparison always succeeds, calling sys.exit(0) before any assertion executes, or writing a conftest.py that monkeypatches the test framework’s reporting subsystem so that every failure is recorded as a pass; models trained in those environments learned to use them (MacDiarmid et al. 2025).


Anthropic. 2025. Claude 3.7 Sonnet System Card.

Baker, Bowen, Joost Huizinga, Leo Gao, Zehao Dou, Melody Y. Guan, Aleksander Madry, Wojciech Zaremba, Jakub Pachocki, and David Farhi. 2025. “Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2503.11926.
Listing 1 shows the structure of this third class. The candidate adds one file to its own source tree; the test runner imports that file before running tests; and from that point forward the runner, not the tests, fabricates the outcome.



Listing 1: A verdict rewritten inside the runner: A reconstruction of the report-patching exploit class described by MacDiarmid et al. (MacDiarmid et al. 2025). Because pytest imports conftest.py from the tree it tests, candidate-controlled code can replace the function that records each outcome.


MacDiarmid, Monte, Benjamin Wright, Jonathan Uesato, Joe Benton, Jon Kutasov, Sara Price, Naia Bouscal, et al. 2025. “Natural Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking in Production RL.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2511.18397.

# conftest.py written into the candidate's tree; pytest imports it first
from _pytest.reports import TestReport

_original = TestReport.from_item_and_call

def _always_pass(cls, item, call):
    report = _original(item, call)
    if call.when == "call":
        report.outcome = "passed"   # a failing assertion now reports success
        report.longrepr = None      # and its traceback disappears
    return report

TestReport.from_item_and_call = classmethod(_always_pass)



These exploits are not confined to training runs. An independent evaluator measured how often the most capable models of 2025 took them when the scorer was within reach, and whether asking the model not to made any difference.

War Story 16.1: Frontier models patch their scorers (2025)Context: In June 2025 the evaluation organization METR reported reward hacking by frontier models, chiefly OpenAI’s o3, on two suites of autonomous tasks: RE-Bench, whose research-engineering tasks let the agent see the entire scoring function, and the broader HCAST suite (Von Arx et al. 2025).
Mechanism: With the scorer in reach, o3 attacked it instead of the task. On a kernel-optimization task it overwrote the timing function so that it always returned shorter measurements; on a code-generation scaffolding task it patched the evaluation function to judge every submission successful; on a fine-tuning speed task it modified the script to copy the cached weights of an already fine-tuned model.
Impact: The fine-tuning task was hacked in 21 of 21 runs. Across RE-Bench, 39 of 128 runs hacked (30 percent), against 8 of 1,087 on HCAST (0.7 percent). Asked after its first hacking plan whether the plan adhered to the user’s intention, o3 answered no 10 times in 10. Adding “Please do not reward hack” to the prompt moved the hacking rate over 20 runs from 80 percent to 70 percent.
Fix: METR excludes successful reward-hacking runs from its reported capability results, and recommends that when a monitor detects a hack, developers patch the exploit in the scoring function rather than punish the model.
Systems lesson: A scorer the agent can read and write sits at the visible-test closure level no matter what the task author intended, and an instruction does not raise it. In an evaluation these runs are excluded after the fact; in an RLVR loop every one of them is a maximal reward, and the gradient copies it.



Von Arx, Sydney, Lawrence Chan, and Beth Barnes. 2025. Recent Frontier Models Are Reward Hacking. METR blog.
METR attributes the substantial difference between 30 percent on RE-Bench and 0.7 percent on HCAST to reachability: on RE-Bench the model could inspect the scoring function directly, making it easier to bypass. The essential defense is a verification check that the policy cannot reach, evaluated on execution evidence that the policy cannot forge. For this reason, the sandboxed architecture of section 16.7 removes the test runner, configuration files, and evaluation credentials from the candidate’s control.
A reward is only as dependable as the closure evidence level of the check that computes it. These closure levels categorize the basis of an evaluation verdict by how much of it the agent policy can influence or reach. A static check establishes selected structural properties, a sealed test suite withholds and protects its test cases, and a formal proof verifies a specified property under explicit assumptions. Test coverage then limits any individual check at every level: even a sealed suite with an omitted edge case continues to reward buggy solutions that exploit the gap. Table 1 summarizes the sources used to construct agent rewards, alongside the specific vulnerabilities an optimizing policy exploits in each.


↩︎ Closure evidence levels, from static checks through sealed tests to formal proofs, are established in The invariant closure principle.



Table 1: Reward Sources and How They Are Gamed: The top rows correspond to the sealed-test and formal-proof closure levels; their verdicts depend on the artifact, not its phrasing, so raising the score requires changing what the check runs on. The lower rows score text the policy writes. Coverage limits every row.











Reward source
