For a coding task with executable behavioral criteria, sealed tests supply the definitive outcome score, while compilation and format checks provide narrower gating signals. The lower rows score free-form text, and because the policy directly controls that text, a learned judge is itself a model with blind spots that gradient ascent can systematically exploit (Gao et al. 2023). The verification asymmetry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)) dictates the role each score can assume: learned assessments can rank candidate trajectories or shape exploration, but wherever a deterministic check exists, that check must govern the final reward. For tasks that lack an executable check, a learned judge can provide the primary reward, provided its calibration error is continuously measured against verified reference outcomes and re-evaluated as the policy distribution shifts. Section 16.7 develops the separate systems requirement of isolating the measurement pipeline from candidate code.



The distinction drawn in Grader error rates between a grader’s false-acceptance rate and the failure rate among accepted outcomes is the same base-rate arithmetic that equation 3.3 applied to a candidate pool. Training changes one thing about it. The policy’s pass rate is no longer a fixed property of the task, so the share of rewards that go to failures moves as the policy learns, and it is largest when true task success is rare. The symbols below map onto those of Grader error rates. Let \(\ReferenceAssessedFailure\) be criterion failure under an independent reference assessment and \(\VerifierVerdict^+\) acceptance by the training verifier (the event written \(\text{Acc}\) there). Let \(\ValidCandidateRate\) be the policy’s current probability that a rollout satisfies the criterion, \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate=\Pr(\VerifierVerdict^+\mid \ReferenceAssessedFailure)\) the verifier’s false-acceptance rate, and \(\VerifierTrueAcceptanceRate\) its probability of accepting a criterion success. Provided verifier acceptance occurs with nonzero probability, the failure rate among accepted rollouts is
\[
\Pr(\ReferenceAssessedFailure\mid \VerifierVerdict^+) = \frac{(1-\ValidCandidateRate)\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate}{\ValidCandidateRate \VerifierTrueAcceptanceRate+(1-\ValidCandidateRate)\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate}.
\tag{1}\]



The rarer true passes are, the more of the reward a small verifier error claims.
Equation 1 defines the false-accept share of the reward: the fraction of all rewarded rollouts that actually fail the task criterion. Because its denominator sums both true positive accepts (\(\ValidCandidateRate \VerifierTrueAcceptanceRate\)) and false positive accepts (\((1-\ValidCandidateRate)\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\)), a small false-positive rate \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\) yields a large false share whenever failures are common. In reinforcement learning on challenging tasks, failure is the default state during early iterations. The same Bayesian arithmetic governs automated tests and learned reward models alike.

Napkin Math 16.1: False accepts in the rewardProblem: A hypothetical batch samples 8 rollouts for each of 1,024 tasks, giving 8,192 rollouts. Suppose 10 percent satisfy the criterion under the reference assessment. The training verifier accepts every criterion success and 2.5 percent of criterion failures. What share of its positive judgments are false accepts?
Math: For \(\BatchRolloutCount\) rollouts, expected true accepts are \(\BatchRolloutCount \ValidCandidateRate \VerifierTrueAcceptanceRate\) and expected false accepts are \(\BatchRolloutCount(1-\ValidCandidateRate)\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\). For this batch these are 819.20 and 184.32, respectively, totaling 1,003.52 expected positive judgments. Applying equation 1 gives 18.4 percent.
Result: 18.4 percent of rewarded rollouts are failures, although the verifier errs on only 2.5 percent of failures. The counts are expectations; an actual batch varies around them.
Systems insight: The false share is set by the ratio \((1-\ValidCandidateRate)\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate/(\ValidCandidateRate \VerifierTrueAcceptanceRate)\), so it moves with the policy’s pass rate as much as with the verifier. In the small-share regime, halving \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\) roughly halves the share; doubling \(\ValidCandidateRate\) has approximately the same effect when \(\ValidCandidateRate\) is also small. For a fixed positive false-acceptance rate, the false share approaches one as true passes become rare. Measure verifier error at the pass rate the policy currently has, and expect the share to fall as training succeeds. The share is not the fraction of the gradient that rewards errors, which also depends on where the false accepts fall within their groups (section 16.5.1).





Suppose a fully assessed rollout receives an observed binary outcome \(\CorrectnessReward(\Trajectory)\in\{0,1\}\). Let \(\FormatComplianceScore(\Trajectory)\in[0,1]\) measure format compliance and let \(\text{len}(\Trajectory)\in[0,1]\) measure generated-token cost relative to an enforced cap. A common terminal score formulation is
\[
\TrajectoryReward(\Trajectory)=\CorrectnessReward(\Trajectory)+\FormatRewardWeight\FormatComplianceScore(\Trajectory)-\LengthPenaltyWeight\text{len}(\Trajectory),
\qquad \FormatRewardWeight\ge 0,\quad \LengthPenaltyWeight\ge 0.
\]
Format compliance encourages well-formed tool calls, and the length penalty favors concise solutions.4 Neither auxiliary term should silently override the core outcome priority. Over their defined ranges, an observed pass earns at least \(1-\LengthPenaltyWeight\), while an observed failure earns at most \(\FormatRewardWeight\). A sufficient condition for every passing rollout to outrank every failing rollout is therefore
4 Reward Shaping: Ng et al. (1999) showed that an added shaping reward is guaranteed to leave the optimal policy unchanged when it takes the form of a difference of potentials over states, and that other additions can change which policy is optimal. Format and length terms are not of that form, so they change the objective itself; their weights therefore need the priority bound derived here rather than an assumption that they merely speed learning. 
Ng, Andrew Y., Daishi Harada, and Stuart J. Russell. 1999. “Policy Invariance Under Reward Transformations: Theory and Application to Reward Shaping.” Proceedings of the Sixteenth International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 278–87.
\[
\FormatRewardWeight+\LengthPenaltyWeight<1.
\]
Allowing equality permits a tie between a maximally penalized pass and a perfectly formatted failure. Strict inequality protects the score ordering, and it holds only while the normalized length penalty \(\text{len}(\Trajectory)\) remains strictly bounded in \([0,1]\). Normalizing by a nominal token budget preserves that invariant only if the execution runtime enforces the cap with hard process termination.
When an unexpected infrastructure failure leaves a required check unavailable, the assessment remains incomplete. Under the four-verdict rule of The four-verdict rule its verdict is unknown, and the reward stays unresolved rather than being converted to \(\CorrectnessReward=0\) or \(\CorrectnessReward=1\). Converting an unexecuted check to failure penalizes valid candidate solutions for harness faults, while converting it to success creates an immediate reward vulnerability; section 16.6.3 develops how a training loop must handle such rollouts. An explicit timeout under the task contract represents a valid failure verdict; a missing result due to test runner crashes does not. Similarly, introducing partial credit (awarding reward for the fraction of unit tests passed, for instance) defines a distinct optimization objective that alters which behavioral changes earn reinforcement, requiring its own priority analysis.
Permissions and hard resource limits must remain strict runtime constraints. A negative reward penalty merely discourages proposing a prohibited action; only the execution harness can enforce the boundary, and a penalty cannot undo an executed side effect. Even a reward function that ranks every unsafe trajectory below every safe one leaves an agent free to explore unsafe actions during policy search. The operational rule is to keep authorization, network isolation, and resource quotas firmly anchored in the container harness, using reward terms strictly to express preferences within that bounded perimeter.
This terminal reward evaluates the rollout trajectory as a complete artifact. Converting that scalar outcome into updates for the individual actions taken along the trajectory introduces the credit-assignment problem.

title: 16 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
text:
With a reward fixed, the credit-assignment problem named in section 16.2.2 becomes concrete. In the connection-pool repair, an agent might run the failing reproducer, read src/pool.py, and correctly identify the missed notification on connection return, only to introduce a syntax error in its final edit. A verifier that evaluates only the end state marks the entire trajectory as failed. That terminal failure characterizes the trajectory as a whole; it does not say that the diagnosis was a mistake.
The estimators that address this problem differ in what they spend to separate the two turns: nothing beyond the sampled return, a trained value model, a denser reward, or additional rollouts. Choosing among them requires keeping two quantities apart, the empirical coefficient applied in a sampled gradient update and the true expected value of an individual action.


Let \(\TurnHorizon\) denote the finite interaction horizon, \(\RolloutTurnIndex \in \{0, \ldots, \TurnHorizon-1\}\) the decision index, and \(\InteractionHistory_k\) the delivered interaction history up to turn \(\RolloutTurnIndex\). Under an undiscounted objective, let \(\TurnReward_k\) represent the reward received immediately after taking action \(\RolloutAction_k\). The remaining return from step \(\RolloutTurnIndex\) onward, often called the reward-to-go, is defined as \(\RemainingReturn=\sum_{j=k}^{\TurnHorizon-1}\TurnReward_j\). In sparse verifiable environments where the environment provides only a terminal reward \(\TrajectoryReward\) at the end of the episode, every intermediate turn sees an identical reward-to-go: \(\RemainingReturn=\TrajectoryReward\) for all \(\RolloutTurnIndex\).
For a trajectory sampled from the current policy, a likelihood-ratio, or score-function, estimator of the REINFORCE form (Williams 1992) is
\[\PolicyGradientEstimate=\sum_{k=0}^{\TurnHorizon-1}\nabla_\ModelParameters\log\Policy(\RolloutAction_k\mid \InteractionHistory_k)\,[\RemainingReturn-\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory_k)].\]
Its expectation equals the gradient of expected total reward under standard regularity conditions: the initial task distribution, environment transitions, and reward mechanism do not depend on \(\ModelParameters\); the differentiable policy has fixed support; and differentiating under the expectation integral is mathematically justified (Sutton et al. 1999). The score \(\nabla_\ModelParameters\log\Policy(\RolloutAction_k\mid \InteractionHistory_k)\) is the sensitivity vector of the sampled action’s log-probability with respect to parameters \(\ModelParameters\). Multiplying this vector by the scalar return \(\RemainingReturn-\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory_k)\) produces a step in parameter space rather than an intrinsic score of action quality (Sutton and Barto 2018).
The baseline \(\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory_k)\) can be fixed, task-specific, or predicted by a learned value model. To maintain an unbiased gradient, \(\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory_k)\) must not depend on the current sampled action conditional on \(\InteractionHistory_k\), and its parameters remain fixed when computing the policy gradient. Subtraction preserves the expectation because the expected score under the policy evaluates to zero:
\[\mathbb E_{\RolloutAction\sim\Policy(\cdot\mid \InteractionHistory)}[\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory)\nabla_\ModelParameters\log\Policy(\RolloutAction\mid \InteractionHistory)]
=\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory)\nabla_\ModelParameters\sum_\RolloutAction\Policy(\RolloutAction\mid \InteractionHistory)=0.\]
A baseline trained on earlier, independent rollouts satisfies this conditional independence property. A baseline computed from the current rollout’s own outcome does not, even if no gradient flows through it, because that outcome depends on the very actions being scored, so the baseline is no longer a constant with respect to them. Group-relative estimators, which compute baselines across multiple rollouts for the same prompt, introduce sample-dependent coefficients that require separate statistical treatment.
Consider the consequences for our connection-pool repair. When an attempt fails (\(\TrajectoryReward=0\)) with a zero baseline, the sampled coefficient \([\RemainingReturn-\PolicyGradientBaseline(\InteractionHistory_k)]\) becomes zero for every turn, yielding zero gradient update. If we instead employ a positive baseline (for instance, an average pass rate of \(0.4\)), the resulting coefficient is negative (\(-0.4\)), penalizing the insightful diagnostic command and the faulty edit alike. The learning algorithm does not assign positive credit to the diagnosis from this single run. Instead, credit for effective diagnostic steps emerges only statistically across many trajectories: actions that systematically lead to successful outcomes appear more frequently in winning runs than in losing ones.
Because every additional interaction turn introduces another score-function term to the summation, the variance of \(\PolicyGradientEstimate\) can grow with the trajectory length \(\TurnHorizon\). Even under a decaying-covariance assumption, the variance bound in Credit assignment variance in trajectory optimization grows linearly with \(\TurnHorizon\), so longer decision horizons can demand substantially more rollouts to extract a clean training signal. Long horizons therefore cost the learner twice. Under the horizon-compounding model (equation 1.1), successful trajectories become exponentially rarer, so fewer rollouts carry a positive signal, and each one that does arrives with a gradient estimate whose variance can grow with \(\TurnHorizon\).



For the same continuation policy and reward definition, define
\[\PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_k)=\mathbb E_\pi[\RemainingReturn\mid \InteractionHistory_k],\qquad
\PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\InteractionHistory_k,\RolloutAction_k)=\mathbb E_\pi[\RemainingReturn\mid \InteractionHistory_k,\RolloutAction_k],\qquad
\PolicyHistoryAdvantage(\InteractionHistory_k,\RolloutAction_k)=\PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\InteractionHistory_k,\RolloutAction_k)-\PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_k).\]
The state value \(\PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_k)\) averages over the policy’s next action and subsequent interaction, whereas the action value \(\PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\InteractionHistory_k,\RolloutAction_k)\) conditions explicitly on that chosen action. Their difference, the advantage, measures expected return relative to the policy’s default behavior at that history. Defining these quantities over interaction histories \(\InteractionHistory_k\) rather than abstract environment states grounds them strictly in the observations and context tokens available to the model.
With terminal value \(\PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_{\TurnHorizon})=0\), the sampled temporal-difference residual (Sutton 1988) is
\[\TemporalDifferenceResidual_k=\TurnReward_k+\PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_{k+1})-\PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_k).\]
Its conditional expectation given \(\InteractionHistory_k\) and \(\RolloutAction_k\) equals the true advantage when the value function is exact and subsequent observations and rewards follow the target environment distribution. A single observed residual is merely a noisy sample of that expectation, and substituting learned value estimates introduces approximation error on top of execution noise;5 dropping \(\TurnReward_k\) is valid only when that immediate step reward is zero. Generalized advantage estimation and KL divergence develops the discounted and multi-step formulations (Schulman et al. 2016).
5 Generalized Advantage Estimation: GAE computes an exponentially weighted average of future residuals parameterized by a decay factor \(\TraceDecay \in [0, 1]\) (distinct from the shaping weights \(\FormatRewardWeight\) and \(\LengthPenaltyWeight\)). At \(\TraceDecay=0\), it uses a single one-step residual, which minimizes variance but incurs substantial bias if the value model contains errors. At \(\TraceDecay=1\), it recovers the empirical return minus the baseline, which is unbiased with respect to the value model but inherits all the variance of subsequent interaction turns (Schulman et al. 2016). For a multi-turn agent with an imperfect critic, \(\TraceDecay\) governs how much credit relies on neural value predictions rather than verified environment execution. 
Schulman, John, Philipp Moritz, Sergey Levine, Michael I. Jordan, and Pieter Abbeel. 2016. “High-Dimensional Continuous Control Using Generalized Advantage Estimation.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
Estimating an existing return differs fundamentally from injecting new reward terms into the training objective. A learned critic acts as an estimator: it approximates the expected continuation return under the current policy without altering the underlying task specification. A process reward model (PRM), by contrast, scores intermediate reasoning steps or tool invocations directly, augmenting the primary objective with synthetic feedback.


↩︎ Process reward models as step-level scorers that prune search at inference time are established in Outcome and step-level evidence.
While dense process rewards can guide search during inference (Lightman et al. 2024; Uesato et al. 2022), training against them directly creates strong incentives for reward hacking. Because the policy generates the very tokens that the process verifier evaluates, systems engineers encounter three common failure modes:

Superficial compliance: The agent generates formulaic boilerplate or ritualistic assertions (such as commenting “carefully verifying pointer bounds before dereferencing”) that satisfy the process model without performing any actual verification.
Locally consistent hallucinations: The agent constructs fluent, step-by-step reasoning that appears rigorous to a local evaluator, even though the derivation rests on an unvalidated or false premise.
Pathological conservatism: The agent avoids exploratory detours, speculative rollouts, or diagnostic failures that temporarily depress step scores, even when those intermediate investigations are necessary to diagnose complex software bugs.

Dense feedback reduces credit variance, but denser feedback is not necessarily correct feedback. Modifying the reward function changes what the policy optimizes, whereas value estimation simply estimates the performance of the policy under the true task metric. Table 2 separates these design choices and their architectural commitments.



Table 2: Reward Definition and Return Estimation: These choices can be combined. Predicting or sampling a declared return does not independently validate the check that defines it.










Choice
Quantity supplied
Main obligation




Terminal check
Observed trajectory outcome
Validate criterion, coverage, and protected assessment


Learned value estimate
Predicted return under a specified policy
Assess prediction error and estimator bias


Process reward
Additional intermediate scoring criterion
Justify the changed objective and assess its errors


Continuation sampling
Empirical return at a declared fork condition
Restore compatible conditions and account for sampling uncertainty and cost









Continuation sampling provides an empirical Monte Carlo estimate of state value by rolling out \(\ContinuationCount\) independent trajectories (in this section \(\ContinuationCount\) counts continuations, not output tokens) from an intermediate execution boundary under a fixed continuation policy and averaging their terminal returns. To accurately estimate \(\PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory)\), the starting state of these continuations must match the true conditional environment distribution given history \(\InteractionHistory\). In interactive environments with latent state (such as unobserved database locks, network traffic, or non-deterministic operating system processes), restoring a single concrete container snapshot conditions on that specific state rather than integrating over all hidden states consistent with \(\InteractionHistory\). A sound fork must therefore explicitly reconstruct the filesystem workspace, container network namespace, delivered context tokens, external mock services, continuation policy version, and verification oracle. Simply copying sandbox memory bytes or disk blocks does not guarantee environmental fidelity.
When individual continuations yield independent bounded returns \(\TrajectoryReward^{(\ContinuationIndex)} \in [0, 1]\), the sample mean \(\EstimatedRemainingReturn = \ContinuationCount^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^\ContinuationCount \TrajectoryReward^{(\ContinuationIndex)}\) serves as an unbiased estimator of the expected continuation return. Because Bernoulli random variables achieve maximum variance at \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.5\) (\(\ContinuationReturnStandardDeviation^2 \le 1/4\)), the estimator’s variance is bounded above by \(1/(4\ContinuationCount)\), corresponding to a standard error of at most \(1/(2\sqrt{\ContinuationCount})\). Halving this uncertainty bound requires a fourfold increase in sampled rollouts. This error bound holds strictly for independently sampled branches; if rollouts share cached environment state or common prefixes, cross-sample correlation increases the variance. Furthermore, estimating action values \(\PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\InteractionHistory, \RolloutAction)\) requires conditioning explicitly on the chosen action \(\RolloutAction\) before rolling out the continuation policy. Consequently, sampling values at selected turn boundaries estimates the net value delta across blocks of turns rather than isolating individual token decisions.
A hypothetical fork makes this estimate concrete. Out of 20 continuations launched from the initial bug report, 1 passes, giving a sampled value of 0.05. In the primary trajectory, the policy then runs a debugger, producing an observation that contains the failing line. Forking 20 continuations from this updated history yields 12 passes, corresponding to a sampled value of 0.60. The estimated value difference for the debugger turn is 0.55, even if the primary trajectory later fails on a subsequent edit. Each sample mean carries a standard error of at most 0.11, and because the two fork estimates are independent their variances add, so the difference has a standard error of at most \(\sqrt2/(2\sqrt \ContinuationCount)\), or 0.16. Treating a difference as resolved only when it is at least twice that bound, here 0.32, the observed 0.55 clears the threshold, so the gain is unlikely to be sampling noise. Resolution against noise does not make \(\FiniteChange \EstimatedRemainingReturn\) an exact advantage, however; it remains an empirical estimate at two particular fork conditions. Of the three ways to connect the terminal failure to earlier turns (figure 1), only the forks separate the debugger turn from the faulty edit on this trajectory, and they do it by paying for extra rollouts rather than by adding a criterion the policy could learn to satisfy.






Figure 1: Three Ways to Connect a Terminal Outcome to Earlier Turns: The same trajectory runs a debugger, makes a faulty edit, and fails the terminal check. (a) With only the terminal check, every remaining return equals the one outcome, so the check alone does not separate the useful turn from the faulty one. (b) Learned step scores supply intermediate feedback by adding a criterion to the objective, one the policy can learn to satisfy without progress on the task. (c) Continuation sampling restores each fork condition and averages the returns of its continuations; the difference between the two means estimates how much the debugger turn raised the chance of passing the declared check, with sampling error and without establishing cause.



These continuation rollouts are expensive. Every branch consumes inference tokens, host memory, and sandbox execution time, and the total depends directly on how many intermediate boundaries the fork schedule samples, which makes the schedule the real design choice.

Napkin Math 16.2: Continuation sampling in tokensProblem: An agent trajectory runs 30 turns of 512 generated tokens each. At each chosen intermediate boundary, the system samples 8 continuations, each running for the remainder of the episode. What generation cost results from sampling every intermediate boundary, compared with sampling only after turns 10 and 20?
Variables: \(\TurnHorizon\) is the trajectory horizon in turns, \(\TurnGeneratedTokenCount\) the generated tokens per turn, \(\ContinuationCount\) the continuations per boundary, and \(\ForkBoundarySet\subseteq\{1,\ldots,\TurnHorizon-1\}\) the index set of completed-turn fork points. Branches are nonrecursive.
Math:
\[\BaseTrajectoryTokenCount=\TurnHorizon\,\TurnGeneratedTokenCount,\qquad
\ForkedTrajectoryTokenCount(\ForkBoundarySet)=\TurnHorizon\,\TurnGeneratedTokenCount+\ContinuationCount\,\TurnGeneratedTokenCount\sum_{k\in\ForkBoundarySet}(\TurnHorizon-\RolloutTurnIndex).\]
When forking at every intermediate boundary, the remaining-turn sum is \(\TurnHorizon(\TurnHorizon-1)/2\), yielding \(\ForkedTrajectoryTokenCount/\BaseTrajectoryTokenCount=1+\ContinuationCount(\TurnHorizon-1)/2\).
Result: The base trajectory generates 15,360 tokens. The multiple-of-base column in table 3 prices the gap: exhaustive intermediate sampling creates severe computational blowup compared with selective boundary evaluation.

Systems insight: Exhaustive forking grows quadratically as \(\ContinuationCount \TurnHorizon^2\,\TurnGeneratedTokenCount/2\), meaning that doubling the horizon quadruples the credit computation bill even though base trajectory generation only doubles. At this horizon of 30 turns, exhaustive forking multiplies token generation by 117. In contrast, sampling only two targeted boundaries costs 9 times the base trajectory. The engineering decision rule is to fork only at a handful of critical boundaries, spending the saved generation budget on exploring a broader diversity of tasks. This inventory tallies generated output tokens alone; context prompt processing, sandbox snapshot restoration, tool execution, and verification add overhead to both configurations, while variable-length continuations shift the exact totals.


Selective forking requires an effective policy for choosing boundaries. Two practical triggers are common in production systems: turn boundaries where the policy’s action distribution exhibits high token entropy (a next-token distribution spread across many candidates, measured in section 16.8.1), indicating a decision among genuine alternatives, and turns that execute state-modifying tool calls such as file edits, database migrations, or network reconfiguration. Forking at two or three such junctures captures targeted empirical credit where trajectories diverge, at a small fraction of the exhaustive cost.
Credit assignment is fundamentally a budget decision across a spectrum of computational cost and statistical fidelity. Fixed baselines incur zero token overhead but offer no step-level resolution; learned value functions reduce variance at the expense of training a secondary critic; and continuation rollouts provide direct empirical value estimates at the price of massive token generation. Group-relative policy optimization represents the minimalist end of this spectrum, comparing complete sampled returns within a task group without spending any additional tokens on intermediate branches.

Checkpoint 16.1: Rewards and credit
A reward is a measurement, and credit is an estimate built on it. Each has a price in errors or tokens.

False-accept estimate: The verifier from the false-accepts notebook keeps its error rate while the policy’s pass rate drops from 10 percent to 5 percent. Does the false share of rewarded rollouts rise or fall, and to roughly what value?
Enforcement: Why must runtime authorization remain in force when unauthorized proposals receive a reward penalty?
Credit: With terminal reward zero, when is the score estimator’s coefficient zero and when is it negative? Why does neither answer identify the faulty turn?
Value sampling: What conditions must continuation forks preserve, and why is a difference between two estimated values not generally an exact advantage?
Credit budget: A trajectory doubles from 30 to 60 turns. By what factor does exhaustive continuation sampling grow, and should the schedule fork at every boundary or at two chosen ones?

title: 16 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
text:
Suppose three fresh rollouts attempt the connection-pool repair under the same fixture, budget, and assessment rule. Their completed terminal rewards are \([0,1,0]\). The successful rollout provides a direct comparison for the two failures without requiring an expert to label each intermediate edit, though this outcome comparison alone cannot identify which specific action caused success. Group relative policy optimization (GRPO) uses such within-task comparisons6 to construct policy update coefficients, replacing a learned value baseline with groups of sampled outcomes (Shao et al. 2024).
6 Sampled Baselines: Scoring each sample against the other samples for the same input predates GRPO. Kool et al. (2019) drew several samples per input and used the others as each one’s baseline, obtaining variance reduction without a learned critic, and Ahmadian et al. (2024) found that such REINFORCE-style estimators could outperform PPO when fine-tuning language models from human feedback. GRPO adds division by the group’s reward dispersion, a weighting choice analyzed in section 16.5.3. 
Kool, Wouter, Herke van Hoof, and Max Welling. 2019. Buy 4 REINFORCE Samples, Get a Baseline for Free!

Ahmadian, Arash, Chris Cremer, Matthias Gallé, Marzieh Fadaee, Julia Kreutzer, Olivier Pietquin, Ahmet Üstün, and Sara Hooker. 2024. “Back to Basics: Revisiting REINFORCE-Style Optimization for Learning from Human Feedback in LLMs.” Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), 12248–67. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2024.acl-long.662.
The trade-off centers on baseline estimation rather than the reward source: proximal policy optimization (PPO) can operate with an external check, just as GRPO can evaluate rollouts against a learned reward model. PPO trains a value function, either sharing parameters with the policy or running in a separate critic network (Schulman et al. 2017). GRPO eliminates that critic alongside its memory and training overhead, paying for the omission with additional rollouts: it samples a group of \(\GroupSize\) attempts per task to estimate empirical group statistics. GRPO serves as our worked optimizer because its systems accounting is straightforward to track, though the execution isolation and trajectory recording requirements that follow apply equally to both approaches. Both optimizers also hold a reference policy, a frozen copy of the starting checkpoint used to penalize drift away from it (section 16.5.2). Table 4 sets the two side by side.



Table 4: PPO and GRPO Compared: The two optimizers differ in the baseline they use, the granularity of their credit, and how they fail. Neither column implies a universal reduction in total memory or compute.










Dimension
PPO
GRPO




Models held

Trained components

Rollouts per task

Characteristic failure

To process a task, the system collects \(\GroupSize\) completed rollouts from a fixed behavior policy \(\pi_{\text{old}}\), the specific model checkpoint, execution environment, and decoding configuration that generated the trajectories. Let \(\TrajectoryReward_i\) denote the terminal reward assigned to rollout \(\GroupRolloutIndex\). For outcome-only verification, the group statistics and advantage coefficients are:
\[\GroupMeanReward=\frac{1}{\GroupSize}\sum_{j=1}^\GroupSize \TrajectoryReward_j,\qquad
\GroupRewardStandardDeviation=\sqrt{\frac{1}{\GroupSize}\sum_{j=1}^\GroupSize(\TrajectoryReward_j-\GroupMeanReward)^2},\qquad
\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i=\frac{\TrajectoryReward_i-\GroupMeanReward}{\GroupRewardStandardDeviation+\AdvantageStabilizer}. \tag{2}\]
The positive stabilizer \(\AdvantageStabilizer\) keeps the expression well-defined when all rollouts receive identical rewards. The denominator uses the empirical population standard deviation with divisor \(\GroupSize\), rather than a Bessel-corrected sample standard deviation with divisor \(\GroupSize-1\). This convention is an integral part of the objective formulation: altering the divisor rescales every coefficient, and neither divisor accounts for unobserved task behaviors outside the sampled group.
During policy updates, the rewards \(\TrajectoryReward_i\) and coefficients \(\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i\) remain fixed constants. Because this scalar is easily conflated with the state-action advantage function discussed in section 16.4, its distinct operational semantics warrant a precise definition.

Definition 16.3: Group-relative advantage
Group-relative advantage is the coefficient \(\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i\) that GRPO attaches to every sampled token of rollout \(\GroupRolloutIndex\): the rollout’s reward minus the mean reward of its task group, divided by the group’s reward dispersion.

Significance: It replaces a learned value function with \(\GroupSize\) rollouts per task. The group size therefore governs both the accuracy of the empirical baseline and the rollout compute budget; on a binary check, a lone pass in a group of \(\GroupSize\) receives a coefficient approaching \(\sqrt{\GroupSize-1}\).
Distinction: The advantage \(\PolicyHistoryAdvantage=\PolicyHistoryActionReturn-\PolicyRemainingReturn\) is an expectation for one action at one history, whereas the group-relative coefficient is an empirical, standardized score broadcast uniformly across all tokens in an entire trajectory. Furthermore, because the group statistics include the rollout being scored, the action-independent baseline argument does not make the standardized estimator unbiased REINFORCE. Centering alone is harmless, since \(\TrajectoryReward_i-\GroupMeanReward\) equals \((\GroupSize-1)/\GroupSize\) times \(\TrajectoryReward_i\) minus the mean of the other \(\GroupSize-1\) rewards, a valid leave-one-out baseline rescaled; the departure comes from dividing by \(\GroupRewardStandardDeviation\), which every reward in the group helps set, and it is a weighting choice recorded with the run rather than an error to be corrected.
Common pitfall: Reading a large positive coefficient as evidence that the rollout was fundamentally sound. The coefficient measures only how the rollout’s reward compared with its group; a false pass receives the exact same coefficient as a genuine success.




Napkin Math 16.3: From three rewards to update coefficientsProblem: Three hypothetical repair rollouts receive terminal rewards \([0,1,0]\), with no intermediate rewards and \(\AdvantageStabilizer=10^{-8}\). What coefficients enter the outcome-only GRPO update?
Math: The mean is \(\GroupMeanReward=1/3\), or 0.333333. The squared deviations are \(1/9\), \(4/9\), and \(1/9\), so \(\GroupRewardStandardDeviation=\sqrt{2/9}\), or 0.471405. Dividing each centered reward by \(\GroupRewardStandardDeviation\) gives \((-1/3)/\sqrt{2/9}=-1/\sqrt 2\) for each failure and \((2/3)/\sqrt{2/9}=\sqrt 2\) for the pass.
Result: Each failed rollout has coefficient -0.707107; the successful rollout has coefficient 1.414214. The three coefficients sum to zero.
Systems insight: The update sign emerges from relative group ranking rather than absolute reward values, and its magnitude scales up as successful trajectories become rarer. However, because every generated token within a rollout receives the identical scalar coefficient, crediting insightful diagnostic steps and mistaken proposals alike, GRPO trades fine-grained temporal credit assignment for substantial algorithmic and computational simplicity.





The rarer the pass in its group, the larger the coefficient it receives.
The group mean acts as an adaptive per-task baseline that absorbs intrinsic task difficulty. When a binary-evaluated group of size \(\GroupSize>1\) produces exactly one pass, the group mean is \(1/\GroupSize\) and the empirical standard deviation is \(\sqrt{\GroupSize-1}/\GroupSize\). Under equation 2, that lone successful rollout receives an advantage coefficient of
\[\LonePassAdvantage=\frac{1-1/\GroupSize}{\sqrt{\GroupSize-1}/\GroupSize+\AdvantageStabilizer}
=\frac{\GroupSize-1}{\sqrt{\GroupSize-1}+\GroupSize\AdvantageStabilizer}, \tag{3}\]
which evaluates to \(\sqrt{\GroupSize-1}\) when the stabilizer is zero and remains slightly below that bound for positive \(\AdvantageStabilizer\). On a difficult task where only one rollout in 16 succeeds, the group baseline drops to 0.0625; the solitary success receives an amplified coefficient of 3.87, while the fifteen failures receive small negative coefficients of 0.26 in magnitude. Conversely, on an easy task where only one rollout in 16 fails, the signs invert, heavily penalizing the isolated failure. In both scenarios, the update amplifies the contrast that separated success from failure on that specific problem instance. The group mean thereby fills the baseline role that a learned value function performs in PPO.
The same arithmetic explains why the false-accept share of equation 1 is not the false share of the gradient. False accepts occur on failing rollouts, which are most common on hard tasks, and on a hard task a false pass is often the group’s only pass, so it receives a coefficient near \(\sqrt{\GroupSize-1}\). A false pass on an easy task, one of many passes in its group, receives only a small positive coefficient, the mirror image of the small failure coefficients above. The same count of false accepts can therefore carry a larger or a smaller share of the update depending on which groups they land in, and the hardest tasks, where the share of equation 1 is also highest, are where each one weighs most.



During optimization, the training engine evaluates recorded trajectory actions under the current policy parameters \(\Policy\). Let \(\SampledPolicyToken_{i,t}\) denote the \(\TokenIndex\)-th sampled policy token in rollout \(\GroupRolloutIndex\), \(\ConditioningTokenPrefix_{i,t}\) its delivered context prefix, and \(\RolloutPolicyTokenCount_i>0\) the total number of sampled generation tokens. While tool outputs, environment responses, and prompt text appear within prefixes \(\ConditioningTokenPrefix_{i,t}\), they are masked out of the policy loss and do not count toward \(\RolloutPolicyTokenCount_i\). At each generated token position, the probability ratio is:
\[\PolicyProbabilityRatio_{i,t}(\ModelParameters)=
\frac{\Policy(\SampledPolicyToken_{i,t}\mid \ConditioningTokenPrefix_{i,t})}
{\pi_{\text{old}}(\SampledPolicyToken_{i,t}\mid \ConditioningTokenPrefix_{i,t})}.\]
Both probabilities must reflect the exact sampling convention used during generation. If generation applied temperature scaling or top-\(\Glyph{k}\) / top-\(\Glyph{p}\) truncation, the recorded behavior probability \(\pi_{\text{old}}\) in the denominator must match the actual sampling distribution and remain strictly positive. Probability support eliminated by decoding filters cannot be restored by downstream loss ratios.
With clipping parameter \(0<\RatioClippingWidth<1\) (kept distinct from the denominator stabilizer \(\AdvantageStabilizer\)), the clipped surrogate objective is:
\[\ClippedSurrogateObjective_{i,t}(\ModelParameters)=\min\left\{
\PolicyProbabilityRatio_{i,t}(\ModelParameters)\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i,
\operatorname{clip}(\PolicyProbabilityRatio_{i,t}(\ModelParameters),1-\RatioClippingWidth,1+\RatioClippingWidth)\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i
\right\}.\]
When \(\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i>0\), the surrogate stops growing once the probability ratio exceeds \(1+\RatioClippingWidth\), removing any gradient incentive to push the current probability higher. When \(\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i<0\), the surrogate flattens once the ratio drops below \(1-\RatioClippingWidth\), avoiding destructive runaway penalties. In contrast, movements in an unfavorable direction, such as reducing the probability of an action with positive advantage, remain unclipped and continue to penalize the surrogate. Clipping caps the gradient incentive on individual tokens rather than creating a true trust region that bounds overall policy shift; parameter sharing across tokens and additional loss terms can still propel \(\PolicyProbabilityRatio_{i,t}(\ModelParameters)\) well outside the clipping interval.7
7 Trust Region: The clipped surrogate originated in trust region policy optimization, which explicitly constrained each policy step to keep the average KL divergence between updated and behavior policies below a target threshold (Schulman et al. 2015). PPO replaced this constrained optimization step with a clipped objective to simplify implementation and distributed scaling (Schulman et al. 2017). Because clipping provides no mathematical guarantee against large policy shifts, production training pipelines must monitor probability ratios and empirical divergence metrics directly. 
Schulman, John, Sergey Levine, Pieter Abbeel, Michael Jordan, and Philipp Moritz. 2015. “Trust Region Policy Optimization.” Proceedings of the 32nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 37: 1889–97.

Schulman, John, Filip Wolski, Prafulla Dhariwal, Alec Radford, and Oleg Klimov. 2017. “Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1707.06347, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1707.06347.
A frozen reference policy \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\), typically initialized from the pre-RL checkpoint, provides an auxiliary regularizer that penalizes excessive policy drift. In distributed pipelines, \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) maintains a distinct model identity from the behavior policy \(\pi_{\text{old}}\) that generated the rollouts. Assuming strictly positive probabilities over shared token support, we define:
\[\ReferenceProbabilityRatio_{i,t}(\ModelParameters)=\frac{\pi_{\text{ref}}(\SampledPolicyToken_{i,t}\mid \ConditioningTokenPrefix_{i,t})}
{\Policy(\SampledPolicyToken_{i,t}\mid \ConditioningTokenPrefix_{i,t})},\qquad
\PerTokenKlEstimate_{i,t}(\ModelParameters)=\ReferenceProbabilityRatio_{i,t}(\ModelParameters)-\log \ReferenceProbabilityRatio_{i,t}(\ModelParameters)-1.\]
The penalty term \(\PerTokenKlEstimate_{i,t}(\ModelParameters)\) is strictly non-negative and vanishes if and only if the current and reference token probabilities coincide. Conditioned on prefix \(\ConditioningTokenPrefix_{i,t}\), the expectation of \(\PerTokenKlEstimate_{i,t}(\ModelParameters)\) over tokens sampled from the current policy \(\Policy\) equals the Kullback–Leibler divergence \(\KlDivergence(\Policy\parallel\pi_{\text{ref}})\), the expected log ratio of the two distributions under \(\Policy\), which is zero only when they agree; the identity is derived in Generalized advantage estimation and KL divergence. The plain log ratio \(-\log \ReferenceProbabilityRatio_{i,t}\) has the same expectation, but a single sampled token can make it negative, so a per-token penalty built on it would sometimes reward drift. Each term \(\ReferenceProbabilityRatio-\log \ReferenceProbabilityRatio-1\) is non-negative, so every token’s penalty pushes toward the reference. Because the tokens in the training batch were originally drawn from the behavior policy \(\pi_{\text{old}}\), evaluating this sample average provides an approximation to the current-policy divergence that degrades as off-policy lag accumulates over multiple gradient steps.
Combining these components yields the empirical GRPO maximization objective:
\[\GrpoSampledObjective(\ModelParameters)=
\frac{1}{\GroupSize}\sum_{i=1}^\GroupSize\frac{1}{\RolloutPolicyTokenCount_i}\sum_{t=1}^{\RolloutPolicyTokenCount_i}
\left[\ClippedSurrogateObjective_{i,t}(\ModelParameters)-\KlPenaltyCoefficient \PerTokenKlEstimate_{i,t}(\ModelParameters)\right],
\qquad\KlPenaltyCoefficient\ge0. \tag{4}\]
Standard deep learning frameworks minimize the negative of \(\GrpoSampledObjective(\ModelParameters)\) as a loss. The hyperparameter \(\KlPenaltyCoefficient\) scales the reference policy penalty. Because reward standardization, probability ratio clipping, and token length normalization collectively depart from the true expected return \(\ExpectedReturnObjective(\ModelParameters)\), production systems record these optimization hyperparameter choices alongside the trained model weights and validate performance through fresh online evaluation trials.



The normalization factor \(1/\RolloutPolicyTokenCount_i\) in equation 4 averages token-level losses within each rollout before computing the group mean. At the start of an update, when the current policy matches the behavior policy and the probability ratios equal one, rollout \(\GroupRolloutIndex\) contributes the following gradient to the reward surrogate:
\[\nabla_\ModelParameters\RolloutSurrogateObjective_i=\frac{\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i}{\RolloutPolicyTokenCount_i}\sum_{t=1}^{\RolloutPolicyTokenCount_i}\nabla_\ModelParameters\log\Policy(\SampledPolicyToken_{i,t}\mid \ConditioningTokenPrefix_{i,t}), \tag{5}\]
initially assigning every sampled token in trajectory \(\GroupRolloutIndex\) an effective scalar weight of \(\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i/\RolloutPolicyTokenCount_i\). This per-sequence divisor exerts asymmetric optimization pressure across different outcome classes (Liu et al. 2025). For failing rollouts (\(\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i<0\)), extending generation length distributes the negative penalty across more tokens, diluting the per-token gradient penalty. For successful rollouts (\(\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i>0\)), producing fewer tokens concentrates the positive advantage on a compact sequence, amplifying the per-token reinforcement. The resulting optimization pressure, known as length bias, systematically favors concise successes and verbose failures.

Liu, Zichen, Changyu Chen, Wenjun Li, Penghui Qi, Tianyu Pang, Chao Du, Wee Sun Lee, and Min Lin. 2025. “Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2503.20783.
Consider two failing rollouts within the same group that receive identical negative coefficients \(\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i\). If one fails after 128 tokens while the second exhausts the context budget at 4,096 tokens, the concise failure absorbs a per-token penalty 32× larger than that of the verbose failure. To eliminate this distortion, alternative implementations replace individual sequence lengths \(\RolloutPolicyTokenCount_i\) with a constant divisor shared across the group or microbatch, such as the mean trajectory length \(\MeanRolloutLength\):
\[\ConstantDivisorGrpoObjective(\ModelParameters)=\frac{1}{\GroupSize\,\MeanRolloutLength}\sum_{i=1}^\GroupSize\sum_{t=1}^{\RolloutPolicyTokenCount_i}\left[\ClippedSurrogateObjective_{i,t}(\ModelParameters)-\KlPenaltyCoefficient \PerTokenKlEstimate_{i,t}(\ModelParameters)\right].\]
Under this constant-denominator objective, every token receives an update weight proportional to \(\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i\) alone, regardless of trajectory length. While these scalar weight comparisons illustrate the gradient mechanics, the actual trajectory length drift depends on how individual token gradient vectors align or cancel across sequences during training, an empirical dynamic examined in section 16.8.
Reward standardization introduces an analogous weighting trade-off across tasks. Dividing by \(\GroupRewardStandardDeviation+\AdvantageStabilizer\) normalizes the scale of centered rewards across groups. As \(\AdvantageStabilizer\to0\), every group without a tie has the same total squared coefficient, \(\sum_i\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i^2=\GroupSize\), whether it holds a single isolated success or an even split between passes and failures. The equality is between whole groups, not individual rollouts. Within the fixed total, a lone pass takes \(\GroupSize-1\) of the \(\GroupSize\) units and its failures share the remaining one, which is the amplification of equation 3, whereas an even split spreads the total evenly. Omitting this dispersion divisor weights tasks strictly by their raw reward spread. Both normalizations represent fundamental objective design choices that must be explicitly logged with the training run alongside the clipping threshold.



When every rollout in a completed group yields the identical reward, the batch constitutes a zero-contrast group. In this scenario, every numerator in equation 2 evaluates to zero, yielding advantage coefficients \(\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i=0\), surrogate terms \(\ClippedSurrogateObjective_{i,t}=0\), and policy gradient contributions \(\nabla_\ModelParameters\ClippedSurrogateObjective_{i,t}=0\). The reward-driven component of the policy gradient vanishes entirely, leaving only the reference policy penalty and any auxiliary regularizers active. Identical rewards do not imply identical behavior: fundamentally different reasoning paths or tool failures collapse into the same uninformative binary score.
Assuming independent rollout attempts on a task with fixed success probability \(\AttemptPassProbability\), a group of size \(\GroupSize\) contains at least one success and at least one failure with probability \(\GroupContrastProbability(\GroupSize,\AttemptPassProbability)=1-\AttemptPassProbability^\GroupSize-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\GroupSize\). This matches the informative-task fraction defined in equation 14.3 with \(\IndependentAttemptCount=\GroupSize\), where the excluded outcomes represent the all-pass and all-fail edge cases. (This contrast probability differs from pass@\(\GroupSize\), which requires only a single pass.)
Computational waste escalates dramatically in difficult task regimes where learning signal is needed most. Sampling groups of 2 on a task with pass rate \(\AttemptPassProbability=\) 0.10 yields a contrast probability \(\GroupContrastProbability\) of only 0.18, leaving 82 percent of generated groups without any policy gradient signal. Even with larger groups of 8, a task solved on 5 percent of attempts produces zero reward gradient 66 percent of the time. Every uninformative group incurs the full systems cost of model inference, containerized tool execution, and reward verification. This binomial model assumes independent trials on a homogeneous task; evaluating a heterogeneous workload requires computing expected contrast per difficulty bucket, as aggregate fleet averages obscure the true zero-contrast rate.



Groups of eight carry a gradient reliably only at mid-range pass rates.
Because binary outcome variance \(\AttemptPassProbability(1-\AttemptPassProbability)\) peaks at \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.5\), active task scheduling based on rolling pass rates maximizes the proportion of informative rollouts. Systems engineers can counter zero-contrast waste using two levers: increasing group size \(\GroupSize\) or filtering task queues by difficulty. These strategies carry starkly different systems costs. Comparing them mirrors the cost-per-accepted-task framework introduced in equation 1.2: the total computational investment per task attempt divided by the probability of producing usable gradient information.

Napkin Math 16.4: Rollouts per informative groupProblem: A hypothetical update samples 8 rollouts for each of 512 tasks, with each rollout executing 30 interaction turns generating 512 tokens per turn. Under the baseline task distribution, the agent policy succeeds on 5 percent of attempts. What is the total generation cost per training step in tokens, and which scaling strategy purchases informative gradient signal more efficiently: doubling group size to 16, or filtering the dispatch queue for tasks where the agent succeeds roughly 50 percent of the time?
Math: Generating a single trajectory consumes 30 \(\times\) 512 = 15,360 tokens, bringing the total generation burden across 4,096 rollouts to 62.9 million tokens per step. With binary outcome probability \(\GroupContrastProbability=1-\AttemptPassProbability^\GroupSize-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\GroupSize\), the amortized rollout cost per informative group is \(\GroupSize/\GroupContrastProbability\), as detailed in table 5.



Table 5: Cost of Reward Contrast: Doubling the group raises contrast but spends more rollouts per informative group; targeting difficulty raises contrast without more rollouts per group, at the price of changing which tasks the policy trains on.

Result: Curriculum difficulty targeting reduces rollout cost per informative gradient by 2.9× compared to the hard baseline mix, whereas doubling group size actually increases the rollout cost per usable gradient. The metric counts informative groups, not the information inside each one; a group of 16 estimates its baseline more precisely than a group of 8, so the verdict holds where the binding problem is obtaining any contrast at all. Targeting also shifts the task mixture, which the run must log (section 16.9.1).
Systems insight: The metric \(\GroupSize/\GroupContrastProbability\) quantifies the computational cost per informative gradient signal: the numerator represents rollout expenditure per group, while the denominator measures the probability that the group yields usable contrast. In regimes with low baseline pass rates, \(\GroupContrastProbability\) dominates system efficiency, and it responds far more dramatically to curated curriculum selection than to expanding group size. When obtaining any contrast is the binding constraint and the changed task mixture is acceptable, the demonstrated curriculum purchases informative groups more cheaply than the larger group. Baseline precision, required task coverage, and measured held-out learning progress can justify other group sizes; the run must record the task-selection distribution as well as the chosen group size.


While group-relative comparisons establish advantage coefficients and optimization weights, every term in the objective ultimately resolves to conditional token probabilities. These probabilities remain valid only if the training engine faithfully reconstructs the precise token contexts seen by the model during inference. In multi-turn agentic workflows, model generations interleave with tool executions, environment state mutations, and dynamic context compaction. Executing GRPO correctly in production therefore requires an exact, immutable log of the tokens passed to and sampled from each model invocation, rather than an unversioned end-of-episode transcript.

title: 16 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
text:
In multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning, an agent alternates between generating actions—such as code edits, shell commands, or structured tool invocations—and consuming external feedback from compilers, test runners, or runtime environments. An environment observation conditions the next proposal, but it is never an action sampled from the policy parameters. As episodes unfold, agent harnesses routinely compact, truncate, or summarize earlier turns to stay within the model’s context window. By the end of an extended trial, the final context window rarely matches the prompt prefixes that originally produced the intermediate turns.
To calculate policy gradients or off-policy importance ratios correctly, the training pipeline must preserve two distinct sources of truth: which tokens the policy actually sampled, and what exact prefix conditioned each token at the instant of generation. Reconstructing training pairs from an end-of-episode chat log fails because it evaluates probabilities on counterfactual context that the policy never saw. While we illustrate these mechanics using group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), this accounting discipline applies universally to any RL algorithm that updates parameters from multi-turn interaction rollouts.


Consider a concrete execution: trial rl_trial_01 running against pool_fixture_v1. In turn 1, the model invokes a test suite. The harness runs the suite and delivers a truncated failure log. In turn 2, the model conditions on that log and proposes a targeted source patch. By turn 4, context window pressure forces the harness to compress the earlier diagnostic logs into a concise two-line summary. If the training pipeline subsequently attempts to reconstruct the rollout from the final episode transcript, it confronts a corrupted causal graph: turn 2 would appear conditioned on the two-line summary rather than the full failure log that actually prompted the patch. Evaluating the model’s action probabilities against that retrofitted context evaluates policy decisions against information states the agent never encountered during sampling.
To guarantee replay fidelity, the rollout recorder must capture each invocation’s delivered input token prefix alongside the exact token IDs emitted by the generator, linking both to a durable interaction record. Storing full token arrays for every step across millions of rollouts would quickly exhaust cluster storage; systems address this using immutable content-addressed storage or prefix-tree references that point to shared parent contexts. The record must register tokenizer versions, chat template metadata, attention visibility masks, rotary position offsets, and compaction decisions. Storing raw UTF-8 text and re-tokenizing it during training is a common architectural anti-pattern: minor discrepancies in BPE merge rules, whitespace handling, or tool-schema formatting can alter token boundaries and shift sequence lengths. The captured token IDs represent the only ground-truth record of the generated trajectory. Table 6 extends the input-fidelity principles established in Serializing Trajectories to the sampling evidence required by multi-turn reinforcement learning.



Table 6: Multi-Turn Rollout Record: Decision inputs, sampled actions, and assessment status are separate evidence. A final transcript or a model-version label alone cannot reconstruct their relationship.










Record component
Contents
Training question it answers




Trial and group identity
Task, fixture and candidate versions; rollout and group IDs; declared initial conditions and split assignment
Which experiment and reward comparison does this sample belong to?


Invocation inputs
Call ID, delivered prefix token IDs or available immutable contents, template/tokenizer versions, attention and position configuration
What could the policy condition on at this decision?


Sampled actions
Original output token IDs, invocation boundaries, mapping from local positions to the rollout’s policy-token index
Which tokens were actually sampled, rather than supplied or reconstructed?


Behavior distribution
Weights/adapters version, sampling configuration and constraints, chosen-token behavior log probabilities
What distribution generated each sampled token?


Observation associations
Tool operation and attempt IDs, delivered result versions, refusals, partial-result status, and input inclusion
Which execution evidence reached which invocation?


Bounds and ownership
Resource limits and usage, stop reason, outstanding work and its owner
Why did collection stop, and what duties remain?


Assessment and learning use
Grader/reward versions, component scores, pending or unavailable findings, group membership and update eligibility
Is a reward known, and how does the declared objective use this record?









To connect multi-turn trajectories to the mathematical objectives developed earlier, we map the episode into the flattened policy-token index \(\TokenIndex=1,\ldots,\RolloutPolicyTokenCount_i\) from section 16.5.2 for rollout \(\GroupRolloutIndex\), while retaining the structural mapping to invocation \(\RolloutTurnIndex\) and the local generation offset. Each conditioning prefix \(\ConditioningTokenPrefix_{i,t}\) consists of the exact input context delivered to invocation \(\RolloutTurnIndex\) concatenated with the preceding policy tokens generated within that invocation. Because context compaction and truncation alter the prompt between turns, \(\ConditioningTokenPrefix_{i,t}\) cannot be inferred by slicing the final transcript.
When computing action-scoring losses, the distinction between conditioning and generation is absolute. Prompts, environment feedback, tool payloads, and harness scaffolding act exclusively as conditioning context. They propagate activations through the model to shape downstream attention and predictions, but they are not sampled policy actions; their token log probabilities must never appear in the loss objective. Consequently, loss normalization denominators must count only the scored policy tokens, while the runtime cost accounting tallies prefill processing and decode generation as separate operational line items.
This action-scoring mask serves a fundamentally different purpose from the imitation masks used in supervised fine-tuning. In the supervised recovery example, the malformed proposal e2 and its refusal stay in the prefix as context but carry a zero loss mask, so they are never imitation targets, because the objective is imitation of curated behavior (Observation Loss Masking). In reinforcement learning, however, the mask identifies the support of the exploration distribution, and verified trajectory post-training (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training}\)) admits every sampled action, weighted by its verified outcome. If the policy samples an invalid JSON schema or an unparsable shell command during exploration, that sequence is an authentic policy action, even if the execution harness subsequently refuses to dispatch it. Masking those tokens out simply because a curator would not present them as demonstrations corrupts the estimator. The malformed tokens escape the negative update, and the failing rollout’s whole negative coefficient lands on its remaining well-formed tokens, so the update pushes down valid syntax in place of the mistake. Similarly, when the model generates an end-of-turn delimiter or stop token, that token is an action that consumed probability mass; by contrast, an abrupt terminator injected by a dataloader when cutting off an execution is harness intervention, not policy choice, and must be excluded. Any partial-action scoring strategy requires an explicit mathematical objective and denominator rather than an ad hoc mask inherited from a supervised training pipeline.
The denominator of the importance-sampling probability ratio must represent the true behavior distribution that generated the token. Inference engines often apply sampling transforms—such as temperature scaling, top-\(\Glyph{k}\) truncation, nucleus (top-\(\Glyph{p}\)) filtering, or grammar-constrained finite-state decoding—that renormalize the distribution over a restricted subset of the vocabulary. The rollout record must therefore store the normalized chosen-token log probability under the active generation configuration, along with the sampling parameters required to reconstruct the sampling state. When computing policy updates, the trainer evaluates the numerator under the target policy \(\Policy\) using the identical prefix recorded during generation. Substituting unconstrained model logits into the denominator treats the behavior policy as an unconstrained softmax; while some systems adopt this simplification to avoid caching rollout probabilities, it introduces estimator bias that must be tracked explicitly as an approximation.
Freezing the policy checkpoint across each episode substantially simplifies this accounting. In high-throughput asynchronous architectures where weight updates occur concurrently with rollout generation, an agent might execute invocation 1 on checkpoint \(\PolicyCheckpoint_1\) and invocation 2 on checkpoint \(\PolicyCheckpoint_2\). If an infrastructure design permits cross-invocation updates within a single trial, the record must associate behavior checkpoints and generation probabilities per invocation; tagging the entire rollout with a single model version misattributes the provenance of later tokens.
Once token log probabilities and behavior distributions are properly recorded, the system links the trajectory-level advantage coefficient \(\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i\) to each sampled policy token. If the system assigns advantages at the turn level rather than across the entire trajectory, it must adhere to the estimator and continuation rules detailed in section 16.4. Two parallel rollouts that happen to reach turn 3 may possess radically different interaction histories, execution latencies, and tool states; comparing intermediate outcomes purely by matching turn indices provides an invalid foundation for relative reward scoring.



A resilient execution harness enforces strict boundaries on wall-clock time, invocation turns, and token counts. How the learning algorithm interprets an enforced stop, however, depends entirely on the task specification. If a task contract defines success as accepted code completion within a declared budget of 10 turns and 5 minutes, exhausting that budget without reaching a solution constitutes an authentic task failure; the policy legitimately receives a zero or negative reward. The rollout record must log the exact termination reason and resource metrics, noting whether the boundary interrupted active model generation or an external tool execution.
Other interruptions stem from external operational limits rather than policy choices. For example, a single tool invocation exceeding a 30 s sandbox deadline produces an error observation from which the agent can still recover. Alternatively, an assessment microservice may crash, leaving the verifier unable to score an otherwise complete pull request. If an orchestration worker aborts an active rollout simply because the cluster scheduler reclaims the node or the batch queue deadline expires before task budget exhaustion, the collector produces a censored rollout. The rollout record must treat budget exhaustion, observation recovery, verifier unavailability, and infrastructure preemption as mutually exclusive execution states. They map onto the four-verdict rule of The four-verdict rule. Budget exhaustion is a fail; a recovered tool error is an ordinary observation inside the trajectory; verifier unavailability and preemption leave the outcome pending while a retry is still possible and unknown once it is not. Throughout this chapter, a censored or unresolved rollout means one in the last two states, whose reward is missing because of the infrastructure rather than the policy.
Mishandling censored rollouts introduces dangerous statistical biases into training pipelines. Silently discarding incomplete rollouts introduces classic survivorship bias, purging complex, multi-turn trajectories from the training set and skewing policy optimization toward trivial, fast tasks. Conversely, assigning a default reward of zero to rollouts interrupted by infrastructure outages penalizes the agent for distributed system failures, teaching the policy to avoid multi-step reasoning. The training pipeline must declare an explicit policy for censored episodes: waiting for asynchronous verifier recovery, scheduling idempotently bounded retries, or applying statistical imputation methods that account for missing outcomes without biasing advantage estimates.
Finally, terminating policy sampling does not automatically stop pending asynchronous operations. Dispatched bash subshells, spawned containers, and cloud API calls remain active until explicitly cancelled. The harness must track resource ownership across the full operational lifecycle, ensuring that abandoned or censored rollouts clean up orphaned processes and container volumes regardless of whether the resulting trajectory is admitted into an optimization batch.



The operational constraints configured in the rollout harness—including context compaction policies, observation truncation limits, tool refusal responses, and resource caps—collectively define the Markov decision process that the policy explores. If the training environment diverges from the intended deployment contract, the agent learns behavioral adaptations that fail in production. For instance, an agent trained with generous 50-turn allowances may learn meandering trial-and-error debugging strategies that collapse when placed under a strict 10-turn production limit. When teams intentionally expand training budgets as an exploratory curriculum to bootstrap discovery in sparse-reward environments, the transfer penalty under tighter deployment constraints must be tracked as an explicit empirical metric.
Decoupling model invocation from episode lifetime is equally critical for cluster efficiency. Tool-heavy agent rollouts can spend most of their lifetime waiting for external work: a policy might generate a tool request in 200 ms, followed by a 45 s wait while an external container compiles code and runs a test suite. An accelerator held for that rollout during the wait would compute for under 1 percent of the episode, and the loss compounds across every rollout in the training cluster. High-throughput collection engines decouple inference serving from episode execution, scheduling active invocations from other ready rollouts onto the accelerator while blocked rollouts wait for external tool observations. This interleaving maximizes hardware utilization without mutating the causal observation stream consumed by any individual trajectory. Section 16.9 develops the bounded queues, group completion barriers, and version-tracking protocols required to coordinate this asynchronous schedule at scale.
A comprehensive rollout record provides a tamper-proof account of what the policy observed, what tokens it generated, and how the environment responded. Whether that recorded trajectory can safely guide policy updates, however, depends entirely on maintaining an uncompromised boundary between the artifacts the policy is permitted to modify and the independent harness that evaluates them.

title: 16 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
text:
Consider the representative trial rl_trial_01, in which an agent submits a candidate patch after running local unit tests against an edited connection pool. The reinforcement learning loop requires an authoritative verdict under the evaluation specification repair_accept_v1, not an unverified self-report from the environment that generated the patch. As the METR evaluations in section 16.3 illustrate, an agent capable of modifying its evaluation environment can bypass the intended task and rewrite its own scoring logic, and where the scorer is within reach it often does.
To prevent this failure mode, the learning loop must integrate the isolated grader boundary as a core systems primitive. We call this architectural guarantee verifier isolation: the assessment harness and its verdict are protected from both the executing agent policy and the candidate code it submits.8 Whereas test coverage determines whether a test suite exercises the required behavioral contract, verifier isolation guarantees that the emitted verdict reflects the actual execution of those tests rather than unauthorized tampering.
8 Complete Mediation of the Verdict: The tool boundary of Complete mediation checks every access to every protected object; verifier isolation applies the same rule, with least privilege, to the reward path. The policy never needs write access to test definitions or score ledgers, so the runtime grants none, and every route to a verdict, including module resolution paths and test runner binaries, passes through the authoritative controller. 
↩︎ The isolated grader boundary, with held-out tests kept by a trusted controller outside the candidate’s sandbox, is established in Grader isolation.



When an agent runs in a shared writable workspace, it can rewrite test assertions, substitute mock runner binaries, or leave persistent configuration flags that alter how verification executes. Scoring an agent within that same environment effectively delegates grading authority to untrusted code. To eliminate this vulnerability, the system enforces a strict dual-workspace architecture, dividing mutable state, assessment authority, and the handoff between the two sides as table 7 lays out. The controller captures the candidate artifact—such as a unified diff or commit object—binds it cryptographically to the rollout identifier and base source revision, and transfers it to a clean assessment workspace. This secondary workspace instantiates a fresh copy of the declared fixture from scratch, discarding all environment variables, running background processes, and temporary files generated during rollout exploration.
Patch admission enforces the task’s modification contract before execution begins. For example, a source-code repair task should restrict modifications strictly to application source files, rejecting any edits to test suites, grading scripts, or container configuration files. When a task legitimately requires modifications to build systems or dependencies, the admission policy must define how those changes are staged and audited. Verifying that a patch applies cleanly with git apply establishes only syntactic compatibility with the base revision; it provides no guarantee that the resulting code is safe or benign to run.



Table 7: Dual-workspace boundaries: Exploration and assessment have separate state and authority. The candidate crosses as untrusted material; separation does not certify its behavior.










Responsibility
Exploration side
Assessment side




Mutable task state
Task-scoped working copy and permitted local diagnostics
Candidate applied to an identified fixture under its own execution limits


Assessment authority
Public feedback, not control of the deciding check
Protected criteria, checker configuration, and authoritative result storage


Handoff
Consistently captured candidate and bounded provenance
Verdict and declared evidence bound to candidate, fixture, and checker versions






The handoff contract summarized in table 7 isolates the file tree, but the candidate code remains untrusted material. As soon as the assessment environment compiles or imports the patch, that code executes. If candidate code shares a Python interpreter or runtime address space with the test runner, it can monkey-patch assertions, inspect in-memory grading structures, or intercept verification hooks. Similarly, mounting hidden test suites directly into the candidate container exposes test logic to inspection, even when mounted with read-only permissions. The assessment controller must isolate test logic and verdict collection in a supervisory process or host, interacting with the untrusted candidate container exclusively across a constrained communication interface, such as standard input and output streams or an isolated IPC socket. When legacy test frameworks demand in-process evaluation, the controller must treat the entire interpreter as tainted. Its exit status and reported pass flags cannot establish success; the controller must independently assess candidate behavior against trusted assertions outside that interpreter. If the framework cannot support that separation, its in-process grading remains an explicitly limited attack surface assessed against known circumvention techniques, rather than an isolated verifier.
Beyond filesystem boundaries, the assessment environment requires strict resource caps and network restrictions. Unfiltered candidate stdout and stderr streams represent raw telemetry, never authoritative verdict strings. The controller collects execution metrics, ties them directly to the candidate artifact and trial identifier through a secured reporting pipe, and distinguishes between deterministic criterion failures and infrastructure failures. If a candidate patch enters an infinite loop and exhausts a 60 s execution budget, the verifier records a valid criterion timeout failure. In contrast, if a grader worker crashes because of an out-of-memory error triggered by host oversubscription, the event leaves the outcome unresolved in the sense of section 16.6.3 rather than penalizing the candidate. The resource caps decide which case applies. A breach of the limits declared for the candidate’s own execution is candidate-induced, whereas a failure of the host or grader while the candidate stayed within those limits is infrastructure. In neither scenario may the system emit a default pass, and both outcomes must be reported distinctly in training telemetry.
Reinforcement learning introduces an adversarial failure mode seldom encountered during offline evaluation: exploiting exception handling in the verification harness. A candidate patch that hangs, triggers an unhandled memory fault, or crashes the test runner can convert an inevitable test failure into a missing verdict. If the training pipeline silently drops rollouts with missing verdicts from batch normalization, or assigns them a default baseline score higher than a failure, the policy learns to generate crash-inducing code rather than viable solutions. The controller must therefore enforce an explicit contract. Any candidate-induced resource exhaustion or process crash, judged against the candidate’s declared limits as above, maps directly to a failure (\(\TrajectoryReward = 0\)) and never outscores an orderly test failure.
MicroVMs (such as Firecracker) and user-space or container sandboxes (such as gVisor) offer distinct isolation trade-offs whose integrity must be rigorously tested. Even with hardware virtualization, however, information can leak through permitted outputs and shared hardware resources, the confinement problem that agent sandboxes already face on their egress channels (Name resolution and local destinations). Even binary pass/fail responses leak information across successive submissions. In multi-turn rollouts, intermediate feedback must never expose hidden test names, assertion details, or internal stack traces. Exposing those details gives the policy a side channel to reconstruct the hidden test suite turn by turn, transforming hidden tests into visible targets. System designers must explicitly declare what training feedback is exposed to the agent, minimize diagnostic leakage, and preserve a pristine held-out evaluation split. Tests queried repeatedly to generate training rewards become de facto training data, meaning unbiased assessment requires evaluation suites that the training loop never executes.


↩︎ The isolation trade-offs among containers, user-space kernels, and microVMs are established in Choosing an Isolation Envelope.



Verifier isolation eliminates deliberate tampering, but it cannot prevent non-deterministic evaluation outcomes.
