Flaky checks—caused by thread scheduling races, network jitter, or asynchronous event loops—can spuriously accept an incorrect patch or fail a valid one, even when the test definitions are completely protected. Repeating the check reduces the rate of accidental acceptance. If a test suite is fundamentally under-specified, however, an incorrect patch that satisfies those partial requirements will pass every repetition.
Let \(\TrialPassProbability\) represent the probability that a fixed candidate patch passes a single verification trial under a specified protocol. Assuming \(\VerificationTrialCount\) independent trials share the same pass probability, the all-pass rule, which requires unanimous success across all \(\VerificationTrialCount\) trials, accepts the candidate with probability
\[\Pr(\text{accept candidate})=\TrialPassProbability^{\VerificationTrialCount}.\]
In this notation, \(\VerificationTrialCount\) denotes the total number of trials conducted, including the first. An initial pass followed by \(\VerificationTrialCount\) additional confirmation reruns would instead yield an acceptance probability of \(\TrialPassProbability^{\VerificationTrialCount+1}\). When trials exhibit statistical dependence, the all-pass probability becomes the product of conditional probabilities \(\prod_{j=1}^{\VerificationTrialCount} \Pr(\text{pass}_j\mid\text{all earlier passes})\), which can diverge sharply from \(\TrialPassProbability^{\VerificationTrialCount}\). Launching fresh container instances with randomized execution seeds promotes independence, whereas a persistent checker bug or shared host-level bottleneck introduces positive correlation across runs.
Group normalization makes a flaky pass as damaging as a tampered one. On a hard task, a lone false pass receives the same near-\(\sqrt{\GroupSize-1}\) coefficient (equation 3) as an authentic solution, so the optimizer spends its largest updates on scheduling luck.

Napkin Math 16.5: The cost of an all-pass ruleProblem: How does requiring repeated passes change accidental reward, false rejection, and verification work?
Variables: In a hypothetical fixture, a fixed incorrect patch has trial pass probability \(\IncorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability\) of 0.20, while a fixed correct patch has trial pass probability \(\CorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability\) of 0.98. Trials are independent under an unchanged protocol. Acceptance requires \(\VerificationTrialCount\) total passes, with \(\VerificationTrialCount\) set to 3; verification stops at the first rejection. A separate illustration considers a group of 16 independently assessed incorrect candidates with the same \(\IncorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability\).
Math: A single trial for each incorrect candidate gives group probability \(1-(1-\IncorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability)^\GroupSize\) of at least one false pass, or 97.2 percent. In the special case of exactly one pass, its standardized coefficient approaches \(\sqrt{\GroupSize-1}\), approximately 3.87, as \(\AdvantageStabilizer\) approaches zero. The all-pass rule lowers each incorrect candidate’s acceptance probability to \(\IncorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability^{\VerificationTrialCount}\), or 0.8 percent, but rejects the correct candidate with probability \(1-\CorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability^{\VerificationTrialCount}\), or 5.88 percent.
Trial \(\VerificationTrialIndex+1\) is needed only if the preceding \(\VerificationTrialIndex\) trials passed. Consequently,
\[\mathbb E[\ExecutedTrialCount\mid \TrialPassProbability]=\sum_{j=0}^{\VerificationTrialCount-1}\TrialPassProbability^\VerificationTrialIndex.\]
For the incorrect patch, \(1+\IncorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability+\IncorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability^2\) gives 1.24 trials; for the correct patch, \(1+\CorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability+\CorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability^2\) gives 2.9404. Running every trial regardless of earlier outcomes instead consumes \(\VerificationTrialCount\) trials per candidate.
Systems insight: Each added trial multiplies an incorrect patch’s acceptance by \(\IncorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability\) and a correct patch’s by \(\CorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability\), so the rule pays when \(\IncorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability\) is far below \(\CorrectCandidateTrialPassProbability\): here 3 trials cut an incorrect patch’s acceptance from a per-trial 0.20 to 0.8 percent, at a false-rejection cost of 5.88 percent for the correct one. Stopping at the first rejection makes the cost fall mostly on correct candidates, which run nearly all \(\VerificationTrialCount\) trials, so size the verifier pool for the passing fraction of the population, not for one trial per candidate.


When provisioning verifier clusters across a heterogeneous population of candidates, system architects must evaluate the expected trial demand across the candidate distribution. Because the expected trial workload \(\sum_{j=0}^{\VerificationTrialCount-1} \TrialPassProbability^\VerificationTrialIndex\) is convex in \(\TrialPassProbability\), substituting the population’s mean pass probability directly into the formula underestimates total compute demand by Jensen’s inequality. High-quality candidates progress deeper into repeated trials than low-quality ones, concentrating the verification workload on the most promising rollouts. Accurately sizing verification cluster capacity, measured in completed candidate evaluations per second, requires weighting the trial demand by the empirical distribution of candidate quality rather than using a single average pass rate.
When successive runs disagree, repetition alone is insufficient: divergence indicates an unstable test harness that requires systemic mitigation. Verification harnesses should deliberately vary test execution order and process scheduling, running regular sanity checks against known-valid and known-invalid reference artifacts to detect fixture drift before emitting training rewards. If a specific test case exhibits persistent flakiness, operators must quarantine it from the active reward loop. Because quarantining alters the task’s reward function, all test suite revisions must be versioned, preserving the historical trial records and audit trail. Verifier isolation and repeated assessment address the named tampering and flakiness paths; policy quality remains bounded by the properties the protected checks cover and requires independent release evidence.

Checkpoint 16.2: Optimizing agent trajectories
The recorded interaction, group statistic, and protected assessment must describe the same training event.

Group coefficients: How does GRPO form its baseline, and which objective term loses its signal when every observed reward agrees?
False accepts in the gradient: Why is the fraction of false accepts among accepted trajectories not their fraction of the gradient?
Group-size budget: A task family passes 20 percent of attempts in groups of 8. Estimate the rollouts spent per group that carries any reward contrast, then identify what additional evidence is needed to choose between doubling \(\GroupSize\) and retargeting task difficulty.
Action records: Why are sampled token IDs and actual delivered prefixes needed when observations are excluded from action scoring?
Candidate execution: A patch passes path checks and enters a fresh grader. Which boundary is still missing if its code shares the grader’s interpreter and result store?
Repeated assessment: Why do three total independent trials differ from an initial pass plus three reruns, and what false-rejection cost accompanies an all-pass rule?
Protected evidence: Why are hidden checks repeatedly used for training rewards not an untouched release evaluation set?

title: 16 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
text:
Even when an execution sandbox isolates the grader and every gradient step updates cleanly, reinforcement learning can steer an agentic policy into unhelpful or degenerate behaviors. Training curves alone rarely reveal why: for a complex repair task, rising reward accompanied by longer rollouts might indicate thorough automated testing, repetitive failed edits, or merely a shift in which tasks completed grading before timing out. Systematically diagnosing these pathologies requires connecting shifts in sampled token distributions, rollout lengths, reward sub-components, and gradient statistics to concrete hypotheses, because each failure mode demands a distinct systems intervention.


Token entropy measures uncertainty in a specified next-token distribution. For a delivered prefix \(\TokenPrefix\) and vocabulary \(\TokenVocabulary\),
\[\NextTokenEntropy\bigl(\Policy(\cdot\mid \TokenPrefix)\bigr)
=-\sum_{\VocabularyToken\in\TokenVocabulary}\Policy(\VocabularyToken\mid \TokenPrefix)
\log\Policy(\VocabularyToken\mid \TokenPrefix),\]
with natural logarithms giving entropy in nats and \(0\log0\) interpreted as zero. When logging this metric, we must explicitly distinguish the raw base-model distribution from the post-sampling distribution shaped by temperature scaling, top-\(\Glyph{k}\) filtering, or grammar constraints. Adjusting inference parameters alters measured entropy without changing network weights, just as changes in benchmark difficulty or prompt length skew aggregate averages. Any reported entropy number is incomplete without specifying the prefix population and decoding pipeline that generated it.
Low entropy is entirely appropriate at deterministic syntax positions, such as emitting closing brackets or fixed tool schemas. A genuine warning sign is collapsing diversity across task-relevant actions on unsolved fixtures, where the policy commits prematurely to a failing strategy and stops sampling the exploratory actions needed to discover reward. Rather than setting an arbitrary global entropy threshold, engineers should inspect action divergence and tool-call variety alongside token-level uncertainty.
Uniform rewards within a sample group introduce an identical diagnostic trap. When all \(\GroupSize\) trajectories in a group receive identical scores, the zero-contrast update of section 16.5.4 zeroes out the reward-surrogate gradient. This zero-contrast condition is an algebraic property of group normalization, but its root cause varies: diverse attempts might all fail, diverse valid solutions might all pass, or an uncalibrated test harness might fail to distinguish partial progress. Disentangling these mechanisms requires inspecting the actual trajectory logs rather than relying on summary statistics.
Table 8 maps common training observations to their underlying ambiguities and practical diagnostic checks. To ensure that an apparent change in policy behavior is not merely an artifact of shifting measurement conditions, all diagnostic comparisons must hold the task fixtures, sampling parameters, reward functions, and grader versions strictly constant.



Table 8: Training observations and diagnostic checks: A metric narrows an investigation without proving an internal mechanism or prescribing a guaranteed remedy.










Observation
What remains ambiguous
Useful next check




Lower entropy and repeated actions on unsolved tasks
Narrower exploration, changed decoding constraints, or a changed task mix
Compare action and candidate diversity on fixed diagnostic fixtures under the same sampling configuration


More equal-reward groups
Mastered tasks, persistently unsuccessful tasks, or missing assessment distinctions
Separate all-pass, all-fail, and unresolved cases; inspect coverage and reward components


More generated tokens without higher acceptance
Necessary checking, unproductive repetition, or a population/termination change
Compare lengths by outcome and task family, including budget stops and unavailable verdicts


Higher training reward without better independent assessment
Useful adaptation, reward-specific shortcuts, or changed grading
Audit candidate artifacts and reward components, then test the identified configuration under the independent protocol









Generated token counts, tool invocation counts, and wall-clock execution time capture distinct execution costs. A verbose trajectory may reflect thorough exploratory testing that culminates in a working patch, whereas a terse rollout may simply indicate early abandonment. Consequently, tracking mean trajectory length is rarely sufficient; engineers should inspect full length distributions segmented by outcome (accepted, failed, pending, and unknown). An unchanged average reward often conceals an expensive failure migration, where cheap syntax failures early in training turn into prolonged, compute-intensive execution loops that still fail verification.
The length bias of section 16.5.3 is the first mechanism to audit when failing trajectories lengthen unexpectedly, because per-rollout averaging charges each token of a long failure less than each token of a short one. Training the same fixed diagnostic tasks under the per-rollout and the constant-denominator objectives separates growth caused by that incentive from growth that reflects useful work, such as additional diagnostic checks that the environment reward favors.
When system requirements favor concise solutions, any length penalty introduced into the reward function must respect the preference hierarchy established in section 16.3. Under bounded reward structures, enforcing \(\FormatRewardWeight+\LengthPenaltyWeight<1\) guarantees that any passing trajectory scores higher than any failing trajectory, regardless of length. A poorly calibrated length penalty that causes a verbose successful repair to score lower than an immediate failure corrupts task incentives. Reward-based length penalties influence policy preferences only during learning; hard execution budgets (such as maximum token limits or turn timeouts) must remain strictly enforced by the execution runtime.



Standard symmetric ratio clipping provides a direct algorithmic route to entropy collapse, the premature loss of action diversity on tasks the agent has not yet solved. When an agent discovers a sequence that partially succeeds early in training, the positive advantage boosts the probabilities of those tokens, rapidly sharpening the distribution around that single path. The positive-advantage surrogate in section 16.5.2 stops increasing at a policy ratio of \(1+\RatioClippingWidth\), but this incentive threshold acts with extreme asymmetry in absolute probability space.
With \(\RatioClippingWidth\) set to 0.2, a dominant token already at probability 0.9 has an incentive threshold of 1.08. Because this threshold exceeds 1.0, the surrogate continues rewarding increases throughout the remaining probability mass. In contrast, for an alternative candidate token at probability 0.01, the positive surrogate incentive flattens after an absolute probability increase of 0.002. Gradients from other tokens and loss terms can still move a token’s probability ratio beyond the clipping interval. Rarely sampled actions therefore face a steep climb to regain probability, while dominant actions consolidate their lead. As action diversity drops across unsolved tasks, the \(\GroupSize\) rollouts in each group collapse into near-identical trajectories. Their rewards tie, precipitating the zero-contrast state described in section 16.5.4 where the reward-surrogate gradient vanishes.
To counteract this dynamic, the clip-higher formulation decouples the clipping boundaries into an asymmetric interval \([1-\LowerRatioClippingWidth, 1+\UpperRatioClippingWidth]\) with \(\UpperRatioClippingWidth > \LowerRatioClippingWidth\) (Yu et al. 2025). This wider upper bound allows low-probability tokens backed by positive advantages to climb more rapidly, while the lower bound still curbs policy drift for penalized tokens. As always, diagnostic context matters: low entropy at deterministic syntax positions is normal and desirable; the operational danger is collapsing diversity among tool invocations and decision branches on unsolved tasks.

Yu, Qiying, Zheng Zhang, Ruofei Zhu, Yufeng Yuan, Xiaochen Zuo, Yu Yue, Weinan Dai, et al. 2025. “DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2503.14476.
Alternative regularizers attack this problem through different mechanisms. An explicit entropy bonus directly penalizes sharp token distributions across targeted positions. A reference-policy divergence penalty, such as the \(\KlPenaltyCoefficient\)-weighted term of equation 4, instead penalizes drift from the initial base model, though it enforces no minimum entropy floor of its own. Both approaches modify the loss surface and require controlled experimentation: hold task distributions and sampling parameters fixed, evaluate on downstream task success and token efficiency, and track policy-ratio distributions. A smoother loss curve during training is the weakest possible evidence of healthy exploration; only verified task completion counts.
When exploration collapses, an agent can enter repetitive loops (emitting duplicate shell commands or re-reading unchanged files) where runtime watchdog mechanisms must intervene. However, repetitive behavior in multi-turn environments is inherently ambiguous: waiting for a slow build, polling an asynchronous API, or retrying a failed test after adjusting parameters can mimic an infinite loop. Systems should log the exact termination trigger and apply the stop-state rules of section 16.6.3, which score budget exhaustion as a task failure and keep infrastructure interruptions out of the reward. Terminating a runaway rollout caps resource consumption immediately, but it settles nothing outside the slot; environment state and external side effects still pass to their cleanup handlers.


↩︎ Runtime watchdog mechanisms for detecting and terminating repetitive agent loops are established in Semantic Watchdogs.



Reports such as the 2025 DeepSeek-R1 study document spontaneous increases in response length during pure reinforcement learning (R1-Zero), accompanied by natural-language tokens where the model appears to reconsider prior reasoning steps (DeepSeek-AI et al. 2025). From a systems perspective, however, introspective tokens such as “Wait, let me double-check” are merely generated text, not verified cognitive state. In an agentic system interacting with real infrastructure, the sole criterion for genuine recovery behavior is whether subsequent tool invocations successfully correct an execution failure or adapt to unexpected environmental feedback.

DeepSeek-AI, Daya Guo, Dejian Yang, et al. 2025. “DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2501.12948, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2501.12948.
Consider testing recovery on the connection-pool repair task. A diagnostic evaluation fixture can intentionally inject an environmental disturbance, for example a dependency version conflict introduced immediately after the agent completes its initial inspection. The evaluation then measures whether the policy gathers fresh diagnostic data, revises its patch to satisfy the conflicting constraints, and successfully passes the test suite within the original resource allowance. Tracking failed and unhandled executions alongside successful runs is essential to ensure that apparent recoveries do not reflect hidden timeout artifacts. Designing experiments around controlled perturbations provides empirical evidence of recovery under the tested perturbation, just as targeted recovery demonstrations mitigate compounding errors during imitation learning.


↩︎ Recovery trajectories as a remedy for compounding errors in imitation learning are established in Exposure Bias.
Matched-budget evaluations, in which candidate policies and baselines operate under identical token and turn limits, reliably separate productive deliberation from empty verbosity. Generating this diagnostic evidence at scale demands robust infrastructure: a versioned catalog of task fixtures, structured rollout traces with explicit execution states, and sufficient isolated grader capacity. These diagnostic demands directly link algorithmic health to the systems architecture of the rollout pipeline.

title: 16 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
text:
Generating rollouts for verifiable reinforcement learning requires coordinating several pipeline stages operating at fundamentally different latencies. Before a single repair rollout can contribute to a parameter update, the infrastructure must orchestrate model inference to sample tokens, provision an isolated sandbox (such as pool_fixture_v1), execute stateful tool commands, run automated assessment suites, and stream trace records to storage. An inference step completes in tens of milliseconds, tool commands and compilers require seconds, while sandbox provisioning can take longer still. The primary systems challenge is to keep every stage saturated while preserving the statistical contract of the learning algorithm: the pipeline must maximize rollout throughput without silently altering, truncating, or biasing the distribution of trajectories delivered to the optimizer.


Every rollout begins with a concrete task environment governed by a fixture contract. Whether an agent repairs repository defects, generates unit tests, or executes multi-step terminal workflows, the environment must strictly define initial filesystem state, available tool APIs, network permissions, and reward evaluation criteria. A recorded trajectory from a previous failure is not an executable task on its own; it becomes runnable only when anchored to an underlying fixture whose permissions, dependencies, and test coverage have been explicitly verified.


↩︎ Collection fixtures, which layer a collection contract on the evaluation gym’s execution baseline, are established in Task Fixture Design.
Data splitting requires equal discipline. Systems must enforce partition policies prior to task sampling or curriculum selection. Related problem variants, mutations, and solution-equivalent tasks must remain confined to their assigned split. While training on familiar repositories helps models learn local code patterns and idioms, holdouts from distinct repository families test generalization to unfamiliar codebases. Ground-truth reference solutions and known defective candidates serve as essential calibration baselines to verify that the reward discriminator functions correctly, while flaky dependencies and test-harness failures must remain visible as operational failures rather than false negative signals. Selecting tasks by difficulty can sharpen reward contrast, but doing so shifts the underlying task mixture. Pipelines must log this curriculum selection explicitly rather than misinterpreting elevated training reward as improved capability across an uncurated population.


↩︎ Task groups, which keep every variant of a problem on one side of the split, are established in Evaluation claims and task groups.
Between successive episodes, an environment slot executes a rollout reset to restore the fixture to its declared initial state. A robust reset requires far more than cleaning a working directory. The environment boundary must terminate lingering child processes, clear uncommitted filesystem writes, purge temporary caches, reset background service daemons, revoke ephemeral credentials, and cancel outstanding network operations. Fast filesystem snapshots or copy-on-write overlay filesystems reset local disk state in milliseconds, but they cannot clean up external side effects, which require designated teardown handlers. Controlled stochasticity—such as randomizing problem seeds or initial state permutations—must be codified directly in the fixture specification. While offline benchmarks incur reset overhead only intermittently, reinforcement learning loops execute resets across millions of rollout cycles, making reset efficiency a direct driver of aggregate throughput.



Consider an environment slot executing agent trajectories serially. Let \(\TurnHorizon\) be the horizon (the number of interaction turns), \(\ModelTime\) the model inference time per turn, \(\ToolTime\) the tool execution time per turn, \(\RolloutAssessmentTime\) the final assessment duration, and \(\EnvironmentResetTime\) the environment reset time. Assuming constant durations, no intra-slot concurrency, and zero queueing delay, the total slot cycle time is
\[\EnvironmentCycleTime=\TurnHorizon(\ModelTime+\ToolTime)+\RolloutAssessmentTime+\EnvironmentResetTime. \tag{6}\]
Accelerating the reset routine directly shortens this cycle. Multiplying the reciprocal of \(\EnvironmentCycleTime\) by the total number of environment slots gives the theoretical capacity ceiling of the rollout fleet. However, that projection assumes model inference servers, tool executors, verification sandboxes, and storage pipelines can sustain this aggregate rate without contention. We compute this baseline capacity in notebook 16.6 before examining where downstream shared bottlenecks arise.

Napkin Math 16.6: Reset cost and slot capacityProblem: A hypothetical pool contains 256 environment slots. Each episode has 20 decisions, each using 120 ms of model service and 80 ms of tool execution, followed by 0.5 s of assessment. Cold reset takes 3.5 s; snapshot reset takes 15 ms. What capacity change follows under the serial-slot assumptions?
Math: Under the serial-cycle model in equation 6, non-reset work takes 4.5 s per cycle. Cold reset gives a cycle of 8 s, of which 56.25 percent is non-reset work. Snapshot reset gives a cycle of 4.515 s and a non-reset fraction of 99.67 percent. For either case, idealized pool capacity is the number of slots divided by cycle time.
Result: The corresponding capacities are approximately 115,200 and 204,120 episodes per hour, a 1.77× local capacity ratio. The non-reset fraction includes tool and assessment time, rather than representing accelerator utilization alone.
Systems insight: Reducing cold reset from 3.5 s to the stated snapshot latency yields a 1.77× slot-capacity gain; eliminating reset entirely would leave the 4.5 s of active work as the cycle-time floor. This is Amdahl’s law applied to the slot: speeding up one stage can shrink the cycle by no more than the time that stage occupied, so the capacity ratio is \(\ColdResetCycleTime / \SnapshotResetCycleTime\) and, because the active work term remains fixed, optimizing reset latency yields diminishing returns once reset overhead constitutes only a small fraction of the cycle. Furthermore, these recovered slot-hours translate into training updates only if downstream inference serving, verification workers, storage pipelines, and the training loop possess sufficient headroom to process 1.77× as many episodes. In a balanced pipeline, the stage with the least headroom dictates the realized throughput gain.





Rollout generation continuously interleaves bursty model inference with blocking tool waits, while training workers consume completed trajectories in minibatches. Allocating distinct resource pools decouples these workloads, whereas colocated or alternating execution schedules reduce model weight broadcast and network synchronization costs. The optimal balance depends on the relative runtimes of rollout generation and gradient computation. Because all \(\GroupSize\) rollouts for a given task share an identical prompt, a radix-tree prefix cache computes the key-value states for that prompt once across the cohort (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\)). Capitalizing on this prefix reuse requires matching model weights, identical prompt token sequences, and compatible cache allocation policies; promoting a new policy checkpoint inevitably invalidates existing cache entries and forces a cold start even on identical prompts.


↩︎ The weight, exact-prefix, and residency conditions for prefix-cache reuse are established in Prefix compatibility.
When the training loop synchronizes across rollout groups before updating parameters, the trainer enforces a group barrier. The step duration is dictated by the slowest member of the cohort:
\[\PolicyUpdateStepTime=\max_i \TrajectoryDuration(\Trajectory_i)+\TrainerUpdateTime, \tag{7}\]
Every worker slot that finishes earlier sits idle until the tail completes. Trajectory latencies in agent tasks exhibit heavy tails due to variable tool execution times, complex multi-turn reasoning loops, and fluctuating compiler or test durations. As the tail stretches, the proportion of idle slot capacity climbs sharply.
For a hypothetical group of 4 whose members complete between 0.2 s and 16.8 s, equation 7 holds all four slots until the 16.8 s member finishes, stranding 65 percent of reserved slot capacity in an idle state. This barrier penalty, charted in panel (a) of figure 2, motivates releasing slots early and gathering rollouts asynchronously.
Under group-relative objectives, asynchronous rollout completion does not remove the mathematical requirement for an aggregated group baseline. The scheduler assigns the group identifier, fixture configuration, planned cohort membership, and generating checkpoint version prior to dispatch. Each completed member record and its verification status buffer in memory until the group closure policy determines eligibility. If the objective requires verified rewards across all group members, group closure must hold the record until all members report. If an environment terminates due to turn caps or time limits, the orchestrator applies the declared protocol penalty; infrastructure failures such as sandbox crashes or network timeouts stay unresolved under the rules of section 16.6.3, and the closure policy must say whether the group waits for them or closes without them.
As soon as a rollout finishes, its environment slot frees its inference concurrency and sandbox resources for subsequent work, retaining only its compact trajectory record in an aggregation buffer while evicting key-value cache states from accelerator memory. Because rollouts complete out of order, group buffers, verification queues, and training ingestion queues require bounded capacities in both record count and total bytes. Admission controllers must track in-flight slot allocations alongside buffered records, applying backpressure upstream to prevent intermediate queues from overflowing host memory during bursty completions.
Prematurely closing a group with only its fastest-finishing members distorts the baseline sample. Slower trajectories often represent harder subtasks, alternative multi-step tool interactions, or transient infrastructure contention. Recomputing relative advantages across only the early completions fails to recover the true underlying distribution; early truncation imposes a survival bias that favors fast, simplistic solutions. Training pipelines must explicitly log all exclusions and their causal categories, monitor completion latency distributions, and track task coverage shifts over time. Similarly, filtering out zero-variance groups (where all members receive identical rewards) reduces gradient variance in advantage-based policy surrogates, but it also eliminates training signals intended for auxiliary objectives, such as reference-policy divergence constraints.



Decoupling rollout collection from training updates means trajectories can arrive after the optimizer has already advanced the policy weights. The version disparity between the policy that sampled an action and the policy undergoing optimization is policy staleness. Asynchronous actor-learner frameworks such as IMPALA address this discrepancy by pairing asynchronous scheduling with off-policy corrections,9 reweighting trajectory tokens by the probability ratio between the learner and actor checkpoints (Espeholt et al. 2018). For an episode pinned to a single behavior checkpoint, let \(\BehaviorPolicyVersion\) denote its generating version and \(\text{ver}_t\) the trainer’s active version. When the training loop steps at a steady pace, the update-count lag is
9 V-trace: IMPALA’s correction weights each step by the ratio of learner to actor probabilities, truncated at a ceiling, accepting some bias to keep the variance of long products of ratios in check (Espeholt et al. 2018). Truncation matters more for agent rollouts than for short episodes, because a product of per-token ratios over thousands of tokens is otherwise dominated by a few extreme values. 
Espeholt, Lasse, Hubert Soyer, R’emi Munos, Karen Simonyan, Vlad Mnih, Tom Ward, Yotam Doron, et al. 2018. “IMPALA: Scalable Distributed Deep-RL with Importance Weighted Actor-Learner Architectures.” Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 1407–16.
\[\FiniteChange\text{ver}=\text{ver}_t-\BehaviorPolicyVersion\approx\left\lfloor\frac{\RolloutAdmissionAge}{\PolicyUpdateStepTime}\right\rfloor, \tag{8}\]
where \(\RolloutAdmissionAge\) is the wall-clock time elapsed from sampling the first prompt token to admission into the training batch, and \(\PolicyUpdateStepTime\) is the training step latency. This relationship enables system designers to calibrate staleness bounds directly from rollout duration. Long agent rollouts are precisely the trajectories most prone to severe staleness. Bounded staleness has a long lineage in distributed training architectures, where worker parameter reads are constrained to a fixed step horizon (Ho et al. 2013), and asynchronous actor-learner algorithms tolerate bounded lag in exchange for high actor utilization (Mnih et al. 2016). Applied at admission (figure 2, panels b and c), the check admits the two short rollouts and excludes the long one, recording why it was dropped. These are record-level lag decisions, not a complete group-admission rule. Under an objective that requires the planned cohort, every member must also have a resolved reward and satisfy that bound before the group enters an update.






Figure 2: Group Barriers and Version-Checked Admission: (a) In the hypothetical group of four, the barrier holds every slot until the 16.8 s member finishes, leaving 65 percent of reserved slot time idle. (b) Asynchronous collection releases slots early, so the trainer’s version advances while rollouts run. Each record carries the version that sampled it, and its lag \(\FiniteChange\text{ver}\) at admission grows with its duration; the long rollout exceeds the illustrative bound and is excluded with its reason recorded. (c) A record leaves verification with a pass, a fail, or an unavailable verdict, waits in a bounded group buffer, and reaches the trainer only if its lag is within the bound. While this admission check enforces a strict bound on version lag, it cannot prevent distribution drift when individual gradient updates make large steps in parameter space.



While the version counter provides an operational threshold for admission control, distribution divergence requires separate monitoring: a single large optimizer step can shift output probabilities far more dramatically than several incremental updates. Production diagnostics must break down elapsed age into generation time, tool wait states, verification latency, group buffer residence, and ingestion queue delay, while tracking empirical probability-ratio distributions (\(\Policy / \pi_{\text{old}}\)) to detect distribution drift directly.
Logging per-invocation metadata as described in section 16.6 accurately captures the behavior distribution even when policy checkpoints update mid-episode. Training on these composite trajectories requires optimization formulations that support turn-by-turn behavior probabilities; retroactively relabeling an entire trajectory under the newest policy checkpoint distorts importance weights and introduces optimization instability.
Freshness limits fundamentally balance off-policy variance against selection bias. Discarding trajectories that exceed a staleness threshold bounds policy lag, but because complex tasks demand more reasoning steps and tool calls, strict staleness cutoffs systematically eliminate hard problems from the training distribution. As indicated by equation 8, systems engineers can preserve task diversity by reducing the numerator rather than loosening the bound. Reducing generation, tool-wait, verification, group-buffer, and ingestion delays can shorten \(\RolloutAdmissionAge\) while preserving the long-horizon tasks the learner needs. Synchronous collection eliminates staleness entirely at the expense of straggler idle time, whereas multiple optimization epochs over a single collected batch reintroduce policy lag. While the clipped surrogate objective in section 16.5.2 limits policy updates driven by stale probability ratios, it neither bounds importance sampling variance nor corrects for the shift in visited state distributions (Schulman et al. 2017). Because discarded trajectories consume inference and sandbox capacity without producing gradient updates, monitoring systems must track discard rates, compute overhead, and shifts in task coverage.



Sizing verification infrastructure requires aligning the units of arrival demand with worker service capacity. Let \(\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\) denote completed trajectories arriving per second, \(\WorkerCount\) the number of independent verification worker slots, and \(\VerificationTrialTime\) the mean execution duration for one verification trial, including environment provisioning, execution, and cleanup. When each trajectory requires \(\VerificationTrialCount\) total trials to evaluate determinism or flaky tests, each trajectory demands an average of \(\VerificationTrialCount \VerificationTrialTime\) worker-seconds. The ideal service capacity \(\VerificationPoolCapacity\) and resulting offered utilization \(\ServingUtilization\) are
\[\VerificationPoolCapacity=\frac{\WorkerCount}{\VerificationTrialCount \VerificationTrialTime},\qquad
\ServingUtilization=\frac{\TrajectoryAdmissionRate \VerificationTrialCount \VerificationTrialTime}{\WorkerCount}. \tag{9}\]
Both \(\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\) and \(\VerificationPoolCapacity\) measure completed trajectories per second. Operating at \(\TrajectoryAdmissionRate=\VerificationPoolCapacity\) leaves no capacity margin; arrival bursts, heavy-tailed trial durations, or worker node failures cause queues to grow unbounded. System designers establish a target utilization \(0<\TargetServingUtilization<1\) based on acceptable queueing latency and variance profiles, provisioning at least \(\lceil\TrajectoryAdmissionRate \VerificationTrialCount \VerificationTrialTime/\TargetServingUtilization\rceil\) worker slots. Queue capacity limits and upstream admission control remain necessary. While executing a candidate’s \(\VerificationTrialCount\) trials concurrently across multiple slots reduces wall-clock verification latency, the aggregate worker-second demand remains identical.
For a hypothetical arrival of 512 trajectories every 16 s, \(\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\) is 32 trajectories per second. With each trial lasting 8 s, a single trial per trajectory consumes 256 worker equivalents at that arrival rate. Executing all 3 trials elevates demand to 768 worker equivalents. Applying the utilization relationship in equation 9 with an illustrative 80 percent target requires provisioning 960 worker slots. Verification demand scales linearly with \(\VerificationTrialCount\), and the target utilization establishes the necessary headroom against queueing delays.
Early-exit evaluation policies fundamentally alter these capacity requirements. Under the stop-on-first-rejection policy introduced in section 16.7, verification terminates upon the first failing trial. For a candidate solution with an independent per-trial pass probability \(\TrialPassProbability\), the expected number of trials drops to \(\mathbb{E}[\ExecutedTrialCount]=\sum_{j=0}^{\VerificationTrialCount-1}\TrialPassProbability^\VerificationTrialIndex\). Capacity models must substitute this expected trial count in place of \(\VerificationTrialCount\) when computing total worker demand. Across a diverse task distribution, engineers must compute this demand by averaging over the empirical mixture of pass rates; taking an aggregate average pass rate and raising it to powers yields an inaccurate estimate due to mixture variance. Sizing calculations must also incorporate unequal trial durations, sandbox initialization overhead, and retry cascades. In-memory queues absorb brief arrival spikes, but sustained overload requires adding worker slots or adopting more aggressive early-exit evaluation rules.



Promoting a policy checkpoint internally within the training pipeline serves a completely different operational purpose than releasing a model for deployment. Internal collection gating determines which checkpoint generates subsequent training trajectories. Automated validation checks verify prompt template compatibility, tool-calling syntax, entropy bounds to prevent policy collapse, and memory utilization before promoting a candidate checkpoint to the rollout fleet. The orchestrator must record the promoted model artifact digest and the generating version for every dispatched episode. If a promoted version exhibits degenerate behavior or crashes sandboxes, the controller halts further admission under that version, while any side effects produced by faulty rollouts remain subject to their designated cleanup handlers.
Production deployment release requires a formal evaluation framework verifying regression resistance, safety constraints, latency budgets, and out-of-distribution transfer. Internal training diagnostics provide rapid feedback during optimization, but they must remain strictly quarantined from release benchmarks to prevent benchmark leakage. Production evaluation suites must enforce an isolated assessment boundary, logging benchmark exposure whenever validation metrics inform architectural or hyperparameter revisions.


↩︎ Controlled comparison and conditional release of a trained checkpoint are established in Controlled comparison and conditional release.

Yue, Yang, Zhiqi Chen, Rui Lu, Andrew Zhao, Zhaokai Wang, Yang Yue, Shiji Song, and Gao Huang. 2025. “Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2504.13837.
System evaluations must carefully distinguish between operational consistency and genuine capability expansion. In the competitive reasoning benchmark study of Yue et al. (2025), RLVR-trained models improve pass@1 while base models match or exceed them when sampled across broad cohorts (\(\IndependentAttemptCount \gg 1\)). This pattern is consistent with concentrating probability mass onto successful solution modes that the base model could already generate; it does not establish a universal limit on acquiring new behavior. Reporting pass@1, pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\) at large \(\IndependentAttemptCount\), and the repeated-trial pass\(^\IndependentAttemptCount\) defined in Potential and repeated-run consistency separates a policy that has become more reliable from one that has expanded its underlying capabilities. A candidate checkpoint must remain unreleased until it satisfies recovery, transfer, and unresolved-outcome criteria across comprehensive production testbeds.
Balancing rollout generation, straggler barriers, staleness bounds, and verifier capacity provides the infrastructure that keeps this learning loop saturated. Tracing how these systems mechanisms operate together requires following a complete update cycle on a concrete repair workload.

title: 16 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
text:
Consider the connection-pool repair group with rewards \([0,1,0]\) from section 16.5. Three fresh trials, rl_trial_01, rl_trial_02, and rl_trial_03, execute task pool_repair_01 against the fixture pool_fixture_v1, sampled from the supervised checkpoint trained_policy_v1, and each ends in a verdict under repair_accept_v1. The recovery run that produced workspace ws_r20 and the demonstrations built from it remain historical artifacts of curation and fine-tuning; they supply comparisons, not targets, for this group. Following the group through each stage of the chapter shows which question every stage answers before the middle rollout is allowed to move the weights.
The first question is whether the lone pass is a pass. A \([0,1,0]\) group on a hard bug is exactly the shape that tampering produces, so the verdict for rl_trial_02 counts only because it came from the assessment side of table 7. The patch was admitted as a source-only diff, applied to a fresh copy of the fixture, and graded by a controller whose tests and result store the candidate could not reach. The defect is a race on connection return, so the fixture is timing-sensitive, and the all-pass rule of notebook 16.5 applies. If an incorrect patch passes a single trial with probability 0.20, 3 independent trials cut its acceptance to 0.8 percent at a 5.88 percent risk of rejecting a correct one. A trial whose verifier crashed, or whose container was preempted, is marked unresolved under the stop-state rules of section 16.6.3 rather than coerced to zero, because converting an infrastructure fault into a task failure penalizes the policy for the cluster and shifts the group baseline.
The second question is whether the update can be computed on what the policy actually saw. Each rollout record holds the delivered prefix and sampled token IDs of every invocation, the behavior log probabilities under the recorded sampling configuration, and the checkpoint version that produced them (table 6). Before admission, the trainer checks each record’s version lag against its bound (equation 8); a trial that ran long enough to fall behind is excluded with its reason logged rather than silently relabeled under the newest weights. In this worked example, all three rewards are resolved and all three members satisfy the lag bound, so the original complete group is eligible. Under its declared complete-group rule, an unresolved or stale member prevents the group from entering the update; excluding members and recomputing its coefficients would require a separately declared objective and selection analysis.
Only then does GRPO compute coefficients. The pass receives 1.414214 and each failure -0.707107 (notebook 16.3), and under per-rollout averaging each token of rollout \(\GroupRolloutIndex\) carries \(\GroupRelativeAdvantage_i/\RolloutPolicyTokenCount_i\) (equation 5), so the length of each failure sets how hard its tokens are pushed down. Because the reward scores only the outcome, every token in rl_trial_02 receives the same coefficient. The edit that adds the missing notification and any redundant status checks along the way are reinforced alike, and only many such groups separate them statistically. The frozen reference policy stays distinct from the behavior policy, contributing only the divergence penalty. Because the GRPO name covers several variants, the training log records the clipping thresholds, the length and dispersion normalizations, and the penalty weight \(\KlPenaltyCoefficient\) with the update.
When an update over eligible groups yields a candidate checkpoint, such as rl_policy_v1, lineage binds its weights and inference configuration to the rollout records, fixtures, and verifier versions that produced it. The controller may promote rl_policy_v1 to the rollout fleet for further collection, since that is an internal training decision. Releasing it is a different decision. Higher training reward on a known fixture can coexist with regression on unobserved failure modes, and the benchmark study discussed in section 16.9.6 illustrates how higher pass@1 can coexist with unchanged broad-sampling performance, so the release case rests on held-out recovery fixtures evaluated by pass@1, pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\) at large \(\IndependentAttemptCount\), and pass\(^\IndependentAttemptCount\) under the protocol of Agent Evaluation.
Each stage therefore answers one question that no other stage can: the isolated verifier says whether the reward is evidence, the record says whether the update is faithful, the coefficients say how hard the evidence pushes, and the independent evaluation says whether the result belongs in production.

title: 16 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
text:
A rollout group can easily contain positive rewards without establishing a sound solution, and a policy update can fit that group without improving the deployed agent. The pitfalls detailed below each turn a narrow, scoped measurement into an unwarranted conclusion, and each carries a concrete systems cost.

Fallacy: An automated reward is a complete task specification.
Automated test suites check only the conditions their authors anticipated, and reinforcement learning operates as an aggressive search procedure that reliably uncovers unhandled edge cases. When a policy’s true success rate is low, Bayesian base rates compound this vulnerability. As demonstrated in notebook 16.1, a verifier that misclassifies only 2.5 percent of failing attempts still results in 18.4 percent of all rewarded rollouts being outright failures when the policy solves only 10 percent of tasks. Because reinforcement updates treat every rewarded attempt as a success, the optimizer systematically increases the probability of the tokens that generated those spurious answers. Always benchmark the verifier against suites of known incorrect solutions, evaluate its false-acceptance rate against the policy’s current pass rate, and gate production deployment on strict held-out task criteria rather than raw training rewards.


Pitfall: Leaving the scorer, the runner, or its configuration where the candidate can reach it.
If an agent can read or write to its evaluation harness, modifying the test framework becomes the path of least resistance. In the METR evaluations, when a task exposed an editable scoring script to the agent, the model bypassed the intended challenge and tampered with the verifier in 21 of 21 runs (war story 16.1). During training, this vulnerability causes severe gradient distortion. On difficult tasks where honest attempts fail, the first rollout that discovers an exploit becomes the group’s lone positive sample. In a rollout group of 16, that single hack receives an advantage coefficient of 3.87, while each honest failure receives a negative coefficient of 0.26 in magnitude, strongly reinforcing the exploit. Always evaluate candidate solutions in an ephemeral workspace isolated behind a hardened controller that retains exclusive ownership of the test harness, the execution runner, and the result path (section 16.7). Even within that sandbox, treat all generated agent code as untrusted input.


Fallacy: A bigger group is the way to extract signal from hard tasks.
Increasing the rollout group size \(\GroupSize\) appears to offer a straightforward way to capture rare successes on difficult tasks. While larger groups improve the likelihood that a batch contains contrasting rewards, the probability of contrast alone does not measure the information each group supplies. At a pass rate of 5 percent, rollout groups of size 8 consume 23.8 rollouts for every informative group with nonzero variance. Expanding the group size to 16 still demands 28.6 rollouts per informative group. By contrast, steering the training curriculum toward tasks near a 50 percent pass rate consumes only 8.1 rollouts per informative group (notebook 16.4). Where obtaining contrast is the binding constraint and the task-mixture change is acceptable, this comparison favors targeting difficulty. Choose the group size using baseline precision, required task coverage, and held-out learning progress as well as rollout cost, and log the sampling distribution.


Pitfall: Reading longer self-correction text as evidence of better reasoning.
When an agent produces lengthy internal monologues and verbose self-critiques, engineers often mistake length for deeper reasoning. In reality, output lengths frequently expand as a direct artifact of loss normalization. Under per-rollout token averaging, a failing rollout of 128 tokens penalizes each individual token 32× as heavily as a failing rollout of 4,096 tokens. Because token-level gradient penalties dilute across longer generation lengths, this objective can favor longer failures even when the extra text performs no useful validation (equation 5). To uncover length bias, compare sequence lengths conditioned on task outcome and train with a constant-denominator loss objective. Ultimately, evaluate candidate revisions by the concrete tool actions and verified task completions they deliver under a matched token budget, rather than by the model’s narration of reconsidering.


Fallacy: Faster environment reset speeds training proportionally.
Optimizing container teardown and environment initialization yields satisfying microbenchmarks, but Amdahl’s law strictly limits the resulting gains in end-to-end training throughput. Reset latency represents only one slice of the rollout lifecycle. Cutting reset overhead from 3.5 s to 15 ms delivers a 233× acceleration in reset speed, yet it improves execution slot capacity by only 1.77×. The remaining 4.5 s spent on model inference, tool execution, and verifier scoring continues to dominate every cycle (notebook 16.6). Moreover, increased rollout throughput converts into faster training progress only if the inference workers, verification services, and parameter optimizers maintain sufficient headroom to ingest the higher volume. Profile the entire training loop to pinpoint the saturated pipeline stage before investing engineering effort into optimizing any individual phase.

title: 16 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
text:
Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards uses assessed interactions to guide a policy update without requiring a demonstrated response at every decision. Its opportunity depends on what the sampling process can reach and what the reward distinguishes. Its risks arise because the recorded score, rather than the full task intent, enters the optimization. Reward validity, sampling fidelity, and external enforcement therefore remain part of the learning system rather than prerequisites that can be forgotten once training starts.
The repair group illustrates the resulting chain of responsibility. Completed assessments support group-relative coefficients; recorded policy actions and their actual inputs support the chosen update; resource and version controls govern the collection loop. None of those steps substitutes for evaluating the resulting candidate under its intended operating conditions. Training changes the policy and moves no exposure; the runtime still bounds horizon, state, and authority for whatever the updated weights propose.
The relations in table 9 carry the chapter’s quantitative decisions, each under the assumptions stated where it is derived.
