Gray, Jim, and Andreas Reuter. 1992. Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques. Morgan Kaufmann.
The economics of budget enforcement and resource consumption descend from transaction processing and utility computing. High-concurrency database systems facing contention on hot account balances introduced escrow transactions to allocate fractional quantities without exclusive record locks (O’Neil 1986), establishing an early paradigm for concurrent budget reservations within the rigorous framework of atomic, durable, and recoverable updates (Gray and Reuter 1992). When compute resources transitioned to on-demand utility pricing, the trade-off between renting vs. owning infrastructure turned on workload variability, average capacity utilization, and which party absorbs provisioning risk (Armbrust et al. 2010). As distributed systems expanded across warehouse-scale infrastructure, Dean and Barroso demonstrated that tail latency across parallel RPCs quickly dominates overall response times (Dean and Barroso 2013), the parallel counterpart of how a multi-step agent trajectory compounds tool and service variability in series.
Machine learning contributed its own lineage of allocating computation adaptively based on instance difficulty. Viola and Jones demonstrated that a cascade of boosted classifiers could deliver real-time visual detection by rejecting straightforward negative examples in early stages (Viola and Jones 2001). That design pattern reemerged for foundation models in the form of cost-aware cascades and learned routers that dispatch queries across heterogeneous model endpoints (L. Chen et al. 2023; Ong et al. 2024). Similarly, speculative execution evolved from blockwise parallel decoding (Stern et al. 2018) into speculative decoding frameworks that pair small draft models with full target-model verification (Leviathan et al. 2023; C. Chen et al. 2023). In agentic workflows, repeated sampling strategies showed that additional generation attempts reliably expand solution coverage whenever verifiers can recognize task success (Brown et al. 2024). These results highlighted a critical requirement for evaluating production agents: benchmark assessments must report task accuracy alongside cumulative expenditure, establishing cost per accepted task as the central engineering metric (Kapoor et al. 2024).

Chen, Lingjiao, Matei Zaharia, and James Zou. 2023. “FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2305.05176.

Ong, Isaac, Amjad Almahairi, Vincent Wu, Wei-Lin Chiang, Tianhao Wu, Joseph E. Gonzalez, M. Waleed Kadous, and Ion Stoica. 2024. “RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2406.18665.

Leviathan, Yaniv, Matan Kalman, and Yossi Matias. 2023. “Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding.” Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning 202: 19274–86.

Further reading.

The Single Server Queue in Heavy Traffic (Kingman 1961). Three pages demonstrating why waiting time, rather than reduced throughput, is the steep price of operating near full capacity.
The Escrow Transactional Method (O’Neil 1986). The database foundation for budget reservations, showing how concurrent transactions can safely allocate portions of a shared balance without global record locking.
A View of Cloud Computing (Armbrust et al. 2010). The definitive analysis of workload variability, capacity utilization, and risk transfer underlying rent vs. own decisions in utility computing.
Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems (Harchol-Balter 2013). A comprehensive guide to queueing theory in computer systems, covering multi-server architectures, heavy-tailed service distributions, and priority scheduling policies beyond basic single-server approximations.
The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso 2013). An essential analysis of why distributed services must optimize against high-percentile latency rather than mean response times when requests fan out across multiple components.
AI Agents That Matter (Kapoor et al. 2024). The empirical blueprint for reporting agent accuracy and operational expense side by side, establishing the evaluation counterpart to cost per accepted task.

Every given below is a hypothetical problem input rather than a price, rate, or measurement of a real system. Each problem ends in a decision, and the calculation exists to justify it.

A cheaper configuration and a moving denominator (Basic). A repair cohort of \(\InitiatedTasks=200\) tickets runs one bounded attempt per ticket under a fixed contract. Configuration A accepts \(120\) tickets; its accepted tasks cost \(\AcceptedTaskMeanCost=\$1.20\) on average and its nonaccepted tasks \(\UnacceptedTaskMeanCost=\$1.80\), since they run to the turn cap. For configuration B under the same contract, accepted tickets cost \(30\) percent less than A’s accepted-ticket mean, and rejected tickets cost \(30\) percent less than A’s nonaccepted-ticket mean.

Compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) for A from the cohort total and again from \(\AcceptedTaskMeanCost+\frac{1-\AcceptanceFraction}{\AcceptanceFraction}\UnacceptedTaskMeanCost\), and state how many nonaccepted tasks each accepted repair carries.
Find the smallest number of accepted tickets at which B costs no more per accepted task than A.
At the reporting cutoff B has \(85\) accepted, \(105\) rejected, and \(10\) pending tickets, with the accepted and rejected groups having B’s stated conditional means. Each of the ten identified pending tickets has final charges of \(\$1.26\), which are not repriced when its verdict arrives. All invoices, cleanup, and other costs are final; only acceptance verdicts remain pending. Compute the range of B’s provisional \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) over the possible verdicts, and decide what the report may claim about B against A before the pending assessments complete. If a pending operation can still incur charges, what liability evidence is needed before this range bounds the final account?

When compaction pays (Basic). A repair trajectory holds \(\SequenceLength=40{,}000\) input tokens at a decision point. Compaction would reduce it to \(\CompactedContextLength=8{,}000\) tokens with a summary call that emits \(\SummaryOutputLength=2{,}000\) tokens, and the first compacted call misses the cache completely. The tariff charges \(\InputTokenPrice=\$3\), \(\CachedInputTokenPrice=\$0.30\), and \(\OutputTokenPrice=\$15\) per million tokens.

Compute the upfront increment \(\CompactionUpfrontCost\), the per-call saving \(\CompactionPerCallSaving\), and the payback horizon \(\CompactionPaybackCallCount\).
Five ordinary calls remain, including the first compacted one. Compute the price difference between compacting and keeping the context, and decide whether to compact on price alone.
The provider halves the cached rate to \(\$0.15\) per million. Recompute \(\CompactionPaybackCallCount\) and decide whether compaction pays with ten calls remaining. Explain why a cheaper cache pushes the profitable compaction point earlier in a trajectory, and name two reasons other than price that could still justify compacting.

How many turns before a person takes over (Basic). A repair loop costs \(\UniformLoopTurnCost=\$0.50\) per reached turn, including assessment and sandbox holding, and stops at the first accepted candidate. Its conditional acceptance probabilities for turns one through five are \(0.50\), \(0.30\), \(0.20\), \(0.10\), and \(0.01\). Every ticket the loop leaves unaccepted goes to an engineer who always resolves it for \(\HumanFallbackCost=\$30\).

Using equation 7, tabulate \(\LoopAcceptanceProbability(\TrajectoryTurnLimit)\), the expected number of turns, and the automated spend per ticket for \(\TrajectoryTurnLimit=1\) through \(5\).
Compute the combined spend per resolved ticket for each \(\TrajectoryTurnLimit\) and choose the cap. Confirm from the table that the chosen cap is the last turn satisfying the marginal rule \(\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_t\HumanFallbackCost>\UniformLoopTurnCost\) of section 18.8, and explain why that rule holds only while the engineer resolves every ticket the loop leaves.
A triage queue replaces the engineer and resolves every rejected ticket for \(\HumanFallbackCost=\$2\). Choose the cap again. Explain why ranking the caps by automated spend per automated acceptance would have chosen wrongly in both cases.

Retry, a stronger model, or a router (Intermediate). A cheap configuration costs \(\MeanAttemptCost=\$0.20\) per assessed attempt and may retry sequentially up to \(\IndependentAttemptCount=4\) times. Half the incoming tasks are easy, which the cheap configuration accepts with \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.8\) per attempt; the other half are hard, with \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.1\). A stronger configuration costs \(\$0.90\) per attempt, is run once, and accepts easy tasks with probability \(0.95\) and hard tasks with \(0.55\). Attempts are conditionally independent given the task.

A planner averages the cheap configuration’s rates to \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.45\). Compute the coverage and cost per accepted task this predicts for sequential retry.
Compute the actual coverage, expected attempts per task, and cost per accepted task for sequential retry over the mixed population, and compare it with running the stronger configuration on every task.
A direct router can identify each task’s class before generation. Price the policy that retries easy tasks on the cheap configuration and sends hard tasks to the stronger one. Decide among the three policies when the declared objective is minimum cost per accepted task subject to at least \(75\) percent coverage, and state what evidence the router’s class labels require before the comparison holds.

Recomputing the critical path (Intermediate). A repair episode has these dependencies and fixed durations. Sandbox creation (\(20\) s) precedes a planning call (\(12\) s). Two branches then run concurrently and must both finish before the test suite: a dependency build (\(60\) s), and static analysis (\(25\) s) followed by a model review of its findings (\(15\) s). The test suite (\(120\) s) is followed by a summary call (\(8\) s) and snapshot export (\(10\) s). For the speculation comparisons in parts (b) and (d), all stated model-call intervals consist entirely of decode with negligible prefill or queueing overhead; every other duration stays fixed.

Compute \(\CriticalPathDuration\) with equation 2, identify the critical path, and compute the model share \(\ModelTimeFraction\) on that path.
A speculative decoder drafts \(\DraftTokenCount=4\) tokens per round at \(\DraftTokenCostRatio=0.1\) of a target step and accepts \(\MeanAcceptedDraftLength=2.2\) tokens per round. Compute \(\SpeculativeDecodingSpeedup\) and its break-even \(\MeanAcceptedDraftLength\), apply the speedup to the model-call intervals under the stated approximation, and compute the new episode time.
A build cache instead cuts the build to \(10\) s. Compute the time saved and explain why it is not \(50\) s.
With the build cache in place, the suite is split into two concurrent shards of \(60\) s plus \(5\) s to merge results. Compute the episode time, then the time with speculation added. Rank the three interventions by elapsed time saved, and name the cost that sharding adds to the account.

A cascade under a deadline (Intermediate). Small repair tasks may run a two-tier cascade. Tier 1 costs \(\CascadeTierCost_1=\$0.05\) and \(\CascadeTierDuration_1=3\) s and accepts \(\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_1=0.50\) of tasks; tier 2 costs \(\CascadeTierCost_2=\$0.60\) and \(\CascadeTierDuration_2=12\) s and accepts \(\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_2=0.80\) of the tasks that reach it. Each gate costs \(\CascadeGateCost=\$0.02\) and takes \(\CascadeGateDuration=30\) s. Direct frontier execution costs \(\$0.62\) with its gate, takes \(42\) s, and accepts \(0.82\) of the full cohort.

Compute the cascade’s expected cost per initiated task, acceptance probability, cost per accepted task, and mean duration, and compare each with direct execution.
A team proposes replacing tier 1’s gate with a lint check costing \(\$0.005\) that exits the same share of tasks, but a fraction \(\LintFalseAcceptFraction\) of those exits violate the independently assessed criterion, each costing \(\$4\) to find and repair. Find the \(\LintFalseAcceptFraction\) at which the harm term erases the gate saving, and evaluate the proposal at a measured \(\LintFalseAcceptFraction=0.04\).
The service now requires \(90\) percent of tasks to finish within \(60\) s. Show that the cascade fails. A router sends \(45\) percent of tasks directly to the frontier tier, where they are accepted with probability \(0.70\); tier 1 accepts \(0.85\) of the rest, and tier 2 accepts \(0.80\) of what it receives. Check the deadline, and compute the routed policy’s cost per accepted task against both alternatives.

The support agent’s binding constraint (Intermediate, second-lighthouse transfer). Apply the chapter’s capacity model to the support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)). The service must deliver trajectory goodput \(\TrajectoryGoodput=30\) accepted sessions per minute at acceptance fraction \(\AcceptanceFraction=0.75\). An admitted session stays present for \(4\) minutes on average, including customer think time, and makes \(5\) serial model calls. Plan the model endpoint as the single-server queue of equation 5 with \(\mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime]=0.25\) s, \(\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2=2\), and \(\ServiceTimeVariationCoefficient^2=1\). The response target is a mean of at most \(1.0\) s of wait plus service per call. Each attempt costs \(\$0.30\) in total.

Compute \(\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\), the mean session concurrency, the call arrival rate \(\ArrivalRate\), \(\ServingUtilization\), and the mean response per call. Decide whether the target is met.
Find the largest \(\ServingUtilization\) that meets the target, and the goodput it permits at \(\AcceptanceFraction=0.75\).
Evaluate three levers: smoothing admissions to \(\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2=1\); smoothing plus raising acceptance to \(\AcceptanceFraction=0.85\); and a second, independent endpoint that takes half the sessions with unchanged variability. State which meet the target, and what happens to \(\ServingUtilization\) if acceptance instead falls to \(\AcceptanceFraction=0.60\) at the same goodput.
Compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) and the probability that a session meets at least one per-call tail delay when each call exceeds its 99th percentile independently with probability \(0.01\), and compare with a \(30\)-call repair trajectory. Explain why this workload’s binding constraint differs from the repair agent’s, and why a design that meets a mean target can still miss a percentile target.

Renting or owning capacity for research fan-out (Advanced, critique and redesign). The research agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}\)) reads \(20\) input tokens per output token, and only \(30\) percent of its input is billed at the cached rate because its sources vary. The API charges \(\$3\) per million uncached input tokens, \(\$0.30\) per million cached input tokens, and \(\$15\) per million output tokens. A matched dedicated deployment costs \(\DedicatedHourlyFixedCost=\$40\) per hour plus \(\DedicatedVariableTokenCost=\$4\) per million output tokens, with a feasible reference output rate \(\FeasibleOutputTokenRate=800\) tokens per second at the latency target. The workload runs at \(\DeliveredCapacityFraction=0.6\) for \(8\) hours a day and is idle otherwise.

Compute \(\EffectiveApiOutputTokenPrice\) per output token including its associated input, and \(\BreakEvenUtilization\) from equation 6.
A colleague argues that because the busy-hour load exceeds \(\BreakEvenUtilization\), the team should commit to dedicated capacity around the clock. Compute the daily cost of the API and of that commitment, and critique the argument.
Redesign the commitment so that owning capacity pays, and compute its daily cost and saving.
Reordering sources to keep a stable prefix raises the cached share to \(80\) percent. Recompute \(\EffectiveApiOutputTokenPrice\), \(\BreakEvenUtilization\), and the saving from part (c). Decide which change the team should make first, and name two conditions the comparison must hold fixed for either conclusion to stand.

A remediation budget under concurrency and cancellation (Advanced, redesign). A remediation task (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) has \(\CostCeiling=\$30\), of which \(\$4\) of diagnosis has settled. Two children, log analysis and canary replay, each request a \(\$15\) allocation at the same moment.

The coordinator reads the free balance, checks it against each request, and then records both reservations. Compute the overcommitment, and state the ledger transition that prevents it and the largest allocation the second child can receive.
After the fix, log analysis receives \(\$15\) and canary replay \(\$11\). Log analysis closes with \(\$9\) settled. An operator then cancels canary replay when it has \(\$3\) settled and a remote load test outstanding with an enforced bound of \(\$6\); that test later bills \(\$4.20\). Tabulate the root’s \(\LedgerSettledCharges\), \(\LedgerReservedFunds\), and \(\LedgerFreeBalance\) at each boundary, and compute what a release at local stop would return against what may safely be returned.
A trailing-window limit allows \(\WindowSpendingLimit=\$8\) of admitted bounds per \(\SpendingWindowDuration=10\) minutes across all children. Requests arrive at minute \(0\) (\(\$3\)), minute \(2\) (\(\$4\)), minute \(6\) (\(\$2\)), and minute \(11\) (\(\$2\)); the first operation settles at minute \(1\) for \(\$1\). Decide each admission, and show what an implementation that credits early settlement back to the window would admit instead.
The agent now proposes renting a load-generation cluster whose provider enforces no duration or spending cap. Redesign the admission path so the task keeps a hard ceiling, and explain why an operator’s approval of the production change does not substitute for a budget reservation.



What’s Next: From priced parts to one trajectoryWho owns each transition between context, tools, execution, assessment, and settlement, and what evidence permits the next one? A policy this chapter justifies on price still crosses every one of those boundaries. Conclusion first returns to the three questions the introduction posed, answering the first with the cost per accepted task priced here. It then follows one remediation incident through the whole system, naming the owner and the record of each transition, putting the attempt on this chapter’s account, and examining the failures that occur at the seams. It ends at the specification boundary, where the runtime can enforce and measure a declared contract but cannot decide whether that contract captures what the task was for.

title: 18 Agent Economics
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can a model with a tenth of the token price make an agent cost more for every task it finishes?
A model whose tokens cost a tenth as much looks like a large saving on the provider’s invoice and can still raise the price of every task the agent finishes. Token charges are only part of the account. An attempt also holds a sandbox open while its tools run, invokes tests and external services, waits for shared capacity, and may end in human review, and an attempt that fails pays for all of it without producing anything that ships. A cheaper model that needs more turns, retries more often, or passes assessment less often spreads those charges across fewer accepted tasks, so the bill per accepted result can rise while the token bill falls. The account that matters is kept over a cohort of tasks under one declared contract. It charges everything every attempt incurred, failed and canceled work included, to the tasks that contract accepted, and it keeps work still pending visible rather than dropping it. Reuse, retries, faster execution, model routing, added capacity, and delegation are each worth buying only when they lower that ratio or meet a deadline the objective values, and which lever matters depends on which term of the account dominates. Capacity enters the same account, because concurrent trajectories hold model servers, sandboxes, and reviewers while they wait, and an undersized pool turns waiting into cost. Horizon, state, and authority each set the closure a task must pay for, and an agent service is sustainable only when the accepted work it delivers covers that price.

Learning Objectives

Calculate cohort cost per accepted task while distinguishing attempt costs, human outcomes, and unsettled liabilities
Evaluate prefix caching, compaction, and retry purchases under explicit billing and acceptance assumptions
Diagnose which acceleration shortens a trajectory by computing its critical path and the model’s share of it
Evaluate model cascades under a common acceptance contract, including assessment costs and false-accept risk
Size resource occupancy and compare provisioning choices under declared workload, quota, and queueing assumptions
Design atomic budget reservations that preserve spending bounds across concurrent work and late settlement
Select a loop cap or architecture by pricing automated and human-completed outcomes under one acceptance contract

title: 18 Agent Economics
text:
A team running the repair agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}\)) is offered a model whose tokens cost a tenth as much. On the provider’s invoice the switch looks like a large saving. On the team’s ledger it can raise the price of every repair that ships. The cheaper model may need more turns to reach a passing patch, and each turn holds a sandbox open and invokes tools. More tickets may fail assessment, and each failure still paid for its model calls, its environment, its checks, and the engineer who triages it. The token discount is real, but it applies to only part of the account.



Horizon, state, and authority each set the closure a task must pay for.
Offers like this one recur, because the price of a fixed capability falls quickly. Epoch AI (2025) track the cheapest model that reaches a fixed score on each of several benchmarks, and figure 1 plots three of those price series.














Figure 1: The Price of a Fixed Capability Falls Fast: Lowest price, in dollars per million tokens on a logarithmic axis, of any model that reaches a fixed benchmark score, plotted at each new low. Each line holds the capability constant, so its descent is price change alone, and the legend gives each series’ fitted decline per year. Prices are the source’s 3:1 blend of input and output rates; the series end in early 2025. Data from Epoch AI (2025).


Epoch AI. 2025. LLM Inference Prices Have Fallen Rapidly but Unequally Across Tasks.


Across all 21 capability thresholds in the source, the fitted decline runs from 9× to roughly 860× per year, with a median of 46×. A falling token price shrinks only the inference terms of the attempt cost. Sandbox lifetime, verification, cleanup, and human review are priced per turn, per check, and per hour of attention, not per token, so each price cut moves a larger share of the bill onto terms the provider’s discount never touches, and onto the acceptance probability in the denominator.
The runtime built so far can already say part of what the team needs. The evaluation discipline of Agent Evaluation decides which repairs count as accepted and how two policies are compared on matched tasks, and the harness’s budget ceilings stop any one task from spending without limit. Single-Agent Baseline Benchmarking joined the two once, deciding for one stated workload whether splitting a migration across workers repaid its coordination tax against a matched single controller. None of these says in general whether a policy is worth running. An accuracy figure reported without its cost cannot rank two designs, which is why cost-controlled evaluation reports the two jointly (Kapoor et al. 2024), and a ceiling that holds says nothing about how much of the spending under it bought accepted work.

↩︎ Per-task budget ceilings and the bounded-liability admission test that enforces them are established in Budgets and Ceilings.

This chapter builds the account that joins spending to accepted outcomes. Reliability and Cost over a Horizon introduced cost per accepted task, the expected cost of an attempt divided by the probability that the attempt is accepted, as one of the book’s two quantitative fundamentals. Here that ratio becomes something a team can measure over a real cohort of tasks. Its numerator holds every charge an attempt incurs, its denominator counts only outcomes accepted under one declared contract, and each lever the runtime controls (reuse, retries, acceleration, routing, capacity, and delegation) is worth buying only if it lowers the ratio or buys a deadline the objective values.
The account comes first, in section 18.2, together with the rules that keep failed, canceled, and still-pending work inside it. Section 18.3 prices what the runtime pays to carry context from call to call and how many attempts it should buy. Section 18.4 finds where faster execution actually shortens a task, and section 18.5 decides which model should attempt the work at all. Section 18.6 sizes the services that concurrent trajectories hold and wait on, and section 18.7 makes spending limits hold across delegated children and late bills. Section 18.8 then compares whole architectures under one contract, and section 18.9 prices all four lighthouse workloads to show that each is bound by a different term of the same account.

title: 18 Agent Economics
text:
Before the team can say which model repairs tickets more cheaply, it must fix what a repair is. A configuration scored against visible tests cannot be compared with one scored against a sealed suite, however carefully the invoices are tallied, because the two denominators count different things. Acceptance is defined only under an explicitly declared contract, checker, and execution environment. Isolating the effect of one policy choice (model selection, prompt construction, or tool scaffolding) therefore takes a matched comparison that holds the task contract, evaluation harness, and resource ceilings fixed while only the policy varies. The ledger also needs an explicit task cohort and a cutoff timestamp. Together they decide which initiated tasks are under review, which outcomes count as accepted before the cutoff, and which operations, assessments, or invoices are still pending.


Across an attempt of \(\TurnHorizon\) turns, an agent system incurs direct inference charges alongside substantial infrastructure costs to maintain the execution environment. Assessment, teardown, and human intervention often continue long after the final token leaves the model server. This chapter numbers turns from one, \(\TurnIndex=1,\dots,\TurnHorizon\), so that the index matches the turn counts in its worked examples. The whole-trajectory cost of an attempt decomposes as
\[\AttemptCost = \sum_{t=1}^\TurnHorizon \left(\TurnInputTokenCost^{(\TurnIndex)}+\TurnOutputTokenCost^{(\TurnIndex)}+\TurnToolFeeCost^{(\TurnIndex)}+\TurnSandboxCost^{(\TurnIndex)}\right)+\AttemptVerificationCost+\AttemptCleanupCost+\HumanReviewCost+\AttemptRuntimeOverheadCost.\]
The input (\(\TurnInputTokenCost^{(\TurnIndex)}\)) and output (\(\TurnOutputTokenCost^{(\TurnIndex)}\)) terms capture inference pricing under the relevant provider rate cards, incorporating tiered rates and prompt-caching discounts. Tool invocation fees (\(\TurnToolFeeCost^{(\TurnIndex)}\)) account for billable external API requests and data lookups. The sandbox charge (\(\TurnSandboxCost^{(\TurnIndex)}\)) reflects the wall-clock lifetime of virtual machines or container environments, including idle wait intervals while external tools execute. Beyond the active turn loop, verification (\(\AttemptVerificationCost\)) covers post-execution checks and test suites not already billed during sandbox execution. Cleanup (\(\AttemptCleanupCost\)) accounts for state reset, storage teardown, or compensating transactions. When rejected attempts or policy escalations trigger human review, \(\HumanReviewCost\) tallies manual engineering time within the declared system boundary. Finally, runtime cost (\(\AttemptRuntimeOverheadCost\)) apportions orchestrator overhead, scheduler queues, and shared network telemetry.
A strict accounting rule governs this ledger: every cost item must map to exactly one category. If an end-of-turn integration test is billed as active sandbox compute time, it must not be double-counted under verification.

Definition 18.1: Whole-trajectory cost
Whole-trajectory cost is the total expense attributed to a single execution attempt across its model calls, environment runtime, validation assessment, and required finalization within a declared accounting boundary.

Significance: It forms the fundamental numerator of cost per accepted task (\(\CostPerAcceptedTask\)), capturing every cost driver that standard per-token pricing hides: container provisioning, external API calls, test-suite grading, state teardown, and human escalation. Crucially, failed attempts accumulate these charges just as relentlessly as successful ones.
Distinction: Whole-trajectory cost measures the expense of an individual attempt, whereas cost per accepted task amortizes all attempted and discarded work across the surviving accepted tasks in the cohort.
Common pitfall: Halting the accounting ledger the instant the agent process emits its final token, ignoring trailing cloud resources, pending cleanup jobs, or downstream engineer triage.



A single initiated task may involve multiple sequential retries or parallel delegated branches. Its task account, denoted \(\TaskCost\), aggregates every attempt, failed branch, and abandoned speculative execution, along with the task’s assigned share of capacity and orchestration overhead. When a sub-agent branch crashes or is canceled, its incurred costs do not vanish; they remain permanently logged against the task.
In production environments, operations are rarely settled instantly. The harness’s reservations hold part of the allowance against work that has been admitted but not yet billed. Because these funds remain committed until all external side effects resolve, any snapshot taken at an intermediate cutoff must distinguish settled expenditures from outstanding liability, the reserved balance backing active, unbilled operations. The settled total serves merely as a lower bound on the final task cost until all pending obligations clear.



For a finite cohort of \(\InitiatedTasks\) initiated tasks with fully resolved accounting, let \(\AcceptedTasks\) represent the number of distinct tasks accepted under the declared contract. If an agent executes three successful retries on a single ticket, the system delivers exactly one accepted task; retries never inflate the denominator. For \(\AcceptedTasks>0\), the cohort cost per accepted task is
\[\CostPerAcceptedTask=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{\InitiatedTasks}{\TaskCost}_i}{\AcceptedTasks}. \]
The numerator aggregates every dollar expended across all \(\InitiatedTasks\) initiated tasks, whether they succeeded, crashed, timed out, or were rejected by validation. Keeping failed and canceled work in the numerator and pending verdicts explicit is exactly what trajectory goodput and the accepted task (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-goodput}\)) demand of any account in this book. Only accepted tasks count as delivered work, and every charge incurred on the way to them stays on the bill. (This chapter defines trajectory goodput formally, as accepted tasks per unit time, when it sizes capacity in section 18.6.1.) If zero tasks are accepted (\(\AcceptedTasks = 0\)), the ratio is undefined; a transparent system report must present the total expenditure and the zero count directly rather than masking the failure behind an artificial floor. Whenever tasks or invoices remain in flight at the accounting cutoff, the report must flag the cutoff timestamp and qualify the calculation as provisional. An unexecuted test suite represents a pending task, not an immediate failure, just as an asynchronous cloud billing adjustment can shift \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) hours after the code artifact is finalized.

Definition 18.2: Cohort cost per accepted task
Cohort cost per accepted task is the total cost of every initiated task in a cohort, within a declared accounting boundary, divided by the number of distinct tasks accepted under one declared contract.

Significance: It provides the empirical, measurable form of this book’s fundamental economic metric \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\). Because the count of accepted tasks divides every item in the numerator, a drop in task acceptance inflates the entire system bill, whereas a token price cut discounts only the inference fraction.
Distinction: Whole-trajectory cost measures the expense of an isolated attempt; cohort cost per accepted task loads all failed, canceled, and abandoned attempts onto the small fraction of work that actually passes inspection.
Common pitfall: Computing the average cost of successful trajectories alone. This survivor bias ignores the graveyard of discarded attempts whose compute and environment bills must be paid by the surviving accepted tasks.



When all tasks in a cohort have reached a terminal state, the cohort acceptance rate is \(\AcceptanceFraction = \AcceptedTasks / \InitiatedTasks\). Let \(\AcceptedTaskMeanCost\) denote the mean cost of an accepted task, and let \(\UnacceptedTaskMeanCost\) denote the mean cost of an unaccepted task (encompassing outright failures, policy cancellations, and timed-out executions). When both subsets are non-empty, partitioning the numerator yields
\[\CostPerAcceptedTask=\AcceptedTaskMeanCost+\frac{1-\AcceptanceFraction}{\AcceptanceFraction}\UnacceptedTaskMeanCost.\]
The cohort fraction \(\AcceptanceFraction\) counts tasks, whereas the per-attempt acceptance probability \(\AcceptanceProbability\) of equation 1.2 counts attempts. When every task gets exactly one attempt, the two coincide, and \(\AcceptanceFraction\) estimates \(\AcceptanceProbability\). When a task may retry, \(\AcceptanceFraction\) estimates task-level coverage, the probability that some attempt on the task is accepted, while the per-attempt planning form stays \(\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability\). Section 18.3.3 connects the two for sequential retry.



Each accepted task carries the rejected ones, and that load explodes as acceptance falls.
The factor \((1-\AcceptanceFraction)/\AcceptanceFraction\) represents the rejection multiplier: the exact number of failed tasks that each accepted task must financially absorb. This expression is an exact accounting identity for the cohort, not an asymptotic model or an assumption that retries will eventually converge. As the acceptance rate \(\AcceptanceFraction\) falls toward zero, this multiplier explodes non-linearly. Whether a steep discount on model tokens yields lower overall operating costs depends on both groups’ costs, which is why no universal threshold decides model selection in isolation. The concrete bug-repair scenario below prices this trade-off directly.

Napkin Math 18.1: The token-price fallacy in automated bug repairProblem: Two hypothetical configurations each process the same 100 tickets, with one bounded attempt per ticket and the same acceptance contract. Every attempt, rejected or not, uses the fixed per-attempt usage that table 1 assumes for its configuration, and all outcomes and charges are settled at the cutoff. The environment charge covers tool use, sandbox holding, and cleanup; the assessment charge covers checking not billed as sandbox time, together with allocated runtime overhead. Which configuration costs less per accepted repair?

Math: Applying the rates and usage in table 1 gives model charges per attempt of $0.240 and $0.069. Adding the other charges gives $0.410 and $0.329, respectively. The complete cohorts therefore cost $41 and $32.888. Dividing each total by its accepted count gives $0.55 and $1.32 per accepted repair. The lower-token-price configuration costs less per attempt but 2.4× as much per accepted task.
Now expand both accounting boundaries to include $10 of engineer triage for each rejected attempt. The frontier configuration has 25 rejected tickets and the other has 75. Total costs become $291 and $782.888; costs per accepted task become $3.88 and $31.32, a ratio of 8.1×. Triage adds no accepted repairs; if engineers also completed tickets, that combined service would need its own named account.
Systems insight: With one attempt per ticket, a cheaper configuration wins only if its attempt cost falls by more than its acceptance does. Here acceptance falls by 66.7 percent, so the low-price configuration needed attempts at least that much cheaper. Its token charges fall by 71.3 percent, but its all-in attempt cost falls by only 19.8 percent, because its extra turns each pay the environment charge. Each of its accepted repairs also carries 3 rejected attempts, against 0.33 for the frontier configuration, so every charge that scales with rejections, such as triage, widens the gap.



Systems Perspective 18.1: Reading a cost-per-accepted-task numberThe cost per accepted task represents a cohort-level ratio of aggregate expenditures to accepted deliverables evaluated at an explicit cutoff timestamp. Engineers must avoid confusing this ratio with the arithmetic mean of individual task expenses; furthermore, in small cohorts, sample variability prevents this ratio from serving as an unbiased estimator of the theoretical planning ratio \(\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability\). To be actionable, any reported \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) figure must be accompanied by its full context: total cohort expenditure, accepted task count with statistical confidence bounds, end-to-end latency distributions, pending execution statuses, and outstanding liabilities. An isolated efficiency number shorn of these context markers cannot support valid comparisons between competing system policies.
A rigorous matched comparison holds the acceptance contract and maximum resource allowances fixed across configurations, rather than enforcing identical expenditures. A more aggressive search policy might intentionally spend more compute per ticket to meet stringent latency deadlines or maximize task coverage, provided the underlying system objective values those gains. Inverting this metric yields goodput per dollar (accepted tasks delivered per unit of currency, the per-dollar counterpart of the trajectory goodput defined in section 18.6.1), which keeps the same accounting boundary but reads it as throughput. In both formulations, acceptance confirms only that an artifact satisfied the automated contract within the designated test suite; it does not guarantee the complete absence of latent defects.




↩︎ Matched-budget comparison, which fixes the acceptance contract and resource envelope while each policy spends it differently, is established in Matched-budget comparison.
Decomposing the account this way shows where a lever can act before anyone pays for it. The dominant term varies across workloads, and section 18.9 prices all four lighthouses to show which term binds each. The levers the runtime controls most directly act on the inference term and on the number of attempts. In automated bug repair, re-sent prompt context makes up most of the inference charge, so prefix caching and context compaction act on that charge, while reasoning limits and retry budgets set how many model invocations an accepted task buys. Whether the inference term is the one worth attacking for a given workload is a separate question, and for the repair agent the answer turns out to be no.

title: 18 Agent Economics
text:
Across the turns of a repair, the same prompt prefix recurs call after call. Context engineering arranges the request so that the stable part comes first, and the serving system keeps the key-value (KV) attention state of that prefix so the next call need not recompute it. Reuse lowers cost, but it is not free, and it competes with two other purchases the runtime can make: compacting the context, which shortens the prompt but discards reusable state, and buying more attempts, which raises coverage but multiplies the bill. Each must be priced under the same acceptance contract before the runtime can tell which one lowers the cost per accepted task.


↩︎ The exact-prefix, execution-parameter, residency, and tenant conditions under which retained attention state may be reused are established in Prefix compatibility.


Evaluating multi-turn agent economics requires distinguishing between logical input, physical computation, and billed tokens. A model provider often retains compatible KV state across calls even when an agent client retransmits the complete conversation transcript on every turn.1 Over an execution trajectory of \(\TurnHorizon\) turns, one call each, let \(\SequenceLength^{(\TurnIndex)}\) represent the logical input length on call \(\TurnIndex\), \(\EligibleCachedPrefixLength^{(\TurnIndex)}\) its eligible cached prefix length, and \(\OutputLength^{(\TurnIndex)}\) its billed output length. Under a published tariff with per-token rates \(\InputTokenPrice\) for fresh input, \(\CachedInputTokenPrice\) for cached input, and \(\OutputTokenPrice\) for generated output, the total token charge is
1 Prefix Reuse: Serving systems make cross-request reuse practical by storing attention state in paged memory blocks that requests sharing a prefix can share (Kwon et al. 2023), and by indexing retained state in a radix tree so subsequent calls locate their longest cached prefix (Zheng et al. 2024). A discounted cached-input tariff reflects this underlying mechanism directly: only an exact, resident token prefix qualifies for the discount.
Kwon, Woosuk, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, and Ion Stoica. 2023. “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention.” Proceedings of the 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 611–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3600006.3613165.

Zheng, Lianmin, Liangsheng Ying, Zhenghao Yin, Cody Hao Liu, Eric Yu, Prakhar Patel, Zhipeng Yang, Anthony K. Joseph, and Ion Stoica. 2024. “SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2312.07104, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2312.07104.
\[
\TrajectoryTokenCost=\sum_{t=1}^{\TurnHorizon}\left[\InputTokenPrice(\SequenceLength^{(\TurnIndex)}-\EligibleCachedPrefixLength^{(\TurnIndex)})+\CachedInputTokenPrice{}\EligibleCachedPrefixLength^{(\TurnIndex)}+\OutputTokenPrice{}\OutputLength^{(\TurnIndex)}\right].
\tag{1}\]
Commercial pricing models often incorporate additional dimensions, including cache-write surcharges, hourly retention fees, and minimum eligible prefix thresholds. In an append-only agent transcript, each turn re-sends the cumulative history alongside newly observed tool outputs and model generations. With an initial prompt of \(\BasePromptLength\) tokens and \(\TurnAppendLength\) tokens appended per turn, the logical input over the whole trajectory is the quadratic re-send total \(\PromptTokensSent\) of equation 2.9, and ideal prefix reuse charges only \(\FreshInputTokenCount=\BasePromptLength+(\TurnHorizon-1)\TurnAppendLength\) of it at the fresh-input rate, once each for the initial prompt and every appended increment. Priced under the tariff, the total input bill is \(\InputTokenPrice{}\FreshInputTokenCount+\CachedInputTokenPrice(\PromptTokensSent-\FreshInputTokenCount)\). Because both \(\CachedInputTokenPrice\) and \(\TurnAppendLength\) remain positive, the quadratic growth term does not disappear; caching merely scales down its cost coefficient from \(\InputTokenPrice\) to \(\CachedInputTokenPrice\). These formulations account for billed input tokens, not the physical accelerator memory required to hold this reusable state across requests.


↩︎ The accelerator memory that retained attention state occupies is established in The Footprint of Retained Attention State.
Prefix hits require strict alignment between the incoming token sequence and the cached execution context, including weights and adapters, token positions, attention masks, and applicable multimodal inputs, together with residency and tenant access conditions (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\)). Reusability breaks at the first altered token. Output sampling settings alone need not change already computed prefix tensors; any additional provider cache-key restrictions belong to the service contract. In production deployments, distributed request routing, memory pressure and cache eviction, and protracted tool execution times degrade realized hit rates. Economic models must therefore price observed, eligible hits under the actual service contract rather than assuming theoretical upper bounds.

Napkin Math 18.2: Pricing an append-only trajectoryProblem: An agent trajectory runs 30 turns, starting with an initial prompt of 8,000 input tokens and appending 1,500 tokens on each subsequent turn. Each invocation generates 200 output tokens. The provider tariff charges $3 per million fresh input tokens, $15 per million output tokens, and 10 percent of the fresh-input price for cached reads, with no separate write or retention fees. How much does ideal prefix reuse reduce the token bill for this trajectory?
Math: Cumulative logical input across all turns reaches 892,500 tokens. Under ideal prefix reuse, only 51,500 tokens are billed at the fresh-input rate. Input processing therefore costs $2.678 without reuse vs. $0.407 with prefix caching. Combining this with the constant $0.090 output charge yields total bills of $2.768 and $0.497, representing a 5.6× cost reduction.
Systems insight: Cache hit rate governs financial efficiency. Because historical context constitutes almost all of this trajectory’s input, even small reductions in hit rate produce large absolute billing increases. If 10 percent of the eligible prefix misses (for example, because a volatile timestamp or session identifier sits near the prompt header), the session cost increases by $0.227, raising the cached bill by 45.7 percent. Prefix caching modifies only the model inference term in effective cost (\(\CostPerAcceptedTask\)): it lowers the cost of carrying context across turns while leaving delivered inputs, outputs, and task acceptance unchanged.





Unlike prefix caching, context compaction actively alters the input transcript. Replacing prior conversation turns with an aggregated summary shortens the active prompt, though it risks invalidating cached attention state. If summarization preserves a stable system prefix, subsequent requests can still reuse those initial blocks. To price the cache-invalidation penalty explicitly, consider the case of a complete cache miss: the first compacted invocation shares no reusable prefix with prior turns, but subsequent calls resume append-only prefix reuse from the compacted prompt. The baseline comparison retains the full uncompacted context over the same remaining turns, holding future token additions and ordinary output lengths constant. This analysis isolates the pure token price of compaction; whether a given summary preserves downstream task acceptance is evaluated separately using the context-policy evaluation of Evaluating Context Policies.
Let \(\SequenceLength\) be the input length at the moment of compaction, \(\CompactedContextLength < \SequenceLength\) the compacted length, and \(\RemainingCallCount \ge 1\) the remaining ordinary invocations, including the first compacted call. Set the two call sequences side by side. Keeping the context makes \(\RemainingCallCount\) ordinary calls, the first of which reads the cached history plus one fresh increment. Compacting makes one summarization call followed by \(\RemainingCallCount\) ordinary calls on the compacted prompt. Assume the summarization call reads exactly what the keep path’s first call would have read, at the same cached and fresh prices; then its input charge equals that call’s input charge, and the two cancel when the paths are differenced. Ordinary outputs are equal call for call. What remains on the compaction side with no counterpart on the keep side is the summary’s generated tokens, \(\OutputTokenPrice{}\SummaryOutputLength\), and the first compacted call, which must send all \(\CompactedContextLength\) tokens as fresh input to rebuild server KV cache state. Relative to keeping the original context, the upfront investment \(\CompactionUpfrontCost\) is therefore
\[
\CompactionUpfrontCost=\OutputTokenPrice{}\SummaryOutputLength+\InputTokenPrice{}\CompactedContextLength,
\]
which combines the output generation fee of the summary with the fresh-input cost of repopulating the cache. Each subsequent call saves \(\CompactionPerCallSaving=\CachedInputTokenPrice(\SequenceLength-\CompactedContextLength)\) under the assumption of equal incremental growth. The cumulative cost difference across \(\RemainingCallCount\) remaining calls is therefore:
\[
\CompactionPathCost(\RemainingCallCount)-\KeepContextPathCost(\RemainingCallCount)=\CompactionUpfrontCost-(\RemainingCallCount-1)\CompactionPerCallSaving,
\qquad
\CompactionPaybackCallCount=1+\left\lceil\frac{\CompactionUpfrontCost}{\CompactionPerCallSaving}\right\rceil
\quad(\CompactionUpfrontCost>0,\ \CompactionPerCallSaving>0).
\]
Here \(\CompactionPaybackCallCount\) represents the payback horizon: the minimum number of remaining invocations required for per-turn cache savings to offset the initial compaction surcharge. When \(\CompactionUpfrontCost \le 0\), compaction pays for itself on the very first call; when \(\CompactionPerCallSaving = 0\) and \(\CompactionUpfrontCost > 0\), compaction never recovers its cost on token pricing alone. Accounting for the first compacted call separately from later turns prevents off-by-one errors when estimating the remaining trajectory budget.

Napkin Math 18.3: Count the first compacted callProblem: In the preceding scenario, suppose the agent triggers compaction at turn 16, compressing 30,500 tokens down to 12,000. The summarization call emits 1,500 tokens under standard cached-history pricing. If 15 ordinary calls remain (including the first compacted turn), what is the minimum remaining horizon required for compaction to cost no more than retaining the full context?
Math: Retaining the uncompressed context incurs $0.24525 in remaining input costs. Compaction incurs $0.19035 across remaining ordinary calls plus $0.03570 for the summarizer, totaling $0.22605. The upfront differential is $0.05850, against which each subsequent turn saves $0.00555. With 11 calls remaining, compaction still costs $0.00300 more than baseline. Reaching 12 remaining calls yields a net saving of $0.00255.
Systems insight: Compaction lowers total expenditure only when the remaining trajectory length meets or exceeds the payback horizon \(\CompactionPaybackCallCount\). Crucially, \(\CompactionPaybackCallCount\) scales inversely with the cached read rate: the upfront cost \(\CompactionUpfrontCost\) depends on \(\InputTokenPrice\) and \(\OutputTokenPrice\), whereas the per-call savings \(\CompactionPerCallSaving\) are proportional to \(\CachedInputTokenPrice\). If the cached read tariff drops from 10 percent to 5 percent of the fresh-input price, the break-even horizon extends to 23 calls. Because only 15 calls remain, compaction under this discounted rate loses money. As KV caching becomes cheaper, compaction must occur earlier in an execution trajectory to justify its cache-invalidation penalty. Late-stage compaction must be justified by context window limits or attention fidelity rather than token savings; an aggressive summary that drops a crucial constraint and lowers acceptance erases any marginal token economy.





An agent runtime can also allocate budget dynamically by purchasing deeper internal reasoning within a single invocation or by funding multiple independent execution attempts. A configured reasoning token limit acts as an upper ceiling rather than a fixed spend. Financial accounting must track actual billed token consumption and its empirical effect on task acceptance under an identical evaluation contract. Because internal deliberation generates tokens serially, systems engineers must evaluate this extra compute against increased turn latency. The retry analysis below prices a reasoning budget too. Deeper reasoning raises the all-in attempt cost \(\MeanAttemptCost\) by the billed price of the extra tokens and is worth buying only if it raises acceptance \(\AttemptPassProbability\) by a larger proportion, so that \(\MeanAttemptCost/\AttemptPassProbability\) falls.


↩︎ The distinction between internal deliberation budgets and external orchestration is established in Internal budgets and external orchestration.
Consider a baseline model of sequential retry with early stopping, in which every attempt on a task exhibits an identical acceptance probability \(\AttemptPassProbability > 0\). Conditioning on a fixed task prompt and external environment, attempts represent independent draws from the same agent configuration, each incurring an all-inclusive cost \(\MeanAttemptCost\) covering model inference, sandbox runtime, and output verification. Sequential retry terminates immediately upon the first accepted result or halts after exhausting a budget of \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) attempts. The overall task acceptance probability (or coverage) is \(\TaskCoverageProbability_k = 1 - (1 - \AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount\), and the expected number of executed attempts is \(\sum_{j=0}^{\IndependentAttemptCount-1}(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\SequentialAttemptIndex = \TaskCoverageProbability_k / \AttemptPassProbability\). Dividing the expected total spend by the expected accepted tasks yields \((\MeanAttemptCost \TaskCoverageProbability_k / \AttemptPassProbability) / \TaskCoverageProbability_k = \MeanAttemptCost / \AttemptPassProbability\). Under early stopping with independent trials, the expected cost per accepted task remains invariant to the attempt cap \(\IndependentAttemptCount\): raising \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) expands overall task coverage, while early termination holds the average cost per successful outcome at exactly \(\MeanAttemptCost / \AttemptPassProbability\), which is the per-attempt form of equation 1.2 with \(\MeanAttemptCost\) as the attempt cost.
In contrast, launching all \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) attempts concurrently in a parallel batch costs \(\IndependentAttemptCount \MeanAttemptCost / \TaskCoverageProbability_k\) per expected accepted task, provided the evaluation harness can identify and return an accepted candidate from the pool. These are the sequential and batch costs of equation 13.6, with the generation and checking charges folded into one attempt cost \(\MeanAttemptCost\). What this chapter adds is the comparison between buying more attempts from a cheap configuration and buying one attempt from a stronger one.

Napkin Math 18.4: What a retry cap buysProblem: A lightweight agent configuration exhibits an acceptance probability of 0.30 at an all-in cost of $0.10 per attempt. A stronger configuration achieves 0.70 acceptance but costs $0.40 per attempt. Allowing up to 5 lightweight attempts under the independent-trials model, which policy achieves the lowest cost per expected accepted task: sequential retry with early stopping, an unconditional parallel batch of 5 attempts, or a single attempt from the stronger model?
Math: Sequential retry achieves an expected coverage of 83.2 percent while consuming 2.773 attempts per task. This produces an expected spend of $0.277 per submitted task and $0.333 per accepted task. Running all 5 attempts in parallel yields identical coverage but requires $0.500 per submitted task, increasing the cost per accepted task to $0.601. A single invocation of the stronger model costs $0.571 per accepted task.
Systems insight: Under early stopping, sequentially retrying a cheaper model outperforms a single call to a stronger model whenever \(\CheapConfigurationAttemptCost/\CheapConfigurationPassProbability < \StrongConfigurationAttemptCost/\StrongConfigurationPassProbability\). In this scenario, sequential retry also delivers superior aggregate coverage (83.2 percent vs. 70 percent). Executing the batch concurrently secures that same coverage at a 1.8× multiplier in cost per accepted task, the ratio of \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) to the expected sequential attempt count. A parallel burst is justified only when strict wall-clock deadlines assign significant value to lower latency, offsetting the substantial financial premium.


Production workloads rarely exhibit a single, uniform success probability \(\AttemptPassProbability\). Difficult tasks maintain persistently low acceptance rates across repeated attempts. Consequently, substituting an average per-task success rate into \(1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount\) systematically overstates aggregate coverage, causing the realized cost per accepted task to drift above the idealized \(\MeanAttemptCost/\AttemptPassProbability\) ratio. Empirical repeated-sampling studies demonstrate this dynamic: on benchmarks with automated verification, task coverage (the fraction of tasks solved by at least one sample) continues to climb across multiple orders of magnitude of generated samples, scaling roughly log-linearly rather than saturating as a single-parameter model would predict (Brown et al. 2024). Environmental feedback, service outages, and shared mutable state further complicate fixed-probability assumptions. Engineers must therefore evaluate retry policies using outcome distributions measured per task over repeated runs.

↩︎ Per-task acceptance probabilities, and the distinction between a task and a repeated run of it, are established in Tasks and repeated runs.

Generating extra candidate solutions also introduces verification risk. As analyzed in Selection and evidence costs, repeated sampling raises the chance of a false acceptance, where a flawed candidate satisfies test assertions without truly solving the underlying task. Passing an automated check provides domain-specific verification evidence rather than an absolute guarantee of correctness. Ultimately, prefix caching, context compaction, and retry policies govern what compute resources an agent runtime purchases; determining how those purchased operations dictate end-to-end latency requires analyzing the critical execution path.

title: 18 Agent Economics
text:
Accelerating a model call rarely yields a proportional reduction in end-to-end task time. In realistic agent workflows, container provisioning, repository setup, test suite execution, tool I/O, and consensus validation often dominate total elapsed time. Evaluating an acceleration technique therefore requires an end-to-end systems perspective that measures how much wall-clock time the proposed change strips from the critical path to a declared endpoint, what compute and memory resources it consumes, and whether the accelerated execution preserves the required acceptance evidence. Tracing exposes where time actually goes, while economic accounting determines whether accelerating that specific span is worth the operational cost.


Distributed tracing distinguishes enclosing parent spans from the nested operations within them. Summing a parent span’s duration with the durations of its children double-counts time. Similarly, simply summing concurrent sibling spans inflates apparent latency, whereas omitting queueing delays, network transit, or uninstrumented runtime pauses undercounts it. When profiling an agent runtime, uninstrumented intervals must remain explicitly accounted for as unexplained gaps rather than arbitrarily attributed to neighboring components.


↩︎ Parent-child span nesting and the double-counting it causes in latency attribution are established in Span overlap and latency attribution.
2 Recovering the Dependency Graph: The critical-path method and its float are introduced with agent traces in Span overlap and latency attribution. What pricing adds is the reconstruction step: distributed-systems work recovered the dependency model of production requests from existing component logs, precisely so that critical-path analysis could say which component’s speedup would shorten end-to-end latency (Chow et al. 2014). An agent trace needs the same reconstruction, from dispatch and join records rather than span nesting, before any acceleration is priced.
Chow, Michael, David Meisner, Jason Flinn, Daniel Peek, and Thomas F. Wenisch. 2014. “The Mystery Machine: End-to-End Performance Analysis of Large-Scale Internet Services.” 11th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 14), 217–31.
Crucially, a span’s parent in a call tree denotes syntactic containment, which does not necessarily reflect an execution dependency. An agent runtime might spawn background log flushes or asynchronous cache warmers that outlive the caller without blocking the next step. Determining end-to-end latency requires constructing a directed acyclic execution graph based on true dispatch and join conditions: a directed edge indicates that the successor task cannot begin until its predecessor completes. Along any path, the critical path counts only disjoint, non-overlapping intervals rather than inclusive parent spans alongside their children. For a directed dependency graph with vertex durations \(\VertexSlotTime(\DependencyGraphVertex)\) and source-to-sink paths \(\SourceSinkPathSet\), the longest path defines the critical path:2
\[\CriticalPathDuration = \max_{\pi \in \SourceSinkPathSet} \sum_{\DependencyGraphVertex \in \pi} \VertexSlotTime(\DependencyGraphVertex). \tag{2}\]
When the graph contains only mandatory computation, equation 2 establishes an idealized lower bound on completion time. The critical path matches the actual observed wall-clock interval only when the dependency graph incorporates real-world scheduling artifacts: thread scheduling delays, resource contention waits, queueing latencies, and sandbox initialization. Furthermore, the boundary of the graph depends on the system contract. Emitting an initial streamed token, evaluating a candidate patch against unit tests, and fully committing a validated pull request represent fundamentally different completion endpoints, each with its own dependency sink.
Accelerating a non-critical branch leaves end-to-end latency unchanged under a fixed schedule, although it may free cluster capacity or reduce hosting costs. Conversely, accelerating an operation on the critical path often shifts the bottleneck elsewhere: once the original limiting path shrinks below a parallel branch, that alternate branch becomes the new critical path. Systems engineers must therefore recompute critical paths dynamically after each proposed optimization, rather than naively subtracting isolated component savings from total elapsed time.




Napkin Math 18.5: How much does faster inference buy?Problem: In a short hypothetical repair episode, far shorter than the 30-turn trajectory priced in notebook 18.2, how much elapsed time does a 4× acceleration of every model call save?
Variables: All intervals execute sequentially, from runtime initialization through final sandbox snapshot export, without queueing, overlapping execution, or uninstrumented gaps. The durations listed in table 2 represent disjoint, non-overlapping sums rather than nested spans. The proposed acceleration modifies only inference latency, leaving model outputs, tool operations, test evidence, scheduling decisions, and finalization unchanged.



Table 2: One serial repair episode: Categories partition elapsed time under the stated assumptions; the total is not an additional interval.

Math: If model execution occupies fraction \(\ModelTimeFraction\) of baseline duration \(\Time\) and accelerates by factor \(\AcceleratorGain \geq 1\), Amdahl’s fixed-work law bounds the new duration: \(\AcceleratedEpisodeTime = \Time[(1-\ModelTimeFraction)+\ModelTimeFraction/\AcceleratorGain]\). This is the delegation bound of equation 17.1 with the overhead term set to zero and the worker count replaced by the acceleration factor; here the accelerated part is the model rather than the parallel work. In this episode, model work accounts for 9.4 percent of elapsed time. A 4× model acceleration reduces the episode to 290.46 s, saving 21.94 s for an overall speedup of 1.08×. Even instantaneous inference (\(\AcceleratorGain \to \infty\)) yields a whole-episode speedup of only 1.10× under these assumptions.
Systems insight: The theoretical speedup ceiling \(1/(1-\ModelTimeFraction)\) dictates whether paying for faster model inference can ever satisfy an operational deadline. Because this ceiling depends only on baseline profile measurements, engineers can evaluate its viability before investing in model optimization or specialized serving infrastructure. In this repair episode, halving test execution duration while maintaining identical coverage saves 122.8 s, far more than the 21.94 s gained from a 4× model acceleration, and it also lowers the sandbox leasing charges in \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\). When an engineering latency target exceeds what \(1/(1-\ModelTimeFraction)\) can theoretically deliver, engineering effort belongs on test execution and environment lifecycle optimizations. In non-linear, branching trajectories, this principle applies directly to the recomputed critical path of equation 2.





Once distributed traces identify the critical path, engineers can target the specific bottlenecks governing each span. Table 3 maps the primary span types of an agent trace to the physical factors governing their duration and the engineering levers available to compress them.



Table 3: Trajectory Span Types: What bounds each kind of span on an agent’s critical path and which techniques shorten it. Each lever is admissible only if the accepted result still meets the same acceptance contract and coverage.
