When tool operations are independent, the runtime can dispatch them concurrently provided security policies, authorization boundaries, and resource reservations permit parallel execution. If three tool calls dispatch simultaneously without I/O contention and all three must complete before the agent continues, the synchronization join waits only for the longest operation rather than the sum of all three. However, concurrency gains diminish when tools contend for local resources, when dispatch is staggered, or when a downstream tool requires the output of an earlier call. In the sandbox domain, warm container pools, pre-baked filesystem snapshots, and persistent build caches dramatically reduce environment initialization spans, subject to strict isolation and teardown guarantees before each reuse.


↩︎ The reset contract that a pooled or snapshot-restored sandbox must satisfy before serving a new lease is established in The reset contract.
Environment preparation can overlap model generation if the runtime executes speculative setup within a sandboxed, isolated scope that commits no external side effects before the full model response is validated and authorized. Streaming tokens from a large language model (LLM) does not constitute an authorized execution intent; even a speculative read operation might violate an access boundary or leak uncommitted state. If the model output subsequently alters the required tool call or aborts, the runtime must discard speculative work, release allocated resources, and record any incurred compute charges in the task account.
Early stopping alters the evidentiary value of an execution as well as its duration. In a validation pipeline, a single failing assertion in a mandatory test immediately proves that a candidate solution is unacceptable, allowing the runtime to short-circuit the remaining suite. Conversely, an early pass confirms only a single check; it provides zero evidence regarding the remainder of the test suite. Intelligent test prioritization and streaming failure detection thus accelerate defect rejection during intermediate iterations. However, final task acceptance still demands full test coverage across the declared verification contract. Furthermore, canceling a running check does not instantly free resources; active worker processes must unwind cleanly, and any intermediate compute costs remain on the ledger until the underlying jobs settle.


↩︎ Cancellation as an asynchronous control action, whose job may finish or keep running after the request and leave cleanup obligations unsettled, is established in Job supervision and cancellation.



Single-stream autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth bound under the serving assumptions developed in Per-call work estimate. Speculative decoding is an inference serving optimization whose latency and throughput depend on drafting accuracy and memory bandwidth constraints. From an agent economics standpoint, speculative decoding represents an engineering trade-off: it is worth deploying only if the resulting end-to-end latency reduction justifies the additional memory footprint and compute overhead.


↩︎ The weight-transfer floor that makes single-stream decoding memory-bandwidth bound is established in Per-call work estimate.
3 Draft-then-Verify Decoding: The idea predates large language models. Blockwise parallel decoding predicted several future positions at once and backed off to the longest prefix a scoring model validated (Stern et al. 2018). Speculative decoding moved the proposals into a separate small draft model and added an acceptance rule under which sampled outputs keep the target model’s distribution, which is why its savings are purely a cost and latency question rather than a quality trade.
Stern, Mitchell, Noam Shazeer, and Jakob Uszkoreit. 2018. “Blockwise Parallel Decoding for Deep Autoregressive Models.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 31 (NeurIPS 2018).
In speculative decoding, a lightweight draft model3 proposes \(\DraftTokenCount\) candidate tokens per speculation round, and the larger target model verifies them in a single forward pass, accepting the longest matching prefix and generating one continuation token of its own (Leviathan et al. 2023; C. Chen et al. 2023). Let the computational cost of generating one draft token equal a fraction \(\DraftTokenCostRatio\) of a standard target decoding step, and let \(\MeanAcceptedDraftLength\) denote the mean number of draft tokens accepted per round. If evaluating \(\DraftTokenCount\) proposed tokens in parallel costs approximately one target step, each round yields \(\MeanAcceptedDraftLength + 1\) verified tokens in the time equivalent to \(\DraftTokenCount\DraftTokenCostRatio + 1\) target decoding steps. The resulting decoding speedup for an isolated stream is
\[\SpeculativeDecodingSpeedup=\frac{\MeanAcceptedDraftLength+1}{\DraftTokenCount\DraftTokenCostRatio+1}. \tag{3}\]
Speculative execution accelerates the generation stream if and only if \(\MeanAcceptedDraftLength > \DraftTokenCount\DraftTokenCostRatio\), that is, when the average number of accepted draft tokens exceeds the amortized drafting cost. When acceptance falls below this break-even threshold, drafting overhead accumulates faster than verification saves time, actively degrading generation latency. Furthermore, the assumption that parallel verification takes no longer than a single decoding step holds only when single-stream generation is memory-bandwidth bound (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}\)). As concurrent serving loads increase and large batch sizes shift accelerator utilization toward compute saturation, evaluating \(\DraftTokenCount\) tokens concurrently incurs substantial arithmetic overhead, eroding the latency advantage.
This break-even condition models arithmetic steps within an isolated model call. In a production agent serving architecture, the end-to-end path incurs additional coordination costs: synchronizing draft and target model processes, memory bus transfers, KV-cache management, and wasted compute when early stopping cancels generation mid-trajectory. Under production fleet load, hosting the draft model also reserves high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and matrix units that could otherwise serve concurrent requests, while variable-length verification batches complicate target scheduler batching. Engineering decisions must therefore be validated under representative production traffic, measuring complete-call latency percentiles, aggregate accelerator utilization, queueing delays, and end-to-end task completion rates against the baseline configuration. A high token acceptance rate \(\MeanAcceptedDraftLength / \DraftTokenCount\) is merely an intermediate serving metric; it does not guarantee economic efficiency at the agent trajectory level.
Speculative decoding shortens the decode portion of a call. Prefill, queueing, and other call overhead remain in the fixed part of the trajectory. The estimate below treats the model intervals in the serial episode as decode time, with negligible nondecode overhead; it is an optimistic approximation of the gain from this serving technique. In the general fixed-work composition, the accelerated fraction is decode time divided by total episode time, and all unaffected intervals remain unchanged.
Evaluating how speculative decoding affects the complete agent workflow requires substituting the decode-stream speedup \(\SpeculativeDecodingSpeedup\) for the acceleration factor \(\AcceleratorGain\) in Amdahl’s formulation from notebook 18.5. Here \(\ModelTimeFraction\) is the decode share of baseline elapsed time. The fixed part includes both non-model spans and nondecode model time, so the maximum trajectory-level speedup remains bounded by \(1/(1-\ModelTimeFraction)\).
Consider a concrete deployment scenario where the draft model proposes 5 tokens per round at a relative cost of 0.08 per token. The break-even threshold requires the mean accepted draft count to exceed 0.4 draft tokens per round. If the draft model aligns well with the agent’s prompt distribution and achieves 3.6 accepted tokens per round, equation 3 yields a decode-stream speedup of 3.29×. Applying this factor to the decode subtotal under the zero-nondecode approximation within the serial episode of table 2 reduces total elapsed time from 312.40 s to 292.1 s, a modest 1.07× speedup for the overall episode. Conversely, if a complex reasoning task drops acceptance to 0.3 tokens per round, the system drops below break-even: decode-stream performance degrades to 0.93× of baseline speed, expanding total episode duration to 314.6 s. Drawn to scale, required tests and sandbox lifecycle operations form a non-model floor that no model acceleration crosses, so even instantaneous inference shortens this episode by less than a tenth (figure 2).






Figure 2: Faster Model Calls, a Barely Shorter Episode: The serial repair episode of table 2 drawn to scale, each bar partitioned into disjoint category sums rather than a chronological trace. Required tests and sandbox lifecycle form a non-model floor that no model acceleration crosses. A 4× model speedup and a 3.29× speculative decode speedup under the negligible-nondecode approximation each shorten the episode by less than a tenth, and even instant model calls stop at the floor. The runtime-status interval is too short to draw at this scale.



Accelerating a component on the critical path directly expands deadline headroom, whereas accelerating an off-critical operation primarily frees hardware capacity or lowers hosting costs. An optimization can justify higher operational expense if shaving critical-path latency satisfies a stringent user-facing service-level agreement (SLA); conversely, an optimization that boosts raw token generation rate should be rejected if interconnect contention or server overhead erases those savings at the workflow level. Deploying speculative decoding in an agent system therefore hinges on two distinct boundaries: the serving engine must satisfy the micro-level condition \(\MeanAcceptedDraftLength > \DraftTokenCount\DraftTokenCostRatio\) under realistic production concurrency, and the overall agent workflow must possess a sufficiently large decode fraction \(\ModelTimeFraction\) to make the macro-level ceiling \(1/(1-\ModelTimeFraction)\) worth pursuing.

Checkpoint 18.1: Cost and time per accepted task
Before routing calls across models, check the account and the clock.

Failed attempts: A policy accepts 25 of 100 tickets. How many rejected attempts does each accepted repair pay for, and which of their charges stay in the numerator if one is canceled before its bill settles?
Cache layout: Which term of equation 1 grows when a timestamp moves from the end of the system prompt to its front, and how does that term’s growth with the horizon change?
Compaction payback: With 11 calls left in notebook 18.3, should the runtime compact for price alone? What else could justify compacting anyway?
Critical-path estimate: Model calls take 9.4 percent of the serial episode. Before reading the table again, estimate the largest whole-episode speedup any model acceleration can buy, and decide whether halving the test interval would beat it.

title: 18 Agent Economics
text:
Critical-path analysis reveals where faster execution accelerates an agent workflow, but routing decides which model configuration should attempt the work in the first place. A small, specialized model often completes a constrained code transformation at negligible cost, whereas a frontier model justifies its higher expense when diagnosing complex, ambiguous system failures. A model cascade4 evaluates a task through a sequence of configurations, beginning with an inexpensive tier and escalating only when necessary; FrugalGPT formalized this architecture for language model APIs (L. Chen et al. 2023). The economic value of a cascade depends directly on three operational quantities: the fraction of requests resolved by cheaper tiers, the overhead of their failed attempts, and the difficulty distribution of tasks that escalate.
4 Generating Cascade: The verifier cascade of Staged Verifier Cascades already borrowed the classifier-cascade economics of cheap early rejection. A model cascade inverts the roles: each tier generates a candidate rather than only filtering one, so a task that escalates has paid for generation at every tier it reached, and the savings come only from a high early-exit rate.Every exit from a cascade must satisfy the same declared acceptance contract. A schema check suffices for a purely syntactic transformation, but it cannot establish that a source patch preserves authentication behavior. An inexpensive tier never earns the right to dilute verification; a tier’s price neither strengthens nor weakens the contract. Passing an assessment gate simply yields an accepted candidate record, while publication and tool execution remain separate runtime decisions governed by effect authorization.
The price spread a router can exploit is wide, and it does not track capability closely. A long-horizon software benchmark runs each configuration five times on every task under a 20-hour budget per trial and reports the mean score, the best and worst of the five, and the average cost and duration of a trial (FrontierSWE 2026). Figure 3 plots those results against cost.














Figure 3: Cost per Trial Barely Tracks Score: Mean score over five trials against the average cost of one trial, on a logarithmic cost axis, for 19 configurations on long-horizon software tasks. Bars run from the worst to the best of the five trials, and parentheses give average hours per trial. Points at similar cost differ by tens of points, and the highest score sits an order of magnitude to the right of nearly equal ones. Data from FrontierSWE (2026) via Epoch AI (2026).


FrontierSWE. 2026. FrontierSWE: Benchmarking Software Engineering Skill at the Edge of Human Ability.

Epoch AI. 2026. Capabilities and Benchmarking.


Cost per trial spans $9 to $1,030 across the 19 configurations, and a single trial runs from 1 to 19 hours. The highest-scoring configuration costs 10× as much per trial as the runner-up for 3 points, while the median gap between a configuration’s best and worst trial is 21 points. Price is therefore a poor proxy for score, and the variation between repeated trials is larger than the difference between the top configurations. That is the opening a router or cascade exploits, and it is also why each tier’s acceptance must be measured on the tasks that actually reach it rather than read from its price.


A direct router inspects incoming task features to select a model configuration upfront, prior to generation. In contrast, a cascade speculatively executes an initial attempt on an inexpensive tier, assesses the candidate against an acceptance contract, and escalates only when that attempt fails. The two architectures incur failure costs in fundamentally different ways. A mistaken direct route either assigns a complex task to an underpowered model (degrading task acceptance) or sends a routine query to an expensive frontier model (wasting budget). Conversely, an ill-fated cheap-first cascade choice always expends budget and latency on an unviable attempt before escalating, even when a higher tier ultimately salvages the task.
For a three-tier cascade, let \(\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_j\) denote the conditional probability of acceptance at tier \(\CascadeTierIndex\), given that the request reached tier \(\CascadeTierIndex\). Assume every task not accepted at a lower tier continues to the next tier, with no additional retry, cancellation, or stopping branch. The reach probabilities, the probability that a task arrives at each tier, are \(\StageReachProbability_1=1\), \(\StageReachProbability_2=1-\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_1\), and \(\StageReachProbability_3=(1-\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_1)(1-\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_2)\). This product reflects the probability chain rule rather than an assumption that tiers fail independently. Because later tiers receive only the tasks earlier tiers failed, a difficulty-filtered remainder, their conditional acceptance rates cannot be copied from full-workload benchmarks.
Let \(\CascadeTierCost_j\) be the mean generation and associated execution cost conditional on reaching tier \(\CascadeTierIndex\), excluding its gate, and let \(\CascadeGateCost_j\) be that gate’s mean cost. Let \(\CascadeTierDuration_j\) and \(\CascadeGateDuration_j\) be the corresponding mean durations. Real systems must budget for prompt caching, sandbox preparation, and environment cleanup within these terms rather than pricing output tokens alone. Linearity of expectation gives
\[
\mathbb{E}[\CascadeTaskCost]=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\StageReachProbability_j(\CascadeTierCost_j+\CascadeGateCost_j),
\qquad \AcceptanceProbability=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\StageReachProbability_j\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_j.
\]
For a serial cascade where all elapsed intervals are represented, the mean duration is
\[
\mathbb{E}[\CascadeTaskDuration]=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\StageReachProbability_j(\CascadeTierDuration_j+\CascadeGateDuration_j).
\]
The final tier must pay for its verification gate as well. With deterministic stage durations, a task reaching every tier takes \(\sum_j(\CascadeTierDuration_j+\CascadeGateDuration_j)\); with variable durations and queueing, characterizing tail percentiles requires the measured empirical distribution. A policy that stops early or leaves assessments unresolved uses its actual reach probabilities and reports those outcomes separately.
The planning metric of cost per accepted task is \(\mathbb{E}[\CascadeTaskCost]/\AcceptanceProbability\), which amortizes the cost of every reached tier across accepted outcomes rather than crediting only successful paths. Evaluating a direct frontier policy requires measuring its baseline acceptance rate across the full target cohort, since its performance on that general distribution is a fundamentally different quantity from its rate on the filtered escalation subset.

Napkin Math 18.6: Price the accepted result at every exitProblem: In a workload of 100,000 code-editing tasks, should an engineering team deploy a multi-tier cascade or route all requests directly to a frontier model to minimize cost per accepted result, and what latency penalty does the cascade incur?
Variables: Each candidate output undergoes an identical verification check. In order of tiers, the cascade’s model invocation and execution costs (excluding gating) are $0.0004, $0.0020, $0.0600 per reached tier, with execution times of 0.25 s, 0.80 s, 4.50 s. Evaluating the verification gate costs $0.0010 and consumes 0.40 s at each reached tier, including the final one. These figures account for container setup, execution, and cleanup overhead; this baseline assumes zero queueing delay and immediate settlement upon completion.
The cascade resolves 60,000 tasks at tier 1. Of the 40,000 tasks advancing to tier 2, it resolves 28,000. Of the 12,000 tasks advancing to tier 3, it resolves 11,400. The resulting conditional acceptance rates are 60 percent, 70 percent, 95 percent, respectively. In comparison, a direct-to-frontier policy resolves 97,000 tasks on an identical cohort. This full-workload rate is an independent baseline parameter rather than an extrapolation from the cascade’s filtered residual. It is lower than the cascade’s total acceptance even though the cascade’s top tier is the frontier model, because the cheaper tiers solve some tasks the frontier model fails (the tiers’ failure sets differ), and every escalated task gets another attempt under the same gate.
Math: The cascade successfully resolves 99,400 tasks (99.4 percent) and leaves 600 unresolved. Across the entire cohort, the cascade expends $992, which is $0.00992 per initiated task and $0.00998 per accepted result. By contrast, direct frontier routing expends $6,100, or $0.06289 per accepted result. Lower-tier cascade attempts must be paid for regardless of whether their candidates pass verification.
Under these deterministic execution times, the cascade averages 1.718 s per task, but tasks that fail all the way through require 6.75 s. Direct frontier routing requires 4.90 s, including verification.
Systems insight: Direct frontier dispatch costs 6.3× as much per accepted result as the cascade because 60 percent of all tasks exit at tier 1, where execution and verification costs represent a negligible fraction of a frontier call. The cascade’s higher acceptance contributes only the ratio of the two accepted counts, 99,400 to 97,000; nearly all of the gap is spend per initiated task. The cascade trades latency for cost: tasks that escalate through all tiers accumulate only $0.0044 in lower-tier tolls, but they incur 6.75 s of serialized latency compared to 4.90 s under direct dispatch. Because cost savings scale with the early exit rate, the critical architectural lever is hybrid routing: dispatching tasks predicted to fail early stages directly to the frontier tier eliminates the latency penalty for time-sensitive tasks while capturing cascade savings across the remaining workload.


The saving comes from the shape of the filter rather than from any one tier’s price. Reach falls tier by tier because accepted results exit where they are produced, while every reached gate charges its assessment whether or not its candidate passes (figure 4). The same structure explains the latency penalty: a task that escalates through every tier pays every gate’s duration in series.






Figure 4: A Gated Three-Tier Cascade: Every tier’s candidate faces the same acceptance contract, and every gate charges its assessment whether or not the candidate passes, including the final gate. Accepted results exit at the tier that produced them and only the rejected remainder escalates, so reach falls from 100,000 tasks to 12,000. The ledger compares cost per accepted result, which charges every rejected attempt to the accepted outcomes, with the separately stipulated direct frontier baseline.






Accounting ledgers record gate verdicts even when a gate is mistaken. An observed accepted result is not automatically a correct result across every operational dimension. To price downstream consequences, define \(\text{FA}\) as the event that an initiated task is accepted by the gate yet violates an independently assessed operational criterion, and define \(\FalseAcceptHarmCost\) as its additional harm or remediation cost not already captured in the execution ledger. The expected cost per initiated task including this risk term is
\[
\mathbb{E}[\HarmInclusiveTaskCost]
=\mathbb{E}[\CascadeTaskCost]+\Pr(\text{FA})\,\mathbb{E}[\FalseAcceptHarmCost\mid \text{FA}].
\]
The harm term complements the cost per accepted task rather than redefining it, with its probability evaluated over initiated tasks. If an engineering team measures a false-accept fraction solely among accepted results, they must multiply that fraction by the overall acceptance probability to recover \(\Pr(\text{FA})\); similarly, the false acceptance rate of Check precision and the candidate pool, evaluated exclusively among invalid candidates, relies on a different conditioning denominator. Catastrophic or irreparable consequences must remain constrained by strict operational authority and safety limits, regardless of their expected monetary value.
When escalating across tiers, the runtime should pass bounded diagnostic evidence and the identity of the failed candidate, treated as untrusted input, rather than forwarding the full conversational transcript. Forwarding full failure transcripts inflates prompt token spend at the expensive tier and risks biasing the stronger model to repeat earlier mistakes. The orchestration layer must also distinguish pending or unavailable assessments from definitive rejections, ensuring that transient infrastructure faults do not trigger unnecessary tier escalation. A passing assessment yields an accepted-candidate record; publication still verifies current dependencies, operational authority, and required effect authorization before applying changes.
A learned router can estimate the probability and cost of each eligible remaining policy from offline evaluation data, for example by training on preference comparisons between stronger and weaker models (Ong et al. 2024). However, training records reflect only the configurations that were actually executed; logs collected under a selective routing policy omit counterfactual outcomes for untried alternatives.5
5 Counterfactual Logs: Learning from the logs of a deployed selection policy is an off-policy causal inference challenge, studied extensively in online ad placement where a platform observes outcomes only for selected actions (Bottou et al. 2013). Estimating what an alternative policy would have achieved requires that the logging policy explored with known, nonzero probabilities: if a router never sends an easy-looking task to the frontier tier, the historical logs contain no empirical evidence about what that frontier route would have achieved. 
Bottou, Léon, Jonas Peters, Joaquin Quiñonero-Candela, Denis X. Charles, D. Max Chickering, Elon Portugaly, Dipankar Ray, Patrice Simard, and Ed Snelson. 2013. “Counterfactual Reasoning and Learning Systems: The Example of Computational Advertising.” Journal of Machine Learning Research 14: 3207–60.
Whatever the estimates come from, the router applies one decision rule. For a simple monetary objective with acceptance probabilities \(\BaselinePolicyAcceptanceProbability,\CandidatePolicyAcceptanceProbability\), expected additional costs \(\BaselinePolicyCost,\CandidatePolicyCost\), and outcome value \(\AcceptedOutcomePayoff\) (with rejected outcomes valued at zero), policy \(\CandidateRoutingPolicy\) is economically preferable whenever
\[
\AcceptedOutcomePayoff(\CandidatePolicyAcceptanceProbability-\BaselinePolicyAcceptanceProbability)>\CandidatePolicyCost-\BaselinePolicyCost.
\]
For direct routing, this decision rule compares two complete end-to-end policies before execution begins. After an initial cheap attempt fails, however, the router compares the remaining escalation policy against stopping or invoking human fallback, treating already incurred spend as a sunk cost. A cheap-then-frontier policy carries its own reach-weighted cost and compound duration, not merely the cheap model’s nominal price. In all cases, the decision rule must operate inside remaining budget, deadline, and operational authority limits; positive expected value never licenses spending past a hard limit or substitutes for explicit authorization.
System load further reshapes this comparison. Waiting for an overloaded model tier consumes wall-clock time and holds open active execution environments, such as containerized sandboxes. When the queue for an inexpensive tier backs up, routing a task directly to an idle frontier model can yield lower total cost and lower wall-clock latency, even at a higher nominal inference price. Production routers must therefore incorporate real-time queue depths and resource contention metrics into their execution-cost and completion-time estimates, linking dispatch decisions directly to underlying queuing and service capacity models.

title: 18 Agent Economics
text:
A routing policy shapes the traffic arriving at each downstream model, tool sandbox, and external API. Sizing the underlying platform requires determining whether those services can sustain the offered load within strict latency and resource budgets. Sizing an agent platform differs fundamentally from sizing traditional stateless services. While the work entering the platform arrives as an end-to-end trajectory, the operations hitting system bottlenecks consist of individual model calls, tool executions, and resource leases. Each internal tier operates with distinct arrival rates, holding intervals, and concurrency limits.


In this capacity model, each admitted trajectory executes one distinct task policy, including its internal retries and delegated calls. For a stable population with finite long-run averages, Little’s law (theorem \(\ref{thrm-05-littles-law}\)) relates the mean number of admitted trajectories present, \(\ConcurrentTrajectories\), to their admission rate \(\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\) and mean time from admission to departure, \(\mathbb{E}[\TrajectoryDuration]\):
\[\ConcurrentTrajectories = \TrajectoryAdmissionRate\mathbb{E}[\TrajectoryDuration]. \tag{4}\]


↩︎ Little’s law, and the residency tax that a tool wait imposes on KV-cache occupancy, are established in Residence time and service rate.
Applying Little’s law requires rigorous accounting of system boundaries. Trajectories rejected at admission never enter the system population, whereas admitted trajectories that eventually fail or abort contribute fully to concurrency while active. Furthermore, different subsystems hold resources over very different horizons. For instance, a trajectory suspended while waiting for human authorization or asynchronous tool execution remains resident in the orchestrator without consuming model accelerator cycles. Little’s law must therefore be applied separately at each resource boundary (sandbox leases, retained key-value cache memory, active model inference workers, and pending external API calls), with the arrival rate and holding interval that govern that boundary.


↪ Little’s law applied per resource boundary to trajectories with tool waits, contrasting live trajectories with the attention-state memory they retain, is developed in Queueing for Trajectories.
Because Little’s law governs only long-run expectations, engineering a platform for high percentiles requires analyzing the underlying occupancy distributions. Peak concurrency and latency tail buffers depend heavily on state-retention policies and burst dynamics. Under stable flow, the overall demand for model calls depends on the average number of invocations per admitted trajectory, including internal retries, reflection loops, and delegated sub-agent calls: \(\ArrivalRate=\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\mathbb{E}[\TrajectoryCallCount]\). In practice, these model invocations rarely arrive as smooth Poisson streams. When an agent cohort encounters a shared external bottleneck or completes a parallel tool phase simultaneously, downstream inference clusters experience severe arrival bursts.
Task acceptance couples operational demand directly to the economic balance sheet. Delivering accepted tasks at goodput \(\TrajectoryGoodput\) when only an acceptance fraction \(\AcceptanceFraction\) of admitted tasks succeeds requires the platform to admit
\[\TrajectoryAdmissionRate=\frac{\TrajectoryGoodput}{\AcceptanceFraction},
\qquad
\ServingUtilization(\AcceptanceFraction)=\frac{\TrajectoryGoodput\,\mathbb{E}[\TrajectoryCallCount]}{\AcceptanceFraction\,\WorkerCount\ServiceRate}\]
for a pool of \(\WorkerCount\) model workers, each completing \(\ServiceRate\) calls per unit time; \(\ServingUtilization\) is then the fraction of the pool’s call capacity the admitted trajectories demand. The trajectory goodput \(\TrajectoryGoodput\) is the primary deliverable of the platform; failed or rejected tasks consume scarce cluster capacity without producing realized value.

Definition 18.3: Trajectory goodput
Trajectory goodput is the number of distinct tasks accepted under a declared contract per unit of elapsed observation time.

Significance: It represents the core throughput metric for sizing an agent platform. At acceptance fraction \(\AcceptanceFraction\), every unit of goodput requires admitting \(1/\AcceptanceFraction\) trajectories, so acceptance governs both the spending multiplier in effective cost \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) and the offered server load \(\ServingUtilization(\AcceptanceFraction)\).
Distinction: Token, call, and raw trajectory throughput measure computational work performed; trajectory goodput isolates accepted outcomes. Similarly, goodput per dollar divides the accepted count by total cost rather than elapsed observation time.
Common pitfall: Counting redundant retries on a single task, or runs that complete outside the declared contract, as incremental goodput.



Which resource binds first under steady-state load is a question for a concrete fleet sized from its trajectory admission rate.

Napkin Math 18.7: One arrival rate, different resource demandsProblem: A hypothetical fleet has a trajectory admission rate of 1 per minute; an admitted trajectory remains present for 20 minutes on average. It makes 60 calls on average, each consuming 30,000 quota-accounted tokens on average across calls. In this scenario the provider counts input and output tokens, including cached input, toward a shared token-rate allowance of 2,000,000 tokens per minute. What mean concurrency and token demand does this imply?
Math: Apply equation 4 to admitted trajectories, and multiply the long-run call rate by mean tokens per call. The token average is call-weighted, not the unweighted mean of per-task averages.
Result: Mean trajectory concurrency is 20, while the mean call arrival rate is 60 calls per minute. The mean token demand is 1,800,000 per trajectory, giving a token rate of 1,800,000 tokens per minute and using 90 percent of the allowance. The quota alone permits a trajectory admission rate of at most 1.11 per minute at this workload mix in the long run.
Systems insight: The token quota sets the admission ceiling calculated here; concurrency, memory, sandbox, reviewer, and model-service limits still require their own checks. Holding goodput fixed, admissions scale as \(1/\AcceptanceFraction\), so a relative drop in acceptance of 10 percent pushes mean demand to the full allowance, leaving no headroom for bursts. A model or prompt change that lowers acceptance is therefore also a capacity change. Analyzing burst fit, deadline feasibility, and sandbox residency requires validating the quota’s actual window semantics against production traces on top of these steady-state means.


Upstream provider quotas count requests, tokens, or concurrent connections across sliding windows of varying duration, and admission control must match the specific contract. For example, while cached input tokens often receive billing discounts, providers typically count cached and uncached tokens equally against rate limits, leaving the throughput ceiling unchanged. Within the platform, reserving capacity for active trajectories can prevent wasted partial work. Such admission and scheduling decisions must depend on forward-looking attributes: remaining resource requirements, deadlines, tenant fairness, and expected task value. Money already spent is a sunk cost and provides no justification on its own for prioritizing a trajectory.



In a shared platform, an agent’s model calls compete in a serving pool alongside every other active trajectory. If the serving cluster runs at 70 percent utilization, pushing utilization to 90 percent lowers the amortized hardware cost per call. The resulting throughput gains appear immediately on the infrastructure bill. The accompanying queue delays do not, because waiting time accumulates silently across every serial step of an active trajectory while sandboxes, execution environments, and attention state remain held.
The simplest model that quantifies this trade-off is a nonpreemptive, first-come-first-served queue fed by a stationary renewal stream. Interarrival times are independent and identically distributed with mean \(1/\ArrivalRate\), and service times \(\RequestServiceTime\) are independent and identically distributed with finite variance. The sequences are mutually independent, with no batching, priority preemption, abandonment, or feedback. Let \(\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2\) and \(\ServiceTimeVariationCoefficient^2\) denote the squared coefficients of variation6 (variance divided by squared mean) of interarrival and service times, and let \(\ServingUtilization=\ArrivalRate\mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime]<1\) denote server utilization.
6 Squared Coefficient of Variation: The scale-free measure of burstiness, defined as \(\IntervalVariationCoefficient^2 = \IntervalStandardDeviation^2 / \IntervalMean^2\). Exponential interarrival or service times, characteristic of a Poisson stream, have a squared coefficient of variation of exactly one, whereas perfectly periodic events yield zero. Values exceeding one describe arrivals and service durations burstier than Poisson, which is the standard profile for agent traffic arriving in cohorts with divergent prompt lengths.7 Heavy Traffic: Kingman’s 1961 note showed that as load approaches saturation (\(\ServingUtilization \to 1\)), the steady-state waiting-time distribution of the single-server queue, appropriately normalized, converges to an exponential distribution (Kingman 1961). This property extends beyond the mean: near saturation, the entire waiting-time distribution, and with it every tail percentile, stretches by the factor \(\ServingUtilization/(1-\ServingUtilization)\), so percentile-based latency targets degrade just as rapidly as the mean.
Kingman, John Frank Charles. 1961. “The Single Server Queue in Heavy Traffic.” Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 57 (4): 902–4. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100036094.
For this single-server system, the Kingman approximation7 (Kingman 1961) estimates the mean waiting time before service begins:
\[\mathbb{E}[\RequestQueueTime] \approx \frac{\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2+\ServiceTimeVariationCoefficient^2}{2}\frac{\ServingUtilization}{1-\ServingUtilization}\mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime]. \tag{5}\]



Near saturation, a little more utilization buys a lot more waiting.

Boon, Marko A. A., Augustus J. E. M. Janssen, and Johan S. H. van Leeuwaarden. 2023. “Heavy-Traffic Single-Server Queues and the Transform Method.” Indagationes Mathematicae 34 (5): 1014–37. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.indag.2023.02.004.
The factor \(\ServingUtilization/(1-\ServingUtilization)\) explains why queueing delays escalate steeply near full utilization. Equation 5 is a heavy-traffic approximation to the mean rather than an exact expectation or a percentile; Heavy-tailed queueing theory derives the corresponding Pollaczek–Khinchine waiting-time formula under general service distributions, and Boon et al. (2023) provides formal derivations and error bounds. Capturing correlated agent bursts, dynamic continuous batching, worker pools, and shared quotas requires queueing networks or trace-driven discrete-event simulations. Crucially, substituting an aggregate cluster service rate into a single-server formula does not turn it into a valid multi-server model. Two workable estimates remain for a pool. When a dispatcher pins each trajectory to one endpoint, every endpoint is its own single-server queue fed by its share of the arrivals, and equation 5 applies per endpoint. When workers share one queue, a trace-driven simulation of the pool, or the multi-server models in the further reading, replaces the single-server estimate.

Napkin Math 18.8: Pricing mean queue delayProblem: In the hypothetical single-server model above, mean service takes 1 second, arrival variability \(\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2\) is 2, and service variability \(\ServiceTimeVariationCoefficient^2\) is 4. A waiting call holds resources costing $0.002 per second. How do estimated mean wait and holding cost change between 70 percent and 90 percent utilization?
Math: Apply equation 5, then multiply mean wait by the stated linear holding rate. The rate covers only resources retained during the queue interval, excluding model service, tool execution, and any separate valuation of user delay.
Result: Estimated mean wait rises from 7 seconds to 27 seconds, and the corresponding holding charge rises from $0.014 to $0.054 per call.
Systems insight: Moving from 70 percent to 90 percent utilization buys 28.6 percent more throughput from the same server, but it multiplies mean wait by 3.9× because the \(\ServingUtilization/(1-\ServingUtilization)\) factor dominates near saturation. While the holding charge for an isolated call appears small, this delay compounds across every serial step of an agent trajectory. Halving the variability term \((\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2+\ServiceTimeVariationCoefficient^2)/2\), for example by smoothing bursty admissions or standardizing prompt lengths, halves the wait at any utilization and provides a cost-effective lever before purchasing reserve capacity. Sizing that reserve ultimately depends on enforcing tail latency targets at measured percentiles.





A one-in-a-hundred delay per call becomes routine across a long trajectory.
Mean metrics also obscure how tail latency compounds across multi-step execution. If each of \(\SerialCallCount\) serial calls independently exceeds its 99th-percentile latency with probability \(\CallTailProbability\), the trajectory encounters at least one such delay with probability \(1-(1-\CallTailProbability)^\SerialCallCount\), which is the horizon compounding of equation 1.1 applied to latency rather than to correctness. For a trajectory of 30 serial calls, each with tail probability 0.01, the probability of experiencing at least one tail delay reaches 0.26. This is the probability of encountering a per-call tail event, not the probability of missing a trajectory deadline; the latter requires the complete duration distribution and the declared deadline. Sizing a fleet solely for acceptable per-call latency can therefore conceal end-to-end delays. This dynamic is the serial equivalent of the fan-out straggler problem in distributed systems (Dean and Barroso 2013). Correlated delays, such as a shared queue that remains backlogged across successive steps, alter the exact probability but preserve the core operational lesson: provision and schedule against trajectory-level percentiles rather than per-call means (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-goodput}\)).


↩︎ The parallel counterpart, an all-results barrier exposed to fan-out stragglers, is established in Hedged requests and speculative work.
Integrating queueing delays completes the model-routing framework of section 18.5. A dynamic router compares eligible remaining paths, each priced with its queue and service delays, retained-resource costs, verification checks, and possible escalations, under an identical acceptance contract. Because dispatching decisions alter the arrival rates that produced the initial delay estimates, the router must refresh queue projections whenever traffic shifts. Separating interactive and batch pools, or enforcing priority scheduling, protects latency-bound work at a quantifiable cost in fairness and cluster utilization.



When an agent application’s token consumption becomes sustained and predictable, engineering teams face a fundamental deployment choice: continue paying on demand via per-token APIs or provision private infrastructure. Consider a dedicated deployment incurring a fixed infrastructure expense of $28 per hour plus $2 per million output tokens in marginal operating costs. Such private infrastructure represents dedicated capacity, a financial commitment paid continuously regardless of whether accelerators are busy or idle. The economic decision therefore turns entirely on sustained utilization.8 This comparison requires a strictly matched workload: equivalent task capability, acceptance criteria, data-privacy constraints, and feasible tail latency under representative traffic mixtures. A shared model architecture or nominal token rate alone does not establish equivalence.
8 Pay-as-You-Go Economics: Mirroring the foundational economic argument for cloud computing, renting capacity on demand can cost less than owning dedicated infrastructure even at a higher hourly rate, because owned capacity must be financed across its average utilization while utility pricing shifts provisioning risk to the provider (Armbrust et al. 2010). A per-token API carries that logic to its finest granularity. Consequently, the utilization break-even point \(\BreakEvenUtilization\) in equation 6, rather than raw token list price alone, dictates the cost-optimal decision. 
Armbrust, Michael, Armando Fox, Rean Griffith, Anthony D. Joseph, Randy Katz, Andy Konwinski, Gunho Lee, et al. 2010. “A View of Cloud Computing.” Communications of the ACM 53 (4): 50–58. https://doi.org/10.1145/1721654.1721672.
Fix the workload’s input/output token ratio and prompt-cache hit rate. Let \(\EffectiveApiOutputTokenPrice\) denote the effective API charge per output token including its associated input tokens, \(\DedicatedVariableTokenCost\) the variable cost per output token on dedicated capacity, and \(\DedicatedHourlyFixedCost\) the complete hourly fixed cost of the private deployment, including amortized hardware leases, provisioned failover headroom, and operational maintenance. Shared application costs cancel only when genuinely identical across both options; differential tool, verification, network egress, or support fees must enter the balance sheet. Let \(\FeasibleOutputTokenRate\) denote the measured feasible output token generation rate (in tokens per second) under the target latency objective, a token rate distinct from the per-worker call rate \(\ServiceRate\) of the capacity model. Let \(\DeliveredCapacityFraction\) represent the fraction of that reference capacity the workload actually delivers. Unlike the queueing utilization \(\ServingUtilization\), which measures offered load against raw service capacity, \(\DeliveredCapacityFraction\) is measured against a rate already chosen to meet the latency target, so \(\DeliveredCapacityFraction=1\) still meets that target by construction. In one hour, the system produces \(3600\FeasibleOutputTokenRate \DeliveredCapacityFraction\) output tokens, costing \(3600\FeasibleOutputTokenRate \DeliveredCapacityFraction\,\EffectiveApiOutputTokenPrice\) via a pay-as-you-go API and \(\DedicatedHourlyFixedCost+3600\FeasibleOutputTokenRate \DeliveredCapacityFraction\,\DedicatedVariableTokenCost\) on dedicated hardware. When \(\EffectiveApiOutputTokenPrice>\DedicatedVariableTokenCost\), the two expenditure curves cross at the break-even utilization
\[\BreakEvenUtilization = \frac{\DedicatedHourlyFixedCost}{3600\FeasibleOutputTokenRate(\EffectiveApiOutputTokenPrice-\DedicatedVariableTokenCost)}. \tag{6}\]



Owned capacity wins only above the load that repays its fixed cost.
If \(\BreakEvenUtilization>1\), the dedicated deployment cannot break even within its physical capacity envelope; if \(\EffectiveApiOutputTokenPrice\le \DedicatedVariableTokenCost\) while \(\DedicatedHourlyFixedCost>0\), self-hosting remains permanently more expensive. Execution deadlines and concurrency limits must be verified separately at the target operating point.

Napkin Math 18.9: Pricing idle capacity and cached inputProblem: Assume a hypothetical matched-capability workload uses 5 input tokens per output token, with 80 percent of inputs billed at the cached rate. API prices per million tokens are $3 for uncached input, $0.3 for cached input, and $15 for output. A dedicated deployment costs $28 per hour for its provisioned capacity and operations, plus $2 per million output tokens for differential variable costs. Its feasible reference output rate is 1,200 tokens/s under the same mix, reserve policy, and latency target. Which alternative costs less at 52 percent of that rate?
Math: Weight the two input prices by their billed volume fractions, then incorporate associated input costs into \(\EffectiveApiOutputTokenPrice\). Apply equation 6. Both options are feasible at this operating point, and shared tool, evaluation, and application costs cancel.
Result: Weighted input costs $0.84 per million input tokens. Factoring in associated inputs, the API costs $19.2 per million output tokens. The cost crossing occurs at 37.7 percent of reference capacity. At the stated load, generating 2,246,400 output tokens per hour costs $43.13 through the API vs. $32.49 on dedicated capacity, saving $10.64 per hour.
Systems insight: The economic break-even threshold shifts directly with the API’s effective token price. Without cached input, the same workload would cross at 23.1 percent of reference capacity instead of 37.7 percent. Aggressive prefix caching by API providers erodes the economic incentive to own capacity. Teams should commit to dedicated capacity only when sustained production load reliably exceeds \(\BreakEvenUtilization\) with the headroom demanded by latency targets. Operating below the crossing wastes capital on idle silicon, while owning hardware places queueing congestion, node failures, and capacity management entirely on internal engineering teams.



Checkpoint 18.2: Check the capacity boundary
Before bounding what an individual trajectory may spend, evaluate the platform capacity model:

Residence vs. service: Why can mean trajectory concurrency remain high while model-worker accelerator occupancy is low?
Queue headroom: With the variability modeled in notebook 18.8, what utilization keeps the estimated mean wait below one mean service time? How does that headroom shift if arrivals come in correlated cohorts?
Acceptance and load: If a model change lowers acceptance while goodput is held fixed, how does offered load \(\ServingUtilization(\AcceptanceFraction)\) scale, and at what relative drop does the fleet in notebook 18.7 exhaust its token quota?
Cache and crossing: Why does cached-input pricing alter the dedicated vs. API break-even crossing without changing a provider’s token-rate quota?



Capacity planning sizes the collective infrastructure required to sustain admitted workload streams. It says nothing about how much any one trajectory, or the tree of children it delegates to, may spend. That bound needs a different mechanism, a transactional admission and settlement ledger.

title: 18 Agent Economics
text:
When a coordinator admits concurrent sub-agents or child tasks, simple balance checks collapse under race conditions. If two children inspect the remaining free balance simultaneously before either records a reservation, both admission checks succeed, yet their combined liability immediately breaches the authorized task budget. Task cancellation introduces a second, equally perilous concurrency bug: returning a stopped child’s allocation to the free pool while its remote service call remains billable allows another worker to spend funds that are already committed to third-party infrastructure. The harness already solved this for one trajectory. Its bounded-liability admission reserves an operation’s maximum charge before dispatch and releases it only at settlement (Reservation and settlement). Trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\)) requires the same invariant to hold when the allowance is split across children, and to stay conserved across concurrent dispatch, node crashes, and late settlement.


Let \(\LedgerSettledCharges(\LedgerEvaluationTime)\) denote gross charges settled into a task’s ledger at time \(\LedgerEvaluationTime\) and \(\LedgerReservedFunds(\LedgerEvaluationTime)\) the funds withheld there for outstanding liabilities, delegated allocations, and protected finalization. A task with authorized budget \(\CostCeiling\) maintains the fundamental invariant
\[\LedgerSettledCharges(\LedgerEvaluationTime)+\LedgerReservedFunds(\LedgerEvaluationTime)\le \CostCeiling.\]
Before admitting any billable operation, the runtime must reserve a strict upper bound \(\OperationChargeBound\) on its maximum possible charge, rather than relying on an expected or average cost. This bound must cover every billing category governed by the provider’s rate schedule. For a foundation model API call, the reservation must account for the prompt token length, cached prefix rates, and the strictly enforced maximum completion token limit across all applicable categories (including hidden reasoning tokens). Similarly, invoking an external tool, provisioning a sandbox container, or renting cloud infrastructure requires enforced caps on execution wall-clock time, network data volume, and total per-call service fees.
Stopping an operation also incurs teardown charges; required cleanup routines and graceful shutdowns must have reserved funds set aside in advance. Relying on a client-side host timeout or an estimated mean cost provides no protection: if an external service continues executing and billing after the client disconnects, the task’s liabilities drift unchecked. Under a strict hard-ceiling policy, the runtime must reject any operation that lacks an enforceable upper bound or substitute a bounded alternative; accepting soft thresholds that permit arbitrary overshoot represents a fundamentally different, weaker operational contract.
Budget enforcement also depends on complete mediation, applied here to money: every billable interaction must pass through the accounting gateway. If worker nodes hold shared credentials that bypass the reservation gate, or if unmonitored retry loops dispatch billable requests off the books, the ledger’s guarantees collapse. Prompt caching and tiered volume discounts present a related operational subtlety: while cache hits reduce final settlement charges, they can reduce the upfront reservation \(\OperationChargeBound\) only if the provider contractually guarantees the discount prior to request dispatch. If a cache miss remains possible, the runtime must withhold the full un-discounted rate.


↩︎ Complete mediation, the requirement that every access pass through one checking point, is established for tool calls in Complete mediation.
The ledger tracks gross liabilities rather than net cash flows. Releasing an unspent reservation simply restores permission to spend money that was never actually charged. Subsequent provider credits, reconciliations, or post-hoc refunds are recorded as separate external adjustments that leave gross spending and historical authorizations intact. Crucially, fresh spending capacity enters the system only through an operator’s explicit budget grant, never through automatic replenishment from error recoveries or the speculative promise of a newly spawned candidate branch.



Each node \(\LedgerNodeIndex\) maintains the same account structure in a runtime-owned ledger, tracking its allocation \({\CostCeiling}_k\), settled gross charges \(\LedgerSettledCharges_k\), reservations \(\LedgerReservedFunds_k\), and free balance \(\LedgerFreeBalance_k\). The local conservation rule requires
\[{\CostCeiling}_k=\LedgerSettledCharges_k+\LedgerReservedFunds_k+\LedgerFreeBalance_k,\qquad \LedgerSettledCharges_k,\LedgerReservedFunds_k,\LedgerFreeBalance_k\ge0.\]
A budget reservation,9 the harness’s bounded-liability reservation applied at node \(\LedgerNodeIndex\), removes funds from the free balance \(\LedgerFreeBalance_k\) before an operation can be dispatched. Multi-agent coordination already partitions consumable budgets into nested subledgers; what this section adds is the settlement side, how a delegated allocation is counted, when it may be released, and what happens when a bill arrives late or exceeds its bound. In a hierarchical agent tree, delegating an allocation \(\DelegatedAllocationAmount\) to a child node withholds those funds in the parent’s reservation pool \(\ParentReservedFunds\) while the child manages them within its own local ledger (\(\ChildBudgetAllocation = \ChildFreeBalance = \DelegatedAllocationAmount\)). The parent’s reservation and the child’s entire ledger thus represent the exact same capital backing viewed from two different levels of abstraction. Naively summing reserved balances across all nodes in the hierarchy would double-count the delegated capital. Conversely, inspecting only the parent’s settled charges \(\ParentSettledCharges\) omits active charges still accumulating in open child accounts. Fleet-wide reporting attributes each charge exactly once through its unique operation record, while the tree hierarchy tracks which branch holds the authority to back it.
9 Escrow at Every Node: The escrow method behind bounded-liability admission (Reservation and settlement) applies unchanged at each node of a delegation tree. Admission durably withholds the backing before dispatch; settlement records the charge and releases the unused backing only upon authenticated finality. That evidence can arrive long after the process that made the request has stopped.The state transitions summarized in table 4 are strictly atomic with respect to competing admissions and control-plane changes. Because spending represents an irreversible external commitment, ledger update records must durably survive the failure domain specified in Durable Intent Before Dispatch before any billable request leaves the runtime. If a worker node crashes, a replacement coordinator reconstructs active reservations directly from this write-ahead log rather than resetting balances because the former worker disappeared. As in multi-agent delegation, budget differs from permission because it is consumed. A child’s read grant leaves the parent’s read access intact, whereas a delegated allocation withholds funds the parent could otherwise spend, which is why the ledger must track it as a reservation.


↩︎ Shared permissions, partitioned consumable budgets, and nested subledgers under delegation are established in Attenuated grants and split allowances.



Table 4: Conserved budget transitions: Each update preserves the allocated total. Closure requires financial settlement, not merely a stopped local process.

Current guards pass; \(\OperationChargeBound\le \LedgerFreeBalance_k\)

Every budget reservation is tied to a unique compound identifier binding the task, logical operation, transport attempt number, pricing tier, and cost bound \(\OperationChargeBound\). When downstream work finishes, settlement requires authenticated usage receipts evaluated against a durable settlement identity, the idempotency key under which the definitive charge posts to the ledger. It is settlement before retry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}\)) applied to money. The operation and attempt identifiers that let a tool call be retried without duplicating its effect also let a bill be redelivered without duplicating its charge. If network retries cause the provider to deliver identical billing evidence multiple times, the runtime applies the state transition at most once, verifying that repeated deliveries contain identical payloads. A conflicting payload under an existing settlement identity indicates a reconciliation fault, which the runtime must neither blindly overwrite nor silently ignore. When long-running services report intermediate consumption, the runtime can incrementally move settled amounts into \(\LedgerSettledCharges_k\) while continuing to withhold a bound on remaining liabilities; it releases the reservation entirely only upon definitive finality. Deduplicating a remote side effect at an API endpoint and deduplicating an internal financial ledger record serve two distinct engineering contracts.


↩︎ Operation and attempt identifiers, which let a retried tool call be recognized as the same logical operation, are established in Operation identity and endpoint contracts.
If an external service reports a charge that exceeds its initial reservation (\(\SettledOperationCharge > \OperationChargeBound\)), the system’s foundational cost invariant has failed. Silently clamping the reported charge to \(\OperationChargeBound\) or allowing the free balance \(\LedgerFreeBalance_k\) to drop below zero would conceal a critical safety failure. Instead, the runtime immediately flags the discrepancy, halts further admissions within the affected subtree, and escalates the incident for reconciliation. Until an administrator or reconciliation procedure resolves the dispute, the system’s strict financial guarantee is temporarily suspended. Provided cost bounds remain valid, admissions execute atomically, and settlements are strictly deduplicated, every state transition preserves non-negative balances (\(\LedgerSettledCharges_k, \LedgerReservedFunds_k, \LedgerFreeBalance_k \ge 0\)) and guarantees that no child sub-agent can spend outside its allocated backing.



The cancellation boundary established in Cancellation context trees immediately prevents a sub-agent from launching new billable operations once control is revoked. However, remote service termination and billing reconciliation operate asynchronously. Even after a local worker halts, outstanding HTTP requests, remote inference batches, or detached cloud instances may continue executing until upstream timeouts trigger or cancellation signals propagate. Consequently, the child’s allocation cannot simply be returned to the parent pool at the moment of local termination; it must remain reserved until all remote obligations settle. If maintaining the inactive child’s ledger in memory is inefficient, the runtime can execute a durable ledger transfer, handing over all known charges, outstanding reservations, and genuinely unencumbered funds to a centralized settlement coordinator. This transfer must preserve the complete lineage of operation identities and backing reservations across all descendants. At no point during the handover may an ownership gap exist where funds could be double-released or where an in-flight liability is left unbacked.
Graceful teardown also requires dedicated resources. Protected finalization routines, such as querying the status of remote jobs, gathering debug telemetry, or shutting down cloud sandboxes, must operate from an isolated sub-allocation within the original budget, the finalization reserve of the harness’s admission test applied at each node. This finalization allowance permits essential status queries after ordinary task admission has closed, without reopening general spending authority. When generating accounting reports across a cutoff boundary, the runtime rigorously distinguishes between settled historical charges and active liabilities held in reserve.
The notebook below traces this distinction for a canceled child sub-agent that receives an unexpected, delayed invoice from an external provider.

Napkin Math 18.10: A canceled child with a late billProblem: A hypothetical repair has a $5 budget. Its planning charge has settled at $0.042, and it allocates $1.20 to trace analysis and $2.50 to fuzzing. The trace child closes with a final charge of $0.38. The fuzzing child has settled $0.85 and holds $1 for a remote operation when its local executor confirms termination. No further child work is admitted. The remote operation later terminates with a final additional bill of $0.70. All other charges and required finalization are included in these records, and neither child has descendants. When can the root release the fuzzing allocation?
Math: The entire child allocation remains reserved at the root until its account closes. Table 5 follows the root’s balances under the same conservation rule throughout.

At local termination, the fuzzing ledger has $0.65 free, but its remote reservation remains outstanding. Final settlement releases the unused part of that reservation, leaving $0.95 to return when the child closes. Re-delivery of the same final billing record changes none of these balances.
Systems insight: A premature release upon local process termination would have returned $1.65 (the allocation minus already-settled charges), even though only $0.65 was truly unencumbered. The subsequent $0.70 bill would then have landed on funds already committed to another child task. The governing invariant upon cancellation is strict: release at most the allocation minus settled charges minus the enforceable upper bound on outstanding work, and return the remainder only as each remote operation reaches final settlement. Financial safety is only as reliable as those upper bounds and the completeness of the ledger records.


The conservation rule shows up as bars of equal length: at every boundary of table 5, funds move among settled, reserved, and free without leaving the root’s budget, and the root’s reservation stays fixed from the fuzzing child’s local stop until its late bill settles (figure 5).






Figure 5: Conservation Across a Canceled Child: The root’s balances at each boundary of table 5, drawn as bars of equal length that always sum to the same budget, with the initial reservation split between the trace and fuzzing children. Expanded beneath the stopped row, the fuzzing child’s own ledger at local stop holds settled charges, a pending remote reservation, and free balance, while the root still sees the whole allocation as reserved. Local stopping leaves the root’s reservation unchanged; only settlement of the late bill moves the fuzzing allocation into settled and free balances.






Even when a cumulative task budget is strictly conserved, an overall ceiling cannot prevent damaging expenditure spikes. If an unconstrained agent launches dozens of model calls concurrently, it can burn through its entire allocation in seconds. A retrospective spending alarm monitors the burn rate by dividing the gross charges settled over a trailing window of duration \(\SpendingWindowDuration\) by \(\SpendingWindowDuration\). However, because external billing is often delayed, a retrospective alarm can stay deceptively quiet while expensive requests are in flight, only to spike violently after execution has already halted. While retrospective alarms are useful for triggering administrative alerts or throttling subsequent work, they act after the fact: the capital they measure has already been spent.
To prevent rapid budget exhaustion, the runtime must enforce proactive admission limits that evaluate new financial commitments, in the form of reservations, before dispatch. For a spending rate limit permitting at most \(\WindowSpendingLimit\) in new liabilities over any trailing window of duration \(\SpendingWindowDuration\), a robust admission policy enforces
\[\sum_{i:\,t-\SpendingWindowDuration<t_i\le t}\OperationChargeBound_i\le \WindowSpendingLimit,\]
where \(\TimeInstant_i\) is the admission timestamp and \(\OperationChargeBound_i\) is the bounded charge of each billable operation.10 Every prospective admission atomically validates both this sliding-window limit and the cumulative ledger balance. This window constraint applies across all child tasks within the coordinator’s scope, rather than granting a fresh window allowance to every newly spawned worker. Delegating an allocation down the agent tree is an internal balance partition, not a newly admitted billable dispatch. Furthermore, retaining \(\OperationChargeBound_i\) in the window calculation until its admission timestamp ages out prevents a rapid sequence of fast-completing calls from triggering an unbounded burst. This policy guarantees a strict upper bound on committed work over the interval, regardless of when external providers finish processing requests or transmit final invoices.
10 Trailing Window vs. Token Bucket: Standard network and API rate limiters often employ token buckets, which permit an initial burst equal to the bucket capacity followed by a steady refill rate; over a short interval \(\FiniteChange \TimeInstant\), maximum consumption can reach capacity plus rate times \(\FiniteChange \TimeInstant\). In contrast, the trailing-window sum strictly caps committed liabilities across every continuous window of duration \(\SpendingWindowDuration\) at \(\WindowSpendingLimit\), irrespective of burst shape, at the modest implementation cost of retaining timestamped admission records until they age out of the window.Rate-limiting policies must also protect capacity and budget for mandatory finalization routines. If an aggressive rate limiter blocks all outgoing traffic during a spending spike, it can starve the very cancellation and status queries required to terminate running tasks and settle outstanding reservations. Dedicating isolated execution lanes or explicit finalization allowances within the accounting policy prevents this deadlock. Furthermore, completing a diagnostic probe or clearing an operational alarm must never prematurely release funds held for unrelated active reservations.
When an agent enters a non-converging loop, evidenced by repeated execution failures or unvarying candidate artifacts, the runtime triggers a spending hold under its semantic watchdog policies. This intervention blocks new ordinary billable work before runaway iterations exhaust the task budget; already-dispatched work may continue accruing charges within its reserved bounds. The runtime enforces the designated cancellation or escalation workflow while preserving all outstanding liabilities on the ledger. Evaluating whether completed work meets task requirements remains the responsibility of the domain acceptance contract, rather than the spending controller.


↩︎ Semantic watchdogs, which detect a non-converging loop from its progress evidence and place the trajectory in an admission hold, are established in Semantic Watchdogs.
Budget reservations turn spending governance from after-the-fact telemetry into an enforceable contract under declared pricing and failure models. They decide what a design may spend, not whether it is worth spending on. With cost, latency, and residual liabilities bounded, the remaining choice is which design delivers enough accepted work for its expense: a deterministic workflow, a single foundation model invocation, a bounded loop, or a delegated tree of agents.

title: 18 Agent Economics
text:
A spending bound makes a proposed architecture admissible under its budget, but the economic ledger determines whether it is worth deploying. When choosing among deterministic code, a fixed model-assisted workflow, a bounded loop, and multi-agent delegation, system architects often frame the decision as an ideological debate between programmatic control and model autonomy. In production systems engineering, however, this decision is fundamentally an empirical optimization problem governed by an acceptance contract. The engineering objective comes first: minimizing expected financial cost subject to a completion requirement selects a fundamentally different architecture than minimizing tail latency or deadline misses under a spending ceiling.


Architectural alternatives differ primarily in who selects the next operation, as table 6 summarizes, but control authority alone reveals little about execution cost, end-to-end latency, or permitted environmental side effects. A sprawling fixed workflow that unconditionally issues calls to a large frontier model can easily cost more than an adaptive, bounded loop that resolves simple instances on its first turn with a lightweight model. Similarly, executing parallel delegated trajectories can slash wall-clock time while dramatically inflating total token consumption. Furthermore, autonomy is orthogonal to authorization: a single model call proposing a database deletion requires the exact same authorization and safety checks as an iterative agentic loop.


↩︎ Foundational trade-offs between fixed workflows and model-directed loops are established in Workflows vs. model-directed loops.



Table 6: Architecture Choices Under One Task Contract: The control structure changes the work to account for, not the required acceptance evidence or authorized effects.
