Every design can carry state, require crash recovery, and demand substantive verification. A rigorous comparison therefore holds the acceptance contract strictly constant across candidate designs. Verification is neither relaxed for a single model call nor tightened for an agentic loop or a delegated system.



The H·S·A exposures that have organized this book, together with the closure evidence the contract demands, do not dictate an architecture. They name the obligations each candidate design must pay for:

Horizon: A longer execution horizon expands the trajectory space, multiplying opportunities for resource consumption, transient network faults, and compounding drift. In an economic ledger, these costs are priced not by hypothetical maximum depth, but by the expected distribution of steps that the runtime policy actually reaches.
State: State incurs retrieval overhead, storage retention, consistency maintenance, and checkpoint recovery mechanisms wherever it resides. An adaptive loop justifies this stateful overhead only when fresh observations yield updates that substantially improve downstream decisions, generating enough value to repay their operational cost.
Authority: The scope of authority determines which operations demand formal admission, evidence collection, and two-phase settlement. Irreversible actions, such as modifying financial records, sending customer emails, or deleting cloud infrastructure, require an explicit authorization and risk policy, often incorporating cryptographic audit trails or human approval gates. Any unresolved effect or outstanding external reservation remains an open liability on the account, regardless of the expected inference bill.
Closure evidence: Closure evidence governs what repeated attempts can actually establish. An automated, executable check, such as a compiler, test suite, or schema validator, supplies fast, inexpensive, and highly specific feedback. The economic value of this feedback depends directly on the test harness coverage and its false-acceptance rate. When no automated check exists, an agent must seek closure through additional observations, queries to independent data sources, or escalation to human review. Human review, however, introduces its own substantial hourly costs, queueing delays, and error rates. Crucially, routing an ambiguous task to a person does not count as completing it; the task counts as completed only when the human reviewer finishes the work and fulfills the acceptance contract.




Consider an automated dependency-upgrade service. The engineering team can deploy a deterministic rule-based rewriter, a single frontier model call, or a smaller, cheaper model that retries for up to three turns within a bounded loop before escalating failed tickets to a human engineer. The deterministic rewriter and the single model call each exhibit a single static acceptance rate. In contrast, the loop’s overall acceptance rate and aggregate spend depend on the exact distribution of turns it reaches before stopping.
For a bounded loop, let \(\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_t\) denote the probability that turn \(\TurnIndex\) produces an accepted candidate, conditional on reaching turn \(\TurnIndex\) after rejections on all preceding turns. Assuming that every reached turn undergoes a complete acceptance assessment, that execution halts immediately upon acceptance, and that the runtime enforces a hard budget of \(\TrajectoryTurnLimit\) turns, the cumulative automated acceptance probability is:
\[\LoopAcceptanceProbability(\TrajectoryTurnLimit) = 1 - \prod_{t=1}^{\TrajectoryTurnLimit} (1 - \StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_t) \tag{7}\]
As with model cascading, this formulation applies the probability chain rule rather than assuming independence across turns. The system reaches turn \(\TurnIndex\) with probability \(\StageReachProbability_t=\prod_{j<t}(1-\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_j)\), where \(\StageReachProbability_1=1\). If \(\LoopTurnCost_t\) represents the comprehensive cost of turn \(\TurnIndex\) (model inference, tool execution, sandbox lease duration, and the assessment check), the expected automated cost per incoming ticket is \(\sum_{t=1}^{\TrajectoryTurnLimit} \StageReachProbability_t \LoopTurnCost_t\). When turns incur an identical per-turn cost \(\UniformLoopTurnCost\), this expectation simplifies to \(\UniformLoopTurnCost \sum_{t=1}^{\TrajectoryTurnLimit} \StageReachProbability_t\), where \(\sum_{t=1}^{\TrajectoryTurnLimit} \StageReachProbability_t\) is the expected number of executed turns. Operational exceptions, such as test harness outages or runtime abandonment triggered by safety filters, introduce distinct terminal states that must be accounted for as separate branches rather than conflated with normal test failures.
Accounting becomes more complex when human escalation enters the operational policy. Suppose an automated tier achieves acceptance probability \(\AttemptPassProbability\) at expected cost \(\MeanAttemptCost\), and routes every rejected ticket to a human fallback workflow that costs \(\HumanFallbackCost\) and achieves conditional resolution probability \(\HumanResolutionProbability\). The expected total expenditure per incoming ticket is \(\MeanAttemptCost+(1-\AttemptPassProbability)\HumanFallbackCost\), while the combined resolution probability across automated and human tiers is \(\AttemptPassProbability+(1-\AttemptPassProbability)\HumanResolutionProbability\). Dividing expected spend by combined resolution yields the true cost per resolved ticket under the end-to-end policy: \[\frac{\MeanAttemptCost + (1 - \AttemptPassProbability) \HumanFallbackCost}{\AttemptPassProbability + (1 - \AttemptPassProbability) \HumanResolutionProbability}\] In contrast, the isolated metric \(\MeanAttemptCost/\AttemptPassProbability\) captures only the cost per automated acceptance. Conflating these two metrics obscures the true cost structure of the system, particularly when automated acceptance is low. Neither ratio is well-defined when its respective denominator reaches zero. The same account sets a bounded loop’s cap. When the fallback resolves everything it receives (\(\HumanResolutionProbability=1\)), the denominator is fixed at one, so adding turn \(\TurnIndex\) changes only spend. The turn costs \(\StageReachProbability_t\LoopTurnCost_t\) and avoids \(\StageReachProbability_t\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_t\HumanFallbackCost\) of fallback spend, so extending the cap from the preceding turn to turn \(\TurnIndex\) lowers expected spend exactly when \(\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_t\HumanFallbackCost>\LoopTurnCost_t\). This adjacent-cap comparison assumes immediate, perfectly resolving fallback and unchanged earlier turns; it is not a general stopping rule for policies with further contingent choices. The executable model in notebook 18.11 illustrates why keeping these accounting ledgers separate is essential for sound architectural selection.

Napkin Math 18.11: Pricing three designs for dependency upgradesProblem: A software engineering team manages an influx of 10,000 dependency-upgrade pull requests each month. Every upgrade requires code modifications that must pass an identical build and regression test suite to be accepted. The team considers three architectural options:

A deterministic rule-based rewriter that costs $0.001 per attempt before verification and achieves automated acceptance on 32 percent of tickets.
A single frontier model call that costs $0.045 before verification and accepts 68 percent of tickets.
A bounded loop powered by a lightweight model that costs $0.006 per reached turn before verification. This loop halts immediately upon acceptance or caps execution at three turns, with conditional acceptance probabilities of 0.55 on turn 1, 0.42 on turn 2, and 0.30 on turn 3.

Every candidate generated by any automated tier incurs an identical $0.002 charge for build and regression testing. Automated costs comprehensively include model inference, process execution, sandbox container reservation, and workspace teardown. Any ticket rejected by automation escalates to a human engineer; human fallback incurs $35 per ticket (including manual triage, debugging, and final verification sign-off) and resolves 90 percent of escalated tickets. Under these population expectations, which architecture minimizes the total cost per resolved ticket while satisfying a mandatory service floor of 95 percent combined resolution?
Math: Applying equation 7, the bounded loop achieves an automated acceptance rate of 81.73 percent while executing 1.711 turns on average per ticket. The multi-tier accounting ledger in table 7 separates automated acceptance from combined resolution, preventing expensive human resolutions from masquerading as automated successes.

Systems insight: When human escalation follows automated rejection, the economics of the system are overwhelmingly dominated by fallback labor costs. Because human handling costs $35, each percentage point of automated acceptance saves $0.35 in expected fallback expenditure per incoming ticket, several times the entire automated spend of any candidate architecture. As a consequence, although the deterministic rewriter appears deceptively attractive under isolated automated accounting ($0.00937 per automated acceptance), it yields the highest combined cost ($25.54 per resolved ticket) and fails to satisfy the 95 percent resolution floor. The bounded loop wins decisively ($6.53 per resolved ticket) because its second and third retry turns successfully salvage rejections that would otherwise trigger human intervention. Across 10,000 monthly tickets, the loop delivers an expected total spend of $64,081.88 for 9,817.3 successfully resolved upgrades. This ranking directly reflects the conditional acceptance yield of subsequent turns relative to human triage costs, relationships that engineering teams must empirically benchmark in production.


This steady-state model assumes that all verification jobs complete cleanly and that all resource charges settle immediately. In a live production evaluation, however, telemetry systems must track in-flight runs, timeout aborts, orphaned sandbox containers, and pending verifier verdicts at the observation cutoff, charging every initiated attempt against the ledger. Crucially, human fallback must be evaluated against the exact same task contract as automation: human reviewers must pass the identical build and regression suite rather than being granted informal operational waivers.
Furthermore, expected cost per resolved ticket does not tell the whole operational story. The model leaves queueing dynamics, completion-time distributions, and human engineering bandwidth unmodeled. If incoming tickets arrive in sudden bursts, or if the engineering staff has fixed capacity, routing even a small fraction of failures to human triage can saturate the queue and introduce catastrophic review latencies. Under stringent service-level agreements or strict staffing limits, a team may deliberately select a direct frontier model call over a bounded loop or rewriter, even at higher automated spend, when measured acceptance is higher and fewer tickets escape to human queues. In the dependency-upgrade scenario, the bounded loop has higher automated acceptance than the single call, so it also sends fewer tickets to human fallback.
Multi-agent delegation obeys this same objective-first economic evaluation when benchmarked against a capable single controller. Decomposing a complex task across a coordinator and specialized child agents pays the coordination tax (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}\)) in two places on the ledger. Handoffs, context delivery, and integration on the critical path enter equation 17.1 as the overhead term that holds any speedup below its serial-fraction ceiling, the same form of ceiling that capped faster inference at \(1/(1-\ModelTimeFraction)\) in notebook 18.5. Token amplification and child work off the critical path enter the numerator of cost per accepted task whether or not they shorten the task. Paying that premium is justified when the multi-agent system unlocks concurrent execution that meets latency deadlines a sequential loop would miss, or when specialized sub-agents achieve higher conditional acceptance on subproblems that confound a monolithic prompt. Economic viability does not require an architecture to dominate every competing design on both cost and latency simultaneously; Pareto dominance is sufficient, but in real systems engineering, meeting a critical operational deadline under an admissible budget is what actually decides the deployment.


↩︎ The matched single-controller baseline against which multi-agent delegation is benchmarked is established in Single-Agent Baseline Benchmarking.

title: 18 Agent Economics
text:
The dependency-upgrade notebook priced three competing architectures for a single, focused task. Real-world systems, however, exhibit vastly different cost structures. The four lighthouse workloads test the chapter’s economic accounting framework under fundamentally different operating stresses. The software repair agent accumulates an expanding workspace context over extended multi-turn trajectories. The research agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}\)) fans out parallel requests across untrusted external sources. The remediation agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) exercises high-privilege authority over live production infrastructure. Finally, the customer support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)) processes high volumes of brief sessions against tight latency targets. Because the dominant cost term differs fundamentally across these four archetypes, each workload responds to an entirely different optimization lever.

Lighthouse 18.1: Cost per accepted task by archetypeEach lighthouse workload executes an attempt under its specific acceptance contract, priced in table 8 using the cost framework developed throughout this chapter. For the repair agent, the execution horizon reflects the step limit of the registry’s reference coding harness, with token costs derived from the prefix-cached, append-only trajectory in notebook 18.2. This repair row is a scenario of its own, independent of the opening cohort of notebook 18.1, whose short attempts and acceptance counts were chosen only to isolate the token-price effect. For the research agent, model costs scale according to the 15× token fan-out multiple reported for a production multi-agent research system (Hadfield et al. 2025), treated here as one measured baseline rather than a universal constant, applied to a standard conversational turn at the chapter’s base tariff. For the remediation agent, human costs reflect an on-call engineer reviewing and approving a high-stakes production patch. For the support agent, every failed or rejected session triggers an immediate escalation handoff to a human representative at $4. The support account counts automated accepted sessions in its denominator and includes handoff setup for rejected sessions in its numerator. Subsequent human resolution, its costs, and its completion delays lie outside this account. A combined service must add those costs and count verified human completions separately, as in section 18.8.3. All remaining inputs represent baseline scenario values.

Systems insight: The economic trade-off between cheaper inference and higher task accuracy follows a direct mathematical relationship. Halving the unit token price saves half of the model’s share of the attempt. In contrast, raising the acceptance probability from \(\AttemptPassProbability\) to \(\AttemptPassProbability+\FiniteChange \AttemptPassProbability\) saves the fraction \(\FiniteChange \AttemptPassProbability/(\AttemptPassProbability+\FiniteChange \AttemptPassProbability)\) across all fixed per-attempt cost components in the repair, research, and remediation rows. Support also saves handoff setup as fewer sessions are rejected. Under these held-cost assumptions, higher acceptance gives the greater reduction whenever the model’s share of total attempt cost falls below \(2\FiniteChange \AttemptPassProbability/(\AttemptPassProbability+\FiniteChange \AttemptPassProbability)\).
For the software repair agent, this decision threshold sits at 40 percent. Because model tokens account for only 33.2 percent of the repair agent’s attempt cost, improving acceptance by 10 percentage points saves more money than cutting token tariffs in half under those assumptions. Selecting an intervention also requires pricing the work and latency that produce the acceptance improvement. In this account, the repair agent is economically bound by holding its sandbox and tools across 30 turns. That is non-model work again, much as tests and sandbox lifecycle rather than model calls dominated elapsed time in notebook 18.5, although here the binding term is residency cost rather than test time.
In fact, each archetype exposes a completely different binding constraint. Only the research agent is truly bound by token expenditure, with model calls consuming 85.7 percent of its attempt cost due to combinatorial sub-agent fan-out; prefix caching, context compaction, and bounded search horizons are its primary economic levers. The remediation agent is dominated by senior engineer approval time. The approval escrow of Held proposals makes each wait cheap to hold but does not shorten it; systems architects shorten review by binding each approval to one exact configuration version and by grouping several reversible actions under one approval, balanced against the expected penalty of irreversible failures. Finally, the customer support agent is dominated by escalation handoffs. Because an escalation fee is incurred whenever a session fails, higher acceptance yields a compounding dividend by directly eliminating human labor. Because the support agent’s cost per accepted task is well under a dollar, its interactive latency objective still requires separate fleet-capacity checks using the queueing models of section 18.6; a small financial ratio alone does not establish fleet saturation.



Hadfield, Jeremy, Barry Zhang, Kenneth Lien, Florian Scholz, Jeremy Fox, and Daniel Ford. 2025. How We Built Our Multi-Agent Research System. Anthropic Engineering Blog.
When transitioning from architectural design evaluations to continuous production monitoring, an engineering team must maintain consistent accounting boundaries within its operational reporting. A complete ledger must track aborted and canceled attempts, idle headroom in shared hosting pools, human review and escalation labor within the task contract, and unresolved liabilities at the accounting cutoff. Preserving this rigorous boundary allows teams to re-evaluate architectural rankings as operating conditions evolve. When an inference provider slashes model pricing, a product release shifts the difficulty distribution of incoming tasks, or an organization updates its safety and approval policies, the matched economic comparison must be re-run. A design that appears cheaper on paper should only be promoted to production after its sandbox environments, test runners, and reviewer pools have been validated under realistic peak admission rates.

title: 18 Agent Economics
text:
An economic evaluation can be mathematically precise yet fundamentally misleading if it tracks the wrong unit of work or quietly shifts the standard of acceptance. In agent systems, these errors typically occur when localized metrics, such as a model’s raw token tariff, an isolated inference speedup, or a child agent’s premature stopping condition, substitute for the end-to-end ledger of completed, accepted tasks.

Fallacy: The lowest token price identifies the cheapest accepted task.
Selecting a model based solely on published input and output token rates ignores the operational overhead of lower model capability. Cheaper models often require longer prompts, take additional interactive turns, invoke tools redundantly, and fail validation gates more frequently. Because every rejected attempt still consumes compute, environment time, and assessment overhead, a low success rate rapidly erodes nominal token savings.
As demonstrated in notebook 18.1, switching to a lower-priced model cuts nominal token charges by 71.3 percent and reduces per-attempt cost by 19.8 percent. However, because its completion rate drops, the system costs 2.4× as much per accepted repair. Factoring in the manual triage required for rejected attempts widens the gap further, driving effective costs to 8.1× the baseline. To measure real economics, systems engineers must evaluate the total cost of all initiated work against the count of accepted solutions delivered under an identical task contract (section 18.2).


Pitfall: Buying faster generation without identifying what delays completion.
Accelerating token generation shortens only decode spans; accelerating complete model calls is a different hypothetical intervention that can also shorten input processing. When an agent spends most of its trajectory compiling code, executing sandbox tests, or waiting on remote APIs, Amdahl’s law strictly limits the returns of a faster model.
Consider the serial software repair episode evaluated in notebook 18.5. Applying a 4× model speedup trims 21.94 s from a 312.40 s trajectory, an overall gain of just 1.08×. In fact, even if complete model calls were instantaneous, the trajectory speedup would cap out at 1.10×. By comparison, simply halving the test execution interval saves 122.8 s. Engineers should map the end-to-end critical path across non-overlapping execution phases, tool interactions, and queueing delays before investing in premium low-latency inference (section 18.4).


Fallacy: Prefix caching makes carried context nearly free.
While prompt prefix caching sharply discounts the cost of reading previously processed tokens, it does not alter the quadratic volume growth inherent to multi-turn interactions. As an agent’s context window expands turn by turn, the append-only input inference bill retains a quadratic growth term whenever the cached-read tariff is positive, even at heavily discounted rates. This need not dominate the complete operational account.
The analysis in notebook 18.2 shows that ideal cache reuse cuts the token bill by 5.6×. Nevertheless, re-reading cached history still constitutes 50.8 percent of the remaining token bill, growing with the square of the trajectory horizon. Moreover, these savings remain fragile: a modest drop of 10 percent in eligible cache hits raises the cached bill by 45.7 percent. Sustained efficiency requires maintaining strict prefix stability across requests and compacting conversational state only when the remaining horizon repays the rebuilding cost or context limits justify it, while preserving task acceptance (section 18.3).


Pitfall: Running shared model capacity near saturation to lower its unit cost.
Maximizing cluster utilization to amortize server hardware yields diminishing economic returns once queueing effects take hold. While throughput scales linearly with load, queue wait times surge hyperbolically as utilization approaches saturation. For multi-turn agents, this latency penalty does not occur in isolation; it compounds sequentially across every turn in the trajectory.
Notebook 18.8 illustrates this trade-off: driving utilization from 70 percent to 90 percent delivers 28.6 percent more throughput, but it multiplies the mean queue wait by 3.9×, and a serial trajectory pays that longer wait on every step. Under the independent per-call tail model, a run of 30 serial calls meets at least one call slower than its own 99th percentile with probability 0.26. This probability does not specify a trajectory deadline-miss rate. Near saturation, the single-server heavy-traffic approximation also predicts longer queue-delay percentiles. Correlated delays and shared serving pools require their own trajectory-level measurements. Infrastructure engineers should provision reserve headroom to satisfy end-to-end trajectory percentiles rather than optimizing for average single-call server utilization (section 18.6).


Fallacy: A cascade’s cheap first tier makes its savings independent of its gate.
Routing tasks to a cheaper model cascade yields net savings only if the validation gate reliably catches defective outputs. When an inexpensive early tier falsely accepts an incorrect result, the downstream cost of detecting and repairing that defect in production quickly outweighs any upstream token savings.
In notebook 18.6, the three-tier cascade saves $0.053 per accepted task over direct frontier model execution. Crucially, this saving assumes that early exits satisfy the exact same acceptance contract as escalated runs. If a relaxed tier-1 gate falsely accepts just 0.9 percent of its exits, and each defective output costs $10 to remediate, the resulting harm wipes out the cascade’s financial advantage entirely. Robust cascade design requires pricing gate evaluation, escalation overhead, and downstream failure remediation together under a unified quality contract (section 18.5).


Pitfall: Returning a canceled child’s unused-looking allowance to the spending pool at local stop.
In distributed multi-agent systems, local process termination does not guarantee remote financial settlement. When a coordinator terminates or cancels a child agent, asynchronous API calls and external tool invocations often remain in flight. Reallocating an agent’s unspent budget back to the common pool the moment it halts locally creates a race condition against incoming delayed charges.
Notebook 18.10 demonstrates this failure mode: releasing funds immediately upon local termination appears to free $1.65, whereas only $0.65 is truly uncommitted. When an in-flight tool run posts a late charge of $0.70, it overdraws funds already promised to a sibling task. Budget coordinators must calculate released funds as the initial allocation minus settled charges minus strict, enforceable upper bounds on outstanding work. Reliable governance depends on atomic budget reservations and idempotent settlement, which prevent concurrent sibling agents from double-spending unsettled allowances; retrospective spend alerts cannot prevent these overages (section 18.7).

title: 18 Agent Economics
text:
An agent service is judged and funded by its accepted outcomes rather than its raw token consumption. Every operational expense the runtime incurs, on successful and failed attempts alike, is amortized across the cohort of accepted tasks under a given service contract. The central economic objective is therefore the effective cost per accepted task, \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\), evaluated across a settled cohort while explicitly accounting for cutoff thresholds and in-flight work. Any proposed optimization earns its keep only if it lowers \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) or meets a latency deadline that the system objective values. Evaluating such changes requires a strictly matched comparison that holds the task contract constant while the underlying policy varies.
The largest cost component identifies a target worth evaluating; the most effective intervention also depends on what it costs to change that component. Token pricing governs the largest cost term only when inference charges dominate the task account. In many production systems, the primary expense lies elsewhere: container sandboxes, test-suite execution, human review, or a depressed acceptance rate that multiplies all other costs. A rigorous cost accounting reveals this governing term before an engineering team spends resources optimizing the wrong bottleneck.

Speculation accelerates decode only when \(\MeanAcceptedDraftLength>\DraftTokenCount\DraftTokenCostRatio\); with \(\ModelTimeFraction\) the decode share, the trajectory gains at most \(1/(1-\ModelTimeFraction)\)
equation 3, section 18.4


\(\mathbb{E}[\CascadeTaskCost]=\sum_j \StageReachProbability_j(\CascadeTierCost_j+\CascadeGateCost_j)\) and \(\AcceptanceProbability=\sum_j \StageReachProbability_j\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_j\)
Reach-weighted price and acceptance of a gated cascade; every reached tier pays for its call and its gate
section 18.5


\(\ConcurrentTrajectories=\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\mathbb{E}[\TrajectoryDuration]\) and \(\ServingUtilization(\AcceptanceFraction)=\dfrac{\TrajectoryGoodput\,\mathbb{E}[\TrajectoryCallCount]}{\AcceptanceFraction \WorkerCount\ServiceRate}\)
Mean occupancy of each held resource, and the offered load a goodput target imposes; lower acceptance raises load as \(1/\AcceptanceFraction\)
equation 4


\(\mathbb{E}[\RequestQueueTime]\approx\dfrac{\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2+\ServiceTimeVariationCoefficient^2}{2}\dfrac{\ServingUtilization}{1-\ServingUtilization}\mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime]\)
Heavy-traffic estimate of mean queue wait at one server; sets the utilization a latency target can afford
equation 5


\(\BreakEvenUtilization=\dfrac{\DedicatedHourlyFixedCost}{3600\FeasibleOutputTokenRate(\EffectiveApiOutputTokenPrice-\DedicatedVariableTokenCost)}\)
Delivered load above which dedicated capacity costs less than a per-token API at a fixed token mix
equation 6


\({\CostCeiling}_k=\LedgerSettledCharges_k+\LedgerReservedFunds_k+\LedgerFreeBalance_k\) with \(\LedgerSettledCharges(\LedgerEvaluationTime)+\LedgerReservedFunds(\LedgerEvaluationTime)\le \CostCeiling\)
Conserved spending across descendants; admission reserves a bound \(\OperationChargeBound\), and only settlement releases it
section 18.7







Key Takeaways: Price the accepted task, not the token

Acceptance divides the whole bill: A token discount reduces only the model’s direct share of an attempt, whereas the acceptance rate \(\AcceptanceFraction\) scales every operational expense. In addition, each successful task must absorb the amortized cost of \((1-\AcceptanceFraction)/\AcceptanceFraction\) nonaccepted tasks. In the repair cohort, the configuration with the lower nominal token price ultimately cost 2.4× as much per accepted repair.
Reuse and retries are investments, not free savings: Prefix caching reduces the slope of quadratic context growth but does not eliminate the re-read penalty. Context compaction pays off only after surviving beyond its payback horizon \(\CompactionPaybackCallCount\). Similarly, when a human fallback resolves every ticket the loop leaves, an additional execution turn makes economic sense only when the fallback spend it expects to avoid, \(\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_t\HumanFallbackCost\), exceeds the full cost of that turn.
Speed pays only on the critical path: Accelerating a model component shortens only its own spans along the trajectory’s execution graph; generation acceleration acts on decode spans. In the hypothetical serial repair episode, a 4× model speedup yielded only a 1.08× end-to-end speedup for the overall episode, because sandbox lifecycle operations and test suite runs formed the dominant latency floor.
A cascade is only as cheap as its gates: Tiered routing saves money only when every exit tier fulfills the identical acceptance contract. If an upstream gate erroneously accepts invalid outputs, even a tiny false-acceptance rate can completely erase the cascade’s cost advantage once downstream remediation and task failure costs enter the balance sheet.
Utilization is paid for in queueing delay: System throughput scales linearly with load, but mean queue wait grows nonlinearly as \(\ServingUtilization / (1 - \ServingUtilization)\). Because an agent trajectory pays this queueing latency across every sequential step, operating at excessive utilization quickly destroys interactive responsiveness. Moreover, falling acceptance forces the runtime to admit \(1/\AcceptanceFraction\) tasks per accepted outcome to sustain target goodput, directly coupling capacity planning to task reliability.
A spending limit holds only if reserved first: Admission control must atomically reserve an enforceable bound before execution begins, releasing unused funds only upon task settlement. Because terminating a child process does not instantly extinguish its pending provider billing, runtime tracking must strictly separate settled costs from in-flight liabilities. Monitoring burn rates merely observes cost overruns after the fact; strict upfront reservation prevents them.
The largest term identifies a target to evaluate: Trajectory horizon, working state size, and external authority determine which subsystem dominates execution cost: token generation in deep research agents, sandbox holding in code repair, human review delays in infrastructure remediation, or cross-system handoffs in customer workflows. An optimization that cuts total cost in half for one agent architecture may yield negligible savings for another.



Evaluating an agent system by trajectory goodput (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-goodput}\)) establishes a rigorous financial metric: the effective cost per accepted task, \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\), and its operational reciprocal, goodput per dollar. This principle requires system designers to account for resource residence and queueing overheads rather than focusing solely on active generation. In parallel, trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\)) preserves spending discipline across child tasks through two-phase reservation and settlement, maintaining an essential separation between reusable operational capabilities and consumable financial budgets.

title: 18 Agent Economics
text:
The principles governing execution time and capacity planning in agent workflows trace directly back to mid-twentieth-century operations research. When project planners needed to isolate which activities determined an overall delivery date, Kelley and Walker introduced the critical-path method to identify the longest chain of dependent tasks (Kelley and Walker 1959). Queueing theory formalized the operational limits of shared capacity. Little proved that mean occupancy equals arrival rate multiplied by mean residence time under remarkably general conditions (Little 1961). In the same year, Kingman showed that waiting times in a single-server queue diverge nonlinearly, in proportion to \(1/(1-\ServingUtilization)\) as utilization approaches unity (Kingman 1961), and Kleinrock later synthesized these results into the queueing theory of computer systems (Kleinrock 1975). When early parallel computers promised order-of-magnitude speedups, Amdahl demonstrated that serial bottlenecks strictly bound the end-to-end performance gains achievable by accelerating isolated subroutines (Amdahl 1967). Each generation encountered the same dilemma confronting modern repair agents: placing a fast component inside a slow end-to-end pipeline yields little return unless engineers account for the performance of the system as a whole.

Kelley, James E., and Morgan R. Walker. 1959. “Critical-Path Planning and Scheduling.” Papers Presented at the December 1-3, 1959, Eastern Joint IRE-AIEE-ACM Computer Conference, 160–73. https://doi.org/10.1145/1460299.1460318.

Little, John D. C. 1961. “A Proof for the Queuing Formula: \(L = \lambda W\).” Operations Research 9 (3): 383–87. https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383.

Kleinrock, L. 1975. Queueing Systems, Volume 1: Theory. Wiley-Interscience.

Amdahl, Gene M. 1967. “Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities.” Proceedings of the April 18-20, 1967, Spring Joint Computer Conference on - AFIPS ’67 (Spring), AFIPS ’67 (spring), 483–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1465482.1465560.

Gray, Jim, and Andreas Reuter. 1992. Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques. Morgan Kaufmann.
The economics of budget enforcement and resource consumption descend from transaction processing and utility computing. High-concurrency database systems facing contention on hot account balances introduced escrow transactions to allocate fractional quantities without exclusive record locks (O’Neil 1986), establishing an early paradigm for concurrent budget reservations within the rigorous framework of atomic, durable, and recoverable updates (Gray and Reuter 1992). When compute resources transitioned to on-demand utility pricing, the trade-off between renting vs. owning infrastructure turned on workload variability, average capacity utilization, and which party absorbs provisioning risk (Armbrust et al. 2010). As distributed systems expanded across warehouse-scale infrastructure, Dean and Barroso demonstrated that tail latency across parallel RPCs quickly dominates overall response times (Dean and Barroso 2013), the parallel counterpart of how a multi-step agent trajectory compounds tool and service variability in series.
Machine learning contributed its own lineage of allocating computation adaptively based on instance difficulty. Viola and Jones demonstrated that a cascade of boosted classifiers could deliver real-time visual detection by rejecting straightforward negative examples in early stages (Viola and Jones 2001). That design pattern reemerged for foundation models in the form of cost-aware cascades and learned routers that dispatch queries across heterogeneous model endpoints (L. Chen et al. 2023; Ong et al. 2024). Similarly, speculative execution evolved from blockwise parallel decoding (Stern et al. 2018) into speculative decoding frameworks that pair small draft models with full target-model verification (Leviathan et al. 2023; C. Chen et al. 2023). In agentic workflows, repeated sampling strategies showed that additional generation attempts reliably expand solution coverage whenever verifiers can recognize task success (Brown et al. 2024). These results highlighted a critical requirement for evaluating production agents: benchmark assessments must report task accuracy alongside cumulative expenditure, establishing cost per accepted task as the central engineering metric (Kapoor et al. 2024).

Viola, Paul, and Michael J. Jones. 2001. “Rapid Object Detection Using a Boosted Cascade of Simple Features.” Proceedings of the 2001 IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. CVPR 2001 1: I-511-I-518. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2001.990517.

Chen, Lingjiao, Matei Zaharia, and James Zou. 2023. “FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2305.05176.

Ong, Isaac, Amjad Almahairi, Vincent Wu, Wei-Lin Chiang, Tianhao Wu, Joseph E. Gonzalez, M. Waleed Kadous, and Ion Stoica. 2024. “RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2406.18665.

Leviathan, Yaniv, Matan Kalman, and Yossi Matias. 2023. “Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding.” Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning 202: 19274–86.

Chen, C., S. Borgeaud, G. Irving, J.-B. Lespiau, L. Sifre, and J. Jumper. 2023. “Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2302.01318.

Brown, Bradley, Jordan Juravsky, Ryan Ehrlich, Ronald Clark, Quoc V. Le, Christopher Ré, and Azalia Mirhoseini. 2024. “Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2407.21787.
Further reading.

The Single Server Queue in Heavy Traffic (Kingman 1961). Three pages demonstrating why waiting time, rather than reduced throughput, is the steep price of operating near full capacity.
The Escrow Transactional Method (O’Neil 1986). The database foundation for budget reservations, showing how concurrent transactions can safely allocate portions of a shared balance without global record locking.
A View of Cloud Computing (Armbrust et al. 2010). The definitive analysis of workload variability, capacity utilization, and risk transfer underlying rent vs. own decisions in utility computing.
Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems (Harchol-Balter 2013). A comprehensive guide to queueing theory in computer systems, covering multi-server architectures, heavy-tailed service distributions, and priority scheduling policies beyond basic single-server approximations.
The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso 2013). An essential analysis of why distributed services must optimize against high-percentile latency rather than mean response times when requests fan out across multiple components.
AI Agents That Matter (Kapoor et al. 2024). The empirical blueprint for reporting agent accuracy and operational expense side by side, establishing the evaluation counterpart to cost per accepted task.


O’Neil, Patrick E. 1986. “The Escrow Transactional Method.” ACM Transactions on Database Systems 11 (4): 405–30. https://doi.org/10.1145/7239.7265.

Harchol-Balter, Mor. 2013. Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems: Queueing Theory in Action. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9781139226424.

Dean, Jeffrey, and Luiz André Barroso. 2013. “The Tail at Scale.” Communications of the ACM 56 (2): 74–80.

Kapoor, Sayash, Benedikt Stroebl, Zachary S. Siegel, Nitya Nadgir, and Arvind Narayanan. 2024. “AI Agents That Matter.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2407.01502.

title: 18 Agent Economics
text:
Every given below is a hypothetical problem input rather than a price, rate, or measurement of a real system. Each problem ends in a decision, and the calculation exists to justify it.

A cheaper configuration and a moving denominator (Basic). A repair cohort of \(\InitiatedTasks=200\) tickets runs one bounded attempt per ticket under a fixed contract. Configuration A accepts \(120\) tickets; its accepted tasks cost \(\AcceptedTaskMeanCost=\$1.20\) on average and its nonaccepted tasks \(\UnacceptedTaskMeanCost=\$1.80\), since they run to the turn cap. For configuration B under the same contract, accepted tickets cost \(30\) percent less than A’s accepted-ticket mean, and rejected tickets cost \(30\) percent less than A’s nonaccepted-ticket mean.

Compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) for A from the cohort total and again from \(\AcceptedTaskMeanCost+\frac{1-\AcceptanceFraction}{\AcceptanceFraction}\UnacceptedTaskMeanCost\), and state how many nonaccepted tasks each accepted repair carries.
Find the smallest number of accepted tickets at which B costs no more per accepted task than A.
At the reporting cutoff B has \(85\) accepted, \(105\) rejected, and \(10\) pending tickets, with the accepted and rejected groups having B’s stated conditional means. Each of the ten identified pending tickets has final charges of \(\$1.26\), which are not repriced when its verdict arrives. All invoices, cleanup, and other costs are final; only acceptance verdicts remain pending. Compute the range of B’s provisional \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) over the possible verdicts, and decide what the report may claim about B against A before the pending assessments complete. If a pending operation can still incur charges, what liability evidence is needed before this range bounds the final account?

When compaction pays (Basic). A repair trajectory holds \(\SequenceLength=40{,}000\) input tokens at a decision point. Compaction would reduce it to \(\CompactedContextLength=8{,}000\) tokens with a summary call that emits \(\SummaryOutputLength=2{,}000\) tokens, and the first compacted call misses the cache completely. The tariff charges \(\InputTokenPrice=\$3\), \(\CachedInputTokenPrice=\$0.30\), and \(\OutputTokenPrice=\$15\) per million tokens.

Compute the upfront increment \(\CompactionUpfrontCost\), the per-call saving \(\CompactionPerCallSaving\), and the payback horizon \(\CompactionPaybackCallCount\).
Five ordinary calls remain, including the first compacted one. Compute the price difference between compacting and keeping the context, and decide whether to compact on price alone.
The provider halves the cached rate to \(\$0.15\) per million. Recompute \(\CompactionPaybackCallCount\) and decide whether compaction pays with ten calls remaining. Explain why a cheaper cache pushes the profitable compaction point earlier in a trajectory, and name two reasons other than price that could still justify compacting.

How many turns before a person takes over (Basic). A repair loop costs \(\UniformLoopTurnCost=\$0.50\) per reached turn, including assessment and sandbox holding, and stops at the first accepted candidate. Its conditional acceptance probabilities for turns one through five are \(0.50\), \(0.30\), \(0.20\), \(0.10\), and \(0.01\). Every ticket the loop leaves unaccepted goes to an engineer who always resolves it for \(\HumanFallbackCost=\$30\).

Using equation 7, tabulate \(\LoopAcceptanceProbability(\TrajectoryTurnLimit)\), the expected number of turns, and the automated spend per ticket for \(\TrajectoryTurnLimit=1\) through \(5\).
Compute the combined spend per resolved ticket for each \(\TrajectoryTurnLimit\) and choose the cap. Confirm from the table that the chosen cap is the last turn satisfying the marginal rule \(\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_t\HumanFallbackCost>\UniformLoopTurnCost\) of section 18.8, and explain why that rule holds only while the engineer resolves every ticket the loop leaves.
A triage queue replaces the engineer and resolves every rejected ticket for \(\HumanFallbackCost=\$2\). Choose the cap again. Explain why ranking the caps by automated spend per automated acceptance would have chosen wrongly in both cases.

Retry, a stronger model, or a router (Intermediate). A cheap configuration costs \(\MeanAttemptCost=\$0.20\) per assessed attempt and may retry sequentially up to \(\IndependentAttemptCount=4\) times. Half the incoming tasks are easy, which the cheap configuration accepts with \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.8\) per attempt; the other half are hard, with \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.1\). A stronger configuration costs \(\$0.90\) per attempt, is run once, and accepts easy tasks with probability \(0.95\) and hard tasks with \(0.55\). Attempts are conditionally independent given the task.

A planner averages the cheap configuration’s rates to \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.45\). Compute the coverage and cost per accepted task this predicts for sequential retry.
Compute the actual coverage, expected attempts per task, and cost per accepted task for sequential retry over the mixed population, and compare it with running the stronger configuration on every task.
A direct router can identify each task’s class before generation. Price the policy that retries easy tasks on the cheap configuration and sends hard tasks to the stronger one. Decide among the three policies when the declared objective is minimum cost per accepted task subject to at least \(75\) percent coverage, and state what evidence the router’s class labels require before the comparison holds.

Recomputing the critical path (Intermediate). A repair episode has these dependencies and fixed durations. Sandbox creation (\(20\) s) precedes a planning call (\(12\) s). Two branches then run concurrently and must both finish before the test suite: a dependency build (\(60\) s), and static analysis (\(25\) s) followed by a model review of its findings (\(15\) s). The test suite (\(120\) s) is followed by a summary call (\(8\) s) and snapshot export (\(10\) s). For the speculation comparisons in parts (b) and (d), all stated model-call intervals consist entirely of decode with negligible prefill or queueing overhead; every other duration stays fixed.

Compute \(\CriticalPathDuration\) with equation 2, identify the critical path, and compute the model share \(\ModelTimeFraction\) on that path.
A speculative decoder drafts \(\DraftTokenCount=4\) tokens per round at \(\DraftTokenCostRatio=0.1\) of a target step and accepts \(\MeanAcceptedDraftLength=2.2\) tokens per round. Compute \(\SpeculativeDecodingSpeedup\) and its break-even \(\MeanAcceptedDraftLength\), apply the speedup to the model-call intervals under the stated approximation, and compute the new episode time.
A build cache instead cuts the build to \(10\) s. Compute the time saved and explain why it is not \(50\) s.
With the build cache in place, the suite is split into two concurrent shards of \(60\) s plus \(5\) s to merge results. Compute the episode time, then the time with speculation added. Rank the three interventions by elapsed time saved, and name the cost that sharding adds to the account.

A cascade under a deadline (Intermediate). Small repair tasks may run a two-tier cascade. Tier 1 costs \(\CascadeTierCost_1=\$0.05\) and \(\CascadeTierDuration_1=3\) s and accepts \(\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_1=0.50\) of tasks; tier 2 costs \(\CascadeTierCost_2=\$0.60\) and \(\CascadeTierDuration_2=12\) s and accepts \(\StageConditionalAcceptanceProbability_2=0.80\) of the tasks that reach it. Each gate costs \(\CascadeGateCost=\$0.02\) and takes \(\CascadeGateDuration=30\) s. Direct frontier execution costs \(\$0.62\) with its gate, takes \(42\) s, and accepts \(0.82\) of the full cohort.

Compute the cascade’s expected cost per initiated task, acceptance probability, cost per accepted task, and mean duration, and compare each with direct execution.
A team proposes replacing tier 1’s gate with a lint check costing \(\$0.005\) that exits the same share of tasks, but a fraction \(\LintFalseAcceptFraction\) of those exits violate the independently assessed criterion, each costing \(\$4\) to find and repair. Find the \(\LintFalseAcceptFraction\) at which the harm term erases the gate saving, and evaluate the proposal at a measured \(\LintFalseAcceptFraction=0.04\).
The service now requires \(90\) percent of tasks to finish within \(60\) s. Show that the cascade fails. A router sends \(45\) percent of tasks directly to the frontier tier, where they are accepted with probability \(0.70\); tier 1 accepts \(0.85\) of the rest, and tier 2 accepts \(0.80\) of what it receives. Check the deadline, and compute the routed policy’s cost per accepted task against both alternatives.

The support agent’s binding constraint (Intermediate, second-lighthouse transfer). Apply the chapter’s capacity model to the support agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}\)). The service must deliver trajectory goodput \(\TrajectoryGoodput=30\) accepted sessions per minute at acceptance fraction \(\AcceptanceFraction=0.75\). An admitted session stays present for \(4\) minutes on average, including customer think time, and makes \(5\) serial model calls. Plan the model endpoint as the single-server queue of equation 5 with \(\mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime]=0.25\) s, \(\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2=2\), and \(\ServiceTimeVariationCoefficient^2=1\). The response target is a mean of at most \(1.0\) s of wait plus service per call. Each attempt costs \(\$0.30\) in total.

Compute \(\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\), the mean session concurrency, the call arrival rate \(\ArrivalRate\), \(\ServingUtilization\), and the mean response per call. Decide whether the target is met.
Find the largest \(\ServingUtilization\) that meets the target, and the goodput it permits at \(\AcceptanceFraction=0.75\).
Evaluate three levers: smoothing admissions to \(\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2=1\); smoothing plus raising acceptance to \(\AcceptanceFraction=0.85\); and a second, independent endpoint that takes half the sessions with unchanged variability. State which meet the target, and what happens to \(\ServingUtilization\) if acceptance instead falls to \(\AcceptanceFraction=0.60\) at the same goodput.
Compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) and the probability that a session meets at least one per-call tail delay when each call exceeds its 99th percentile independently with probability \(0.01\), and compare with a \(30\)-call repair trajectory. Explain why this workload’s binding constraint differs from the repair agent’s, and why a design that meets a mean target can still miss a percentile target.

Renting or owning capacity for research fan-out (Advanced, critique and redesign). The research agent (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}\)) reads \(20\) input tokens per output token, and only \(30\) percent of its input is billed at the cached rate because its sources vary. The API charges \(\$3\) per million uncached input tokens, \(\$0.30\) per million cached input tokens, and \(\$15\) per million output tokens. A matched dedicated deployment costs \(\DedicatedHourlyFixedCost=\$40\) per hour plus \(\DedicatedVariableTokenCost=\$4\) per million output tokens, with a feasible reference output rate \(\FeasibleOutputTokenRate=800\) tokens per second at the latency target. The workload runs at \(\DeliveredCapacityFraction=0.6\) for \(8\) hours a day and is idle otherwise.

Compute \(\EffectiveApiOutputTokenPrice\) per output token including its associated input, and \(\BreakEvenUtilization\) from equation 6.
A colleague argues that because the busy-hour load exceeds \(\BreakEvenUtilization\), the team should commit to dedicated capacity around the clock. Compute the daily cost of the API and of that commitment, and critique the argument.
Redesign the commitment so that owning capacity pays, and compute its daily cost and saving.
Reordering sources to keep a stable prefix raises the cached share to \(80\) percent. Recompute \(\EffectiveApiOutputTokenPrice\), \(\BreakEvenUtilization\), and the saving from part (c). Decide which change the team should make first, and name two conditions the comparison must hold fixed for either conclusion to stand.

A remediation budget under concurrency and cancellation (Advanced, redesign). A remediation task (lighthouse \(\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}\)) has \(\CostCeiling=\$30\), of which \(\$4\) of diagnosis has settled. Two children, log analysis and canary replay, each request a \(\$15\) allocation at the same moment.

The coordinator reads the free balance, checks it against each request, and then records both reservations. Compute the overcommitment, and state the ledger transition that prevents it and the largest allocation the second child can receive.
After the fix, log analysis receives \(\$15\) and canary replay \(\$11\). Log analysis closes with \(\$9\) settled. An operator then cancels canary replay when it has \(\$3\) settled and a remote load test outstanding with an enforced bound of \(\$6\); that test later bills \(\$4.20\). Tabulate the root’s \(\LedgerSettledCharges\), \(\LedgerReservedFunds\), and \(\LedgerFreeBalance\) at each boundary, and compute what a release at local stop would return against what may safely be returned.
A trailing-window limit allows \(\WindowSpendingLimit=\$8\) of admitted bounds per \(\SpendingWindowDuration=10\) minutes across all children. Requests arrive at minute \(0\) (\(\$3\)), minute \(2\) (\(\$4\)), minute \(6\) (\(\$2\)), and minute \(11\) (\(\$2\)); the first operation settles at minute \(1\) for \(\$1\). Decide each admission, and show what an implementation that credits early settlement back to the window would admit instead.
The agent now proposes renting a load-generation cluster whose provider enforces no duration or spending cap. Redesign the admission path so the task keeps a hard ceiling, and explain why an operator’s approval of the production change does not substitute for a budget reservation.



What’s Next: From priced parts to one trajectoryWho owns each transition between context, tools, execution, assessment, and settlement, and what evidence permits the next one? A policy this chapter justifies on price still crosses every one of those boundaries. Conclusion first returns to the three questions the introduction posed, answering the first with the cost per accepted task priced here. It then follows one remediation incident through the whole system, naming the owner and the record of each transition, putting the attempt on this chapter’s account, and examining the failures that occur at the seams. It ends at the specification boundary, where the runtime can enforce and measure a declared contract but cannot decide whether that contract captures what the task was for.

title: Inference Cost Foundations
text:
This appendix supplies the serving arithmetic behind model-call latency, attention-state storage, and resource occupancy. It provides reusable estimates for comparing prompt processing with generation, sizing retained state, and separating average demand from capacity guarantees. Each estimate states its assumptions so that a reader can substitute another model, serving configuration, or workload without treating the reference values as universal performance claims.


Start from the agent-level question in table 1 and jump to the section that derives its answer.



Table 1: Question-to-Derivation Lookup: Agent-level questions and the sections that derive their answers.










If you need to know…
Jump to…
What you get




When output generation and prompt processing have different per-token costs
section 1.1
Conditional compute and bandwidth floors, not measured service latency


When attention work matters in long-context prefill
section 1.1
The attention term and the length at which it matches the weight term


How batching changes amortized serving time and per-stream latency
section 1.1
Weight reuse across streams and the limits of a weight-only estimate


How sampling placement, grammar masks, and speculative verification add work
section 1.2
Transfer and storage formulas, plus the conditions for exact speculative sampling


How much memory a trajectory’s context occupies, and how attention design changes it
section 1.3
Bytes per token from model geometry, multi-head versus grouped versus multi-query attention


How tool waits change live state and how load changes waiting
section 1.4
Little’s law with matched boundaries and a scoped single-server waiting approximation


Which model, accelerator, and node values the book assumes
section 1.5
The reference inputs, ready to substitute









Prompt processing can reuse a model’s weights across many token positions, whereas unbatched generation uses those weights for one new position at a time. That difference can make prefill arithmetic-bound and decode bandwidth-bound. Neither regime follows from the phase name alone. Prompt length, batching, attention traffic, and the serving implementation determine which resource limits an actual call. A weight-only estimate isolates the reuse effect before adding those complications.
A model call processes the uncached prompt during prefill and generates new tokens during decode. Both phases use the same weights, but the reference calculation yields a ratio of about 295 between the unbatched weight-transfer floor per output token and the arithmetic floor per prompt token. We compare these conditional floors to explain the bandwidth constraint (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}\)), not to predict the ratio of measured call latencies or token prices.


An accelerator has two limits, the rate \(\PeakRate\) at which it performs arithmetic (operations per second) and the rate \(\Bandwidth\) at which its memory delivers data (bytes per second). A computation’s arithmetic intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) is the number of operations it performs per byte it moves. The roofline model (Williams et al. 2009) gives a performance ceiling \(\AttainableComputeRate\) from whichever limit binds first:

Williams, Samuel, Andrew Waterman, and David Patterson. 2009. “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” Communications of the ACM 52 (4): 65–76. https://doi.org/10.1145/1498765.1498785.
\[\AttainableComputeRate = \min\left( \PeakRate, \; \ArithmeticIntensity \cdot \Bandwidth \right)\]
The two ceilings meet at the ridge point \(\RooflineRidgePoint = \PeakRate / \Bandwidth\). Below the ridge, bandwidth supplies the lower ceiling; above it, arithmetic supplies the lower ceiling. Actual performance can fall below either ceiling because of implementation and scheduling overhead. For the reference accelerator at 8-bit precision, \(\PeakRate\) = 1,979 trillion operations per second and \(\Bandwidth\) = 3.35 TB/s, so \(\RooflineRidgePoint \approx\) 591 operations per byte.



A dense transformer with \(\Parameters\) active parameters performs about \(2\Parameters\) weight-related operations per token, one multiply and one add per weight. Its weight payload is \(\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize\) bytes, where \(\WeightElementStorageSize\) is bytes per parameter. The approximation counts this payload once per pass; prefill and decode differ in how many tokens share that read. Sparse activation and weight reuse from another cache level require a different traffic count.
In the weight-only model, prefill shares each weight read across \(\SequenceLength\) prompt positions, giving intensity \(2\Parameters \SequenceLength / (\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize) = 2\SequenceLength/\WeightElementStorageSize\). When that intensity exceeds the ridge and arithmetic approaches the stated peak, the per-token time approaches the following floor. Small prompts, kernel tiling, attention, and additional memory traffic can invalidate those assumptions.
\[\PerTokenPrefillTime \approx \frac{2\Parameters}{\PeakRate} \tag{1}\]
Ordinary decode for one stream generates one token per pass, with each token depending on the preceding prefix. If the weights must be read from the modeled memory on every pass, the weight-only intensity is \(2/\WeightElementStorageSize\), or 2 operations per byte at 8-bit precision, about 0.34 percent of the ridge. Streaming those weights imposes a time floor even before attention-state traffic and overhead:
\[\PerTokenDecodeTime \ge \frac{\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize}{\Bandwidth} \tag{2}\]
For the reference model, with \(\Parameters\) = 70.6 billion parameters at 8-bit precision, equation 2 gives a decode floor of 21.1 ms per output token, and equation 1 gives about 71 µs per prompt token. In the following comparison only, the time symbols denote these weight-only estimates rather than observed times:
\[\frac{\PerTokenDecodeTime}{\PerTokenPrefillTime} = \frac{\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize / \Bandwidth}{2\Parameters / \PeakRate} = \frac{\PeakRate \, \WeightElementStorageSize}{2 \Bandwidth} = \frac{\WeightElementStorageSize}{2} \, \RooflineRidgePoint \tag{3}\]
which is 295 for the reference configuration. Model size cancels in this approximation because both estimates count the same dense-model weights. The result assumes weight-dominated unbatched decode, peak-rate prefill, and negligible attention and serving overhead; it is not a measured ratio shared by every model on the accelerator. Within that model, the same number gives the number of tokens per pass at which arithmetic time meets weight-transfer time, a threshold used in the batching and speculative-decoding estimates below.
The estimate separates two quantities an agent engineer can influence. Shorter output reduces generation work, and avoiding repeated processing of an unchanged input prefix reduces prefill work. Which change matters more depends on the request lengths, serving configuration, and measurement boundary; token counts alone do not determine a service bill. The Cost of a Model Call prices a bounded example under explicit assumptions. A localized edit illustrates the output-side choice by omitting unchanged file contents, without implying that every compact serialization improves task success.



Equation 1 counts only the weights. Attention adds work that grows with the context itself. The token at position \(\CausalTokenPosition\) compares its query with \(\CausalTokenPosition\) earlier keys and combines \(\CausalTokenPosition\) earlier values, about \(4 \LayerCount d \CausalTokenPosition\) operations for a model with \(\LayerCount\) layers and width \(\HiddenDimension\). Summed over a causal prefill of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens, attention adds about \(2 \LayerCount d \SequenceLength^2\) operations to the \(2\Parameters \SequenceLength\) of the weights, so
\[\PrefillTime(\SequenceLength) \approx \frac{2\Parameters \SequenceLength + 2 \LayerCount d \SequenceLength^2}{\PeakRate} \tag{4}\]
The quadratic term equals the linear one at \(\SequenceLength^* = \Parameters / (\LayerCount \HiddenDimension)\), about 108,000 tokens for the reference model, with \(\LayerCount\) = 80 and \(\HiddenDimension\) = 8,192. At 32,768 tokens, attention adds about 30 percent to the prefill arithmetic, and beyond \(\SequenceLength^*\) it dominates. Under this fixed-throughput approximation, prefill time grows faster than linearly with length. Observed time to first token also depends on queueing, reuse, and the serving schedule. The logical selection problem in Usable Working Context determines which information the request needs; the estimate here prices the processing work without establishing an optimal context length or task-quality threshold.



A server can batch decode steps from several trajectories. If one weight read serves \(\BatchSize\) streams, the step produces one token for each stream. Ignoring the attention state each stream also reads, the time of one step is
\[\BatchedDecodeStepTime(\BatchSize) \approx \max\left( \frac{\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize}{\Bandwidth}, \; \frac{2 \Parameters \BatchSize}{\PeakRate} \right) \tag{5}\]
and the step stays at the memory-bound floor until \(\BatchSize\) reaches \(\PeakRate\,\WeightElementStorageSize / 2\Bandwidth\), the ratio of equation 3. Within this weight-only approximation, adding streams up to that threshold leaves step time unchanged, while step time divided by the number of generated tokens falls as \(1/\BatchSize\) toward \(2\Parameters/\PeakRate\). This is amortized serving time, not the latency of one stream or the price charged by a service. Repeated input adds prefill work when the prefix cannot be reused, but the bill also depends on utilization and the service’s accounting rules.
A trajectory cannot batch a future call whose input depends on an observation it has not received. Its current call can nevertheless share a physical serving batch with calls from other trajectories. That batching can change queueing and per-step latency; a dependent client stream is not evidence that the server runs at batch size one. The weight-only estimate also omits attention-state traffic. Each stream reads its own keys and values, approximately \(\SequenceLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\) bytes for a context of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens (section 1.3). Long contexts can therefore bind bandwidth or capacity before the arithmetic threshold in equation 5 is reached. Section 1.4 relates resident state to the number of live trajectories.



A large admitted prefill can delay decode work sharing its execution resources. Chunked prefill divides that work into bounded token slices that the scheduler can interleave or co-schedule with decodes (Agrawal et al. 2024). The token budget limits admitted token positions, not elapsed iteration time; realized gaps and prompt-completion time depend on context lengths, batching, resource contention, and implementation overhead. The weight-only estimate in equation 5 explains one opportunity for amortization, not a latency guarantee. Chunked Prefill Scheduling develops the policy trade-off.

Agrawal, Amey, Nitin Kedia, Ashish Panwar, Jayashree Mohan, Nipun Kwatra, Bhargav S. Gulavani, Alexey Tumanov, and Ramachandran Ramjee. 2024. “Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve.” 18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 24), 117–34.




Token selection, optional grammar constraints, and speculative verification add work beyond the model’s forward pass. Their placement determines which data crosses a device boundary and which dependencies remain on the generation path. The formulas below separate payload sizes from synchronization and computation costs; a small payload alone does not establish a low latency.


At each step the model produces one logit per vocabulary entry. Let \(|\TokenVocabulary|\) be the vocabulary size and \(\LogitStorageSize\) the bytes stored per logit. One vector occupies \(|\TokenVocabulary|\LogitStorageSize\) bytes. If \(\BatchSize\) streams each emit \(\PerStreamTokenRate\) tokens per second and transfer one full vector per token to a host sampler, the logit payload rate is \(\BatchSize \PerStreamTokenRate|\TokenVocabulary|\LogitStorageSize\) bytes per second. Batching transfers can reduce the number of transfer operations, but not that payload under these assumptions.
Sampling on the accelerator permits an interface that transfers only the selected token identifier. If each identifier occupies \(\TokenIdentifierSize\) bytes, its payload rate is \(\BatchSize \PerStreamTokenRate \TokenIdentifierSize\), giving a payload ratio of \(|\TokenVocabulary|\LogitStorageSize/\TokenIdentifierSize\). Neither expression counts protocol framing, requested log probabilities, or synchronization. Those costs must be measured on the actual path before choosing a placement. The calculation concerns an internal serving interface, not the application response format. A service may decode and buffer tokens into response chunks whose boundaries need not match tokens; The Invocation Contract specifies how the runtime handles that response.



A grammar-constrained decoder needs the legal tokens for its current parser state at every step (Grammar-Guided Decoding). With one bit per vocabulary entry, a dense mask occupies \(\lceil |\TokenVocabulary|/8 \rceil\) bytes. If the constraint has a finite-state representation with state set \(\AutomatonStateSet\), a byte-aligned dense table needs \(|\AutomatonStateSet|\lceil |\TokenVocabulary|/8 \rceil\) bytes, excluding transitions and metadata. This formula lets us compare a proposed vocabulary and state count with the memory budget without assuming that every grammar has a small finite-state representation.
Whether the table fits and remains resident in on-chip cache depends on the accelerator and competing working sets. Precomputation permits lookup and filtering during sampling, but table size alone establishes neither the lookup latency nor a required device placement.
A host-mediated implementation may instead transfer the selected token to a host process, advance its grammar state, and return the next mask before sampling continues. The cost depends on the implementation and on how much work overlaps model evaluation. Recursive grammars require additional parser state, while compressed structures and precomputation can reduce masking work. The legal-token mask must be available when selection uses it. Architectural Criteria for Constrained Decoding considers when constraining is worth its cost; Finite-state constrained decoding gives the masking argument, whose complete-output guarantee requires reaching an accepting state under the specified grammar and decoder assumptions. An interrupted legal prefix need not parse as a complete object.



Exact speculative sampling preserves a specified target distribution while checking several draft positions in a target-model pass (Leviathan et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2023). A draft distribution \(\DraftSamplingDistribution\) proposes \(\SpeculativeDraftTokenCount\) tokens \(\DraftCandidateToken_1, \dots, \DraftCandidateToken_k\) autoregressively. The target computes the distributions needed to verify them and to sample after the full draft. Both \(\TargetSamplingDistribution\) and \(\DraftSamplingDistribution\) below are normalized distributions at the same prefix after their sampling transformations, including any grammar masks. Scanning left to right, candidate \(\DraftCandidateToken_j\) is accepted with probability

Leviathan, Yaniv, Matan Kalman, and Yossi Matias. 2023. “Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding.” Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning 202: 19274–86.

Chen, C., S. Borgeaud, G. Irving, J.-B. Lespiau, L. Sifre, and J. Jumper. 2023. “Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2302.01318.
\[\DraftPositionAcceptanceProbability = \min\left(1, \frac{\TargetSamplingDistribution(\DraftCandidateToken_j \mid \cdot)}{\DraftSamplingDistribution(\DraftCandidateToken_j \mid \cdot)}\right) \tag{6}\]
At the first rejection, the remaining drafts are discarded and one replacement token is drawn from the normalized residual distribution
\[\ResidualSamplingDistribution(\VocabularyToken) = \frac{\max\left(0,\; \TargetSamplingDistribution(\VocabularyToken) - \DraftSamplingDistribution(\VocabularyToken)\right)}{\sum_{\NormalizerTokenIndex \in \TokenVocabulary} \max\left(0,\; \TargetSamplingDistribution(\NormalizerTokenIndex) - \DraftSamplingDistribution(\NormalizerTokenIndex)\right)} \tag{7}\]
If every draft is accepted, the sampler draws one bonus token from the target distribution after the full draft. Otherwise, equation 7 applies at the first rejected position; its denominator is positive when rejection has positive probability. Together with equation 6, this rule preserves the target sequence distribution under exact sampling and consistent prefix state. It does not promise the same sample for the same random seed. Termination or an output limit may shorten an iteration that otherwise emits between one and \(\SpeculativeDraftTokenCount+1\) tokens.
Weight reuse in equation 5 explains why verification can cost less than separate target passes. Actual benefit depends on draft cost, acceptance, attention traffic, batch composition, and verification overhead. Those terms can erase the saving; the weight-only threshold is not a speedup guarantee. Profitability boundaries for speculative decoding compares the resulting work and latency at the trajectory boundary.




For the full-attention decoder considered here, generation uses keys and values associated with earlier token positions. The serving system caches those derived vectors rather than recomputing them at each step. Autoregressive Generation introduces this reuse within a call; the storage estimate here follows from the model’s geometry and retained sequence length.


For a decoder with \(\LayerCount\) layers, \(\KvHeadCount\) key-value heads per layer, head dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension\), and \(\KvElementStorageSize\) bytes per stored element, each token stores one key vector and one value vector per layer and key-value head:
\[\KvCacheBytesPerToken = 2 \cdot \LayerCount \cdot \KvHeadCount \cdot \AttentionHeadDimension \cdot \KvElementStorageSize \tag{8}\]
and a context of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens occupies
\[\KvCacheMemory = \SequenceLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\]
For the reference model, with \(\LayerCount\) = 80, \(\KvHeadCount\) = 8, \(\AttentionHeadDimension\) = 128, and 16-bit storage, \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\) = 327,680 bytes, so a 32,768-token context occupies about 10.7 GB. The Footprint of Retained Attention State turns this into the number of trajectories one node can hold.



The number of key-value heads is a design choice, and it changes \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\) directly. Multi-head attention gives every query head its own keys and values. Multi-query attention shares one key-value head across all query heads (Shazeer 2019). Grouped-query attention sits between them, sharing each key-value head across a group of query heads (Ainslie et al. 2023). Table 2 applies the three designs to the reference model’s other dimensions.

Shazeer, Noam. 2019. “Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head Is All You Need.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1911.02150.

Ainslie, Joshua, James Lee-Thorp, Michiel de Jong, Yury Zemlyanskiy, Federico Lebr’on, and Sumit Sanghai. 2023. “GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints.” Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP).
