Storing each key and value element at 8 rather than 16 bits halves the element payload, to 163,840 bytes per token for the grouped design, before scale, metadata, or layout overhead. Lower precision and selective removal of entries require task-quality and implementation validation. The remaining cache alone does not recover a discarded entry, although retained inputs and compatible configuration may permit recomputation. These storage approximations are distinct from changing the model architecture (The Footprint of Retained Attention State).



Memory occupancy depends on how much is held and for how long. A trajectory whose attention state stays resident through a tool wait of length \(\ExternalWait\) occupies
\[\MemoryHoldDuringWait = \KvCacheMemory \cdot \ExternalWait\]
byte-seconds while generating nothing. When a tool wait exceeds the active generation interval and holds the same footprint, idle occupancy exceeds active occupancy. The relevant inputs are the actual retained bytes and their holding interval, which makes the retain, evict, recompute, or offload decision of Paused-State Policies a per-wait decision rather than a fixed property of agents.



Reserving a contiguous region for each trajectory’s maximum context leaves unused capacity when its retained length is below that cap. Paged storage divides a pool into interchangeable fixed blocks of \(\KvBlockSize\) tokens and maps each trajectory’s positions to blocks through a table (Kwon et al. 2023). Allocation on demand removes variable-extent external fragmentation within that pool; it does not eliminate metadata, temporary allocations, or unused final-block slots. If sequence lengths have uniformly distributed remainders modulo \(\KvBlockSize\), the mean unused tail payload is

Kwon, Woosuk, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, and Ion Stoica. 2023. “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention.” Proceedings of the 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 611–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3600006.3613165.
\[\mathbb{E}[\text{waste}] \approx \frac{\KvBlockSize - 1}{2} \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\]
per sequence. Without that distributional assumption, the unconditional bound is at most \(\KvBlockSize - 1\) unused token slots in a final block. Compatible blocks can also be shared, allowing branches and requests with a common prefix to use one physical copy under the serving system’s ownership rules (Paged KV Allocation).




An agent can remain live while it consumes no accelerator execution time. A retained cache, sandbox lease, and harness record can each span a different interval of that trajectory. Capacity estimates therefore begin by choosing the resource and its acquisition-to-release boundary. Little’s law relates average occupancy to that boundary; a separate queueing model estimates waiting under stated arrival and service assumptions.
The worked case assumes an unchanged context footprint and no extra waiting. Its averages compare two retention policies; they do not determine peak provisioning or prove that the model-serving system can sustain the offered rate.


A server batches decode steps from many trajectories (equation 5). In a fixed-membership batch, finished requests cannot be replaced until the batch drains, although their results need not be withheld. Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries (Yu et al. 2022). A returning trajectory can enter a later iteration when memory, token budgets, and scheduling policy permit; a released slot does not promise admission on the immediately following step.

Yu, Gyeong-In, Joo Seong Jeong, Geon-Woo Kim, Soojeong Kim, and Byung-Gon Chun. 2022. “Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models.” 16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 22), 521–38.
Batch slots are not independent servers. Their occupants share weight reads, arithmetic, memory bandwidth, and iteration time, so one request can change another’s service rate. Little’s law still applies to a stable measured boundary, but the number of slots cannot be substituted for the number of independent servers in a queueing formula. Predicting delay requires a model or measurements that capture the batching policy and workload mix.



For a stable system with well-defined finite long-run averages, the mean number of items inside a boundary equals their entry rate times their mean time inside that same boundary (Little 1961):

Little, John D. C. 1961. “A Proof for the Queuing Formula: \(L = \lambda W\).” Operations Research 9 (3): 383–87. https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383.
\[\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \cdot \RequestTimeInSystem \tag{9}\]
A trajectory of \(\TurnHorizon\) turns spends each turn in a model call and then in a tool, so its trajectory duration is
\[\TrajectoryDuration = \sum_{t=0}^{\TurnHorizon-1} \left( \ModelTime^{(t)} + \ToolTime^{(t)} \right)\]
under the simplifying assumption that model calls and tool operations run sequentially, with no additional approval, queueing, or runtime delay. As a worked case, let trajectories start at 2 per second, each running 15 turns of 4 s of model time and 20 s of tool time. Each lives 360 s, about 6 minutes, so equation 9, in its trajectory form \(\ConcurrentTrajectories = \TrajectoryAdmissionRate\,\mathbb{E}[\TrajectoryDuration]\), gives 720 live trajectories. Only 17 percent of each trajectory’s time is spent in a model call, so on average 120 of them are calling the model at any moment.
The gap between those two numbers measures the effect of holding state through tool waits in this workload. If every live trajectory keeps a 32,768-token context resident, the attention state totals about 7.7 TB, about 15 nodes’ worth of the reference pool of section 1.5. Holding the same footprint only during the stipulated model-call intervals gives about 2.4 nodes’ worth. Reloading or recomputing on resumption adds time and work omitted from this comparison; recomputing those intervals may change the averages. Paused-State Policies develops that policy choice.
Harness records and sandbox leases require their own acquisition rates and holding times, not the whole trajectory lifetime by default. If footprints vary, average memory occupancy follows the byte-time held by each arrival, rather than an unqualified product of mean footprint and mean lifetime. Headroom and admission additionally require variability, reclamation behavior, and resource-specific limits (Capacity for Trajectories, Sandbox Pools and Reset).



A single-server queue isolates how variability and load contribute to waiting. Consider first-come, first-served service with independent, identically distributed interarrival times, independent, identically distributed service times, independence between the two sequences, finite variances, and utilization \(\ServingUtilization < 1\). Let \(\mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime]\) be mean service time and \(\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2\) and \(\QueueServiceVariationCoefficient^2\) the squared coefficients of variation of interarrival and service times. Kingman’s heavy-traffic result motivates the following finite-load approximation to mean waiting time; it is not an identity or a tail bound.
\[\QueueWaitTime \approx \frac{\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2 + \QueueServiceVariationCoefficient^2}{2} \cdot \frac{\ServingUtilization}{1 - \ServingUtilization} \cdot \mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime]\]
With interarrival variability \(\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2\) = 2 and service variability \(\QueueServiceVariationCoefficient^2\) = 1, the variability factor is 1.5. Substitution gives approximate waits of 1.5, 3.5, and 13.5 service times at 50, 70, and 90 percent utilization. These are selected comparison points, not a universal utilization knee or an operating recommendation.
Batching, correlated fan-out, retries, and state-dependent service rates can violate the model. Infinite service-time variance also invalidates the finite-variance calculation. The derivation and its limits follow the single-server heavy-traffic analysis of Boon et al. (2023); multiple-server pools need a separately justified model. Measured deadline compliance, workload mix, and admission policy determine usable capacity. Heavy-tailed queueing theory distinguishes mean waiting from tail behavior.

Boon, Marko A. A., Augustus J. E. M. Janssen, and Johan S. H. van Leeuwaarden. 2023. “Heavy-Traffic Single-Server Queues and the Transform Method.” Indagationes Mathematicae 34 (5): 1014–37. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.indag.2023.02.004.



For a server with memory \(\NodeHbmCapacity\), weights of \(\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize\) bytes (16-bit here, whereas the time floors assume 8-bit weights), and a runtime reserve \(\RuntimeReserveMemory\), the memory left for attention state is
\[\KvPoolMemory = \NodeHbmCapacity - \Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize - \RuntimeReserveMemory \tag{10}\]
and a mean-footprint estimate for contexts of average length \(\MeanContextLength\) is
\[\MaxResidentContextCount = \left\lfloor \frac{\KvPoolMemory}{\MeanContextLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken} \right\rfloor \tag{11}\]
An average footprint does not guarantee that a particular set of requests fits. For the reference node and equal-length unshared contexts, equation 10 leaves 526.0 GB and equation 11 gives 48 resident contexts at 32,768 tokens, before allocator overhead and additional headroom. This is the payload bound derived in The Footprint of Retained Attention State, not an admission or throughput guarantee. When a new allocation cannot fit, the service may queue or reject work, reclaim dormant state, or move or drop eligible state.
A restricted comparison estimates reconstruction of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens by the linear weight-work term \(2\Parameters \SequenceLength/\PeakRate\) and reload by \(\SequenceLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken / \HostLinkBandwidth\), assuming the stated sustained compute and transfer rates. It omits the attention term of equation 4, queueing, allocation, and other overhead. Within that model alone, reconstruction has the smaller estimated duration when
\[\frac{2 \Parameters}{\PeakRate} < \frac{\KvCacheBytesPerToken}{\HostLinkBandwidth}\]
The cancellation of context length follows from those two linear estimates, not from a general property of serving latency. The pause policy in Paused-State Policies additionally considers uniquely reclaimable state, competing demand, resumption likelihood, host and link resources, and the permitted resume delay.




The worked estimates use the MLSysIM entries Models.Language.Llama3_70B, Hardware.Cloud.H100, and Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100. These identify a reference configuration, not a current-product recommendation. Table 3 collects their values and the local precision and reserve assumptions so that a reader can audit or replace them. The ratio of equation 3 isolates weight reuse; equation 8 sizes the attention payload.
The two calculations have different placement boundaries. Per-token floors use one accelerator’s compute rate and bandwidth with 8-bit weights. The memory pool instead aggregates 8 accelerators, totaling 687.2 GB, and subtracts one 16-bit model copy and a node-wide reserve. It assumes a feasible sharding arrangement without counting communication time or per-device imbalance. Multiplying memory capacity does not establish an equivalent latency speedup. Memory quantities below use decimal GB consistently with the pool arithmetic, rather than the accelerator’s branded capacity label.

title: Inference Cost Foundations
text:
Prompt processing can reuse a model’s weights across many token positions, whereas unbatched generation uses those weights for one new position at a time. That difference can make prefill arithmetic-bound and decode bandwidth-bound. Neither regime follows from the phase name alone. Prompt length, batching, attention traffic, and the serving implementation determine which resource limits an actual call. A weight-only estimate isolates the reuse effect before adding those complications.
A model call processes the uncached prompt during prefill and generates new tokens during decode. Both phases use the same weights, but the reference calculation yields a ratio of about 295 between the unbatched weight-transfer floor per output token and the arithmetic floor per prompt token. We compare these conditional floors to explain the bandwidth constraint (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}\)), not to predict the ratio of measured call latencies or token prices.


An accelerator has two limits, the rate \(\PeakRate\) at which it performs arithmetic (operations per second) and the rate \(\Bandwidth\) at which its memory delivers data (bytes per second). A computation’s arithmetic intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) is the number of operations it performs per byte it moves. The roofline model (Williams et al. 2009) gives a performance ceiling \(\AttainableComputeRate\) from whichever limit binds first:

Williams, Samuel, Andrew Waterman, and David Patterson. 2009. “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” Communications of the ACM 52 (4): 65–76. https://doi.org/10.1145/1498765.1498785.
\[\AttainableComputeRate = \min\left( \PeakRate, \; \ArithmeticIntensity \cdot \Bandwidth \right)\]
The two ceilings meet at the ridge point \(\RooflineRidgePoint = \PeakRate / \Bandwidth\). Below the ridge, bandwidth supplies the lower ceiling; above it, arithmetic supplies the lower ceiling. Actual performance can fall below either ceiling because of implementation and scheduling overhead. For the reference accelerator at 8-bit precision, \(\PeakRate\) = 1,979 trillion operations per second and \(\Bandwidth\) = 3.35 TB/s, so \(\RooflineRidgePoint \approx\) 591 operations per byte.



A dense transformer with \(\Parameters\) active parameters performs about \(2\Parameters\) weight-related operations per token, one multiply and one add per weight. Its weight payload is \(\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize\) bytes, where \(\WeightElementStorageSize\) is bytes per parameter. The approximation counts this payload once per pass; prefill and decode differ in how many tokens share that read. Sparse activation and weight reuse from another cache level require a different traffic count.
In the weight-only model, prefill shares each weight read across \(\SequenceLength\) prompt positions, giving intensity \(2\Parameters \SequenceLength / (\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize) = 2\SequenceLength/\WeightElementStorageSize\). When that intensity exceeds the ridge and arithmetic approaches the stated peak, the per-token time approaches the following floor. Small prompts, kernel tiling, attention, and additional memory traffic can invalidate those assumptions.
\[\PerTokenPrefillTime \approx \frac{2\Parameters}{\PeakRate} \tag{1}\]
Ordinary decode for one stream generates one token per pass, with each token depending on the preceding prefix. If the weights must be read from the modeled memory on every pass, the weight-only intensity is \(2/\WeightElementStorageSize\), or 2 operations per byte at 8-bit precision, about 0.34 percent of the ridge. Streaming those weights imposes a time floor even before attention-state traffic and overhead:
\[\PerTokenDecodeTime \ge \frac{\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize}{\Bandwidth} \tag{2}\]
For the reference model, with \(\Parameters\) = 70.6 billion parameters at 8-bit precision, equation 2 gives a decode floor of 21.1 ms per output token, and equation 1 gives about 71 µs per prompt token. In the following comparison only, the time symbols denote these weight-only estimates rather than observed times:
\[\frac{\PerTokenDecodeTime}{\PerTokenPrefillTime} = \frac{\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize / \Bandwidth}{2\Parameters / \PeakRate} = \frac{\PeakRate \, \WeightElementStorageSize}{2 \Bandwidth} = \frac{\WeightElementStorageSize}{2} \, \RooflineRidgePoint \tag{3}\]
which is 295 for the reference configuration. Model size cancels in this approximation because both estimates count the same dense-model weights. The result assumes weight-dominated unbatched decode, peak-rate prefill, and negligible attention and serving overhead; it is not a measured ratio shared by every model on the accelerator. Within that model, the same number gives the number of tokens per pass at which arithmetic time meets weight-transfer time, a threshold used in the batching and speculative-decoding estimates below.
The estimate separates two quantities an agent engineer can influence. Shorter output reduces generation work, and avoiding repeated processing of an unchanged input prefix reduces prefill work. Which change matters more depends on the request lengths, serving configuration, and measurement boundary; token counts alone do not determine a service bill. The Cost of a Model Call prices a bounded example under explicit assumptions. A localized edit illustrates the output-side choice by omitting unchanged file contents, without implying that every compact serialization improves task success.



Equation 1 counts only the weights. Attention adds work that grows with the context itself. The token at position \(\CausalTokenPosition\) compares its query with \(\CausalTokenPosition\) earlier keys and combines \(\CausalTokenPosition\) earlier values, about \(4 \LayerCount d \CausalTokenPosition\) operations for a model with \(\LayerCount\) layers and width \(\HiddenDimension\). Summed over a causal prefill of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens, attention adds about \(2 \LayerCount d \SequenceLength^2\) operations to the \(2\Parameters \SequenceLength\) of the weights, so
\[\PrefillTime(\SequenceLength) \approx \frac{2\Parameters \SequenceLength + 2 \LayerCount d \SequenceLength^2}{\PeakRate} \tag{4}\]
The quadratic term equals the linear one at \(\SequenceLength^* = \Parameters / (\LayerCount \HiddenDimension)\), about 108,000 tokens for the reference model, with \(\LayerCount\) = 80 and \(\HiddenDimension\) = 8,192. At 32,768 tokens, attention adds about 30 percent to the prefill arithmetic, and beyond \(\SequenceLength^*\) it dominates. Under this fixed-throughput approximation, prefill time grows faster than linearly with length. Observed time to first token also depends on queueing, reuse, and the serving schedule. The logical selection problem in Usable Working Context determines which information the request needs; the estimate here prices the processing work without establishing an optimal context length or task-quality threshold.



A server can batch decode steps from several trajectories. If one weight read serves \(\BatchSize\) streams, the step produces one token for each stream. Ignoring the attention state each stream also reads, the time of one step is
\[\BatchedDecodeStepTime(\BatchSize) \approx \max\left( \frac{\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize}{\Bandwidth}, \; \frac{2 \Parameters \BatchSize}{\PeakRate} \right) \tag{5}\]
and the step stays at the memory-bound floor until \(\BatchSize\) reaches \(\PeakRate\,\WeightElementStorageSize / 2\Bandwidth\), the ratio of equation 3. Within this weight-only approximation, adding streams up to that threshold leaves step time unchanged, while step time divided by the number of generated tokens falls as \(1/\BatchSize\) toward \(2\Parameters/\PeakRate\). This is amortized serving time, not the latency of one stream or the price charged by a service. Repeated input adds prefill work when the prefix cannot be reused, but the bill also depends on utilization and the service’s accounting rules.
A trajectory cannot batch a future call whose input depends on an observation it has not received. Its current call can nevertheless share a physical serving batch with calls from other trajectories. That batching can change queueing and per-step latency; a dependent client stream is not evidence that the server runs at batch size one. The weight-only estimate also omits attention-state traffic. Each stream reads its own keys and values, approximately \(\SequenceLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\) bytes for a context of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens (section 1.3). Long contexts can therefore bind bandwidth or capacity before the arithmetic threshold in equation 5 is reached. Section 1.4 relates resident state to the number of live trajectories.



A large admitted prefill can delay decode work sharing its execution resources. Chunked prefill divides that work into bounded token slices that the scheduler can interleave or co-schedule with decodes (Agrawal et al. 2024). The token budget limits admitted token positions, not elapsed iteration time; realized gaps and prompt-completion time depend on context lengths, batching, resource contention, and implementation overhead. The weight-only estimate in equation 5 explains one opportunity for amortization, not a latency guarantee. Chunked Prefill Scheduling develops the policy trade-off.

Agrawal, Amey, Nitin Kedia, Ashish Panwar, Jayashree Mohan, Nipun Kwatra, Bhargav S. Gulavani, Alexey Tumanov, and Ramachandran Ramjee. 2024. “Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve.” 18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 24), 117–34.

title: Inference Cost Foundations
text:
Token selection, optional grammar constraints, and speculative verification add work beyond the model’s forward pass. Their placement determines which data crosses a device boundary and which dependencies remain on the generation path. The formulas below separate payload sizes from synchronization and computation costs; a small payload alone does not establish a low latency.


At each step the model produces one logit per vocabulary entry. Let \(|\TokenVocabulary|\) be the vocabulary size and \(\LogitStorageSize\) the bytes stored per logit. One vector occupies \(|\TokenVocabulary|\LogitStorageSize\) bytes. If \(\BatchSize\) streams each emit \(\PerStreamTokenRate\) tokens per second and transfer one full vector per token to a host sampler, the logit payload rate is \(\BatchSize \PerStreamTokenRate|\TokenVocabulary|\LogitStorageSize\) bytes per second. Batching transfers can reduce the number of transfer operations, but not that payload under these assumptions.
Sampling on the accelerator permits an interface that transfers only the selected token identifier. If each identifier occupies \(\TokenIdentifierSize\) bytes, its payload rate is \(\BatchSize \PerStreamTokenRate \TokenIdentifierSize\), giving a payload ratio of \(|\TokenVocabulary|\LogitStorageSize/\TokenIdentifierSize\). Neither expression counts protocol framing, requested log probabilities, or synchronization. Those costs must be measured on the actual path before choosing a placement. The calculation concerns an internal serving interface, not the application response format. A service may decode and buffer tokens into response chunks whose boundaries need not match tokens; The Invocation Contract specifies how the runtime handles that response.



A grammar-constrained decoder needs the legal tokens for its current parser state at every step (Grammar-Guided Decoding). With one bit per vocabulary entry, a dense mask occupies \(\lceil |\TokenVocabulary|/8 \rceil\) bytes. If the constraint has a finite-state representation with state set \(\AutomatonStateSet\), a byte-aligned dense table needs \(|\AutomatonStateSet|\lceil |\TokenVocabulary|/8 \rceil\) bytes, excluding transitions and metadata. This formula lets us compare a proposed vocabulary and state count with the memory budget without assuming that every grammar has a small finite-state representation.
Whether the table fits and remains resident in on-chip cache depends on the accelerator and competing working sets. Precomputation permits lookup and filtering during sampling, but table size alone establishes neither the lookup latency nor a required device placement.
A host-mediated implementation may instead transfer the selected token to a host process, advance its grammar state, and return the next mask before sampling continues. The cost depends on the implementation and on how much work overlaps model evaluation. Recursive grammars require additional parser state, while compressed structures and precomputation can reduce masking work. The legal-token mask must be available when selection uses it. Architectural Criteria for Constrained Decoding considers when constraining is worth its cost; Finite-state constrained decoding gives the masking argument, whose complete-output guarantee requires reaching an accepting state under the specified grammar and decoder assumptions. An interrupted legal prefix need not parse as a complete object.



Exact speculative sampling preserves a specified target distribution while checking several draft positions in a target-model pass (Leviathan et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2023). A draft distribution \(\DraftSamplingDistribution\) proposes \(\SpeculativeDraftTokenCount\) tokens \(\DraftCandidateToken_1, \dots, \DraftCandidateToken_k\) autoregressively. The target computes the distributions needed to verify them and to sample after the full draft. Both \(\TargetSamplingDistribution\) and \(\DraftSamplingDistribution\) below are normalized distributions at the same prefix after their sampling transformations, including any grammar masks. Scanning left to right, candidate \(\DraftCandidateToken_j\) is accepted with probability

Leviathan, Yaniv, Matan Kalman, and Yossi Matias. 2023. “Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding.” Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning 202: 19274–86.

Chen, C., S. Borgeaud, G. Irving, J.-B. Lespiau, L. Sifre, and J. Jumper. 2023. “Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2302.01318.
\[\DraftPositionAcceptanceProbability = \min\left(1, \frac{\TargetSamplingDistribution(\DraftCandidateToken_j \mid \cdot)}{\DraftSamplingDistribution(\DraftCandidateToken_j \mid \cdot)}\right) \tag{6}\]
At the first rejection, the remaining drafts are discarded and one replacement token is drawn from the normalized residual distribution
\[\ResidualSamplingDistribution(\VocabularyToken) = \frac{\max\left(0,\; \TargetSamplingDistribution(\VocabularyToken) - \DraftSamplingDistribution(\VocabularyToken)\right)}{\sum_{\NormalizerTokenIndex \in \TokenVocabulary} \max\left(0,\; \TargetSamplingDistribution(\NormalizerTokenIndex) - \DraftSamplingDistribution(\NormalizerTokenIndex)\right)} \tag{7}\]
If every draft is accepted, the sampler draws one bonus token from the target distribution after the full draft. Otherwise, equation 7 applies at the first rejected position; its denominator is positive when rejection has positive probability. Together with equation 6, this rule preserves the target sequence distribution under exact sampling and consistent prefix state. It does not promise the same sample for the same random seed. Termination or an output limit may shorten an iteration that otherwise emits between one and \(\SpeculativeDraftTokenCount+1\) tokens.
Weight reuse in equation 5 explains why verification can cost less than separate target passes. Actual benefit depends on draft cost, acceptance, attention traffic, batch composition, and verification overhead. Those terms can erase the saving; the weight-only threshold is not a speedup guarantee. Profitability boundaries for speculative decoding compares the resulting work and latency at the trajectory boundary.

title: Inference Cost Foundations
text:
For the full-attention decoder considered here, generation uses keys and values associated with earlier token positions. The serving system caches those derived vectors rather than recomputing them at each step. Autoregressive Generation introduces this reuse within a call; the storage estimate here follows from the model’s geometry and retained sequence length.


For a decoder with \(\LayerCount\) layers, \(\KvHeadCount\) key-value heads per layer, head dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension\), and \(\KvElementStorageSize\) bytes per stored element, each token stores one key vector and one value vector per layer and key-value head:
\[\KvCacheBytesPerToken = 2 \cdot \LayerCount \cdot \KvHeadCount \cdot \AttentionHeadDimension \cdot \KvElementStorageSize \tag{8}\]
and a context of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens occupies
\[\KvCacheMemory = \SequenceLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\]
For the reference model, with \(\LayerCount\) = 80, \(\KvHeadCount\) = 8, \(\AttentionHeadDimension\) = 128, and 16-bit storage, \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\) = 327,680 bytes, so a 32,768-token context occupies about 10.7 GB. The Footprint of Retained Attention State turns this into the number of trajectories one node can hold.



The number of key-value heads is a design choice, and it changes \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\) directly. Multi-head attention gives every query head its own keys and values. Multi-query attention shares one key-value head across all query heads (Shazeer 2019). Grouped-query attention sits between them, sharing each key-value head across a group of query heads (Ainslie et al. 2023). Table 2 applies the three designs to the reference model’s other dimensions.

Shazeer, Noam. 2019. “Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head Is All You Need.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1911.02150.

Ainslie, Joshua, James Lee-Thorp, Michiel de Jong, Yury Zemlyanskiy, Federico Lebr’on, and Sumit Sanghai. 2023. “GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints.” Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP).

Storing each key and value element at 8 rather than 16 bits halves the element payload, to 163,840 bytes per token for the grouped design, before scale, metadata, or layout overhead. Lower precision and selective removal of entries require task-quality and implementation validation. The remaining cache alone does not recover a discarded entry, although retained inputs and compatible configuration may permit recomputation. These storage approximations are distinct from changing the model architecture (The Footprint of Retained Attention State).



Memory occupancy depends on how much is held and for how long. A trajectory whose attention state stays resident through a tool wait of length \(\ExternalWait\) occupies
\[\MemoryHoldDuringWait = \KvCacheMemory \cdot \ExternalWait\]
byte-seconds while generating nothing. When a tool wait exceeds the active generation interval and holds the same footprint, idle occupancy exceeds active occupancy. The relevant inputs are the actual retained bytes and their holding interval, which makes the retain, evict, recompute, or offload decision of Paused-State Policies a per-wait decision rather than a fixed property of agents.



Reserving a contiguous region for each trajectory’s maximum context leaves unused capacity when its retained length is below that cap. Paged storage divides a pool into interchangeable fixed blocks of \(\KvBlockSize\) tokens and maps each trajectory’s positions to blocks through a table (Kwon et al. 2023). Allocation on demand removes variable-extent external fragmentation within that pool; it does not eliminate metadata, temporary allocations, or unused final-block slots. If sequence lengths have uniformly distributed remainders modulo \(\KvBlockSize\), the mean unused tail payload is

Kwon, Woosuk, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, and Ion Stoica. 2023. “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention.” Proceedings of the 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 611–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3600006.3613165.
\[\mathbb{E}[\text{waste}] \approx \frac{\KvBlockSize - 1}{2} \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\]
per sequence. Without that distributional assumption, the unconditional bound is at most \(\KvBlockSize - 1\) unused token slots in a final block. Compatible blocks can also be shared, allowing branches and requests with a common prefix to use one physical copy under the serving system’s ownership rules (Paged KV Allocation).

title: Inference Cost Foundations
text:
An agent can remain live while it consumes no accelerator execution time. A retained cache, sandbox lease, and harness record can each span a different interval of that trajectory. Capacity estimates therefore begin by choosing the resource and its acquisition-to-release boundary. Little’s law relates average occupancy to that boundary; a separate queueing model estimates waiting under stated arrival and service assumptions.
The worked case assumes an unchanged context footprint and no extra waiting. Its averages compare two retention policies; they do not determine peak provisioning or prove that the model-serving system can sustain the offered rate.


A server batches decode steps from many trajectories (equation 5). In a fixed-membership batch, finished requests cannot be replaced until the batch drains, although their results need not be withheld. Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries (Yu et al. 2022). A returning trajectory can enter a later iteration when memory, token budgets, and scheduling policy permit; a released slot does not promise admission on the immediately following step.

Yu, Gyeong-In, Joo Seong Jeong, Geon-Woo Kim, Soojeong Kim, and Byung-Gon Chun. 2022. “Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models.” 16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 22), 521–38.
Batch slots are not independent servers. Their occupants share weight reads, arithmetic, memory bandwidth, and iteration time, so one request can change another’s service rate. Little’s law still applies to a stable measured boundary, but the number of slots cannot be substituted for the number of independent servers in a queueing formula. Predicting delay requires a model or measurements that capture the batching policy and workload mix.



For a stable system with well-defined finite long-run averages, the mean number of items inside a boundary equals their entry rate times their mean time inside that same boundary (Little 1961):

Little, John D. C. 1961. “A Proof for the Queuing Formula: \(L = \lambda W\).” Operations Research 9 (3): 383–87. https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383.
\[\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \cdot \RequestTimeInSystem \tag{9}\]
A trajectory of \(\TurnHorizon\) turns spends each turn in a model call and then in a tool, so its trajectory duration is
\[\TrajectoryDuration = \sum_{t=0}^{\TurnHorizon-1} \left( \ModelTime^{(t)} + \ToolTime^{(t)} \right)\]
under the simplifying assumption that model calls and tool operations run sequentially, with no additional approval, queueing, or runtime delay. As a worked case, let trajectories start at 2 per second, each running 15 turns of 4 s of model time and 20 s of tool time. Each lives 360 s, about 6 minutes, so equation 9, in its trajectory form \(\ConcurrentTrajectories = \TrajectoryAdmissionRate\,\mathbb{E}[\TrajectoryDuration]\), gives 720 live trajectories. Only 17 percent of each trajectory’s time is spent in a model call, so on average 120 of them are calling the model at any moment.
The gap between those two numbers measures the effect of holding state through tool waits in this workload. If every live trajectory keeps a 32,768-token context resident, the attention state totals about 7.7 TB, about 15 nodes’ worth of the reference pool of section 1.5. Holding the same footprint only during the stipulated model-call intervals gives about 2.4 nodes’ worth. Reloading or recomputing on resumption adds time and work omitted from this comparison; recomputing those intervals may change the averages. Paused-State Policies develops that policy choice.
Harness records and sandbox leases require their own acquisition rates and holding times, not the whole trajectory lifetime by default. If footprints vary, average memory occupancy follows the byte-time held by each arrival, rather than an unqualified product of mean footprint and mean lifetime. Headroom and admission additionally require variability, reclamation behavior, and resource-specific limits (Capacity for Trajectories, Sandbox Pools and Reset).



A single-server queue isolates how variability and load contribute to waiting. Consider first-come, first-served service with independent, identically distributed interarrival times, independent, identically distributed service times, independence between the two sequences, finite variances, and utilization \(\ServingUtilization < 1\). Let \(\mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime]\) be mean service time and \(\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2\) and \(\QueueServiceVariationCoefficient^2\) the squared coefficients of variation of interarrival and service times. Kingman’s heavy-traffic result motivates the following finite-load approximation to mean waiting time; it is not an identity or a tail bound.
\[\QueueWaitTime \approx \frac{\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2 + \QueueServiceVariationCoefficient^2}{2} \cdot \frac{\ServingUtilization}{1 - \ServingUtilization} \cdot \mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime]\]
With interarrival variability \(\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2\) = 2 and service variability \(\QueueServiceVariationCoefficient^2\) = 1, the variability factor is 1.5. Substitution gives approximate waits of 1.5, 3.5, and 13.5 service times at 50, 70, and 90 percent utilization. These are selected comparison points, not a universal utilization knee or an operating recommendation.
Batching, correlated fan-out, retries, and state-dependent service rates can violate the model. Infinite service-time variance also invalidates the finite-variance calculation. The derivation and its limits follow the single-server heavy-traffic analysis of Boon et al. (2023); multiple-server pools need a separately justified model. Measured deadline compliance, workload mix, and admission policy determine usable capacity. Heavy-tailed queueing theory distinguishes mean waiting from tail behavior.

Boon, Marko A. A., Augustus J. E. M. Janssen, and Johan S. H. van Leeuwaarden. 2023. “Heavy-Traffic Single-Server Queues and the Transform Method.” Indagationes Mathematicae 34 (5): 1014–37. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.indag.2023.02.004.



For a server with memory \(\NodeHbmCapacity\), weights of \(\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize\) bytes (16-bit here, whereas the time floors assume 8-bit weights), and a runtime reserve \(\RuntimeReserveMemory\), the memory left for attention state is
\[\KvPoolMemory = \NodeHbmCapacity - \Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize - \RuntimeReserveMemory \tag{10}\]
and a mean-footprint estimate for contexts of average length \(\MeanContextLength\) is
\[\MaxResidentContextCount = \left\lfloor \frac{\KvPoolMemory}{\MeanContextLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken} \right\rfloor \tag{11}\]
An average footprint does not guarantee that a particular set of requests fits. For the reference node and equal-length unshared contexts, equation 10 leaves 526.0 GB and equation 11 gives 48 resident contexts at 32,768 tokens, before allocator overhead and additional headroom. This is the payload bound derived in The Footprint of Retained Attention State, not an admission or throughput guarantee. When a new allocation cannot fit, the service may queue or reject work, reclaim dormant state, or move or drop eligible state.
A restricted comparison estimates reconstruction of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens by the linear weight-work term \(2\Parameters \SequenceLength/\PeakRate\) and reload by \(\SequenceLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken / \HostLinkBandwidth\), assuming the stated sustained compute and transfer rates. It omits the attention term of equation 4, queueing, allocation, and other overhead. Within that model alone, reconstruction has the smaller estimated duration when
\[\frac{2 \Parameters}{\PeakRate} < \frac{\KvCacheBytesPerToken}{\HostLinkBandwidth}\]
The cancellation of context length follows from those two linear estimates, not from a general property of serving latency. The pause policy in Paused-State Policies additionally considers uniquely reclaimable state, competing demand, resumption likelihood, host and link resources, and the permitted resume delay.

title: 1 Reference Architecture
text:
This appendix is a reference for assigning responsibilities across an agentic machine learning system. Its maps connect task requirements to state owners, interfaces, and evidence obligations, so a design review can identify missing ownership without prescribing a particular implementation stack. The chapters teach the mechanisms; this reference helps a reader locate their boundaries and check the assumptions connecting them.


Consult the entry matching the design decision or missing record:

When a responsibility has no clear owner, section 1.1 maps it to a logical component.
When deciding which mechanisms a task requires, section 1.2 links contract conditions to design obligations.
When an operation crosses component boundaries, section 1.3 traces the records needed at each handoff.
When choosing an execution boundary, section 1.6 collects the compatibility and isolation questions.
When deciding where information lives and who may change it, section 1.5 distinguishes state ownership and reconstruction contracts.
When placing components or investigating a deployment symptom, section 1.12 identifies assumptions and measurements to check.

The maps describe logical responsibilities. One process may implement several rows; distributing a row across services does not remove its ownership requirement.



A design can contain a tool gateway yet leave retry ownership undefined. Naming a component therefore does not establish its contract. The responsibilities in table 1 identify the records or decisions that need an owner when that function is present.

For each applicable row, record the actual owner, its inputs and outputs, and the assumptions under which its boundary holds. Information-flow policy also crosses the rows: a permitted read can still disclose sensitive data through a later output or tool call. Information-Flow Policy develops the provenance and permitted-flow checks needed at those handoffs. No single row establishes end-to-end correctness.



A short task can issue an irreversible action, while a long task can remain disposable and read-only. Horizon alone cannot select durability or recovery mechanisms. H·S·A identifies exposures to examine; the adopted task contract determines permitted effects, failure tolerance, resource limits, and completion evidence (The H·S·A Exposure Space). Table 2 records conditional obligations rather than minimum stacks for exposure levels.



Table 2: Contract-Driven Design Obligations: Conditions that make particular responsibilities necessary. Several conditions can apply to one operation; none uniquely determines a deployment topology.

Apply the rows to operations and retained records, not merely to a task’s largest exposure label. A local patch needs a workspace boundary; publishing it adds source-side authorization and concurrency requirements. Publication does not imply that reversal is safe, available, or equivalent to undoing its consequences. If the task does not permit publication, withholding that capability removes the need to manage that particular effect without removing obligations for local execution and evidence.



A tool-using turn in a crash-recoverable task provides a bounded interface check. Assume that the harness owns admission, the endpoint exposes an operation contract, and the runtime retains the inputs required for its promised recovery. The sequence below follows one admitted model call and one proposed external operation; answer-only turns, parallel calls, and approval waits take different paths.

Admit the turn. The harness considers a READY trajectory, checks current grants and control state, and reserves the proposed bounded liability against actual consumption and existing reservations while preserving finalization resources. Admitted work moves to CALLING_MODEL (Trajectory States).
Assemble the context. The assembler selects applicable source material and observations within the input budget. Record the delivered input or retained artifact references needed by the recovery contract; a hash identifies content but cannot reconstruct missing bytes.
Call the model. The model service receives the call with an output ceiling and a deadline, reuses the cached prefix where it can (Prefix Caching Across Turns), and returns a proposal with a stop reason and token usage (The Invocation Contract). The log records the reply.
Validate and grant. The tool gateway validates the proposal and applies runtime policy to the session, target, operation, and current preconditions. A discovered descriptor does not confer permission (Interoperable Tool Discovery). Calls requiring approval go to the approval gate before dispatch (Approval Gates).
Write intent, then dispatch. The trajectory log makes the intent durable under the declared storage failure domain before dispatch (Durable Intent Before Dispatch). Where the workflow supplies a compensating operation, its recovery plan is recorded as well (The Trajectory Saga Pattern). The gateway dispatches under the task’s enforced grant and execution limits, preserving a logical operation identity where the endpoint supports that retry contract (Capabilities and Credentials, Retrying Uncertain Actions).
Wait without holding more than needed. The harness moves the trajectory to WAITING_TOOL. The serving memory decides whether the trajectory’s attention state stays resident, is evicted and recomputed, or is offloaded for the length of the wait (Paused-State Policies).
Record the outcome and shape the observation. The gateway correlates returning evidence with its call, preserving known results, partial effects, or unresolved status. Late outcomes can matter for reconciliation even when they should not resume the model. The log records this disposition and the bounded observation (Observation Stream Truncation).
Check progress and continue. Recovery compares task-scoped observations with recent history to assess possible nonprogress (Semantic Watchdogs). The harness applies its guarded continuation or finalization decision. Evaluation assesses acceptance under the declared criteria, including any required residual-duty evidence; its final verdict need not be available when finalization begins (The Task Acceptance Contract).

At each handoff, the receiving owner needs an identity, applicable version, and disposition, not merely a text description of the preceding step. Diagnostic spans can correlate observed calls and outcomes, but only the records and artifacts covered by the durability contract support promised recovery. A final acceptance decision can occur after this turn and can require evidence from outside its trace.



An interrupted response needs a different disposition from a complete proposal. The invocation contract therefore identifies the model and call configuration, input format, output limit, status, and available usage evidence (The Invocation Contract). Deadlines and cancellation specify what the client can stop admitting or consuming and what termination the provider confirms. A local timeout does not prove that generation stopped or that its charge is settled. Token usage is one accounting input; task budgets can also constrain money, elapsed time, tool work, and other resources.
Prefix caching is an optional performance facility rather than a correctness requirement. If it is available, record compatibility, sharing, residency, and routing assumptions before relying on its savings. Session affinity can improve reuse but can also concentrate load; a changed prefix can reduce hits without changing the task’s validity. Prefix Caching Across Turns supplies the reuse conditions, while The Size of the Attention State supplies the memory-sizing model. Behavioral suitability still requires task-level evaluation independently of this interface contract.



An agent’s state lives in several places that differ in who may write them, how long they last, and what maintains their validity. The architecture needs an owner for each, and it must distinguish a derived copy from its source (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)). Table 3 maps these responsibilities to components. The persistent-record roles in Roles of persistent records further distinguish the claims and evidence retained in durable stores.

Three architectural rules follow from the table. First, a trajectory log records the events captured under its durability and retention contract; it does not establish every claim made in a logged response. Second, reconstruction requires retained inputs and a compatible reconstruction procedure. An index can be rebuilt from available sources, but a preference or observation cannot be recovered merely because an agent originally wrote it. Losing its only retained evidence can change later behavior. Third, the model proposes writes through mediated tools; workspace containment and memory admission enforce different boundaries on those operations. The context assembler selects from these records, and the retrieval contract (The Retrieval Contract) governs how durable information re-enters a call, preserving its applicability, provenance, and retrieval limitations.



The tool gateway mediates requests and returning evidence; the isolation envelope constrains execution reach. The gateway validates arguments, applies session policy and action-time checks, dispatches permitted calls, and returns bounded observations. Retry behavior depends on operation semantics and the endpoint’s supported identity, effect, and result contract. A timeout may remain unresolved; a key alone does not make repetition safe (Tool Calling). The envelope enforces the implementation’s permitted resource access, credentials, workspace effects, network reach, and resource use (Agent Sandboxes). Neither a grant nor a descriptor enforces those limits merely by naming them.

Provisioning also depends on lifetime policy. A warm lease, a fresh restore, and a verified reset are different events. Pool capacity needs an explicit reserve, replenishment concurrency, admission policy, and memory ledger; average arrival rate alone does not establish that an environment is ready when needed (Sandbox Pools and Reset).
Supporting services enforce distinct boundaries. A credential broker withholds selected secrets from the guest and checks authorized use, while task data and returned observations may still be sensitive (Credential brokering). Egress controls constrain actual routes, destinations, and supported request semantics; permitted requests can still carry inappropriate disclosures (Egress Control). Security develops provenance and information-flow policy for those remaining cases (Information-Flow Policy).



The harness record connects an admitted call to its trajectory identity, current version, grants, budgets, pending work, and retained artifacts (The Trajectory Record). Check that every writer of this record passes through guarded transitions. A model-proposed plan update must not directly grant authority, release a reservation, or mark an unknown effect settled.
The control interface distinguishes holding new work from terminating existing work. Pause, cancellation, approval, and resume each need an explicit disposition for outstanding calls and liabilities. An authenticated late result may settle an effect without becoming eligible input to an obsolete continuation. Trajectory States supplies the transition guards; the reference-design question is which owner applies them when control requests and results arrive concurrently.



A surviving event record is useful only if the required history and referenced artifacts also survive. The recovery interface specifies the authoritative history, acknowledgment rule, compatible checkpoint boundary, retained bytes, and ownership-transfer mechanism. An incomplete replica cannot establish that an absent intent was never dispatched. Resuming a Trajectory develops the validation and fencing needed before a new owner admits work.
Diagnostic traces have a different contract. Sampling or redaction can be acceptable for measurement while making a record insufficient for recovery. For each retained field, distinguish its recovery, replay, and diagnostic uses, with the completeness and lifetime promised for each (Log Retention and State Compaction). One storage service can support several uses, but its most permissive sampling policy must not silently determine all of them.



An unknown tool outcome enters recovery as an unresolved operation, not as a failed call that can automatically be repeated. The recovery interface needs operation identity, available source evidence, permitted repeat behavior, and the owner of any remaining duty. Where compensation is supported, record its template and binding rule before forward dispatch; bind returned resource identities only from adequate evidence (The Trajectory Saga Pattern).
Recovery also consumes authority and resources. Its contract specifies which retries, revised proposals, cleanup, or escalation remain permitted after normal model-directed admission stops. Progress detectors and dependency breakers can limit further work without establishing the fate of prior effects. Tool Circuit Breakers supplies those containment boundaries.



An acceptance result needs a binding to the task contract, candidate version, checks, and evidence scope. Record the evaluator’s authority to publish that result and the uncertainty or residual duties it leaves. The Task Acceptance Contract defines the distinction between local checks and task acceptance; a completed trace alone satisfies neither.
The evaluation boundary protects grading logic and authoritative results from the acting agent and from candidate code executed during grading. Read-only test storage does not prevent in-process interference. Shared isolation infrastructure is possible under explicit credentials, execution, and observation boundaries; the fixture description must still state which production behaviors it omits.



Training is optional. When a system learns from its trajectories, the data interface must bind each admitted artifact to its source, transformations, intended use, and split policy (Trajectory Curation). A recovery log, an accepted task, and a usable policy target are different objects; none automatically qualifies as another.
The return path identifies the changed model and the behavioral evidence supporting its release. A changed policy may alter trajectory length, state use, and requested effects without acquiring additional authority. The existing runtime bounds still apply, and the release decision needs renewed evaluation rather than an assumption that training improves every task.



A logical component map does not prescribe machine pools. A model service may be remote or local; a harness worker may retain live state while relying on durable records for recovery. Hardware virtualization is one possible isolation boundary, not a property of every sandbox. Placement should name the trusted components, reachable services, failure domains, and credentials rather than equating separate hosts or networks with adequate protection.
Resources held throughout a trajectory depend on its lifetime, not merely the duration of one model call. Under stable flow, Little’s law relates mean live trajectories to admitted arrival rate and mean lifetime (Capacity for Trajectories; Queueing for Trajectories). That product is not a hard admission limit or a guarantee against reserve exhaustion: bursts, variability, outstanding work, and reclamation require additional accounting. Across agents, typed task envelopes carry scoped authority and budgets (Typed Task Envelopes), reservations account for concurrent spending (Spending Governance), and cancellation requires supervision of the work and effects it reaches (Bounding In-Flight Work).

Components can be combined, distributed, or omitted when the task does not require their function. Across agents, typed task envelopes carry scoped authority and budgets (Typed Task Envelopes), reservations account for concurrent spending (Spending Governance), and cancellation requires supervision of the work and effects it reaches (Bounding In-Flight Work).

title: 1 Reference Architecture
text: The reference is complete for a particular design when each applicable obligation has an owner, an interface, and stated assumptions. Components can be combined, distributed, or omitted when the task does not require their function. The remaining review is about the boundaries between them: preserved identities and evidence, current authority, resource liability, and responsibility for unresolved work.

title: 1 Agentic Failure Taxonomy
text:
A failed agent task can leave a responsive process, successful tool calls, and an unsupported completion report. Diagnosing it requires relating the task’s acceptance criteria to evidence distributed across model inputs, runtime decisions, and external effects. This appendix supplies a symptom-based reference for classifying failures, distinguishing competing explanations, and designing regression tests. It supports project work and the main text’s worked examples without replacing their explanations of the underlying mechanisms.


Begin with an observed mismatch between the task contract and the recorded outcome. A category is an investigation aid, not proof of a unique cause; several categories can apply to one trajectory.

Use table 1 to match a symptom to a diagnostic entry and identify the evidence worth inspecting.
Use section 1.10 when the category remains uncertain or the failure crosses several components.
Use section 1.11 to record a tested explanation, a scoped correction, and the limits of its regression evidence.

The chapter links in each entry identify where the book teaches the mechanism. A confirmed enforcement defect requires repair at the responsible boundary; a proposal-quality failure can motivate context, interface, or learning changes according to comparative evidence. The alternatives are not mandatory rungs in a response sequence.



Table 1 separates symptoms from the evidence needed to investigate them. The relevant H·S·A exposures depend on the actual task and effects. A retry storm can stress both horizon limits and controls on authorized effects, for example, while a misleading reward can select poor behavior at any exposure. Neither the category nor its symptom establishes that a particular principle was violated.



Table 1: Taxonomy of Agentic Failure Modes: Observable mismatches direct evidence collection; they do not uniquely identify causes or guarantee a remedy.










Failure mode
Observable mismatch
Evidence that distinguishes explanations




No-progress loop (section 1.2)
Activity continues without demonstrated task progress
Candidate revisions, scoped check results, pending work, and newly obtained information


Context overflow and dilution (section 1.3)
Requests exceed capacity, or decisions degrade as the working context changes
Exact delivered input, omissions, token accounting, reuse, and matched context-policy comparisons


Reward hacking and verifier gaming (section 1.4)
A score improves without corresponding task improvement
Reward and grader versions, candidate artifacts, protection boundaries, and independent assessment


Confused deputy and injection (section 1.5)
A proposed or executed action exceeds the requester’s permitted scope
Source provenance, effective grants, admission decisions, destinations, and actual effects


Correlated agreement (section 1.6)
Several reviewers accept the same incorrect result
Independent task evidence, reviewer inputs, shared information, and the evaluated review procedure


Environment desynchronization (section 1.7)
An action relies on an obsolete or mismatched observation
Source versions, observation dependencies, concurrent writes, and operation identities


Lost progress and repeated effects (section 1.8)
A restart loses recorded work or dispatches an already performed effect
Durable history, checkpoint coverage, dispatch records, and endpoint outcome evidence


Retry storm (section 1.9)
Attempts amplify dependency load while tasks exhaust allowances
Attempts per logical operation, retry owners, arrival rates, and outstanding remote work









A trajectory repeatedly edits and reverts the same patch, or repeats a tool request without obtaining evidence that advances the task. Rising activity with unchanged check results suggests a no-progress loop. An unchanged workspace alone does not establish one. Useful inspection, a pending external job, or justified backtracking can leave the same bytes in place.
Compare candidate revisions with the exact checks and observations attached to them. Inspect whether a repeated request encounters unchanged conditions, whether previous failures remain available in context, and whether the tool response contains enough information to support a different proposal. Missing capture can make apparent repetition indistinguishable from useful investigation.
Enforce the existing task budget while testing the explanation. A progress monitor can withhold further work, request investigation, or trigger another permitted response; it cannot guarantee that a revised proposal will succeed. Stopping new admissions does not settle outstanding effects. Semantic Watchdogs develops progress signals, false alarms, and bounded interventions, while Budgets and Ceilings supplies the cumulative resource limits.



A request rejected for exceeding the configured input limit establishes a capacity problem. Ignored constraints or poor tool arguments establish a behavioral problem whose cause remains open. The required evidence might be absent, truncated, obsolete, poorly organized, or present but inadequately used. Longer context alone does not distinguish these cases.
Inspect the actual delivered request rather than a reconstructed transcript. Record selected source versions, omission markers, token counts, and the serving policy’s reuse accounting. Longer uncached inputs add processing, but prefix reuse and context replacement change repeated work. Neither full retransmission nor a universal loss of information from the middle of the input should be assumed. Compare alternative context policies on matched tasks with quality, latency, and cost outcomes; Usable Working Context distinguishes nominal capacity from measured usability.
The response should address the observed defect. Restore missing task evidence, repair silent truncation, or test a bounded compaction policy that preserves required constraints and provenance. Reducing tokens is not a successful correction if acceptance deteriorates. Memory pressure in the serving layer is a separate diagnosis from proposal quality; The Footprint of Retained Attention State explains its capacity accounting. Evaluating Context Policies provides the task-level comparisons needed to assess a context-policy change.



A policy receives higher reward while independent assessment shows no corresponding improvement. Candidate diffs may weaken tests, special-case exposed examples, or optimize a judge’s preferred style instead of the declared criterion. Candidate selection can expose the same mismatch without changing model weights.
A widening training–evaluation gap is not by itself proof of verifier gaming. Task mix, grader revisions, sampling variation, and differences between the measured criteria can also produce divergence. Compare candidate artifacts and reward components under recorded configurations. Establish whether the policy or submitted code could modify protected grading logic, and whether the checks actually cover the claimed outcome. Reading a permitted development test is not equivalent to tampering with an acceptance test.
Repair an established protection or coverage defect and reassess the affected candidates. Protected tests still have limited coverage, and a learned judge needs calibration against independent assessment. Grading Trajectories explains these measurement obligations; Training Pathologies distinguishes training observations from their possible explanations. A decision to continue, suspend, or change training requires that evidence rather than an automatic diagnosis from the gap.



An agent processing an issue proposes sending private repository content to an unrelated recipient after reading instructions embedded in the issue. This is evidence of an out-of-scope proposal. Whether the runtime dispatched it, and whether data left the boundary, are separate findings. An approved destination can still receive information the task was not permitted to disclose.
Compare the trusted task instructions with the third-party content, delivered context, effective grants, and admission record. Check the actual operation and its arguments, not only the tool name. A policy configuration error, an adapter that drops provenance, or incorrect tenant scoping can also permit an unauthorized effect without an injected instruction. The model’s account of why it acted does not establish causation.
Withhold affected new actions while preserving authorized investigation and any outstanding recovery duties. Repair the boundary shown to be defective, such as object scoping, recipient checks, credential mediation, or approval binding. Model-visible source labels support interpretation but do not enforce those policies. The Adversarial Threat Model distinguishes hostile influence from delegated authority, and Information-Flow Policy develops the provenance and information-flow checks needed at use.



Several reviewers approve the same incorrect patch or repeat the same unsupported answer. Their agreement is observable; the dependence structure of their errors is not established by that incident alone. Identical model weights do not by themselves prove dependence between independently randomized outputs for a fixed input.
Inspect the evidence each reviewer received, whether reviewers saw prior conclusions, and whether the acceptance criterion was incomplete or ambiguous. Shared candidate difficulty can associate errors across a task population even when reviews are conditionally independent. Correlated failures in multi-agent quorum voting supplies a model of that distinction. An interactive debate is a different procedure from isolated reviews and needs its own evaluation.
Preserve the task’s required acceptance evidence and publication authority instead of replacing either with a vote. Test whether different evidence sources or independent initial reviews improve the selected result under matched budgets. Distinct reviewer names are not evidence of useful diversity, and a passing check establishes only its covered criterion. Correlated Ensemble Failures explains how to assess review dependence and retain a separate integration boundary.



An agent edits a file using a stale listing, retrieves a superseded record, or treats a late result as evidence for a newer operation. A missing path can also reflect a wrong workspace, an incorrect argument, or an access restriction. The failure category applies when the observation used for a decision does not match the relevant source state or operation.
Compare observation identities and source versions with the state at the attempted use. Include concurrent writers, index-update coverage, and the dependencies of derived summaries. A successful earlier read establishes the observation then, not its continued validity. Historical information can remain correct as history while being unsuitable for a current-state decision.
Invalidate or restrict the affected use, obtain an authorized current observation where possible, and enforce the endpoint’s applicable version condition on mutation. Workspace isolation limits interference only within its stated boundary. A late reply may be ineligible to continue an obsolete branch yet remain important evidence for settling an unresolved operation. Context Invalidation develops dependency-aware invalidation, and Optimistic Concurrency Control treats concurrent publication.



After a worker restarts, the trajectory repeats completed analysis or sends a second external request. A missing progress record suggests a durability problem, while a second request suggests a repeat-safety problem. Neither observation alone establishes whether the external effect occurred twice.
Inspect the surviving authoritative history and its declared failure domain, the checkpoint boundary and referenced artifacts, and each logical operation’s dispatch attempts. An intent without adequate outcome evidence remains unresolved. A complete recorded history can reconstruct known decisions; a fresh model response cannot reconstruct a missing historical observation. Missing logs may reflect retention or capture limits rather than absence of execution.
Restore compatible recorded state where supported and reconcile unresolved operations through the endpoint’s result-recovery or repeat contract. A deduplication key has value only under the endpoint’s enforced semantics; an unchanged-state probe cannot exclude a delayed effect. Withhold repetition when the available contract and evidence do not establish its safety. Durable Intent Before Dispatch explains durable intent before dispatch, and Retrying Uncertain Actions distinguishes safe repetition from unresolved outcomes.



Many trajectories exhaust their allowances while a shared dependency receives repeated attempts. A slowdown alone does not establish a retry storm. Sequential clients that wait for replies can reduce their request rate as latency rises; amplification requires added attempts, overlapping remote work, synchronized arrivals, or another source of increased load.
Group transport attempts by logical operation and identify every retry owner, including client libraries and gateways. Compare attempted and admitted rates with dependency outcomes, queue occupancy, and unresolved remote work. Several layers can each obey a local retry allowance while multiplying total attempts. Changing argument wording can also disguise repetitions generated by the agent itself.
Coordinate retry ownership and enforce scoped admission and capacity limits. A circuit breaker can withhold new dispatches but cannot cancel every earlier remote operation. Backoff and jitter change timing without guaranteeing a peak-load bound or making a mutating retry safe. Tool Circuit Breakers develops these controls and their evidence requirements. Preserve the distinction between withheld new work and unresolved old work when recording the response.



Before testing an explanation, preserve the available evidence and apply any necessary containment under the task’s authority. A student experiment should use an isolated fixture with live effects disabled unless those effects are explicitly part of the authorized test. Table 2 organizes the evidence by the question it can answer; its rows are not a mandatory incident sequence.



Table 2: Diagnostic Evidence Checklist: Each evidence set answers a bounded question and leaves explicit uncertainty for the investigation.










Investigation focus
Evidence to retain or compare
Limit of the finding




Task outcome
Acceptance criteria, candidate revision, scoped checks, and unresolved outcomes
A runtime completion label does not establish task acceptance


Admission and effects
Proposals, current grants, decisions, dispatch identities, and endpoint evidence
A blocked proposal differs from an unauthorized executed effect


Progress and context
Delivered inputs, omission metadata, versioned observations, checks, and pending work
Repetition or a missing fact does not identify a unique cause


Source state and durability
Source generations, concurrent changes, surviving history, and checkpoint coverage
A missing record does not prove that an operation never occurred


Load and resources
Logical operations, attempts, reservations, charges, queues, and remote obligations
Local request completion does not prove that remote work ended


Assessment and intervention
Grader configuration, candidate artifacts, comparison fixtures, and all trial outcomes
A successful correction on one fixture is not a general reliability guarantee






Reconstructing history, replaying captured inputs against harness code, and running a changed continuation answer different questions. Missing capture limits replay; changing an input creates an experiment rather than a recovered historical outcome. Incident Postmortems develops these distinctions and controlled comparisons. Keep both established defects and competing explanations in the report until the evidence supports a narrower conclusion.



A useful project report should let another reader locate the evidence, understand the tested correction, and reproduce the relevant check without repeating a live harmful effect. Table 3 is a reusable form for that record. It separates an observed contract violation from the hypothesis that a particular change will improve task outcomes.



Table 3: Failure Report Template: A project can instantiate these fields without claiming a unique cause or a universally effective repair.









Record field
Material to supply




Task and symptom
Intended outcome, acceptance criteria, observed mismatch, task and candidate identities


Evidence and coverage
Exact artifact or record references, configurations, retained interval, redactions, and missing inputs


Findings and alternatives
Established boundary defects, plausible contributors, competing explanations, and evidence still needed


Controlled comparison
Starting fixture, intervention, unchanged conditions, allowed randomness, common outcome criteria, and effect isolation


Regression checks
Deterministic boundary tests where applicable; repeated task-level trials with failures, budget stops, and unavailable verdicts retained


Decision and limits
Tested revision, supported claim, untested conditions, outstanding effects and their owners, and evidence required before broader use






For a silently truncated tool response, a boundary regression can verify that the revised adapter supplies a partial-result marker and a valid continuation handle. Separate task-level trials assess whether the revised interface improves accepted repairs. Neither result establishes that every future task will succeed. The appendix’s diagnostic categories help choose those tests; the evidence, not the category name, supports the correction.
